en: Oṃ, homage to the glorious Great Buddha and to all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
The Beginning of the Mahāvastu.
These four are the bodhisattva practices of bodhisattvas.
Which four?
The practice of the fundamental nature, the practice of the vow, the practice of conformity, and the practice of non-retrogression.
Homage to the Tathāgata Aparājitadhvaja, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One,
in whose presence this very Blessed One Śākyamuni first planted roots of merit while he was formerly a universal monarch engaged in the practice of natural conduct.
Homage to the past Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni,

in whose presence this very Blessed One Śākyamuni first made his root-of-merit vow while initially engaging in the conduct of the vow as a merchant-leader, saying: "O, may I become a Buddha, a Tathāgata, in a future time!"
"Just as this Blessed One Śākyamuni is a Worthy One, a Perfectly Awakened One, so too shall my name be Śākyamuni in detail; and may I also have the city of Kapilavastu."

Homage to the Tathāgata Samitāvin, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened Buddha, in whose presence this very Blessed One Śākyamuni, while he was a universal monarch (cakravartin) established in the practice of conformity, made a conforming vow—
[what is the practice of turning back?].
Homage to Dīpaṃkara, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha,
by whom this Blessed One was first thus prophesied:
"Young man, in a future time, after immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless eons, you shall become a Tathāgata named Śākyamuni, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha."
I shall set forth in detail the prophecy concerning the young brahmin Megha from the *Dīpaṃkara-vastu*.
From that time forth, while engaged in the practice of non-retrogression, he was prophesied by Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata and by immeasurable Tathāgatas thereafter, saying: "You shall become a Buddha."
Thereafter, the Blessed One Sarvābhibhū also gave a prediction concerning him.

"O monk Abhijit, in a future time, after a hundred thousand kalpas, you shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni"— thus I shall proclaim in detail the prophecy concerning the monk Abhijit.
Homage to Vipaśyin, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Homage to Krakucchanda, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Homage to Kāśyapa, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha,
by whom this very Blessed One Śākyamuni was prophesied and consecrated as crown prince:
"Jyotiṣpāla, in a future time, immediately after me, you shall become a Tathāgata named Śākyamuni, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha"— thus [the Blessed One] spoke in detail concerning Jyotiṣpāla.
The prophecy concerning the monk.
Thus, homage to the perfectly awakened ones of the past, future, and present.
The introductory salutations are completed.
The beginning of the Mahāvastu, according to the recension of the Vinaya Piṭaka of the noble Mahāsāṃghikas, the Lokottaravādins of the Middle Country.

There are four kinds of full ordination (*upasampadā*): full ordination by one's own [vow], full ordination by the "Come, monk" formula, full ordination by a group of ten, and full ordination by a group of five.
There, they were ordained by their own self-ordination in the presence of the Blessed One at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
Those who, having undertaken them, abide by the ten paths of wholesome action, become much closer to enlightenment.
And even there, he is preeminent.
Thus, through his practice in these well-performed deeds for the sake of being disciplined by a Buddha, he approached Dīpaṃkara;

and having seen him in succession among tens of millions of living beings— wonderful to behold, serene in every way, inspiring confidence, and surrounded by a community of disciples— he conceived a heart of longing for him.
It would be well if I, having overcome the world itself, were to move through the world for the sake of the world and be born for the benefit of this world.

Having understood his attainment of perfect enlightenment and his firm resolve, the Self-Existent One briefly prophesied [his future] based on his equality with himself and his equality with all self-arisen ones.
"In a future time, immeasurable [henceforth], you shall become a Buddha, a son of the Śākyas in the Śākya clan, for the sake of gods and humans."
Thus predicted by the Blessed One, the Lion among Men, as one who would attain the state of the Supreme Person, he was a foremost man, a true man, and he practiced the conduct of the Supreme Person.
Thus, seeking the welfare and happiness of sentient beings, the Bodhisattva wanders through cyclic existence for the sake of the world and for his own sake.
Seeking the benefit of the world, he practices some degree of generosity, ethical discipline, self-restraint, and the observance of fasts, being free from stinginess.

Furthermore, the Victor has prescribed that one should gather sentient beings by means of the four bases of sympathy: generosity, pleasant speech, purposeful conduct, and sharing in both joy and sorrow.
There was nothing that he did not give away which was present at hand;

and upon seeing a supplicant, his mind becoming even more serene, he repeatedly gave away his eyes, his flesh, his wife and children, his wealth, his grain, his very self, and even his life— by this means, throughout many hundreds of thousands of millions of births.

The Bodhisattva wanders through existence, contemplating the welfare of sentient beings; knowing the right time and the proper occasion, skilled in discerning the superior and inferior qualities of individuals, and awaiting the opportune moment, he approached the Tuṣita realm.
In the Tuṣita abode, the Sugata—who brings an end to becoming—cultivating the realization that existence is impermanent, entered his final birth.

For the sake of liberation from existence, the Blessed One practiced difficult austerities, eating only a single sesame seed or grain of rice, becoming extremely emaciated and inflicting the utmost pain upon his body. Knowing, "This is not the path to liberation," at the time of the river’s flow, he bathed in the Nairañjanā River and sat down at the supreme city called Gayā. Like an undaunted lion, during the first watch of the night, having thoroughly purified the stainless divine eye, the Blessed One directly realized the various destinies and transmigrations of sentient beings.
During the middle watch, you recollect your former abodes; you have supernormal knowledge of the various modes of former dwellings of others and of yourself.

And in the final watch of the night, whatever is to be known by the Charioteer of Men to be tamed, all that the Self-Existent One fully awakens to in a single moment, as being equal [to his own realization].
The introductory verses of the glorious Mahāvastu are completed.

The Blessed One, the perfectly enlightened one, having accomplished the purpose for which he had come, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery—the teacher of gods and humans; [the text continues] with the detailed introduction and the circumstances.
Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana frequently went on a journey through the hells.
There he sees beings in the eight great hells, each with its sixteen secondary hells, experiencing many kinds of thousands of hellish sufferings.

And I, the Venerable Elder Kolita, while wandering on my journey through the hells, beheld beings experiencing many sufferings in the hells; in the Saṃjīva hell, they were with their feet up and heads down, being destroyed by adzes and axes.
Others too, with mutually corrupt intentions, tear each other apart with iron claws and sharp sword-leaves.
Weapons appear in their hands with which they cut one another's limbs, yet they do not die as long as their evil karmas have not been fully exhausted.
In the Kālasūtra Great Hell, he saw beings whose limbs were marked with black threads, being struck and destroyed by axes, split apart by adzes, and torn asunder by saws.
And although their bodies are cut and hacked, they heal again; they experience unpleasant sensations, yet they do not die because they are sustained by karma.

In the Saṃghāta great hell as well, he saw thousands of beings being crushed by mountains that were blazing, flaming, and turned into masses of fire; rivers of blood flowed forth, and those mountains repeatedly closed in upon them; yet they did not die for such a long time because they were propped up by their own karma.

He saw thousands of beings cast into the Ekāntaraurava hell, amidst dense masses of copper that were ablaze, fiercely flaming, radiant with light, and thick with smoke, experiencing thousands of sufferings;

and he heard the sound of those cast into the fire of Mahāraurava— which was ablaze, fiercely flaming, and radiant with light— as they cried out with great screams, resounding even beyond the Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa mountains.
It is obstructed by mountains, through which [the sound] reaches the range of hearing of humans in the four great continents— Jambudvīpa, Pūrvavideha, Aparagodānīya, and Uttarakuru.
In the Tapana hell, he saw many thousands of beings experiencing exclusively agonizing sensations;

from their heels up to the nape of their necks, they were being pounded with iron hammers and undergoing thousands of other sufferings, yet they did not die so long as their karma remained obstructive.
In that great hell, which was ablaze, fiercely burning, and turned into a mass of fire, many thousands of beings were reborn, experiencing painful sensations.

In that great hell, which is a hundred yojanas on all sides, thousands of flames arise from the eastern wall and strike against the western wall; thousands of flames arise from the western wall and strike against the eastern wall; arising from the southern wall, they strike against the northern wall.
Rising up toward the north, they strike back toward the south;
rising up from the ground, they strike against the surface; rising up from the surface, they strike back down upon the ground.
Those thousands of beings fall down on all sides, yet they do not die for such a long time because they are propped up by their karma.
In the Pratāpa great hell, mountains are blazing, aflame, and set ablaze;
those mountains are traversed by the hell-beings who are impaled upon stakes.
They experience such sufferings, yet they do not pass away for so long because they are propped up by their karma.

Released from that great hell, they plunge into the *kukkula* (boiling embers). There, being burned in the *kukkula*, those people run about, yet they do not die because they are sustained by their karma.
Released from the Kukkula hell, they plunge into the Kuṇapa hell;
there they are devoured by black creatures with iron mouths, yet they do not die because they are propped up by their karma.

Released from the heaps of corpses in hell, they see delightful trees and the edges of forests; seeking happiness, they run toward those forest edges. There too, hawks, vultures, crows, and owls with iron beaks tear away the flesh from the fresh trees and eat it, until only their bones remain; yet once more, skin, flesh, and blood are produced for them.
And they do not die in this manner because they are supported by their karma.
Terrified of those birds, perceiving a place of refuge where there is no refuge, they enter the Forest of Sword-leaves and the Hell-pot.
Furthermore, for those who have entered there, winds blow that cause those sharp sword-leaves to fall;

they strike the limbs of those beings so that not even a single part of their bodies remains unscarred, not even a space the size of the tip of a hair. Yet, because they are sustained by their karma, they do not die in this manner.

Wounded and lying there, their bodies smeared with blood, those beings plunge into the Vaitaraṇī river, a harsh river of alkaline water that pierces their tender limbs; yet they do not die, because they are propped up by their karma.

Then those wardens of hell, having pulled them out with iron hooks onto the bank of the river, onto ground that was ablaze, burning fiercely, and glowing with heat, spoke thus to those who were being dragged along.
"Aha! O men, what do you desire?"
They spoke thus.
We are hungry; we are thirsty.
Then those wardens of hell, having forced open their mouths with iron wedges, heat iron bars until they are ablaze, fiercely burning, and full of radiance; then,
having caused their own mouths to gape open, they cast into them glowing, fiercely burning, and radiant iron balls.
May you all enjoy it.
And they cause him to drink molten copper and iron.
May you drink.
That which, while being blown, burns the lip; having burned the lip, it burns the tongue; having burned the tongue, it burns the palate;
having burned the palate, it burns the throat; having burned the throat, it burns the intestines;
having burned the intestines, it takes up the mesentery and passes out through the lower part. Yet they do not die at that time because they are propped up by their karma.

Thus, having seen sentient beings experiencing thousands of sufferings within the eight great hells, the Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana thought, "Alas, what misery! and, returning to the Jetavana, he related the matter in detail to the fourfold assembly.
Thus, sentient beings experience thousands of various sufferings within the eight great hells and their sixteen secondary hells.
Therefore, I say that one must know, attain, understand, fully awaken to, perform what is wholesome, practice the holy life (brahmacarya), and not commit any evil deed whatsoever in the world.
Having thus heard the words of the Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana, many thousands of beings, both gods and humans, were struck with wonder.
Such, in brief, is the description of hell.
I shall also describe it in detail.
The Fully Awakened One himself beheld this world and the world beyond, the coming and going of beings, and the cycle of death and rebirth.

Reflecting upon the fruitfulness of actions dependent on living beings and their maturation according to their respective places, the Sage himself realized this; having understood it through direct knowledge, Gautama proclaimed the eight hells.
The Blessed One has directly perceived the Dharma; he possesses the eye regarding all phenomena.
Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, and the two Rauravas;
then there is the great Avīci, as well as Tapana and Pratāpana.
Thus these eight hells have been described, difficult to escape,
teeming with those of fierce karma, each having sixteen secondary hells.
It has four sides and four gates, divided and measured into sections;
it rises one hundred yojanas high and extends for one hundred yojanas all around.
Encircled by iron walls and arched over with iron,
their ground is made of iron, blazing and filled with fiery heat.
The dwellings were spacious with ploughs made of iron, difficult to approach,
hair-raising in appearance, terrifying, formidable, and painful.
All of them are most terrifying, filled with hundreds of flames;
each one shines forth intensely, extending for a hundred yojanas.
Where many beings, fierce and doers of great evil,
suffer for a long time, even for hundreds of years.
With iron staffs, the thick-walled guardians of hell strike those enemies who have committed evil deeds.
I shall proclaim their names to you in due order;
listen with respect and attention as I speak.
In the Saṃjīva hell, sentient beings are suspended with their feet upward and heads downward,
and are then carved with adzes and axes.
Then, driven by the power of anger and filled with rage, they quarrel with one another using their own sharp, self-arisen iron claws.
And another [weapon] arose in their hands, sharp as a donkey's ear,
with which men, possessed of corrupted minds, cut one another down.
With their minds corrupted, their limbs wither as a cold wind blows upon them;
yet all their limbs burn due to the ripening of their former karma.
Thus the Teacher, the Tathāgata, having understood it as it truly is,
has declared Saṃjīva to be the abode of those who commit evil deeds.
Released from Saṃjīva, they plunge into Kukūla;
being struck down, they gather together upon that which is long, vast, and extensive.
They indeed run there for many yojanas, being burned by the glowing embers and experiencing manifold suffering.
Released from the Kukkula hell, you plunge into the Kuṇapa hell,
your manly vigor destroyed, upon that long and exceedingly vast expanse.
Then those black insects, harsh with mouths as sharp as fire and feeding on flesh and blood, pierce his skin and devour him.
Having emerged from the corpse-pit, the beautiful trees,
green and covered with foliage, appear; those seeking happiness approach them,
while hawks, vultures, and iron-beaked crows pursue him.
And avoiding fresh trees, they eat those wounded by blood.
And when they have been devoured until only the bones remain,
their skin, flesh, and blood arise once again.
Terrified, they leapt up, perceiving a place of refuge where there was no refuge, and approached the horrific Forest of Sword-Leaves while being struck down.
Then, wounded, afflicted, and smeared with much blood,
they emerge from the forest of sword-leaves and go toward the Vaitaraṇī river.
Therefore, they plunge into that river of scalding alkaline water,
and their limbs and members are pierced and wounded.
Then the henchmen of Yama, having pierced them with iron hooks and lifted them up, force them to eat iron balls on the banks of the river.
They cause copper and bronze to be melted down;
having taken that [liquid], it passes through their intestines and out through the lower part of the body.
Having committed these evil deeds and following the wrong path, you shall go to the hells, having failed to perform wholesome action.
And those who thoroughly avoid evil deeds and whose conduct is exclusively wholesome do not go to an unfortunate rebirth.
Therefore, since karma has two aspects— the auspicious and the evil—
one should avoid all evils and practice what is auspicious and beautiful.
In the Kālasūtra hell, they are stripped like moist trees; having been marked with lines, their limbs are cut with adzes and axes.
Then iron plates, heated for a long time,
were wrapped around his limbs, burning and afflicting them.
Having burned and crushed them, the iron plates are beaten together;
they tear away the skin and flesh, and cause the blood to flow forth.
Then, having split [the body] from the heels up to the nape of the neck,
he crushes many [beings] together in the Kālasūtra hell.
In that terrifying darkness where no news can be seen,
amidst a mass of smoke, they descend into that hell.
And they run there for many yojanas,
trampling one another with supreme skill in binding mantras.
Thus the Teacher, the Tathāgata, having understood it as it truly is,
shall speak this *Kalaśūtra*, the dwelling place of those who commit evil deeds.
And in the Saṃghāta hell, great mountains descend from above; into the space between them, sentient beings are driven like deer.
Those mountains, having come together through the causal power of the karma of sentient beings,
afflict many living creatures like masses of fire.
From their tormented limbs, much blood flowed forth;
and amidst the agitation of their bodies, rivers of pus began to flow.
And in iron troughs with iron pestles,
enemies shall be crushed for even many hundreds of years.
Thus the Teacher, the Tathāgata, having understood it as it truly is,
has declared this confluence to be the dwelling place of those who perform evil deeds.
In the Raurava hell, a great multitude of people are confined;
as the fire blazes forth, they utter a terrifying cry.
And when the fire goes out, they then become silent;
but when the fire flares up again, they cry out with a great sound.
And the second is also declared to be Raurava, which causes the hair to stand on end;
it is a hell with shoreless banks, profound and impossible to cross.
There, having seized their staffs, the coarse wardens of hell torment their enemies for many hundreds of years.
Thus the Teacher, the Tathāgata, having understood it as it truly is,
declared Raurava to be the dwelling place of those who commit evil deeds.
And in the Tapanīya hell, heated iron is raised up;
and the tormented beings, crying out, are as painful as a mass of blazing fire.
There, a great multitude of people of evil conduct,
who have committed sinful deeds and are guilty of transgressions, are confined and cooked.
As soon as it is cooked and softened, many dogs—
large-bodied, powerful, and feeders on flesh and blood— devour it.
And when they have been devoured until only the bones remain,
then their skin, flesh, and blood are produced once more.
Thus the Teacher, the Tathāgata, having understood it as it truly is,
declared this place of torment to be the dwelling of those who perform evil deeds.
In the Pratāpana hell, there are iron-tipped spears with sharp points;
there is a mountain of terrifying dread, consisting of a great mass of fire.
There, the multitude of people who engage in evil conduct is vast;
they wander about with their ends occupied by evil deeds, like cats moving through a heap of gravel.
Thus the Teacher, the Tathāgata, having understood it as it truly is,
declared Pratāpana to be the dwelling place of those who commit evil deeds.
Beyond that is the Avīci hell, which is exclusively and intensely bitter suffering;
it is vast, scorched by heat, and enveloped by a multitude of masses of flames.
Just as iron balls heated in a fire,
so too [is it] in the Avīci hell— below, above, and on all sides.
The bodies of those dwelling in hell are equal to fire;
they perceive the firmness of their own karma, and therefore there is no escape for them.
And seeing the door opened, they rush toward it,
for even there is an exit for those who seek liberation.
And those for whom evil karma previously committed has not yet ripened do not obtain release from hell, due to the condition of that karma.
Thus the Teacher, the Tathāgata, having understood it as it truly is,
has declared Avīci to be the dwelling place of those who commit evil deeds.
It is named Saṃjīva.
By the ripening of what karma are beings reborn there?

Here, those who have been rivals, or those who harbor enmity, or enemies— whether enemies over land, enemies over property, or enemies over embankments— or rival kings, or thieves, having gone into battle and established minds of mutual hostility toward one another.
When they die, through the ripening of that karma, sentient beings are reborn there.
Furthermore, this is indeed merely the predominant condition for rebirth there;
those born there also experience the ripening of other sinful and unwholesome karmas.
As the ripening of what karma do they diminish?
Those living beings who, while alive here, have been carved with adzes, axes, and hatchets, are carved as the ripening of that karma.
As the ripening of what karma does a cold wind blow upon them?

Those who, in this world, have provided fodder and food for jackals, buffaloes, pigs, and chickens— having raised them with the thought, "I shall slaughter them for their meat"— as the ripening of that karma,
iron claws or iron rods grow upon their hands.
Just as weapons and vehicles have been given here, so you, with these very weapons, must destroy such-and-such a village,
city, or town, or kill humans or animals. As the ripening of that karma, staves and swords will grow from their hands.
By whom was this Saṃjīva [revived]?
There, those denizens of hell think to themselves: "This is the Saṃjīva [hell], consisting of the Kālasūtra and other such places; therefore, this is the Saṃjīva hell."
It is called Kālasūtra.
That hell extends as far as those with weapons in hand, even unto where it becomes filled with light.
There, the hell-guardians, having placed those denizens of hell against a moist tree, saw them with the black-thread device, carving them into eight parts, six parts, or four parts.

Now, some go along cutting [the bodies] from the heels up to the nape of the neck, just like stalks of sugarcane; others, however, go along cutting from the nape of the neck down to the heels, just like stalks of sugarcane.
Being in such a state, they experience excessively painful sensations, yet they do not die as long as that evil karma has not been exhausted.
As the ripening of what karma are beings reborn there?
Those who here are bound by means of elephant-irons and other such fetters, or are made to perform labor, [are told]:

"Cut off so many hands, cut off so many feet; pull out the noses of so many, tear out the sinews and flesh of so many, tear out the arms of so many, and the back-flesh of so many—five times or ten times for that work."
Beings are reborn there as a result of karmic maturation.
Furthermore, this is indeed merely the dominant condition for rebirth there.
Having been reborn there, they also experience the ripening of other evil and unwholesome karmas.
There, those denizens of hell, being beaten and reviled by the guardians of hell, cried out, "May it be well! (subhassu).
Terrified, many thousands of living beings remain as if they were no longer alive.
Then, many thousands of cloths belonging to the guardians of Yama— hot, blazing, and set ablaze with fire— move through the air before them; as they approach, they make a sound, crying out,
"These are coming!"
Having arrived, they each enveloped their bodies.
There they burn their skin; they burn the hide, the flesh, and even the sinews, until everything has been completely consumed by fire.
Then their swollen flesh and blood are completely consumed by fire.
Being in such a state, they experience extremely intense painful sensations, yet they do not die as long as that evil karma of theirs has not been exhausted.
Moreover, this is indeed merely the predominant condition for rebirth there;
those born there also experience the ripening of other evil and unwholesome karmas.
As the ripening of what karma are sentient beings reborn there?
Those by whom many living beings have been caused to be killed here while they were still alive, or those who, as beggars, eunuchs,
all types of outcasts, or those of immoral conduct, have made use of robes or waist-bands belonging to renunciants—
by the ripening of that karma, sentient beings are reborn there.
Furthermore, this is indeed merely the dominant condition for rebirth there;
those born there also experience the ripening of other sinful and unwholesome karmas.
Now others tore her apart from the heels up to the nape of the neck.
Now, others were tearing them apart from the nape of the neck down to the heels.
Now, others made garments of bark from the nape of the neck down to the hips.
Being thus situated, they experience intense sensations.
As the ripening of what karma are beings reborn here?
Those who here have had *erakavārṣika* garments made, or *cīrakavārṣika* garments made, by the ripening of that karma, beings are reborn there.

The mass of smoke and darkness that surrounds the hell—that smoke is sharp, pungent, and terrifying; having pierced the outer skin, pierced the inner skin, pierced the flesh, pierced the tendons, and pierced the bone, it emerges from the marrow right through the flesh.
All bodies, becoming faint, dissolve away there.
There, wandering for many hundreds of yojanas and trampling one another, they fall back.
Being in such a state, they experience intense sensations, yet they do not die as long as that evil karma of theirs has not been exhausted.
As the ripening of what karma are sentient beings reborn there?
Those who, in this world, having burned incense in holes, burrows, prisons, or cages— whether belonging to *sāhika* creatures, *kiṃpuruṣas*, rats, cats, or pythons— thereby guard the doors,
or those who harass honey-bees with smoke, are reborn there as a result of the maturation of that karma.
Furthermore, it is indeed due to the ripening of various kinds of evil and unwholesome karmas that sentient beings are reborn there.
Furthermore, this is indeed merely the dominant condition for rebirth there;
those reborn there [experience] the full details of other [conditions] as well.
By what means is this Kālasūtra [hell] produced?

There, the hell-wardens, having fixed the denizens of hell against a moist tree, carve them according to the black line; for this reason, it is called the Kālasūtra Hell, named after that which is to be done.
[The hell] named Saṃghāta.
That hell is situated between mountains, made of iron, blazing and fiercely aflame, radiant with light, and extending for many hundreds of yojanas.
There, the hell-wardens, with weapons in their hands, point them out to those denizens of hell.
Then, terrified, they entered that mountain cleft.
Then a fire appeared before them;
they were terrified and turned back,
and then the fire appeared behind them.
Then those rocks came together with one another;
as they were coming, they made a sound, saying, "They are coming! They are coming!"
When they have come together, they crush them just like sugarcane.
Then those rocks rose up into the air.
They enter beneath them;
once they have entered, many thousands of living beings are then pressed together by those rocks like stalks of sugarcane, and rivers of blood flow forth.
They discard the skeletons, devoid of flesh and bound together only by sinews.
Experiencing such sensations, they do not die as long as that evil karma of theirs has not been exhausted.
As the ripening of what karma are beings reborn there?

Those who here have caused insects to be crushed, or have had floors trampled, or likewise have caused living creatures such as lice, nits, or bugs to be tormented on the sword-leaf trees of the gods, or have been pinched with nails— by the ripening of that karma, beings are reborn there.
Furthermore, this is indeed merely the dominant condition for rebirth there;
those reborn there also experience the ripening of other evil and unwholesome karmas.
Those skeletons of bones, [they throw] into iron vats that are blazing, aflame, and glowing, with iron pestles that are blazing,
aflame, and glowing, for five hundred years.
Being in such a state, they experience painful sensations that are thus intense.
As the maturation of what karma are sentient beings reborn there?

Those beings are reborn there as the ripening of that karma by which living creatures here were pierced with spears while still alive, or afflicted with clubs and swords; or by which, having slain living creatures with blazing [weapons], they were crushed with mortars and pestles.
By what is this called a "composite"?
In that place, the beings of hell undergo compression; therefore, this hell is called Saṃghāta.
... there those hell-beings, many thousands in number, each individually confined within small cells, go about with their modes of conduct (īryāpatha) broken.
Fire blazes forth from their hands;
as the fire blazes, so they make a sound,
and as the fire goes out, so they become silent.
Being thus, they experience intense sensations.
As the ripening of what karma are sentient beings reborn there?
Those by whom people here have been made defenseless and without protectors, having been forced to perform labor,
or who have set fires to houses, or set fires to forests, or who have placed [beings] in vulnerabilities,
or in watchtowers, or in prisons, or in bonds— whether they be *sāhikas*, or *kiṃpuruṣas*, or rats, or cats, or pythons.
Or, having set fire to the hollows of trees so that the doors [of the hives] are guarded, or having had honey or betel leaves destroyed by fire—
by the ripening of that karma, beings are reborn there.
Furthermore, this is indeed merely the dominant condition for rebirth there;
those born there experience the ripening of other sinful and unwholesome karmas. ...
[The hell] named Mahāraurava.
That hell was vast, made of iron, blazing, fiercely aflame, and glowing with light, extending for many hundreds of yojanas.
There, the hell-wardens of those hells, with mallets in their hands, point them out.
Then, being terrified, some ran, some fled, some did not flee, some retreated somewhere, some did not retreat, and some, trying to appease him as best they could, went out to meet him.
Then those hell-wardens strike them, asking, "Whom are you addressing here as you come forward? and they are shattered and destroyed just like jars of curd.
Both those who run and those who do not run, being in such a state, experience painful, harsh, and bitter sensations.

As the ripening of what karma are beings reborn there? It is those who, having obstructed the sun and moon here, have constructed prisons and, having cast them inside, release them [with the command]: "Do not look at the sun and moon here! As the ripening of that karma, beings are reborn there.
As the ripening of what karma do the heads of those beings fall off?

Those by whom the heads of living creatures here—of snakes, scorpions, and centipedes—were crushed while they were still alive, as a result of the ripening of that karma, their own heads are crushed; why is it called Raurava?
There, those denizens of hell, weeping, are unable to address their kinsmen as "Mother" or "Father."
Therefore, this is designated as Raurava.
The Tāpana hell.
There, those hell-beings—many thousands of living beings—are confined and remain.
Now they eat them, having avoided those that are still moist.
When they have become fleshless, mere skeletons held together by sinews, then, having fainted, they fall down with a single convulsive sensation.
Then, as a result of the ripening of their karma, a cool wind blew upon them.
By that means, their skin, flesh, and blood are produced.
Then they ushered those who were in such a state before him.
As the ripening of what karma are sentient beings reborn there?

Those who have prepared houses here that are without doors—their walls become covered with living creatures due to the fault of their construction; or else, they are pierced there by knives as a result of that karma, and beings are reborn therein.
In that regard, as the ripening of what karma are they devoured?
Those living beings who were made to be eaten here by lions, tigers, leopards, bears, and hyenas while they were still alive, are devoured as the ripening of that karma.
As the ripening of what karma does a cold wind blow upon them?

For those by whom fodder and food were given here for deer, buffalo, pigs, and chickens, with the thought, "I shall slaughter them for the sake of their thick flesh," a cold wind blows upon them as the ripening of that karma.
By whom was this scorcher created?
The denizens of hell are burned; therefore, this hell is named Tapana (the Heating), for they are pierced on all sides by glowing iron spikes.
There, some of those hell-beings are impaled and cooked on a single stake; some on two, and some even up to ten stakes.
When one side has become cooked and expanded, then [he should proceed] with the second side.
Furthermore, some denizens of hell, due to the ripening of their excessive evil and unwholesome karmas, undergo transformation by themselves.
Being thus situated, they experience intense sensations.
As the ripening of what karma are sentient beings reborn there?
Those who here have caused living beings to be impaled on stakes—such as sheep—due to the ripening of that karma, those sentient beings are reborn there.
Furthermore, this is indeed merely the dominant condition for rebirth there;
those born there also experience the ripening of other evil and unwholesome karmas. ... Why is this called "Avīci"?
From its eastern wall, the flames strike against the western wall;
from the western wall, the flames strike against the eastern wall; from the southern wall, the flames strike against the northern wall;
and from the northern wall, the flames strike against the southern wall.
The flames arising from the ground are repelled by the surface; the flames falling upon the surface are repelled by the ground; that entire hell is thus enclosed by flames.
There, those denizens of hell, numbering many thousands of beings, are cooked in various ways just like pieces of wood.

Being thus situated, they experience painful, intense, harsh, and bitter sensations, yet they do not pass away for as long as that evil karma of theirs has not been exhausted; such is that which was previously performed and undertaken by them while in human form, which must necessarily be experienced.
Furthermore, this is indeed merely the dominant condition for rebirth there;
those born there also experience the ripening of other evil and unwholesome karmas.
As the ripening of what karma are beings reborn there?

Those who here are killers of their mothers, or killers of their fathers, or killers of Arhats, or those with malicious intent who draw blood from a Tathāgata— all such beings are reborn there as the ripening of these various unwholesome courses of action.
Furthermore, it is indeed through the ripening of various kinds of evil and unwholesome karmas that sentient beings are reborn there.
Therefore, this is called Avīci.

There, those denizens of hell experience bitter, intense, and harsh sensations in the Avīci hell that are not experienced in other hells; there, the hell-wardens, being terrified, compel them to perform tasks, and a cold wind blows there as it does nowhere else.
Indeed, here in the great hell Avīci, they experience painful, intense, harsh, and bitter sensations; for that reason, this great hell is named Avīci.
Thus ends the sutra titled "The Chapter on Hell" in the glorious Mahāvastu-Avadāna.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana frequently went on journeys among the animals.
He sees beings born in the animal realm experiencing various kinds of suffering.

The Venerable Elder Kolita, while wandering on a tour among the border regions, saw beings in the animal realm who were extremely miserable; they were consuming dry and moist grass by licking it up with their mouths and drinking cold and warm water,
yet they knew neither mother nor father, nor brother nor sister, nor teacher nor one in the position of a teacher.
A friend, a kinsman, or a blood relative.
They devour one another, they drink each other's blood, they kill one another, and they tear one another apart.

They go from darkness to darkness, from the states of woe to the states of woe, from miserable rebirths to miserable rebirths, from ruin to ruin; they experience thousands of various sufferings and with great difficulty emerge from the animal realms.
Having seen that great danger in the animal realms, go to Jeta’s Grove and announce it in detail to the fourfold assembly.
In this way, those beings who have been reborn among the animals experience various sufferings and thousands of miseries, and they struggle with great difficulty to survive within the animal realm.
Therefore, I say that one must know, one must attain, one must understand, one must fully awaken; the holy life must be practiced, and nothing whatsoever evil should be done in the world.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana frequently went on journeys among the hungry ghosts.
He sees beings reborn in the world of hungry ghosts, undergoing various thousands of sufferings.
While wandering on a journey among the hungry ghosts, the Venerable Elder Kolita saw in the world of the hungry ghosts certain pretas who were extremely miserable;
they had massive bodies and needle-like mouths, their throats were completely constricted, and though they were constantly consuming food, they never attained satisfaction.

How much more so for those who have not performed meritorious deeds, by whom nothing at all is obtained—those who are ill-favored, unsightly, foul-smelling, poorly endowed, of little renown, and repulsive to behold; naked and uncovered, tormented by hunger and thirst, they longingly crave excrement, urine, spittle, snot, pus, and blood.

Due to the ripening of their karma, a wind blows for them, crying out, "There is water! There is water! There is rice! There is gruel! Hearing that sound, they go leaping over rivers and mountains, thinking, "Here we shall eat;
here we shall feast; here we shall drink."
Thus, having previously formed their hopes, they become hopeless.
A wind blows saying "it does not exist, it does not exist"; hearing that sound, they lose hope and fall headlong right there.
The female preta spoke this verse:
For five hundred years, this cry has been heard by me:
"Behold how exceedingly difficult it is to find even water in the world of the pretas!"
[_Mvu_1.29_] Another female preta recites this verse:
For five hundred years, this cry has been heard by me: "Cruel is the world for a preta! Behold how very difficult it is [to escape]."
Another female preta spoke this verse:
For five hundred years, I have heard this cry in the world of the hungry ghosts: "O porridge! Behold how exceedingly difficult it is to obtain!
Another female preta spoke this verse:
The thirsty approach the river, yet the shifting sands turn away; the scorched seek shade, yet the shifting heat turns away.
Another female preta spoke this verse:
Fie on this life, lived by you who do not give within it;
while wealth exists, you do not provide a lamp.
Having seen that great peril in the world of hungry ghosts, he returned to Jetavana and proclaimed it in detail, in many ways, to the fourfold assembly.
Thus, beings born in the world of hungry ghosts experience thousands of various sufferings.

Therefore, I say that one must know, one must attain, one must understand, one must fully awaken; one must perform what is wholesome and practice the holy life, and no evil deed whatsoever should be committed in the world.
Having heard the Elder, many thousands of living beings, both gods and humans, attained the Deathless.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana frequently went on journeys among the asuras.

He sees that in the city of the asuras, the asuras have massive bodies, are fierce in appearance, and are full of malice; having passed away from among the asuras, they cause others to fall into states of ruin.
The Venerable Elder Kolita, while wandering on a tour among the asuras, saw the five hosts of asuras who were deeply afflicted by malice toward the devas.
It occurs to them:
"We are below; the gods are above."
Then they become agitated, fall into malice, overflow with resentment, and manifest anger, rage, and lack of confidence.
Having arrayed their fourfold army— having arrayed the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry—
they break through the divine outposts, namely the yakṣas called Karoṭapāṇis, the yakṣas called Mālādhāras, and the yakṣas called Sadāmattas.
Having broken through these divine outposts, they engage in battle with the Trāyastriṃśa gods.

Indeed, having harbored malice toward the gods of the Thirty-three—who are of great renown and have performed meritorious deeds—they, upon the dissolution of the body after death, are reborn in states of woe, in evil destinies, in perdition, and in the hells.
Having seen that great peril for the asuras, he came to the Jeta Grove and proclaimed it in detail to the four assemblies.
In this way, sentient beings in the city of the asuras within the great ocean experience various sufferings.
Therefore, I say that one must know, one must understand, one must attain, one must fully awaken to; one must practice the holy life, and no evil deed whatsoever should be committed in the world.
Having heard the Elder, many thousands of beings, both gods and humans, attain the deathless.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana frequently went on a tour among the gods of the Four Great Kings.

There he sees the gods of the Four Great Kings, who have performed meritorious deeds, who are of great renown, long-lived, beautiful, and possessed of abundant happiness; they are recipients of divine life-span, beauty, happiness, sovereignty, and retinue; they are recipients of divine forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, divine garments, and divine ornaments.
Ornaments bound on the front appear at the back, and those bound on the back appear at the front;

even their shadows are not seen. They are self-luminous, moving through the air, going wherever they desire, with abundant food and plentiful drink. In celestial palaces made of jewels, they are fully provided with the five divine strands of sensual pleasure.
Having become united, they played, took delight, and enjoyed themselves.
The elder perceives that prosperity ends in misfortune.
Then, falling from among the Cāturmahārājika gods, the Svayaṃprabhas are reborn in the hells; they are reborn among animals; they are reborn among the hungry ghosts and among the hosts of asuras.

Then the Elder, having seen that suffering of change among the gods of the Four Great Kings, thought, "Alas, what a hardship! and returning to the Jetavana, he announced this in detail to the four assemblies:
"In this way, through the ripening of wholesome karma, sentient beings are reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings."
Having experienced divine prosperities there, when they pass away from that state, they are reborn in the bodies of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, or asuras.
Even the gods are impermanent, unstable, and subject to the nature of transformation.

Therefore, I say that one must know, one must attain, one must understand, one must fully awaken; one must perform what is wholesome and practice the holy life, and no evil deed whatsoever should be done in the world.
Having heard the Elder, many thousands of living beings, both gods and humans, attain the deathless.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana frequently went on a tour among the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
There he sees the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, who have performed meritorious deeds, are of great renown, long-lived, powerful, and abound in happiness;
they possess divine lifespan, strength, happiness, sovereignty, and retinues;
they enjoy divine forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and textures, as well as garments, ornaments, and the qualities of sensual pleasure, and are self-luminous.

Moving through the atmosphere, dwelling in happiness, going wherever they desire, with abundant food and plentiful drink, they reside in celestial palaces made of jewels and in the eight great gardens: Vaijayanta, Nandāpuṣkariṇī, Pāripātra,
Kovidāra, Mahāvana, Pāruṣyaka, Citraratha, Nandana, Miśrakāvana, and other such jewel-adorned places.

And in their celestial palaces, they were endowed with and possessed of the five divine strands of sensual pleasure, playing, sporting, and enjoying themselves. Śakra, the lord of the gods, too, in the Vaijayanta palace, surrounded by eighty thousand apsarases, was endowed with and possessed of the five divine strands of sensual pleasure, playing, sporting, and enjoying himself.

The Elder, having seen such prosperity of those Trāyastriṃśa gods, having seen their divine wealth, having seen the celestial city Sudarśana, having seen the arrangement of that celestial city Sudarśana made of the seven precious gems, and having seen the celestial assembly hall Sudharmā, which was entirely made of beryl and measured one thousand yojanas, [reflected].

There, the Trāyastriṃśa gods and Śakra, the lord of the gods, were seen seated and assembled in the outer divine council hall for matters concerning the gods; and the Trāyastriṃśa gods, seated in the Sudharmā divine council hall,
saw the entire city of Sudarśana.
Thus, having seen the entire prosperity of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, the Elder returned to the Jeta Grove and announced it in detail to the four assemblies.
Thus, through the ripening of wholesome karma, sentient beings are reborn among the Trāyastriṃśa gods and experience divine prosperities.
That too is impermanent, unstable, and subject to change.
Falling away from there, they are reborn among hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts.

Therefore, I say that one must know, one must attain, one must understand, one must fully awaken; one must do what is wholesome, one must practice the holy life, and no evil deed whatsoever should be committed in the world.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana frequently went on a tour of the Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmitavaśavartin, and Brahmakāyika deities, up to the Śuddhāvāsa deities.
He sees the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host, who have performed meritorious deeds, who are of great renown, long-lived, beautiful,

abounding in happiness, self-luminous, moving through the atmosphere, feeding on joy, dwelling in bliss, going wherever they desire, free from passion, gods who are arhats, who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, whose nature is not to return to this world, and who are unmixed with all foolish ordinary people.
Having seen such splendor of the gods, the Elder returned to the Jeta Grove and reported it in detail to the four assemblies.
In this way, through the ripening of wholesome karma, sentient beings experience the prosperities of the gods among the devas;
yet even that is impermanent, characterized by suffering and subject to change.
The entire world is a danger; the entire world is ablaze;
the entire world is set on fire; the entire world is trembling.
The Buddhas teach the Dharma— unshakable, immovable, and practiced by those who are not ordinary beings— for the attainment of the supreme goal.

Therefore, I say that one must know, one must attain, one must awaken, one must do what is wholesome, one must practice the holy life (brahmacarya), and no evil deed whatsoever should be committed in the world.
Having heard the Elder, many thousands of beings, both gods and humans, attained the deathless.

The Blessed One, the perfectly enlightened one, having accomplished the purpose for which he had come forth, was dwelling at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain— the teacher of gods and humans, honored, revered,
esteemed, worshipped, and venerated, having attained the highest gain and fame, and receiving the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick.

There, unstained like a lotus in water, establishing beings who possess merit in merits, settling beings who possess the fruit in the fruits, and placing beings who possess latent tendencies in those very tendencies; distributing the rain of ambrosia among gods and humans, he leads thousands of living beings to the attainment of immortality, [delivering them] from the terrible wilderness of cyclic existence— beginning with birth, old age, and death, which has no beginning or end— and from the harsh grasp of the wilderness of cyclic existence, such as the hells and other miserable realms.

Having rescued them from the great precipice and established them in the secure, firm ground of peace, auspiciousness, and fearlessness— namely, in Nirvana— he won over Aṅga, Magadha, Vajji, Malla, Kāśi, Kośala, Ceti, Vatsa, Matsya, Śūrasena, Kuru, Pañcāla, Śibi, Daśārṇa, Aśvaka, and Avantī; and having exerted his prowess in matters of knowledge, the Self-Become One dwelt in divine abidings and imperturbable abidings.

Through continuous abidings, the Buddha abides by means of the abidings of a Buddha; through the abidings of a Victor, the Jina abides by means of the abidings of a Jina; through the abidings of one who knows, the Knower abides by means of the abidings of one who knows;

and through the abidings of the All-Knowing One, the All-Knowing One abides by means of the abidings of the All-Knowing One. Furthermore, having attained mastery over the mind, the Buddha, the Blessed One, abides by whichever abidings he desires to abide in.
Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having dressed early in the morning, set out for the city of Rājagṛha for alms.
Then, not long after the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had departed, this thought occurred to him:
It is indeed far too early to wander for alms in the city of Rājagṛha; what if I were now to approach the Śuddhāvāsa realm of the gods?
For a long time, I have been approaching the divine assembly of the Śuddhāvāsa deities.
Then, indeed, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, by means of his supernormal power, set out for the Śuddhāvāsa host of gods with a stride.
A great many sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host saw the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana approaching from afar; having seen him, they went out to meet the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
"Here, here is the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
Welcome to the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana; we rejoice at the arrival of the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
It has been a long time since the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana made an occasion to come here."
Then those many sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host bowed their heads at the feet of the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana and stood to one side.
Thereupon, a certain son of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host said this to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"It is marvelous, noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana! It is wonderful, noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana! How difficult it is to attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, even after such a vast number of eons!
Then, O Blessed One, that son of the gods from the Śuddhāvāsa realm addressed the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
For a hundred thousand eons, there was a monk named Abhiya who possessed lust, hatred, and delusion.

Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana, at that time there was a city named Vasumata, which was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, crowded with people, inhabited by happy people, populous, free from violence and civil unrest, with thieves well-restrained, and perfected in its legal administration.

Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana, in the great city of Vasumatī there was a guild-president named Uttiya, who had performed meritorious deeds, was of great renown, wealthy, possessed of vast riches and great enjoyments, with abundant property, abundant wealth, grain, treasuries,
and storehouses, abundant gold, silver, assets, and utensils, and abundant elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep, as well as numerous female and male slaves, laborers, and servants.

Having gained faith and clarity in the teaching of the Blessed One Sarvābhibhū, he took refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha as his auspicious path, and was deeply devoted to the monks beginning with Nanda.
Then, Maudgalyāyana, the monk Nanda and the monk Abhiya went to the house of the merchant Uttiya.
Monk Nanda Maudgalyāyana was honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated in that guild-president’s family, whereas monk Abhiya was not so treated.
Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana, the daughter of the merchant Uttiya was the wife of a certain wealthy householder in the great city of Vasumata;
she, Maudgalyāyana, was exceedingly devoted to the monk Nanda.
Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the monk Abhiya, out of a jealous disposition, slandered the monk Nanda with a false accusation of unchaste conduct.

The monk Nanda was unchaste, possessed of evil qualities, unrestrained, and one whose sinful deeds were concealed; he had committed a grave offense with the daughter of the merchant Uttiya. This conduct of his in the great city of Vasumatī was such that the great multitude of people considered it something they ought to hear and believe.

Then indeed, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the brahmins and householders in the great city of Vasumata, as well as the merchant Uttiya, no longer thought that the monk Nanda was to be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped in the same manner as before.
It is possible that virtuous persons return [to the right path] and become remorseful because of unwholesome karma.
Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, this thought occurred to the monk Abhiya:

The bhikṣu Nanda was free from passion, free from hatred, and free from delusion; he was an Arhat of great merit, yet I, being by nature envious, have falsely slandered him with a charge of unchastity.
I have produced much demerit.
What if I were now to ask the monk Nanda for forgiveness and confess my transgression in the presence of the Blessed One, Sarvābhibhū?
Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the bhikṣu Abhiya asked the bhikṣu Nanda for forgiveness and confessed his transgression in the presence of the Blessed One Sarvābhibhū.
Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the monk Abhiya approached the merchant Uttiya and said this to him:
"Householder, I wish to perform a service for the Blessed One Sarvābhibhū together with his community of disciples; grant me the necessary means."
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the merchant Uttiya gave abundant gold and bullion to the monk Abhiya, as did other wealthy householders.
Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, in the great city of Vasumata, there were two chief perfumers who were full of faith in the monk Abhiya.
Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the monk Abhiya, with a hundred thousand hands, approached those two chief perfumers and said this to them:

"O Vasiṣṭhas, I desire this: having set aside one hundred thousand [pieces] of the *keśara* flower, I shall perform a service for the Blessed One, the All-Conqueror, together with his community of disciples."
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, those two chief perfumers avoided the *śatasahasrakeśara* [flower].

Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the monk Abhiya, having satisfied and served the Blessed One Sarvābhibhū together with the community of disciples with abundant solid food, soft food, and delicacies, and knowing that the Blessed One had finished eating,
had washed his hands, and had put away his bowl, [offered] that hundred-thousand-petaled kesara flower to the Blessed One Sarvābhibhū.
He scattered [flowers] over him along with the community of disciples, he strewed them, he showered them; having scattered, strewed, and showered them, he gave rise to this thought:

"O, may I too in a future time become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, just as this Blessed One Sarvābhibhū is now."
May I likewise be endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man, my body adorned with the eighty secondary characteristics,
possessed of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, strong with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and confident with the four grounds of self-confidence.
Just as this Blessed One, the Conqueror of All, is now a seer.

And may I thus set in motion the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, which has not been set in motion by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world in accordance with the Dharma; and may I maintain a harmonious community of disciples just as this Blessed One Sarvābhibhū does now.
And thus gods and humans will consider that what is to be heard and believed is just as it is now for the Blessed One Sarvābhibhū.
"Thus, having crossed over, may I help others cross; being liberated, may I liberate others; being comforted, may I comfort others; having attained final nirvana, may I lead others to final nirvana.

May that be for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of the great multitude of beings, both gods and humans."
Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Blessed One Sarvābhibhū, having understood this kind of aspiration made by the monk Abhiya, said this:

Abhiya, in a future time, after a hundred thousand kalpas have passed, you shall become a Tathāgata named Śākyamuni— an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha (samyaksaṃbuddha), endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans— just as I am now, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.

He was endowed with a body resplendent with the eighty minor marks; he was endowed with the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; he was powerful through the ten powers of a Tathāgata and perfectly confident through the four grounds of self-confidence—just as I am now.
And thus you shall turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, which has not been turned by any ascetic, god, Māra, or anyone else in the world, in accordance with the Dharma.
And thus you will maintain the entire community of disciples,
just as I do now.
And those gods and humans will think that what you say is to be heard and believed, just as they do now of me:

"Having crossed over, you will help others cross; being liberated, you will liberate others; being comforted, you will comfort others; having attained final nirvana, you will lead others to final nirvana—just as I do now.
Thus you will be for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of a great multitude of beings, both gods and humans.

And immediately after the monk Abhiya had been predicted by the Perfectly Enlightened One Sarvābhibhū for supreme perfect enlightenment, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, this trichiliocosm world-system shook, trembled, and quaked violently in six ways;
the eastern direction rose up while the western direction sank, and the eastern direction sank while the western direction rose up.

The southern quarter rises up and the northern quarter rises up; the southern quarter sinks down and the northern quarter sinks down; it rises up from the center and sinks down at the edges; it rises up from the center and sinks down at the edges.
And the gods of the earth raised a cry and made their voices heard.

This monk Abhiya has been prophesied by the Blessed One, the All-Conquering One, the Perfectly Awakened One, for unexcelled perfect awakening; he will exist for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, welfare, and happiness of the great mass of beings, both gods and humans.
Having heard the cry of the gods of the earth, the gods who move through the atmosphere, the gods of the Four Great Kings, the gods of the Thirty-three,
the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, and so on up to the gods of the Brahma-realm, raised their voices and proclaimed this sound.

"Thus, friends, the monk Abhiya has been prophesied by the Blessed One, the All-Conqueror, for unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. This will be for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare,
and happiness of a great multitude of beings— both gods and humans— and for the sake of an immeasurable, sublime, and great illumination."
There was an appearance in the world;
and those intermediate spaces between worlds which are shrouded in darkness, plunged in gloom, enveloped in obscurity, dismal, unknown,
and never before perceived— even where these very suns and moons, so possessed of great supernormal power and majesty, cannot reach with their light— there was an appearance in the world.
They could not perceive light with light even at the wrong time; nevertheless, they were suffused by that radiance.
And those beings who were born there also [spoke] to one another in conversation.
"Indeed, sirs, other beings too have been reborn here; indeed, sirs, other beings too have been reborn here; indeed, sirs, other beings too have been reborn here."

Furthermore, at that very moment and instant, all sentient beings became endowed with absolute happiness— even those reborn in the great Avīci hell— surpassing indeed the splendor of the gods, the splendor of the nāgas, and the splendor of the yakṣas.
And the palaces of Māra became darkened, devoid of splendor, and joyless;

fragments measuring one *krośa* fell down, fragments measuring two *krośas* fell down, fragments measuring three *krośas* fell down, fragments measuring one *yojana* fell down, and fragments measuring two or five *yojanas* also fell down.
And Māra the Evil One became sorrowful, dejected, full of regret, and consumed by the burning sting within him.
Verses sung in response.
Having given that gift, he made this aspiration: "May I become a leader of the world, a teacher of gods and humans, and may I proclaim the noble Dharma."
I shall wander with the torch of Dharma, beat the drum of Dharma with its banner,
raise the noble standard of Dharma, and blow the conch shell.
And thus, through this revelation and teaching of the Dharma to me,
may I establish many sentient beings in the noble Dharma.
And thus may gods and humans hear these well-spoken words of mine;
and thus do I set in motion the wheel of Dharma for the benefit of many beings.
For those beings fallen into hardship, afflicted by birth and old age, subject to the nature of death,
and blinded by existence, I would establish them in the aggregate of wisdom and lead them away from the lower realms.
In Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, and Avīci—
may I liberate those scattered throughout the six realms of existence from the cycle of becoming.

May I liberate from the cycle of existence those who have been cooked and ripened in hell, who are oppressed by the states of woe, subject to the nature of death, and for whom pleasure is slight while suffering is abundant.
I shall act for the welfare of the world, teaching the Dharma to gods and humans;
thus may I discipline sentient beings just as this Light of the World does.
Thus may I wander through this world just as he wanders with a mind free from attachment;
may I turn the wheel like him, peerless and without equal.
Well-honored and worshipped by gods and humans.
And knowing his vow, the Jina Susamudgata,
with all the necessary causes present,
gave him a prediction that was unbroken, flawless, and without blemish.
The wise one who perceives the meaning.
In the future, after hundreds of thousands of eons, you shall become a Buddha, a leader of the world,
a Śākyan in the place called Ṛṣivadana in Kapila.
Then this vow will reach its fruition.
Then the earth, together with its oceans, trembled, and amidst the hosts of gods in heaven,
a proclamation arose for that radiant one, rising up as a resounding voice.
This Abhiya has been prophesied by the Blessed One—the Sage who has overcome all, whose banner is the song of most excellent speech: "You shall become a Victor."
For the sake of the welfare and happiness of the world including the Brahmās, gods, and asuras, you shall become [the refuge];
the host of asuras will diminish, while the assembly of humans and gods will increase.

Then indeed, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, those two chief perfumers, having heard the prophecy of Abhiya’s unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, were thrilled, satisfied, delighted, and filled with joy and gladness; they conceived this thought:

"When the monk Abhiya has awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, may we then become his foremost disciples— the excellent pair, the auspicious pair— just as this pair of disciples of Sarvābhibhū was: one foremost in wisdom and one foremost in supernatural power."
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the daughter of the merchant Uttiya heard that the monk Abhiya had been prophesied by the Blessed One, the All-Conqueror, for unexcelled perfect enlightenment.

Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the daughter of the merchant Uttiya, having honored, revered, esteemed, worshiped, and venerated the Blessed One together with the community of disciples, made this aspiration:
By the monk Abhiya, who was of an envious nature, a false accusation was made against me.
"By whatever merit I have acquired by performing service for the Blessed One Sarvābhibhū together with his community of disciples,
through this root of merit, wherever the monk Abhiya may be reborn, there I shall falsely accuse him with an untruthful charge, until he has attained supreme perfect enlightenment."
"It might be," Mahāmaudgalyāyana, that he should think thus:
"At that time, on that occasion, that disciple named Abhiya who belonged to the Blessed One Sarvābhibhū was someone else."
This should not be viewed in such a way.
For what reason?
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, at that time and on that occasion, I was a disciple of the Blessed One Sarvābhibhū named Abhiya.
"It might be," said Mahāmaudgalyāyana, "that it might occur to him thus:
'Those two who were the chief perfumers in the great city of Vasumata at that time and on that occasion were others.'"
Indeed, this should not be viewed in such a way.
For what reason?
Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, you two were those two chief perfumers at that time and on that occasion.
That is your original vow.
"Perhaps, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, it might occur to you thus: 'Was she someone else at that time, on that occasion, who was the daughter of the merchant Uttiya? ... [She was not. ... "
Because of that vow, this woman of the heretics will give me false accusations wherever I am reborn, even until I have attained supreme perfect enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, it might occur to you thus:
'Was that merchant named Uttiya in the great city of Vasumata at that time and on that occasion someone else?'"
Indeed, this should not be viewed in such a way.
This very son of the gods from the Śuddhāvāsa realm, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, was at that time and on that occasion the merchant named Uttiya in the great city of Vasumata.
He remembers a hundred thousand of these eons; he recollects the Dharma.
Thus ends the *Abhiyavastu* with its accompanying verses in the glorious *Mahāvastu-Avadāna*.
"O Mahāmaudgalyāyana, from this point back, immeasurable and incalculable eons have passed since I first made my vow for enlightenment."
I have made offerings to immeasurable Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, yet I have not received a prophecy.
Maudgalyāyana, three hundred Buddhas named Puṣpa were honored by me, yet I was not prophesied by them.
For immeasurable and incalculable eons I have wandered and transmigrated, and immeasurable perfectly awakened Buddhas have been honored by me, yet I was not prophesied by them.
There are, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, four practices of a bodhisattva here in this world.
Which are the four?
Namely: the practice of the natural state, the practice of aspiration, the practice of conformity, and the practice of non-retrogression.
And what, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, is the practice of natural disposition?
In this regard, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, such is the very nature of a bodhisattva.

They are respectful toward their mothers and fathers, respectful toward ascetics and brahmins, and they honor the elders of the family; having undertaken the ten paths of wholesome action, they abide in them and teach them to others, saying, "Give gifts! Perform meritorious deeds!
They honor the Buddhas while they remain and honor the Śrāvakas as well, yet for all that, they do not yet generate the mind set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Those of great renown first worship the Tathāgatas with great reverence; yet they do not yet give rise to pride in their minds.
O supreme among men, you have attained the state of the foremost person.
Tens of millions of those who have attained mastery worship them, for they have long ago reached the perfection of mastery; even then, they do not give rise to a conceited mind.
The leaders who ferry [beings] across the ocean of gnosis.
And those millions of Pratyekabuddhas, persons of ultimate reality, honor them;
yet they do not give rise to even a thought of pride.
They are wise because they have knowledge of all phenomena.
This, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, is the practice of natural disposition.
And what, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, is the practice of the vow?

From this point, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, immeasurable and incalculable eons ago, there arose in the world a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni— one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Śākyamuni’s city was named Kapilavastu, [which was] extensive.
At that time, I was a guild-leader.
Having drunk the gruel, he made a resolution for awakening.
When they have accumulated a vast store of merit and have cultivated their bodies and minds,
they approach, bearing excellent forms.
They direct their minds toward awakening.
By whatever merit I have previously acquired,
may I attain omniscience;
and may my aspiration never fail.
May this very vow that he has made come to pass.
May whatever accumulation of roots of merit I have become great for all living beings; and whatever unwholesome karma I have committed, [may it be exhausted].
That bitter fruit shall be mine alone.
Thus may I wander through this world just as he wanders with a mind free from attachment;
may I set in motion the wheel that is without equal.
Duly honored, he is worshipped by gods and humans.
He was the one who first gave a drink of rice gruel to the supramundane Buddha, the Blessed Śākyamuni, in an incalculable eon ago from this time.
That was my first vow at that time.

"Mahāmaudgalyāyana, in an immeasurable and incalculable eon from now, a Tathāgata named Samitāvin arose in the world— an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed,
a teacher of gods and humans."

Furthermore, at that time, the Bodhisattva was a universal monarch (cakravartin), ruling over the four continents, victorious, endowed with the seven treasures, righteous, a king of Dharma who practiced the undertaking of the ten paths of wholesome action.

These were his seven treasures, namely: this wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh; and he had a full thousand sons.
There were heroes, brave men of excellent form, who crushed the armies of their enemies.

Thus, having conquered this entire earth— bounded by the oceans and mountains, including these four continents, namely Jambudvīpa, Pūrvavideha, Aparagodānīya, and Uttarakuru— free from thorns, free from distress, and without punishment or weapons, he dwells there, ruling by means of the Dharma without oppression.

Then indeed, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, King Cakravartin attended upon the Perfectly Awakened One Samitāvin and his community of disciples with every requisite— robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal provisions for the sick—
and he had a palace constructed out of the seven precious substances: gold, silver, pearl, beryl, and crystal.
Of musāragalva and red coral, eighty-four thousand pillars were made, each pillar being fashioned with half [of its material] from crores of gold;
he had eighty-four thousand gabled chambers constructed, variegated and beautiful, made of the seven precious substances, namely: gold, silver, pearl, beryl, crystal, musāragalva, and coral.
To Lohitikā.
Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having had a palace built with such characteristics, the wheel-turning monarch presented it to the Perfectly Awakened One Samitāvin and made this aspiration:
"O, may I in a future time become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world,
an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, just as this Blessed One is now."

At present, Samitāvin is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, his body adorned with the eighty minor characteristics, possessed of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, powerful through the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and perfectly confident through the four grounds of self-confidence— just as this Blessed One, Samitāvin, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is.
Now that I have thus crossed over, may I help others cross; being comforted, may I comfort others; having attained final nirvana, may I lead others to final nirvana.

May I become one who acts for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, benefit, and happiness of the great multitude of beings—both gods and humans.
Thus, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, this was the vow of the Tathāgata.
Thus may I wander through this world as he wanders with a mind free from attachment;
may I set in motion the wheel, peerless and without equal.
May I be honored by gods and humans.
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to the Samyaksambuddha Samitāvin:

"Indeed, after I have entered final nirvana, and these disciples have also entered final nirvana, and this proclamation of the Dharma has disappeared— after how much time from now will a Buddha, a Blessed One, appear in the world?"
In one eon he did not see him;
in two eons he did not see him;
only after a thousand eons does he behold a Buddha in the world.
Then indeed, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, great compassion for sentient beings arose within the Perfectly Awakened One Samitāvi, who was endowed with great mercy.
And the five activities of a Buddha must necessarily be performed.
Which five?

The wheel of Dharma must be set in motion; the mother must be converted, the father must be converted, and those beings who are to be converted by a Buddha must be converted; the crown prince must be consecrated.

"This one shall become a Buddha in the world after my passing, just as I am now; even so, this Bodhisattva Ajita shall become a Buddha in the world after my passing—Ajita by name, Maitreya by lineage—in the royal capital of Bandhumā."
What if I were now to remain here for a hundred thousand eons?
Then indeed, the perfectly enlightened one Samitāvin addressed the monks.
Here, as I was alone in seclusion, withdrawn in meditation, this kind of reflection arose in my mind.

"Indeed, after I have attained final nirvana, and these assemblies of disciples have also attained final nirvana, and this proclamation of the Dharma has disappeared—after how much time from now will a Buddha appear in the world?
He did not see [one] within a single eon.
For two eons he did not see [him].
For three eons he did not see [it].
Only after a hundred thousand eons do I behold a Buddha in the world.
I have five tasks of a Buddha that must necessarily be performed; furthermore, that being who is to be consecrated as the crown prince has been reborn among the long-lived gods.
"What if I were to wish to remain for a hundred thousand eons? O monks, do you wish to remain for a hundred thousand eons? Who will remain with me?"
In that regard, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, that world was upheld by eighty-four hundred thousand monks, all of whom had attained mastery through power.
We shall remain, O Blessed One; we shall remain, O Sugata.
Then indeed, the Perfectly Enlightened One Samitāvin and those disciples remained for a very long time.

At the time of the world's dissolution, when humans pass away, they are reborn in the Ābhāsvara realm of gods; when the king passes away, he too is reborn in the Ābhāsvara realm of gods; and the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, goes to the Ābhāsvara realm of gods.

When the period of evolution has arrived and the world-system has been established, beings, due to the exhaustion of their lifespan, pass away from the Ābhāsvara host of gods and come into this state of existence.

The Bodhisattva, having passed away from the Ābhāsvara host of gods and come to this world of men, becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin), a conqueror of the four continents; having completely subdued these four great continents by means of righteousness alone, he dwells therein.

When human beings become limited in lifespan and aging, sickness, and death become known, then the Blessed One, having subdued his enemies, comes to Jambudvīpa together with the community of disciples.
Having arrived, he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings.
In the same way, King Cakravartin attended upon the Perfectly Enlightened One Samitāvin with all requisites— robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick—
