and having had a palace made of the seven precious gems constructed exactly like that, he presented it to the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
By this means, for a hundred thousand eons, the Perfectly Awakened One Samitāvin remained together with his community of disciples; for a hundred thousand eons,
he was attended by the Bodhisattva, and in every single eon, having caused a palace made of the seven precious gems to be constructed in that very manner, he presented it to Samitāvin.
Of the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Desiring unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, while being a wheel-turning monarch, I gave hundreds of thousands of palaces made of jewels to those who were self-controlled and tranquil.
In an incalculable eon from now,
having given that gift, he made this aspiration: "May I become a leader of the world,
a teacher of gods and humans, and may I proclaim the noble Dharma."
And thus, through this revelation and teaching of the Dharma to me,
may I establish many beings in the noble Dharma.
And thus may gods and humans hear these well-spoken words of mine;
and thus may I set in motion the wheel of Dharma for the benefit of many beings.
I shall wander with the torch of Dharma; I shall beat the drum of Dharma with its banner;
I shall raise the noble banner of Dharma; I shall blow the conch shell.
In a world fallen into hardship, afflicted by birth and old age, and subject to death— with the eye of existence blinded— I would establish the mass of wisdom within the lower realms.
In Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, and Avīci—
may I liberate those scattered throughout the six realms of existence from the cycle of becoming.

May I liberate from the cycle of existence those who have been cooked or not yet fully cooked in hell, who are tormented by the states of woe, whose nature is subject to death, and for whom pleasure is slight while suffering is abundant.
I shall act for the benefit of the world, teaching the Dharma to gods and humans;
thus I shall discipline sentient beings, just as this Light of the World [the Buddha] has done.
That was his second vow at that time.
He gave eighty sandalwood palaces to the world-transcending Buddha, his teacher.
I was the Blessed One in this [eon] from that incalculable age.
That was his third vow.
King Arka gave eighty thousand caves made of the seven precious gems to the one named Parvata.
At that time, there was a fourth vow.
For six years he practiced the perception of impermanence, having been instructed by Ratnendra regarding the signs of desire.
Then there was the fifth vow.
Thus ends the Bahubuddhasūtra in the glorious Mahāvastu-Avadāna.
Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha on the Vulture Peak Mountain.
Then, indeed, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having dressed early in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, set out for the city of Rājagṛha for alms.
Then, not long after the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had departed, this thought occurred to him:
"It is still too early to wander for alms in the city of Rājagṛha;
what if I were now to approach the Śuddhāvāsa realm of the gods?"

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, in a single moment and with a single stride, rose up into the air from Rājagṛha and alighted in the realm of the Śuddhāvāsa devas.
The sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm saw the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana approaching from afar.
Having seen him, he approached the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, bowed his head at the feet of the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, those many sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm addressed the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana in verses:
Having coursed through hundreds of thousands of eons for the ripening of enlightenment, after a very long time, the Buddha Anantaratna has appeared in the world.
Having spoken thus, those many sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host bowed their heads at the feet of the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, she vanished.
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
Thus, enlightenment is indeed difficult to attain, for it requires hundreds of thousands of eons.

Then, indeed, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana— just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm— in that single moment, vanished from the Śuddhāvāsa host of gods and reappeared in the city of Rājagṛha.

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having walked for alms in the city of Rājagṛha, returned from his alms-round after his meal; having set aside his bowl and robe and washed his feet, he approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he sat down to one side; and as he was seated there, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the Blessed One in this way.
"Here, Blessed One, having dressed early in the morning and taken my bowl and robes, I set out for the great city of Rājagṛha for alms."
"Lord, not long after I had departed, this thought occurred to me:"
It is not yet time for me to wander for alms in the great city of Rājagṛha;
what if I were now to approach the Śuddhāvāsa realm of the gods?
It has been a long time since I last approached the Śuddhāvāsa realm of the gods.
Then, as quickly as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, in that very instant I rose up from Rājagṛha into the air and alighted in the Śuddhāvāsa host of gods.
"Lord, many sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host saw me coming from afar; having seen me, they approached where I was, bowed their heads at my feet, and stood to one side."
Standing to one side, those many sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host addressed me in verse:
Having pursued the ripening of enlightenment for hundreds of thousands of eons,
after a very long time, the Buddha Anantaratana has appeared in the world.
Having spoken thus, those many sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host bowed their heads at my feet and departed.
Then, Blessed One, this thought occurred to me:
"Since unexcelled perfect enlightenment is so difficult to attain— that it indeed takes a hundred thousand eons—
what if I were now to go to where the Blessed One is and ask him about this matter?
I shall retain it exactly as the Blessed One explains it to me."
What did the Blessed One say in this regard?
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the number of gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host is indeed limited to one hundred thousand.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, for immeasurable and incalculable eons, they have planted roots of merit under immeasurable Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, while aspiring for future enlightenment.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, I recall thirty koṭis of Buddhas named Śākyamuni whom I, while having been a universal monarch, honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated together with their communities of disciples, desiring future enlightenment; and those Blessed Buddhas gave me prophecies.

In a future time, you will become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, and a teacher of gods and humans.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, I recall that I have honored, revered, respected, worshipped, and venerated eight hundred thousand Buddhas named Dīpaṃkara, together with their assemblies of disciples, while I was a universal monarch (cakravartin) aspiring for supreme enlightenment; and those Blessed Buddhas gave me prophecies.
As it was done in the first chapter, so it should be done everywhere.
In a future time, you shall become [a Buddha].
I recall, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, five hundred Buddhas named Padmottara.
It must be performed everywhere:
"In a future time, you shall become [a Buddha]."
I recall, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, eight thousand Buddhas named Pradyota.
I recall, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, three hundred million Buddhas named Puṣpa.
I recall, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, eighteen thousand Buddhas named Māradhvaja, under whom I practiced the holy life while aspiring for future awakening, and those Blessed Buddhas gave me their prophecies.
I recall, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, five hundred Buddhas named Padmottara whom I honored together with their assemblies of disciples.
I recall, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, ninety thousand Buddhas named Kāśyapa.
I recall, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, fifteen thousand Buddhas named Pratāpa.
I recall, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, two thousand Buddhas named Kauṇḍiṇya.
I recall, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, eighty-four thousand pratyekabuddhas.
I recall, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha named Samantagupta.
I recall, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, a thousand Buddhas named Jambudhvaja.
I recall, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, eighty-four thousand Buddhas named Indradhvaja.
I recall, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, fifteen thousand Buddhas named Āditya.
I recall, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, sixty-two hundred Buddhas with various names.
I recall, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, sixty-four Buddhas named Samitāvin.

Mahāmaudgalyāyana, it was at the time of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Suprabhāsa that the Bodhisattva Maitreya first planted the roots of merit, while he was King Vairocana, a universal monarch (cakravartin) aspiring for future perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when Suprabhāsa was a Tathāgata, the lifespan of human beings was eighty-four thousand koṭis of years, though there were occasional fluctuations in that lifespan.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, there were three assemblies of the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha Suprabhāsa.

The first assembly of disciples consisted of ninety-six koṭis, all of whom were arhats whose taints were exhausted, who had lived the holy life, who were liberated through perfect knowledge, whose fetters of existence were completely destroyed,
and who had attained their own goal.

The second assembly of disciples consisted of ninety-four koṭis, all of whom were arhats whose taints were exhausted, who had lived the holy life, who were liberated through perfect knowledge, whose fetters of existence were completely destroyed,
and who had attained their own goal.

The third assembly of disciples consisted of ninety-two koṭis, all of whom were arhats who had destroyed their outflows, lived the holy life, were liberated through perfect knowledge, had completely exhausted the fetters of existence,
and had attained their own goal.
Then indeed, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, upon seeing that Blessed One Suprabhāsa, King Vairocana experienced a sublime joy, a sublime surge of gladness and rapture.
For ten thousand years, he honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated that Blessed One together with his community of disciples.
Honoring and revering that assembly, favoring that community of disciples, and favoring that lifespan, he generated this thought:

"O, may I too in a future time become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, just as this Blessed One Suprabhāsa is now."
In this way, may I teach the Dharma endowed with all excellent aspects and fulfilled in all its aspects, just as the Blessed One Suprabhāsa does here at present.
In this way, may I maintain the entire community of disciples just as the Blessed One Suprabhāsa does now.
And thus may gods and humans consider me worthy to be heard and worthy to be trusted, just as they now do for the Blessed One Suprabhāsa.
May that be for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of the great mass of beings, both gods and humans.
And thus he spoke, O Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and even more than this, something else.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, it was only after Maitreya the Bodhisattva had already been set out for forty-four kalpas that he subsequently generated the mind for enlightenment.

Mahāmaudgalyāyana, there was a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Aparājitadhvaja, whose Saśrāvakasaṃgha I— while seeking future perfect enlightenment as King Dṛḍhadhanu, a Cakravartin— honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated for a thousand years, together with five great [offerings].

And this, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, was his constant and perpetual vow.

At whatever time sentient beings might be without a refuge, without protection, without a shelter, without a resort; being full of greed, full of hatred, and full of delusion; persisting in the undertaking of unwholesome dharmas; and for the most part filling the states of woe—at that time, at that moment, may I awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Maudgalyāyana, in an immeasurable and incalculable eon from now, there was a perfectly awakened one named Ratna, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans.
At that time, I was a universal monarch (cakravartin).

Then, for this Blessed One Ratnavat, eighty-four thousand gabled pavilions were constructed by me—variegated, beautiful to behold, and made of the seven precious substances: gold, silver, pearl, beryl, crystal, musāragalva, and ruby.

when the world was dissolving, the Blessed One went with those eighty-four thousand disciples to the Ābhāsvara realm of the gods; when the world was evolving, he returned here and taught the Dharma here.
"May I once again become a universal monarch;

This, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, is the practice of the vow.
And what is the practice of conformity?

This, Mahāmaudgalyāyana,
is the irreversible practice.

Homage be to the Buddhas; homage be to the Arhats.
The peerless vision of the Dharma belongs to those on the ten stages who have cultivated themselves for a hundred eons; it does not belong to others.
The ten stages of the glorious Victors,
by which the wise always exercise their miraculous powers.
Completely freed from pride, arrogance, intoxication, and delusion,
endowed with equanimity and gentleness,
and having generated reverence for all the All-Seeing Ones.
Listen to the teaching of the Supreme Victor.
When the Tathāgata, who brings joy to the Śākyas and resembles a heap of gold, has entered into parinirvāṇa,
the earth, along with its mountains and forests, trembles.
Clad in the garment of the ocean, together with its mountains.
Having observed that terrible earthquake, which caused the ground to tremble and produced extreme horripilation,
Kāśyapa, who had reached the further shore of the excellence of the ascetic qualities (dhūtaguṇa), [spoke].
At that time, he was one who had attained mastery over his mind.
Why indeed does the earth, together with its mountains, wearing the ocean as its garment, the bearer of wealth, tremble today with such an exceedingly dreadful sound?
Surely the Tathāgata has attained final nirvāṇa.
And he, possessing divine vision, beheld the Tathāgata— who puts an end to all the bonds of existence— being venerated by the foremost of gods and kinnaras.
He has attained final nirvana between the twin śāla trees.
Indeed, it is not fitting for me to follow the Tathāgata Gautama by means of supernatural power; let me instead approach the Sage, the best of speakers, on foot alone.
In order to behold the Peerless One, I am going forth into homelessness.
Knowing this, the venerable Kāśyapa, that monk of the highest rank, hurried with a stirred mind,
surrounded by many monks.
He gradually arrived at the realm of Nirvāṇa.
And he made this supreme vow at the feet of the Jina Kāśyapa:
"May I [worship] those two feet of the Great Sage."
Having pressed his head to the ground, he prostrated himself in worship.
Then, having taken up a large torch, four powerful Mallas approached,
who were fanned by a supreme Malla attendant.
They blew upon the burnt embers.
{Lies: dagdha-ulkāṃ}:
A burning torch was brought by those chariot-heroes, who possessed the strength of valor, toward the funeral pyre.
And she was extinguished at that very moment,
like a torch upon being doused with water.
Having approached Aniruddha, who possesses divine vision, the Mallas— humble with respect and well-disciplined— lowered their heads into the midst of his doubt and uncertainty.
I ask this question. . . . I inquire about this.
What indeed is the cause here, and what is the condition,
by which these sons of the Conqueror have been brought to this state,
having entered into extinction like extinguished torches?
Tell me the reason here, O Noble One, exactly as it is.
The deities are indeed well-disposed toward Kāśyapa;
this is surely his cultivation of supernatural power.
The fire will not burn at all yet.
Until he who has reached the further shore of the supreme has arrived.
And this vow of that glorious Kāśyapa, who maintains the dhuta-precepts, is being fulfilled:
those two feet of the one endowed with the ten powers.
For indeed, O Great Sage, [I come] to worship with my head.
And that Kāśyapa, the son of the Conqueror, whose dust was shaken off, surrounded by a multitude of monks,
approached the pyre of the Conqueror with palms joined in reverence.
With his head bowed in reverence, his mind was humble.
Seeing the Tathāgata, who possessed a most excellent form, situated upon that heap of wood,
he uttered these words: "Fie on you!"
[She] who has revealed the characteristics of the state of primordial nature.
Who indeed is that living being who, having approached existence, shall not fall under the power of death—
[he] in whom this [body], resembling blazing gold, [shall remain]?
He is extinguished like a flame without fuel.
Having joined his palms in reverence, the highly renowned Kāśyapa prostrated with his head at the feet of the Jina, the Great Seer.
This final [verse] is offered in homage to the Sage.
And those two feet, marked with the excellent wheel and worshipped by the best of gods and dānavas,
likewise emerged after rending that funeral pyre.
They were empowered by the majesty of gods, yakṣas, and serpents.
Placing those two feet upon his head and supporting them with his hands, O Sage,
he addressed the great seer Śrutidhara.
Then Kāśyapa was one who dwelt nearby.
[ Mvu 1.68 ] But why, O bearer of the sacred tradition, have these two feet of the Sage become dark and lost their luster? Speak the cause in its entirety; call it forth!
By which these two do not delight the eyes.
Having heard this collection of teachings, the wise Śrutasaṃcayadhara spoke thus to Kāśyapa,
his voice choked with a torrent of tears as he grieved:
These two feet have been crushed by your weeping.
Therefore, O Great Sage, these two excellent feet of yours, tormented by the weeping of the people,
do not shine as they did before.
Behold this thus, O you of noble vows.
Bowing his head again and again, he pressed those two feet, marked with the signs of the excellent wheel, against the palms of his hands, O Sage.
To the mind that is devoted to reverence for the Teacher.
And those two feet of the Teacher were saluted by Guṇadhara, who upholds the dhuta-precepts,
with the splendor of the wood used for the funeral pyre of the Lord of the World.
It blazes when shaken by the force of the wind.
While the body of the Conqueror-Candra was being cremated,
those five hundred who had attained mastery approached together and spoke.
At the time of the parinirvāṇa, [he performed] the communal recitation.
The Teacher, who possesses the most excellent marks and is the leader of gods and asuras, has attained final nirvana;
what merit is there in dwelling here for a long time?
We too shall cast off this body today.
Having attained the deathless, sorrowless, and infinite state, we have in every way completed our task and have transcended all states of existence and becoming.
Right here, we shall attain final liberation.
When this had been said, Kāśyapa, purified by the ascetic virtues (dhutadharma), then spoke to those who had attained mastery:
"Indeed, you have not yet attained liberation through the destruction of the acquisitions (anupādhi-vimukti)."
Having attained nirvāṇa right here.
The heretics and those who follow external paths would find fault with the peerless teaching,
saying it is like smoke for a *śramaṇa*.
And this alone is what must be protected by us.
O Protector of the World, may many lions among men, who are wise and heroic, and those of great intelligence yet to come,
arise for us with exalted minds.
If the teaching of the Teacher had not been compiled.
Therefore, being unimpeded and perfectly united,
sing the supreme teaching of the Sugata,
so that this may be well-chanted according to its true meaning.
He shone for a very long time among men and gods.
"So be it," they replied, honoring the words of Kāśyapa who had attained mastery; they then directed their minds toward this question: "Where now?"
There should be a regional enumeration of those who uphold the Dharma.
May it be in Rājagṛha, the excellent city of the Magadhan king of Magadha, within his most flourishing and beautiful groves and forests.
In the cave named Saptaparṇa.
On the northern shore of Mount Vaihāyasa, on its excellent flank,
amidst various trees and upon a ground of stone slabs.
In this portion, let there be a discourse on the Dharma.
And those sons of the Conqueror, established in the power of mastery over supernatural faculties, rose into the path of the sky;
at that very moment, they vanished.
Like a flock of swans at Lake Mānasa.
Having approached that forest on the side of the most excellent mountain peak, they settled there and sat down,
established in the well-proclaimed teaching of the Sugata.
Multitudes of divine drums resounded.
And they, the executors of the Sugata’s teaching, having heard the drum resound with its roar and having observed the terrible trembling of the earth, [were filled with wonder].
They spoke these words to Kāśyapa, whose dust had been shaken off:
But, O bearers of the dhuta-qualities, the earth with its rivers and oceans trembled,
and the delightful sounds of celestial drums resounded.
And there is a scattering of divine garlands.
Kāśyapa, who was endowed with the dhuta-precepts, spoke to those disciplined daughters of the Jina:
"These hosts of gods have assembled."
Having heard the excellent teaching, which is perfectly complete.
Those hosts of gods, possessing all the excellent marks and filled with joy through their reverence,
perform worship for the Peerless One.
May you all hear the teaching in its entirety.
For he has long since thus undertaken this for the sake of the welfare and happiness of the multitudes of men and gods throughout many hundreds of existences and eons.
Having been fully liberated, I shall liberate all beings.
Having attained the supreme truth, which is sorrowless and the cessation of the suffering of existence in all states of being,
[he dwelt] in the city of Kāśī for the benefit of gods and men.
I shall turn the wonderful, supreme wheel.
Together with those five sages, the Leader,
the best among those who teach discipline,
[guided] many millions of billions of beings.
Lift me up from birth, birth, and death!
Thus the Lion among Men, having now crushed all opposing disputants, brings joy to men and gods and liberates those who delight in worldly existence.
But the Blessed One has entered parinirvāṇa, being free from all concern.
Having heard these delightful words of Kāśyapa, who upholds the dhuta-precepts,
the hosts of gods stood rejoicing in the sky.
They utter speech that is delightful to the mind.
Excellent, excellent, O you who are skilled in the dhuta-precepts!
You speak of the infinite qualities of the Buddha, acting according to the Teacher’s instruction without deviation.
In the Jeta Grove, humans and gods were well-satisfied.
For he is the supreme among gods and men; for he is the foremost person, the Great Sage;
for he is the Lord, the highest refuge.
Having seen what was to be seen, he acts for the benefit of living beings.
Therefore, the Knower, the One Possessing the Ten Powers, has taught that the aggregates are like lightning and bubbles, and like a mass of foam, luminous in nature.
Of whom this discourse on virtues proceeds.
Likewise, O Kāma, these have been taught by the Supreme Person to be like the head of a black cobra,
and like weapons, disease, and jars of poison.
Of whom this discourse on virtues proceeds.
By him, through views that are supremely virtuous, was seen the immovable, supreme bliss;
it was revealed by him who was free from envy.
That which was experienced by one who delights in sharing.
Just as when the sun has risen, a glowworm becomes lusterless and does not shine,
so it is when the Sun-like Victor has risen.
Lacking splendor, belonging to another faction, and unrestrained.
Having reached the perfection of the power of the bases of psychic mastery, the Lord, possessing the eye through the power of the Victor—
behold the eye of the Blessed One!
He is extinguished, resembling a golden image.
Fie upon existence, which resembles an autumn cloud or the city of the Gandharvas,
wherein there is indeed no accumulation of wholesome merits!
He has attained nirvāṇa, an ocean of supreme wisdom.
Having observed existence as being without another death, the Leader roars the roar of a lion among men by means of hundreds of reasons and causes.
It has been said that for him, no interval exists.
The sky, adorned with the finest divine flowers and perfumed by the essence of celestial sandalwood, shines as the praises of the Sugata are proclaimed.
The sky shines with the fragrance of nectar.
Then, indeed, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the venerable Mahākāśyapa.
O Son of the Conqueror, establish those who have attained mastery so that they may discern the minds of those in the assembly who have fallen into doubt.
Then Kāśyapa spoke to Aniruddha, Upāli, the Elder, Alakuṇḍalabhaṭṭiya, and Sundarananda.
O sons of the Conqueror, look upon the minds within this assembly;
ask whatever doubts you may have, wherever they may arise.
Having promised "So be it," those experts in the teachings of the Jina perceive the minds of others as clearly as an *āmalaka* fruit in the palm of their hand.
To him who had long arms and was self-mastered, Kāśyapa said this:
"Upon the peak of Gṛdhrakūṭa, you should quickly create light earth."
Eighteen thousand people assembled in the assembly;
he manifested such supernatural power that they all recognized him as such.
Having reflected upon the mango tree and attained mastery, Kāśyapa spoke these words:
"I shall lightly create clouds in the sky consisting of the waters of the Gaṅgā."
And let various fragrant flowers blow from all sides;
quickly cause the raw stench of humans to disappear.
Kāśyapa spoke thus to the one named Haryakṣa, who had attained self-mastery:
"O son of the Sugata, quickly produce such a concentration that the possessions of householders do not pass away to another state."
Kāśyapa spoke thus to the one named Varuṇa, who had attained mastery:
"May I turn back gadflies, mosquitoes, and other pests that cause distress to human beings."
Kāśyapa spoke thus to Ajakarna, who had attained self-mastery:
"Avert hunger, thirst, and disease for human beings."
Having promised "So be it" to Kāśyapa, those sons of the Jina attended to the places as they were commanded and remained watchful as instructed.
Then the Elder Kāśyapa said to Kātyāyana:
"Proclaim the life-stories of those great-souled kings of Dharma."
When this had been said, the one of great wisdom born of the Kātyāyana clan spoke regarding the conduct of the Buddhas as Kāśyapa was inquiring.
Listen, O sons of the Conqueror, to the conduct of the all-seeing Buddhas, whose practice and conduct are pure, as it truly and sequentially unfolds.
Indeed, O sons of the Conqueror, there are ten stages of the bodhisattvas.
What are these ten?
The first stage is taught as "Difficult to Ascend";
the second is named "Firmly Established," and the third is "Adorned with Flowers."
The fourth is named Rucirā, the fifth is Cittavistarā; the sixth is named Rūpavatī, and the seventh is known as Durjayā.
The eighth is designated as birth, the ninth as the state of crown prince, and the tenth as consecration;
these are the ten stages.
When he had spoken thus with these verses, the wise Kāśyapa then addressed this peerless speech to Kātyāyana:
Proclaim accurately the transformations of the stages,
and how those of great renown evolve as they wander through saṃsāra.
Speak also of how those who are the essence of beings evolve,
and declare their high resolve exactly as it is.
And how beings endowed with sentient life conceive things,
and how they give gifts— all that I shall proclaim.
Having seen it thus, and speaking what is pleasing to the mind, the Fully Awakened Ones likewise describe the arising of perception; Kāśyapa spoke this.
Having heard these words of yours, those self-controlled Great Beings have stood ready with reverence toward the Great-Souled Perfect Buddhas.
When this had been said, Kātyāyana spoke to Kāśyapa.
Indeed, O Son of the Conqueror, it is not possible to measure the stages (bhūmi) of the Bodhisattvas as being "only this many eons" or "infinite.
For Bodhisattvas, the entirety of saṃsāra is conceived as a stage through the perception of it as a single fragment; therefore, they are called "stages."
When this had been said, the venerable Ānanda spoke to the venerable Kātyāyana.
"O Son of the Victor, if one stage is immeasurable,
how then will there be the inclusion of the remaining stages?"
When this had been said, the venerable Kātyāyana addressed the venerable Ānanda in verses:
Just as an immeasurable eon has been revealed by the Knower himself, who speaks without error,
so too is there teaching throughout many eons.
This indeed, O sir, is the teaching of the Best of Men.
Thus, the immeasurable stages have been revealed by the one who possesses unimpeded intelligence;
likewise, they proceed through the remaining stages.
An investigation of general conventions.

O Son of the Conqueror, Bodhisattvas dwelling on the first stage are indeed ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), yet they have attained the fruit [of their practice] and are worthy of offerings (*dakṣiṇīya*) by the worlds; they shine forth and become preeminent therein.
Through their renunciation, these Bodhisattvas, perfected in giving and possessed of great fame, illuminate the worlds like the radiant moon and sun with their rays.
For bodhisattvas abiding on the first stage, there are eight modes of conduct.
Which eight?
Namely: renunciation, compassion, indefatigability, absence of pride, study of all treatises, valor, compliance with the world, and steadfastness.
And in this regard,
there are these verses: Those who delight in sharing, feeling compassion for the masses of suffering, [are the followers] of the Blessed Ones who possess sweet voices.
The wise attain satisfaction through words and virtues;
such beings practice in this way on the first stage of the earth.

having gone forth and considered this world to be like a blade of grass, they renounce it.

For one reason, Bodhisattvas regress from the second stage.
By which one?
They conceive a sense of relish toward states of existence.
For two reasons, bodhisattvas regress from the second stage.

Furthermore, by three modes, bodhisattvas regress from the second stage.
By which three?

Bodhisattvas established on the first stage fall back from it to the second stage due to six factors.
By which six?

they abound in resentment and possess stubborn enmity.
They become abundant in sloth and torpor,
and they become devoted to worldly affairs.

O sons of the Conqueror, those bodhisattvas who have turned back, are turning back, or will turn back— all of them have turned back, are turning back, or will turn back by means of these twelve modes; there is nothing beyond this.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.

"O Son of the Victor, how much merit do these Bodhisattvas— both those who are subject to regression and those who are irreversible— generate when they first produce the thought, 'May we become perfectly awakened Buddhas'?"
When this had been said, the venerable Kātyāyana spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.

Behold, O Son of the Conqueror: one who would give Jambudvīpa, filled with a collection of the seven jewels, to those endowed with the ten powers, generates far more merit for the sake of awakening by making the vow for enlightenment.

"I shall endure that bitter fruit."

One should explain that stage of the Bodhisattvas as it truly is.
Then the Elder Kātyāyana spoke thus to Kāśyapa:
"I shall proclaim the delightful exposition of the Bodhisattvas."
As they proceed toward the second [stage], weariness with existences arises first in the Bodhisattvas; of this there is no doubt.
O Son of the Conqueror, for Bodhisattvas dwelling on the second stage, these resolute intentions arise: namely,
they possess a virtuous resolute intention, a gentle resolute intention, a sweet resolute intention,
a sharp resolute intention, a vast resolute intention, and a diverse resolute intention.

And they possess profound resolve; they possess inexhaustible resolve; they possess unimpaired resolve; they possess uncommon resolve; they possess lofty resolve; they possess noble resolve; they possess non-miserly resolve; they possess irreversible resolve; they possess uncontrived resolve; and they possess pure resolve.
And they possess firm resolve, they possess natural resolve, they possess satisfied resolve, they possess resolve directed toward persons, and they possess infinite resolve.
"How, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, do bodhisattvas come to possess a virtuous resolute intention? It is said:
They do not have any doubt whatsoever regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha;
thus, their resolute intention is taught to be virtuous.
"How, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, do bodhisattvas come to possess a gentle resolute intention? It is said:
Even when their limbs are being severed, their minds do not become angry;
thus, their resolute intention is taught to be affectionate and gentle.
And how, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, do bodhisattvas come to possess a sweet disposition? It is said:
"The supreme among men cultivate wholesome deeds within;
thus, the inner dispositions of those whose intellects are purified by ascetic practices become sweet."
"How, O bearer of the ascetic qualities (dhutadharma), do bodhisattvas come to possess sharp resolve? It is said:
Those endowed with pure intention awaken thus, both in the world and likewise in the supramundane; in this way, the higher intentions of those whose actions are purified become sharp.
And how, O bearer of the ascetic virtues (dhutadharma), do bodhisattvas come to possess vast resolute intention? It is said:
"For the sake of the welfare of all beings, they accumulate much merit;
thus the resolute intentions of the supreme sages become vast."
"How, O bearer of the ascetic virtues (dhutadharma), do Bodhisattvas come to possess diverse resolute intentions? It is said:
Free from envy, they give various delightful gifts;
thus the noble intentions of the supreme Seers become manifold.
And how, O bearer of the ascetic virtues (dhutadharmadhara), do bodhisattvas become those whose resolute intention (adhyāśaya) is inexhaustible? It is said:
Their minds are inexhaustible, and they possess the prowess of penetration;
thus, their resolute intention is said to be inexhaustible.
And how, O bearer of the ascetic virtues (dhutadharmadhara), do bodhisattvas become those whose resolute intention (adhyāśaya) is unimpaired? It is said:
They cannot be led astray by anyone with a wicked mind;
thus, their resolute intention is never impaired.
"And how, O bearer of the ascetic qualities (*dhutadharmadhara*), do Bodhisattvas come to possess uncommon resolute intentions? It is said:"
When no other aspiration whatsoever arises in a being except for the sake of the happiness of all beings, they know that to be uncommon.
And how, O upholder of the ascetic virtues, do bodhisattvas come to possess a lofty resolve? It is said:
Having heard the doctrines of other non-Buddhist teachers, contempt does not take root; by that, they become lions among men, possessing an exalted resolve.
And how, O bearer of the ascetic virtues (dhutadharma), do bodhisattvas come to possess a noble intention that is free from meanness? It is said:
The wise do not accumulate merit for the sake of enjoying the qualities of sensual pleasure;
therefore, their higher aspirations remain forever free from meanness.
And how, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, do Bodhisattvas become irreversible in their resolute intention? It is said:
Those who have made a firm resolve for Buddhahood are not overwhelmed by sensual desires;
therefore, their resolute intentions are known as "irreversible."
And how, O bearer of the ascetic virtues (dhutadharmadhara), do bodhisattvas come to possess an uncontrived resolute intention? It is said:
They do not desire the state of Pratyekabuddhas in any way;
thus, their resolute intention remains forever uncontrived.
And how, O bearer of the ascetic virtues (dhutadharmadhara), do bodhisattvas come to possess pure resolute intention? It is said:
"Having renounced gain and honor, those who long for the ultimate truth possess pure higher resolve"— thus it is taught.
And how, O bearer of the ascetic virtues (dhutadharmadhara), do bodhisattvas become firm in their resolute intention? It is said:
"Though assailed by the worlds, they do not withdraw their vigor from the Dharma;
such is the firmness of the high resolve of those great seers."
And how, O bearer of the ascetic virtues (*dhutadharmadhara*), do bodhisattvas come to possess a resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) that is their very nature? It is said:
"Overwhelmed, they do not eat the food of others, for they have lost their appetite;
such is the noble praise of their natural disposition and high resolve."
And how, O bearer of the ascetic virtues (dhutadharmadhara), do bodhisattvas become possessed of a satisfied resolute intention? It is said:
They do not flow toward sensual pleasures here, but always delight in renunciation;
thus the resolute intention of a satisfied bodhisattva is praised.
And how, O bearer of the ascetic virtues (dhutadharmadhara), do bodhisattvas come to possess the resolute intention regarding persons? It is said:
The wise long for the state of being self-arisen and all-seeing;
through their resolute intention toward the person, they thus become peerless and steadfast.
"And how, O bearer of the ascetic qualities (*dhutadharma*), do Bodhisattvas come to possess infinite resolve? It is said:"
Through the perfection of the quality of non-giving, they do not seek great enjoyments;
thus, these supreme among men possess infinite resolute intention.
Endowed with all these twenty qualities, those excellent persons are skilled in all dharmas and possessed of auspicious, sublime intentions.
Indeed, O bearer of the ascetic qualities (dhutadharma), it is by means of these twenty resolute intentions that Bodhisattvas become endowed with them.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
"O Son of the Conqueror, in how many ways do bodhisattvas, while abiding on the second stage, fall back from the third stage?"
When this had been said, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke to the Venerable Mahākāśyapa.
O upholder of the ascetic virtues, for twenty-eight reasons, bodhisattvas dwelling on the second stage regress from the third stage.
By which twenty-eight aspects?
That is to say: they become those who value gain; they become those who value honor;
and they become those who are intent upon fame and renown.
They are deceitful, they pursue gain through dishonest means, and they are intent on speaking harsh and angry words.
They do not bestow gifts with abundant reverence toward the Three Jewels; they do not seek out the conduct of a bodhisattva;
and having reached the stage of a bodhisattva’s conduct, they do not honor it.
They do not take up a burden that is obtainable through excessive worship; and having taken up a burden that is unobtainable, they cast it off.
Furthermore, they are not distressed by living in a crowded dwelling.
They wear garlands, garments, ornaments, jewelry, and ointments,
yet they are satisfied with only a few virtues.
They constantly delight in what is pleasing to the world,
yet they do not conceive that all elements are impermanent;
moreover, they hold themselves in high esteem on account of their own complexion and form.
They do not abandon their perverted views,
nor do they fulfill the words and syllables as they were taught; moreover, they become stingy regarding the teaching.
They regard those who are unworthy recipients,
they do not bestow gifts upon worthy recipients,
and they possess a harsh disposition.
And they act without due reflection.
"O upholders of the ascetic virtues (dhutadharma), whatever bodhisattvas abiding on the second stage turn back from the third stage, they all turn back by means of these twenty-eight modes.
In this regard, it is said as follows:"
Thus is described this second stage of the Bodhisattvas,
who possess various treasuries of wholesome qualities and act for the welfare and happiness of the world.
For those who are joined with faults turn back in such a manner;
but the wise, though they may likewise turn back [from worldly things], do not turn back [from their spiritual goal].
Those who are steadfast in their burden undertake a heroism that is difficult to ascend;
and for the sake of compassion for the world, they practice it despite its many sufferings.
All those Tathāgatas are to be honored by both gods and humans;
for they undergo various forms of suffering preceded by wisdom.
The wise conform to this world of manifold elements;
therefore, their fame has spread throughout the world, including the realms of gods and humans.
Thus ends the second bhūmi in the glorious Mahāvastu-avadāna.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
"O Son of the Best of Men, what kind of mind arises in Bodhisattvas who are transitioning from the second stage to the third stage?"
Then the Elder Kātyāyana said this to Kāśyapa:
"Listen to the unsurpassed mind of transition belonging to the Bodhisattvas."
The mind of the Bodhisattvas, O friend, is inclined toward renunciation as they proceed from the second to the third stage, O Son of the Conqueror.
These lords of men bring happiness to all sentient beings as they abide;
yet they do not do so for the sake of their own pleasure, nor for the sake of enlightenment in any way whatsoever.

They would purchase even a single well-spoken verse with their children and wives. Long ago, while that virtuous Bodhisattva was ruling his kingdom, he underwent the hardships of the forest, the hardships of the army, and the hardships of the mountains, through acts of renunciation and grasping.
But the human thickets are forests where uneven ground is interspersed with settlements.
Thickets of grass, shrubs, thorns, and creepers, as well as dense forests where trees are difficult to grasp, are but minor obstacles;
however, the thickets of humans—consisting of deceit, malice, and slander—are far more treacherous. "Tell me, O Brahmin," said Bhaṇḍin.
A single well-spoken verse was [offered] by the Bodhisattva;
that [verse] was purchased by the Bodhisattva, who longed for the ultimate truth.
This well-spoken verse was acquired with great effort from the hand of a snake-charmer:
"As long as one lives, whatever evil deed has been committed remains within this very body."
Having approached the lord of men, the divine seer, the brahmin, with a joyful heart, spoke these well-spoken words: "She exists."
"The price for that is your head," he said, "having offered your head.
"Speak quickly, O Brahmin, this well-spoken verse to me."
Even if they should occasionally practice something unwholesome while longing for the conduct of a perfectly awakened bodhisattva,
it is like an oil lamp shrouded by the rays of the sun.
It does not shine when overcome by the power of vast merit.
A rākṣasa said this to the lord of the earth named Surūpa:
"There is a well-spoken verse for sale, if you will purchase it."
Its price would be that it might devour the prince, the queen, and you as well;
let it be taken if you have need of it, for this verse is indeed consistent with the Dharma.
That handsome king, free from attachment and out of reverence for the Dharma, said:
"Let it be taken; let the verse be given; let it be fitting; do not delay."
Then, on this occasion, the rākṣasa spoke this well-spoken verse:
"Better to dwell in the hells than to take up residence in the company of wicked men— those who tremble at lamentation, who suffer from union with the unpleasant, and who are bereft of what is dear."
A piśāca spoke these words to the minister named Saṃjaya:
"Give me your own heart; listen to this well-spoken verse."
"I give you my own heart; speak a well-spoken verse," said the hero Sañjaya, free from all suffering, to the Piśāca.
Then the piśāca spoke this well-spoken verse:
"A blazing fire is never extinguished by grass and wood;
likewise, thirst for sensual pleasures is never quenched by enjoyments."
A poor man spoke thus to the merchant named Vasundhara:
"This well-spoken verse shall be given in exchange for my entire possessions."
The Bodhisattva said:
"I give you everything; recite a well-spoken verse. The virtuous praise that which is well-spoken among all things."
Then the poor man recited this well-spoken verse:
Where beings are foolish, even crowded places are empty;
yet even a single person who possesses true knowledge makes a place full, though it be empty.
A man said this to King Surūpa:
"It is possible to hear well-spoken words at the price of all of Jambudvīpa."
The Bodhisattva said:
I give you all of Jambudvīpa, whatever you desire;
speak quickly your well-spoken words, speak the truth of what you wish.
Then a man spoke this well-spoken verse:
Wherever the conceits of "I" and "mine," as well as various forms of pride,
have arisen, there the Tathāgatas appear for the sake of bringing that pride to cessation.
The hunter spoke thus to the deer named Satvara:
"This is a well-spoken verse; give me your flesh and listen to it."
If I may hear a well-spoken word in exchange for this flesh subject to decay, I will give you my flesh; speak quickly that well-spoken word!
Then the hunter spoke this well-spoken verse:
The dust from the feet of the virtuous is better than a mountain made of gold;
that dust removes sorrow, while that mountain increases it.
A slave said this to the king named Nāgabhuja:
"It is possible to obtain well-spoken words even through a kingdom over the four continents."
The Bodhisattva said:
"I give you sovereignty over the four continents; speak quickly!
Do not delay; tell me these well-spoken words."
Thereupon, his slave recited this well-spoken verse:

The wise say that the agitation of a learned person is equal to the plucking out of body hair; therefore, having attained the power of knowledge, one should uproot the defilements. Having severed them with a mind free from faults, the pure Saṅgha shines forth.
The Teacher of the World shines forth for the virtuous, following them, having not laid down his burden, and being pure.
Thus, for the sake of a well-spoken word, he fell once more into a precipice;
and again, for the sake of a well-spoken word, he abandoned his ship in the great ocean.
Having heard a well-spoken verse, he again gave up his eyes;
and having heard a well-spoken verse, he fell once more into a mass of fire.
For the sake of the well-spoken teachings, the highly renowned bulls among Jinas undertake many such difficult practices.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
Furthermore, O Son of the Conqueror, how do those bodhisattvas who abide on the third stage regress from the fourth stage?
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.
O bearer of the ascetic virtues, by fourteen modes, bodhisattvas abiding on the third stage fall back from the fourth stage.
By which fourteen?
They are devoted to the practice of gambling with crooked dice;
they resort to seclusion far too frequently;
and while exercising their rule, being overcome by greed, they seize all the property of the inhabitants of the conquered territories.
Without investigating the offense, they inflict capital punishment;
they do not protect those deserving of execution,
and they subject men to castration.
They fall into error and,
while possessing wealth, do not share it for the maintenance of their livelihood;
and having gone forth, they do not master the great learning spoken by the perfectly enlightened Buddhas.
Furthermore, despite their former vows, they do not teach the vast learning they have acquired;
they associate with those bound by material gain rather than those bound by the Dharma;
and they do not frequently speak in praise of the Buddha.
They teach that the perfectly awakened ones are equal to the world,
and they do not lead others to perceive the perfectly awakened ones as being supramundane.
O bearer of the ascetic qualities, by these fourteen modes, bodhisattvas abiding on the third stage fall back from the fourth stage.

"O Dhātudharmadhara, whatever bodhisattvas, while abiding on the third stage, have turned back, are turning back, or will turn back from the fourth stage, all of them do so for these fourteen reasons and no more."
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.

Furthermore, O Son of the Conqueror, when those irreversible Bodhisattvas first generate the mind directed toward awakening, with what kind of happiness are they endowed, and how many beings become possessed of the essence of happiness?
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana addressed the venerable Mahākāśyapa in verses:
When that which is inconceivable and marvelous arises— the birth of the minds of the great seers— then all sentient beings come to be endowed with the essence of happiness.
Consisting of the cultivation of the path to enlightenment.
And those who have the certainty that it is for seven nights,
even those who dwell in the terrible abodes of hell,
and those living beings in the realms of the hungry ghosts—
And they are indeed called happy beings.
For seven nights, living beings do not pass away out of the Bodhisattva’s skillful compassion;
and the earth, together with the oceans, trembles.
Radiant with light, he wanders upon the summit of Mount Meru.
This [wind] operates at the joints of the earth; it is as immovable as space, of this there is no doubt.
Within those [joints], for all the masses of virtuous karma, it [remains].
It revolves everywhere, continuously pervaded by splendor.

Then indeed, the Bodhisattva who had been a Trāyastriṃśa deity named Nāmatideva, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder and extending his joined palms toward where the Blessed One was seen, praised the Blessed One in the presence of the assembly of those who have attained self-mastery with these verses:
His form has the luster of gold, with a body as unassailable as the rising sun, shining with splendor;
it is fully endowed with the thirty-two perfect marks of a Great Man as described by those who practice virtue;
he is supreme in conduct, possessed of a complete radiance, with strength greater than that of the mountains of the earth, and the bearer of the highest power.
I pay homage to you, who are peaceful, who are self-controlled, who are skilled in mindfulness and discipline, and who are honored by gods and asuras.

For a long time, the Sage— desiring the destruction of existence, possessing various noble and diverse virtues preceded by loving-kindness, and having produced manifold roots of merit— was intent upon tranquility; he, the wise one, abandoned his permanent residence, honored by both asuras and devas, though it was comfortable, for the sake of awakening sentient beings.
Born in the lineage of the Ikṣvākus, he descended to the surface of the earth, established in glory, and possessed of unshakable fortitude.

That excellent one, resembling a white lotus and possessing the form of an elephant, entered the womb of Queen Māyā; thus did the Illuminator of the World, departing from his residence in the sublime Tuṣita heaven,
come here to uplift all beings who are intoxicated, blind, and fallen upon the treacherous path of doubt.
At that time, the earth, strewn with jewels and filled with heaps of various treasures, trembled;
and it paid homage to that Great Sage, the Lord of the Śākyas, who was rich in conduct, steadfast in mindfulness, and endowed with supreme virtues.

Whether in the upper story of the palace or in the preeminent abode of the Lord of the Gods, the Queen Māyā dwells in happiness, attended by dances, songs, graceful movements, and instrumental music— delightful to the ear, heart, and eye— just like a goddess among the immortals.
That queen said to the king who was despondent, "O Lord of the Earth, I wish to go to that excellent forest, if you so desire."
The Lumbinī grove was strewn with flowers, filled with the sweet warbling of cuckoos, and was a delight to the heart and soul.

Having gone there, he wandered about with his women, joyful and happy in the forest out of a longing for the woods; and as she was wandering through the grove, she then beheld the Lumbinī tree, which bore young creepers and tender sprouts.

Grasping a branch of that tree, she stood there gracefully, filled with the joy of supreme delight; while protecting that branch, she gave birth to the Jina, the Great Sage of unsurpassed excellence, whose mind is unconquerable.

There, the gods bathed the Jina with two streams of water, one cold and one warm, filled with the finest flowers— the King who was honored in the realm of the gods as soon as he was born, the Great Lord of the three worlds,
compassionate, transcendent of the world, a refuge here in heaven and on earth, and the ender of old age and death.
That steadfast one, whose eyes resemble lotus petals and who brings joy to both gods and asuras, has not yet reached the ground.
All the gods, joyful and satisfied, descended from their abodes beginning with the Heaven of the Thirty-three, intending to enter the forest.
Born of the lineage of the Ikṣvākus, he descended to the surface of the earth, established in glory and possessing immovable steadfastness.
With his seven strides complete, like the mind of a king of deer or a bull, he moved with a majestic retinue.
I am the eldest, the most excellent, the foremost in the world; for me there is no more birth, old age, or death, and the affliction of existence has been destroyed.

A celestial parasol, strewn with jewels, variegated with flowers as beautiful as crystal, and possessing the white luster of a pale cloud, was released from his hand and spontaneously covered the prince in the sky as he rose;
it was fashioned by the denizens of heaven, incomparable, and adorned with soft, fierce hairs resembling the whorls of a conch shell.
The white horse, adorned with jewels and gold, wanders about while being fanned by beautiful whisks and bearing a high-raised staff.
The great-sounding drums, thundering like clouds, resound through the wind, the birds, and the sky;
and divine showers of flowers, mixed with sandalwood powder, are released by the gods and celestial beings into the mouth of the Victorious One, the supreme in power.
With minds filled with extraordinary joy, the gods and celestial beings cry out "Victory! hundreds of times to him who brings happiness to all beings.
The oceans on earth, filled with various jewels, were agitated and brought near [to dry up] by the splendor of the Tathāgata, both in their depths and in their waters.
Thus ends the third bhūmi in the glorious Mahāvastu-avadāna.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
Furthermore, O Son of the Conqueror, as for those bodhisattvas who are established in the state of non-retrogression, how many kinds of actions do they perform that are considered impossible?
Then the elder Kātyāyana, who was learned in the teachings of the Jina,
addressed Kāśyapa, the observer of the dhuta-precepts, with these verses:
Understand those actions which bodhisattvas practice;
understand those which they do not practice because they are improper.
Bodhisattvas of great renown do not deprive even their mother, their father, or likewise an Arhat, of life.
They do not cause a schism in the Saṅgha, nor are they destroyers of stūpas;
they do not, in any way whatsoever, harbor malice toward the Tathāgata.
Those who do not pursue evil deeds due to their perverted views do not let even a small deed go to waste; how much less so for me, who has done much?
And while wandering through cyclic existence, they are never attached to the objects of their views, nor to merit preceded by knowledge, for the sake of the Dharma.
In the shade of whichever tree they sit and lie down,
there is no injury to its leaves, nor do they cause harm when provoked to anger.
The supreme among men practice the ten wholesome paths of action;
they do not employ mantras that destroy the bodies of others.
Relying upon their karma and relying upon curiosity,
they do not despair in times of adversity, nor do they rejoice in times of prosperity.
Physical action, verbal action, and likewise mental action,
as well as purified higher intentions and the perfection of generosity;
Having reached the eighth stage and beyond, they are irreversible;
honored by the world, they practice wholesome deeds with single-minded devotion.
Starting from the first stage up to the seventh,
these best of people practice mixed karma on these stages.
Practicing such deeds as these, great beings fulfill the ten stages for the sake of compassion toward the worlds.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
Furthermore, O Son of the Conqueror, do those irreversible Bodhisattvas go to the miserable states among the ordinary worldlings, or not?
Do they go to the various inferior destinies among the ordinary worldlings, or not?
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.

"O bearer of the ascetic qualities, those bodhisattvas who possess the nature of non-retrogression never, in any way, at any time, or by chance, go to hell, or go to the animal realm, or become poor, or weak, throughout the seven stages."

Furthermore, there are brahmins, whether individual brahmins or [those belonging to the classes of] Indras, Upendras, lords of yakṣas, yakṣas, nāgas, nāga kings, gandharvas, lords of gandharvas, universal monarchs, regional kings,
chief ministers, guild-leaders, prominent men of the countryside, and princes.

They become sons of guild-masters and sons of chief queens; they become leaders, possessing all forms of heroism and valor, endowed with strength, worthy of being looked up to, worthy of being gazed upon, worthy of salutation, their words worthy of being accepted, beloved by many people, dear to many people, pleasing to the minds of many people, worthy of praise, and worthy of gladdening.
And they become very wealthy, possessing great opulence, having large retinues, and being full of great energy and great splendor.
If some, for whatever reason, revile the noble ones while abiding on the seven stages, they go to the great Avīci hell; indeed, they go to individual hells.
They are not reborn among the pretas with their extremely coarse bodies, nor are they reborn among the asuras.
They do not go to the lowly animal realm;
they are not reborn in Uttarakuru;
and they do not undergo female birth.
They do not become impotent.
Furthermore, in all ten stages, there are persons who are endowed with all major and minor limbs and possess unimpaired faculties.

And whichever bodhisattva deprives another bodhisattva of life— whether it be a disciple of a perfectly awakened Buddha, a stream-enterer, or those beings destined for the state of a pratyekabuddha— that person, having deprived such an individual of life, goes to hell.

Whatever killing or taking of what is not given Bodhisattvas may commit while on the seven stages, or whatever fully completed unwholesome karma they may perform, it is not capable of leading that Bodhisattva to hell.

Furthermore, whatever unwholesome karmas were accumulated by Bodhisattvas prior to their initial vow remain obstructed by that first production of the thought of awakening (*prathamacittotpāda*), like a herd of deer blocked by a great mountain.
Yet, until that vow-mind is attained, those karmas ripen during the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh births—even down to the point of causing a headache.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.

Furthermore, O Son of the Conqueror, when those irreversible Bodhisattvas, having propitiated the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, go forth from the home life into homelessness, with what kind of instruction do those Tathāgatas instruct them?
Then the Elder Kātyāyana spoke thus to Kāśyapa:
"Indeed, through these distinct discourses given in proper sequence..."
Those skilled in the Jātaka and other supreme teachings proclaim the conduct of Bodhisattvas, which brings great benefit, as well as self-control, generosity, and restraint.
They are the sovereigns of the assembly of bodhisattvas.
The wise Tathāgata thus regards that Supreme among Men who, for the benefit of the great multitude, practices incomparable deeds.
He speaks to the assembly of bodhisattvas.
Such a lord is called a Blessed One; he undertakes what is difficult with prior knowledge.
In this world, one who is his equal is very hard to find.
In the teaching, "bodhisattva" refers to the Victor.
"O bearer of the dhuta-dharmas, it is in this manner that the Perfectly Awakened Ones teach the Dharma to the assembly of bodhisattvas."
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke thus to the venerable Mahākātyāyana:
"O Son of the Victor, from what point onward are these Jātaka stories spoken by the Victor to be understood?"
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke thus to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.
"O bearer of the ascetic virtues, these Jātaka tales spoken by the Victor pertain to this eighth stage."
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke thus to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
From what point on, O Son of the Conqueror, do Bodhisattvas relinquish all their possessions and perform difficult acts of renunciation?
When this had been said, Mahākātyāyana spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.
"O bearer of the ascetic virtues, from the eighth stage onwards, Bodhisattvas relinquish all their possessions and perform difficult acts of renunciation."
"O bearer of the dhuta-precepts, from the eighth stage onwards, Bodhisattvas are to be honored with the same honor as a perfectly enlightened Buddha."
In this regard, it is said:
From the eighth stage onward, O Bodhisattvas, sons of the Conquerors, they are to be regarded as perfectly enlightened Buddhas; from this point forward, they are irreversible.
From this point on, they attain profound meditations;
from this point on, refined knowledge arises within them.
From this time forth, they speak words preceded by wisdom;
from this time forth, the wise abandon their life out of contempt for it.
From this point on, they follow whatever pure birth they obtain;
from this point on, they experience whatever pure form they possess.
From this time forth, whatever *liṅga* they desire, they become that;
from this time forth, whatever deity they desire, they become that.
From this point on, they become either world-renouncers or destroyers of existence;
from this point on, they loathe sensual desires and praise nirvana.
From this time forward, there will be many preeminent speakers,
disciples of the glorious, perfectly awakened Buddhas, the gods beyond gods.
Then, having passed away, they will be exhorted by the Buddhas who illuminate the Dharma:
"O wise ones, teach the Dharma; receive the banner of the sages."
From this time forth, they will discipline a great many people in Arhatship;
from this time forth, they will discipline many people on the stage of training (śaikṣa).
From that time forth, the gods, yakṣas, and guhyakas followed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva until he attained the state of a Self-Existent One (Svayaṃbhū).
From that time forth, his form became preeminent in the world including the gods;
from that time forth, even his complexion, as well as his splendor, fame, renown, and strength,
became incomparable to the world, being supreme among Bodhisattvas.
And because the Buddhas have not arisen, they possess the five superknowledges;
seeing the faults in sensual desires, they praise renunciation.
From that time forward, both the gods and the asuras, together with Brahmā,
came with palms joined in reverence, being attracted by their virtues.
Whatever the activity of those who have attained mastery, such is the activity of Bodhisattvas;
likewise, whatever the activity of those on the eighth stage (bhūmi) may be, such it becomes for them as well.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.

"O Son of the Conqueror, what kind of Dharma do these irreversible Bodhisattvas teach to sentient beings while exercising the sovereignty of universal monarchs? In the absence of Buddhas, by what kind of gathering do they gather sentient beings,
and what kind of people do they disregard?"
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.
O bearer of the ascetic qualities, those irreversible bodhisattvas who exercise the sovereignty of universal monarchs teach the Dharma to sentient beings in this way.
They demonstrate to sentient beings that which is conjoined with the ten paths of wholesome action.

"May there be no killing of living beings; may there be no taking of what is not given; may the wives of others be protected; and may falsehood, slander, harsh speech, frivolous chatter, covetousness, malice, and wrong views be abandoned"—thus they teach.
Having set out heaps of bullion, gold, wealth, and dwellings before them, they spoke thus: "Whoever needs what from this, let him take that wealth;
my possessions were acquired through righteousness, so do not despair, sirs."
"I give you garlands, perfumes, incense, and delightful powders; do not despair, sirs, but enjoy yourselves."
When this had been said, Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
By what kinds of actions do the seven jewels come to belong to those bodhisattvas who exercise the sovereignty of a universal monarch?
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana addressed the venerable Mahākāśyapa in verses:
Just as the bull among men, a king of the four continents with abundant wealth and treasuries, obtains the seven jewels— so shall I proclaim this.
The best of men obtains the precious wheel, which resembles the orb of the rising sun, is beautiful with its collection of a thousand excellent spokes, and is born from his former roots of merit.
When one gives a gift accompanied by the proper method of service with an irreproachable intention,
that best of men obtains the wheel, which is unconquered and unimpeded.
He obtains the marvelous elephant-treasure, white as a mass of snow or a kumuda lily, established on seven limbs, with a speed equal to the force of the wind.
Having established a bridge across difficult and uneven terrain,
that slayer of enemies obtained the precious jewel of a supreme elephant capable of traveling through the path of the sky.
Then the king, through his accumulation of merit and wholesome deeds, obtains a jewel of a horse, dark as a bumblebee, golden-hued, with a mane swift as the wind, and with its hooves raised.
When he has carried his mother, father, elders, and likewise his teacher on excellent vehicles,
by that merit he obtains the wonderful jewel of a horse as king.
A woman obtains a jewel-gem of incomparable color, surpassing even the brilliance of beryl; she gains a beloved woman through infinite strength and vigor, the most excellent of jewels.
For in a previous existence, while dwelling there, he was devoted to self-restraint and contentment with his own wife;
and because he was a lord of men, he obtained that jewel of a woman.
The king, possessing great mastery, obtains as his noble householder-jewel one who is wealthy with various excellent riches and endowed with a vast accumulation of hoarded treasures.
A giver of various stores of wealth, endowed with profound respect for his teachers,
he thereby obtains the treasure of the householder, which is skilled in abundant riches.

The king who has desisted from unwholesome conduct obtains the excellent jewel of a counselor, one who is wise, discerning, clearly manifest as a leader’s banner, and capable of governing the four continents.
Having set out upon the path, he shows the way to those who have lost their way and whose eyes have been struck down;
by that, he obtains the jewel of the excellent guide, the supreme leader.
By means of these actions, those who uphold the ascetic virtues (dhuta-dharma) produce jewels;
and by that very same principle, the Lord of Men rules the earth with righteousness.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
"O Son of the Conqueror, by how many modes do these Bodhisattvas who have first produced the thought of awakening, while abiding on the fourth stage, fall back from the fifth stage?
When this was said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke thus to the venerable Mahākāśyapa:

O upholder of the ascetic qualities, those bodhisattvas who have first generated the thought of awakening, while abiding on the fourth stage, fall back from it to the fifth stage due to seven factors.
By which seven?
They become defilers of nuns,
they become defilers of men,
and they become defilers of paṇḍakas.
Moreover, by the power of mantras, they cause others to contract diseases that do not exist;
they cause those who possess good conduct to fall away from their ethical discipline,
and they become shameless.
And they become free from fear.

O bearer of the ascetic virtues (dhutadharma), whatever bodhisattvas first produce the thought of awakening, if they abide in these seven ways while on the fourth stage, they turn back from the fifth stage.
Thus, O son of the Sugata, this fourth stage has been taught,
which is delightful for those Bodhisattvas who are intent upon awakening.
Thus ends the fourth bhūmi in the glorious Mahāvastu-avadāna.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke thus to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
"O sons of the Conqueror, for those irreversible Bodhisattvas who pass from the fourth stage to the fifth stage, what is their state of mind at the transition?"
When this had been said, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke to the Venerable Mahākāśyapa.
They see all states of existence as ablaze due to passion, hatred, and delusion;
the transitional consciousness, which occurs immediately after the fourth or fifth [moment of consciousness], is without refuge and devoid of joy.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
Furthermore, O Son of the Conqueror, regarding those Perfectly Enlightened Ones who were honored by the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, while he was on the fifth stage—
what were the names and lineages of those Perfectly Enlightened Ones, and how large were their assemblies of disciples? How many were they?
The lifespan of the Prabhā-kalpa is one kevatika.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana addressed the venerable Mahākaśyapa in verses:
There was a supreme Victor named Śākyamuni, surrounded by ten million self-controlled ones;
he possessed a fathom-wide radiance, was as solid as a mountain, resembled a mountain of gold, and had vanquished all enemies.
At that time, the lifespan of that Supreme among Men was six thousand years;
his name was Yaśavrata, and he was an exceedingly beautiful Buddha.
By virtue of his lineage he was Gautama, and this Blessed One was then the son of a merchant who,
having given a gift of rice-gruel to the Buddha and his retinue, made a formal aspiration.
Whatever merit has been accumulated by me through giving to the Saṅgha of Arhats with full devotion—by that may I become a seer of the ultimate truth; may all my merit be entirely mine.
The final incarnation will be a beautiful lion among men named Sudarśana;
he will belong to the Bhāradvāja gotra, and his radiance will extend for ten yojanas.
The retinue of that essence of beings, who had attained mastery, consisted of ten million;
the lifespan of that subduer of Māra was ten thousand years.
And there was a wheel-turning monarch named Dharaṇīdhara;
he spoke thus to that Jina Sudarśana, together with his community of disciples:
"I give everything as a support for welfare," so the wise one spoke;
and thus he made this supreme vow: "May I become a king."

May I ferry across the people who have not yet crossed the ocean of old age and death. At that time, the Blessed One was named Nareśvara; he was of the Vāsiṣṭha lineage, and his radiance extended for ten yojanas. His roots of merit remained unimpaired.
He had a retinue of twelve koṭis of those who had attained mastery;
at that time, the lifespan of human beings was nine thousand years.
And there was a universal monarch named Aparājita;
with a clear and devout mind, he spoke these words to the Lord of Men, the One Possessing the Ten Powers:
I give these eighty-four monasteries to you, adorned with the limbs of the seven precious gems and endowed with many varieties of jewels.
Having given that gift to that lord of men, he made this aspiration:
"May I become thus; may I attain the powers of a Jina."
Formerly, there was a Jina named Suprabha, who had a minister named Vijaya;
he belonged to the Kāśyapa clan, and his radiance extended for ten yojanas.
And his community of disciples consisted of eighteen koṭis of those who had shaken off all dust;
at that time, the lifespan of human beings was twenty thousand years.
Having thus paid homage to that supreme Jina, Vijaya invited him who destroys existence;
the Daśabala then consented, and Vijaya was filled with joy.
Having satisfied him with excellent, refined food and delicacies of exquisite flavor, you then made this subsequent vow: "I have followed [him]; may I likewise attain such a state."
May I too become thus, honored by the best of men, a benefactor to humans and gods;
may I also become a supreme leader, a possessor of the ten powers, a tiger among speakers.
In former times, there was a Buddha, a Tathāgata named Ratanaparvata;
he belonged to the Gautama clan, and his radiance extended for ten yojanas.
There was an entourage of thirty million people whose minds were disciplined;
at that time, the lifespan of human beings was twenty thousand years.
At that time, there was a universal monarch named Acyuta;
pressing his feet to the feet of the Victor, he spoke these words to the best of men and gods:
"O Nara-nāga, I give eighty-four thousand palaces,
all beautifully adorned, to you and your community of disciples."
Having understood the King’s acceptance, he, with a joyful mind,
made a vow in the presence of the one who bears the excellent marks.

By this merit, may I become a protector for those without a protector, possessing the conduct of those who have accumulated the most excellent roots of virtue, and whose deeds are characterized by tireless vigor.
The Perfectly Awakened One named Kanakaparvata, whose mind was as pure as the expanse of the sky, existed;
he was honored by the best of men and was known by the clan name Kauṇḍinya.
The radiance of his body, born of his auspicious karma, extended for six yojanas,
and he had a retinue of five million self-controlled ones.
At that time, the lifespan of human beings was ten thousand six hundred years, and there were fourteen thousand [beings] of thirty-seven thousand years each.
At that time there was a universal monarch (cakravartin) named Priyadarśana,
radiant with the seven treasures, the protector of the earth who ruled over the four continents.
Having prostrated at the excellent feet of the Fully Awakened One, Kanakavarṇa, he,
together with his assembly of ministers and the inner court, made this request and spoke while holding a pearl necklace.
O Hero, I give to you, along with your assembly of disciples, my kingdom filled with cities and towns, as well as the four great and wealthy islands; I am without attachment to them.
Whatever food belongs to the seers, whatever clothing, and whatever medicinal preparations;
and whatever beds and seats there are, even those found in the most excellent palaces.
Everything is already bestowed for your enjoyment in its twelvefold form;
O you who possess the most excellent form, out of compassion, show mercy to me.
Having given this gift, that protector of the earth,
with a joyful mind, made a vow in the presence of Saṃpūrṇakuśala.
Perceiving the ultimate truth, having attained the supreme perfection of fearlessness,
may I thereby become an excellent leader who brings about the destruction of all substrates of existence.
The Blessed One, who bore the thirty-two marks, was named Puṣpadanta;
he was a perfectly awakened one (saṃbuddha) of the Vatsa clan, a seer of the ultimate truth.
The bodily radiance of that most excellent Jina extended for nine yojanas,
and thirty-four koṭis of those who had attained mastery were attached to the One Possessing Ten Powers.
And the measure of the lifespan of human beings was fifty thousand years;
thus, one should not entertain doubt regarding that instruction.
And at that time there was a king, a lord of men named Durjaya;
having approached Puṣpadanta, he paid homage at his feet along with his retinue.
With palms joined in reverence and full of faith, the Lord of Men said this to Puṣpadanta:
"May the Daśabala accept my provision of food for seven days."
Perceiving his acquiescence, King Durjaya-ṛddhibala [or Durjaya-ūrdhvabala] covered the surface of the earth with beautiful golden bands.
There he sets out variegated seats made of jewels,
and he prepares a diverse array of food, fragrant and freshly prepared.
Eight hundred men and gods, wearing ornaments and bearing various beautiful decorations, hold parasols made of the seven precious gems.
Thus, for each one who has attained mastery, they hold in their hearts a variegated jewel-umbrella, stainless and resembling the surface of the moon or a conch shell.
Having fully gratified the Sugata named Puṣpa along with his retinue, the king then made a mental aspiration, and at that very moment, he fulfilled that aspiration.
"Just as you, may I too become a perfectly awakened one and proclaim the Dharma to humans and gods. ...
[There was] a Blessed One named Lalitavikrama, a perfectly awakened one who bore the thirty-two marks, a destroyer of existence, of the Vāsiṣṭha lineage, who had shaken off all afflictions.
And from his own body there issued forth a radiance for thirty-two *yojanas*,
