and the retinue of that best of men consisted of thirty million self-mastered ones (*vaśibhūta*).
At that time, the lifespan of humans was eighty-four thousand years;
and there was a king then who possessed the fourfold army and was beloved and pleasing.
The protector of the earth had forty million palaces made of many jewels constructed,
as well as one preeminent palace.
The king causes vast and irreproachable lodgings and seats to be made, and he provides for the sages food and medicinal requisites suitable for them.
Having offered [this] to the Blessed One together with his community of disciples,
the king, with a joyful heart, made this aspiration in the presence of the One Possessing the Ten Powers.

May I become one like the rare and peerless One of Ten Powers, who crushes the delusions of old age and death; may I be the supreme among men and gods, crushing the words of the hosts of evil factions.
The Blessed One, possessing the thirty-two marks, was named Mahāyaśas;
by lineage he was Kāśyapa, one of vast renown and immeasurable fame.
The body of that merit-filled one was fifty yojanas in radiance,
and he had fifty-five koṭis of those who had attained mastery.
At that time, the measure of the lifespan was eighty-four thousand years;
this eighty-four [thousand] was fourfold for human beings at that time.
At that time, there was a king named Mṛgapatisvara,
the sovereign of the four continents, possessed of vast and excellent power, whose wheel was unconquered.
The lord of the earth had a forest grove constructed, ninety-six yojanas in extent, with branches like heaps of jewels, most excellent and covered with choice cloths.
Having made the earth have a surface of lapis lazuli gems, adorned with various ornaments,
scented with the fragrance of the finest aloe-wood incense, and its surface strewn with fragrant flowers;
There, the protector of the earth, with a serene mind, gratified that lion among speakers, that bull among men, with exquisite food for seven days.
Then, with a joyful heart, he offered that forest— which was like the grove of the best of gods— as a daytime retreat for the Daśabala, the essence of all beings.
Having given [this] to the one of great renown together with his community of disciples,
the king, with a joyful mind, then made this secondary vow.
May I be honored by many people, self-become, not led by others, and omniscient;
for through that merit of mine, may I become one who possesses the power of a Tathāgata.
The Victorious One Ratnacūḍa was a treasury of vast strength and merit, a knower of right and wrong policy,
possessed of deep blue eyes, a steadfast one who was a collection of incomparable virtues.
And his radiance extended for a hundred yojanas all around his body;
at that time, he was Sarvadarśin, of the Bhāradvāja lineage.
His Saṅgha consisted of ninety-nine koṭis of those who had shaken off the dust [of defilements],
and at that time, the lifespan was eighty-four thousand years.
At that time, there was a universal monarch, a powerful ruler of the four continents,
named Maṇiviṣāṇa, who governed the people according to the Dharma.
The protector of the earth had ninety-two billion palaces of manifold forms constructed, dedicated to that Jewel-like Victor.
He fed for ten years without ceasing Ratnacūḍa— who resembled excellent gold and was honored by the hosts of gods and men— along with his retinue.
And on the first day, having fed the Sugata together with the community of disciples,
the best of men presented magnificent palaces to the Possessor of Virtue.
Having given that gift to that Great Being, the excellent king,
with a mind full of serene faith, makes a vow in the presence of the Victor.
With the net of delusion severed, with a serene mind and unimpeded eloquence,
he shall ferry across all people fallen into the great ocean of saṃsāra.
In this very way, on the fifth stage, there are immeasurable lions among men:
Pratyekabuddhas, as well as those sons of the Conqueror who are still in training and those beyond training.
These and all other Tathāgatas have been fully honored by the Blessed One;
thus has the root of merit been accumulated for the sake of the entire world.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
O sons of the Conqueror, by how many modes do those bodhisattvas who have made the vow for enlightenment, while abiding on the fifth stage, turn back from the sixth stage?
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.

O Son of the Conqueror, bearer of the ascetic virtues, there are four ways in which Bodhisattvas who have made the vow for enlightenment, while abiding on the fifth stage, fall back from the sixth stage.
By which four?
Having gone forth in the instruction of the Perfectly Enlightened One, they associate with practitioners of yoga (*yogācāra*).
While on the eighth stage, though greedy for the sensations of ascetic purification (*dhuta*), they are terrified of meditative cultivation;
yet they frequently dwell in abundance in the cultivation of tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
They conceptualize the mind that takes an object as its object according to its causes.

For indeed, O bearer of the ascetic qualities (dhutadharmadhara), whatever bodhisattvas, having made the vow for awakening, while abiding on the fifth stage, turn back from the sixth stage— all of them have turned back, do turn back, or will turn back by means of these four modes.
Thus, O worthy one, this fifth stage has been explained and demonstrated for those Bodhisattvas who possess manifold merits.
Thus ends the fifth bhūmi in the glorious Mahāvastu-avadāna.
Then the Elder Kāśyapa spoke to Kātyāyana:
"What is the mental state of the wise Bodhisattvas in the fifth [stage]?"
Then the Elder Kātyāyana addressed the sage Kāśyapa, who maintained the dhuta-precepts, with a verse:
Bound by a mere trifling taste, this worldly cycle is exceedingly terrible;
[from it] one is born again and again.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
"The field."
Then the Elder Kātyāyana spoke to Mahākāśyapa:
"Listen to the field of the Lords of the World, which is grounded in the true meaning."
And I shall describe the secondary field (*upakṣetra*) of those supreme speakers;
having heard those words and the teaching, O best of men.
A buddha-field is examined as being sixty-one thousand [yojanas];
the secondary field (upakṣetra) of that same kind should be known as four times that size.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
Furthermore, O Son of the Conqueror, do perfectly awakened Buddhas arise in all Buddha-fields, or do they arise only in some?
When this had been said, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana addressed the Venerable Mahākāśyapa in verses:
Only a very small portion of the field remains non-empty, filled by those who possess incomparable forms;
for there are many millions of billions of fields.
They are empty of the most excellent of men.
For rare indeed is one who bears the excellent marks, whose awakening has been fully realized over a long period of time,
who is skilled in all dharmas, and possesses supreme splendor.
"The being who is the foundation for the happiness of all beings."
When this had been said, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the Venerable Mahākātyāyana.
Indeed, O Son of the Conqueror, what is the cause and what is the condition that two Perfectly Enlightened Ones do not appear simultaneously in a single field?
When this had been said, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana addressed the Venerable Mahākāśyapa in verses:
Whatever task there is that is most difficult to accomplish—the work of a Buddha—that he fulfills entirely; this is the natural law of the Buddhas.
If one who possesses the eye were to be incapable regarding the qualities of a Buddha,
then two Great Beings, Tathāgatas, would arise.
And they avoid that coexistence of two [Buddhas] who are incapable [of teaching simultaneously]; therefore, two bulls among men are not born in the same field.

It is never heard that the Buddhas, those supreme among men and sons of the Victors, have entered parinirvāṇa while the Buddha-qualities remain incomplete, even though they have passed away in the past.
“Those Perfectly Awakened Ones who have not yet come, those who have passed away, and those who exist at present—
the supreme among men— attain nirvana through the Dharma of a Buddha.”
When this had been said, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the Venerable Mahākātyāyana.
"O Son of the Victor, which other Buddha-fields are there at present where the Perfectly Awakened Ones are currently teaching the Dharma?"
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana addressed the venerable Mahākāśyapa in verses:
In the eastern direction, there is a Buddha-field called Sunirmita;
there dwells the preeminent Victor named Mṛgapatiskandha.
In the eastern direction lies the Buddha-field named Kṛtāgada;
there dwells the Victor named Siṃhahanu, endowed with the thirty-two marks.
In the eastern direction, there is a Buddha-field called Vibhūṣita;
there dwells the Great Sage named Lokaguru, the all-seeing one.
In the eastern direction lies the Buddha-field called Akantaka;
there, the Teacher named Jñānadhvaja instructs living beings.
In the eastern direction, a buddha-field was beheld;
there dwells a Jina named Sundara, who has the luster of a golden image.
In the southern quarter lies the buddha-field named Drumadhvaja;
there dwells the perfectly awakened one named Anihata, who is gladdened by the gods.
In the southern direction, there is a delightful Buddha-field;
there dwells the Great Sage, the Perfectly Awakened One named Cārunetra.
In the southern direction lies a Buddha-field free from mire;
there dwells the Perfectly Awakened One, the Guide named Mālādhārī.
In the western direction lies the Buddha-field named Avigraha;
there dwells the Perfectly Awakened One named Ambara, the destroyer of existence.
In the northern quarter of the world, there is a delightful buddha-field;
there dwells a perfectly awakened one named Pūrṇacandra, who is learned in the ritual procedures.
In the downward direction lies a well-established Buddha-field;
there dwells the Perfectly Awakened One, the Tathāgata named Dṛḍhabāhu.
In the region above, in the direction of the zenith, there is a Buddha-field named Anuddhṛta;
there dwells a fortunate Buddha known by the name Arisūdana.
Beyond this, there are many thousands of Buddha-fields;
beyond those thousands of Buddha-fields, no further ten million is known.
No end to the millions of empty buddha-fields can be discerned;
no end to the millions of thousands of world-systems can be discerned.
Just as the prior limit of the wheel of saṃsāra is not known,
even so the prior limit of world-systems is not known.
The prior limit of the Buddhas who have passed away is not known;
the prior limit of those making vows for enlightenment is not known.
The prior limit of those possessing the qualities of non-retrogression is not known;
the prior limit of those who have attained the stage of consecration is not known.
For those dwelling among the Tuṣita gods, no prior limit is known;
for those passing away from the Tuṣita gods, no prior limit is known.
For those lying within the mother’s womb, no prior limit is known;
indeed, for those staying within the mother’s womb, no prior limit is known.
The prior limit of heroes being born is not known;
the prior limit of world-protectors who have been born is not known.
For those being held on their laps, no prior limit is known;
for those taking steps, no prior limit is known.
The prior limit of those laughing with great laughter is not known;
the prior limit of those surveying the directions is not known.
No prior limit is known for those being carried on the hip;
no prior limit is known for those being led away by the Gandharvas.
The prior limit of those going forth from the cities is not known;
the prior limit of those approaching the foot of the Bodhi tree is not known.
For those who have attained the wisdom of the Tathāgata, no prior limit is known;
for those who turn the wheel of Dharma, no prior limit is known.
For those who are training millions of beings, no prior limit is known;
for those who roar the lion’s roar, no prior limit is known.
For those relinquishing the formative forces of life, no prior limit is known;
for those heroes who enter parinirvāṇa, no prior limit is known.
For those who have attained extinction and are lying in peace, the prior limit is not known;
for those heroes who are blazing in meditation, the prior limit is not known.
Understand this as it truly is: the host of Teachers;
for in various places, the Perfectly Awakened One is seen within the Buddha-fields.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.

"O sons of the Conqueror, if there are this many perfectly enlightened ones, and each single perfectly enlightened one brings immeasurable beings to final nirvana, will they not, in a short time, bring all beings to final nirvana?
Thus, this world would become entirely empty in every respect, devoid of all beings."
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana addressed the venerable Mahākāśyapa in verses:
May it always be empty, completely filled with immediate succession;
may it always be established as non-abiding and without objective support.
"However small the element of earth may be, sentient beings are more numerous than that;
thus were ordinary persons described by the Seer of the Ultimate."
"For those many beings who hear the teaching of the Best of Men, how could there ever be an end?"— thus it was said by the Great Seer.

When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana: "O Son of the Conqueror, by how many factors do those beings who have made the vow for perfect enlightenment, while abiding in the sixth stage, fall back from the seventh stage?"
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.

Indeed, O bearer of the ascetic qualities (dhutadharma), there are two conditions by which bodhisattvas who have made the vow for awakening, while abiding on the sixth stage, fall back from the seventh stage.
By which two?

They long for the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, and at the time when the Perfectly Awakened Ones, through their thorough knowledge of sentient beings, [declare], "I am the Great-Souled One who brings peace," they listen with attentive ears, honoring the deity.

"O bearer of the ascetic qualities, whatever bodhisattvas there may be who, while abiding on the sixth stage, have turned back, are turning back, or will turn back from the seventh stage— all of them do so, have done so, or will do so by means of these two modes."
Thus is this sixth stage of those excellent qualities of the lords of deer, the beneficial great seers, the bodhisattvas.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the glorious Mahāvastu-Avadāna.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.

"O bearer of the ascetic qualities (dhutadharma), what kind of transitional consciousness (sandhicitta) arises for those bodhisattvas who are irreversible and pass from the sixth stage to the seventh stage?"
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana addressed the venerable Mahākāśyapa in verses:
The mind of the supreme great person proceeds toward self-restraint for the benefit of others;
that which transitions from the seventh stage to the [subsequent] stages is called the "connecting mind" (*saṃdhicitta*) among the stages.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.

O Son of the Conqueror, as for these irreversible Bodhisattvas, from the first bhūmi onwards, with what kind of bodily action are they endowed? With what kind of verbal action are they endowed? With what kind of mental action are they endowed?
With what kind of nature are they endowed?
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.
O bearer of the ascetic qualities, for those bodhisattvas who are irreversible, these actions occur starting from the first stage.

They abstain from taking life and speak in praise of abstaining from taking life; they commend those beings on the stages who, through their resolute intention, do not deprive any living being of life, even by association with evil friends.
But after they have developed compassion for those beings who are crying out across the seven earths, and having undertaken the precepts,
renounced their kingdom or whatever sovereignty they possessed, and gone forth from the home life into homelessness,
they extensively teach the Dharma of abstaining from taking life.
Furthermore, O bearer of the dhuta-precepts, in the past, while dwelling on the seventh stage, this Supreme Person became a king named Kuśa.
He had a queen named Apratimā, who was this very Yaśodharā, the mother of Rāhulaśrī.
And he who was the wicked man Devadatta at this time was then the regional king named Jaṭhara.
Having heard of that peerless goddess, sensual desire overwhelmed his mind.
He dispatched a messenger to King Kuśa.
"Give me the peerless goddess; she shall be my wife.
If you do not give her, then prepare for battle and get your mounts ready."
"O King, send to me that which you have resolved;
otherwise, if you do not send it to me, you shall come under my power along with your entire kingdom."
Having heard this, King Kuśa said this to his wife:
"Listen, O Queen, to the words of your womb; speak your certain conclusion."
Then the queen, shedding a torrent of tears, spoke to King Kuśa.
"O noble one, O lord of men, though you have not surpassed me with your weapons, I have reached the further shore in being cut and in being pierced."
"O King, behold the head of Jaṭhara, severed by me with its crown level; drenched in blood, let it roll at your feet."
But this arrow, released by me as a living being and made to take away his life,
having pierced his belly and its own body, shall further pierce the earth.
On the back of a horse, on a chariot, or on the shoulder of an elephant, and at the forefront of the best of warriors, I have brought about the end of many bellies.
I am the mantra, I am the twilight prayer, and I am the speaker of words;
likewise, by means of reasons and causes, I cause even that which is not to be killed to be killed.
I alone, who am peerless, shall bring liberation through both;
for my illusions are indeed incalculable, and the world is as straw to me.
"How might the king, wearing perfumes and garlands, dwelling upon the palace roof and surrounded by thousands of women, become free from longing? [Mvu 1.130]
Then, O Son of the Conqueror, Queen Apratimā employed such a stratagem that, by means of it, King Jaṭhara became confident and entered the inner apartments of King Kuśa,
falling under the power of Queen Apratimā.
Then that peerless queen, having placed her right foot upon the heart of King Jaṭhara and resting her left foot upon his ankle, sang these verses:
O base man, you have never before heard the description of that flowering forest creeper whose blossoms at the arrival of spring are drunk by bees with wings variegated by floral pollen.
Other bees do not show affection for this [place].
O base man, you have never before heard of that lotus pond which a wild elephant, his body afflicted by passion, once climbed upon though it was submerged in mud and churned by water.
Other wild elephants do not show such affection here.
O you of faultless limbs, you who have resolved upon the lotus-like Kamalā, she who sports at night like a string of pearls upon the chest of the king honored by the earth.
As if standing upon the surface of the earth to reach the full moon.
Then indeed, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, King Jaṭhara cried out at that time.
"Be gracious, O Goddess; grant us refuge! they said.
King Kuśa spoke to that incomparable queen.
"O Goddess, grant fearlessness to this coward who has come to you for refuge;
for to one with palms joined in supplication, it is indeed the duty of the virtuous to do so."

"Long ago, O bearer of the dhuta-precepts, this Blessed One was a nāga king named Ugra; having been brought under control by a snake-charmer through the power of mantras and medicinal herbs, he fell into great distress."
And due to negligence, that snake-charmer became one whose spells had failed.
Then this thought occurred to that Naga king Ugra:
"Indeed, it would be easy for me to reduce this wretch to ashes;
however, this is not worthy of us who are devoted to the protection of Dharma."
He spoke these verses.
"Even though you were capable of reducing me to ashes by your own power, since your mantra has failed, I grant you safety; live long for me."
Long ago, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, this very Blessed One was Siṃha, the king of beasts, and this wicked man Devadatta was that hunter.

Then, while he was dwelling in a grove suitable for a lion’s training, wandering in the forest, solitary, sitting in confidence, motionless, at peace, and not looking around, a hunter— whose enmity had been nurtured by former intentions— pierced him with a poisoned arrow.
Though pierced, he remained motionless, endowed with profound fortitude, established in his own strength, and undaunted;
with his neck slightly raised, he then perceived that wicked man, terrified and having sought refuge, and fell into reflection.
"Indeed, this base man is within my reach to slay, even though he has fled to a mountain peak, a cave, a tree, or the subterranean realm;
nevertheless, considering that 'enmities are not stilled by enmity,' he spoke this verse."
"I have been pierced by a poison-smeared arrow that strikes the vital organs;
today, let it be so for him who is afraid, but there is no fear for you."
In the past, O upholder of the ascetic virtues, this very Blessed One was a highly esteemed caravan leader.
And this caravan, with that very evil man Devadatta acting as its guide—having been instigated by bandits—set out upon a path through a wilderness.
With his mind bound by the persistence of former enmity, he approached in order to have that caravan leader killed by bandits.

Those merchants, led by the caravan leader, captured the bandits; and as they were being led toward execution with the guide at their head, crying out in distress and without refuge, they sought protection from the caravan leader alone. And the guide, having offended against others, joined his palms in reverence and begged the caravan leader for safety.

In him, who dwells in compassion, compassion had been cultivated through hundreds of thousands of existences; it arose within him, and having granted fearlessness even to those who were life-threatening, he spoke to the guide:
"Smoke released by me with the wind would destroy the entire region;
therefore, I grant life to the guide along with the thieves."

Furthermore, O upholder of the ascetic virtues (dhutadharma), when he was a king, this Blessed One granted inconceivable safety to his chief queen, who had committed a great offense and had been brought to the place of execution.
Having consoled the chief queen— who was endowed with gentleness and straightforwardness accumulated from former lives— he spoke this verse:
"Come now, let me cause the weapon to fall from her body with an unbaked clay vessel;
I grant you safety, and that place shall be as it was before."

O bearer of the dhuta-precepts, hundreds of thousands of such difficult deeds have been performed by Bodhisattvas who are irreversible, in this way with the body, in this way with speech, and in this way with the mind.
Bodhisattvas wander through cyclic existence endowed with manifold virtues;
nevertheless, having come under the influence of karma, those bodhisattvas perform actions that are celebrated for their condensed virtues.
They possess firm valor, are endowed with fortitude, are true to their vows, upright, and free from deceit.
They are not miserly;
they are not fickle;
and they are gentle.

They are compassionate, capable of enduring conflict, possessed of inexhaustible minds, and unmoved in mind; they are invincible, difficult to conquer, endowed with courage, perfected in renunciation, and perfected in their vows.
They are eloquent, possessed of diverse eloquence, endowed with vision, and free from craving.
They become attached to the ultimate truth; they grasp at what has been gathered;
and they maintain pure conduct.
They possess unshakable minds;
they are endowed with extreme reverence;
and they are perfected in the proper conduct toward elders and virtuous persons.
They are skilled in means;
they are those who bring about the connection and integration of all undertakings,
and they are experts in the coordination of steps regarding royal affairs.
They possess speech that does not falter in an assembly and are patient with harsh words; they have wisdom as their banner and are skilled in gathering a great multitude of people;
they maintain an even mind and their conduct is such that it cannot be censured.
They are accomplished in their professional activities and skilled in providing assistance;
they are also skilled in attending to the sufferings of others.
They are firm and sweet in their appreciation of the perils [of sensory pleasures] and the like; they are skilled in uprooting faults regarding what is contemptible to behold;
they are untiring in concealing the private failings of others;
and, having no desire for the attainment of fruits, they possess roots of virtue characterized by the discernment of passion, hatred, and delusion.
They become skilled in the exhaustion and pacification of the afflictions;
they become free from doubt regarding all that is beneficial;
and they become possessed of tireless resolve toward all dharmas.
They become endowed with aspiration for the profound teachings of the Buddha; they become untainted in their bodily, vocal, and mental actions regarding the realization of the ultimate truth;
and they become those whose virtuous karma is not clung to within the reality of existence and the living being.
They possess supreme knowledge and unafflicted eloquence;
they aspire to the domain of the Buddhas and are intent on never turning back.
Having wisdom as their banner, they are tireless in speech and skilled in exhortation.
They come to possess a nature free from corruption, they become devoid of defeat,
they become free from fault,
and they become transformed by the three kinds of non-distraction.
They become steady in speech and free from lustful desires;

they do not engage in sexual intercourse and do not disparage the gathering of all sentient beings. Having entered into the world, they possess the strength of firm resolve and are skilled in various matters of what is possible and impossible regarding all activities. Thus, they become endowed with such qualities as these.
The preeminent ones, steadfast in their countless virtues, possess an even-mindedness toward all sentient beings;
regarding this, it is said:
It is not possible for all the birds to reach the end of the sky;
likewise, it is not possible for all sentient beings to know the qualities of the Self-Arisen Ones.
And whatever mantras or medicines, O bearer of the ascetic qualities (*dhutadharmadhara*), are fashioned for the benefit and happiness of the world to assist sentient beings,
all of them have been brought forth by Bodhisattvas.
And whatever medicines circulate in the world for the sake of the welfare and happiness of sentient beings, all of those have been handed down from the Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, whatever treatises circulate in the world that are endowed with the determination of reality, all of them were composed by Bodhisattvas.
Whatever enumeration, calculation, and numerical positions exist here in this world—all these are the method of the bodhisattvas.

Or whatever designations exist in the world, such as Brāhmī, Puṣkarasārā, Kharoṣṭī, Yāvanī, Brahmavāṇī, Puṣpalipi, Kutalipi, Śaktinālīpi, Vyatyastalipi, Lekhalipi, Mudrālipi, Ukara, Madhura, Darada, Cīna, Hūṇa,
Apīra, Vaṅga, Sīphala, Tramida, Dardura, Ramaṭha, Bhaya, Vaicchetuka, Gulmala, Hastadā, Kasūla, Ketuka, and Kusuva.
Even when the soles of the feet are worn out, they are bound to the axle; this is the entire policy of the Bodhisattvas.
Gold, silver, tin, copper, lead, gems, jewels, and all types of fields—these are the domain of the Bodhisattvas.
Whatever causes there may be that are devised for the benefit of the world, all of these are brought forth by the Bodhisattvas.
In this regard, the following is said:
Those foremost among men, who understand the welfare of the world,
move through the cycle of existence as unequaled beings;
they practice what is most beneficial for gods, humans, and guhyakas.
For the supreme attainment belongs to the lords.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
O son of the Conqueror, what thought arises in those who are irreversible?
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.
"O bearer of the ascetic qualities (dhutadharmadhara), when those irreversible Bodhisattvas pass from the seventh stage to the eighth stage, a mind associated with great compassion arises.
Thus, this is called the seventh stage of the Bodhisattvas."
Thus ends the seventh bhūmi in the glorious Mahāvastu-avadāna.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.

"O Son of the Victor, by the Blessed One, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni, while abiding in the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh stages, in which Samyaksaṃbuddhas was merit planted? What are the names of those Samyaksaṃbuddhas?"
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.

O bearer of the ascetic virtues (dhutadharma), hear first the names of those Perfectly Awakened Ones, the Blessed Ones born of the Śākya royal lineage, by whom roots of merit were accumulated— those of vast power, excellence, and fame: Satyadharmavipulakīrti, then Sukīrti, Lokābharaṇa, Vidyutprabha, Indratejas, Brahmakīrti, Vasundhara, Supārśva, Anupavadya, Sujyeṣṭha, Sṛṣṭarūpa, and Praśastaguṇarāśi.
Meghasvara (Cloud-Voiced), Hemavarṇa (Golden-Colored), Sundaravarṇa (Beautiful-Colored), Mṛgarājaghoṣa (Roar of the King of Beasts), Āśukārī (Swift-Acting), Dhṛtarāṣṭragati (Gait of Dhṛtarāṣṭra),

Kokābhilāṣita (Longed-for by the Cakravāka Bird), Jitaśatru (Conqueror of Enemies), Supūjita (Well-Worshipped), Yaśarāśi (Mass of Glory), Amitatateja (Immeasurable Radiance), Sūryagupta (Protected by the Sun), Candrabhānu (Moon-Light), Niścitārtha (One of Certain Meaning), Kusumagupta (Protected by Flowers), Padmābha (Lotus-Like), Prabhaṃkara (Light-Maker), Dīptateja (Blazing Radiance), and Satvarāja (King of Beings).
Gajadeva, Kuñjaragati, Sughoṣa, Samabuddhi, Hemavarṇalambadāma, Kusumadāma, Ratnadāma, Alaṃkṛta, Vimukta, Ṛṣabhagāmī, Ṛṣabha, Devasiddhayātra,
Supātra, Sarvabandha, Ratnamakuṭa, Citramakuṭa, Sumakuṭa, Varamakuṭa, Calamakuṭa, Vimalamakuṭa, and Lokandhara.

Vipuloja, Aparibhinna, Puṇḍarīkanetra, Sarvasaha, Brahmagupta, Subrahma, Amaradeva, Arimardana, Candrapadma, Candrābha, Candratejas, Susoma, Samudrabuddhi, Ratanaśṛṅga, Sucandradṛṣṭi, Hemakroḍa, Abhinnarāṣṭra, Avikṣiptāṃśa, Puraṃdara, Puṇyadatta, and Haladhara.

Ṛṣabhanetra, Varabāhu, Yaśodatta, Kamalākṣa, Dṛṣṭaśakti, Naraṃpravāha, Pranaṣṭaduḥkha, Samadṛṣṭi, Dṛḍhadeva, Yaśaketu, Citracchada, Cārucchada, Lokaparitrātā, Duḥkhamukta, Rāṣṭradeva, Rudradeva, Bhadragupta, Udāgata, Askhalitapravarāgra, Dhanunāśa, and Dharmagupta.
Devagupta, Śucigātra, and Praheti constitute the first hundred of the noble faction.
The Blessed One is Dharmadhātu, Guṇaketu, Jñānaketu, Satyaketu, Puṣpaketu, Vajrasaṃghāta, Dṛḍhahanu, Dṛḍhasandhi, Atyuccagāmī, Vigataśatru, Citramāla, Ūrdhvasadhni, Guṇagupta, Ṛṣigupta,
Pralambabāhu, Ṛṣideva, Sunetra, Sāgaradharapuruṣa, Sulocana, Ajitacakra, and Unnata.
Ajitapuṣyala, Purāṣa, Maṅgalya, Subhuja, Siṃhatejas, Tṛptavasantagandha, Avadhyaparamabuddhi,
Nakṣatrarāja, Bahurāṣṭra, Āryākṣa, Sugupti, Prakāśavarṇa, Samṛddharāṣṭra, Kīrtanīya, Dṛḍhaśakti,
Harṣadatta, Yaśadatta, Nāgabāhu, Vigatareṇu, Śāntareṇu, and Dānapraguru.
He was of sublime complexion, strong-armed,

of immeasurable vigor, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, desired by the world of the gods, of fresh appearance, protected by the king of the gods, Dāmodara, King of Dharma, with a square face, radiant for a league, with a lotus-like crown protrusion, of manifest prowess, and walking like a royal swan.

Adorned with his own distinctive marks, with a dark-blue crest and a jeweled crown, of excellent complexion, wearing divine ornaments and clad in garments from the wish-fulfilling tree, of noble form and unimpaired intellect, a lotus among men, profound in wisdom, Śakrabhānu, Indradhvaja, Dānavakula, Manuṣyadeva,
Manusyadatta, Somacchatra, Ādityadatta, Yāmagupta, Nakṣatragupta, and Sumitrarūpa.
Satyabhānu, Puṣyagupta, Vṛhaspatigupta, Gaganagāmī, Śubhanātha, Suvarṇa, Kanakākṣa,
Prasannabuddhi, Avipranaṣṭarāṣṭra, Udagragāmi, Śubhadanta, Suvimaladanta, Suvadana, Kulanandana, Janakṣatriya, Lokakṣatriya, Anantagupta, Dharmagupta, and Sūkṣmavastra.
The second hundred belongs to the side of the Noble Ones.
Pratyāsannabuddhi, Satvasaha, Manuṣyanāga, Upasena, Suvarṇacārī, Prabhūtavarṇa, Subhikṣākānta, Bhikṣudeva, Prabuddhaśīla, Nahīnagarbha, Anālambha, Ratnamudra, Hārabhūṣita, Prasiddhavedana,
Sugandhivastra, Suvijṛmbhita, Amitalocana, Udāttakīrti, Sāgararāja, Mṛgadeva, and Kusumahestha.
Ratnaśṛṅga, Citravarṇa, Padmarajavarṇa, Samantagandha, Udāragupta, Praśāntaroga, Pradakṣiṇārtha, Saṃkṣiptabuddhi, Anantacchatra, Yojanasahasradarśin, Utpalapadmanetra,
Atipuruṣa, Anivartikabala, Svaguṇaśākha, Saṃcitoraḥ, Mahārāja, Cārucaraṇa, Prasiddharaṅga, and Trimaṅgala.
Suvarṇasena, Vartitārtha, Asaṃkīrṇa, Devagarbha, Suprītyarati, Vimānarāja, Parimaṇḍanārtha, Devasattva, Vipulatarāṃśa, Salīlagajagāmī, and Virūḍhabhūmi.

Thus ends the eighth chapter in the glorious Mahāvastu-Avadāna. Then, O bearer of the dhuta-precepts, immediately thereafter, the Blessed One [was born as] Citrabhānu, Cārubhānu, Dīptabhānu, Rucitabhānu,
Asitabhānu, Hemaratha, Cāmīkaragaura, Rajakaratha, Suyakṣa, and Akṣobhya.
Apariśrotavāhana, Devālaṃkṛta, Subhūṣitakhaṇḍa, Śithilakuṇḍala, Maṇikarṇa, Sulakṣaṇa, Suviśuddha,
Vimalajendra, Devacūḍa, Mandāravagandha, Pataṅgacara, Cārugandha, Indracūrṇa, Śailarājaketu, Arimardana, Maṇicakra, Vimalottarīya, Satyābharaṇa, Dṛḍhavīrya, and Nandigupta.
Ānandamāla, Cakravālagupta, Dṛḍhamūla, Ānandacandra, Brahmadhvaṃsadeva, Saumyavatsabāhu,
Samīkṣitavadana, Satyāvatāra, Supratiṣṭhitabuddhi, Hāraśītalāṅga, Sukhaprabha, Bhūrisattva,
Bhadragupta, Candraśubha, Bhadratejas, Iṣṭarūpa, Cakravartidatta, and Suvicakṣaṇagātra.
King Vaiśravaṇa; Samṛddhayajña; Saṃmataraśmi; Darśanakṣama; Srajamālādhārī; Suvarṇaviṣāṇa; Bhūtārthaketu; Ratnarudhiraketu; Mahārṣacūḍa; Tejagupta; Varuṇarāja; Udāttavastra;
Vajragupta; Dhanyabhānu; Uttaptarāṣṭra; Viśālaprabha; Lokasundara; Abhirūpa; Hiraṇyadhanyaśirika; and Prabhūtadehakarṇa.

Prāgajita, Vicitramakuṭa, Dānavagupta, Rāhuvamī, Puṇyarāśi, Salilagupta, Śamitaśatru, Ratnayūpa, Suvikalpāṅga, Ajitabala, Satyanāma, Aviraktarāṣṭra, Vaiśvānaragupta, Madhuravadana, Kusumotpala, Uttarakururāja, Añjalimālādhārī, Dhanapatigupta, and Taruṇārkabhānu.
Anurūpagātra, Ratnakaraṇḍaketu, Mahākośa, Bahulakeśa, Puṣpamañjarimaṇḍita, Anapaviddhakarṇa, Anāviddhavarṇa, Sitāsitalocana, Araktapravāḍa, Siṃhoraska, Ariṣṭanemi, and Bahurāja.
In the ninth stage, there is first a hundred [qualities] on the side of the noble ones.
Bhūmideva, Puṇḍarīkākṣa, Sādhuprabha, Jyotigupta, Bahuprabha, Satyavacas, Bhavadevagupta,
Saṃvṛttatejas, Nirupaghāta, Jānutrasta, Ratnaśayana, Kusumaśayana, Citraśayana, Dantaśayana, Supratiṣṭhitacaraṇa, Sarvadevagupta, Arajottarīya, Svāyaṃbhavendra, and Prasannavarṇa.
Bhavaketu, Kṣīrapūrṇāmbhas, Anantabuddhi, Kanakanāgarājatejas, Bandhanāntakara, Anugravarṇakṣemagupta, Jinakāntāra, Vimala, Marīcijāla, Ajitasenarāja, Kanakarāśi, Gaura, Padmamāla, Rājakṣetragupta,
Samapakṣa, Cāturdeva, Devagupta, Puṣkalāṅga, Dvijātirāja, Bahusena, and Kumudagandha.
Śabalāśva, Ṣaḍviṣāṇapāta, Surabhicandana, Rājā Sahasradātā, Abhayadeva, Arinighnā,
Vimalaśikhara, Durārohabuddhi, Yajñakoṭigupta, Ratnacaṅkrama, Jālāntara, Pariśuddhakarma, Kāmadeva, and Gururatna.
Śatasahasramātā, Śucipraroha, Stimitarāja, Vṛddhadeva, Gurujanapūjita,
Jayantadeva, Sujātabuddhi, Samīkṣitārtha, Ujjhitapara, Devābhika, Asuradeva, Gandharvagīta,
Vīṇāravaghoṣa, Śuddhadanta, Sudanta, Cārudanta, Amṛtaphala, Mārgodyotayitā, and Maṇikuṇḍaladhara.

Hemajālaprabha (Golden Net Radiance), Nāgabhogabāhu (Arm Like the Coil of a Serpent), Kamaladhara (Holder of the Lotus), Aśokasattva (Being Free from Sorrow), Lakṣmīputra (Son of Fortune), Sunirmitarūpa (Well-Fashioned Form),

Īśvaragupta (Protected by the Lord), Lokapālarāja (King of the World-Guardians), Sunidhyāna (Deep Meditation), Agrapuruṣa (Foremost Person), Anihitavarṇa (Unassailable Color), Kundapuṣpagandha (Scent of the Kunda Flower), Aṅkuśa (The Hook), Ārdravallipratirūpa (Resembling a Fresh Creeper), Kāryatāvicāra (Discernment of Duty), Svatejadīpta (Blazing with One’s Own Splendor), Prakāśadharma (Radiant Dharma), and Āryavaṃśaketu (Banner of the Noble Lineage).
Devarājaprabha, Pratyakṣadeva, Ahibhānurāga, Kusumottarīya, Avirasa, Prathamarāja, Puṇḍarīkarāja, and Subhikṣarāja.
The second noble category [is found] on the ninth stage.
One with smooth limbs, a being of ultimate reality, one whose limbs are unmoistened, a hero of Dharma, a good ford, a wrestler established in the illumination of the world,

having the fragrance of kunda flowers, unrestrained, one whose limbs are not scorched, a king among preceptors, one of supreme and foremost intelligence, one of unconquered fame, one whose grasp is never severed, a teacher of the gods, a flower of jewels, a being of purity, a peak of lapis lazuli, and one adorned with variegated garlands.

Sugandhakāya (Fragrant Body), Anantakośa (Infinite Treasury), Samamathita (Equanimous), Satyaprabha (Light of Truth), Adīnagāmī (One Who Proceeds Without Despair), Suvikrānta (Well-Valiant), Asambhrāntavacana (Unconfused Speech),

Gurudeva (God of Teachers), Naradeva (God of Men), Naravāhana (Carried by Men), Ratnahasta (Jewel-in-Hand), Lokapriya (Beloved of the World), Parinditārtha (Entrusted Purpose), Aviśuṣkamūla (Undried Root), Aparitṛṣita (Unsatiated), Sarvaśilparāja (King of All Arts), Grahakośa (Treasury of Planets), Anuraktarāṣṭra (Loving Realm), Śivadattamāla (Garland Given by Śiva), and Śikharadatta (Given by the Peak).
Citramāla, Mahāvimāna, Anotaptagātra, Citrahemajāla, Śāntarajas, Saṃgṛhītapakṣa, Aprakṛṣṭa, Raktacandanagandha, Acalitasumana, Upacitahanu, Jvalitayaśas, Racitamāla, Śirasamukuṭa, and Tejaguptarāja.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the glorious Mahāvastu-Avadāna.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.

Furthermore, Bhojinaputra, those bodhisattvas who have fully ripened their roots of merit, who have accomplished their tasks, and who— having transcended the ninth stage and fulfilled the tenth stage— have gone to the Tuṣita heaven and, desiring human existence, descend into the womb of a mother; proclaim such things as these concerning the Supreme Persons, beginning with their non-returning [to saṃsāra].
These are marvelous and extraordinary qualities, uncommon to Pratyekabuddhas and others, as well as to the hosts of those who have attained mastery, and to those in training or ordinary worldlings.
When this had been said, Mahākātyāyana spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.
The perfectly awakened ones are endowed with excellence in their descent into the womb;
they are endowed with excellence in their stay in the womb and in their birth;
and the perfectly awakened ones are also endowed with excellence in their mother.
The perfectly awakened ones are perfected in their great departure;
the perfectly awakened ones are perfected in vigor;
and the perfectly awakened ones are perfected in the attainment of knowledge.
"How, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, do the perfectly awakened ones become endowed with the excellence of descent into the womb?"
Śrīghana, the hero who has accumulated a store of former roots of merit, gazes with exceptional intensity from the Tuṣita heaven at the worlds during the time of his passing.
Thus does the Benefactor, the Great Being, the teacher of the hosts of gods, surrounded by the foremost of immortals, contemplate this thought that brings welfare to men and gods.

Now indeed is the time for me to pass away; for these beings have fallen into great darkness, with their eyes destroyed and their vision clouded—it is by attaining me that they shall be liberated from it.
Who now is this woman who delights in such restraint of moral conduct and tranquility—
she of noble birth, pleasant speech, and endowed with generosity, joy, and gentleness?

And she is radiant... who indeed is she, whose darkness of passion and hatred has been destroyed, who has reached the perfection of beauty and virtue, whose conduct is faultless, and who possesses abundant merit?
Who is capable of bearing me for ten months, and who can provide the happiness of privacy?
Who might be my mother, and into whose womb shall I enter today?
While gazing about, he saw among the harem of King Śuddhodana a woman resembling a celestial nymph, like a flash of lightning— Māyā.
Having observed his mother, he addressed the immortals:
"I shall descend, entering my final dwelling in a womb for the sake of the welfare of gods and men."
To him, the host of gods, wearing exquisite ornaments and with palms joined in reverence, said:
"O Supreme Person, may your vow, endowed with undiminished virtue and merit, be fulfilled!"
We too, for the benefit of the world, having renounced manifold delightful sensual pleasures,
shall dwell in the world of men for the sake of honoring the Blameless One.
Furthermore, O Teacher of the multitude of beings, although we do not wish for separation from you,
nevertheless, O lotus-eyed one, you will become the refuge for humans and gods.
Thus indeed, O bearer of the ascetic qualities (dhutadharma), the Perfectly Awakened Ones are endowed with the excellence of the descent into the womb.
And how, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, do the perfectly awakened ones become endowed with the perfection of dwelling in the womb?
Indeed, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, when Bodhisattvas have entered their mother’s womb, they remain supported by the mother’s birth canal;
they remain supported by the mother’s back;
they remain supported by the mother’s belly.
They remain leaning against their mother's side.

"O bearer of the dhuta-precepts, it is like a false sūtra that, while clinging to a coral and vaidūrya gem, cannot be found anywhere; yet there is a certain region where this is so. In the same way, O bearer of the dhuta-precepts, Bodhisattvas do not remain in their mother’s womb, and yet they do remain.

Furthermore, O bearer of the dhuta-precepts, when a Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, hosts of gods approach him and, bowing with palms joined in reverence, ask: 'Is this a favorable moment? Is this an auspicious day?'"
With joyful minds, the Bodhisattvas greet those hosts of gods who thus inquire of them; raising their right hands, they do not cause any distress to their mother.

Furthermore, O bearer of the ascetic qualities (dhutadharma), Bodhisattvas who have entered their mother’s womb do not remain in a squatting position, nor on their side, nor in any other manner whatsoever;
rather, O bearer of the ascetic qualities, Bodhisattvas sit cross-legged and do not cause any distress to their mother.
Furthermore, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, while still in their mother’s womb, Bodhisattvas indeed discourse on the nature of existence by virtue of their roots of merit.

Furthermore, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, for the sake of honoring the Bodhisattva while he was in his mother’s womb, divine musical instruments were played constantly and continuously; they never ceased, whether by day or by night.

And, O bearer of the ascetic virtues (dhutadharmadhara), for the sake of honoring the Bodhisattva while he is in his mother’s womb, hundreds of thousands of apsarases manifest themselves, and divine showers of flowers and divine showers of powders never cease.
From the time the Bodhisattvas first enter their mother’s womb until they have attained final nirvāṇa, the divine incense of agallochum never ceases for those endowed with the ten powers.
Indeed, O bearer of the dhuta-precepts, Bodhisattvas are not produced from a mother and father;
rather, they are spontaneously born through the perfection of their own virtues.
In this regard, the following is said:
Then that dark-complexioned Māyā, whose eyes were like lotus petals, being pursued by the many arms of the Gandharvas, spoke these very sweet words to Śuddhodana: "Together with him..."
This I undertake: non-violence toward living beings and celibacy;
I also abstain from taking what is not given, from intoxicants, and from idle chatter.
O best of men, I shall likewise abstain from harsh speech and from slander;
O lord of men, I shall abstain from false speech—this is my resolve.
I shall not give rise to envy toward the desires of others, nor shall I harbor malice; with a mind of loving-kindness toward all beings, I abandon wrong views.
"O Protector of the Earth, I practice the elevenfold morality throughout this entire night;
such is the desire that arises within me."
Moreover, O protector of the earth, let there be no thought of sensual desire regarding me;
look upon me so that no unrighteousness may befall me, who am a practitioner of the holy life.
Desiring to fulfill his resolve, the king spoke these words to his wife:
"Take your pleasure here in this excellent palace; both I and the kingdom are at your disposal."
Taking with her a thousand foremost women who were devoted to her, she ascended that excellent celestial palace and sat down, surrounded by a retinue that was pleasing and complete.
For some time, she spent that period upon a couch resembling a snow-white lotus,
devoted to tranquility and self-restraint through silence.
Then, their minds filled with curiosity, many celestial maidens wearing exquisite garlands approached the Mother of the Jina, desiring to see her; they stood upon the beautiful summit of the palace.
Having approached and beheld Māyā reclining on her bed, radiant like a sublime flash of lightning,
he experienced vast joy and bliss, and then rained down celestial flowers.
Even such a human form as this, so well-born, is indeed a marvel! Were it to remain for even a short time within [this world], it would not be equal to the wives of the gods.
"Behold, O friends, the playful grace of this woman, such as it is and appropriate to her;
reclining upon the bed, she shines, captivates the mind, and gleams like the very essence of gold."

She shall bear that Great Man, who delights in ultimate generosity, self-control, and virtue, who brings an end to all outflows, and is free from passion; O Queen of the King of Men, what is lost to you?

The Blessed One, the Giver of Boons, has taken up residence here in this belly of a woman— resembling the interior of a bow, with palms-like sides, possessing a row of excellent hair, and adorned with beautiful markings— untouched by impurity.
"You are a woman of corresponding excellence, your mother is preeminent, and your son is a supreme man who brings an end to existence; O consort of a lord of men, what is lacking for you?"

Furthermore, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, in whatever birth the mothers of Bodhisattvas bear a Bodhisattva in his final existence, in that birth the supreme women possess a celibacy that is completely pure,
perfect, and unbroken.
Not even in their minds did passion arise for any other men among those most excellent women, starting with their own husbands as the foremost.

Furthermore, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva’s mother possesses a body clothed in divine garments and wears divine ornaments; and hosts of Apsarases attend to the Bodhisattva’s mother with bathing, anointing, massaging, and sprinkling.
When the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva’s mother shares in laughter together with hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens.
Likewise, celestial maidens, having reached the full bloom of their prime youth, fanned the sleeping Bodhisattva’s mother with garlands of mandārava flowers.
And when the Bodhisattva descends into the womb of that most excellent woman, the mother of the Bodhisattva does not experience any sufferings as other women do.
Beginning with the Tuṣita heaven, for all bodhisattvas, the five hindrances are suppressed even before they have attained the sovereignty of Dharma.
And when ten months are complete, all Bodhisattvas manifest from the mother’s womb through her right side, yet that side is not pierced;
nor does any delay occur therein, for as soon as they are born, it is thus: "He has been born."
In this regard, the following is said:
Then, when the tenth month was complete, the mother of the one of abundant merit,
her purpose fulfilled, approached Śuddhodana and spoke as follows:
"O lord of men, the thought of going to the park has arisen in me; quickly prepare my vehicle as well as the appropriate guard."
Having heard these words, King Śuddhodana, with a well-pleased mind,
the protector of the earth, spoke with longing to his excellent retinue.
"Quickly prepare my vast army, abounding in elephants and horses and crowded with foot soldiers, adorned with various spears, arrows, and javelins, and report to me when it is ready."
Let ten hundred thousand horse-chariots with four horses each be yoked—
excellent chariots with the sweet, resonant sounds of golden bells.
Quickly prepare ten million elephants, resembling dense clouds of collyrium and clad in armor, in great numbers and fully equipped.
Let the brave warriors, clad in armor and mail, become ready and irreversible;
let those twenty thousand of them quickly prepare themselves.
Let the women, wearing excellent garlands and garments, carry the noble horse-chariot for the queen— a chariot resplendent with a golden lattice and the widespread tinkling of small bells.
And quickly make the Lumbinī grove free from grass, dust, leaves, and refuse; well-cleansed and pleasing, like a celestial abode for the queen.
And fashion each excellent tree from *kukūla*, silk, wool,
and *kośikāra* fibers, like the wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*) belonging to the preeminent god in heaven.
Having promised "So be it," and acting upon the word of that scion of kings,
it was reported to the king that everything had been done as commanded without delay.
She, whose face was charming with grace, the mother of the one who crushes the host of Māra,
ascended those delightful vehicles together with her retinue.
Adorned with various ornaments and crowded with multitudes of foot-soldiers and chariots,
that well-advanced army of the preeminent among men shines resplendently.
Having entered that excellent grove, the Mother of the Jina, accompanied by her illusory friends,
wanders about like the wife of a chief of the immortals in Citraratha, knowing the ways of pleasure.
Having approached for the sake of sport, she grasped a branch of the Plakṣa tree with her arms and gracefully yawned at the time of the birth of that illustrious one.
Then twenty thousand incomparable, excellent *apsarases*,
stretching out their limbs, joined their palms with ten fingers pressed together and, having greeted Māyā, spoke thus:
Today you shall give birth to one who crushes old age and birth, as delicate as the offspring of the immortals—
a queen who brings welfare to gods and men, honored in heaven and on earth, and a benefactor to both humans and deities.
Do not give way to despondency; we shall perform the necessary preparations for you. Tell us what must be done; let it be seen that it is already accomplished—do not worry.
Without causing pain to his mother, the Sage, the supreme speaker, appeared from the right side of Māyā, mindful and fully conscious.
Then, when the supreme lord of men had appeared, thousands upon thousands of cities filled with heaps of various jewels blazed forth, and a stainless radiance manifested.

Indeed, O bearer of the dhuta-precepts, there is no being within the realm of sentient beings who, having been born in their final birth, is capable of prophesying the Bodhisattva immediately upon his birth, except for the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven.
In this regard, it is said:
With his head finely wrapped in a cloth, eight thousand of the best of Maheśvaras,
wearing the guise of brahmins, approached the city of Kapilavastu.
Wearing excellent garments and bearing exquisite ornaments, those best of beings approached the gate of the royal palace with joyful minds and spoke to the doorkeeper.
"Go to Śuddhodhana and say: 'These eight thousand who know the rules for the qualities of the marks stand here; they would enter [the city] if it is your consent.'"
Having heard these words, the doorkeeper approached the excellent king;
with palms joined in reverence and bowing down, he spoke thus to the lord of men:
O you of incomparable strength and radiant splendor, rule the kingdom happily for a long time with your enemies destroyed;
gods resembling immortals stand at your gate, desiring to enter.
With perfectly full and stainless eyes, moving with the sweet voice of an elephant in rut—of them I have no doubt; they are not humans, they are sons of the gods.
As they walk back and forth, the dust of the earth does not scatter beneath their excellent steps,
nor is the sound of their joints ever heard while they are walking.
With profound and sweet gestures, noble appearance, and a tranquil range of vision,
they produce vast joy in people who behold them with longing.
Without doubt, O best of men, these excellent sons have come to see you—
the god among gods and men, the lion among humans— in order to pay homage and rejoice.
Having heard these words, the lord of men said to the doorkeeper: "O sir, having received my permission, let them enter the noble residence."
Those foremost hosts of immortals, resembling the sky and pure in their conduct, entered the royal family of that preeminent leader of an undiminished lineage.
King Śuddhodana, having observed Maheśvara from afar,
rose from his seat along with his retinue out of a sense of reverence.
The lord of men greets everyone with a welcome and with affection; "I am delighted by the sight of you, and by your power of tranquility and self-restraint."
These excellent seats, fashioned from exquisite materials, are available;
please, sirs, sit upon them out of favor toward us.
Then, upon those excellent seats with feet variegated with the colors of gold and silver,
they sat down comfortably, free from intoxication, pride, and arrogance.
Having sat down for just a short while, they said to the lord of men:
"May your majesty hear the purpose for which we have come here."
Your son has been born with all limbs faultless,
having attained the perfection of the [major] marks.
We too are skilled in marks; we discern faults and virtues by means of marks.
If it is not a burden to you, we would like to see your son’s form of a Great Man.
He says: "Come, behold my son, who is secure in his excellent reputation;
he is renowned for his fame among gods and men, and has reached the perfection of the qualities of the marks."
Then the excellent king brought forth the Sugata, who possesses a golden complexion and reclines upon a soft bed of kācalindika wool, and who is venerated by humans and gods alike.
Having beheld from afar the supreme feet of the Best of Men, the Great Lords,
with their crowns slipping from their heads, prostrated themselves upon the surface of the excellent earth.
Having established upon the surface of the earth a head as pure as cow’s milk or the moon,
they remained for a very long time, rejoicing in the One Possessing Ten Powers, who was longed for.
Indeed, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, once born, Bodhisattvas practice all human arts and crafts even without a teacher.
Indeed, O bearer of the dhuta-precepts, Bodhisattvas do not indulge in sensual pleasures from the time they depart from the Tuṣita heaven.
"O Son of the Conqueror, what is the cause, what is the condition, that although their afflictions have not been abandoned, Bodhisattvas do not indulge in sensual pleasures, and how was Rāhula born?"
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.

Because they have accumulated the wholesome, Bodhisattvas do not indulge in sensual pleasures; because of their noble resolve (*kalyāṇādhyāśaya*), supreme resolve (*agrādhyāśaya*), and sublime resolve (*praṇītādhyāśaya*), Bodhisattvas do not indulge in sensual pleasures;

because they do not desire what is desired by others, because they possess the banner of knowledge (*jñānadhvaja*), because they do not take that as their ultimate refuge, and because longing does not arise within them, Bodhisattvas do not indulge in sensual pleasures.

Because they are noble (*ārya*), because they are not base, and because they are thoroughly cultivated by the wholesome, Bodhisattvas do not indulge in sensual pleasures; and because they are esteemed by the world as beings who will become perfectly awakened Buddhas.
Then Rāhula, having passed away from the Tuṣita realm, descended into the womb of his mother, Yaśodharā, the daughter of a kṣatriya.
Thus it is heard, O bearer of the ascetic virtues.
The universal monarchs were of spontaneous birth.

They were as follows: Kusumacūḍa, Hemavarṇa, Gāndharva, Sumāla, Ratnadaṇḍa, Suvimāna, Ārjava, Māndhātā, Sunaya, Suvastra, Bahupakṣa, Toragrīva, Maṇiviraja, Pavana, Marudeva, Supriya, Tyāgavān, Śuddhavaṃśa, and Durāroha; such were the hosts of universal monarchs (cakravartin).
They were all of spontaneous birth, but Rāhulabhadra was not so.
"O bearer of the ascetic virtues, how do bodhisattvas become perfected in their great departure?"
Long ago, O Son of the Conqueror, the Bodhisattva went forth into the religious life.
Having entered the royal palace, he addressed Chandaka with a verse:
"Quickly, Chandaka, bring Kaṇṭhaka; do not delay for long!
Today I shall conquer the invincible battle; be alert!"
With his face filled with tears and sighing deeply,
Chandaka uttered these sorrowful cries and shed these tears in order to awaken him.
While the people of the earth were asleep...
Why now have you fallen away, your noble burden of self-restraint dissolved, submerged in a flood of tears, overcome by passion,
at this very time of longing, sorrow, and lamentation?
Now that we have awakened from sleep, there is no fixed place or time.
Even the Queen herself, having remained awake for a very long time, now lay down, her form resembling a flash of lightning,
at the moment of the departure of the Supporter of Men.
In the excellent city of the gods, she is like a celestial nymph, full of grace.
Then his queen, the mother of that lord of men, whose eyes were large, beautiful, and full of affection,
beheld with compassion this separation from her beloved.
Overcome by sleep, he does not recognize one who is speaking to him.
Where does that army dwell— filled with excellent elephants, horses, and warriors, and equipped with various armors, iron arrows, spears, shafts, and javelins— and what benefit does it provide?
She who does not perceive the Bull of the Śākyas as he is departing.
Whom shall I awaken? Who indeed might be my companion?
What shall I do when even the day has vanished? Alas! I am truly deprived of that which resembles molten gold.
The king, together with his kinsmen, will cast off his body.
The host of gods spoke to him with sweet speech:
"Chandaka, why do you lament? Why are you distressed?
Even if the sons of Māra were to rise up against him..."
How much less could they possibly create an obstacle for you?
Even if someone were to sound thousands of drums, mṛdaṅgas, and conchs for the sake of awakening Kapilavastu,
it would not awaken him, even by the likes of the Lord of the Immortals.
He indeed entered that excellent city, which was well-fortified and prosperous.
Behold now in the sky the gods with crest-jewels of precious gems, who, living in obedience to him who is honored in heaven,
bow down with heads bowed and palms joined in reverence.
Worshipping you, they say, "You are our kinsman; you are our refuge."
Therefore, bring forth Kaṇṭhaka, the leader, that horse born with him whose body is like gold and cow’s milk;
for there exists no other such steed on earth or in heaven for this noble lord of men.
Whoever should create an obstacle, bring the best of horses here!

Thus, spurred by the words of that possessor of great virtues, he mounted his own horse, which was as white as a bed of blooming night-lotuses or kunda flowers and possessed a body like the full moon.
Performing service, he brings [it] while weeping.
This is he, O Lord, whose limbs are adorned with the excellent marks,
who is ready, whose feet shine brightly, and who moves with graceful gait;
he whom you have now resolved upon, O bearer of the most excellent form.
May that be fulfilled for you, O lady with the broad expanse between your shoulders.
And your enemy, O one of foremost strength, being broken by his own weakness and scorched by your superior splendor, shall quickly be consumed;
and this aspiration of yours, O support of men, is endowed with great purpose.
Let it be filled completely, resembling a mountain of gold.
May those who create obstacles for you depart;
may they instead bring about your welfare and obtain great strength. And may you reach the further shore of whatever vow you undertake.
Go, you who move with the playful gait of a noble, rutting elephant!
And the jeweled pavement of the royal palace, struck by Kaṇṭhaka’s hooves,
resounded sweetly through the night, emitting a marvelous sound.
And the four world-protectors, with their crowns slipping and their excellent garlands hanging down,
placed their hands— resembling red lotuses— at the neck and the feet [of the horse].
In front goes Indra, the lord of the thirty-three gods, the bearer of the excellent vajra, with a jeweled crest bound upon his head and a thousand eyes, leading the way before the Best of Men.
"This is merely a matter of designation that Kaṇṭhaka carries the tiger among speakers;
the gods carry him who is borne by the most excellent hand, like a rain of the finest rays."
Having departed from this excellent city, the lion among men gazed back at the great city and said:
"I shall not enter it again until I have reached the further shore beyond old age and death."
Thus, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, the perfectly awakened Buddhas are indeed perfected in their Great Renunciation.

"O bearer of the dhuta-precepts, I am indeed not capable of describing in detail the Bodhisattva’s descent into the womb, starting from that event up until his Great Departure, even for an eon or the remainder of an eon; nor is it possible to fully fathom his virtues in every respect."
Thus, the perfectly awakened ones are endowed with many excellent qualities.
Having approached the foot of the Bodhi tree, even before attaining omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), they become endowed with the five eyes.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
"O Son of the Victor, proclaim in detail the five eyes; the assembly, crowded with gods and humans, and the hosts of all beings, have their ears attentively tuned."
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.
"O bearer of the ascetic qualities, these five are the eyes of the perfectly enlightened ones."
Which five?
The fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the Buddha eye.

"O bearer of the ascetic qualities (dhutadharmadhara), these five eyes belong to the perfectly enlightened ones (samyaksaṃbuddhas); they are not shared with pratyekabuddhas, arhats, those in training (śaikṣas), or with any ordinary worldlings (bālapṛthagjana)."
In that regard, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, this is the fleshly eye of the Tathāgatas.
That fleshly eye, which is endowed with such radiance, endowed with such subtle vision, and endowed with such vision of reality, does not exist in the body of any other being;
and having attained the state of all-seeing, whatever extent of space the Bodhisattvas wish to survey, their vision operates there without obstruction.
What is the reason?
Because of having accumulated vast wholesome merit.

Just as, for example, by the power of supernatural faculties, a universal monarch together with his fourfold army travels through the air from continent to continent, so too should this be understood.

In the conduct of the perfectly enlightened ones (*samyaksaṃbuddhas*), when they traverse the firm earth by the power of their supernatural faculties (*ṛddhibala*) without desiring to do so— such that the high ground sinks and the low ground rises— it should be understood in this same way;
thus, by such mere characteristics, the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*) of the perfectly enlightened ones is described.
And even in an eon, it is not possible for the fleshly eye to reach the limit of the qualities of the perfectly awakened ones.
What is the reason?
For there is nothing whatsoever of the perfectly enlightened ones that is equal to the world.
Indeed, everything belonging to the great seers is entirely supramundane.
For in this way, the realization of the perfectly awakened ones is also supramundane.
And that color and location of the fleshly eye of the perfectly enlightened ones have arisen just as they do for other beings within their own bodies.

With that eye by which the terrestrial gods, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and the gods of the desire realm and the form realm [perceive], the divine eye of the perfectly awakened ones is even more distinguished, more vast, and more clearly manifest.
That [consciousness] has proceeded toward forms consisting of mind.

By means of which eye of wisdom (*prajñācakṣus*) those individuals who are endowed with it—beginning from the person of the eighth stage (*aṣṭamaka*) up to the person who is an Arhat—are examined through the investigation of their vision; therefore, the eye of wisdom of the Perfectly Enlightened Ones (*samyaksaṃbuddha*) is even more distinct than that.
In this regard, what is the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*) of the Perfectly Enlightened Ones?
That is the mental mastery over the ten powers.
In that regard, what are the ten powers? They are as follows:
first, the power of those with immeasurable buddhi, which knows what is possible and what is impossible;
and second, the power which knows the path leading everywhere.
They know the world to consist of various elements; this is known as the third power.
They know the diversity of inclinations; this constitutes the fourth power.
He knows the skills of other men; that is the fifth power. They recognize the power of karma, both auspicious and inauspicious; that is the sixth power.
He knows the purification from afflictions; this is the seventh power. He knows the meditative absorptions and attainments; this is the eighth power. He knows former abodes in their many varieties.
The ninth power is that they possess the completely pure divine eye;
the tenth power is that they attain the destruction of all afflictions.
These are the powers of mental mastery by which he who sees all things, whose fame has spread throughout heaven and earth, is thus designated as the "One Possessing the Ten Powers."
That mental discernment-knowledge which exists within these ten powers is called the Dharma-eye.
In that regard, what is the Buddha-eye?
The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

That is to say: the Tathāgata’s unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the past; his unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the future; and his unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the present.
All bodily action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge;
all vocal action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge;
all mental action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge.
There is no decline of zeal; there is no decline of energy;
there is no decline of mindfulness.
There is no decline in concentration;
there is no decline in wisdom;
there is no decline in liberation.
There is no stumbling; there is no clamor;
there is no loss of mindfulness.
There is no unconcentrated mind; there is no equanimity lacking discernment;
there is no perception of diversity.
The knowledge regarding these eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is called the "Buddha-eye."
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Mahākātyāyana.
Furthermore, O Son of the Victor, does this designation belong to you regarding the prophecy of such stages, or rather does it belong to the Perfectly Awakened Ones?
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.
At one time, O bearer of the ascetic virtues, the Blessed One was dwelling at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana, honored by twenty-eight hundred self-controlled ones.

In that regard, the Blessed One has analyzed the eighteen qualities of a Buddha; since the perfectly enlightened ones possess unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the past, he proclaimed the ten stages.
Beginning with the perfectly enlightened Śākyamuni, these ten stages were taught.
In this regard, the following is said:
The one with vision, wandering through existence with a mind long purified, gives away beloved things;
from that, he awakens to the supreme, dear knowledge.
The Tathāgata himself has come to this circle of the earth.
With a deeply satisfied mind, he gives women adorned with various garments and ornaments;
his wondrous vow is truly marvelous.
It is stirred up by the fruit of that karma.
As he wandered through various states of existence, he did not hurl spears, iron arrows, javelins, or *tomara*s at sentient beings;
likewise, his path was free from grass, clumps of earth, and thorns.
Wandering through villages and cities, he brought suffering upon them.
He listens with respect even to the words of his own servant if they speak according to the Dharma, and does not interrupt him; thus,
as that person speaks the Dharma before the great assembly, he [listens].
No one finds delight in us, nor is anyone satisfied with us.
He gives excellent gifts;
from that very act, he removes longing and doubt.
Then, from his body, [rays] resembling blazing flames emerge.
A cool radiance arises.
No supplication made by any petitioner shall be in vain when addressed to one who has entered the state of a god among men;
therefore, his teaching shall never be fruitless.
That was a marvel in the crushing of Māra’s forces.
With minds full of joy, they offer beautiful golden palm leaves to the Jinas;
thereafter, those kinsmen of the world become visible even in the lightless realms.
And this is always a marvel throughout the worlds.
With a mind always full of contentment, he constantly gives sandals made of jewels and wooden shoes;
thereafter, that best of men always practices walking meditation.
Without touching the ground by four finger-breadths.
When addressed with harsh words again and again by others, the Lord, remaining composed, endures them and does not retaliate;
therefore, even as he walks, the earth together with its mountains is dear to him.
The earth sinks where it is elevated and rises where it is depressed.
By means of his policy, he gathers the distressed;
he rescues the great multitude who are falling away;
from that, there arises for him a heap of jewels consisting of precious gems.
When it sinks down, the earth rises up.
And by means of proclaiming his own qualities, the Perfectly Awakened One taught the Dharma discourse named "Recollection of the Buddha."
At the conclusion of that, the Venerable Vāgīśa praised the Perfectly Awakened One to his face.
Homage be to you, O Buddha of infinite vision, whose eye is all-pervading, who bears the marks of a hundred merits,
who is compassionate for the welfare of others, and skilled in the ultimate truth.
I bow to you, O Gautama, with my charming speech.
Having crossed over yourself, O Great Sage, you ferry across the people;
O Supreme Person who brings security, you do not fear as you reveal the state exactly as it is.
Lead many people to the truth, which is the deathless.
The morality of the Great Seer, who possesses infinite vision,
is profound, noble, vast, and well-spoken;
you are preeminent in morality, O crusher of enemies.
In this world and in the next, he is one of noble vows.
O Great Sage, your conduct is unbroken, flawless, stainless, unblemished, and free from taint;
it is ever pure, having attained supreme purification.
I shine upon the mountain peak like a fire.
O person, although you have reached the perfection of stability of mind and are a master in meditative concentration,
you have attained supreme mastery over the mind itself.
Free from crookedness and open space, you shine forth.
According to your wish, you practice the peaceful concentration free from conflict (araṇa-samādhi),
which is honored among gods and men;
you dwell [there], possessing the radiance of a golden garland.
Homage be to you, O Gautama, whose valor is truth!
Just as Virocana shines in the sky, or like the moon on the fifteenth day in a pure, cloudless sky,
so do you shine while established in meditative concentration.
In this regard, individuals are like refined gold.
Desirous and dejected, deluded beings do not understand the all-encompassing exertion of one who cultivates blissful concentration free from conflict.
Homage be to you, who are worshipped by gods and humans!
When you look upon the one who goes like a Naga,
and when he has come to the further shore beyond death—
endowed with intelligence and mindfulness, with a stainless mind.
Then this earth, the supporter of beings, trembles.
Having personally realized the truth through direct vision, and having previously heard it through supernormal knowledge,
O Supreme Person, utter these words.
Like Maghavan with his thousand eyes, you shine forth.
This great calamity and terrible danger have come to an end; henceforth there shall be no further occurrence of it,
for its obstruction now proceeds downward.
He passes away like the sound of the wind, as does a ripe fruit.
For one whose mind is liberated, the vision of liberation is inconceivable, not dependent on the path of reasoning;
it shines forth through the fearless words of the Hero.
That which is the auspicious hour, gentle, and born of truth.
And you should proclaim those words that are free from agitation in the presence of people; for they,
having heard your sweet and well-spoken speech, [will be inspired].
They drink as if afflicted by thirst at the ocean of water.
Cultivate loving-kindness toward sentient beings who harbor hatred;
you have indeed reached the further shore of sovereignty, miraculous power, supreme eloquence,
and the most excellent dharmas.
Just as there is no one else whatsoever in this world-system.
And you possess supreme wisdom, O Sage, peerless and incomparable in all the world;
you alone are the most excellent among all living beings.
Just as Mount Meru is among the masses of rocks.
There is no one equal to you, no one similar or like you; how could there be anyone superior in qualities to you, O bearer of virtues? You alone are the most excellent person in the ultimate sense.
The immovable bliss of all phenomena is like nirvana.
Having abandoned passion and delusion, hatred, pride, and the ensnaring thirst,
you shine forth with a mind liberated from aversion.
Just as the full moon in a clear sky.
That which you seek here as truth is the straight, great bridge frequented by noble beings;
utter these words, O foremost of persons!
And you, the thousand-eyed Maghavan, shine forth.
Cultivating this concentration, which is liberated from afflictions, stainless, and perfectly peaceful— the refuge of all beings—
you shine forth as a conqueror for the welfare of living creatures.
Just as Ravi is honored by gods and humans.
Unattached both here and in the hereafter,
you delight in meditative absorption while established in meditation;
many gods have gathered together to pay you homage.
With palms joined in reverence, they paid homage to the Great Sage.
The eye becomes manifold and of many kinds for those of pure vision— the Buddhas who crush old age and death, the tamers of the untamed.
The conduct of the Blessed One is supramundane; his roots of merit are supramundane.
The walking, standing, sitting, and lying down of the Sage are supramundane.
That which is the body of the Sugata, which brings about the destruction of the bonds of existence—even that, O friend, is supramundane; herein no doubt should be made.
The wearing of robes by the Sage is supramundane; there is no doubt about this.
Furthermore, the taking of food by the Sugata is likewise supramundane.
The teaching of the human-nagas is considered entirely transcendent of the world;
I shall proclaim, according to reality, the majesty of those possessed of supreme intelligence.
Having taken account of the influence of place and time, as well as the ripening of karma,
the Leaders teach the Dharma that is true or has been fully realized.
The Buddhas conform to worldly convention in order to follow the ways of the world; they conform to conventional designations just as they do to that which is supramundane.
The four Supreme Persons display the modes of deportment,
yet no exhaustion arises for those who perform virtuous deeds.
They wash their feet, yet no dust adheres to them;
their feet have the luster of lotus petals—this is their conformity with the world.
The perfectly awakened ones indeed bathe, yet no impurity exists in them; this bathing upon their bodies, which shine like golden images, is merely conformity with the ways of the world.
They use tooth-sticks and their mouths have the fragrance of a blue lotus;
they put on lower garments and wear upper robes and the triple set of robes.
Having caused the winds to blow upon their garments, they do not disturb their bodies;
this is the conformity with the world practiced by those lions among men.
They sit in the shade, yet the heat of the sun does not oppress them;
this is the conformity with the world of the Buddhas, who are the outpouring of merit.
They partake of medicine, yet no disease exists for them;
this great fruit of the Leaders is their conformity with the world.
The Lords are able to prevent karma, yet the Jinas demonstrate karma;
they conceal their sovereignty—this is their conformity with the world.
They indeed take food, yet hunger does not afflict them;
they do so for the sake of providing for the people—this is their conformity with the world.
They indeed drink water, yet thirst does not afflict them;
this is the wonder of the great seers—this conformity with the ways of the world.
They put on robes, yet the Jina is always clothed;
whatever form a god might have—that is his conformity with the world.
They cause their hair to grow long, yet the razor does not cut it;
the hair resembles dark collyrium—this is their conformity with the world.
