They demonstrate old age, yet for them no old age exists;
these Victors, endowed with the qualities of a Victor, act thus in conformity with the world.
Having reached the perfection of merits over incalculable millions of eons, they demonstrate the undertaking [of practice]; this is their conformity with the world.
The exalted body of the Sugata was not produced through sexual union, yet they point to parents as its source; this is his conformity with the ways of the world.
Since the time of Dīpaṃkara, the Tathāgata has been free from passion;
yet he displays Rāhula as his son—this is his conformity with the world.
Having traversed the perfection of wisdom for incalculable millions of eons, they manifest the state of a fool; this is their conformity with the world.
Having uttered improper mantras in this world together with its gods, they seek again at various shrines; this is merely following the ways of the world.
Having awakened to incomparable enlightenment for the sake of all sentient beings, they demonstrate a lack of zeal; this is their conformity with the world.
All perfectly awakened ones are endowed with supreme qualities and are perfected in speech.
The speech of the perfectly awakened ones is endowed with sixty qualities.
By which sixty?
The speech that issues from the words of the best of men is as sweet as the sound of song;
the voice of the Sugata is like the resonance of the lute and the flute, and like the cry of the swan.

The speech of those of supreme intelligence is as sweet as the roar of clouds, its resonance equal to the song of the cuckoo or the clatter of chariot wheels, and it possesses the power of the ocean’s thundering and the cry of the crane.

The speech of those who bear the excellent marks is like the song of the *kinnara* and the *kalaviṅka*, like the sound of the voice of the best of clouds, like the cry of the noble elephant, and like the roar of the bull and the king of beasts.
The voice of the leaders of men and gods was as deep as the sound of a drum, a resonance shaken by the forest deities and the wind, a roar that caused the earth to tremble.

From the mouth of the Jina, whose voice is like that of a fivefold musical instrument and who is free from the agitation of swans and peacocks, there issues forth speech from lips as red as the *bimba* fruit and a slender tongue.
The speech of those preeminent in excellent qualities is sweet as the song of the Gandharvas, its sound like the falling of torrents of rain, neither too diffuse nor too condensed.
The sound of excellent men, produced by the playful jingling of small bells, resembling the resonance of golden nets,
and arising from the clashing of ornaments, prevails both on earth and in heaven.

Neither too rapid, not faltering, uninterrupted, and sweet, their speech— possessing a collection of well-delivered words— revolves with the excellent characteristics of those who bear the marks of excellence.
He follows every single assembly, even if it consists of millions of world-systems;
with most sweet speech, he makes himself understood by the entire assembly of those who possess the ten powers.
Among the Śakas, Yavanas, Cīnas, Ramaṭhas, Pahlavas, and Daradas, as well as among the assemblies of bandits,
she is called by a single name while wandering through all regions.
The speech emerging from the best of men does not overstep the assembly;
the voice of the Ten-Powered Ones, steady in its rhythm, neither increases nor diminishes.
It does not break, it does not push back, nor is it distressed; it does not falter or produce harsh, grating sounds—the voice of the Sugata is a resonant melody.
And she does not use corrupt words, nor is she deficient in speech; she employs every word with complete application.
Skilled in all words, whether wholesome or unwholesome, she gladdens the entire multitude of people.
When the speech of those who possess virtuous qualities issues forth from their mouths, which have perfectly pure teeth,
the flocks of birds dwelling in the sky and those dwelling in the forest become intoxicated with joy.
Whatever sound is pleasing to anyone, that voice— arisen from the words of the Sugata and moving through the assembly— fulfills his intention.
Accompanied by excellent perfumes, its resonance like the roar of a mountain river, pure,
and echoing with the cries of cranes and *kurara* birds, this voice arises as the source of all sublime sounds.

The voice of the Jina, like the song of the *śakunta* and *jīvañjīvaka* birds, and like the sound of golden palm leaves, possesses an resonance equal to the charming tones of sharp-sounding drums, kettledrums, and clay drums.
The speech of those who have reached the supreme perfection is to be known and understood; it is profound and awe-inspiring in form, yet pleasant to the ear, ever reaching the heart.
And their speech, worthy of being heard from lute-players, was lovely and possessed of virtues;
it belonged to all those who had accumulated a vast store of merit and possessed infinite fame.
The speech has been taught according to reality.
The perfectly awakened ones teach the Dharma in this way.
"Monks, I do not teach those phenomena which are impermanent as being permanent;
nor do I teach those phenomena which are permanent as being impermanent;
nor do I teach those phenomena which are suffering as being happiness."
Nor do I teach that those phenomena which are pleasant are suffering;
nor do I teach that those phenomena which are not self are the self;
nor do I teach that those phenomena which are self are not-self.
Nor do I teach that those phenomena which are impure are pure; nor do I teach that those phenomena which are pure are impure;
nor do I teach that those phenomena which are material are immaterial.
Nor do I teach that those dharmas which are wholesome are unwholesome;
nor do I teach that those dharmas which are unwholesome are wholesome;
nor do I teach that those dharmas which are untainted are tainted.
Nor do I teach that those phenomena which are with outflows are without outflows;
nor do I teach that those phenomena which are determinate are indeterminate;
nor do I teach that those phenomena which are indeterminate are determinate.
Nor do I teach that those dharmas which are inferior are superior,
nor do I teach that those dharmas which are superior are inferior;
nor do I teach that those dharmas which rely on the household life rely on renunciation.
Nor do I teach that those phenomena which are based on renunciation are based on the household life.

Furthermore, O bearer of the ascetic qualities (dhutadharma), the Perfectly Awakened Ones are speakers of truth, speakers of the timely, speakers of reality, speakers of the meaningful, speakers of the suchness, speakers of the non-otherwise, speakers of the non-false, speakers of the Dharma, and speakers of the Vinaya.

[ Mvu 1.174 ] Once upon a time, O bearer of the ascetic virtues (dhutadharmadhara), a son of the gods belonging to the Tuṣita heaven, named Śikharadhara, who was a Bodhisattva, spoke face-to-face to the Blessed One— the Perfectly Awakened One— who had arrived at Ṛṣivadana in Vārāṇasī on the day of setting in motion the excellent Wheel [of Dharma] in that preeminent forest.
He addressed him with reverence, with respect, bowing low with palms joined in homage.
Excellent! Your speech, O you who possess a virtuous form, is not obstructed;
excellent is your delightful speech, which is meaningful and purposeful.
Excellent! Your speech is well-composed with melodious sounds and endowed with the qualities of phonetic euphony; excellent, O Great Sage, that you proclaim the Four Truths.
Excellent, O Deva-Gandharva, as they drink in your sweet speech;
excellent that you here set in motion the peerless wheel that follows its course.
In this world, there is no one equal to you in form, complexion, lineage, or strength; nor in deportment, vigor, meditative concentration, knowledge, tranquility, or self-control.
Today, O Hero, ten crores of them, delighted,
have been disciplined in the first fruit within the teaching of the Son of the Gods, the first Sage.
O Lord, O Hero, you have guided thirty million beings to the first fruit;
and in the second teaching, you have likewise guided men and sons of gods.
Moreover, O Sage, fifty billion sons of gods were further disciplined in the third teaching of yours and liberated from the states of woe.
Furthermore, eighty koṭis were established in the fruit of stream-entry;
having been tamed within the fourth teaching, they were liberated from the miserable destinies.
Therefore, O Supreme among Men, there is no one equal to you in loving-kindness;
O Bull among Men, having become compassionate, you are even more so in compassion.
Joyful, tigers among men, born as the most beautiful in the world,
they wander for the benefit of all sentient beings, O Great Sage.
After a very long time, O bull among men, you have been born as a prince—
the leader of those who have gone astray, the delighter of the eyes of the afflicted.
May the true teacher and protector never disappear;
O kinsman of the world, may your station be boundless.
O Self-Existent One, by your splendor the states of woe have been thinned;
O Supreme Person, having attained you, the heavens have been made spacious.
O person, this individual who belongs to the group destined for falsehood will,
upon reaching you— who belong to the indeterminate group— be brought to fulfillment.
O you who are praised by the gods, even that person whose destiny was uncertain will, upon encountering you,
fulfill their potential as one born of a family endowed with perfect splendor.
And the purification of marvelous qualities is attained by reaching you, O Sun among men, the destroyer of darkness, the infallible one.
O Bull among Conquerors, O Great Sage, as you speak these true dharmas,
the worlds, including Indra, rejoice in your words.
Thus do the hosts of gods, with joyful minds, praise the giver of boons,
the supreme among men, who is endowed with infinite virtues and worthy of hymn of praise.

O upholder of the ascetic virtues (dhutadharma), the Perfectly Enlightened Ones are perfected in the rules of conduct; they are capable in the knowledge of the proper time, possess pure vision, and behold things without partiality. They are endowed with the methods of the past, have raised the banner of the Dharma, and possess a banner that is peerless.

They are sharp-witted in overcoming strife and conflict, learned in the teaching, and possess inexhaustible knowledge. Furthermore, O friends, they bring those who lack right vision to maturity at the proper time.
They are instigators, those who follow wrong paths, and revilers.
In this regard, the following is said:
Endowed with all excellent qualities, all of them are certain regarding all objects;
they are the leaders and guides, the Buddhas honored by wise men.
With unconfused knowledge and a purified mind,
they shine throughout the three worlds like the full moon in the sky.
With their beautiful and virtuous feet, beloved by the noble, these leaders,
born from the perfect arising of merit, let out a great roar.
The heroes, firm in their conduct, instruct the people;
seeing reality as it is, they crush the disputes of other beings.
Born in the world, O best of men, yet you are not defiled by the world;
having transcended all conventional designations, you are masters whose domain is profound.
Having taken up the heavy burden, the wise do not despair;
acting exactly as they speak, their conduct is beyond reproach.
Having burned that terrible poison of [wrong] views with the fire of knowledge,
the Lord utters to living beings words that are neither terrifying nor causing alarm.
Having crossed the wilderness and reached safety, those wise leaders among men call out: "This very place is now free from fear!"
The arising of old age, death, and disease does not exist here;
the occurrence of exhaustion and sorrow is not found here.
Having heard his sweet words, those gods and humans,
acting in accordance with his instruction, attain that happiness.
Therefore, they possess extensive and supreme fame throughout the three worlds;
honored by the virtuous, they continue their practice and do not cease.
Moreover, O bearer of the dhuta-precepts, the Perfectly Awakened Ones offer gifts to sentient beings for the sake of their welfare.
For example, the Blessed One spoke concerning the offering made by Queen Kusumā to the King of Kaliṅga, and the Blessed One spoke concerning the verbal offering made by the merchant Dhruva.
And in that very way, in Rājagṛha, the best of cities,
the Blessed One engaged in the offering of others;
he, skilled in his own methods, caused them to excel.
Upāli [received] that offering of words.

Likewise, that lion among debaters, the self-controlled master of those who have attained mastery, the Blessed One, accepted the offering from the other monk who had arrived on the slopes of Mount Meru.
The Great Sage spoke this to the Saṅgha.
I shall proclaim all these delightful offerings;
listen to the auspicious play of that preeminent being.
When that best of men had appeared and the Wheel of Dharma had been set in motion,
the King of Kaliṅga ruled over a prosperous kingdom free from thorns.
There was one named Abhaya; this was his view:
he held the certainty that there is no fruit for wholesome or unwholesome actions.
Likewise, there is no other world, nor is there anywhere the fruit of giving,
for one who is free from passion, free from hatred, and free from delusion does not exist.
Having attained that vision, he would assemble the multitude,
proclaim his own view, and thereafter never turn back from it.
If my father were to speak thus to me in person, having approached me himself, then I would believe it as such.
At all times he was then possessed of virtue and a mind of loving-kindness;
if there is fruit for that, his destination shall be the city of the gods.
"Having known me as one who has become a god, he shall liberate me from this view.
Having said this, [the Buddha declared]: "There is a world beyond; abandon this evil view."
Since the occurrence of that other world is not perceived, may my father come and gladden my mind.
Then, out of compassion for the world, the Sage, who is great and fearless,
himself manifested the form of the King of Kaliṅga.
Having ascended the excellent palace and likewise entered the inner apartments,
he showed the inner apartments to those who were there for the purpose of seeing the common people.
Then that emanated king, standing poised in the sky,
the wise and supreme among men, spoke these words of fearlessness to the king.
Having abandoned one's own duties and being occupied with the affairs of others,
that which is joined with false views is called "kingless," though it bears the name of a kingdom.
Today, your destination in this world will be a great and terrible hell;
and for those who shall point it out to you, their destination shall be the same.
For one who has been struck down strikes others; one who is ruined causes others to perish;
and one who is himself blinded out of shame for his blindness blinds others as well.
Having already plundered one, you plunder another; having killed one, you cause others to die. O evil-minded one, you bring suffering even to those beings who are happy.
Sunk in the mire of sensual desire, greedy for and infatuated with these pleasures,
the king— who wished to see the next world— [sought] the method of the teachings.
It is impossible, O Lord of the Earth, that you, being devoted to sensual pleasures and incapable of it, should go from this world to the next, O Master.
Having understood both the gratification in sensual pleasures as well as their defects,
and knowing the escape from sensual pleasures, I truly know your successive lineage.
Having heard this, Abhaya, the best of men, trembled with fear;
bowing low, he spoke thus to Sudarśana in the sky:
I have faith in you, O God; it is even so and not otherwise.
Be gracious to me, O Lord; deliver me from fear.
Therefore, having entered the inner apartments, tell my teacher, that peerless person:
"I am under your discipline, as are you and many other people."
This "offering to others" was performed by that one of supreme intelligence and excellent wisdom for the sake of bestowing grace upon sentient beings.
The queen of King Kusumbha was renowned as Kusumā;
she was the beloved of King Kusumbha and the most excellent among thousands of women.
His mother and father, both aged and dependent on staffs, spoke thus to their daughter: "O Kusumē, my daughter, listen!"
"We are old, while you are young and agitated by passion;
we desire to release you, and we desire our own death."
Having heard these words, Kusumā formed this thought: "If my mother and father are to be killed because of this dispraise of me, [what is the point?]"
"I shall give them most dreadful food mixed with poison,
by eating which both of these will undoubtedly die."
When her mind had become fixed upon her parents with such cruelty,
the Teacher then gave rise to compassion toward Kusumā.
Then the Teacher, the Perfectly Awakened One, causes the mother and father of Kusumāyus to disappear and establishes two other emanations in their place.
Kusumā obtained that food mixed with poison;
she said to the emanated beings, "Mother and Father, please eat this food."
Created by the Jina, they eat their food without wavering;
nothing at all afflicts their bodies, for they are indeed emanations.
On the second day, and likewise on the third, fourth, and fifth,
having eaten food mixed with poison, they sustained themselves as if it were nectar, being sustained by their magical power.
Then, having joined her palms in reverence, Kusumā said:
"If I am worthy of your favor, please reveal yourself to me."
To Kusumā, who was thus entreating him with palms joined, Nirmita said:
"Whatever offense you recognize yourself to have committed, acknowledge it accordingly."
The Buddha is a tiger among men, endowed with the thirty-two excellent marks;
he has arisen from a noble lineage and is possessed of all branches of knowledge and virtues.
Everything—past, future, and present—has become a quality of that Lion of Speakers; it is known by him. Abandon your doubt in this matter.
Having ascended the excellent palace together with his women's quarters, that king requested:
"We desire to see you, O Seer of All Aims."
Having paid homage to him who is endowed with all virtues, go for refuge;
then the Jina will speak to you regarding whatever you ask us about right there.
Having promised "So be it" to the emanated being,
the king, together with his harem, then quickly ascended the palace.
Immediately, that king, together with his wives and attendants, bowed low with palms joined in reverence;
accompanied by Kusumā, the king spoke these words.
To those who are endowed with all virtues and compassionate toward the worlds— to them,
with palms joined, I offer this expression of joy.
Then the Teacher addressed his disciples who delight in the teaching—
Cāruvarṇa, Siṃhahanu, Dṛḍhabāhu, and Anindita.
Kīrtimant, Mahānāga, Cāturanta, Mahābala, Nīlakeśa, Buddha, Śānta, and Sāstraviśārada.
Likewise, Śārasa, Atulya, Guptakāma, Anindita,
Siṃhanandin, and Viśālākṣa— this is the supreme mark of excellence.
"O monks, I am going; follow after the Teacher!
Placing Kusumā at my head, I shall lead many people."
Having promised "So be it" to the Self-Existent One who had attained mastery,
they surrounded the Perfectly Awakened One and spoke these words:
O heroes, our feet too shall traverse the midst of the sky;
we shall follow the Perfectly Awakened One, the Seer, wherever he goes.
In the twinkling of an eye, the Blessed One, surrounded by his disciples, arrived at the city of Kusumapura out of compassion for living beings.
The Leader, skilled in meditation, mentally emanated the form of Vajrapāṇi and visualized the host of deities with his mind.
He emitted a circle of light extending for fourteen yojanas,
and the deities paid homage to the journey of him who possesses supreme intelligence.
Then Queen Kusumā, bowing low, spoke to the Sugata:
"O Protector, with palms joined in reverence, I wish to worship your feet."
Then the Teacher, the bringer of glory, having established himself upon the summit of the excellent palace,
surpassed all the directions with his radiance.
Then Queen Kusumā, together with the king,
paid homage at the feet of the Jina, and the queen’s retinue also paid homage to the Bull among Men.
O best of men, honored by the gods, we go to you for refuge.
What kind of fruit does one obtain after killing both mother and father?
Listen, Kusuma, to the truth regarding the fruit of killing one's mother and father:
immediately thereafter, one is reborn in the Great Avīci Hell.
Then, through the power of the Buddha, the Teacher, the Guide skilled in speech,
revealed the Great Avīci hell to Kusumā.
Then Queen Kusumā, terrified of the dreadful hell and shedding a torrent of tears, spoke these words:
O compassionate one, what kind of fruit arises in the next world for one with a wicked mind toward his mother and father? Speak that which is true.
For one with a wicked mind, that very thought regarding a flower would become unreleasable;
indeed, through such violence, that same [state] becomes the immediate fruit in the next world.
Then, filled with joy and happiness, Kusumā relinquished her cruel intent before the King of Dharma.
Then the All-Knowing One speaks of the gratification of sensual pleasures,
and the Supreme among Men speaks of the danger of sensual pleasures.
Then, he of inconceivable prowess speaks of the transcendence of sensual desires;
seeing reality as it is, he proclaims the marvelous qualities of nirvana.
Making Kusumā the foremost, the Sage disciplines twelve koṭis of humans, thinking, "This is an offering."
In the city of Kāśivardhana, there was a merchant named Dhruva;
this sinful vision of his occurred during a gathering with his mother and father.
He who, having gathered together his mother and father— who have grown old and whose youth has passed—
as well as his circle of kinsmen, should satisfy them with various kinds of food and drink;
When the mass of fire is blazing, one should cause both ancestors to be cremated;
an offering should be presented to it, and its merit is infinite.
He manifested thousands of rākṣasīs,
who stood before Dhruva as he slept upon his excellent palace.
With staffs in hand, with whips in hand, and likewise with spears in hand;
with axes in hand, with swords in hand, and likewise with torches in hand.
Then, with lances in their hands and hundreds of iron arrows in their grasp,
and with spears and mallets in their hands, they stood before the merchant.

O lowest of men, you have attained a view that is repeatedly censured; having encountered this censured false doctrine, you ought not to place your trust in it. Those who performed difficult deeds for you, those who were your former benefactors—[how can you disregard them?]
Toward those who have entered into a state of loving-kindness, you desire their slaughter.
You desire the slaughter of those whom it is impossible to repay in any way by offspring, even if one were to give them all manner of jewels.
Death would be better for you than life, were it not for such a sight as this—
that you should reject the vision practiced by the noble beings.
Today your life ends—along with that of your wife, your kinsmen, your servants, and your sons; and after death, your destination shall be hell.
Indeed, O worthy ones, may it be well with you;
[behold] this man who is possessed of false views, whose mind is deluded and conceited as a scholar.
Furthermore, we shall surely destroy that merchant, who possesses evil views, who leads other people astray, and who reviles the noble vision.
Having heard these words, Dhruva became distressed in mind; with his limbs perspiring and bowing low, he was filled with trepidation.
With a bewildered mind, looking about in all directions, his heart became terrified; joining his palms in reverence, he spoke these words:
May the hosts of rākṣasas be propitiated, as well as my retinue;
you are my goal, my shelter, and indeed my refuge.
Command me: what must I do today so that fearlessness may come to me and my circle of kinsmen, and so that we may not fall into an evil rebirth?
And those hosts of spirits, stationed in the sky, said to Dhruva, the merchant leader:
"Do not go to us for refuge; go to him alone for refuge."
To the Buddha, who desires the welfare of all beings, who is honored by those who have shaken off the defilements,
who has transcended the entire world, the Teacher, the Lion of the Śākyas, the delightful one.
Where indeed is that Blessed One, honored by all beings?
We too would go for refuge to that Sage, the best among men.
Endowed with all virtues, he was in the city of Ratnakholaka,
in the Gandhamādana garden, which was strewn with various flowers.
Honored by ninety thousand who have attained mastery,
the wise Sage, skilled in the monastic life, dwells there.
Go for refuge to him together with all your kinsmen;
behold that sun among men and abandon that [wrong] view.
And whatever auspicious Dharma he teaches, established through parables, behold that with wisdom; in this way your life shall be meaningful.
And if you do not go, O merchant, you will certainly not attain [the goal];
this death of yours is immediate, so act with faith in that.
Then the merchant, together with his kinsmen, having become deeply dejected in mind,
prostrated himself on the ground with his head where that Supreme Person was.
O Sage endowed with all excellent qualities, possessed of great compassion, together with your circle of kinsmen; O one of great renown, I go to you for refuge.
O ender of fear for the frightened, you ought to grant me fearlessness; O Great Being, I am one who has taken refuge in fear, yet I have found my protector in you.
"I wish to worship the feet of the Teacher, O best among debaters;
I wish to see that True Person, if we are worthy of his grace."
Then the Teacher, the Leader, who has attained mastery and is surrounded by his followers, arrived in the twinkling of an eye out of compassion for sentient beings.
Seeing him standing in the sky— tamed, patient, and honored—
a sense of joy arose in the merchant together with his kinsmen.
The merchant approached that tiger among speakers for refuge;
and the merchant attained the state of one who possesses a beautiful appearance.
Having fully understood its transcendence, the Tathāgata, the best of men,
the truth-speaking sage, proclaims the four truths.
The All-Pervading One, the Sun among men, reveals in detail the fruit of both auspicious and inauspicious deeds, like a lion roaring in the forest.
Having heard this lion’s roar, the merchant, together with his attendants,
attains the sweet fruit of truth in the very first moment.
Whatever preparation was made for him by the great seer,
those who are skilled in all dharmas call that an "offering" (upahāra).
There was once a king named Taru on a certain island in the ocean;
in him arose a wicked vision, beloved by the foolish.
He who, having invited a brahmin, a śramaṇa, or even another mendicant,
does not feed them— they call him one possessing the mark of excellence.
Having invited a great multitude of people, including many Śūdras and Brāhmaṇas,
he brings them to hunger by subjecting them to imprisonment.
Upon going to Uttarakuru, he is reborn there as one of noble family, of great power, and of great fame, possessing abundant clothing and ornaments.
The king causes the people to believe thus with an evil mind;
having heard his words, the great multitude places its trust in them.
Having understood this vision, the Sage, who is worshipped by gods and gandharvas,
instantly manifested five thousand monks.
Having reached that island where the lord of men was ruling his kingdom, those groups of self-controlled ones began to walk about there.
But the lord of men, having seen those created beings described by the monk,
crossed over from his vehicle, prostrated at his feet, and spoke.
"O sages, I invite you with sincere devotion;
may the sages accept my invitation if we are worthy of their favor."
Knowing that he had consented, he then ran out once more;
having prostrated at the feet of the sages, he went to his own royal palace.
Perceiving that the night had turned to dawn, he said to the king’s man:
"Go, approach the seer, and invite him on my behalf."
And they were ushered by the king into the most wonderful hermitage of the seer,
which was a refuge endowed with all virtues and secured by firm bolts and excellent mechanisms.
When the seven days had passed, the king inspected them;
and those described by the monks were meditating with their facial complexions free from dejection.
Having further avoided those emanations, O lord of men,
he transcends the second [dhyāna] and contemplates within the second.
On the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, ninth, and tenth week, he spoke these words:
Gods, nāgas, gandharvas, yakṣas, guhyakas,
and asuras have come in the form of sages for the purpose of inspiring spiritual urgency in me.
Declare yourselves if we are to be favored; or if you are to be favored by us, declare yourself.
"You are worthy of favor, O lord of the earth," he said these words to him:
"Act exactly according to the word that we speak."
This Teacher is in the city of Kāśī, in the auspicious grove at Vārāṇasī;
he has reached the further shore of all phenomena and is the destroyer of all doubts.
Having ascended the excellent palace, I, together with my kinsmen, bow low and entreat you:
"O Best of Men, we wish to behold the Peerless One."
Having heard these words, he replied, "So be it.
Then the Teacher, by means of his supernatural power, approached that island through the air.
And the four who had attained mastery— Kuñjara, Karabhoja, Vāraṇa, and Mahādhyāyin— along with Manāpa, all came together.
Having seen the Perfectly Awakened One shining with the luster of the moon,
they praised him— the Teacher of the true nature of reality— with palms joined in reverence.
With a serene mind and a joyful heart, endowed with all forms of virtue,
O Protector of gods and humans, homage to you, the one who supports humanity!
Who are you, O Great Being, of great majesty and great splendor, of great intelligence and mighty arms? Speak according to the truth.
Born of a royal lineage, established in the kingdom of Dharma,
and the refuge of all beings— I am known as the Buddha.
I am the lord, the leader, and the physician of gods and humans;
I am the Perfectly Awakened One, the ender of doubt, who is honored by the gods.
Having heard this, the king of trees spoke thus to the Fully Awakened One:
"Homage to you, O tiger among speakers, destroyer of all doubts!"
Having ascended the excellent palace together with our kinsmen, our followers, and the entire kingdom, we go for refuge; O Holy One, be our refuge.
And the king explained his own view to the great seer;
having heard that, the tiger among men spoke thus to the king:
"O lord of the earth, it is no gain for you that you place your trust in evil which leads to miserable rebirths; abandon this pernicious view."
Having relinquished that view, the king spoke these words:
"O wise one, teach me the Dharma, wherein suffering is brought to an end."
And that Supreme among Men, confident in the Buddha-dharma, cultivated for all sentient beings that which is connected with the Dharma and conducive to their welfare.
Having understood that Dharma, the king, together with his attendants,
abandoned the three fetters and attained the first fruit.
And an incalculable multitude of people attained the first fruit;
behold, O King, the supreme power of loving-kindness, O virtuous man!
Those monks who were manifested there are not considered to be actual monks;
the Jinas, who are experts in the teachings, declare this to be a mere offering.
It is simply impossible, O Son of the Victor, that the Tathāgatas could have attained omniscience previously, while still remaining on the coarse stages.
These tigers among speakers, these supreme among men, do not let time pass by in vain; they reveal [the truth] through the fully perfected stages.
Having gone to the forest at Vārāṇasī, the Leader, preceded by the Buddha-dharma,
extensively proclaimed the ten stages.
The perfectly awakened ones, who know right and wrong conduct, understand all supreme intentions;
they examine the resolute intentions of all living beings through their birth stories.
By means of sweet song and skillful method,
the Fully Awakened One, who perceives virtues and understands all beings, has well-disciplined a great multitude of people.
Having encountered the supreme friend, they are disciplined by one of excellent intelligence; they are not born, they do not age, and they do not die in any way whatsoever.
The wise understand one another’s profound conduct;
they all possess infinite eloquence and are beautiful in every limb.
Thus ends the tenth stage, named Abhiṣekavatī, in the glorious Mahāvastu-Avadāna.
On the peak of Vulture Mountain, in the assembly of five hundred who had attained mastery, he spoke the introductory discourse on the teaching named "The Ten Stages."
The *Daśabhūmika* is completed.
Those beings who aspire to Buddhahood should be instructed in this; it should be given to Bodhisattvas of the ten stages and to those who have seen the truth and possess faith, but not to others.
For these [latter] would have faith in this matter, while others would fall into doubt.
Thus concludes the first stage up to the tenth stage, the ten stages, which form the vicinity of the Mahāvastu.
The story of Dīpaṃkara and so forth.

Mahāmaudgalyāyana, in an immeasurable and incalculable kalpa from now, there was a king named Arcimat, a wheel-turning monarch who had performed meritorious deeds, possessed great majesty, endowed with the seven treasures, ruler of the four continents, a conqueror, beloved by his citizens and countryfolk, righteous, a king of dharma, and one who lived having undertaken the ten paths of wholesome action.

He possessed the seven precious treasures, namely: the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure—such were his seven treasures.
And he had a full thousand sons, who were brave, heroic, possessed of excellent physical forms, and crushers of enemy armies.

Thus, having completely conquered these four great continents, bounded by the oceans and mountains—entire, free from thorns, and without punishment, without the use of weapons, and without oppression—he dwells there through righteousness alone.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, King Arcimat had a royal capital named Dīpavatī; it was twelve yojanas in length from east to west and seven yojanas in width from south to north, and it was surrounded by seven walls.
It was surrounded by golden [railings] covered with gold.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the royal capital Dīpavatī was surrounded by seven rows of palm trees,
variegated and beautiful, made of the seven precious substances: gold, silver, pearl, beryl,
crystal, musāragalva, and ruby.
The golden *tāla* trunk had leaves and fruit made of silver;
the silver *tāla* trunk had leaves and fruit made of pearl;
and the pearl *tāla* trunk had leaves and fruit made of beryl.
The trunk of the palm tree made of beryl had leaves and fruit made of crystal;
the trunk of the palm tree made of crystal had leaves and fruit made of musāragalva;
and the trunk of the palm tree made of musāragalva had leaves and fruit made of ruby.
The trunk of that palmyra tree was made of ruby, while its leaves and fruit were made of pearl.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when those palm trees are stirred by the wind and struck together by the wind, a sound issues forth that is lovely, charming, delightful, and not unpleasant to hear.
Just as, for example, when a five-piece musical ensemble is skillfully played by expert performers, a sound issues forth that is lovely, charming, delightful, and not unpleasant to hear—
even so, O Mahāmaudgalyāyana, at that time and at that season,
the people in the royal capital of Dīpavatī were intoxicated; they [indulged] in the five strands of sensual pleasure with that sound like the rustling of palm leaves.
Being fully devoted and united with one another, they played, took delight, and enjoyed themselves.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the royal capital Dīpavatī was surrounded by seven networks of railings,
variegated and beautiful to behold, made of the seven precious substances: gold, silver, pearl, beryl,
crystal, white coral, and ruby.
The golden foot had a silver pin, a support,
and a base;
the silver foot had a pearl pin, a support, and a base.

The base of the one made of pearls was made of beryl; that of the one made of beryl was made of crystal; that of the one made of crystal was made of musāragalva; that of the one made of musāragalva was made of ruby;
and for the base made of ruby, the needle and the support were made of gold.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, those railings and lattices were covered with two nets of gold: one net made of gold and one made of silver.
The golden net had silver bells,
and the silver net had golden bells.
Furthermore, in that royal capital of Dīpavatī, there were three gates on each side, variegated and beautiful,
made of the seven precious substances: gold, silver, pearl, beryl, crystal, musāragalva, and ruby.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, those gates had thresholds made of two kinds of precious substances, gold and silver;
they had balances made of two kinds of precious substances, gold and silver;
and they had crossbars made of two kinds of precious substances, gold and silver.
The panels were made of two types of material: crystal, and gold and silver.
The inlays on the panels were of two types: gold and silver.
The decorative filigree was of four types: gold, silver, pearl, and beryl.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, those gates had door-bolts made of two kinds of metal: gold and silver.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, those four gates had door-bolts of four kinds: gold, silver, pearl, and beryl.
The two kinds of doors were of gold and silver.
The two kinds of bolt-chains were of gold and silver.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, in front of those gates, arrows were set up— three men in height, three men in width, and twelve men in depth— which were variegated, beautiful to behold, and made of seven precious substances: gold, silver, pearl, beryl, and crystal.
Of musāragalva and red coral.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, those gates were each covered with two golden nets: one made of gold and one made of silver.
On the golden net there were silver bells, and on the silver net there were golden bells.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when those golden nets are stirred by the wind and struck together by the wind, a sound issues forth that is lovely, charming, delightful, and not unpleasant to hear. Just so, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when those golden nets are stirred by the wind and struck together by the wind, a sound issues forth that is lovely, charming, delightful, and not unpleasant to hear.

Furthermore, O Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the royal capital Dīpavatī was indeed not empty of such sounds as these: namely, the sounds of elephants, the sounds of chariots, the sounds of infantry, the sounds of kettledrums, the sounds of clay drums, the sounds of small drums, the sounds of conchs, the sounds of flutes, the sounds of lutes, the sounds of singing, and the sounds of musical instruments—eat! drink! enjoy yourselves!
"Eat! Drink! Give gifts! Perform meritorious deeds! Practice the Dharma toward śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas! May it be well with you!"—with these words [he called out].
Furthermore, in the center of that royal capital Dīpavatī, there was a sacrificial pillar named Valguyā, variegated and beautiful to behold,
made of seven precious substances— gold, silver, pearl, beryl, crystal, musāragalva, and ruby—
twelve yojanas in height and four yojanas in its base-width.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, King Arcimat had a chief queen named Sudīpā, who was gracious, beautiful to behold, of noble presence, and endowed with the most excellent and abundant beauty of complexion.
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana, twelve years from now, the Bodhisattva Dīpaṃkara will descend from the Tuṣita heaven;
the Śuddhāvāsa gods announce this to the Pratyekabuddhas."
The Bodhisattva will descend; leave the Buddha-field!
From the Tuṣita heaven, the one of exceeding fame, who possesses infinite knowledge and vision, will descend;
leave the buddha-field for him who bears the excellent marks.
Having heard the word "Buddha" from the supreme Maheśvaras, those Pratyekabuddhas,
self-arisen ones who have mastery over their own minds, attained nirvāṇa with liberated hearts.
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana, twelve years from now, the Bodhisattva Dīpaṃkara will descend from the Tuṣita heaven.

The Śuddhāvāsa gods, having assumed the guise of brahmins, will teach the mantras, the Vedas, and the thirty-two marks of a Great Man to those brahmins, so that they may prophesy when the Bodhisattva arrives here."
Then indeed, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, at the time of his passing away from the Tuṣita abode, the Bodhisattva performed four great surveys:
namely, the survey of the time, the survey of the region, the survey of the continent, and the survey of the family.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Bodhisattvas are born into two types of families: either in a kṣatriya family or in a brāhmaṇa family.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the family in which Bodhisattvas are born is endowed with sixty qualities.
With which sixty factors is it endowed?
And that family, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, is well-known;
that family is thoroughly understood;
and that family provides no opportunity for the base.
He is endowed with noble birth,
endowed with a distinguished lineage,
and endowed with a succession of ancestors renowned from former generations.
It was endowed with the excellence of a great and ancient lineage; it possessed many women and many men.
Neither restless,
nor greedy,
nor fearful.
And one who is not dejected,
and one who possesses wisdom,
and one who possesses ethical discipline.
And while not looking after his own property,
he enjoys that family's wealth;
furthermore, that family becomes a firm friend to him.
Grateful,
knowledgeable of the proper method,
not acting out of desire, and not acting out of hatred.
And [he is] one who goes without delusion, one who goes toward fearlessness,
and one who fears reproach.
And Sthūlabhikṣa,
Puruṣakāramati, and Dṛḍhavikramaṇa.
One who worships a shrine,
one who worships the gods,
and one who worships his ancestors.
And those devoted to ritual action, those devoted to renunciation, and those devoted to ascetic observances.
He is one who has attained both the prior and the subsequent;
he is proclaimed by a voice surpassing that of the gods;
and he is the eldest of the family.
And one who is the best of families, the most excellent of families,
and one who has attained mastery over the family.
And it is renowned,
and has a great retinue,
and its retinue is untiring.
And having a devoted retinue, and an unbreakable retinue,
and one who knows how to revere his mother.
And that which is known by the fathers;
and the state of a śramaṇa; and the state of a brāhmaṇa.
He honors his elders of the family;
he possesses abundant wealth and grain;
and he has ample treasuries and storehouses.
It possesses abundant elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep;
it has numerous female and male slaves, laborers, and servants;
and that family becomes invincible against others who are adversaries or enemies.
In whatever family, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Bodhisattvas are born, that family is endowed with these sixty qualities.
Those beings who are endowed with a noble lineage—beings of such a kind—attain great compassion.
Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, at the time of his passing away, the Bodhisattva made a great final arrangement.
Thousands of sons of gods were addressed by the son of a god.

"Be born in the sixteen great provinces of the Middle Country, in families of great kṣatriyas, in families of great householders, in royal families, and in families of royal ministers; when you have been disciplined, the great mass of people will come to discipline."
At the time of his passing away, the Bodhisattva surveys: "Where shall I be reborn?"

"This King Arcimat has performed meritorious deeds, is of great renown, and is a universal monarch, the lord of the four continents; he is worthy to be my father. He then searched for a mother who would be gracious, of noble birth, pure of body, with little passion, and short-lived—such that only seven nights and ten months of her lifespan remained.
After giving birth to all those supreme among men, the Bodhisattvas,
on the final seventh day, the mother gives up her life.
What is the reason for this, O omniscient mothers, that having given birth to the best of men, you so quickly abandon your lives?
While in the Tuṣita realm, the Bodhisattva, through his pure karma, attains great mindfulness as he examines the mother who shall give birth to him.
If there should remain for a woman here a remnant of life,
it shall descend upon her breast for seven days and ten months.
For what reason? Because it is improper for one such as me to engage in sexual intercourse after having maintained the unsurpassed [vows] at a later time.
Even if they were to indulge in sensual desires with the mother of the Sugata,
he would not be called one of broken conduct by the hosts of gods.
The Blessed One indeed constantly speaks of the faults of sensual desires;
yet the mother of the Lord of the World indulges in sensual desires.
And those jewel-caskets situated in the palaces of kings—
O Best of Men, the Jewel is the Mother of the Jinas, and this is her vessel.
While searching, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Bodhisattva saw him.
In the royal capital of Dīpavatī,

Queen Sudīpā— the consort of King Arcimat— was gracious, of noble birth, pure of limb, and of little passion; yet she was short-lived, having only seven nights remaining out of ten months of her life-span.
While surveying the world from the enclosure of Arcimat’s palace,
he saw a woman who resembled the consort of an immortal, glowing like a flash of lightning or a brightly lit lamp.
Having observed his mother, Amarā, he addressed her: "I shall descend;
I will enter my final dwelling in a womb for the sake of the happiness of gods and men."
To him, the host of gods, wearing exquisite ornaments and with palms joined in reverence, said:
"O Supreme Person of undiminished virtue and form, may your vow be fulfilled!"
We too, for the benefit of the world, having renounced delightful sensual pleasures,
shall dwell in the human world for the sake of making offerings to you, O Supreme God.
With uplifted minds, they rained down a shower of Mandārava flowers of stainless, radiant color from the sky, accompanied by pure and very sweet words.

That you do not rejoice in nor indulge in sensual pleasures— which are delightful even to the inhabitants of the immortal realms, yet are intermingled with grief and suffering— this is a marvel in your case.
That you, having surpassed the host of Maruts, illuminate the ten directions with a radiance like Mount Jambunada— O Bull among Gods, this is a marvel!
You surpass the hosts of gods, including Maheśvara and the dānavas, as well as the assemblies of Māra and the hosts of stars that move through the sky; O Amitamati, this too is a marvel.
Moreover, O Teacher of the multitude of beings, although we do not wish for separation from you,
nevertheless, O lotus-eyed one, you shall become the refuge for humans and gods.
Then, at the time of his passing away, the host of gods, filled with joy, proclaimed throughout all the directions: "He whose eyes are like pure hundred-petaled lotuses!"
While this conversation was taking place in the city of Tuṣita, that peerless and most excellent Sudīpā,
the queen of King Arcimat, approached the king and said this:
That dark-complexioned woman, with eyes like those of a young deer and resembling a pure Gandharva maiden,
being well-lit, spoke these very sweet words to Arcimat.
O bull among kings, with arms adorned by ornaments and wearing exquisite garments, my desire is to spend this night with my friends in your absence.
The best of men, Śataraśmi, ascended to the highest floor of his excellent palace,
where there was a supreme couch, stainless and resembling a garment of white water-lilies.
Pleased by those agreeable words of the goddess Arcimat,
the excellent man, his resolve uplifted, addressed his retinue.
Let them quickly announce to me that Śataraśmi is covered with excellent flowers;
scatter loose blossoms over him, making him like a divine realm in heaven.
Adorned with hanging silk streamers, let the hundred-rayed chariot shine forth with agility,
covered by a net of excellent gold and resembling the peak of the noble Mount Sumeru.
And let a fourfold army, variegated with spears, iron arrows, and javelins,
swiftly surround the delightful host of Śataraśmi.
The command having been issued by the king, and everything having been made ready,
his own family approached the king there and said this:
May the protector of the earth preserve his life for no less than a thousand years;
your excellent celestial palace stands ready, inspiring joy.
Then that queen, resembling a celestial consort, having risen from her excellent seat,
spoke to the best of kings just as the sun had set.
I undertake this: non-violence toward living beings and the holy life;
I also abstain from taking what is not given, from intoxicants, and from idle chatter.
O best of men, I likewise desist from all slanderous speech;
O lord of men, I desist from harsh speech—this is my resolve.
I shall not give rise to envy toward the desires of others, nor shall I harbor malice; I shall cultivate benevolence toward all beings and abandon perverted views.
"O Protector of the Earth, I practice the elevenfold morality throughout this entire night; such is the aspiration that arises within me."
Moreover, O protector of the earth, do not harbor thoughts of desire toward me;
do not send me away, lest demerit accrue to you on account of me, a woman living the holy life.
"I shall fulfill all your desires," said the king;
"rejoice, having entered this most excellent palace; both I and the kingdom are at your command."
Taking with her a thousand foremost women who were devoted to her, she ascended that excellent celestial palace and sat down there, her desires fulfilled and pleasing.
For some time, she spent that period in silence upon her couch, which resembled a snow-white water lily or a white lotus, finding delight in tranquility and self-restraint.
Then, having laid down her excellent body on her right side,
she lay upon her bed entwined like a flowering creeper around a noble tree.
Then, beholding the goddess lying upon her bed, resembling a celestial maiden in form,
the hosts of gods descended from the Tuṣita abode and stood upon the roof of the palace.
All those gods, their heads bowed and filled with joy, with palms joined in reverence,
paid homage to that goddess of vast merit, the mother of the Conqueror, as she lay upon her bed.
Then, filled with great curiosity, many daughters of the gods, wearing pure garlands and longing to see the Mother of the Jina, approached and took their places upon the roof of the palace.
Having approached and beheld the queen reclining upon her bed, who resembled a flash of excellent lightning,
he experienced vast joy and bliss, and then rained down celestial flowers.
"Even among humans, such a well-formed beauty as this is indeed a marvel!
Were she to remain within for some time, she would not be equal even to the wives of the gods."
O friends, behold the playful grace of this young woman, which is so appropriate for her;
she shines upon her couch, captivating the mind like a radiant streak of gold.
She shall bear that Great Man, who delights in ultimate generosity, self-control, and virtue, who brings an end to all outflows, and who is free from dust; O Queen of men, what is lost to you?
In this beautiful belly, curved like a bow, resembling the palm of a hand, and adorned with a wonderful line of hair,
that one of infinite intelligence shall dwell, ever unstained by impurity and pure.
For this woman, there is vast and supreme wholesome merit accumulated over a very long time; she shall uphold him who possesses infinite qualities and the power of merit gathered over many nights.
You are a woman worthy of him, the most excellent mother; and he is that preeminent man, a son free from craving and stainless. O queen, what is lacking for you? What is lost to you?
Then the Rākṣasas, assuming various forms and commanded, swiftly stationed themselves all around in the sky:
"O you who bear excellent weapons, remain here and make all directions unobstructed!"
Immediately following them, hosts of double-tongued serpents stand in all directions for the sake of protection;
even at the mere sound of a stirring wind, their anger flares up like fire.

Stationed immediately behind them were the Yakṣas, with blazing crests and deformed features; they, being of malicious intent, were told: "Drive them back, and do not commit the slaughter of anyone at all."
Standing immediately behind them were powerful hosts of Gandharvas, possessing beautiful forms;
for the sake of protection, they bore splendid bows, were endowed with excellent marks, and possessed vast intelligence.
The four Lords of the World, together with their own retinues, have themselves established themselves in the sky;
today, it is said, the Blessed One, who increases the welfare and happiness of the world, will descend.
Standing in the intermediate space together with the gods of the Thirty-three, the foremost of the Thirty-three, the bearer of the excellent wheel,
will before long undergo his final passing away, desiring incomparable bliss.
At the foot of the Goddess, many hosts of gods, having joined their ten fingers and bowing toward her,
uttered sweet words while gazing upon the Jina in the Tuṣita heaven.

O you whose power of merit is accumulated through purification, the time has indeed come for you to reach the end of existence; wait but a moment, for your mother is ready, so now show compassion toward the suffering people.
"I am passing away," he uttered these auspicious words, and proclaimed this pure speech.
Then, at that very moment, the Mother of the Victor beheld a dream, the fruit of excellent ripening.
Resembling snow and silver, with six tusks, beautiful feet and lovely arms, and a deep red head—
this preeminent elephant has entered her womb, possessing a graceful gait and flawless joints of the limbs.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Bodhisattvas do not descend into their mother’s womb during the dark fortnight;
rather, Bodhisattvas descend into their mother’s womb on the full moon of the month of Pūrṇamāsī, when it is conjoined with the Puṣya constellation.

When a woman has observed the *upoṣadha* vows, is endowed with height, endowed with girth, well-proportioned, having reached the full bloom of the prime of youth, is disciplined, learned, mindful, clearly conscious, possesses a mind that is skillful in every respect, is suitable in every way, and is the most excellent of women— into the womb of such a mother do Bodhisattvas descend.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva had gone to the Tuṣita heaven, at the time of his descent, he emitted a radiance by which the entire Buddha-field was illuminated.
One son of the gods asks another son of the gods.
For what reason has the Suravara emitted this radiance,
cooler than the rays of the moon and as bright as gold,
by which the hosts of Asura lords and the lords of men [are illuminated]?
And the hells, which were like the flames of a blazing fire, were completely cooled.
Then he said:
Those who protect the people here and there—
who are trapped in the cage of saṃsāra and overcome by passion—
by means of their great fame, they bring about their liberation.
For the purpose of addressing him, a radiance was emitted by the Sinless One.
The Bodhisattva said:
O immortals, do not abandon the cities; this is surely no time for merriment.
This is the time to shatter the city of old age and death with the blow of wisdom.
The Bodhisattva, mindful, clearly comprehending, and with a favorable mind, descended into his mother’s womb.
Thus, at the time of his passing, that lion among men let out a lion’s roar by the river;
vanishing in an instant, he was reborn in the palace of the lord of men.
He who illuminates the Tuṣita realm with his beautiful complexion,
that unsurpassed light of the world, was passing away from the city of the gods.
Together with Brahmā, the world, and all beings including recluses and brahmins,
he— the unsurpassed one, the light of the world— illuminates them with his splendor.
Behold this wonder and marvel: how the Teacher, possessed of great supernormal power, mindful and clearly comprehending, has entered his mother’s womb.
And for as long as that most excellent of men, endowed with the supreme marks,
remained in his mother’s womb, he was mindful, possessed of intelligence, and fully conscious.

And immediately after the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva had entered his mother’s womb, O Mahāmaudgalyāyana, this great earth shook, trembled, and quaked violently in six ways; it shook in a manner that was thrilling, beautiful, exhilarating, gladdening, affection-inspiring, refreshing, beyond description, and worthy of being gazed upon.
It was refreshing, not disagreeable, pleasing, expansive, free from agitation, and free from terror.
And even while trembling, it does not harm any living being, whether moving or stationary.
Then this earth, together with its oceans and the circle of Mount Meru, shook in six ways;
and the world was made stainless and delightful.
By the splendor of him who dispels the great darkness.
Thus this one of great majesty, mindful, having descended from the Tuṣita heaven,
assumed the form of an elephant with six tusks, resembling a white boar.
While she was observing the poṣadha, lying on her side in the heroic posture (vīrāsana) and dressed in pure garments,
he— mindful, clearly conscious, and skillful— descended into his mother’s womb.
And at the break of that night, she told her beloved husband:
"O best of kings, a white lordly elephant has entered my womb."
The king, having summoned the five classes of diviners, addressed them: "Listen to this dream;
tell me the true result and ripening of everything that occurred within it."
There, when the soothsayers were questioned by the king himself, they said:
"One who bears the thirty-two marks has entered the womb of the queen."
O best of men, you are joyful that one who upholds a hundred thousand marks has arisen in your family—
O bearer of the earth, a noble embryo, an incomparable being, a great being.
Just as I have personally received from the ancient teachers,
O tiger among the heroes of men, there are two other destinies for him that are not different.

If he shall dwell in the household, he will become a lord of the earth, possessing the seven treasures and great supernatural power, ever victorious and surrounded by a retinue of hundreds of thousands of kings.
Then, indeed, having abandoned the earth consisting of the four continents, he will go forth into homelessness;
by that [act], he will become a Buddha who cannot be led by others among men and gods.
All the dragon kings and lords of dragons, as many as there were, applied themselves with zeal to provide protection, defense, and guardianship for the Bodhisattva.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, all the kings of Suvarṇa and lords of Suvarṇa apply themselves with zeal for the sake of the Bodhisattva’s protection, defense, and guardianship.
The four great kings also applied themselves with zeal for the protection, defense, and guardianship of the Bodhisattva.
The four world-protectors also provided protection for the Lord of the World,
so that no one seeking harm might injure the dispeller of Namuci’s power.

Śakra, the lord of the gods; the divine son Suyāma; the divine son Saṃtuṣita; the divine son Sunirmita; the divine son Vaśavartin; Mahābrahmā; and the divine son Śuddhāvāsa—all applied themselves with zeal for the sake of protection, defense, and guardianship for the Bodhisattva while he was in his mother’s womb.
Thousands of contented gods,
possessing excellent wisdom, have approached the city of Arcimat for the sake of protection, as if it were the city of the immortals.
The supreme city of Dīpavatī,
made enchanting by the hosts of immortals who enter it with mind-made strides and movements, shines resplendently.
Surrounding the goddess, it is said that eight thousand hosts of Maheśvara, situated in the expanse of the sky, sat poised in the air.
Now, behind them, many thousands of Indras with stainless peaks sat down for the purpose of guarding the one of manifold virtues.
Now, behind those lords of the gods, thousands of myriads of gods belonging to the realm of desire were seated in the supportless sky.
Behind those hosts of gods were the asuras, and behind the asuras were the hosts of double-tongued serpents.
And yakṣas of deformed appearance and hosts of rākṣasas were seated there.
By this rite, the glorious sky, crowded with hundreds of thousands of immortals, became utterly pure; for merit was accumulated by one free from passion.
Mahābrahmā said:
"In a dream, a certain woman saw the sun entering her womb from the sky."
She gives birth to one whose limbs bear excellent marks; he becomes a king, a powerful universal monarch.
The woman who, in her dream, beheld the moon entering her womb from the sky,
shall give birth to a son who is a god among men.
He becomes a king, a supreme universal monarch.
The woman who, in her dream,
saw a white elephant enter her womb shall give birth to one endowed with the essence of the nature of an elephant.
Thus he becomes a Buddha, one who has awakened to the meaning of the Dharma.
He questioned the queen.
What do you carry?
She said:
"A universal monarch," he said.
I bear within my womb a universal monarch, a supreme man, a tiger among kings, whose body is golden-hued and endowed with the most excellent marks, illuminating the interior.
The gods raised their voices in the sky, proclaiming the word of the Blessed One.
He will become a Buddha, not a king who is a wheel-turning monarch of power.
Mahābrahmā spoke this verse:
You are the elephant, the most excellent of jewels, who removes the force and speed of passion;
you are the lamp of the world that dispels the darkness, gloom, and delusion;
you are the treasury of virtues, possessing a mine of immeasurable jewels.
O royal seer, you bear an unimpeded wheel and the splendor of the immortals.
The queen said:
"Now that I have perceived the embryo of the lord of men, passion and hatred no longer overcome me;
there will undoubtedly be one of equal splendor, just as these words issue forth."
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva’s mother moves, stands, sits, and lies down with ease, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva.
No weapon can penetrate her body; neither poison, nor fire, nor lightning can prevail against her, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, celestial maidens attend to the Bodhisattva’s mother with divine ointments, massages, and requisites; by the very power of the Bodhisattva, she becomes clothed in divine garments and adorned with divine ornaments.
By the very power of the Bodhisattva, she becomes a recipient of divine scents, divine garlands, divine ointments, and divine essences.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, those who are her inner circle of attendants think that she must be served and listened to with extreme care, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, those who see the Bodhisattva’s mother approach her and invite her with words concerning her needs,
solely through the power of the Bodhisattva.
Nothing whatsoever goes above it, not even a bird, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva’s mother is free from illness and free from affliction; she possesses a digestive system that is well-balanced and capable of transformation, neither too cold nor too hot, due to the very power of the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva’s mother enjoys exquisite foods— both solid and soft— as well as the finest and most fresh flavors,
solely through the power of the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva’s mother becomes free from passion;
she practices a holy life that is unbroken, flawless, unspotted, untarnished, completely pure, and perfect.
Not even in her mind did passion arise for that most excellent of women toward any man whatsoever, including even King Arcimat.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva’s mother abides having undertaken the five precepts, and these have been undertaken by her from time immemorial.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, as many as there are Nāga kings and lords of Nāga kings—
Whether they be born from eggs, born from a womb, born from moisture, or born spontaneously, they approach the dwelling and scatter divine sandalwood powders.
Thus they scattered powders of agallochum and loose flowers; and for the sake of its completion, they honored it with worship; and for the sake of its fulfillment, they honored it with worship;
and for the sake of its utter purity, they honored it with worship.
Having scattered divine sandalwood powders, they scattered saffron powders, tamāla-leaf powders, and loose flowers.
They honored him with perfect worship; they honored him with complete worship; they honored him with pure worship.
Having performed worship with complete offerings, having performed worship with pure offerings, having scattered divine sandalwood powder,
having showered, strewn, and overspread divine aloe-wood powder, saffron powder, tamāla-leaf powder, and loose flowers,
and having circumambulated the Bodhisattva’s mother three times to the right, they departed as they pleased.
They set out by the very power of the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, all the golden kings and golden lords—

whether born from eggs, from a womb, from moisture, or by spontaneous birth— enter his dwelling and scatter divine sandalwood powder, scatter many kinds of divine powders, and scatter divine saffron powder.
They scattered divine *tamāla* leaf powder; they scattered divine flower powder.
And they honored him with a completed worship, they honored him with a perfect worship, and they honored him with a completely pure worship.
Having scattered divine powders— powders of agallochum, powders of saffron, and powders of *tamāla* leaves—
and having scattered divine loose flowers, they circumambulated the mother of the Bodhisattva three times to the right and departed as they pleased, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva had entered his mother’s womb, the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmitavaśavartin, Brahmakāyika,
and Śuddhāvāsakāyika gods entered his dwelling and scattered divine sandalwood powder and divine aloe-wood powder.
They scattered divine *tamāla* leaf powder and loose flowers over it; they honored it with a completed offering,
they honored it with a perfectly fulfilled offering, and they honored it with a completely pure offering.

Having scattered divine sandalwood powder over her, having strewn divine aloe-wood powder, divine saffron powder, divine *tamāla* leaves, and divine loose flowers, and having honored the mother of the Bodhisattva with that worship— worshiping her with complete worship, worshiping her with perfect worship, and worshiping her with utterly pure worship— [they departed].
Having circumambulated him three times, they proceeded wherever they desired, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when a bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, he does not remain too low, nor does he remain too high; he does not remain hunched over, nor on his back, nor on his left side, nor in a squatting position.
Then, indeed, he remained standing on his mother's right side with his legs crossed in the paryanka posture.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, he does not remain there defiled by bile, phlegm, blood, or any other impurity;
rather, with his limbs cleansed, bathed, and pure, the Bodhisattva dwells within his mother’s womb.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Bodhisattva, while dwelling within his mother’s womb, beholds his mother.

The mother of the Bodhisattva also sees the Bodhisattva within her womb like a form of gold; having seen him illuminating her womb like a form of gold—as a beryl gem placed in a crystal casket—just so does the mother see the Bodhisattva illuminating her womb like a form of gold.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, hosts of gods come to inquire after her pleasant nights and pleasant days; and the Bodhisattva welcomes them by raising his right hand, without causing any discomfort to his mother.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, dānavas, rākṣasas,
and piśācas do not leave him by day or by night; nor is there any talk of attachment spoken there, whether connected with sensual desires or any other kind of false speech.
They speak of nothing other than the praise of the Bodhisattva, according to his form, his being, his splendor, his color, his fame, and his roots of merit.
The worship of the Bodhisattva while he is in his mother’s womb does not cease.
Divine musical instruments resounded; divine aloe-wood incense was burned; a rain of divine flowers fell, and a rain of divine powder fell.
And thousands of apsarases sing and dance before him.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva’s mother engages in laughter and conversation with thousands of celestial maidens.
And while the Bodhisattva’s mother was asleep, celestial maidens fanned her with garlands of māndārava flowers through the power of the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, this is the unsurpassed perfection of the descent into the womb within this trichiliocosm, the great thousandfold world system.
And behold now another marvel of that divine assembly,
so vast was the conversation that arose, generating supreme joy.
For them there was no talk of sensual pleasures, nor talk of apsarases, nor talk of singing;
there was no talk of instrumental music, nor talk of food, nor talk of drinks.
No talk of ornaments arose among them, nor did talk of clothing ever occur; even the thought of vehicles or pleasure gardens never occurred to their minds.
What is the discourse on the garden?
It is this: "The splendor of the Leader, who possesses the power of merit, is excellent and incomparable; it surpasses the world including the gods, and this discourse flourishes therein."
"Excellent is the peerless descent into the womb of him who has reached the perfection of form"—
thus did various discourses blossom forth in the midst of this assembly.
The virtuous, free from worldly attachment, pass that time through terms of correct understanding;
this discourse of theirs, characterized by supreme wisdom, also blossoms in the midst of the assembly.
And thus, speaking many kinds of discourse, the hosts of gods take delight,
recounting the form, complexion, splendor, and strength of Viraja.
The mothers of all bodhisattvas give birth when the tenth month is complete.
When the tenth month was complete, the queen named Sudīpā said to King Arcimat:
"Your Majesty, it is my intention to go out to the Lotus Grove park."
Having heard this from Queen Sudīpā, the king said to his ministers:
"I shall go out to the Lotus Grove park with my harem for the sake of recreation."
Make the lotus grove very swift-moving, cleared of grass, debris, and leaves,
filled with heaps of excellent fragrant flowers, and scented with perfumed water.
And let the breezes from the lotus grove, their bodies perfumed with the scent of *tāla* leaves,
sprinkle her with the fragrance of nectar and drive away those things that cause intoxication.
May the clouds from the sky, filled with the finest incense of aloe-wood,
quickly descend and cover that grove of lotuses, which is overflowing with the essence of excellent powders.
"And fashion each excellent tree from *dukūla*, *paṭṭa*, wool, and *kośikāra* silk,
making them like the wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*) of the preeminent god in heaven."
The gods and goddesses, taking perfumes and garlands, came to the Padminīvana garden to visit Arcimat.
Wearing earrings of crystal jewels, with garments slipping off and long necklaces of gems dangling, they take up perfumes and garlands and, moving along the path of the sky, they draw near.
One [chariot] was filled with māndārava flowers; another, having been filled with saṃgerī flowers; one with yellow sandalwood; and another again with kalpavṛkṣa garments.
Taking garlands born of land and water, as well as jewels and ornaments, the Apsarases, with joyful hearts, headed toward Jambudvīpa.
Eighty-four thousand celestial maidens, not fewer,
taking up parasols made of gold and jewels, dissolve into the sky.
The atmosphere was filled with hundreds of gabled pavilions, variegated with crystal and jewels, smeared with plaster, and adorned with hundreds of banners raised aloft on fine cloth.
Resembling the breath of an elephant, the autumn clouds shine forth,
fragrant with the scent of excellent, sweet-smelling flowers, intermingled with lotuses, water-lilies, and campakas.
Even the lords of the serpents, filled with joy, showered the sky with clouds laden with fragrant water,
along with hundreds of other wonders.
Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, King Arcimat, with great royal majesty, great royal power, and great splendor, went out to the lotus grove garden accompanied by his harem.
Having entered that excellent forest, the Queen, the mother of the Conqueror, surrounded by her female companions,
roamed about like a celestial nymph skilled in the arts of love in the Citraratha grove.

Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Queen Sudīpā, surrounded by her female companions, sported upon the boats at the eastern and western embankments of the lotus pond— boats which were covered with canopies, draped with variegated cloths, hung with bundles of silk ribbons and garlands, smeared with ointments, perfumed with incense, strewn with loose flowers, enclosed by latticed railings, and adorned with raised parasols, banners, and flags.
Then, as Queen Sudīpā was being dragged along by the boat, it is said that this thought arose in her:
"I shall disembark from the boat."

And through the power of the Bodhisattva, an island appeared in the middle of the lake—level and even, strewn with golden sand; and soft, blue grasses grew there, like cotton to the touch and resembling the neck of a peacock, which would sink four finger-breadths into the earth when a foot was placed upon them; and trees appeared there, laden with fruit and most delightful.
The goddess was established on that island.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the mother of a Bodhisattva does not give birth to the Bodhisattva while lying down or sitting;

nor, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, does the mother of a Bodhisattva give birth to a Bodhisattva who is defiled by bile, phlegm, blood, or any other kind of impurity. On the contrary, [the Bodhisattva] emerges with his limbs cleansed, bathed, and pure.
...she gives birth to the Bodhisattva himself.
With her body exhausted, she supported herself by grasping a branch of a tree with her arm;
she yawned gracefully at the time of the birth of that illustrious one.
Then twenty thousand daughters of the gods quickly assembled;
with their hands joined in reverent salutation and their intentions purified, they spoke thus to the goddess.
Today you shall give birth to one who will destroy old age and disease— one as delicate as the offspring of the immortals,
a goddess honored in heaven and on earth, the benefactor and well-wisher of both humans and gods.
Do not give way to despondency; we shall perform your preparations. Speak whatever must be done, and see how all of that is already accomplished.
Then the four world-protectors, together with their retinues, very quickly assembled;
with divine hair-braids in their hands, they approached the Queen from the right side.
All the hosts of gods, having surrounded the goddess in the sky,
stood there with garlands and perfumes in their hands, gracing themselves along with their retinues.
Mindful and clearly comprehending, the Bodhisattva appears from the mother’s right side without causing her any pain.
For indeed, the best of men are born from the right side;
all those tigers among men become dwellers therein.
Why was that side of the Mother of the Victor not pierced,
and why did no pain arise in her who gave birth to the Best of Men?
The Tathāgatas appear in a mind-made form;
thus their sides are not broken, and no pain arises.
Exhausted from dwelling in the womb, he strides seven steps upon the earth;
he gazes toward the directions and lets out a great laugh.
What is the reason stated here for why one traverses seven steps, neither eight nor sixty? Listen now to the traditional teaching on this matter.
Exhausted by dwelling in the womb, the Sage, who is the benefactor of the entire world,
then departed with speed from that final residence in the womb.
When his feet were placed upon the ground for the seventh time, the hosts of gods prostrated themselves;
suddenly, the Sage was supported by the laps of the world-protectors.
Then a rain arose, consisting of sprays of celestial flowers,
strewn with the finest mandārava blossoms and thick with divine sandalwood.
For a long time, the foremost of the gods released intense and sublime incense as an ornament for that one of supreme intelligence.
I shall now declare the scripture and the delightful instruction regarding that purpose for which the Peerless One surveys the directions.
Among beings, both among gods and humans,
there exists no one for whom such a birth and even such an entry into the womb could occur.
When the Omniscient One is being born in his final existence, the side of the Mother of the Jina becomes radiant like a firefly or gold.
As soon as he was born, that mind of the Preeminent Speaker arose:
"Is there anyone who possesses an intellect equal to mine?"—
this was his thought for the purpose of dispelling such conceit.
Some suffer from the noose of saṃsāra just as I do;
for this purpose, the Sun of Men gazes upon all directions.
