Then, surveying the directions, the best of speakers beheld thousands of millions of deities; therefore, he let out a laugh.
As soon as he was born, the deities belonging to Māra’s host said:
"You shall become a universal monarch with a great treasury over the four continents."
Then a smile arose upon his face: "O beings, you do not recognize me;
I shall become the Supreme Person, omniscient and all-seeing."
Thus do the distinguished instructors praise this;
for in this way has the teaching of the Lions among Men been fully revealed.
I pay homage to that unsurpassed Jina, whom his mother gave birth to while standing amidst blossoming śāla trees, as she supported her body.
As soon as he was born, the Sugata stood upon level ground;
he took seven steps and gazed toward all directions.
As he was walking about in meditation, they followed him with a fan and a parasol,
lest gadflies and mosquitoes should alight upon the body of that knower of the supreme state.
The gods first received the Sugata, the Jina, as soon as he was born; afterwards, humans held that unsurpassed one in their arms.
The gods received the Sugata, who displayed the thirty-two marks;
and afterwards, humans carried that unsurpassed one on their laps.
The lamps of men were extinguished, and the world was illuminated when the Sugata was born, like a torch-bearing festival for gods and men.
As soon as the Sugata was born, those seeking water ran forth;
then, wells in front of them became full and overflowed from their mouths.
Two streams of water welled up— one cool and one warm—
whereby they bathed the Sugata, who was like a statue of refined gold.
Immediately upon the birth of the Sugata, the Bodhisattva’s mother remained unhurt and unscarred, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva himself.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, as soon as the Bodhisattva was born, the Bodhisattva’s mother’s womb remained completely full, yet it was not constricted, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva himself.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, as soon as the Bodhisattva was born, a sandalwood forest appeared on the intermediate island, which served for the Bodhisattva’s enjoyment and use through the very power of the Bodhisattva himself.
There, hundreds of thousands of sons of gods went along together, holding perfumes and garlands in their hands for the sake of worshipping the Bodhisattva.
A son of the gods asked another son of the gods, "Where will you go? He said to them:
This most excellent consort of a king shall give birth to that supreme child, as fair as the interior of a blossomed, choice lotus—
the one who will attain the highest goal upon the circle of the earth.
Having defeated Māra along with his army, I approach that Hero.
His limbs were unstained by the impurities of the womb,
like a supreme lotus born in the water;
his radiant body possessed the brilliance of the morning sun.
He surpasses the immortals together with Brahmā.
Then, as soon as he was born into the family of Arcimat,
the wise one took seven steps here,
and having surveyed the directions, he uttered a lion’s roar.
"Now this is my final existence."
And from that [tree] there appeared a single, brilliantly shining parasol, adorned with the finest jewels and pearls, outshining all others by its splendor,
and fanned by a wreath of mandārava flowers.
Many sons of the gods held it up in the sky.
They held aloft in the sky an excellent golden parasol, its color resembling the sun, a conch shell, or silver;
then, fans were released and began to whirl about.
Taking hold of the Jina with their hands, they fanned him.
Then there arose fragrant, pleasantly warm, abundant, light, lovely, beneficial to humans,
auspicious, delightful, and yet accompanied by coolness.
Two streams of water rose up into the sky.
Then, from the peak of Mount Meru, various kinds of upper garments were released, forming waves on all sides; they were intensely perfumed by the wind with the scent of every fragrance.
They caused the firm earth to tremble with its sixfold movement.
In celestial palaces made of gold, silver, and beautiful jewels, the gods, accompanied by the sounding of musical instruments,
gazed upon the Jina who was well-born and born in accordance with his nature.
They would beautify the sky, including the moon, sun, and stars.
"This great seer, having crossed the great flood of the world— including its gods, nāgas, and yakṣas—
will then reach the secure and solitary state."
The gods, greatly rejoiced, proclaimed this from the sky.
King Arcimat gave the command.
"Lead the prince here to pay homage at the feet of this very queen."
"In what kind of vehicle does the prince sit?"
The gods fashioned a palanquin made of jewels.
"Who will carry this palanquin?"
The four great kings stood in attendance.
"We shall carry the Bodhisattva, the essence of beings, as well as Queen Sudīpā and the Bodhisattva’s nurse."
Seated upon the palanquin were Śakra, the lord of the gods, and Mahābrahmā; they made way for him.
Thus, with great splendor, great prosperity, great divine power, and great royal majesty, the Bodhisattva was conducted from the lotus grove garden into the capital city of Dīpavatī,
where he was brought into the presence of the Queen.
When the Great Lord of the World, the Teacher of the lords of men, entered the shrines without desire,
they caused him to be saluted with their heads.
Then his feet appeared.
Then a deity said this to another deity:
"It is not fitting that he should worship me;
for if he were to offer salutation to anyone else,"
"May his head split into seven firm pieces! he said.
As soon as the prince was born, all beings as far as the Avīci hell became successful in their aims and happy;
and all the gods paid him homage, being filled with great joy.
[_Mvu_1.224_] When the prince had entered the royal palace, the king said to the domestic priest:
"Quickly seek out brahmins who are skilled in the qualities and the rules of physiognomy."
And having understood that, the gods named Maheśvaras, who have mastery over their own minds, [will protect him];
let not the hosts of twice-born ones, being unskilled in the marks, engage in conceptualization.
Free from intoxication, pride, and arrogance, eight thousand of the most excellent Maheśvaras approached the newborn,
who was being honored by the hosts of gods.
Standing at the gate of the royal palace, dressed in pure and excellent garments and maintaining absolute silence,
they addressed the doorkeeper with voices as sweet as the song of the kalaviṅka bird.
"Approach the excellent king and say: 'These eight thousand men, who are experts in the rules for the marks and qualities, stand waiting; they would enter if it is your pleasure.'"
Having assented with "So be it," the gatekeeper entered the royal palace and,
with palms joined in reverence and a joyful mind, spoke to the protector of the earth.
O you of incomparable strength and radiant fame, rule the kingdom for a long time with your enemies destroyed;
gods resembling immortals stand at your gate, desiring to enter.
Those with perfectly full and stainless eyes, who move with the sweet voice of an elephant in rut—of them I have no doubt; they are not humans, but sons of gods.
As they walk back and forth, the dust of the earth does not soil their excellent feet;
nor do I see any footprints of theirs upon the ground—this too is a marvel.
With profound and steady gestures, noble appearance, and a gaze that is perfectly tranquil,
they generate vast joy in the people who behold them.
And another marvel occurred: no shadow of their bodies was seen, nor was any sound of their joints heard as they walked about.
O lord of the best of men, you have undoubtedly come to see your excellent son;
having greeted him and paid homage, behold the gods who are not born from a womb.
With hands holding choice garlands and perfumes, their graceful movements and bodies enchanting, those excellent Maruts shine as if with splendor; of this there is no doubt.
Having heard those words of Arcimat, his body trembling with joy, he spoke very hurriedly:
"O messenger, let them enter the magnificent palace!"
For what reason? Such features do not belong to ordinary persons;
nor does such supernatural power as you describe belong to humans.
Then that doorkeeper, having approached the Maheśvaras, spoke thus:
bowing low with palms joined in reverence, he paid homage, joyful and delighted in heart.
The lord of men rejoices: "May you enter, sirs, the palace of the bull among kings, which is like a city of the gods, with the permission of the sovereign."
Having heard these words, the eight thousand excellent Maheśvaras entered the royal palace of the foremost of the unconquered lineage.
Then King Arcimat, having observed Maheśvara from afar,
rose up with his retinue, his body suffused by the power of reverence.
The bull among kings said to them: "Welcome to you all with such affection;
I am pleased by the sight of you and by your power of tranquility and self-control."
"These excellent seats of ours are available;
please remain here, sirs, for the sake of showing us favor."
Then, free from intoxication, pride, and arrogance, those whose actions were blameless sat down upon those seats, which had variegated feet made of many pure jewels.
After waiting for some time, they said to the lord of men:
"May your majesty listen to the purpose for which we have come here."

O Lord of Men, it is said that a son has been born to you, whose every limb is irreproachable, who is the most beautiful in the world, and who has reached the perfection of the qualities of the marks.
We too are skilled in marks and capable of discerning the characteristics of virtues and faults;
if it were not for our regard for your status, we would behold the form of a Great Man.
He said: "Come, behold my son, who is secure in his noble reputation, who brings joy to gods and men, and who has reached the perfection of the qualities of the marks."
Then, having taken Guṇadhara upon a soft kācilindika woolen rug,
he presented the moon among speakers upon his hip to the best of the gods.
Having beheld from afar the noble strides of the One Possessing Ten Powers, the great lords,
with their diadems slipping from their heads, fell upon the earth in rapture.
Then they informed the king.
It is a gain for you, Great King, it is well-acquired by you, that such a Great Being has been born in your family, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Being. They are as follows:

The feet are even, broad, long, and tapered, with high ankles; the calves are like those of the eneya antelope, the thighs are large, and while standing, he reaches his knees with his hands; these are his ten [marks], including the sheathed organ and the nyagrodha-like body.

The hands and feet are soft and webbed; the fingers and toes are full; the fifth [mark] is that the heels are high; the skin is smooth; there is a space between the fingers like those of a swan; and the body is well-proportioned—these are the ten [marks].
Rasa, Suvarṇa, Siṃha, and the fifth, Samā; Samāprabhūta, Brahmā, Nīla, and Gopakṣma—these are the ten.
The Lord, possessing the thirty-two marks, has the *ūrṇā*, the *uṣṇīṣa*, and the crown of the head;
then those brahmins were addressed by King Arcimat.
"Give the prince a name that is appropriate for him."
Those brahmins said:
"Great King, when the prince was born, a lamp appeared and a great radiance shone; therefore, let the prince be named Dīpaṃkara."
In this way, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa realm, having manifested in the guise of brahmins, gave the prince the name Dīpaṃkara.
Suitable nurses attended upon the prince and raised him.
And when the Bodhisattva had reached his youth, the king had three palaces built for the prince’s play and enjoyment, and a vast harem was established for his service.
The Bodhisattva, accompanied by his harem, went out to the lotus grove in the park for the sake of recreation, with great royal majesty, great royal supernatural power, and great royal splendor.
King Arcimat commanded the women of the inner apartments.
"Play well with the prince."

The Bodhisattva descends onto the shore from the boats, which have railings at the front and rear, are surrounded by networks of railings, are covered with canopies, draped with variegated cloth, hung with bundles of silk ribbons and garlands, perfumed with incense, strewn with loose flowers, beautifully adorned with necklaces, half-necklaces, and crescent ornaments, and from which umbrellas, banners, and flags are raised— boats that are devoid of men.

The harem, exhausted and fast asleep, was such that one woman was clutching her jaw, another was embracing a *paṇava* drum, another a flute, another a *vīṇā*, another a *vallakī*, another a *sughoṣakī*, another an anklet, another a *mṛdaṅga* drum, and another a lute-case.
Upon seeing that, the perception of a cemetery arose in the Bodhisattva.
In the middle of the lotus pond, a lotus appeared with a pericarp as large as a chariot wheel, surrounded by thousands of other lotuses.
The Bodhisattva sat cross-legged upon that lotus, and that lotus, having closed up, remained situated like a gabled chamber.
All the marks of a householder disappeared from the Bodhisattva, and saffron robes appeared.

Then indeed, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Bodhisattva Dīpaṃkara, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, entered and dwelt in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion.

With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, through internal clarity and the unification of the mind, he entered and dwelt in the second dhyāna, which is without applied or sustained thought, born of concentration, and characterized by rapture and happiness.
Through the fading away of joy, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body;
he attains and dwells in the third dhyāna, which the Noble Ones describe as "equanimous, mindful, and dwelling in happiness," being free from joy.

And through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and through the previous disappearance of mental joy and dejection, you dwell having attained the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness.

With his mind thus concentrated— purified, cleansed, stainless, free from defilements, supple, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability— he directed and inclined his mind during the first watch of the night toward the attainment of the divine eye for seeing.
With the divine eye, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—fair and ugly, in happy states and miserable states; he understands beings according to their karma.

With his mind thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from secondary defilements, supple, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he would, during the middle watch of the night, recollect his manifold past abodes,
such as one birth, two births, three births, four births, or five births.
For ten, twenty, thirty, forty, or fifty births; for a hundred births, a thousand births, many hundreds of births,
many thousands of births, and even many hundreds of thousands of births, as well as the aeons of dissolution.
or eons of evolution, or eons of both dissolution and evolution, many eons of dissolution, many eons of evolution,
and many eons of both dissolution and evolution.

"In that place I was, with such a name, such a clan, such a caste, such food, such a limit to my lifespan, and such an experience of pleasure and pain"— thus he recollects his manifold past abodes with their modes and details.

Thus, with a mind thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from defilements, steady, and attained to imperturbability, during the last watch of the night, at the time of dawn when the night was turning into day, whatever [was to be known] by that elephant among men, lion among men, bull among men, lotus among men, white lotus among men—

By that bull among men, that true man, that noble steed among men, that unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed— one who possesses movement, mindfulness, steadfastness, and intelligence— he has fully known, attained, awakened to, and perfectly realized all that is to be known, attained, awakened to, and perfectly realized in every way and everywhere, through wisdom conjoined with a single moment of mind, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
And this great earth shook, trembled, and quaked in six ways; and the gods on earth raised a cry and made their voices heard in the sky.

"O worthy one, this Blessed One Dīpaṃkara will awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment for the benefit of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, benefit, and happiness of the great multitude of beings, both gods and humans."
Having heard the cry of the gods of the earth, the gods who move in the intermediate space— the Trāyastriṃśas, Yāmas, Tuṣitas, Nirmāṇaratis,
and Paranirmitavaśavartins— at that very moment, at that very instant, the sound rose up as far as the Brahma-realm.

"O worthy one, this Blessed One Dīpaṃkara will become a perfectly awakened Buddha; he will do so for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, benefit, and happiness of a great multitude of beings, both gods and humans."
An immeasurable, sublime, and great radiance appeared in the world.

To whatever extent there are in the world the intermediate spaces between worlds— regions of darkness enveloped in darkness, gloom enveloped in gloom, abysses that have existed as abysses since time immemorial— where even these suns and moons, so possessed of great supernatural power and such great majesty, do not reach one another with their radiance, nor pervade one another with their light, even those [spaces] by that...
They became suffused with radiance.

Those beings who were reborn there also recognized one another, saying: "Indeed, friends, other beings have been reborn here; indeed, friends, other beings have been reborn here; indeed, friends, other beings have been reborn here."
And furthermore, at that very moment, at that very instant, all sentient beings became endowed with exclusive happiness.
Even those who have been reborn in the great Avīci hell surpass the divine power of the gods, the power of the nāgas, and the power of the yakṣas.
And the palaces of Māra became darkened, lusterless, devoid of splendor, and joyless.
There, fragments measuring one *krośa* fell; there, fragments measuring two *krośas* fell;
there, fragments measuring three *krośas* fell; there, fragments measuring one *yojana* fell;
even the tips of banners fell there.
And Māra the Evil One became sorrowful, dejected, full of remorse, and consumed by the burning sting within him.

And there, Maudgalyāyana, in that very Lotus-Peaked Pavilion, the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara was surrounded by the four Great Kings, Śakra the lord of the gods, the divine son Suyāma, the divine son Saṃtuṣita, the divine son Vaśavartin, and Mahābrahmā, together with a retinue of many hosts of gods.
A magnificent worship was performed for the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara.

Having scattered, strewn, and profusely showered the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara with divine mandārava flowers, mahāmandārava flowers, karṇikāra flowers, rocamāna flowers, bhīṣma flowers, mahābhīṣma flowers, samantagandha flowers, mahāsamantagandha flowers, sandalwood powder, agallochum powder, keśara powder, and tamāla-leaf powder, [he honored him] with thousands of divine musical instruments.
Having honored him right there, Mahābrahmā requested him to turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara consented to Mahābrahmā by remaining silent.
The gods, perceiving his acceptance, were thrilled, satisfied, elated, and filled with joy, gladness, and mental well-being;
they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara, circumambulated him three times, and vanished right there.
At the end of that very night, the Blessed One arose from his seclusion and set out on a journey through the countryside.
The sun-like Dīpaṅkara, of excellent complexion, arose like a youth in the sky; filling a hundred yojanas with his radiance, he stood there.

The Blessed One Dīpaṃkara, while wandering on his journey and performing acts of benefit for a great multitude of people— both gods and humans— arrived at the royal capital of Dīpavatī together with eighty thousand monks, out of compassion for his father Arcimat and his kinsmen.
King Arcimat heard it.
The Blessed One Dīpaṃkara, together with eighty thousand monks, was coming to the royal capital of Dīpavatī out of compassion for his kinsmen.
And they prepared the road for ten *krośas*, from Dīpavatī as far as the Padminīvana park; it was made level like a chessboard, even as the palm of a hand, sprinkled and swept,

with canopies spread overhead, draped with various fine cloths, hung with bundles of silk ribbons and garlands, perfumed with incense, and adorned in the ten directions by actors, dancers, athletes, wrestlers, and musicians.
Furthermore, the city of the universal monarch was adorned with hundreds of lotuses.
King Arcimat took up abundant perfumes and garlands; likewise, a great multitude of people gathered perfumes and garlands from all around for twelve yojanas.
The king, together with eighty thousand vassal kings and other people, went out to meet the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara.

Another [man] was a learned Vedic scholar, one who knew the six auxiliary sciences, had mastered the three Vedas along with their phonetic refinements, and was a teacher of five hundred young students— students who included the histories as the fifth and the glossaries and ritual manuals; he was skilled among the Brahmin deities and caused the five hundred students to recite the Vedic mantras.
There were two young brahmins there who were friends and dear to one another: a young brahmin named Megha and a young brahmin named Meghadatta.
The young brahmin Megha was wise, steadfast, intelligent, and possessed of sharp discernment.
Not long after that, he had mastered all the mantras.
Having now completed his study of the Vedas, he descended from the Himalayas to the countryside, thinking, "I shall seek the teacher's fee for my preceptor."
Taking his staff, water-pot, parasol, sandals, and bathing-cloth, whichever village, city,
or town boundary he enters becomes free from calamity and free from affliction through the power of the young brahmin Megha’s element of fire.
The traveler addressed the man.
Thus, five hundred purāṇas were given by him.
Then this thought occurred to him:
"What if I were now to go to the royal capital of Dīpavatī, the city of the universal monarch made of the seven precious gems, so that I might behold it in its delightful splendor?"
Having now entered the royal capital Dīpavatī, he beheld the royal capital Dīpavatī adorned.
This thought occurred to him:
What is this? Is there today in the capital city of Dīpavatī a festival, a performance, or a celebration?
Then King Arcimat heard that the young brahmin Megha, having completed his studies of the Vedas, had descended from the Himalayas into the countryside and would come to the royal capital of Dīpavatī;
therefore, he said, "Let this excellent city be adorned."
Whosoever among the people enters that city goes pure, and he asks someone there.
There, another young woman—gracious, beautiful to behold, not fickle, not arrogant, and not impudent—was going along carrying a water-jar and seven lotuses.
She was questioned by him.
Today there is a festival in the city.
Then the young woman Prakṛti addressed the young man Megha with these verses:
But you are no young man, O youth; you have come here from another city, you who do not recognize that the Benefactor of the World, the Light-maker, has arrived at Dīpavatī.
Dīpaṃkara, the leader of the world, the son of Arcimat, the one of great fame—the Buddha will enter the city; for his sake, the city has been adorned.
She was questioned by him.
"How did you buy these blue lotuses?"
She said to him:
For five hundred purāṇas, five lotuses were purchased; two of them were obtained by me for Maitra.
The young brahmin Megha said:
"I will give you five hundred purāṇas; give me those five blue lotuses. With these five blue lotuses, I shall worship the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara;
you, indeed, may worship with two."
She said:
"On this condition, I shall give you these five lotuses:
if you take me as your wife, wherever you may be reborn, I shall be your wife and you shall be my husband."
The young brahmin Megha said:
I shall generate the mind set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; how shall I generate the mind toward union?
She said:
Give birth; I will not create any obstacle for you.
It was accepted by that young brahmin, Megha.
I take your wife for the sake of those lotuses.
I shall worship the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara and generate the mind set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Having given five hundred purāṇas, he took five lotuses, and a sublime joy and gladness arose in his body upon hearing the word "Buddha" from the young woman Prakṛti.
If you wish to worship the Leader of the World with delightful lotus garlands,
take me as your wife this very day.
I shall always be devoted with love.
Just as the flower of the udumbara tree is rare and only occasionally appears in the world, O young man,
so too is it with the Buddhas of great renown.
Sometimes there is the arising of Tathāgatas.
Worship the Buddha, the charioteer who tames men,
with delightful lotus garlands;
this shall become the cause for your awakening.
And I shall be your wife there, in each and every place.
Megha said:
Today I take your beautiful wife for the sake of the water-born flowers;
I shall worship the Buddha, the charioteer who tames men.
It will become the cause for my awakening.
She became joyful and gave him lotuses,
knowing him to be moved by affection and love; as he was departing, she followed him on his journey.
For the young man was indeed situated at the crossroads.

The Blessed One, surrounded by eighty thousand monks, set out for the royal capital of Dīpavatī together with King Arcimat, eighty thousand minor kings, many thousands of great Kṣatriya householders, and various ascetics, brahmins, and followers of other sects.
At the time of the Blessed One’s departure, thousands of deities assembled,
taking with them thousands of parasols made of the seven precious gems.
Then he, the possessor of great virtues, set out at the head of the excellent assembly;
he moved with the gait of an elephant in rut, his body overspread with a network of rays.
The sons of the gods hold up parasols for the Pure God, with handles well-fashioned from beryl, crystal, and solid gold.
Created by the gods in the sky, resembling the orb of the young sun,
they were beautiful with golden bells and produced excellent, joyful sounds.
And the King of the Thirty-three held over him in this world a divine parasol made of the seven precious gems, adorned with celestial flowers, while he stood as the parasol-bearer for the World.
And they followed the Lord of Men, fanning him with a stainless, excellent yak-tail whisk that had a well-crafted handle of solid gold from the three-thousandfold world system.
The ground that was exceedingly high sank down, and even that which was low became level as the Blessed One entered, through the majestic power of the Ten Powers.
Immediately thereafter, the Blessed One withdrew his right foot, which was like a golden lotus, from the threshold; at that moment, a wondrous sound arose.
Kettledrums, clay drums, and tabors resounded without being struck;
conchs, cymbals, and flutes played as he, the best of men, entered.
Whatever jewels were deposited in the city, contained within chests and caskets,
they too jingled as the Knower of the Best Jewels entered.
Then they spread out pairs of soft, costly garments on the road for the Blessed One—
various kinds of Kāśī silk and dukūla cloth dyed in many colors.

The Leader of the World was adorned with Kośikāraka linen, cotton, Kācilindika cloth, antelope skins, and woven rugs; with garments from Vanarusta, Tamakūṭa, Ātapakoṭṭavaka, and Subhūmi; and with wool from Toṣala and Kolama, as well as fresh and dyed red silk of five kinds.
From the eastern garden as far as the king's inner apartments,
the royal road shone, strewn with hundreds of thousands of fine cloths.
Then the women, having entered the grove, showered the lion among men;
taking handfuls of flowers, they scattered them over him who resembled a mountain of gold.
In whatever manner the Greatly Powerful One, the Compassionate One, approaches Dīpavatī,
in that same manner do your glorious ones release a shower of flowers.
And those fragrant flowers of five colors, released from his hands,
formed a floral mantle for the Blessed One, the Protector of the World.
In the path of the sky, which is without support, there are fragrant inner thorns;
stand firm and scatter these flowers in circumambulation, moving clockwise.

When he moves in circumambulation, they follow; when the Light of the World stands still, they stand. They do not abandon the deportment of the one possessed of supernormal power, the Conqueror of All.
Even if the winds of universal destruction were to blow across this triple-thousandfold world system, they could not disturb it; how much less could they carry away that flower-garment?
Having seen the Blessed One, who resembles gold, the most excellent gold, with a complexion like the finest sugarcane, the hosts of gods in heaven then exclaimed: "Aho! The Dharma!"
The sky was strewn with scattered flowers, and floods of blossoms covered the earth;
the flowers shone knee-deep, and a floral mantle hung in the air.
The sounds of "Hikka," mingled with the music of instruments, resounded everywhere; "Aho! Dharma!
they cried out as the Bull among Men entered the excellent city.
In Dīpavatī, the sweet voices of swans, kalaviṅkas, peacocks, and cuckoos, along with the humming of bees,
are heard mingled with the sounds of the treasures and jewels.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the young brahmin Megha saw the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara coming from afar,
endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, his body adorned with the eighty minor characteristics,
possessed of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, powerful with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and [endowed] with the four [assurances].
Endowed with the grounds of self-confidence,

like an elephant who has performed his task, he stands with his faculties turned inward and his mind not wandering outward; having attained the state of the Dharma, with tranquil faculties and a tranquil mind, he has reached the supreme perfection of self-mastery and tranquility— a guarded elephant, with senses conquered, like a lake.
It was clear, unclouded, serene, pleasing, beautiful to behold, delightful, not disagreeable to look upon, illuminating for a distance of a league with its radiance.
And having seen it, moreover, the perception of non-duality arose in him.
I too shall become a Buddha in the world.
Then, Maudgalyāyana, at that time the young brahmin Megha spoke this verse:
After a long time, the eye has arisen in the world; after a long time, the Tathāgatas have appeared;
after a long time, my vow has been fulfilled.
"I shall become a Buddha; of this I have no doubt."

Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the young brahmin Megha, having generated a sublime sense of rapture and agitation, as well as sublime joy and gladness, threw those five lotuses toward the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara.
They remained there, surrounding the orb of his face with a network of light.
The young woman Prakṛti also threw those two blue lotuses,
and they too remained suspended in the air.
The Buddha Bhagavāns discipline sentient beings by means of three miracles: the miracle of supernatural power, the miracle of mind-reading, and the miracle of instruction.

The canopy of flowers over the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara— consisting of those five lotuses thrown by the young brahmin Megha, those thrown by the young woman Prakṛti, and those thrown by other people— was sustained by his supernatural power for the sake of training sentient beings; it was beautiful and lovely to behold, intended to produce joy and gladness in the young brahmin Megha.
It had four pillars, four doors, and was adorned with hanging bundles of cloth-festoons.
When Megha saw those lotuses standing all around above the Blessed One’s halo, beautiful and inspiring confidence, joy and rapture arose in his body, and a noble intention manifested.

Having set aside his water-pot in a secluded spot and spread out his deerskin, he prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara and, while stroking the soles of the feet with his hair, formed this thought:

"O, may I too in a future time become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, just as this Blessed One Dīpaṃkara is now."

May I likewise be endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man, my body adorned with the eighty secondary characteristics; may I be endowed with the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, powerful with the ten powers of a Tathāgata,
and perfectly confident with the four grounds of self-confidence— just as this Blessed One Dīpaṃkara is now.
And may I thus set in motion the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, just as this Blessed One Dīpaṃkara does now.
In this way, I would maintain the entire community of disciples.
And thus gods and humans would think that this is worth hearing and worth having faith in;
thus, having crossed over myself, may I help others cross; being liberated, may I liberate others; being comforted, may I comfort others—just as the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara does now.
May I exist for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, benefit, and happiness of the great multitude of beings, both gods and humans.

Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara, having known through his unsurpassed Buddha-knowledge the great attainment of the young brahmin Megha, and having known his accumulation of roots of merit and his mental vow, prophesied his unsurpassed perfect enlightenment— [an enlightenment] that is unbroken, flawless, unblemished, and without blemish.

"Young man, in a future time, after an immeasurable and incalculable eon, in the city of Kapilavastu among the Śākyas, you will become a Tathāgata named Śākyamuni— an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans— just as I am now."

Now, he is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, his body adorned by the eighty minor characteristics, possessed of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, strong with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and perfectly confident through the four grounds of self-confidence.

Thus, having crossed over, you will cause others to cross; being liberated, you will liberate others; being comforted, you will comfort others; having attained final nirvāṇa, you will lead others to final nirvāṇa, just as I do now.
And in this way, you will set in motion the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma; and in this way, you will guide a harmonious community of disciples.
And thus gods and humans will think that this is worth hearing and worth having faith in,

just as I do now: "You shall become [a Buddha] for the benefit of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, benefit, and happiness of the great mass of beings, both gods and humans."

And immediately after he was thus prophesied by the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara for unexcelled perfect enlightenment, Māṇava Megha rose into the air to the height of a palm tree, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, joined his palms in reverence,
and paid homage to the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara and the community of his disciples.
And at that very moment, at that very instant, this great earth shook and trembled violently in six ways;
and from the earth, the gods raised a cry and made their voices heard.

Thus was the young brahmin Megha prophesied by the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; this will be for the benefit of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, benefit, and happiness of a great multitude of beings, both gods and humans.
Having heard the cry of the gods of the earth, the gods who move through the intermediate space— the Cāturmahārājika gods, the Trāyastriṃśa gods,
the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods— at that very moment, at that very instant, the cry rose up as far as the Brahmakāya realm.

"In this way, friends, the young brahmin Megha has been prophesied by the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; he will exist for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, benefit, and happiness of the great multitude of beings, both gods and humans."
And there was the manifestation in the world of an immeasurable, vast, and great radiance.

Even those intermediate spaces between worlds— which are dark, shrouded in darkness, gloomy, enveloped in gloom, wretched, and where such things have never occurred before, where even these suns and moons, so powerful and majestic, cannot reach with their radiance nor pervade with their light— even those were suffused by that illumination.
And those beings who were reborn there also recognized one another.
"Indeed, sirs, other beings too have been reborn here; indeed, sirs, other beings too have been reborn here."
At that very moment, at that very instant, all sentient beings became endowed with absolute happiness—
even those reborn in the great Avīci hell surpassed the splendor of the gods, the splendor of the nāgas, and the splendor of the yakṣas.
And the palaces of Māra became darkened, lusterless, devoid of brilliance, and unpleasant;
even fragments of them a *krośa* in size fell down,
and even fragments of them two *krośas* in size fell down.
Fragments of it fell measuring three krośas;
fragments of it fell measuring one yojana;
even the tips of its banners fell.
And Māra the Evil One became sorrowful, dejected, full of remorse, and consumed by the burning sting within.
Having spread out his deerskin and set down his water-pot to one side,
he cast a handful of blue lotuses and fell at the feet of the Visionary One.
And those fragrant flowers of five colors, released from his hand,
formed a floral mantle for the Blessed One, the Protector of the World.
In the path of the sky, which is without support, fragrant flowers with inward-pointing thorns remained,
having been placed to the right for the purpose of circumambulation.
When the Light of the World walks, they walk; when he stands, they stand;
they do not abandon the deportment of the one possessed of supernormal powers, the conqueror of all.
Even if the winds of universal destruction were to blow across these three thousandfold worlds, they could not disturb it; yet when those winds blew, that flower-robe was carried along.
Then, having seen the Blessed One— who resembles gold, who is the most excellent gold, and whose complexion is like that of the finest sugarcane—
the hosts of gods in heaven exclaimed: "O, the Dharma!"
Then, when the prophecy had been delivered, the earth with its oceanic garment trembled, and in the heavens among the hosts of gods, a marvelous sound arose.
This Megha was prophesied by the Sage Dīpaṃkara, who raised the banner of exclusively well-spoken words: "You shall become a Jina."
You will act for the benefit and happiness of the world, including its Brahmās, gods, and asuras;
the lower realms and hells will diminish, while the heavens will increase.
An incalculable eon ago from now, there was a Teacher named Dīpaṃkara, who was an island, a refuge, and a final resort.
The Blessed One, the Lord of Men, has well-expounded the Dharma.
Having realized the supreme goal, the wise one fearlessly set in motion the wheel of Dharma;
mindful and established in truth and the Dharma.
Rescue the people from great fear and from adversity.
Megha beheld the leader of the host of ascetics, Dīpaṃkara, who possessed the most wonderful marks;
having purified his mind toward the Jina, he paid him homage.
Thus, while paying homage, he made this aspiration.
Thus may I wander through this world just as he wanders with an unattached mind;
may I set in motion the wheel that is peerless and without equal.
Well-refined, it is honored by gods and humans.
I shall act for the benefit of the world; I shall teach the Dharma to gods and humans.
Thus I shall discipline sentient beings, just as this Light of the World does.
And having known his vow, which is joined with non-attachment and established through all causes— the Jina [knows it] to be unbroken, flawless, stainless, and without blemish.
The wise one, who perceives the true meaning, gave a prophecy.
"You, young man Megha, shall become a Buddha in the future, after immeasurable eons;
you, a Śākyan, in the hermitage of the sages at the place called Kapila."
Then you too shall attain the fruition of your vow.
He sent another five hundred purāṇas to the teacher.
Having delivered all such things, he informed Meghadatta.
Thus was the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara honored by me, and he granted me the prophecy of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
"Let us then go into the presence of the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara; there we shall practice the holy life and experience that assembly."
He said:
Since I have not yet completed my study of the Vedas, I am unable to go there.
Just as a piece of wood is carried away in the great ocean of water and perishes upon colliding with another, so too is the meeting with loved ones.
Megha went into the presence of the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara and went forth as a monk.

Having approached such spiritual friends, having propitiated and honored immeasurable and incalculable thousands of millions of Buddhas along with their assemblies of disciples, and having honored immeasurable trillions of Pratyekabuddhas, they experience divine and human prosperity until they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
He who, having heard that form is the charioteer of men to be tamed, would neither go to form nor to grasping, nor to me, nor to what is grasped.
But he said this:
This cloud is exceedingly inclined toward bowing its head.
Having heard the word "Buddha" from the young brahmin Megha, he was not joyful;
due to his association with evil friends, he committed the five deeds of immediate retribution.
Addicted to another's wife, he goes there at either the proper time or the improper time.
His mother, out of affection for her son, tried to dissuade him, thinking, "Lest they kill him there, taking him for an adulterer."
One who is passionate does not know the goal; one who is passionate does not see the Dharma.
When passion overcomes a person, he then exists in darkness.
Having had his mother killed, he went to the woman with whom he was infatuated and explained the whole matter to her.
Thus you are dear to me, for it was on your account that I deprived my mother of life.
That woman became agitated.
She said to him:
Do not come to me again.
He was attached to another mother.
Then that stepmother said to her:
"Come, deprive my father of life, and you shall be my master."
By him, his father was now deprived of life.
Thus, he became loathsome in that place.
Friends and kinsmen avoid them.
Then, having moved from that location to another location, he thought: "No one here will know of me."
A certain monk who had been a family attendant to his parents—a noble one of great spiritual power—while wandering on a journey through the countryside, arrived at that very residence.
Then, that son of a donor was seen by the monk there in that location.
Seeing that monk, he also became suspicious, thinking, "May this monk not defile this place of mine."
By him, that arhat monk was now deprived of life.
Now, he has gone forth in the teaching of him who was then the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Having now gone forth into that teaching, he caused a schism in the Saṃgha and drew the blood of the Buddha.
Having committed these five actions of immediate retribution, he was reborn in the great hells.

Having thus run and wandered for a very long time through the eight great hells and their sixteen secondary hells, when the Blessed One Śākyamuni had awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and set the wheel of Dharma in motion, he was born as a species of fish named Timitimiṅgila in the great ocean, with a body many hundreds of yojanas in length.

When the householder Sthapakarṇi, with five hundred followers and his ship, had entered the great ocean, then that [creature] who had become a makara, being hungry and seeking food, opened its mouth wide; thereupon the ships belonging to the householder Sthapakarṇi rushed toward where that makara’s mouth was.
Niryātamukha said:
"Householder, these ships have fallen into the mouth of the submarine fire; now do whatever must be done, for there is no life left for you."
Then they paid homage to their respective deities:

some to Śiva, some to Vaiśravaṇa, some to Skanda, some to Varuṇa, some to Yama, some to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, some to Virūḍhaka, some to Virūpākṣa, some to Indra, some to Brahmā, and some to the deities of the ocean.
When the venerable Pūrṇaka directed his attention, he saw that the householder Sthaparakarṇika, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred, was seized by doubt.
Having risen into the air from Mount Tuṇḍaturika, he stood suspended in the sky above the ship of Thapakarṇika upon the great ocean.
All those five hundred merchants, having joined their palms and stood up, said: "Blessed One, Blessed One, we have gone for refuge to you."
The Elder said:
"I am not the Blessed One; I am his disciple."
All of you, with one voice, utter "Homage to the Buddha!"
All those five hundred merchants cried out, "Homage to the Buddha!"
The sound of the word "Buddha" reached the range of that *timitimiṅgila*'s ears.

Having heard that sound of his, the sound of the name of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara— which he had previously heard from the young brahmin Megha during an immeasurable and incalculable eon— became manifest to him as he had become a *timitimiṅgila* fish in the great ocean.
"The word 'Buddha' is not in vain."
Then this thought occurred to that being Timitimiṅgila:
The Buddha has appeared in the world, yet we have fallen into the states of woe.
Then, being deeply moved, he closed his mouth once again.

Having died without food while recollecting that sound of "Buddha," immediately upon his death, he was reborn in a brahmin family in the great city of Śrāvastī; at that time and on that occasion, a young boy was born.
As it was said by the Blessed One: "O monks, I do not speak of anything other than karma."
Then, the name Dharmaruci was given to that boy.
When he had grown up, he then went forth into homelessness in the teaching of the Blessed One.
By applying himself, striving, and exerting effort, he realized the three knowledges, the six superknowledges, and mastery over the powers.
Three times a day he approaches to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One.
To whatever extent he approaches, to that extent the Blessed One exhorts and reminds him: "After a long time, Dharmaruci; after a very long time, Dharmaruci!"
He too said:
"So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata.
It has been long, Blessed One; it has been very long, Sugata."
The bhikṣus, with doubt, questioned the Blessed One.

Three times a day Dharmaruci approached the Blessed One, and the Blessed One said to him, "After a long time, Dharmaruci! After a very long time, Dharmaruci! He replied to the Blessed One, "So it is, Blessed One;
so it is, Sugata. It has been a long time, Blessed One; it has been a very long time, Sugata. Yet, Blessed One, we [have not known] this..."
We understand the meaning of what has been spoken.
The Blessed One related this matter in detail to those monks, beginning from the time of Dīpaṃkara.
I was the young brahmin named Megha, and this Dharmaruci was Meghadatta.
Thus, monks, the sound of "Buddha" is not in vain; it leads even to the destruction of suffering.
At that time, the Elder Dharmaruci approached the Teacher;
he bowed at the feet of the Jina and said, "It has been a very long time, Dharmaruci."
After a very long time, Dharmaruci addresses the Teacher, the Leader of the World:
"Knowing [the answer], why does the Jina ask, 'Why have you come after so long?'"
He spoke again: "Formerly, I was a *timitimiṅgila* fish in the salt ocean; overcome by the weakness of hunger, I was searching everywhere for food."
At that time, many millions of living beings entered my physical body;
likewise, five hundred merchants also entered by means of their vehicle.

And as the bowl was being brought in, all those who were afflicted by the fear of being unprotected, having fallen into calamity, spoke with one voice: "Homage to the Buddha, the One Endowed with the Ten Powers!"
Having heard the sound "Buddha," which I had never heard before, I became joyful;
thrilled and elated in heart, I quickly closed my eyes.
Tens of millions of beings in the animal realm and hundreds of merchants heard the voice of the One Possessed of Ten Powers; at that time, I arose from the miserable states.
"By that merit, O Blessed One, this human state has been attained by me;
through the fruit of that well-practiced conduct, my name is Dharmaruci."
For that very reason, O Self-Existent One, I went forth into homelessness in your teaching;
not long after going forth, I became an Arhat, one whose defilements were shaken off.
Having wandered through endless saṃsāra for many billions of kalpas, I now call to mind the Sugata, saying: "After a very long time, the Benefactor of the World has appeared!"

After a very long time, the eye of Dharma has been purified; the doubt regarding the Dharma, which was shrouded by the darkness of delusion, has been severed; and I have dwelt for a long time in the states of woe.
By that merit, the cataract was removed and passion and hatred were uprooted;
the rivers of the stream of existence have been dried up without remainder—this is my final birth here.
Even for this Timitimiṅgila, hearing the Buddha brought great fruit;
how much more, O Blessed One, would hearing this now bring the deathless?
Therefore, having abandoned the five hindrances that obstruct the mind,
one should listen to the word of the Buddha, conceiving the thought that it is difficult to encounter.
Difficult is the attainment of human birth and the avoidance of the forest of insubstantial forms; rare is the appearance of Buddhas, and rare too is faith and the state of nirvāṇa.
Thus ends the *Dīpaṃkaravastu* in the glorious *Mahāvastu-Avadāna*.
From this *Bhadrakalpa*, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, after an immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite number of eons following Dīpaṃkara, there appeared a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha named Maṅgala.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, during the time of that Samyaksambuddha Maṅgala, the lifespan of human beings was one hundred thousand million years.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the perfectly enlightened Buddha Maṅgala had three assemblies of disciples.

In the first assembly of disciples, there were one hundred thousand times ten million [arhats]— all of them arhats whose taints were exhausted, who had lived the holy life, whose minds were well-liberated through right knowledge, whose fetters of existence were completely destroyed, and who had attained their own goal. In the second assembly of disciples, there were ninety times ten million [arhats]— all of them arhats whose taints were exhausted, who had lived the holy life, whose minds were well-liberated through right knowledge, and whose fetters of existence were completely destroyed.
For those who had attained their own goal,

there was a third assembly of disciples consisting of eighty koṭis; all were arhats, whose taints were exhausted, who had lived the holy life, whose minds were well-liberated through right knowledge, whose fetters of existence were completely destroyed,
and who had attained their own goal.

Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Perfectly Enlightened One Maṅgala had a pair of disciples named Sudeva and Dharmadeva; they were a supreme pair, an auspicious pair—one was foremost in wisdom, and the other was foremost in supernormal powers.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the perfectly enlightened Buddha Maṅgala had two chief female disciples: a nun named Śīvālī and Aśokā;
one was foremost in wisdom and the other in supernormal power.
Now, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Perfectly Awakened One Maṅgala had a monk named Pālita who served as his attendant.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Bodhi tree of the Perfectly Enlightened One Maṅgala was a Nāga tree.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the city of the Perfectly Enlightened One Maṅgala was indeed named Uttara;
it was twelve yojanas in length from east to west and seven yojanas in width from south to north.
It was surrounded by seven walls made of gold with golden roofs.
It was surrounded by seven long ponds, variegated and beautiful to behold, made of the seven precious substances: gold, silver, pearl, beryl, crystal, emerald, and ruby.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, those long ponds had stairways of two kinds: gold and silver;
and the steps of the stairways were of four kinds: gold, silver, pearl, and beryl.
Those long ponds were covered with blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water lilies, white lotuses, nalini-lotuses, and fragrant saugandhika-lotuses.
Those long ponds were shaded by such trees as these, namely:
shaded by mango, rose-apple, breadfruit, lakucha, bhavya, and pālevata trees.
Furthermore, on the banks of those long ponds, there were such terrestrial and aquatic garlands as these:
namely, *atimuktaka*, *campaka*, *vārṣika*, *vātuṣkāra*, *indīvara*, *damanaka*, and those brought from the gods.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the city of Uttara was indeed surrounded by seven rows of palm trees.
The royal capital Dīpavatī should be described in detail as follows.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the father of the Perfectly Awakened One Maṅgala was a kṣatriya named Sundara, a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the mother of the Perfectly Enlightened One Maṅgala was a queen named Śrī.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, I was a dragon king named Atula, one who had performed meritorious deeds, possessed great majesty, and had accumulated a vast store of wholesome roots.

Then I honored, revered, respected, and worshiped that Blessed One Maṅgala together with his community of disciples; having offered him a pair of fine cloth garments as a covering, I made a vow for enlightenment.
By him also I was prophesied: "In a future time, after immeasurable and incalculable eons, you shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni."
To the north of Dīpaṃkara, there will be a leader named Maṅgala;
having destroyed the darkness in the world, he shall kindle the torch of the Dharma.
His splendor was incomparable, surpassing that of other Jinas;
eclipsing the radiance of ten million suns, he shone with a thousand rays.
And that Buddha proclaimed the four supreme truths; having drunk that essence of truth, they dispelled the great darkness.
Having awakened to incomparable enlightenment, at his first teaching of the Dharma, there was the initial realization of hundreds of thousands of millions of gods.
When...
[the time had come], then the Perfectly Awakened One struck the excellent, supreme drum of the Dharma.
Furthermore, when he revealed the Truths at the time of the gods,
there was a second realization involving ninety billion beings.
When Sunanda became a universal monarch and approached the Buddha’s Dharma,
then the Perfectly Awakened One struck the supreme, most excellent drum of the Dharma.
The multitude of followers of Sunanda numbered ninety koṭis;
all of them, without exception, became disciples of the Buddha.
Furthermore, at the time of the gods, when he revealed the Truths, there was a third realization of eighty koṭis; this was the third assembly.
When the householder Uttara approached to behold the Buddha,
then the Perfectly Awakened One struck the supreme, most excellent drum of the Dharma.
There were eighty koṭis of followers who followed after him;
all of them, without exception, became disciples of the Buddha.
There were three assemblies of the great seer Maṅgala—
those whose taints were exhausted, who were free from passion, whose minds were peaceful, and who were disciplined.
The first assembly consisted of one hundred thousand times ten million;
the second was ninety crores, and the third was eighty.
At that time, I was a nāga king of great supernatural power, named Atula, so called because of my abundant accumulation of merit.
With divine musical instruments, the nāgas honored the great seer Maṅgala;
having offered him garments, they went to him for refuge.
Thus the Buddha Maṅgala, the leader of the world, prophesied to me:
"After immeasurable eons from now, you shall become a Buddha in the world, in the delightful and prosperous city of the Śākyas called Kapilavastu."
Your mother shall be named Māyā;
your father, Gautama, shall be named Śuddhodana.
Kolita and Upatiṣya shall be the foremost among the male disciples;
Kṣemā and Utpalavarṇā shall be the foremost among the female disciples.
One named Ānanda shall be your attendant; the Bodhi tree under which you shall attain enlightenment will be the noble Aśvattha tree.
Having heard that prophecy from the great seer Maṅgala,
and having exerted my vigor and made my mind firm,
I shall practice the conduct of awakening and never abandon anyone.
The city was named Uttara; the Kṣatriya father was named Sundara;
and the mother of the great seer Maṅgala was named Śirikā.
Sudeva and Dharmadeva were the foremost male disciples;
Śīvālī and Aśokā were the foremost female disciples.
The attendant of the great seer Maṅgala was named Pālita;
his Bodhi tree was a Nāga tree, and that Bodhi tree was in full bloom.
The assembly of that great seer numbered hundreds of thousands of millions;
while remaining present, the Great Hero delivered many people.
Having caused the teaching to spread widely, he shall deliver many people,
like a blazing mass of fire or like the risen sun.
Just as the waves of the ocean cannot be counted,
even so the sons of the Blessed One cannot be counted.
That Blessed Buddha, the True Dharma, and the supreme Assembly—all have passed away one after another; indeed, all conditioned phenomena are now depleted.
Thus ends the narrative of Maṅgala in the glorious Mahāvastu-Avadāna. Now begins the narrative of the parasol.
On the slopes of the Himalayas, there dwells a yakṣiṇī named Kuṇḍalā.
Then she gave birth to five hundred sons at equal intervals;
having given birth to a thousand sons, she passed away.
They too were dispatched as vitality-seizers to Vaiśālī.
Having gone to Vaiśālī, they steal the vital energy of human beings.
There are two types of disease-epidemics: the *maṇḍalaka* and the *adhivāsa*.
The *maṇḍalaka* disease-epidemic, whichever family it falls upon, leaves nothing remaining; it carries everything away.
The *adhivāsa*, on the other hand, is the disease-epidemic that carries off only a specific region.
At that time, the people of Vaiśālī, afflicted by a prevailing epidemic, were dying.
They pay homage to the God of Gods.
This thought occurred to them:
Upon whose arrival, indeed, would the affliction of the people of Vaiśālī be pacified?
Then they sent a message to Pūraṇa Kāśyapa.
"Come! A non-human affliction has arisen among the people of Vaiśālī; upon your arrival, it will be pacified."
Kāśyapa Pūraṇa came to Vaiśālī, yet he did not alleviate that illness.
This thought occurred to them:
Kāśyapa has arrived, yet the non-human affliction of the people of Vaiśālī is not being pacified.
Then they sent [this] to Maskari Gośāliputra.
He too arrived, yet the non-human plague among the people of Vaiśālī was not alleviated.
Then they sent a message to Kakuda Kātyāyana.
He too arrived, yet the non-human affliction of the people of Vaiśālī was not alleviated.
Then they sent a message to Ajita Keśakambala.
He too arrived, yet the non-human affliction of the people of Vaiśālī was not alleviated.
Then they sent a message to Sañjayin Veraṭṭiputra.
He too arrived, yet the non-human affliction of the people of Vaiśālī was not alleviated.
Then they sent a message to the Nirgrantha Jñātiputra.
He too arrived, yet the non-human plague of the people of Vaiśālī was not alleviated.
Among those kinsmen and blood relations of the people of Vaiśālī, some who had passed away were reborn among the gods.
One of those deities informed the people of Vaiśālī.
"These who have been brought by you are not teachers, nor do they profess to be teachers; they are indeed not capable of bringing to an end the non-human affliction of the people of Vaiśālī."

This Buddha, the Blessed One, has fully realized awakening through incalculable eons; he is an Arhat, a perfectly awakened one, possessing knowledge and vision without remainder, endowed with great supernatural power and great majesty, omniscient and all-seeing.
In whatever village or field boundary he dwells, there all plagues, strife, clamor, calamities, and misfortunes are pacified.
"Bring him here;
once he has arrived, the non-human plague of the people of Vaiśālī will surely be pacified."
He dwells in Rājagṛha, the city of the palace, as delicate as the interior of a choice lotus;
by him, who has conquered the afflictions, all strife and quarrels have been stilled.

Wherever he goes— whether to a village, a market town, or a city— even if it is beset by calamities— he, who resembles gold, pacifies the plagues there, just as a powerful downpour of water settles the dust.
Bring him who is pale-colored yet resembles gold, whose beautiful face is like the full sun, and who possesses the fragrance of excellent and sweet morality; then the disease shall be pacified.
In Vaiśālī, there was a Licchavi chief named Tomara, who had a great faction, a large retinue, and was wise.
Thus, having been requested by the community, he was sent forth.
Go to Rājagṛha; there the Buddha, the Blessed One, resides.
He dwelt in a dwelling provided by Śreṇiya Bimbisāra.

Having gone there, speak words of greeting on behalf of the Licchavis of Vaiśālī; inquire after the health, the freedom from illness, the freedom from distress, and the state of dwelling in comfort of the Blessed One together with his retinue, and speak as follows:
"Lord, a non-human plague has arisen among the Licchavis of Vaiśālī, and many thousands of living beings are meeting with misfortune and ruin.
It would be well, O Blessed One, if you, who desire their welfare and seek their benefit, would come to Vaiśālī out of compassion."
Then Tomara, having given his promise to the Licchavi assembly, mounted auspicious vehicles together with a suitable retinue, departed from the city of Vaiśālī, and set out for the city of Rājagṛha.

Then Tomara the Licchavi, having gone to and entered the city of Rājagṛha, proceeded toward the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground, in order to see, approach, and attend upon the Blessed One.

Now at that time, on the fifteenth day of the month, during the Uposatha ceremony on the full moon, the Blessed One was teaching the Dharma— good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the correct meaning and phrasing, entirely complete and pure— to an assembly of five hundred monks and many thousands of other people.
He proclaims the holy life that is completely pure and utterly cleansed.
Then Tomara the Licchavi, having traveled by carriage as far as the ground would allow for a vehicle, alighted from the carriage and approached the Blessed One on foot.
Now, being unable to force his way through the great assembly that had gathered, he was not able to approach the Blessed One by force.
Then, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder and extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, he addressed the Blessed One in verse:
On the fifteenth day of the Upoṣadha for the sake of purification, those seers have assembled to observe the fast;
and Śakra, the god who is the lord of the Thirty-three, has also come.
Placed at their head, he endured what was otherwise unbearable.
Shining brightly, you proclaim the supreme state;
through the Dharma, you satisfy this vast multitude of beings, as a great cloud satisfies the earth with water.
Having heard these sweet words of yours, they...
O Great Sage, we who bear no enmity, having paid homage and saluted you with joined palms,
go to you for refuge— you who endure what is unbearable.
For them, it is well-gained and a true welcome.
I am near those who,
being full of faith, go for refuge and are then heedful in the teaching of the Sugata.
They will bring about the end of birth and death.
At the conclusion of the verse, a great multitude of people made way for him.
Then Tomara the Licchavi approached the Blessed One, bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet, and said this to the Blessed One:
"O Blessed One, the Licchavis of Vaiśālī— both the elders and the youths, those from within Vaiśālī and those from outside Vaiśālī—
bow their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and his community of disciples, inquire after his well-being and comfort, and speak as follows:"

"Lord, in Vaiśālī a non-human plague has arisen, and many thousands of living beings are meeting with misfortune and ruin; yet the Blessed One is compassionate and merciful toward the world including the devas."
"It would be well if the Blessed One would come to Vaiśālī, out of compassion for the people of Vaiśālī."
The Blessed One said:
The Tathāgata is staying at the residence requested by King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra; please grant him permission to depart.
Then Tomara the Licchavi, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and having circumambulated the Blessed One and the community of monks three times, departed toward Rājagṛha.
Then Tomara the Licchavi, having approached King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra and having greeted King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra most courteously and thoroughly,
said this to him:
"Great King, a non-human plague has arisen in Vaiśālī, and many thousands of living beings are meeting with misfortune and ruin."

There, the six teachers who were highly esteemed were brought together: Kāśyapa, Pūraṇa, Maskarī Gośālīputra, Ajita Keśakambalin, Kakuda Kātyāyana, Saṃjayin Vairaṭṭikaputra, and Nirgrantha Jñātiputra.
Even with these having arrived, the non-human affliction of the people of Vaiśālī was not pacified.
Then, O Great King, the deities informed the Licchavis.

This Buddha, the Blessed One, has indeed arisen through the power of incalculable qualities; he is the shelter, the protection, the refuge, and the final resort for the world including its gods— the god beyond gods, the teacher of gods and humans, and [the protector] of nāgas, asuras, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and kumbhāṇḍas.

Thus, wherever he enters the boundary of a village or field, there all calamities, strife, and misfortunes are pacified through the power of the Buddha, the power of the Dharma, and the power of the Saṅgha.
"Bring him here; for when he has arrived, the non-human plague of the people of Vaiśālī will be pacified."
"Excellent, Great King! Out of compassion, please grant the Blessed One permission to go to Vaiśālī."
Thus addressed, King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra said this to the Licchavi Tomara:

"Vāsiṣṭha, if the Licchavis of Vaiśālī should come out to meet the Blessed One as he travels from Rājagṛha to Vaiśālī as far as their own territory, just as I have escorted him as far as my own territory, then I shall request the Blessed One’s permission to proceed from Rājagṛha to Vaiśālī."
Then Tomara the Licchavi, having received word from King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra, dispatched messengers to the Vaiśālī assembly.
Thus, O Vāsiṣṭhas, King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra speaks.
Then those messengers, having given their word to the Licchavi Tomara, went to Vaiśālī and informed the Licchavi assembly.
Thus, O Vāsiṣṭhas, King Śreṇika Bimbisāra spoke to Tomara the Licchavi:

"If the Licchavis of Vaiśālī were to come out to meet the Blessed One as he travels from Rājagṛha to Vaiśālī as far as their own territory, just as I follow him as far as my own territory, then I would desire it."
I would have the Blessed One permit me to go from Rājagṛha to Vaiśālī.
When this had been said, the Licchavis of Vaiśālī [addressed] those messengers...
"O Vasiṣṭha, this should be said to King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra on behalf of the Licchavi assembly."
"O Great King, the Licchavis of Vaiśālī will go out to meet the Blessed One as far as the territory of the Licchavis."
Then those messengers, having given their assent to the Licchavi assembly, went to Rājagṛha and announced [the matter].
Then Tomara the Licchavi, having heard the words of the messengers, approached King Śreṇika Bimbisāra and said this to King Śreṇika Bimbisāra:
"O Great King, the Licchavis of Vaiśālī will go out to meet the Blessed One."
"Please, Blessed One, grant us permission to go to Vaiśālī out of compassion."

Now the Blessed One, having been granted permission by King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra to go to Vaiśālī, commanded his ministers: "From Rājagṛha as far as the Ganges ferry, prepare the road so that it is level like a chessboard, even, smooth as the palm of a hand, covered with canopies, draped with variegated cloth, hung with bundles of silk ribbons and garlands, and perfumed with incense."
"Have a bridge constructed, sprinkled and swept, strewn with loose flowers,
by which the Blessed One, together with the community of disciples, shall cross the Ganges on its way to Vaiśālī.
And at intervals of half a yojana, have pavilions prepared and provisions of food and drink made ready."

And he made all arrangements for the bedding and seating of the Blessed One together with the community of disciples, providing every comfort so that the Blessed One, along with the community of disciples and the assembly of monks, might travel easily from Rājagṛha to Vaiśālī.
"By means of the mind for the gods, by speech for kings,
by action for the wealthy, and by physical labor for the poor."
The king gave the command, and the ministers prepared everything exactly as ordered.
The Blessed One set out together with the community of monks.

King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra, accompanied by his chariots, army, and mounts, together with his queens, princes, ministers, and retinue, followed the Blessed One as he was proceeding toward Vaiśālī, with five hundred royal parasols being held aloft— adorned with hanging clusters of silk streamers and tassels, and equipped with flags and banners— displaying great royal majesty, great royal power, and great splendor.
With a resting place every half-yojana, he proceeded toward his own territory on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
The Licchavis of Vaiśālī heard that King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra was making a ceremonial procession for the Blessed One as he was coming from Rājagṛha to Vaiśālī.
And having heard this, they prepared the road from Vaiśālī as far as the Ganges Ferry— within that interval, the territory of the Licchavis of Vaiśālī—
leveling it like a checkerboard, making it even, smooth as the palm of a hand,
sprinkled and swept, strewn with loose flowers, covered with canopies, draped with variegated cloths, hung with bundles of silk ribbons and garlands, and perfumed with incense.
And from various regions, they stationed actors, dancers, athletes, wrestlers, and musicians;

and at intervals of half a *yojana*, they had pavilions constructed, as well as arrangements for beds and seats, arrangements for drinking water, and arrangements for food, for the Blessed One together with the community of his disciples.
From within Vaiśālī, eighty-four thousand chariots were yoked, and another eighty-four thousand chariots [were prepared].
Having caused [the chariots] to be yoked— adorned with victory banners, resounding with joyful cries, decorated with flower garlands, and equipped with parasols, standards, and flags—

and having taken abundant perfumes and garlands, they mounted their respective auspicious vehicles and proceeded with great royal majesty, great royal power, and amidst the clamor of a vast multitude of people shouting "Hakkā! and "Hikkā!", and the sound of kettledrums, clay drums, cymbals, small drums, and conch shells.
Departing from the city of Vaiśālī, they went out to meet the Blessed One as far as the Ganges ford in order to pay homage to the Blessed One.
For them also, such a form of arrangement came to pass.

There, there are Licchavis with blue horses, blue chariots, blue reins and whips, blue staves, blue garments, blue ornaments, blue turbans, and blue parasols; they possess blue swords, jewels, sandals, and yak-tail fans—this is what is said regarding them.
The horses are blue, the chariots are blue, and blue are the reins, the goad, and the turban;
the five crests are blue, as are the garments and ornaments.

There are Licchavis here who have yellow horses, yellow chariots, yellow reins, whips, and staves; they wear yellow garments, yellow ornaments, yellow turbans, and yellow parasols; their swords, jewels, and sandals are all yellow.
In this regard, the following is said:
The horses were yellow, the chariot was yellow, and yellow were the reins, the whip, and the turban;
the five crests were yellow, as were the garments and ornaments.
There are Licchavis here with crimson horses, crimson chariots, crimson whips and staves, crimson garments, crimson ornaments, crimson turbans, and crimson parasols;
they have crimson jewel-studded sandals and fly-whisks.
In this regard, the following is said:
Mañjiṣṭhā, horse-chariots, Mañjiṣṭha, reins, goads, and staffs; Mañjiṣṭha, the five humps, Mañjiṣṭha, garments and ornaments.

There are Licchavis here with red horses, red chariots, red whips and staves, red garments, red ornaments, red turbans, and red parasols; they have red swords, jewels, sandals, and yak-tail fans. Regarding this, it is said:
The horses are red and the chariots are red; the reins, whips, and staffs are red;
the five humps are red, as are the garments and ornaments.

There were Licchavis here with white horses, white chariots, white whips and staves, white garments, white ornaments, white turbans, white parasols, white swords, and white jewels, sandals, and yak-tail fans;
concerning this, it is said:
They have white horses, a white chariot, and white reins, whips, and staffs;
their five humps are white, as are their garments and ornaments.

There are Licchavis here whose horses are green, whose chariots are green, and whose reins, whips, and staffs are green; they wear green garments, green ornaments, green turbans, green parasols, and green swords; and their jewels, sandals, and yak-tail fans are green.
In this regard, it is said:
The horses are green, the chariot is green, and the reins, the goad, and the staff are green;
the five crests are green, as are the garments and ornaments.
There are Licchavis here whose horses are disheveled, whose chariots are disheveled, whose reins, whips, and staves are disheveled,

whose garments are disheveled, whose ornaments are disheveled, whose turbans are disheveled, whose parasols are disheveled, whose swords are disheveled, and whose jeweled sandals and fly-whisks are disheveled.
In this regard, it is said:
The horses and chariots were scattered; the reins, whips, and staves were scattered;
the five crests were scattered; and the garments and ornaments were scattered.
There are Licchavis here with golden parasols, riding upon elephants adorned with various ornaments.
There are Licchavis here in golden palanquins adorned with every kind of jewel.
There are Licchavis here with golden chariots, adorned with victory banners, making joyful sounds, with hooves like bells, and with parasols, flags, and pennants raised aloft.

With such power, by such means, with such an assembly, with such royal majesty, with such prosperity, and with such an array of ornaments as had come to pass, the Licchavis of Vaiśālī, along with Gośṛṅgī and Āmrapālikā, and that great multitude of people, set out in eighty-four thousand vehicles.
They went out to meet the Blessed One as far as the Ganges landing-place.
The Blessed One, on the further bank of the Ganges, having instructed, exhorted, and gladdened King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra and the Magadhan brahmins with a discourse on the Dharma,
established eighty-four thousand of those Magadhan brahmins in the realization of the Dharma, and [proceeded] toward where the Licchavis of Vaiśālī were.
Having looked around, he addressed the monks.
"Monks, you have never before seen the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven departing from the city of Sudarśana for the pleasure groves."
Behold now these Licchavis of Vaiśālī!
For what reason?
And by such miraculous power, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven depart from the city of Sudarśana to the pleasure groves.
Relatives who govern flourishing kingdoms do so by bringing them to peace;
likewise, these [Licchavis] abide amidst the Licchavis.
The Teacher made this analogy for the sake of the gods.
For those Trāyastriṃśa gods who had never before seen [this] as they were departing for the pleasure groves,
such was their assembly.
Just as this prosperity belongs to the Licchavis.
Some [came] with golden parasols and elephants,
others with palanquins made of gold,
and still others with chariots made of gold.
The Licchavis went out to meet him.
All gathered together with their kinsmen and relatives— the young, the middle-aged, and the elderly—
adorned and dressed in garments dyed with lac.
And they, moving with various gaits, went forth to meet him.

Now, on that Ganges River, King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra had a causeway for boats built; the inhabitants of the inner Vaiśālī had a causeway for boats built; the inhabitants of the outer Vaiśālī had a causeway for boats built; and the Nāgas of the Ganges, Kambala and Aśvatara, had a causeway for boats built.
"The Blessed One will cross over by means of our [raft]."
Śuka invited the Blessed One, together with the community of disciples, for a meal on the following day by means of Gośṛṅgī’s words; and the Blessed One consented to this by remaining silent.
By that silence of the Blessed One, the parrot understood his consent through the Buddha’s manner of being.
Having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and circumambulated the Blessed One and the community of monks, he returned.
Having approached the Blessed Lady Gośṛṅgī, he said:

The Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one, together with the community of disciples, was invited for a meal on the following day by your word; the Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
The Blessed One then ascended the boat-bridge.
King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra saw the Blessed One on his own bridge of boats.
And the Vaiśālakas from within [the city] beheld the Blessed One together with the community of disciples upon their own bridge of boats.
The Vaiśālakas from outside saw the Blessed One together with the community of disciples on their own bridge over the water.
