Kambala and Aśvatara, the great nāgas of the Gaṅgā, also beheld the Blessed One together with the community of disciples upon their own bridge-causeway.

As he was crossing over, having seen five hundred parasols belonging to King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra with those Kambala-Aśvatara Gāṅgeyakas, and having also seen five hundred parasols belonging to the people of Vaiśālī, they held up five hundred parasols for the Blessed One as he was crossing;
and the yakṣas also held up five hundred parasols.
The Four Great Kings also held up five hundred parasols;
the divine son Sunirmita likewise held up a parasol even more distinguished than those;
and the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, as well as the Four Great Kings, also held up five hundred parasols.
The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven also held up five hundred parasols;
Śakra, the lord of the gods, also held up a parasol;
and the divine son Suyāma also held up a parasol.
Five hundred parasols were held aloft by the Tuṣita gods;
the divine son Saṃtuṣita held up a parasol even more excellent than those.
Five hundred parasols were held aloft by the Brahmakāyika gods.
Mahābrahmā also held up a parasol even more distinguished than that;
and by the Śuddhāvāsa deities, five hundred parasols were held up for the Blessed One as he was crossing the Gaṅgā.
The divine son Maheśvara also held up a parasol for the Blessed One as he was crossing the Ganges.
By whom were all those thousands of parasols belonging to gods and humans eclipsed?
The kings who perform their daily duties and are descended from noble lineages deserve it;
and this illustrious bull among men truly deserves the royal parasol.
Those outsiders who, having conquered hosts of enemies, enjoy an unconquered kingdom and are endowed with all perfections— even those men deserve the parasol.
How much more so for him by whom all afflictions have been conquered everywhere without remainder?
Moreover, Namuci with his entire army has been defeated, yet the Blessed One is not one who requires even a hundred parasols.
Taking five hundred parasols with handles of vaidūrya gem, whose light flickers like stars and whose forms do not appear within the sky;
King Bimbisāra followed behind the One Possessing the Ten Powers;
and the Blessed One set out toward the Vajjis together with his retinue.
The Blessed One, having boarded the boat, has crossed over the flood of existence;
and on the further shore, the Licchavi hosts held up five hundred parasols.
Then the Nāgas, dwelling in the great mountain Mahāmahīdhara and possessing great strength, as well as those residing in the Gaṅgā, held up five hundred parasols for the Lord of the Earth.
Possessing supernatural powers and radiance, dwelling upon the paths of the earth and abiding in great strength,
even the Yakṣas and Asuras there, filled with joy, held up five hundred parasols.
With flower garlands and pearls falling away, their faces as beautiful as the full moon of the lord of stars,
even the gods there, filled with joy, held up five hundred parasols.
The four world-protectors as well, with joyful minds and free from intoxication and pride,
acting like stage-managers who clear away the dust, bore [the Buddha] who was equal to the upholder of the earth.
Then that lord of the thirty-three gods held over the head of the Conqueror a parasol made of a well-fashioned, excellent net of gold, jewels, and gems, and a well-fashioned garland of red flowers.
Having approached the Lord of the Yāmas, who is worshipped by Yama, Varuṇa, and the Nāgas, Vasuyāmā bore him—
who was as white as an autumnal water-cloud— moving with the speed of a dense wind.
Furthermore, the Lord of the Tuṣita abode, free from delusion, approached the Blessed One;
with a serene mind, he held a parasol, his body possessing a form as firm as a diamond.
Sunirmita held the parasol, which had a well-crafted handle of beryl, was variegated with a thousand prongs of coral,
and had its surface strewn with full-blown flowers.
The Paranirmitavaśavartin [deity] fashioned a parasol for Trailokyakīrti, covered with a load of excellent gold and adorned with hanging strings of jewel necklaces.
Brahmā, with a serene mind and a heart as pure as the wind-path,
held the moon-like parasol for the crusher of opposing disputants.
Furthermore, Maheśvara held the parasol— the secret of parasols— adorned with garlands made of divine flowers and consisting of the seven precious gems.
Thus this assembly of the realm of desire was convened by the Lord of the Gods;
it was a great gathering by Maheśvara for the sake of honoring the one who possesses incomparable power.
As many parasols as there were, so many Buddhas were manifested by the Blessed One.
They do not see the Blessed One one after another.
To each and every one of them, this thought occurred:
Under my very parasol stands the Protector; the Sugata stands; the Banner stands.
By the power of the Buddha, both gods and humans see as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
Then the Blessed One, the Moon among Men, manifested those Perfectly Awakened Ones through his supernatural power;
the Blessed One displayed them, yet they did not see one another.
But the Buddhas endowed with the ten powers, having gone to the Akaniṣṭha realm, [purify] the clear sky.
They shine in the expanse of the sky like a sacrificial pillar variegated with jewels.
All were golden-colored; all were endowed with the thirty-two marks;
all resembled mountains of gold; and all possessed the gait of a noble elephant.
All possess pleasing forms, and for all, a web of radiance shines;
all are bearers of immeasurable virtues, and all are generators of joy.
Having seen the expanse of the sky graced by those possessed of the ten powers, the gods and humans, filled with exceeding joy and rapture, raised a cry of "Hāhā! in celebration.
Filled with the clamor of clapping hands and shouts of joy, they advance;
remaining in the sky, they release a fragrant cloud of excellent powdered incense.

Having seen such a miraculous display of the Buddha’s supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) by the Blessed One, the gods paid great honor to the Blessed One with *māndārava*, *mahāmāndārava*, *karkārava*,
*mahākarkārava*, *rocamāna*, *mahārocamāna*, *bhīṣma*, *mahābhīṣma*, *samantagandha*, and *mahāsamantagandha* flowers.
With flowers from the Pāriyātraka tree— golden flowers, silver flowers, and white silver flowers— and with powders of sandalwood, agallochum, and saffron,
they scattered and showered them over the Blessed One from all sides for sixty yojanas; and a flood of divine fragrant powders arose, reaching up to the knees.
The monks said to the Blessed One:

"Lord, what is this? Is it the power of the gods, the power of the nāgas, or the power of the yakṣas, by which these thousands of parasols are now being held aloft by the gods, the nāgas, and the kings?"
The Blessed One said:
Monks, this is the power of the Tathāgata’s ancient wholesome qualities.
If the Tathāgata had not awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, then as he wandered through saṃsāra, he would have exercised as many reigns as universal monarchs as there are these parasols.
And yet, furthermore, the Tathāgata’s final nirvāṇa will occur through the exhaustion of all merit and demerit.
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Vagīśa.
May the former life of the Tathāgata be revealed to you, O Lord of Speech.
"Very well, Blessed One," the venerable Vāgīśa replied to the Blessed One, and at that moment he spoke this verse:
In the past, there was a teacher, a brahmin free from all fear;
having abandoned rebirth, that brahmin was perfected in the holy life.
Having seen sentient beings suffering, afflicted by the nature of suffering,
you turned the wheel of Dharma and produced unsurpassed light.
Having set in motion the wheel of Dharma and having produced unsurpassed radiance, the Perfectly Awakened One, the Great Seer whose rebirth is exhausted, shall pass into final nirvana.
His disciples, who were fearless from any quarter— both those still in training and those who were supreme and self-controlled— erected a stūpa for him as a cause for his renown.
The kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, and vaiśyas performed worship for the great seer,
accompanied by dance, instrumental music, and song, and gathered with various garlands.
The brahmin, the wise father of the Buddha, also reflected:
"What if I were now to have a parasol made, fashioned from jewels, auspicious and bright white?"
Having placed a stainless parasol upon the stūpa that had been constructed,
the father, shedding tears, paid honor to his son.
Having performed that virtuous deed praised by the Buddha, the brahmin passed away; such is the natural law for all who are born.
Through that deed, for eighty cycles of dissolution and evolution, he did not encounter an unfortunate rebirth; this is the fruit of the parasol.
Then, among human beings, ruling the kingdom with righteousness,
he was a world-conquering universal monarch (cakravartin) of great power upon the earth.
O Kṣatriyā, the country was variegated and your retinue was vast;
you honored him alone, providing comfort by granting him the white parasol.
And having passed away from there as well, he was reborn among the gods;
he became the most excellent of the Maruts, honored by the hosts of deities.
Honored by the hosts of gods and established in the mantle of sovereignty, you dwell here even now; this is the fruit of that white parasol.
You were the highest among the gods, and you were the highest among humans;
everywhere you were the highest, both of gods and of men.
Having been the highest among the gods and the highest among humans,
and having abandoned even that state and come to this final existence,
you have become a perfectly awakened one, O Seer, whose rebirth is exhausted.
Thus, having directly known that path leading to the pacification of suffering—
the attainment of which brings an end to suffering— [he proceeds].
And regarding this, the Buddhas of the past and that heroic, powerful one—all possess equal virtue and wisdom; there is no difference between the Buddhas.
And those who are fully awakened from time to time— of this there is no doubt—
all of them go to a happy rebirth, reaping the fruits of their own actions.
There was a Brahmin who possessed sight, and I was his pupil;
urged by you, O Hero, I have come to recollect my former birth.
It was exactly so, as you have spoken, O Lord of Speech;
I was indeed a brahmin at that time, and you were my pupil.
Being thus exhorted by me, you shall remember your former birth;
therefore, one should cause a banner, a flag, and a white parasol to be made.
One should also construct a railing around the stupas to the extent of five finger-breadths;
thus, the donor attains excellent, vast, and wholesome merit.
This and whatever other worship is performed in honor of the Buddha—
all of it becomes fruitful, productive, and leads to the deathless.
Indeed, I do not see any worship in this world equal to it, much less superior;
yet, by worshipping another, you attain even greater merit.
Even if every deity in this world were always to honor me with all manner of jewels, it would not be a sufficient recompense for him.

Thus, those of great fame and great compassion, who act out of pity for the welfare of others, are indeed not easily seen; for the Perfectly Awakened Ones are as rare as the flower of the udumbara tree.

Furthermore, those who speak my praise on account of my concentration, ethical discipline, wisdom, realization, renunciation, application, birth, and true nature— being of great renown and having performed merit in various births— they become persons whose words are authoritative and who are celebrated by many people.
By that very root of merit having been planted,
their physical covering thereafter becomes one of little difficulty.
Therefore, one should perform meritorious deeds as an accumulation for the future life;
for in the world beyond, merit is the ultimate refuge for living beings.
The Blessed One had crossed the Ganges and stepped upon the boundary of Vaiśālī.
By the Blessed One, those non-human beings were put to flight.

As the Blessed One was proceeding, Māra the Evil One caused the entire road—which had been prepared by the Licchavis, sprinkled with water, swept clean, and strewn with loose flowers—to appear covered with living creatures; he did this by manifesting himself as a wandering mendicant named Kuṇḍala.
As the Blessed One was going along that path, he said to him: "Turn back."
The earth is covered with many living beings— minute, large, and middling;
when the Buddha walks upon that ground strewn with creatures, [he does so without harm].
From that, suffering arises when one is attacked.
The Blessed One said:
The touch of the Tathāgatas is as soft as that of a gentle breeze; for such is the nature of the supreme Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
Upon obtaining a body, death comes into being.
Free from fear or malice toward living beings, that Blessed One proceeds without obstruction to the grove of sacrificial offerings among all creatures.
The Blessed One created a verdant expanse of green grass.
The Blessed One sat down, as did the community of monks.
Those Licchavis questioned the Blessed One.
Whose house has been accepted by the Blessed One for tomorrow—the house of those from within Vaiśālī or those from outside Vaiśālī?
The Blessed One said:
For indeed, O Vāsiṣṭhas, the Tathāgata has not accepted the invitation of the Vaiśālīans from within, nor that of the Vaiśālīans from without.
A parrot capable of human speech was sent by Gośṛṅgī to the far bank of the Gaṅgā;
he invited the Tathāgata, together with the community of disciples, for a meal on the following day, in the name of Gośṛṅgī.
The Tathāgata consented.

Then those Licchavis, the inhabitants of internal Vaiśālī, eighty-four thousand kings, and the great multitude of people— including the great kṣatriya families and the great householder families— were filled with wonder, asking, "How does the parrot speak?"
The Blessed One said:
What is so wonderful about this? Śuka speaks with human speech to Gośṛṅgī; moreover, Vāsiṣṭha, there were others who, having become birds, administered kingdoms.

Long ago, Vāsiṣṭhas, in times past, in the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi, a king named Brahmadatta reigned. He was one who had performed meritorious deeds, was illustrious, possessed great strength, a vast treasury, and many mounts.
His kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and teeming with people; it was crowded with a great multitude of men.
And it was filled with happy people and men, where punishment and civil unrest were stilled, where thieves were well-restrained, and which was prosperous in its legal affairs.
His harem was extensive, yet he was childless.
The thought occurs to that king:
How might I have a son?
He hears [the report] from the ministers.
"In a hermitage in the Himalayas dwell sages of great power who possess the five superknowledges and have attained the four meditative absorptions; they should be asked how a son might be obtained."
Those sages of great power will explain how he shall become the son of a god.
Then the king, together with his harem, his princes, his ministers, and his army and vehicles, set out for the hermitage of those seers.
The king, together with his army, his vehicles, and his harem, arrived at a place to stay on the intermediate road.
There he saw three birds emerging from the hollow of a *sāmbali* tree: an owl, a myna, and a female parrot.
Then, having seen that, curiosity arose in the king.
He commanded a man: "Go and find out what is there in this hollow."
Having climbed up, he gazes intently and sees three eggs.
He said:
"O King, there are three eggs."
The king said:
Bind them individually in separate containers and bring them down so that they do not perish.
That man, having tied them separately in a bundle, brought them down unharmed.
The ministers are questioned.
"Whose eggs are these?"
The ministers said:
Indeed, these fowlers are questioned;
this is their domain here.
The fowlers were summoned.
The fowlers were questioned by the king.
The king said:
"O, tell me, do you know whose eggs these are?"
Those fowlers dwelling there were experts in the methods of all species of birds' eggs, and they were also experts regarding the birds themselves, knowing exactly what kind of bird each one was.
They said:
"Great King, these three eggs belong to an owl, a śārikā bird, and a parrot respectively."
The king said:
Are these eggs capable of hatching?
They said:
They have been brought down successfully, O Great King,
without being damaged.
The king asks.
What is the proper care for these eggs so that, being thus cared for, they may thrive and safely reach hatching?
The fowlers said:
"Your Majesty, the cotton should be spread out upon both supports."
There, these eggs, having been smeared with honey and ghee, should be placed; on top, a layer of crushed cotton should be laid down, and that will nourish them for the sake of their development.
Those eggs were deposited exactly as those fowlers had instructed.
The king arrived at that hermitage of the seers in due course.
Having stationed his army and mounts in a secluded place, he approached the hermitage of the seers together with his harem.
Seeing the king, the sages went out to meet him according to the customary conduct toward sages.
Welcome, Great King; you are most welcome, Great King. Please be seated, Great King, upon these seats.
The king, together with his harem, having bowed at the feet of the seers, sat down.
The most eminent among the sages, the patriarch of the clan.
Having exchanged greetings with that king, he asked him:
"Great King, what purpose do you have for yourself in seeking the presence of the seers?"
The king said:
I have a vast harem, yet I am childless; no one has a son for me. Please instruct me on how I may obtain a son.
The eldest of the seers said:
"Great King, those three eggs which were brought down from that hollow of the *śāmbalī* tree—have them incubated; from them your sons will be born."
The king was struck with wonder.

"Highly fortunate are these seers that they know of him whom those three eggs—brought forth from that hollow of the *śāmbalī* tree from such-and-such a place—are destined for while they dwell here in this hermitage."
These sages are highly fortunate.
Having prostrated at the feet of the sages, he set out once more for Vārāṇasī;
traveling by stages, he entered Vārāṇasī.
In due course of time, all three of those eggs were hatched.
From the first [egg] an owl chick was born, from the second a myna chick was born, and from the third a parrot chick was born.
By the king's command, they are brought up and nourished.
At that time, when they had all grown up, the three wise and intelligent ones engaged in conversation and discourse with one another using human speech and the language of men.
Then King Brahmadatta, having recognized their power of intellect, questioned each of them individually regarding the duties of a king.
And having known them, they give predictions.
Having heard the prophecy concerning all three of them, King Brahmadatta became filled with joy.
In Vārāṇasī there was a powerful king named Brahmadatta;
that king had three wise sons who were like birds.
The first was Kauśika, the second was Śārika, and the third was Śuka; all were of a wise nature.
Having ascertained their intellectual power, the king, the lord of men, was pleased;
he intended to question them all individually in private regarding the duties of kingship.
First I shall ask Kauśika; O Śakunta, may it be well with you.
Son, what do you consider to be the duty of one who governs a kingdom?
Kauśika said:
"Ah, after a long time indeed, my father asks me about the duties of kings!
Well then, I shall explain them to you; listen with a one-pointed mind."
One should not fall under the power of anger; rather, one should restrain that anger.
For neither profit nor dharma comes to one who is angry, O King.
For when a king is free from anger, O lord of men, his wealth and his dharma prevail;
wisdom triumphs everywhere, therefore one should restrain anger.
Then, when a dispute has arisen, he should remain impartial toward both sides;
having heard the statements of both, he should act in accordance with the Dharma.
O King, neither out of desire, nor hatred, nor fear, nor delusion,
but having heard the words of both parties, should one act in accordance with the Dharma.
That wise man does not suffer loss, O King, for he acts for the sake of his true interest; guarding his fame and renown, he seeks the heavenly realm.
Therefore, O King, having avoided unrighteousness, rule according to the duties of kings; O protector of the earth, by doing so you shall go there.
Do not indulge excessively in delightful sensual pleasures;
for when one is intoxicated by sensual desires, the enemy becomes all the more powerful.
Then he should follow all the customs of the city;
thereafter, he should follow the customs of the countryside in accordance with the Dharma.
He should sustain the realm of city-dwellers and country-folk with virtues,
by the granting of wealth and goods, and by the performance of their necessary tasks.
Then, one should win over the entire retinue by means of a gift; through the bestowal of wealth and goods, he shall become an inseparable man.
O King, you know all those who are devoted and all those who are disaffected—
among the vanguard of the army, the dependents, and the people of both the city and the countryside.
Having examined the affairs of state, he should grant rewards according to reality;
avoiding violence toward all, he should assign the fruits [of labor] in accordance with the Dharma.
O King, act in such a way that you establish the vast multitude of people who have come here, just as it was established by previous kings, and settle the kingdom accordingly.
O lord of men, always bestow favor upon the distressed and provide protection for the wealthy among those who dwell within your conquered realm.
A king who delights in gambling with wealth and is constantly devoted to the wives of others becomes disliked by his kingdom and quickly loses his life.
Furthermore, O dear one, the wise man who is free from greed and always abstains from the wives of others becomes beloved by the kingdom and lives for a very long time.
And do not form bonds of enmity with rival kings, O King;
for those who are enemies, O protector of the earth, hand over their enmity to other enemies.
And you should form alliances with neighboring kings, O King;
for kings who possess firm friendships honor their subjects.
O lord of men, in this month, you should utter mantras at the proper time, joined with reasons and causes, for the sake of all purposes, without skipping any part.
O King, always maintain the secret meaning and restrain it; for kings who disclose their counsel, O lord of kings, suffer many calamities.
By keeping a secret matter concealed, one obtains vast prosperity;
one does not fall under the power of enemies, nor does one later feel regret.
O Lord of Men, those people whose counsel is not deluded, whose speech is not scattered, and who are disciplined in matters of purpose,
do not provoke anger in their enemies.
Just as there are hundred-killers with jeweled horns.
The man who maintains a secret matter connected with wealth remains like a slave to him out of fear of the enemy’s treachery.
O King, you should always provide protection for those established in the Dharma;
for it is by relying on the wheel of power that the wheel of Dharma turns.
By the power of those established in the Dharma, all calamities are pacified;
by their agreement, the gods send rain, and there the crops flourish.
"O Great King, that which is done for those possessed of virtue results in benefit in this very life and happiness in future lives."
Therefore, O King, you should protect that [dharma] through righteousness;
for that is beneficial to you as a king and it is also beneficial to the kingdom.
For she is a prudent manager in all matters, O lord of men; therefore, be vigilant and provide for both the granary and the treasury.
This much is my meaningful instruction;
having grasped all of it, O King, act accordingly.
For you who practice in this way, fame and renown shall arise;
the kingdom will become secure, prosperous, flourishing, and densely populated.
Having heard the excellent words of Kauśika, which were consistent with both dharma and artha, I likewise ask Śārika: "Tell me of the duties of kings."
The young sarika bird said:
"Ah, after a long time indeed, my dear son, you ask me about the duties of kings.
Well then, I shall explain them to you; listen with a one-pointed mind."
But by two factors, my dear, this world is established:
the acquisition of what has not been gained, and the preservation of what has been acquired.
Therefore, O lord of men, for the sake of acquiring wealth and for the protection of what has been acquired, you should exert firm effort in accordance with the Dharma.
O Lord, that ruler of the earth who governs by unrighteousness finds his kingdom weak and riddled with vulnerabilities on all sides.
And that lord of the earth, O King, who rules according to the Dharma,
his kingdom becomes stable, prosperous, flourishing, and teeming with people.
Restrain those who should be restrained; uplift those worthy of being uplifted; gather those who should be gathered; and be one who delights in showing favor.
That lord of men who does not know how to restrain or to encourage, nor even how to gather or favor his subjects, falls away from his goals.
Do not treat as your masters even your sons, your brothers, or those who are brave, daring, or powerful— whether they be in the village or in the countryside.
O King, a ruler should show favor for the sake of his mother and father;
for heirs who have been insulted become enemies who are distraught.
Your kingdom may become divided into five realms, served by crooked enemies;
do not place your trust in them there, and do not set out upon a wrong path.
A kṣatriya who has set out on a wrong path and follows his passions falls under the power of his enemies and later regrets it.
O lord of men, weigh [the matter] for the sake of attaining strength for yourself, for the suppression of enemies,
and out of compassion for the kingdom.
Speak only after careful consideration, whether by night or by day; for there are eavesdroppers who stand nearby, and having heard you, they will act against you.
A hero is quickly turned back; a wealthy man gathers an army.
One who possesses wealth and the power of counsel can seize wealth from one who is angry, but you cannot.

Therefore, one should banish the Brahmin for the sake of the [king's] interest, along with his sons and wife; likewise, the wealthy Vaiśya who possesses excellent mantras, or even a deceitful person, whether he be small or great.
O King, you should appoint as minister a wise man who considers state affairs,
who is free from greed, devoted [to the king], and a leader of the realm.
The kingdoms of those who possess ministers of poor wisdom, who lack discernment,
flourish in suffering along with their sovereign.
O King, through the brilliance of the wisdom of wise ministers,
kingdoms flourish in happiness along with their sovereign.
O lord of men, a minister who is greedy and of little intelligence is of no benefit to the king,
nor is he beneficial to the kingdom.
Therefore, O lord of men, one should appoint as the leader of the kingdom a minister who is free from greed, wise, and devoted to counsel.
There is no eye equal to a spy, and there is no policy equal to spying;
therefore, a lord of men should employ spies in all his affairs.
O King, encompassing all your attendants and the kingdom, as well as the elite forces and those who depend upon you, consider what ought and ought not to be done, O Ruler of the Earth.
Therefore, O King, you should appoint a wise doorkeeper;
he will ensure vigilance for you, which brings about your happiness.
This instruction of mine is so meaningful;
having grasped it all, O King, act accordingly.
For you who practice in this way, there will be fame and renown;
the kingdom will be secure, prosperous, flourishing, and densely populated.
Kauśika was also questioned by them, and they gave me answers;
now, O parrot, you ask me about the duties of kings exactly as they are.
O wise one who considers the king's welfare, how many kinds of power does a king possess?
Tell me truly how the duties of a king are to be desired.
The parrot said:
O lord of men, a king should desire five kinds of power;
having become one-pointed in mind, listen to my words.
The first strength is that which is innate, the second is the strength of one's sons,
and the third, O lord of men, is the strength of kinsmen and friends.
O King, the fourfold army is the fourth power;
know that the fifth power is the unsurpassed power of wisdom.
O lord of men, for whoever possesses these five kinds of power,
his kingdom becomes stable, prosperous, flourishing, and teeming with people.
Furthermore, O lord of men, the power of wisdom among these is supreme;
by the power of wisdom, one discerns what ought to be done and what ought not to be done in the governance of people.
He avoids what ought not to be done and performs what ought to be done,
bringing happiness to himself, his kinsmen and friends, and the kingdom.
For even one of noble birth, O lord of men, if he lacks wisdom for the sake of the king's affairs,
is of no benefit to the king nor is he dear to the realm.
But a kingdom is quickly destroyed by rival kings, O King,
when the subjects become disaffected and seek another master.
A wise man who considers his own welfare is highly honored;
moreover, he appoints those who are excellent—brave, heroic, and discerning.
Having completely abandoned unrighteousness, he always practices righteousness, thereby attaining fame in this world, in the life hereafter, and a heavenly rebirth.
Practice righteousness toward your parents, O Great King, O Ruler;
having practiced righteousness here in this world, a king shall go to heaven.
Practice the Dharma, O Great King, toward your children and wife, O lord of men;
having practiced the Dharma here in this world, a king shall go to heaven.
Practice the Dharma, O Great King, toward your friends and ministers, O lord of men;
having practiced the Dharma here in this world, a king shall go to heaven.
Practice the Dharma, O Great King, toward recluses and brahmins alike;
having practiced the Dharma here in this world, a king shall go to heaven.
Practice the Dharma, O Great King, both in the city and in the countryside.
Having practiced the Dharma here, the king will go to heaven.
Practice the Dharma, O Great King, in this world and in the next;
having practiced the Dharma here, a king shall go to heaven.
This instruction of mine is so meaningful;
having grasped it all, O King, act accordingly.
For you who practice in this way, fame and renown shall arise;
the kingdom will become secure, prosperous, flourishing, and densely populated.
To them, the powerful King Brahmadatta spoke thus:
"O sons, you are all-wise, skillful, and deliberators of state affairs."
I shall carry out the words of you all as my instruction;
I have seen for you the purpose that accords with the Dharma and pertains to the future life.
Recalling his former dwelling and former birth, the Blessed One,
the Teacher, related this Jātaka in the presence of the monks.
In this beginningless and endless saṃsāra where I formerly dwelt,
I was then Śuka and Śāriputra was Sārika.
Ānanda was Kauśika, and Śuddhodana was Brahmadatta;
thus was this immeasurable and manifold suffering, this ancient conduct of high and low status.
Free from fever, free from fear, and without sorrow, the Blessed One relates his own birth story in the midst of the community of monks.
Thus ends the Jātaka named Triśakunīya in the glorious Mahāvastu-Avadāna.
Then the Bodhisattva, having abandoned that existence as a parrot, became a prince and taught the ten paths of wholesome action.
The ten masteries have been proclaimed by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun;
listen to me as I speak of them for the sake of the heroic Bodhisattvas.
The venerable ones are self-controlled and wise; likewise, they have attained mastery over eloquence, rebirth, karma, and thought.
Mastery over the Dharma, mastery over supernormal powers, and likewise mastery over intention;
mastery over time and place—the wise one possesses these ten masteries.
Having established themselves in these ten masteries,
the fearless bulls among men bring to maturity thousands of millions of sentient beings.
The Bodhisattvas, the leaders, purify the Buddha-field;
these Bodhisattvas are radiant and have attained great compassion.
At the conclusion of that Jātaka, eighty-four thousand living beings were ripened there and realized the Dharma.
When the Buddha, the Blessed One, stepped across the boundary of Vaiśālī, all the non-human beings fled.
A great multitude of people, filled with joy, questioned the Blessed One.
Behold, Blessed One, how all the non-human beings fled the very moment the Blessed One stepped across the boundary of Vaiśālī!
The Blessed One said:
What is so wonderful about this, O Vāsiṣṭhas, that when the Tathāgata—the god beyond gods who has attained supreme perfect enlightenment—merely stepped across the boundary, all non-human beings fled?
On another occasion as well, when I had become a rishi and was entering the city of Kampilla, all the non-human beings fled at the mere crossing of the boundary.
The Licchavikas said:
At another time as well, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
Or at any other time as well, O Vasiṣṭhas.

Once upon a time, Vāsiṣṭhas, in the past, in the kingdom of Pañcāla, in the city of Kampilla, a king named Brahmadatta reigned. He was well-supported by his retinue, possessed of a nature inclined toward generosity and sharing,

and his realm of Kampilla was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, crowded with many people, inhabited by happy folk, free from violence and civil unrest, with thieves well-restrained, and rich in commerce.

Now, King Brahmadatta had a son of the family priest named Rakṣita, who was of great renown, who lived having undertaken the ten paths of wholesome action, who saw the peril in sensual pleasures, who possessed wisdom regarding the means of escape, who was full of spiritual urgency,
and whose intention was directed toward renunciation.
Having seen the danger in sensual pleasures, he went to the Himalayas and went forth into the wandering life of a seer.

Then, having established a hermitage there in the Himalayas and constructed huts of grass and leaves, he lived as an outsider, subsisting on roots, leaves, flowers, and fruits, devoted to the practice of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night, and attained the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
And the five supernormal powers were produced and realized.

Now that prince— who had attained the four dhyānas, possessed the five superknowledges, lived in accordance with the undertaking of the ten paths of wholesome action, and was a celibate practitioner— sat cross-legged in his hermitage and personally touched the orb of the moon and the orb of the sun with his hand; indeed,
that rishi of fierce austerity and great fortune brought even the hosts of the Brahma-world under his control.
Once, in the great city of Kampilla and its surrounding countryside, a terrible non-human plague broke out.
Touched by that non-human affliction, many thousands of living beings met with misfortune and ruin.
Having seen that great danger in Kampilla, King Brahmadatta dispatched a messenger to Rakkhita in the Himalayas.
In Kampilla, such a non-human affliction has arisen that many thousands of living beings are meeting with ruin and disaster.
"It would be well, Blessed One, if you would come to Kampilla out of compassion."
Having heard the words of the messenger, the seer came from the Himalayas to Kampilla.
When that seer entered the boundary of Kampilla, all those non-human beings fled.
There in Kampilla, the seer performed a rite of auspiciousness and taught the ten paths of wholesome action to eighty-four thousand living beings.
What is that man’s discourse on the inconceivable time,
what is his knowledge, and what is his gift,
that he may travel toward happiness in this world and in the world beyond?
How does one act to be protected? They say that is the way to attain well-being.
He who constantly disregards the perfected deities, all men, his kinsmen, and living beings,
and [disregards] the blazing, sharp [fire].
Compassionate toward living beings, he is protected; they call that a blessing.
Or rather, he who would endure ill-spoken words,
accepting them through the power of patience even upon hearing harsh and undesirable speech.
They say that protection through acceptance is a blessing.
Or those who can endure ill-spoken words, those who have always been affectionate friends,
and those who are confident and non-deceptive.
One who betrays friends and fails to share equally with them,
yet always shows compassion toward friends with his wealth—
he is protected among friends; they call that true well-being.
He who, in the midst of kinsmen and in the midst of companions, always shines forth through his virtue, wisdom, and self-mastery— indeed, he shines at all times.
Thus protected in the midst of kinsmen, they say that is his auspicious blessing.
In whomsoever the king, the lord of the earth, has confidence, and who possesses truth and prowess—
such a person is incapable of being harmed here or in the past.
He is protected in the midst of kings; they call that a blessing.
She who, being affectionate toward her offspring and compassionate toward her children,
gives birth to one who is beautiful and virtuous.
They say that protecting one's household is a blessing.
Those who praise the Buddha with noble Dharma, being virtuous, they attend upon him and serve him;
they are learned, have crossed over doubt, and are liberated.
Being protected among the Arhats, they call that a blessing.
With minds full of faith, they give food, drink, Kāśī sandalwood, perfumes, and garlands at the proper time to śramaṇas and brahmins.
That which is protected in the middle of the village, they call that *svastyayana*.
Slander, lying, taking the wives of others, likewise the taking of life, and intoxicants—
having abandoned these, you will go to the heavenly realm.
That which is protected in the middle of the village, they call that a blessing.
Now, Vāsiṣṭhas, it might occur to you that at that time, on that occasion, the seer named Rakṣita was someone else;
however, it should not be viewed in this way.
And for what reason?
O Vāsiṣṭhas, at that time and on that occasion, I was the seer named Rakṣita.
At that time, on that occasion, he who was the king named Brahmadatta in the city of Kampilla was someone else.
Indeed, this alone is not how it should be viewed.
This King Śreṇika Bimbisāra was, at that time, a king named Brahmadatta in the city of Kampilla.
Even then, when I was an ṛṣi entering the boundary of Kampilla, all the non-human beings fled.
Even now, as soon as I stepped across the boundary of Vaiśālī, all the non-human beings fled.
Moreover, it is not only now that all non-human beings have fled as soon as I stepped across the boundary; on another occasion as well, they fled as soon as I stepped across the boundary.

Long ago, Vāsiṣṭhas, in times past, in the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi, there reigned a king who had performed meritorious deeds, was illustrious, possessed great power, a great treasury, and many mounts; he was by nature disposed toward generosity and sharing.
His city, Vārāṇasī, in the kingdom of Kāśi, was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with people.
Now, that king’s state elephant was one who had performed meritorious deeds, possessed of great renown, great majesty, and great power; by virtue of his majesty and power,

Vārāṇasī and the Kāśī country were free from pestilence and free from calamity, such that even those other villages and districts whose boundaries he entered likewise became free from pestilence and free from calamity.
Once, in Mithilā, the city of Videha, a non-human plague broke out, and many thousands of living beings met with ruin and calamity.
They heard that the elephant-king of the King of Kāśī was one who had performed meritorious deeds, possessed great renown, great majesty, and great power;
and that whichever village or city his boundary entered became free from pestilence and free from calamity.
Then that king of the Vaidehakas spoke to another brahmin.
Go to Vārāṇasī; that King of Kāśi is one who gives everything away and is habituated to generosity and sharing.
Inform him of this nature of yours and request that noble elephant from him.
By that nāga having come here, every non-human affliction shall be pacified.
Having heard the king's words, that brahmin gradually arrived at Vārāṇasī.
And the brahmin entered Vārāṇasī.

And this King of Kāśi, departing from Vārāṇasī to the outskirts of the city with great royal majesty and great royal power, proceeded with that noble elephant— adorned with every ornament, covered with a golden net, and blazing with splendor— at his front.
That brahmin, standing before the King of Kāśī, congratulated him with cries of victory.
The king, having seen that brahmin, stood still.
"O Brahmin, what is your need? What shall I give to you?"
The brahmin reported all of that non-human affliction in Mithilā to the King of Kāśi.
"Great King, out of compassion for Mithilā, please give this noble elephant to me."
The king was compassionate and devoted to the welfare of others.
He gave that noble elephant to that brahmin, adorned just as it was.
"I give this elephant to you, O brahmin— adorned, covered with a net of gold, worthy of a king, fit for royal enjoyment, noble, and accompanied by its driver.
Go wherever you desire."

Now, Vāsiṣṭhas, it may be that you think the king who was in Vārāṇasī at that time and on that occasion was someone else. But it should not be seen so. Why is that? It was indeed I myself who was the king in Vārāṇasī at that time and on that occasion.
This should not be viewed in such a way.
At that time, on that occasion, King Śreṇika Bimbisāra was the King of Kāśī.

Now, Vāsiṣṭhas, it might occur to you that the king who was ruling in Mithilā at that time and on that occasion was someone else. But it should not be viewed in this way. Why is that? Because he, indeed, was the king of Mithilā at that time and on that occasion.
This should not be viewed in such a way.
For what reason?
This General Siṃha was, at that time and on that occasion, the king.
That other person is a brahmin; this Tomara is a Licchavi.
That elephant-king becomes something else.
Furthermore, it should certainly not be viewed in this way.
At that time, on that occasion, I was the royal elephant of the king.
Even then, having become an elephant-king, I caused all the non-human beings in Mithilā to flee.
Even now, as soon as I have stepped across the boundary of Vaiśālī, all the non-human beings have fled.
But, O Vāsiṣṭhas, it was not only now that all non-human beings fled as soon as I stepped upon the boundary.
On another occasion as well, when he was the Ṛṣabha and merely stepped across the boundary, all the non-human beings fled.

Once upon a time, Vāsiṣṭhas, in the distant past, there was a king ruling in the city of Rājagṛha. He was one who had performed meritorious deeds, possessed great majesty, and maintained a well-gathered retinue; he was disposed toward giving and sharing, and possessed great strength, a great treasury, and a great army.
His kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, crowded with people, and teeming with many inhabitants.
And it was filled with happy people, where punishment and civil unrest were stilled, thieves were well-restrained, and legal affairs were successfully conducted.
There, a non-human affliction arose, and many thousands of living beings met with ruin and calamity through that non-human affliction.
And among the kings of Aṅga, he was Ṛṣabha—gracious, handsome, one who had performed meritorious deeds, and possessed of great majesty.
By the power of his majesty, the entire region of Aṅga became free from pestilence and free from calamity.
The brahmins and householders of Rājagṛha heard [this].
Such was the bull of the King of Aṅga— gracious, beautiful to behold, meritorious, and of great renown;
by the power and majesty of his splendor, the entire realm of Aṅga became free from calamity and free from affliction.
They informed the king.

"Great King, listen: such is this bull of the King of Aṅga—so pleasing, beautiful to behold, meritorious, illustrious, and of great majesty—that whatever village or city boundary he enters becomes free from calamity and free from affliction."
"Great King, bring Ṛṣabha; by his being brought, the non-human plague in Rājagṛha will be pacified."
King Rājagṛhaka sent a brahmin to the King of Aṅga.
"Go, and having made the King of Aṅga aware of this danger in Rājagṛha, beg that bull from him."
Then that brahmin, having replied "So be it" to the king, traveled from Rājagṛha by stages until he arrived at the city of the King of Aṅga.
Having approached the King of Aṅga and greeted him with cries of victory, he reported in full detail everything regarding the non-human plague in Rājagṛha and requested the bull.
And that king was both compassionate and devoted to benefiting others.
Having heard of that great danger facing the people of Rājagṛha, he gave that bull to the brahmin.
Go, brahmin; may all the people of Rājagṛha and all sentient beings be happy.
Taking that bull, the brahmin went from the region of Aṅga to the region of Magadha.

And immediately after, Vāsiṣṭhas, the boundary of Rājagṛha was overrun by Ṛṣabha, and all those non-human beings fled; thus the district of Rājagṛha became free from pestilence and free from calamity.
It may be, Vāsiṣṭhas, that you might think that at that time, on that occasion, the King of Aṅga in the city of Aṅga was someone else. [But it was not so.]
Furthermore, it should certainly not be viewed in this way.
For what reason?
O Vāsiṣṭhas, at that time and on that occasion, this King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra was the King of Aṅga.
He who was the king in Rājagṛha at that time and on that occasion was someone else.
This should not be viewed in this way.
For what reason?
This is the general Siṃhasena.
That brahmin from Rājagṛha who brought that bull at that time and on that occasion was someone else.

It should not be viewed in this way. For what reason? O Vāsiṣṭhas, this Tomara the Licchavi was, at that time and on that occasion, the brahmin in Rājagṛha by whom the bull was brought from the presence of the King of Aṅga to Rājagṛha.
Now, Vāsiṣṭhas, it might occur to you that at that time, on that occasion, the bull was someone else; however, he was indeed the king of Aṅga.
Indeed, this should not be viewed in such a way.
For what reason?
O Vāsiṣṭhas, at that time and on that occasion, I was the bull belonging to the King of Aṅga.

Even then, when I had become a bull and was merely crossing the boundary of Rājagṛha, all the non-human beings fled; and now, too, as I have attained supreme perfect enlightenment and am merely crossing the boundary of Vaiśālī, all the non-human beings have fled.
Thus ends the Jātaka of Ṛṣabha in the glorious Mahāvastu-Avadāna.
Then the Blessed One, proceeding by stages, arrived at Vaiśālī.
Now the Blessed One performed a rite for well-being throughout Vaiśālī, both within and without,
and he spoke these verses of well-being.
Homage be to the Buddha; homage be to Awakening; homage to the Liberated One; homage to Liberation;
homage be to Wisdom; homage be to the Wise One.
Pay homage to the one who is the most excellent pinnacle of the world.
Whatever beings have gathered here, whether they belong to the earth or to the atmosphere,
let them all become joyful in mind.
May they hear this auspicious prayer spoken by the Jina.
Whether in this world or in another,
or again in the heavens, whatever jewel is most excellent,
there is nothing equal to the Tathāgata.
By this truth— that the Buddha, the supreme among gods, the best of men, has brought forth this most excellent jewel of a Buddha— may there be great well-being.
Whether from humans or from non-humans...
this too is a sublime jewel of the Dharma. By this truth, may there be well-being.
Whether from humans or from non-humans.
That which the Best of Buddhas has praised as pure,
which they call the "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*) concentration—
there exists no concentration equal to it.
This too is a sublime jewel among the teachings;
by this truth, may there be well-being from humans or from non-humans.
Those individuals who are always praised as the eight,
consisting of these four pairs—
they have been declared by the Sugata to be worthy of offerings.
These gifts bestowed yield great fruit;
this jewel is also most excellent within the Saṅgha.
By this truth, may there be well-being.
Whether from humans or from non-humans.
For one who possesses the excellence of vision, all these three qualities are abandoned:
the view of a self-identity and doubt.
And whatever moral conduct and vows there may be—
this too is a sublime jewel in the Saṅgha;
by this truth, may there be well-being.
Either from humans or from non-humans.
Furthermore, even if a learner (śaikṣa) commits an evil deed by body, speech, or even by mind,
he is incapable of concealing it.
Inability [to attain the fruits] on the noble paths has been declared;
this too is a sublime jewel in the Saṅgha. By this truth, may there be well-being.
Either from a human or from a non-human.
Just as a city-gate pillar, firmly established in the earth, would be unshakable by the four winds,
even so do I describe the true person.
He who, having understood and seen the well-taught Noble Truths of profound meaning—
this too is a sublime jewel in the Saṅgha.
By this truth, may there be well-being from humans or from non-humans.
Those who clearly discern the Noble Truths well-taught by one of profound wisdom—
even if they should become greatly negligent— will not fall away.
Those venerable ones do not cling to the eight [worldly conditions].
This too is a sublime jewel in the Saṅgha;
by this truth, may there be great well-being.
Whether from humans or from non-humans.
Those practitioners of yoga who, with a well-directed mind, are intent on renunciation within the teaching of Gautama—
they have attained what was to be attained, having plunged into the deathless.
With minds liberated, enjoying nirvāṇa—
this too is a sublime jewel in the Saṅgha;
by this truth, may there be well-being.
Whether from a human or from a non-human.
The old is exhausted and no new accumulation exists; they are liberated from future existence. Having exhausted the seeds, they are of a nature that does not sprout again.
The wise pass away like oil lamps;
this too is a sublime jewel in the Saṅgha. By this truth, may there be well-being.
Whether from humans or from non-humans.
Just as a blazing fire that has arisen with great force subsides when its fuel is exhausted,
so do the sons of the Buddha who practice such meditation.
Having grasped the latent tendency of passion through wisdom, they go beyond the sight of the King of Death;
this too is a sublime jewel in the Saṅgha.
Whether from humans or from non-humans.
In the first month of summer, Caitra,
the forest thickets with their flowering tops waft a fragrant scent when stirred by the wind.
In this way, the sons of the Buddha who meditate and are endowed with virtue emit a fragrant scent;
this too is a sublime jewel within the Saṅgha.
By this truth, may there be well-being from humans or from non-humans.
Whatever beings have gathered here, whether they belong to the earth or to the atmosphere,
may they always treat human beings with loving-kindness.
Day and night they carry away your tribute;
therefore, protect it with vigilance,
just as a mother protects her son out of compassion.
By this truth, may there be well-being from humans or from non-humans.
In Vipaśyin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, Bhāmaka, Kanakamuni, the highly renowned Kāśyapa, and Śākyamuni Gautama;
May those deities who have placed their faith in these Buddhas of great supernatural power protect you thoroughly and act for your benefit.
It is a source of well-being for human beings;
therefore, protect it with heedfulness,
just as a mother protects her son out of compassion.
This too is a sublime jewel in the Saṅgha;
by this truth, may there be well-being from humans or from non-humans.
He who, out of compassion for all beings, turns the Wheel of Dharma in the world having overcome it—
such is the supreme among gods and humans.
I pay homage to the Buddha; may there be well-being.
I pay homage to the Dharma; may there be well-being. I pay homage to the Saṅgha; may there be well-being.
Either from humans or from non-humans.
Having provided a meal for the community of monks headed by the Buddha at Gośṛṅgī, she offered the Śāla grove as a gift.
This thought occurred to the Licchavis:

Each one of us is capable of attending upon the Blessed One together with the community of disciples for as long as we live, providing robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
Nevertheless, let it be done in such a way that the great multitude may be endowed with merit.
Let the grain of humanity be carried away.
By them, the human-grain was discarded, and twenty-five or more varieties of grain were produced.
In this way, they attended upon the Blessed One together with the community of disciples for seven days.
They attend upon the Fully Awakened One— who is glorious, of great authority, beautiful in form, and renowned— just as the hosts of stars attend upon the moon.
Clad in yellow ornaments and garments, like blossoming *karṇikāra* trees,
they wait upon the Perfectly Awakened One, wearing heavy armlets.
Their limbs were anointed with yellow sandalwood paste, and they wore the finest garments of Kāśī;
[they beheld] that assembly of gods who had gathered together—
pure, well-born, and endowed with the marks of a hundred merits.
The Buddha surpasses all in splendor,
like the king of the stars among the constellations.
Just as the moon, the maker of light, shines amidst the hosts of stars in a cloudless sky,
so too does he shine among these kṣatriya rulers of the earth.
In every respect, the Buddha surpasses all by his splendor.
Just as the sun prevails in the atmosphere and shines while stationed upon the path of the Ādityas,
even so [do you shine] over these kṣatriya rulers of the earth.
The Buddha surpasses all by his splendor.
Just as the sun blazes in the atmosphere and shines while stationed upon the path of the Ādityas,
so too [does he shine] over these kṣatriya rulers of the earth.
In every respect, the Buddha surpasses them in splendor.
Just as a well-born *kokanada* lotus, radiant, in full bloom, and endowed with fragrance—
so too [is this] the Kṣatriya protector of the earth.
The Buddha surpasses all by his splendor.
Just as Śakra, the crusher of the hosts of asuras,
shines forth with a thousand eyes among the thirty-three gods,
so too [does he shine] over these kṣatriya rulers of the earth.
In every respect, the Buddha surpasses all by his splendor.
Just as Brahmā, out of compassion for living beings, outshines all the splendor of the gods with his majesty,
so too does he [outshine] these kṣatriya rulers of the earth.
In every respect, the Buddha surpasses all by his splendor.
Then, having realized the pure glory endowed with ten attributes and the grace of the nectar of immortality,
he disciplined these kṣatriya rulers of the earth.
I shall show this Dharma as clearly as if it were in the palm of one's hand.
Thus was the Blessed One praised by the Venerable Ānanda.

The Blessed One, having instructed, inspired, and gladdened the Licchavis of Vaiśālī with a discourse on the Dharma, converted many hundreds of thousands of living beings; such was the gift and the religious offering of the Licchavis of Vaiśālī, for which this expression of appreciation was made.
Just as those bees, having gathered together and taken various kinds of flower nectar,
collect it with their mouths and feet... [and bring it to one place].
When there is a combination of flavor, fragrance, and color,
that which is prepared becomes excellent honey,
endowed with color, fragrance, and flavor.
And he approaches him during his meals of medicine.
In that very village or town where he has arrived, there is a great multitude of people—
men and women, along with their sons and wives.
They have a common desire for virtuous deeds.
Having gathered together, they give drink; they provide meals for the Saṅgha and rice-gruel,
as well as drinks and various wholesome hard foods.
And they give flavors approved by the noble ones.
According to their faith and according to their power,
having offered many gifts even for an entire eon, they give again and again with minds full of serene confidence.
The mass of merit goes toward accumulation.
Salutation and the act of joining the palms, rising from one's seat and offering a seat,
as well as service and rejoicing in the Dharma.
The great multitude, being joyful, performs meritorious deeds.
Having given gifts and performed meritorious deeds,
they were either led away by speech or by the very nature of their shared karma.
They all go to the heavenly realm.
Endowed with divine forms, they sport together with hosts of apsarases;
having abundant food, they enjoy excellent meals and drinks.
Having ascended the most excellent celestial palaces, they take their delight.
And when they come to the world of humans,
they are all born into wealthy families— prosperous, flourishing, and possessing great riches.
In places crowded with many women and men.
This honey has been prepared, praised by holy men,
and brings happiness through all its flowers; whatever purpose was prayed for with the mind, [it has been fulfilled].
May he attain all supernatural powers according to his wish.
Having gathered for the sake of all, may you attain the peace that destroys all conditioned phenomena and afflictions;
thus the Great Lord, the benefactor of the world, has praised it.
Together with their sons, wives, kinsmen, and relatives.
Then those Licchavis said to the Blessed One:
"Lord, this great park among our parks, namely this Great Forest together with its gabled hall,
we give to the Blessed One and present it to him along with his community of disciples."
The Blessed One then addressed the monks.
"Therefore, monks, I authorize [the use of it] for the sake of a monastery, for the sake of a dwelling, and for the sake of a ritual enclosure."
The Blessed One has now come from the Great Forest to the Cāpāla Shrine.
The Licchavis asked.
Where is the Blessed One?
The monks said:
"O Vāsiṣṭhas, this Blessed One has departed from Mahāvana for Cāpāla Shrine in order to dwell there during the day."
Then those Licchavis said:
We offer the Cāpāla Shrine of the Blessed One, together with the community of disciples.

At a later time, the Licchavis came to the Great Forest to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One; meanwhile, the Blessed One, having finished his meal, went to the Saptāmra Shrine for his midday rest.
The Licchavis asked the monks.
"Noble lady, where is the Blessed One?"
The monks said.
"Vasiṣṭha, this Blessed One, having finished his meal, has gone toward the Saptāmra Shrine for his midday rest."
Then those Licchavis approached the Saptāmra-cetiya, bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Venerable Sir, we offer the Saptāmra-caitya to the Blessed One together with his community of disciples."
Likewise, there is the Bahuputra-caitya, the Gautamaka-caitya, and the Kapinahya-caitya.
Furthermore, the Blessed One, having finished his duties regarding the meal, departed from the Great Forest and proceeded to the shore of the Markaṭahrada cetiya for his midday rest.
The Licchavis came to the Great Forest to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One.
They ask the monks.
"Noble lady, where is the Blessed One?"
The monks said.
"Vāsiṣṭhas, this Blessed One, having finished his meal, has gone to the bank of the Markaṭahrada for his midday rest."
Then, having approached the shrine on the bank of the Markaṭahrada lake and bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they said this to the Blessed One:
Let us go to the Dema Markaṭahrada shrine and present it to the Blessed One together with his community of disciples.
After Āmrapālī had provided a meal for the Blessed One together with the community of disciples, she offered the mango grove as a gift.
After the girl had provided a meal for the Blessed One together with the community of disciples, she offered her own skin.
Thus ends the Chapter on the Parasol in the glorious Mahāvastu-Avadāna.
Now, may the protector of the ninefold treasury of the Dharma of the teaching of King Aparimitayaśas,
this excellent community, endure for a long time.
He is the most excellent in glory, immovable like Mount Sumeru.
In the absence of the appearance of Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas arise in the world.
Beautiful in silence, of great majesty, wandering alone like the horn of a rhinoceros, they subdue themselves alone and attain final nirvana.

Now, another Pratyekabuddha entered a village for alms in the forenoon within the lands of Kāśi; he was graceful in his advancing and retreating, in his looking ahead and looking aside, and in his drawing in and stretching out [his limbs], and in his manner of wearing the outer robe, bowl, and inner robe.
Like an elephant who has performed its task, with his senses withdrawn within and his mind not directed outward, he remained established in the nature of reality.
Looking only a yoke's length ahead.
And the village headman ran out from the village into the forest to inspect his work, being handsome and inspiring faith in gods and men.
The Pratyekabuddha, having wandered for alms through that village in proper sequence, departed from that village with his bowl as clean as when it was washed.
The time for alms has almost passed, yet no one has given any alms.
The village headman, having inspected his works, entered the village again and saw that pratyekabuddha departing from the village.
The thought occurs to him:
The time for food is nearly at hand.
"I shall first find out what alms have been obtained by this renunciant."
The village headman approached the Pratyekabuddha and asked:
"Noble one, alms have been obtained."
The Pratyekabuddha, beautiful in his silence, showed the empty bowl to the village headman.
The village headman, seeing the Pratyekabuddha’s empty bowl, said to him:
How is it that people who are by nature ungenerous allow such a worthy recipient of offerings to depart from this great village with his alms-bowl as empty as when he first washed it?
What do these people enjoy while illuminating [the world]?
He said:
"O Blessed One, please come; I shall give you food."
Having taken that Pratyekabuddha, he entered that village.
Standing at the crossroads of the four great paths, he cried out, "Avidhāvidhā!"
When the village headman residing there heard the sound "avidhāvidha," the entire village, including women and men, assembled together.
Having approached the village headman, they asked him.
"What is security? Why do you cry out, 'What is not a calamity, what is a calamity'?"
The village headman said:

I lament because these people do not delight in sharing nor have they the habit of sharing, since from such a large village as this, a single monk departs with his bowl as clean as when it was washed.
Then those elders in the village, having heard that from the village headman, thought that they should honor that pratyekabuddha.
The village headman, having invited the Pratyekabuddha into his home and honored him with food, entreated him to remain for as long as he lived.
"I invite the Noble One for as long as I live, with every provision for comfort."
One who has been taught by oneself is a *saṃveditā*.
In this way, you shall attend upon that noble one with food on that day.
The girl became joyful and satisfied.
A beautiful and auspicious deed has been performed by me.
Then, she attended upon that pratyekabuddha with food every day; she was pleasing and inspiring faith in gods and humans alike.
The Pratyekabuddha, who has fully understood food and whose impurities are entirely exhausted, is one of great fortune.
Then, having seen that conduct of the Pratyekabuddha, a noble faith arose in the daughter of that village headman.
Likewise, other people also became inspired with faith.
Then that Pratyekabuddha, through his faith in that village headman, attained final nirvana right there in the village field, without further clinging.
Then, having cremated that Pratyekabuddha, the village headman constructed a stūpa, neither too small nor too large, coated with plaster and clay.
Then that daughter of the village headman worshipped that stūpa daily with a bronze vessel, using perfumes, garlands, and incense.
Afterwards, that various kind of garland was then blown away from the stūpa by the wind.
Then, having gathered that garland together with her maidservants, she fashioned a long, thick wreath composed of various flowers.
There, that garland completely encircled the entire stūpa of that pratyekabuddha.

Seeing that garland of hers remaining there upon the stūpa— standing there, outshining all other garlands in both form and brilliance, and shining even after the divine lifespan among the gods had been exhausted— an exceeding clarity of mind arose within her.
Then, with a serene mind, she made this aspiration:
"May such a garland as this garland shines here upon this stūpa appear upon my head wherever I may be reborn."

Having performed that wholesome deed, she passed away from there and was reborn among the gods, adorned with a garland of jewels. Once reborn there, she was attended by a retinue of a hundred thousand apsarases.
Passing away from there as well, she was reborn in Vārāṇasī in the womb of the chief queen of King Kṛkī.
After the lapse of nine or ten months, a daughter was born to the queen, who was gracious and beautiful to behold, adorned with a necklace of jewels.
The name Mālinī was given to her.
She was dear and pleasing to King Kṛkī, as well as esteemed by his entire retinue; she was a girl of such merit that she was beloved throughout the whole city.
A pratyekabuddha may enter a village for alms; having received his food, he should then depart from that village with his bowl as clean as when it was washed.
Having seen him, the awakened one, the village headman said this: "Is the Blessed One free from illness? May he obtain almsfood."
Then, O Blessed One, he presented his bowl to the village headman;
yet he did not see any alms-food therein, and the village headman felt dejection.
This world is blinded, forever struck down by wrong views;
it does not worship such a worthy recipient of offerings as they deserve.
Having approached the edge of the village and standing at the crossroads, he cries out, "Avidhāvidha!"; then the people gather together.
The great multitude, both women and men, having gathered together, approached the village headman and asked, "What shall we do? What is the proper course of action?"
The village headman said:
"Surely it must be that among you there is no one who delights in sharing;
for in this village, this one monk alone is being harassed."
Having heard the words of the village headman, the entire village, including the women,
repeatedly performed acts of cordial welcome toward the Perfectly Awakened One.
Then the village headman, together with his wife and his sons,
invited the Tathāgata to dwell in every comfort.
The village headman’s own daughter, dressed in pure garments and fragrant perfumes,
endowed with proper conduct and virtues, attended upon the Tathāgata.
Through the favor of the village headman, in that very village,
the perfectly awakened one, Suvrata— the seer whose rebirth has been exhausted— entered final nirvana.
Having meditated upon him as having entered parinirvāṇa, the village headman had a stūpa constructed;
he performed worship for the Great Seer with dance, instrumental music, and song.
Having gathered white flowers blown by the wind,
one should collect them into a single heap and weave them into a long garland.
Just as that variegated garland was placed upon him right there,
may such a garland as this be upon my head.
Wherever I may be reborn here, may this [vow] of mine be fulfilled there.
Having performed that virtuous deed praised by the Buddha,
she was then reborn among the Trāyastriṃśa gods as an apsaras.
And having placed a hundred thousand apsarases before her, she stood there;
she was the most excellent and distinguished among them, a woman beautiful in every limb.
Then, having passed away from there, those highly powerful celestial maidens were reborn in the womb of King Kṛkī’s wife.
When twelve months had passed, the king’s wife gave birth to a daughter named Mālinī, a woman beautiful in every limb.
She was of exceeding complexion and exceeding beauty;
she was the most excellent among the daughters of kings, the daughter of the King of Kāśi.
Endowed with the virtues of proper conduct, wearing clean garments and fragrant perfumes,
she stands before King Kṛkī with her palms joined in reverence.
The king said to her as she stood with palms joined in reverence:
"O blessed lady, feed my brahmins without weariness."
Having heard her father’s words, Mālinī fed no fewer than twenty thousand brahmins with all the objects of their desire.
Seeing her, who resembled an Apsaras, on the Mālinī river, those brahmins,
their minds seized by passion, called out to her again and again.
Seeing her agitated, haughty, fickle, and with unrestrained senses, Mālinī reflected: "These are not worthy of offerings."
Having ascended the palace, she looked all around and beheld a disciple of the Blessed One, the glorious Fully Enlightened One.
Seated upon the excellent palace, anointed with the finest sandalwood from Kāśī,
the daughter of King Kṛkī gazed out toward all directions.
She saw the disciples of the Buddha entering with graceful movements— those who had cast out evil and were in their final bodies.
She sent a maidservant with this message: "Offer salutations to these seers;
and having saluted them, say: 'Enter, venerable sirs, and be seated.'"
That maidservant, having approached and bowed at the feet of those of cultivated self, spoke with palms joined: "Enter, O Venerable Ones; please be seated."
Having transcended passion, confident, the foremost wise ones in the world— these disciples of the Buddha have cast out evil and possess their final bodies.
They entered that white, well-constructed inner palace with beautiful archways, guarded by swords and daggers, to please the daughter of the king.
He sat upon a seat that had been prepared, spread with a Kāśika cloth, adorned with many variegated bundles, embellished with jewels, and strewn with various flowers.
Like a lotus of auspicious luster, like a water-born flower unsullied by the water,
so may you sit there with an unsullied mind, free from delusion.
She personally offers them, according to their pleasure, the method of preparing rice from fine śāli grains, served at the proper time and accompanied by various side dishes.
Those monks said: "The Teacher is the foremost wise man in the world;
let that Great Hero eat his first meal."
Having heard the word "Buddha"—a sound never before heard in the world—she became even more serene, thinking: "He is indeed superior to these [others]."
That Mālinī said, "Having eaten, take the food for the Teacher;
and offer my salutation in my name to the Lord of the World."
The Blessed One consented to the meal, together with the community of monks,
for the sake of the King’s daughter, who was pleasing to him, within the inner apartments.
Then those two chief disciples of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, Tiṣya and Bhāradvāja, having finished their meal at Mālinī’s house, took the meal for the Blessed One Kāśyapa and set out for Ṛṣivadana.
Having offered the alms-bowl to the Blessed One Kāśyapa, they paid homage to the Blessed One Kāśyapa on behalf of Mālinī, saying: "We offer our salutations."
“Lord, Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi, the daughter of the Blessed One, sends her greetings and asks after the welfare of the Blessed One and his community of disciples.
She invites you, together with the community of monks, for a meal tomorrow; may the Blessed One, out of compassion, consent to this invitation in the inner apartments of King Kṛkī.”
The Blessed One Kāśyapa consented out of consideration for those to be converted.
The men who had gone with those great disciples, taking the instruction of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, went and informed Mālinī.
The Blessed One Kāśyapa accepted [the invitation], saying, "Tomorrow, together with the community of monks, I shall partake of the meal."
Having heard this from those men, Mālinī prepared an abundance of solid and soft food that very night, and had the time announced to the Blessed One Kāśyapa.
The Blessed One knows the right time, knows the proper occasion, knows the appropriate moment, knows individuals, and knows the superior and inferior qualities of individuals.

Having dressed early in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, when the time for wandering had arrived, while it was still morning mealtime in Māgadha, he entered the city of Vārāṇasī together with twenty thousand monks.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, enter a city like a flight of swans.
On the right side is the great śrāvaka Tiṣya.
On the left side is the great śrāvaka Bhāradvāja.
Behind them were four great śrāvakas; behind those four were eight; behind those eight were sixteen; behind those sixteen were thirty-two; and behind those thirty-two were sixty-four.
Thus the Blessed One, preceded by twenty thousand bhikṣus,
entered the inner apartments of King Kṛkī.
As the Blessed One was entering the city, the sunken ground rose up and the surface of the earth became level and even.
Impure stones, pebbles, and gravel enter the earth, and the ground remains strewn with scattered flowers.
The trees laden with flowers blossomed, and the trees laden with fruit bore fruit.

Along that path, to the left and to the right, there were ponds and lotus-pools filled with cool water, covered with blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lilies, pink lotuses, nalini-lotuses, and fragrant saugandhika-lotuses;
from the mouths of the wells, the water flowed forth.
The horses neigh, the bulls bellow, and the elephant-kings let out their trumpeting cries.
Immediately, he stepped over the threshold with his foot, and the entire city trembled; the blind saw light, the deaf heard sound, the insane regained their mindfulness,
the sick were freed from their ailments, pregnant women gave birth without illness, clothing appeared for the naked, and those bound in fetters were released.
The bindings burst open; the jewels enclosed in boxes and caskets clash together, and the vessels ring out.
Whatever lutes, harps, flutes, vīṇās, mṛdaṅgas, bherīs, and paṇavas there are in the city, they sound forth spontaneously, even though unstruck and unplayed.
Parrots, mynas, cuckoos, swans, and peacocks utter their respective cries.

He walks without touching the ground by a distance of four finger-breadths, and upon the surface of the earth, wheel-marks appear with a thousand spokes, hubs, and all features perfectly complete; and in the sky, the gods play thousands of divine musical instruments and rain down showers of celestial flowers.

The Blessed One Kāśyapa, together with his community of disciples, entered the inner palace of King Kṛkī, being honored by gods and humans with such rites, such adornments, such a gathering, such supernatural power, and such magnificence.

The Blessed One, together with the community of disciples, was served there in that inner four-hall residence with great honor, with abundant, excellent, savory food— both soft and solid— that was upright in flavor, unadulterated in flavor, and fresh in flavor.

The Blessed One, having eaten with the community of disciples, having washed his hands and set aside his bowl, instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened Mālinī with a discourse on the Dharma; then, rising from his seat, he departed.

Those twenty thousand brahmins who were the regular guests of Kṛkī, the king of Kāśi, became incensed because the Blessed One Kāśyapa, together with his community of disciples, had been served in the royal palace with great hospitality and great honor by Mālinī.
By them, the entire assembly of brahmins was convened, consisting of many thousands of brahmins.
At that time, at that period, the earth was overrun by brahmins.
They gathered together, desiring to have Mālinī killed.
This very person has arisen here in the royal court as a thorn to the brahmins.
King Kṛkī was devoted to the brahmins; twenty thousand brahmins ate daily at his court, and this woman had been appointed to serve those brahmins with the instruction, "Feed these brahmins every day.
Yet, having shown contempt for these brahmins, she admitted the śramaṇas into the royal palace and rendered such honor and hospitality to them.
This is that [which she does]: she diverts to the ascetics for the sake of honor and hospitality what was the livelihood of the brahmins from the royal court, thinking, "They are to be honored."
Those brahmins made this resolution: "Mālinī must be killed."
And Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi, had gone out to inspect his realm.
Those brahmins sent a messenger to King Kṛkī.
Such was the disrespect that arose in Mālinī toward the brahmins;
having brought Kāśyapa along with his community of disciples into the royal palace and having offered such honor and hospitality, she would not even grant an audience to the brahmins.
He does not act in accordance with what was commanded by the Great King.
Furthermore, even the regular provision for twenty thousand brahmins at the royal court was no longer maintained.
Mālinī did not even grant an audience to the brahmins.
As soon as the king heard this, he came from the countryside to Vārāṇasī and saw many thousands of brahmins assembled together.
He went straight to where the brahmins were.
The brahmins also went out to meet the king, and after congratulating him with cries of victory, they reported all this news concerning Mālinī to King Kṛkī.
"Your Majesty, this Mālinī has arisen as a thorn to the brahmins; it is not possible for the brahmins to accept a regular endowment from the king as long as Mālinī has not been put to death."
This determination has arisen within this entire assembly of brahmins.
The king and the brahmins as well—
this conduct of the assembly of brahmins must be followed.
If your status as a brahmin has not been abandoned, then renounce Mālinī;
but if Mālinī has not been renounced by you, your status as a brahmin does not exist.
As he was following the ritual proceedings of the assembly of brahmins, this thought occurred to that king:
"This earth is overrun by brahmins; it is filled with many brahmins.
If I do not abandon Mālinī, there will be a riot.
Mālinī will not be like this, nor shall I."
One should abandon an individual for the sake of the family; one should abandon a family for the sake of the village;
