one should abandon a village for the sake of the country; and one should abandon the whole earth for the sake of the self.
Then Mālinī was abandoned by the King of Kāśi.
Let it be according to the intention of the assembly of brahmins.
Then those brahmins said:
If Mālinī has been abandoned, let her be summoned by the king.
Then, while standing at the base of some brahmins outside the city, he dispatched a messenger.
"Come, bring Mālinī! he said.
By the king's command, the messenger arrived at the royal palace.
"Come, Mālinī! You have been abandoned by your father;
you shall be deprived of life by the brahmins."
Mālinī went to her mother and let out a cry, and the entire harem did likewise.
All the people in the city were distressed and thrown into agitation by that sound of lamentation.
There was great weeping.
Mālinī was sent out from Vārāṇasī by messenger to the presence of her father.
Then, having been expelled by the messengers, she went to her father.
This, O Great King, is the Mālinī.
With a tearful throat and a weeping face, the king gave Mālinī to the Brahmins of the great multitude and relinquished her to his father.
Then, at the time when Mālinī was abandoned by her father, she became subject to the commands of the brahmins.
Then Mālinī, having joined her palms in reverence, prostrated before the assembly of brahmins.
"I wish for one formal authorization: that the assembly of brahmins be considered authoritative."
They said:
Speak whatever petition you have.
He said:
I was abandoned by my father among the brahmins; I have now come under your power.
In the assembly of brahmins, there was this very resolution: "Mālinī must be put to death."
Therefore, I wish to live for seven days right here in the presence of this assembly of brahmins; I shall give gifts and perform meritorious deeds.
I have performed services for the brahmins, and by my father’s command, I have also caused the brahmins to be served.
Then, after the passing of seven days, you may kill me, or do whatever you deem fit.
A thought arose among those elder brahmins.
It is exactly as Mālinī says: for a long time, at her father’s command, she attended upon and fed these brahmins;
subsequently, however, an evil thought arose in her, whereby she abandoned the brahmins and became devoted to the śramaṇas.

Therefore, she ought not to give further gifts to the śramaṇas; this [gift] has been relinquished to those brahmins alone, and she will give it as a gift for seven nights. Let this request be granted: let her be released for seven nights, for at the end of the seventh day, she will be executed.
For this reason, since this resolution has arisen among the assembly of brahmins, it must be carried out while Mālinī is still alive.
A request was made to her by those brahmins.
"Having been granted leave for seven nights from the presence of this great multitude of brahmins, may there be heedfulness; may it not be violated even for those seven nights."
Now, although she had been dismissed, she surely entered the royal palace again, surrounded by a great multitude of people, and made her request to her father.
I desire to give gifts and perform meritorious deeds for these seven days, according to my own intention.
The king said.
"Let it be so; perform, daughter, the merit in which you have interest."
She said:
"I shall serve the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the perfectly awakened one, together with his community of disciples, for seven days here in the royal palace."
The king said:
Rejoice in it!
The Blessed One Kāśyapa, together with the community of his disciples, was invited by the royal family for a meal for seven days.
Out of compassion, and out of consideration for those to be trained, the Blessed One Kāśyapa consented, thinking that a great multitude of people would come to be disciplined.
Those brahmins, being greatly incensed, desired to kill her while she was still alive.
Mālinī joined her palms in reverence.
Please wait for seven days while I bestow gifts.
O Brahmins, as you give, it is your own free will.
On that first day, the Teacher was fed together with his assembly in the midst of the inner apartments, in the presence of both her mother and father.
And the Teacher spoke to the king a discourse that inspires serene confidence.
And the king, together with his inner court, realized the Dharma that is free from hindrances.
On the second day, he converted five hundred sons.
And on the third day, there was also their retinue.
On the fourth day, the Perfectly Awakened One instructed the king and his ministers.
And in the fifth watch, the Teacher established the foremost of the assembly in the first fruit.
On the sixth day, the Perfectly Awakened One instructed the royal preceptor.
And in the seventh [chapter], the Nigamas, regarding the fruit of stream-entry in the Vinaya.
The king also, with a joyful heart, having beheld the Perfectly Awakened One together with his assembly, invited the Blessed One Kāśyapa for a meal of the finest food.
On the seventh day, Mālinī, having learned that the Blessed One Kāśyapa had finished his meal and had set aside his bowl, formed this aspiration:
"Without delay, may I bring an end to suffering;
may I become such a son as this Blessed One Kāśyapa is, who practices for the welfare of gods and humans."

"In this way, may my son, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, practice the conduct that benefits gods and humans. Mālinī’s brother, the prince named Aniyavanta, also made this aspiration: "May I too [attain it]."
"May my father be such as this Blessed One Kāśyapa is now;
and may I bring an end to suffering there."

Thus, by the Blessed One Kāśyapa, Kṛkī the King of Kāśi, together with his harem, five hundred princes, the ministers, the chief of the army, and for the most part all the townspeople, were disciplined in the noble dharmas; and this thought occurred to them:
Our spiritual friend Mālinī, having come to us, has purified our Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.
The brahmins will deprive her of life.
"Would that we might even sacrifice ourselves rather than Mālinī."
They sent a message to those brahmins.
"We have come here together with Mālinī; Mālinī is our spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra). You are not capable of depriving Mālinī of life while we are still alive."
When we are all gone, you will then be able to deprive that Mālinī of her life.
Then, together with their retinues and their armies and vehicles, they set Mālinī at their head, departed from Vārāṇasī, and proceeded toward where those thousands of brahmins were.
Seeing that infinite army approaching together with Mālinī, those brahmins were afraid and terrified.
They sent a messenger to the king as well.
Let Mālinī go forth and be released on that day; and she who has been struck with the rod—let her be granted sight by her father and be released from the rod.
"This Mālinī has not offended us;
it is Kāśyapa, along with his retinue, who has offended us, and we shall inflict punishment upon him."

Then, ten men equipped with armor and carrying a thousand-fold array were dispatched to Ṛṣivadana with the command: "Deprive the ascetic Kāśyapa, together with his community of disciples, of their lives."
Having been suffused with loving-kindness by the Blessed One Kāśyapa, they were established in the noble dharmas.
Those brahmins dispatched twenty other men, clad in armor and mail, saying, "Deprive the ascetic Kāśyapa of his life."
Those men, equipped with armor and weapons, went to the hermitage of the seer.

The Blessed One, having suffused them with loving-kindness, established them in the noble Dharma. In this way, whether thirty, forty, or fifty—however many were sent—they were all suffused with loving-kindness by the Blessed One Kāśyapa and established in the noble Dharmas.
This is the summoning of the Buddhas.

In order to attract those beings who were to be disciplined by the Blessed One, as many as there were thousands of brahmins there who were to be disciplined by a Buddha, they were all dispatched by him; and they were all disciplined by the Blessed One through the noble dharmas.
The remaining many thousands of living beings have entered upon a wrong path.
For those who have been disciplined by the noble dharmas, this occurs.
These brahmins do not know the greatness of the Buddha;
if they were to approach the Blessed One Kāśyapa, they would be endowed with great benefit.
They sent a messenger to those brahmins.
The Blessed One Kāśyapa, the perfectly enlightened one, was a great soul, possessed of great compassion, and engaged in favoring the world.
Sirs, do not harbor malice toward the Blessed One Kāśyapa or the community of monks.
Thus, having abandoned pride and arrogance, all of you come to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One Kāśyapa; you will be endowed with great benefit.
The speech of the Buddha is truthful, free from malice, meaningful, pure, sweet to others, clear, and gentle.
Satisfying, free from harshness, and destroying all burning afflictions—
such is the gentle speech of the Buddha, possessing a beautiful complexion and a pleasing appearance.
The Buddha’s gentle speech is free from stammering, unerring, truthful, not otherwise than it is, exactly as it is, and beyond conceptual construction.
The speech of the one of immeasurable wisdom is unarisen regarding the object of knowledge and its cognition, without end, incomparable, not subject to human control, and perfectly articulated.
He speaks truthfully and without malice,
and is further possessed of a mind of loving-kindness toward all; he acts for the benefit of others and with ultimate purpose.
This indeed is the supreme well-spoken word.
He speaks whatever is uttered by the possessed one— whether high, low, or even middling—
following word for word and syllable for syllable with perfect purity.
This indeed is the supreme well-spoken word.
He utters words endowed with supreme compassion, arising from reason, possessed of the ten fruits,
and characterized by eight qualities and four modes.
This indeed is the supreme well-spoken word.
He speaks words that are fivefold meritorious,
well-ascertained, or further, those that sever doubt;
he does not perform any evil action whatsoever.
Such is the state of supreme manliness.
Thus, having renounced his excellent kinsmen who were like jewels, he instructs this assembly of great splendor, which is endowed with the supreme marks of excellence.
And having experienced abundant delight, go forth.
Having observed that son of Nanda, who desired to conquer the state of immortality, who was like the essence of trees and possessed supreme, excellent fragrance,
and who had undergone various transformations, [the Buddha]—
Then he cooked the rice with that very same [fuel].
In this way, Kāśyapa, people of limited wisdom revile the great seer here,
whose words are well-spoken and beyond reproach.
The non-transgression of the conduct befitting a man.
Having abandoned both merit and evil,
delighting in the destruction of the fetters of existence,
he is peaceful and possesses a perfectly composed mind.
People blame that one who is free from blemish.
And these monks and lay followers, O Kāśyapa, are greatly devoted to the teaching;
they are like a blazing fire with its crest of flames.
Come, let us go together and pay homage to Kāśyapa.
This supreme among bipeds, the Guide who bestows vision,
has utterly abandoned pride and arrogance.
Come, let us go together and pay homage to Kāśyapa.

All those brahmins were fixed in the category of the eternal; even if a thousand Buddhas were to teach the Dharma, they would be incapable of understanding it or of gaining faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Then, with clubs and sticks in their hands, they rushed toward where the Blessed One Kāśyapa was.
The Blessed One addressed the Earth Deity.
Then, with a body as tall as a palm tree, she stood before the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said to that Earth Deity:
And who are those brahmins there?
Then she said:
These are my slaves, produced from the earth.
The Blessed One said:
Therefore, exert yourself just as servants are made to exert themselves.
Then, having uprooted a large palm trunk, she went out to meet those brahmins.
That palm trunk fell upon the earth with a crashing sound.
Those brahmins, terrified, perished and were destroyed.
Thus ends the story of Mālinī in the glorious Mahāvastu-Avadāna.

Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour among the Kośalas with a great community of monks, five hundred monks in all, arrived at a market town of the Kośalas called Mārakaraṇḍa and stayed there in a certain grove.

Then, at the time of evening, the Blessed One arose from his seclusion, went out from the monastery, looked upward, surveyed the quarters of the sky, looked downward, and gazed upon the level ground; then, manifesting a smile, he walked a long distance on the walking-path.
Then, at the time of evening, the venerable Ānanda saw the Blessed One rising from his seclusion, looking upward, surveying the quarters of the sky, looking downward,
and gazing upon the level ground, as he displayed a smile and walked a long distance in meditation-walking.
Having seen him, he approached where many monks were and said this to the monks:
In the evening, this Buddha, the Blessed One, having arisen from his seclusion, looked upward,
surveyed the quarters of the horizon, gazed downward, and beheld the level ground; then, manifesting a smile,
he walked a long distance in the walking meditation.
Furthermore, friends, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas do not manifest a smile without cause or condition.
But why, friends, should we not approach the Blessed One where he is and ask him about this matter?
We shall retain it exactly as the Blessed One will explain it.
"Very well, venerable sir," those monks replied to the venerable Ānanda.
Then indeed, the Venerable Ānanda, together with those monks, approached the Blessed One; having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
Here, in the evening, I saw the Blessed One emerging from his seclusion, coming out of the monastery,
looking upward and looking downward, surveying the various directions, gazing upon the level ground, manifesting a smile, and walking a long walk.
Furthermore, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas do not manifest a smile without cause or condition.
"O Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition, for manifesting a smile?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda.
"And do you, Ānanda, see this spot of earth?"
For it is even so, Blessed One.
Ānanda, on this spot of earth there was the site of the arrival of the Blessed One Kāśyapa.
"Do you see this spot of earth, Ānanda?"
For it is even so, Blessed One.
Ānanda, on this very spot of earth was the site of the hut of the Blessed One Kāśyapa.
"Do you see, Ānanda, this spot of earth?"
For it is even so, Blessed One.
Ānanda, on this spot of earth there was a walking path of sixty [leagues] belonging to the Blessed One Kāśyapa.
"Do you see this spot of earth, Ānanda?"
For it is even so, Blessed One.

Ānanda, on this very spot of earth there were the seats of three Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones: of the Blessed One Krakucchanda, of the Blessed One Kanakamuni, and of the Blessed One Kāśyapa.
Then the venerable Ānanda, filled with wonder and amazement, his hair standing on end with agitation, quickly and with great haste went to that spot of earth.
Having spread out a fourfold-layered robe upon that spot of earth and having bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One, he addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"May the Blessed One sit here on this very seat that has been prepared."

This spot of earth will have been frequented by four Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones: by the Blessed One Krakucchanda, by the Blessed One Kanakamuni, by the Blessed One Kāśyapa, and by the Blessed One here and now.
"May the Blessed One please sit upon the seat already prepared."
The venerable Ānanda, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, sat down to one side.
Those monks also, having bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, sat down to one side.
When the venerable Ānanda was seated to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
Furthermore, Ānanda, do you wish to hear the Tathāgata speak a discourse on the Dharma concerning his former abodes, beginning with this very city of Mārakaraṇḍa?
When this had been said, the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One in this way:
Now, Blessed One, this is the time; now, Sugata, this is the occasion for the Blessed One to speak on this matter to the monks.
The monks, having heard it in the presence of the Blessed One and having grasped it in his presence, will retain it as suchness.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda.
"Once upon a time, Ānanda, during the time of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, this market town of Mārakaraṇḍa was a brahmin village named Veruḍiṅga."
In the brahmin village of Veruḍiṅga, Ānanda, there was a potter named Ghaṭikāra who was an attendant to the Blessed One Kāśyapa.

Furthermore, Ānanda, Ghaṭikāra the potter had a young brahmin friend named Jyotipāla, a childhood companion who played with him in the dust; he was dear and pleasing to him, and was the son of the noble brahmin Ajanya.

Then, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa, while wandering on a tour among the Kośalas with a great community of monks— seven thousand monks in all— approached the brahmin village of Veruḍiṅga in the Kośalas; having arrived there, he stayed right there in this very forest grove.
"Ānanda, Ghaṭīkāra the potter surely heard that the Blessed One Kāśyapa, while wandering on a tour among the Kośalas,
had reached the brahmin village of Veruḍiṅga in the Kośala country and was staying right there in a certain grove."
Then, Ānanda, Ghaṭikāra the potter approached the young Brahmin Jyotipāla and said this to him:
This has been heard, Samyagjyotipāla:

it is said that the Blessed One Kāśyapa, while wandering on a tour among the Kośalas with a great saṅgha of monks— seven thousand monks in all— proceeded toward and arrived at Veruḍiṅga, a brahmin village of the Kośalas.
He dwelt right there in a certain forest grove.
Furthermore, O Samyagjyotipāla, why should we not approach the Blessed One Kāśyapa—wherever he may be—in order to see the Blessed One Kāśyapa, to pay him homage, and to attend upon him?
When this had been said, the young brahmin Jyotipāla spoke thus to Ghaṭikāra the potter:
"Ghaṭikāra, what have I to do with those shaven-headed ascetics coming to see me for the sake of paying their respects?
A second and even a third time, Ānanda, Ghaṭikāra the potter said this to the young man Jyotipāla.
"Tell me, Ghaṭikāra, what is the use of my approaching those shaven-headed ascetics for the purpose of seeing them or for attending upon them?"
Then, Ānanda, this thought occurred to Ghaṭikāra the potter:

"What indeed might be the means by which the young brahmin Jyotipāla would approach the Blessed One Kāśyapa for the purpose of seeing him and for attending upon him? Then, Ānanda, this thought occurred to Ghaṭīkāra the potter:
Indeed, not far from that very grove there is a lotus pond named Sumukā; what if I were now to go with the young Brahmin Jyotipāla to the lotus pond named Sumukā in order to bathe my head?
Then, Ānanda, Ghaṭīkāra the potter approached the young brahmin Jyotipāla and said this to him:
Furthermore, O Samyagjyotipāla, shall we go to the lotus pond named Sumukā in order to bathe our heads?
When this had been said, Ānanda, the young brahmin Jyotipāla spoke thus to Ghaṭikāra the potter:
"In that case, my dear Ghaṭikāra, be happy; do as you deem it the right time to do."
Then, Ānanda, Ghaṭikāra the potter, taking his head-bathing cloth, went together with the young brahmin Jyotipāla to that lotus pond in order to bathe.
Then, Ānanda, the young brahmin Jyotipāla, having washed his head, stood on the bank of the water arranging his hair.
Then, Ānanda, Ghaṭīkāra the potter said this to the young brahmin Jyotipāla:
"Samyagjyotipāla, this Blessed One Kāśyapa is in this very grove; why then, Samyagjyotipāla, should we not approach the Blessed One Kāśyapa to see him and to attend upon him?"
When this had been said, the young brahmin Jyotipāla spoke thus to Ghaṭikāra the potter:
"Ghaṭikāra, what need have I for those ascetics coming to see me or to pay me homage?"
Then, Ānanda, Ghaṭīkāra the potter took the young man Jyotipāla by the neck and said this to him:

"Samyagjyotipāla, this Blessed One Kāśyapa is right here in this very grove; why then, Samyagjyotipāla, should we not approach the Blessed One Kāśyapa, go to see the Blessed One Kāśyapa, and attend upon him?"
Then indeed, Ānanda, the young brahmin Jyotipāla, having shaken off Ghaṭikāra the potter, departed.
Then Ghaṭikāra the potter, having run after him and seized him by his matted hair, said this:
"Samyagjyotipāla, this Blessed One Kāśyapa is dwelling right here in this forest grove; why then, Samyajjyotipāla, should we not approach the Blessed One Kāśyapa to see him and pay him homage?"
Then, indeed, venerable Ānanda, this thought occurred to the young brahmin Jyotipāla:
It is certainly not without reason that Ghaṭikāra the potter, though being my equal in low birth, touches me on the hair of my head when I have bathed my head and am wearing a turban.
"In that case, my dear Ghaṭikāra, be happy; do as you now think best."
Then, Ānanda, Ghaṭikāra the potter, together with the young brahmin Jyotipāla, approached the Blessed One Kāśyapa;
having paid homage at the feet of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, Ānanda, Ghaṭīkāra the potter said this to the Blessed One Kāśyapa:

"Lord, this young brahmin Jyotipāla is my childhood friend, one who played with me in the dust; he is dear and pleasing to me, being the son of the noble Brahmin. May the Blessed One exhort and instruct him.
Then, Ānanda, the Blessed Kāśyapa caused the young brahmin Jyotipāla to undertake the three refuges and the five precepts.
Then, Ānanda, the young brahmin Jyotipāla said this to the Blessed One Kāśyapa:
"O Blessed One, I shall not, for now, cause all five precepts to be undertaken."
"I have indeed one man who is a harasser and an irritant, and he must be deprived of life."
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the young brahmin Jyotipāla:
Furthermore, Jyotipāla, who is that one man who is a harasser and an irritant, and who is to be deprived of life?
When this had been said, Ānanda, the young brahmin Jyotipāla spoke thus to the Blessed One Kāśyapa:
"Lord, this is Ghaṭikāra the potter, who at that time stroked my head with his hair when I had just bathed."
Then I spoke as follows.
Let us approach the Blessed One Kāśyapa in order to see him and to attend upon him.
...and furthermore, may the venerable Ghaṭikāra the potter be happy; here I undertake all these five precepts.
Then, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened Ghaṭikāra the potter and the young brahmin Jyotipāla with a discourse on the Dharma, dismissed them.
Then, Ānanda, Ghaṭikāra and the young brahmin Jyotipāla bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One Kāśyapa and departed.
Then, Ānanda, not long after he had departed, the young brahmin Jyotipāla said this to Ghaṭikāra the potter:
"Tell me, Ghaṭikāra, do you understand the perfectly taught Dharma of the Blessed One Kāśyapa just as I do?"
When this had been said, Ānanda, Ghaṭikāra the potter spoke thus to the young brahmin Jyotipāla:
When this had been said, O Samyagjyotipāla.
I too understand the perfectly taught Dharma of the Blessed One Kāśyapa exactly as you do.
When this had been said, Ānanda, the young brahmin Jyotipāla spoke thus to Ghaṭikāra the potter:
"But why, Ghaṭikāra, do you not go forth from the home life into homelessness in the presence of the Blessed One Kāśyapa?"
When this had been said, Ānanda, Ghaṭikāra the potter spoke thus to the young brahmin Jyotipāla:
"Jyotipāla, I have parents who are aged and elderly, with failing sight; they have no other attendant."
Therefore, I did not go forth from the home life into homelessness in the presence of the Blessed One Kāśyapa.
Then indeed, Ānanda, before long, a distaste for the household life arose in the young brahmin Jyotipāla, and his mind was inclined toward going forth.
Then, Ānanda, the young brahmin Jyotipāla approached Ghaṭikāra and said this to Ghaṭikāra the potter:
"Come, Ghaṭīkāra, let us together make a formal aspiration in the presence of the Blessed One Kāśyapa for the sake of going forth; I shall go forth from the home life into homelessness."
Then, Ānanda, Ghaṭīkāra the potter, taking the young brahmin Jyotipāla with him, approached the Blessed One Kāśyapa;
having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, Ānanda, Ghaṭikāra the potter said this to the Blessed One Kāśyapa:
"Venerable Sir, this young brahmin Jyotipāla is my childhood friend, one who played with me in the dust; he is dear and pleasing to me, being the son of the noble brahmin Ajanya."
May the Blessed One grant him the going-forth and confer full ordination upon him.
Then, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa addressed the monks.
"Monks, let the young brahmin Jyotipāla go forth; let him receive full ordination."
Then, Ānanda, the monks ordained the young brahmin Jyotipāla.
Then, Ānanda, not long after the monk Jyotipāla had received full ordination, the Blessed One Kāśyapa set out on a wandering tour among the Kośalas and the Kāśīs.

Then, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa, while wandering on a tour among the Kāśīs together with a great community of monks— seven thousand monks in all— approached the city of Vārāṇasī in the land of the Kāśīs; having arrived there,
he stayed right there in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana.

Ānanda, King Kṛkī indeed heard that the Blessed One Kāśyapa, while wandering on a tour among the Kāśīs with a great saṅgha of seven thousand bhikṣus, had reached the city of Vārāṇasī in the land of the Kāśīs and was staying right there in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana.
Then, Ānanda, Kṛkī, the King of Kāśī, addressed a certain man.
"Come, my good man, go to where the Blessed One Kāśyapa is, and in my name offer salutations to the Blessed One Kāśyapa."

Kṛkī, the King of Kāśī, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, inquired after his freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, strength, well-being, and comfortable dwelling; he then invited him, together with the community of monks, for a meal at his residence on the following day, and the Blessed One Kāśyapa accepted his invitation.
When this had been said, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa spoke thus to that man.
"May Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi, together with his son and his retinue, be happy;
now do as you deem timely."
Then that man, having understood the Blessed One’s consent, set out for the city of Vārāṇasī.
Then, Ānanda, that man went to where Kṛkī, the King of Kāśī, was.
He spoke thus to Kṛkin, the king of Kāśī:
"O Great King, I have conveyed your salutation to the Blessed One Kāśyapa."

Inquiring after his freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, well-being, strength, and comfortable dwelling, he invited him, together with the community of monks, for a meal on the following day.
And the Blessed One Kāśyapa consented, saying, "Do now as you deem it timely."
Then, Ānanda, on that very night, King Kṛkī of Kāśi had abundant and exquisite food, both hard and soft, prepared; and when that night had passed, he addressed a certain man.
"Come, my good man, go to where the Blessed One Kāśyapa is, and having approached the Blessed One Kāśyapa, speak to him thus:"
"It is time, Blessed One; it is the time for the Blessed One to accept a meal at the residence of Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi, if the Blessed One deems it the right occasion."
"Very well, Great King," that man replied to Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi, and having departed from the city of Vārāṇasī, he set out for the Ṛṣivadana Deer Park.
Then, Ānanda, that man approached where the Blessed One Kāśyapa was, prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, and said this to the Blessed One Kāśyapa:
"It is time, Blessed One, for the meal at the residence of King Kṛkī; now, Blessed One, please do as you deem fit."

Then, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa, having given his assent to that man, dressed early in the morning, took his bowl and robe, and, surrounded and preceded by the community of monks, set out for the city of Vārāṇasī.

At that time, Ānanda, Kṛkī, the King of Kāśī, surrounded by his princes and ministers, stood at the gate of his own palace, waiting for the Blessed One Kāśyapa together with his community of disciples.
Ānanda, King Kṛkī of Kāśi indeed saw the Blessed One Kāśyapa approaching from afar together with his community of disciples.

Having seen him, he approached where the Blessed One Kāśyapa was together with his community of disciples; having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One Kāśyapa and his community of disciples, and having placed the Blessed One Kāśyapa and his community of disciples in front of him, he led them into his own residence.
Now at that time, in the residence of Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi, there was a palace named Kokanada, newly built and recently completed, which had not yet been used by any ascetic or brahmin.
Then, Ānanda, Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi, said this to the Blessed One Kāśyapa:
“Blessed One, in my residence there is a new palace named Kokanada, recently completed and never before occupied by any ascetic or brahmin; may the Blessed One be the first to enjoy it.”
"After the Blessed One has partaken, we shall partake afterwards."
When this had been said, the Blessed One Kāśyapa spoke thus to Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi.
Therefore, O Great King, may you be happy; do now as you deem timely.
Then indeed, Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi, had seats prepared in the Kokanada palace and had hard and soft foods served.
Then the Blessed One, having ascended the Kokanada palace, sat down upon the seat that had been prepared, as did the community of monks upon their respective seats.
Then indeed, Ānanda, King Kṛkī of Kāśi personally satisfied and served the Blessed One Kāśyapa with various kinds of solid and soft food.
And for each one, seven men [prepared] with sevenfold mortars and with rice from the *parṇakulaka* variety.

Then King Kṛkī of Kāśi, knowing that the Blessed One Kāśyapa had finished his meal, had washed his hands, and set aside his bowl, took a certain low seat and approached the Blessed One Kāśyapa; having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, he sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, Ānanda, Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi, said this to the Blessed One Kāśyapa:
May the Blessed One consent to spend the rains retreat in the city of Vārāṇasī.

“Blessed One, I shall have a monastery built, and in it I will provide seven thousand gabled chambers, seven thousand seats, seven thousand walkways, seven thousand horses, and seven thousand monastery attendants, who shall each individually serve the community of monks.”
"With such service as this, they shall attend upon the Blessed One and the community of monks. When this had been said, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa spoke thus to Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi:
For it is not possible, Great King, that my rainy-season retreat will take place among the Vajjis.
A second and a third time, it should be done in exactly the same way.
Then, Ānanda, King Kṛkī of Kāśi, thinking, "The Blessed One Kāśyapa does not consent to spend the rains retreat in the city of Vārāṇasī," wept and shed tears.
Then, Ānanda, Kṛkī, the king of Kāśi, said this to the Blessed One Kāśyapa:
Furthermore, does the Blessed One have another attendant such as I am?
When this had been said, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa spoke thus to King Kṛkī.
"Indeed, O Great King, you are an incomplete attendant to me."
When this had been said, Ānanda, Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi, spoke thus to the Blessed One Kāśyapa.
But who is my attendant who serves me more fully and more perfectly than Pūrṇa?
When this had been said, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa spoke thus to Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi:
"Great King, there is indeed in your own realm a brahmin village named Veruḍiṅga."
There, Ghaṭīkāra was my attendant.
When this had been said, Ānanda, Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi, spoke thus to the Blessed One Kāśyapa:
But of what kind, Blessed One, were Ghaṭīkāra’s riches, with which he serves the Blessed One and the Saṅgha?
When this had been said, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa spoke thus to Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi:

Great King, Ghaṭikāra the potter has for as long as life lasts abstained from taking life; for as long as life lasts he has abstained from taking what is not given; for as long as life lasts he has abstained from unchaste conduct; for as long as life lasts he has abstained from false speech;

for as long as life lasts he has abstained from fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which cause heedlessness; and for as long as life lasts he has abstained from dancing, singing, and instrumental music.

He is abstinent for as long as life lasts from the wearing of perfumes, garlands, and cosmetics; he is abstinent for as long as life lasts from high and luxurious beds; he is abstinent for as long as life lasts from eating at improper times; and he is abstinent for as long as life lasts from the acceptance of gold and silver.
"Indeed, Great King, Ghaṭikāra the potter does not dig the earth himself.

Rather, he takes clay from those places where it has been thrown up by mice, or where it has been deposited by water, or where it has been cut away by water; having taken that clay and fashioned vessels, he sets them down at the crossroads."
Those who have need of those vessels fill them with either split mung beans, split black gram, or split rice, pour them out, take their vessels,
and depart without even a look back.
Such, O Great King, were the enjoyments of Ghaṭikāra the potter, with which he served both the Tathāgata and the Saṅgha.
And his parents were aged, elderly, and weak of sight.
"Once upon a time, Great King, I was staying at Veruḍiṅga, a brahmin village."
Therefore, Great King, having dressed early in the morning and taken my bowl and robe, I set out for the brahmin village of Veruḍiṅga for alms.
Thus, Great King, while wandering for alms with a formal declaration in the brahmin village of Veruḍiṅga, I approached the dwelling of Ghaṭīkāra the potter and stood at the entrance.
At that time, Ghaṭīkāra the potter had just come out from his own dwelling.
Then, O Great King, the mother and father of Ghaṭīkāra the potter said this to the Tathāgata:
"Your attendant has departed, Blessed One."
"Here in the upper storeroom are both soup and rice; may the Blessed One partake from this."
Therefore, O Great King, having had the soup and rice from the upper storehouse accepted by the deities and having partaken of it myself, I departed.
Then, O Great King, Ghaṭikāra the potter went to his own residence.
Indeed, Great King, Ghaṭikāra the potter, having seen that the soup and rice from the upper store-room had been consumed, spoke thus again to his parents:
"Father, by whom were these side-dishes, broth, and rice from Ghaṭīkāra’s upper storehouse consumed?"
When this had been said, O Great King, the parents of Ghaṭikāra the potter spoke thus to Ghaṭikāra the potter:
By the Blessed One, the son of Kāśyapa.
Then, indeed, O Great King, this thought occurred to Ghaṭikāra the potter:
Moreover, it is a great gain for me that I have obtained, since even a single person has become so exceedingly trusting in me, as has the Blessed One Kāśyapa.
And thus, for half a month, the bliss of joy did not leave his body; and for seven days, it remained with his parents, who were aged, elderly, and weak of sight.
Once, Great King, at a time when the thatch for the Tathāgata’s forest hut was being repaired, the grasses could not be found.
Therefore, O Great King, I addressed the monks.
"Go, monks, to the house of Ghaṭikāra the potter and bring some grass."
Then indeed, O Great King, those monks approached the dwelling of Ghaṭīkāra the potter.
Furthermore, Great King, at that time Ghaṭīkāra the potter had gone out from his own dwelling.
They did not see any grass there; they saw a newly thatched workshop hall.
Then, O Great King, those monks approached the Tathāgata, bowed their heads at the feet of the Tathāgata, and addressed the Tathāgata as follows.
"O Blessed One, your attendant has departed; there is no grass here at all, but there is a newly thatched workshop shed."
When this had been said, O Great King, he spoke thus to that bhikṣu:
"Go, monks, to Ghaṭikāra the potter’s workshop with its new roof; strip off the thatch and bring the grass here."
Then, O Great King, those monks approached the dwelling of Ghaṭikāra the potter and cleared away the grass from Ghaṭikāra the potter’s newly thatched workshop.
Then, O Great King, the parents of Ghaṭikāra the potter said this to those bhikṣus:
"Who is this who, having stripped the new roof of Ghaṭikāra the potter's workshop, is carrying away the straw?"
When this had been said, O Great King, those monks said this to the parents of Ghaṭīkāra the potter:
Venerable sir, wherever the monks lack sufficient grass for covering the forest huts of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, there these grasses are taken.
When this had been said, O Great King, the mother and father of Ghaṭīkāra the potter spoke thus to those monks.
Take them, take them, and your own as well!
Then, Great King, Ghaṭīkāra the potter went to his own dwelling.
"Indeed, Great King, Ghaṭikāra the potter saw that the new-roofed workshop had been stripped of its straw; and seeing that the straw had been taken away, he said this to his parents:
'Father, by whom has this new-roofed workshop of Ghaṭikāra the potter been stripped of its straw and the straw removed?'"
When this had been said, Ghaṭikāra’s parents spoke thus to Ghaṭikāra the potter:
The grasses in the forest hut of the Blessed One Kāśyapa’s son are no longer growing; those grasses have been carried away by the monks.
Then, indeed, O Great King, this thought occurred to Ghaṭikāra the potter:
Well-gained indeed are my gains, since even this Blessed One Kāśyapa has become so exceedingly trusted by me, even to the point of being like one of my own people.
And for one month, the bliss of joy did not leave his body; and for half a month, it did not leave that of his blind parents.

Furthermore, Great King, I do not recall Ghaṭikāra the potter ever experiencing such dejection as you have now, namely that the Blessed One Kāśyapa did not consent to spend the rainy season retreat in the city of Vārāṇasī.
Then, Ānanda, this thought occurred to Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi:
It is a great gain for me, truly well-obtained, that such a practitioner of the holy life dwells within my domain—he who is a field of merit among two-legged beings.
Then, Ānanda, King Kṛkī of Kāśi sent a hundred wagons to Ghaṭikāra the potter, who lived in a house of leaves, carrying fresh water and boiled oil and salt.
Then, Ānanda, Kāśyapa, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened Kṛkī, the King of Kāśi, with a discourse on the Dharma, rose from his seat and departed.
Then, Ānanda, after the meal, when he had returned from his alms-round, the Blessed One Kāśyapa addressed the monks.

"Sit down, monks; assemble, monks! Bind yourselves in the cross-legged posture. For I shall remain bound in this cross-legged posture until the minds of these seven thousand monks, seated upon these very seats, are liberated from the outflows through non-clinging."
"Very well, Blessed One," those monks replied to the Blessed Kāśyapa, and they sat down together, assembled, and took their seats cross-legged.
Then, Ānanda, while the monk Jyotipāla was alone in seclusion and in retreat, this reflection arose in his mind: "O, may I in a future time become a Tathāgata,
an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed."
The Teacher of gods and humans.
Thus, having directly known this world— with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, and this generation with its ascetics and brahmins,

its gods and humans— I shall set in motion here in Vārāṇasī, at the Deer Park in Ṛṣivadana, the Wheel of Dharma in its twelve aspects, which cannot be turned back by any ascetic, brahmin, god, Māra, or anyone else in the world in accordance with the Dharma.
And may I thus teach the Dharma, endowed with all aspects and complete in all aspects, just as the Blessed One Kāśyapa does now.
And thus gods and humans will consider that what was to be heard and believed in the time of the Blessed One Kāśyapa is likewise [to be heard and believed] now.

May I become that for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, welfare, and happiness of the great mass of beings, both gods and humans.
The hosts of asuras diminished, and the divine hosts increased.
Then, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa, having known with his own mind such a reflection that had arisen in the mind of the monk Jyotipāla, addressed a certain monk.
"Come, monk, go to where the monk Jyotipāla is, and having approached him, speak thus to the monk Jyotipāla."
"Venerable one, the Teacher calls you;
approach where the Tathāgata is."
Having received the command of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, he approached the monk Jyotipāla and said this to him:
The Teacher addressed the Venerable Jyotipāla: "Go to where the Blessed One is."

"Very well, venerable sir," the venerable Jyotipāla replied to that monk, and having approached the Blessed One Kāśyapa, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One Kāśyapa and sat down to one side.
When the venerable monk Jyotipāla was seated to one side, the Blessed One Kāśyapa said this to him:
"Was it not, Jyotipāla, that while Jyotipāla was alone, in seclusion, and withdrawn in meditation, this kind of reflection arose in his mind?"

"O, may I in a future time become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans!"

Thus, having directly known this world and the world beyond, including the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, and this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, may I set in motion right here in Vārāṇasī, at the Deer Park in Ṛṣivadana, the Wheel of Dharma—
threefold in its revolutions and twelvefold in its aspects— which cannot be turned back by any ascetic, brahmin, or Māra.
or by Brahmā, or by anyone else in the world, together with justice.
And may I teach the Dharma endowed with all aspects and perfected in all aspects, just as the Blessed One Kāśyapa does now.
And thus may I maintain the entire community of monks just as the Blessed One Kāśyapa does now.
And thus may both gods and humans consider me worthy to be heard and believed, just as they do now for the Blessed One Kāśyapa.
May that be for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of the great multitude of both gods and humans.
The hosts of asuras diminished, while the divine hosts increased.
Thus addressed, Ānanda, the bhikṣu Jyotipāla said this to the Blessed One Kāśyapa:
"So it is, Blessed One."
When this had been said, Ānanda, the Blessed One spoke thus to the monk Jyotipāla:

Therefore, Jyotipāla, give this golden seat and pair of fine cloths to the community of monks headed by the Buddha; having performed this merit, both gods and humans will consider it worthy of being heard and believed.
Ānanda, the monk Jyotipāla indeed gave a golden seat and a pair of fine garments to the community of monks headed by the Buddha.
Then, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa, having manifested a smile, gave a prophecy concerning the monk Jyotipāla.

Jyotipāla, in a future time you shall become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed,
a teacher of gods and humans.
Having directly known this world and the world beyond, including the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās,

and this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, you shall set in motion right here in Vārāṇasī, at the Deer Park in Ṛṣivadana, the Wheel of Dharma— threefold in its revolutions and twelvefold in its aspects— which has not been set in motion by anyone.
Neither by a śramaṇa, nor by a brāhmaṇa, nor by a deva, nor by Māra, nor by anyone else in the world, can it be overturned in accordance with the Dharma.
And thus you shall teach the Dharma, endowed with all aspects and complete in every aspect, just as the Blessed One Kāśyapa does now.
And in this way, you will lead the entire community of disciples, just as the Blessed One Kāśyapa does now.
And thus those gods and humans will consider that which is to be heard and believed, just as they do now for the Blessed One Kāśyapa.

You will become one for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, welfare, and happiness of the great mass of beings, both gods and humans.
The hosts of asuras will diminish, and the divine hosts will increase.
Then indeed, Ānanda, when the Blessed One Kāśyapa had prophesied concerning Jyotipāla, the gods of the earth raised a cry.

"Friends, this monk named Jyotipāla has been prophesied by the Blessed One Kāśyapa: 'In a future time, he will become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans.'"
Having directly known this world and the world beyond, having directly known the world with its gods, its Māras, and its Brahmās,

and this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans— right here in Vārāṇasī, at the Deer Park in Ṛṣivadana, he will set in motion the Wheel of Dharma, which has three turnings and twelve aspects, and which cannot be turned back by any ascetic or [brahmin].
Neither by a brahmin, nor by a deva, nor by Māra, nor by Brahmā, nor by anyone else in the world, can it be [overturned] in accordance with the Dharma.
In this way, he will teach the Dharma endowed with all excellent aspects and complete in all its aspects, just as the Blessed One Kāśyapa does now.
That will be for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of the great multitude of beings, both gods and humans.
The hosts of asuras will diminish, and the divine hosts will increase.
Having heard the sound of the gods of the earth, the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, the Nirmāṇarati, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin [gods] [heard it as well].
At that moment, a cry rose up from the Brahmakāyika host of gods.

"Venerable sir, this monk named Jyotipāla has been prophesied by the Blessed One Kāśyapa: 'In a future time, he will become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans.'"
Having directly known this world and the world beyond, having directly known the world with its gods, its Māras, and its Brahmās,

and this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, he will here in Vārāṇasī, at the Deer Park in Ṛṣivadana, set in motion the Wheel of Dharma— threefold in its revolutions and twelvefold in its aspects— which cannot be turned back by any ascetic.
or by a brahmin, or by a deva, or by Māra, or by Brahmā, or indeed by anyone else in the world, together with reason.
And thus he will teach the Dharma, endowed with all aspects and complete in all aspects, just as the Blessed One Kāśyapa does now.
And thus gods and humans will think that what is to be heard and believed is just as it was for the Blessed One Kāśyapa in the present.
That will be for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of the great multitude of gods and humans.
The hosts of asuras will diminish, and the divine hosts will increase.
Then, Ānanda, when that sound had vanished, the Blessed One Kāśyapa instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened those monks with a discourse on the Dharma.
"Monks, reflect in this way; do not reflect in that way. Attend to your minds in this way; do not attend to them in that way."

Monks, dwell with yourselves as an island and no other island; with yourselves as a refuge and no other refuge. Dwell with the Dharma as an island and no other island; with the Dharma as a refuge and no other refuge.

Then indeed the Blessed One, with his body blazing, flaming, and turned into a mass of light, rose into the air to the height of a palm tree and instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the monks with a discourse on the Dharma.

"Thus, O monks, reflect; do not reflect thus. Attend to this; do not attend to that. Monks, dwell with yourselves as your island, not another as your island; with yourselves as your refuge, not another as your refuge; with the Dharma as your island, not another as your island;
with the Dharma as your refuge, not another as your refuge."
Then, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa rose up into the air from one palm-tree height to two palm-tree heights;
from two to three, from three to four, from four to five, from five to six, and from six to seven palm-tree heights.
Standing at the height of seven palm trees, he instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened those monks with a discourse on the Dharma.
He encourages and gladdens them.
"Monks, think thus; do not think thus. Attend to this; do not attend to that."

"Monks, dwell with yourselves as your island, not with another as your island; with yourselves as your refuge, not with another as your refuge; with the Dharma as your refuge, not with another as your refuge."

Then, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa, descending from the height of seven palm trees to six, from six to five, from five to four, from four to three, from three to two, from two to one, and finally from one palm tree down to his own seat, sat down and instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened those monks with a discourse on the Dharma.
"Monks, reflect in this way; do not reflect in that way. Attend to things in this way; do not attend to them in that way."

"Monks, dwell with yourselves as your island and not another as your island; with yourselves as your refuge and not another as your refuge; with the Dharma as your island and not another as your island; with the Dharma as your refuge and not another as your refuge."
Then, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kāśyapa, breaking his cross-legged posture, addressed those monks.
"Monks, I break the cross-legged posture of all these seven thousand monks while they remain seated on these very seats, as their minds are liberated from the outflows through non-clinging—
with the exception of the monk Jyotipāla."
He too has been prophesied by me for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, Ānanda, it might occur to you that the monk named Jyotipāla at that time and on that occasion was someone else. But it should not be thought thus.
This should not be viewed in such a way.
At that time, on that occasion, I was the monk named Jyotipāla.
The Blessed One spoke thus; the Venerable Ānanda, being uplifted in mind, and those seven thousand monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
Thus ends the Jyotipālasūtra in the glorious Mahāvastu-avadāna.

After the monk Jyotipāla had prepared a drink of rice gruel for the Blessed One Kāśyapa and his community of disciples, he purchased saffron for one hundred thousand [pieces of gold] and sprinkled it over the Blessed One Kāśyapa and his community of disciples; he also gave a golden seat and a set of fine garments to the Blessed One Kāśyapa.
And thus he made this aspiration:

Just as this Blessed One Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, his body adorned with the eighty minor characteristics, endowed with the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha,
powerful with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and confident with the four grounds of self-confidence— oh, may I too in the future [be so].
May I become, in the course of time, a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly enlightened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world,
an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, just as this Blessed One Kāśyapa is now.
And thus may I set in motion the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, with its three turnings and twelve aspects, just as the Blessed One Kāśyapa does now.
And in this way I would maintain a community of disciples, just as the Blessed One Kāśyapa does now.
And thus both those gods and humans will consider me worthy of being heard and worthy of being trusted, just as they do now for the Blessed One Kāśyapa.

"Thus, having crossed over, may I help others cross; being liberated, may I liberate others; being comforted, may I comfort others; having attained final nirvāṇa, may I lead others to final nirvāṇa, just as this Blessed One Kāśyapa does now."

May I become that for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, welfare, and happiness of the great multitude of beings, both gods and humans.
Jyotipāla was prophesied by Kāśyapa for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Jyotipāla, in a future time, you shall become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha (samyaksaṃbuddha), endowed with knowledge and conduct (vidyācaraṇasampanna), a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, and a teacher of gods and humans; in this very Fortunate Aeon (bhadrakalpa), immediately following [me], you shall be endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty [minor marks].

His body was adorned with the secondary marks; he was endowed with the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, powerful through the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and confident through the four grounds of self-confidence.

Thus, having crossed over, you will help others cross; being liberated, you will liberate others; being comforted, you will comfort others; having attained final nirvana, you will lead others to final nirvana, just as I do now.

Thus you shall be for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of a great multitude of people, out of compassion for the world, and for the sake of both gods and humans.
As soon as the monk Jyotipāla had been thus predicted by the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Awakened One,
this great earth shook, trembled, and quaked violently in six ways; and the gods of the earth raised a cry and made their voices heard.
It should be explained in detail as it is in other grammatical treatises, for such is the Blessed One’s own vow.
Having gone forth as a follower of Kāśyapa, Jyotipāla the Bodhisattva was instructed by the Perfectly Awakened One: "Cleanse the monastery and provide water."
Jyotipāla, the Bodhisattva, desiring the cessation of existence, gave rice gruel to drink, along with a golden seat and a pair of garments.
Having given that gift, he made this aspiration: "May I become a leader of the world, a teacher of gods and humans, and may I proclaim the noble Dharma."
And thus may there be this revelation of the Dharma for me, and thus may I establish many beings in the noble Dharmas.

And thus may gods and humans hear my words; and thus may I set in motion the wheel of Dharma for the benefit of many; may I kindle the torch of Dharma, beat the drum of Dharma, raise the banner of Dharma with its pennants, and blow the conch of Dharma, for those fallen into hardship, oppressed by birth and old age, subject to death, and blinded by existence.
I would establish them with the eye of wisdom regarding the states of woe.

In the Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, and Avīci hells, and throughout the six realms of existence, may I liberate those who are scattered; those who are cooked and ripened in hell, oppressed by the lower realms, subject to death, and possessing little happiness and much suffering—
may I liberate them from the cycle of existence.
I shall act for the benefit of the world, and I shall teach the Dharma to gods and humans.
In this way, he disciplines sentient beings, just as this Light of the World does.
"You shall become a Buddha, a leader of the world, in this future Fortunate Aeon; you,
a Śākyan, in the place called Kapila at Ṛṣivadana."
Then the fruition of your vow will come to pass.

Having practiced the holy life (brahmacarya) that was unbroken, flawless, unspotted, untarnished, complete, and utterly pure, he passed away and was reborn in the divine realm named Tuṣita as a son of the gods named Śvetaketu, possessing great psychic power and great majesty; he surpasses other gods in ten divine respects: in divine lifespan, divine complexion, and divine happiness.
With divine sovereignty, with a divine retinue, with a divine form, with divine sounds, with divine fragrances, with divine tastes, and with divine objects of touch.
Other sons of the gods also questioned him regarding whatever was to be asked.

This son of the gods named Śvetaketu is learned, discerning, confident, skillful, and wise; he has followed the religious life under forty thousand Buddhas and has performed services for eighty-five thousand Buddhas—not to mention the ninety-six million Pratyekabuddhas and the great powerful Śrāvakas.
Forty thousand Buddhas, leaders of the world, have entered parinirvāṇa—
those under whom the Jina practiced the holy life, seeking the cessation of existence.
Fifty thousand Buddhas, the leaders of the world, have entered parinirvāṇa—
those Victors through whom the Jina brought about his passing, seeking the cessation of existence.
Ninety-six koṭis of self-arisen Pratyekabuddhas have entered parinirvāṇa,
during whose time the Jina passed away, seeking the cessation of existence.
While those immeasurable millions of Arhats, great meditators, were passing away,
the Jina met his end, seeking the cessation of existence.
Among these, the former practices of the Teacher, the One Possessing the Ten Powers, have been proclaimed.
Few have been spoken of, many remain unsaid, among whom the Jina passed away while seeking the cessation of existence.
Thus ends the prophecy concerning Jyotipāla in the glorious Mahāvastu-Avadāna.
The beginning of the royal lineage.
Monks, there comes that time, there comes that occasion, when, after the passing of a long period, this world undergoes dissolution.
Furthermore, monks, when the world is undergoing dissolution, for the most part sentient beings are reborn in the Ābhāsvara host of gods.
Monks, there comes that time, there comes that occasion, when after the passing of a long period, this world evolves.

Furthermore, monks, when the world is evolving and the configuration of the world has been established, certain beings, due to the exhaustion of their lifespan and the exhaustion of their karma, pass away from the Ābhāsvara host of gods and come into this state of existence.
Those beings are self-luminous, moving through the air, made of mind, feeding on joy, abiding in happiness, and going wherever they desire.

Furthermore, monks, it is the natural law (dharmatā) that for those beings who were self-luminous, moving through the air, made of mind, feeding on joy, abiding in bliss, and going wherever they desired; [this was their nature].
These two, the moon and the sun, would not be discerned in the world.
When the moon and sun were not perceived in the world, the forms of the stars were not perceived in the world.
When the forms of the stars were no longer discernible in the world, the paths of the constellations could not be discerned in the world;
when the paths of the constellations were no longer discernible in the world, night and day could not be discerned in the world;
and when night and day were no longer discernible in the world, months and fortnights could not be discerned in the world.
When months and half-months are no longer known in the world, the seasons and years are not known in the world.
It is indeed the natural law, monks, that for those beings who are self-luminous, who move through the air, and who go wherever they desire, [this occurs].
This great earth, too, would emerge like a pool of water.
And it was endowed with excellent color and endowed with excellent flavor; its taste was just like pure, small-cell honey, and its appearance was just like a stream of milk or a stream of ghee.
Then, monks, a certain being who was fickle and of a greedy nature tasted that essence of the earth with his finger.
He relishes it for its color, its fragrance, and its flavor as well.
Other beings also, having seen that being, fall into imitation of him.
They too tasted the essence of the earth with their fingers.
He causes them to taste it as well, even to the extent of its flavor.
Then, monks, at a later time, that being took that essence of the earth as food, making it into morsels.
Other beings also, having seen that being, fall into imitation of him.
They too took that essence of the earth as food, making it into morsels.

And when, monks, those beings took that essence of the earth as food in mouthfuls, then heaviness, coarseness, and hardness came upon their bodies; and that which they had previously possessed—their self-luminosity, their movement through the air, their mind-made bodies, their feeding on joy, their abiding in happiness, and their ability to go wherever they wished—that disappeared.

[When beings] possessed self-luminosity, moved through the air, were mind-made, fed on joy, and went wherever they desired, the sun and moon became manifest in the world; when the sun and moon were manifest in the world, the forms of the stars became manifest in the world; when the forms of the stars were manifest in the world, the paths of the constellations became manifest in the world.
When the paths of the constellations are known in the world, day and night are known in the world;
when day and night are known in the world, months and fortnights are known in the world;
and when months and fortnights are known, the seasons and years are known in the world.
Then, monks, those beings, consuming that essence of the earth as their food, remained for a very long time, having that as their color, that as their nourishment, and that as their sustenance.
Those among them who took much food became ill-favored in complexion, while those who took little food were possessed of a beautiful complexion.
Those who were beautiful in color looked down upon those beings who were ill-favored in color.
We are beings possessed of beautiful color, while these others are of ugly color.
While they were dwelling thus, characterized by pride and arrogance, and conditioned by their physical appearance and secondary marks, the essence of the earth (pṛthivīrasa) disappeared.
A crust of earth would appear, having a color and appearance just like that of a mushroom.
And it was endowed with excellent color and endowed with excellent fragrance; its taste was just like that of pure, small-bee honey.
Then, monks, when that essence of the earth had disappeared, those beings uttered this inspired exclamation:
"Oh, what flavor! Oh, what flavor!"
Just as, monks, people nowadays, having eaten good food and being happy after their meal, utter this inspired utterance (udāna).
"Oh, what flavor! Oh, what flavor!"
They approached that very same ancient, imperishable, and unchanging fire, yet they did not discern its true meaning.
Then, monks, those beings, consuming that food of earth-crust, remained for a very long time, having that as their color, that as their nourishment, and that as their sustenance.
Those among them who consumed much food became ill-favored in appearance, while those who consumed little food became possessed of a beautiful complexion.
Those who possessed a beautiful complexion despised those beings who had an ugly complexion.
"We are beautiful in color, while these beings are ugly."
As they dwelt there, characterized by pride and arrogance based on their physical appearance and complexion, the crust of earth disappeared and forest creepers appeared.

Just as a *kalambukā* plant possesses such a brilliant appearance, and is perfect in color, perfect in fragrance, and perfect in flavor— its taste being just like that of pure, unadulterated honey— so too [is this].
Then, monks, when the crust of earth had disappeared, those beings lamented.
"O, he speaks! O, he speaks!"

Monks, it is just as if beings at present, when touched by some painful condition, were to groan, "Aho! Aho!"—uttering that very same ancient, unchanging sound—which they would not understand in its true meaning.
In the same way, monks, when that crust of earth had disappeared, those beings lamented.
"O, he speaks! O, he speaks!"

Then, monks, when that crust of earth had disappeared, those beings, subsisting on forest creepers as their food, possessing that same color, eating that same food, and consuming that same sustenance, remained for a very long time.
Those among them who ate much food became ill-favored in appearance, while those who ate little food became possessed of a beautiful complexion.
Those beings despised her because of her ugly appearance.
"We are beautiful in color, while these beings are ugly."

When those [beings], who were characterized by pride and arrogance based on their physical appearance and complexion, had disappeared, the forest creepers vanished. Then rice appeared—without husks, without powder, fragrant grain—which, when harvested in the evening, was found in the morning to have grown, ripened, and sprouted again, such that no trace of its having been cut was even discernible.
Even that which is harvested in the morning becomes grown, ripened, and fully developed by evening, and no trace of its cutting is perceived.
Then, monks, when that forest creeper had disappeared, those beings lamented.
"Alas, I say! Alas, I say! he cried.
Just as, monks, beings nowadays, when touched by some such painful condition, would lament.
They approached that very same ancient, imperishable, and unchanging fire, yet they did not discern its true meaning.
Then, monks, when that forest creeper had disappeared, those beings remained for a very long time subsisting on that rice which was without powder or husk, consisting of fragrant grains of rice.
And when, monks, those beings took as food that rice which was without powder or husk, consisting of fragrant grains,
then the female characteristics appeared among the women and the male characteristics appeared among the men.
With minds excessively impassioned, they gazed intently at one another.
With hearts full of passion for one another and gazing intently at each other, they became mutually enamored; being thus mutually enamored, they violated one another.
Furthermore, monks, those beings who saw others being violated there would throw sticks at them, they would throw clods of earth, and they would even throw dust.
"Friends, unrighteousness has appeared in the world; friends, the false dharma has appeared in the world, in that a being indeed defiles another being."

Monks, it was just as if, when a girl is being carried away in marriage today, people were to hurl sticks at her or even clods of earth at her; yet that very ancient syllable would fall upon her fire-pit, and they would not discern its meaning.
At that time, monks, it was indeed considered contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the sacrifice, and contrary to the Vinaya;
but now, monks, it is indeed considered in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the sacrifice, and in accordance with the Vinaya.
Then, monks, those beings, distressed and repelled by that unrighteousness, lived apart for one day, they lived apart for two days,
they lived apart for three days, they lived apart for four days, and they lived apart for five days, for a fortnight, and even for a month.
They went away and had even household chores performed, solely for the purpose of concealing that very unrighteousness.
Then, monks, it occurred to a certain being who had gone to fetch rice:
"What is his name? Why do I toil? How did I toil in the past? For evening meals in the evening, and for morning meals in the morning."
"What if I were now to carry all at once the rice for both the morning and the evening meal?"
Monks, that being indeed gathered the divine rice all at once, both for the evening and for the morning.
Then, monks, a certain being said this to that being:
"Come, O being, let us go to gather rice."
When this had been said, monks, that being spoke thus to that other being:
Go now, O being; I have brought rice that provides for both evening and morning all at once.
Then, monks, this thought occurred to that being as well:
Even if it is done in this way, it is excellent;
what if I were also to carry that rice all at once for two days' or three days' supply?
Monks, that being indeed brought forth rice for two days or three days at a single time.
Then, monks, a certain being said this to that being:
"Come, O being, let us go to gather rice."
When this had been said, that being spoke thus to that being:
"Go, O being! I have brought for you at once rice that ripens in two or three days. Then, monks, this thought occurred to that being as well:
Even so, being done now, it will be excellent.
"What if I were now to bring back rice sufficient for four or five days?"
Monks, that being indeed brought forth rice for four days or five days at a single time.

And when, monks, those beings began to consume that rice— which was without powder and without husk, consisting of fragrant grains— by means of storing it up, then indeed powder and husk appeared upon that rice.
Even that which was harvested in the evening would, by morning, not have sprouted, nor ripened, nor grown, yet its cut surface would still be visible.
Then, monks, those beings ran together; having run together and assembled, they deliberated with incantations.
Sirs, we are self-luminous, moving through the air, made of mind, feeding on joy, abiding in happiness, and going wherever we desire.
For us—who were self-luminous, moving through the air, mind-made, feeding on joy, abiding in happiness, and going wherever we desired—the moon and sun were not perceived.

When the moon and sun were not perceived in the world, the forms of the stars were not perceived; when the forms of the stars were not perceived in the world, the paths of the constellations were not perceived in the world;
and when the paths of the constellations were not perceived in the world, night and day were not perceived.
When nights and days were no longer discernible, months and fortnights were not discerned;
when months and fortnights were not discerned, seasons and years were not discerned.
This great earth also rises up like a pool of water.
Just as, for example, a stream of ghee or a stream of milk, so too did they appear in color, being perfect in color, perfect in fragrance, and perfect in taste;
their flavor was just like that of pure, small-bee honey.
Then, indeed, O sirs, a certain being who was fickle and of a greedy nature tasted that essence of the earth with his finger.
He relishes it for its color, its fragrance, and its flavor.
Then, indeed, O sirs, that being at a later time took that essence of the earth as food, making it into morsels.
Having seen that being, we too would adopt his imitation and take that essence of the earth as our food, making it into morsels.
But from the time we, sirs, began to take the essence of the earth as food in morsels, heaviness, coarseness, and hardness came upon our bodies.

That which he formerly possessed—his self-luminosity, his movement through the air, his mind-made body, his feeding on joy, his dwelling in happiness, and his power to go wherever he desired—that all disappeared.

Because those beings possessed self-luminosity, the ability to travel through the air, bodies made of mind, the consumption of joy, abiding in happiness, and the power to go wherever they desired, the moon and sun became manifest in the world.
When the moon and sun were made manifest in the world,
the forms of the stars became manifest.
As the forms of the stars became manifest, the paths of the constellations became manifest;
as the paths of the constellations became manifest, night and day became manifest;
as night and day became manifest, months and fortnights became manifest.
When months and half-months were discerned, the seasons and years became discernible.
Sirs, consuming that essence of the earth as our food, having that as our color, that as our nourishment, and that as our sustenance, we remained for a very long time.

And when some evil, unwholesome qualities became manifest among them, and when, sirs, some evil, unwholesome qualities became manifest among us, then that essence of the earth disappeared and a crust of earth appeared.
Just as a mushroom, so too was its appearance: it was perfect in color and perfect in fragrance.
Just as, for example, the taste of pure, unfermented honey, such is its flavor.
Thus, sirs, subsisting on that earth-crust as our food, having that as our color, that as our nourishment, and that as our sustenance, we remained for a very long time.
And when certain evil, unwholesome qualities became manifest among them, then that crust of earth disappeared and a forest creeper appeared.
Just as, for example, a *kalambukā* plant appears with such a color, so too was it endowed with excellence of color, excellence of fragrance, and excellence of flavor.
Just as if it were small, pure honey—such is its taste.
Thus, sirs, consuming that forest creeper as our food, having its color, eating its substance, and taking it as our sustenance, we shall remain for a long period of time.
But when some evil, unwholesome qualities became manifest among them, and when, sirs, some evil, unwholesome qualities were manifested by them, then that forest creeper disappeared,
and rice— without powder, without husk, fragrant and yielding grains— appeared.
That which is harvested in the evening becomes grown, ripened, and fully developed by the morning, and no trace of its having been cut is discerned.

"Venerable sirs, consuming that rice— free from red powder and husks, with fragrant grains as its fruit— as our food, we remained for a very long time, of that same color, subsisting on that, and nourished by that."
And because some evil, unwholesome qualities became manifest among them, then the husk and the chaff enveloped the grain of rice.
And that which was harvested this evening is not yet grown, nor ripened, nor sprouted by morning, and its cut-off portion is still clearly visible.
Even that which was harvested in the morning is not grown, nor ripened, nor sprouted by evening, and its mark remains clearly visible.
"What if we were now to divide the rice fields and establish boundary markers?"
"Let us measure out this rice field for you, sirs, and this one for us."
Then, monks, those beings established boundaries for the fields of rice.
"This rice field belongs to you; this one belongs to us."
Then, monks, it occurred to a certain being who had gone to gather rice:
What indeed shall I become? By what means indeed shall I sustain my life when my own portion of rice has been exhausted?
"What if I were now to take some ungiven rice belonging to another?"
Then, monks, that being, while guarding his own portion of rice, would take a portion of rice belonging to another that had not been given.
Monks, another being saw that being taking rice that had not been given and belonged to another; having seen him, he approached that being and said this to him:
"O being, have you perhaps taken this rice belonging to another which was not given?"
When this had been said, monks, that being spoke thus to that being:
Therefore, O being, it shall not happen again in this way.
Monks, for a second time, as that being had gone to gather rice, this thought occurred to him:
"What indeed shall I become? By what means indeed shall I maintain my livelihood now that my own portion of rice has been exhausted?"
"What if I were now to take some ungiven rice belonging to another?"
And a second time, monks, that being, while guarding his own portion of rice, took rice belonging to another that had not been given to him.
Monks, that being saw that second being taking rice that was not given and belonged to another.
And having seen him, he approached that being and said this to him:
"Is it true, O being, that for a second time you have taken rice that was not given and belonged to another?"
A second time, monks, that being said this to that being:
Therefore, O being, it shall not happen thus again.
Monks, when that being had gone to fetch rice, this thought occurred to him for the third time:
"What indeed shall I become? By what means indeed shall I provide for my livelihood now that my own portion of rice has been exhausted?"
"What if I were now to take some ungiven rice belonging to another?"
Monks, even on the third day, that being, while guarding his own portion of rice, took the rice of another which had not been given.
Monks, that being saw that third being taking ungiven rice belonging to another.
Having seen him, he approached that being and, striking that being with a staff, spoke thus:
"Is it true, O being, that you have taken this ungiven rice belonging to another, even as many as three times?"
Then indeed, monks, that being, raising both his arms, wailed and cried out.
"Friends, unrighteousness has appeared in the world; friends, the false dharma has appeared in the world, in that indeed the taking up of the rod is known in the world."
Then, monks, that being, having writhed upon the ground and raised both his arms, wailed and cried out.
"Sirs, unrighteousness has appeared in the world; sir, the false dharma has appeared in the world, in that indeed theft and false speech are known in the world."
And furthermore, monks, it was in this very way that these three evil, unwholesome states first appeared in the world: namely, taking what is not given, false speech, and the taking up of the staff.
Then, monks, those beings ran together and assembled; having run together and assembled, they deliberated.
"Friends, what if we were now to appoint that being among us who is the most handsome and the most influential,
who would restrain those among us deserving of restraint and honor those deserving of honor, and who would direct each of us to give his share of rice from his own rice-field?"
Then, monks, those beings elected that being who had been the most pleasing to all and the most influential of all.

"May you restrain those among our beings who deserve restraint and favor those who deserve favor; we shall appoint you as the foremost of all beings, and in our respective rice fields, we shall give you a sixth share of the rice."
Because he was approved by a great body of people, the designation "Mahāsammata" (Greatly Approved) arose.
