Because he was worthy of receiving a share of the rice from the rice-fields, the designation "King" arose. Because he protected and preserved [the people] perfectly as one consecrated by coronation, the designation [“King”] arose. Because he was like a mother and father to the townspeople and countryfolk, the designation “One who has attained the power and vigor of the countryside” arose.
Therefore, I am a consecrated Kṣatriya king who has attained the power and heroism of the realm.
The son of King Sammata was Kalyāṇa; the son of Kalyāṇa was Rava; the son of Rava was Upoṣadha; and the son of Upoṣadha was King Māndhātṛ.
King Māndhātṛ had many thousands of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and further descendants;
the last of these was a king of the Ikṣvāku lineage named Sujāta, who ruled in the great city of Śāketa.
King Ikṣvāku Sujāta indeed had five sons: Opura, Nipura, Karakaṇḍaka, Ulkāmukha, and Hastikaśīrṣa;
and he had five daughters, the princesses Śuddhā, Vimalā, Vijitā, Jalā, and Jalī.
The prince named Jenta was the son of a courtesan.
His mother was named Jentī.
King Sujāta was won over by her through the arts of women;
the king became delighted with her.
The delighted king invited Jentī to choose a boon.
I invite you with a boon, O Jentī; whatever boon you ask of me, that boon I grant to you.
Then she said:
"Your Majesty, as soon as I have taken leave of my parents, I shall then request a boon from Your Highness."
She informed her parents.
"The king has invited me; therefore, what boon should be requested for you? What boon shall I ask of the king? Then each of them spoke according to his own wish.
"Ask for an excellent village," he said.
There was another female wanderer there who was wise, skillful, and intelligent.
She said:
"Who are you? You are the daughter of a courtesan; your son has no authority over even a small amount of paternal wealth, much less over a kingdom."
These five princes, sons of a Kṣatriya maiden, have authority over their father's kingdom and his wealth.

You have been invited by the king to choose a boon, and King Sujāta is one who does not refuse a request, who speaks the truth, and who acts exactly as he speaks; therefore, you should ask the king for a boon.
"Having banished these five princes from the kingdom, you must consecrate my son, Prince Jenta, as the crown prince."
"After the passing of this god, he will become king in the great city of Śāketa; then everything will belong to you."
King Sujāta was thus entreated for a boon by her.
"Great King, having banished these five princes from the kingdom, consecrate Prince Jenta as the crown prince,
so that upon Your Majesty’s passing, he may become king in the great city of Śāketa."
May the king grant this boon to me.
Having heard this, Sujāta became dejected out of affection for those princes; yet, having granted the boon, it was not possible to make it otherwise.
The king said to Queen Jentī.
So be it; let this boon be granted.
The citizens and the people of the countryside heard the granting of this boon: that after having the princes exiled, he would consecrate Jenta, the son of Vailāsikā, as the crown prince.
In that assembly of people, there was longing because of the greatness of the princes' virtues; "Whatever is the destiny of the princes, that shall be our destiny."
King Sujāta heard that a great multitude of people from the country of Śāketa would go into exile together with the princes.
He had a proclamation made in the great city of Śāketa.
Whoever shall depart from Śāketa together with the princes, whatever he may have need of for his royal duties shall be given to him from the treasury.
For those who have need of elephants, horses, chariots, draft animals, vehicles, carts, oxen, mules, goats, sheep, wealth,
or anything else such as clothing, ornaments, male slaves, or female slaves— all these royal requirements shall be supplied from the treasury.
While they were living abroad together with the princes, by the king’s command the ministers released the treasuries and granaries so that whatever anyone requested was given to them.

Thus those princes, together with many thousands of countryfolk and a great military force, and with many thousands of wagons, carriages, and vehicles, departed from the city of Śāketa and set out toward the north.
She was taken up by King Kāśikośala.
The princes were virtuous, illustrious, sheltered from harm, pleasant to touch, meritorious, and righteous.
All the people of Kāśi and Kośala were delighted with them from the very beginning.
"Oh, how truly excellent are these princes, and how righteous they are!"
Regarding that king, it was as the Blessed One has stated in the *Śakrapraśna* [Sūtra].
Gods, humans, asuras, garuḍas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, and whoever else there may be among the various beings, are all associated with the fetters of envy and avarice.
Envy arose within that King of Kāśi and Kośala.
Just as this body of people has taken to heart the virtues of these princes, it is possible that they might deprive me of life and consecrate these princes in the kingdom.
Then they were banished by that King of Kāśi and Kosala as well.
To the north of the Himalayas there dwelt a seer named Kapila, who possessed the five superknowledges, had attained the four meditative absorptions, and was of great psychic power and great majesty.

His hermitage was very extensive and delightful, provided with roots, flowers, leaves, fruits, and water, and adorned with thousands of root-stocks; and there, in that grove of *śākoṭa* trees, those princes were then settled.
There, the merchants set out and traveled toward the districts of Kāśī and Kośala.
Those merchants were asked by the people, "From where have you come?"
They said:
From such-and-such a Śākoṭa forest grove; merchants from Śāketa and Kośala also go there to that Śākoṭa forest grove.
They, too, are questioned.
"Where will you go? he asked.
They also said:
The Śākoṭa forest grove along the Himalayas.
Then those princes, fearing that there might be a corruption of their lineage, and out of dread of such a corruption, married one another's own maternal sisters.
King Sujāta asked his ministers:
"O ministers, where do the princes dwell?"
The ministers said.
"Great King, beyond the Himalayas there is a great forest tract of Śākoṭaka trees; there the princes dwell."
The king questioned his ministers.
From where were the wives brought by the princes?
The ministers said:

"Great King, we have heard that out of fear of the corruption of their lineage, the princes have each married their own maternal sisters as wives to one another, thinking, 'Lest there be a corruption of our lineage.'"
Then King Sujāta questioned the domestic priest and other learned brahmins.
It is possible to do this very thing in the same way that it was done by those princes.
Those brahmin scholars, headed by the family priest, said:
It is possible, Great King, that the princes are not stained by fault on account of that cause.
Having heard this from the learned brahmins, King Sujāta was thrilled, delighted, and elated, and he uttered this inspired utterance:
Furthermore, sirs, the princes are capable.
Then, for those princes, the designation, appellation, and conventional term "Śākyas, the Śākyas" arose.
Then this thought occurred to those princes:
"For how long shall we make our dwelling in this grove of Śākoṭaka trees?"
And this great multitude of people is approaching.
"What if we were now to have a city built?"
Then those princes went into the presence of the seer Kapila.
Having prostrated at the feet of the seer, they said:
"If the Blessed One Kapila would grant us permission, we would build this city named Kapilavastu after the name of the seer."
The seer said:
"If you build a city by making this hermitage my royal palace, then I shall grant you permission."
Those princes said to the seer:
We shall do exactly as the seer intends.
Having made this hermitage a royal palace, we shall build a city there.
The seer took a water-pot and gave water to those princes for that purpose.
The princes also, having made that hermitage of the seer their royal palace, had a city constructed.
Because it was given as a dwelling place by the seer Kapila, the name Kapilavastu arose.

Thus the great city of Kapilavastu became prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, crowded with people, populous, filled with happy inhabitants, and surrounded by a vast retinue of people; it became renowned in every direction and intermediate direction, abounding in festivals and assemblies, dear to merchants, and perfected in commerce.
Now, among those five princes—Opura, Nipura, Karaṇḍaka, Ulkāmukha, and Hastikaśīrṣa—the prince Opura was the eldest.
Thus he was consecrated in the kingdom at Kapilavastu.
Opura had a son named Nipura; Nipura, the king, had a son named Karakaṇḍa; Karakaṇḍa, the king, had a son named Ulkāmukha; Ulkāmukha’s son was Hastikaśīrṣa;
and Hastikaśīrṣa’s son was Siṃhahanu.
King Siṃhahanu had four sons—Śuddhodana, Dhautodana, Śuklodana, and Amṛtodana—and a daughter named Amitā.

Now, at that time, there was another Śākyan elder whose daughter was gracious, beautiful to behold, of noble presence, and endowed with supreme beauty; however, a disease of leprosy arose in that girl.
Now she was seized by that disease of leprosy.

Physicians apply themselves; all treatments are administered, yet there is no improvement. Ointments and counter-ointments are applied, and emetics and purgatives are given, but the disease of leprosy does not subside.
The entire body is a single wound.
Upon seeing her, compassion arises in every person.
Then, having been placed in a carriage by her brothers, she was taken away toward the Himalayas.

There, having had a cave excavated on Mount Utsaṅga, that girl was placed inside; and having provided an abundance of food and drink, water, bedding, and clothing, they firmly closed the door of the cave, piled up a great heap of dust over it, and entered the city of Kapilavastu.

Now, as that girl lived there in the cave, due to the lack of wind, the confinement, and the heat of that cave, her entire leprosy disease vanished; her body became clean and free of sores, endowed with supreme beauty,
such that it was no longer even known whether she was a human being.
Then, at that very spot, a tiger came wandering about.
"Beasts see with their noses; Brahmins see with the Vedas;
kings see with their spies; and other subjects see with their eyes."
Then that tiger smelled the scent of a human being.
Then, having smelled that human scent, he pushed aside that great heap of dust with his feet.
And not far from there lived a royal seer named Kola, who possessed the five superknowledges and had attained the four meditative absorptions.
His hermitage was delightful, provided with roots, leaves, flowers, fruits, and water, and endowed with various kinds of trees.
Then that seer, while walking about and wandering through the hermitage grounds, came to that place where the Śākya maiden had been placed within the cave.
That tiger also dragged away the entire heap of dust with his paw until nothing remained but wood.
Then that tiger, seeing the seer, was driven back by the seer.
Seeing that dust being swept away by a tiger, curiosity arose in the seer.
Then that seer removed those logs and opened the door of the cave.
By him, through his supreme vigor, the Śākya maiden was seen, yet she was not even recognized as a human being.
This seer asks.
"Noble lady, who are you?"
The human woman said:
"I am the daughter of such-and-such a Śākya from Kapilavastu."
I, Jīvantikā, being thus afflicted here by the disease of leprosy, have been rejected in this way.
Upon seeing that Śākya maiden of supreme beauty, a fierce passion arose within him.
Even if one has long practiced the holy life,
if the latent tendency of passion has not been eradicated,
that poison of passion will flare up once again.
Just as one remains standing, like a piece of wood that has not been moved.
Then that royal seer, having entered into union with that Śākya maiden, fell away from his meditative absorptions and superknowledges.
Then, taking that Śākya maiden, he went to his hermitage.
Now that Śākya maiden lived there in that hermitage together with the royal seer Kola.
Sixteen twin sons were born to her.
There were thirty-two young sages, gracious and beautiful to behold, wearing deerskins and matted hair.
Then, when those young seers had grown up, they were sent by their mother to Kapilavastu.
"Go, my sons, to the great city of Kapilavastu; there is a Śākyan named so-and-so who is your father and my maternal grandfather."
The sons of that such-and-such person are your maternal uncles; for the most part, they are Śākya elders and kinsmen, and your family lineage is great.
They will provide for your livelihood.
She was instructed according to the customary conduct of the Śākyas.
In this manner, you should approach the assembly of the Śākyas.
In this manner one should perform the salutation;
in this manner one should sit down.
Having been instructed in all the customary practices of the Śākyas, they were dismissed.
Having paid homage to their mother and father and circumambulated them clockwise, they departed and in due course arrived at Kapilavastu.
All of them entered Kapilavastu one after another, according to their respective lifespans.
Seeing those young sages, the great multitude of people took them to heart.
"Oh, how pleasing and beautiful these young sages are, wearing deerskins and matted hair!"
Then, surrounded by a great multitude of people, they approached the assembly hall of the Śākyas.
And about five hundred Śākyas were seated together, assembled in the assembly hall for some particular business.
Then, having been instructed by their mother, they approached the assembly of the Śākyas with that same deportment.
The assembly of Śākyas, seeing that conduct of the young seers, was filled with wonder.
Then those Śākyas questioned the young seers.
"From where have you come?"
They reported all that matter to her exactly as she had been instructed by her mother.
"In the Himalayas, from such-and-such a hermitage, the daughter of a certain Śākya and the son of the royal seer Kola is my mother."
Just as that Śākya maiden had been sent away to that place, so too, having heard it from their mother, those Śākyas reported everything to her.
The Śākyas, having heard this, were delighted.
Their maternal grandfather, Śakyamahattaraka, was also living, as was a great family lineage.

That royal seer Kola, having consecrated his eldest son to the kingship in Vārāṇasī, went forth as a seer; that great-souled royal seer became renowned for his super-knowledges and full realizations throughout the quarters.
Then those Śākyas became joyful, thinking, "These have been born from a royal seer, not from an ordinary man."
This thought occurred to those Śākyas.
"These princes are well-born to us; let these Śākya maidens be given to them, as well as a means of livelihood."
They gave those Śākya maidens to those princes, and they gave them the ploughed lands together with their surrounding districts.
Namely, the hermitages, market towns, and villages of Sumukta and Karkarabhadra, as well as other cultivated lands together with their districts, and abundant wealth.
They are known as Koliyas because they were born from the seer Kola; and they are known as Vyāghrapadyas because [they descended] from Vyāghrapatha.
Thus ends "The Origin of the Koliyas" in the glorious Mahāvastu-Avadāna.
Now, there was a market town of the Śākyas named Devaḍaha.
There was a leading Śākya named Subhūti; he brought home as his wife a Koliyan maiden from a certain town.
To him were born seven daughters: Māyā, Mahāmāyā, Atimāyā, Anantamāyā, Cūlīyā, Kolīsovā, and Mahāprajāpatī.
The arising of illusion.
King Siṃhahanu, the Śākya king, had four sons and one daughter: Śuddhodana, Śuklodana, Dhautodana, Amṛtodana, and the daughter Amitā.
When King Siṃhahanu had passed away,
Śuddhodana obtained the kingdom.
King Śuddhodana commanded his ministers: "Bring me a maiden who is suitable—one who is both beautiful and of noble birth."

Those ministers dispatched on all sides Brahmins who were wise, highly learned, and experts in the rules for discerning the characteristics of women, the characteristics of men, and the characteristics of maidens.
"Go and find a girl who would be suitable for King Śuddhodana."

While those brahmins were searching through villages, market towns, cities, and provinces, they saw the seven daughters of Subhūti the Śākyan in the Śākya town of Devaḍaha; of those seven daughters, Māyā was the most excellent, and such a maiden is very difficult to find in all of Jambudvīpa.

They informed the king: "In the town of Devadaha, Subhūti the Śākyan has seven daughters who are gracious and beautiful to behold; among these seven sisters, one is preeminent in beauty, in splendor, and in wisdom, being endowed with all virtues, and her name is Māyā."
"However many villages, towns, cities, and districts we have searched, we have never before seen a maiden like Māyā, the daughter of the Śākya Subhūti."
Śuddhodana sent [this] to Subhūti.
"Give me your daughter Māyā to be my wife; she shall become my chief queen."
Subhūti said to the messengers:
When Māyā’s six daughters, who are her elder sisters, have been married off, then Māyā herself shall be given to the Great King.
Those messengers informed King Śuddhodana.
"Great King, Subhūti the Śākya spoke thus."
"When these six elder daughters have been married off, then Māyā shall be given to the Great King."
King Śuddhodana again dispatched a messenger to Subhūti the Śākyan.
Give me all seven of your daughters.
Those messengers informed Subhūti the Śākyan.
King Śuddhodana said:
"Give me all seven of your daughters."
Subhūti the Śākyan sent a message to King Śuddhodana.
"Great King, let them be granted to you."
Then all those seven girls were brought from the town of Devaḍaha to Kapilavastu by King Śuddhodana with great royal majesty, great royal power, and great royal prosperity.
King Śuddhodana caused his two daughters, Māyā and Mahāprajāpatī, to enter his own inner apartments.
The five maidens were given to the five brothers.
In twelve years, the Bodhisattva will descend from the Tuṣita heaven.
The Śuddhāvāsa gods announce to the Pratyekabuddhas in Jambudvīpa: "The Bodhisattva is about to descend; vacate the Buddha-field!"
From the Tuṣita heaven, the one of exceeding fame, possessing infinite knowledge and vision, will descend;
leave the Buddha-field for him who bears the excellent marks.
Having heard the word "Buddha" from the supreme Maheśvaras, those Pratyekabuddhas—
self-arisen ones who have mastery over their own minds— extinguished [their defilements] with liberated hearts.
Then those Pratyekabuddhas, having each delivered their own individual prophecies, passed into final nirvana.
At a distance of one and a half yojanas from Vārāṇasī, there was a great forest grove where five hundred pratyekabuddhas resided.
They too, having each given their own individual prophecies, entered final nirvana.
Having attained vigor, constantly engaged in practice, with an uplifted mind, not dwelling in indolence,
firm in prowess, and endowed with the power of energy.
They wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.
Having risen into the air and entered the fire-element, they attained final nirvana without further clinging.
The flesh and blood were consumed by the fire-element within his own body,
and his physical remains fell away.
Cultivating equanimity and compassion,
and practicing sympathetic joy at the proper time,
one should possess a mind of loving-kindness, compassionate for the welfare of others.
One should wander alone, like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having laid aside the rod toward all living beings, he does not harm even one among them;
having cast aside the rod toward both the mobile and the immobile, he is free from violence.
One should wander alone, like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having cast off the marks of a householder, like a *pāripātra* tree with its leaves withered away,
he went forth, clothed in saffron robes.
One should wander alone, like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having cast off the marks of a householder like a peacock into ashes, he went forth alone,
clothed in saffron robes.
One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
For one who cultivates intimacy, excessive affection may arise; from this affection, this suffering follows.
But for one who cultivates intimacy while maintaining revulsion [for passion], [suffering does not arise].
One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
For one who cultivates close association, excessive affection may arise;
from this affection, suffering follows. Thus, one should feel revulsion toward excessive attachment to what is dear.
One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
For one who cultivates intimacy, excessive affection may arise;
from this affection, suffering follows.
Fearing separation from what is dear, one becomes repelled by it.
One should wander alone, like the horn of a rhinoceros.
For one who cultivates close association, excessive affection may arise;
from this affection, suffering prevails.
Reflecting upon the danger inherent in friendships, [one should remain detached].
One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
For one who associates closely with others, excessive affection may arise;
from this affection, suffering follows.
Reflecting upon the dangers inherent in children, [one should remain detached].
One should wander alone, like the horn of a rhinoceros.
One whose mind is bound [to them] loses wealth while looking toward sons and companions;
one should not desire a son, much less companions.
One should wander alone, like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Looking toward relatives and companions, one whose mind is bound loses wealth;
how could one who does not desire relatives ever desire companions?
One should wander alone, like the horn of a rhinoceros.
The entire Khaḍgaviṣāṇa-gāthā should be recited in detail.
Each of the five hundred pratyekabuddhas has one verse.
The sages fell here; thus it is called Ṛṣipatana.
In that forest grove, a king of deer named Rohaka tended a herd of a thousand deer.
He had two sons, named Nyagrodha and Viśākha.
Then that king of deer gave five hundred deer to one son and gave five hundred deer to the other son.
Brahmadatta, the king of Kāśi, used to go out frequently for the hunt, roaming all around that forest grove and killing the deer there.
He does not himself subsist on as many deer as those that, having entered into forest thickets, deep woods, reed-beds, cane-beds, and thorn-beds, perish after being struck down.
There they were devoured by crows and birds.
Nyagrodha, the king of deer, said to his brother Viśākha:
"Viśākha, let us make this request to the King of Kāśi."
You do not personally subsist upon as many deer as those that, having entered into dense thickets, die or are devoured by crows and birds after being struck down.
"We shall provide the king with one deer daily, which shall enter the kitchen of its own accord."
And this herd of deer will not thus fall into misfortune and ruin.
His brother Viśākha said:
So be it; let us inform him.
Then the king went out on a hunt.
Those leaders of the herds, the kings of deer, saw the king from afar as he approached with his army and mounts, surrounded by those bearing swords, bows, spears, and lances.
Then, seeing the king, they went out to meet him, facing toward where the king was, fearless and undaunted, having surrendered their own lives.
Then, the King of Kāśi saw the two kings of deer approaching from afar, coming directly toward him.
He gave an order to his own vanguard of troops.
"No one should harass these deer as they approach; who knows what the reason here might be, that seeing this vanguard of my army, they do not flee but instead come right toward me?"
The vanguard of their army was deployed between those deer; that vanguard was positioned on both the left and the right.
Those deer, having approached the place where the king was, prostrated themselves at the king's knees.
The king questioned those kings of deer.
What is your request? Let it be made known what business you have.
Then they informed the king with human speech.
O Great King, we inform you.
We were born and raised here in your kingdom, in this forest grove, as were many hundreds of other deer.
"Among those deer, we two brothers, who are leaders of the herd, dwell here within the domain of this great king."

Just as the cities, towns, villages, and districts of the Great King are adorned by the people, by oxen and bulls, and by thousands of other living beings— both bipeds and quadrupeds— even so are these forest groves, hermitages, rivers, and springs adorned by these deer and birds.
Thus, Great King, this is the adornment of this empowerment.

"O Great King, all these bipeds and quadrupeds, however many there may be dwelling within Your Majesty’s realm—whether they be in villages, in the forest, or on the mountains—they have all gone for refuge to the Great King; therefore, O Great King, they are all to be cared for and protected."
And the great king has authority over them; no other king does.
Whenever the Great King goes out for a hunt, many hundreds of deer then fall into misfortune and ruin.
"Great King, those who become your dependents do not equal in number those who, struck by arrows here in these forest thickets,
reed thickets, *śara* grass beds, and *kāśa* grass beds, enter them and die, being devoured by crows and birds; and the Great King becomes tainted by unrighteousness."
"If Your Majesty would grant us favor, we two leaders of the herd will each send one deer daily for Your Majesty.
From one herd, we shall send one deer on the first day; from the second herd, we shall send one deer on the second day.
Thus, there will be no lack of deer meat for Your Majesty to eat, and these deer will not fall into such misfortune and ruin."
Then the king granted a request to those leaders of the deer herds.
"Let it be as you intend; go, dwell without fear or terror, and release one deer from my herd for me every single day."
Having granted their request, the king said to his ministers:
No one shall harass the deer.
Having thus given his command, he entered the city.
By those herd-leaders, all those deer were brought together and comforted.

"Do not fear; we have petitioned the king in such a way that the king will no longer go out for the hunt, nor will he ever again harass the deer. Furthermore, one deer must be surrendered to the king every day—one from one herd on one day, and another from another herd on the next day."
Those deer, having counted all those deer in both herds, established a rendezvous from one herd to another.
From one herd, a deer goes to the king’s kitchen for one day; from another herd, it goes for another day.
Once, it was the turn of a pregnant doe from Viśākha’s herd to go to the king’s kitchen.
Then that doe was addressed by the deer who had been sent as a messenger.
"Today is your turn; go to the king's kitchen."
She said:
"I am pregnant and there are two fetuses within my womb; for now, please command someone else, and when I have given birth, I shall go."
Now, for the sake of one person, we shall pursue the threefold set of goals.
It will be your turn only after a very long time, once these two young ones have been born.
That commanding deer reported this matter to the leader of the herd.
The leader of the herd said:
"Command another deer who is between this doe and you."
"This doe, having given birth, will go away afterwards."
That messenger-deer, having bypassed that female deer, was commanded to go to the king’s kitchen along the path between her and himself.
He also said:
"It is not my turn today; it is the turn of such-and-such a doe today. In this way, I shall live for a while longer."
In this way, others and yet others are spoken to, and they do not depart without having confessed;
everyone speaks.
"It is the turn of such-and-such a doe; let her go."
That doe said:
"Lady, no one wishes to go without being in turn.
It is your turn; you yourself must go to the king's kitchen."
Then, at the time when she could not be released, out of affection for her young ones and fearing that they too would be killed due to her capture, she went to that second herd of deer.
Having gone, she prostrated herself before that leader of the herd.
Then that leader of the herd asked them.
"What is this, noble lady? What do you command? What is the task?"
She said:
Today, therefore, it was my turn from this herd to go to the king’s kitchen; and since two calves were in my womb, I made a request to that leader of the herd, Viśākha.
"Today is my turn, and these two young ones are within my womb;
send another [on my behalf], for when I have given birth, I shall go."
And those others who were commanded by that leader of the herd also did not wish to go, saying, "It is not our turn; it is the turn of such-and-such a doe; let her go."
I am not released by them; I am told, "It is your turn, go! Therefore, I desire that the king of deer release another deer instead of me. At the time when I have given birth, then I shall depart.
Then the king of deer said to the doe:
"Do not be afraid; I shall send another."
That king of deer commanded an attendant deer: "From this herd, direct whichever deer's turn it is; I have granted safety to this doe."
That overseer then directs whichever deer's turn it is.
Go to the king’s kitchen.
He too said:
Today is not our turn for the herd; today is the turn of Viśākha’s herd.
Then that commanding deer said:
"Today is the turn from Viśākha’s herd; as for that doe whose turn it is, she is pregnant with two young ones in her womb.
She cannot be spared; it is your turn, so you must go."
And while that doe was not yet released from there, she came here to the herd and informed Nyagrodha, the leader of the herd.
The leader of the herd, Nyagrodha, granted safety to that doe.
It was commanded by the leader of the herd.
"Release him who is the one whose turn it is to go from this herd."
It is your turn to leave this herd; you should go.
He said:
Today is the turn of the second; I would not go when it is not my turn.
In this way, whoever was commanded likewise did not wish to go to Anosara.
That messenger-deer reported [the matter] to Nyagrodha, the lord of deer.
No one wishes to go without a turn; they say, "It is not our turn today; it is the turn of the second deer herd; today is their turn."
The king of deer said:
"I have granted safety to this doe by the thousands;
she cannot be sent back to the kitchen there again.
I shall go myself."
Then that king of deer, having descended from that forest thicket onto the path, went toward Vārāṇasī.
Whichever person saw that king of beasts as he was going, each of them followed after him.
The deer was beautiful in form, variegated and adorned, with red hooves and eyes as dark as collyrium, radiant and lovely to behold.

Placed at the head of a great multitude of people, he proceeded until he entered the inner city, where he was seen and recognized by the citizens as that king of deer. When that king of deer was seen by the great multitude of people, they were filled with longing for him;
that entire herd of deer had been destroyed, yet here was the leader of the herd himself come.

"Let us go and petition the king so that this king of deer may be released and not killed; for his ornament has become a delight to the eyes of this city as he runs about in the parks and by the ponds."
Having seen that deer, they experience delight for their eyes.
Together with that very same chief minister and a great multitude of people, he entered the royal palace following behind the king of deer.
The king of beasts entered the kitchen, and while the king was seated in the court of justice, he was informed by these citizens.
"Great King, that entire herd of deer has been completely exhausted."
Harmless, they feed upon dry and fresh grass and do not offend anyone; yet they have all been destroyed, and here is that very leader of the herd who has come in person.
"O Great King, such a king of deer is rare—one so gracious, beautiful to behold, and a delight to the eyes of people."

When people go out from the city to a garden, a pond, a grove, or a lotus pool, they too become joyful upon seeing that king of deer, who serves as an ornament to the city park; if it were Your Majesty’s pleasure, this king of deer might be released alive.
The king commanded his ministers.
"Go and bring that king of deer from the kitchen."
So, having gone with those ministers, he was brought from the kitchen into the presence of the king.
The king questioned that king of deer.
"Why have you come yourself? There is no longer any other deer for you to pursue, since you have come here in person."
Then the king of deer said:
For it is not the case, O Great King, that there are no other deer.
But today is the turn of the second herd of deer.
In that place, it happened that a certain doe whose turn had come was pregnant with two young ones in her womb.
That doe was told, "Go to the bathhouse; it is your turn today."
In the second deer herd, Viśākha is the leader of the herd.
She went to him and said:
"Today is my turn to go to the king’s kitchen; however, I am pregnant and have two children in my womb. I wish for another to be sent instead, so that when I have given birth, I may then go."
Then, whichever other deer was commanded went, but he did not wish to go; he spoke, saying, "It is this doe's turn; let her go. Because of that, he was not released by those deer.
"Today is your turn; you should go. But she did not let them go, and she came before me.

I was petitioned by her: "Today is my turn from that herd. I have two fawns in my womb, and I cannot be parted from them. Therefore, I wish for the king of deer to command another from this herd who might go to the king's kitchen."
I shall go from there to wherever I am to give birth.
I granted safety to that doe; furthermore, whichever deer I commanded was not willing [to go].
"It is not our turn; it is the turn of the second herd. Thus, whomever was commanded did not wish to come here while it was not his turn.
"I know that I myself have granted safety to this doe; therefore, I am coming here in person. Thus, I have come of my own accord.
When the king heard this from that deer, he and the entire assembly of people were struck with wonder, exclaiming, "Oh, how righteous is this king of deer!"
It occurred to that king of Kāśi:

"This one is not a beast, for this deer, for the sake of another, sacrifices himself; he knows the Dharma. We are beasts, we who do not know the Dharma, and who would conceive malice toward such jewels among beings who are free from harm."
He said this to that king of deer:
I am pleased with you; you are compassionate and high-minded, since, even while in the form of a deer, you granted safety to that female deer who was your own servant.
I too, having come to you and by your word, grant safety to all the deer.
From this day forward, I grant safety to all those deer who are in that region; go and dwell there, free from fear and unafraid.
The king had a proclamation made by the sounding of a bell throughout the city.
"No one in my realm shall harm the deer," [he declared], because that king had granted them the gift of fearlessness.
...up to the point that a cry arose among the gods.
Śakra, the lord of the gods, created many hundreds and thousands of deer for the purpose of testing the king.
The entire Kāśi countryside was swarming with deer; there was no field where there were no deer.
The king was petitioned by the people of the countryside.
Then that female deer was addressed by Nyagrodha, the king of deer:
"O auspicious lady, go to the troop of Viśākha."
She said.
O King of Beasts, I will not go; it is better to die at your feet than to live at the foot of Viśākha.
Then that doe spoke this verse:
"One should resort to the *nyagrodha* tree alone; one should not long for the *viśākha*.
Death under the *nyagrodha* is better than life under the *viśākha*."
The people of the countryside, O King, make this representation.
The countryside is being devastated and the prosperous kingdom is perishing;
deer are devouring the grain—restrain them, O lord of men!
"Let the countryside be devastated and let the prosperous kingdom perish;
yet, having granted this boon to the king of beasts, I shall certainly not speak a falsehood."
A gift of deer was given [there], thus it is called "Deer Park" (Mṛgadāya), the Abode of Sages (Ṛṣipattana).

Twelve years hence, the Bodhisattva will descend from the Tuṣita heaven; thus thinking, the Śuddhāvāsa deities assumed the guise of brahmins and taught the Vedas, the mantras, and the thirty-two marks of a Great Man to those brahmins, so that they might prophesy when the Bodhisattva had arrived here.
[_Mvu_2.1_] Then, at the time of his descent from the Tuṣita heaven, the Bodhisattva performed the four great observations: namely,
the observation of the time and the observation of the place.
The examination of the continent; the examination of the family.
Bodhisattvas are born into two families:
either a kṣatriya family or a brāhmaṇa family.
When the earth is ruled by kṣatriyas, they are born into a kṣatriya family.
When the earth is overrun by brahmins, then they are born into brahmin families.
And, monks, whatever family the Bodhisattvas are born into, that family is endowed with sixty qualities.
Which sixty?
It is well-known.

That family enjoys its wealth, being noble in conduct, endowed with a good birth, endowed with a noble lineage, endowed with a succession of generations of men, endowed with a succession of generations of men renowned from of old, having many women, having many men, not fickle, not deficient, not lowly, not dejected, possessed of wisdom, possessed of virtue, not looking for honor, and that family possesses steadfast friends.

That family is one that is grateful and knows the proper rites, and does not act according to its own whims; it does not follow anger, nor folly, nor fear; it is wary of blame, practices generous almsgiving, possesses a mind intent on manly effort, and is firm in valor, excellent in valor, and supreme in valor; it honors shrines and honors the deities.
And that family is one that honors former friends, is devoted to ritual action, and is devoted to generosity; it is one where the lineage is continuous from past to present,
which is proclaimed by its renown, proclaimed by the fame of gods and others,
and which is the eldest of families, the best of families, the most excellent of families, and has attained mastery over the family.

...attained and renowned, with a great retinue, a retinue free from fatigue, a devoted retinue, an indivisible retinue; respectful toward mothers, respectful toward fathers, possessing the virtues of a recluse and a brahmin, honoring the elders of the family, possessing abundant wealth and grain, possessing abundant treasuries and granaries, and possessing many elephants, horses, goats, and sheep.
That family in which Bodhisattvas are born possesses abundant female and male slaves, laborers, and servants, and it becomes invincible to others, adversaries, and enemies;
that family is endowed with these sixty qualities.
Those beings who are endowed with a noble lineage—such beings as these attain great compassion.
At the time of his passing from the Tuṣita abode, the Bodhisattva makes a great preparation;
at the time of the Bodhisattva’s passing, thousands of gods, beginning with those of the Four Great Kings, all belonging to the realm of desire, assemble in the Tuṣita abode.
He said to Bimbisāra and the others,
"Be born in Rājagṛha;
once you have been disciplined, the great mass of people will follow the path of discipline."
In this way, the caravan leader Abhaya Sahasodgata, as well as other great householders and great brahmins, [were established].
"Udayana, the King of Vatsa, is called [to you]. Be reborn in Kauśāmbī;
once you have been disciplined, the great mass of people will follow the path of discipline."
The householder Ghoṣila and likewise other great kṣatriya householders and great householder householders—

by this method, thousands of sons of gods who had been companions to the Blessed One as he wandered through *saṃsāra* were reborn in Jambūdvīpa within the sixteen great provinces into families of great kṣatriyas and families of great brahmins.
"Without a doubt, once you have been disciplined, the great multitude will follow the path of discipline through your example, O householders of the great śāla clan."
The Bodhisattva looked to see where he should be reborn:
"This King Śuddhodana is a suitable father for me."
He seeks a mother who is graceful, of noble birth, pure of body, possessing little passion, and short-lived, such that only ten months remain of her life span, including seven nights.
After giving birth to the Supreme among Men, the mother of all Bodhisattvas loses her life on the final seventh day.
What is the cause here, O mothers of the All-Knowing One, that having given birth to the Supreme among Men, you so quickly abandon your lives?
While dwelling in the Tuṣita realm, the Bodhisattva, through his virtuous karma, maintains this mindfulness as he examines prospective mothers.
For whichever woman here might have life remaining,
seven days and ten months shall descend upon her breast.
For what reason? Because it is improper for one such as me, having maintained the unsurpassed [teachings], to engage in sexual intercourse at a later time.
Even if they were to indulge in sensual pleasures with the mother of the Sugata,
that would not cause the father of the hosts of gods to be considered one of broken conduct.
The Blessed One indeed constantly speaks of the faults of sensual desires;
yet the mother of the Lord of the World indulges in sensual desires.
And those jewel-caskets that exist in the palaces of kings—
the jewels, the best of men, the vessels that are the mothers of enlightenment.

Searching for one of short lifespan on earth, the Bodhisattva saw the chief queen of Śuddhodana in Kapilavastu— gracious, of noble birth, with pure limbs, possessing little passion, and short-lived; of her,
ten months plus seven nights remained of her life-span.
This thought occurred to the Bodhisattva:
This mother of mine is worthy.
Looking out, he beheld in King Śuddhodana’s harem a woman resembling the wife of an immortal, like a flash of lightning, like an illusion.
Having perceived his mother, he addressed her: "O Maruṇā, I shall descend;
entering my final dwelling in a womb for the sake of the happiness of gods and men."
To him, the host of gods—wearing exquisite ornaments and with palms joined in reverence—said:
"O Supreme Person, whose form possesses undiminished virtues, may your vow be fulfilled!"
We too, for the benefit of the world, having renounced many delightful sensual pleasures,
shall dwell in the human realm, O blameless one, for the sake of honoring you.
With uplifted minds, they released from the sky a rain of large, beautiful-colored mandārava flowers, praising him with sweet words.

That you behold the desires which are as delightful as the abode of the immortals yet so charming in their tranquility, and that you neither indulge in them nor even look upon them amidst the mixture of grief and suffering— this is truly marvelous in you.
That you, O Bull among Gods, having surpassed the host of Maruts and shining with a brilliance like a mountain of Jambunada gold, illuminate the ten directions— this too is a marvel.

O you of immeasurable intellect, that you surpass the hosts of gods, including Maheśvara and the Dānavas, as well as the assemblies of Māras and the hosts of stars moving through the sky— this too is a marvel.
Although we do not desire separation from you, O Teacher of the multitude of beings, nevertheless,
O lotus-eyed one, you shall become the refuge for humans and gods.
Then, at the time of his passing away, the hosts of gods, filled with joy, proclaimed from all directions to him whose eyes were like pure hundred-petaled lotuses:
While this conversation was taking place in the Tuṣita heaven, Queen Māyā, who was peerless, approached King Śuddhodana and said this:
[Mvu 2.5] That Śyāmā Māyā, with eyes like those of a young deer and resembling a pure Gandharva maiden, spoke these very sweet and harmonious words to Śuddhodana.
With arms adorned by ornaments and wearing exquisite garments, together with her friends,
she desires to spend this night without you, O Joy of the Śākyas.
O best of men, ascend to the highest floor of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s excellent palace,
to that preeminent couch which is stainless and resembles a garment of white water-lilies.
Pleased by those agreeable words of the queen, Śuddhodana,
the best of men, with uplifted resolve, addressed his retinue.
Let them quickly inform me that Dhṛtarāṣṭra has been covered with the finest flowers and strewn with loose blossoms; make it like a celestial palace in heaven.
And let Dhṛtarāṣṭra, adorned with hanging silk streamers, shine forth with its swift movement,
covered by a noble lattice of gold and resembling the peak of the excellent Mount Sumeru.
And let the fourfold army, variegated with spears, iron arrows, and javelins,
swiftly protect Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who possesses a charming assembly.
As soon as the command was issued by the king, they made everything ready; having performed their duties skillfully there, they approached the king and said this:
O Great Protector of the Earth, may you protect your subjects for no less than a thousand years;
your excellent celestial palace stands ready, inspiring great joy.
Then Māyā, resembling a celestial nymph, rose from her excellent seat and spoke to the son of the lord of the earth just as the sun had set.
This I undertake: non-violence toward living beings and celibacy;
I also abstain from what is not given, from intoxicants, and from unrestrained speech.
O best of men, I desist from all idle talk;
likewise, O lord of men, I desist from slander and harsh speech—this is my resolve.
May I not conceive envy toward the desires of others, nor even malice; may I cultivate a sense of kinship toward all beings and abandon distorted views.
"O Protector of the Earth, I practice the elevenfold morality throughout this entire night;
such is the aspiration that arises within me."
O protector of the earth, let there not be even the slightest thought of desire toward me;
do not long for me, lest demerit accrue to me, who am a practitioner of the holy life.
"I shall fulfill all your intentions," the king said.
"Take your pleasure within this excellent palace; both I and the kingdom are at your disposal."
Accompanied by her full retinue of thousands of women, she immediately took that excellent celestial palace, ascended it, and sat down there, her heart's desire completely fulfilled.
For a short while, she spent that time in silence upon that couch, which resembled snow, the white water-lily, and the lotus, delighting in tranquility and self-restraint.
Then she laid down her excellent body on its right side,
reclining upon the bed like a flowering creeper entwined around a noble tree.
Then, having observed that queen— who resembled a celestial maiden— lying upon her bed,
the hosts of gods descended from the Tuṣita abode and stationed themselves upon the roof of the palace.
[ Mvu 2.7 ] All those immortals, filled with joy, bowed their heads and joined their palms in reverence;
they paid homage to Māyā, the mother of the Jina, who possessed vast merit as she lay upon her bed.
Then many celestial maidens, wearing pure garlands, were overcome with great curiosity.
Desirous of seeing the Mother of the Conqueror, they approached and stood upon the roof of the palace.
Having approached and beheld Māyā reclining upon her bed, who resembled a flash of sublime lightning,
he experienced vast joy and happiness, and then rained down celestial flowers.
"Even among humans, such a well-formed beauty as this is indeed a marvel!
May she remain within for some time;
she shall have no equal among the women of the gods."
O friends, behold the playful grace of this woman, which is so appropriate;
reclining on her bed, she shines, captivates the mind, and gleams like the very essence of gold.
But since she shall bear a Great Man who delights in ultimate generosity, self-restraint, and virtue,
who brings an end to all outflows and is free from passion— what is lost for you, O Queen?
In this beautiful belly, curved like a bow, measured by the palm of the hand, and adorned with a magnificent line of hair,
that one of infinite intelligence shall dwell— ever unstained by the impure and pure.
The wholesome merit accumulated by this woman over a very long night is vast and supreme;
she shall uphold that which possesses infinite qualities and the power of merit gathered over a long period.

You are a woman worthy of him, the most excellent mother; and he is indeed the most excellent of men, a son whose cravings have been abandoned and who is free from passion. O queen of kings, what is lacking for you?
Then the Rākṣasas, assuming various forms and commanded, swiftly took their positions throughout the sky;
"O you who bear excellent weapons, remain and leave no part of any direction unguarded!"
Immediately after them, hosts of double-tongued serpents stood in all directions for the sake of protection;
even upon hearing the sound of a slight breeze stirring, they rose up in fury like blazing fires.
Standing immediately behind them were stationed yakṣas with blazing crests and deformed features, who said:
"O you of evil intent, turn back! Do not commit the slaughter of anyone at all!"
Standing immediately behind them were many hosts of Gandharvas bearing beautiful forms,
holding auspicious bows for the sake of protection, at the moment of the passing away of the one possessed of stainless wisdom.
The four Lords of the World also stood in the sky together with their own retinues;
today, it is said, the Blessed One will descend, he who increases the welfare and happiness of the world.
Standing in the sky together with the gods of the Thirty-three, the foremost of the Thirty-three, the bearer of the excellent wheel,
will before long undergo his final passing, desiring incomparable bliss.
With their ten fingers joined at the base of Māyā’s feet, the great hosts of gods bowed toward her;
gazing up at the Jina in Tuṣita, they uttered these sweet words.
O you whose power of merit is accumulated through purification, this is the time; enter your final existence.
Your mother is now ready; out of compassion, look now upon the suffering people.
"I am passing away," he uttered these auspicious words;
at that very moment, the mother of the Jina beheld a dream, the fruit of excellent ripening.
Resembling snow and silver, with six tusks, beautiful feet and lovely arms, and a crimson head— this preeminent elephant, with its graceful gait and faultless joints of limb, has entered my womb.
Indeed, Bodhisattvas do not enter their mother's womb during the dark fortnight.
Then, indeed, on the full moon night of the month of Pūrṇa, when it was conjoined with the Puṣya constellation, the Bodhisattvas descend into their mother’s womb.
[She was] one who observed the *upoṣadha* vows,

the most excellent of women, joyful, free from embarrassment, not of lowly conduct, inspiring confidence, pure of limb, with little passion, endowed with noble birth, endowed with family, endowed with beauty, and endowed with complexion.

When a woman is endowed with a noble name, endowed with height, endowed with girth, distinct, having reached the full bloom of prime youth, renowned, wise, mindful, self-possessed, possessing a favorable disposition, perfected in every aspect, complete in every quality— the supreme among women— it is into her womb that Bodhisattvas descend.
The Bodhisattva emitted a radiance by which the entire Buddha-field was illuminated;
then one son of the gods asked another son of the gods:
For what reason has the god-superior emitted this radiance,
cooler than the rays of the moon and as bright as gold,
by which the hosts of asura lords and the lords of men [are illuminated]?
And the hells, which were like blazing fires, were completely cooled.
Then he said:
Those of great renown who, here and there, protect the people trapped within the cage of saṃsāra and overcome by passion, by means of bringing them liberation;
For the purpose of addressing him, a radiance was emitted by the Sinless One.
The Bodhisattva said:
"O immortals, do not leave your cities; this is surely no time for joy.
This is the time to shatter the city of old age and death with the blow of wisdom."
Mindful, clearly comprehending, and with a right-minded heart, the Bodhisattva descended into his mother’s womb.
Thus, having let out a lion’s roar by the river, that lion among men vanished at the moment of his passing and was reborn in an instant within the palace of a king.
I pay homage to that most excellent Jina, who illumined the Tuṣita realm with his beautiful complexion and who is now passing away from the city of the gods.
The unsurpassed illuminator of the world outshines with his radiance the entire world, including the Brahmās, and all beings, including recluses and brahmins.
Behold this wonder, this marvel: how the Teacher, possessed of great supernormal power, mindful and clearly comprehending, has descended into his mother’s womb!
And for as long as that best of men, endowed with the supreme marks,
remained within his mother’s womb, he was mindful, possessed of intelligence, and fully conscious.
And as soon as the Bodhisattva had descended, this great earth shook, trembled, and quaked violently in six ways; it shook in a manner that was thrilling,
gladdening, exhilarating, marvelous, wonderful, and enchanting.
And it was not disagreeable, but rather delightful, inspiring confidence, free from agitation, and devoid of fear;
moreover, even while trembling, it did not harm any sentient being, whether moving or stationary.
Then this earth, including the circles of Sāgara and Meru, shook in six ways;
the worlds were made stainless and delightful.
By the splendor of him who dispels the great darkness.
To whatever extent the dragon kings and lords of dragons applied themselves with zeal for the sake of protection, defense, and guardianship.
The four world-protectors also provided protection for the Lord of the World,
lest anyone seeking harm should injure him, the dispeller of Namuci’s power.
Śakra, the lord of the gods; Suyāma, the son of the gods; Saṃtuṣita, the son of the gods; Sunirmita, the son of the gods;

Vaśavartin, the son of the gods; Mahābrahmā; and the Śuddhāvāsa gods—all applied themselves with zeal for the sake of protection, defense, and guardianship for the Bodhisattva while he was in his mother’s womb.
Then thousands of millions of gods, being well-pleased, approached the city named Kapila to protect the one of excellent wisdom.
The supreme city of Kapila, made like the city of the gods,
shines brilliantly with hosts of immortals who enter it, possessing the power and speed of thought.
Having surrounded Māyā, it is said that thousands of Maheśvara’s hosts,
swiftly freed from all stains, seated themselves in the sky.
Now, behind them, many thousands of Indras with stainless peaks sat down for the purpose of guarding the one of manifold virtues.
Now, behind those lords of the gods, thousands of myriads of gods belonging to the realm of desire sat in the sky, unsupported by anything.
Behind the hosts of gods were the asuras, and behind the asuras sat the throngs of double-tongued serpents,
along with yakṣas of deformed appearance and multitudes of rākṣasas.
By this rite, the glorious sky became crowded with hundreds of thousands of immortals;
for indeed, the Giver of Boons has accumulated merit that is utterly pure.
Thus, that one of great majesty and mindfulness, having passed away from the Tuṣita heaven,
assumed the form of an elephant with six tusks, resembling a white boar.
While she was lying on her heroic bed, observing the poṣadha vow and dressed in pure garments,
he— skilled in mindfulness and clear comprehension— descended into his mother’s womb.
And at the break of dawn, she told her beloved husband:
"O best of kings, a white royal elephant has entered my womb."
And having heard that, the king spoke to the assembled fortune-tellers:
"Tell me the true result and ripening of all these dreams he had."
There, when questioned by the king himself, those diviners reflected:
"One who bears the thirty-two marks has entered the womb of the queen."
Be joyful, O best of men, for you have been born into such a lineage:
a sustainer of the earth, a hero’s womb, an incomparable being, a great being.
Just as I have personally acquired from the ancient teachers,
O tiger among the heroes of men, there are two infinite destinies for him.
If he shall dwell in a house, he will become a lord of the earth, possessing all treasures and great supernatural power, ever accompanied by victory and surrounded by hundreds of thousands of kings.
Then, indeed, having abandoned the earth consisting of the four continents, he will go forth into homelessness;
he will become a Buddha, a leader of humans and gods, who cannot be led by another.
[The Śākyan lady related her dream to her beloved husband:
"A white lordly elephant, having split my womb, has entered within."
Having heard this, the king spoke to the assembled fortune-tellers:
"Tell me everything regarding his dream exactly as it is, along with its true result and ripening."
There, when questioned by the king himself, those interpreters of signs reflected:
"One who bears the thirty-two marks has entered the womb of the queen."
If, however, he dwells in the midst of a household, he will conquer the entire earth;
he shall obtain a thousand sons who are brave and such heroic men.
Then, having abandoned the earth filled with an infinite mine of jewels, he went forth into homelessness;
he will become a Buddha in the world, omniscient and all-seeing.
Thus spoke Mahābrahmā.
In her dream, she saw the sun entering her womb from the sky;
she shall give birth to a fortunate jewel among women.
The lord of this [world] becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin).
The woman who, in a dream, saw the moon entering her womb from the sky,
shall give birth to a son who is a god among men.
He becomes a king, a wheel-turning monarch of power.
The woman who, within a dream, saw the sun enter her womb from the sky,
shall give birth to one whose limbs are marked with excellence.
He becomes a king, a wheel-turning monarch of power.
That woman who, within a dream, beheld a white elephant enter her womb,
shall give birth to one who possesses the essential strength of an elephant.
Thus he becomes a Buddha, one who has awakened to the Dharma that is the goal of awakening.
The goddess is questioned.
What do you carry?
She said:
"A wheel-turning monarch."
I bear within my womb a universal monarch, a supreme man, a tiger among kings, whose golden body illuminates the belly and who is endowed with the most excellent marks.
The gods raised their voices in the sky, proclaiming the words of the Blessed One.
He will become a Buddha, not a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Mahābrahmā spoke this verse:
You are the elephant, the most excellent of jewels, who removes the force and speed of passion;
you are the lamp of the world that dispels the darkness, gloom, and delusion;
you are the treasury of virtues, possessing a mine of immeasurable jewels.
You bear the royal seer Samaruci, whose wheel is unimpeded.
The goddess said:
Just as passion and hatred do not overcome me upon perceiving the embryo of the Lord of Men,
there is no doubt that he will become one of equal radiance, just as these words issue forth.
Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, she moves with ease, stands with ease, sits with ease, and lies down with ease, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva himself.
Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, no weapon can penetrate the body of the Bodhisattva’s mother.
Neither poison, nor fire, nor lightning can prevail against a bodhisattva, solely through his own splendor.

Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, celestial maidens attend to the Bodhisattva’s mother with divine ointments, massages, and perfumes, keeping her awake through the power of the Bodhisattva himself.

Moreover, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva’s mother has her body clothed in divine garments and wears divine ornaments, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva himself.

Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, the mother comes to possess divine fragrances, divine garlands, divine ointments, and divine nourishment, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana,

when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, those who constitute his mother’s inner circle consider what he says to be most worthy of being heard and believed, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva.
They invite him with matters concerning what is to be done, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva himself.
Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva beholds the Bodhisattva-mother.
Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, no one at all passes above the Bodhisattva’s mother— not even a bird; she is free from illness and free from affliction,
and she is endowed with a digestive system that is well-balanced and capable of transformation.
Neither was it too cold nor too hot due to the change of seasons, but solely through the power of the Bodhisattva himself.

Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva’s mother becomes a recipient of exquisite foods— both hard and soft— to eat, which are of the finest flavor, the most excellent flavor, the most attained flavor, and the most fresh flavor,
solely through the power of the Bodhisattva.

Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva’s mother becomes free from passion; she practices a celibate life that is unbroken, flawless, unspotted, untarnished, completely pure, and perfect.
Not even in her mind does passion arise for that supreme woman toward any man, including even King Śuddhodana, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva himself.

Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva’s mother abides having undertaken the five precepts, and she maintains them because they were already undertaken previously through the very power of the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, all those dragon kings and lords of dragons— whether born from eggs,
born from a womb, born from moisture, or born spontaneously— all approach his dwelling and scatter divine sandalwood powder, divine *tamāla* leaf powder, and divine aloe-wood powder.
They scattered divine powders of saffron filaments and scattered divine flowers;
they honored him with that worship until it was completed, and they honored him with that worship until it was fully perfected.
Having scattered divine sandalwood powders, they scatter divine aloe-wood powders, divine kesara flower powders, and divine tamāla leaf powders.

Having scattered divine loose flowers and honored her with complete worship, and having honored her with perfect worship, they circumambulated the mother of the Bodhisattva three times and departed as they pleased, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva.

Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, as many kings of the Suvarṇas and lords of the Suvarṇas as there are— including the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmitavaśavartin, and Brahmakāyika realms— all of them approach the dwelling, scatter divine sandalwood powder, and [scatter] divine...
They scattered powders of agallochum;
having scattered divine *tamāla* leaf powders and divine loose flowers, they honored him with complete worship, they honored him with perfect worship, and they honored him with utterly pure worship.
Having circumambulated the Bodhisattva’s mother three times, they departed as they pleased, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva.

Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, he does not remain too low, nor does he remain too high; he does not remain hunched over, nor on his back, nor on his left side, nor in a squatting position.
Then, indeed, he remained standing with his body folded crosswise on the right side.
Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, he remains there unstained and pure, untainted by bile, phlegm, blood, or any other impurity.
Then, indeed, with his body cleansed, bathed, and purified, the Bodhisattva remained within his mother’s womb.

Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva has entered his mother’s womb, he beholds his mother, and the Bodhisattva’s mother also beholds the Bodhisattva within her womb like a form of refined gold; seeing him illuminating her womb like a form of refined gold, she becomes filled with joy.
Just as a beryl gem placed within a crystal casket upon the lap of one's waist would appear, even so does the mother behold the Bodhisattva,
illuminating her womb like a statue of refined gold.

The hosts of gods, with joyful minds, come to inquire after the Bodhisattva’s good night and good day; and as those hosts of gods thus inquire, the Bodhisattva greets them in return by raising his right hand, yet he does not cause his mother any discomfort.

The gods, nāgas, yakṣas, maruts, rākṣasas, and piśācas do not leave the Bodhisattva while he is in his mother’s womb, by day or by night; nor is there any talk of attachment spoken there, whether concerning sensual desires or any other kind of untruthful speech. On the contrary, they speak only of the praise of the Bodhisattva—his form, his being, his splendor, his complexion, his fame, and his roots of merit.
The worship of the Bodhisattva while he was in his mother’s womb did not cease:
there were divine musical instruments, divine aloe-wood incense, a divine rain of flowers, and a divine rain of powders.
And thousands of apsarases sing and dance around him.
The Bodhisattva’s mother engages in laughter and conversation with thousands of celestial maidens.
And while the Bodhisattva’s mother is fast asleep, the celestial maidens, being agile, fan her with garlands of *mandārava* flowers through the very power of the Bodhisattva himself.
Moreover, this is the unsurpassed perfection of the descent into the womb within this triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system.
And behold now another marvel in that assembly of gods:
how vast was the conversation that took place, which gave rise to supreme joy.
For them there is no talk of sensual pleasures, nor talk of apsarases, nor talk of singing;
for them there is no talk of instrumental music, nor talk of food, nor talk of drink.
No talk of ornaments arose among them, nor did any talk of clothing; even the thought of vehicles or gardens did not occur to their minds.
Excellent! This radiance of the Leader, who possesses the power of merit, surpasses the world together with its gods; this story of his blossoms forth there.
"How excellent is the descent into the womb, so consistent with the karma of one who has reached the further shore!"—
thus did various kinds of discourse blossom within that assembly.
"Excellent!"—with such disinterested words of praise they pass that time;
even this discourse of the one of supreme intelligence blossoms in the midst of the assembly.
Thus, speaking in many such ways, the hosts of gods delight themselves,
recounting his form, complexion, splendor, excellence, and heroic conduct.
The mother of all bodhisattvas gives birth when the tenth month is complete.
The Śākya Subhūti sent word to the king: "Let the queen come here; she shall give birth here."
The king awakens him.
He will come and he will fashion a Salabhanjika.
Make the Lumbinī grove very beautiful, cleared of grass, stumps, leaves, and debris; cover it with heaps of excellent fragrant flowers and make it sweet-smelling with scented water.
Or rather, let the winds in the Lumbinī grove blow, their bodies perfumed with the scent of *tāla* leaves;
let them carry the fragrance of nectar and cause intoxication, and let [all other scents] flee away.
May clouds from the sky, laden with the fragrance of the finest aloe-wood incense,
quickly descend to cover that Lumbinī grove, which is overflowing with the essence of excellent powders.
And for each one, fashion excellent walking-grounds from fine linen, silk, wool, and *kośikāra* fibers,
just like the wish-fulfilling trees of the preeminent gods in heaven.
The gods and the celestial maidens, taking perfumes and garlands, came to the Lumbinī grove.
Wearing earrings of crystal and gems, with garments slipping off and long strings of pearls hanging down,
they fly through the path of the sky, carrying perfumes and garlands.
One [woman] took a basket filled with mandārava flowers;
another took yellow sandalwood, and yet another took garments from the Kalpa-tree.
Taking garlands born on land and in water, as well as jewels and ornaments, the Apsarases, with joyful hearts, turned their faces toward Jambudvīpa.
Eighty-four thousand celestial maidens, not fewer, taking up parasols made of gold and jewels, fly through the sky.
And the atmosphere was filled with variegated crystal, maṇi, and musāragalva jewels resembling gabled chambers,
with hundreds of fine cloth banners raised aloft.
Resembling the breath of an elephant, the autumn clouds shine in the path of the birds,
bearing the excellent fragrance of fragrant flowers mixed with lotuses, blue water-lilies, and campakas.
The lords of the serpents, greatly rejoicing, showered the city with clouds laden with fragrant water,
along with hundreds of other wonders.
Having entered that excellent forest, the Goddess Māyā, the mother of the Jina, surrounded by her companions,
wanders in the chariot of the mind like a celestial nymph skilled in the arts of love.
Having approached for the sake of sport and grasped a branch of a *pilakṣa* tree with her arm,
she gracefully yawned at the time of the birth of that illustrious one.
Then ninety thousand daughters of the gods gathered together very quickly;
with palms joined in reverence and with pure intentions, they spoke these words after manifesting a magical display.
Today you shall give birth to one who crushes old age and disease, as delicate as the offspring of the immortals—
a queen who has brought forth a benefactor, honored in heaven and on earth, and a bringer of welfare for both gods and men.
Do not indeed give way to despondency; we shall perform your consecration. Speak whatever must be done, and see how all that has already been accomplished.
Then the four world-protectors, together with their retinues, quickly assembled;
carrying divine bundles of hair in their hands, they approached the Queen from the right side.
All the hosts of gods, having sported with Māyā in the sky,
stood there, adorned by their retinues, holding garlands and perfumes in their hands.
Furthermore, the mother of a bodhisattva does not give birth to the bodhisattva while lying down or sitting, as other women do.
Then indeed, while remaining standing, the Bodhisattva’s mother gave birth to the Bodhisattva.
Mindful and clearly conscious, the Bodhisattva emerges from his mother’s right side without causing her any pain.
For indeed, the best of men are born on the right side;
all those tigers among men become dwellers in this [place].
Why was her side not pierced, and why did no pain arise,
after she had given birth to that Supreme among Men, the progenitor of the Victors?
The Tathāgatas manifest in a mind-made form;
thus, their side is not broken, nor does pain arise.
The Bodhisattva, weary from dwelling in the womb, takes seven steps.
As soon as he was born, he took seven strides upon the earth;
he gazed toward the quarters and let out a great laugh.
In this regard, what is the reason it is said that one takes seven steps, neither eight nor sixty? Listen here to the traditional account.
Exhausted by his dwelling in the womb, the Sage, who brings benefit to the entire world,
then proceeded with great speed toward his final residence in a womb.
But as soon as those seven steps were taken, the hosts of gods gathered around;
the Sage was suddenly held in the arms of the World-Protectors.
Then a rain arose, a spray of divine flowers,
strewn with the finest māndārava blossoms and filled with divine sandalwood.
For a long time, the exalted and foremost of gods released supreme incense as an ornament for him of the highest intelligence.
And for whatever purpose the Peerless One gazes upon the directions,
regarding that as well I shall declare the tradition and the delightful instruction.
Among beings, whether among gods or humans, there exists no one for whom such an origin occurs,
nor even the descent into the womb.
When the Omniscient One is born in his final existence, the side of the Mother of the Jina shines with the luster of a firefly or gold.
As soon as he was born, that mind of the Preeminent Speaker arose:
"Is there anyone who possesses an intellect equal to mine?"—this was his thought for the purpose of turning back [such] speculation.
Some suffer from wandering in saṃsāra just as I do;
for this purpose, the Sun among Men gazes upon all directions.
Then, looking toward the directions, the best of speakers saw thousands of millions of gods and let out a laugh.
As soon as I was born, the deities belonging to the host of Māra said to me:
"You shall become a universal monarch with a great treasury over the four continents."
Then a smile arises in him: "Beings do not understand me;
I shall become the All-Knowing, the All-Seeing, the Supreme among Men."
Thus do the teachers of the doctrine praise this ripening of karma; for in such a way has the teaching of the lions among men been well-proclaimed.
I pay homage to that most excellent Conqueror, whom his mother, while standing amidst blossoming *śāli* rice fields, gave birth to as a hero, supporting her body [with the stalks].
Immediately upon being born, the Sugata stood upon the earth with level feet;
he took seven steps and gazed toward all directions.
And as he was walking, a fan and a parasol followed him,
so that gadflies and mosquitoes might not fall upon the body of the Knower of the Best.
Immediately upon the birth of the Sugata, the gods first received the Jina; afterwards, humans held him, who is unsurpassed, in their arms.
The gods welcomed the Sugata, who was endowed with the thirty-two marks;
afterwards, humans carried him, the unsurpassed one, upon their laps.
The lamps of men were extinguished, yet the world was illuminated when the Sugata was born, like a torch-bearing light for humans and gods.
When the Sugata was born, his kinsmen ran about seeking water;
then, from the front, wells full to the brim began to overflow from their mouths.
Two streams of water welled up— one cool, one warm—
whereby they bathed the Sugata as if he were an image of gold.
Furthermore, when the Sugata had been born, the Bodhisattva’s mother remained indeed unhurt and unscarred, solely through the power of the Bodhisattva;
the Bodhisattva’s mother’s womb remained completely full and yet was not distended.
Furthermore, as soon as the Bodhisattva was born, in the midst of four hundred million continents, a preeminent aśvattha tree-staff appeared upon the surface of the earth;
and in the intermediate island, a sandalwood forest appeared.
These came to serve as the Bodhisattva’s enjoyments and requisites, through the very power of the Bodhisattva himself.
There, thousands of sons of gods and thousands of apsarases came, bringing perfumes and garlands for the purpose of honoring the Bodhisattva.
A son of the gods asks another son of the gods.
"Where will you go? He replied:
This supreme consort of the lord of men shall give birth to that excellent son, whose womb is as fair as a blossomed, choice lotus—
the one who shall attain the highest goal upon the circle of the earth.
Having subdued Māra together with his army, I approach that Hero.
His limbs were unstained by the impurities of the womb,
like a supreme lotus born in the water;
he was handsome, with a complexion radiant as the morning sun.
He surpasses the immortals together with Brahmā.
Then, as soon as he was born into the family of the Śākyas, the steadfast one took seven strides here,
and having surveyed the directions, he uttered a lion’s roar.
"This is now my final existence, the last one."
In the sky, however, there was a brilliantly shining parasol, adorned with the finest jewels and pearls, outshining all others,
and hung with a garland of swaying mandārava flowers.
Many sons of gods held [it] in the sky.
They held aloft in the sky an excellent golden parasol, its color resembling the sun, a conch shell, or silver;
then, fans were released and began to whirl about.
Having grasped the Victor with their hands, they fanned him.
Then there arose a fragrant, pleasantly warm, abundant, light, lovely, and beneficial breeze for human beings—
a propitious, delightful wind laden with coolness.
Two streams of water rose up from the sky.
Then, from the peak of Mount Meru, various kinds of upper garments were released, arising as waves on all sides.
Strongly perfumed by the scent of various fragrances and carried by the wind, they caused the firm earth, with its sixfold foundation, to tremble.
In celestial palaces made of gold, silver, and beautiful jewels, the gods, accompanied by music,
proclaimed their praise as they gazed upon the Victor, born of noble birth.
They beautified the sky, including the moon, the sun, and the stars.
"This great seer, having crossed the great flood of the world— including its gods, nāgas, and yakṣas—
will thereafter reach the secure state in one direction."
The gods, being greatly delighted, proclaimed it in the sky.
When the Bodhisattva was born, there were five hundred Śākya youths headed by Sundarananda,
five hundred maidens headed by Yaśodharā,
and five hundred servants headed by Chandaka.
Five hundred horses, headed by Kaṇṭhaka;
five hundred young elephants, headed by the young elephant Candana;
and five hundred treasures appeared.
Five hundred kings were sent for the sake of increasing his victory.
King Śuddhodana issues a command.
Turn the queen back from this very place.
Someone will carry the Bodhisattva away.
A jeweled palanquin was fashioned by Viśvakarman, the son of the gods.
"Who will carry this palanquin?"
The four great kings stood by [and said],
"We shall carry the essence of beings.
And the Bodhisattva, together with his mother Māyā, ascended a palanquin.
Śakra, the lord of the gods, and Mahābrahmā both clear the way.
King Śuddhodana commanded his ministers.
"From here, lead Prince Śākyavardhana to the temple to pay homage at the feet of Queen Abhayā."
At the king’s command, those ministers led the prince Śākyavardhana from that very place to the temple to pay homage at the feet of Queen Abhayā.
Thinking, "Now we shall have them bow their heads at the feet of Queen Abhayā," the prince's feet appeared before Queen Abhayā;
then Queen Abhayā bowed her head at the prince's feet.
