When the Great Lord of the World, the Teacher of the lords of men, entered the shrines without desire,
and they caused him to be saluted with their heads, then his feet would appear.
Then the goddess Abhayā said: "It is not fitting for him to bow to me;
if he were to offer salutation to another, his head would surely split into seven pieces."
As soon as the prince was born, all sentient beings, down to those in the Avīci hell, became prosperous and happy;
the gods offered him homage, and the fearless queen, greatly rejoiced, paid him homage.
Verses for Awakening.
When he, the preeminent one in the world, was born, all matters became favorable for the king;
therefore, the name of that support of men was Sarvārthasiddha.
[_Mvu_2.27_] When the prince had entered the royal palace, the king said to the domestic priest:
"Quickly seek out brahmins who are skilled in the qualities and the rules of the marks."
And having understood that, the gods named Maheśvaras, who have mastery over their own minds, [said]:
"O assembly of brahmins, do not conceptualize based on faulty characteristics."
Free from intoxication, pride, and arrogance, eight thousand of the foremost Maheśvaras approached the Teacher of gods and men who had just been born, with their palms joined in reverence.
Clad in pure garments and standing at the gate of the royal palace, they spoke to the doorkeeper in hushed voices,
their tones as sweet as the song of the karaviṅka bird.
"Approach Śuddhodana and say: 'These eight thousand who are experts in the rules for the qualities of the marks stand here; they shall enter if you grant your permission.'"
Having promised "So be it," the gatekeeper entered the royal palace and,
with palms joined in reverence and a joyful heart, spoke to the protector of the earth.
Rule the kingdom for a long time, O slayer of enemies, with incomparable, excellent, and radiant glory;
at your gate stand those like the immortals, desiring to enter.
Those with perfectly full and stainless eyes, possessing sweet voices and the gait of an elephant in rut—of them I have no doubt; they are not humans, but sons of gods.
As they walked back and forth, the dust of the earth did not touch their excellent feet, nor was any footprint of theirs seen upon the ground; this too is a marvel.
With profound and steady gestures, noble appearance, and a gaze that is perfectly tranquil,
they produce vast joy in people who behold them with longing.
Furthermore, another marvel occurred: no shadow of their bodies was seen, nor was any sound of their joints as they walked heard at all.
Without doubt, O lord of the best of men, you have come to see the most excellent of sons;
rejoice and pay homage, and behold the gods who are not born from a womb.
O excellent Maruts, you whose hands hold choice garlands and perfumes, whose playful gestures and bodies are enchanting,
and who shine as if with splendor— of this there is no doubt.
Having heard these words, Śuddhodana, his body trembling with joy, said: "Speak quickly! Let them enter my magnificent palace."
For what reason? Because such characteristics do not belong to ordinary persons, nor does such supernatural power as you describe belong to humans.
Then that doorkeeper, having approached Maheśvara, spoke these words,
bowing low with palms joined in reverence, joyful and delighted in heart.
Rejoicing, the king said, "May you enter the palace of the bull among kings, which is like a divine city,
having been authorized by the lord of men."
Having heard these words, the eight thousand foremost Maheśvaras entered the royal palace of the chief of the unconquered lineage.
King Śuddhodana, having observed Maheśvara from afar,
rose with his retinue, his body imbued with the power of reverence.
The bull among kings said to them: "Welcome! May there be affection for all of you.
We are pleased by the sight of you and by your power of tranquility and self-control."
"We have these excellent seats available for us;
please, sirs, remain here for the sake of showing us favor."
Then, free from intoxication, pride, and arrogance, those whose deeds were blameless sat down upon those seats, which had legs variegated and pure with many jewels.
Having waited for a certain period of time, they said to the lord of men:
"May your majesty hear the purpose for which we have come here."
O Lord of Men, a son has indeed been born to you, whose every limb is faultless, who is the most beautiful in the world, and who has reached the perfection of the qualities of the marks.
We too are skilled in marks and capable of discerning the characteristics of virtues and faults;
yet we would not have seen this form of a Great Man had we not regarded you as our teacher.
He said: "Come now, behold my son, who brings security through his excellent reputation;
he brings joy to gods and men, and has reached the perfection of the qualities of the marks."
Then, having taken Guṇadhara in a soft Kācalindika woolen garment,
he presented the Moon of Speakers upon his hip to the best of the gods.
Having beheld from afar the prowess of the One Possessing Ten Powers, the Great Lords,
thrilled with joy, cast their crowns from their heads and fell upon the surface of the earth.
They then informed the king:
"It is a gain for you, Great King, a great blessing for you, that such a Great Man has been born in your family, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man. They are as follows:"
Even, neither too short nor too long, with broad heels and a fifth [mark] being the high-shouldered chest;
with thighs like those of an antelope, a large foundation, a sheathed [organ], and the nyagrodha-tree proportions—these are the ten.
The webbed hands and feet are soft and full; the fingers and toes are five with tips pointing upward;
the skin is smooth; there is a web between the toes like that of a swan; and these are the ten protuberances.
The sense of taste, the golden lion, the even [teeth], and the white [tongue]—these five are equal;
the broad [tongue], Brahmā, and the blue eyes like a cow’s—these ten;
the ūrṇā hair, the uṣṇīṣa on the head—the Protector possesses these thirty-two marks.
In the southern region, there was another young Brahmin, the son of a wealthy Brahmin from Ujjayinī; he was dark and black in complexion, wise, skillful, and possessed of great intelligence.
From his teacher’s household, he had studied the *devas*, the *mantras*, and the *śāstras*.

Having now completed his studies of the Vedas, he departed from his home, went to the Vindhya Mountains, and entered the ascetic life of a seer, subsisting on roots, fruits, and leaves, living a life of austerity.

Having established a hermitage there on the Vindhya mountain, by applying himself, striving, and exerting effort along the path of practice, he accomplished the four dhyānas and realized the five superknowledges (abhijñās).

He was a master of the four dhyānas and possessed the five superknowledges; he was highly learned, having reached the further shore of the Vedas. This seer Asita was renowned and well-known everywhere. The seer Asita, celebrated throughout the heavens, moving through the air, endowed with great supernatural power and majesty, dwelt in that hermitage together with about five hundred disciples and Nālaka.
Thus, seeing the earthquake that occurred at the moment the Bodhisattva was born, seeing the great radiance,

hearing the delightful and non-human sounds of song and instrumental music, and seeing divine showers of flowers falling as thousands of koṭis of gods and thousands of apsarases traveled through the sky with celestial garlands and perfumes in their hands—
Seeing hundreds of other wonders as well, such as those rushing toward him from the east, his hair stood on end with thrill.
"What is this that has happened today in Jambudvīpa?
By whose power does the earth tremble today, and why have hundreds of wonders appeared?"

Then that seer, with his divine eye, surveyed the whole of Jambudvīpa: "Whose is this power of majesty? From whence do such delightful sounds of singing and instrumental music issue forth? Why are hundreds of divine musical instruments heard? Why are gods and celestial maidens seen? And why do divine showers of flowers rain down, as if from thousands of suns and moons?"
And in thousands of hells, fire was no longer seen blazing;
moreover, sentient beings became endowed with exclusive happiness.
Thus, with his divine eye, he saw.

Previously, in the city of Kapilavastu, a son was born to King Śuddhodana—one who had performed meritorious deeds, possessed great renown, and was of great majesty; through the power and influence of his splendor, hundreds of such wonders as these appeared throughout Jambudvīpa.
"At the proper time and place, I shall see the prince."

Then, knowing the proper time and occasion, surrounded by a great many disciples, he arrived through the air by means of his supernormal power at the gate of King Śuddhodana’s inner apartments in order to see the prince.
The minister and the doorkeeper, upon seeing the seer, rose up and asked:
"What does the Blessed One command? For what purpose have you come?"
The ṛṣi said:
Announce to Śuddhodana that the seer Asita desires an audience.
The doorkeeper informed the king.
The seer Asita was desirous of seeing him.
King Śuddhodana, having heard of the arrival of the seer Asita—who was renowned, famous, and highly distinguished—spoke to the doorkeeper.
"Let the seer enter," [he said].
The gatekeeper, having run out, informed the seer:
"May your honor enter."
The seer entered;
seeing the seer, the king, together with his harem, rose to meet him.
Let us pay homage to the Blessed One; may the Blessed One be seated.
The seer, having congratulated the king with cries of victory, sat down.
The king asks.
"O Blessed One, what is the purpose of your coming?"
The seer said:
I desire to see your son.
And at that time, the prince entered a certain peaceful meditative absorption.
This thought occurred to them:
"The prince is fast asleep."
Then the king said to the seer:
"Venerable One, wait a moment; the prince has just now fallen asleep."
The seer said:
"Great King, the prince does not shiver."
The king approached the prince's feet and saw that the prince was awake.
The king was amazed by the seer;
the seer was highly distinguished.
The king commanded:
"Bring the prince to the seer."
The prince, taking hold of a fine deerskin rug, presented it to the seer.
Seeing from afar the marks of a Great Man upon the body of the young seer, he placed his joined palms to his head and rose up to meet him.
Having paid homage, the prince was accepted by the seer.
The seer examined the thirty-two marks of a Great Man on the prince.
And there in the royal palace, the seer heard the word "cakravartin" being applied to the prince;
for the fortune-tellers had prophesied that the prince would become a universal monarch.
It occurs to the seer:
He will not become a universal monarch;
he will become a Buddha in this world.
Having seen those marks, the seers said, "These are not the marks of a universal monarch; such are the marks of Buddhas.
This one will become a Buddha in the world.
And I shall pass away before long."
And I shall not behold this jewel;
I shall not hear his Dharma, nor shall I behold the supreme assembly.
The seer wept and shed tears.
When King Śuddhodana saw the seer Asita weeping, he became agitated along with his entire harem.
"Why do you weep upon seeing the Blessed One, the Prince? Do you perceive some misfortune for the Prince?"

As soon as the prince was born, the earth shook in six ways; a radiance appeared in the world; he was honored by thousands of gods; divine showers of flowers fell, and thousands of divine musical instruments were played, and their sounds resounded.

As soon as the prince was born in Kapilavastu, five hundred princes were born; five hundred maidens, five hundred male slaves, and five hundred female slaves appeared; five hundred young elephants, five hundred horses, and five hundred treasures manifested; and five hundred kings sent greetings of victory and prosperity, along with other wonders and marvels.
And the Blessed One, seeing the prince, wept. "Tell me this, Blessed One: do you see some misfortune befalling the prince?"
The seer said: "Great King, I see no misfortune for the prince.
Great King, such great beings as these appear in the world only occasionally and in some place."
"This Great Person has appeared; he will become a Buddha in the world.
Yet I am old and shall not see him.
He will teach the Dharma that leads to peace, to the noble state, and to Nirvana, but I shall not hear it."
"I shall not see his excellent assembly, nor shall I see the miraculous transformations of the Buddha.
Therefore, O Great King, seeing this great misfortune of my own, I weep."
Having unilaterally prophesied that the Bodhisattva would become a Buddha in the world for four reasons, the seer departed.
Having abandoned the hindrances, listen to me with a one-pointed mind,
how Asita lamented when the Śākyan prince was born.
There was a great seer named Asita who dwelt in the region of the Vindhya mountains;
he was a high-souled one of fixed resolve, whose body-hair was like that of the great Kapila.
Skilled in the forest scriptures and possessing the five superknowledges,
he dwelt on the peak of Mount Kailāsa like Dhanapati, the lord of the Guhyakas.
Thus he dwelt at the head of the forest, subsisting on a harsh livelihood of uncultivated roots and fruits,
together with his disciple Nālaka and many others.
Practicing the ten wholesome actions, delighting in tranquility and self-restraint, he instructs others;
having reached the perfection of divine qualities, the seer is endowed with supreme virtue.
A vast radiance appeared, and supramundane joy arose without confusion;
beings experienced absolute happiness, and the earth trembled.
Seated there, he saw mandārava flowers and divine kalpa-flowers fallen upon the surface of the earth.
And Asita saw in the sky the masses of ornaments scattered about,
and thousands of celestial maidens rushing through the expanse of the heavens.
In the mountain caves, he hears the sweet songs of the kinnarīs;
he calms the mountain rivers flowing along their banks, whose currents are filled with blossoms.
And he beholds a vast radiance spreading everywhere in the ten directions,
suddenly surging upward like the rays of the rising sun.
Having seen these and many other wonderful things,
Asita’s hair stood on end and his mind became filled with reflection.
But indeed, the earth trembled and in the vault of the sky drums resounded;
the world was illuminated and a rain of flowers fell.
The moon and sun do not shine; the salt-water ocean of dark waters is agitated;
and masses of lotuses, like upper garments, are seen amidst the flood of waters filled with flowers.
And all these excellent trees, though not their season for flowering, are covered with blossoms;
today they are laden with fruit and flowers, and fragrant scents waft abroad.
Today, within a single day, the fires in the thousands of hells do not blaze forth,
nor do the beings perishing in the intermediate spaces between worlds experience suffering.
Furthermore, neither hunger nor thirst arises in my body as it did before;
my heart is joyful—what indeed will happen today?
But why indeed do these divine maidens, with laughter overflowing, run toward the eastern quarter while carrying sandalwood powder?
Who indeed has been born today in Jambudvīpa, possessed of such great majesty? By whose fame does this illustrious one possess such a magnificent power?
In this world, such a sign occurs for anyone at all;
when Buddhas appear, such portents come to pass.
He hears the hosts of immortals in the sky as they descend toward the earth:
"A Lord of the World has arisen; he will become an unleadable Buddha."
Then, with a joyful mind, having heard the hosts of gods in the expanse of the sky, he [thought]:
"Today, the Buddha, the essence of the heroes among men, has appeared in the world."
Then the seer surveyed the whole of Jambudvīpa with his divine eyes;
he saw him who was born in the clan of the Śākyas as the son of Śuddhodana.
Having seen this, a great rumor concerning enlightenment has arisen in all directions;
that sound of "Buddha" circulates there, and I shall see him in due time.
And they too, with axes in their hands, wearing well-made upper garments of black antelope skin and clad in robes of bark and rags, arrived bringing fruits and water.
In the sky, without support, along the path of the wind, the seer set forth;
having manifested supernatural power, he arrived at Kapilavastu in an instant.
At the foot of the Himavat mountains, he beheld a delightful city protected by the Kinsman of the Sun (the Buddha),
unassailable by enemies, as exceedingly beautiful as the city of the Thirty-three gods;
there the seer entered the city of the gods for the purpose of seeing the Śākyas.
He entered the city, which was filled with people intent on buying and selling in the marketplaces,
and crowded with joyful people and throngs of delighted horses, elephants, chariots, and infantry.
Approaching with his mind, he entered the gate into the inner apartments of Śuddhodana’s residence, which was like the abode of the king of the gods.
He beheld that palace-tower, with its excellent windows and latticed balconies fully blossomed,
shining in the sky like a mountain peak fallen from the heights.
In that preeminent celestial palace, gabled chambers possessing the splendor of silver shine forth; their finials resemble the blazing flames of a sacrificial fire.
The inner chambers are auspicious and resemble bright conch shells and pearl necklaces;
they shine with the brilliance of the stainless sun, fashioned like moons.
There, they are seen upon well-crafted slabs of beryl,
with rows of house-needles, possessing the colors of lightning and rain-clouds.
They behold archways made of gold, resembling flames of fire;
they shine with the brilliance of the stainless sun and are fashioned like moons.
In some places, even those intoxicated like dark clouds at the end of an eon seem to pour forth water; in other places, resembling the sun, they emerge together with stars, resting upon it.
In various places, even kittens suddenly pounce there,
and in various places they are terrified by peacocks flying together.
In various places, cuckoos within their cages warble sweetly; in other places, parrots and mainas are distracted by the tinkling of their ornaments.
Pure, square, and extending in the ten directions, it was well-constructed and beautifully adorned; it was unassailable by enemies and perfectly laid out according to the measuring line.
Upon this ground of many variously arranged masses, for the sake of a great collection of jewels, a lion sits; he trembles at the rising sun when it has already set.
Accompanied by female attendants and musicians, he entered that place— which was devoid of vehicles and carriages,
variegated with the color of saffron robes, and crowded with eunuchs.
Accompanied by a hundred servants and vehicles, crowded with noble people, pure and fragrant,
the matted-haired ascetic entered the palace gate without obstruction.
And in the assembly hall, the woman was seen standing in agitation,
her hand grasping a sword, yet speaking with words of exceeding sweetness and beauty.
He was unattached, discerning, profound, and well-versed in the proper methods of all treatises;
he said to the doorkeeper, "Announce me to the King of the Śākyas."
I am the renowned Kāla; I am Bhāradvāja by lineage. I was born in the noble region of Ārya, and I dwell upon the peak of the Vindhya mountains.
"Very well, noble sir," Śrutadhara replied, and having heard those words of the king in their entirety, he brought them [to the queen] and caused her to enter.
Having been granted leave, he entered the celestial abode of Siṃhahanu,
which was crowded with throngs of apsarases, like Indra gone to the Nandana grove.
Asita by name caused them to be increased with cries of victory and presented fruits;
the king accepted them and said, "Welcome, Blessed One."
Then, having been invited, he sat down upon that excellent seat which was made of gold with eight legs, adorned with variegated kilañja grass, and embellished with jewels.
Seated upon his couch, the great-attained seer endowed with the five supernormal powers was invited for a meal by King Śuddhodana himself.
"Abundant food has been prepared; please accept it, O Blessed One, for you are free from illness.
We wish to see your son, the prince, if it should be agreeable to you."
Welcome and with affection to you! Prince Priyadarśin has been sleeping for some time; once he has awakened, you shall see him like a statue made of gold.
And when the prince had awakened, they presented him with a fine woolen blanket adorned with the eight auspicious symbols,
and showed him the sun appearing through a gap in the clouds.
Having seen him placed upon the fine woolen blanket like an earring, that best of sages rose up quickly and received the prince in his arms.
Taking him on his lap and observing that he was endowed with the thirty-two marks as well as the secondary characteristics, he, equal to Indra, wept.
To him, whose eyes were filled with tears, King Śuddhodana said this:
"Why has this dejection arisen in you now upon seeing the prince?"
O Brahmin, having seen him who, on the very day he was born, took seven steps facing north—why do you weep? I wish to hear [the reason].
On the very day he was born, having taken up a parasol and a fan, they stood in the air; seeing this, O Brahmā, why do you weep?
O Brahmin, I wish to hear why you weep upon seeing him, on whose birth this entire world was illuminated.
O Brahmin, I wish to hear why you weep upon seeing him, on whose day of birth two wells of water rose up from the sky.
O Brahmin, I wish to hear why you weep upon seeing him on whose day of birth the gods held up a parasol in the sky.
O Brahmin, I wish to hear why you weep upon seeing him, on whose day of birth the gods scattered mandārava flowers.
O Brahmin, I wish to hear why you weep upon seeing him, on whose day of birth the unconscious earth itself trembled.
O Brahmin, on the day he was born, the salt-water ocean of dark waters was agitated; having seen that, why do you weep? I wish to hear [the reason].
O Brahmin, I wish to hear why you weep upon seeing him, on whose birth day the celestial drums resounded in the sky.
O Brahmin, on the very day he was born, five hundred sons of the Śākyas were also born; having seen him, why do you weep? I wish to hear [the reason].
On the day he was born, five hundred Śākya maidens were also born.
"O Brahmin, having seen him, why do you weep? I wish to hear [the reason].
On the day he was born, five hundred slaves were born for me;
O Brahmin, having seen him, why do you weep? I wish to hear [the reason]."
"O Brahmin, on the very day he was born, five hundred of my slave-girls were also born; having seen him, why do you weep? I wish to hear [the reason]."
"O Brahmin, on the very day he was born, five hundred horses were born for me; having seen him, why do you weep? I wish to hear [the reason]."
O Brahmin, on the very day he was born, five hundred young elephants were also born; having seen him, why do you weep? I wish to hear [the reason].
O Brahmin, on the day he was born, five hundred treasuries revealed their openings; having seen him, why do you weep? I wish to hear [the reason].
O Brahmin, I wish to hear why you weep upon seeing him, on whose birth day the kings of the mandala bowed down before me.
"O Brahmin, I wish to hear why you weep upon seeing that king, to whom the royal preceptors come for an audience."
O Brahmin, having seen whom men become joyful, happy, and elated—having seen that very person, why do you weep? I wish to hear [the reason].
"O Brahmin, dispel your sorrow; become joyful in mind and obtain happiness.
This one shall become a king, a protector of the earth possessed of the seven treasures."
When this had been said, Asita spoke these words to the one called Śveta:
"Wiping away his tears, he said: 'He has been prophesied by the seers.'"
Resembling the fire of bliss and the rising sun, that lion among men will not remain a mere lord of men;
he will become a Teacher, unconquered by any.
For by means of these three stages, having leaped over the triple world without remainder,
he will attain the supreme Dharma— auspicious, immortal, and free from obstacles.
"I am aged and my life has passed; the Supreme among Men is young and has been born but recently.
I shall have met my end by the time the Prince attains enlightenment."
"This one will become a Buddha, omniscient and a master of all dharmas;
and I am old in this well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya—thus I weep."
Nor do I have any fear of death; for where has a human being ever been born who does not die?
But it is because I shall no longer behold the peerless Buddha that I weep.
Indeed, I have no fear of death; for where is there a human being who is born and does not die? But it is because I shall not hear the Dharma that leads to peace that I weep.
Truly, I have no fear of death; for where is there a mortal who is born and does not die?
It is because I shall not see the Saṅgha, that ocean of virtues, that I weep.
He who, as a Buddha, will awaken this generation long asleep in worldly enjoyments—he has now appeared; but I am old, and therefore I weep.
He who, being himself liberated, will liberate this generation bound by the fetters of passion—he has now appeared; yet I weep because I am old.
"He who, being himself liberated, will liberate this people bound by the fetters of delusion—he has now appeared; yet I weep because I am old."
He who, being himself liberated, will liberate this generation from passion, hatred, and delusion—he has now appeared; yet I weep because I am old.
He who, having become free from illness himself, will also make others free from illness—
he has appeared today, yet I weep because he is old.
He who, having become sorrowless himself, will also make others sorrowless—he has appeared; as for me, I weep because I am old.
"He who, having himself become free from the arrow, shall also make others free from the arrow—he has appeared; alas, I weep because he is old."
These humans and gods in Kāśipur are happy, for they shall behold the King of Dharma setting the wheel of dharma in motion; but I weep because I am old.
These happy humans and gods shall behold him standing in the midst of the excellent assembly, distributing the deathless nectar; but I weep because I am old.
Sickness, old age, and death are many obstacles for human beings;
though I have arisen as a source of consolation, I weep because I myself am not consoled.
Then, having spoken thus to the Sage, feeling great compassion and trembling,
he praised him with words upon seeing that Tamer of Men, the Best of Beings.
From the eastern direction he spoke, having come here searching for the Supreme among Men:
"For the arising of Buddhas, the tamers of the untamed, is not easily found."
Having now circumambulated the Bodhisattva many times from left to right, he addressed the lord of men: "I am going; may your majesty grant me Snigdhavatī."
Having heard the Buddha’s voice, you shall go into the presence of the Supreme Guide;
there you shall practice the holy life and become an attendant to his word.
Having promised "So be it" to Asita, Nārada—
having gone forth— became the elder of the community, an Arhat who had shaken off all defilements.
Pay homage to the Elder Nārada, who is of the same lineage as Kātyāyana, the son of the Jina, a forest-dweller who has attained final nirvāṇa.

Pay homage to that Elder who has attained final nirvana— tranquil, perfectly peaceful, free from the substrata of existence, liberated through the exhaustion of all substrata, and transcending all conceptual proliferation.
For four reasons, the Bodhisattva was declared with certainty by Asita that he would become a Buddha.
By which four?
For the clarity of the characteristics, for their well-differentiated nature, for their profundity, and for their unimpaired excellence.
The Blessed Buddhas possessed eighty secondary marks.

The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have high nails, copper-colored nails, and glossy nails; their fingers are rounded, beautiful, and tapering with beautiful proportions. Their veins are without knots and hidden, their ankles are concealed, their joints are firm, and their feet are level and even.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, possess fully developed secondary characteristics (*vyañjana*), are radiant on all sides, and have limbs that are soft, pure, and free from dejection.
Her limbs are well-knit, her body is compactly formed,
and her major and minor limbs are well-proportioned.

Furthermore, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, possess entirely faultless bodies; their limbs are free from moles and dark spots, and their hands are as soft as cotton wool. Their lines on the palms are deep, unbroken, and continuous.
Her lines on the palms are gradual; her lips are like the *bimba* fruit; and her speech issues from the region of the navel.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have tongues that are soft, thin, and red;
their voices are like the roar of an elephant or the sound of thunder,
and their speech is melodious with a sweet resonance.
He walks with the stride of an elephant,
he walks with the stride of a bull,
and he walks with the stride of a lion.
She walked with a graceful, rightward-turning gait; she was well-proportioned and possessed of a serene beauty on all sides;
and her conduct was pure.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have body hairs that are supremely pure and clean, and they possess a pervasive radiance free from darkness; their limbs are straight.
Her limbs are soft and well-proportioned;
her waist is shaped like a bow, being beautiful, smooth, and unbroken;
and her navel is deep.
And his navel is unbroken; and his navel is uninterrupted;
and his navel curls to the right.
And his kneecaps are well-rounded.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have rounded fangs and sharp fangs.
And his canine teeth were unbroken; and his canine teeth were unsevered; and his canine teeth were not uneven.
She has a prominent nose, a nose that is not too long,
and dark eyes.
And his eyes are like dark and white lotuses;
the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have dark eyebrows and smooth-haired eyebrows;
and his ears are not small.

The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have ears that are symmetrical, free from defects of the ears, unimpaired, undefiled, with tranquil faculties, and possess faces and foreheads that are most excellent and sublime.
With black hair,
with thick hair,
and with variegated hair.
Her hair is well-arranged and unbroken;
her hair is uncut and not coarse;
her hair is glossy and fragrant.
The hair of the Blessed Buddhas is curled at the tips, well-formed at the roots, and resembles the finest swastikas, nandyāvartas, and strings of pearls.
These are the eighty secondary marks on the body of the Buddha of immeasurable wisdom,
by which his body is constantly adorned.
Of the god beyond gods, the supreme among men.
He possesses thirty-two excellent secondary marks upon his body,
and from all sides, a fathom-wide radiance issues forth.
How indeed could a wise person not have faith in the Victor?
By taking up a hundred times the merit of all sentient beings,
one may produce a single excellent mark upon his body.
King Śuddhodana, together with his harem and accompanied by the prince, set out for the park grounds.
While the Bodhisattva was walking about in the park grounds, he arrived at a farming village.
There he saw plows being drawn;
by those plows, both the long snake and the frog were lifted up.
The frog was seized for the sake of food.
Dīrghaka, too, was thrown by the prince.
The Bodhisattva saw it, and upon seeing it, a great sense of spiritual urgency arose within him.
Granted, my body and life are equally tormented; yet today I shall attain the deathless state, liberation from existence—
for it is impossible for me to withdraw my vigor.
And at the appointed time, he [restrained] the force of the waters, just as Anarva did.
While the Bodhisattva was seated in the shade of a rose-apple tree, as the forenoon passed and the sun moved on, the shadow did not leave the Bodhisattva;
having attained and abided in the first dhyāna, accompanied by applied and sustained thought.
From the side of the Himavat, five sages were traveling through the air toward the Vindhya mountains;
they were unable to pass over the Bodhisattva there.

Like an elephant breaking through a thicket of mango branches and a multitude of trees, we have here repeatedly burst forth from Mount Meru, which is crowned with jewels and diamonds, rising high and extending exceedingly far in every direction.

We were capable of going even to the city of the immortals and ascending into the heights of the sky, taking refuge in the abodes of gods and gandharvas; yet now, having reached this mere grove of trees, we despair—alas, whose splendor causes the power of our supernatural success to turn back?
The gods recite this verse:

Born into the lineage of the lords of kings, the son of the Śākya king was wise and possessed the radiance of the rising sun; his limbs were marked with excellent physical characteristics and the splendor of his complexion surpassed even the light of the young sun at dawn.

This king, having taken refuge here in the forest and being devoted to meditation and reflection, has been increased by hundreds of millions of virtues; let his majesty turn back the power of his supernatural success.
For this lamp has appeared in the blinding darkness;
he shall attain that Dharma which will bring breath to the world.
The Great Sage has appeared in a world scorched by the fires of affliction;
he shall attain that Dharma which will bring joy to the world.
This supreme vehicle has appeared in the wilderness of the ocean of sorrow;
he shall attain that Dharma by which he will deliver the world.
The One with Vision will teach this supreme and most excellent path to the three worlds, which have become lost in the great wilderness of saṃsāra.
For a long night this progeny has been bound in the prison of saṃsāra;
this King of Dharma will bring about both their bondage and their liberation.
When reviled, people always desire a hero; they honor a companion who is skilled in counsel, treating him with great affection by providing him with food and drink.
At the time for the meal, the king asked the prince:
"Where will the prince take his food?"
Having heard this from the king, the chamberlains, the eunuchs, the Kirātas, and the dwarfs ran out in all directions, searching for the prince.
The prince was seen by his chamberlain meditating in the shade of a rose-apple tree; even as the sun turned, the shade of the rose-apple tree did not leave the prince.
Seeing this, the chamberlain was struck with wonder: "How extraordinary is this prince, whose shadow remains conscious and never leaves him!"
The chamberlain informed King Śuddhodana.
When the orb of the dispeller of darkness had set,
[he saw] the Lord of Men, possessing the supreme auspicious marks, with a dark radiance,
meditating as motionless as a mountain.
The shade of the rose-apple tree does not leave one who has achieved their purpose.
Having heard this from the chamberlain, the king approached the place where the prince was and saw the shade of a rose-apple tree [covering him].
Amazed, the king said:
Like a sacrificial fire upon a mountain peak, or like the moon surrounded by a host of stars,
he gladdens the limbs of those who behold him.
Established in meditative absorption, he is like a lamp filled with oil.
The king said: "This one is truly fortunate, since even these inanimate things bow down before him."
King Śuddhodana prostrated at the feet of the Bodhisattva as he sat within the shade of the rose-apple tree.
This thought occurred to King Śuddhodana:
Since the prince’s mind delights in peaceful meditations, that prediction made by the seer Asita will indeed come true.
That king provided the prince with an extensive harem so that the prince might take delight in the domestic life.
For the sake of the maidens, the king had various kinds of Aśoka ornaments made in many different ways.
And in the city of Kapilavastu, a proclamation was made:
"All the maidens must go out to the royal park; Prince Sarvārthasiddha will distribute ornaments to the girls."
By the king's command, many thousands of maidens were sent out from Kapilavastu to that park.
The daughter of the Śākya Mahānāman, named Yaśodharā, having been brought forth amidst great prosperity, approached the Prince with a bashful demeanor.
When the Blessed One had gone forth, attained unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, and set in motion the sublime wheel of Dharma, that was heard by the monks.
While the Blessed One, still a youth, was in a pleasure grove distributing ornaments to the maidens, Yaśodharā, feeling bashful, approached the Prince.
A monk asked the Blessed One.
"How was it, Blessed One, that Yaśodharā, feeling bashful, clung to the Blessed One when he was still a youth?"
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now that Yaśodharā has clung to me out of shame;
on another occasion as well, she clung to me out of shame."
The monks said.
At other times as well, Blessed One?
The Blessed One said:
On another occasion as well, monks.
Once upon a time, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi, there was a brahmin of the Kauśika clan.
Having seen the peril in sensual pleasures, he went forth into the life of a seer in the Himalayas.

Having established a hermitage there on the banks of the Gaṅgā in the Himalayas, he dwelt devoted to the practice of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night. By means of the path already traversed, he produced the four dhyānas and realized the five super-knowledges (*pañcābhijñā*).
He became a seer (*ṛṣi*) of great psychic power and majesty, capable of touching the sun and moon, yet he was not disposed toward sharing his wealth.
Now, after the dissolution of his body, that kinsman was reborn among the Gandharva-bodied gods as a son of the Gandharvas named Pañcaśikha.
Having become a god, he remembers that Kauśika:
"Where in the sky is Kauśika—has his life proceeded or has he died?"
He reflected and saw that Kauśika, having gone forth into the renunciant life of a seer,
was dwelling in a hermitage on the bank of the Gaṅgā in the Himalayas, being of a nature that did not share his possessions.
He informed Śakra, the lord of the gods.

He who was my kinsman when I was a human being—dear and pleasing to me—has gone forth into the wandering life of a seer and dwells in a hermitage on the bank of the Ganges in the Himalayas; since he is of a nature that does not share his possessions, let us approach him for the sake of benefiting him and establish him in the practice of sharing.
Then Śakra, for the sake of favoring the seer Kauśika, at the time and place for taking food, together with the moon and the sun,
and with Mātali as his charioteer and the divine son Pañcaśikha, having assumed the guise of brahmins,
approached the hermitage of the seer Kauśika one by one at the time for taking food.
And that dog displayed various kinds of high and low colors.
Kauśika said:
I neither buy nor sell,
nor do I have any store of goods; this food of mine is of a very limited quantity.
This Nala is a man of evil conduct who stole a prastha of syāmāka grain.
The dog said:
From a small amount one should give a small portion; from a moderate amount a moderate portion; from a large amount one should give a large portion. It is not right to give nothing at all.
Having paid homage, O Kauśika, I say: eat and give;
one who has entered upon the Noble Path finds happiness exclusively.
The Moon also approached.
Kauśika said:
I neither buy nor sell,
nor do I have any store of goods; this food of mine is of very limited quantity.
A prastha of syāmāka grain is equal to three nalas of sheep's wool.
Candra said:
He swallows a hook made of iron with a long line— namely,
he who eats his meal while a guest is seated, having given nothing to him.
Having paid homage, O Kauśika, I say: eat and give;
one who has entered upon the Noble Path finds happiness single-mindedly.
The sun also approached.
Kauśika said:
I neither buy nor sell,
nor do I have any store of goods;
this food of mine is of limited measure.
A prastha of syāmāka grain is equal to four of each of these: nala and meṣa.
The Sun said:
Vain is his oblation, and vain is his concentration,
who eats his meal without giving to a guest who is seated.
Having paid homage, I say to you, Kauśika: eat and give;
one who has entered the Noble Path finds happiness in its entirety.
Mātali also approached.
Kauśika said:
I do not buy, nor do I sell,
nor do I have any store of goods whatsoever;
this food of mine is of limited quantity.
A prastha of syāmāka grain is equal to five nalas of sheep's wool.
Mātali said:
The offering of one who eats his meal only after giving food to a guest seated before him becomes true, and it is truly well-concentrated.
Having paid homage, O Kauśika, I say: eat and give;
one who has entered upon the Noble Path finds happiness single-mindedly.
Śakra also approached.
Kauśika said:
I do not buy, nor do I sell,
nor do I have any store of goods whatsoever; this food of mine is of a limited form.
A prastha of syāmāka grain is the measure for six [persons].
Śakra said:
He offers the Sarasvatī sacrifice and causes it to reach even those who have not sacrificed,
he who, when a guest is seated, eats his meal only after having given [food] to him.
Having paid homage, O Kauśika, I say: eat and give;
one who has entered the Noble Path finds happiness as a single certainty.
Kośika said:
"These brahmins are of noble appearance,
yet what is the reason for this dog of yours?
I shall demonstrate to you the various grades of physical appearance."
Tell me, sirs, who indeed might you be?
Śakra said:
The Moon and the Sun have come here,
as has Mātali, the divine charioteer;
and I am Śakra, the lord of the thirty-three gods.
And this is that Pañcaśikha... [so it was said].
In former births you were our kinsman; you, Kauśika, were a miserly person of evil character. It is out of compassion for you that we have come here.
O you of evil nature, do not go forth in vain.
Those who are stingy, possessed of the evil qualities of anger and malice, who harbor hatred toward śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas,
and who have performed sinful deeds—
Having passed away from here, they go to hell.
And those wise ones here who give gifts with a serene mind to ascetics and brahmins,
having performed meritorious deeds in this world of the living—
Passing away from here, they go to a happy rebirth.
Kauśika said:
"Today I shall perform such merit;
I will give gifts to ascetics and brahmins.
Through these [means], I shall provide food and drink."
I shall not drink even the nectar without having given it away.
And as I give in this way at all times,
all my enjoyments will be exhausted;
therefore, I shall go forth into a happy rebirth.
Having abandoned sensual desires as well as those that are excessive.
On Gandhamādana, the best of mountains, the sons of the supreme lords of gods rejoice;
all the excellent sages have arrived to pay him honor.
Take hold of the branch of the best of trees, which is in full bloom.
"O worthy one, let them offer a branch that is pure, fragrant, honored by the thirty gods, beautifully blossomed, and frequented by the best of immortals; homage be to you!"
Just as you are, Śakra, so indeed are you.
"O Brahmin, you said that you would look after her as she was begging; why then do you incite this quarrel? I have no need for these flowers here."
"Let whichever of you is more excellent take it."
Therefore, O Brahmin, you yourself must examine this and discern for us, O worthy sir, which of us is indeed superior;
to whomever among us, O worthy sir, you shall grant it.
She alone will become even more excellent for us.
"This is an improper statement," said the fair-limbed woman;
that brahmin uttered words of anger:
"Go and ask the Lord of Beings!"
He alone will know for you which of these two is indeed better.
Even then, those who perceive the ultimate truth, being noble and desiring the most excellent praise,
went and spoke to the Lord of the Thirty-three.
Know us, O noble sir; what indeed is better?
Seeing them, Purandara was not pleased;
he spoke thus:
"Among all of you, none are as well-proportioned as she."
Who would incite a quarrel preceded by malice?
The Great Sage who wanders throughout the entire world, he whose name is Nārada and whose valor is truth—
on Mount Gandhamādana, he spoke.
Having gone there, indeed ask the Lord of Beings.
From here, in the northern direction,
on the bank of the Gaṅgā at the side of the Himavat,
there is that Kauśika, for whom food and drink are difficult to obtain.
The charioteer of the gods sent nectar to him.
Just as the sun, the dispeller of darkness and illuminator of the world, shines when it rises and offers oblations into the fire,
so too do you conduct yourself in the realm of the sun.
"Which deity are you? For what purpose have you come here?"
Resembling a conch shell, with a brilliance like incomparable snow, possessing a pleasing fragrance and a lovely appearance—
such as this has never before been seen by my eye.
Who is your deity, and what indeed do you give to me?
"O great seer, I have been sent by Mahendra and have come swiftly to you, the stealer of nectar;
know me to be Mātali, the charioteer of the gods."
May I enjoy these supreme pleasures as I desire.
Having experienced cold for twelve [years], those who have committed evil deeds [endure] hunger,
thirst, discontent, and fever in succession; as well as anger, enmity, strife, and slander.
And it is the supreme state, free from cold, heat, and lassitude.
"O Mātali, it does not befit me to eat without first having given; thus he spoke of the unsurpassed [gift].
Nor is it praised for me to give to only one."
For one who does not share finds no happiness.
Those who are friends, those who provide means, and those who strike down enemies or kill women for the sake of wealth—
all of them are considered equal to a miser.
If one does not give away what has been obtained, even the nectar of immortality will perish.
Thus sent by the King of the Gods, his four daughters, resembling molten gold,
took with them nectar worthy of being received as a gift.
To that hermitage where Kauśika had been.
But having seen those four women standing in the four directions, illuminating everything and stationed immediately adjacent to one another, the wise Arthadarśa [reflected].
Then, O Kauśika, he addressed him thus.
O goddess, you stand in the eastern direction,
adorned like the excellent star and the medicinal herb;
I ask you, O you whose form is like a golden altar.
"Tell me, which deity are you?"
I am the foremost among women, esteemed for my noble character;
always devoted to service,
I have come into your presence seeking happiness.
O one of excellent wisdom, grant me that nectar as my portion.
Endowed with virtue, endowed with conduct, endowed with wisdom, and endowed with excellent deeds—
you are possessed of a glorious birth and majesty.
One who possesses enjoyments and lives in happiness sends [others] away like a slave.
Moreover, even a man who is a slave, lazy, unskilled, or wretched and deformed, if he is endowed with you, who possess the nature of glory, [he becomes noble].
This which has been done by you is improper.
O illustrious one, illuminating the delightful quarters of the world with your fame,
I ask you, O lady whose form is like a golden altar.
Tell me, which deity are you?
"I am Faith, esteemed among men; I always serve those of noble character. Seeking happiness, I have come into your presence."
O one of excellent wisdom, grant me that nectar as my portion.
My wife too was indeed worthy of me, honored, possessed of virtuous qualities, and devoted to her husband;
she left behind her own family and her daughters.
He again produces faith in Kumbhakāśī.
Even when morality, learning, self-restraint,
faith, and truthfulness are present at one time,
this [state] is not seen to be impaired by anything blameworthy.
This which has been done by you is improper.
Even though you speak in my presence, I know that you are deluded and follow after rogues;
such a person as you does not deserve a seat or water.
"Whence do you come for nectar? You do not please me."
The night departs when the dawn has risen;
you stand there like the best of stars, O herb.
I ask you, O you whose form is like a golden altar.
Tell me, which deity are you?
Like a doe wandering, abandoned and driven away by a wild bull, you gaze about me with a faint smile;
who is your companion, O lady of delicate limbs?
Are you not afraid, being all alone, O goddess?
No companions have come here with me, O Kauśika;
I am a preeminent deity.
I have come here for the sake of nectar.
Therefore, O one of excellent wisdom, grant me a share of that ambrosia.
Out of hope, farmers plow their fields;
together with their sons and wives, they gather in one place.
Yet the rain carries them away, and the lightning bolt has arisen.
This which has been done by you is improper.
Some men, seeking wealth out of hope, board a ship and cross the ocean; yet they sink there, failing to find a firm support.
Those whose merit is destroyed fall into suffering.
Even though you are in my presence, you speak falsely; I know you are a fool who follows after rogues.
One such as you does not deserve a seat or water.
"Whence do you come for nectar? You do not please me."
Who are you that have been seen with a cluster of blossoms bound upon you?
With lion-like shoulders, wearing a girdle polished like gold, with earrings well-fastened and red as the tips of kusha grass,
you shine with splendor, possessing the hue of uśīra root.
Just as in the rainy season, so now in autumn,
the river adorned with red garlands flows here;
I ask you, O lady whose form is like a golden altar.
Tell me, which deity are you?
I am Hiri, esteemed by men,
always serving noble beings;
seeking happiness, I have come into your presence.
But I am not able to entreat you, O great seer.
"In this world of dark complexion, no woman is found; I know you by your virtue, O fair-limbed one. Since they do not ask for her, I shall give her to you."
I give you that nectar, which is life itself.
Having addressed you alone, whose form is like a golden altar, I shall enter the hermitage;
I shall honor you alone with every virtue.
Without giving you the nectar, it is not enough for us either.
She of beautiful complexion entered that hermitage, which was strewn with various flowers and resounded with the sweet voices of birds.
It was filled with water and adorned with fruits and roots.
Many of the foremost trees were in full bloom:
*sāla*, *piyāla*, *panasa*, and *tinduka* trees;
*śobhāñjana*, *lodhra*, and *pāṭala* trees.
And the Mucilinda trees, which possess most excellent fragrances.
There were many *kuvala* and *tamāla* trees in the dwelling,
as well as *aśvattha*, *nyagrodha*, and *udumbara*; likewise, there were *tilaka*, *kadamba*, and *campaka* trees.
There, the rice grains were *prasātika* and *śyāmaka*.
There, wrapped in a garment of *kuśa* grass, possessing a most auspicious fragrance, and clad in a deerskin,
he sat and dispelled the cold.
Sit upon this seat with auspicious happiness.
For him, Kauśika, who was seeking this [medicine] for his son Kuśin, conquered those [demons] with wealth;
he himself gave nectar from golden vessels.
She spoke hurriedly to the great sage.
"Take him now with a joyful heart," said the delighted wearer of matted locks to Kauśika; "you have performed worship for me."
Now I go to serve the Thirty-three gods.
Permitted by the radiant Kauśika, she approached the gods with the desire for victory;
having gone there, she spoke to the Thousand-eyed One.
O Vāsava, this victory of mine is indeed nectar.
Thus, Mātali, having been sent there, returned to the front of the assembly hall of the gods;
by what cause was Sudhā obtained by Hiri?
Having called out thus once more, you spoke as follows.
He would turn back that chariot from the ford— a chariot made of Jāmbūnada gold,
resembling refined gold, blazing like the rays of the sun.
Adorned and variegated with golden images.
And elephants, monkeys, tigers, leopards, and deer made of vaidūrya gemstone arrived;
they were abundant, auspicious, and composed of jyotīrasa gems.
And such [palaces] are made of mani-jewels and lapis lazuli.
With a lower floor and an upper terrace,
adorned with golden moons, Mātali approached that most excellent chariot. Having ascended it, Mātali—
He would cause the ten directions and the earth to rejoice.
He quickly and with great haste approached the earth, including its mountains, crags, and lordly trees, as it trembled along with the oceans.
To that hermitage where Kauśika had been.
Thus Mātali...
"I am a messenger; Purandara asks after you, out of regard for your glory, your faith, and your hope."
"By what quality do you consider shame (*hirī*) to be superior? ... [O Mātali,] glory (*śrī*) appears to me; faith (*śraddhā*), however, is impermanent, O charioteer of the gods."
My hope is restrained by that which is deceptive.
Modesty is pleasing, pure, and absolute; though not delighting in the forefront of battle, it has been renounced.
Seeing clearly, the fragrant one is beset by calamity.
Modesty restrains one's own mind.
O Mātali, among men, shame is the highest;
it is desired by both the young and the old,
and it makes even a fierce kinsman dear.
Modesty restrains one's own mind.
"Who is it, Kauśika, who has seen this?
For either Indra is formidable, or else Sahāmpati;
O you of the same lineage as Indra, Indra desires [this] from you."
O younger brother of Bhāvasahavrata!
Having abandoned that pride, Kauśika, endowed with virtuous conduct and becoming peerless,
performed vast meritorious deeds in the hermitage.
Upon the dissolution of the body, he rejoices in the heavenly realms.
"Furthermore, monks, it might occur to you that at that time and on that occasion, the seer named Nārada, of the Kauśika clan, was someone else.
But this should not be viewed in such a way. And why? Because it was I."
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, there was a seer named Nārada, of the Kauśika clan.
"Furthermore, monks, it might occur to you that at that time, on that occasion, Śakra, the lord of the gods, had a daughter named Hirī.
But it should not be viewed in this way. For what reason, monks?"
At that time, on that occasion, this very Yaśodharā was the daughter of Śakra, the lord of the gods, named Hrī.
Even then, she approached me while feeling bashful; even now, she approaches me while feeling bashful.
Thus ends the Mañjarī Jātaka.
The monks said to the Blessed One:
"How is it, Blessed One, that Yaśodharā cannot be satisfied?"
While the Blessed One, in his state as a prince, was distributing ornaments even to the girls, he gave a necklace worth a hundred thousand to Yaśodharā;
and she said,
"I am worthy of only this much."
The prince gave him a ring worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], yet even so, he was not satisfied.
How is it that Yaśodharā, being insatiable, is unable to please him?
The Blessed One said:
Monks, it is not only now that this Yaśodharā is insatiable; on another occasion as well, she was insatiable.

Once upon a time, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi, there was a king named Suprabha who ruled the realm. He had a son named Sutejas, who was meritorious, illustrious, modest, pleasant to touch, the first to speak, and sweet-spoken; he was beloved and highly esteemed by his ministers, the army commanders, the guild-leaders, the merchants, and by everyone.
A thought arose in the king:
"This entire body of people has been won over by the prince's virtues; perhaps they might deprive me of my life and establish the prince in the kingdom.
Therefore, the king sent that prince away into exile.

Then the prince, together with his wife, dwelt in a certain forest grove in the Himalayas, having constructed a grass hut and a leaf hut; he lived there subsisting on roots, leaves, fruits, and water, while consuming the meat of deer and boar that were easily obtained.
Now, as he had departed from his hermitage, a cat killed a fat lizard, placed it before his wife, and went away.
She did not even touch that lizard with her hand.
The prince, having taken roots, leaves, and fruits, went to the hermitage; there in the hermitage he saw that fierce and sluggish iguana.
He asked the princess, "Where did this iguana come from?"
She said:
This was brought by a cat.
The prince said:
Is this iguana now accomplished?
She said to him:
Because it is considered cow dung, it is not established [as such].
The prince said:
This iguana is not inedible; it is edible for human beings.
Then that iguana was skinned by the prince, cooked,
and after being cooked, hung upon a tree branch.
And his wife, taking a jar, went to fetch water, thinking:
"I am going; I shall fetch water, and then I will prepare food."
When those women saw that lizard—cooked, well-prepared, excellent in color and fragrance, choice, and fresh—a longing arose within them.
It occurred to the prince’s wife as well:
"This princess does not wish to touch this lizard with her hand even while it is uncooked."
And when it was cooked at the proper time, he rejoiced to eat it.
[He thought: "If she had any love for me, then this iguana would have been prepared by her while she went to gather fruit;
I shall not share any of this iguana with her, but I will eat the iguana myself."
While the princess had gone to fetch water, she was eaten by that lizard; the princess returned, carrying the water-jar.
Then she said to the prince:
"Noble son, where is that lizard?"
The prince said:
She fled.
She thought:
"How did the cooked lizard escape after clinging to the branch of the tree?"
This thought occurred to the princess: "I am not beloved by the prince."
That dejection entered her heart.
All sentient beings shall die, for life ends in death;
they will act according to their karma, experiencing the fruits of merit and evil.
Those of evil deeds go to hell, those who have performed merit go to a heavenly realm,
and others, having cultivated the path, will attain nirvana, free from outflows.
Then King Suprabha was joined with the law of time;
the ministers brought Prince Suteja from the forest and consecrated him in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
In the presence of Queen Sutejas, the king had nothing withheld;
there was nothing in that kingdom considered a jewel that he did not offer to the queen.
Whatever garments were magnificent, whatever ornaments, and whatever necklaces and half-necklaces, he presented them all to the queen, yet he was unable to please her.
And a lizard had entered her heart.
It occurred to King Sutejas:
"There is no kind of virtue that I do not practice for the sake of the queen, nor is there any affection that I do not display; yet I am unable to satisfy her."
He said to her:

"O Queen, there is no kind of virtue that I do not practice for you, nor is there any affection that I do not display; yet I am unable to satisfy you and I do not understand what the obstacle here is.
Let the Queen speak."
Then that queen addressed King Suteja with a verse:
Even now, O Kṣatriya, I recognize him in that forest: you, with bow in hand and quiver fastened to your back,
from whose grasp a lizard clinging to a tree branch fled when it was cooked.
The king said:
I shall honor one who honors me; I shall act for the benefit of one who acts in accordance with my wishes; and I shall not associate with one who does not honor me.
One should not do what is beneficial for one who desires what is harmful.

One should always abandon that which abandons; one should not go toward it with a sense of attachment, nor dwell with it with a sense of intimacy— just as a twice-born man, having found a tree whose fruit has perished, [leaves it].
I shall examine another, for the world is indeed great.
"Furthermore, monks, it might occur to you that at that time, on that occasion, the king named Sutejas was someone else.
You must certainly not view it in this way."
For what reason?
At that time, on that occasion, I was the king named Sutejas in Vārāṇasī.
"That queen who was the chief consort of King Sutejas was someone else"—
indeed, it should not be viewed in this way.
Monks, she was none other than Yaśodharā, who was the queen and chief consort of King Sutejas.
Even then she was insatiable and could not be satisfied;
even now she is insatiable and cannot be satisfied.
Thus ends the Śrī Godhājātaka.
The monks said to the Blessed One:
"When the Blessed One was a youth, while distributing ornaments to the maidens in the park, he gave the most to Yaśodharā alone."
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now that I have given much to Yaśodharā."
The monks said.
At other times as well, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
On another occasion as well, monks.

Long ago, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi, there reigned a king who was meritorious, of great power, surrounded by a retinue, habituated to giving and sharing, possessed of great strength, a great treasury, and many mounts. His kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with people.
And it was a land where the people were mostly happy, where violence and civil unrest were pacified, where thieves were well-restrained, and which was prosperous in its legal affairs.
Now that king had a harem of five hundred women.
Among them, his chief queen was preeminent over the entire harem; she was exceedingly gracious and beautiful to behold, wise, skilled in ritual procedures, and endowed with all artistic talents.
That king frequently distributed garments and ornaments to the women of the inner apartments.

That king also wore a necklace worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], and in the center of that necklace was a precious gem wherein the four great continents were visible: Jambudvīpa, Pūrvavideha, Aparagodānīya, and Uttarakuru.
And Sumeru, the king of mountains,
was that jewel-gem of many hundreds of thousands of values situated in the center of that great necklace.
Distributing ornaments, he questioned that goddess.
"O Queen, you captivate my mind exceedingly.
What is the means by which you, O Queen, captivate my mind?"

Then the queen addressed the king with a verse: "O King, women are fickle; they fall in love for three reasons: through gestures and playful conduct, through the perception of signs, and through curiosity."
"Furthermore, monks, it might occur to you that the King of Kāśī at that time and on that occasion was someone else.
But this should not be viewed in such a way.
And for what reason?"
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, I was the King of Kāśi;
and she who was the chief queen of the King of Kāśi at that time and on that occasion—
indeed, it should not be viewed in this way.
For what reason?
This very Blessed Lady Yaśodharā was, at that time and on that occasion, the chief queen of the King of Kāśi;
even then, much was given by me to her.
Thus ends the Jātaka of the Gift of the Necklace to the illustrious Yaśodharā.

When the Bodhisattva, having abandoned the sovereignty of a universal monarch that was held in his hands, and having abandoned his noble household life, went forth from home into homelessness despite his unwilling parents who were weeping with tearful faces, then Yaśodharā was addressed by Devadatta:
"My brother has gone forth; come, you shall become my chief queen."
She did not desire him at all, longing instead for the Bodhisattva alone.
Sundarananda also said to her, "My brother has gone forth into homelessness; come, you shall be my chief queen."
He does not desire even that; he desires only the Bodhisattva.
When the Blessed One had set the Wheel of Dharma in motion, the monks heard this.
The monks asked the Blessed One:
"How is it, Blessed One, that Yaśodharā, though being courted by Sundarananda and Devadatta, does not desire them but desires only the Blessed One?"
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now that Yaśodharā, when courted by Sundarananda and Devadatta, did not desire them but desired only me;
on another occasion as well, when she was courted by these two, she did not desire them but desired only me."
Once upon a time, monks, in the distant past, there was a gathering of all four-footed creatures at the foot of the Himalayas.
We have no king; let a king be established for us among the four-footed creatures.
There, the thought arose among them: "Let him be appointed as the king of the four-footed creatures."
They said:
"Who now shall be established as the king of the four-footed creatures?"
Then this thought arose among them:
"Whosoever among us goes first to the Himalayas, the king of mountains, on the seventh day from now, he shall become the king of quadrupeds."
Having thus made this agreement, they ran from that place toward the Himalayas, the king of mountains.
Having placed all of them on her back, she reached the Himalayas, the king of mountains.
The tigress, having gone to Himavat, the king of mountains, roars for the sake of the four-footed creatures.
And all four-footed creatures reached the Himalayas, the king of mountains;
and there they saw that tigress guarding her offspring.
Then those four-footed animals, seeing that tigress, became distressed and dejected;
they thought, "We have been defeated by a female, for nowhere is a female king; everywhere it is males who are kings."
So that it may not be false for us, and that this man may become king.
They said that to the tigress.
"O blessed lady, the husband you desire shall become the king of the four-footed creatures."
The bull approached that tigress.
"O blessed lady, choose me as your husband!
I am an auspicious being in the world; with my cow dung, temples shall be smeared and divine rites shall be performed."
Then that tigress said:
I would not desire you as my husband—you who are constantly broken and stuck by plows and carts!
The elephant king also approached that tigress and said:
"O auspicious lady, I am strong and my body is fully developed; I am undefeated in battles, so take hold of me."
The tigress said:
For you do not flee when a lion roars, nor when it voids excrement and urine.
The lion, the king of beasts, also drew near.
"O blessed lady, choose my husband; all the herds of deer are terrified of me."
The tigress said:
Even if it falls upon the head of the king of beasts, I accept it.
A great assembly of all four-footed creatures gathered together;
"This land of ours is without a king—who shall become the king here?"
"He who shall be the first among us to go to Himavat, the king of mountains,
seven days from now, he shall become the king."
Lions, tigers, deer, elephants, bulls,
and wolves were unable to follow her once she had gone first to the mountain.
Having gone to the Himalayas, the best of mountains— gracious and beautiful to behold— the tigress first scouted it for four-footed creatures.
Having gone there on all fours, they all saw the tigress;
and having seen her, they were overcome with distress, for they had been defeated by the female.
"There are no kings among women, nor shall there be any falsehood in this:
he whom the tigress desires as her husband, he shall become the king."
"My ritual duties for the gods are performed with my cow dung.
The bull said to her there, "O blessed lady, choose me as your husband."
The tigress said:
One who is constantly rising up yet always exhausted by carts and plows—
one should not desire such a husband, even if he were to exist among men in this world.
The elephant king said:
Accompanied by my followers, I am undefeated in battle; there, O blessed lady, let me choose you as my husband, I who am like a powerful elephant-king.
The tigress said:
While the lion roars, you flee in fear, voiding nothing but vomit and excrement; I would not desire such a man as my husband.
The lion said:
With shoulders well-formed in succession,
I am a lion whose domain is the mountains;
all the herds of deer tremble before me.
"O blessed lady, choose my husband."
The tigress said:
One should desire such a husband, endowed with all excellent qualities, as if he had come to her of his own accord; she would receive him even upon her head.
"Furthermore, monks, it might occur to you that at that time, on that occasion, the lion, king of beasts, was someone else.
It should not be viewed in this way. For what reason? Because [it was I]."
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, I was that lion, the king of beasts.
He who was the bull at that time and on that occasion was not anyone else;
indeed, it should not be viewed in this way.
And for what reason?
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, Sundarananda was that bull.
"Furthermore, monks, it might occur to you that at that time, on that occasion, the elephant king was someone else.
But this should not be viewed in such a way. For what reason?"
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, Devadatta was that elephant king.
"Furthermore, monks, it may be that you think thus: 'At that time, on that occasion, she who was the tigress was someone else.
But she was none other than this Yaśodharā."
Even then, though she was courted by these men, she did not desire them but desired only me; even now, though she is being courted by these men, she does not desire them but desires only me.
Thus ends the Jātaka of the illustrious Yaśodharā, who had become a tigress.
While the Bodhisattva was distributing jewels among the maidens in the park, Yaśodharā arrived last of all, after all the ornaments had already been distributed.
King Śuddhodana commanded his ministers:
"Which maiden here catches the prince's eye?"
When the prince saw Yaśodharā, his gaze fell upon her.
The precious necklace that had been fastened upon the prince, worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], was removed by the prince and given to Yaśodharā.
As she was sending him away, she said:
"I am worthy of this much," [she thought].
The prince, laughing, removed a ring worth a hundred thousand [pieces] from his finger and gave it to him.
Thus, having bestowed the jewels upon the maidens, the prince entered the royal palace.
The king asks his ministers.
Upon which maiden did the prince’s gaze fall?
The ministers said:
O Great King, she was the daughter of the Śākya Mahānāman, named Yaśodharā;
there the prince’s gaze fell upon her.
King Mahānāma sent word:
"Give my daughter Yaśodharā to my son, Prince Sarvārthasiddha."
Mahānāma sends word to King Śuddhodana.

"I am unable to give Yaśodharā to the prince. For what reason? The prince has been raised within the inner apartments; he has not gone anywhere regarding the arts, nor archery, nor elephant-riding, nor the use of the bow, nor the royal sciences. The prince has attained no proficiency in anything at all."
Upon hearing this from King Śuddhodana, dejection arose within him: "It is exactly as Mahānāma says;
out of excessive affection, I have not left the prince deficient in any craft whatsoever."
Then the king, dejected in mind, entered his home;
there he was seen by the prince, his father.
The prince asked his father,
"Father, why are you so dejected?"
The king said, "Let it be so, my son; what use have you for this?"
The prince said:
For indeed, father, it is not necessarily something that must be told.
Seeing that the prince was distressed, and being questioned by him again and again, [the minister] explained [the matter].
"Thus and so has Mahānāma the Śākya informed me on your behalf as he was requesting Yaśodharā:
'Your son, raised within the inner apartments, has not been left deficient in any skill—whether in the arts, in the knowledge of archery, or in the management of elephants, chariots, or the bow.
Therefore, I would not give him my daughter."
The prince, having heard this, said to his father:
"Let my father not be anxious.
Have a proclamation made throughout the city and the countryside: 'On the seventh day, the prince will grant an audience.
Whoever is skilled therein—whether in the knowledge of crafts, in the knowledge of archery, or in combat or wrestling—let him come.'"
Or in cutting, or in splitting, or in speed, or in cloud-formation, or in elephants, or in horses, or in chariots, or in archery, or in swordsmanship, or in discursive thoughts.
Upon hearing this, King Śuddhodana became filled with joy.
Therefore, an announcement was caused to be made in the city of Kapilavastu and throughout the countryside: "On the seventh day, the prince will give a demonstration.
Whoever is skilled therein—whether in the knowledge of crafts or in the knowledge of archery—let him come."
Messengers were also dispatched by other means with this message:
"Prince Sarvārthasiddha will grant an audience to Śuddhodana on the seventh day;
whoever is trained therein, let him come."
From Kapilavastu, a multitude of people rushed forth, and people from the countryside also arrived; from other districts as well, those filled with curiosity came, thinking,
"We shall behold the splendor of the Śākya princes, and we shall behold the strength and prowess of the prince Sarvārthasiddha."
There, many thousands of people had gathered, and the princes were rushing out from Kapilavastu.
Another elephant-king, sixty years of age and endowed with supreme strength, having gone astray, was entering Kapilavastu from outside the city;
and Devadatta, mounted upon the back of a noble elephant, was rushing out from Kapilavastu toward that place where the spectacle was held.
That elephant-king, having gone astray, charged directly toward him.
Enraged by this, Devadatta struck that sixty-year-old elephant with a single blow of his palm and killed it right there at the city gate;
having slain that noble elephant, he rushed out through that gate.
There, a great crowd of people gathered together, and the youth Sundarananda arrived.
He asked: "O friend, why is there this gathering of people at the city gate?"
The people said:
As Devadatta was running away, he struck this noble elephant with a single blow of his palm.
That elephant then blocked the city gate in such a way that Devadatta was unable to pull it away from the gate; having leaped over it, the elephant passed through.
Then Sundarananda, descending from his vehicle, dragged that elephant seven paces away from the gate.
Seeing this, the great multitude let out a shout of acclaim:
"Oh, how great is the enthusiasm of Prince Sundarananda!"
Sundarananda also, having drawn that noble elephant seven paces back from the gate, passed beyond it.
The Bodhisattva arrived with great magnificence.
The Bodhisattva asked:
"For what reason is there this great gathering of people at the city gate?"
They said:
Prince Devadatta was departing from Kapilavastu when a mad elephant entered the city gate and charged directly toward Devadatta.
Enraged, he struck the elephant with a single blow of his palm and killed it; that elephant fell, blocking the city gate.
Devadatta was unable to drag the elephant away from the gate, so he leaped over it and passed beyond.
Dragged by seven paces by Sundarananda,
this mass of people is somehow being driven out in a crowded throng.
At that time, on that occasion, Kapilavastu was surrounded by seven walls.
Having descended from his vehicle, the Bodhisattva, by the power of his parents, hurled that noble elephant beyond those seven walls of the city.
Seeing that enthusiasm of the Bodhisattva, many thousands of gods and humans let out shouts of acclaim, and the Bodhisattva also rushed forth.
King Śuddhodana, surrounded by the circle of Śākyas, and the Śākya Mahānāma also rushed out.
There, Prince Sarvārthasiddha gave his consent, and all the spheres of arts and crafts were demonstrated by the prince.
There was no one at all equal to Prince Siddhārtha, whether in combat or in wrestling; indeed, there was no one at all who could match the prince.
In the western illustration, arrows pierce [the targets].
There, these ten *krośas* contained seven palm trees;
seven palm trees were planted at intervals of one *krośa*, and before each of the seven [trees], a drum was raised.
There, one man struck through the trunk of a single *tāla* tree, while another struck through two *tāla* trunks.
Devadatta’s arrow, having struck through two *tāla* trunks, became stuck in the third *tāla* trunk.
Sundarananda’s arrow, having struck through three *tāla* trunks, fell to the ground between the fourth *tāla* trunk.
The Bodhisattva had a bow brought there from the royal palace of his grandfather, King Siṃhahanu.
Thus, that bow was placed there in the middle of the arena.
Whoever is able to string this bow and wield it.
That bow was examined by the multitude of people with their hands, yet no one was able to string it. It was examined by all the Śākya youths, but not one was able to string it.
It was examined by the Koliyan youths, by the Licchavi youths, and by other youths as well, but no one was able to string it.
Afterwards, the Bodhisattva took it up;
out of reverence for his grandfather, the Bodhisattva honored that bow with perfumes and garlands and drew it to its full extent.
As he was drawing that bow, the entire city of Kapilavastu was made aware by the sound, and gods and humans let out shouts of acclaim.
Thus, having struck seven palm trees with a single arrow, the Bodhisattva also struck that drum; and having struck the drum, it entered the subterranean realm.
A cry of acclaim was released by gods and humans,
and thousands of deities let fall a rain of divine flowers from the sky.

Having seen the prince’s strength, prowess, and power of intellect, and having witnessed his mastery everywhere through his physical might, supernatural powers, and wisdom, all the Śākya kingdom as well as other kings became filled with joy. "A great gain has been obtained by the Śākyas and by King Śuddhodana, for such a Great Being has been born to them! they exclaimed.
When the Bodhisattva had gone forth, attained unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, and set in motion the supreme wheel of Dharma,
the monks heard this account.
The monks said to the Blessed One:
The Blessed One has recognized the long-lost "fist of the Śākyas."
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it was not only now that I recognized the long-lost 'Shakya-fist'."
On another occasion as well, I discovered the long-lost "fist" of the Śākyas.
The Blessed One said:

Long ago, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi, a king named Brahmadatta reigned. He had subdued his adversaries and vanquished his enemies; his realm was well-governed, and he was disposed toward charity and distribution. He was meritorious, illustrious, possessed of great strength, a vast treasury, and many mounts.
His kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and teeming with people.

That king had a domestic priest named Brahmāyu, who had mastered the three Vedas along with the Nighaṇṭus and Kaṭhas, including the Itihāsas as the fifth; he was no small scholar in phonology, word-analysis, and grammar.
This teacher was skilled in the Brāhmaṇa-Vedas and the Śāstras, possessed a nature inclined toward generosity and sharing, and lived having undertaken the ten paths of wholesome action.
His son was a young brahmin named Dharmapāla.
It occurred to that Brahmāyu:
