"It is time for my son Dharmapāla to study the Vedas; yet he is not fit to study the Vedas from me. Even out of trust in his father, he will not study; therefore, I shall send him to a teacher's household."
This brahmin, a master of the Vedas, was residing in a hermitage in the Himalayas and was teaching the Vedas to five hundred young students.
Therefore, Dharmapāla was entrusted by him with the task: "Teach the Vedas to this [young man]."
Now, not far from that hermitage, there was a great pool of water, and in that pool lived a water-rākṣasa who repeatedly killed people as they were bathing.
Thus the young brahmin Dharmapāla bathed repeatedly in that lake of water.
It occurs to that brahmin:

"In this water-pool there dwells a water-rākṣasa who repeatedly kills people; yet this Dharmapāla, the son of the royal chaplain, bathes there in that water-pool. If he were now to be devoured by the water-rākṣasa while bathing there, our chaplain would become dissatisfied with us. Why did you not prevent him from the water-pool?"
Then that preceptor summoned the young brahmin Dharmapālaka and said to him:
Do not bathe here in this pool of water; a fierce rākṣasa dwells in this pool of water. Lest you be devoured by that water-rākṣasa!
And in that lake lived a nāga of great power with a vast retinue; the son of that nāga king took pleasure in friendly conversation with the young brahmin Dharmapāla,
and by him, the young brahmin was brought into the interior of the nāga abode.
That nāga youth took delight in conversing with that young brahmin, and there in the nāga abode, the young brahmin Dharmapāla taught the ten paths of wholesome action.
And another young man, of the same age and similar appearance as Dharmapāla, was traveling along that same road from another village when he was bathing in the water of that lake.
Having been killed by that water-demon, he was seen floating in that pool of water, half-eaten, by another young man.
Having gone to the hermitage, he informed the preceptor: "Dharmapāla has been devoured by a water-rākṣasa."

Then that brahmin, together with all those five hundred young students, went to that lake and saw the youth floating there, half-eaten by the water-demon; when they saw him, they all let out a great cry.
Then, having lifted him out from the water and gathered wood together, they cremated him.
Having placed those bones in a small jar, he went with his retinue to Vārāṇasī to the presence of Brahmāyus.
With a throat choked with tears and a face weeping, he approached Brahmāyus and said:
That Dharmapāla was killed by an aquatic rākṣasa;
these are his bones.
He said to the brahmin Brahmāyu:
"This is not so," said Dharmapāla; "in our family, no one has ever died while still young."
Then the brahmin Brahmāyu addressed that preceptor of Dharmapāla with a verse:
One should not harm living beings, nor take what is not given;
one should not perform an evil deed even with the mind.
We shall avoid all that is unrighteous.
Therefore, indeed, from this [state], the young person does not die.
Never do we have anger,
nor do we ever become angry;
even when others are angry, we do not give way to wrath.
Therefore, indeed, from this [state], the young person does not die.
We hear the Dharma of both the wicked and the virtuous,
yet we do not find pleasure in the Dharma of the wicked; indeed,
we take pleasure only in that which belongs to the wicked among the wicked.
Therefore, indeed, from this [state], the young one does not die.
We have given many gifts on many occasions, and the one who begs from us is never unpleasant to us; having given these gifts, we do not feel any regret.
Therefore, indeed, from this [state], the young person does not die.
Those brahmins who possess learning and virtue, seeking renown and approaching as supplicants—
may their hearing of us and their sight of us be pleasing.
Therefore, indeed, from this [state], the young does not die.
Those brahmins who possess learning and virtue,
who wander about seeking fame as beggars—
them we shall satisfy with food and drink.
Therefore, indeed, from this [state], the young person does not die.
And whatever beggars come to us— blind, helpless, miserable, and leaderless—
we satisfy them with food and drink.
Therefore, indeed, from this [state], one who is young does not die.
We do not transgress against our wives, nor do our wives transgress against us; therefore,
we practice the holy life.
Therefore, indeed, from this [state], a young person does not die.
Whoever is born becomes virtuous in conduct, well-restrained, observant of vows, upright in nature,
a teacher who has mastered the words of the scriptures.
Therefore, indeed, from this [state], the young person does not die.
Mother, father, sister, brothers,
and those kinsmen who are not on the opposing side—
we practice the Dharma for the sake of the next world.
Therefore, indeed, from this [state], the young one does not die.
Mother, father, sisters, brothers,
and those who are family servants—
we practice the Dharma, seeing the world beyond.
Therefore, indeed, from this [state], the young person does not die.
For indeed, Dharma protects the practitioner of Dharma,
just as a great umbrella [protects] during the rainy season.
This is the benefit when Dharma is well-practiced.
One who practices the Dharma does not go to an evil rebirth.
For whatever destination a heedless man who practices unrighteousness goes,
that practiced unrighteousness destroys him.
Like a black snake caught by its own neck.
For neither dharma nor adharma both have an equal ripening;
adharma leads to hell, while dharma attains the heavenly realm.
For Dharma indeed protects the practitioner of Dharma,
just as a great umbrella [protects] in the rainy season;
protected by Dharma, I am a guardian of Dharma.
The prince is well; he has [recovered] the bones of another.
Having fed that brahmin along with his retinue, he was dismissed by the brahmin Brahmāyu. That brahmin then went to the hermitage and saw the young man Dharmapāla there at the hermitage;
they were all amazed, for the domestic priest had indeed understood it perfectly.
The Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, monks, it might occur to you that at that time, on that occasion, the brahmin named Brahmāyus was someone else. But it should not be viewed in this way.
And why is that?"
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, I was the brahmin named Brahmāyus.
"Furthermore, monks, it may be that you think thus: 'At that time, on that occasion, the son of the brahmin Brahmāyus named Dharmapāla was someone else.
It should not be viewed in this way;
at that time, on that occasion, Rāhula was the son of Brahmāyus."
There was a son named Dharmapāla;
even then he was recognized by me, and now too, this long-lost handful of Śākyas has been recognized by me.
Thus ends the Jātaka of the illustrious Dharmapāla.
The monks said to the Blessed One:
The arrow shot by the Blessed One traveled a great distance.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it was not only now that I shot an arrow a great distance."
At another time as well, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
For it was also at another time, monks.

Once upon a time, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi, there was a king who reigned, possessing great power, a great treasury, and many mounts; he was one who had performed meritorious deeds and was of great majesty.
His kingdom was now so vast that it extended as far as Takṣaśilā, which he governed by his command.
Having established his younger brother in the kingdom, he came from Vārāṇasī to Takṣaśilā.
He was now living in Takṣaśilā when he was besieged by another king from Vārāṇasī with a fourfold army.
His brother sent a messenger from Vārāṇasī to Takṣaśilā, saying:
"Come here; I am besieged by this hostile army."

Having heard this from the messengers while staying in Takṣaśilā, that king wrote the name of that [other] king on a birch-bark leaf, wrapped it around his own thigh, bound it securely with thread, and threw it toward Vārāṇasī.
That arrow, having come to rest at the foot of the king, shattered the king's footstool into pieces.
The king was amazed by that man, exclaiming, "Oh, what energy and what precision of aim! For while standing in Vārāṇasī, he has indeed shot an arrow [that has reached here]."
"He has come such a great distance and fallen at my feet upon a wooden plank; thus, I have not been killed by him."
Then that king, having released it from the arrowhead, read that birch-bark, and upon that very birch-bark it was written as follows:
This man here in Takṣaśilā stands ready to hack off your feet;
if you do not wish to die, withdraw from my kingdom.
Then, becoming even more afraid and terrified, he thought,
"I know that this arrow has come from Vārāṇasī," and because of that,
I was struck with wonder.
And this was thrown by him while staying in Takṣaśilā.
Having built a temple for Devaśara at that very spot and having enshrined that arrow within the temple, he performed worship and honors, and then departed.
The Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, monks, it might occur to you that the King of Kāśi at that time and on that occasion was someone else who, while stationed at Takṣaśilā, shot an arrow at Vārāṇasī.
But it should not be viewed in this way."
For what reason?
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, I was the King of Kāśī.
Even then, I shot an arrow a great distance; and now, too, I have shot an arrow a great distance.
Thus ends the Jātaka of the Noble Arrow-Throwing.
The monks said to the Blessed One:
How was Yaśodharā obtained by the Blessed One through his skill?
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now that Yaśodharā was won by me through my skill; on another occasion as well, Yaśodharā was won by me through my skill."
The monks said:
At another time as well, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
On another occasion also, monks.
Once upon a time, monks, in the distant past, half a yojana from Mithilā there was a village named Yavakacchaka.
Outside of that Yavakacchaka, there was a village of smiths.
There, the daughter of the village blacksmith, named Amarā, was gracious and beautiful to behold, wise, and endowed with eloquence.

The village headman of Yavakacchaka had a son named Mahauṣadha, who was gracious, handsome, meritorious, and of great renown. While wandering through the fields and forests, he saw Amarā, the daughter of a smith, going along carrying food.
Mahauṣadha questioned her.
"Noble lady, what is your name? What is your name?"
Amarā said:
By which [he is called] "Tathāgata."
Mahauṣadha said:
"O blessed lady, to whom do you belong?"
She said:
Of those who have approached me, I am their [refuge].
Mahauṣadha said:
"Noble lady, where are you going?"
She said:
I shall go to that which is the umbrella.
Mahauṣadha said:
"O blessed lady, where are you going?"
Amarā said:
Having taken refuge [in him], she went there.
Then indeed, Mahauṣadha, the foremost scholar, addressed Amarā, the smith’s daughter, with a verse:
"O immortals, you are surely the daughters of the smith;
with your minds you truly know the field that lies in the direction of your sacrificial fee."
Now that girl had her head and eyes anointed, her clothes were clean, and she held a small pot of thin gruel in her hand.
Then indeed, Mahauṣadha, the foremost scholar, addressed Amarā, the smith’s daughter, with a verse:
By what has your head been anointed? By what have your eyes been anointed?
By what are your clothes pure? And by what is this thin gruel yours?
Then the smith’s daughter Amarā addressed the greatly wise Mahauṣadha with a verse:
Sesame oil, [the head], anointing, and dancing;
nakedness and clothing, pure [food], rice gruel, coarse food, and no water.
Then, monks, the greatly wise Mahauṣadha addressed Amarā, the smith’s daughter, with a verse:
If indeed that oil and collyrium were for you,
and those garments and festive ornaments were for you, then only a small amount would have been rained down by the god.
Then that smith’s daughter, taking a vessel of savory broth covered with a white cloth, went out in the rain.
Then indeed, Mahauṣadha, being of great wisdom, addressed Amarā, the smith’s daughter, with a verse:
As for this pond covered with snow-white [ice] that you carry for the sake of life,
I ask you about this matter.
Whose food do you steal, O charming one?
Then, monks, Amarā, the smith’s daughter, addressed Mahauṣadha, the one of great wisdom, in verse: “... I bring food from the tree.”
Then, monks, the greatly wise Mahauṣadha replied to Amarā, the smith’s daughter, in verse:
"Your father was thirty years old when he became a householder, and your grandfather was the same; you are ten years of age by birth—thus do I understand it, girl."
Mahauṣadha said:
When he has gone forth, his mother becomes suffering and dejected;
she and his mother search for him, asking, "Where has he gone, [this] immortal one?"
Then, monks, the smith’s daughter Amarā addressed Mahauṣadha, who possessed great wisdom, with a verse:
Where the dead sigh and the burnt are burned again,
where a kinsman is slain by kinsmen— there has my father gone.
Then, monks, the greatly wise Mahauṣadha replied to Amarā, the smith’s daughter, with a verse: [_Mvu_2.86_] Then, monks, the greatly wise Mahauṣadha addressed Amarā, the smith’s daughter, in verse.
The bellows of karma breathe; the charcoal burns again;
iron is forged with iron; my father has gone to the smithy of karma.
Being asked for the way, tell me of the secure, straight, and direct path, free from thorns, O blessed lady; I shall go to Yavakacchaka.
Then, monks, the smith’s daughter addressed Mahauṣadha, the one of great wisdom, with a verse:
By whom trees were made to have seven branches and double trunks,
by him you were not seen, nor did he see you.
This is the path to Yavakacchaka; if you are wise, know it.
Then, monks, the greatly wise Mahauṣadha replied to Amarā, the smith’s daughter, in verse:
Since the barley, the kadā plants, and the kovidāra trees have all blossomed,
I shall take the left-hand path and go to Yavakacchaka.
Then, monks, Amarā, the smith’s daughter, addressed Mahauṣadha, the one of great wisdom, with a verse:
"Go, Brahmin, by the path; you shall eat him as your food.
Sons are perfected by their fathers; in a month, you shall eat them."
Then, monks, the greatly wise Mahauṣadha replied to Amarā, the smith’s daughter, with a verse:
Dry fuel is found there among the bamboos and *karīra* stalks; with these I shall prepare my meal for a month. I shall go to your home.
Then, monks, Amarā, the smith’s daughter, addressed Mahauṣadha, the very wise one, with a verse:
"Stay, O Brahmin, in my house; there a sacrifice will take place here.
My mother will perform a great sacrifice with the King of the Gods."
Then, monks, the wise Mahauṣadha replied to Amarā, the smith’s daughter, with a verse:
O mother, that sacrifice which your brother-in-law, the king of gods, has performed or will perform, I shall attend; I am going now to your house.
Then, monks, the wise Mahauṣadha requested Amarā, the smith’s daughter, from her parents for the sake of a wife.
They said to their parents, Amarāyī:
"We do not give our daughter to one who is not a smith."
And, monks, Mahauṣadha was greatly wise and skilled in all arts;
this thought occurred to him:
What is the work of smiths? All types of powder-work and needles. A smith who is able to even make a needle is a master craftsman.
By means of the great medicinal herb, a needle is placed within a sheath; seven needles are placed within a single sheath, and all those eight needles become one needle,
and that one needle also becomes eight needles.
Mahauṣadha took that needle and went to that village of smiths to sell it.
Having gone by the road of the smith-village headman, he proclaims:
The needle is for sale; whoever has need of it, let him buy it.
With its handle removed, well-crafted, sharp-pointed, and round—this needle I am selling in the village of smiths; buy it from me!
[ _Mvu_ 2.88] Having heard the voice of Mahauṣadha, that girl ran out;
she addressed Mahauṣadha with a verse:
Here spears are being fashioned, as well as iron arrows and javelins;
right here they are being made, along with needles and fish-hooks.
"You are a madman, O man, or perhaps you are deranged,
you who wish to buy needles in a village of smiths."
Then indeed, Mahauṣadha, being possessed of great wisdom, addressed Amarā, the smith’s daughter, with a verse:
A needle should be sold in a village of smiths by one who understands;
for it is the masters alone who know whether a task is easy or difficult to perform.
If your father, O lady, were to know that this needle was made by me,
he would himself offer me a boon, and he would grant you a favor.
Then, monks, Amarā, the smith’s daughter, addressed her father in verse:
"Father, listen to this as the artisan speaks—
the skillful and clever son of a smith, a maker of needles."
Then, monks, when Amarā’s father, the smith, saw that needle, he was filled with wonder.
Taking his daughter with him, he addressed the highly wise Mahauṣadha in verse:
"Never before have I heard of or seen such a needle;
I am pleased by this deed and shall give this maiden to you."
The Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, monks, it may be that you think thus: 'At that time, on that occasion, Mahauṣadha the greatly wise was someone else.
Indeed, it should not be viewed in this way. For what reason?"
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, I was the one named Mahauṣadha.
"Furthermore, monks, it might occur to you that at that time, on that occasion, the headman of the smith-village was someone else.
But it should not be viewed in this way. And why is that?"
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, this Śākya Mahānāma was that village headman of the smiths.
"Furthermore, monks, it might occur to you that at that time, on that occasion, she who was the daughter of the village headman of the smiths named Amarā was someone else.
But this should not be viewed in such a way. And why is that?"
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, this very Yaśodharā was the daughter of a smith.
Even then she was obtained by me through my craft, and now as well she has been obtained by me through my craft.
Thus ends the Jātaka of Amarā, the daughter of a smith.
The monks said to the Blessed One:
Through his vigor, the Blessed One won Yaśodharā.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now that Yaśodharā was obtained by me through diligence; on another occasion as well, she was obtained by me through diligence."
The monks said to the Blessed One:
At another time as well, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
On another occasion as well, monks.

Monks, once in the past, in the city of Vāravālī, there was a brahmin who had mastered the three Vedas, along with the glossaries (Nighaṇṭu), the ritual manuals (Kaṭha-bhāṇa), and the histories as the fifth; he was skilled in phonology, word-formation, and grammar.
As a teacher of the brahminical Vedas, he taught the Vedas and mantras to five hundred young students.
Now that brahmin had a daughter named Śirī, who was gracious, beautiful to behold, and endowed with the most excellent beauty and lotus-like complexion.
Now, while that brahmin was having a sacrifice performed at Samudrapaṭṭana, he sent a message to his teacher:
"Either come yourself or send someone; I will give you whatever wealth you require."
He said to those five hundred young novices:
"Who among you is willing to go to the seaport to the presence of such-and-such a caravan leader?
To whoever goes, I shall give my daughter Śirikā Māṇavikā."
In that regard, the young brahmin was wise, industrious, and energetic; he felt an exceeding love for his teacher’s prosperity,
and being encouraged, he said, "Teacher, I shall go."
Having been given a letter by that preceptor, he boarded a ship and was sent away.
Thus, having traveled by stages, he arrived at a seaport city;
there he presented that letter to the caravan leader.
That caravan leader, having read the letter from his preceptor and having given him jewels, gold, and bullion, dismissed him.

Then, at whatever time he set out from that seaport for Vāravālī by means of a ship, he arrived at Vāravālī by that ship in due course. Now, as he was about to board a small boat to depart from that ship,
and while there was a great crowd, that bundle fell into the ocean.
The thought occurred to that young man:
"Having brought this from the seaport with such great effort and boarding a small boat here, it has fallen into the ocean. What means might there be by which I could recover this wealth?"
There is no other means; there is nothing else but that I shall empty this ocean.
Taking his heated iron hammer, he came to the shore of the ocean.
Having set down the hammer on the seashore, he girded his loins; then the deity of the ocean, approaching in the guise of a brahmin, said:
What is this?
The young man said: "I shall empty the great ocean."
The brahmin said:
"Mahodaka will not be able to collect it. The young brahmin said:
For Brahmā, a day and night is long;
for one who is diligent and heedful, such as Dakṣa, glory is not difficult to attain.
Listen to the heroism, the strength, the power, and the prowess of the Supreme Person,
which even as a young man he displayed in former births.
For his sake, he descended into the ocean.
At that time, his jewel had been lost; he spoke thus: "I shall dry up the ocean;
exert yourselves so that I may recover the jewel."
Do not be indifferent, lest you come to suffer.
The golden nāgas, asuras, yakṣas, and rākṣasas who dwell within the midst of the ocean became terrified,
just like agitated clouds.
They emit a resonant and thundering sound.
Then the goddess emerged from the ocean;
terrified, she looked toward the four directions and saw the young man exerting himself.
To scoop up and to exhaust the ocean.
Having crossed over, she spoke to him from the front: "What do you seek from the ocean, young man?
Tell us, and we too shall [follow]."
We shall give it, even if we encounter obstacles or suffer setbacks.
"O deity, my jewel has been lost here;
I am searching for it in the great ocean.
Having exhausted the waters, may I recover the jewel."
He emptied the great ocean of its water.
Many fools wander in the world,
utterly deluded regarding both material wealth and the true Dharma;
you too, O youth of supreme intelligence, [are such].
That which is difficult to find in the world, you seek.
Eighty leagues and four waters flow forth from it, yet even by that [water] it is not known;
and below the water is the infinite abyss.
How indeed do you venture to exhaust it?
Where many rivers flow in and endless rain falls, the ocean is reached;
it is the dwelling place of those of great supernatural power.
But how is it that the Dharmaśāstra is set aside?
You, who are evil-minded, perform this deed though your limbs are exhausted; before long you shall come to ruin,
for you are not able to dry up even a mere pond.
But this is not at all fitting for you, young man.
O deity, regarding that which you have reproached and censured, I see your meaning as one who has cut through the ocean:
he would not dig a channel, nor would he uproot the source.
But he for whom there is no interval, nor a further shore to cross over.
I am not indolent; I would not abandon my own jewel.
Having taken away their wealth, I shall exert my vigor.
Let all beings here carry out my word!
I would speak thus, I would not speak otherwise;
I would not bow before a blazing fire, nor would I overturn the earth together with its moon and stars.
That deity thought there:
"I must give that jewel to the young man, so that he does not exhaust the ocean."
And having taken this excellent jewel, young man, go forth with your vessel ready for success.
Everywhere the energetic person is virtuous, while the indolent person lives in misery;
by the power of his energy, he takes wealth and departs.
Recalling his former residence and former birth, the Blessed One,
the Teacher, related this Jātaka in the presence of the monks.
Referring to those aggregates, those elements, and those sense-bases,
as well as to the self, the Blessed One explained that meaning.
"In the beginningless cycle of existence where I formerly dwelt,
I was then a young brahmin and Śirī was Yaśodharā.
Having understood this matter, you should thus remember this Jātaka."

Thus, free from fever, free from fear, and free from sorrow, the Blessed One recounted this ancient Jātaka of his own—immeasurable and full of many sufferings, involving conduct both high and low—in the midst of the community of monks.
The Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, monks, it might occur to you that the young brahmin to whom that wealth fell in the great ocean at that time and on that occasion was someone else.
Indeed, it should not be viewed in this way. For what reason? [Because he was I myself]."
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, I was that young brahmin.
"Furthermore, monks, it may be that you think thus: 'At that time, on that occasion, was she not the daughter of the brahmin named Śiri in the city of Vāravālī?
But it should not be viewed in this way. And for what reason?
Monks, she who was Yaśodharā at that time and on that occasion was the daughter of a brahmin named Śiri in the city of Vāravālī.
Even then she was won by me through my vigor; even now she has been won by me through my vigor.
Thus ends the glorious Śirijātaka.
The monks said to the Blessed One:
Yaśodharā was obtained by the Blessed One with great effort.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now that Yaśodharā was obtained with difficulty; on another occasion as well, she was obtained by me with great difficulty, great exertion, and great vigor."
The monks said.
On another occasion as well, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
On another occasion as well, monks.

Long ago, monks, in times past, a king named Subāhu reigned in Hastināpura. He was one who had performed meritorious deeds, possessed of great majesty, great strength, a great treasury, and many vehicles; he was the lord of sixty thousand cities.

He had an only son, a prince named Sudhanu, who was gracious, handsome, beautiful, meritorious, illustrious, virtuous, and filial toward his mother and father; he was established by his father Subāhu as the crown prince.
Together with his ministers, he protected those thousands of paternal cities.
King Subāhu, having laid down the burden of royal duties, was sitting at ease, composed, in his excellent upper palace within the royal compound.

Now, King Subāhu had a close friend and neighboring king named Sucandrima, who ruled the kingdom in the city of Siṃhapura; he was one who had performed meritorious deeds, was illustrious, possessed great power, a vast treasury, and a great army.
Now, a great sacrifice was prepared for King Sucandrima;
he intended to perform the sacrifice with all living beings.
He gave an order to all the hunters dwelling within his realm.
"I shall perform a sacrifice with all beings.
Whatever living creatures there are that move on land—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed—bring together all those species of living beings."
The Niṣādas have also been designated;
whatever creatures live in the water, with those you shall provide the sacrifice, for I will perform the sacrifice with all living beings.
"By the mind for the gods, by speech for kings,
by action for the wealthy, and by poverty for the destitute."

At the mere word of the king, hunters and fishermen brought together all species of living beings, both those that move in water and those that move on land; having constructed a large enclosure, they confined those terrestrial creatures therein,
and having likewise brought together the aquatic creatures, they confined them in a lotus pond.
With the exception of the kinnarīs, all species of living beings were assembled.
Then, at the time when King Sucandrima’s sacrificial enclosure had been prepared with all the necessary implements,
he bathed his head, put on fresh garments, and having ascended to the upper story of his excellent palace, he made an offering of perfumes, flowers, and incense.
Having extended his joined palms in salutation toward the four directions— the east, south, west, and north— he paid homage to the Blessed Ones in those directions.

I invite those seers who have attained the four dhyānas, possess the five superknowledges, are of great psychic power and great majesty, and travel through the atmosphere, to my sacrificial enclosure.

Then those seers there, who had attained the four dhyānas, possessed the five superknowledges, and were of great psychic power and great majesty, having focused their attention, went to the sacrificial enclosure by means of their miraculous power through the air.

Then King Sucandrima, seeing those seers who had arrived at the sacrificial enclosure, was filled with joy and a sense of gladness and satisfaction; having prostrated at their feet, he spoke as follows.
May the Blessed Ones inspect the sacrificial enclosure to see whether it is complete or not.
Then those seers, having reflected, said this to King Sucandrima:
"Your Majesty, the entire sacrificial enclosure is complete, lacking only one thing."
The king said:
By which factor is it deficient?
The sages said:
"O King, she is lacking a kinnarī."
Then King Sucandrima said to the hunters:
Those seers, the Blessed Ones, said: "There is need for a kinnarī at the sacrificial enclosure; go and exert yourselves so that you may bring a kinnarī to me."
Now, among those thousands of hunters, there was one who was the most eminent in terms of valor, gain, and manliness; he was encouraged by all those hunters as a group:
"You are capable and competent to bring back the kinnarī."
Encouraged by his group and by King Sucandrima, that hunter took up his bow and quiver and entered the Himalayas.
There, in the Himalayas, he saw a certain delightful hermitage of a seer, provided with roots, leaves, and fruits.
He approached that seer, and having paid homage at the seer's feet, he stood there. The seer addressed him, saying, "Come, welcome! Welcome to you; sit down upon this palanquin."
The seer performed a hospitable reception for that hunter,
offering him fruits and water according to the dharma of seers.
Having now eaten the fruits and drunk the water, he sat there;
and there, at the foot of the seer, he heard the sound of sweet singing such as he had never heard before.
He asked that seer.
"Blessed One, whose is this so pleasing sound of song, [belonging] to the daughters of the gods or the daughters of the nāgas?"
The seer said:
This is not the sound of song from the daughters of the gods, nor is it the sound of song from the daughters of the nāgas or the kinnarīs.
He then questioned that seer.
"Blessed One, this sound of singing is heard, yet they are not seen;
where, indeed, are they singing?"
The seer said:

On the northern side of this hermitage is a great lotus pond where there are blue, white, red, and white lotuses, as well as fragrant lilies, belonging to all seasons and blooming throughout the year.
There, from Mount Kailāsa, the daughter of Drumā, the king of the kinnaras, named Manoharā, comes to play in this lotus pond surrounded by many kinnaras and kinnarīs;
that wise hunter questioned the seer with a stratagem.
He said:
"Lord, it is heard that there are certain men who sport and dally with kinnarīs.
How do those men come to be under the power of the kinnarīs?"
The seer said:
Bound by this word of truth, they are unable to vanish.
And because of his sweetness of character, the seer spoke with sincerity without having reflected; he did not know that this was for the sake of the kinnarī.
Then that hunter, having paid homage to the seer, went to the lotus pond where Druma, the king of the kinnaras, had his daughter playing.
Now those kinnarīs were distracted by their singing and their playing of the water-drums, and they did not see that hunter;
and there, Manoharā was the most distinguished of all in both beauty and voice.
Standing within earshot, that hunter bound Manoharā with a word of truth.
"You are the illustrious daughter of Druma, the king of the kinnaras;
by this word of truth, remain bound, O kinnarī!"
Just as you are the daughter of the king of trees, raised by King Druma,
by the power of your word of truth, O auspicious Manoharā, do not go to that place!
Then Manoharā, bound by that hunter’s word of truth, was unable to vanish;
all those other kinnaras and kinnarīs, however, disappeared completely.
Then that Manoharā was brought by that hunter to Siṃhapura;
she was introduced there into the sacrificial enclosure.
Upon seeing the kinnarī, King Sucandrima and the great multitude of people became filled with joy toward that hunter.
The hunter was greedy for a large cloak.
Bound by snares, she was brought to Sucandrima’s Siṃhapura; it became a city of brahmins, and she was led into the sacrificial enclosure.
King Sucandrima, having prepared the requisites for the sacrifice, dispatched a messenger to King Subāhu in Hastināpura:
"I shall perform a great sacrifice for all beings; come here and rejoice in it."
King Subāhu dispatched his son, Prince Sudhanu, saying:
"Go to Siṃhapura; King Sucandrima will perform a sacrifice there, so offer your approval for it."
Prince Sudhana arrived at Siṃhapura along with many hundreds of other kings;
and among them all, Prince Sudhana was preeminent in beauty, in majesty, in retinue, and in fragrance.
Prince Sudhanu entered that sacrificial enclosure, surrounded by many hundreds of kings.
There, in that sacrificial enclosure, he saw those many thousands of wicked land-dwelling and water-dwelling creatures,
and he also saw that kinnarī.
Even as Prince Sudhanu was looking on, a noble love fell upon the Kinnarī, and a love for Sudhanu also fell upon the Kinnarī.
As it was said by the Blessed One in the words of a sutra:
Whether through former cohabitation or through present benefit,
love for all beings arises, just as a lotus grows in the water.
Thus, by the mere sight of one another, affection arose among them.
Prince Sudhanu questioned King Sucandrima.
For what reason have these many thousands of living beings been confined within the sacrificial enclosure?
Then the king said:
"With these I shall perform the sacrifice, and with this abundant food to be chewed and eaten. The prince asked:
"What is the fruit of this sacrifice? What is the accomplishment of its qualities? Of what kind is the sacrificial merit he will accomplish by committing such slaughter of living beings?"
The king said:
"Whichever species of living beings are slaughtered here in this sacrifice, they shall all go to heaven;
and as many times as these living beings are slaughtered here in this sacrifice, so many times do I myself arise in heaven."
The prince said:
"Great King, it is not so; this is a false view that non-violence is the supreme Dharma."

Taking life is non-dharma; abstaining from taking life is dharma. Taking what is not given is non-dharma; abstaining from taking what is not given is dharma. Sexual misconduct is non-dharma; abstaining from sexual misconduct is dharma.
The drinking of *surā*, *maireya*, and intoxicants is unrighteousness; abstaining from the drinking of *surā*, *maireya*, and intoxicants is righteousness.
False speech is unrighteousness; abstaining from false speech is righteousness. Malicious speech is unrighteousness; abstaining from malicious speech is righteousness.
Frivolous speech is non-dharma; abstaining from frivolous speech is dharma.
Ignorance is non-dharma; abstaining from ignorance is dharma. Malice is non-dharma; abstaining from malice is dharma.
False view is non-dharma; right view is dharma.
The ten wholesome paths of action are the Dharma.
Great King, beings endowed with the ten unwholesome paths of action are reborn in the hells;
beings endowed with the ten wholesome paths of action are reborn in the heavens.
Thus, Great King, this is not the path to the heavens that has been taken by you; rather, this is the path taken for going to the hells.
Having thus heard the Dharma teaching of Prince Sudhanu, King Sucandrima and all those kings, along with the entire great multitude of people, were filled with joy.
Having heard the Dharma teaching of Prince Sudhanu, King Sucandrima released all those species of living beings, both those that move in water and those that move on land.
The kinnarī Manoharā was attached to Prince Sudhanu;
because of her love for him, the entire kinnara realm no longer occupied his mind.
Even for Sudhanu, other playful diversions no longer occupied his mind because of his love for Manoharā.
King Sucandrima also performed a sacrifice that was free from obstacles and blameless, exactly as it had been instructed by Prince Sudhanu.
Many thousands of ascetics, brahmins, the destitute, and beggars were fully satisfied with food and drink and clothed in garments.

When the sacrifice was concluded, Prince Sudhanu, mounted upon the back of a noble elephant together with Manoharā, departed from Siṃhapura for Hastināpura accompanied by a great retinue, with great prosperity, with great abundance, and with great splendor.

As the prince was entering Hastināpura, the city of Hastināpura was adorned: canopies were spread out, it was surrounded by variegated cloths, bundles of silk ribbons and garlands were suspended, it was sprinkled and swept, incense was burned, and flowers were strewn about; and in various places there were actors, dancers, athletes, wrestlers, musicians, and water-carriers.
Thus, Prince Sudhana, with great prosperity and a vast retinue, mounted upon the back of a noble elephant together with Manoharā, entered Hastināpura.
That prince dismissed all the princesses and played together with Manoharā alone.
In King Subāhu’s sixty thousand cities, thousands of affairs were neglected and many thousands were brought to a standstill.
The merchants and the people of the countryside petitioned King Subāhu:

"Great King, Prince Sudhanu is infatuated with the kinnarī Manoharā; he does not attend to matters of state, royal affairs are falling into neglect, and from the sixty thousand cities, many thousands [of subjects] are turning back."
King Subāhu summoned Prince Sudhana.
"Son, the people of the realm cry out;
you do not attend to their affairs as you did before. You dwell intoxicated with the Kinnarī Manoharā. Son, dismiss this Kinnarī and grant her permission to depart."
Bound by the net of craving for Manoharā, the prince would not release her.
His father, however, urged him again and again:
"Son, let go of this Kinnarī; I will bring you as many royal maidens as you wish to name."
Although the prince was told thus again and again by his father, he did not desist.
And the ministers informed King Subāhu again and again.
"Great King, Prince Sudhanu, being infatuated with the Kinnarī Manoharā, does not attend to his royal duties; many royal affairs are falling into neglect."
And the king commanded his ministers, "Surround the prince!"
Thus he was restrained by the ministers at the king's command.
Because the prince was detained, the household has fallen into misfortune and all its prosperity has vanished.
Manoharā herself has been permitted by Subāhu to go to Nirati, the city of the Kinnaras.
"Manoharā, you are permitted to go; go to your parents' presence, where the forests are pleasant and cool."
Then, adorned with all her ornaments, she descended from that palace.
As she was descending, many thousands of women wept out of grief for Manoharā at the sight of Sudhanu.
There was no space left in the city of Hastināpura, whether on the left or the right, as Manoharā departed from the city.

Receiving thousands of salutations with joined palms from the left and right, being honored with perfumes and garlands, and followed by thousands of women and a great multitude of people, she then departed from Hastināpura; having bid farewell to the crowd, she set out facing north, directed toward the Himalayas, the king of mountains, and proceeded northward.
And he looked toward Sudhanu in the direction of Hastināpura.
And there, in the foothills of the Himalayas on the bank of the river Śatadru, two sons of hunters were hunting deer;
one hunter’s son was named Utpalaka, and the second hunter’s son was named Mālaka.

They saw the Kinnarī Manoharā approaching from afar, adorned with all ornaments, anointed with exquisite unguents, wearing unfading fragrant garlands, and coming while looking back again and again over her shoulder.
By them, that kinnarī was recognized.
With palms joined in reverence, they prostrated and asked:
They go; you look back, they look back; you are going.
Why do you look back, noble lady? Where will you go?
Manoharā said:
I long for both: the city of the Kimpuruṣas;
I behold Sudhanu and I long for Nirati.
Then those sons of hunters said:
Prince Sudhanu has women among the Kurus and Pañcālas;
sporting with them, he will not remember you.
Manoharā said:
"I shall bring Sudhanu under my control by a mere glance and a smile;
he will become submissive like an aged elephant."
She gave those sons of hunters a finger-ring worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] and a garland of *tālīsa* wood, saying:
"If Prince Sudhana should come along behind me searching for me, you must give him this token of recognition and, in my name, ask after his welfare;
he should be told:"
"Turn back from this very place; beyond this point, it is difficult for humans to traverse.
Separation from humans is certain for me."
Having thus instructed the sons of the hunters, Manoharā crossed the Śatadrū river without touching the water with the soles of her feet.
When King Subāhu knew that Manoharā had departed, he then summoned Prince Sudhana and had him sit upon his own lap, as well as upon the laps of his father and mother.

"Do not, my son, remember the kinnarī. Your harem is vast, consisting of many thousands of maidens; I shall have others brought to you as well. Sport, delight, and enjoy yourself with them. What do you want with a kinnarī? You are a human being."
The king comforted the prince, and he commanded his ministers:
"Decorate the prince's residence."
He gave this instruction to the women of the inner apartments:
"Entertain the prince so well that he may not even remember Manoharā."
By the mere word of the king, the prince’s house was adorned with everything imaginable, just like a celestial mansion.
In the seven gate-halls, jars of fine powder were placed, unbroken grains were placed, and whatever other things are esteemed as auspicious by the world were all placed there.
Thousands of brahmins were stationed at the prince's gate, as was another multitude of people, all waiting for the prince.

The prince, too, having been comforted by his father, was dismissed with these words: "Go home; attend to your duties; bathe, anoint yourself, wear garlands and ornaments, play, enjoy yourself, divert yourself, and oversee the affairs of state."
Having thus instructed his father, Prince Sudhanu was dismissed.
Having thus departed from the royal palace, together with his single attendant Vasantaka who was devoted to him, he set out from the city of Hastināpura toward the Himalayas, the king of mountains,
for the sake of Manoharā.
The prince did not set his mind upon those sixty thousand prosperous cities of his father’s, with their towns and districts, nor upon his extensive harem;
he grieved for and remembered only the kinnarī Manoharā.
At the moment he beheld the king’s lamentation, he gave away that entire kingdom;
having cast it aside, he departed, taking with him his unwashed, soiled garment.
Having taken along a single attendant who possessed a state of devoted affection,
he set out toward the Himalayas, facing the king of mountains.
Before long, Sudhanu went to the Himavat, to the lovely slopes of that mountain;
there he saw two hunters, Utpalaka and Mālaka.
And he beholds the Śatadru river, which is constantly radiant with pure and stainless crystal;
it is auspicious, with very cool waters, flowing forth, soft, fresh, and well-formed; that river, with its lush grassy banks and gentle ripples, carries hundreds of akṣauhiṇīs.
Sudhanu said: "O hunters, did you see a certain dark-complexioned woman, anointed with unguents that were not of inferior quality, wearing unfading perfumes and garlands, as she was walking along?"
The son of the hunter said: "She whom you ask about departed from here long ago;
having crossed the river, she went to the Himalayas by this time."
"For she spoke of one named Sudhanu following behind me;
if the son of the hunter comes, give him this token of recognition."
"O sons of the hunter, give me this ring and this tālīsa-scented garland; you are my husband, my lord, and my master."
And hunters, at my word, you should say to my master:
"Go back to Hastināpura; our meeting was destined by fate, yet it has ended in separation."
Rejoicing, he accepted the garland and took up the ring, saying:
"I would even accept death itself rather than being separated from Manoharā."
Those hunters said to Sudhanu: "Turn back from here;
what unenjoyed life would there be for you in the city of Hastināpura?"
Neither did it enter his heart, nor did he hear their words;
he was solely resolved to go and had already crossed the great river Śatadru.
The hunters were also stationed there, thinking, "The king’s wrath will fall upon us if we abandon Sudhanu in such a transgression."
They too descended into that river, which resounded with the cries of herds of tigers, lions, and elephants;
which was frequented by deer and birds; and which was delightful with the calls of ruddy geese.
At that very moment, they crossed the great river, which resounded with the cries of swans and cranes,
was filled with networks of waterfalls, and was most delightful with its wild beasts and kinnaras.

Then the prince, Vasantaka the attendant, Utpalaka the son of a hunter, and Mālaka the son of a hunter, having thus resolved their intent, entered the Himavat, the king of mountains, by way of Manoharā’s footprints. Manoharā, too, went along, gathering and binding together choice flowers of various colors that were hanging down.
Having seen those flowers later, they followed them;
having rested here, Śyāmā went from this place.

"Here she sat for a moment; here are her heaps of flowers; here are the beautiful garlands and her discarded wreaths from when she wore choice blossoms as ear-ornaments. In various places they see and recognize these signs: 'The dark-complexioned woman has gone this way,' and thus they follow her path. They see her various kinds of ornaments fallen upon the road, they see them caught upon the branches of the forest trees, and they see other identifying marks."
And as they entered further and further into the Himalayas, so did they behold many precious jewels.
They see mountains with golden peaks; they see mountains with silver peaks; they see mountains of iron; they see mountains of copper;
they see mountains of brass; they see mountains with tin peaks; they see mountains of antimony; they see mountains of red arsenic;
and they see pairs of kinnaras sporting together.
They behold many hundreds of other wonders and marvels; in various places they hear the sounds of kinnarīs singing, and they hear the sounds of lions roaring, the sounds of tigers roaring,
and the roars of leopards.
They hear the cries of various kinds of deer; they hear the cries of yakṣas and rākṣasas;
and they hear the cries of piśācas and kumbhāṇḍas.
They see thousands of various kinds of medicinal herbs, and they see the vidyādharas.
As they were going along, they saw the hermitage of the seer Kāśyapa, which was endowed with many roots, leaves, flowers, and fruits, covered by thousands of trees, and well-supplied with water.
Having now entered that hermitage, they saw there in the hermitage the aged and illustrious seer Kāśyapa, together with his retinue, seated nearby.
Having then paid homage to the seer, they stood before him together with their retinue.
It occurs to the seer:
"This prince who has entered this hermitage must be a great-souled one, one who has performed meritorious deeds and is possessed of merit;
for this region was not reached with safety."
By that, the prince was delighted.
Welcome to the prince; please be seated on these couches.
The prince sat down with his retinue;
the seer offered him fruits resembling small honeycombs and water.
At the place where the fruits had been eaten and the water drunk by the prince, the seer questioned him.
What is the purpose of the prince’s coming here, he who has been brought up in comfort?
The prince said:
"O Blessed One, have you seen such a woman as this passing by?"
The seer said:
"I have seen her; having approached this hermitage of mine and paid homage at my feet, she has gone along the slopes of the great mountain.
Therefore, let the prince turn back from this hermitage.
A difficult task has been performed by the prince in coming thus far; what more, then, could be gained by going further? That place is inaccessible to men. Turn back from here."
The prince said:
"I am not able to turn back, Blessed One.
Wherever that Manoharā has gone, by that very same path I shall go."
The seer said:
The realm of the kinnaras is one thing, and that of humans is another.
Even birds cannot reach the realm of the kinnaras, let alone humans;
even birds can only reach that region with great difficulty.
Where the *kinnaras* go, rejoicing and experiencing the delights of pleasure—O Prince, that place is inaccessible by human paths;
therefore, turn back from this hermitage.

"Your father is indeed the lord of sixty thousand cities; surely the prince should sport, delight, and enjoy himself with noble pleasures. It is impossible for you to go to such an inaccessible region."
The prince said:
O Blessed One, one must face either death or that [state].
The illustrious seer, dwelling in great loving-kindness and being compassionate,
thinks to himself:
If the prince were to go to a place that is inaccessible, his body might perish.
That seer said:

"O Prince, spend this night here in this hermitage until we reach that place where monkeys dwell. The leader of their troop is devoted to me; he comes to me every day, bringing fruits resembling small honeycombs.
I shall request that king of the monkeys [to assist you]."
He will lead you to the Kinnara city named Nirati, belonging to Druma, the king of the Kinnaras.

By the word of the seer, the prince stayed that night in the hermitage; and when the night had turned to dawn, the prince heard the sound of a lion approaching. The prince asked the young seers, "Whose sound is this of one approaching?"
The young seer said:

As the lord of monkeys was thus approaching, this sound was constantly heard here at this time: "He comes, descending from tree to tree, gathering fruits as sweet as honey, coming toward the feet of our preceptor."
Then, as if out of curiosity, he rose up and gazed toward the direction from which the sound of that approaching monkey came.
By him, that king of monkeys was seen coming along, leaping from tree to tree.
That king of monkeys, having come to that hermitage and placed fruits resembling small bees before the seer, sat down.
The seer said:
O King of Monkeys, perform my service.
The king of the monkeys said:
"O Blessed One, I shall do so; please command me."
The seer said:
Taking this prince as the fourth, they went to the Kinnara city named Nirati, belonging to Drumā, the king of the Kinnaras.
The monkey said:
Blessed One, it is so.
Then the lord of monkeys, mounting the prince as the fourth person on his back, traveled from peak to peak of the mountains and from tree to tree;
before long, he arrived at the city of Druma, the king of the *kiṃnaras*, upon the summit of Mount Kailāsa.

And he beheld upon the summit of Mount Kailāsa the city named Nirati, belonging to the king of the kinnaras, which was fashioned from all manner of gold and auspicious craftsmanship; it was adorned with thousands of gardens and embellished with lotus ponds and reservoirs made of every kind of jewel, featuring steps with beryl fruit-stones, surrounded by railings of the seven precious gems, and covered with blue lotuses, red lotuses, night-blooming water lilies, white lotuses, and fragrant saugandhika flowers.

It was covered with thousands of trees laden with various kinds of flowers, leaves, and fruits, and adorned with *atimuktaka*, *campaka*, *vārṣika*, *mallikā*, *sumana*, *navamālikā*, and *yūthikā* blossoms; it was filled with boats made of jewels, joined by jeweled banks, variegated with diverse gems, floating upon the water, and with various kinds of colorful, spring-like rafts drifting about.
There they saw thousands of pairs of kinnaras sporting about;
some were playing *jaladardara* drums, some were playing various kinds of musical instruments, and others were singing enchanting songs with sweet voices.
And within the city, they hear the sounds of hundreds of musical instruments and they hear the sweet sounds of songs.

Then, while standing in the grove outside that city of the Kinnaras, many Kinnarīs— gracious, beautiful to behold, adorned and bedecked with ornaments, carrying golden water-jars in their hands— were seen approaching the lotus pond where Sudhanu stood drawing water.
Sudhanu asks her this.
What festival is there in this city that such a joy as this exists?
Then they said:

Today there is no festival nor any celebration; however, the daughter of Druma, the king of the kinnaras, had been taken away by humans, and having returned after many years, Druma, the king of the kinnaras, and the entire city were filled with joy upon her arrival— this is the cause of such great rejoicing here.
Sudhanu asks.
Where will this water be carried?
They said:
That Manoharā will bathe you;
she will remove the human odor from you.
The prince threw the ring into the last water-jar so that it was not seen by those kinnarīs.
As Manoharā was bathing, the ring fell from her hand into her lap from the water-jar while she was bathing.
When Manoharā saw that ring, she recognized it,
and this thought occurred to her:
"Prince Sudhana has come for my sake."
How has the delicate prince come to this inaccessible region?
Then, having put on her clothes with great haste, her throat choked with tears and her face weeping, she prostrated before her parents and said:
"He who was my husband in Jambudvīpa has arrived; he is the prince named Sudhanu, the only son of King Subāhu."
Druma, the king of the kinnaras, did not believe it, saying:
"Daughter, it is not possible for humans to come to this region."
Manoharā said:
For he has not come manifestly, my dear.
Druma, the king of the kinnaras, asks:
"Was this seen by you yourself, or was it heard from another?"
She said:
"I have not seen it myself, nor have I heard of it from another; however, while she was bathing, Sudhanu’s ring fell into her lap."
Druma, the king of the kinnaras, summoned the water-carriers;
having summoned them, he then questioned them.
"Have you seen a man anywhere while you were gone fetching water?"
They said:
"Your Majesty, the Kinnara youth was seen—gracious and beautiful to behold—standing on the bank of the lotus pond with three others as the fourth."
This occurs to him.
Thus did this prince [behave] toward Manoharā.
How could he possibly come to this region?
Then he asked that daughter:
O Manoharā, let Prince Sudhanu enter this royal palace.
She said:
Father, please enter.
Thus, he has come here out of love for me, and because of me, he has experienced much unpleasantness and disrespect from his father;
he has endured the suffering of imprisonment and execution, yet I have never once abandoned him.
Then, Prince Sudhanu, having been imprisoned by his father Subāhu in the prison-house, I was sent away;
now that he has been released, he has come after me.
Druma, the king of the kinnaras, commanded his ministers.

"Quickly have the city decorated, from the royal palace as far as the Asura pond; have canopies spread over it, surrounded by variegated flowers, hung with bundles of silk ribbons and garlands, sprinkled and swept clean, strewn with loose flowers, and drenched with all kinds of fragrant water."
"Let all those who are the principal men in my city and the fourfold army go forth to meet my son-in-law, taking with them parasols, banners, and flags."
At the mere word of the ministers, everything was prepared; they went out to meet him with great magnificence.

Manoharā also, clothed in a magnificent garment and adorned with all her ornaments, surrounded by many thousands of kinnaras and accompanied by the sounding of thousands of musical instruments, went out to meet him.
Then, having seen Sudhanu, she fell at his feet with her head, and she rubbed his feet all over with her face and her hair.

Thus, Sudhanu was led with great splendor and great prosperity into the city of Druma, the king of the kinnaras; he was welcomed by Druma, the king of the kinnaras, at the royal palace, where he was seated upon his lap and comforted.

"This city of yours is made entirely of gold, adorned with a thousand parks, and possesses infinite excellence; here, together with my daughter Manoharā, sport, enjoy yourself, and take your pleasure."

Now Sudhanu, having resided in the city of the Kinnaras for many years, having played, delighted, and enjoyed himself, and having experienced all that was conducive to pleasure in every garden, addressed Manoharā:
"Manoharā, do you not know how I am the beloved and dear only son of my parents? Out of love for you, I have not taken leave of them."
Having abandoned everything belonging to my mother and father, and having made the sacrifice myself, I have come here; it has been many years since I first dwelt here.
Therefore, take leave of my parents, for I shall go to Hastināpura.
Manoharā informed her parents.
Druma, the king of the kinnaras, questioned Sudhanu.
"O Prince, you shall go into the presence of your mother and father."
The prince said:
If it is your wish, father, then I shall go.
The tree said:
"I shall dismiss them."
The yakṣas called Yambhakas are the executors of the commands of the kinnaras.
The king commanded the Yambhaka yakṣas.
"Take my son-in-law, together with his retinue and Manoharā, to Hastināpura, and bring back a great abundance of precious jewels."

By them, Prince Sudhanu together with his retinue and Manoharā were lifted up from the city of the Kinnaras while she was still lying on her bed; and having brought a great abundance of precious jewels to Hastināpura, they were established in the royal park.
When the night had turned to dawn, Prince Sudhanu awoke and heard the sound of kettledrums in Hastināpura as well as the clamor of the people.
The thought occurs to him:
"Where have I been brought? To Hastināpura!"
He beheld this royal park,
those couches made of jewels arranged as they were, that enchanting retinue consisting of the three groups, and the abundant treasure;
the prince became filled with joy and returned to his own city as he had desired.
After the prince had departed from Hastināpura, King Subāhu caused a search to be made with great effort.
When the king could not obtain any news of the prince, he thought:
"The prince must have died while searching for Manoharā."
That king had the funeral rites performed for the deceased prince Sudhanu.
He becomes the presiding authority over everything;
Sudhanu has died.

Then, from the main gate of the royal park, the park-keepers rushed out and were raising banners in the park; having arrived, they saw Sudhanu and Manoharā, as well as that retinue consisting of the three groups,
the couches made of jewels, and the great heap of gems, and upon seeing them, they ran back.
They entered Hastināpura.
A great multitude of people asked after his welfare;
they replied,
"It is well, for Prince Sudhanu has arrived."
Thus he becomes joyful.
Having gone to the royal palace, those gardeners informed King Subāhu.
"O Great King, by good fortune there is prosperity; Prince Sudhanu has arrived."
The king and the entire royal family became delighted merely by hearing this,
and a vast gift was bestowed upon those garden-keepers.
King Subāhu, along with his ministers and retinue, Queen Sudhanus’s mother, and the entire harem,
rushed out to the park to see the prince; and the whole city, having heard the news of Prince Sudhanu’s arrival and that of Manoharā, did the same.
There was no interval for the king’s business from Hastināpura for one rushing out to the park to see the prince and Manoharā.

Upon seeing his parents, Sudhanu prostrated himself with his head at their feet; and Manoharā, upon seeing her mother-in-law and father-in-law, likewise prostrated herself with her head at their feet.
The prince, together with his father Subāhu, mounted a noble elephant adorned with gold and covered with a golden net;
accompanied by great royal majesty, great royal power, a vast array, and great splendor, he was led into Hastināpura.
In this way, may all sentient beings be separated from everything dear to them, once they have abandoned [the pursuit of] awakening.
Just as at that time Sudhanu met with the Kinnarī.
The Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, monks, it might occur to you that at that time, on that occasion, the prince named Sudhanu was someone else.
It should not be viewed in this way."
For what reason?

"Monks, you should not view it thus: that at that time, on that occasion, the prince named Sudhanu was someone else; nor that the king named Subāhu was someone else. It was I who, at that time, on that occasion, was the prince named Sudhanu."
For what reason?
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, this King Śuddhodana was the king named Subāhu.
[_Mvu_2.114_] "She who was Sudhanu’s mother at that time and on that occasion was not someone else;
it should not be viewed in this way. For what reason? Because..."
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, this Queen Māyā was the mother of Sudhanu.
"Furthermore, monks, it may be that you think the one who was Sudhanu’s attendant named Vasantaka at that time and on that occasion was someone else.
It should not be viewed in this way. And why is that?"
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, this Chandaka was the attendant of Sudhanu.
That hunter’s son named Uppalaka at that time and on that occasion was someone else;
it should not be viewed in this way.
And for what reason?
Monks, this Rāhula was formerly a hunter's son named Uppalaka.
It should not be viewed in this way that at that time, on that occasion, the hunter’s son named Mālaka was someone else.
For what reason? Because [he was I].
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, this Elder Ānanda was the hunter's son named Mālaka.
That seer named Kāśyapa who existed at that time and on that occasion was not someone else;
it should not be viewed in this way. For what reason?
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, this elder Mahākāśyapa was a seer of the Kāśyapa clan living in the vicinity of the Himalayas.
That monkey king in the Himalayas at that time and on that occasion was someone else;
it should not be viewed in this way. For what reason?
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, this Kaṇṭhaka, the king of horses, was the king of the monkeys in the Himalayas.
That Kinnara king named Druma who, at that time and on that occasion, was on the summit of Mount Kailāsa, was not anyone else.
It should not be viewed in this way. For what reason?
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, this Śākya Mahānāma was the Kinnara king Druma.
It should not be viewed in this way that she was Manoharā’s mother at that time and on that occasion.
For what reason? Because it was I myself.
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, this mother of Yaśodharā was the mother of Manoharā.

It should not be viewed in this way that at that time, on that occasion, she was the kinnarī Manoharā. For what reason? Because it was I myself who was the kinnarī Manoharā at that time, on that occasion.
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, Yaśodharā was the Kinnarī Manoharā;
even then, she was obtained by me with great effort.
One who delivers diverse and profound discourses, is widely learned,
destroys the afflictions, and crushes the arguments of opponents.
That monk would shine within the teaching of the Self-Existent One, like the full-orbed moon in the sky.
Thus ends the Śrīkinnarījātaka.

The Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, having accomplished the purpose for which he had come, was dwelling at Śrāvastī as the teacher of gods and humans; having related the introduction in detail, he addressed the monks.
Monks, I was delicate, exceedingly delicate.

Monks, for me, who was so delicate, my Śākya father had three palaces built—the winter palace, the summer palace, and the rainy-season palace—for my own sake, for play, for pleasure, and for enjoyment.
Monks, I was delicate, exceedingly delicate.

Monks, for me— who was delicate, most delicately nurtured— my Śākya father had palatial gabled chambers constructed upon those mansions; they were plastered and whitewashed, provided with lattices to ward off the wind, their windows closed, perfumed with incense, hung with bundles of silk ribbons and cords, and strewn with loose flowers, all for my own sake, for play, for pleasure, and for diversion.
I was delicate, monks, most exceedingly delicate.

Monks, for me— who was so delicate, indeed supremely delicate— my Śākya father had couches made for those gabled chambers, fashioned of gold, silver, and jewels; they were spread with sixteen-fold woolen rugs,
cotton coverlets, variegated carpets, and silk cloths, provided with pillows at both ends, red cushions, and white counter-spreads.
It was for my very own amusement, for pleasure, and for diversion.
I was delicate, monks, supremely delicate.
Monks, for me— who was delicate,
most delicately nurtured— my Śākya father had canopies made over those couches to keep away dust and dirt for my play, pleasure, and enjoyment;
for I, monks, was delicate, most delicately nurtured.
Monks, for me— who was delicate, most delicate— my Śākya father provided various ointments, such as aloe-wood, sandalwood, kālānusārin, and tamāla leaves, solely for my play, pleasure, and enjoyment.

"Monks, I was delicate, exceedingly delicate. For me, monks, being so delicate and exceedingly delicate, my Śākya father provided various garments, such as fine cloth from Kāśī and fine woolen blankets, for the sake of my play, for the sake of pleasure, and for the sake of enjoyment."
"Monks, I was delicate, exceedingly delicate.
For me, monks, who was so delicate and exceedingly delicate, my Śākya father provided various garlands, namely:
atimuktaka, campaka, vārṣika, vātuṣkārī, indīvara, damanaka, and those brought from the gods—all for my own sake, for play, for pleasure, and for diversion."
"Monks, I was delicate, exceedingly delicate.
For my sake, monks, my Śākya father provided various kinds of food:
rice of many colors and grains, accompanied by numerous soups, stews, and condiments, solely for my play, for my pleasure, and for my enjoyment."
"O monks, I was delicate, most delicately refined. O monks,

while I was thus delicate and most delicately refined, my father, the Śākya, immediately after eating, would offer me a garland fit for a universal monarch, solely for my amusement, pleasure, and enjoyment."
"Monks, I was delicate, exceedingly delicate. For me, monks, who was so delicate and exceedingly delicate, my Śākya father provided the five strands of sensual pleasure—
namely, dance, song, instrumental music, orchestral music, and women— for my play, for my delight, and for my enjoyment."
"Monks, I was delicate, exceedingly delicate. For me, monks, who was so delicate and exceedingly delicate, my Śākya father provided various vehicles—
namely, elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, boat-vehicles, and palanquin-vehicles— for my very own play and for my enjoyment."

Monks, I was delicate, indeed most delicate. For me, monks, being so delicate and most delicate, my father, the Śākya, would provide a variegated rug bordered with lion skins, tiger skins, and leopard skins.
Covered with white woolen blankets, making joyful sounds, and adorned with victory banners, they were for my very own amusement, pleasure, and diversion.
"Monks, I was delicate, exceedingly delicate. Monks, for me— who was so delicate and exceedingly delicate— my Śākya father had a parasol held over me as I went out,
lest the heat, dust, or grime should scorch my body, for the sake of my play, my pleasure, and my diversion."
"Monks, I was delicate, exceedingly delicate.
For me, monks, being so delicate and exceedingly delicate, he had gardens constructed in the four directions for my own sake—for play, for pleasure, and for diversion."
"Monks, I was delicate, exceedingly delicate. For me, monks, being so delicate and exceedingly delicate, my Śākya father had lotus-pools constructed in the four directions within those gardens,
covered with blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lotuses, and fragrant water-lilies, for my very own pleasure."
For the sake of delight and for the sake of thorough investigation.
“Monks, I was delicate, exceedingly delicate.

Monks, for me—who was so delicate and exceedingly delicate—my Śākya father had palaces built in the four directions within those gardens: high, large, and lofty, for my very own sake, for play, for pleasure, and for diversion.”
"Monks, I was delicate, exceedingly delicate.
Monks, as I was so delicate and exceedingly delicate, this thought occurred to me:"
Furthermore, this life in a household is crowded, whereas the life of one who has gone forth is open space.

It is not possible for one dwelling at home to practice the holy life (brahmacarya) that is utterly refined, utterly blameless, completely pure, and perfectly bright; what if I were now to go forth from the home into homelessness?
Monks, against the wishes of my parents—who had tearful throats and weeping faces—I indeed went forth, leaving behind no wealth.
Having abandoned the household life and the sovereignty of a universal monarch as if they were a mere trifle held in his hand, he went forth from the home into homelessness;
and being thus ordained, he proceeded toward the city of Vaiśālī and arrived there.
[ Mvu 2.118 ] Now at that time, Ārāḍa Kālāma was residing in the great city of Vaiśālī, honored, revered, and esteemed by three hundred disciples.
He taught the Dharma for the sake of the practice of the "vow of suspicion" among the disciples of the Jina.
He spoke to those disciples of the Jina as follows:
Behold, behold! Abandon, abandon!
Those disciples also spoke to him in this way:
We see, we see; we abandon, we abandon—both ourselves and others.
Then, monks, this thought occurred to me:
"What if I were now to practice the holy life under Ārāḍa?"
Then, monks, having approached where Ārāḍa Kālāma was, I said this to Ārāḍa Kālāma:
I wish to practice the holy life under the Blessed One Ārāḍa.
When this was said, monks, Ārāḍa Kālāma spoke as follows:

Go forth, O Gautama! Such is this Dharma and Vinaya that a faithful son of good family may lead the holy life (brahmacarya), and while leading it, he may further accomplish wholesome states (kuśalā dharmāḥ).
Then, monks, this thought occurred to me.

Indeed, I too have the desire, the strength, and the energy; what if I were now, for the sake of attaining and realizing this very Dharma, to dwell alone, vigilant, ardent, resolute, and withdrawn, so that before long I might master and realize this Dharma?
Then, monks, I approached Ārāḍa Kālāma and said this to him:
"Such is the Dharma as it was realized, personally attained, taught, and proclaimed by the Blessed One through Ārāḍa."
When this had been said, monks, Ārāḍa Kālāma spoke as follows.
"So it is, Gautama; such is this Dharma which has been realized, personally attained, taught, and established by me."
When this had been said, monks, I spoke thus to Ārāḍa Kālāma:
"In that case, friend Ārāḍa, this Dharma has also been realized and personally attained by me."
When this had been said, monks, Ārāḍa Kālāma spoke thus to me:
"Therefore, O Gautama, whatever Dharma I know, that Dharma you, Gautama, know; and whatever Dharma you, Gautama, know, that I know.
Let us both, then, lead the community of disciples together in this way."
Thus, monks, that Ārāḍa Kālāma honored me with the highest honor and praised me with the highest praise.
And having established such a view, one should place it for the sake of common purpose.
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
"This Dharma of Ārāḍa does not lead one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering;
what if I were now to seek further?"
Monks, being thus desirous of seeing him, I went toward the city of Rājagṛha; having arrived there, I stayed right there in the city of Rājagṛha.
Now at that time, Udraka Rāmaputra was residing in Rājagṛha;
he was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by seven hundred disciples.
Thus, he teaches the Dharma to the disciples of the Jina for the sake of practicing in accordance with the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
He spoke thus to the disciples of the Jina.
Behold, behold! Abandon, abandon!
And those disciples also spoke thus:
We see, we see; we abandon, we abandon—both ourselves and others.
Then, monks, this thought occurred to me:
"What if I were now to lead the holy life under Udraka Rāmaputra?"
Then, monks, I approached where Udraka Rāmaputra was and said this to Udraka Rāmaputra:
"Venerable Udraka, I wish to lead the holy life under you; may the venerable Udraka grant me permission to do so."
When this had been said, monks, Udraka Rāmaputra spoke as follows.

"In that case, go forth, O Gautama; dwell, O Gautama! Such is this Dharma and Vinaya wherein a faithful son of good family may practice the holy life (brahmacarya), and while practicing it, he may attain wholesome states."
Then, monks, this thought occurred to him.
Indeed, I too have the desire, the strength, and the vigor;
what if I were now to dwell alone, heedful, ardent, resolute, and withdrawn, for the sake of attaining and realizing this very Dharma?
Monks, for the sake of attaining and realizing that very Dharma, I dwelt alone, diligent, ardent, resolute, and secluded; and before long, I attained and realized that Dharma.
Then indeed, monks, I went to where Udraka Rāmaputra was and said this to him.

"Venerable sir, such is the Dhamma that has been realized, personally attained, taught, and proclaimed by you, the venerable Uddaka Rāmaputta—namely, this sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
When this had been said, monks, Udraka Rāmaputra spoke as follows.
"Venerable Gautama, this much has been realized, witnessed, and declared by your venerable Rāma—namely, this very sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
Then, monks, I said this to Udraka Rāmaputra:
"In that case, Uddaka, this Dharma has been attained and realized by me as well."
When this was said, monks, Uddaka Rāmaputra spoke as follows.
"In that case, Gautama, whatever Dharma the venerable Rāma knows, you, venerable Gautama, know that same Dharma.
Therefore, let the venerable Gautama himself now lead the community of disciples."
Thus, monks, that Udraka Rāmaputra indeed honored me with the highest honor and praised me with the highest praise; he regarded me as his equal and placed me in the position of a teacher.
Then, monks, this thought occurred to me.
"And this dharma of that Rāma does not lead to the complete destruction of suffering for one who practices it;
what if I were now to undertake a further search?
Monks, being thus disposed from having seen that [truth], I proceeded toward the city of Gayā.
Having attained that, I dwell right there.
While staying on Gayāśīrṣa mountain, three similes occurred to me—previously unheard, never heard before, unknown, and never known before.
What are these three?
For whatever venerable ascetics or brahmins dwell with their bodies not withdrawn from sensual pleasures and their minds not withdrawn from them,

even those discursive thoughts of sensuality, those attachments to sensuality, those fevers of sensuality, and those obsessions with sensuality remain unremoved for them; and furthermore, these venerable ascetics or brahmins [engage in] self-mortification and bodily torment.
They experience painful, intense, harsh, and bitter sensations.
Indeed, they are truly incapable of the knowledge, vision, and awakening that constitute the state of a superhuman being.

Just as if, for example, a man were to come here seeking fire, searching for fire, and looking for fire, and while rubbing together wet wood that is moist and full of sap, with a lower fire-drill that is wet and contains water within it, he would be incapable of producing heat or making fire appear; even so, sirs, are those ascetics or brahmins.
They experience painful, intense, harsh, and bitter sensations that originate from themselves and afflict the body.
Indeed, they are truly incapable of the knowledge, vision, and awakening that constitute the superhuman state.
"Monks, while I was dwelling on Mount Gayāśīrṣa, this first simile occurred to me— something never heard before, never heard by anyone in the past, unknown before, and never known by anyone."
"Monks, this thought occurred to me."
For whatever ascetics or brahmins, sirs, dwell with their bodies withdrawn from sensual pleasures but whose minds are not withdrawn,
even for them those thoughts of sensuality, those affections for sensuality, those fevers of sensuality, and those attachments to sensuality remain unremoved; and furthermore, they...
"Sirs, whether they be ascetics or brahmins, they experience painful, intense, harsh, and bitter sensations that involve self-exertion and torment the body."
Indeed, they are incapable of the knowledge, vision, and awakening that belong to the superhuman state.

It is just as if a man here were to come seeking light, searching for light, and looking for light, yet while rubbing together a piece of moist, sap-filled wood with a wet upper fire-stick on dry ground, he would be incapable of producing heat.

Just as for the purpose of producing light and making it manifest, even so, whatever ascetics or brahmins dwell with their bodies withdrawn from sensual pleasures but whose minds are not withdrawn— those discursive thoughts of sensual pleasure, those attachments to sensual pleasure, those fevers of sensual pleasure,
and those fixations on sensual pleasure remain unremoved within them, even though those venerable ones are ascetics or brahmins.
Or they experience painful, intense, harsh, and bitter sensations that arise from self-inflicted exertion and torment the body.
Indeed, they are truly incapable of knowing, seeing, or awakening to the superhuman state.
"Monks, while I was staying on Mount Gayāśīrṣa, this second simile occurred to me—previously unheard, never before heard, unknown, and never before known. Then, monks, this thought arose in me:"
Whosoever, sirs, are those ascetics or brahmins who dwell with bodies withdrawn from sensual pleasures and with minds withdrawn from them,

even those thoughts of sensuality, attachments to sensuality, fevers of sensuality, and obsessions with sensuality that exist— these too have been thoroughly subdued by them. Furthermore, although those worthy ascetics or brahmins [engage in] self-inflicted hardship and bodily mortification...
They experience painful, intense, harsh, and bitter sensations.
Indeed, they are capable of knowing, seeing, and awakening to the state that transcends human conditions.
