Just as if, for example, a man were to come here seeking light, searching for light, and pursuing light, and while rubbing dry wood that is free of sap with a dry upper fire-stick on dry ground, he would be capable of producing heat and manifesting light; even so, those who...
There are certain venerable recluses or brahmins who dwell with their bodies withdrawn from sensual pleasures and their minds withdrawn from them;
even those thoughts of sensuality, attachments to sensuality, fevers of sensuality, and fixations on sensuality that they may have are thoroughly subdued in them.
Furthermore, although those venerable recluses or brahmins [practice] self-assault and bodily mortification...
They experience painful, intense, harsh, and bitter sensations.
Indeed, they are capable of the knowledge, vision, and awakening pertaining to the state beyond that of ordinary humans.
"Monks, while I was dwelling on Mount Gayāśīrṣa, this third simile occurred to me—previously unheard and never before heard."
"Monks, while I was dwelling on Mount Gayāśīrṣa, three similes occurred to me—previously unheard, never heard before; previously unknown, never known before."
Then, monks, this thought occurred to me:
Indeed, I shall dwell with my body withdrawn from sensual pleasures and my mind withdrawn; even those discursive thoughts of sensuality,

those attachments to sensuality, those fevers of sensuality, and those obsessions with sensuality have been subdued by me, even though I experience painful, intense, harsh, and bitter sensations that involve self-exertion and torment the body.
Then indeed, I am capable of the knowledge, vision, and awakening regarding the state of being superior to human conditions.
Monks, having thus seen it as it truly was, I set out for Uruvilvā, the village of the general, and arrived there.

There he saw the roots of trees that were pleasing, beautiful to behold, remote, secluded, free from calamity, and devoid of human habitation; they possessed delightful ponds for reclining and were suitable for solitary meditation.
Furthermore, on all sides there were villages within the range of alms-gathering, neither too far nor too near, well-suited for coming and going.
He also saw the level ground and the river Nairañjanā, which was even, provided with embankments, abundant in its purpose, and possessed of pure, excellent water.
And seeing her flowing [with milk] once more, my mind was exceedingly gladdened.
Enough now with my exertion for the sake of abandonment as a son of good family who has gone forth out of faith; what if I were to practice abandonment right here?
Indeed, monks, with my mind I thus restrained and oppressed this very body.

Monks, as I thus restrained and oppressed this very body with my mind, sweat was released from my armpits and fell upon the ground, becoming warm and steaming; sweat was released from my mouth and forehead and fell upon the ground, becoming warm and steaming.
Just as if, monks, a strong man were to seize a weak man by the neck and press him down,
crush him; even so, monks, as he pressed down and crushed this very body with his mind in such a way,
sweat fell from his armpits onto the ground and emitted heat, and sweat was released from his face and forehead and fell onto the ground.
They were heated and steamed.
Then, monks, this thought occurred to me:
"What if I were now to practice the breath-holding meditation (āsphānaka-dhyāna)?"
Indeed, monks, I completely stopped the inhalation and exhalation through my mouth, nostrils, and ears.
Monks, when the inhalations and exhalations were obstructed at my mouth and nostrils, a loud and great sound issued forth from both the openings of my ear canals;
just as a blacksmith’s bellows produce a loud and great sound when blown, even so, monks,
did a loud and great sound issue from both the openings of my ear canals when the inhalations and exhalations were obstructed at my mouth and nostrils.
They moved about with loud noises and great clamor.
Then, monks, this occurred to me: "What if I were now to practice the breath-holding meditation (āsphānaka-dhyāna) to an even greater degree?"

"Monks, I indeed obstructed the inhalations and exhalations through my mouth, through both nostrils, and through the openings of both ear canals. Monks, when the inhalations and exhalations were thus obstructed through my mouth, nostrils, and both ear canals, winds would have struck upward against the skull of my head."
They crossed over.
Monks, it was just as if a butcher or a butcher’s apprentice were to split, thoroughly split, cut, and completely cut away the skull of an ox with a sharp butcher’s knife. Just so.
Thus, when inhalation and exhalation were obstructed from the mouth, the nostrils, and both ear canals,
the winds would strike and shatter the skull above.
Then, monks, this thought occurred to me.

There are some here who prescribe purification; they eat jujube fruit as food, they eat the husks of jujube fruit as food, they drink jujube water, and they subsist on various preparations of jujube fruit. What if I were now to take a single jujube fruit as my sole food, without a second?
Indeed, monks, I took a single jujube fruit as my sole food.
This body of mine had become exceedingly emaciated; it had become exceedingly emaciated.
Just as if they were the joints of a blackwood tree, even so did my limbs become; just as if they were the hoof of a goat or the hoof of a camel, even so did my ribs become.

Just as in a carriage-house with its sides open on both parts, where the gaps between the rafters are exposed and visible through, even so did the spaces between my ribs become exposed and visible through.
Just as a braid of hair is uneven with rises and dips, even so the vertebrae of his back were uneven with rises and dips;
just as in the last month of summer the stars reflected in a well appear far away and deep down.
They appear as if difficult to see; even so, the pupils in my eyes became distant and deep-set, appearing as if difficult to see.
Just as an autumnal bitter gourd, cut while still green, becomes withered, shriveled, and shrunk, even so my skull became withered and shriveled.
It is produced from a casket.
"Indeed, monks, thinking, 'I shall grasp the front part of my body,' I would pull back the back; as I was about to straighten up, I would fall right there, bent double."
Indeed, monks, having thoroughly and well rubbed my dust-covered limbs with effort, I would wipe them with my hand.
Monks, as I was rubbing my dust-covered limbs with my hand, the hairs on my body, rotten at their roots, fell away.
For indeed, in the countryside villages, women and men spoke thus: "He has been conquered!"
"The ascetic Gautama is now dark; the ascetic Gautama is now dusky; the ascetic Gautama is now the color of a madgura fish."
And even this beautiful complexion of my body has vanished because of such harsh asceticism.
"Monks, this thought occurred to me."

There are certain venerable ascetics and brahmins who prescribe purity through a diet of rice; they consume rice as food, they eat rice powder, they drink rice-water, and they subsist on various preparations of rice. What if I were to take a single grain of rice, without a second, as my food?
Indeed, monks, while I was taking a single grain of rice as my sole food, this body of mine reached an extreme state of emaciation.
Just as black joints or joints that have not yet matured, such were my limbs and members;
just as, for example,
the spaces between the rafters in a carriage-house shed with its sides open on both sides.
They opened wide and displayed their sides, and likewise they opened wide and displayed the spaces between their ribs;
just as one might see the hoof-print of a goat or the footprint of a camel, so too were their armpits and chests, all of them possessing unsurpassed firmness.

Just as a braided rope is undulating with highs and lows, even so did my vertebrae become; just as in the last month of summer the stars reflected in a well appear far away, deep down, and visible only with difficulty, even so did the pupils in my eyes become— far away and deep down.
They manifested a sight of great suffering.
Just as an autumnal bitter gourd, cut while still green, becomes withered, shriveled, and shrunk into a hollow shell, even so his skull became withered,
shriveled, and shrunk into a hollow shell.
Indeed, monks, thinking, "I shall restrain my upper body," I would grasp only the backbone; as soon as I tried to lift it up, I would fall right there, bent over backward.
"Monks, having risen with great effort and care, I would rub my dust-covered limbs with my hand.
As I rubbed my dust-covered limbs, monks, the hairs on my body, rotten at the roots, would fall away."
For even the neighboring villages and the people of the surrounding hamlets—both women and men—spoke thus:
"The ascetic Gautama is now dark-skinned; the ascetic Gautama is now dark-brown; the ascetic Gautama is now the color of a madgura fish.
That beautiful complexion of mine has vanished because of such harsh asceticism."
"Then, monks, this thought occurred to me."
For there are some venerable recluses and brahmins here who proclaim purification through a diet of sesame;
they consume even sesame as food, they drink sesame powder and sesame water, and they subsist on various preparations of sesame.
"What if I were now to take a single sesame seed as my sole food?"
Indeed, monks, I would take a single sesame seed as my sole food, without a second.

Monks, as I took that single sesame seed as my sole food, this body of mine became exceedingly emaciated. My limbs and members became like the joints of a withered tree or the joints of a shriveled creeper;
indeed, my jaw became just like the hoof of a goat or the foot of a camel.

Just as, for example, in a carriage-house with both sides open, one might look through and see the spaces between the rafters, even so my ribs and the spaces between my ribs were visible; just as, for example,
a braided rope is uneven, rising and falling, even so were my vertebrae.

Just as in the last month of summer, the reflections of stars in a well appear far away, deep down, and are visible only with difficulty, even so the pupils of my eyes appeared far away, deep down, and were visible only with difficulty. Just as a bitter gourd cut while still green becomes withered, shriveled, and shrunk up, even so my skull became withered and shriveled.
"Indeed, monks, thinking, 'I shall grasp the front of my body,' I instead grasp only the backbone; as they lift me up, I fall back down right there, bent over."
"Monks, having exerted myself with great care and effort, I would raise up my dust-covered limbs and rub them with my hands.

As I rubbed my dust-covered limbs with my hands, monks, the hairs on my body, rotten at their roots, fell away. Indeed, the women and men from the neighboring villages where I went for alms said this:"
"The ascetic Gautama is now dark; the ascetic Gautama is now dark-complexioned; the ascetic Gautama is now the color of a madgura fish.
Even that beautiful complexion of mine has vanished through such harsh exertion."
Monks, this thought occurred to me.
Indeed, there are some venerable recluses and brahmins here who prescribe purification through total abstention from food; what if I were now to practice total abstention from food?
Monks, as I was practicing for total abstention from food, this body of mine became exceedingly emaciated. My limbs and members became like the joints of a blackwood tree or a śīta-tree;
my jawbones became like those of a camel or a goat.

Just as in a carriage-house stable with its sides open, one looks through and peers between the gaps in the rafters, even so my ribs and the spaces between my ribs were visible, looking through and peering out.
Just as a braided rope is uneven, rising and falling, even so did the vertebrae of my spine become.

Just as in the last month of summer, the reflections of stars in a well appear far away, deep down, and are visible only with difficulty, even so the pupils in my eyes appeared far away, deep down, and were visible only with difficulty.
Just as an autumnal bitter gourd, cut while still green, becomes withered, shriveled, and shrunk together, even so my skull became withered,
shriveled, and shrunk together.
"Indeed, monks, thinking, 'I shall grasp my front body,' I instead grasp only my backbone;
as they pull it upward, I fall right there, bent over."
"Monks, having raised myself up with great effort and care, I would wipe my dust-covered limbs with my hand.

As I was wiping my dust-covered limbs, monks, the hairs at their roots, being rotten at the base, would fall away. Indeed, the women and men from the neighboring villages where I went for alms said this:"
"The ascetic Gautama is now dark; the ascetic Gautama is now sallow; the ascetic Gautama is now the color of a madgura fish.
Even that beautiful complexion of mine has vanished because of such harsh exertion."
"Monks, this thought occurred to me."

Whosoever, sirs, are those ascetics or brahmins who experience painful, intense, harsh, and bitter sensations resulting from self-inflicted violence and bodily mortification— to this extent they have reached the limit, yet even this they do not fully attain.

Monks, in the past, and even now, monks, in the present time, whatever recluses or brahmins there may be who experience painful, intense, harsh, and bitter sensations resulting from self-inflicted violence and bodily mortification— this much they have not mastered, nor do they attain this perfection by any means.

Furthermore, I do not recall that by means of this practice of austerities I was able to realize any superhuman state, any noble knowledge and vision, or any distinguished attainment; this is not the path to awakening.

Indeed, I recall that formerly, before I had gone forth, while still at home, I sat cross-legged in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree in my father the Śākyan’s park; secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, I entered and dwelt in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and filled with the joy and happiness born of seclusion.
Indeed, that path would truly lead to awakening.
"Monks, as I was dwelling there, a consciousness following that [practice] attended upon me;
that very path leads to awakening.
However, that path cannot indeed be attained by one who is emaciated, or weak, or whose body is overcome [by suffering], or by one who has undertaken a total fast from food."
"What if I were now to take solid food...? ...by that coarse practice of mine, you will maintain your conscious life."
As they fly away, we shall withdraw their divine vitality from within the pores of their skin.
Then, monks, this thought occurred to me:

"I indeed declare myself to be entirely without food. Even in the nearby villages where I seek alms, women and men perceive me thus: 'The ascetic Gautama is without food. And these deities, who are devoted to austerity and have faith in austerity, infused divine vitality through the pores of my skin. If that were so, it would be a conscious lie on my part."
Monks, being terrified of the fear of conscious lying, and loathing conscious lying, thinking "enough of this," I rejected that deity and partook of substantial,
solid food at my ease.
Indeed, monks, I ate there preparations of mung bean soup, as well as pea soup and hareṇuka soup.

"Monks, having gradually regained my physical strength and vigor, I took honeyed milk-rice from Sujātā, the village headwoman, and at the time when the elephants rejoice, I went to the river Nairañjanā.
Having cooled my limbs in the river Nairañjanā, I approached Svastika the grass-cutter and [spoke to] Svastika."

Having requested a handful of grass from a grass-cutter, he approached the Bodhi tree, spread out a seat of choice grass before the Bodhi tree, circumambulated the Bodhi tree three times to the right,
and sat down cross-legged, with his body held straight, facing eastward, and with mindfulness directed before him.

Having established [myself], O monks, being secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, I entered and dwelt in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion.

With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, through internal tranquility and the unification of the mind, I enter and abide in the second dhyāna, which is without applied or sustained thought, born of concentration, and characterized by rapture and happiness.

Through detachment from joy, I dwell in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending; I experience happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones declare: "He who dwells in equanimity and mindfulness lives happily. Thus, having attained the third dhyāna, I dwell therein.

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and dejection, I entered and dwelt in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness.
Indeed, monks, with my mind thus concentrated, I directed it toward the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, I saw beings passing away and being reborn—beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, lowly and exalted; I understood how beings fare according to their karma: "These worthy beings, endowed with misconduct of body, revilers of the noble ones..."
Those who held wrong views, because of their undertaking of actions based on wrong views— for that cause and by that condition— after the breaking up of the body,
after death, were reborn in states of woe, in miserable destinies, in perdition, in the hells.
Furthermore, these beings, sirs, being endowed with good conduct of body and endowed with good conduct of mind,

not reviling the noble ones and possessing right view, on account of undertaking actions based on right view— due to that cause, due to that condition— after the breaking up of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world, among the gods.

Monks, with my mind thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from defilements, supple, wieldy, stable, and attained to imperturbability, during the first watch of the night, I directed and applied my mind toward the attainment of the knowledge and vision that recollects past lives; I recollected my manifold past lives.
Namely: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births;
even many aeons of dissolution, many dissolutions, many evolutions, and many aeons of both dissolution and evolution.

"In that place I was, with such a name, such a clan, such a birth, such food, such a limit to my lifespan, and such an experience of pleasure and pain. Passing away from there, I was reborn elsewhere; passing away from there, I came here. Thus, with its aspects and details, I recollect my manifold past abodes.

Monks, with my mind thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from secondary defilements, supple, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, in the last watch of the night, at the time of dawn when the night was ending, whatever [was to be realized] by a true man, a bull among men, a lion among men, a leader among men— [that I realized].
By means of that thoroughbred man, that lotus among men, that white lotus among men, that true man, that great man, that unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed—
possessed of movement, mindfulness, intelligence, steadfastness, and splendor— he [the Buddha] has,
through wisdom conjoined with a single moment of mind, known, attained, and fully awakened to everything that is to be known, attained, and fully awakened to in every way and in all respects.
He has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Blessed One said this; with joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.
Then Śuddhodana saw a dream.
O son, I saw in a dream a preeminent elephant, covered with a net of jewels, emerging from a boat that had plunged into the water.
And in the middle of the city, standing upon the road at night, he rushed out from the excellent city, trembling violently.
Having seen that in my dream, a vast laughter arose within me,
as well as immeasurable weeping.
My body trembles and is thoroughly consumed by fever; a burning sensation rises from within—what indeed will become of me today?
Then the World-Protectors spoke to the foremost of men:
"Do not fear, O Lord of the Earth; give rise to joy!"
Come, listen to the fruit of this dream, its reality that has arisen for the purpose of awakening many people.
This possessor of great virtues, having abandoned his kingdom, as well as his two wives and his own prosperous kinsmen, has departed.
Without doubt, disregarding even his excellent strength, he will depart from this preeminent city; let this be known to him.
When he has departed, many kinds of suffering will arise; that which was laughed at in the dream is the truth.
Having heard that infinite bliss which exists even in dreams, O Heaven and Earth, there will now be victory over the host of enemies who have been conquered.
The mother’s sister also sees a dream.
The mother’s sister said, "O you who have the color of a heap of gold,
my son, I see in a dream a well-born bull."
White, with beautiful and well-proportioned horns, possessing exceptionally prominent peaks, moving with the grace of the erotic sentiment, and having a perfectly formed body.
Thus he roars most sweetly, charging forth from the city named Kapila,
stealing away the very hearts and the range of vision.
And no one was able to roar back at him as he roared, for he was well-born and resembled a mass of white water-lilies.
Those gods, O King of Devas, spoke to him as he wept piteously:
"Do not weep, O you who have been born as the joy of the Śākya clan."
I shall speak to you words that are unerring and free from deception;
produce within yourself the joys born of gladness.
He whose conduct is utterly pure and who is endowed with virtue—
this bull among men knows the way for those possessed of supreme intelligence.
Having abandoned the people and gone forth from the city, that best of lions among men aspired to the state of a bull among men.
He too, with his perfectly purified eye, [attained] the deathless, the immovable, the unshakable, the imperturbable, the incomparable Nirvana.
Having proclaimed that lion’s roar of a man, which, upon being heard, causes the hosts of heretics to flee in all directions, the Great Seer [spoke].
Yaśodharā also saw a dream.
Then his mother, her heart bound by a passion exceeding even [the love of] Maitra, spoke this to Rāhula:
"O King, listen to how a delightful dream was seen by me today, and may its fruit come to pass for me."
It is said that King Śuddhodana’s royal palace was completely enveloped in an instant by a cloud of human lords.
Possessing powerful clouds, emitting a beautiful sound, and illuminating many worlds with the light of lightning, he shines throughout the three realms.
Having rained down cool, stainless, incomparable, and clear water, he roared sweetly.
While it rains, Sāgaradhara spends the summer on his bed; he too is inwardly happy, like a lord of the Sahā world.
Then Brahmā, having approached, said this to the mother of Rāhula: "Listen; do not despair."
This dream of yours portends a desired fruit of great significance; it shall be fulfilled very swiftly—therefore, give rise to joy.
This son of Śuddhodana, with his beautiful eyes,
rains down upon the three worlds like a cloud.
Having generated the constant, compassionate, and incomparable Dharma, he will refresh those scorched by great suffering.
The Bodhisattva also saw five great dreams;
having attained supreme perfect enlightenment, he explained them to the monks at Śrāvastī.
Monks, before the Tathāgata had fully awakened to enlightenment, he saw five great dreams.
Which are the five [powers] of the Tathāgata?
"Monks, before the Tathāgata had awakened to supreme enlightenment, this great earth served as his high bed and grand couch; Sumeru, the king of mountains, was his pillow;
his left arm rested upon the eastern great ocean, and his right arm rested upon the western great ocean."
Monks, in the past, before he had fully awakened to supreme enlightenment, the Tathāgata saw this first great dream: both soles of his feet were placed upon the southern great ocean.
Monks, before the Tathāgata had fully awakened to enlightenment, a species of grass called *kṣīrikā* sprang up from the circle of his navel, rose up, and remained suspended as far as the sky.
Monks, before the Tathāgata had fully awakened to enlightenment, he saw this second great dream.
"Monks, formerly, before the Tathāgata had awakened to perfect enlightenment, red creatures with black heads stood covering him from the soles of his feet up to his knees.
Monks, before the Tathāgata had awakened to perfect enlightenment, he saw this third great dream."

Monks, before the Tathāgata had awakened to perfect enlightenment, four birds of various colors and many hues came from the four directions through the air, smelled the soles of the Tathāgata’s feet, and cast off all their black feathers. Monks, before the Tathāgata had awakened to perfect enlightenment, he saw this fourth great dream.
Monks, in the past, before he had fully awakened to enlightenment, the Tathāgata walked back and forth upon a great mountain of excrement without being soiled.
Monks, in the past, before he had fully awakened to enlightenment, the Tathāgata saw this fifth great dream.
“Monks, before the Tathāgata had previously awakened to full enlightenment, this great earth served as his high bed and grand couch;
Sumeru, the king of mountains, was his pillow;
his left arm rested upon the eastern great ocean, his right arm rested upon the western great ocean, and both soles of his feet rested upon the southern great ocean.”
Monks, that the Tathāgata has not yet fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment—this is the ripening of that great dream.
"Monks, that species of grass called *kṣīrikā*, which, before the Tathāgata had fully awakened to supreme enlightenment, sprang up from the circle of his navel and reached as far as the sky,
stood there— monks, by the Tathāgata, having directly known this world and the world beyond, including the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, and the generation of recluses and brahmins..."
In Vārāṇasī, at the Deer Park in Ṛṣipatana, he set in motion for the sake of all beings, including gods and humans, the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma—
threefold in its revolution and twelvefold in its aspects— which had never before been set in motion by any ascetic, brahmin, god, Māra,
or anyone else in the world in accordance with the Dharma; that is to say, the Four Noble Truths.

Namely: this is the noble truth of suffering, this is the noble truth of the origin of suffering, this is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and this is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
And furthermore, monks, having heard such a teaching of the Dharma from the Tathāgata, the gods of the earth raised a cry:
"Friends, this unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma has been set in motion by the Blessed One at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana."

It has been set in motion—having three revolutions and twelve aspects—which has not been set in motion by any ascetic, or brahmin, or deva, or Brahmā, or Māra, or indeed by anyone else in the world, in accordance with the Dharma: "This is suffering;
this is the origin of suffering; this is the cessation of suffering; this is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
That will be for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of a great multitude of beings— both gods and humans.
Having heard the cry of the terrestrial gods, the gods who roam the atmosphere— the Cāturmahārājikas, the Trāyastriṃśas, and the Yāmas— [will rejoice].
At that very instant, at that very moment, the Tuṣitas, Nirmāṇaratis, and Paranirmitavaśavartins raised a cry as far as the Brahma-world:

"O worthy ones, this unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma—having three revolutions and twelve spokes—has been set in motion by the Blessed One at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana; it has not been set in motion by any ascetic or anyone else."

Whether by a brahmin, a deva, Māra, or anyone else in the world, it cannot be contested according to the Dharma that "this is suffering," "this is the origin of suffering," "this is the cessation of suffering," and "this is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
This is the fruition of that great dream.
"Monks, that which red creatures with black heads stood covering the Tathāgata’s feet up to his knees before he had previously awakened to full enlightenment—

monks, this is the ripening of that dream: that many people nowadays, having performed meritorious deeds toward the Tathāgata, after the breaking up of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world, among the gods."

"Monks, before the Tathāgata had awakened to supreme enlightenment, four birds of various colors came through the air from the four directions, smelled the soles of the Tathāgata’s feet, and all became pure white. Monks, what are these four castes? They are the Kṣatriyas, the Brāhmaṇas, the Vaiśyas, and [the Śūdras]."
Those śūdras, having practiced the holy life under the Tathāgata, realize the unshakable liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom;
this is the ripening of that great dream.

Monks, before the Tathāgata had awakened to supreme enlightenment, while he was walking back and forth upon a great mountain of dung that was being smeared [with it], even there in the eastern direction, monks, the Tathāgata dwelt; and there too he was honored, revered, esteemed, worshiped, and respected, and he obtained the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal supplies for the sick.
Unattached, uninfatuated, and with a mind unstained— monks,

the Tathāgata dwells in the southern direction as well, where he is honored, revered, esteemed, worshiped, and venerated, and where he receives the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal supplies for the sick.
Unattached, uninfatuated, and with a mind unstained— O monks,

the Tathāgata also dwells in the western direction, where he too is honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated, and receives the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal supplies for the sick.
Unattached, uninfatuated, and with a mind undefiled, monks,

the Tathāgata dwells in the northern direction as well; there too he is honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated, and he receives the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick.
"Without attachment, without infatuation, and with a mind undefiled—
this, O monks, is the fruition of that great dream which the Tathāgata saw in the past before he had fully awakened to enlightenment."
The Blessed One said this, and those [monks], being uplifted in mind, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.
Thus ends "The Five Great Dreams of Śuddhodana" in the glorious Mahāvastu-Avadāna.
Then this thought occurred to the Bodhisattva:
"It is difficult for one dwelling in the midst of a household to practice the holy life (brahmacarya) that is exclusively refined, exclusively blameless, exclusively pure, and completely purified.
What if I were now to go forth from the home into the homeless state?"
The Bodhisattva addressed the king, saying, "I shall go forth into the religious life. The king said:
O lotus-eyed one of beautiful form, do not now fall into vast grief, being separated from you.
And if my mother were to undergo this death so difficult to encounter,
then what kind of happiness would this be, even if it were so distinguished?
For the sake of whom you will abandon your own kin and your own kingdom, that separation will indeed be full of great suffering.
All the directions appear confused to me; every part of the ground is afflicted by cold, heat, gadflies, mosquitoes, and biting insects.
He was terrified in the forests by those who slaughter deer and elephants,
amidst great terrors accompanied by the terrifying cries of jackals.
"O my son, having formed the thought of liberation in your mind through constant reflection, first follow the path; be gracious,
so that I may live as long as I do, and she remains right here."
For what reason? Upon perceiving your departure, my body will surely meet its destruction.
[ _Mvu_ 2.141] The king then sent word to five hundred kings: "Come, the prince desires to go forth."
Then they arrived and entreated the prince in many ways, saying,
"Do not go forth!"
Then the Bodhisattva spoke thus to the king and those other kings:
"If, O Great King, you will provide me with four conditions as a guarantee, I promise you, O King, that I shall not depart from this excellent city."
The king said:
"I shall be your guarantor for the four steps; quickly, my son, speak before your life-breaths depart. The prince said:
While I am still in my youth, let old age not come upon me.
While I am abiding in health, let no disease come upon me.
While I am still living, let death indeed not come upon me.
While prosperity is still delightful, let misfortune not yet arrive.
Then the hosts of gods let out shouts of "hikkāra" and "hakkāra."
Excellent, excellent, Great Being! Excellent, O Peerless One!
This assembly, including Brahmā, has heard these well-spoken words of yours.
They were all thrilled, joyful at heart, and filled with the bliss of rapture.
Then King Śuddhodana was pierced by the arrow of suffering.
With eyes filled with tears, he spoke this to the Bodhisattva:
O son, you yourself must know for whom this does not exist.
Neither old age, nor sickness, nor death, nor calamities shall be my fate.
The prince said:
Come now, O Great King, stand as a guarantor for these three points.
Therefore, there shall never be separation from me for you.
The king said:
O son, I grant you the status of a guarantor for these steps.
Therefore, O Bhava, withdraw your mind from that which you are reciting at the root.
The prince said:
May the qualities of sensual pleasure be divine for me, and may they always be sources of happiness.
And may they be eternal here; be my guarantor in this matter.
The apsarases sang sweetly in the sky, [praising] the most excellent, supreme, and preeminent one of excellent wisdom.
The sweet water was pleasant and refreshing, adorned with excellent anklets and ornaments.
Indeed, the mind of a virtuous person is not attached to intoxicants in the manner that he describes them.
He will abandon the earth, which resembles a golden image and is strewn with manifold acquired riches.
And thus, the king, being distressed, spoke this to the prince:
Be gracious, my son; for whom are sensual pleasures truly pleasant or auspicious?
The prince said:
"Come now, O lord of the earth, you shall speak two other words."
Since you desire this very thing, act as my guarantor for them.
The king said:
I firmly accept this; I shall stand as your guarantor.
Speak to me in two words, and do not abandon me.
May the notions of "I" and "mine" never arise at any time.
Whether it be great or small, O protector of the earth, be my guarantor in this matter.
Then the Maheśvaras, standing in the sky, uttered these words:
"You shall indeed become a perfectly awakened Buddha, the destroyer of all bonds."
For what reason? Because, indeed, among those words [spoken] in the world with its gods, [there is no contradiction].
In this world, there exists a speaker such as you, O one possessed of vision.
Then King Śuddhodana was pierced by the arrow of suffering.
With eyes filled with tears, he spoke this to the Bodhisattva:
O Supreme among Men, I do not even know their names.
Regarding those words which you proclaim, I have no confidence in them.
The prince said:
Enough with delay; give your pledge on a single word.
Therefore, I shall dwell right here in this delightful place called Kapila.
Now, my son, may I be at your side in this very life.
O surety, speak quickly; I have come here together with him.
The prince said:
While I am dwelling right here in this most excellent palace.
May my mind proceed under its own control, free from all obstructions.
Then the gods, the yakṣas, the gandharvas, and the dānavas—
And the hosts of nāgas and rākṣasas cried out, "Aha! The Dharma!"
Oh, what a supreme speaker is he, who longs for the ultimate truth!
Clearly, the supreme words manifest themselves again and again.
Then, with a dejected mind, the king spoke thus to the prince:
"My son, I shall not dwell here; I shed a torrent of tears."
Then, [he spoke] words that produce joy for gods and humans.
The Bodhisattva, raising his voice, addressed his father with these words:
I am agelessness, health, and immortality, O best of kings.
I shall approach the unconditioned, which is free from the fear of misfortune.
O King, whatever is eternal, whatever is happiness, and whatever is auspicious—that has been attained by me myself.
There is no doubt that what is to be attained will come; cast off your fortitude and take up [the opposite].
Then King Śuddhodana, seeing that the prince was meditating in the shade of the rose-apple tree, entered an ocean of anxiety.
If the prince’s mind delights in peaceful meditations, then let the prophecy of the seer Asita not come true for the time being.

"What if I were now to provide the prince with an extensive harem and have various pleasure gardens constructed, wherein the prince might play, delight, and divert himself, so that he would not set his mind on going forth?"
Then indeed, Śuddhodana established an extensive harem for the prince, providing many thousands of women;

and he had various pleasure pavilions of diverse kinds constructed, hung with bundles of silk ribbons and strewn with loose flowers, wherein the prince would play and divert himself, and would not set his mind upon going forth.
Then King Śuddhodana gave instructions to the women of the inner apartments.
"Entertain the prince well with dance, song, and instrumental music, so that the prince may not set his mind upon renunciation."

Now the prince, seeing the peril in sensual pleasures and finding no purpose in any enjoyments of desire, found no delight even in such gardens resembling the abodes of the gods, or in the inner apartments filled with women like apsarases.
His mind delighted in going forth; nor did the Bodhisattva need to be urged by anyone that this saṃsāra is suffering.
Having attained mastery over all phenomena, he becomes detached by himself through right understanding; with a mind full of agitation, he causes his own mind to be agitated:
"Alas! Saṃsāra is suffering by its very nature; it displays immeasurable hundreds of calamities."

Then the prince, having gone up and sat upon the roof-terrace of the palace, remained there with his mind fixed on that very same meditation which he had attained under the shade of the rose-apple tree.
He took no pleasure in the sound of singing, nor the sound of the noise of dancing, nor the sight of the beautiful throngs of women;
reflecting only on that [meditation], he remained seated.
Then King Śuddhodana asked a certain man:

"What is this, my good man? Why is the sound of singing not heard within the prince's inner apartments, nor the sound of dancing, drums, clay drums, lutes, flutes, and cymbals? Is there some mental distress in the prince?
Then the deity who dwells in the Lumbinī grove, standing in the air, spoke to King Śuddhodana.
"Great King, reflect upon the prince!

Your son has become dispassionate toward all delights of the sensory qualities; before long, he will sever the entire bond of craving without remainder and go to the forest of asceticism, where he will cultivate that which is well-restrained.

For now, O King, Siddhārtha—though belonging to a royal lineage and currently situated within the excellent palace surrounded by a host of women—is discoursing upon impermanence, suffering, and selflessness regarding the body."
Then King Śuddhodana, having heard this from the presence of the deity, with a dejected complexion and afflicted by grief, approached the Prince and said this:
"What is this, my son? Why do you sit here with a dejected face, afflicted by grief? Do you perceive some physical ailment?
Do you observe a loss of wealth? Or has the fear of an enemy army approached? Tell me quickly, my son, for what reason."
The prince said: "Father, I perceive affliction within this body. Disease assails health; death assails life. Therefore, father, I contemplate the decay that lies between birth and death.

All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) perish, as flickering as the water of a mountain river; they are subject to the nature of supreme exhaustion. Life wanes with the passage of seasons and years; it draws near to death. Father, I perceive this very affliction within the body."
"Father, I see the decay of wealth; I see every phenomenon as empty, vain, pithless, like an illusion, deceptive, and unreliable. There is no stability in wealth;
it either perishes or passes from one person to another.
Father, I see this decay of wealth."

There is the fear of an enemy army; there is seen the fear of the defects resulting from the conditioning of phenomena—such as the cutting off of hands, the cutting off of ears, and the cutting off of heads. In many ways and through various means, manifold sufferings of these kinds migrate into this body.
Father, it is this fear of an enemy army that I perceive.
King Śuddhodana said:

"Enough, my son; do not think such thoughts. You are currently young and have entered the first bloom of youth; experience the duties of royalty. Your harem is vast and full of women endowed with youth; sport, delight, and enjoy yourself with them. Do not set your heart on the life of a renunciant."
The prince said:
"Father, if you grant me eight boons, then I shall no longer think upon this matter."
The king said:
"Tell me quickly, my son, what kind of eight boons you desire; if there is power or strength [in me], I shall grant them to you.
Why, my son, would my kingdom be lost if I do not grant you a boon, my son?"
The prince said: "Father, grant me these eight boons."
If old age would not overcome my youth; if illness would not overcome my health;
if death would not take away my life.
If there were no separation for me from you,

and if such an inner court like the Apsarases, and an extensive circle of kinsmen, were not to enter into decline, and if there were no transformation or state of suffering regarding my kingdom and sovereignty;
and if for all those beings who were invited by the bliss of the Deathless (amṛta) at the very moment of my birth, there were also the pacification of all their afflictions (kleśa).
May there also be an end to my birth, aging, and death.
King Śuddhodana said:
"My son, from where would such power or strength come to me that I might grant these eight boons?

Even those former kings, my son, who were long-lived—such as King Mahāsammata, Mahātejas, Dṛḍhadhanu, Śatadhanu, Niśāntāyus, Yugandhara, and others of noble royal lineage—all of them, my son, have been brought to their end by the force of impermanence; they remain now as nothing more than mere names."
"Son, from where do I have the strength or the power to grant you these eight such boons?"
The prince said:
"Father, if you do not venture to grant me these eight boons, then I invite you: may there be an end to old age and death for you."
The king said:
"I am worn out, aged, and my youth has passed; therefore, after I have died, you may go forth into the religious life."
The prince said:

"Rejoice greatly, dear father; while you are still living, you shall see me here—liberated from all states of existence, severed from all craving, free from all suffering, no longer enveloped by the flames of afflictions, and cultivating the jewels of all the factors of enlightenment."
Then the king showed him his groups of women: "My son, here are these noble women with eyes like broad, pure lotuses, with beautiful and full breasts,

limbs radiant as semen, adorned with various ornaments, their hands and feet scented with fine perfumes, their hair as delicate and excellent as black bees, draped in red silks and bound with bracelets, jewels, pearls, and necklaces."
They produce the sounds of the five types of musical instruments—the clinking of the tips of balances, bracelets, and anklets.
"O son, take delight in these; do not long for the life of a renunciant."
The prince said:
Behold, father, whoever here would be attached to what is designated as "woman," would conceptualize it, or would be intoxicated by it, would become one who possesses the notion of a woman.
The king said:
What kind of perception do you have?
The prince said:
In this regard, I have a perverted perception.
The king said:
"My son, what kind of perverted perception do you have?"
The prince said:
"O Father, such is my perverted perception:

that this body, to which [the notion of 'I'] is attached, comes and goes, stands and sits, exerts itself and remains silent; wherein the external is empty, effortless, weak or strong, and like an illusion that deceives."
They declare that everything is indeed the dharmakāya.
King Śuddhodana said:
"My son, if you do not take delight in beauty, why do you take delight in this which is devoid of manliness? What kind of vision do you perceive?"
The prince said:
"Father, I perceive this drama of saṃsāra which, through the mechanical skill of its actors, produces the transformations of sensation;

the triple world is its stage, where beings enter the performance amidst various changes and associations, while the depth of the hundreds of afflictions is the excellence of the moisture of craving."
Thus, no prior limit is discerned; it is a mutual drama of sentient beings, characterized by deception, grasping, and destruction.

There is no being, nor any collection of beings, who has not been humiliated or deceived by conditioned phenomena, and likewise by those who are venerable. Therefore, my dear son, experience this with exaltation; having turned back from the drama of saṃsāra, I shall enter the city of the peace of nirvāṇa, where old age and death do not assail. I shall first seek out that very path which was sought by the Tathāgatas of the past.
It has been thoroughly sought after by the Arhats and the Perfectly Enlightened Ones.

The king said: "My son, this palace of yours is like the abode of the gods, prosperous and abundant; your inner apartments are likewise, and you yourself, my son, are handsome, endowed with the marks of a thousand merits. Why is it, my son, that you find no pleasure here, but instead desire only to go forth, abandoning the city and its towns? The prince replied:
With a mind terrified of the realms of existence, listen to me, my dear father, as to why I have no delight [in them].
Old age and disease are enemies, and death is the third; they crush me, and therefore I have no delight.
If eternal happiness were to belong to the self, or if the power of suffering did not exist for the self.
If this were not conditioned by formative factors,
then why would there be no delight for me?
The body is perceived as being like a basket,
and within the body, [the elements] are perceived as being like snakes.
Since the aggregates are perceived to be like enemies,
how could there be any delight in them for me?
If the body were not like a basket,
or if there were no snakes within it;
If the aggregates were not like enemies,
then why would there be no pleasure for me in them?
If... there were no production of suffering.
If birth, old age, and death did not exist,
then why would there not be delight in saṃsāra?
If he were not one whose dwelling is in the empty village,
and if he were not the slayer of passion;
If the realm of conditioned phenomena were not a commitment (samaya),
then why would I not find delight in it?
If this were not a goad for the disciple,
and if there were no fear of the royal family.
If there were no fear at all in the three realms of existence,
I would have no delight in my renunciation.
Then, when King Śuddhodana was unable by every possible means to turn the prince's mind away from his purpose, the king thought to himself:

"If I am unable to turn the prince's mind away by any other means, what if I were now to show the prince every single girl who exists in the city of Kapilavastu? Perhaps his mind might find delight in none of them."
The Bodhisattva addressed his father, saying, "I shall go out to the park grounds."
King Śuddhodana commanded his ministers.

"From the royal palace as far as the pleasure grove, prepare the area in between: sprinkle it with water, sweep it clean, spread out canopies, surround it with variegated cloths, hang bundles of silk ribbons and streamers, burn incense, and scatter loose flowers.
In various places, set up incense burners and garland displays, and station actors, dancers, athletes, wrestlers, musicians, and drummers."
"Present agreeable forms, sounds, and smells, and remove those that are disagreeable,
so that when the prince has gone out to the park grounds, he may not see anything unpleasant."

Thus, by the mere word of the king, the ministers prepared the road as commanded, from the royal palace as far as the prince’s park grounds; and men were stationed at various places so that nothing would appear before the prince— neither one who was decrepit, aged, or diseased, nor one who was blind, lame, leprous, afflicted with skin eruptions, or scabby.
Or one with eczema, or anyone else unpleasant, should stand before the prince as he was departing for the park.

Thus, as the prince was departing for the pleasure grove in a magnificent carriage adorned with the seven precious gems, accompanied by great royal majesty, great royal power, and great splendor, the king’s men went along on both the left and right, clearing the way so that the prince might not see anything unpleasant.

Thus, as the prince was departing from Kapilavastu for the pleasure grove— beholding pleasing forms, hearing pleasing sounds, smelling pleasing scents, receiving hundreds of thousands of salutations with joined palms on both his left and right sides, and receiving various showers of powdered incense— he was accompanied by Ghaṭikāra the potter, who had become a son of the Śuddhāvāsa devas.

Likewise, other sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host manifested before him an aged man— an old man, decrepit, advanced in years, having reached the end of his life’s journey, with white hair, a body covered in freckles, hunched like a roof-rafter, stooping forward, and leaning upon a staff for support.
Moving along on their limbs.
Having seen him, the Bodhisattva asked the charioteer:

"What is this man? Why is he so repulsive—worn out, aged, and decrepit; having reached the end of his journey through life, with white hair, a body covered in spots, broken, hunched like a roof-rafter, leaning forward, and walking while supporting himself on a staff, his limbs trembling?"
The charioteer said:
"Prince, what is the use of this question? This man is called 'old,' his body overcome by age.
Let us go to the pleasure grove; there, O divine prince, play, delight, and enjoy yourself with the five strands of sensual pleasure."
The prince said:
"O, tell me, charioteer, we too are subject to old age; we have not transcended the nature of aging.
Since old age is indeed perceived for one who is born, what pleasure can there be for a wise man in this?"
The prince said:
"Charioteer, turn back the chariot; enough of going to the park."
The prince, having turned back again, entered his home.
King Śuddhodana asked his ministers:
"O friend, why has the prince returned again and not gone out to the pleasure grove?"
The ministers said.
"O Great King, having seen an aged man, the prince went out and has not gone forth to the pleasure grove again."
The king thought: "May it not indeed come to pass exactly as the young man was prophesied by the seer Asita."
The king gave an instruction to the prince’s harem:
"Amuse the prince well, delight him, and entertain him with dances, songs, and instrumental music, so that the prince may find pleasure at home."
Just as it was in the world of the gods, so too did such musical performances take place within the prince’s inner apartments;
yet the prince’s mind found no pleasure in these concerts,
for he remembered only that aged man.
At another time, the prince said:
"I shall go out to the park grounds."
The king said:
"Provide pleasing forms and sounds so that the prince, when departing for the pleasure gardens, may not see anything unpleasant."

Thus, at the mere word of the king, the ministers had the road prepared as commanded from the royal palace all the way to the prince’s park grounds; and men were stationed in various places so that as he was departing for the park, no one aged would appear anywhere before him.

Or whether he be old, or diseased, or one-eyed, or lame, or a dwarf, or itchy, or scabby, or afflicted with eczema, or whatever else may be unpleasant— none such shall stand before the prince as he goes forth to the park grounds.

Thus, as the prince was departing for the park in a magnificent carriage adorned with the seven precious gems, accompanied by great royal majesty, great royal power, and great splendor, the king’s men went along, clearing the way to the left and right, so that the prince might not see anything unpleasant.

Thus, as the prince was departing from Kapilavastu for the pleasure grove— beholding pleasing forms, hearing pleasing sounds, smelling pleasing scents, receiving hundreds of thousands of salutations with joined palms from both the left and right, and receiving various showers of flowers— he was accompanied by Ghaṭikāra the potter.

Having become a son of the gods from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven, as well as other sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host, he manifested before him a diseased man with swollen hands and feet, a swollen face, a yellowish-pale complexion, suffering from dropsy with a stream of water flowing from his navel, being eaten by thousands of flies— an unsightly sight that inspired a sense of spiritual urgency.
Having seen him, the Bodhisattva asked the charioteer:

"O, tell me, charioteer, why is this man so repulsive— yellowish-pale in color, with swollen hands and feet, and with the color of his face broken, as thousands of flies devour him while a stream of excrement flows from his navel?"
The charioteer said:
"Prince, what is the use of this question? This man's body is overcome by disease; let us go to the park grounds, where Your Majesty may play, enjoy yourself, and take your pleasure."
The prince said:
"O charioteer, tell us: are we also subject to illness, have we not transcended the nature of being subject to illness?"

Where indeed birth is known to be followed by old age and sickness, what delight can there be for the wise man? It is the ruin of beauty, the crushing of strength, the destruction of all the senses, the source of sorrows, the cessation of pleasures, the treasury of mental afflictions, and the abode of diseases; it is that which drinks up the world and consumes the body.
Who would not tremble at a disease that seizes one?
The prince said:
"Charioteer, turn back the chariot; enough for me of going to the park."
The prince, however, turned back and entered his home.
King Śuddhodana questioned his ministers.
"O friend, why has the prince returned? Has he not gone out to the pleasure grove?"
The ministers said:
Your Majesty, having seen a sick man, the prince turned back and did not go out to the pleasure grove again.
It occurs to the king:
Do not think so; it will be exactly as the seer Asita prophesied concerning the prince.
The king sent word to the prince's harem.
"Play well with the prince, delight him, and entertain him with dances, songs, and instrumental music, so that the prince may find pleasure at home."
In this way, just as in the world of the gods, such musical performances were held in the prince’s inner apartments;
yet the prince’s mind did not take pleasure in those concerts, for he kept recollecting that very same man who was old and diseased.
At another time, the prince again asked his father:
"Father, I wish to go out to the park grounds for the sake of seeing [the sights]."
The king gave this command to his ministers:

"The prince shall go out to the park; therefore, have the park grounds adorned, prepare the road, and decorate the city, from the royal palace all the way to the prince’s park grounds, sprinkling and sweeping them clean."
"Spread out a canopy, encircle it with variegated cloth, hang bundles of silk ribbons and garlands, burn incense, and scatter loose flowers.
In various places, set up flower-machines, as well as actors, dancers, athletes, wrestlers, musicians, and drummers;
and present all manner of pleasing sights, sounds, and scents, so that when the prince goes forth to the park grounds, he perceives nothing [unpleasant]."
He might see something unpleasant: one who is aged, or diseased, or one-eyed, or lame, or afflicted with ringworm, or itchy, or scabby, or blind, or sickly.
Act in such a way that the prince may not see anything unpleasant.

At the mere word of the king, the ministers carried out his instructions; men were stationed on the left and right to clear the way for the people, so that as the prince was departing for the park grounds,
he might not see anything unpleasant.

Thus the prince, in a vehicle variegated with the seven jewels, with a canopy spread above, with bundles of hanging silk streamers, covered with a golden net, adorned with victory banners, accompanied by the sound of joyful drums, with hooves like coral, and with flags and pennants raised high— attended by his ministers and retinue,
with great royal majesty, great royal power, great splendor, and a great assembly on both sides.
Receiving hundreds of thousands of salutations with joined palms from both left and right, he departed from Kapilavastu for the pleasure grove.
Then Ghaṭikāra the potter, who had become a son of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, along with other sons of the Śuddhāvāsa gods,
conjured a dead man before the prince, placed upon a bier, and being carried away by men.
With kinsmen whose throats were choked with tears, their faces weeping, their hair disheveled, beating their breasts and uttering lamentations.
Having seen it, the prince asked the charioteer.
"O, tell me, charioteer, what is this? Why is this man being carried on a litter by his kinsmen, who have tearful throats, weeping faces, disheveled hair, and are beating their breasts?"
The charioteer said:
"Prince, this man has died; his kinsmen, with tearful throats, weeping faces, disheveled hair, and beating their breasts, have placed him upon a bier and are carrying him to the cemetery."
"O, tell me, charioteer, does this man see his father or mother, or brother or sister, or kinsmen, friends, or blood relations, or the wondrous Jambudvīpa once again?"
The charioteer said:
"Indeed, Prince, this man shall no longer see his mother, nor his father, nor his brother, nor his sister, nor his friends, kinsmen, or blood relations, nor the wondrous Jambudvīpa. The prince said:
"The prince said: [he repeated the same].
Death is equal for both you and me; it is neither enemy nor friend, but like the changing of the seasons—difficult to conquer and difficult to restrain.
He takes no account of the noble, nor the lowly, nor those who have protectors;
like the sun, he proceeds fearlessly along this path.
The charioteer said:
Ask her about the fulfillment of desires, royal fortune, pleasure, and glory— her who is the foremost in all the worlds.
What is this terrible thing for you, the root of the torment of disease— that death which, when seen, brings destruction to men?
The Bodhisattva said:
He who, upon seeing the decrepit, the diseased, and the dead, does not feel revulsion for this cycle of existence—
that dull-witted man is to be pitied, like a blind man who has lost his way on a road.
The prince said: "O driver, we too are subject to death; we have not transcended the nature of mortality.
Since for one who is born, illness is known to occur and death is known to occur, what pleasure can there be for a wise man in this?
Turn back my chariot from going to the pleasure grove."
Then the prince, having thus turned back, went home once again.
King Śuddhodana asked his ministers:
"Why has the prince been turned back again; why has he not gone out to the pleasure gardens?"
The ministers said:

"Your Majesty, the prince saw a dead man being placed upon a bier and carried to the cemetery by his kinsmen, who— with tearful throats, weeping faces, disheveled hair, and chests heaving with grief— were crying out in piteous tones. Upon seeing this, a sense of spiritual urgency arose within him."
He then turned back from that very place.
This thought occurred to King Śuddhodana:
"Let it not be that the word of truth spoken by those Brahmins who are experts in omens— who said, 'The prince will go forth into the religious life'— should prove false."
Then the king sent a messenger to the prince’s harem, saying:
"O eunuchs and chamberlains, entertain the prince well with dance, song, and instrumental music, so that the prince may be delighted."

Then those women of the harem delighted the prince thoroughly with dances, songs, and instrumental music; yet the prince’s heart or mind was not there, for he remembered nothing other than those who were aged, afflicted, and dead.
At another time, the prince again asked his father:
"Father, I shall go out to the park grounds to see them."
The king said:
O Prince, do as you deem timely.
The king commanded his ministers:

"Have the grounds of the pleasure garden adorned like the Nandana grove of the King of the Gods; and have the city decorated as well, from the royal palace all the way to the prince's pleasure garden, sprinkled and swept, and provided with spread canopies."

Have it prepared with variegated cloth draped around it, hung with bundles of silk ribbons and garlands, perfumed with incense, and strewn with loose flowers; and in various places, set up flower-machines and incense-machines, and have actors, dancers, athletes, wrestlers, musicians, and drummers attend to it,
providing delightful forms, sounds, and scents so that when the prince goes out from Kapilavastu to the park grounds, [he may enjoy them].

May you not see anything unpleasant—whether one who is aged, diseased, or dead; or one who is blind, one-eyed, lame, afflicted with ringworm, itchy, scabby, or suffering from eczema; act in such a way.

As soon as the ministers were commanded, everything was prepared exactly according to the king’s instructions; and men were stationed in various places so that the prince, while departing from Kapilavastu for the pleasure grove, would not see anything unpleasant.

Then the prince, accompanied by his ministers and retinue, set out in a chariot variegated with the seven precious gems, covered with a golden lattice, well-adorned, beautifully decorated, equipped with victory banners, making a joyful sound, with hooves like coral, and with flags and pennants raised high; he did so with great royal majesty, great royal power, great array, and great prosperity.
For the sake of adornment, he departed from Kapilavastu for the pleasure grove.

As he was departing, Ghaṭikāra the potter—who had become a son of the gods in the Śuddhāvāsa heaven—along with other sons of the gods from the Śuddhāvāsa realm, manifested before the prince a renunciant clad in saffron robes, whose faculties were tranquil, who was perfect in his deportment, and who looked only a yoke’s length ahead. On that royal road of Kapila, amidst thousands of people, the prince then saw this renunciant; having seen him, his mind became serene once more.
Oh, the wisdom of the one who has gone forth!
Seeing him gone forth, the prince asked:
"Noble one, for what purpose has he gone forth?"
The renunciant said:
Young man, he has gone forth for the sake of self-taming, tranquility, and final nirvana.
Having heard those words of the one who had gone forth, the prince became filled with joy.
The prince said:
Truly, one who has gone forth is preeminent by virtue of wearing the excellence of saffron-dyed robes; he stands apart from the throngs of people on the royal highway,
his body covered with much dust and pollen like a solitary cakravāka bird in a forest of reeds.
Mṛgī, the Śākya maiden and mother of Ānanda, saw the prince departing from Kapilavastu with such splendor and such adornment; she praised the prince with these verses:
Truly, your mother and father have attained nirvana; furthermore, they are at peace. Moreover, that woman who shall become your wife has also attained nirvana.
Upon hearing the word "nirvāṇa," the mind of the bodhisattva becomes serene toward nirvāṇa itself; it remains there and leaps forward into it.
Having heard the sound of nirvāṇa, one directs the ear toward nirvāṇa;
having seen the unsurpassed nirvāṇa, one meditates on that which is free from fear from any quarter.
While the Prince was meditating on that Nirvana, he neither looked at nor spoke to the Śākya maiden Mṛgī.
Then, dejection arose within that Śākya maiden, Mṛgī.
"In the midst of such a great multitude of people, I have praised the prince, yet he has not even looked at me."
King Śuddhodana had a gate named Ṣaḍvālaka constructed for the prince, which was opened by five hundred men.
As he was being unrobed, the sound went forth for a yojana in every direction.
Five hundred kings stood surrounding the city.
The king had the vessels for the consecration prepared,
intending to consecrate the prince under the Puṣya constellation.
The Bodhisattva also thought thus:
"They shall go forth under the Puṣya constellation."
The Śuddhāvāsa gods said to the Bodhisattva:

At the right time, O Great Being, you descended from the Tuṣita realm; at the right time, you entered your mother’s womb; at the right time, you were born; and it is the right time for you to go forth.
You are endowed with the excellence of the right time, O Great Being, and many people long for you, just as farmers long for a great rain-cloud when they have examined the water.
The divine son Īśvara spoke this verse:
Reflect correctly; thus do the wise Bodhisattvas reflect:
"Roots of virtue have arisen in you, since you reflect with such wisdom."
Maheśvara spoke this verse:
Go forth, O Great Hero; go forth, O Great Sage!
For the sake of the entire world, awaken to the deathless state.
Mahābrahmā said:

"If, Great Being, you do not go forth today, on the seventh day seven treasures will appear, and you will become a universal monarch (cakravartin), a conqueror of the four continents, righteous, a king of Dharma, endowed with the seven treasures. From the sky these seven treasures made of precious gems will appear, namely: the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure."
In this way, the seventh [month] shall be fulfilled; you will have a full thousand sons who are heroic, brave, possessed of excellent physical forms, crushers of enemy armies, and preeminent.

Thus, having completely conquered these four great continents— namely Jambudvīpa, Pūrvavideha, Aparagodānīya, and Uttarakuru— bounded by the oceans and mountains, making them whole, free from thorns, without punishment, without weapons, and without oppression, you shall dwell there through the Dharma.
Rāhula, having descended from the Tuṣita heaven, entered his mother’s womb at the hour of midnight.

The Bodhisattva, having awakened, saw the inner apartments fast asleep: one woman was embracing a lute, another a flute, another a *nakula*, another a *sughoṣa*, another a *tūṇaka*, another a *caṇḍīsaka*, another a *saṃbhārikā*, another a *mahatī*, another a *vipañcikā*, another a *ḍhakkapaṭaha*, another a *vallakī*, and another a *mṛdaṅga*.
One [girl] [embraced] Mukunda; one [played] a *paṇava* drum; one [played] a *jharjharaka* drum; one [embraced] an *āliṅga* drum; one [played] a *parivādinī* lute;

one placed her hand on his neck; one placed a *mṛdaṅga* drum upon her head; one placed her head in another's lap; one placed her arm upon another's shoulder; one embraced another; and one [did so] from the left and right.
The limbs of some were disheveled, and saliva flowed from their mouths.
When the Bodhisattva had thus seen the women of the harem as they truly were, according to their nature, the perception of a cemetery arose within him regarding that harem.
The Bodhisattva, having risen from his cross-legged posture, took fine Kāśika garments from a casket and had his attendant Chandaka dress him in them.
"Chandaka, bring me the horse Kaṇṭhaka."
Chandaka said:
"Prince, it is the hour of midnight; why is there a need for horses at such a time and place?"
This residence is like the palace of Vaiśravaṇa; take your delight here—what need have you for horses at this time and place?
This inner harem is like a host of apsarases; take your delight here—what need have you for horses?
Thus Chanda now addressed him in many ways: "Prince, this is not the time for horses; Prince, it is the time for beds worthy of a king. This is the time for sleep; what need is there for horses now?"
The prince said:
"Chandaka, now bring me the horse; present Kaṇṭhaka to me."
Chandaka thought: "Just as the prince has [prepared] Kaṇṭhaka at this time and place while the people are sleeping soundly, surely the prince desires to go forth."
Then, as he was saddling Kaṇṭhaka, he let out a cry at a loud voice so that the king and all the people in Kapilavastu might wake up;
yet, because of Chandaka’s voice, no one there woke up,
for the gods had cast a veil over all the people, both those within and those without.
As Kaṇṭhaka was being led toward the Bodhisattva, he let out a loud neigh; yet by the sound of that neighing,
King Śuddhodana did not wake, nor did the multitude of people, for although the sound reached a full yojana in every direction, no one was awakened.
Thousands of millions of deities gathered at Kapilavastu, bringing perfumes and garlands for the purpose of honoring the Bodhisattva as he was departing.
The Bodhisattva, mounted upon Kaṇṭhaka, the king of horses, was showered with a rain of flowers by thousands of gods who had ascended into the sky:
*maṇḍārava*, *mahāmaṇḍārava*, *karkārava*, *mahākarkārava*, *rocamāna*, *mahārocamāna*,
*mañjūṣaka*, *mahāmañjūṣaka*, *bhīṣma*, *mahābhīṣma*, *samantagandha*, and *mahāsamantagandha*.
There were divine *pārijātaka* flowers, divine golden flowers, divine silver flowers, and divine jewel-flowers;
there was divine sandalwood powder, divine aloe-wood powder, divine saffron powder, and divine *tamāla* leaf powder;
and divine, cool perfumed water rose knee-deep for sixty *yojanas* all around Kapilavastu.

A divine mass of flowers fell from all sides for sixty *yojanas*, and the ground became covered with mud made of divine scented water; thousands of millions of billions of divine sounds resounded, celestial music was performed, and thousands of *apsarases* raised their voices in song.
And they sang; the Four Great Kings took hold of Kaṇṭhaka’s hooves.
If Pelavaka, who follows Kaṇṭhaka’s birth and runs by his ear, has not emerged with equal speed, then I am no [true] horseman.
A yakṣa named Supratiṣṭhita, born at the same time as Chandaka, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred,
opened the gate of Ṣaḍvālaka and suppressed the noise.
Then the Bodhisattva, having abandoned a great body of elephants, went forth from home into the homeless state;

having abandoned a great body of infantry, having abandoned a great mass of wealth, having abandoned great sovereignty, and having abandoned a great circle of kinsmen, he went forth from home into the homeless state.
A Bodhisattva, weary of birth, goes forth from home into the homeless state for the sake of attaining the path that transcends birth;

leaving behind a great body of horses and foot-soldiers, leaving behind a great body of chariots, leaving behind a great body of infantry, leaving behind a great mass of wealth, leaving behind great sovereignty, and leaving behind a great circle of kinsmen.
Having abandoned the household life, he goes forth into the homeless state.
The Bodhisattva, being distressed by birth and distressed by death, goes forth from the home to the homeless life for the sake of attaining the path that transcends death.
Afflicted by sorrows and afflicted by anxieties, he goes forth from the home to the homeless life for the purpose of attaining the path that transcends anxiety.
Furthermore, monks, it was not because he was worn out by old age that the Bodhisattva went forth from the home life into homelessness;
rather, monks, it was while endowed with the very highest prime of youth that the Bodhisattva went forth from the home life into homelessness.
"Monks, it was not because he was worn out by the affliction of disease that the Bodhisattva went forth from the home life into homelessness.
Rather, monks, it was while endowed with the foremost and supreme health that the Bodhisattva went forth from the home life into homelessness."
"Furthermore, monks, it was not because of the loss of wealth that he went forth from home into the homeless state.
Rather, monks, the Bodhisattva went forth from home into the homeless state after having abandoned a vast mass of wealth."
Furthermore, monks, it was not because of the loss of his kinsmen that the Bodhisattva went forth from home into the homeless state;
rather, monks, it was after abandoning his great circle of kinsmen that the Bodhisattva went forth from home into the homeless state.

The mountains shook, the waters surged, and the ocean, though immeasurable, was stirred; and the gods scattered divine sandalwood powder, divine aloe-wood powder, divine kesara powder, divine tamāla-leaf powder, and divine rains of loose flowers.

This great earth shook, trembled, and quaked violently in six ways through the very power of the Bodhisattva; and there appeared in the world an immeasurable, sublime, and vast radiance. Even those intermediate spaces between worlds—regions of darkness plunged in darkness, of gloom plunged in gloom, desolate and never before perceived—were illuminated.

Where even these very moon and sun, possessing such great supernatural power and such great majesty, do not overcome one another with their radiance, nor pervade one another with their light— even those regions were suffused by that illumination; and the beings who had been reborn there also recognized one another.
"Indeed, O sir, other beings have also been born here;
moreover, at that very moment, at that very instant, all beings became endowed with absolute happiness."
Even those who had been reborn there in the great Avīci hell, having surpassed the divine power of the gods, the power of the nāgas, and the power of the yakṣas,
found that the palaces of Māra had become gloomy, lusterless, devoid of splendor, and joyless.

In this place, fragments fell for the distance of one *krośa*; in this place, fragments fell for the distance of two *krośas*; in this place, fragments fell for the distance of three *krośas*; and in this place, fragments fell for the distance of a full *yojana*.
Even the tops of banners fell down here.
And Māra the Evil One became sorrowful, dejected, remorseful, and consumed by the burning pain of a thorn lodged within.
Furthermore, monks, when the Bodhisattva was departing, the eastern direction became exceedingly pure and clear;
the southern direction became exceedingly pure and clear;
and the western direction became exceedingly pure and clear.
The northern direction became exceedingly pure and radiant;
the downward direction and the upward direction likewise became exceedingly pure and radiant.

The risings of the moon and sun became exceedingly pure and bright; the journeys on the paths became exceedingly pure and bright; the floods became exceedingly pure and bright; the constellations became exceedingly pure and bright;
and the forms of the stars became exceedingly pure and bright.
The abodes of the gods of the Four Great Kings became exceedingly pure and radiant;
the abodes of the gods of the Thirty-three, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, the Nirmāṇarati, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods also became exceedingly pure and radiant.
The abodes of Māra became exceedingly gloomy;

the tops of the banners of the gods belonging to Māra’s host became discolored and lusterless; and Māra the Evil One was sorrowful, dejected, and full of remorse, his complexion darkened, born of an internal sting and a burning fever.
The abodes of the Brahmakāyika gods became completely pure and utterly radiant;
the abodes of the Śuddhāvāsa gods became completely pure and utterly radiant.

Likewise, within those Śuddhāvāsa heavens, the walking-places, sitting-places, and sleeping-places empowered by the Perfectly Awakened Ones of Limited Radiance (Parīttābha) also became exceedingly pure.
completely purified.
The Śuddhāvāsa gods became exceedingly joyful, exultant, delighted, and filled with gladness and cheerfulness.
Furthermore, monks, when the Bodhisattva was going forth, as many lords of the nāgas and nāga kings— whether born from eggs, from a womb, from moisture, or by spontaneous birth— as there were,
having conjured up a great fourfold army and having conjured up a vast body of elephants, a body of horses, a body of chariots, and a body of infantry, escorted the Bodhisattva alone from his home.
To go forth into the homeless life.
Furthermore, monks, when the Bodhisattva was going forth, all those who were lords of gold and kings of gold—
whether born from eggs, born from a womb, born from moisture, or of miraculous birth— they manifested a great fourfold army;
having manifested a vast body of elephants, a body of horses, a body of chariots, and a body of infantry, they placed the Bodhisattva at their head.
The city deity, standing before the Bodhisattva as he was departing, spoke with a dejected mind:
O Naga, O Naga, look upon me; O Simha, O Simha, look upon me.
O Essence of Beings, look upon me;
O Caravan Leader, look upon me.
Having departed from the city named Kapila and gazed back at that excellent city, the lion among men, who brings joy to the Śākya clan, uttered these words:
I would rather fall into hell and eat poison as my food.
But not again, having entered here, without reaching the further shore of old age and death.
This, monks, is the perfection of the Bodhisattva’s Great Departure.

The Bodhisattva, escorted by thousands of gods and the four Great Kings, was led twelve yojanas south from Kapilavastu to a town called Anomiya in the realm of the Mallas, not far from the hermitage of the seer Vasiṣṭha.
There the Bodhisattva remained, as did Chandaka.
The Bodhisattva gave the ornaments and the horse Kaṇṭhaka into the hands of Chandaka,
and he sent a message to his father Śuddhodana, to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, and to all his circle of kinsmen.
