"O Kauśalya, you speak skillfully; having accomplished my purpose, I shall return once the excellent Wheel of Dharma has been set in motion."
Chandaka said:
May you have no longing for mother or father.
The Bodhisattva said: "Chandaka, it is for this very purpose that I perceive your fault; for the sake of liberation, I abandon my kinsmen with a mind set on release."
How could one who has been born experience separation from beloved kinsmen once again in this cycle of rebirth?
If death had not occurred, nor sickness, old age, and the like;
and if there were neither the abandonment of the beloved nor the encounter with the unpleasant.
And if hope were not fruitless, and if happiness were not fickle, then this delight in various sense-objects here among humans might indeed exist.
Chandaka said:
"Noble son, it was prophesied by those skilled in all the treatises that you would become a traveler through the four continents;
that is not true."
The Bodhisattva said:
"O, tell me, Chandaka, what else was said by those skilled fortune-tellers?"
The time for truth is indeed at hand, if you have any regard for me.
Chandaka said:
This I declare:
or else, having abandoned the earth, he goes forth as a wanderer and becomes a destroyer of the passion for existence, seeing everything without exception; this is the second [verse].
This thought occurred to the Bodhisattva:
"How can there be both the going forth and the tonsure?"

The Bodhisattva cut off his topknot with a sword-blade, and that topknot was received by Śakra, the lord of the gods, and is worshipped in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven; furthermore, the festival of the topknot is celebrated there.
Kaṇṭhaka licked the Bodhisattva’s feet equally on all sides;
the Bodhisattva, however, departed without looking back.
I shall proclaim the going forth, just as the One with Vision went forth.
Seeing him decayed and deceased, the sage attained a sense of spiritual urgency.
Having attained a sense of spiritual urgency through proper reflection, he is one of great wisdom and profound insight.
Having seen the peril in the world, he went forth into the homeless life.
Having abandoned his mother and father, as well as his circle of kinsmen.
Having mounted the horse Kaṇṭhaka, you departed from Kapilavastu.
Having abandoned Aśvajit and Chandaka, and having severed the bonds of home and kin, [he departed].
Having relinquished all this, one should proceed indeed without regard for anything.

Now, after the Bodhisattva had gone forth from the city of Anomiya, Chandaka was sent back not far from the hermitage of the seer Vaśiṣṭha; there he returned the ornaments and the horse Kaṇṭhaka, and conveyed greetings of well-being to King Śuddhodana, to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, and likewise to his other kinsmen.
He did not send word to Yaśodharā.
When the Blessed One had set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dharma, the monks heard of it;
the monks then said to the Blessed One:
How was it that you departed without regard for Yaśodharā?
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it was not only now that I departed without regard for Yaśodharā; on another occasion as well, I departed without regard for her."
The monks said.
On another occasion as well, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
On another occasion also, monks.

Once upon a time, monks, in the past, in the northern region there was a city named Takṣaśilā. There, a son of a guild-leader named Vajrasena was traveling from Takṣaśilā to Vārāṇasī with horse-merchandise for the purpose of trading in horses.
Now, as he was traveling, another caravan at Vārāṇasī was plundered by bandits;
the merchants were slaughtered and scattered, and all the horses were carried off.
Then that caravan leader, having covered himself with the corpse of a dead man, lay down; thus he was not killed.
When those thieves had killed and struck down that caravan leader and taken his goods and departed, then Vajrasena, the horse merchant, having entered the city of Vārāṇasī by mistaking it for water,
lay down in an empty house.
On that very night, thieves broke into the royal palace in the city of Vārāṇasī and carried off a great deal of wealth.
When the night had turned to dawn, the breach in the royal palace was discovered by the ministers.
They informed the king.
"Your Majesty, the alliance within the royal family has been severed."
They were commanded by the king.
Examine the royal palace.
While the ministers were conducting an investigation, they saw that a great deal of property had been stolen.
They informed the king.
"Your Majesty, a great deal of property has been taken from the royal household."
The king commanded his ministers.
Search for that thief.
By the king's command, the thieves were pursued throughout Vārāṇasī at that very moment; all houses were searched, as were the temples and empty dwellings.
Those royal officers, searching for him, entered an empty house where Vajrasena, the horse-dealer, lay struck down by the thieves.
Now, exhausted by the fatigue of the journey, by staying awake through the night, and by anxiety, he fell fast asleep and did not wake even when the sun had risen.

While those royal officers were searching for the thieves, they saw him lying there with his body and clothes drenched in blood, yet still in possession of his goods; and upon seeing him, this thought occurred to those royal officers:
This man is a thief, a plunderer of the royal palace.
Then, struck by a kick from the king’s servant, he was raised up [and told]:
"Arise, you wicked thief! Is it truly the case that you are plundering the royal palace?"
Then that horse-dealer, frightened and terrified, rose up and thought, "What is this?"
Then those royal messengers said:
You are indeed a wicked thief by name, for you even assault the royal palace!
Then he said:
"Noble ladies, be gracious; I am no thief, I am a horse-dealer."
Then those royal messengers said:
Such is a horse-dealer as you are—a wicked thief you are!
Having been bound by them with his arms behind his back while he was still crying out, he was presented to the king.
"Thus, Your Majesty, while lying in an empty house, he was found."
The king was also fierce and of harsh commands;
he gave this order.
"Go, take him to the Atimuktaka cemetery and impale him alive on a stake."
Then, with his arms bound behind his back, drinking from a vessel of clay, his neck encircled by the garland of a condemned man,

and accompanied by the harsh-sounding drum being beaten, surrounded by thousands of people and executioners bearing swords, spears, and lances, he was led out to the Atimuktaka cemetery; and having reached the street of the courtesans, he arrived there.

And there was a chief courtesan named Śyāmā, who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and a vast treasury, with abundant gold, silver, and utensils, and many female and male slaves, laborers, and servants.
Then, as that caravan leader was being led to his execution, he was seen by Śyāmā, the chief courtesan;
at the mere sight of him, love for that caravan leader descended upon the courtesan.
As it was said by the Blessed One:
Either through former habitual tendencies or through benefit in the present.
In this way, love is born, just as a lotus arises in water.
Through living together, through dwelling together, through being observed, and through smiling.
In this way, affection arises among humans and among wild animals.
Wherein the mind enters or the consciousness becomes serene.
A wise person should go everywhere; indeed, there may be familiarity in the city.
Now, that courtesan had been bound by affection for that horse-dealer through thousands of lifetimes;
thus, an exceedingly great love for him arose within her.
Then this thought occurred to her:
"If I do not obtain this man, I shall die."
Then, at that very moment, she said to her maidservant:
"Go to such-and-such a place and, in my name, say this to the executioners: 'I will give you this much gold and bullion; do not kill this man.
Another man will come who is of the same complexion and appearance as he; seize him and kill him.'"
And so you speak; [yet] the second does not know.
Then that maidservant went and reported to those assassins exactly as she had been instructed.
Her executioners said to her:
"Very well, let it be so."
Now they go toward the needle of the end-maker.
Now, in that family of courtesans, the merchant’s only son had entered into a twelve-year contract; ten years have passed and two years remain.
As it has been said:
A hundred [is the lifespan] of Kṣatriyas; for Brāhmaṇas, it is two hundred.
A thousand are the illusions of kings, but the illusion of women is indeed endless.
Then that courtesan Śyāmā cleared away the food and the side dishes from before the merchant’s son.
The merchant’s son asked:
What will become of me in this situation?
She said:
"Noble son, upon seeing that man who was to be executed, compassion arose in me,
and this thought occurred to me:"
I myself shall take this food.
The merchant’s son said:
Do not go yourself; send a maidservant instead.
She said.
"Who knows whether she will give or not? Perhaps the maidservant will not give;
I shall go and fetch it myself and give it."
Then that merchant’s son said: "Bring me; I will go myself. Do not go yourself."
Then she displayed even greater illusion and said:
"No, let my noble son not go; I shall go."
The merchant’s son also said:
Do not go; I shall go.
The courtesan said:
"Let it be as the noble son intends; either I shall go, or the noble son himself."
Then that merchant’s son took that food and set out.
Then that courtesan spoke to her maidservant.
"Go; when this merchant's son has been killed, then bring that man secretly so that no one may see him, until the sun sets."

The entire multitude of people had turned back, and those executioners had reached the cremation ground; the merchant’s son arrived carrying that food. He offered that food to the man condemned to death.
Then, after those executioners had killed the merchant’s son, they released the horse-dealer.
Thus, he was now introduced secretly by that maidservant into the courtesan's household.
Then, at that very moment, the horse-dealer was raised up, bathed, dressed in costly garments, seated upon a magnificent couch, and provided with perfumes, garlands, and food;
he was thus endowed with and fully possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure.
Both play, delight, and take pleasure together.
Now, that first son of the guild-president was ten years old when he was executed;
even then, for two years, all his requisites were brought from the presence of his parents.
Then that horse-dealer, seeing such a state of affairs, was overcome with grief and became pale of complexion;
he would not even eat the food set before him, thinking, "Lest I too be destroyed in this very same way as that former son of the merchant."
Then that courtesan questioned that horse-dealer.
"Noble son, it has been this long since you entered here, yet I do not see you joyful or elated.
What is your deficiency? What do you desire? For what is your longing? You shall obtain it."
Then the horse-dealer said:

That city of ours, Takṣaśilā, was adorned with parks and lotus ponds; there, people frequently went out on excursions to the parks for the sake of sport. I recall those parks, that pleasure in the parks, and the water-sports.
The courtesan said:

"Noble son, here in Vārāṇasī as well, there are gardens, lotus ponds, and groves endowed with flowers and fruits that are delightful; if it is your noble son's intention to go to a garden, let us go out to the park grounds for the sake of sport."
He said:
"Very well, we shall run."
Then that courtesan had a certain park grounds sprinkled and swept;
having placed that horse-dealer in a covered carriage and taking food, drink, perfumes, and garlands, she set out preceded by her maidservants.
Then Vajrasena, the merchant’s son, said to that courtesan:
Have this lotus pond enclosed with curtains; we shall play at water-sports in confidence so that no one sees us.
It occurred to that courtesan:
The noble son speaks well; we shall play there with confidence, and no one will recognize us.
Then that courtesan had the lotus pond covered with curtains;
they then played, sported, and dallied in the water, both groups together, numbering no more than two.
Then that horse-dealer thought:
"If I do not escape today, it will no longer be possible for me to escape."
He then placed the drink before her and made the courtesan drink it, thinking: "When she becomes intoxicated, I will then be able to escape."
The courtesan also looked at him with affection, thinking, "The noble son makes me drink.
Then, as she drank, she became intoxicated.
Then that horse-dealer said to those maidservants:
"Go, you stay by the goods; we, being confident, shall play in the water."
Then that maidservant sat down to one side at the base of the goods.
Then those two descended into the lotus pond to play in the water.
Then that horse-dealer, having embraced Śyāmā around the neck, turned her back; having held her back for a moment, he exerted himself.
Śyāmā knew, "The noble son is playing in the water.

Thus, by that horse-dealer Vajrasena, she was repeatedly and for a long time held back and restrained, while Śyāmā was tormented and Vajrasena, having submerged her there in the water, made her [exert herself] with little strength.
That which has arisen.
Vajrasena thought:
"This Śyāmā is dead; this is the time for my escape."
Having then recognized that Śyāmā was dead, he placed her on the steps of the lotus pond, looked here and there to ensure she was not seen by anyone, and fled.
It occurred to those maidservants:
"The noble son and the noble daughter are churning here in the lotus pond for the sake of sport, yet we do not hear any sound from them as they play; let us go and find out."
Having approached the lotus pond, they saw Śyāmā there in the pond, lying on the mud at the foot of the steps;
they somehow managed to revive her.
Then Śyāmā was made to hang upside down by those maidservants for a moment, and all the water came out of her mouth.
Then, when Śyāmā had recovered her breath, she asked the maidservants, "Where is the noble son?"
The maidservants said:
"Noble daughter, the noble son is certainly not to be seen anywhere; he must have fled."
She said:
Do not delay; we shall enter the city.
Then they entered the city.
Then, at that very moment, the courtesan Śyāmā, having summoned the Caṇḍālas, said:
"I shall give you this much and that much gold for your livelihood; I desire that a fresh corpse be brought here, one that has not been bitten by animals."
They said.
"Certainly, it shall be brought."
Having gone to the cremation ground, they bring back a recently deceased man who has not been bitten by any creature, so that he is seen by no one.
Then those caṇḍālas were dismissed after being provided with a means of livelihood.
Then Śyāmā, having bathed that dead man with scented water, anointed him with perfumes, wrapped him in robes worthy of an Arhat, placed him in a coffin, secured it firmly,
and spoke to those maidservants.
All of them, with one voice, wept and spoke thus: "The noble son has passed away! The noble son has passed away!"
Those maidservants wept exactly as they had been instructed by Śyāmā.
A great multitude of people, having heard the sound of weeping at the house of the courtesan Śyāmā, cried out, "The merchant's son has died!
His parents also heard that their only son, the merchant's son, had passed away.
Then, weeping, they went to that courtesan’s household along with their entire circle of kinsmen and the people from the street of courtesans.
They said.
Withdraw this army; let us behold our son for the last time.
Then it occurred to that courtesan:
"If they carry him away, then they will become wise; therefore, I shall cut them into pieces."
She said to them:
Do not carry off Camū.
They said:
What is the reason?
She said:

At the time when the noble son was ill, I said to him, "Noble son, go to the family of your mother and father. He then replied, "I have not gone for all these years; I will not go now. Once I have recovered my health, then I shall go to see my mother and father."
Now, when he no longer recovers and is seized by disease, I have been instructed by him: "Do not show me [the corpse] once I am dead, nor my parents, nor my kinsmen; do this much for me as a favor.
And I have made a vow to my noble husband: "Noble husband, I shall not show the corpse to anyone—not to my parents nor to my kinsmen."
"I would rather approach my own death than show myself before the body of the noble son.
Therefore, if you carry away the army in this manner, I shall approach my own death;
for such was the vow I made to the noble son at the time of his passing."
It occurs to the merchant:

"It is exactly as she says; for this reason, she was exceedingly dear and pleasing to my son, such that even at the time of death he did not abandon her. She too was devoted to my son’s welfare and desired his well-being. Furthermore, our deceased son cannot be recovered; this is the fact, even if we were to [recover] this son."
We do not find the dead; therefore, we shall withdraw the army.
The merchant ordered.
Do not take away the army; let it be as was the intention of my son at the time of his death.
Then, having been escorted out of the city with great honor, he was made to meditate in a secluded place.

Then that courtesan wept most piteously, grieved, lamented, and displayed many deceits; though being restrained, she ran toward the funeral pyre, desiring to throw herself into it, even as she was being held back by all the people from falling into the pyre.
Then this thought occurred to the parents of that merchant’s son:
"This courtesan Śyāmā was dear and beloved to our son, and our son was likewise dear and beloved to her. What if we were now to bring this Śyāmā into our home, so that she may see our son?"
Then that merchant, having obtained permission from the royal court, brought Śyāmā into his house.
Now, having removed her jewels and gold and wearing white garments, she sat there mourning Vajrasena, the horse-dealer, with her hair in a single braid.
And this thought occurred to the parents of the merchant’s son:
"She is the [wife] of our only son."
[_Mvu_2.175_] He grieves. Now that merchant, together with his wife, treats Śyāmā exactly as he would his own little son.
Once, some actors from Takṣaśilā arrived in Vārāṇasī;
then those young actors, seeking alms, entered that merchant’s house.
Then Śyāmā took up the dialect of the Northern Region (Uttarāpathaka) from those young actors;
she asked those young actors,
"Where are you from?"
They said:
We are people from the Northern Path.
She said:
From which basis?
They said:
From Takṣaśilā.
She said:
"Yonakas, do you recognize him? He is Vajrasena by name, the son of a guild-president in Takṣaśilā, and a merchant in horses."
The young actors said:
Yes, we recognize it.
She said:
Are you able to perform my task?
They said:
"Certainly, we are able; what should be done?"
She said:
Recite this verse in the presence of Vajrasena, the son of the guild-president.
You [beheld] Śyāmā, dressed in silk, amidst those blossoming *sāla* trees.
Pressing you firmly with her embrace, she asks after your welfare.
Then those young actors, having arrived at Takṣaśilā in due course, approached the horse-dealer Vajrasena and said:
You [behold] Śyāmā, clad in silken garments, amidst these blossoming *sāla* trees.
Pressing you firmly with her embrace, she asks after your welfare.
Then Vajrasena, the merchant’s son, having heard that verse, addressed the young actor with a stanza:
Overcome by passion, those who desire to repay a favor done for them do not sleep in peace.
Grateful men do not sleep in peace;
those addicted to enmity do not sleep in peace.
I do not believe that for you, even as the wind might blow away a mountain.
How could that mortal woman speak of my skill?
Then those young actors said:
That woman neither dies nor does she desire another;
wearing her hair in a single braid, the young girl desires only you.
Vajrasena, the son of the guild-president, said:
I am unacquainted with that which is long-acquainted;
one should certainly not construct the impermanent by means of the impermanent.
Even if I were to go much further from here,
she would not create another for me.
"O monks, it may be that you think thus: 'At that time, on that occasion, he who was the horse-dealer named Vajrasena was someone else.
It should not be viewed in this way.
And why is that?"
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, I was the horse-dealer named Vajrasena.
That courtesan named Śyāmā who lived in the city of Vārāṇasī at that time and on that occasion was not someone else;
it should not be viewed in this way. Why is that?
Monks, she who was the chief courtesan named Śyāmā in the city of Vārāṇasī at that time and on that occasion was this very Yaśodharā.
Even then I was indifferent toward her; even now I am indifferent toward her.
_____Thus concludes the Jātaka of Śyāmā.
Then the monks said:
The Blessed One was saved while being led to his execution by Yaśodharā;
Yaśodharā was of great service to the Blessed One as he wandered through saṃsāra when he was a bodhisattva.
The Blessed One said:
"Truly, monks, Yaśodharā was of great service to the Tathāgata as he wandered through saṃsāra.
On another occasion as well, I was protected from falling into the hands of my enemies by this very Yaśodharā."
The monks said.
At another time as well, Blessed One?
The Blessed One said:
On another occasion also, monks.

Long ago, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi, a king named Ugrasena reigned. He was one who had performed meritorious deeds, possessed great majesty, maintained his retinue well, was disposed toward giving and sharing, and possessed a vast treasury and a great number of mounts.

His kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, crowded with people, and filled with happy subjects; it was free from violence and civil unrest, thieves were effectively restrained, and it was perfected in its legal administration.

Now, in that country there lived a dragon king named Campaka, who had performed meritorious deeds, accumulated a vast store of wholesome roots, and was attended by a retinue of many hundreds of thousands of nāgas.

Now, the palace of that Naga king Campaka was like a celestial abode; it contained palaces made of the seven precious gems, with flowers and fruits of every kind available at all times, and lotus ponds made of jewels covered with blue, red, white, and yellow lotuses.
Not far from that lotus pond was a palace made of jewels with pillars of beryl, its floor paved with emerald.
And that king had a harem of sixteen thousand naga maidens.
Now, in that abode of the nāgas, he rejoices just like a king of the gods.
Now, on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the fortnight, he observed the *upoṣadha* three times each fortnight at the crossroads;
endowed with the eightfold [precepts], he dwelt with his body surrendered.
[ Mvu 2.178 ] Now, while that Nāga king had undertaken a fast at that crossroads of the four great roads, he was spotted by a snake-charmer.
That snake-charmer seized Campaka, the Nāga king, from that crossroads of the four great roads and placed him in a snake-basket.

Yet the Nāga king—possessing great power and great majesty—did not become angry with that snake-charmer, nor did he vanish; rather, he intended to reduce Vārāṇasī, along with its countryside, to ashes.
There, in that snake-basket, he remained guarding that herd.
That Naga king also explained the signs to his retinue: "If anyone should harm me while I am observing the fast here at this crossroads, then signs will appear in that Naga abode.

If the trees here in this Naga abode wither away, and these blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lotuses, water lilies, and fragrant lilies [wither], then you should know that the Naga king has been bound."
If all these trees were to have their leaves completely withered, and these lotus ponds were to become devoid of water, then you should know that the Naga king has been slain.
Then, while the nāga king Campaka was bound in a snake-basket by the snake-charmer, these omens appeared there in that abode of the nāgas.
Then those nāgas and nāga maidens, having seen those omens there in the nāga abode, all became anxious, thinking, "The nāga king is bound;
what will come of it?"
Each one individually was capable of liberating that nāga king from the hands of the snake-charmer, yet they did not devour that nāga king.
For this reason, the Naga King previously instructed his retinue:
"If anyone should seize or bind me while I am observing the fast, none of you should do anything unpleasant or harmful to him;
for this is my supreme vow."
Now, the chief queen of that Naga king [was the foremost] among sixteen thousand women...
And she, having gone to Vārāṇasī, reported the capture of the Naga king—along with its circumstances—to King Ugrasena, who was staying in his excellent upper palace.
King Ugrasena, having heard that praise of the virtues of the nāga king Campaka from the presence of that female nāga, became joyful.
The king said to that nāga maiden:
"Either sit down or go to your own abode until the messengers have searched for that Naga king and returned."
The nāginī said:
"Great King, having satisfied the snake-charmer with either a choice village or gold and bullion, release that Naga king; do not act by royal decree alone."
The king said:
"O Nāginī, let it be so; having satisfied the snake-charmer with either an excellent village or gold and bullion, I shall release the Nāga king named Campaka."
Then that Naga maiden spoke to Ugrasena, the King of Kashi.
"O Great King, King Campaka, together with sixteen thousand women, has gone for refuge to you."
Having spoken thus, that Naga maiden disappeared.
King Ugrasena dispatched messengers in all directions, saying:
"The Naga king Campaka, who was observing a fast, has been seized by a snake-charmer; bring him here!"
By the mind of the gods, by the speech of kings,
by the action of the wealthy, and by the labor of the poor.
At the mere word of King Ugrasena, royal messengers brought the snake-charmer together with the king of the nāgas.
The king, having gratified that snake-charmer, bestowed the excellent village, along with silver and gold, upon the nāga king Caṃpaka.
As soon as he was released, the Naga king Campaka became a domain of the king of the gods, and his naga abode became as it was before,
resembling a celestial palace; and when the retinue of that naga king saw their abode restored to its former state, they became joyful and satisfied.
The Naga king was liberated.
Then the Naga king sat on a single seat together with Ugrasena, the King of Kāśi.
He invited the King of Kāśi, saying, "Great King, I desire that you, together with your retinue, should visit my abode."
The king said:
"You nāgas are of fierce venom and prone to anger;
I am unable to go to the nāga abode."
The Naga king said to him:
"Great King, he who would do harm to one such as you, our former benefactor, would fall alive into the great hell with his very body;
even the earth, together with its moon and stars, might fall, and the rivers might flow upstream."
Indeed, I would not speak such a falsehood, nor would I fail to recognize what has been done for you.
The king said:
"Let it be as the Naga King desires;
I shall see your abode."
King Ugrasena commanded his ministers:
"Prepare chariots, elephants, horses, and various vehicles; we shall go to see the palace of the Naga King."
At the mere word of the king, the ministers attended to him.
The king, together with his ministers, retinue, chariots, troops, and mounts, mounted the same vehicle as Campaka, the Naga king.

With great royal majesty and great royal power, amidst the shouts of "Hakkāra" and "Hikkāra," the sound of drums, kettledrums, and conchs, and accompanied by a vast multitude of people, he departed from the city of Vārāṇasī and proceeded toward the abode of Campaka, the Naga king.
Having traveled by vehicles as far as the ground permitted for vehicles, he and his retinue entered the abode of the nāga king Caṃpaka on foot.

Then he beheld that palace of the nāga king Campaka, which resembled the abode of the gods; it was adorned with thousands of trees laden with flowers and fruits, perfumed with various kinds of garlands, and graced by lotus ponds made of jewels, covered with blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lotuses, water lilies, white lotuses, and fragrant lilies, and variegated in many ways.
And with gabled halls made of jewels and palaces with pillars of beryl and floors spread with musāragalva stone.
There, the King of Kāśi was seated upon a jeweled couch by the Naga king Campaka.
Those sixteen thousand Naga maidens approached Caṃpaka, the Naga king, and asked:
"How was your dwelling among enemies? How were your hunger and thirst dispelled? And how did your liberation from there come about?"
The Naga king said:
I have obtained food and drink as was fitting, and I have been liberated by this King of Kāśī.
Then those sixteen thousand daughters of the nāga kings became joyful and satisfied with King Ugrasena, and they gave him five hundred loads of pearls mixed with beryl.
The Naga king Campaka beheld King Ugrasena’s palace in its every aspect, resembling the abode of the gods.
The royal palace was well protected; when a conflagration broke out, it was extinguished by the naga king Campaka.
Thus ends the section on the mental projections of the illustrious Campaka, the king of the nāgas. Now, who is it that shines like lightning in the lake, like stars?
Or like a copper-stemmed tree in full bloom within a forest.
You were born in the Nandana grove, born in the Citraratha forest.
Are you a goddess or a Gandharvī? For you are certainly not human.
The Naga maiden said:
I am not a goddess, nor a gandharvī, nor am I a human woman, O Great King.
"I am a Naga maiden; may it be well with you; I have come here from Avīci."
The king said:
Your mind is distracted by various objects and your senses are agitated; why is it that tears are flowing from your eyes?
For I have come here seeking something that has been lost; do not speak of it at length.
The nāga maiden said:
O Lord of Men, that which people call "a serpent" because of its fierce splendor, they also call "an elephant."
"O Lord, release my husband from his bonds while he still possesses his life, before anyone seizes him."
A nāga, being thus endowed with such power, could reduce even a city to ashes.
But this Naga, while requesting the Dharma,
has come into the state of being a hand for the mendicant.
The king said:
How may I recognize that one who has seized the naga, possessed of fierce splendor and endowed with strength and power?
Difficult to approach and difficult to withstand, the serpent has come into the hand of the beggar.
The Naga maiden said:
On the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day, the Naga king goes to the crossroads.
Wandering with his body cast off, the Naga may become the hand of a beggar.
Thus you should understand that he is like a captured elephant,
possessing fierce splendor and having attained strength and power.
Difficult to approach and difficult to withstand, the serpent has come into the hand of the beggar.
The king said:
"O Nāgī, sit down, or stand, or go for now to your own dwelling."
Meanwhile, the messengers went and searched for the illustrious king of the nāgas, saying, "Let him be brought here."
The Naga maiden said:
Release him according to the law, without violence, for a village, a gold coin, and a hundred cows.
Having relinquished his body and subdued the serpent,
may the Naga King, seeking merit, be released.
The king said:
I shall release you by means of dharma, without violence, for a village, a gold coin, or a hundred cows.
And having cast off his body, let the serpent depart;
let the Naga king attain joy.
The Nāginī said:
Sixteen thousand women were adorned with jeweled earrings.
O Noble One, we who dwell in this water-retreat house have come to you for refuge.
The royal messengers brought both the snake-charmer and the king of the nāgas.
King Ugrasena said:
She obtained fifty niṣkas and large jeweled earrings.
And four hundred couches, resembling flowers bound with garlands.
And let the Lord of Serpents release his consort, a goddess worthy of himself.
The snake-charmer said.
But without a gift, O lord of men, this righteous Naga king will not release him from his word.
He is of great majesty, a seer of the world beyond, and possessed of great power; he is not to be harmed.
The Naga Campaka, having been released, spoke to the King of Kāśi.
Homage to you, O King of the Kāśis; homage to you, O Increaser of the Kāśis.
I join my palms in reverence to you; O King, behold my dwelling.
"Where is my residence?
King Ugrasena said.
"O Naga, a most difficult task has been performed by me for you; you have been released from suffering and from bondage."
And having been born into the world, one does not know what has been done;
do not be distressed, O Naga, for I do not know what has been done.
The Naga king said:
May he live for a long time in hell as he pleases; may he not obtain even the slightest bodily well-being.
He who would harm a king who has performed good deeds in the past—
such as you, I do not know how he could have acted toward you.
The king said:
Indeed, you are my nagas— possessing sharp venom, noble, of great strength, and quick to anger.
I do not believe this;
you are not a human being who is angry with a human.
The Naga king said:
He shall fall into hell upon the surface of the iron spikes,
with his feet upward and his head downward.
He who oppressed King Pūrvakari—
such as I am— I do not know what was done for you by him.
Even the wind might blow away a mountain,
and even the moon and the sun might fall to the earth.
And all rivers would flow upstream;
yet, O King, I would never speak a falsehood.
The king said:
O Lord of Serpents, let it be exactly as the Naga King desires.
Just as you request, I shall show you your dwelling.
King Ugrasena said to his ministers:
May your most variegated royal chariots be yoked, and your excellent Kamboja horses be well-tamed.
And let the elephants be harnessed with golden parasols;
I shall behold the dwellings of the Nāgas.
The ministers said:
These variegated horse-chariots are yoked; they are drawn by excellent, well-trained Kamboja horses.
And let the elephant, equipped with golden parasols, go forth with great force, O lord of kings!
Then the king went forth, accompanied by his fourfold army.
Surrounded by friends and ministers, and preceded by his kinsmen.
Kettledrums, clay drums, tabors, conchs, and flutes were sounded for King Ugrasena.
The king goes forth with a great force,
placed in the midst of a multitude of women.
Having gone to the abode of the Naga king in Kāśī, the King [of Kāśī]...
He saw it like the celestial abode of the Naga king.
It was covered with mango and rose-apple trees and frequented by flocks of cuckoos.
The King of Kāśi went to the residence of the Naga king Addarśa.
On all sides, the forest thickets were in bloom throughout every season.
They waft a delightful fragrance throughout the abode of the Naga King.
Lotus ponds with stairways of gold and silver were manifested.
Covered with lotuses and water lilies, it is frequented by various birds.
The palaces have pillars of beryl and floors spread with musāragalva.
The King of Kāśi went to the residence of the Naga king Addarśa.
Having entered the abode of the Naga king, the King of Kashi [proceeded].
He sat down upon a beautiful couch made of gold.
And having seen that Naga king Campaka arrive.
And together with the King of Kāśi, they bowed with palms joined in reverence.
The Naga maiden asks: "When you were in the midst of enemies..."
Then, how shall I dispel my thirst and hunger there?
The Naga king said:
One obtains food and drink as is appropriate for the purpose of dispelling hunger and thirst.
And may this Kāśi king, my...
quickly be released from his bonds.
Then those sixteen thousand Naga maidens praised Ugrasena, the king of Kāśi.
Thus rejoice, O King of Kāśi; may it be well with you and your kinsmen.
Just as we rejoice today upon seeing the Lord of Nagas.
Thus, O King, rejoice together with all your kinsmen.
Just as we rejoice today, all together with our husband.
You indeed give five hundred pearl-adorned horses, set with beryl, to the king.
For in the inner apartments, the ground is strewn with carpets, free from mire, radiant, and shining like water.
Then the king, having seen that inner palace which was like a celestial chariot of the gods, beheld it as such.
Being attended by a multitude of women,
he governed the prosperous city of Kāśī.
King Ugrasena said:
Wearing a robe of fine cloth and a tunic, you dwell there with incomparable complexion.
O Naga, why do you wander upon the earth when you are endowed with divine pleasures?
The Naga king said:
Otherwise, there is no human being who would intentionally seek such a meeting with him even for a single day.
Desiring a human womb,
I am practicing asceticism for that purpose.
King Ugrasena reflects.
A male nāga and a female nāga were seen, both longing for human existence.
What auspicious deed shall I perform to completely transcend the lower realms?
The Blessed One, recollecting his former abodes and former births, [attained knowledge].
The Teacher related this Jātaka in the presence of the monks.
Those are the aggregates, those are the elements, and those are the sense-bases.
And concerning himself, the Blessed One explained that matter.
In this saṃsāra without beginning or end, where I formerly dwelt.
At that time, I was the Naga king Campaka, possessed of great supernatural power.
Yaśodharā is indeed a Naga maiden; thus should you remember this Jātaka.
Thus is this immeasurable, manifold suffering, the ancient course of life, high and low.
Free from fever, free from fear, and without sorrow,
he relates his own birth story in the midst of the community of monks.
The Blessed One said:
Even then, monks, when I had become a nāga and was bound by a snake-charmer for the sake of my flesh, I was released by Yaśodharā;
and even when I was born as a horse-dealer in Vārāṇasī, I was released.
Thus ends the Jātaka of the noble Campaka Nāga King.
When the Bodhisattva was departing, Chandaka was sent back from Anomiya; both Chandaka and Kaṇṭhaka returned to Kapilavastu.

When King Śuddhodana heard that Chandaka had arrived bringing Kaṇṭhaka, along with the parasol and the ornaments, he rushed out from the royal palace to the outer gate-hall together with his harem; Yaśodharā also, embracing Kaṇṭhaka by the neck and weeping aloud, said:

"Where has the prince Kaṇṭhaka been taken? What offense have I committed against you and Chandaka, that you have departed taking the prince while I was sleeping soundly, leaving me and the sixty thousand women of the inner court to become widows?"
Chandaka said:
"What offense have we committed that I too must cry out at such a loud voice?
When the prince was departing, Kaṇṭhaka made a loud sound of neighing, yet not one of you was awakened."
Thousands of millions of deities have assembled in the sky.
He was led to this wrestling ground, a settlement named Anomiya, not far from the hermitage of the seer Vasiṣṭha.

The prince, having given his Kāśika garments to the hunter, took the saffron robes for himself; he then cut off his own topknot with a sword-blade, and that topknot was received by Śakra, the king of the gods.
Then the prince gave her ornaments and sent her back,
instructing her thus: "Inquire after the welfare of my father, my maternal aunt, and the entire circle of my kinsmen."
Having accomplished my task and fulfilled my resolve, I shall return.
Yaśodharā, the sixty thousand women of the harem, and the entire Śākya kingdom, having wept and lamented, went each to their own dwellings.

Having brought Chandaka into the royal palace, excellent food, drink, and delicacies fit for a king were served to him. For Kaṇṭhaka as well, sweetmeats smeared with honey were presented, as well as other various kinds of food and delicacies fit for a king; these were piled up in heaps before Kaṇṭhaka, yet Kaṇṭhaka did not eat them.
Constantly recollecting the Bodhisattva, they shed tears at all times.

The women of the inner apartments wiped the tears from Kaṇṭhaka with fine silks, dukūla fabrics, and costly garments made of silk and wool—robes fit for a king; some wiped his head, others his neck, and others his back.
Some wipe away the shoulder; some wipe away the arm; some wipe away the joint;
some wipe away the hair of the head; some massage the feet; some place morsels smeared with honey into the mouth;
some place various kinds of snacks into the mouth; others place cakes into the mouth.
Others were partaking of sweetmeats, and drinks worthy of a king, served in vessels made of gold and silver and variegated with jewels, were being enjoyed; yet Kaṇṭhaka took no food.
Out of grief for the Bodhisattva, Kaṇṭhaka remained without food and passed away, not seeing the Bodhisattva.
When he had passed away, King Śuddhodana performed the funeral rites for his body with great royal magnificence.
Immediately after passing away, he was reborn among the Trāyastriṃśa gods, arising as the son of the divine son Śikhaṇḍin;
there he became a divine son named Kaṇṭhaka, possessed of great supernatural power and great majesty, who surpassed other thousands of previously reborn divine sons by means of ten divine qualities.
That is to say: with divine lifespan, divine complexion, divine happiness, divine sovereignty, divine retinue, and divine forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles.

When the Blessed One had set in motion the most excellent wheel of Dharma and his teaching had become widespread, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, while wandering on a tour among the gods, saw the divine son Kaṇṭhaka; having seen him, he addressed him with a verse:
Just as on the fifteenth day the moon, surrounded by the constellations,
illuminates all directions while the stars have vanished from the sky.
In this same way, this divine mansion of yours in the city of the gods is ablaze with color; you shine like the sun.
The ground is variegated and well-prepared with musāragalva, pearls, and red gems; moreover, no dust rises there.
Those palaces are delightful, with beautiful locations consisting of gabled chambers made of beryl, gold, crystal, and silver.
And not far from the palaces were well-constructed lotus ponds,
with steps made of lapis lazuli slabs and strewn with golden sand.
And on their banks grow well-formed trees with great,
lofty branches that rise up toward the city of Brahmā from the sky.
Stirred by the wind, they blow in all directions.
And upon their banks, well-grown trees with massive,
towering branches stand in full bloom, illuminating the four directions.
Proclaimed by the twice-born with melodious voices.
Covered with white lotuses, red lotuses, blue lotuses,
and flowers of various colors, the winds blow in every direction.
To each single musical instrument, sixty apsarases dance;
and as they dance, those divine maidens are in the grove.
A divine sound issued forth, like that from a host of young brahmin maidens,
as he sat upon a couch with golden legs fashioned of jewels.
When your conditioned existence has been well relinquished, you rejoice in a celestial body upon a couch fashioned of jewels with legs of gold.
Surveying all directions, you, Brahmā,
shine forth upon that couch spread with cotton down.
Adorned celestial maidens fan you with yak-tail whisks;
these hosts of apsarases, adorned with nets of gold, attend upon you.
Throwing out their arms, they dance and sing with beautiful instrumental accompaniment;
some apsarases there sing along and play musical instruments.
Some danced while beautiful music was played,
and others emitted lovely sounds from all their limbs.
From some of them, superhuman fragrances waft from every pore;
that residence of yours is endowed with celestial maidens who are more beautiful than Padumā.
"Ah, this palace is adorned with celestial nymphs and possesses the splendor of a golden casing!
What karma did you perform in previous births?"
By what root of merit are you reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven?
What action did you perform previously in a human existence,
and by what root of merit do you now experience this ripening?
By what means was this mastery over life, fame, strength, supernatural power, and retinue obtained by you, that you enjoy such superhuman excellence?
What auspicious deed did you perform in other births? By what wholesome action do you experience this ripening result?
By what holy life, by what self-restraint, and by what self-control,
and by what wholesome deed do you rejoice in the heavenly realm?
By what means has such radiant power and beauty been kindled in you? By what virtuous deed do you illuminate all directions?
"O son of the gods, being questioned, tell me: of what karma is this the fruit? Thus questioned by Maudgalyāyana himself, that son of the gods answered the question; so I have heard from the Elder.
I was in Kapilavastu, the supreme city of the Śākyas,
which was constructed with watchtowers and bastions, and possessed strong walls and gateways.
In the residence of the Śākya chief, which had archways with lion-head spouts, sturdy bolts, doors, and gate-towers, and which was frequented by horses, elephants, and chariots.
In the city, well-constructed and crowded with people,
there was a horse named Kaṇṭhaka, born at the same time as the son of Śuddhodana.
And when that supreme among men went forth into the homeless life,
he then spoke these words, uttering many truths.
Having heard those words together with her speech, with a heart born of joy and impelled by fervor,
I would pay homage and carry the Supreme among Men.
Having gone to the realm of others when the sun had risen,
he departed without looking back, leaving behind my desire and Chanda.
Licking with my tongue his feet, which have copper-colored nails,
I shall gaze up with tears at that Supreme Person as he departs.
Through not seeing that very glorious son of the Śākyas,
the affliction of a hoof-wound shall arise, and then I shall pass away.
By his very power, I dwell in this celestial palace,
a most excellent gabled chamber filled with throngs of the finest women.
"If you go, venerable sir, to the presence of the Lion of the Śākyas,
Kaṇṭhaka shall speak these words to the Supreme among Men:
'And I too shall come to pay homage to the Supreme among Men.'"
Truly auspicious is the sight of such great seers;
by that [favor] I have obtained this longevity, beauty, fame, and strength,
and I enjoy superhuman supernatural power and retinue.
Through this celibate life, through self-restraint and self-control,
such superhuman psychic power has arisen in me, which is irreversible.
Having performed that wholesome deed which was accumulated in the past,
I am now experiencing the ripening of that wholesome karma.
Whatever enjoyments have arisen for me that are dear to my mind,
even the gods pay homage to me, and I am honored by them.
In such a one worthy of offerings, you should set your mind upon faith.
He sees the auspicious karma accumulated by him while he was a yakṣa.
Thus ends the prediction concerning Kaṇṭhaka in the narrative of the glorious Mahāvastu-Avadāna.
By the Śuddhāvāsa devas, a hunter clad in saffron robes was manifested there in that forest retreat;
he was then seen by the Bodhisattva.
There in the forest, he saw a hunter clad in saffron robes.
Having approached him there, he spoke these words:
"Taking these two Kāśika garments, give me your saffron robe.
Having taken those two Kāśika garments, the hunter gave him his saffron robe.
Then, having taken the saffron robes, he became satisfied and joyful, thinking:
"This steadfast one is my excellent guide for the attainment of the supreme goal."
The Bodhisattva entered the forest of Dharma, the hermitage of the seer Vasiṣṭha.

The seer Vasiṣṭha, too, seeing the Bodhisattva, was struck with wonder: "Who might this be? Is he a human, or a god, or Śakra, or Brahmā—by whose bodily radiance this entire grove of asceticism is illuminated?"
All those young boys, upon seeing the Bodhisattva, ran very hurriedly to their respective leaf-huts; taking various kinds of fruits and water, they approached the Bodhisattva.
There he saw the eldest, most wise, and excellent ascetic, named Vasiṣṭha by lineage, and having seen him, he went toward him.
With matted hair as red as copper smoke, he appeared like a flame;
he saw that sage sitting unperturbed, like a windless ocean.
Having approached that sage, the righteous bull of the Śākyas,
being permitted to enter, sat down upon the ground.
As deep as the ocean and as steadfast as the Himalayas,
the great seer was filled with wonder upon seeing the son of the Śākya king.
Who indeed is this glorious one, blazing with incomparable splendor in his form,
golden-hued and free from smoke like a radiant fire?
Broad-chested and long-armed, with well-praised fingers and toes,
his flanks are even and smooth, and his hips are like those of the ena deer.
Resembling a pillar of gold, with eyes like those of a bull and great splendor, he has the shoulders of a tiger or a bull; sinless, his hands and feet are like lotuses.
With the marks upon his body, accumulated through a hundredfold qualities of his birth,
his body shone like the moon among the stars.
No ornaments were fashioned upon his limbs that were truly fitting;
rather, it is the auspicious marks that adorn the body of this Great-Souled One.
As he proceeded with the gait of an elephant, his essence being like the core of Mount Meru,
the earth seemed to resound as it was suddenly trodden upon by his feet.
With a voice that is smooth, deep, and resonant,
he commands the entire three worlds by his majestic power.
For by the secondary marks and the primary characteristics that I perceive in him,
he is joined with the status of the Lord and Sovereign of all beings in the three worlds.
With the radiance rising from his own body,
he fills this entire grove of ascetics, like the sun as it rises.
Endowed with eighty secondary marks and possessing the thirty-two excellent primary characteristics, this radiant youth is like Sanatkumāra.
Approaching that great seer, I would question the youth who is endowed with all auspicious marks and is captivating to the hearts of all beings.
Resembling a Gandharva or the moon, like the offspring of a god, and full of youth—
whose son are you, or for what reason have you come to this forest of asceticism?
With speech that followed the truth, which was the self of all beings,
gentle, and pleasant to hear, that prince spoke.
Born of the Ikṣvāku lineage, the son of King Śuddhodana,
having abandoned the earth and renounced his kingdom, he has set out for liberation.
Having thus seen the world overwhelmed by many sufferings—
birth, disease, old age, and so forth— he went forth for the sake of liberation.
I pray for that state wherein nothing exists, wherein everything ceases,
and wherein everything is stilled.
When this had been said, the great-souled seer Satyavāk, possessed of great wisdom,
spoke to the best of speakers, who was born of the Śākya royal lineage.
O fortunate one, by such conduct, by such livelihood, by the perfection of my characteristics,
and by my wisdom, there is nothing that I cannot attain.
Then the Bodhisattva went to Vaiśālī and approached Ārāḍa Kālāma;
having realized that this was not the path leading to liberation, he departed from there and went to Rājagṛha.
And having gone to Rājagṛha in the mountain caves of the Magadhas, he,
endowed with excellent marks, went forth for alms.
Śreṇiya, the lord of Magadha, saw him from the palace;
having seen him with a clear mind, he spoke thus to his ministers:
"Behold this being, sirs, endowed with excellent marks;
he is perfect in his proportions and gazes only a yoke's length ahead."
"With eyes cast down and full of wisdom, this man is not born of a low family;
let the king's messengers follow him to see where he will take up residence."
Then those messengers, having been thus instructed, followed after him, [inquiring]:
"Where will the monk go? Where will he take up residence?"
Having wandered for alms and departed from the city, the Sage headed toward Pāṇḍava; here he will find lodging.
Having learned that he had arrived at his lodging, one messenger sat down,
while another, returning quickly, then informed the king.
"O Great King, this monk is seated there at the foot of a tree in the city of Pāṇḍava, one-pointed and well-composed."
Then the king, hurrying, addressed his ministers:
"Quickly clear the path; we shall behold the Supreme among Men."
Then those illustrious royal messengers and high ministers quickly cleared the road, thinking, "The king himself will come here."
Then those illustrious royal messengers and high ministers went and reported to the king: "O Lord, your son Pāṇḍava is pure."
Then the king set forth with his fourfold army,
surrounded by friends and ministers, and preceded by a host of kinsmen.
Having descended from his vehicle, he approached on foot;
after exchanging friendly greetings, he sat down to one side.
Having sat down facing the king, he addressed the Bodhisattva:
"You are as exultant as King Selaka, the horseman."
"I give you enjoyments; enjoy them and tell me your lineage when you are asked.
The Bodhisattva said:
O King, his own territory was on the slopes of the Himalayas;
endowed with wealth and prowess, he resided among the Kośalas.
He was Āditya by clan (gotra) and Śākyan by birth (jāti).
Therefore, having gone forth from my family, I do not long for sensual pleasures;
I shall go to the palace made of jewels in order to abandon them.
"May it indeed be so for him; may he touch Nirvāṇa and, having attained awakening,
return once more and preach the Dharma to me as well, O Gautama."
Having heard which, may I go to a heavenly rebirth.
The Bodhisattva said:
"Indeed, Great King, it shall be so:
I will touch enlightenment; of this I have no doubt.
And having attained enlightenment, I will return again."
"I promise that I shall teach you the Dharma."
The Bodhisattva approached Udraka Rāmaputra, but realizing, "This is not the path leading to liberation," he departed from there and went to Gayā.
On Mount Gayāśīrṣa, three similes appeared to him.
Then he went to Uruvilvā and entered it for alms.
Pūraṇa Kāśyapa entered Uruvilvā for alms.
Having abandoned all hindrances, listen all of you with one-pointed minds to how the illustrious Bodhisattva met with the former Victors.
Having entered the religious life under Arāḍa and Udraka in the forest, being dissatisfied,
he set out toward the southern direction, to the land frequented by the former Victors.
Wandering for alms, he who resembles a golden ornament reached Uruvilvā;
at the proper time, he came to the householder’s home, which was crowded with men and women.
Then the village headman’s daughter, named Sujātā— wise and of noble birth—
seeing that prince, trembled with a surge of joy.
Standing before him with her husband, full of reverence, she shed tears;
she addressed the prince, saying, "O best of men, do not turn back!"
O you whose face is like the full moon, do not go away forever;
for my eyes, O Hero, remain unsatiated as they gaze upon you from every side.
But why indeed, O you of most graceful gait, beautiful form, auspicious marks, and wearer of excellent ornaments,
do you depart while I am still unsatisfied, you who have made my heart entirely dark with longing?
She heard the voices of the deities speaking from the sky:
"This is indeed the excellent son of King Śuddhodana from Kapilavastu."
Driven by her thirst to see him, she rushed forth and proclaimed his hundreds of virtues:
"O noble man, how did you fare when separated from your own kinsmen?"
Surrounded by a multitude of women, they weep and follow after the Golden-Hued One as he enters the mouth of the forest wilderness, lamenting piteously.
Happy in the forests are the herds of deer, the forest deities, and the lords of the woods,
who gaze upon that hero, the best in the forest, whose gait is like that of a royal swan.
With your delicate, blossoming body and jewel-like feet resembling lotus petals,
how can you tread upon this earth, so difficult to traverse and strewn with grass, *kuśa*, and reeds?
Having been nourished by the essence of refined foods and having had your body sustained by the excellence of various flavors,
how will you subsist on roots, fruits, and leaves at the edge of a forest waterfall?
Having slept upon a bed with legs of gold and ivory, covered with excellent rugs and strewn with flowers,
how will you sleep on surfaces spread with grass, *kuśa*, and reeds?
O best of men, having heard the music of drums, lutes, and songs in your palace,
you shall hear harsh and terrifying sounds, like the roar of an enraged elephant.
May the quarters of the sky be filled with roots, fruits, leaves, and sap for you and the herds of non-cruel wild animals;
O forest-dweller, may the sun not scorch your body with its heat while you are thirsty and hungry.
For you who are tormented by the summer heat, let there be a grove with a pavilion containing water;
and in the winter, let the cloudless sun shine within the mountain caves.
Your retinue consists of rākṣasas, yakṣas, and serpents; you are as delicate as a divine infant, the most excellent among the stars and the moon, with a body that delights the heart and the eyes.
Thus, like a noble elephant longing for a lotus pond, he enters the edge of the ascetic grove at the foot of the Vindhya mountains; now hear of the various wonders of that excellent forest.
In some places the forest was filled with creepers of red sprouts and handfuls of blossoms from very young trees;
in some places it was scorched by forest deities, and in others it was trampled by wandering elephants.
In some places it was adorned with trees inaccessible due to their vast, dense foliage and hanging fruits;
in other places, its base was covered by shrubs and forest trees, including withered hollow trunks.

In some places there are beautiful lotus ponds; in others, forests with the sound of mountain streams; in some places, hermitages of ascetic families; and in others, songs sung by cuckoos, parrots, and peacocks.
In some places it was filled with hollows, grass, and arid wastes; in others, it was dyed red by the shoots of *śara* reeds;
in some places there were *ruru* deer, yak-cows, and buffaloes; and in others, the roars of tigers and lions resounded.
In some places, various creepers with red shoots hung down from young trees,
like women exhausted from going to a garden, falling asleep.
In some places, the tops of the *kuravaka* trees were in full bloom, their flowers clearly and perfectly awakened,
like women who have just woken from sleep with eyes still heavy from slumber.
In some places, the branches of various trees, variegated with blossoms and stirred by a sweet breeze,
lean gracefully against one another like playful women leaning upon each other.
In some places, a flowering branch of the *kupyaka* forest tree, unable to bear its own weight,
sways as if it were an affectionate woman bending under the burden of her own sister.

In some places, within the forest groves of rows of trees, there were blossoming *kiṃśuka* flowers; or else, in what seemed like a great schoolhouse, there were women with large eyes, like young ladies wearing red garments as upper cloths.
In some places, a region of the earth was covered with freshly blossomed flowers,
like a young bride adorned with a full load of ornaments, dressed in fine garments, and resting gracefully upon her bed.
In some places there were hard thorny creepers, the dwelling-places of the tracks of deer, buffaloes, and boars,
drenched with the blood of deer struck by the arrows of the Śabaras.
In some places, heaps of elephant skeletons cover the ground like white cloth coverlets;
in other places, tigers, lions, poisonous snakes, men, elephants, and boars have been slain.
In some places there are the ravings of *rākṣasas* and the terrifying cries of *piśācas* and *kumbhāṇḍas*;
in other places, the utterances of *guhyakas* circulate through the groves during the nights.
At times during the nights the clouds thunder, and the hosts of beasts of prey rejoice;
they assume many forms that are terrifying to behold.
He who desires the welfare of the entire world dwells in that forest grove,
which is delightful because it has stripped away the pride of fierce beasts and rākṣasas.
Just as the Lord of Beasts seeks the welfare of the entire world for his own sake, so too does the Essence of Beings seek it especially for sentient beings; that too is a marvel of self-control.
If I must experience suffering for an incalculable number of eons for the sake of liberating each and every single being among all sentient beings, I shall deliver them all; this is my firm resolve.
Having practiced austerities for six years in the forest, Satvasāra attained mindfulness through the exhaustion of karma, realizing: "The path by which I have gone is not the way to liberation."
I remember that in the past, while the Śākya king was in the Jambudruma grove, he attained the first dhyāna; that shall become the path to awakening.
And it is not possible for one who is weak, emaciated, with blood and flesh completely dried up, to attain awakening; therefore, I shall take food once again.
The deities said: "Do not exert yourself; let not your glory diminish.
We shall infuse vital energy into your limbs."
"I am known by everyone as one who is constantly without food;
yet the vital energy they have offered to me is false for her."
Thus, fearing false speech, he rejected that deity,
saying "Enough," and consumed a soup made of *phāṇita* from the broth of a *mudra*, a *kulaccha*, and *hareṇu*.
Having gradually restored strength and vigor to his body,
he sought out food and approached Uruvilvā properly.
Then Sujātā, his mother from a previous birth, who was of noble family and wise,
stood at the foot of a nyagrodha tree holding honeyed milk-rice.
"O Brahmacārin, why is your body so emaciated and exhausted?
Having given the milk-rice, announce it to the prince."
And for that royal seer, there was well-prepared honeyed milk-rice there;
the prince said to him, "For what purpose do you give this gift?"
She who had been the mother of that pure being throughout hundreds of births spoke sweetly: "I make this request; may it be fulfilled for me."
At the foot of the Himalayas stands the city known as Kapila,
renowned throughout every direction and sub-direction, crowded with joyful men and women.
In that city lived the prince, the son of Śuddhodana the Śākya;
having abandoned his royal power and left behind his circle of kinsmen, he went to the forest.
As he wandered for six years in that fierce and terrifying penance grove,
my vow was fulfilled through his act of giving.
"May that excellent goal which he seeks through this asceticism be fulfilled for me;
may I too proceed along that same path with that most eminent of great men."
Then a non-human voice arose from the sky:
"O well-born lady, this is that wise one, born of the Śākya royal lineage."
By him were practiced these austerities, difficult and hair-raising,
of various kinds in the penance grove, until his blood and flesh were dried up.
Leaving those useless things behind, they proceed toward the excellent tree;
here, past Buddhas attained supreme enlightenment.
Then, filled with joy, she shed tears;
trembling, she spoke to that tiger among men with her palms joined in reverence.
O lotus-eyed one, you have been seen arising from fierce asceticism in the Bhairava forest;
seeing you, my heart, which was tormented by grief, now experiences joy.
For six years, this couch has never before been slept upon for pleasure by me,
as I contemplated your asceticism with the burning heat of the arrows of grief.
Hearing that you have reached the end of your asceticism, the people, the king, your father, and your mother’s sister, who is so deeply affectionate toward you, will become joyful and glad at heart.
In the city of Kapila, the palaces will resound with the music of hundreds of instruments;
they will be filled with joy and delight, and the throngs of men and women will be laughing.

Having partaken of the honeyed milk-rice, you who destroy existence through the power of your former births attained the deathless state of sorrowlessness beneath the king of trees in the grove on earth.
The Lamp of Men prophesied: "For five hundred births you were my mother;
in a future time, you shall become a Pratyekabuddha named Jinavrata."
Thus ends the Prediction concerning Sujātā from the glorious Mahāvastu.
Then the Bodhisattva, having received his alms from Senāpati Village in Uruvilvā with his bowl filled with various kinds of cakes, set out; and Pūraṇa Kāśyapa set out with his bowl empty.
Thus he was questioned by the Bodhisattva.
"Venerable Kāśyapa, alms can be obtained."
Then Kāśyapa addressed the Bodhisattva with this verse:
Praskandaka, Balākalpa, Ujjaṅgala, and Jaṅgala—
in these wretched villages, not even a single alms-meal could be obtained.
Then the Bodhisattva replied to Pūraṇa Kāśyapa with a verse:
Praskandaka, Balākalpa, Ujjaṅgala, and Jaṅgala—
from these villages of the Bhadras, behold how the bowl has become full.
When the Bodhisattva had gone forth despite his unwilling parents, whose throats were choked with tears and whose faces were weeping, King Śuddhodana dispatched men, saying:
"Bring me daily news of the prince's activities."
Then, news arrived that the prince had gone to Anomiya, to the hermitage of the seer Vasiṣṭha.
When he had gone from the hermitage of the seer Vasiṣṭha to Vaiśālī, news of this reached King Śuddhodana.
News has also arrived from when he approached Araḍa Kālāma at Vaiśālī.
When he went from Vaiśālī to Rājagṛha, news also arrived from there.
News has also arrived from that water at Rājagṛha where he approached the son of Rāma.
News also arrived that King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra had invited him with abundant offerings.
When he went from Rājagṛha to Mount Gayāśīrṣa, news also arrived from there.
When he had gone from Mount Gayāśīrṣa to Uruvilvā, to the grove of Uruvilvā on the bank of the river Nairañjanā, news of him reached King Śuddhodana.
When he performs fierce austerities and applies himself to exertion in the grove of Uruvilvā, from that [exertion] spiritual progress proceeds.

When the Bodhisattva practiced the *āsphānaka* meditation with such austerity that he had blocked the inhalations and exhalations through both the nostrils and the openings of the ear-canals, those men thought, "The prince has passed away; he neither breathes in nor breathes out. Having gone to Kapilavastu, they [informed] the king...
It was reported to Śuddhodana:
"Great King, the prince has passed away."
The king did not believe it;
he questioned those men:
"How do you know that the prince has passed away?"
They said:
"Your Majesty, through fierce asceticism and the consumption of coarse food, he has passed away; he neither breathes in nor breathes out, but remains like a piece of wood.
Therefore, we thought that since the prince neither breathes in nor breathes out, and his body is emaciated and weak, the prince must have died."
Then this thought occurred to King Śuddhodana:

Such was the descent of the prince into the womb, such was the worship performed by thousands of gods for his walk in the womb, and such was the manner in which the prince was born in the Lumbinī grove park; and as soon as he was born, he took seven steps upon the earth, surveyed the directions, laughed a great laugh, and uttered these words: "I am..."
He is the foremost, the eldest, the most excellent, and the one worthy of worship among both gods and humans. Just as there were marvelous and wondrous miracles when the Prince was born—
such as the insentient earth trembling and worship being performed by thousands of gods— and just as there was the perfection of his Great Departure, such Great Beings do not have short lifespans.

"It must be that the prince, as in the past, will have gone forth into homelessness; while not yet having gone forth, he will sit cross-legged in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree and enter into peaceful meditative concentration.
Therefore, these people think, 'The prince has passed away.'"
Then he spoke to those men.
"Go to the presence of the prince; the prince has not passed away, he has entered into a peaceful meditative absorption. Bring me news of the prince's daily activities."
Then those men went back again to Uruvilvā and entered the penance grove, where they saw the prince healthy and well, having arisen from his meditative concentration.
Then those men were amazed, thinking, "King Śuddhodana is wise."
When the Blessed One had set in motion the most excellent wheel of Dharma, the monks heard this account.
The monks questioned the Blessed One.
"How is it, Blessed One, that King Śuddhodana, having heard from those messengers that the prince has passed away, does not believe it?"
The Blessed One said:
Monks, it is not only now that King Śuddhodana, upon hearing that I have passed away, does not believe it; on another occasion as well, having heard that he had passed away, he did not believe it.
The monks said.
At another time as well, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
At another time as well, monks.
Long ago, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi, there was another brahmin.
For forty-eight years he practiced celibacy from his youth and studied the Vedas.

Having now practiced the celibate life of a youth for forty-eight years and having studied the Vedas, that Brahmin thought: "In this world, there is no spiritual merit for one who remains childless; therefore, I have taken a wife and fathered offspring. I have enjoyed human pleasures; it is now time for me to go forth into the religious life."
Then that brahmin addressed his brahmin wife:
"Lady, I bid you farewell; I shall go forth into the religious life."
She said to him:
"Whether it be for a Brahmin's son or for me, who will decide?
If it is your intention to go forth, I too shall go forth; I too shall practice austerities; I too shall lead the holy life.
Just as you shall practice austerities, so too shall I practice austerities."
The brahmin said: "Let it be so; you too should go forth into the religious life."
Then they departed from Vārāṇasī.
On the slopes of the Himalayas, there is a hermitage named Sāhañjanī.
There dwells a great seer named Gautama, who is accompanied by five attendants, has attained the four dhyānas, and possesses the five superknowledges.
Then that brahmin, having gone with his brahmin wife to the Sāhañjanī hermitage, went forth in the presence of the seer Gautama;
and the brahmin woman also went forth.
Then, not far from that hermitage, he constructed a hermitage, building both a grass hut and a leaf hut;
for the female ascetic Pāragā, a grass hut was made in a secluded spot.

Then, while dwelling there in that hermitage, applying themselves, striving, and exerting themselves along the external path, they realized the meditative absorptions and the supernormal powers; having attained the four dhyānas and the five abhijñās, they became highly fortunate practitioners of celibacy, relying on fierce asceticism.

Whatever root-preparation or fruit-preparation, or *kodrava* grain, or *śyāmāka* millet, or *priyaṅgu*, or hemp, or savory vegetable, or radish the seer brings, he shares it with that pregnant woman who has gone to the far shore.
The thought occurred to them: "What shall be the name of this young man?"
This thought occurred to them:
"This young man has a dark complexion; let the name of this young man be 'Śyāmaka'."
Then those parents gave that young brahmin the name Śyāmaka.
In that hermitage, the young boy was reared;
thus, as time passed and he grew up until he could walk on his own feet, he played in this manner together with the young deer.
The highly fortunate sages dwell in loving-kindness;
the deer and birds are not afraid of them.
That hermitage was graced by thousands of deer and birds.
Whenever those young fawns drank from their mothers' teats, Śyāmaka likewise drank from the teat of that same doe along with them.
Whichever doe he approached, she would suckle him; just as she would suckle her own fawn, so too did she suckle Śyāmaka.
He suckled him. Thus did that young seer Śyāmaka grow up in that hermitage together with those fawns and birds.
Wherever the young deer and the birds ran, there the young seer Śyāmaka ran, surrounded by those deer and birds;
and those deer and birds also took delight together with the young seer.
Whenever the young seer was lying in his hut, many young deer and various kinds of birds would gather at the entrance of the hut; then, as soon as the young seer Śyāmaka emerged from the hut,
they would scatter throughout the vicinity of the hermitage.
Śyāmaka took delight in the hermitage together with those deer and birds, and the deer and birds also took delight there in the hermitage together with Śyāmaka.
Even when the young seer was lying down in the hermitage, the fawns, the deer, and the birds would sit surrounding him;
whenever the fawns and the birds wished to go out, they would wake the young seer Śyāmaka by nuzzling him with their snouts.
In this way, that young seer grew up in the hermitage together with those deer and birds.
When the young seer had grown up, he was then clothed and covered with the skins of deer.

Whatever root-preparation or fruit-preparation was there in that hermitage— whether it be *kodrava*, *śyāmaka*, *cinnaka*, *priyaṅgu*, *bhaṅga*, *prāsādika*, vegetables, or radishes— he would bring them and present them to his parents.
He brought water, he brought wood, and he constructed grass huts and leaf huts.
He sprinkles that hermitage site and sweeps it clean.
He attends upon his parents with the utmost reverence;

first he serves his mother and father, and only afterwards does he take food for himself. From the time the young seer reached the age of discretion, from that point on, he never once [ate] without having given [to them].
[Mvu 2.212] Having previously prepared food for his parents, Śyāmaka the young seer himself took his own meal; thus he attended upon his parents there in that hermitage.
Time passed for the young seer as he attended upon his mother and father with what was desired, lovely, dear, and pleasing.

His parents, dwelling there in that hermitage, had grown old and their bodies were frail; they were deprived of sight and dependent on others, unable to provide for their own food, unable to go out for water, and unable to repair the grass hut or the leaf hut themselves.

The young seer Śyāmaka attended to those elderly parents—who were aged, infirm, physically weak, and blind—by providing every kind of beneficial service; he lived having undertaken the ten paths of wholesome action.
This handsome young seer was pleasing to behold, brought forth by auspicious karma; he was devoted to his parents and practiced the celibate life from his youth.

Resorting to fierce asceticism, dwelling in remote lodgings and seats, he was highly distinguished and beloved by the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, kinnaras, kinnarīs, wild animals, birds, and indeed all living beings.
Wherever the young seer went— whether to gather roots, or leaves, or flowers, or fruits— there he went surrounded by deer and birds, and by gods, nāgas, kinnaras, and kinnarīs.
So now, taking his water-jar and surrounded by deer, birds, gods, nāgas, kinnaras, and kinnarīs, he descended to the mountain river to fetch water; there he filled his water-jar.
Meanwhile, the King of Kāśi named Peliyakṣa—possessing great strength, a vast treasury, and a large retinue—while hunting, was pursuing a deer on a horse as swift as the wind.
Having abandoned his army and mounts, no one else reached that place.
As it was said by the Blessed One in the Dharmapada:
The wind is the course of wild animals; space is the course of birds;
Dharma is the course of those who seek distinction; and Nirvana is the course of Arhats.
That deer vanished right there in that very forest thicket.
Then, in that forest grove, the king heard the sound of the sage Śyāma filling a water-jar from the mountain stream.
It occurred to him: "This is the sound of a deer; this forest is not frequented by humans."
Then, from the direction where the seer Śyāma was carrying his water-jar, he discharged a razor-headed arrow.
Then that poisoned arrow struck the heart of the young seer.
At the sound of that poisoned arrow and by the scent of the one who shoots by sound, those deer and birds fled in the ten directions.
The seer Śyāmaka, having set down his water-pot on the riverbank, lamented piteously.
For the sake of meat, deer and boars are killed;
for the sake of hides, lions, tigers, and leopards are killed;
for the sake of their tails, yaks are killed.
Elephant-kings are killed for the sake of their tusks;
partridges and francolin pheasants are killed for the sake of medicine.

But for us, it is not possible to accomplish anything with meat, nor with hide, nor with hair, nor with tusks. For what purpose, then, are we—harmless, innocent, and blameless—being struck by a single arrow?
Three people have been killed;
alas, how righteousness has been utterly consumed by fire!
While the young seer Śyāma was thus lamenting, the King of Kāśi arrived at that place and saw the illustrious young seer lamenting, wearing deerskin, matted hair, and bark garments,
with tears streaming down his face.
When the king saw that the young seer had been struck by the razor-edged arrow, he became terrified and filled with dread, thinking:
"Lest he should indeed reduce my city and its countryside to ashes with his curse!"
Then, having dismounted from his horse, he prostrated himself with his head at the feet of the young seer Śyāma.

"O Blessed One, this arrow was shot by me under the perception that it was a deer, acting without knowing [the truth]. I ask the Blessed One for forgiveness. These teardrops that fall upon the earth would burn the entire Jambudvīpa; how much more so, then, those of fools like us?"
Regarding that which the Blessed One said—"With a single arrow, one strikes down the three"—I do not understand this. The Blessed One is one, not a triad;
how then were three people struck down by a single arrow?
The young seer said:

"Great King, my parents are aged, elderly, weak of body, and sightless; they are celibate, highly fortunate, worthy of offerings from the world including the gods, and dependent on others for their livelihood. I am their attendant;

first I provide for their food, and afterwards I take whatever remains for myself. I perform every service for them until the end of their lives; there is no one else who might attend to them. Therefore, by my being slain, they too are slain."
"If I were dead, they would not have lived;
for that reason I say that by a single arrow three people were killed."
The King of Kāśi said to the young seer Śyāmaśrī:
"I have struck you in the heart with an arrow made of sharp poison, unknowingly as I was; I now know that there is no life left for you. Therefore, I promise you this one truth:
having abandoned my prosperous and flourishing kingdom, I shall serve your venerable father and mother."
