Just as it has been practiced, so shall I practice.
The young seer said:
"Great King, by that [explanation], the dart of grief has been removed from my heart."
Having heard these words, O protector of the earth, act in such a way that you remain true to your promise toward my elders; great merit will accrue to you.
Having performed service and attendance upon those illustrious ones, O Great King, take this water-jar and go by this footpath to the hermitage of my parents. In my name, offer them my salutations.
Śyāmaśrī sends his greetings and says this:

"Your only son is dead; you should not grieve, nor should you weep. For one born into the world of the living, death is inevitable. That state cannot be avoided, and it cannot be attained by weeping or grieving; it is impossible [to alter] what has been done by oneself."
It is impossible to escape from the results of one's actions.
Nor is death for me alone; all sentient beings are subject to the nature of death.
Therefore, do not grieve, and do not be distressed.
There is separation and parting from all that is dear and beloved.
O Great King, act in such a way that you remain true to your promise toward me, as you are toward your teachers.
Having understood this, the young seer, his body transformed, passed away.

The king, having learned that the young seer had passed away, wept and lamented; wiping away his tears, he took that water-jar and proceeded along that same footpath as instructed by Śyāmakaśiri toward that hermitage.
Immediately after the King of Kāśi had departed from the presence of Śyāmakaśiri, Śyāmakaśiri himself, surrounded by hundreds and thousands of beasts and birds,
as well as by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, kinnaras, kinnarīs, and other beings,
gathered around the young seer and broke into great lamentation, raising a mighty cry.

Surely that evildoer will go from darkness to darkness; he will go from one state of woe to another state of woe, by whom an offense has been committed against one who was harmless, innocent, and blameless.
The entire forest grove, those mountain caves, and that hermitage were resounded by the cries of spirits and filled with the calls of beasts and birds.
Having heard those cries of the spirits and having heard the sounds of the beasts and birds, Śyāmakaśiri’s parents fell into anxiety:

"What is this? Never before have we heard such cries from spirits, nor have we ever heard such sounds from beasts and birds; could it be that Śyāmakaśiri has been seized by a lion, a tiger, or some other [beast]?"
Or perhaps he has been harmed by a predatory beast.
Such are these omens, and such is our heart’s lack of peace, and such is the way my eyes are throbbing.
And they, not having attained such a state of cessation through body and mind, were thinking of Śyāmakaśiri; meanwhile,
the King of Kāśi arrived at that hermitage, and hundreds of deer and birds fled from that hermitage, uttering terrifying cries.
The sages were even more terrified by this.
The King of Kāśi, having tied his horse to a tree trunk at one side and taking that water jar, approached the presence of Śyāmakaśiri’s parents.
I pay homage to you, Blessed One.
They ask, rejoicing.
Who are you?
The king said:

"Blessed One, I am the Kāśi king named Peliyakṣa. Does the Blessed One dwell happily here in this penance grove, frequented by fierce beasts and devoid of humans? Do roots and fruits appear here; is *kodrava* and *śyāmāka* grain, as well as vegetables and roots, obtained with little effort?
Is there little illness in the body, and do few contacts from gadflies, mosquitoes, and reptiles fall upon the person?"
Then they said:

Indeed, O Great King, we live happily here in this forest hermitage, frequented by wild beasts and devoid of humans; roots, leaves, fruits, and grains such as kodrava, śyāmaka, and radish are obtained with little effort, illness in the body is slight, and few contacts from gadflies, mosquitoes, and reptiles afflict the body.

"Is it well with you too, Great King? Is there security, freedom from calamity, and absence of affliction within your inner apartments, among your princes and ministers, and in your forces, vehicles, treasury, and granaries? Do the people of the city and the countryside remain obedient? Do rival kings cause no offense? Does the rain fall from the sky in due season? Do the crops flourish? And is your kingdom secure, well-supplied with food, and free from distress?"
Then he said:

Indeed, Blessed One, within the inner apartments, among the princes and ministers, the military forces, the vehicles, the treasury, and the granaries, all is secure, free from calamity, and free from affliction.
The citizens and countryfolk remain loyal; rival kings do no wrong; the Lord rains in due season; the crops flourish; and the kingdom is secure, well-supplied with food, and free from distress.
Then they said:
"Great King, sit upon these litters until Prince Śyāmaka returns from his water-gathering; then he will offer you fruit and water."
And when he was thus addressed by those seers, the king wept aloud.
They ask.
"Great King, why do you weep?"
The king said:

"Venerable Sir, he of whom you speak—the one named Śyāmakaśiri who was to come and offer fruit and water—has passed away. This water-jar has been sent with me in my hand, and he greets you with salutations and instructs you thus:
'You must not grieve; you must not weep.'"
There is no purpose served by grieving or weeping;
everyone who is born must inevitably die.
Death does not belong to me alone; all sentient beings are subject to death and subject to passing away. It is impossible to escape from the results of one's own actions.
They ask.
"Great King, how did Śyāmaśrī pass away?"
The king said:
While hunting, pursuing a deer with a horse as swift as the wind, I arrived at that place near the water where Śyāmāśrī was filling her jar;
and there, in the dense forest thicket, that deer vanished.
I heard the sound of that Śyāmaśiri carrying that water-jar,
and it occurred to me: "That very deer is going with water."
As I was going along and hearing that sound, a poisoned razor-headed arrow was shot by me in the direction of that sound;
it struck Śyāmakaśiri in the heart,
and this young seer has passed away.
Having heard this from the king, they wept with choked voices and tearful faces, lamenting.
"Great King, deer and boars are killed for the sake of their meat; lions, tigers, and leopards are killed for the sake of their skins; elephants are killed for the sake of their tusks;
and partridges and mongooses are killed for the sake of their medicinal properties. But for us, Great King, there is no need for meat, nor for skin, nor for hair, nor for tusks."
For what reason? We were harmless, innocent, and blameless, yet three people have been killed by a single arrow.
The King of Kāśi, having prostrated himself, asked for forgiveness from the sages.
"Blessed One, these tears of yours that fall upon the ground would burn even the entire Jambudvīpa for an aeon, let alone foolish people like us."
"Having abandoned my kingdom, along with my own people and kinsmen, I shall attend upon you here; I will serve you just as I served Śyāmakaśiri."
Then they said:
"Great King, we are blind and deprived of sight; we are not capable of going to that place without a guide.
Therefore, Great King, lead us to that place where Śyāmakaśrī is."
We shall restore that young seer by means of a truthful word, and by means of a truthful word we shall destroy that deer-poison.
The thought occurred to that king:
"These highly fortunate seers are capable of attending upon him."
He said:
I shall lead you to that blessed place where Śyāmakaśiri is.
Then, placing their hands upon the shoulder of that king, they went to that place.
Placing the head of the seer Śyāmaka on her lap, Pāragā, the mother of the illustrious Śyāmaka, stroked his face with her hand and wept and lamented in many ways.
"The hermitage will become empty, deprived of the illustrious Śyāmaka;
the forest deity, having lamented piteously, will depart.
Even the beasts and birds, not seeing the illustrious Śyāmaka, will depart from the hermitage, lamenting piteously."
The seer said: "Pāraga, do not weep; do not grieve. What purpose is served by weeping or by being mangled?"
"We too have practiced excellent vows through fierce asceticism and are celibate practitioners; we are capable of raising him up by means of a declaration of truth.
Let us make that declaration of truth by which we shall destroy his animal venom and restore his life."
Then, by his word of truth, that deer-poison was destroyed.
Just as you, my son, have never conceived anything unrighteous toward anyone, but have been friendly-minded toward all sentient beings, so may the poison of the deer be neutralized for you.
Just as you have never taken food for yourself without first giving to your parents, so may this deer-poison be destroyed for you.
Just as your parents, my son, always maintain perfectly pure conduct,
so may the poison of the deer you have killed be neutralized for you.

Then, by the power of his parents' majesty, by the power of his word of truth, and by the power of his own well-performed conduct, that young seer stretched himself like a man who has been asleep and awakens;
thus it was said by the Blessed One.
"Furthermore, monks, it may be that you think thus: 'At that time, on that occasion, the young seer Śyāmaka was someone else. "
This should not be viewed in such a way.
For what reason?
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, I was the young seer named Śyāmaka.
That seer who was Śyāmaka’s father at that time was this very King Śuddhodana. He was Śyāmaka’s father back then.
She who at that time, on that occasion, was the mother of the young seer Śyāmaka named Pāragā,
was this very Māyādevī.
That other one who was named Peliyakṣa was the King of Kāśi.
This should not be viewed in such a way.
For what reason?
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, the Elder Ānanda was the King of Kāśī named Peliyakṣa.

"Even then, monks, when King Śuddhodana heard that he had passed away on my account, he did not believe it. [The deer said: 'O Great King, he has not passed away; Śyāmakaśiri was merely deluded by the deer-poison.
Do not go to that place of ours; we shall destroy that deer-poison with a word of truth and we shall raise up Śyāmakaśiri.'"
Even now, having heard that King Śuddhodana has passed away for my sake, he does not believe it.
Thus ends the narrative of the Śyāmaka-jātaka.
I shall proclaim the former conduct of the Blessed One, the virtuous one, the World-Protector of immeasurable fame in the world, who has transcended the world.
For the conduct of a Bodhisattva cannot be surpassed by anyone in the world of gods, gandharvas, and humans; therefore, the One Possessing the Ten Powers is unconquerable.
Whatever power of mindfulness the Tathāgatas possessed in each of those various births,
as they compassionately felt sympathy for the world through loving-kindness and compassion;
I shall proclaim that well-practiced conduct of the Blessed One, who accumulated merit for hundreds of thousands of eons; give your attention with reverence.
At that time, the Blessed One was reborn as a being endowed with perfect wisdom in a family of forest-dwelling ascetics, which was utterly pure.
His parents had grown old and were deprived of their sight;
for their benefit, he was born as one who transcends the world.
With all limbs faultless, possessed of supernormal powers, gentle, and large-eyed,
his name at that time was indeed Śyāma.
It is a marvel that whether a human or a god, whoever beholds the young seer who has reached the perfection of beauty and virtue, is never satiated while gazing upon him.
The Bodhisattva himself, seeking what is wholesome, undertakes it;
he takes up that pure, wholesome dharma and abides by it.
Unbroken, stainless, and completely pure, he avoids evil deeds and laziness;
he himself practices the holy life and establishes others in it as well.
The hero, having attended upon his mother and father, serves them with intense devotion;
as a celibate practitioner, he himself observes the vow of celibacy.
He made this vow regarding his beloved parents:
"I must certainly not engage in conceptual proliferation toward those who are blind and dependent on others."
Gathering roots and fruits, I shall serve my teachers with love and reverence, honoring them as they are sick, infirm, and advanced in years.
With food and drink, by providing medicine for the sick,
with clothing, and with bedding and seats, I shall attend upon my mother and father.
Moreover, in this matter, the Bodhisattva said to his parents: "Do not be distressed;
indeed, you should not grieve, for I am your attendant."
Śyāmasundarī said to him: "May neither Cīrabhājī nor any spirits cause you harm, for you have gone upon a path that is not the way."
May even the lions seeking flesh and blood, and the exceedingly powerful elephants, move away from the path; and may no beings cause you fear.
He dwells together with young fawns in delightful hermitages;
like a deer, the young seer lives among the deer in the forest.
While he was dwelling in that hermitage, practicing patience, self-control, and renunciation, he felt compassion for the world through loving-kindness and pity.
There appeared the King of Kāśi, a monarch of great power and high renown;
he terrified the deer and the birds in that hermitage.
The king saw herds of deer within the forest;
having seen them, he very hurriedly drew his bow and fixed sharp-tipped arrows upon it.
This horseman has released a steed with the speed of the wind toward the deer— a preeminent horse among all steeds, with flowing mane and moving with great haste.
And now the young seer, taking his water-pot, set out for the water;
he entered the mountain river, while the deer and birds were terrified.
Then that king, provoked to the highest pitch of anger,
pursuing deer with his drawn bow, did not see the young seer, being himself filled with rage.
He fixed an arrow to the bow of the deer, by which Śyāma was struck;
pierced by that poison-smeared shaft, he fell down, though he remained unperturbed.
Being struck, he said: "By whom am I, who have done no wrong, being killed? Father, mother, and one arrow—three have been slain; once again, unrighteousness has flared up."
For the sake of their tusks, elephants are killed; for the sake of their meat, deer;
for the sake of their hair, the yak; and for the sake of their hides, the leopard.
But for me, there are no teeth, nor skin, nor hair, nor even flesh;
for what purpose indeed would we, who are harmless, be killed?
Having heard those words and approached that young seer,
the king consoled him and asked for his forgiveness, saying, "The Blessed One was struck by me in ignorance."
This was not an arrow intentionally aimed; you were struck by me unknowingly.
Whatever wound has been caused by me through ignorance, let that indeed be forgiven.
And as for what you said while lamenting—"Three were struck by a single arrow"—explain this, O practitioner of the holy life; tell me the meaning of this.
The Bodhisattva spoke to his beloved parents,
creating a pretext, and uttered these words:
They have long been my practitioners of the holy life—my mother and father, aged and decrepit;
for them, being sightless, I alone am their refuge and their protector.
Death without a protector has come upon them; because of that, O King, I grieve.
They, who have not been cared for by me, will die a death without a protector.
For this reason I say that the three are slain;
yet while nourishing you, I shall not be slain by anything.
The Lord of Kāśī, who possessed sharp intelligence, also honored his purpose;
having bowed his head at the feet of that young seer, he spoke to him.
"I shall fall into hell for having killed this innocent son of a seer;
for having committed such a deed, one cannot be released from the hells."
Even the drops of tears that fall from you, whose being is utterly pure, could burn the world; how much more so those of fools like us?
I speak the truth: even if my life were to end through yours, I would sacrifice even my own breath; yet such a thing is simply impossible.
O son of a seer, you have been struck in the heart with a sharp poison;
I know that there is no life left in you, yet it is not pleasing to me.
And so, O you of great renown, I shall grant you my promise; have confidence in me.
For truth is established in the world of the living; this is the ultimate reality.
Having abandoned my prosperous kingdom and having renounced women and sensual pleasures,
I shall serve your parents by gathering roots and fruits.
The Bodhisattva said to him: "O elephant among kings, by uttering these words, you are removing this harsh burning pain of my grief-stake."
"Taking this very water-pot, go along these footpaths to our hermitage and speak these words on my behalf."
Again and again you said, "Greet my mother and father;
your son has passed away, and he sends his greeting to you."
One should not grieve in any way, nor is there any purpose in grieving like a wretch;
everyone born into the world of the living must inevitably die.
This indeed is the natural order: the life of humans is not very long;
death is the ultimate end for both the wealthy and the destitute.
Nor is it possible to escape from the fruit of one's own actions;
for upon the turning of the wheel, both happiness and suffering fall upon one.
Nor have I heard from those endowed with wisdom, nor do I myself know,
the instability of that which is momentary, weak, and subject to conditioned formations.
Nor is there death, nor is such suffering mine alone;
this truth has been experienced, for there is nothing in the world that is not accessible.
This is my dart of grief, that they— old and deprived of sight—
will become overwhelmed with sorrow upon hearing your news.
"O Kāśivardhana, look now; may you be one whose promise is true.
O lord of men, that shall serve as my service to my gurus."
The wise praise that person of great purpose even when they are aged and weak;
for, O Lord of Men, he possesses all three of those qualities through his service.
There shall indeed be merit, renown, fame, and roots of wholesome action;
O King of Kāśi, ask for this word and attend upon him.
Having heard "So be it," the King of Kāśī, dejected and wiping away his tears,
departed, realizing that Śyāma was dead.
And now the King of Kāśi has departed, along with many hundreds of deer;
flocks of birds and even deities have surrounded Śyāma.
Having seen him fallen and lying there on the riverbank, unconscious,
even the deities and many hundreds of beasts and birds wept.
Truly, that evildoer goes from darkness to deeper darkness, from one miserable state to another miserable state, who thinks evil thoughts toward you, whose nature is free from evil.
There was the clamor of beings in the sky and a roar upon the earth;
winds blew violently, and the seer thought, "Alas, what a calamity!"
Surely the young seer has been harmed, judging by what is seen:
these many fierce and piteous sounds of "ruta-ruta" cries.
The winds blow most painfully, and the birds utter harsh cries; my heart is unsettled and my entire body is restless.
These mental discursive thoughts were occurring when he named Peliyaśa departed for his hermitage, and the flocks of birds and herds of deer were terrified.
Terrified and afflicted by fear, even the deities fled in all directions; yet, recognizing [the situation], they became even more despondent as they watched, their hopes extinguished.
Neither a human nor even a non-human has ever come from anywhere to this region;
nor have the hosts of deer and birds ever felt fear upon seeing the young seer.
Without a doubt, there will be a great and hair-raising being,
at the sight of whom the herds of deer and the flocks of birds will be terrified.
Having approached his parents who were already aware of what was known,
he greeted them with sweet words, even though they were terrified that he might take their lives by not returning.
He said to them, "Welcome to you! From where have you come, or whose messenger are you?
We are blind and sightless; Śyāma has gone to fetch water."
The king said: "I went out from the city of Kāśī for a hunt with my army;
by the name of Peliyakṣa, I was wandering about searching for deer."
O elephant among kings, does the rain fall for you, and does the seed sprout? Is the inner harem free from disease, and are my princes and the elite of the army well?
In my cities and provinces there is security, and the subjects are devoted;
enemies do not increase, and the entire treasury grows.
Among the śramaṇas and the brāhmaṇas, there is righteous protection for the people in the provinces;
[the realm] increases and does not decline, and I give gifts with due respect.
Even in your forest, where many thieves, tigers, and wild beasts roam,
no beings cause harm to one another, as if they had strayed onto the wrong path.
When there is abundant *puṣpa-kala* rice and plenty of *śyāmāka* grain, vegetables, and radishes, one can obtain them with little effort; thus, there will be few diseases in the body.
Before long, the prince arrived; sit down upon these leaf-litters, which are worthy of one who is fortunate, righteous, and exceedingly pleasing to the mind.
Then, shedding tears, the king uttered words that were poisonous, undesirable, and life-threatening to that community of ascetics.
"The one you speak of, the son of a seer, a practitioner of the holy life, a follower of the Dharma, and a practitioner of equanimity—he has just now passed away; he sends his salutation to you."
One should not grieve in any way, nor is there any purpose served by lamenting for the mutilated;
everyone born into this world of the living must inevitably die.
Having heard those words— unwanted, unpleasant, and disagreeable—
they said, "You are indeed cutting short my life," speaking thus.
He said: "This matter has arisen through my conduct when I committed evil while ignorant; may the gods thus forgive me."
I too have come here for this very purpose; whatever burden the young seer bears, I shall bear it as well, and I, O gods, shall attend upon him.
His mother laments, recollecting the former smiles and speech of her beloved son, who possessed a complexion as beautiful as a well-blossomed blue lotus.
Alas, beloved Syāmasundara! In the past, the arising of separation from you will burn my heart, just as fire consumes dry grass and wood.
This hermitage appears empty, terrifying and fearsome, and unpleasant; it is bereft of that noble, righteous, and sublime seer.
"Surely he has exhausted all our power; by that very means, let there be peace for him.
This is better for me than such suffering ever beingfalling upon him."
I believe that various and manifold ascetic practices were performed by us that were inferior [to his];
this is their ripened fruit, that we are deprived of our beloved son.
Distressed and exhausted by the lamentations of Ruṇḍa,
she remembered the hundreds of virtues of this righteous man.
He said to the King of Kāśī, "Thus have we been entreated there:
'We are blind and sightless; we are not capable of going there.'"
He said, "I shall indeed go to that place where the young seer dwells;
perhaps that youth may still live, though he has been struck down by the poisons of the wild beasts."
That king of Kāśi, proceeding by the same path by which he had come,
before long arrived at that place where the young seer was.
Seeing him fallen and lying there on the riverbank, unconscious,
his mother, weeping, stroked his face-jewel with her hand.
Alas, beloved only son! You are the kinsman of us who are destitute, poor, and friendless; how have you been harmed, my child?
Even the forest deities have no concern for those who are non-human;
they see nothing [to fear] among them, for the dark-skinned calf was not restrained even slightly.
The food for the journey was difficult to endure, consisting of many hundreds of grains;
it was [prepared] by one who was virtuous and worthy, yet deprived of his beloved son.
Surely those deer and birds in the hermitage grove,
not seeing the glory of Śyāmaka and finding no delight, are crying out most piteously.
Do not grieve, Pāraga; there is no purpose whatsoever in grieving for Ruṇḍa.
Everyone born into this world of the living must inevitably die.
"We too are celibate, having long abstained from sexual unions.
We shall utter a word of truth, and by that we will destroy his poison."
Just as your mind, O handsome one, never clings to evil, so too has the deer-poison been destroyed; arise by the power of this word of truth!
Just as your parents maintain a morality that is eternally pure, so too has the deer-poison been destroyed; arise by means of this word of truth!
Just as you have no wrong view, pride, intoxication, or hypocrisy, so too has the deer-poison been destroyed; arise by means of your word of truth!
Then, as the deer-poison had subsided, he arose while yawning,
through the power of his parents, the power of his own well-practiced conduct, and his own inherent strength.
Seeing him risen by that word of truth, the king,
his hair standing on end with joy, fell at his feet and asked for forgiveness.
The Bodhisattva said to him: "O Great King, may you be happy, together with your yoked draft animals and your troops, along with your queens, and including your cities, market towns, and provinces."
Behold, O Kāśivardhana, the outflow of reverence for one's mother and father,
just as the poison of the deer was completely eradicated by Suvākya through the power of his well-practiced conduct.
O Kāśivardhana, those who desire to go to heaven must perform service for their mother and father, as well as offer salutations with joined palms.
"Having brought all the jewels from this Jambudvīpa in order to go to heaven,
honor your mother and father; one should not act with ingratitude toward one's parents."
Thus, O Great King, I say that it is not easy to repay one's mother and father;
have compassion for them as the ancient teachers did for the world.
One should bow down to those human deities as if they were gods;
those whose parents receive honor from them are not to be grieved for.
She who was his mother at that time was Māyā then;
King Śuddhodana was the father of the Blessed One at that time.
By that word of truth which was uttered, he who had arisen with great majesty was the Blessed One Bodhisattva Śyāma at that time.
He who was the king at that time was Ānanda;
for many thousands of births, he was a kinsman and a servant of the Blessed One.
This was not something he realized anywhere else, nor was it a knot he untied by himself;
for it was indeed the perfection of the Dharma through the Blessed One’s own past conduct.
The Śyāmaka-jātaka is concluded.
While the Bodhisattva was practicing austerities in the penance grove at Uruvilvā,
subsisting on a single jujube fruit per day, he remained committed to his diet of jujubes for eighteen months.
Sustaining himself for a day with a single sesame seed, he practiced the taking of sesame seeds for eighteen months;
sustaining himself for a day with a single grain of rice, he practiced the taking of rice for eighteen months;
and for eighteen months he practiced complete non-intake of food.
His food consisted of a single jujube fruit and a single sesame grain.
In some cases, the wisdom of a perfectly awakened Buddha does not reside in one who lacks diligence.
Just as all the limbs of a black snake become cold, so it was with his limbs.
At that time, her jaw was like the footprint of a camel on the crossbar.
Like the interior of a dilapidated cow-pen, with its sides fallen apart.
Thus was the body of the great seer completely withered by his ascetic heat.
It is long, like a braided coil, and undulates with rises and falls.
In this way, his back and neck became alternately raised and depressed.
His eyes shine like stars in a water well.
His deep inhalation was like the bellows of smiths.
Or like an autumnal *ālambu* flower that has withered after being cut while still green.
Thus, the head of the great seer was withered by his ascetic heat.
The Great Hero, with body stilled, has realized the unheard-of state of his own mind.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he practices fierce asceticism.
And it is not possible to fully proclaim it even by speaking with every voice.
That which is difficult to perform, the Hero does it upon seeing sentient beings who are suffering.
Or just as a bird does not find a limit in the sky.
Just as the water in the ocean is immeasurable, so too is the great deep.
Thus [it is] regarding the Buddhas, the lamps of the world, the kinsmen of the sun.
It is not possible to express the limit of his qualities with all speech.
His outer skin is unstained, yet his back is smeared with [filth].
All their limbs have fallen away, yet they do not exert themselves to move.
Having grasped the front part of the body, one takes hold of the back part.
When you arise with speed, O Sage, may you fall into happiness.
The four deities, seeing the body of the hero to be weak, [approached].
They said, "The Sage has passed away," yet he does not cease through his vigor.
While the Supreme Person was practicing such fierce asceticism.
The world, including its gods, asuras, and humans, was struck with wonder.
[ _Mvu_ 2.233] Having heard from the messengers he had dispatched that the prince was engaged in such fierce asceticism, King Śuddhodana, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, Yaśodharā,
and the entire Śākya kingdom were filled with longing,
thinking: "May the prince indeed emerge safely from this severe austerity."
It occurred to Yaśodharā as well:

"It would not be good for me, nor would it be fitting, that while my noble son is suffering, practicing austerities, sleeping on a bed of grass, and subsisting on coarse food, I should here in the royal palace enjoy foods fit for a king."
I would drink drinks worthy of a king, I would wear garments worthy of a king, and I would prepare beds and seats worthy of a king.
"What if I were now to take coarse food, wear ordinary clothes, and prepare my bed even upon a layer of grass?"
She then took coarse food, wore common clothes, and made her bed upon a layer of grass.

And when the Blessed One, having set in motion the most excellent Wheel of Dharma, was dwelling in Rājagṛha surrounded by a retinue of twelve hundred and fifty monks, then King Śuddhodana dispatched Chandaka and Kālodāyin as messengers to the Blessed One in Rājagṛha, [saying]:
"The Blessed One has shown compassion toward gods and humans; may the Blessed One also show compassion toward his kinsmen."
And do whatever the Blessed One may say.
They too arrived at Rājagṛha from Kapilavastu and approached the Blessed One; they reported to the Blessed One the entire message of King Śuddhodana and of his entire circle of kinsmen.
And the Blessed One, knowing the right time, knowing the hour, and knowing the occasion, awaited the proper time, hour, and occasion for going to his birthplace.
The Blessed One addressed Chandaka and Kālodāyin.
Chandaka and Kālodāyin, you two shall go forth into the religious life.
They said:
King Śuddhodana commanded: "Whatever the Blessed One may say to you, you must do."
And when they saw that there was neither a barber there nor any saffron robes with which they might be clothed and go forth, they followed the Blessed One and said:
We shall go forth into homelessness, Blessed One.
Then they were addressed by the Blessed One with the "Come, monk" formula.
"Come, monks, Cchanda and Kālodāyin; lead the holy life under the Tathāgata."
Now, as soon as they were addressed by the Blessed One with the "Come, monk" formula, whatever marks of a householder, banners of a householder, protections of a householder,

or conventions of a householder they had all vanished; three robes appeared, a bowl was provided, their hair remained in its natural state, and their deportment became established just like that of monks who had been ordained for a hundred years.
This, venerable ones, is the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk for Chanda and Kālodāyin.
The Venerable Udāyī said to the Blessed One:

"Lord, Yaśodharā followed the Blessed One’s vows; while the Blessed One was practicing austerities in the forest of penance, Yaśodharā also took coarse food, wore common garments, and having abandoned beds and seats worthy of a king, she prepared her bed upon a layer of grass."
The monks questioned the Blessed One.
"How is it, Blessed One, that Yaśodharā follows the Blessed One's vows?"
The Blessed One said:
Monks, it is not only now that Yaśodharā has been devoted to me.
On other occasions as well, Yaśodharā has been devoted to me.
The monks said:
At another time as well, Blessed One?
The Blessed One said:
For it was also on another occasion, monks.

Once upon a time, monks, in the distant past, there lived in a certain forest retreat a deer named Śiriprabha. He was gracious, beautiful to behold, and possessed a well-proportioned body; with his hooves and feet red and his eyes anointed [with pigment], he led a herd of five hundred deer.
Now, that king of deer had a chief queen;
she was devoted to his power and faithful to him.
He does not experience separation from that deer even for a moment.
And there was another hunter named Nīlaka;
he had set snares for deer in that forest retreat.
Thus Śrīprabha, surrounded by that great herd of deer while wandering there in the forest retreat, was captured.
When all the male and female deer saw the king of the deer bound, they fled; however, one female deer who was devoted and faithful to that king of the deer remained and did not flee.
And that female deer addressed Śiriprabha with a verse:
Exert yourself, Śiriprabha; exert yourself, O lord of beasts!
Before that hunter arrives who set this snare, cut the leather bond of the snare; I shall find no pleasure without you.
Then, monks, Śiriprabha, the king of deer, addressed that doe with a verse:
I am trying to stride forward, yet I am unable; I fall to the ground with great force.
Firm is the leather strap of the tether, and it cuts into my foot.
The forests, mountains, and groves are delightful;
you shall enjoy them, O blessed lady, together with another husband.
Then, monks, that doe replied to the king of deer with a verse:
Delightful are the forests, mountains, and groves;
I shall take my pleasure with you even in other births.
And having heard them lamenting and wailing,
that hunter, an evildoer of most cruel deeds, went there.

Then the king of deer saw that hunter approaching from afar— black, with white teeth, red eyes, resembling a man-eater, and wearing blue garments— and having seen him, he addressed the doe again in verse:
"Here comes that hunter, dark and clad in blue garments,
who will cut my skin and flesh and kill me."
Not far from him, that doe went out to meet the hunter where he was and addressed him with a verse:
"Spread out the palāśa leaves, O hunter, and draw forth your sword;
having first struck me down, you may afterwards kill the great deer."
Then, monks, this thought occurred to that hunter:
"Deer flee from me even from afar and go out of sight; yet this doe, being utterly unafraid, comes forward facing me after sacrificing her own life—she neither fears nor flees."
Then that hunter, seeing the conduct of that doe, was struck with wonder and filled with amazement:
"Such as this doe is,
we do not possess those virtues which they have."

They are not animals who possess such greatness of virtue, such firmness of mind, such gratitude, and such devotion. We are the ones who are truly animals— those who, while seeking food with our own mouths, would cause harm to such a noble-souled deer as this.
I will not carry this deer away from the snare.
Then the hunter replied to that doe with a verse:
I have neither heard nor seen a female deer speak in human language.
And you, O blessed lady, be happy; I release this great deer for you.
Then that hunter released Śiriprabha, the king of deer, who had been bound by the snare.
Then that doe, seeing the king of deer released, was uplifted, joyful, and filled with gladness and happiness; she addressed the hunter in verse:
In this way, O hunter, rejoice together with all your kinsmen.
"Just as I rejoice today upon seeing the great deer set free,
so too the Blessed One, recollecting his former dwellings and former births,
related this Jātaka in the presence of the monks."
Those aggregates, those elements, and those sense-bases—
the Blessed One explained this matter with reference to the self.
In this beginningless and endless saṃsāra where I formerly dwelt,
I was Śrīprabha and Yaśodharā was a doe.
Ānanda was once a hunter; thus you should remember this Jātaka.
Thus is this ancient cycle, encompassing much suffering and characterized by high and low states of existence.
Free from fever, free from fear, and without sorrow,
he relates his own birth-story in the midst of the community of monks.
Thus concludes the Jātaka of the illustrious Prabhāsa, the King of Deer.
Then, as the Bodhisattva was practicing austerities in the forest of penance at Uruvilvā on the bank of the river Nairañjanā, Māra the Evil One approached him and spoke.
"What will you achieve through renunciation? Dwell in the midst of a household; you shall become a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Perform great sacrifices: the horse sacrifice, the human sacrifice, the Soma-drinking sacrifice, the Nirargada, the Paduma, and the Puṇḍarīka."
Having performed these sacrifices, after death you will rejoice in the heavens and produce much merit;
yet, the abandonment [of worldly life], which is difficult to perform and difficult to attain, is the blameless, meritorious relinquishment and the dwelling in the holy life (*brahmacaryavāsa*).
The Bodhisattva said:
"O Evil One, I have no need for merits;
having seen the delightful forests and groves,
I have directed my exertion toward the vicinity of Uruvilvā."
Having approached him as he was exerting himself to attain the supreme goal,
Namuci came here, speaking words of compassion.
"You are emaciated and ill-colored; death is near for you.
Cease this great exertion; there is no hope for your life."
Life is beneficial and supreme for you; while living, you shall perform meritorious deeds.
Perform those meritorious deeds by which you will not grieve after passing away.
"By practicing the holy life and offering the fire sacrifice, infinite merit is produced; what will you achieve by mere renunciation?"
"Far is the abandonment of hope; it is difficult and hard to accomplish"—this was the speech Māra spoke in the presence of the Bodhisattva.
To Māra, who was thus [addressed], the Bodhisattva then spoke:
"O evil one, kinsman of darkness, I have not come here seeking merit."
O Māra, I have no need for even atom-sized merits;
but as for those who do have need of merits, how is it that you, O Māra, do not know them?
I do not think "I am immortal," for life indeed ends in death;
I shall go forth irreversibly, devoted to the holy life.
This wind might even dry up the currents of the rivers;
why then would it not dry up the blood of me who have exerted my soul?
The body dries up—the bile, the phlegm, and that born of wind;
let the flesh and the blood now waste away.
As the [defilements of] fleshly desires diminish, the mind becomes even more serene;
mindfulness, vigor, and concentration become further established.
And for him who dwells thus, having attained the supreme state, look at the purity of this being; here, this body is not subject to injury.
I possess desire, energy, and wisdom;
I see no one in the world who could turn me back from my exertion. This life-destroying [battle] is at hand; fie upon this vulgar life!
Therefore, being mindful, alert, and free from acquisitions... [the wise one attains final liberation].
Having cultivated both my own mind and that of the other in battle,
and having shattered the forest with my strength, I have accomplished what was to be accomplished.
Beneath the Bodhi tree, before I had attained the state of immortality,
I beheld the army of Namuci, armored and with banners unfurled.
"I shall go forth to battle; I did not sit down for the sake of a place to stay.
I shall bring back that army of yours in due order."
Sensual desires are your first army; the second is said to be discontent;
the third is hunger and thirst; and the fourth is said to be craving.
The fifth is sloth and torpor; the sixth, O timid one, is said to be fear.
The seventh is doubt for you, and the eighth is the purpose of pride.
Greed, fame, honor, and whatever reputation is wrongly acquired—these are [the ninth].
This is the army of Namuci, armored and with banners raised;
here some ascetics and brahmins are seen to be deeply entangled.
The coward does not conquer it, or having conquered it, he grieves;
I shall shatter that [craving] with wisdom, as one breaks an unbaked clay vessel with water.
Having brought them under control and having made the thorn [of defilement] removed,
remaining with mindfulness well-established and possessing attained vigor, I shall indeed discipline my disciples as well.
Foolish people of weak intellect are devoted to negligence;
I shall go for you, even against your will, to where suffering ceases.
While he was overcome with grief, his prosperity went to ruin;
then the yakṣa Surmana vanished right there.

Just as the Bodhisattva, being afraid of intentional lying and loathing intentional lying, rejected that feeling thinking "enough," and then consumed solid, coarse food for his comfort; thereupon the group of five auspicious companions, becoming disillusioned, withdrew from him, saying:
"The ascetic Gautama has fallen away from concentration; he has become lax and has again consumed solid, coarse food."
Māra, the Evil One, followed closely behind the Bodhisattva for six years while he was practicing austerities, seeking an opportunity and searching for a vulnerability.
He too, having followed the Bodhisattva for six years, finding no opportunity, finding no foothold, and finding no basis for attachment, became disillusioned and withdrew.
The world together with its gods honors him who drives away the King of Death— that one whom Māra cannot overcome, just as the wind cannot shake the Himalayas.
The monks said to the Blessed One:
With the intention of liberation, the Blessed One practiced what is difficult to perform.
The Blessed One said:
Monks, it was not only now that I practiced austerities with the intention of liberation.
The monks said.
At other times as well, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
On another occasion as well, monks.

Once upon a time, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi, there was a fowler who would capture birds in forest regions, confine them with nets, snares, and cages, nourish them with fodder and water, and having raised them to great size, sell them for a high price.
There, another bird, having been caught, was confined within a cage.
Now that wise bird saw those birds who had previously been cast into the cage and fattened on grain; when they were grown, people bought them and pulled them out from the cages.
Seeing this, the wise bird thought:
"This man does not provide us with grain or water out of a desire for our welfare; he provides us with grain or water only for the sake of profit, once we have become fully grown."
"Then they would sell it for a desirable price.
Therefore, I shall act in such a way that no one will buy it from me; even when offered an opportunity, no one at all will take it."
I shall take such food as that I shall neither increase in this way nor die.
He now consumes such food and drinks such water that he neither gains in bulk nor dies.
A man, a buyer of birds, is coming.
Then that bird stood right there in front of the door of the cage.
Then that bird-seller, having thrust his hand into the cage, felt for the bird, yet he did not grasp its flesh with his hand; he weighed it, and it was not heavy.
Then, having set it aside to one side from the cage, other birds—those that were large and strong—took up their dwelling there;
yet, regarding that bird as withered and diseased, no one took hold of it.
The fowler also sees:
"This bird must be ill; when it has become ill and is released, it will eat much more of the bait and drink much more water, and then, having become fat, it will grow strong."

"Lest he should make other birds ill through this association; having been taken out from the cage, he is being fed outside the cage, receiving separate food and separate water. When he becomes fat, he will then be sold."
That wise bird also gained the confidence of that fowler;
whenever the fowler opened the door of the cage for the sake of the birds— for the sake of food or water— that bird would enter the cage as if it were unknown to him.
When he is out of sight, he then enters that cage of his own accord;
and when he wishes to go out from the cage, he then runs out by himself.
No one prevented him on the grounds that he was ill.

Now that bird’s body had become so weak that it could enter and exit the cage even through what was not a door; moreover, because they thought the bird was ill, they neglected it. Then, when the bird realized, "These fowlers trust me," it began to consume more fodder and drink more water until it was able to fly far away and escape.
Then, at the moment he became emboldened, thinking, "This is my time to flee," he stood above that cage and at that very moment spoke this verse in front of those birds:
A person who does not reflect does not attain distinction;
see how, through the power of reflection, I have been liberated from my own bondage.
Having spoken this verse, that bird flew up from the fowler's house and returned once more to the forest.
The Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, monks, it might occur to you that at that time, on that occasion, the wise bird was someone else;
it should not be viewed in this way.
And for what reason?
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, I was that wise bird.
That fowler at that time and on that occasion was someone else;
it should not be viewed in this way.
And for what reason?
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, this Māra, the Evil One, was that fowler.
Even then, with the intention of liberating this bird-catcher Māra from his cage, I performed difficult austerities.
Thus ends the Śakuntakajātaka.
The monks said to the Blessed One:
By means of his extraordinary wisdom, the Blessed One—though having become like a bird, fallen into the hands of Māra, and confined within a cage—was liberated.
The Blessed One said:
On another occasion as well, by means of his superior intelligence, he was liberated from having fallen into the hands, the power, and the basket of this Māra.
The monks said.
At other times as well, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
On another occasion as well, monks.
Once upon a time, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi, there was a river named Paripātrikā.
On its bank was Vanamāla, the garden of another florist.

At that time, the florist, having come from the flower garden for the sake of garlands, gathered flowers and took his flower-basket; he emerged from the florist's workshop and set out toward the village.
Not far from that florist, a tortoise emerged from the river and was eating cow dung.
He was seen by that gardener,
who thought to himself:
"This tortoise will make an excellent dish for me today."
Then, having set that flower-basket aside in a secluded spot, he caught the tortoise.
He then placed him there in the flower-basket,
and that tortoise spoke to him in human speech.
"I am smeared with mud; therefore, this flower of mine will be ruined by the mud. Wash it here in the water and place it in the casket;
then these flowers will not be spoiled."
Then that gardener saw it.
"This tortoise is indeed beautiful; I shall go and wash him here in this water, so that these flowers will not be ruined by the mud."
Thus, having stretched out his limbs with the five parts including the trunk upon the paternal domain, he fell from the hand of that gardener.
Standing firmly in that water, having risen onto the bank not far from that river, he addressed the florist with a verse:
“O Pāripātrī, you are free from disease; and as for the farmer, he has done his work by the riverbank according to his strength.
O garland-maker, I am covered in mud; wash me and place me in the basket.”
Then, monks, that gardener addressed the tortoise with a verse:
"Much has been accumulated by me for the king; a great multitude of the three classes has assembled there.
There, O tortoise, you shall sport in a basket fashioned as a palanquin."
Then, monks, that tortoise addressed the garland-maker with a verse:
"O garland-maker, you have many flowers accumulated; the king has brought a large crowd of his three classes together.
You are prattling drunk—eat the auspicious tortoise in oil!"
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it may be that you think thus: 'At that time, on that occasion, the auspicious tortoise was someone else.
It should not be viewed in this way.
For what reason? Because at that time, on that occasion, I myself was that auspicious tortoise."
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, I was that tortoise.
That florist at that time and on that occasion was someone else;
indeed, it should not be viewed in this way. For what reason?
Monks, this very Māra, the Evil One, was at that time and on that occasion that florist.
Even then, I was liberated from the hands of this florist through the excellence of my intelligence;
even now, I am liberated from the realm of this Māra through the excellence of my intelligence.
Thus ends the Kacchapa-jātaka.
Moreover, monks, it was not only now that he was released from this man's domain; on another occasion as well, when I had fallen into his hands, I was released from his domain.
The monks said:
At another time as well, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
On another occasion also, monks.

Once upon a time, monks, in the distant past, on the shore of the ocean there was a great forest tract adorned with various groves and trees of diverse colors, laden with flowers and fruits, and abounding in udumbara trees.
There lived a monkey who was the leader of a large troop of monkeys.
Thus he dwelt there in that forest grove together with that troop of monkeys, in a place that was peaceful, secluded, frequented by many hundreds of deer and birds, and uninhabited by humans.
And that lord of monkeys, there on the seashore, was eating udumbara fruits from a large udumbara forest tree that was thick with branches and foliage.
And then, a great crocodile emerged from the ocean and came to that place.
He was sitting there on the seashore,
and he was seen by that lord of monkeys.
Seeing that crocodile, compassion arose within him:
"Where in the midst of the ocean can these aquatic creatures find flowers or fruits?
What if I were now to give this one some udumbara fruits from here?"
Then he threw down from that udumbara tree very large, ripe udumbara fruits, perfect in color and perfect in flavor; and he ate the udumbara fruits as they fell one after another before him.
In this way, the crocodile came again and again to that place near the monkey.
Thus, that lord of monkeys would cause the udumbara fruits to fall from the tree for every visitor who arrived.
Then both of them, the monkey and the crocodile, became affectionate toward one another.
Now, the wife of that crocodile, not seeing her husband, was filled with longing.
"It must be that my husband has taken another female crocodile;
therefore, he has gone to her side and is sitting with her."
Then she asked her husband:
Where have you gone from my presence to sit?
He said to her:
"On the shore of the ocean, in such-and-such a place, in a great forest tract, there dwells my monkey friend; I sit there in conversation and discourse with him."
Then this thought occurred to that female crocodile:
"As long as that monkey lives, this master of mine will continue to go there and engage in conversation with the monkey.
Therefore, I shall have that monkey killed; once he is killed, my master will no longer go to that place."
Then that female crocodile remained there, having feigned illness.
Then the crocodile asked her:
"O blessed lady, what is your business? What is your suffering? What is your desire? Tell me; what shall I give? Command me."
She said to him:
"Noble son, I have a pregnancy longing for a monkey's heart.
If I obtain a monkey's heart, I shall live; if I do not obtain it, there is no life for me."
He said to them:
"Please grant me your favor; how could there be any movement of a monkey here in the ocean? If you have another intention regarding a water-dweller, I shall provide one for you."
Then she said:
I have no other intention; my intention is for the monkey's heart. Bring that to me if you wish me to live.
Thus he instructs them again and again.
Be gracious, O blessed lady; how could there be a monkey here in the midst of the water?
Then she...
Bring the heart of that monkey who was your friend on the seashore.
He said:
"Please show me favor; that monkey was my companion and my friend—how could I possibly tear out his heart?"
Then she said:
If you are unable to bring my monkey-heart before me, there is no life for me.
Then that crocodile, being well-cared for by that female crocodile, said:
I am an aquatic creature, while that monkey is a land-dweller and a forest-roamer; wherever he roams, there I have no access.
How then can I possibly bring the heart of that monkey?
As it has been said by the wise:
There are one hundred [wives] for Kṣatriyas and two hundred for Brāhmaṇas.
"The illusion of kings is a thousandfold; the illusion of women is endless."
Then she said to that crocodile:
"Tell that monkey, who eats fruit and craves fruit, 'Friend,
here on the far side of the ocean are trees of various colors, laden with the weight of clusters of flowers and fruits of many kinds— mangoes, rose-apples, breadfruits, bhavyas, pālevatas,
kṣīrakas, tindukas, and pippalas.'"
"Come, I will lead you there; you shall enjoy various kinds of fruits.
Then, when he has fallen into your hands, you must kill him and bring his heart."
Then that crocodile agreed.
I shall bring the heart of a monkey from the future; be joyful, do not feel longing any longer, and do not grieve.
Then, having comforted his wife, the crocodile went to that place where the lord of monkeys lived in the forest grove.
Then that lord of monkeys saw the otter;
having seen him, the monkey greeted the otter joyfully and asked:
"Friend, why have you come to visit us after such a long time? Is all well with you, or has there been some affliction to your body?"
Then he said:
"Friend, all is well; there was no affliction whatsoever to my body even after going to the far shore of the ocean and returning."
He asks him: "What is the shore beyond the ocean like?"
The crocodile said:

"Friend, the shore of the ocean is beautiful, adorned with thousands of various kinds of trees endowed with auspicious fruit; it is graced by mangoes, rose-apples, jackfruit, *bhavya* fruits, and *pālevata* trees; and by citron, *tinduka*, *piyāla*, *madhuka*, and *kṣīrika* trees, as well as other species of fruit whose like are not found here."
If it is your intention to come and enjoy various kinds of fruits, then let us go there.
Now, having heard of various kinds of fruits from that monkey who had eaten fruit and was greedy for fruit, the thought arose in him to go there across the ocean.
He then said to that crocodile:
"How can a land-dweller go to the far shore of the ocean?"
The crocodile said:
"I will carry you; climb onto my neck here and lie down, holding on with both hands to the water-jar."
Then that monkey said:
"Let it be so; I shall go, if you so intend."
Then the crocodile said:
Come down; I will lead you away.
Then that monkey, having descended from the udumbara tree, climbed onto the neck of that crocodile and clung to the water-jar with both hands.
Then that crocodile, having seized the monkey, went out into the ocean and, not very far from the sea, made the monkey move about in the water.
Then that monkey said to him:
"Friend, why have you now stirred up water for me?"
He said to him:
"Friend, do you not know for whose sake I have brought you here? My friend has a pregnancy-longing (*dohada*) for a monkey's heart;
therefore, it was for the sake of a monkey's heart that you were brought by me."
"My friend, that wife of mine will devour your heart;
it was for this reason that you were brought by me."
Then that monkey said:

"Friend, my monkey-heart has been placed upon an udumbara tree so that I might cross the ocean more lightly and it may not become too heavy a burden. Therefore, if you have an absolute necessity for a monkey-heart, let us turn back; then, having removed that monkey-heart from the udumbara tree, I shall give it to you."
As that monkey was speaking in this manner, the crocodile believed him.
Then that crocodile, having seized him, turned back and in a short while reached that same region of the forest grove.
Then the monkey, having leaped up from the neck of that crocodile, departed with that udumbara fruit.
Then the crocodile said:
Friend, descend here; take the heart from this udumbara tree.
Then, monks, that monkey addressed the crocodile with verses:
"You are both round and old, yet wisdom is not found in you;
O fool, you do not understand that there is no one anywhere who is without a heart."
One should not disclose a secret matter regarding current affairs;
the wise obtain wisdom like a monkey in the midst of water.
Enough with these mangoes, rose-apples, and jackfruits; what need have I for those that are on the other side of the ocean, when this ripe udumbara fruit is here?
The Blessed One said:
"O monks, it may be that you think thus: 'At that time, on that occasion, was he not some other monkey dwelling in the forest grove on the seashore?
But it should not be viewed in this way. And for what reason? Because..."
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, I was that monkey dwelling in a forest grove on the shore of the ocean.
That one who, at that time and on that occasion, was the crocodile in the great ocean—
it should certainly not be viewed in this way.
And why is that?
At that time, on that occasion, this very Māra the Evil One was the crocodile in the great ocean.
Even then, having fallen into his hands and come under his power, I transcended the realm of that particular Buddha; and now as well, I have transcended the realm of this evil Māra.
Thus ends the Markaṭajātaka.
The monks said to the Blessed One:

Behold, Blessed One, how this Māra, the Evil One, followed behind the Blessed One while he was practicing austerities in the forest of asceticism, seeking an opportunity and searching for a flaw; and finding no such opportunity, he turned back in despondency.
The Blessed One said:

“Monks, it is not only now that this Māra, the Evil One, has followed closely behind me, seeking an opportunity, searching for an opening; and finding no opening, he has turned away in disappointment.
The monks said to the Blessed One: [“Is it so, Blessed One?”]
For it was also at another time, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
At another time as well, monks.
Once upon a time, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi, a fowler set black snares in a forest glade for the sake of birds and scattered bait.
Then, having gone to a secluded spot, he sat within the range of sight of those snares.
And there, another bird, being of a wise nature, was tending a great flock of birds in a forest retreat.
By virtue of that leader of the flock’s exceptional intelligence, that flock of birds increased and did not diminish;
he protected those young birds from the root— from the hands of fowlers, from the hands of outcasts, from the hands of deer-hunters, and even from the hands of cats, jackals, mongooses, and snakes.
Now, while dwelling in that forest region together with a flock of birds from which the fowler had departed,
he arrived at that spot where the fowler had laid those black snares and scattered that bait.
As those birds were wandering in that region, they smelled the scent of sesame, rice, kodrava, and śyāmāka.
Then, having smelled the scent of that bait, as they looked here and there, they saw that bait; and in that place, they saw it surrounding them on all sides.
Those birds addressed that leader of the flock.
"O leader of the herd, let us go to this region where there are sesame and rice, as well as kodrava and śyāmāka grains, and let us eat them."
Then that bird said to those little birds:

"Do not go to this forest retreat; there is no sowing here of rice, *kodrava*, or *śyāmāka*. Furthermore, these and other kinds of crops grow in fields, but they do not exist in any forest retreat. Surely, in this place, bird-catchers have set a death-trap for the sake of the birds and scattered bait; do not settle here."
Practice in whatever manner I practice according to my instruction.
That fowler observed that great flock of birds there in the forest retreat;
thereafter, day after day, he went to various different locations.
In those very places where those birds used to go and roam, on that day snares were set and bait was scattered.
And the leader of the flock of birds, from all sides, drove those birds away from those various spots by means of those black snares and the bait.
In this way, they go forth, longing for the noose of time.
While that fowler was exerting himself there in the forest region within the range of that flock of birds for the sake of baiting them—tormented by hunger and thirst—it occurred to him:
"Now they will be caught; in a moment they will be caught; these birds are coming close to these snares."
Those birds move behind the leader of the flock, keeping close to the perimeter of those death-traps;
they see the bait, yet they do not step onto the ground where the bait and traps are set. Moving at all times, they protect themselves from the death-traps and from the bait.
Then a certain fowler also sees those birds moving about in the vicinity of those dark snares, and this thought occurs to him:
"These are gathering; they will be caught at the wrong time; they will be caught now; they will be caught in a moment."

Thus, in that forest retreat, the fowler— tormented day after day by hunger and thirst for the sake of that flock of birds, with a parched mouth and cracked lips, burning with the cold in the winter season and scorched by the heat in the summer season, and consumed by wind and sun— became exhausted and constantly waited for the wrong time [to hunt] with his bow.
If one goes home with [the object] in hand, one becomes struck down.
But he, seeing that the flock of birds was not weary of him, would constantly come into the range of that flock of birds, cast snares of death, and scatter bait.

Then, in the last month of summer, having gone to that forest retreat, he again set a black snare within the range of that flock of birds, scattered bait, and went to a secluded spot where he remained within the line of sight of the black snare.
And that leader of the flock, while protecting his flock of birds, moved about together with that great flock of birds all around those snares of Death and the bait;
the little birds saw those sesame and rice grains again and again, and having seen them repeatedly, they questioned the leader of the flock.
Let us go and gather these sesame seeds and rice grains.
The leader of the herd speaks.
"Do not settle here! How could there be an abundance of sesame or rice in this wilderness? Sesame comes from fields, and rice, paddy, and other varieties of grain come from cultivated plots.
Do not settle; depart from this place!"
Then that fowler saw him as well.

Thus, for a long time here in this forest retreat, while I was wearying myself for the sake of these birds— setting snares, scattering bait, and spreading nets— in this very region of the forest, over such a vast expanse where I have set my snares and scattered my bait, they have never once appeared.
The little birds here cling to these death-traps or feed upon the offerings.

For many years, while I was suffering— tormented by the cold during the winter season, scorched by the heat during the summer season, struck by wind and sun, and withered by hunger and thirst as I wandered about— it never once happened that, even after wandering for all these years, a single bird from such a vast flock of birds came into my hand.
"What means might there be by which I could bind these little birds with those black snares?"
This thought occurred to him:
"What if I were now to wrap myself in leaves and branches and wait for this flock of birds right where those black snares are?"

Then, monks, at the end of the last month of summer, that fowler, tormented by the summer winds and heat and overcome by hunger and thirst, wrapped himself in leaf-branches and drove that great flock toward those black snares.
Then, monks, those birds, seeing that leader of the flock approaching from a great distance while completely enveloped by the branches of the tree, addressed him.
"Head of the herd, this tree passes by the outermost edge of this flock of birds."
Thus, monks, that leader of the flock, the bird, addressed those birds with a verse.
I have seen in the forest trees such as the aśvakarṇa and the vibhītaka;
likewise the karṇikāra, the mucilinda, and the ketaka.
Those born in the forest remain there, yet this tree is departing;
it is not merely this single tree, for there is something else right there as well.

Then, monks, at that time, that fowler— tormented, exhausted, broken, and overwhelmed by the summer winds and heat in the last month of summer— uttered this verse: "This ancient partridge, having broken through the cage and come forth,
skilled in the snares of death, speaks as he steps forward and backward."
The Blessed One said:

"Furthermore, monks, it might occur to you that at that time, on that occasion, the leader of those flocks of birds, the one who drew them together, the wise bird, was someone else. It should not be viewed in this way."
For what reason?
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, I was a bird, a leader of a flock, one who draws others along, and of a wise nature.
That fowler was someone else;
it should not be viewed in this way.
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, this Māra the Evil One was the fowler.
Even then, having cast my snares, nets, and bait, he followed closely behind me for a long time, seeking an opportunity and looking for a flaw; but finding no opportunity, he withdrew in defeat.
Now too, while I was practicing austerities in the forest of penance for six years, he followed closely behind me, seeking an opportunity and looking for a flaw; but finding no opportunity—
Having become disenchanted, he has turned back.
Thus ends the Śakuntaka-jātaka.
The monks said to the Blessed One:
For the sake of the well-spoken word of the Blessed One, he renounced his own flesh and blood.
The Blessed One said:

Monks, it is not only now that my flesh and blood were sacrificed for the sake of a well-spoken word; on another occasion as well, my flesh and blood were sacrificed by me for the sake of a well-spoken word.
The monks said.
At another time as well, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
On another occasion also, monks.

Long ago, monks, in times past, there lived in the Himalayas a deer named Surūpa. He was handsome, pleasing, and possessed of a delightful body, with red hooves, red antlers, and eyes anointed [with pigment].
With his variegated and well-adorned body, he led a great herd of deer; he was wise, intelligent, and sustained by the merit of very wholesome roots.

By virtue of that deer’s accumulation of merit, the entire herd of deer lived happily there in the Himalayas, grazing on various kinds of food and drinking cool waters; they dwelt there fearless and undaunted, incapable of being harmed by anyone— neither by humans nor by predatory beasts— and were endowed with a capable leader.

In the cold season, he draws that herd of deer toward warm regions; in the hot season, he draws that herd of deer toward cool forest groves. He is beloved by the gods, the nāgas, the yakṣas, the kinnaras, the forest deities, the deer, and likewise by other beings as well.
Then, monks, Śakra, the lord of the gods, desiring to test that deer, transformed himself into the guise of a hunter; having approached the handsome king of deer, he said to that king of deer:
"I have a well-spoken verse; if you will sacrifice your own flesh, then I shall cause you to hear it."
Having heard the words of that hunter, the king of deer became joyful, thinking, "If I hear this well-spoken word even through this nature of destruction, I shall be favored by a great favor.
Then the king of deer said to that deer-hunter:
I sacrifice my own flesh for the sake of the well-spoken word; let me hear the well-spoken word quickly and without obstacle.
Śakra, the lord of the gods, became filled with joy because of that king of deer’s reverence for the Dharma.
He said that to him.
"It would be better to have the dust from the feet of such virtuous persons than a mountain of gold;
for the dust from the feet of virtuous persons leads to the destruction of sorrow, whereas even a mountain of gold leads to the increase of sorrow.
Having thus tested the king of beasts, Śakra, the lord of the gods, vanished on the spot.
A hunter spoke thus to a deer named Surūpa:
"There is a verse of well-spoken words; give me your flesh and listen to me."
If I may hear a well-spoken word in exchange for this flesh subject to decay, I shall give you my flesh; speak quickly that well-spoken word!
The hunter said:
The dust from the feet of the virtuous is better than a mountain made of gold;
that dust leads to the destruction of sorrow, while that mountain increases sorrow.
The Blessed One said:

"Furthermore, monks, it may be that you think thus: 'At that time, on that occasion, was the leader of the deer herd named Surūpa, who lived in the Himalayas, a puller [of the string], and a righteous deer someone else?
It should not be viewed in this way."
For what reason?
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, I was that righteous king of deer named Surūpa, the leader of the herd who drew [the animals] together in the Himalayas.
Just as I sacrificed my flesh and blood for the sake of a well-spoken word at that time, so too have I now sacrificed my flesh and blood for the sake of a well-spoken word.
The Jātaka of Surūpa, the King of Deer, is completed.
Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain together with a great community of monks, with five hundred monks.

Then indeed, the divine son Nanda, the divine son Sunanda, the divine son Sumana, the divine son Īśvara, the divine son Maheśvara, and these and many other divine sons belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host—
possessing surpassing beauty— at the end of the night, having illuminated the entire Gṛdhrakūṭa mountain with their radiance, approached.

Having approached where the Blessed One was, she bowed her head at the Blessed One’s feet and stood to one side, full of reverence and respect, with her robe arranged over one shoulder and her palms joined, paying homage to the Blessed One alone.
As the divine son Nanda stood in a secluded place, this kind of reflection arose in his mind.

This exposition called the Avalokita was spoken and previously spoken by former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones; it would be well if the Blessed One were also to speak it now for the monks.
Having heard it in the presence of the Blessed One and having received it in his presence, they will uphold it in accordance with suchness for the benefit of many,
for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of the great multitude of gods and humans.
Out of compassion, the Blessed One consented to the request of the divine son Nanda by remaining silent.

Then indeed, the divine sons Nanda, Sunanda, Sumana, Īśvara, and Maheśvara, perceiving the Blessed One’s acceptance through his silence, bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated him three times, and vanished on the spot.
Then, indeed, at the end of that very night, the Blessed One approached where the many monks were and sat down on the seat that had been prepared.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed those monks.
Monks, the sons of the gods Nanda, Sunanda, Sumana, Īśvara, and Maheśvara—
possessing transcendent beauty— when the night had passed, illuminated the entire Gṛdhrakūṭa mountain with their radiance and approached the Tathāgata. Having approached the Tathāgata...
Having touched his feet with her head, she stood to one side, full of reverence and respect, with her robe arranged over one shoulder, paying homage to the Tathāgata alone.
Monks, as the divine son Nanda stood to one side, this kind of reflection arose in his mind:
This prophecy named Avalokita was spoken by former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones, and it has been spoken before.
Then, monks, the divine son Nanda addressed the Tathāgata in this way:
"Blessed One, this prophecy named 'Avalokita' has been spoken and previously spoken by former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas."
"It would be well, Blessed One, if you were now to speak to the monks;
having heard it from the presence of the Blessed One, the monks will retain it as such.
That will be for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of a great multitude of beings, both gods and humans."
Out of compassion, monks, the Tathāgata consented to Nanda, the son of the gods, by remaining silent.

Then, monks, the divine son Nanda, the divine son Sunanda, the divine son Sumana, the divine son Īśvara, and the divine son Maheśvara, perceiving through the Tathāgata’s silence that he had consented, were thrilled, satisfied, elated, joyful, delighted,
and filled with gladness.
Having bowed their heads at the feet of the Tathāgata and having circumambulated the Tathāgata three times, they vanished right there.
Then those monks said this to the Blessed One:
"It would be well, Blessed One, if you would explain this matter to the monks; having heard it from the presence of the Blessed One and received it, the monks will retain it as such."
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to those monks:
"O monks, listen well to this exposition of the Avalokita; listen attentively and pay close attention, and I shall speak."
"Excellent, Blessed One," those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this to her.
Monks, when the Bodhisattva gazes from this shore toward the further shore,

as he is being perfected by those qualities that precede his vision, even those gods of great power worship the Tathāgata with the highest and most supreme worship, and honor him with the highest and most supreme honor; and so too do the eighteen Śuddhāvāsa gods.
They obtain the qualities that are to be delighted in.
Which are the eighteen?
The Śuddhāvāsa gods obtain a joyful Dharma [thought], thinking: "The Great Śramaṇa is endowed with the perfection of former yoga.

And they think: "He has attained preeminence through the perfection of prior arising; he is endowed with the perfection of arising as the peerless one in the world, endowed with the perfection of arising as the auspicious one, endowed with the perfection of arising as the foremost, endowed with the perfection of arising as the eldest, and endowed with the perfection of arising as the most excellent."
Endowed with the prior arising of his vow, endowed with his reliance, endowed with his equipment, endowed with his support, and endowed with the provisions,
the Great Śramaṇa will teach the Dharma that is unerring, leading to liberation, supramundane, uncommon, of invincible renown,
and profound in appearance; he will teach the Dharma that is complete in all aspects and pure in all aspects.
Thus, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa realm obtain a dharma that brings joy.
Monks, when the Bodhisattva gazes from this shore toward the further shore, as he is being perfected by those qualities preceded by such gazing,
even those sons of the gods who possess great power pay the Tathāgata the highest, supreme, and most excellent honor.
The Śuddhāvāsa deities honor those who have honored [the Buddha], and they obtain these eighteen qualities that cause joy.
For even the gods, O monks, including Indra, Brahmā, and Prajāpati, obtain a cause for great rejoicing;
yet, O monks, as long as Bodhisattvas are alive, they are not yet fully endowed with all physical strength, nor are they yet fully endowed with all vocal strength. Nor, for that long, are they...

Monks, Bodhisattvas are not yet endowed with all mental qualities in every respect; nor, monks, do Bodhisattvas walk, stand, or sit upon a spot of earth until, monks, having sat down upon that spot of earth, [they have realized their goal].

They slay the great yakṣa, they defeat the great army, they cross over the great flood, and they attain the state of being the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed; they attain the state of being the unsurpassed excellence in the world;
they attain the state of being the unsurpassed source of well-being; and they attain the state of being the unsurpassed recipient of offerings.
They attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; they attain what was spoken just as it was performed; they attain incomparability; they attain peerless sweetness; they attain incomparable likeness;
they attain the basis for great praises, and the praises of reality.

They attain the objective support; they attain the cause for the arising of great things; they attain the cause for the arising of the elements; they attain the state of having laid down the burden; they attain the state of having accomplished what was to be done;
they attain a mind like the earth; and they attain a mind like water.
And they attain it; they attain a mind like fire, they attain a mind like wind, they attain a mind like one terrified by a cat, they attain a mind as soft as kācilindika cloth,
they attain a mind like Indra’s pillar, and they attain the perfection of the faculties.

They attain perfection of strength and they attain perfection of vigor; they attain perfection of wealth and they attain perfection of bedding; they attain self-mastery and physical confidence, and they attain verbal confidence and mental confidence, and they attain vast confidence.
They attain the perfection of wisdom and they attain the perfection of mastery over all wholesome dharmas.
And because, monks, Bodhisattvas are endowed with physical strength in every respect,
endowed with vocal strength, and endowed with mental strength,
they therefore proceed by relying upon that spot of earth, even on whatever spot of earth it may be.

Having sat down, the Bodhisattvas slay the great yakṣa, defeat the vast army, cross over the great flood, and attain the state of being the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed; they attain the state of being the unsurpassed excellence in the world, the state of being the unsurpassed eldest in the world, and the state of being the unsurpassed source of well-being for the world.
They attain unsurpassed worthiness as recipients of offerings; they attain unsurpassed perfect enlightenment;
