they attain acting in accordance with what was spoken and speaking in accordance with what was done;
they attain incomparability; they attain peerless sweetness; and they attain incomparable likeness.
And they attain the objective support of great colors; they attain the objective support of the colors of the elements;
they attain the cause of great arisings; and they attain a mind equal to the earth, they attain a mind equal to water, and they attain a mind equal to fire.

They attain a state of mind equal to the wind; they attain the cause of the arising of those things that serve as objects for the mind; they attain the state of having laid down their burden; they attain the state of having accomplished what was to be done; they attain a state of mind like a pillar trembling with fear of a cat;
they attain a state of mind as soft as kācilindika cloth; and they attain a state of mind like Indra’s pillar.

And they attain the perfection of the faculties, the perfection of strength, the perfection of stamina, the perfection of wealth, the perfection of seating, and the perfection of bedding; they attain self-mastery, confidence of body, confidence of speech, confidence of mind, vast confidence, the perfection of wisdom, and the perfection of mastery over all wholesome dharmas.

Monks, that spot of earth where Bodhisattvas sit and slay the great yakṣas and so forth becomes endowed with sixteen qualities... [and] they attain the perfection of mastery over all wholesome dharmas.
By which sixteen?

Monks, when the world is being destroyed, the region of the earth is the very first to be consumed by fire; and when the world is evolving again, monks, the region of the earth is the very first to be established, and it is established there as something exquisite. Furthermore, monks, that region of the earth is not established in the outlying borderlands; rather, monks, that region of the earth is established in the central lands.
It is established.
Indeed, monks, that region of the earth is not established among the lands of the Mlecchas; rather, monks, that region of the earth is established among the lands of the Āryāvarta.
And that region of the earth, monks, is level, well-prepared, unaltered, and like the palm of a hand.
Even in waterless places, variegated blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lotuses, and fragrant lilies come into being.
And, monks, that region of earth becomes well-known;
and, monks, that region of earth becomes distinguished.
Monks, that region of earth is frequented by beings of great majesty;
monks, that region of earth is difficult to assail;
and monks, that region of earth is unconquerable.
Furthermore, monks, no being whatsoever—whether it be Māra or one belonging to Māra’s host—can gain entry to that spot of earth.
Monks, that spot of earth is not seized by the gods;
rather, monks, that spot of earth is reckoned as the "lion-throne" within the circle of the earth.
And that spot of earth, monks, becomes like a diamond.
And on that spot of earth, monks, there grow grasses only four finger-breadths in height—blue, soft, resembling the neck of a peacock, auspicious, and curling to the right.
Even those universal monarchs, monks, occupy that spot of earth for no other purpose than for the sake of a shrine.

Thus indeed, monks, that spot of earth becomes endowed with sixteen qualities upon which the Bodhisattvas sit and slay the great Yakṣa, and so forth, until they attain mastery and perfection in all wholesome dharmas.

Then, monks, the Bodhisattva, having practiced austerities at Uruvilvā and having taken the honeyed milk-rice from Sujātā, the daughter of the village headman, approached the river Nairañjanā; having cooled his limbs on the bank of the river Nairañjanā, he ate the honeyed milk-rice of Sujātā, the daughter of the village headman.
Having floated a bronze bowl down the Nairañjanā River and having spent the day’s rest right there, he regained his mindfulness at the Nyagrodha tree.
Then, monks, at the time of the dragon’s delight, the Bodhisattva approached the river Nairañjanā; having cooled his limbs in the river Nairañjanā, he proceeded toward the Bodhi tree.
Monks, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva saw between the Bodhi tree and the river a Svastika grass-seller with a heap of grass and a bundle of grass.
Then, monks, the Bodhisattva approached Svastika the grass-cutter and asked him for some grass.
Monks, Svastika gave grasses to the Bodhisattva.
Then, monks, the Bodhisattva, taking a handful of grass, approached the Bodhi tree; yet Māra the Evil One did not see him as he went.
Immediately thereafter, monks, mindfulness returned to Māra the Evil One.
Recalling that mindfulness, he saw the Bodhisattva advancing with fearless prowess.
He strode with the stride of a lion; he strode with the stride of one difficult to overcome; he strode with the stride of an elephant.

He strode with the stride of a lion, he strode with the stride of a bull, and he strode with the stride of a swan; he was the foremost birth, the eldest birth, the birth of the pair, and the birth preceded by his vow.
He strode with the prowess that crushes enemies; he strode with the prowess of the unconquered;
he strode with the prowess of a noble thoroughbred.
He strode with the stride of a Great Being,
seeking the welfare of others, for the sake of accomplishing infinite deeds, for victory in the great battle, and for the attainment of unsurpassed immortality.
Then, monks, as the Bodhisattva was taking his great stride, five hundred peacocks circumambulated the Bodhisattva as he went and followed after him;
five hundred woodpeckers circumambulated the Bodhisattva as he went and followed after him;
and five hundred curlews circumambulated the Bodhisattva as he went.
Five hundred *jīvañjīvaka* birds followed the Bodhisattva as he went, circumambulating him to the right;
five hundred cranes followed the Bodhisattva as he went, circumambulating him to the right.

Five hundred full water-jars followed the Bodhisattva as he went, keeping him to their right in circumambulation; five hundred maidens followed the Bodhisattva as he went, keeping him to their right in circumambulation.
Then, monks, this thought occurred to the Bodhisattva:
And just as these prior arisings and just as these prior signs [indicate] that I shall fully awaken to unimpeded, unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Monks, the nāga king named Kāla saw the Bodhisattva advancing with fearless prowess, and having seen him, he spoke as follows:
"Come, Great Śramaṇa! By whichever path you go, Great Śramaṇa, by that very path the Blessed One, the Great Śramaṇa Krakucchanda, went; he awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
You too, Great Śramaṇa, go by this path; you too, Great Śramaṇa, shall today awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
"The Blessed One, the Great Śramaṇa Konākamuni, also went by this path; he fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Great Śramaṇa, go by this path; you too, Great Śramaṇa, shall today fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
The Blessed One, the Great Śramaṇa Kāśyapa, also went by this path and awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;
you too, Great Śramaṇa, go by this path, for today you too, Great Śramaṇa, shall awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
When this had been said, monks, the Bodhisattva spoke thus to Kāla, the king of the nāgas:
"So it is, O Naga; so it is! Today I shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
Then, monks, the Naga king Kāla praised the Bodhisattva as he was departing with these appropriate verses spoken in his presence:
Just as Krakucchanda, Konākamuni, and Kāśyapa went, so do you go, O Great Hero; today you shall become a Buddha.
Just as you lift up your right foot, O Supreme among Men,
there is no doubt, O Great Hero, that today you shall become a Buddha.
Since this earth resounds like a struck vessel of bronze,
there is no doubt, O Great Hero, that today you will become a Buddha.
And just as my dwelling, which has been shrouded in darkness for a month,
is now filled with light in its entirety, so shall you become a Buddha today.
Just as a treasure remains clearly manifest through its radiance, O wise one,
there is no doubt, O Great Hero, that today you will become a Buddha.
Just as the winds blow, just as the trees sway,
and just as the birds warble, today you shall become a Buddha.
Such is the arising of the Buddhas, and such is enlightenment adorned;
without doubt, O Great Hero, you shall become a Buddha today.
And just as the calyx stands filled with blossoms, O Wise One,
there is no doubt, Great Hero, that today you will become a Buddha.
Just as five hundred cranes are circumambulating you to the right,
there is no doubt, O Great Hero, that today you will become a Buddha.
Just as five hundred peacocks circumambulate you to the right,
there is no doubt, O Great Hero, that today you will become a Buddha.
Just as five hundred pheasants circumambulate you to the right,
there is no doubt, O Great Hero, that today you will become a Buddha.
Just as five hundred cranes are circumambulating you to the right,
there is no doubt, O Great Hero, that today you will become a Buddha.
Just as five hundred swans are circumambulating you to the right,
there is no doubt, O Great Hero, that today you will become a Buddha.
Just as five hundred cranes are circumambulating you to the right,
there is no doubt, O Great Hero, that today you will become a Buddha.
Just as five hundred full jars perform a circumambulation of you,
there is no doubt, O Great Hero, that today you will become a Buddha.
Just as five hundred maidens circumambulate you to the right,
there is no doubt, O Great Hero, that today you will become a Buddha.
Since you possess the thirty-two marks of a Great Man upon your body, O Great Hero, you shine forth without doubt after having conquered the Yakṣa.
Then, monks, the Bodhisattva strode forth with a fearless stride, a stride free from distress, a stride free from dejection, a stride invincible, a stride like a lion’s,
a stride like an elephant’s, a stride like a bull’s, and a stride like a swan’s, for the sake of the supreme birth.

They stride for the sake of generating the eldest; they stride for the sake of generating the most excellent; they stride for the sake of generating the foremost; they stride for the sake of generating the pair; they stride for the sake of subduing enemies; they stride for the sake of invincibility; they stride with the stride of a noble steed (*ājāneya*);
they stride with the stride of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*); they stride for the sake of bringing about the infinite performance of those who desire welfare.
Displaying great valor for the sake of seizing the unsurpassed nectar— the supreme victory over the great village of Māra—

he approached the Bodhi tree; having spread a seat of *samantabhadra* grass at the inner edge of the Bodhi tree, he circumambulated the Bodhi tree three times with the same reverence shown to former Victors.
He sat down, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him, facing straight toward the east.
And as soon as he was seated, monks, the Bodhisattva attained five perceptions.
Which five?
The perception of security, the perception of happiness, the perception of purity, and the perception of benefit: today I shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
And immediately after sitting down, monks, the Bodhisattva attained these five perceptions.

Then, monks, Māra the Evil One— suffering, dejected, and consumed by an internal sting of anguish— approached the Bodhi tree, stood before the Bodhisattva, and sang as if a great song and made a gesture as if throwing off a great cloak; yet he did not gain the Bodhisattva’s attention.
Then, monks, Māra the Evil One—suffering, overcome by dejection, and consumed by the internal sting of anguish—laughed a tenfold great laugh while mocking the Bodhisattva.
Monks, how did Māra the Evil One, suffering, dejected, and consumed by the internal sting of anguish, break into ten kinds of great laughter?

"I possess great supernatural power, O Great Śramaṇa; I am of great majesty. You shall not escape me, O Śramaṇa! Thus spoke Māra the Evil One. Suffering, born of dejection, consumed by the internal sting of anguish, and vexed at the Bodhisattva, he let out a great, mocking laugh.

"I am of great power, O ascetic; you shall not escape me, O ascetic! Thus spoke Māra the Evil One. Suffering, overcome by dejection, and consumed by the internal sting of anguish, he reviled the Bodhisattva and let out a great, mocking laugh.

"I am of great majesty, O ascetic; you shall not escape me, O ascetic! Thus spoke Māra the Evil One, who, becoming sorrowful and dejected, consumed by the internal sting of anguish, and vexing the Bodhisattva, let out a great, mocking laugh.

"I am the great bull, O ascetic; you shall not escape me, O ascetic! Thus spoke Māra the Evil One, miserable, born of dejection, consumed by the burning of an internal sting, and grinding his teeth against the Bodhisattva, he let out a great, loud laugh.

"I am the great victor, O ascetic; you shall not escape me, O ascetic! Thus spoke Māra the Evil One, miserable, born of dejection, consumed by the internal sting of anguish, and vexing the Bodhisattva, he let out a great, mocking laugh.

“I have a great army, O ascetic; you shall not escape me, O ascetic! Thus spoke Māra the Evil One, miserable, born of dejection, born of the burning of an internal sting, and writhing against the Bodhisattva, as he let out a great, mocking laugh.

"I am possessed of great power, O Śramaṇa; you shall not escape me, O Śramaṇa! Thus spoke Māra the Evil One, who was pained, filled with dejection, and consumed by the internal sting of anguish; and as he tormented the Bodhisattva, he let out a great, mocking laugh.

“You are a human being, O ascetic; I, however, am a son of the gods. You shall not escape me, O ascetic! Thus spoke Māra the Evil One, miserable, born of dejection, consumed by the internal sting of anguish, and vexed toward the Bodhisattva, as he let out a great, mocking laugh.

"The body of a śramaṇa is born of mother and father, a heap of boiled rice and gruel, subject to anointing, rubbing, sleep, breaking, scattering, and destruction; but my body is mind-made. O Śramaṇa, you shall not escape from me! Thus spoke Māra the Evil One, who, becoming sorrowful and dejected, consumed by the internal sting of anguish, and vexed at the Bodhisattva, let out a great, mocking laugh.
Thus, monks, Māra the Evil One, miserable and dejected, consumed by the internal sting of anguish, and vexed by the Bodhisattva, let out a great burst of laughter.
Then indeed, monks, the Bodhisattva— fearless, undaunted, and with his hair standing on end from joy— roared at Māra the Evil One in fourteen ways.
And thus, monks, the Bodhisattva, fearless, undaunted, and with his hair standing on end from joy, roared confidently at Māra the Evil One in fourteen ways.
Therefore, O Evil One, I shall destroy you!
Just as a strong wrestler destroys a weak wrestler, so shall I destroy you, O Evil One!
Just as a powerful bull would crush a weak bull, so indeed, O Evil One, shall I crush you.
Just as a noble elephant would crush a plantain tree or an asārikā creeper, so indeed shall I destroy you, O Evil One!
Just as a powerful wind might strike down a weak tree, so indeed shall I crush you.
Just as the rising sun outshines all fireflies, even so, O Evil One, shall I overcome you.
Just as the rising moon outshines all the forms of the stars, even so, O Evil One, shall I overcome you.
Just as Himavat, the king of mountains, surpasses all other mountains at all times, so indeed, O Evil One, shall I overcome you.
Just as a universal monarch [conquers] many individual kings, so too, O Evil One, shall I completely conquer you.
Just as a noble, well-bred horse [surpasses] all other horses, so indeed, O Evil One, shall I terrify you.
Just as the lion, the king of beasts, [overpowers] all small animals, so indeed, O Evil One, I shall cut through your net of delusion.
Just as a strong man [easily tears] a weak net, so indeed, O Evil One, shall I burn away that net of delusion of yours.
Just as a fire [consumes] its fuel, so indeed, O Evil One, shall I reduce you to ashes.
Just as this is connected with its natural outflow, by that means, O Evil One, I shall overcome you.
Just as this is so, O Evil One, being endowed with higher wisdom, I shall indeed cross over, bind you, terrify you, and conquer you;
and here, O Evil One, there shall be no further path for you.
Thus indeed, monks, the Bodhisattva—fearless, undaunted, and free from terror and horripilation—roared back at Māra the Evil One face-to-face in fourteen ways.
The monks questioned the Blessed One.

"Behold, Blessed One, how the householder Jyotiṣka’s home was endowed with such prosperity, possessing unique wealth; and how the Blessed One was propitiated, and he obtained the going-forth and full ordination, and attained the state free from defilements.
Blessed One, whose is this ripening of the fruit of karma for the householder Jyotiṣka?"
The Blessed One said:
Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, ninety-one eons ago from now, there was a king named Bandhuma.
Furthermore, monks, King Bandhuma had a royal capital named Bandhumatī;
it was a city of a wheel-turning monarch in its full extent.
Furthermore, monks, King Bandhumat had a son named Vipaśyin.
Then, monks, the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin went to another region, left the household life for homelessness, and fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Then, at one time, King Bandhuma sent a messenger to the Blessed One Vipaśyin.
"Come, Blessed One, to your own birthplace for the sake of compassion toward us."
Then, monks, having heard the words of the royal messengers, the Blessed One Vipaśyin proceeded toward his own birthplace together with sixty-eight thousand arhats.

At that time and on that occasion, in the royal capital of Bandhumatī, there was a guild-president named Anaṅgaṇa, who was wealthy, possessed of great riches, and endowed with abundant and diverse resources.
The householder Anaṅgaṇa heard that the Blessed One Vipaśyin was approaching together with sixty-eight thousand arhats.
Then this thought occurred to him: "What if I were to go first of all to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One?"
Then the householder Anaṅgaṇa, hurrying with great haste, approached to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One.
The householder Anaṅgaṇa saw the Blessed One Vipaśyin approaching from afar, inspiring confidence, and so forth, surrounded by the community of monks.
Then the householder Anaṅgaṇa approached the Blessed One and, having arrived,
said this to the Blessed One:
"May the Blessed One accept from me, together with the community of monks, a meal for three months," [and he consented] by remaining silent.
King Bandhumā heard that the Blessed One Vipaśyin was approaching with a great saṅgha of monks, sixty-eight thousand arhats; he said, "Therefore, decorate the city!"
(As far as) with great royal majesty (as far as) he saw him who was pleasing to behold (as far as) he invited him (as far as).
"I have accepted, O Great King, the three-month meal-offering from the householder Anaṅgaṇa, together with the community of monks."
Having heard this, the king became filled with longing.
The householder Anaṅgaṇa, without having consulted or looked back upon me, and having shown no respect, approached the presence of the Blessed One and invited the Blessed One;
this was not good.
The Blessed One was addressed by the king.
"Let one daily meal be mine, and the second be his."
The Blessed One said:
If Anaṅgaṇa permits it, then it may be obtained in this way.
Then the king sent a messenger to Anaṅgaṇa, [and so on] until he had arrived.
The king said:

"Householder, the time has come for you, which you have reached, that you act in opposition to the king; you invited me without having asked my permission. You do not know that my son, Vipaśyin, has arrived."
Serve the Blessed One food for three months, together with the community of monks.
The householder said:

"It is not that I lack great respect for Your Majesty; rather, is Your Majesty superior in merit, or am I? I am not superior. However, I shall do exactly as Your Majesty desires. Thus was the Blessed One invited by me.
Then, this thought occurred to Bandhumat:
"If I say, 'Householder, do not do this yet,' he will not grant me permission, the Blessed Vipaśyin will not be pleased with me, and he will not consent [to my request]."
As he was reflecting in this way, he addressed the householder.
"In that case, householder, I shall take turns for the meal;
let it be my turn one day, and yours the second day. He replied, "Certainly!
Why should that not be possible?"
One day's meal was set aside for the king, and the second for Anaṅgaṇa.
Now, the householder Anaṅgaṇa, whatever amount of food he provides for the king on a single day, Anaṅgaṇa necessarily makes it superior to that of another.
Then King Bandhuma addressed his chief minister.

Now, village headman, this householder Anaṅgaṇa’s wealth is much greater than mine; whatever food accrues to the householder does not accrue to me. Therefore, seeing that it is the king’s last day, he makes a special distinction.
Therefore, village headman, you must act in such a way that there will be an expulsion of the householder Anaṅgaṇa, so that he will be restrained.
He was unable to do anything until the three-month period was completed; only two days remained—the fourteenth being the king’s day for receiving alms and the fifteenth being the householder’s.
Now, King Bandhuma had a pleasure grove named Munihata, which was large, extensive, cool, fragrant, serene, and beautiful to behold.
Then, on the fourteenth day of the latter fortnight, the king had the entire sandalwood grove sprinkled and swept,
hung with bundles of silk streamers and garlands, perfumed with incense, and strewn with loose flowers; for each individual sandalwood tree,
he prepared a seat worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold for each individual monk.
Four boys, adorned with all kinds of ornaments, fanned him with a fly-whisk that was entirely white and had a handle made of gold and silver.
On one side, young maidens adorned with every ornament grind together hundreds of thousands of fragrant preparations for ointments;
on the other side, majestic elephants adorned with every ornament and covered with golden nets hold up white parasols.
"By the king's command, throughout the twelve yojanas surrounding Bandhumatī, no one at all shall sell a *śalākā*. Whosoever buys or sells it shall be subject to the penalty of death.
Behold! Even though he was thus restrained, what will that householder do? He cooks his food without being stopped by anyone."
No one shall purchase it; [and so on,] up to: the punishment for execution shall be imposed;
[and so on,] until it is no longer possible to prepare even a hundred varieties of condiments without being obstructed.
From where did the householder have the garden-prepared seats brought? ... (and so on) ... from where did he have the elephant brought?
Then, having heard of such prosperity from the householder Anaṅgaṇa, his heart pierced by the arrows of grief, he remained plunged into an ocean of anxiety.
He now broods with compassion.
He then reflected:

If I do not obtain wood, it is possible to provide even just the tooth-sticks; and if I do not obtain them for the sake of condiments, it is also possible to provide this, having prepared other condiments that are beautiful and excellent.
"Moreover, I do not possess such a sandalwood grove, nor will my arrangement of seats be like that;
I shall have no four sons and one daughter, and I shall have no noble elephants."
In that way, he was filled with longing.
By the power of his merit, Śakra, the lord of the gods, approached and spoke from before him.
"Householder, do not be anxious; prepare the food, attend to the meal, and look after everything—it shall all be provided for.
I will arrange the seating, I will have that circular pavilion measured out, and I will have it made beautiful and well-adorned."
The householder said:
Who are you, worthy sir?
He said:
I am Śakra, the householder, the lord of the gods.
The householder Mudita prepared a sauce with sandalwood wood;
having filled a vessel with ghee and oil, he then had it boiled until it was well-cooked, and with that he prepared the meal.
Śakra, the lord of the gods, addressed Viśvakarman, the son of a god.
And provide for the Blessed One and the community of monks a great circular hall and excellent lodgings and seats.
"Very well, worthy sir," [he replied], and having assented,
the divine son Viśvakarman then manifested a great circular pavilion with sixty-eight thousand [pillars].
Having miraculously created a grove of palm trees— with a trunk made of gold having leaves, flowers, and fruit made of silver, and so on,
up to a trunk made of ruby having leaves and fruit made of beryl, and so forth—
Seats were prepared for each individual monk at the foot of each pillar;
four sons of gods, adorned with every ornament, stood to the left and right fanning them with peacock-feather fans, while four celestial maidens,
likewise adorned with every ornament, ground divine unguents downwind.

For each individual monk, there was a single elephant-nāga like Erāvaṇa following behind, holding a supreme parasol made of the seven precious gems with handles made of beryl; and the elephant-nāga Erāvaṇa held a parasol over the Blessed One.
That great maṇḍala-mansion was strewn with divine flowers as high as the knees, and soft breezes blew;
and when that grove of palm trees was stirred by the wind, a divine sound issued forth.
(As far as) they announce the time to the Blessed One;
(as far as) he enters.
The Blessed One sat down; thereupon, the householder sent a messenger to the king.
"Come, Your Majesty; this very day, on our final day, we shall serve the Saṅgha together."
Then the king, having mounted an excellent vehicle, set out.
King Bandhumat saw from afar an all-white elephant-nāga approaching; having seen it, this thought occurred to him:
"Without a doubt, the householder has had this elephant-nāga made entirely out of alms-food."
Having now arrived and entered, and seeing such a manifold array of splendors, he was struck with wonder and thought, "This marvel has arisen through the power of the householder’s merit."
Now, even a man from the village brought a jar of curd as a gift.
He was asked by Krīyaka for five hundred purāṇas.
Then that village man, filled with agitation, saw:
"Let it not be that these [men],
while they are still in the process of drawing out their wealth, or while they are still in the process of making a decision, or while they are still within the entire Saṃgha..."
Having requested exactly that much wealth.
Then King Bandhuma said to Anaṅgaṇa, the leader of the Māṇavas: "And what about these five hundred purāṇas? What will come of this?"
He then asks:
What will this be?
They said:
The Blessed One Vipaśyin was being served by sixty-eight thousand arhats.
He then thought:
"The appearance of Tathāgatas, up to and including Fully Enlightened Ones, in the world is rare."
"What if I were now to serve this pot of curd myself to the Buddha and the rest of the assembly?"
Then he himself, having requested as much as needed from the entire Saṅgha, [received] exactly that amount.
Then King Bandhuma, together with the householder Anaṅgaṇa and such a retinue, served the Blessed One along with the community of disciples.
When the Blessed One had finished eating, washed his hands, and set aside his bowl, the householder then made a formal vow.

"Whatever outflow of merit, whatever outflow of virtue, and whatever foundation of happiness may arise for me from this relinquishing of my gift of Dharma, may that become a divine enjoyment not shared [with others]. May I please such a Teacher who might teach the Dharma, and may I understand it; having gone forth, may I become free from the afflictions."
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it might occur to you that at that time, on that occasion, the merchant named Anaṅgaṇa was someone else.
It should not be viewed in this way.
The householder Jyotiṣka was, at that time and on that occasion, the householder named Anaṅgaṇa... [up to] his vow was fulfilled by Sarvārthasiddha."
Then indeed Māra the Evil One, suffering, overcome by dejection, and consumed by the internal sting of anguish, uttered a great lamentation endowed with sixteen aspects.
And how, monks, did Māra the Evil One, suffering, dejected, and consumed by the internal sting of anguish, utter his great lamentation endowed with sixteen aspects?

"Alas, while I am possessed of such great supernatural power (*maharddhika*), may it not be that this ascetic will overcome me! Thus Māra the Evil One, suffering, filled with dejection, and consumed by the internal sting of anguish, uttered a great lamentation.
"Alas, while I am possessed of such great majesty (*mahāprabhāva*), may it not be that... [he continued].

Thinking, "Lest the ascetic Gautama should overcome me," Māra the Evil One, suffering, born of dejection, and consumed by the internal sting of anguish, uttered a great lamentation. Thinking, "Alas, though I am of such great power, lest the ascetic Gautama should overcome me," Māra the Evil One, suffering, born of dejection, and consumed by the internal sting of anguish, uttered a great lamentation.

"Alas, he possesses such great majesty! May the ascetic Gautama not overcome me, who am his equal! Thus Māra the Evil One, suffering and filled with dejection, consumed by the internal sting of anguish, uttered a great lamentation. "Alas, he possesses such great bull-like prowess! May the ascetic Gautama not overcome me, who am his equal! Thus Māra the Evil One, suffering and filled with dejection, consumed by the internal sting of anguish, uttered a great lamentation.

Lamenting with great wailing: "Alas! Though I possess such great prowess, may the ascetic Gautama not indeed overcome me!"—thus Māra the Evil One, miserable, born of dejection, and born of the burning pain of an internal sting, lamented with a great lamentation.

"Alas, my great power is equal [to his]; let it not be that the ascetic Gautama will overcome me! Thus Māra the Evil One, suffering, born of dejection, and born of the burning of an internal dart, uttered a great lamentation. "Alas, my great strength is equal [to his]; let it not be that the ascetic Gautama will overcome me! Thus Māra the Evil One, suffering, born of dejection, and born of the burning of an internal dart, uttered a great lamentation.

Lamenting, Māra the Evil One—thinking, "Gautama the ascetic has become a human being, whereas I am the son of a god; let it not be that Gautama the ascetic shall overcome me"—became sorrowful, dejected, and consumed by the internal sting of anguish, and he uttered this great lamentation: "In lamentation: Gautama the ascetic has become a human being, while I am the son of a deity. Let it not be that Gautama the ascetic shall prevail over me! Thus Māra the Evil One, miserable and dejected, born of the burning pain of an internal thorn, uttered this great lamentation.

"The body of the ascetic Gautama is born of mother and father; it is coarse, a mass of boiled rice and sour gruel, subject to covering, rubbing, pressing, breaking, scattering, and destruction. But my body is mind-made. Let it not be that the ascetic Gautama should overcome me! Thus Māra, the Evil One, became sorrowful and dejected.
Born from the burning pain of an internal thorn, he uttered a great lamentation:

"Even those who are heroes, champions, and supreme men do not know how to cast off this human state, lest the ascetic Gautama should overcome me. Thus Māra the Evil One was miserable, filled with dejection, and born from the burning pain of an internal thorn.
I lamented with great lamentation:

"In whatever way I think, 'Today I shall overcome the ascetic Gautama,' in that very way my mental preoccupation is quickly extinguished; may it never be that the ascetic Gautama [should overcome me]."
Thinking, "He will overcome me," Māra the Evil One, miserable and born of dejection, consumed by the internal sting of anguish, uttered a great lamentation.

And as his army was falling into ruin, thinking, "May this ascetic Gautama not indeed overcome me," Māra the Evil One, miserable and born of dejection, consumed by the internal sting of anguish, uttered a great lamentation.

"Alas, my limbs are failing me! May the ascetic Gautama not overcome me! Thus Māra the Evil One, miserable and dejected, burning with the internal sting of grief, uttered a great lamentation: "Alas, my exertion is in vain! Alas, my labor is in turmoil! May the ascetic Gautama not overcome me! Māra the Evil One was thus miserable and dejected, burning with the internal sting of grief.
He lamented with a great lamentation:
"Even those sons of the gods belonging to my own domain and body are now part of the inner retinue of the ascetic Gautama;
let it not be that the ascetic Gautama shall overcome me! Thus Māra the Evil One became sorrowful, born of dejection, and consumed by the internal sting of anguish.
He lamented with a great lamentation.
In this way, monks, Māra the Evil One, suffering, born of dejection, and consumed by the internal sting of anguish, uttered a great lamentation endowed with sixteen modes.
Then indeed, monks, the Bodhisattva— fearless, undaunted, and free from terror and horripilation— grasped the noble arrow, which was endowed with thirty-two characteristics.
And how, monks, did the Bodhisattva—fearless, undaunted, and free from terror and horripilation—assume the noble pride endowed with thirty-two aspects?
A bodhisattva who aspires to a great purpose maintains noble pride;
a bodhisattva who aspires to a fulfilled purpose maintains noble pride;
a bodhisattva who aspires to a sublime purpose maintains noble pride.
Seeking a completely pure meaning, the bodhisattva maintains noble pride;
seeking an unerring meaning, the bodhisattva maintains noble pride;
seeking a previously unknown meaning, the bodhisattva maintains noble pride.
Seeking the meaning of definitive deliverance, the bodhisattva maintains noble pride;
seeking the supramundane meaning, the bodhisattva maintains noble pride; seeking the uncommon meaning, the bodhisattva maintains noble pride.
Seeking an indestructible goal, the bodhisattva maintains noble pride;
seeking a future goal, the bodhisattva maintains noble pride;
there is no happiness that he has not relinquished for the sake of attaining that goal—the bodhisattva maintains noble pride.

There is no happiness in the world beyond this world that I have not renounced for the sake of attaining that goal; for the sake of attaining that goal, the Bodhisattva maintains noble pride. There is no suffering in the world that I have not taken upon myself for the sake of attaining that goal; for the sake of attaining that goal, the Bodhisattva maintains noble pride.
There is no delight in the world that I have not renounced for the sake of attaining that goal; for the sake of attaining that goal, the Bodhisattva maintains noble pride.

There is nothing in the world that the Bodhisattva does not relinquish for the sake of attaining that goal; he maintains noble pride for the sake of attaining that goal. There is no sovereignty in the world that the Bodhisattva does not relinquish for the sake of attaining that goal; he maintains noble pride for the sake of attaining that goal.
Furthermore, it is certainly not for the sake of delighting in sensual pleasures that the Bodhisattva maintains noble pride.

Then indeed, being detached from all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), the Bodhisattva, thinking "I shall bring about the transcendence of all conditioned phenomena," exerts noble pride (*āryamāna*).
Endowed with prior arising, the Bodhisattva exerts noble pride; endowed with foremost arising, the Bodhisattva exerts noble pride.
The Bodhisattva, perfected in his vow, maintains noble pride;
the Bodhisattva, perfected in his reliance, maintains noble pride;
the Bodhisattva, perfected in his conduct, maintains noble pride.
A bodhisattva endowed with support maintains noble pride; a bodhisattva endowed with the accumulations maintains noble pride;

thinking, "I am one who has firmly undertaken [the practice] regarding wholesome qualities, and that undertaking was never broken by me before, nor shall I break it," the bodhisattva maintains noble pride.

"I am one of firm mind, of stable mind; indeed, I shall attain that stage which is to be attained by one of firm mind and stable mind"—thus does the bodhisattva grasp noble pride. "I am a great tree, of immeasurable mind; indeed, I shall attain that stage which is to be attained by a great tree of immeasurable mind"—thus does the bodhisattva grasp noble pride.
“I shall attain the supreme stage through supreme vigor; my vigor is supreme,” thus the bodhisattva exerts noble pride.
“I shall attain that stage, having attained which I will accomplish the welfare of the great mass of people,” thus the bodhisattva exerts noble pride.
In this way, monks, the Bodhisattva—fearless, undaunted, and free from terror or horripilation—assumed the noble pride endowed with thirty-two aspects.
Then, monks, the Bodhisattva—fearless, undaunted, and free from terror and horripilation—manifested a fivefold noble smile.
And how, monks, did the Bodhisattva, fearless, undaunted, and free from fear and horripilation, manifest the fivefold noble smile?
Namely: that supported by zeal, supported by energy, supported by mindfulness, supported by concentration, and supported by wisdom.
In this way, monks, the Bodhisattva—fearless, undaunted, and free from terror and horripilation—manifested the fivefold noble smile.
Then, monks, the Bodhisattva— fearless, undaunted, and free from terror or horripilation— cast about with the fourfold gaze of a noble great lion.
And how, monks, does the Bodhisattva, fearless, undaunted, and free from terror or horripilation, perform the fourfold noble great lion’s gaze?
That is to say: he looks about without agitation, he looks about without fear,
and he looks about without terror.
And he beheld him free from fear and with the hair of his body no longer bristling.
In this way, monks, the Bodhisattva gazes with the fourfold gaze of the noble great lion.
Then, monks, the Bodhisattva—fearless, undaunted, and free from terror or horripilation—performed the fourfold yawn of the noble great lion.
And how, monks, does the Bodhisattva, fearless, undaunted, and free from terror and horripilation, display the fourfold noble great lion’s yawn?
That is to say: he yawns fearlessly, he yawns without agitation, he yawns without trepidation; and furthermore, terrifying both Māra and the assembly of Māra, he yawns with the yawn of a great lion.
And thus, monks, the Bodhisattva performed the fourfold noble great lion’s yawn.
Then, monks, the Bodhisattva—fearless, undaunted, and free from terror or horripilation—uttered a great lion’s roar.
And how, monks, did the Bodhisattva, fearless, undaunted, and free from terror or horripilation, utter the roar of the noble great lion?
That is to say: he coughs fearlessly, he coughs without agitation, he coughs without terror, and he coughs without trepidation.
Moreover, monks, this was the noble lion’s roar of the Bodhisattva;
all the people throughout the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system heard that sound.
Thus indeed, monks, the Bodhisattva—fearless, undaunted, and free from terror or horripilation—uttered the fourfold noble lion’s roar.
Then, monks, Māra the Evil One— suffering, overcome by dejection, and consumed by the internal sting of anguish—
arrayed a great fourfold army and approached the foot of the Bodhi tree;
standing before the Bodhisattva, he raised a great clamor and a loud, thunderous shout.
Namely: "Take this away, carry this out, kill this! O hosts of Māra, may it be well with you!"

Then, monks, the Bodhisattva— fearless, undaunted, and free from terror or horripilation— drew forth his gold-colored arm from his robe. With his jewel-like right hand, which was webbed, possessed copper-colored nails with beautiful lines, had the hue of a coating of lac-juice, was soft like the touch of cotton, and was endowed with the roots of merit accumulated over many millions of eons, he [stroked it] three times.
Having stroked his head with his right hand and having smoothed his couch, he strikes the earth with his right hand.

Then, monks, when the Bodhisattva touched his head with his hand, touched his cross-legged posture with his right hand, and struck the earth with his right hand, this great earth resounded and reverberated with a deep and terrifying sound.
It was just as if, monks, a great Magadhan bronze gong were struck upon a stone slab within a mountain cave.
Just as when a great drum is struck, a deep and terrifying sound resounds and reverberates, even so, monks,
when the Bodhisattva touched his head with his right hand, touched his cross-legged posture with his right hand, and struck this earth with his right hand,
this great earth resounded and reverberated with a deep and terrifying sound.

That army of Māra, though so well-provided and so well-equipped, became afraid, terrified, distressed, and agitated; their hair stood on end as they wandered about and dissolved away. Even their elephants sank down, their horses sank down, their chariots sank down, their foot soldiers sank down, and even their weapons sank down.
Others stretched out their hands;
others fell head-first; others fell with their backs bent forward; others fell face-up; others fell on their left sides; others fell on their right sides.
And Māra the Evil One, miserable and dejected, consumed by the internal sting of anguish, sat brooding at one side, scratching the ground with a stick.
"The ascetic Gautama will overstep my domain."

Then, monks, the Bodhisattva— fearless, undismayed, and free from fear and horripilation— dwelt having attained the first dhyāna, which is secluded from sensual desires, secluded from evil and unwholesome states, and characterized by applied and sustained thought, born of seclusion, and filled with zest and happiness.

With the subsiding of applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), through internal clarity and the unification of the mind, one enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is free from applied and sustained thought, born of concentration, and characterized by rapture and bliss.
With the fading away of rapture, one dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, experiencing bliss in the body.
That which the noble ones describe as "dwelling having attained the third dhyāna, equanimous, mindful, and abiding in happiness"—

by the abandoning of pleasure and the disappearance of all prior joy and dejection, he dwelt having attained the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness.

Then, monks, the Bodhisattva— fearless, undismayed, free from terror and horripilation— directed his mind toward the realization of the knowledge and vision of the divine eye during the first watch of the night.

He directs his attention; with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn— fair and ugly, in happy states and miserable states, lowly and exalted— and he understands all of them according to their karma.
These beings, sirs, were possessed of misconduct of body, possessed of misconduct of speech, and possessed of misconduct of mind;

they were revilers of the noble ones and held wrong views. Because of their undertaking of actions based on wrong views, and for that cause and that condition, upon the breakup of the body after death, they have been reborn in states of deprivation, in miserable destinies, in perdition—in the hells. These...

Furthermore, sirs, those beings who are endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech, and endowed with good conduct of mind; who do not revile the noble ones and possess right view; because of their undertaking of actions based on right view, and by reason of that cause and that condition, after the breaking up of the body, after death, they are reborn in a heavenly world among the gods.
With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—beings who are beautiful or ugly, in happy states or miserable states, lowly or exalted;
he knows beings according to their karma as they go.
Then, monks, the Bodhisattva— fearless, undaunted, and free from terror and horripilation— at the middle watch of the night, directed his mind toward the knowledge of recollecting former existences;
he recollected various former existences,
such as one birth, two births, three births, four births, or five births.

For ten births, or twenty births, or thirty births, or fifty births, or a hundred births, or a thousand births, or a hundred thousand births; or for a kalpa of dissolution, or a kalpa of evolution, or a kalpa of both dissolution and evolution;
or even for many kalpas of dissolution, many kalpas of evolution, or many kalpas of both dissolution and evolution.

"I was there, with such a name, such a clan, such a caste, such food, such a limit to my lifespan, and such an experience of pleasure and pain"— thus he recollects his manifold past abodes with their modes and details.

Then indeed, monks, fearless, undaunted, and free from fear and horripilation, during the last watch of the night at the time of dawn, when the night was smiling with joy, whatever [is to be achieved] by a man who is a true man,
a great man, a bull among men, a substance among men, a hero among men, a warrior among men, an elephant among men, a lion among men—
[He is] a lotus among men, a white water-lily among men, a white lotus among men, a thoroughbred among men, a leader among men,

the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed; having gone forth, being valiant, having exerted himself, seeking the goal, vigilant, ardent, resolute, dwelling in seclusion, possessed of wisdom, mindfulness, and fortitude.
By one who is wise and possessed of insight, everything must be known, attained, understood, and fully awakened to in every respect and for all purposes;
and by means of wisdom conjoined with a single moment of mind, he has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment—namely:
"This is suffering, this is the origin of suffering, this is the cessation of suffering, and this is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
These are the taints; this is the origin of the taints; this is the cessation of the taints; this is the practice leading to the cessation of the taints.
Here, the taints are ceased without remainder, completely extinguished, abandoned, and brought to an end.
That is to say: when this exists, that comes to be; when this does not exist, that does not come to be.
"From the arising of this, that arises;
from the cessation of this, that ceases. Thus:

with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises; with name-and-form as condition...

The six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases is contact; conditioned by contact is feeling; conditioned by feeling is craving; conditioned by craving is clinging; conditioned by clinging is existence; conditioned by existence is birth; and conditioned by birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair come into being.
Thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.

Thus, with the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations, the cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, the cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, the cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases, the cessation of contact;
with the cessation of contact, the cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling, the cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving, the cessation of clinging.

From the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of becoming; from the cessation of becoming comes the cessation of birth; from the cessation of birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
Thus occurs the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all conditioned phenomena are suffering; all dharmas are without self.

This is peaceful, this is sublime, this is as it truly is, this is unerring: namely, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the stilling of all formations, the cutting off of phenomena, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, which is Nirvana.
Then, monks, at that time the Tathāgata uttered this inspired utterance:
The ripening of merit is happy, and one's intention succeeds;
quickly one attains supreme peace and nirvana.
Whatever obstacles there may be before them, even deities belonging to the host of Māra, are truly unable to create any hindrance for one who has performed meritorious deeds.
Those obstacles that exist for one of little merit do not exist for the meritorious person. One's meditative concentration (*samādhi*) becomes powerful through the accumulation of merits.
Whatever a person who has performed merit desires—whether in the world of the gods or among humans who possess sovereign power—it is accomplished for them accordingly.

Or rather, he who aspires to Nirvana—the deathless state, free from sorrow—attains the path that pacifies suffering. With little exertion, supreme enlightenment has been touched by me here; through wisdom and vigor, suffering has been liberated, the heavy burden of delusion cast off, and omniscience attained. Māra, along with his army and mounts, has been struck down and reduced to ashes; I stand at that most excellent Bodhi tree, having brought an end to Death itself.
For seven days, they worshipped [him] while seated on a single seat, making offerings to thousands of millions of deities.
Upon that seat they scattered divine sandalwood powder and scattered māndārava flowers;

divine musical instruments resounded above without being struck. Then the gods scattered divine sandalwood powder from above, as well as divine aloe-wood powder, divine keśara powder, and divine tamāla-leaf powder.

They rained down divine *māndārava* flowers, great *māndārava* flowers, *karkārava* flowers, great *karkārava* flowers, *rocamāna* flowers, great *rocamāna* flowers, *bhīṣma* flowers, great *bhīṣma* flowers, *samantagandha* flowers, great *samantagandha* flowers,
*mañjūṣaka* flowers, great *mañjūṣaka* flowers, divine *pārijātaka* flowers, and divine golden flowers.
Golden flowers,

silver flowers, and flowers made of every kind of jewel rained down; thirty million divine flowers made of jewels appeared in the sky and covered the body of the Jina, which was like a mountain composed of precious gems.
Or a stūpa made of gold, endowed with the roots of merit from many millions of eons.
Then, monks, many gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host approached the Tathāgata;

having bowed their heads at the feet of the Tathāgata, they stood to one side, full of reverence and respect, with their robes arranged over one shoulder and their palms joined, paying homage to the Tathāgata alone.
Standing to one side, those many monks and sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm roared at Māra the Evil One face-to-face in eighty ways.
By which eighty?
"Indeed, O Evil One, it did not occur to you:
'I do not see any point of defeat for the ascetic Gautama among gods or humans; what if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"
"O Evil One, did it not occur to you:
'These sons of the gods belonging to my own domain, who are the inner retinue of the ascetic Gautama—what if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"
"O Evil One, did it never occur to you that beings such as these are perfected through their past applications, such that I should now become disillusioned with the ascetic and depart?"
"O Evil One, did it not occur to you that beings of such a nature are close to nirvāṇa, such that I should now become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?"
"O Evil One, it did not occur to you:
'Beings of such a nature are endowed with such radiance; what if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"
"O Evil One, did it not occur to you that beings of such a kind, endowed with perfect conduct, do not become weary of the ascetic Gautama and depart from him?"
"Indeed, Evil One, did it not occur to you:
'Beings of such a kind are endowed with a perfect descent into the womb; what if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart? Indeed, Evil One, did it not occur to you?"
Beings of such a nature are endowed with a perfected stay in the womb; what if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?
"O Evil One, it did not occur to you:
'Beings of such a kind are endowed with noble birth; what if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"
"O Evil One, did it not occur to you that beings of such a kind are endowed with noble lineage, such that I should now become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?"
It did not occur to you, O Evil One, that this was so.
Beings of such a kind become endowed with the marks; what if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?
O Evil One, did it not indeed occur to you?
Beings of such a kind are endowed with the secondary marks; what if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?

"O Evil One, did it not occur to you that such beings as these— having performed their duties and being endowed with the Dharma— are those from whom I should now become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?"
"O Evil One, it did not occur to you that beings of such a kind are endowed with excellence; 'What if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"
"O Evil One, it did not occur to you:
'Beings of such a kind are endowed with beauty; what if I were now to depart after causing dissension among the ascetic Gautama?'"
O Evil One, did this thought not even occur to you?
Beings of such a kind are endowed with excellent appearance and complexion; what if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?
"O Evil One, it did not occur to you that beings endowed with such high resolve could exist; otherwise, you would surely have become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and departed."
Surely, O Evil One, this thought did not occur to you:
Beings of such a kind are endowed with true excellence; what if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?
"O Evil One, did it never occur to you that beings of such a nature are endowed with every excellence, such that I should now become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?"
"O Evil One, did it not occur to you:
'Beings such as these are perfected in their bodily actions; what if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"
"It did not occur to you, O Evil One, that beings endowed with such verbal action as these exist;
'What if I were to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"
"O Evil One, it did not occur to you:
'Beings such as these are perfected in the work of the mind; what if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"

"O Evil One, did it not occur to you that beings of such a kind are endowed with the very essence of sentient beings, such that you thought, 'What if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"

"O Evil One, it did not occur to you that beings of such a nature are endowed with the most excellent essence, such that you thought, 'What if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"
"O Evil One, it did not occur to you:
'Beings of such a nature are endowed with the quality of non-retrogression; what if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"
"O Evil One, it did not occur to you:
'Beings such as these are endowed with such beauty; what if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"
"O Evil One, did it not occur to you that beings of such a kind are endowed with the means of subsistence, so that I might now become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?"
"O Evil One, it did not occur to you that beings of such a nature are endowed with such conduct, that I should now become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart."
"O Evil One, it did not occur to you that beings of such a kind are endowed with great compassion, such that I might now become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart."
"O Evil One, it did not occur to you:
'Beings of such a kind possess a perfect dwelling; what if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"
"O Evil One, it did not occur to you:
'Beings of such a kind are endowed with great majesty; what if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"
"O Evil One, did it not occur to you:
'Beings of such a kind are endowed with mastery over the Dharma; what if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"
"O Evil One, it did not occur to you that beings of such a kind are endowed with the Great Dharma; therefore, why should I now become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?"
"Indeed, O Evil One, this thought did not occur to you."
Beings of such a kind are successful in the world; what if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?
"O Evil One, did it not occur to you:
'Beings of such a kind are endowed with the investigation of the world; what if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"

"O Evil One, did it not occur to you that beings of such a kind are endowed with the discernment of the world, such that you thought: 'What if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"
"O Evil One, did it not occur to you that beings of such a kind possess such supernatural power, that I should now become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?"

"O Evil One, it did not occur to you that beings endowed with such factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣika-dharma) exist, such that you thought, 'What if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"
It did not occur to you, O Evil One,
that beings of such a kind are endowed with such exertion, that I should now become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart.
"O Evil One, it did not occur to you that beings of such a nature are endowed with vigor, such that you thought: 'What if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"
"O Evil One, it did not even occur to you:
'Beings such as these are endowed with mindfulness; what if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"

"O Evil One, it did not occur to you that beings of such a kind are endowed with meditative concentration, such that you thought, 'What if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"
"O Evil One, it did not occur to you that beings endowed with such wisdom are like this, and that you might now become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart."
"O Evil One, it did not even occur to you:
'Beings of such a nature are endowed with liberation; what if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"
"O Evil One, did it not occur to you:
'Beings such as these are endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation; what if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"
"O Evil One, it did not occur to you that beings such as these are endowed with such eloquence; why then should I not become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?"
"O Evil One, it did not occur to you:
'Beings of such a nature are endowed with the [ability for] prophecy; what if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"
"O Evil One, it did not occur to you:
'Beings such as these are endowed with the perfection of the teaching of the Dharma; what if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"
"O Evil One, it has not occurred to you that beings such as these are endowed with the teaching of the blameless Dharma; why then should I become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?"
"O Evil One, did it never occur to you that beings endowed with such wisdom exist, that I should now become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?"
"O Evil One, did it never occur to you that beings of such a nature are endowed with true vision, such that I should now become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?"
"O Evil One, did it not occur to you that beings endowed with such knowledge and vision exist, such that I should now become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?"
"O Evil One, did it not occur to you:
'Beings of such a kind are endowed with imperturbability; what if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"
"O Evil One, did it not occur to you that beings of such a nature are endowed with protection, such that I should now become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?"
"O Evil One, did it not occur to you that beings such as these have been perfected since their previous births, such that I should now become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?"

"O Evil One, did it not occur to you that beings endowed with such qualities as these arise only at the appearance of a [Buddha] Yuga? 'What if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"
"O Evil One, it did not occur to you that beings of such a kind are endowed with the excellence of noble birth, that I should now become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart."
"O Evil One, it did not occur to you that beings of such a nature are endowed with the excellence of being foremost; 'What if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"

"O Evil One, it did not occur to you that beings such as these are endowed with the excellence of being the eldest-born, such that you thought: 'What if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"

"O Evil One, it did not occur to you that beings of such a kind, endowed with the excellence of a supreme birth, could exist; therefore, why should I not become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?"
"O Evil One, did it not occur to you that beings such as these are perfected by the prior generation of their vows, such that I should now become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?"
"O Evil One, it did not even occur to you that beings of such a kind are endowed with supreme excellence, that I should now become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart."
It did not occur to you, O Evil One,
that beings of such a kind are endowed with such an accumulation of merit, that I should now become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart.
"O Evil One, did it not occur to you that beings such as these are skilled in providing support, so that I might now become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?"
"O Evil One, did it not occur to you:
'Beings such as these are endowed with such accumulations; what if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"

"O Evil One, did it not occur to you that beings of such a nature are endowed with the noble five-limbed concentration, such that you thought, 'What if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"

"O Evil One, did it not occur to you that beings of such a nature—endowed with the noble Great Five-Limbed Samādhi—are not to be treated thus? Why then should I become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?"

"O Evil One, did it not occur to you that beings of such a kind, endowed with the five noble lineages, do not become weary of the ascetic Gautama, and that you should therefore depart from him in disillusionment?"

"O Evil One, it did not occur to you that beings such as these, endowed with a noble and great family of five, could exist; therefore, why should I now become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?"
"O Evil One, it did not occur to you:
'Beings of such a kind possess one-pointedness of mind; what if I were now to depart from the ascetic Gautama in disillusionment?'"

"O Evil One, did it not occur to you that beings of such a nature are endowed with the state of being free from conflict (*araṇā*), such that you thought: 'What if I were now to depart from the ascetic Gautama in disillusionment?'"
"O Evil One, did it not occur to you:
'Beings of such a kind as these are endowed with the power to crush the armies of their enemies; what if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"
"O Evil One, it did not occur to you that beings of such a nature are perfected by themselves; 'What if I were now to depart from the ascetic Gautama in disillusionment?'"
"O Evil One, did it not occur to you that beings such as these are endowed with the nature of self-arisen dharmas, such that I should now become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?"
"O Evil One, did it not occur to you:
'Beings of such a nature are endowed with the foremost and supreme Dharma-nature; what if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"
"O Evil One, did it never occur to you:
'Beings of such a kind are endowed with the perfection of merit; what if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"
"O Evil One, did it not occur to you:
'Beings such as these are endowed with the foremost and supreme perfection of complexion; what if I were now to become disillusioned with the ascetic Gautama and depart?'"
"O Evil One, did it not occur to you that beings of such a form are endowed with beauty? Furthermore, O Evil One, such beings are difficult to overcome.
Behold, O Evil One, how great this transgression is!"
Standing to one side, the monks who were among the Śuddhāvāsa deities roared directly at Māra the Evil One with these eighty modes.
The Blessed One said this while staying at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain.
And as this exposition was being spoken, the minds of five hundred monks were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging.
With uplifted hearts, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.
The Sūtra named Avalokita is completed.
Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was staying in Vaiśālī at the Āmrapālī grove together with a great community of monks and a great host of bodhisattvas.

Then the monk Viśuddhamati rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows:

May the Blessed One explain that which was surveyed by the Blessed One while he was a bodhisattva, having approached the seat of awakening and stood upon the seat of awakening for the benefit of the entire world and for the happiness of the entire world; that will be for the welfare of many people,
for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, and for the sake, benefit, and happiness of the great mass of beings, including the gods.
A great light of Dharma will be made for human beings, bodhisattvas, and mahāsattvas, and comfort will be granted.
Then, at that time, the monk Viśuddhamati spoke this verse:
How did you, O Lamp of the World, immeasurable and free from substrate,
cross over the Nairañjanā river for the benefit of all living beings?
O Great Hero, Tathāgata, Great Sage, please explain those signs that appeared there when the Supreme among Men was crossing over.
O Lamp of the World, just as the seat of enlightenment has been adorned by you,
so please speak to me when asked, for you are the one who brings about welfare, benefit, and happiness.
Just as supreme enlightenment was attained by you, O shrine of the world,
so too did you slay the Evil One, the kinsman of darkness, together with his army.

O Self-Existent One, Essence of Beings, you possess ten unsurpassed powers. O Great Seer, honored a hundred times over by men and gods as the Caravan Leader, you radiate supernatural power and heat all directions.
You stride like a king of swans, white as the finest snow, pure as a Dhārtarāṣṭra goose, the best of excellent deities, with a body free from fatigue.
As you travel from one direction to another, the hosts of gods, asuras, nāgas, and yakṣas, having made all the crooked-colored pillars into celestial mansions,
[behold them]; just as a golden image outshines a burnt pillar, so does the Teacher outshine the entire world.
The body of jewels is in full bloom with the marks [of perfection], filling the sky as it were with stars;
there is no limit to the hundreds of thousands of millions of merits belonging to the Sugata, even for a single name.

There is no one at all equal to you in the entire world; how much less anyone superior? You illuminate all ten directions on every side, just as the sun with its thousand rays shines throughout the sky.
O Daśabala, your person is adorned with the thirty-two marks; like the full moon in the month of Kārtika, it shines forth, liberated from all clouds.

Just as there were eighty thousand Tārakas and another eighty-four [thousand] who followed the Teacher, by whom the Blessed One’s voice was grasped through its thousandfold components in its entirety; and by whom the fragrance of the Blessed One’s sandalwood-like mouth wafted forth,
filling the incomparable, immeasurable, and infinite Buddha-field, it pacifies the stubbornness, hatred, and delusion.
Even if the entire trichiliocosm were filled with mustard seeds, O Śikhin,

a wise person might be able to count those mustard seeds in a single moment; but it would not be possible to count all the infinite and boundless realms of sentient beings in the ten directions who, having smelled it, perceive the fragrance of the Blessed One’s sandalwood.

O steadfast one on the stage of patience, incomparable hero of great compassion, possessed of great majesty and power, physician of sentient beings; O Protector, unstained, worthy of offerings, refuge for those who approach you, supreme Victor, Self-Arisen One!
For who, indeed, could find satisfaction while praising you?
For thus the power of the Blessed One is immeasurable.
We go for refuge to you, the one of infinite splendor, whose passion is destroyed, whose mind is tranquil, the conqueror who is unconquered.
The sky might come to an end for one who traverses it, and even the ocean might be exhausted; but it is not possible to exhaust the measure of power of the Jina,
for the Fully Awakened One has attained such strength.
I ask the lion among men, the one endowed with the ten powers, the immeasurable one.
O Hero, whose passion is destroyed, whose mind is peaceful, and who has purified the ten directions through wisdom by means of non-attachment—O Benefactor, please explain this question of mine.
For immeasurable and inconceivable thousands of millions of eons,
the Omniscient One, the supreme among bipeds, has practiced for the sake of others' welfare.
Generosity, ethical discipline, patience, and meditative absorptions were practiced,
and wisdom was cultivated in the past for many hundreds of millions of eons.
Whatever radiance belongs to fire-precious gems, or that of lightning in the sky,
or even the radiance of the stars— all these become dull in color.
There is no god, nor nāga, nor yakṣa, nor kumbhāṇḍa, nor rākṣasa,
whose body is such as yours, O Leader of Men.

Worthy of worship by the best of gods and asuras, honored and saluted by teachers, revered by the great seers, O Radiant One, Lord of Bipeds, Essence of Beings, Supreme Bull among Men, you are a shrine for humanity.
On the forehead between the eyebrows, the mark of the *ūrṇā* shines with perfectly pure rays like the sky; it gleams like the stainless full moon in the month of Kārtika.
The Leader’s eyes are blue and stainless; his pure and auspicious radiance resembles the color of a beautiful, blooming lotus.
These teeth of the Lord of Men, which produce happiness for men and women, are stainless white, well-formed, even, and closely set, resembling the finest snow;
O Daśabala, his mouth is thus bright and shines like a blooming lotus petal.
The tongue of the Guide, covered with youthful and delicate rays, shines with excellent flavor; its color is equal to a young sprout, divine, and it brings conviction to many people.
Your forehead, adorned with a web of light, and your face with its eyebrows, bestow happiness and shine like the moon;

O Blessed One, Possessor of the Ten Powers, the dark-blue hairs on the head of the Lion of the Śākyas are beautifully arranged in harmony. O Victor, your neck shines like a golden conch shell, equal to the neck of a noble steed.

Indivisible, with the body of a lion as its foremost part, the Blessed One’s physical form illuminates the world in all directions. O you of distinguished speech, ocean of the incomparable, bring about the ripening of karma while speaking these words; the entire world bows down to you, won over and made submissive, having asked with palms joined in the ten-fingered salutation.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the monk Viśuddhamati:

"Excellent, excellent, monk! It is indeed excellent for you, monk, that you consider it necessary to ask the Tathāgata about this matter. Your eloquence, monk, is admirable; your inquiry is noble, since you have such insight, monk.
Indeed, monks, the maturation of karma will manifest even for those sons of good family who shall come to possess this Dharma-discourse."
They shall not fall under the power of Māra, the Evil One;
nor shall humans or non-humans find an opportunity to harm them.
For what reason?
Those monks are indeed practitioners of noble roots of virtue; those beings are indeed such that for their sake you ask about this matter concerning the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas.

O monk, you consider it necessary to ask the Tathāgata about this matter for the sake of beings—namely, regarding the Bodhisattvas who are leaders of the world and have set out upon the distinguished conduct toward all beings.
O monk, [you ask] the Tathāgata for the sake of beings...

[_Mvu_2.298_] You ask this of the Tathāgata for the sake of the monks who are beings— that is, for the sake of the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, the leaders of the world, who have set out endowed with skill in cutting through and analyzing all doubts. You ask about this matter concerning the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, the leaders of the world, who are devoted to the excellence of giving, devoted to the excellence of patience, and devoted to the excellence of meditation.
For those who are devoted to the excellence of wisdom.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke this verse:
Having descended from the divine Tuṣita abode, he became a six-tusked elephant like a snowy mountain;
he entered the womb of the king’s chief queen, and then the three-thousandfold world system trembled.
Then, a vast radiance, golden in color, blazed forth throughout this entire thousandfold world system,
reaching upward as far as the peak of existence, when the Victor entered the womb with full awareness.
Hundreds of thousands of Śakras, along with millions of Brahmās, constantly pay homage to the Jina while he is within the noble womb;
they approach him by day and even at midnight, yet they never depart until they have been dismissed.
And musical instruments resounded a hundred thousand times, filling the sky above with all the deities;
others, having cast aside celestial sandalwood powder, held banners and parasols in their hands.
...divine and excellent flowers of the blue lotus rained down,
as did bees, kalaviṅka birds, and golden garlands, until the Jina entered the womb with full awareness.
When you were born as a Buddha, the essence of beings, Indra, the lord of the gods,
joyfully held for you a distinguished and most beautiful garment of Kāśī silk, resembling the color of Jāmbūnada gold.
And when the Bodhisattva, standing on the ground, took seven steps with a joyful heart, he thought:
"I shall indeed bring about that which is peerless in the world—the end of old age and the process of death."
Then the earth shook in six ways, and a light was released in all directions;
divine sounds resounded in the sky, and there were eighty thousand deities.
And divine powders of sandalwood, beautiful as gold, rained down from the sky by the sons of the gods;
filled with joy and delighted in heart, the Maruts strewed mandārava flowers over the Bodhisattva.
Having reached the age of twenty-nine and having brought the world to maturity, the Bodhisattva renounced his kingdom and the seven excellent jewels; clad in saffron robes, he became a Bodhisattva.
Having gone forth, that wise Bodhisattva practiced austerities for twelve years;
he entered the realm of Māgadha, where the village head’s daughter beheld the Bodhisattva.
Then, with a joyful heart, the Bodhisattva Rishi took up a golden vessel and a water-pitcher variegated with jewels; endowed with the eight qualities and perfectly pure, he then sipped the water.
One should bring food endowed with strength, delicious, well-prepared by the gods, and fragrant;
and thus, generating an intense and impetuous aspiration, one should think: "May I become a Buddha, armored with the primary marks."
Having abandoned this base state of desire, may I practice the pure and unblemished holy life;
avoiding sensual pleasure, which causes suffering and is the root of disease, may I serve the Buddhas who have destroyed passion and are free from defilements.
Having spoken such a verse as this, the daughter of the general, with a joyful heart, paid homage to the Bodhisattva with palms joined; shedding tears, she spoke these words:

King Bimbisāra has obtained a great gain; he has attained freedom from sorrow, his command being increased, since this Bodhisattva dwells within his realm and today shall attain supreme, incomparable enlightenment.
Having eaten my meal, Krakucchanda, the Self-Existent One, shall go to the tree, the lord of trees,
illuminating the ten directions on all sides like a sacrificial pillar of Jāmbūnada gold.
Whose name is Konāka, the one most worthy of great offerings—having eaten his meal, he proceeds to the seat of awakening;
with a mind undepressed, immovable and unshakable, his body is adorned with the primary marks.
The name of him whose body is like refined Jāmbūnada gold is Kāśyapa;
having eaten my meal, that wise one, the essence of beings, shall go of his own accord to the best of trees, the lord of plants, the self-existent one.
