Those wise ones who, in this Fortunate Aeon, shall become incomparable objects of veneration—steadfast, with passion destroyed and free from defilements—I shall honor them all for the sake of incomparable awakening; indeed, I have no other desire whatsoever.
Those sons of the gods who were here in the atmosphere sprinkled the Bodhisattva with sandalwood powder;
having given rise to a surge of joy, they spoke these words: "The daughter of the general has obtained her great gain!"

You remember your former lives, O Sujātā; having conceived pure love for the Bodhisattva, thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, having partaken of my food, have gone to the foot of the tree of enlightenment.
Then the Bodhisattva approached the Nairañjanā River and stood for a moment;
with the soles of his feet level, he caused the earth to tremble.
Then, at that time, there occurred a great earthquake— terrifying and hair-raising—
by which this trichiliocosm became as level as the palm of a hand.
Sumeru, the king of mountains, the Cakravāḍas and Mahācakravāḍas, and the mountains Nimiṃdhara, Yugandhara, Īṣādhara, Khadiraka, and Aśvakarṇa were likewise leveled.

By the power of the Bodhisattva, the seven mountains— Vinataka and Sudarśana— as well as other Kāla mountains that separate the continents, became submerged in the earth; and by the power of the Bodhisattva, the great oceans were stirred up and became visible.

Furthermore, at that time, this great trichiliocosm was covered with lotuses made of Jāmbūnada gold, each as large as a cartwheel, with hundreds of thousands of petals; they were composed of blue beryl,
musāragalva, and śirigarbha-piñjala, and were arranged in a checkerboard pattern across the vast expanse.
A radiance appeared, by which radiance the terrifying great hells were pacified;
all beings in the hells became happy,
and all those who had gone to the animal realm became happy.
All beings in the world of Yama became happy and possessed minds of mutual loving-kindness through the power of the Bodhisattva;
and by a great radiance, the entire trichiliocosm was illuminated.

Furthermore, at that time, all the abodes of the lords of gods, the lords of nāgas, the lords of yakṣas, and the lords of garuḍas throughout this triple-thousand great-thousand world system became illuminated by a single radiance.
Everywhere, they perceive the Bodhisattva as having attained the state of a physical body.

Furthermore, at that time, all the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas throughout the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system found no pleasure in their respective seats because of the majestic power of the Bodhisattva.

Unable to endure the splendor of the Bodhisattva, they all approached the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), carrying flowers, garlands, perfumes, parasols, banners, musical instruments, incense, and ointments.

Then, at that time, Bodhisattvas of surpassing beauty from incalculable and immeasurable Buddha-fields, having manifested themselves in the form of deities, stationed themselves in the sky above, holding divine blue, red, and white lotuses.

Furthermore, at that time, this great trichiliocosm was completely filled from the surface of the earth up to the peak of existence with hundreds of thousands of *jāmbūnada* gold lotuses, each the size of a cartwheel, with stalks of blue beryl, myriads of filaments, and calyxes like the interior of a *śirīṣa* flower— lotuses that had appeared from elsewhere.

From the surface of the earth up to the peak of existence, the world was filled with visiting bodhisattvas and with devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, who were like the interiors of śirīṣa flowers with their filaments.
Then indeed, the Bodhisattva crossed the river Nairañjanā in front of a great host of deities.
Furthermore, at that time, eighty koṭis of parasols made of Jāmbūnada gold appeared over the Bodhisattva by the river Nairañjanā and remained there; eighty koṭis of parasols made of silver,
eighty koṭis of parasols made of emerald (aśmagarbha), eighty koṭis of parasols made of elephant-essence (hastigarbha), and eighty [koṭis of parasols made of]...
Eighty koṭis of parasols made of red precious gems and eighty koṭis of parasols made of jewels appeared and remained above the Bodhisattva.

And eighty koṭis of nāgas, each nāga accompanied by a retinue of eighty koṭis of nāgas, carrying red pearl flowers, approached the place where the Bodhisattva was and honored the Bodhisattva through their prior accumulation of merit.

Then indeed, the nāga king Kāla, accompanied by his own retinue, emerged from his own abode and approached the Bodhisattva; having bowed his head at the feet of the Bodhisattva and gazing upon him with palms joined in reverence, he addressed him in verses:
Seeking awakening, the Bodhisattva, full of confidence,
having traversed the Nairañjanā River, approached the foot of the tree of awakening.
Resounding with the cries of various flocks of birds, adorned with excellent trees,
and endowed with choice flowers and fruits, extending as far as the triple-thousandfold world system.
Where those illuminators of the world came and attained awakening—
Krakucchanda, Konākamuni, and the great sage Kāśyapa.
The Light of the World, the Leader of the World, that supreme Sage of the Śākyas, the kinsmen of the Sun, approached that place.
All those hosts of gods, joyful and with delighted minds,
made that earth like a mass of clouds of flowers.
Having come to their own abodes, the Śuddhāvāsa deities assemble and pay homage to the Leader of the World, the Bodhisattva, by circumambulating him.
Adorn the seat of awakening with divine and human mandārava flowers— costly and most excellent.
Then all the trees in the forest at the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa) bowed down toward that preeminent region where former Buddhas had dwelt.
And the deity who was dwelling upon the tree at the seat of awakening,
seeing the Bodhisattva, uttered a superhuman cry.
She waved a celestial garment and released divine sandalwood powder;
she scattered divine jewel-dust over that bull among men.
And winds carrying various kinds of fragrances— both divine and human—
blowed toward the seat of awakening from all four directions.
And divine, beautiful musical instruments were played in the sky,
performing various kinds of music that were sweet-sounding and enchanting.
A most great radiance arose from the rays of the seat of awakening,
by which the entire world of the gods was immediately suffused.
The divine palaces made of jewels, though possessing celestial colors,
became dull-hued by the rays of the Bodhisattva’s Jāmbūnada gold.
Thousands of sons of gods, possessing great supernatural power, stood in the sky and showered the Bodhisattva with mandārava flowers.
Having heard the incomparable voice of the Great Seer, the Naga Kāla was thrilled,
delighted, and satisfied, escorted by his daughters of the Naga race.
Having abandoned all divine pleasures of play and delight, he arrived and,
looking toward the four quarters, beheld the bull among men.
Having honored Vairocana in the sky, who is surrounded by all rays of light,
the Bodhisattva, joyful and satisfied, addressed him.
O Supreme among Men, what were the marks of the former Buddhas— of Krakucchanda, of Konākamuni, the best of men, and likewise of the Jina Kāśyapa, the Tathāgata, the Supreme among Men?
The feet of those great seers are even, webbed, and well-set; they have the color of lac-dye and are marked with wheels. Beneath the soles of their feet, they are adorned with svastikas.
Upon all the toes of their feet, the *nandyāvarta* patterns are raised;
they shine as the Lords of the World traverse the variegated earth.
O Lord, your feet are unrestrained, just like you yourself;
they do not shine with ankles, yet the toes are well-proportioned.
The feet of the Lords of the World, as they traverse the variegated earth, have long toes, copper-colored nails, webbed fingers, and prominent ankles.
Your shanks shall be like those of an antelope, resembling the interior of a golden vessel;
with hidden knees and concealed ankles, you shall likewise become a benefactor to the world.
The arms of those great seers were like the trunks of elephants;
their upper bodies were like those of lions, and they were well-proportioned like the banyan tree.
Like refined gold, beautiful with a golden complexion,
she touched her knees with her hands while her body remained unbent.
For the king of deer, their hips were likewise rounded and well-proportioned;
their sheathed private parts and genitals were just like those of a noble horse.
Their conduct was pure white, their knees were well-formed, and they had deep navels; such were those former Buddhas, the great seers.
The bodies of those great seers were untouched by even a speck of dust;
those protectors had smooth skin, just as you do.
Each of your hairs grew singly; the rows of hair on your body pointed upward; and they were blue and curled to the right, O Benefactor of the World.
Their shoulders were well-rounded and their eyebrows were like those of a bull; these lords had limbs that were supple and straight, and they possessed these prominent [marks].
With arms like the coils of a serpent, tapering and free from arrogance,
you possess such a Nārāyaṇa-like firmness as one such as you alone has.
With prominent nails and copper-colored nails, resembling the peaks of Mount Kailāsa,
their bodies were exceedingly beautiful, adorned with these elevated marks.
Their necks are like conch shells, rising in smooth succession; those Protectors have jaws like a lion's and likewise possess the foremost of all tastes.
Those great seers had forty perfectly rounded teeth;
their white tusks were just like yours, O Blessed One.
With his broad and slender tongue, he could cover his entire face;
he also wiped both the tips of his ears and his nose.
The speech of those great seers, who possess all-seeing vision, is perfectly complete in its eight qualities; it is true and should be understood by all living beings.
And your voice was like that of Brahmā, with a tone like the song of the kalaviṅka bird;
it had the resonance of a drum and was truly lovely.
Just as a golden lotus shines,
so did the faces of the Protectors, the kinsmen of the Sun, radiate light.
The eyes of those great seers were long and deep blue;
their noses were prominent and beautiful, like golden sacrificial posts.
Between the eyebrows of those great seers of noble birth,
there appeared a radiant *ūrṇā*, soft like cotton.
And his face became like a great flame, or like the full moon on the night of the full moon;
and all the quarters of space were illuminated by him as if by fires of jewels.
Your hair is blue-black and soft, resembling kācilindika cloth;
all the hairs curl to the right, for you, O Benefactor of the World, are thus.
O Protector, those whose heads are crowned with usnīṣas are just like you;
their heads are not to be looked upon even by gods or asuras.
For those Buddhas possess great radiance; they surpass all with their rays of light, just as the moon is surpassed by its own brilliance when eclipsed by Keturāja.
Having observed these and other signs and characteristics of the Bodhisattva, he spoke these words:
Since those sons of the gods have emerged for the sake of honoring you,
O Great Hero, there is no doubt that today you will become a Buddha.
With a concentrated mind, having taken up the weapon of wisdom, you shall cut through the unvanquished, ensnaring craving that leads to further existence— the bond of Māra.
Today, O Supreme among Men, having attained enlightenment, you will utterly shake off the fire of passion that completely envelops all remaining afflictions.
The outer robe, the bowl, and likewise the color of the monastic garment—
just as they were seen by me in the case of the Protectors, so too are they yours, O benefactor of the world.
All such persons as you are turn to the right; just as you walk like a lion today, so shall you become a Buddha.
Like a mountain, unshakable, and like a Victor in his meditative concentration,
having stood at the seat of awakening, he exerted himself with firm vigor.
Having heard those words spoken by the naga Kāla,
he was satisfied and, with an uplifted and joyful mind, approached the foot of the Bodhi tree.
Having heard that incomparable sound, the mighty Naga Kāla emerged from his abode with great speed toward the Bodhisattva.
Having joined his palms with all ten fingers extended,
he praised the Heroic Buddha as he was proceeding toward the seat of enlightenment.
Just as these gentle winds will always blow pleasantly—
possessing fragrant and delightful scents, neither too hot nor too cold.
And just as these deities rained down this shower of flowers, [they proclaimed]:
"O Sugata, O supreme among bipeds, you shall attain the state of an Arhat."
"O noble one, turning clockwise, satisfied, thrilled, and delighted,
with a joyful mind and uplifted, go forth while emitting bliss."
Just as a thousand musical instruments resound, filling the sky above with the voices of the deities,
you will be born with a surge of joyful and delighted mind, becoming a Buddha, preeminent in all the world.
Just as no other light shines above the celestial palaces and they are rendered dull in color,
and just as the earth trembles in six ways, so shall you today become an incomparable object of offerings.
And as they joyfully wave their garments, having shattered the host of Māra, and hold up parasols, banners, and flags, they say: "You shall become a Buddha; I have no doubt."
Just as sweet drums resound, filling the entire expanse of the sky with their sound through the heavens,
and just as the host of gods rains down flowers, so shall you become a self-arisen one (*svayaṃbhū*) in the world, including the realm of the gods.
And as thousands of gods, with joyful hearts, joined their palms together in the sky and offered praise:
"O one of golden radiance, most distinguished, you shall become a Buddha, a supreme field of merit for humanity, a speaker of the unsurpassed truth."
Then the Bodhisattva approached the foot of the tree. At that time, the entire seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa) was draped with bundles of hanging silk streamers;

it was adorned with raised banners and pennants, decorated with millions of parasols, variegated with jeweled threads, perfumed with incense, surrounded by jewel-trees, strewn with spread-out robes, sprinkled with sandalwood powder, and made magnificent by a profusion of jewels.
Furthermore, at that time, many hundreds of thousands of deities, stationed in the sky above, paid homage to the Bodhisattva while holding incense.
Holding parasols, banners, and flags, they paid homage to the Bodhisattva.
Holding divine blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water lilies, and white lotuses, they paid homage to the Bodhisattva.
Holding divine sandalwood powder, they pay homage to the Bodhisattva;
holding divine jewel powder and divine jewel flowers, gazing with unblinking eyes, they pay homage to the Bodhisattva.

Other deities perceive that Bodhi tree as being made of gold, according to their own respective inclinations; other deities perceive the Bodhi tree as being made of silver; and other deities perceive the Bodhi tree as being made of beryl.
Some gods perceive the Bodhi tree as being made of crystal; some gods perceive the Bodhi tree as being made of emerald; and some gods perceive the Bodhi tree as being made of the seven precious gems.
Other gods perceive the Bodhi tree as consisting of hundreds of thousands of jewels;

indeed, according to their respective inclinations, other gods perceive the Bodhi tree as being made of red sandalwood, while other gods perceive the Bodhi tree as being made of aloe-wood sandalwood. Other gods...
Some perceive the Bodhi tree as consisting of the jewels they each desire;
other gods perceive the Bodhi tree as being of yellow sandalwood; still other gods perceive the Bodhi tree as being of lion-sandalwood.
Other gods perceive the Bodhi tree as sandalwood of exquisite fragrance.
For instance, according to their respective inclinations, some gods perceive the Bodhi tree as being made of *girisāra* sandalwood;
other gods perceive the Bodhi tree as being made of divine *aguru* sandalwood; and other gods perceive the Bodhi tree as being composed of precious jewels.
Some gods perceive the Bodhi tree as adorned with all kinds of jewels;
other gods perceive the Bodhi tree as variegated with precious gems;
and other gods perceive the Bodhi tree as adorned with divine blue beryl.
Some gods perceive the Bodhi tree as variegated with musāragalva gems;
some gods perceive the Bodhi tree as variegated with emerald (*asmagarbha*) jewels;
and some gods perceive the Bodhi tree as variegated with *hastigarbha* jewel-gems.
Some gods perceive the Bodhi tree as variegated with mani-jewels;
some gods perceive the Bodhi tree as adorned with mani-jewels of excellent radiance;
some gods perceive the Bodhi tree as embellished with mani-jewels of immortal emerald.
Some gods perceive the Bodhi tree as adorned all around with moons;
other gods perceive the Bodhi tree as adorned with beautiful moons; other gods perceive the Bodhi tree as adorned with the radiance of suns.
Some gods [saw it] variegated with crystal; some gods [saw it] adorned with the splendor of the sun; some gods [saw it] adorned with the radiance of the moon;
and some gods [saw it] adorned with the light of the stars.
Some gods [beheld it] adorned with lightning-like radiance;
some gods [beheld it] adorned with jewels that illuminate all directions;
and some gods [beheld it] adorned with jewels possessing the luster of pearls.
Some gods perceive the Bodhi tree as adorned with jewel-gems of unimpeded radiance;
other gods perceive it as adorned with a towering mass of jewels; and other gods perceive it as adorned with jewel-gems that are the most supreme in all the worlds.
Some gods [saw it] adorned with precious jewels fixed to Śakra;
other gods [saw it] adorned with jeweled leaves;
other gods [saw it] adorned with *uragagarbha* precious jewels.
Some were adorned with sandalwood-fragrance gems;
others were adorned with red-eye gems;
others were adorned with lordly elephant-gem jewels.
Some were adorned with precious gems given by Maheśvara;
others were adorned with *rasaka* stones;
others were adorned with *gomedaka* precious gems.
Some gods perceive the Bodhi tree as adorned with *śaśa* jewel-gems;
others perceive it as adorned with *lālāṭika* jewel-gems;
others with *śirigarbha* jewel-gems; others with *tālika* jewels; and others perceive the Bodhi tree as adorned with these and various other divine jewel-gems.
Those gods for whom, on that account, the roots of merit would ripen for unsurpassed perfect enlightenment perceived the Bodhi tree according to those roots of merit—

with blue pearl necklaces, red pearl necklaces, white pearl necklaces, neck-ornaments, golden threads, earrings, signet rings, bracelets, bangles, anklets, headbands, finger-seals, armlets, and jeweled pendants.

They perceived the Bodhi tree as adorned with these and other divine ornaments: garlands of fine cloth, flower garlands, golden armlets, jewel necklaces, pearl necklaces, mandārava flower garlands, swan garlands, lion-creeper vines, diamond-shaped patterns, and svastikas.
Those gods for whom roots of merit arise upon seeing the Bodhi tree perceive the Bodhi tree as beautifully adorned;
others perceive the Bodhi tree as fully adorned with these and other ornaments, just as they have been described.
In that regard, some gods perceived the Bodhi tree as being one yojana in height;
other gods perceived it as being five yojanas in height.
Others are ten yojanas in height.
Some were twenty yojanas in height; others were thirty yojanas in height;
others were forty yojanas in height.
Some gods perceive the Bodhi tree as being fifty yojanas in height;
others perceive the Bodhi tree as being one hundred yojanas in height.
Each perceives the Bodhi tree in height according to their own respective knowledge.
There are gods who perceive the Bodhi tree as being one thousand yojanas in height;
there are long-lived gods who, having performed meritorious services for previous Victors, perceive the Bodhi tree as being one hundred thousand yojanas in height;
and there are sons of gods who, having brought forth roots of goodness, perceive the Bodhi tree as being as high as the very peak of existence.
There, some gods saw at the foot of the Bodhi tree a lion throne made of every kind of jewel;
it was divine, many yojanas in height, spread with divine cloth, covered with a net of jewels, and adorned with a network of tinkling bells.
Other gods saw a lion throne a hundred thousand yojanas in height.
Some gods saw a lion throne one thousand yojanas in height; some gods saw a lion throne two hundred and fifty yojanas in height;
other gods saw a lion throne two hundred yojanas in height.
Some gods saw the lion throne as being one hundred yojanas in height;
other gods saw the lion throne as being fifty yojanas in height;
and other gods saw the lion throne as being forty yojanas in height.
Some gods saw the lion throne as thirty yojanas in height;
other gods saw the lion throne as twenty yojanas in height;
still other gods saw the lion throne as ten yojanas in height.
Some gods saw the lion throne as four yojanas in height;
some gods saw the lion throne as three yojanas in height;
other gods [saw it] as two yojanas.
[In Mvu 2.313] some saw the lion throne at a height of one *yojana*; other gods saw the lion throne at a height of one *yojana*;
still other gods saw the lion throne at a height of three *krośas*.
Some gods saw the lion throne at a height of two krośas;
other gods saw the lion throne at a height of one krośa;
and other gods saw the lion throne at a height of seven tālas.

Some gods saw a lion throne at the foot of the Bodhi tree six *tālas* in height; other gods saw it five *tālas*, others four *tālas*, others three *tālas*, others two *tālas*, and others saw it only one *tāla* in height. Still other gods saw a lion throne seven *pauruṣas* in height.
Some gods saw the lion throne at the foot of the Bodhi tree as being six *pauruṣas* in height;
others saw it as five *pauruṣas*, others as four *pauruṣas*, others as three *pauruṣas*, and others as two *pauruṣas*.
Still other gods saw the lion throne at the foot of the Bodhi tree as being only one man’s height in height.
There, those beings who were inclined toward austerity saw the Bodhisattva seated upon a bed of grass;
they thought, "Seated upon this bed of grass, the Bodhisattva will awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Then, moreover, the Bodhisattva, having approached the foot of the Bodhi tree in the presence of the world with its gods, humans, and asuras, and having circumambulated the Bodhi tree three times, sat down cross-legged at the root of the Bodhi tree, recollecting the former Tathāgatas, having set his body straight and established mindfulness before him.
And there, as the Bodhisattva sat thus at the foot of the Bodhi tree, his facial orb shone, blazed, and radiated,
just like the solar orb spread across the great trichiliocosm;
by its brilliance, the entire great trichiliocosm was rendered lusterless in comparison.
Just as, for example,

before a polished image of Jāmbūnada gold, a charred pillar— black and resembling soot— does not shine, does not gleam, and does not become radiant, even so [the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system] appeared before the Bodhisattva.
The world-system was overwhelmed by its brilliance.
There, those sons of the gods as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven saw the Bodhisattva seated above them; however, the gods of that level saw the Bodhisattva as being on their own level.

Likewise, as far as the gods of the Cāturmahārājika, Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmitavaśavartin realms, up to the abode of Māra in the intermediate space, they perceived the Bodhisattva seated upon his lion throne.

In this way, Brahmā, the gods of the Brahmakāyika realm, the Brahmapurohita gods, the Mahābrahmā gods, the Ābhā gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Śubha gods, the Parīttaśubha gods, the Apramāṇaśubha gods, the Śubhakṛtsna gods, the Bṛhatphala gods, the Avṛha gods, the Atapa gods, the Sudarśana gods, and the Akaniṣṭha gods perceived the Bodhisattva seated upon his lion throne.
And all those beings dwelling at the very limits of the triple-thousand great-thousand world system who were endowed with roots of merit perceived the Bodhisattva seated upon the lion throne.

Those beings who have planted roots of merit and performed services for previous Victors, though they are included within the realm of desire, do not see or perceive Māra as they perform worship and pay homage to the Bodhisattva through the power of the Bodhisattva.
Then indeed, Māra the Evil One perceived his own power to be dimmed and saw that the entire great trichiliocosm had bent toward where the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva was; and he reflected thus:
"I shall not attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment so long as I have not [conquered] Māra the Evil One."

"I shall defeat him as he arrives, fully armed, together with his army, lest beings should think: 'It is no marvel that Māra was subdued by one who has attained awakening. Rather, the Bodhisattva desires to demonstrate before the world, including the gods, his own power through a miracle of supernatural might, so that they may think, 'The Bodhisattva has thus attained such firm strength, momentum, and supernatural power,' and having trained under me for unexcelled perfect awakening..."
They will generate the thought [of awakening].
Then indeed Māra the Evil One, suffering, dejected, and pierced by the arrow of grief, conceiving the notion of a rival king toward the Bodhisattva,
mobilized the fourfold army of Māra, marched many hundreds of yojanas, and approached the foot of the Bodhi tree, thinking, "We shall see the Bodhisattva."

He was unable to see the Bodhisattva, having fallen into a visual delusion. If the Bodhisattva were to open his mouth, by the power with which the Bodhisattva was endowed, he could— if this triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system were composed of solid diamond mountains—
shake that world system as if it were like a single atom of dust and hurl it across incalculable world systems.
And not even a single atom of dust coincides with a second atom of dust.

And then the Bodhisattva saw many beings within the assembly of Māra who possessed roots of merit, thinking: "Upon seeing such a miraculous display of supernatural power by the Bodhisattva, they will resolve their minds toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
Perceiving this significant point, the Bodhisattva reflects: "I shall not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening until I have conquered Māra along with his army and his vehicles."
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke this verse:
Just as the Self-Existent One, the King of the Śākyas, a being of perfect purity, stood at the foot of the Bodhi tree,
beautiful to behold like a golden image.
Made of Jāmbūnada gold, he is free from all afflictions.
The quarters of the world became filled with radiance,
and Māra was terrified, fallen into distress,
thinking: "What indeed will happen to me?"
I find no delight in this celestial palace.
All the celestial palaces were the color of the sky;
they were the finest mansions made of excellent sandalwood,
adorned with golden threads, crystal, and coral.
May I not indeed fall from this place today!
The windows are clearly manifest with beautiful half-moons, and the inner chambers are inlaid with musāragalva; such is the preeminent palace of Vairocana for the sake of the world.
Was it light that was, or will it be? But what is it today?
The crown has fallen from my head,
and today my auspicious radiance has vanished; the celestial music of the apsarases has ceased for me.
May I indeed not fall from this state today!
Just as celestial mansions made of Jāmbūnada gold cause the colors of the sky to appear dull,
so too are these divine mansions.
She became dejected when the Bodhisattva had departed.
And you have seen the Blessed One, the Self-Existent, seated like an invincible lion,
the pure essence, the essence of the beings of the world.
Like a sacrificial pillar made of Jāmbūnada gold, it shines.
The gods, established in heaven, wearing necklaces of liberation, beautiful with golden shells, and charming,
were filled with joy as they took up golden threads.
They adorn the Bodhi tree of the Blessed One.
And auspicious svastikas, half-moons,
and lion-vines adorned the Bodhi tree; and having seized jewels with the brilliance of lightning, they shone.
The joyful sons of the gods adorn [it].
Having taken hold of moonlight gems,
having taken hold of sun-crystal gems,
and having taken hold of Vairocana precious gems;
They adorned the Bodhi tree of the Blessed One.
And taking up pearls and gems that were radiant,
beautiful to behold, and illuminating,
they became filled with joy, their hearts glad and thrilled.
They adorned the Bodhi tree of the Blessed One.
Having taken up *samantacandra* gems and a string of jewels most beautiful and lovely to behold,
and having taken up *gomedaka* gem-jewels—
They adorn the Bodhi tree of the Blessed One.
Others, having taken hold of beautiful red-eyed [beings],
and having taken hold of pure Ratana from the womb of Śiri,
adorned the Bodhi tree of the Blessed One.
And those with red limbs, having taken up rucakas,
were Maheśvaras of most beautiful complexion;
and having taken up karketana gems, they shone.
They adorned the Bodhi tree of the Blessed One.
Seeing blue pearls, as well as white pearls, red pearls, and those of auspicious color,
they were moved by joy and overcome with excitement.
They adorned the Bodhi tree of the Blessed One.
And having taken up the *jyotikā* jewel-gem,
those who surpass the sun and moon in brilliance—
having taken up such distinguished jewel-gems— [shine forth].
They adorned the Bodhi tree of the Blessed One.
And the Naga-maṇīs of beautiful complexion, pure-eyed and secret,
rejoicing and possessed of supernatural powers, stood then in the sky.
They adorned the Bodhi tree of the Blessed One.
Brahmā approached the seat of awakening with thousands [of followers],
as did Śakra, the lord of the gods, and the Guhyakas—
those by whom the former Protectors of the World had been seen.
And those deities bowed down before the Self-Existent One.
The sons of the gods from the Ābhāsvara realm have arrived, as well as the Śubha and Śubhakṛtsna sons of the gods,
and those from the Rūpa and Bṛhatphala realms.
The Atapa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha [deities] adorn the Bodhi tree of the Blessed One.
The entire Bodhi tree was completely covered as it scattered thousands of immeasurable rays of light;
with divine jewels, it illuminated the Buddha-field.
He overcomes the entire Sahā world-system.
Thus he thought to himself: "May this negligent kinsman not cause me to fall from my position;
may he indeed become the king of the gods."
And there is no one equal to him in the entire world.
Furthermore, even if the Buddha, the Lord of Dharma,
were to exist while the celestial palaces of the gods were empty,
he would teach the path that is auspicious, peaceful, and secure.
I shall no longer possess lordship over existence.
He will bring about a Buddha-field that has attained excellence, subduing millions of Māras;
he is girt with armor, clad in mail.
At the time of battle, be vigilant.
Having mobilized his army of Māra and approached the supreme lord of trees,
Kṛṣṇa likewise beheld the Bodhisattva.
Like a thousand suns within the atmosphere.
His very mind became trembling,
thinking: "Having seized this jewel, which is so highly esteemed in the world, I am not able to withstand his assault."
Having generated a desire that is indifferent to sovereignty.
And having taken divine powder of excellent sandalwood, and that which consists of jewels from Jambūnada gold, and divine, excellent, and precious fragrances;
Thus, overcome by emotion, he overwhelmed the Bodhisattva.
Having arranged his garment over one shoulder, with palms joined in reverence, he circumambulated [him], knelt upon the ground,
and gazed at him with joy and unblinking eyes.
At that time, he praised the Bodhisattva.
In form you are peerless, and in merit no one has been found equal to you;
fully self-possessed, you are worthy of worship by the gods.
The sole hero of the world stood at the foot of a tree.
There is no one equal to you; how could there be anyone superior—whether a god, a nāga, or a human—in this world?
You surpass all directions with your splendor.
Like the moon in the sky when freed from thick clouds.
For these seven most excellent and supreme jewels of yours are worthy of worship; enjoy them!
Set the wheel of dharma in motion and dwell upon the earth.
O possessor of jewels, rule over the four continents!
And you have arrived, surveying the directions with an undaunted mind and infinite splendor;
surpass the light of thousands of gods with your radiance.
Just like a polished pillar or a golden image.
Adorned with the thirty-two marks, your body shines forth, O Essence of Beings; you appear resplendent, remaining vigilant while established in your kingdom.
O fathers, govern your sons.
You dwelt as a sovereign over the four continents, yet you did not exercise dominion here;
having attained supernatural powers, you wander throughout the world.
May I become your disciple, like an only son.
Sporting with thousands of women like a king of the gods who has attained glory and supernatural power,
I shall give you the seven jewels.
Become a wise universal monarch, a Cakravartin!
There shall be a thousand sons born to you— heroes, warriors of great strength,
with excellent limbs and forms, who will crush the armies of your enemies.
May he conquer this world as far as the edge of the ocean.
And behold these many daughters of Māra, clothed in pure garments, holding flowers and excellent sandalwood in the sky before you.
In song and in the arts, she has attained the ultimate truth.
Taking up lutes, hand-drums, clay drums,
conchs, flutes, and sweet-sounding instruments, as well as sambhārikas, nakulakas, and kiṃphalas.
At that time, she was being sung to at the foot of the tree.
Others, remaining in the sky and flying about,
scattered powdered supreme sandalwood and [powder] made of Jāmbūnada gold and jewels.
They all throw powder upon you.
O Prince, enjoy yourself in this most excellent palace amidst the sounds of the *hāhā* cry, the kettle-drum, the conch, and the *paṇava* drum; here you have flowers, perfumes, and ointments.
"Eat there; I shall be your attendant."
A wheel, an elephant, a noble horse with beautiful mane, a distinguished beryl jewel,
a preeminent woman, a treasury of wealth, and a sword held in hand.
The seven treasures include the counselor as one of them.
O Prince, dwelling under your sovereignty and serving you who speak so gently,
I shall become happy upon hearing your words.
And I do not speak falsely to you in such a manner.
Abiding in truth, may I obtain a beautiful body, distinguished and clearly adorned with the primary marks,
as well as the secondary and minor marks.
Shining brightly, adorned with the distinct marks.
Then Mañjughoṣa, speaking with a sweet and melodious voice,
looked toward all directions and uttered speech endowed with the eight qualities.
Listen, O Yakṣa, to my words as I speak them.
"I shall become a king in all the world, having awakened to the enlightenment that is sovereign, peaceful, and secure;
and my sons shall be vigilant beings."
Having heard my instruction, they will act accordingly.
When I have awakened to supreme enlightenment, seven excellent jewels will also be mine—
those seven factors of awakening praised by the former Victors.
Having obtained that, one becomes heedful.
Having awakened to the four bases of psychic power, the measure of meditative concentration, the supreme path, and the all-encompassing wisdoms of the truths, I [attained this].
He has arrived, intending to conquer the quarters.
Desirable desires are indeed loathsome and devoid of happiness;
herein the wise find no benefit.
For this path leads to hell and the animal realm.
In the world of Yama, in the world of many pretas.
Desiring what is unrighteous, they delight in sexual intercourse;
they are bent all around in the blinding darkness,
deprived of sight, and fallen away from the pure Dharma.
Such are the men who indulge in sensual desires.
Foul-smelling, putrid, impure, and ignoble—
pure beings never take delight therein;
only the fool conceives a notion of distinction regarding it.
A wise person would not conceive a desire for that.
Just as a thunderbolt or a wheel of fire might fall upon a prosperous, ripened field of rice,
even so do the pure dharmas of the ultimate truth [perish].
With desire as their cause, they become fruitless.
But ordinary people, delighting in what is inferior and serving the base, are like those blind from birth; being ignorant, they become attached.
They become attached with an ignorant mind.
A bodhisattva does not generate craving for sensual pleasures.
Just as when a buddha-field is undergoing destruction and the fire has blazed up in the sky,
even the delightful radiance [of the world] becomes soot or ash.
In the same way, one who doubts regarding sensual pleasures [does not possess] pure dharmas.
Just as one condemned to death by a king might obtain release, prosperity, and well-being,
so too would he who does not indulge in base desires.
May I obtain the wealth authorized by the Jinas.
Excrement, when dry and being burned,
is loathsome, utterly foul-smelling;
a prince does not feel elated there.
In the same way, sensual pleasures are censured by the wise.
Just as in the last month of summer, the salt water produces thirst in men,
even so one who indulges in sensual pleasures experiences suffering.
One who has fallen into ignorance generates the thirst of the net.
That which is pus from their liver, kidneys, and lungs, as well as excrement and other things adhering within the body,
flowing out through the openings of the physical frame.
In this matter, there is no joy for a wise person.
Nasal mucus,
saliva, and an abundance of phlegm, as well as bile that has spread through the head causing disease— these flow constantly, being impure and loathsome.
In this matter, there is no joy for a wise person.
Driven by desire, men fall into miserable states and experience various degrees of suffering,
like mung beans and black grams caught in a mortar.
In the same way, sentient beings are exhausted within the hells.
Their bodies are cut in many ways by swords,
and further pierced by spears and arrows;
fools thus perform the threefold undesirable [karma].
A bodhisattva should never take delight in this.
Carried away by forms and born of delusion, that person of little wisdom generates craving for sensual pleasures;
he himself serves the very root of disease that produces suffering.
Just as a jackal [in] a cemetery [approaches] a corpse, so too,
O kinsman of darkness, do not praise sensual pleasures for my sake; they are condemned by the wise.
Just as one would avoid a pit filled with glowing embers, even so does the Bodhisattva renounce sensual desires.
For one who indulges in sensual desires would not frequent this place,
which is crowded with birds and filled with blossoming trees,
nor indeed would one who possesses such auspicious marks.
Having indulged in sensual pleasures, one obtains this physical existence.
Having guarded their ethical discipline and practiced the stainless holy life, having served the Buddhas who have destroyed passion and are free from defilements,
and having cultivated patience for many millions of eons.
One's physical form becomes distinguished (and radiant).
In a former life, he was one whose conduct was flawless,
endowed with patience, always vigilant,
and having purified the manifold, infinite path.
Thus, today I shall attain the supreme, excellent enlightenment.
The caravan leader, acting for the welfare of the Blessed One, stood alert before him and said: "O Kṛṣṇabandhu,
listen, dear father, to my words as I speak them."
Do not conceive of any fault or lack of faith in this matter.
When this one was born, peerless and meritorious, the earth with its mountains shook in six ways,
and the ten directions were illuminated.
And divine musical instruments resounded spontaneously, even without being struck.
O sons of gods, hold up divine parasols;
the Buddha-field is filled with banners and flags.
The hosts of Māras and the assemblies of gods waved their garments.
O beings who are not disheartened, generate heedfulness!
He will become the eye for the entire world, becoming a source of light by destroying the cataracts;
he will dispel the darkness of those who are suffering.
Do not produce lack of faith, O one of childish intellect!
For he will indeed become a shelter for the entire world, a protection, an island, a refuge, and the ultimate resort—
for those who have not yet produced faith toward him, whether they be humans or gods.
They go to the terrible Avīci hell.
For he is indeed peerless in this world as one worthy of offerings;
for he is ever compassionate toward the welfare of the world. Having served him, the multitudes of men and women—
Having passed away, one will become happy here in all the world.
Whoever conceives pride here and does not find faith in the Lion of the Śākyas— who is endowed with merit and has shaken off all dust—
shall never possess well-being.
And having passed away, one quickly falls into miserable states of existence within the Vraja.
Having lifted up this mountain army of snow,
he would hurl it from the ocean and cast it across millions of billions of fields.
In this world, there is no army equal to him in strength.
This one of firm vows, being heedful, could dry up the entire ocean— the water-bearing sea filled with liquid, the abode of asuras, the great deep of universal splendor.
For he indeed overcomes the entire army of Māra.
He surpasses Brahmā, Śakra, the Guhyakas,
Nāgas, Asuras, humans, and Mahoragas,
like a polished golden image set upon a sturdy pillar.
O Jina, you whose body is as firm as a cloud, you have overcome Nārāyaṇa in battle.
Having seized this supreme mountain Cakravāḍa,
he could reduce it to fine dust with the palm of his hand; yet he cannot be overcome when he has approached the foot of the Bodhi tree.
The hero of firm vows, being heedful, is unable to be shaken.
The moon might fall from the sky to the earth,
and this very earth might stand in the sky by its own power,
and all rivers might flow upstream.
And he, firm in his vows, cannot be shaken at all.
Just as a mighty lordly elephant, sixty years of age, a six-tusked naga with its body raised high,
breaks an unbaked clay vessel with its foot without being discouraged; so too [should one act].
In that very same way, he will treat the entire army of Māra.
For Māra, distressed, spoke thus to the Caravan Leader:
"Why do you terrify me, you of childish intellect?
My army is fully arrayed, clad in armor and mail."
I shall create an obstacle for this one of firm vows.
He whom I have indeed nourished for thousands of years— he who is called my eldest son here—
has become an attendant to Gautama here.
Intending to subdue the army of Māra.
Just as the flower of the udumbara tree, when it has appeared, is endowed with color, most beautiful, and sweetly fragrant;
so too are these Buddhas, whose dust is destroyed and who are free from afflictions.
They exist for tens of billions of nayutas of eons.
Having generated pure compassion, he would lead his father— who lacks faith and has failed in moral conduct— [to virtue];
such is the natural disposition of sons.
I am compassionate; I am not an enemy.
If a man, having climbed to the summit of Mount Sumeru, were to throw himself down upon the surface of the earth,
he might obtain some relief for his body as it falls.
One does not [attain it] by doing what is harmful to a bodhisattva.
A man of childish intellect, having fallen into a pit of glowing coals that is completely full,
might find pleasure in his body.
One does not [attain this] by doing what is harmful to a bodhisattva.
Having taken a well-sharpened sword, polished with oil,
and placed it in his mouth, he might draw it out; he would obtain happiness and thereby attain a state of well-being.
One should not speak harsh words to a bodhisattva.
If one were to tread upon a path made of razors for a thousand years or even ten million years,
one might thereby obtain happiness and attain well-being.
One should not speak harsh words to a bodhisattva.
A person of little intelligence might find happiness while drinking molten metal when his stomach is fiercely ablaze,
even as his intestines, liver, kidneys, and lungs are being torn asunder.
One should not speak harsh words to a bodhisattva.
One might even find happiness while swallowing a blazing iron ball when one's stomach is on fire,
even as the liver, kidneys, and lungs are being torn apart.
One should not speak harsh words to a Bodhisattva.
Just as if a great mountain like Cakravāḍa were thrown from the sky and fell upon a man's head,
he might experience happiness and thereby attain a state of well-being.
One should not speak harsh words to a bodhisattva.
Pits of glowing coals, arrows, swords, and javelins, though hurled from the sky, would fall upon my body;
yet they would produce only happiness, and from that, a state of well-being would arise.
One should not speak harsh words to a bodhisattva.
It would be possible to hold this world-system in one's hand for ten million eons,
and to know the various thoughts of human beings.
Not for the sake of moving the sage from his seat.

It is possible to ignite a mass of fire in the midst of the waters of the ocean that sustains all beings— a blazing mountain of flame as vast as Sumeru, a smoke-bannered conflagration that illuminates the world.
Not for the sake of moving the sage from his seat.
Endowed with virtue, peerless in patience, austerity, and religious observance, he had long ago reached the further shore;
like a lion, the lord of beasts, he was possessed of innate vigor.
The Victor, roaring his roar amidst the army of Māra.
Just as a being born blind, having fallen here into a great well, though moving about,
has reached the edge but does not know the direction.
In that same way, Māra, your army shall be.
Behold them, dear father— those sons of gods endowed with beauty, who have performed meritorious deeds,
holding powders of excellent sandalwood.
With uplifted minds, they showered the Bodhisattva.
All the thousands of deities, having abandoned their celestial palaces, arrived;
standing in the sky, they scattered flowers and powders.
The delighted ones shower the Bodhisattva with offerings.
Do not give rise to an evil thought, O one of vast intelligence;
for the great caravan leaders are difficult to approach,
lest you fall into the dust of the miserable realms.
"Father is not drinking; he is suffering and has fallen into distress."
Those beings who here generate love and reverence, and those who go for refuge to this [teaching],
will before long abandon the states of woe.
All touch that which is ageless and sorrowless.
The son of Janī, possessed of vast intelligence, took various beautiful and charming flowers and, having scattered them over the Essence of Beings in the World, spoke to his father.
At the very end, one should reduce the entire army to ashes.
Just as there would be no fault for blind beings who, having found a treasure, do not see it,
so it is with you who have found one most worthy of offerings.
O kinsman of negligence, you produce lack of faith.
Like a child of immature intellect in his house, raining down a stream of gold as thick as an axle,
he would go about crying out, "I am falling! even while he was about to fall.
In that very same way, my father could not endure the great seer.
Having obtained a celestial palace made of sandalwood,
delightful with its fragrant scent and beautiful to behold,
he then emerged from it and fell here into this well.
In that very same way, my father could not endure the great seer.
Just as one might rise from a lion throne within a beautiful, radiant jeweled palace and,
having stepped out, fall headlong into a pit of glowing coals.
In that very same way, my father could not endure the great seer.
Just as one who, having obtained a palace made of beautiful and auspicious Jāmbūnada gold,
should then depart and fall into the ocean.
In that very same way, my father could not endure the great seer.
Just as one might cast off golden neck-ornaments from one's neck and wear copper in this world,
even so it is with having encountered a Sage worthy of offerings.
O kinsman of negligence, you produce lack of faith.
Just as a person of childish intellect, having cast away a vessel of nectar, might drink from a vessel of poison,
even so is he who, having obtained one worthy of great offerings...
Having fallen into negligence, you produce lack of faith.
Just as one of childish intellect, having obtained beautiful blue eyes, might pluck them out by oneself;
In that very way, having obtained a sage worthy of offerings,
you, whose kinsman is negligence, produce a lack of faith.
O Māra, take up this divine, exquisite pearl necklace of mindfulness;
it illuminates all directions with its radiance.
Do not, my dear, give rise to lack of faith.
And just as he, assuming a beautiful form, illuminates this entire world-system here,
having split Mount Meru and the great Cakravāḍa mountains.
Like the king of mountains in the midst of the ocean.
And just as he stands here at the foot of the tree,
surpassing the sons of the gods on the summit of Sumeru,
so he who indulges in sensual pleasures does not stand in this place.
Do not cause lack of faith, O kinsman of Kṛṣṇa!
There is no being, my dear, in the three worlds who possesses such merit as you,
appearing like the invisible king of rays.
Thus sat the Sage at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
Just as the Jina Krakucchanda sat at the foot of a tree, illuminating the directions,
so too was his body adorned with the primary marks.
Do not, dear father, harbor ill-will toward these people here.
May he whose name is Konāka, like the Lord of the World with pure vision who destroys the darkness,
shine forth with glory throughout the quarters.
He too is seated here at the foot of this tree.
He whose name was Kāśyapa, the one with all-seeing eyes, worthy of the supreme gift—
he too is seated here at the foot of this tree.
O Hero, you awaken to the supreme and excellent enlightenment.
Those Lords of the World, the sages, the gods of gods, who attained perfect enlightenment in this Fortunate Aeon—
those who previously sat here at the foot of this tree.
May the heroes awaken to the auspicious, supreme enlightenment.
Indeed, four thousand Jinas sat here previously beneath this sovereign lord of excellent trees;
likewise will the future world-protectors who act for the benefit of the world.
They too shall attain the supreme, excellent enlightenment.
Having spoken this verse of such a kind,
he who bore the excellent name Mahāsmṛti cast a necklace of liberation upon Gautama.
With an uplifted mind, he was born with excellent vigor.
The supreme son of Māra, established in knowledge,
having taken a divine, auspicious, and well-fashioned silken garment,
gazed upon the Sage, the Bodhisattva.
With an uplifted mind, I praise [you] at the seat of awakening.
The essence of beings uttered a cry of pleasing sound;
there is no one equal to you in the entire world— thus you have practiced in the past, O Great Seer.
In the past, you were a renunciant who practiced infinite contemplation; you abandoned your distinguished royal capital,
along with its multitudes of elephants, horses, and many meritorious vehicles.
By that, O Essence of Beings, you illuminate the directions.
Having abandoned his wife, as well as his own flesh, his sons and daughters, his eyes and his own flesh,
and having previously sacrificed his beloved head.
By that, you illuminate all directions on every side.
Having abandoned pure celestial jewels and various palaces inlaid with radiant gems—
[palaces] with the luster of stars and the brilliance of lightning in the sky—
You shine forth before all people.
Having spoken such a verse as this,
the other son of Māra, Vidyupratiṣṭha,
[offered] thousands of nayutas of kotis of garments.
He was cast down by the king, having been born of supreme speed.
His spiritual friends also supported him,
lest he should give rise to a lack of faith toward the many Buddhas;
for this great-souled one, Vimalaprabha, cannot be overcome.
To move the Sage once more from his seat.
Disbelieving these words, that evil-minded one,
a kinsman of Kṛṣṇa, gave rise to envy and anger;
he was born with a wicked mind and devoid of wisdom.
To a greater degree, he produces lack of confidence among people.
Having arrayed hundreds of millions of Māras,
and having marshaled his vast army of Māras, Māra then desired to create an obstacle to enlightenment.
That person of inferior intellect generates a sinful mind.
Thousands of nayutas of kotis of yakṣas,
as well as nāgas, asuras, humans, mahoragas,
and sons of gandharvas who have attained strength and power.
They approached that lord of trees.
Having seized a rock of most terrible form,
clad in armor and with a most fearsome appearance,
he hurled lightning bolts and rained down thunderbolts.
Approaching the preeminent lord of trees.
Seizing spears and javelins, and grasping swords with razor-sharp edges,
they hang garlands and shout "ki-li-ki-la! in joy.
They set out toward the lordly elephant Siṃhapāda.
Lions, tigers, horses, elephants, camels, cows, donkeys, and others of various forms,
with heads grasped by venomous serpents;
They approached from where the Bodhisattva was.
Others, seizing great masses of fire, had their heads ablaze and their natures distorted; some moved about with razor-sharp blades, while others had their noses shattered.
The armies of Māra stood at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
Thousands of chariots at the seat of enlightenment,
along with banners and flags resounding with joyful noise, were indeed beautiful to behold and auspiciously proclaimed.
And at the very top of the banner-pole, there was a joyful sound.
For thirty yojanas all around,
it was filled with thousands of most terrifying yakṣas,
in the four directions and above in the sky.
Those hosts of yakṣas were of most exceedingly terrible form.
Grasping a sharp, keen sword,
the kinsman of darkness approached at a distance of a yoke’s length;
with a malevolent mind, he spoke to the Bodhisattva.
Arise quickly from this seat!
For thirty yojanas all around, it was filled with thousands of most terrifying yakṣas;
it was not possible for any monk to go forth anywhere.
Today I shall cut you down, just like a section of bamboo.
Then the Bodhisattva uttered speech endowed with eight qualities— sweet, melodious, and resonant—
even if all those beings were to become Māras.
And they are not able to move even a single hair of mine.
You stand alone, O monk, at the foot of a tree,
and there is no army such as this for you;
by whose power would it not be capable [of harming you]?
That army of Māra is not even able to cause a single hair of yours to quiver.
In generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, and meditation, for many millions of eons,
[he practiced] in immeasurable and supreme wisdom.
There is no one equal to me in the entire world.
Dwelling in loving-kindness, dwelling in compassion,
practicing the conduct of awakening for the sake of sentient beings, having awakened, one attains awakening and the knowledge of a Buddha.
I shall liberate all beings, O Kṛṣṇabandhu!
In previous existences, throughout infinite millions of billions of eons, he was of flawless conduct,
concentrated, and as indestructible as a diamond.
Thus, today I shall attain the supreme, excellent enlightenment.
O kinsman of Kṛṣṇa, however many armies you may have, should they all come under your power and sovereignty,
they would be like the Cakravāḍa mountains when faced with weapons.
And they are not able to move even a single hair of mine.
Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness have been cultivated;
there is no perception of a sentient being... nor perception of Māra, nor perception of harm.
While you remain thus, you are weak, O evil one!
There is no perception of form, nor even perception of sound, nor perception of taste, nor perception of smell;
there is no perception of the tangible... [and so forth].
While you are situated thus, you are powerless, Māra.

I have no perception of the aggregates, nor do I have any perception of the elements; the perception of an internal self has been eliminated by me, for it is like the sky, which is devoid of intrinsic existence.
For all phenomena indeed have such a nature.
With his variegated right hand,
the Bodhisattva struck the earth;
that world-system shook in six ways.
And at that time, there was a sound like the form of Bhīṣma.
Just as a man, having seized Kaṃsa’s gong, might strike it with a sweet sound,
so too in the world-system of battle.
When the Bodhisattva struck Vasumatī.
Then Māra’s army became terrified; frightened, they fled for many yojanas,
looking about in all four directions.
They behold the Buddha, like the king of rays.
Others fell from their chariots onto the earth like thundering clouds in the sky,
or like great elephants in the vast ocean.
In the same way, all [of them] have destroyed the armies of Māra.
The gods scattered divine flowers and rained down sandalwood powder;
they strewed mandārava blossoms over the Bodhisattva.
It extends for thirty yojanas all around.
Thousands of gods in the sky waved their garments;
others threw down pearl necklaces;
and still others praised him with verses and songs.
But Kṛṣṇa’s kinsman, sorrowful, brooded in silence.
For a full seven days, Māra’s army remained distressed at the foot of the tree, fallen into misery,
like those born blind, unable to discern the directions.
And the Buddha shines like the king of rays.
Seeing hundreds of chariots being shattered and the earth trembling as it was struck down,
they manifested themselves with distorted forms.
They approached the lordly king of trees;
they did not regain their former appearance, and all became filled with terror.
Just as a bird bound to the ground remains there,
so too did the Kinsman of the Kṛṣṇas remain upon the surface of the earth for a full seven days, together with his army and his host.
One born with delusion is not able to go forth.
All the sons of the gods who had gathered from the realm of form, being entirely assembled and filled with a surge of joy,
scattered showers of powder as fine as the tip of a hair.
Divine, distinguished, and made of excellent sandalwood.
The sons of the gods raised thousands of millions of billions of banners into the sky;
the Buddha-field was filled with fluttering flags and streamers.
When the Bodhisattva struck Vasumatī.
Divine musical instruments resounded in the sky, and a celestial concert of the deities arose;
sons of the gods rained down flowers from the heavens.
When the Bodhisattva struck Vasumatī.
As many trees as there were upon the earth, all became possessed of infinite fragrances of flowers;
they were empty, signless, and their aspirations had been fully realized.
He utters a sound of such a nature.
In the divine palaces situated above the clouds,
likewise in the palaces of the nāgas within the ocean,
and in the cities of the asuras, there are sounds of pleasing resonance.
When the Bodhisattva struck Vasumatī.
At the time when the Bodhisattva emits a ray from the palm of his hand, which is variegated with auspicious signs, then, setting aside the desire for the end of hell, [he brings about its cessation].
He falls into the worlds of Yama in every world.
They saw the earth, the bearer of wealth, become utterly distraught; ten million Māras were falling upon the ground,
and they saw the Sage who had attained perfect awakening.
Like a thousand moons in the sky.
Then, having risen from the earth, they rose up even more toward one another like variegated silk cloths cast into the sky.
In that very way, Māra’s army then became [powerless].
The supreme Bodhisattva, being undaunted, free from fear, and incomparable field of merit,
having previously practiced the most excellent and sublime Dharma, [attained this state].
You shine in the world like the king of rays.
This is suffering, and this is its origin;
likewise its cessation, and the supreme path.
When this exists, that appears.
When this is lost, that comes to an end.
Ignorance is the cause of the conditioned formations of existence; it serves as the condition for their arising.
With consciousness as the cause, name-and-form exists within existence.
And that becomes the condition for the six sense faculties.
The six sense faculties arise, and from them contact is born;
contact is the cause of feelings.
Experiencing these, one becomes possessed by craving.
With craving as condition, clinging comes to be.
They recollect existence as the cause of grasping,
and likewise birth, old age, death, and disease;
there are also sorrows and lamentations.
Exertions lead to suffering and mental distress.
The Bodhisattva, having investigated the phenomenon of dependent origination,
perceives their cessation within unimpeded omniscience;
thus he beholds their very nature.
He has attained the incomparable, supreme, and excellent awakening.
And when the Jina has attained the supreme enlightenment, the unsurpassed and immeasurable, possessing the pure eye,
his knowledge having proceeded throughout the directions without attachment;
The sound traveled through the three worlds in succession.
The immeasurable drum was struck, and at that time an immeasurable sound arose;
the multitudes of men and women attained freedom from sorrow.
The gods, nāgas, humans, and mahoragas.
Infinite thousands of millions and billions of sons of gods, pure in their dwellings, have arrived;
they join their palms with ten fingers extended.
He praised the One Possessing Ten Powers, who has reached the further shore.
Like the king of mountains in the midst of the ocean,
like Vaijayanta upon the summit of Sumeru,
or like a thousand suns in the sky.
Thus did the Jina shine at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
For whose sake generosity was given in previous existences, and for whom pure morality was guarded in the past; for whose sake supreme wisdom was cultivated— [for that person's sake].
O best of lords of men, you have attained awakening.
The one with vision who destroys cataracts,
the destroyer of the nature of decay, the essence of beings;
the self-become one who has attained [enlightenment], the caravan leader among the best of men.
There is no one at all equal to you in the entire world.
All world-systems have been illuminated by you with a dense radiance, like the moon when it is released;
just as the divine splendor of the various gods blazes forth.
And of the nāgas, asuras, and mahoragas.
It might be possible to weigh Sumeru, the king of mountains,
by reducing it to dust; one could even divide it into as many equal portions as there are mustard seeds.
It is impossible to exhaust the praise of the Buddhas, the Victors.
Just as the drops of water in the great ocean, though filled with water, can be grasped by the hand and counted—
thousands of koṭis, nayutas, and hundreds.
It is impossible to fully describe the qualities of the Victors.
It might be possible to know everything here within this trichiliocosm up to the peak of existence— the earth, the trees, the wind, the fire,
and the number of grasses, creepers, medicinal herbs, and their potencies.
The praise of the Buddha cannot be fully exhausted.
Even if one were to pierce through a hundred or a thousand layers of clouds, it would be possible to count the sky and the highest reaches of the firmament,
as well as these hundreds of directions in the four quarters.
The praise of the Buddha cannot be fully exhausted.
Even if one were able to count all the realms of sentient beings, and even all the body hairs and the hair on their heads,
those bodies of theirs would still be more numerous than those of the past.
It is not possible to exhaust the praise of the Victors.
Those beings who, having heard such qualities as these, with serene minds remember the Lord of the World,
for them there is a great gain, and they shall abandon the miserable states of existence.
And their enlightenment is considered to be not far off.
Furthermore, monks, after the Tathāgata had fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, he spent seven days in a single cross-legged posture.
Then indeed, the gods who dwell on the earth, the gods who move through the atmosphere, the gods of the Four Great Kings, the gods of the Thirty-three,

the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, Mahābrahmā, the Brahmakāyika gods, the Brahmapurohita gods, the Brahmapāriṣadya gods, and the Ābhāsvara and Parīttābhā gods—
And the gods of the Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Śubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Vṛhatphala, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa,
up to the Akaniṣṭha heavens, honored the Tathāgata for a full seven days while he was at the supreme seat of enlightenment.
They honored, revered, and worshiped him; and the entire trichiliocosm remained adorned with a single ornament for a full seven days.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke this verse:
Having awakened to supreme enlightenment, the Perfectly Awakened One, the shrine of the entire world, did not rise from his seat for seven full days.
Thousands of millions of deities gathered in the sky and rained down a shower of flowers for no less than seven nights.
There the gods rained down blue lotuses, red lotuses, campaka flowers, white lotuses, and delightful thousand-petaled blossoms of exquisite beauty.
And Māra was dejected; he scratched the earth with his arrow:
"I have been conquered by the God of Gods, the Scorching Lion of the Śākyas!"
The Trāyastriṃśa gods, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, and those who are Nirmāṇarati, as well as the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods— all those established in the realm of desire.
Divine red sandalwood, aloeswood, and campaka flowers,
as well as divine showers of blossoms, were scattered from the sky;
this buddha-field was drenched by streams of water as thick as axle-trees.
Thousands of millions of Brahmās assembled in the sky and rained down a fine powder of divine red sandalwood.
Beginning with the gods of the earth up to the Śuddhāvāsa gods who are self-luminous,
the succession of deities was thus completely filled.
With parasols, banners, and flags, they completely fill the sky,
performing the most excellent worship for the glorious, perfectly awakened Buddha.
A vast radiance was released, completely illuminating the Buddha-field;
even the world-systems up to the peak of existence became of one uniform color.
The hells became completely pacified throughout this buddha-field;
the glowing coals were turned cold, and sentient beings became happy.
For those whose hellish suffering has been completely exhausted,
those beings in the hells will be reborn among the gods.
In Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Tapana, Pratāpana,
and Raurava, the fire was extinguished by the rays of the Lord of the World.
Then, in the Avīci hell, in Saṃghāta, and in the individual hells,
the fire was completely extinguished by the rays of the Lord of the World.
In as many world-systems as there were individual hells,
the fire was entirely extinguished by the rays of the Lord of the World.
And those who belong to the animal realm, feeding on flesh and blood,
were suffused with loving-kindness by the Buddha so that they do not harm one another.
The Bodhi tree was adorned with parasols, banners, and flags;
it was covered with gabled pavilions fashioned by the sons of the gods.
Stumps, thorny thickets, gravel, and even sand were established all around the seat of awakening, down to the ground below.
The seat of enlightenment was completely covered by ground made of jewels,
which had been fashioned here in this buddha-field by the sons of the gods.
Thousands of sons of gods stood upon the earth;
taking up incense burners, they paid homage to the Leader of the World.
And the entire ground below was completely covered with lotuses made of Jāmbūnada gold, which had arisen through the splendor of the Buddha.
And those beings who were diseased, suffering, and without refuge,
became healthy and happy, suffused by the rays of the Buddha.
Those born blind shall see forms once they have obtained confident vision;
and they shall converse with one another when the Protector has attained awakening.
At the time when the Lion of the Śākyas, the Great Seer, attained enlightenment, passion, hatred, and delusion were rendered minute.
The palaces, together with their celestial mansions and delightful gabled houses,
were all oriented toward the Bodhisattva, the Protector.
As many men, women, and kinnaras as there were within the Buddha-field,
they all turned their faces toward the Bodhisattva, the Protector.
The deities, the sons of gods, and the beautiful daughters of gods were all turned toward that direction where the Great Seer’s enlightenment lay.
Then the nāgas, gandharvas, yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, and rākṣasas—
all turned their faces toward where the Great Seer’s awakening was located.
The girls and boys as well, having lain down upon their beds and seats,
remained with their faces turned toward where the Great Seer’s awakening was.
And whatever divine ornaments, distinguished and made of jewels,
were worn by the gods, they all turned toward him.
Then all the ornaments of the nāgas, yakṣas, piśācas, and rākṣasas went toward where the Bodhi tree was located.
Then the celestial palaces of the gods, the nāgas, the yakṣas, and the rākṣasas were turned toward that direction where the Great Seer’s awakening was located.
Ankle-bells, bracelets, or even armlets—
by means of these, the robe of the Buddha who has attained awakening becomes hanging down.
Necklaces for people, beautiful golden coins on their necks,
and ornaments fastened by men— by which unshakable enlightenment [is attained].
Necklaces of pearls were fastened, along with various jeweled earrings,
bracelets, and rings, by which unshakable awakening was attained.
However many inconceivable realms of truth there are within the Buddha-fields— whether they know it or do not know it— by this, awakening is unshakable.
And cool winds, fragrant and delightful,
shall blow throughout the entire buddha-field for that Protector who has attained awakening.
As many gods, nāgas, and humans, asuras, kinnaras, and yakṣas as there are within the Buddha-field, they all behold the Leader.
Having taken up incense burners, they all remained in comfort and paid homage to the Lamp of the World, who was established at the seat of awakening.
They paid homage with joined palms and praised him with verses;
established at the seat of awakening, they offered worship to the Buddha.
Everyone sees the Lord of the World, the Illuminator, as being near; no one perceives him as distant, for he stands as if at a distance of only one fathom.
No one in the world-system sees the Buddha from behind;
for in every direction, he is seen face-to-face by all who look upon him.
From the left or right side, no one perceives the Leader of the World;
yet all behold the Great Hero, the Guide.
In that buddha-field there was incense burning, and immediately thereafter,
tens of millions of buddha-fields were filled on all sides with its fragrance.
It is not possible to calculate how many millions of beings,
having beheld the glory of the Buddha, have set out toward perfect enlightenment.
The grasses, the wood, the herbs, and the forest trees—
all of them were turned toward that direction where the Great Seer’s enlightenment was located.
Who, having heard such teachings as these shown by the Lord of the World, would not be satisfied, except for one who belongs to the faction of Māra?
It is not possible to fully describe with speech, even by one possessing supernatural power,
the glory that belonged to the Buddha, the Protector, when he had attained awakening.
And those wise ones who have seen the Perfectly Awakened One established at the seat of enlightenment, and who have honored the Great Hero, are filled with joy upon hearing this.
And those monks who are well-established in the aggregate of ethical discipline that is without flaw,
having heard this sutra, will experience auspicious joy.
Endowed with patience and gentleness, their bodies and minds undaunted,
and seeking the wisdom of a Buddha, they shall find satisfaction.
When I have awakened to supreme enlightenment, those beings whom I have comforted and who are being born [in my realm] shall attain joy.
Those best of the twice-born who have honored previous Buddhas,
those great seers, will be filled with joy upon hearing this sutra.
Those wretched beings who were satisfied by you with food and drink,
having heard this sutra, will show reverence toward the Buddha.
Those destitute beings who were previously covered by riches,
having heard this sūtra, will show reverence toward the Buddha.
And those by whom beautiful shrines for the Buddhas were previously constructed— having awakened with supreme faith, they indeed shall become joyful.
Those who in the past upheld the true Dharma of the Lord of the World,
having renounced gain and honor, will indeed be filled with joy.
Those who possess unconditioned life and are free from punitive actions will indeed perform worship to the breast-born sons of the Lord of the World.
Those who, having seen the perfectly awakened Maitreya, the supreme among bipeds,
shall perform extensive worship, they will experience great joy.
Those who, having seen you— the lion, the great elephant, the shrine of the world—
shall perform extensive worship, for them there will be joy.
For those who perform worship of Ketu, the Lord of the World,
and who seek the wisdom of a Buddha, there will be joy.
And those who shall perform worship for the Buddha Pradyota,
being seekers of the Buddha’s wisdom, will experience great joy.
And those who, having seen the Buddha Aparājita, the Holder of Light,
shall perform great worship, for them there will be joy.
Those who, having seen Sunetra, the illuminator of the world, shall honor him,
will experience joy through immeasurable worship.
There will be two Buddhas named Kusuma, Tathāgatas who are protectors of the world;
those who see them and honor them will experience great joy.
Those who, having seen Maru, the best of bipeds, the perfectly awakened one, the foremost of speakers, shall honor him, will experience great joy.
And those who, having seen the Flower, the Perfectly Awakened One, the supreme among bipeds,
shall offer the highest worship, for them there will be joy.
Those who are greedy for gain and honor, relying on crooked wisdom, will be terrified upon hearing about that state of having few desires.
And those who delight in company and are established in living in groups— upon hearing of the Buddha’s solitude, they feel no distress.
Having heard what was thus spoken by the Buddha, those of immoral conduct will bow down before the Lamp of the World and show intense reverence.
Those future bodhisattvas who have been prophesied by the Buddha—
those who are gentle and pleasant to dwell with— they shall experience joy.
Those for whom there is no turning back at all from the Buddha-knowledge—
those people, having heard this sutra, will become happy.
Those former Buddhas, the essence of beings, who were honored, revered, and worshipped as lords of men—
before them he bowed his mind, being instructed in the Buddha-knowledge.
Having heard [this], O one of the finest complexion among men, they become joyful.
And those who are unimpaired, completely pure, endowed with hundreds of millions of excellent qualities,
and those by whom you uphold the Dharma while it is decaying—
With a joyful mind within the teaching of the Sugata.
And those who are not fickle— steadfast, not loquacious, and whose speech is not scattered—
and who are not possessed by pride.
Having heard the excellent description of the Conqueror, they become joyful.
Those who have not abandoned the wisdom of the Buddha— this stainless, incomparable, and infinite enlightenment—
and who practice their vows with vigilance;
Having heard the excellent praise of the Victor, they become joyful.
Endowed with four qualities, O monks, the Tathāgata, while formerly practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, attained preeminence over the entire world.
By which four?
With an unbroken aggregate of ethical conduct...
[Mvu 2.357] ...with a mind intent on the welfare of all sentient beings and a mind intent on the benefit of all sentient beings.
Monks, endowed with these four qualities, the Tathāgata, while formerly practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, attained this kind of omniscience.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke this verse:
In the teaching of the Lord of the World, the aggregate of ethical discipline is the supreme wealth;
neither gold nor silver is described as the wealth of a monk.
One who is well-established in the Teacher’s dispensation should honor ethical discipline;
one who is immoral and trembling is far from being a disciple of the Buddha.
Having guarded their moral discipline without flaw, the supreme among bipeds— the Lords of the World, the great heroes endowed with the thirty-two excellent marks— behold them.
One who is intent on the aggregate of virtue through loving-kindness, who delights in dwelling in the forest,
and who is gentle and pleasant to dwell with— this is the wealth of the ascetic life.
Having little desire, being easily satisfied, gentle, well-composed, and endowed with moral shame and dread of blame— this is the wealth of the ascetic life.
For monks of virtuous conduct, having severed the ensnaring net of craving, cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment; this is the wealth of the ascetic life.
The Sage meditates on emptiness and peace, and is detached from existence;
this wealth of the ascetic life is free from much suffering and devoid of essence.
He who practices in this way becomes very wealthy;
indeed, that monk who is perfected in practice is truly great in wealth.
The monk who is perfected in virtue is said to be wealthy;
for a monk does not become great in riches merely by means of pearls and coral.
A virtuous monk who practices non-violence is pleasant to dwell with;
for it is not by the acquisition of robes that a monk goes to a heavenly state.
Having practiced pure ethical discipline, he avoids all unfavorable conditions;
the Teacher does not praise a monk who seeks gain from his kinsmen.
Having applied effort toward ethical conduct, heaven is not difficult to attain;
wherever one is reborn, one becomes beloved and pleasing to all.
A wise person, seeking three kinds of happiness— praise, the attainment of mental peace, and rejoicing in heaven after death— should guard their virtue.
Ethical discipline is the most excellent garment; it is a radiant ornament.
A monk adorned with ethical discipline does not suffer when giving.
Through perfectly pure ethical discipline, the body becomes radiant;
and when death has arrived, no burning pain arises for him.
When morality is completely pure, the attainment of its fruit is not difficult;
