how much more so, then, that one attains the heavenly realm and beholds the Lord of the World!
A monk adorned with pure morality and gentle in nature is truly praised;
for one does not become a praiseworthy monk merely by speaking in a loud voice.
Possessing virtue and being undaunted, he never fears at any time; he never goes to a miserable rebirth among beings for having committed transgressions.
One who possesses virtue has few concerns and little business, delights in spiritual qualities,
quickly attains meditative concentration, and also gains serene confidence.
A monk who is protected by the aggregate of ethical discipline becomes confident;
his vision is never impaired when he beholds the disciples of the Jina.
And having purified his moral conduct, O monk, he remembers his former dwellings for thousands of millions of eons, being fully conscious and mindful.
And this is the natural outflow of his virtue:
that the Great Hero, the shrine for all the world, gazes upon the Brahma-world as he passes by.
Through completely pure ethical discipline, the divine eye becomes purified;
for such a person, there is no further coming at all into any of the Buddha-fields.
Through his perfectly perfected morality, the immeasurable Tathāgata,
the Leader, knows the passing away and rebirth of all sentient beings.
One who possesses ethical discipline, wandering through the world heedful and striving with diligence,
for such a person it is not difficult to hear the delightful voice of the Buddha.
One who possesses ethical discipline becomes dear to all beings and is honored everywhere;
being respected and esteemed, he is pure of heart and free from blemish.
By means of perfectly pure ethical conduct, a person sees, as they are about to pass away,
a radiant and excellent celestial mansion frequented by hosts of apsarases.
By means of perfectly pure ethical conduct, a person beholds one passing away and being reborn upon the beautiful summit of Mount Sumeru, in the abode of the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
Through perfectly pure morality, he beholds the Yāma deities and that very divine city, filled with apsarases.
Through perfectly pure ethical conduct, one beholds the Tuṣita deities;
one beholds their celestial palaces, variegated and composed of jewels.
Through completely pure ethical discipline, one beholds the Nirmāṇarati gods and beholds the well-adorned sons of the Sunirmita gods.
Through perfectly pure ethical discipline, one beholds the beautiful gods established in their celestial palaces as masters of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin realm.
Through perfectly pure ethical discipline, one beholds Māra’s abode,
covered with canopies of jewels and frequented by hosts of apsarases.
Having applied effort toward ethical conduct, one beholds the Brahmās and the deities,
as well as palaces of Jāmbūnada gold adorned with jewels.
The virtuous monk beholds the gods of the Brahma-realm and the gods who are the Ministers of Brahma, established within their celestial palaces.
A virtuous monk beholds the gods of the Brahma-parishadya realm and the Mahābrahmā deities established in celestial palaces.
Endowed with the aggregate of ethical discipline, one sees the radiance of the deities;
one beholds their distinguished palaces made of jewels.
The virtuous monk sees the auspicious gods of great psychic power;
he also sees the Śubhakṛtsna gods and the Apramāṇābha gods.
Having guarded pure ethical discipline, one beholds the Parīttaśubha deities and thousands of sons of gods established in the realm of form.

Through perfectly pure morality, one sees the Bṛhatphala heaven; likewise, through perfectly pure morality, one sees the Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, and Sudarśana heavens, and one also sees the Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
Those who attain final nirvana there, like a fire extinguished by water—
those monks also see this, having guarded excellent moral discipline.
In former lives, he was always unstained in his conduct and distinguished by his marks;
therefore, he approaches the Teacher, the One Possessed of Ten Powers.
His body shines with the [major] marks.
The Jina has always practiced with heedfulness in ethical discipline and meditative concentration throughout infinite past eons;
by that, he becomes the Lord of the world's dharmas.
Just as the sun, the king of rays, situated in the sky.
Having thus practiced such perfectly pure ethical discipline for immeasurable and likewise infinite eons,
the Sugata, adorned with the marks, shines with splendor.
From his mouth wafts the fragrance of sandalwood.
Constantly perceiving these virtues and maintaining the ethical discipline praised by the supreme Victors,
dwell in the forest with uplifted minds.
That which is honored by the best of sages is indeed sublime.
I have seen former Buddhas, the caravan leaders, who had destroyed the passions and were honored and worshipped by themselves; thus,
the aspiration for supreme enlightenment has been generated.
Having heard of these qualities, the Bodhisattvas become uplifted.

Furthermore, monks, the Tathāgata is pure in ethical discipline; the Tathāgata is pure in concentration; the Tathāgata is pure in wisdom; the Tathāgata is pure in liberation; the Tathāgata is pure in the knowledge and vision of liberation; the Tathāgata, monks, is pure in patience; the Tathāgata, monks, is also pure in gentleness; the Tathāgata, monks, is pure in loving-kindness; and the Tathāgata, monks, is pure in compassion and sympathetic joy.
And so too, monks, is the Tathāgata.

Thus, for a monk who is completely pure, it is impossible to reach the limit of the merit of one who would pay honor to the Tathāgata with flowers, garlands, perfumes, banners, flags, music, and ointments;
nor can that mass of merit ever be exhausted except by means of one or another of the three vehicles until final nirvāṇa, at which point its limit is reached.
For what reason?
Just as the Tathāgata, O monk, is immeasurable in all his qualities, even so, O monk, an offering established for the Tathāgata is immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable,
incomparable, unfathomable, infinite, and ineffable.
Furthermore, O monk, if someone were to honor, revere, respect, and worship the Tathāgata while he is currently living and maintaining his life—

honoring him with flowers, perfumes, garlands, parasols, banners, flags, musical instruments, incense, ointments, food, drink, vehicles, and clothing— and if another were to [honor] even a relic the size of a mustard seed from one who has entered final nirvāṇa, [the latter would generate greater merit].
"To honor" is equal to "equal."
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke this verse:
Having directed the mind toward awakening for the benefit of all living beings,
whoever performs a circumambulation of the stūpa of the Lord of the World, [attains great merit].
Possessing mindfulness, possessing intelligence, and possessing merit,
one becomes confident in all births while practicing the conduct of awakening.
Having performed a circumambulation of a stūpa, one becomes honored everywhere among all births by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas.
One should avoid the eight inopportune states that have been taught by me in any way,
and instead cultivate the single opportune state, the most beautiful arising of a Buddha.
Endowed with excellent complexion and form, adorned with the primary marks,
he was possessed of a sublime appearance and a mind free from dejection.
He becomes wealthy, possessing great riches and merit, and free from envy;
having seen the Light of the World, he honors him again and again.
Having seen selflessness and emptiness in all phenomena, he is not deluded regarding those phenomena;
he quickly attains serene confidence and becomes skilled in the Dharma.
He is reborn into wealthy and prosperous merchant families;
he is a heroic master of giving, one who practices relinquishment and is free from envy.
Whosoever among those distinguished and illustrious families in Jambudvīpa—
therein that hero is born, and he avoids those who are lowly.
A wealthy householder, empowered by the splendor of Śrī,
becomes honored everywhere for having circumambulated a stūpa.
A great brahmin family will be wise and learned,
and a great kṣatriya family will be wealthy and possess great riches.
The king too becomes righteous, a lord over Jambudvīpa,
and he rules this entire earth encircled by mountains.
A universal monarch of great supernatural power, lord of the seven treasures,
established in his kingdom, repeatedly pays honor to the Buddha.
Having passed away, one who has faith in the Buddha's teaching goes to heaven;
even Śakra becomes the lord of the gods, the sovereign on the summit of Mount Meru.
He becomes Suyāma, the lord of gods, and also Saṃtuṣita;
he becomes Nirmita, the lord of gods, and Vaśavartin, the sovereign.
Even Brahmā becomes a wise lord in the Brahma-world,
honored by tens of millions of gods, having circumambulated a stūpa.
It is not possible to exhaustively describe, even in hundreds of millions of eons,
those who perform circumambulations of the stupa of the Lord of the World.
Having directed the mind toward awakening, whoever pays homage to the shrine of the Teacher shall never become blind or one-eyed for tens of millions of eons.
By performing a circumambulation of the shrine of the Lord of the World, one obtains pure, wide eyes that are beautiful with their dark blue hue.
Endowed with strength and vigor, he does not fall into indolence;
having circumambulated the stūpa, he becomes ever vigilant.
Possessing firm vigor, firm strength, a leader, and firm prowess,
one quickly attains skillfulness by performing circumambulation of a stūpa.
The wise person never dies by fire, poison, or weapons;
he meets his end only when his full lifespan has been exhausted.
Proclaimed throughout the royal capitals, kingdoms, and market towns:
"By means of beauty, wealth, and enjoyments, one should perform circumambulation of the stūpa."
With pure body and pure clothing, established in the white dharmas,
he does not indulge in sensual desires while practicing the conduct of awakening.
Having fashioned a garland of flowers and offered it at a stūpa,
having directed the mind toward awakening, one shall never suffer defeat.
Having passed away from here and died, he indeed goes to the Trāyastriṃśa heaven;
there he quickly obtains a celestial palace made of various jewels.
Having offered garlands upon a stūpa, one enjoys celestial palaces and gabled mansions frequented by hosts of apsarases among the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
May I obtain a divine lotus pond, complete with the excellence of the eight qualities, strewn with golden sand, and covered with lapis lazuli and crystal.
Having enjoyed divine wealth and having fulfilled [his merit], the wise one,
passing away from the world of the gods, becomes a human being possessed of riches.
And by that root of merit, the heedful and wise one propitiates the Tathāgata and honors the Best of Bipeds.
Having worshipped the Supreme among Bipeds, he is not conquered by passion, nor is he humiliated by hatred; he never becomes deluded.
Having honored the Leader of the World, one becomes free from passion, free from hatred, and free from delusion, with sense faculties restrained in all births.
For hundreds, thousands, and millions of billions of births,
one will be honored everywhere after having offered a garland at a shrine.
Having offered a garland at a caitya, one becomes even a universal monarch, or Śakra the lord, or even Brahmā in the Brahma-world.
Having offered a silk ribbon at the stūpa of the Lord of the World,
all one's aims are fulfilled— both those that are divine and those that are human.
He avoids low-born families and is not reborn there;
rather, he becomes wealthy, possessed of riches, and a lord in Jambūdvīpa.
Having made offerings to the Tathāgata, one becomes distinguished everywhere in terms of physical form, enjoyments, complexion, and supernatural power.
He becomes one who remembers his past lives and is not led astray by passion;
knowing the fault of sensual desires, he undertakes the holy life.
Unconquered by forms, sounds, and tastes,
he commits no evil deed after having worshipped the Supreme among Bipeds.
Having honored the Leader, he is never repelled by fragrances or by tactile objects; he becomes possessed of mindfulness and clear comprehension.
Neither thieves nor kings can seize his mass of wealth, nor does fire consume it, once he has paid homage to the Tathāgata.
Having offered a silk ribbon and flowers to the Leader of the World, he never again falls into sorrow or the weariness of grief.
In all his births, he shall be free from sorrow and unharmed;
having honored the Light of the World, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch of great supernatural power.
With hands and feet well-knit, he attains beauty of limb;
endowed with excellence of complexion and form, he honors the Leader of the World.
Avoiding evil karma while practicing the conduct of awakening,
one beholds those supreme among bipeds who are so difficult to find in the world.
Having enjoyed happiness for hundreds, thousands, and nayutas of millions of eons, that wise one awakens to supreme enlightenment.
Having constructed a garland-monastery for the relics of the Lord of the World, the king becomes possessed of great supernatural power, surrounded by an invincible retinue.
One avoids those unwholesome states that have been shunned by the Noble Ones,
and practices those wholesome states that have been praised by the Buddhas.
He becomes beloved, dear, honored,
and praised by the gods, the nāgas, and those who are wise in the world.
Accompanied by a magnificent and vast retinue, the one of great power worships the Buddha, the unconquered and supreme among bipeds.
In whatever house he is born, empowered by the splendor of his merit,
that family becomes honored by both the kingdom and the town.
Having constructed a flower garland monastery, one should direct the mind toward awakening;
this is the accomplishment for him that has been praised by the Buddhas.
Neither humpbacked, nor lame, nor stumbling in his gait is he;
wherever he is reborn, he is adorned with the [major] marks.
Seeing poor beings, he covers them with wealth;
and while practicing the conduct of awakening, he remains unassailable.
Having renounced this entire earth, the one of great intelligence becomes undaunted in mind; he never desponds.
Having cast aside his sons, daughters, and even his auspicious and blessed wife,
he who has set out for awakening departs.
He is one who initiates conversation first, possessing a pleasant countenance and being easy to look upon;
he is never overcome by envy nor ever by pride.
Thus, one who is free from envy and gentle, who has reached the perfection of patience,
who desires the welfare of others and is endowed with virtues, is one who has set out toward awakening.
A jewel in all the world, his appearance is difficult to find—
he who is irreproachable, worthy of offerings, and has set out for enlightenment.
A child might be able to count the stars in the sky in a single blink of an eye,
but it is not possible to describe the limit of his virtues with words.
It is possible to know the minds of all sentient beings throughout the three times,
but it is not possible to describe the limit of his virtues with words.
The four great oceans, the sands likewise,
and thousands of millions of nāgas cannot describe his virtues.

Even if one were able to count, in a single blink of an eye, all the hairs on the bodies of every sentient being throughout the six realms of existence in the world, it would still be impossible to describe his virtues.
Wherein this entire earth is established upon the mass of water—
no fool is able to create such a thing, nor can its qualities be fully described.
Starting from the temple of the gods, those trees that live for an eon, those that exist in the interval here, and those on the earth yet to come.
It might be possible for one who possesses knowledge to count the flowers and fruits [of a tree],
but it is impossible to describe the limit of the virtues of that son of the Buddha.
They might speak a delightful garland of praise for that hero,
yet it is not possible to describe the limit of the virtues of a son of the Buddha.
He who would do what is unpleasant for hundreds of thousands of births—
having avoided gods and humans, hell shall be his domain.
He becomes blind and sightless, suffering and without refuge—
whosoever, being ignorant, causes oppression to the Bodhisattvas.
Having passed away, he would go to Avīci, which is terrible and fearsome;
with a massive physical form, he experiences agonizing sensations.
There he is reborn with a body one *yojana* in height,
surrounded on all sides by a circle [of flames] and scorched from every direction.
Five thousand heads were established upon his body,
and on each single head there were no fewer than five hundred tongues.
A hundred tongues are placed upon a single tongue-tip;
he who cooks them experiences that most terrible fruit of his evil karma.
Having passed away from the Avīci hell, as well as from the Tapana and Pratāpana hells,
the man of dull wit experiences there the results of his former evil deeds.
The ignorant person who causes oppression to the sons of the Buddha will never again find it easy to obtain a human birth.
For hundreds of thousands of births, for hundreds and for millions,
one experiences painful sensations and is tormented on that account.
He becomes a consumer of marrow, a poison, a terrifying oppressor,
having caused affliction to the sons of the Buddha, the protectors.
Having encountered hunger and thirst, that is the fruit of evil karma;
even after obtaining food, he never eats with satisfaction.
Having passed away from there, one is devoured in great cauldrons in the world of Yama;
having caused oppression to monks, one never finds any protection.
Having passed away from there and reached the end of his life, he comes to the world of humans;
he is born blind, dull-witted, with a perverted view, and unrestrained.
Speech that is ill-spoken becomes untrue and evil-sounding;
having passed away from among humans, one quickly goes to an evil destination.
For thousands of millions of eons, one who is unrestrained and causes harm to the sons of the Buddha shall never behold a Buddha.
O sons of the Buddha, by providing righteous protection for things,
one avoids all miserable rebirths and swiftly goes to a heavenly realm.
One becomes wealthy, possessing great riches, powerful, and confident;
endowed with mindfulness and wisdom, one is happy and free from affliction.
And when the illuminators of the world have entered final nirvana,
they behold the stupas of the Buddhas and pay them honor again and again.
Who, having heard such teachings spoken by the Buddha,
would not repeatedly develop serene confidence in the sons of the Buddha?
And whoever should honor hundreds, thousands, and nayutas of Buddhas— as many as there are grains of sand in the Ganges— for so many eons;
And whoever should uphold for even a single night and day the True Dharma shown by the Lord of the World as it is perishing, his merit will be superior.
I am honored when established in the wisdom of a Buddha;
and those Buddhas are also honored when the Dharma is maintained during its decline.
He who protects the Teacher’s instruction while the True Dharma is perishing shall never suffer harm for thousands of millions of eons.
He is physically happy and does not fall ill;
he is never overwhelmed by thousands of unpleasant things.
Endowed with patience, gentle, amiable, and mild,
and possessing a mind of loving-kindness toward all beings, he protects the teaching of the Teacher.
Happy and joyful,
he attains the rejection of what was previously seen as cessation;
he abandons all unfavorable conditions without remainder.
Having upheld the Dharma of the Supreme Victor while it was being destroyed.
He is always armored with the primary marks, just as the sky is filled with stars;
he possesses sweet speech and a pleasing voice.
Having upheld the Dharma of the supreme Jina while it was decaying.
He becomes one who is free from low-born families;
he is happy among those who possess neither ease nor mental joy.
He becomes wealthy, happy, and possessed of enjoyments.
Having upheld the Dharma of the Supreme Victor while it was being destroyed.
Possessing supreme strength and vigor, he wanders undaunted across the entire earth,
honoring hundreds of thousands of Buddhas.
Having upheld the Dharma of the Supreme Victor while it was being destroyed.
Possessing mindfulness, intelligence, and insight, they become endowed with merit and receive the highest honor among humans and gods;
such wise ones are most highly praised in Jambudvīpa.
Having upheld the Dharma of the Supreme Victor while it was being destroyed.
Extremely beautiful and lovely to behold, he becomes dear to men, women, and gods;
radiant, praiseworthy, and possessed of merit.
Having upheld the Dharma of the Supreme Victor while it was being destroyed.
Even if one were endowed with the stability of virtues for a full hundred thousand billion kalpas, possessing infinite knowledge,
one could not exhaust all its benefits.
Having upheld the corrupted teaching of the supreme Victor.
For those people to whom the Teacher, the God of Gods, the possessor of the ten powers, has revealed this foremost sūtra,
there shall be unshakable joy.
It will come to pass in the future time, when it is present.
And he shall proclaim the Dharma of the supreme Jinas who have attained nirvāṇa; with faith and reverence, he upholds it;
and he gives gifts at immeasurable shrines.
He honors the Saṅgha out of reverence for the Blessed One.
While the teaching of the best of Jinas is being utterly destroyed,
he upholds the Teacher’s supreme guidance of the Dharma;
yet, having failed to perform that most excellent virtuous deed, [he falls].
He did not perform any auspicious act at the time of his death.
And may all sentient beings become protectors of the world, possessing universal vision, with dust removed and free from afflictions;
may they [remain] for thousands of nayutas of kotis of eons.
They would speak praise for the Supreme Victor when flowers were offered.
He abandons evil action at all times and,
with a joyful mind, practices the supreme Dharma; having long practiced for the sake of the goal throughout his various wanderings.
Thus he becomes a Buddha, incomparable in the world.
Whoever takes even a minute amount of incense, as small as a mustard seed, and offers its fragrance at the shrines of the Blessed One—
listen to me as I speak of the benefits for that person.
With a serene mind, abandon the afflictions.
Thus the merit-filled one wanders through the directions,
free from illness, firm in his vows, and heedful;
he guides the worlds as he carries out his journey.
He becomes dear and pleasing to people.
Having attained sovereignty, the Victorious One, the Greatly Powerful and Wise Wheel-turning King, golden-hued and radiant with the marks of excellence, pays honor.
One obtains pleasing fragrances at all times.
He has no suffering or mental distress;
he distributes even inferior enjoyments during his travels.
He becomes wealthy, possessing riches and abundant enjoyments.
Having attained the state where nothing remains, he wanders through all worlds.
He approached many people, inquiring about the distinguished Dharma within the teaching of the Jina;
speaking with words, he dispelled their doubts.
And having heard the Dharma, one obtains gladness.
One of inferior intellect does not perform evil deeds;
rather, having realized supreme knowledge, the distinguished one performs that which is divine, auspicious, and lovely.
It purifies the eye and dispels darkness.
One does not possess intense passion, nor intense hatred, nor intense delusion in the world of humans,
while practicing pure and unblemished holy conduct.
It accomplishes immeasurable and infinite benefit.
No one ever becomes ill-disposed toward him,
nor does he ever suffer a loss of wealth;
no distress from people ever comes upon him.
Having offered incense at the shrines of the Victorious One.
With a pure mind, stainless, having shaken off all evil, peaceful, thoroughly calmed, and endowed with supreme tranquility,
he practiced for hundreds of millions of billions of eons.
With an undaunted mind, he touches incomparable awakening.
Having established thousands of nayutas of kotis of beings on the supreme path free from sorrow,
he shall turn the peerless wheel in all the world.
Having destroyed the dust of passion and being free from defilements, he shall later enter nirvāṇa.
Having offered a banner at the stūpas of the Blessed One, one should generate the aspiration: "How may I become a Buddha in the world?
Thus, one becomes worthy of worship by the people.
May he practice the supreme conduct of the Victors.
His fame resounds, he is praised by the wise, and he obtains a pure and utterly purified physical form;
he becomes one who is looked up to by the people.
He is the teacher of the gods and the nāgas, and is honored by them.
His physical form is always golden-hued,
and he obtains beautiful robes—
whether made of cotton or woolen blankets.
And of linen, fine silk, and those made of *kauśika* fiber.
Those who in Jambudvīpa are the best of families—
wealthy, magnanimous, and possessing great riches and property—
it is precisely there that his rebirth occurs.
They avoid those families that are low and poor.
By this, sovereignty over him arises in some place,
and no sentient being becomes ill-disposed toward him;
he also censures the evil karma of others.
He possesses pure morality, is ever vigilant,
is free from stinginess, and is without grasping; he is one who practices liberality and has attained freedom from sorrow.
He does not produce [teachings] for the sake of a livelihood;
his voice is proclaimed afar and he is always praised.
Having seen the Buddha, the Great Caravan Leader,
he always performs worship with a joyful heart,
using parasols, banners, flags, perfumes, and garlands.
Always practicing the unblemished holy life.
Having been honored and venerated in the world of men,
one obtains among the gods a supreme celestial palace,
of pleasing color and most beautiful to behold.
Covered with silver and adorned with jewels and crystals.
[He attains] wondrous sovereignty upon the summit of Sumeru;
all the gods bow down before him as his disciples.
Through the Dharma, he generates gladness in them.
He never becomes utterly heedless.
Having passed away from there, he will become a supreme king, an excellent universal monarch (cakravartin) in the world of humans;
no sentient being whatsoever shall produce evil toward him.
One becomes dear and pleasing to people.
Having obtained happiness for many thousands of nayutas of kotis of eons in the world of mortals,
he went to the place where the former Victors had arisen.
Thus he awakened to enlightenment—ageless, deathless, and free from sorrow.
Having raised the banner for the sake of the essence of beings whose dust has been destroyed,
one will before long obtain that which is born;
possessing abundant treasure, one becomes one of incomparable wisdom.
His retinue is one whose mind is undaunted.
Having obtained wealth, he distributes it and enjoys it;
for him there is no fear, nor is there any dejection.
The king, being pleased, bestows villages and kingdoms upon him.
He never gives rise to an evil thought toward him.
A merchant becomes distinguished with abundant wealth, and a householder whose body is adorned with jewels;
or else he becomes a son of the king, or a minister.
And he becomes a powerful universal monarch.
Having obtained a jewel of a family with distinguished wealth, he avoids all low-born families;
always heedful, his mind is never dejected.
One should avoid sensual desires as one would a jar of excrement.
One obtains an excellent form and auspicious moments, becomes a lord in a preeminent family,
and one's retinue becomes indivisible.
And he is held in high esteem by the people.
With a mind full of faith toward the Buddhas and always heedful, he does not produce mental anguish;
neither fire nor weapon can overcome him.
One who possesses merit is always worthy of being looked upon with reverence.
That meritorious man does not engage in negligence; always fully aware,
he is well-restrained and his mind is liberated.
There is no end to that Dharma.
The Blessed One, the speaker of truth, possesses exceptionally sharp limbs and a most purified mind.
May I bring joy to those afflicted by fear among the people, and may I act as their protection and their ultimate refuge.
Having indeed performed many deeds for humanity and established himself in the great mass of wisdom,
he went to the excellent king of trees at the site of enlightenment.
In the Buddha, he is incomparable for the supreme, foremost enlightenment.
Taking from below up to the peak of existence,
this Buddha-field filled with Jāmbūnada gold—
such glory as this could be exhausted.
Not equal to one who offers a single lamp at a stupa of the Buddha.
His body does not become discolored;
he remains firm upon his seat. Having attained light, he moves through the entire world.
Having offered lamps at the stupas of the Blessed One.
And when the appearance of a Jina occurs,
it becomes imminent for the Tathāgata.
Whether it be a son, a brother, or even a father, such a kinsman will before long attain the aggregate of knowledge.
If there were thousands of millions of immeasurable Buddha-fields filled with mustard seeds,
it might be possible to count, weigh, or know them.
Not one who offers even a single lamp at a stupa of the Buddha.
The Buddha is the most worthy recipient, the one to whom the best offerings should be given;
having practiced the most excellent conduct,
he has performed worship for that ocean of virtues.
Its ripening is supreme and incomparable.
If this entire Sahā world-system were filled with lapis lazuli gems and jewels,
it would be possible to exhaust such glory as this.
Not for one who maintains even a single lamp at a stupa of the Buddha.
It would be possible to exhaust such glory as this by means of kārṣāpaṇa coins, filling the entire world-system from its base up to the peak of existence.
Not equal to one who maintains a single lamp at a stūpa of a Buddha.
It would be possible to exhaust such glory as this by using excellent sandalwood to fill thousands of world-systems from the bottom up to the peak of existence.
Not equal to one who holds up even a single lamp at a stupa of the Buddha.
Even if there were thousands of fields filled with many garments— such as the fine cloth found in the auspicious world of the gods—
it would be possible to exhaust such glory as this.
Not equal to one who offers even a single lamp at a stupa of the Buddha.
It would be possible to exhaust such glory as this among the gods and their divine, variegated jewels,
and among the nāgas, asuras, humans,
and mahoragas.
Not for one who maintains even a single lamp at a Buddha-stūpa.
If the divine fragrances found in the worlds of humans and gods were to completely fill this Sahā world,
it would still be possible to exhaust such splendor as this.
Not [is it equal to] holding up even a single lamp at a stupa of the Buddha.

It might be possible to know the measure of this element of space in all directions and intermediate points, saying "it is this much," but it is not so for one who maintains even a single lamp at a stupa of the Buddha.
It would be possible to calculate the measure of that mass of merit.
Having inspired faith in his mind toward that supreme among men, he offered a parasol to the Blessed One, the best of Buddhas, the bull among humans, as he was proceeding through the Māruta grove.
O King of Rays, do not scorch the Buddha-body.
Having performed that supreme Dharma, Śakra among the Maruts said, "I have spoken a hundred thousand times;
I was also Brahmā in the world of Brahmā."
Having given a hundred thousand parasols to the Jina.
I was once a universal monarch, a wheel-turning king who traveled through the ten directions a hundred thousand times; furthermore, I was a wealthy merchant with vast treasuries.
The householder was wealthy and meritorious.
And twenty koṭis of the most excellent Sugatas have come to me, and I have honored, revered,
and venerated them with beds and seats.
Their monasteries were smeared with fragrant scents;
all foul odors have departed from me,
and heat and cold have been eliminated for me.
And you are satisfied, with a most exalted mind,
performing worship for those most supreme ones,
having adorned them beautifully and in a pleasing manner.
Having offered a parasol at the shrines of the Jinas.
His own body also becomes beautiful, adorned with the thirty-two marks,
by which his body shines eternally.
Like a distinguished sacrificial post made of gold,
like one of Jāmbūnada gold, beautiful to behold, unblemished, and radiant with its distinctive marks.
Having attained the superknowledges, he becomes the best of physicians as he practices the victorious conduct of the Conquerors;
he never lacks for enjoyments.
One becomes a teacher to the gods and is honored by them.
He who possesses pure morality and always practices the holy life does not take delight in the enjoyment of sensual pleasures,
having undertaken the practice and gone forth into homelessness.
His meditative concentration is unfailing, and he has attained a most distinguished state.
He never suffers a loss of meditative concentration,
nor does he ever abandon the thought of awakening;
dwelling always in loving-kindness, his mind is ever joyful.
Having offered a parasol at the shrines of the Victorious One.
Having honored the Bull among Men with musical instruments,
the arrows of sorrow do not overcome him;
his voice is delightful throughout the world of men.
And his voice becomes pure.
With a pure stream and an uplifted mind, with pure vision and full awareness,
he becomes well-endowed with the faculty of hearing.
Having played musical instruments at the shrines of the Conqueror.
His tongue becomes slender and beautiful, radiant like a lotus,
as red as coral, like that of the gods.
Whatever beautiful sound he emitted was lovely to behold.
He does not become dull-witted, nor tongueless, nor hunchbacked, nor lame, nor even with severed limbs; he becomes distinguished,
a preeminent self, possessing a preeminent physical form.
Having played musical instruments at the shrines of the Jina.
No person— whether gods, nāgas, humans, or mahoragas— would be displeased with him;
having attained consolation, he may wander through the entire world.
Having played musical instruments at the shrines of the Jina.
He shall never be ill, nor suffer from jaundice, nor be afflicted by leprosy, nor even by skin diseases;
he shall obtain a praiseworthy physical form.
Having played musical instruments at the shrines of the Victorious One.
With a vast mind and an unbent body, his complexion is radiant like a golden image;
he possesses firm concentration and is unshakable.
Having played musical instruments at the shrines of the Jina.
Indeed, among the gods he possesses lordship;
having gone even to the world of humans, he is worthy of worship;
he becomes one of refined vigor, invincible.
Having played musical instruments at the shrines of the Conqueror.
He never shows lack of faith toward anyone,
nor does he speak anything harsh;
the speaker of truth abandons all slanderous speech.
Having played musical instruments at the shrines of the Victorious One.
Having adorned the shrines of the Jinas and bathed the stūpas of the Tathāgatas,
one who possesses pure speech shall likewise bathe the stūpa.
Washing away the dust by means of mindfulness of the dust-free one.
Having practiced the Dharma and the conduct of a practitioner, one who has attained health may wander through the entire world,
becoming an object of praise for the people.
Having offered cow-dung fuel at the shrines of the Jinas.
Possessing unbroken virtue and unfailing meditation,
having attained service and irresistible wealth,
he exercises great authority over the people.
Having offered cow-dung fuel at the shrines of the Victorious One.
He conceives the perception of a cemetery even toward bricks;
he has no desire for the world of sense-pleasures nor a mind stained by passion; he abandons all longing for gain without remainder.
Having offered cow-dung fuel at the shrines of the Victorious One.
He does not cause mental distress to others,
nor does he produce joy in people merely by means of food and drink;
he is neither poor nor diseased.
Having offered cow-dung fuel at the shrines of the Victorious One.
He has no side of enemies,
and he constantly worships the Buddhas; he is indivisible [in his devotion] toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the disciples of the Jina.
Having offered cow-dung fuel at the shrines of the Victorious One.
Even if there were many thousands of infinite fields, entirely filled with Jāmbūnada gold,
it would be possible to exhaust such glory as this.
Nor by offering a single drop of oil at a stūpa of the Jina.
He is always master of his own mind and never acts impulsively;

Having been repelled by the Bodhisattva, Māra returned to his own abode and informed his retinue.
"O worthy one, this Bodhisattva is seated at the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), desiring to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
He must be made to fall from his position; lest he lead the great multitude of people beyond my domain."
Then his son, named Janīsuta, said:
"Father, do not create an obstacle for him regarding his unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; let him awaken!

Just as I have realized it—my descent into the womb, my birth, my renunciation, and how he has now approached and sat at the seat of awakening—he shall today awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
There is no being, nor any collection of beings, capable of creating an obstacle for a bodhisattva regarding his attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Seated at the foot of the tree like an invincible lion, he illuminates the directions;
yet this is never to our liking.
That you have thus assailed such a seer as this.
Endowed with virtue, patience, and austerity, he has reached the supreme goal;
such as he is, his banner is raised high.
Just as an elephant will break its own bonds.
Behold him, the supreme among all bipeds, who shines like the full moon on its auspicious day;
for how could the mind proceed without wisdom?
He who undergoes such an affliction.
No one would fall into a pit of glowing coals, nor would anyone touch a venomous snake with their hand;
even one born blind would be terrified by dogs on his back.
Thus, being sightless, he would fall into a blind well.
Thus these ones become limited in mind;
for such as they, there is no mantra [suitable] regarding that which is such a perfectly pure sphere of activity.
Those lacking faith and devoid of vision fall away.
If you do not accept these words,
you who stand on the path will go astray; as you flee in the four directions, you will remember [this].
Just as, for example, a fallen jackal.
The minister Kāla recited this verse:
Everyone, when their own purpose is fully accomplished,
falls into delusion with a bewildered mind;
O King, as this man here is now without conviction.
The son of Janī applies his intellect improperly.
Then Māra, having donned his great armor, came into the presence of the Bodhisattva.
And it was shattered by the sound of the Bodhisattva’s cough.
Again, Māra, having donned his great armor, approached the Bodhisattva at the seat of awakening with a vast fourfold army consisting of kumbhāṇḍas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas.

Having pervaded the area for thirty yojanas on all sides, he mounted a vehicle yoked to a thousand horses; bearing a variegated bow, clad in armor and mail, with banners and flags raised high, he was surrounded by a terrifying and hideous army of spirit hosts, accompanied by the resounding noise of many kettledrums, clay drums, *marupaṭaha* drums, small drums, and conchs, emitting shouts of joy and war-cries.
It is as follows:
Some had the faces of horses, some the faces of camels, some the faces of donkeys, some the faces of goats,
some the faces of rams, some the faces of deer, some the faces of lions, some the faces of tigers, some the faces of leopards, some the faces of bears,
some the faces of dogs, some the faces of pigs, some the faces of cats, some the faces of crows, some the faces of cocks, and some the faces of vultures.

Some had faces like ospreys; some were headless trunks; some had a single head, some many heads, and some two heads; some were eyeless, some had only one eye; some were handless, some were footless, some were armless, some had ten arms;
some carried swords, some carried spears, some carried javelins, some carried slings, and some carried tridents.
Some held tridents, some held plows, some held wheels, some held clubs, some held mallets, some held axes, some held swords, and some held skeletons.
Some vomited fire from their mouths, some vomited snakes, and others whirled razor-edged wheels above in the sky.
Some, seizing an elephant by its foot, rushed toward the Bodhisattva;
others, seizing a camel; others, seizing a horse; others, seizing a donkey; others, seizing a headless trunk;
others, seizing skeletons; others, seizing venomous serpents; others, seizing lions; others, seizing tigers.
Some, seizing leopards; others, seizing bears; others, seizing gayals; others, seizing buffaloes; others, seizing human skulls; others, seizing mountain peaks; others, seizing trees with their roots;
some cause a rain of embers to fall from the sky; others cause rains of venomous serpents to fall; others cause rains of stones to fall.

Some mounted on elephants, some on horses, some on camels, some on buffaloes, some on donkeys, some on gayals, some on deer, and others mounted on boars, rushed toward the Bodhisattva; yet not even a single hair of the Bodhisattva’s body stirred, nor did his mind undergo any change.
Then he, having conjured up an army equipped with many horses, elephants, chariots, and oxen,
advanced toward the supreme seat of the Bodhisattva.
Mounting a vehicle yoked with a thousand horses and wielding a variegated bow, he uttered these fierce words: "Slay! Slay! Seize him quickly!"

With faces like elephants, donkeys, and horses, and with mouths like camels, these fierce hosts of *rākṣasas* wander about, maces in hand, terrifying as they move wherever that slayer of enemies goes.
Other headless trunks, like venomous serpents, rise from the earth; "Kill him! Seize him! they cry out with a terrible sound of distress.
Others vomit serpents, fire, and poison from their mouths;
hosts of piśācas seize lordly elephants by the foot and rush toward them.
Others, vomiting forth mountain peaks, rush toward the Sage;
other hosts of piśācas rain down showers of glowing coals from the sky.
Others whirl wheels with razor-sharp edges in the midst of the sky;
and in the firmament, they crackle and produce a terrible sound like a thunderclap.
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva stroked his head three times and stroked his cross-legged posture three times;

with his right hand-jewel— variegated with beautiful lines, colored like the application of liquid lac, soft as the touch of cotton, with copper-colored nails, and endowed with the roots of merit from many millions of eons— he struck the earth, and it resounded deeply.
A subtle sound resounded and reverberated;
just as, for example, a Magadhan bronze vessel struck against a mountain peak resounds and reverberates with a deep tone,
even so [did it happen] by means of the Bodhisattva’s right hand-jewel, with its copper-colored nails and beautifully variegated lines.

The earth was struck by him with a hand that had the color of lac-juice sprinkled upon it, was soft like the touch of cotton, and was endowed with the roots of merit accumulated over many millions of eons;
and by that sound of the earth, the earth was shattered, broken apart, utterly destroyed, and transformed.
Their elephants collapsed, their horses collapsed, their chariots collapsed, their feet collapsed,
and their hands collapsed; their weapons fell away, they lost their sense of direction, and they plunged into the Nairañjanā River where there was no ford.

Some fell on their left sides, others on their right sides; some fell face upwards, others fell on their feet, others on their knees; some fell with their heads downward, others fell headfirst; terrified and trembling, they cried out to one another.
Then that Lord of Men struck the earth with his trunk, which was like soft cotton;
the earth, together with its oceans and mountains, trembled.
By him the army of Namuci was shattered.
And then, as they moved about by the power of the Bodhisattva, they abandoned their many horses, elephants, and warriors near the Bodhi tree.
They plunged into the sacred ford named Nairañjanā.
With their horses, chariots, and weapons fallen and crushed,
Māra and his hosts of rākṣasas fled in all directions,
unaware of the name "Nairañjanā."
Having crossed over, he is free from weapons; he has reached the further shore.
The Rakshasa army, terrified by the power of his supernatural faculties, fled for a distance of a thousand yojanas;
yet even so, they did not tremble out of fearlessness.
"By good fortune, you live; you have been released from danger."
Other hosts of *rakṣasas*, with their necks entwined,
wept aloud; and the gods rained down *mandārava* and *karkārava* flowers.
With joyful minds, they uttered these words:
There was victory for the king, and in the sky there was the sound of kettledrums and the roar of "Hikkāra";
when the triple world resounded, it trembled.
The Teacher’s victory was like the stainless sky.
The son of a god, having gone to the world of the gods, said:
That state of the Supreme Being when he was struck down on the banks of the Nairañjanā cannot be described even in hundreds of years.
I shall proclaim a mere portion [of it].
I saw him, shining like Jāmbūnada gold, with the radiance of the sky and limbs adorned with the marks;
he had set out, traveling alone.
From the Nairañjanā River as far as the seat of enlightenment.
As he placed his steps, which shone like lotus petals,
upon this earth,
so did that delightful land tremble.
The earth is delighted by manifold sounds.
I have seen Māra’s army assembled from all sides— thousands of millions of yakṣas;
they cause terror and my heart trembles.
They do not cause the Essence of Beings to waver.
And his existence on earth was not known by the thousands of millions of gods all around;
yet they raised their voices, saying, "The Victor shall come to be."
Rejoicing, they waved their garments.
As I was setting out, I saw five hundred jīvajīvaka birds, peacocks, swans, kalaviṅkas, and cuckoos,
all uttering a single sound together.
From the Nairañjanā River as far as the seat of enlightenment.
I have seen the path fashioned by the immortals,
from the Nairañjanā river as far as the seat of awakening,
[strewn] with incense, flowers, and garlands.
It was filled with various flowers and possessed a most delightful fragrance.
When Māra is utterly broken and his splendor destroyed,
one should purify the eye in the first watch;
and in the middle watch, one is the slayer of Māra.
You remember your past lives and former deeds.
And when the dawn had risen,
you attained the supreme awakening— whatever has been awakened by previous Buddhas— and you reached mastery over the qualities of a Buddha.
The Lord of the World, who has destroyed the passion for existence.

In the last watch of the night, at the time when the dawn is breaking, during the "Joyful Face" of the night, whatever [is achieved] by a man who is a true man, a great man, a bull among men, a substance among men, a hero among men,
an elephant among men, a lion among men, a king among men, a lotus among men, a water-lily among men, a white lotus among men, and a bull among men—

By one who is a thoroughbred among men, a leader of men, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed; by one who is valiant, courageous, solitary, vigilant, ardent, secluded, resolute, possessed of gait, mindfulness, steadfastness, intelligence, and wisdom; by one who is purposeful and zealous, in every way and everywhere, regarding that which is to be known and to be awakened to.
Having fully awakened to all that is to be fully awakened through wisdom conjoined with a single moment of mind, he has realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The sons of the gods stood holding perfumes and garlands, wondering: "Has the Blessed One’s mind indeed attained liberation?"
The Blessed One, having known the minds of those deities with his own mind, at that time spoke this inspired utterance (udāna) to those deities for the purpose of cutting through their doubts.
Having cut off craving, I have abandoned passion; the dried-up influxes do not flow, and the severed path does not turn. This indeed is the end of suffering.
Then, multicolored masses of flowers— exceedingly variegated and fragrant— fell,
released from the palms of the hands of the sons of gods.
They circumambulated the king of the gods, keeping him to their right.
Of him whose vigor is like the essence of a mountain, incomparable, who is always like a flame of supreme splendor from his lineage,
and who is honored by gods and men—
Offer salutation with palms joined to the Peerless One.
When these phenomena appear to the ardent, meditating brahmin,
then all his doubts vanish away.
When one understands phenomena together with their causes.
This is dependent origination in its forward order.
When these phenomena appear to the ardent, meditating brahmin,
then all his doubts vanish away.
One understands the exhaustion of conditions.
This is dependent origination in reverse order.
Māra the Evil One created living beings who tore at the Blessed One’s couch;
as the sun was rising, they all melted away.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance:
When these phenomena appear to the brahmin who meditates with arduous exertion,
the armies of Māra stand defeated.
The atmosphere was illuminated by the sun itself.
Then, indeed, at that time when he had first attained awakening, the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance:
The maturation of merits is pleasant, one's intentions are fulfilled,
and one quickly attains supreme peace and nirvana.
Whatever obstacles there may be before them— whether from deities or the hosts of Māra— they are truly unable to create any hindrance for one who has performed meritorious deeds.
The conflicts that arise for one of little merit do not become powerful;
however, for those who possess the accumulations and are endowed with merit, their meditative concentration becomes powerful.
Whether one is in the world of the gods or among the Vasavartin [deities], or even as a human—
if one seeks after anything that ought not to be done, it will not succeed for him in any way whatsoever.
Or again, if one aspires for nirvāṇa, the unshakable state free from sorrow,
one attains the path that pacifies suffering with little difficulty.
Then the Blessed One said:
He enters the meditative absorption named "Victory over the World."
This world, born of torment and stilled by contact, experiences passion for itself;
for by whatever means they become intoxicated, it does not turn out otherwise.
This world is attached to existence, stained by existence, and delights in existence.
Where there is existence, there suffering comes to be.
Moreover, monks, it is for the sake of abandonment that the Tathāgata leads the holy life.
For whoever says that there is an escape from existence by means of existence, I declare that all those existences are not an escape.
And furthermore, O monks, whoever says that there is liberation from existence by means of existence, I declare that all those existences are not liberated.
Dependent upon acquisitions, there is the arising of suffering; through the destruction of all acquisitions, monks, there is no arising of suffering.
Behold this vast world, enveloped by ignorance, consisting of beings and born of beings, and not yet liberated.
Whatever existences there may be, all indeed proceed toward the three realms;
all those existences are impermanent, characterized by suffering, and subject to transformation.
Thus one sees this as it truly is with right wisdom.
The thirst for existence is exhausted; one no longer delights in existence in any way whatsoever. The destruction of thirst is nirvana.
Monks, for him who has attained extinction, there is no further becoming.
Māra has been overcome, the battle won, the enemies conquered, and all existence has been renounced.

The Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, having accomplished the purpose for which he had come, shattered Māra the Evil One— along with his army and his mounts— at the foot of the Bodhi tree by the sound of his coughing;
and having awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dharma, he dwelt at Rājagṛha after having assembled a great assembly.
The Teacher of gods and humans was honored, revered, esteemed, worshiped, and venerated; he attained the highest gain and supreme fame;
he was a recipient of the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick.
Yet, he remained unsullied therein, like a lotus by water, establishing beings who were partakers of merit in meritorious deeds.
Establishing beings who partake of the fruits in those very fruits; settling beings who partake of the latencies in those very latencies;
distributing the nectar of immortality in no small measure among gods and humans; causing hundreds of thousands of millions of living beings to attain the nectar of immortality;

and having rescued them from the vast wilderness of the cycle of birth, old age, and death that has no beginning or end, and from the great abysses of the miserable states such as the hells—he is established in patience.

Establishing [beings] in the auspicious, level, fearless state of Nirvana, having won over Aṅga, Magadha, Vajji, Malla, Kāśi, Kośala, Kuru, Pañcāla, Ceti, Vatsa, Matsya, Śūrasena, Aśvaka, and Avanti; one who has personally realized the prowess of knowledge throughout the ten directions, dwelling in divine abidings, dwelling in brahmic abidings,
dwelling in imperturbable abidings, dwelling in noble abidings, and dwelling in continuous abidings.

The Buddha dwells with the dwellings of a Buddha; the Conqueror dwells with the dwellings of a Conqueror; the Knower dwells with the dwellings of a Knower; the All-Knowing One dwells with the dwellings of the All-Knowing One.
Furthermore, having attained mastery over the mind, the Buddha, the Blessed One, dwells in whichever dwellings he desires by means of those very dwellings.
The monks heard this account of how, at the foot of the Bodhi tree, Māra the Evil One, together with his army and his mounts, was defeated by the sound of the Blessed One’s coughing.
Those monks said to the Blessed One:
Behold, Blessed One, the marvel of the Man-Lion, the subduer of pride and anger! How was Māra, together with his foremost host, conquered by the Blessed One with a mere cough?

By that single, wise one, unaided and possessing a mind of loving-kindness, many millions of yakṣas were conquered with a mere cough; and the Evil One—whose methods are evil and whose toil consists of wicked conduct—was conquered by the Moon-Faced One along with his foremost host of lions, tigers, hyenas, leopards, and elephants.
How was he, together with the vanguard of his army, conquered by a mere clearing of the throat?
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, what is the wonder here that the Tathāgata, having attained supreme enlightenment at the foot of the Bodhi tree, defeated Māra the Evil One along with his army and vehicles by the sound of a cough?
On another occasion as well, when I was still a prince, I conquered this Evil One together with the vanguard of his army by the sound of a cough."
The monks said.
At another time as well, Blessed One?
The Blessed One said:
On another occasion also, monks.

Once upon a time, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi, there was a king named Subandhu. He was one who had performed meritorious deeds, possessed great majesty, great strength, and a vast treasury; he ruled over a kingdom of sixty thousand cities that was prosperous, flourishing, with suppressed punishment, legal disputes, and thieves—a realm secure, well-supplied with food, free from calamity, and free from affliction.
It was crowded with people.

Now, King Subandhu had sixty thousand elephants equipped with ivory tusks, covered with golden nets, adorned with gold ornaments, with coral-like hooves, and accompanied by their riders, who held arrows and spears in their hands; he also had sixty thousand horses.

There were sixty thousand chariots from Sindh, swift-moving and adorned with every ornament, covered with lion skins, tiger skins, and leopard skins; they resounded with joyful cries, were equipped with victory banners, had coral-like hooves, and bore raised flags and pennants. There were also sixty thousand cows, all of which yielded every desire, and sixty thousand women.
There were sixty thousand couches adorned with all ornaments and wearing jeweled earrings, made of gold, silver, and ivory;
sixty thousand golden vessels, sixty thousand vessels made of jewels, sixty thousand treasuries,
and twenty thousand brahmins provided with constant meals.

Abundant wealth, grain, treasuries, and storehouses; abundant female and male slaves, laborers, and servants; abundant ministers, soldiers, and the vanguard of the army; and abundant collections of machines, bows, and arrows.
Now, in the bedchamber of King Subandhu, a great clump of sugarcane appeared.

In the midst of that clump of sugarcane, a single stalk of sugarcane appeared that was most beautiful of all; it surpassed the other stalks of sugarcane in strength, in color, in luster, and in foliage.
Then King Subandhu, having seen the clump of sugarcane, was struck with wonder and entered into an ocean of anxiety.
To whom will this be a sign—whether auspicious or evil?
Then King Subandhu, having summoned the brahmin domestic chaplain and the royal preceptors, addressed them.

"Gentlemen, in my bedchamber a great sugarcane clump has appeared. In the midst of that sugarcane clump, one single sugarcane stalk has appeared that is most beautiful of all; it surpasses all the others in color, in luster, and in foliage. Gentlemen, examine it and find out whose omen this is—whether it is auspicious or evil—and then do whatever you must do."

Then those brahmin chaplains and royal preceptors examined that stalk of sugarcane; they saw it as marvelous, serene, beautiful, and pleasing to the eye. Having seen it, they congratulated King Subandhu on his victory and said this:
"By good fortune, O Great King, there has appeared an auspicious omen in the inner apartments;

therefore, O Great King, from this clump of sugarcane a prince shall be born to you— one who has performed meritorious deeds, who is of great renown, of great majesty, difficult to approach, invincible, unassailable, gracious, and beautiful to behold for both gods and men."
May that be dear to the god.
Then those brahmins, having been thoroughly satisfied and served with choice hard and soft foods by King Subandhu, were dismissed after he had placed handfuls of gold and bullion in their laps.
Then, after growing for a day and night, that stalk of sugarcane became a large stalk of sugarcane over time;
even that middle stalk of sugarcane grew into a large sugarcane the size of a bamboo pole— tender, beautiful to behold, and thick— which surpassed all other stalks of sugarcane.
Now, King Subandhu’s chief queen was named Surucirā; she was gracious, beautiful to behold, noble in appearance, and endowed with the highest excellence of radiant complexion.

Then King Subandhu lay upon a royal bed together with his chief queen, Suruci; the bed was draped with bundles of silk ribbons, perfumed with incense, strewn with loose flowers, and surrounded by golden and silver lamp-stands, while hunchbacks, dwarfs, Kirātas, eunuchs, and chamberlains remained awake.

Then, indeed, during the last watch of the night, at the time when the dawn was breaking, a prince emerged from the root-stalk of that sugar-cane thicket— gracious, beautiful to behold, with a noble presence, and endowed with the highest excellence of golden hue.
Then that prince was received by Queen Surucirā.
Then King Subandhu, seeing that the prince had emerged from the stalk of sugarcane, was struck with wonder:
"How marvelous! What kind of being will this one be, who has appeared from a stalk of sugarcane?"
Then King Subandhu performed delightful birth-rites for the prince for seven nights;

for seven days he distributed food, drink, solid food, soft food, perfumes, garlands, ointments, and garments among ascetics, brahmins, the poor, beggars, and the great multitude of people, and channels of oil and channels of ghee were set flowing.
Various kinds of drinking conduits were set flowing;
a great circle of kinsmen had assembled, many hundreds of kings had assembled, and many thousands of brahmins had assembled;
a great celebration was taking place in the house of Subandhu.
Hundreds of musical instruments resound, and hundreds of songs are performed.
The entire city was honored for seven days.
Then King Anupātra, having performed the birth-rites for seven days, at the end of those seven days, King Subandhu addressed the brahmins, the domestic chaplains, and the royal preceptors.
"Sirs, give the prince a name that is suitable for him."
Then it occurred to them: "This prince was born from a sugarcane; let his name be Ikṣvāku."
Then those brahmins informed the king:
"Great King, since this prince was born from a sugar-cane stalk, let the name of this prince be Ikṣvāku."
Then King Subandhu, having heard the name of the prince from the presence of the brahmins, became joyful;
he established a name for the prince that was appropriate to him.
Others also, having heard the name of the prince, became joyful.
Then King Subandhu, having provided those brahmins with abundant solid and soft food and having served them, gave them much gold and bullion and dismissed them.

Then King Subandhu appointed four suitable nurses along with their attendants for the prince; one would rub him down and put him to sleep, another would suckle him at the breast, another would remove his excrement and urine, and another would hold him in her lap.

Thus, now that the prince Ikṣvāku was being properly attended to and properly cared for by four nurses, he grew like a blue lotus, a red lotus, a white water lily, or a great white lotus on the banks.
As it was said by the Blessed One:
For one who has performed merit grows like a banyan tree in fertile soil;
but one born on a roadside, having little merit, withers away like a tree.
Thus, as the prince was being raised, when he had reached the age of seven or eight years,
he then trained himself in writing, scripts, arithmetic, calculation, sealing, memorization, and in the management of elephants,
horses, bows, and bamboo-poles; and in running, jumping, sprinting, and leaping.

He was thoroughly proficient in the knowledge of archery and weaponry, in combat, in cutting and piercing, at the front of battle, and in royal illusions; he was universally esteemed for his established virtues, respectful toward his mother, honorable toward ascetics and brahmins, habitually offering salutations, prostrations, and rising to greet others; he was endowed with the power of attraction, possessed of gentleness, neither harsh nor abrasive, free from turbulence, pleasant to live with, the first to speak, speaking kindly, and beloved by the king.
He was beloved by the queen, the women of the harem, and the ministers; he was beloved by the entire army and the vanguard of the troops;
he was beloved by the domestic chaplain, the guild-leader, the merchants, and the people of the countryside; he was beloved, dear, and pleasing to rival kings.
He was free from illness and possessed a digestive system that was well-balanced, capable of properly digesting food, neither too cold nor too hot.
Due to the change of seasons, though long-lived, the measure of their lifespan was eighty-four thousand years.
As it was said by the Blessed One:
All sentient beings will die, for life indeed ends in death.
They will go according to their karma, experiencing the fruits of their merit and demerit.
Those of evil deeds go to hell, while those who have performed meritorious acts go to a good rebirth.
And others, having cultivated the path, attain final nirvana as those free from outflows.

Then King Subandhu, having ruled the kingdom righteously for a long time and a great duration, passed away according to the law of time after the lapse of eighty-four years; Prince Ikṣvāku then obtained the kingdom.

Then the king ruled his kingdom in Vārāṇasī over the sixty thousand ancestral cities; he had laid aside the rod of punishment, overcome his adversaries, and subdued his enemies. He was free from thorns, beloved by the people, possessed of great strength, a vast treasury, and many mounts.
His harem was extensive, consisting of many thousands of women, all of whom were yet childless.
No one has a son or a daughter.
Then, after some time had passed while King Ikṣvāku was ruling his kingdom, he entered into an ocean of anxiety:
"I have a vast kingdom and a vast harem, yet I have no son; let it not be that I should pass away childless, for then enemies would invade this realm of mine."
Then King Ikṣvāku, together with his domestic priest, extended an invitation.
"How might I have a son? he thought.
The domestic priest said to him:

"Great King, this women's quarters must be vacated three times each fortnight—on the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth day. Then a prince will be born to you, and the Ikṣvāku lineage will become widespread."

Then King Ikṣvāku, having heard these words from his domestic priest, established Queen Alindā as the chief queen in the royal palace; as for those other many thousands of women, he dismissed them three times during the fortnight, saying:
"Go, let each woman sport with whomever she desires."

Thus, now many thousands have rushed out from the royal palace with joyful minds, adorned with all their ornaments; like terrified does, they have arrived at every gate— some speaking enticingly, others laughing, and others running and chasing after one another.
All stumbled and all fainted;
in the city of King Ikṣvāku, the people, together with those royal wives, rolled about and fell unconscious.
Now, another man, a kinsman born into the family of Subandhu, being a human being endowed with good conduct of body,
endowed with good conduct of speech, and endowed with good conduct of mind, having lived by undertaking the ten paths of wholesome action,
passed away from among humans and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa host of gods as the divine king named Śakra.
He then reflected:
"Where is King Subandhu now? Is he still existing in his body—alive or dead?"

He then saw that King Subandhu had passed away, and his son named Ikṣvāku had obtained the kingdom. A wicked, improper, and unsuitable course of action had been given by the domestic priest of King Ikṣvāku; for three times, the harem was to be abandoned for the sake of the subjects, though it did not befit the family of Subandhu. Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, having manifested himself in the guise of a brahmin, appeared as one who was aged, decrepit, and infirm.
Having reached old age, his body covered with wrinkles, his head gray and his limbs marked with spots, he went to the gate of King Ikṣvāku and said:
I desire to see Ikṣvāku.
The doorkeeper entered the royal palace and announced [the matter] to King Ikṣvāku.
"Your Majesty, a brahmin is standing at the gate and wishes to see the king."
King Ikṣvāku said:
Welcome to the brahmin; please enter.
Then that doorkeeper ushered the brahmin into the royal palace.
Seeing the aged brahmin, the king rose from his seat.
Welcome to you, O brahmin; please sit down, here is a seat for you.
Then that brahmin, having congratulated him with cries of victory, sat down.
The king asks him.
"Brāhmaṇa, from which direction have you come? What do you seek? What is pleasing to you? What shall I give to you?"
The brahmin said:

"Great King, I have come from a distant land having heard your noble fame, renown, and verses. It is said that Ikṣvāku empties his harem three times a fortnight for the sake of progeny; therefore, O King, seeking a wife, I have come from a distant land. Consequently, grant me a share of a woman."
Then the king, having heard the words of the brahmin, became joyful and satisfied, and addressed the chamberlain.
"Hey, chamberlain! Quickly show this brahmin my harem;
give him whichever woman he pleases."
Then that chamberlain led the brahmin into the inner apartments, into the midst of many thousands of women.
"Brāhmaṇa, this is the harem of King Ikṣvāku; take whichever woman you desire and go."
Then that brahmin seized from among those many thousands of women the queen named Alindā, who was the chief consort of King Ikṣvāku and never before had stepped out from the royal palace, saying:
"Let her be mine."
Then the queen wept, thinking:
"This brahmin is either my grandfather, or my great-grandfather, or perhaps even my superior.
May King Ikṣvāku, who is firm in his commitment to his vows, not indeed surrender me to the service and attendance of this brahmin."
Now, while that hunchbacked female garland-maker was weaving a garland for Alindā,
she spoke to that brahmin.
"Brāhmaṇa, you are old, aged, and decrepit, yet you desire a young woman.
No young woman would ever touch you with her hand or her foot; go away! What do you have to do with Queen Alindā, who has not been abandoned by King Ikṣvāku?"
Then that brahmin said to the hunchbacked woman:
"O hunchback, you have little concern; weave a garland for me as you would for Queen Alindā, and not for anyone else."
Now, Queen Alindā had another maidservant who was a pigment-grinder;
she then spoke to that brahmin.
"Brahmin, you are worn out, aged, decrepit, smelling of straw and cloth, and foul-smelling; the queen would not even wish to look at you, let alone speak with you.
Go away! What have you to do with Alindā, who is not abandoned by King Ikṣvāku?"
Then that brahmin said to the maidservant:
"You are a servant with little concern; grind the cosmetic paste. I am as dear to Queen Alindā as you are to no one else."
Then Queen Alindā said:
By no means whatsoever will this brahmin be able to subdue me.
Then that queen wept aloud;
as she was weeping, her retinue also wept,
and a great sound of lamentation arose there in the inner apartments.
King Ikṣvāku, having gone to the excellent upper palace, heard the loud noise and great clamor of the harem. He then questioned the eunuchs and the chamberlains.
"O friend, what indeed is this sound of women's wailing that is being heard?"
Then those eunuchs and chamberlains said:
"Your Majesty, Queen Alindā was taken by that brahmin.
King Ikṣvāku offered me a choice, saying, 'Take whichever woman pleases you.
Therefore, let her be mine."
Then Queen Alindā wept, and as the queen was weeping, her retinue also let out a cry.
Having now promised them, he entered his own inner apartments and spoke to that brahmin.
"Brāhmaṇa, you are worn out, aged, and elderly; if you wish to eat as a regular guest in the royal household, I shall provide that for you. What do you want with Queen Alindā? Take another woman."
He then said: "Great King, I am old and aged, and suffering from a cough; I faint moment after moment.
I am unable to rise by myself, and I urinate upon my own bed. Therefore, give her to me; she will help me up and she will attend to me."
"May you, O Ikṣvāku, not feel regret later after having offered me to a woman.
Now, I say this so that you, O Ikṣvāku, do not make a false request; I shall depart."
The king said:
"O Brahmin, I do not make false requests, nor do I regret having given; however, you are aged, old, and advanced in years, while this queen is young, delicate, and does not desire you.
Furthermore, your harem is extensive with many thousands of women; take whichever woman pleases you and enjoy yourself with her—she will attend to you."
The brahmin said:

"Enough, Great King! Let her alone be mine who stands there, proud, remaining, with faultless limbs, gazing gently. Let her alone be mine who stands there, proud, remaining, with faultless limbs, gazing with the demeanor of a doe.
Let her be mine who stands there, proud, remaining, with faultless limbs, shedding tears of joy."

"Enough for me, Great King, with a woman from the inner apartments; let this queen alone be mine. She shall rouse me, she shall attend to me, and she shall serve me. Do not, O Ikṣvāku, feel regret after having offered me a woman.
Now, I am going."
King Ikṣvāku said:
"Even though you are worn out, aged, and decrepit, this queen is young and delicate; she does not desire you.
This low-caste hunchback is desirous of sexual union; let her be your slave. Take her wherever you wish; she shall attend to you."
The hunchback said:
"Great King, this brahmin is putrid and wrinkled, with a grey-haired face; he is as foul-smelling as a jujube flower and reeks like a goat.
O Lord, if you give him to me, I shall die after consuming poison. I will kill this old man with broken limbs when we are in private."
Then that brahmin said:
I have enmity toward all hunchbacks, whoever they may be, who dwell upon the earth.
Where this low-caste hunchback woman wishes to have me killed.
"Enough, Great King, with this hunchbacked woman! Let this queen alone be mine; she shall attend to me and she shall serve me.
Do not, sir, feel regret after having offered me your wife.
Since you are making a false request, I bid you farewell; I am going."
The king said:
"O Brahmin, I do not make a false request, nor do I regret having given.
However, you are old, aged, and infirm, while this queen is young and delicate; she does not desire you.
If you were young, this queen might well have yearned for you. But I do not make a false request: go, take Queen Alindā and lead her wherever you wish."
Then that brahmin, having given his word to King Ikṣvāku, became thrilled, satisfied, and joyful.
Having embraced Queen Alindā and ushering her inside, he fell right on top of her; a loud roar of laughter was let out by the thousands of women:
"A virtuous and worthy man has been found for the queen!"

Queen Alindā, too, with a throat choked with tears and a face weeping, lamented as she was seized by the hand by the brahmin; she was dragged along, pulled hither and thither, and clung to him. Sighing and gasping, with tears streaming down, her voice faltering, and wetting the ground at every step, she was firmly grasped and driven out from Rājagṛha without support, until she became utterly distraught.
That brahmin, having constructed a crooked and dilapidated hut in a poor village along the city wall, spread grass and leaves upon a rickety couch and set down a broken pot for water.

There, Queen Alindā was ushered in with her garments ruined and lost, her ornaments shattered and scattered, and with nothing remaining but the barest remnants; she had never before touched the ground with her feet, yet now her sandals were fallen away and her feet remained uncovered, wounded and mangled.
Then that brahmin, having sat down there in the midst of the dilapidated shed, said:

"O auspicious lady, having dressed yourself well, wash my feet and wash your own feet; then enjoy yourself. I am well-pleased by you, O auspicious lady; enjoy yourself thoroughly. Make me happy, O auspicious lady; make me happy for me, O auspicious lady;
make me happy with playful charm, O auspicious lady."
Thus, throughout that entire night, the goddess said, "Delight me thus! Delight me thus! Raise me up!

Lay me down! When the night had passed and at the time of the rising of the dawn, Śakra stood there in his own form, wearing armlets and divine earrings, his body adorned with celestial ornaments, illuminating everything with his sublime radiance, and bearing exquisite, stainless earrings.
Having become a king of the gods, she emitted her own radiance, and by her color, the entire surrounding hall was illuminated.
Then Queen Alindā, seeing Śakra, the lord of the gods, in his own form, was overcome with passion and thought,
"What have I done that I have not enjoyed myself with him?"
Śakra, the lord of the gods, offers a boon to Queen Alindā.
I am Śakra, the Indra of the gods, the lord of the Trayastriṃśa.
Choose a boon from me, O blessed lady, whatever you desire in your heart.
Then Queen Alindā, having joined her palms in reverence toward Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this:
Śakra restrains me with a boon; thus I say: "My son is my boon."
Then Indra gave her a medicinal pill, saying:
"Mix this pill with water and drink it; from that, you will have a son who will be like a lion, powerful, and a crusher of enemy armies.
In his energy, there will be no one in the world equal to him."

"However, he will be ugly in complexion and form because I did not present myself before you when you were joyful. Then Indra, having granted a boon to Queen Alindā and caused the Jarjara Hall to disappear, returned to the realm of the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
Then Queen Alindā, having tied that medicinal pill to the corner of her silken garment, entered the royal palace with a face the color of a lotus and with perfectly pure faculties, thinking:
"In this vast inner apartment, such shall be my son."
Then Queen Alindā was seen by King Ikṣvāku from afar as she was entering the gate-hall, with her face the color of a lotus and her sense-faculties completely pure.
The king then questioned the queen.

"Your face has the color of a lotus, your faculties are completely purified; you have slept happily during the night, or have experienced the delights of play; have you obtained something noble and auspicious?"
Then that queen said:
"Great King, where could I have found the comfort of sleep, or experienced the delight of play?
That was Śakra, the lord of the gods, who, having assumed the guise of a brahmin, came here.
Therefore, he kept me awake the entire night, making me rise and lie down again; when the night had passed and it was the time of dawn, at the moment the sky was breaking, [he departed]."

Having made that brahmin disguise disappear, Indra stood in his own form, illuminating all directions with his radiance, and said: "I have been invited to choose a boon; choose a boon, O blessed lady!
I am Śakra, the Indra of the gods, the lord of the Trāyastriṃśa."
"Choose a boon from me, O blessed lady, whatever you desire in your heart."
In that regard, O Great King, having requested the boon of a son, [he said: "Grant me the boon of a son."
Śakra gave me this medicinal pill, saying: "Mix this pill with water and drink it;

from that a son will be born who shall sit upon a lion-throne, be powerful, and crush the armies of his enemies. In energy, there will be no one in the world equal to him; however, he will be ugly in complexion and form, which is why I did not attend upon you with joy and satisfaction."
Then the king, having heard this, became angry with the queen.
