Now that you have been permitted by me, why did you not attend upon him with joy and satisfaction?
Then the king, out of anger, snatched away a medicinal pill from the queen.
Then the king ground the medicinal pill on a stone, mixed it with water, and gave it to the five hundred queens, the daughters of Māna, for them to drink from the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass.
However, Queen Alindā did not receive any of that medicinal pill to drink, [thinking]: "Lest this queen give birth to an evil son."
Then Queen Alindā questioned her maidservants.
Where was that medicinal pill made?
The maidservants said:
"O Queen, that medicinal pill of yours was taken by the king, ground in Niṣadhā, and given for the drinking of five hundred female attendants."
The goddess asks.
On what kind of seat was that medicinal pill ground?
The maidservant said:
O Queen, that medicinal pill was rubbed upon this Niṣadha stone.
Then that queen, having made a drop of water into a hollowed leaf and having placed the tip of her tongue at the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass, consumed it;
she too conceived in her womb.
In this way, five hundred queens became pregnant.
Then those five hundred queens, after the lapse of nine or ten months, gave birth;
four hundred and ninety-nine princes were born, handsome, beautiful to behold, with noble proportions, endowed with the most excellent and abundant beauty of complexion.
To Queen Alindā also a son was born, but he was ill-favored and unpleasant to look upon, with thick lips, a thick head, thick feet, a large belly, and black as a heap of soot.
Then those eunuchs and chamberlains informed the king.
"Great King, forty-nine hundred queens have given birth, and forty-nine hundred princes have been born, handsome and beautiful to behold;
yet to Queen Alindā a son has been born who is ill-favored and ugly to look upon, with thick lips, a thick head, thick feet, and black as the color of a heap of soot."
Upon hearing this, King Ikṣvāku became enraged and fell into a state of dejection, thinking:
"Since I did not give the queen a pill to drink, lest she should give birth to a son, how is it that such a son has been born to her?"
The eunuch chamberlains said:
"Great King, at the spot where the Lord ground that medicinal pill for Niṣadha, Queen Niṣadhā took a drop of water with the tip of a blade of kuśa grass and placed it on the tip of her tongue;
from that, a son was born to the queen."
The king said:
"May my son never stand before the Queen; I do not wish to see such a thing."
Then Ikṣvāku, having heard of the beauty and form of those five hundred princes minus one, was thrilled and delighted.
Having set aside the son of Alindā among those handsome princes, for seven days he performed delightful birth-rites and distributed food,
drink, solid food, and delicacies to ascetics, brahmins, the poor, beggars, and other people.
Food, clothing, perfumes, garlands, and ointments were provided; channels of oil and channels of ghee were set flowing, and various kinds of channels for drinks were set flowing.
For each prince, four nurses were appointed:
one to bathe and put him to sleep, another to remove his excrement and urine, another to give him the breast, and another to hold him in her lap.
The nurses were not assigned to Queen Alindā’s son;
instead, Queen Alindā’s own personal attendants were assigned to him.
In this way, those princes were now reared and brought up.
Then King Ikṣvāku gave names mixed with the word *kuśa* to all those five hundred princes:
some were named Indrakuśa, some Brahmakuśa, some Devakuśa, some Ṛṣikuśa, some Kusumakuśa, some Drumakuśa,
some Ratnakuśa, some Mahākuśa, some Haṃsakuśa, some Kroñcakuśa, and some Mayūrakuśa.
In this manner, names mixed with *kuśa* grass were given to all of them; however, for Queen Alindā, the name "Pure *Kuśa*" (*śuddha-kuśa*) was given.
Now King Ikṣvāku gave various kinds of children's toys to all four hundred and ninety-nine princes, but he did not give a toy to Prince Kuśa, the queen’s son. Thereupon,
whichever toy Prince Kuśa desired, he would take it from his brothers, play with it and enjoy himself, and then give it back.

Thus, King Ikṣvāku now gave various kinds of play-vehicles to those princes— elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, and various other noble vehicles worthy of kings— but he did not give a vehicle to Prince Kuśa.
Yet whatever vehicle Prince Kuśa desired, whether an elephant-vehicle, a horse-vehicle, or a chariot-vehicle, [he received].

Having seized their carriages, palanquins, chariots, gallīs, half-gallīs, leaf-carriages, or sky-chariots, he would carry them away and then give them back, saying: "What is the use of guarding these?"
Thus, as those princes grew up and reached the age of discretion— whether seven or eight years old—
they were then trained in writing, scripts, arithmetic, calculation, sealing, memorization,
and in the management of elephants, horses, chariots, and bows; and in running, racing, leaping, and in the science of archery.
Whether in combat, or wrestling, or in cutting, or in piercing, or in striking, or at the head of a battle, they have attained a certain mastery in all the practices of royal illusion.
No one taught the craft to Prince Kuśa; yet, by his own intellect, his own wisdom, and his own diligence, he became well-trained beyond all his brothers and the rest of the great multitude of people.
He was highly skilled in the science of archery and weaponry, and in all other various fields of craftsmanship; in all these respects, Prince Kuśa excelled them all.
Then this thought occurred to King Ikṣvāku:
"What if I were now to examine these five hundred princes to see which among them shall become king after my passing?"

Then King Ikṣvāku had five hundred sweetmeats made; he placed one large sweetmeat in the middle of those sweetmeats and covered it with the other sweetmeats, thinking: "Whosoever shall take this large sweetmeat, him I shall know."
After my passing, he shall become the king.
Then King Ikṣvāku, having made that heap of sweetmeats into a single mass, summoned his five hundred princes and addressed them:
"Quickly, with three claps of the hand each, take one sweetmeat from this heap."
Then all those princes ran first, and afterwards the prince ran after them;
that prince, having grasped all his brothers with his left and right hands, took hold of that large sweetmeat.
This thought occurred to King Ikṣvāku:
"This Prince Kuśa shall become king after my passing.
But he is ill-colored, unsightly, with thick lips, a thick head, thick feet, and a large belly; he is black, the color of a heap of soot, unpleasant, and repulsive to behold.
Who will accept him as king?"
"What if I were now to test these princes a second time? At the time and place for their meal, I shall have them served in my presence;
whichever among them receives the first portion of food, I shall know that he will become king after my passing."

Then King Ikṣvāku, at the time and place for taking food, summoned those five hundred princes, had them sit before him, and served the meal. Those princes also waited for the food. Prince Kuśa, however, received that food on the ground; with as much food as he desired, he made a heap of boiled rice upon the ground.
Right there, above, he desires condiments; he eats while supported by the earth.
Then this thought occurred to King Ikṣvāku:
"This Prince Kuśa, after my passing, will become king; as a lord of the earth, he shall enjoy that which rests upon the earth."
Then, at another time, King Ikṣvāku asked his domestic priest:
"Preceptor, which of these princes will become king after my passing?"
The domestic priest said:
"Great King, this Prince Kuśa will indeed become king after the passing of Your Majesty;
he possesses the marks of royalty."
Then King Ikṣvāku,
having heard this from the domestic priest, became distressed.
"What means might there be so that this Prince Kuśa shall not become king after my passing?
What if I were now to bury great treasures in various secret places throughout the royal palace, unseen by anyone?
Whoever, after my passing, should discover, perceive, and dig up these treasures, he shall be the king; perhaps in this way another prince might become king."
Then, by that King Ikṣvāku, a great treasure was buried in secret locations throughout various parts of the royal palace, unseen by anyone.
Then, after the passing of a long time, at the moment of his death, King Ikṣvāku instructed his ministers.
"O ministers, listen! Among these five hundred princes, whoever shall know, discover, and excavate these treasures after my passing—him you must consecrate with the kingdom.
There is a treasure at the end, a treasure outside, and a treasure neither at the end nor outside; four treasures beneath the four king-śāla trees;
a treasure in the ocean, a treasure in the sea, a treasure at the distance of a yojana, a treasure at the place of release, a treasure at the top of a tree, and a treasure on the mountain."
"Wherever the sun of Vairocana rises, there is a treasure; wherever the light-making sun sets, there is a treasure;

and even where the gods are honored, there too a treasure lies buried. O ministers, whoever among you knows these treasures and can have them excavated without being instructed—him you shall consecrate with the kingdom."
He shall indeed become a king.
Then King Ikṣvāku, having thus instructed his ministers, was joined with the law of time and passed away.

Now, when their father had passed away, those five hundred princes, for the sake of the kingdom, quarreled with one another, each saying, "I am king! I am king! Yet, because they were righteous, they did not harm one another;
then the ministers spoke to the princes.
"O princes, do not quarrel! You have received the command of King Ikṣvāku. At the time of his death, the father gave this instruction: 'He who shall know the father's instruction shall become king.'"
The princes said:
"O ministers, you must indeed report this message to us, just as it was given to our father."
Then those ministers proclaimed that message of King Ikṣvāku before the five hundred princes:
"There is a treasure at the end; there is a treasure outside; there is a treasure neither at the end nor outside—four treasures beneath the four king-śāla trees;
a treasure in the ocean; a treasure in the sea; a treasure at the league-mark; a treasure at the place of release; a treasure at the tip of a tree; a treasure on the peak of a mountain."
Where the sun, the son of Virocana, rises, there is a treasure; where the light-making sun sets, there is a treasure;
and where the gods offer worship, there too a treasure is deposited.
O Prince, this was the message given to you by your father Ikṣvāku: "Whosoever among you recognizes these deposited treasures and digs them up, he shall become your king."

The four hundred and ninety-nine princes did not know or understand when the treasures were being proclaimed; but Kuśa, possessed of great intelligence and a great investigator, understood the entire matter and was completely purified.
Then he said:
O friend, I shall report these words of my father there.
Whatever treasures have been proclaimed by you, all of those I shall cause to be excavated.
As for what was said by my father: "The treasure is at the end; the treasure is placed inside the threshold at the entrance of the royal palace."
The ministers had that spot excavated, and a great treasure was revealed.
As for what was said by my father— that a treasure was deposited outside his very own dwelling—
that great hoard too has been caused to be excavated by the prince.
As for what my father said— that there is no treasure neither inside nor outside— that treasure was placed beneath the threshold at the middle gate;
that great hoard was also caused to be dug up by the prince.
As for what my father said regarding the four treasures beneath the four king-śāla trees— wherein King Ikṣvāku’s bedstead,
made of śāla wood and covered with golden feet, was laid out; beneath those feet of the bedstead were the four treasures— and those great treasures were also caused to be excavated by the prince.
As for what my father said regarding the treasure in the ocean: there was also a treasure deposited in the pleasure pond belonging to the royal Aśoka grove;
that too was caused to be drawn out from the pleasure pond by the prince.
Regarding what was said by the father concerning the "ocean-treasure": there was a well in the bathing hall of King Ikṣvāku, and a treasure was deposited there as well;
that great treasure was caused to be excavated from the well by the prince.

Regarding what was said by my father, "There is a treasure at the yoking-place," in whatever place King Ikṣvāku’s vehicle— whether an elephant-vehicle, a horse-vehicle, or a carriage— was yoked, even that spot was had the great treasure excavated by the prince.

As for what was said by my father regarding "the treasure at the place of release": in whatever place the king Ikṣvāku’s vehicle is released—whether it be an elephant-vehicle, a horse-vehicle, or a chariot-vehicle—a treasure is deposited there.
That great treasure has been caused to be excavated by the prince.
Regarding what was said by my father, "the treasure is at the top of a tree": in the audience hall of King Ikṣvāku, there is a great tree;
where the first shadow falls as the sun rises, and where the final shadow falls when the sun has set—in that very place the treasure is deposited.
Those two great treasures were also caused to be excavated by the prince.

Regarding what was said by my father concerning the treasure on the mountain: on that stone slab where the head-bath of King Ikṣvāku is described and where his ointment is ground, a treasure was deposited beneath it;
that great treasure has also been excavated by the prince.

As for what my father said, "Where Vairocana rises, there is a treasure," that treasure was also deposited where my father Ikṣvāku was born from a sugar-cane; and that great hoard was also caused to be excavated by the prince.
As for what my father said—that where the light-making sun sets, there a treasure is buried—where Ikṣvāku passed away, there too a treasure was buried;
that great treasure has also been caused to be excavated by the prince.

As for what my father said—that where the gods are honored, there too a treasure was deposited; and where King Ikṣvāku had five hundred princes served, there too a treasure was deposited—that great treasure was also caused to be excavated by the prince.
Thus, as those treasures were being excavated by Prince Kuśa, the ministers, the princes,
the domestic priests, the brahmins, the royal preceptors, the army commanders, and the people of the towns and countryside— all were filled with wonder as Prince Kuśa dug up those treasures.

"Oh, how great is the wisdom and the profound discernment of Prince Kuśa! For he has now discovered all those great treasures that were deposited here and there within the royal palace of King Ikṣvāku, and he has caused them all to be excavated.
He shall be the king."
Then it occurred to those ministers:
"Lest Prince Kuśa should hear this from others; let us test him further and again under another pretext."
Then those ministers of the princes spoke.
"O princes, whichever among you shall first pay homage to all the gods and sit upon the lion throne, he shall become the king."
Then those four hundred and ninety-nine princes, having mounted various kinds of vehicles, ran with great haste and speed toward the temple of the gods to pay homage to the deities.

Then Prince Kuśa approached the all-golden consecration lion-throne; having extended his joined palms toward the gods of the four directions and circumambulated that lion-throne out of reverence for former kings, he sat down upon it.
For Kuśa was consecrated in the kingdom by the princes, the ministers, the army commanders,
and the people of the towns and countryside, because they considered him wise; he was honored as king by all the sixty thousand cities, towns, and provinces, and by the royal ministers and princes.
Thus, now Prince Kuśa has obtained the kingdom.
Thus, when King Kuśa had obtained the kingdom, he paid homage to his mother, Queen Alindā;

having honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped her, King Kuśa ruled the kingdom righteously for a long time. Then, at another time, he made this request to his mother, Queen Alindā: "Mother, let my wife be appointed as the chief queen."
Bring her who is gracious and beautiful to behold, such that no other woman is her equal.
Queen Alindā said:
"My son, who will give you a beautiful and pleasing wife in exchange for your ugliness? I shall bring you a wife who is indeed ugly in form, one who will not bring you joy."
King Kuśa said:
"Mother, if you bring me a wicked wife, I shall not touch that wicked wife with either foot or hand.
Bring me a wife who is gracious and beautiful to behold.
Mother, I have neither heard nor seen it said that a king is wicked, nor that a king takes pleasure with a wicked woman; therefore, mother, bring me a beautiful wife."
Queen Alindā said:
O son, husband and wife live together happily when they possess similar characteristics, and they do not hold contempt for one another.
A wife of beautiful form holds her husband in high regard because of his beauty;
a husband of beautiful form holds his wife of evil form in high regard.
"Son, I will bring you a wife such as is suitable for you—one who, being wicked in appearance, my son, will not be pleasing to you."
King Kuśa said:
"Mother, I have no need for this wicked wife;
bring me a wife who is my equal in beauty."
Queen Alindā said:
"My son, who will give you a wife of beautiful form for the sake of your evil form?"
King Kuśa said:
"Mother, from afar bring me a wife of auspicious form, by means of expenditure of wealth, bullion, and gold."
Then Queen Alindā, having summoned the ministers and the domestic chaplains, addressed them.
"Gentlemen, find out who is the wife and chief queen of King Kuśa—one who, among the many thousands of women in the royal court, would be the chief queen and the eldest."
Then those ministers and domestic priests, having given their assent to the queen, dispatched brahmins and messengers throughout the cities and the countryside:
"Go, sirs, and find such a maiden as would be suitable for King Kuśa, the son of Ikṣvāku."
Then those brahmins and messengers, searching through the sixteen provinces, arrived at the city named Kaṇṇakubja in the province of the Śūrasenas.
There, a king of the Madrakas named Mahendraka ruled.
He had a daughter named Sudarśanā, who was gracious and beautiful; in all of Jambudvīpa, there was no other maiden equal to her in beauty.
Then that princess, having mounted a four-horsed chariot with great royal splendor, great royal majesty, and a vast retinue, and surrounded by her female companions and maidservants,
went out to the pleasure gardens;
she was seen by those brahmins and messengers.
Then it occurred to them:
"This princess is truly serene and beautiful to behold; she is worthy to be the chief queen of King Kuśa."
Then those brahmins and messengers, having dressed and put on their robes early the next morning, stood at the gate of the royal palace.
At the time when King Mahendraka was seated in the audience hall, those brahmins and messengers greeted the king and stood before him.
Then that brahmin, having congratulated King Mahendraka on his victory, said this:
"Great King, in Vārāṇasī there was a king named Kuśa, the son of Ikṣvāku; he requested your daughter Sudarśanā as his wife."
Now King Kuśa was distinguished in such a way that he ruled over the sovereignty of sixty thousand cities.
This occurs to that Mahendraka.
Such a connection is worthy of a person like this.
Then King Mahendraka spoke to that brahmin and the messengers.
"Gentlemen, King Kuśa is my friend; I give him my daughter to be his wife."
Then that brahmin, having purchased sweetmeats and summoned the brahmins, offered them the sweets, saying:
"Gentlemen, Mahendraka, the king of Madra, is offering his daughter Sudarśanā as a wife for King Kuśa, the son of Ikṣvāku;
therefore, gentlemen, offer him water."
Then those brahmins and messengers, having carried out the brahmin’s instructions and taken leave of King Mahendraka,
set out and in due course arrived at Vārāṇasī.
Then those brahmins and messengers informed the ministers and the domestic priests.
Such a maiden was obtained, to whom no other maiden in all of Jambudvīpa is equal in beauty.
In the district named Śūrasena, there is a city named Kanyakubja; there lived a king of the Madrakas named Mahendraka.
His daughter was named Sudarśanā, who was gracious and beautiful to behold.
Having heard this, those ministers and priests then informed Queen Alindā.
Such a maiden was obtained; among all other maidens in Jambudvīpa, there is none equal to her in beauty.
In the district named Śūrasena, there is a city called Kanyakubja. There dwelt a Madra king named Mahendraka.
His daughter, named Sudarśanā, was gracious and beautiful to behold.
Upon hearing this, Queen Alindā became thrilled and joyful,
thinking, "I have obtained a peerless wife for my son."
Then Queen Alindā took a liking to her son Kuśa.
"My son, such a maiden has been found as whom no other maiden in all of Jambudvīpa is her equal in beauty.
In the province named Śūrasena, there is a city called Kanyakubja; there dwells a king of the Madrakas named Mahendraka, and his daughter is named Sudarśanā—gracious and beautiful to behold."
Then King Kuśa, having heard his mother’s words, became thrilled and joyful.
He addressed his ministers, courtiers, brahmin chaplains, and royal preceptors:
"Sirs, in the district called Śūrasena there is a city named Kanyakubja; there resides a Madra king named Mahendraka, and he has a daughter named Sudarśanā.
Go and bring her here for my sake."
Then those ministers, assembly members, brahmin chaplains, and royal preceptors, having given their assent to King Kuśa, arrayed a fourfold army and set out with great prosperity and great splendor.
Then, as they were setting out, this thought occurred to Queen Alindā:
"What indeed might be the means by which that princess Sudarśanā would not know what the king Kuśa is like in complexion and form?"
Then, this thought occurred to Queen Alindā: "Thus it is."
"What if I were now to have a private inner chamber built, where King Kuśa might sport, enjoy himself, and dally with his wife, and yet she would not know what King Kuśa looks like?"

Then Queen Alindā had such a private chamber prepared— smeared and plastered, hung with bundles of silk ribbons and garlands, perfumed with incense, and strewn with loose flowers— wherein King Kuśa would play, delight, and enjoy himself.
Then those ministers, assembly members, brahmin chaplains, and royal preceptors, traveling by stages, arrived at the city named Kanyakubja in the Śūrasena country.
Then, having approached Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, and having congratulated the king with cries of victory, they stood before him and said this.
"Great King, your son-in-law, King Kuśa, inquires after the welfare of the King of Kauśala and his retinue; he requests that you grant him your daughter Sudarśanā, whom you promised, to be his wife."

Then King Mahendraka, having greeted and exchanged friendly greetings with those ministers, courtiers, brahmin chaplains, and royal preceptors, gave them garments, ornaments, and articles of enjoyment befitting kings.
Then those ministers and assembly members, having stayed there for some days, addressed King Mahendraka.
"Great King, we have been gone for a long time; let the marriage be performed, we must go."
Then King Mahendraka,

with great royal splendor and great royal majesty, amidst the shouts of "Hakkā! and "Hikkā!", and the resounding noise of kettledrums, *bherī*, *bhṛdaṅga*, *paṭaha*, and conchs of a vast multitude of people, performed the marriage ceremony and gave his daughter Sudarśanā as a wife to King Kuśa.
Then those ministers and priests, having performed the marriage rites and taken leave of King Mahendraka, set out;
in due course, they arrived at a park on the outskirts of Vārāṇasī.
Thus, Sudarśanā, the king’s daughter, was now escorted into the city of Vārāṇasī with great honor and a grand assembly.
Then that Princess Sudarśanā was ushered into the royal palace.
Having approached where his mother-in-law, Queen Alindā, was, he bowed his head at his mother-in-law's feet and stood before her.
Then Queen Alindā, seeing that bride, became joyful, filled with gladness and happiness.
Then King Kuśa, together with the princess Sudarśanā, remained in that inner chamber devoid of light, sporting, delighting, and enjoying himself with magnificent articles of luxury and enjoyment.
Then, while that princess Sudarśanā was playing, sporting, and enjoying herself with King Kuśa there in the inner chamber where there was no light, this thought occurred to her:

"This royal lineage of Kuśa, of the Ikṣvāku clan, is prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and a mine of infinite jewels; yet this bedchamber of ours is without light, and even the lamps do not burn.
Indeed, we cannot see one another’s eyes, nor do I know what King Kuśa is like in complexion and form, nor does King Kuśa know what Queen Sudarśanā is like to me in complexion and form."
"I do not understand this matter: for what reason are there no lamps burning in our bedchamber, neither by night nor by day?
Then Queen Sudarśanā questioned King Kuśa in private.

"Great King, this royal palace is prosperous, flourishing, and a mine of countless jewels; yet in our bedchamber, neither by night nor by day do lamps burn. We dwell together as if in darkness, unable to see one another with our eyes.
I do not know what my husband is like, nor does Your Majesty know what Queen Sudarśanā is like."
I do not understand this reason: for what purpose are the lamps not burning in our bedchamber?
King Kuśa said:
The queen said, "I too do not know for what reason the lamps are not burning in our bedchamber.
My mother will know; go and ask her."
Then, at dawn, when King Kuśa had gone forth, Queen Sudarśanā, the king’s daughter, dressed herself in garments, put on her ornaments, and approached the great queen Alindā to pay homage at her feet.
Then Sudarśanā, having bowed at her mother-in-law's feet, said:
"Madam, this royal palace is prosperous and flourishing, a mine of endless jewels;

yet in our bedchamber, neither by day nor by night do lamps burn. We dwell together just as we would in darkness, unable to see one another with our eyes. What is the reason that lamps do not burn in our house?"
Queen Mahādevī said:

"Daughter Sudarśanā, both you and your husband are of noble form; in beauty, I see no one else who is their equal. Therefore, lest you two, upon seeing each other's noble forms, should fall into madness, let it be so: I have made this vow to the gods for a long time that when my daughter-in-law Sudarśanā shall have a son or a daughter, then in the twelfth year [they shall be united] with one another."
You shall see.
This is our family tradition.
Then that princess Sudarśanā said:
Indeed, it was a wicked thing that the noble lady made this vow to the gods, that we should not see one another for a long time.
Queen Mahādevī said:
"Daughter, what can I do? Such was my vow to the gods: 'I shall protect even you; let it not be that, upon seeing one another's noble complexion and form, you should fall into madness.'"
Thus, Sudarśanā, the king’s daughter, was now reconciled with her mother-in-law, the chief queen Alindā.
Then, after a long time, Sudarśanā, the king’s daughter, prostrated herself before her mother-in-law and made this request.
"Master, I wish to see my lord."
Queen Mahādevī said:
Be it so, daughter; you shall see him in due time.
Then Sudarśanā entreated her mother-in-law again and again:
"Madam, I wish to see him for one more time."
Then this thought occurred to Queen Alindā:
"This Princess Sudarśanā wishes to see Kuśa; if I do not dispel her curiosity, it will become very great.
Then Queen Alindā said:
"Daughter Sudarśanā, very well; tomorrow I shall show King Kuśa to you in the hall of audience, and he shall be granted an audience by the people."
Then Queen Alindā addressed King Kuśa.

"Son, this Sudarśanā, the king’s daughter, desires to see you; yet you are ill-favored in appearance. Lest Sudarśanā, upon seeing such a form as yours, experience a change of heart, let him who is the most handsome and the most pleasing among all those five hundred princes sit upon the royal throne, making him the king."
Then he should be shown to Sudarśanā, saying, "This is King Kuśa.
Then Sudarśanā will recognize that King Kuśa is like this, and her heart will not turn back [from him].
King Kuśa said:
Mother, let it be done thus.
Now, among those princes, Prince Kuśadruma was gracious and beautiful to behold.

Then, having adorned Kuśadruma with garments and ornaments worthy of a king, he was dressed like a king and seated upon the lion-throne in the audience hall for royal business as if he were the king; and all those princes, likewise adorned and well-decorated, were seated each upon their own respective seats.
The assembly, including ministers, chaplains, the vanguard of the army, guild-leaders, merchants, village-heads, and country-folk, together with the king, shone like the assembly of the gods.
Then King Kuśa, taking the parasol, held it over his left side for his brother, Prince Kuśadruma, who was seated upon the royal throne.
At that time, Queen Alindā, accompanied by her daughter-in-law Sudarśanā and surrounded by many hundreds of other queens, emerged from the palace and stood at the lion-window.
Then indeed, the Great Queen Alindā pointed out Prince Kuśadruma, who was seated upon the royal throne, to her daughter-in-law Sudarśanā.
"Daughter Sudarśanā, this is your husband; look upon him."

Then Sudarśanā, seeing Prince Kuśadruma seated upon the royal throne, was delighted in mind and thought: "Great is my gain, that my husband is so handsome, pleasing, and beautiful to behold; he surpasses the entire assembly of kings in physical form."
Then Sudarśanā, the king’s daughter, surveyed the assembly until, by her intuition regarding a thousand women, she saw that royal parasol-bearer.
Now, when Sudarśanā saw that royal parasol-bearer, her heart was struck, and she became filled with pain and dejection.
He speaks to his mother-in-law, the great queen Alindā.
"O Queen, King Kuśa shines, as do the princes who have performed meritorious deeds; and the entire royal assembly is beautiful, like an assembly of gods.

Yet this parasol-bearer is unsightly and unfit for a king such as he, who is equal to a son of the gods; such a parasol-bearer is deformed in appearance—stout-lipped, stout-headed, stout-footed, pot-bellied, dark, and the color of a heap of soot."
By this parasol-bearer, the entire majesty of the royal assembly has been eclipsed;
for in such a vast kingdom, there is no other man who may hold the king's parasol.
"If my husband wishes to do what is pleasing to me, then let this umbrella-bearer not stand near the king; let him have another man hold the umbrella."
Queen Alindā said:

"Daughter Sudarśanā, do not speak thus! It is not by physical appearance that one's purpose is fulfilled. Although this umbrella-bearer is ugly in appearance, he is great-souled in his virtues; he is virtuous, truthful, righteous, meritorious, powerful, and a crusher of enemy kingdoms.
By his majesty, no adversary whatsoever causes harm to our sixty thousand cities, including their towns and provinces."
By the power of this, we all live in happiness.
In this way, Sudarśanā was thus instructed by Queen Alindā.
Then Sudarśanā, having gone into private with King Kuśa, spoke to him.
"Great King, in your vast kingdom there is no other man who could serve as your umbrella-bearer;
such an umbrella-bearer as this one is truly unsightly.
If you wish to do what is pleasing to me, then dismiss this umbrella-bearer and appoint another man as your umbrella-bearer."
The king said:
"Do not revile this umbrella-bearer; what need is there for outward appearance?
What will his appearance do for him who is endowed with virtue?
This noble umbrella-bearer is excellent in virtue and possesses great strength. By his power, no adversary whatsoever can cause harm to these sixty thousand cities."
Thus, Queen Sudarśanā was now persuaded by King Kuśa.
Then King Kuśa, desiring to see Queen Sudarśanā, made a request to his mother, Queen Alindā:
"Mother, it is my wish that I might see Queen Sudarśanā."
Queen Alindā said:
"My son, you are ugly in appearance; if Sudarśanā were to know that King Kuśa is such in color and form, it is possible that she would take her own life by some means."
King Kuśa said:
"Mother, what can be done?
A stratagem must be devised so that I may see Sudarśanā and yet she does not know who I am."
Queen Ālindā said:

"My son, there is this means: when Princess Sudarśanā goes out to the park together with the other queens and all the women of the inner apartments to see the blue lotuses, red lotuses, and various flowers, you should go to the park beforehand, descend into the lotus pond up to your neck, and sit there with your head covered by a lotus leaf."

"We shall act in such a way that, in whichever place you remain upon the lotus pond, Sudarśanā will descend by those very steps for the sake of the lotuses; for since Sudarśanā is exceedingly fond of flowers and fond of leaves, you will see her according to your desire."

[ Mvu 2.449 ] Now, at that time, various kinds of blossoming flowers—blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lotuses, and fragrant lilies—as well as diverse types of garlands, were being brought into the royal palace by florists.
Seeing those blossoming blue and red lotuses, Sudarśanā then made a request to her mother-in-law, Queen Alindā.
"Madam, I wish to see the ponds filled with blooming blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water lilies, and great white lotuses."
Queen Mahādevī said:
"Son, look well; we shall all run out from the ponds."
Then Queen Alindā informed King Kuśa.
"My son, you should know that Sudarśanā, the daughter of the king, will go out with the women of the inner court to see the ponds.
If you wish to see her, then go to the park grounds beforehand and stay in such a place that Sudarśanā does not recognize you as King Kuśa."
Then King Kuśa, having promised his mother, went to the park grounds at dawn in his ordinary attire.
While waiting for the women of the harem, King Kuśa descended by that staircase where there were the greatest number of red and white lotuses; he sat there, concealing himself with a lotus leaf.
And all the women of the inner apartments rushed out;
just as the Nandana grove shines when filled with throngs of apsarases, so did that park shine with the king’s harem.
Then Queen Sudarśanā, having seen the lovely blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water lilies, and white lotuses in full bloom within those ponds, spoke to the other queens.
"O ladies, come! We shall gather lotuses from the ponds."
The goddesses said to them:
"Very well, O Queen,
we shall take the lotuses."
Then Queen Sudarśanā, together with the other queens, went down by that same staircase where King Kuśa was standing, placing Sudarśanā at their head.
Then Sudarśanā extended her hand for the sake of the lotuses, thinking, "I shall take a lotus";
thereupon, King Kuśa suddenly embraced her.
Then this thought occurred to Queen Sudarśanā: "I have been seized by the water-demon."
Then, crying out "Help! Help!", she was cast in; she cried, "I am being devoured by a water-demon! I am being devoured by a water-demon!"
Then all those women of the harem stood aside at one spot, thinking, "King Kuśa will sport with the queen. Then Queen Sudarśanā cried out, "Help! Help! as she was being devoured by the water-demon.
Then, when those women of the harem knew that King Kuśa had acted according to his intention, they performed an auspicious rite together with Queen Sudarśanā’s retinue:
"The ladle has been extinguished; your evil is pacified and stilled. By good fortune, you have been released by the water-demon!"
Then Sudarśanā, together with those other queens, having played, enjoyed herself, and amused herself there at the lotus pond during the day, entered the royal palace at eventide.
Then Queen Sudarśanā entered King Kuśa’s bedchamber.
The king speaks.
"The queen went to see the lotus pond but did not bring me any lotuses;
am I not dear to you, my beloved?"
The goddess said:

"Great King, from where would I have lotuses? Thinking, 'I shall take lotuses from the pond,' I was embraced by a water-rākṣasa; I was nearly devoured by the water-rākṣasa, and then I was rescued by the women of the inner apartments."
"O Great King, such as that umbrella-bearer of yours is, such is the water-demon in that lotus pond; I consider them to have been born of the same mother."
Then King Kuśa said:
"O Queen, do not go out again to see the lotus pond;
I too was there at that pool, for I have been devoured by a water-rākṣasa."
Then, at that mango season, various kinds of mangoes were brought into the royal palace by the king’s mango-keepers.
Then Queen Sudarśanā, having seen those various kinds of mangoes, made a request to her mother-in-law, the Great Queen Alindā.
"Madam, I wish to see the mango groves."
Queen Alindā said:
Daughter, look well; tomorrow I shall cause the mango groves to be cleared away.
Then Queen Mahādevī Alindā summoned Āmrapālā and gave her this command.
"Tomorrow the princess Sudarśanā will go out from the inner apartments together with her retinue to see the mango groves; therefore, have the mango grove sprinkled and swept.
Wrap the mango trunks in variegated spring-colored cloths, hang clusters of silk ribbons and garlands, burn incense, and adorn the mango grove by scattering loose flowers."
Then those garden-keepers, at the mere word of the Great Queen Alindā, adorned that mango grove park.
Then Queen Alindā informed King Kuśa.
"My son, tomorrow indeed Princess Sudarśanā will go out from the inner apartments together with her retinue to visit the royal mango grove.
If you wish to see Princess Sudarśanā, then go there beforehand and stand in that spot so that Sudarśanā does not recognize you as King Kuśa.
Having assented to his mother’s words, he went to the mango grove in his ordinary attire and stood beneath the most beautiful mango tree in the entire park.
Then Sudarśanā, surrounded by the women of the harem and with great royal splendor and great royal majesty, mounted various kinds of highly variegated royal chariots.
Then Queen Sudarśanā, having descended from her vehicle and surrounded by many hundreds of queens, entered that mango grove.

Just as the *yātraka* and *kovidāra* trees surrounded by deities shine in the Citraratha and Miśrakāvana groves of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, so too does the royal mango grove shine when surrounded by those women of the king’s inner court.

Then Queen Sudarśanā, wandering and strolling together with her companions through that mango grove, picking the finest mangoes and eating the mango fruits, and gathering various kinds of flowers, eventually arrived in the middle of the mango grove where King Kuśa was staying.
Then King Kuśa, having risen from the foot of the mango tree, was embraced by Queen Sudarśanā, who had thrown her head back.
Then Sudarśanā, terrified and trembling, realized, "I have been seized by a forest piśāca!"
Then, being pushed in with the cry of "Avidhāvidha!", she cried out, "I am being devoured by a forest piśāca! I am being devoured by a forest piśāca!"
Then those women of the harem fled here and there.

King Kuśa was sporting, enjoying himself, and diverting himself with Sudarśanā in the mango grove; and Sudarśanā would cry out, "Help! Help! and run, saying, "O women of the harem, I am being devoured by a forest-demon!"

Then, when those women of the inner court realized that King Kuśa had finished playing, sporting, and enjoying himself with Sudarśanā according to his desire, they took various kinds of flowers in their laps and went to that place.
Then those many hundreds of queens showered handfuls of flowers over King Kuśa and raised a cry:
"Shame on this demon! Shame on this demon!"
Then Kuśa, having abandoned Queen Sudarśanā, entered the royal palace.
Then, Queen Sudarśanā’s retinue performed a propitiatory rite;
they held up a ladle and cried out, "The evil has been appeased and pacified! By good fortune, you have been released alive by the forest piśāca!"
Then Queen Sudarśanā, having spent the day as she pleased in that mango grove with the other queens—sporting, delighting, and enjoying herself—entered the royal palace at the wrong hour.
She then entered King Kuśa’s bedchamber. The king said: "The queen went out to look for mangoes; neither were those mangoes brought back, nor am I dear to her."
The goddess said:
"Your Majesty, where would I have mangoes?
I ran out to look for mangoes, and then I was embraced by a forest piśāca; I was nearly devoured by that forest piśāca.
Thereupon, I was rescued from the hands of the forest piśāca by the women of the harem."

"Great King, such as your umbrella-bearer is, and such as the water-demon of the lotus pond is, such too is the forest-piśāca in the mango grove; I believe all three persons were born of one mother, for they are all exactly alike.
King Kuśa said:
"O Queen, do not go again to see the mango grove;
I too was devoured by a forest piśāca in that mango grove."
Then, at another time, Queen Sudarśanā made a request to her mother-in-law, the Great Queen Alindā.
It is my intention to see King Kuśa’s elephant corps;
I have heard that King Kuśa possesses an extensive elephant corps of sixty thousand elephants.
Queen Alindā said:
"O daughter, tomorrow you shall go out to see the king's elephant-division."
Then Queen Mahādevī Alindā summoned the chief elephant-keeper and gave him this command:
"Tomorrow the princess Sudarśanā will go out together with the women of the inner apartments to view the royal elephant stables;
therefore, decorate both the elephant and the elephant stables."
Then the elephant mahout, having heard the command of Queen Alindā, prepared the entire elephant force—
sixty thousand elephants adorned with every ornament, covered with golden nets, with ivory trappings and trunk-ornaments, and with hooves like coral.
And that elephant stable was sprinkled and swept, strewn with loose flowers, draped with bundles of hanging silk ribbons, and perfumed with incense.
Then Queen Alindā addressed King Kuśa.
"My son, you must know that tomorrow the princess Sudarśanā will go out from the inner apartments together with her retinue to visit the royal elephant stable.
Therefore, go to the elephant stable beforehand and stay in that place so that Sudarśanā does not recognize you as King Kuśa."

Then King Kuśa, having given his word to his mother, went at dawn, disguised as an elephant-keeper, directly to the elephant stable and remained there at the foot of the elephants, waiting for Sudarśanā.
Then Sudarśanā, accompanied by her mother-in-law Alindā and surrounded by all the women of the inner apartments, mounted royal horse-chariots and entered the elephant stable.
Then, having descended from her horse-chariot and surrounded by many hundreds of maidservants, she entered the elephant stable.
King Kuśa, meanwhile, remained at the foot of the elephants, acting as an elephant-keeper while gazing intently at Sudarśanā.

Then, as Queen Sudarśanā was walking back and forth, pacing about there in the elephant stable together with the women of the inner apartments, at the moment she turned back thinking, "I am going to the royal palace," King Kuśa struck Queen Sudarśanā from behind with fresh, steaming elephant dung.
Those garments worthy of a king were ruined by elephant dung.
Then Sudarśanā, the king’s daughter, made a request to her mother-in-law, the great queen Alindā.
"Madam, punishment must be meted out to this royal elephant-keeper.
He is capable of striking the chief queen of King Kuśa with elephant dung."
Then Queen Alindā said:
"Be it so, daughter; let him go. This royal elephant-keeper is not to be killed; what can be done?"
Thus, Sudarśanā was now persuaded by her mother-in-law.
Then, at another time, Sudarśanā made a request to her mother-in-law, the great queen Alindā.
"Madam, it would please me to see King Kuśa’s cavalry."
Queen Alindā said:
"Very well, daughter; go out tomorrow to see King Kuśa’s horse-riding display. Then Queen Mahādevī Alindā summoned the chief grooms and gave them her command.
"Tomorrow the King’s daughter Sudarśanā will go out with her retinue of women to view the royal horse-enclosure.
Now, decorate all sixty thousand horses, and have the stable sprinkled, swept clean, and strewn with loose flowers."
Having heard the command of the Great Queen Alindā from those horse-keepers, all sixty thousand horses were adorned with every kind of ornament;
and that stable was sprinkled and swept, and strewn with loose flowers.
Then Queen Alindā informed King Kuśa.

"My son Kuśa, you should know that Sudarśanā, the king’s daughter, will go out together with the women of the inner apartments to view the royal horse-herds. If you wish to see her, then go directly to the stable and stand in such a place that Sudarśanā does not recognize you as King Kuśa."
Then King Kuśa, having assented to his mother’s words, at the break of dawn assumed the guise of a horse-keeper; scattering fodder for the horses, he sat there waiting for Sudarśanā.
Meanwhile, Princess Sudarśanā, together with her mother-in-law, Queen Alindā Mahādevī, and all the women of the inner apartments, mounted a jeweled palanquin and set out for the stable.
Then Sudarśanā, having descended from the palanquin and surrounded by many hundreds of queens, entered the stable.
King Kuśa also stood behind the horses, gazing intently at Sudarśanā.

Then Sudarśanā, having wandered about and roamed through that horse stable together with other women of the harem, at the moment she was turning back to go toward the royal palace, she was struck on the back by King Kuśa with fresh, steaming horse dung.
Those garments worthy of a king were ruined by horse dung.
Then Sudarśanā, the king’s daughter, said to her mother-in-law, the chief queen Alindā:
"Madam, punishment must be meted out to this horse-keeper."
"It is possible for this man to strike the chief queen of King Kuśa with a horse-dung pellet."
Queen Alindā said:
"Daughter, be patient; these royal horse-guards are not to be slain. What can be done?"
Then, at another time, Sudarśanā made a request to her mother-in-law, the queen-mother Alindā.
"Madam, it is my intention to see King Kuśa’s chariot-army;
I have heard that King Kuśa’s chariot-army is vast, consisting of sixty thousand chariots."
Queen Mahādevī said:
"Very well, daughter; tomorrow go out to see King Kuśa’s procession of chariots."
Then Queen Alindā summoned the charioteers of King Kuśa and gave them this command.
The king’s daughter Sudarśanā, together with her retinue of women from the inner apartments, will go out to see King Kuśa’s chariot procession.

Then, having heard the words of the Great Queen, those chariot-guards prepared six thousand chariots from the day before yesterday; they were yoked, covered with lion skins, island-deer skins, and tiger skins, draped with white woolen blankets, making a joyful sound, adorned with victory banners, with coral-like hooves, and with flags and pennants raised high.
Then Queen Alindā informed King Kuśa.
"My son, you should know that tomorrow the princess Sudarśanā will go out with her retinue from the inner apartments to view the royal chariot procession.
If you wish to see her, then go to the chariot shed this very evening and stand in such a place that Sudarśanā might not recognize you as King Kuśa."
Then Sudarśanā, the king’s daughter, together with Queen Mahādevī Alindā and the entire harem, mounted royal chariots and set out for the chariot shed.
King Kuśa, having given his promise to his mother, went at dawn to the chariot-house by his own nature; he sat at the base of the chariots in the guise of a chariot-attendant, waiting for Sudarśanā.
Then Sudarśanā, the king’s daughter, having descended from her horse-drawn chariot and surrounded by many hundreds of queens, entered the chariot-house.

Then, after Sudarśanā, the king’s daughter, had wandered about the chariot-shed together with the other queens and was turning back to go toward the royal palace, King Kuśa struck her on the back with a fresh lump of steaming cow dung.
Those garments worthy of a king were ruined by a lump of cow dung.
Then Sudarśanā, the king’s daughter, said to her mother-in-law, the chief queen Alindā:
"Minister, punishment must be inflicted upon this Rathapāla;
he deserves to strike the chief queen of King Kuśa with a lump of cow dung."
Queen Alindā said:
"Daughter, forgive him; this is the king's chariot-guardian, the king's chariot-treasury keeper, who is not to be slain. What can be done?"
Then Sudarśanā was thus instructed by Queen Alindā.
Then, at another time, a fire was set in the royal elephant stable, and a great conflagration blazed up.
Thousands of elephant-keepers, chief mahouts, and a great multitude of other people gathered at the elephant stable, thinking,

"We shall extinguish this fire," yet they were unable to extinguish that conflagration; the entire harem, too, became terrified and trembling with fear of that fire, thinking, "May it not burn down this royal palace as well!"
Then all those women of the harem were running out from where the elephant stable was, saying, "Who is able to extinguish this burning fever of the elephant?"
The great multitude of people grew weary, yet they were unable to extinguish that conflagration, nor were they able to bring down those thick, massive, and many-layered roofs of the elephant stables.
And at that time, King Kuśa was walking and wandering about outside the city when he was noticed.
Then, a man who was a minister reported this to the king.
"Great King, you should know that the royal elephant stable has indeed caught fire."
And having heard this, King Kuśa, mounted upon the back of a noble elephant, arrived with his retinue at that elephant stable with great speed.

All the women of the inner apartments saw the king rushing toward them; as he charged, with a single effort, that king cast those flaming bundles—along with their wings, stalks, and thorns—from the elephant stable out through the main gate.
For even those elephants that are bound with leather thongs, he cuts those bonds with his hand by snapping his fingers;
and even those noble elephants seized by fire, he lifts them up and casts them to one side out of fear of the flames.
Thus, in that very moment, King Kuśa extinguished the elephant stable and rescued the entire elephant corps from the conflagration; not a single elephant was burned or harmed.
Then, seeing such valor and prowess of King Kuśa, many hundreds of thousands of millions of people raised thousands of shouts of acclaim.
Even the women of King Kuśa’s harem, seeing such manly prowess, were all joyful and satisfied, exclaiming, "Oh, the strength of King Kuśa! Oh, his prowess!"
Then another hunchbacked woman, thrilled and filled with excitement, cried out "King! King! to Kuśa.
Possessing a lion-like, excellent seat, powerful, beautiful, vast, and great,
he shines like the moon in the sky, perfectly circular in every direction.
With eyes as long and copper-red as those of a cakora bird, he shines like the god of love;
the king, a bull among men endowed with great power, has set the elephants free.
Then King Kuśa, being pleased with that hunchbacked woman, gave her a gift, entertained her, and granted her a boon.
"Truly, this hunchback who praises the king is fortunate;
I shall give you four garments of Kāśī cloth."
Then, having heard that hunchback woman speaking in praise of Kuśa, it occurred to Sudarśanā, the king’s daughter:
"This man shall become King Kuśa; this hunchbacked woman speaks his praise."
Then, having seen such a complexion and form of King Kuśa, the princess Sudarśanā’s heart was struck with emotion, and she became filled with pain and dejection.

"Let it not be that such a man is my husband—one so ill-colored and hideous, with thick lips, a thick head, thick feet, and a large belly; black as the color of a heap of soot, there is no difference whatsoever between him and this *piśāca*."
Then Queen Sudarśanā, enraged at that hunchbacked woman, said:
Truly, there is no one who would cut out the tongue of this hunchback with a very sharp blade for praising the king.
Then that hunchbacked woman addressed Queen Sudarśanā with a verse:
Kings threaten with imprisonment or execution;
therefore, I speak in praise of this [virtue] so that one may protect one's own life.
Then Queen Sudarśanā, seeing King Kuśa in such a state— discolored and hideous—
found no pleasure there in that royal palace, which was so delightful as to resemble the abode of the gods and was a mine of endless jewels; she felt no desire even for food and drink.
"I will not eat, I will not consume; what is the use of my life, since I must dwell together with a piśāca?"
Then Sudarśanā, the king’s daughter, made a request to her mother-in-law, the chief queen Alindā.
"Madam, release me; I shall go to my mother and father in Kanyakubja."
If you do not release me, I will take my own life and kill myself within a moment.
Then this thought occurred to the Great Queen Alindā:
"It is better that this princess lives than that she should die."
Then Queen Alindā said:
Daughter, go wherever you desire.

Then Sudarśanā, the king’s daughter, accompanied by the hunchback, mounted a horse-chariot, departed from Vārāṇasī, and set out; traveling by stages, she arrived at Kanyakubja, in the presence of her mother and father.
Then King Kuśa, having entered his bedchamber at an improper hour, did not see Queen Sudarśanā;
though they searched throughout the royal palace, she was not seen anywhere.
Now King Kuśa, not obtaining Queen Sudarśanā, was longing, grieving, and tormented;
though his harem was so extensive, he did not find another woman to his liking.
When it became known to him that Queen Sudarśanā had gone to her kinsmen's home accompanied by the hunchback, King Kuśa then made a request to his mother, Alindā.
"Mother, I too shall go to Kaṇṇakubja, to the presence of my father-in-law Mahendra, the king of the Madrakas, and I will bring Queen Sudarśanā back."
Then Queen Alindā, having heard the words of her son Kuśa that he would go to Kanyakubja, fainted from affection for her son and thirst for the kingdom; she stumbled, fell broken upon the ground,
overcome with grief for her son.
"Alas, what a calamity for me, unfortunate as I am!
Since I have sought her out and brought here this Sudarśanā, the daughter of Mahendraka, the Madra king of Kanyakubja, I do not know how it will turn out for my son, King Kuśa."
Then Queen Alindā spoke to her son Kuśa.

"My son, you are the son of King Ikṣvāku, delicate and raised in comfort; whereas the people of the countryside eat parched grain, wear woolen blankets, and have coarse food from their daily labor—how will your journey on the road be possible?"
King Kuśa said:
"Mother, I shall go, providing for my own livelihood through dancing, singing, instrumental music, and various other illusions and diverse means; let not my mother grieve."

King Kuśa, having thus consoled his mother, established his brother Kuśadruma upon the throne. He said, "Brother, exercise sovereignty over these sixty thousand cities, along with their market towns and provinces.
Here are sixty thousand elephants for you, adorned with every ornament, covered with nets of gold, and having coral tips on their tusks."

Sixty thousand horses, all from Sindh, swift-moving and adorned with every ornament; sixty thousand chariots covered with lion skins, tiger skins, and leopard skins, draped in white woolen blankets, making a joyful sound, equipped with victory banners, with coral-like hooves, and with parasols, standards, and flags raised high— these are your vehicles.
Protect this kingdom until my return shall take place.
Then King Kuśa gave instructions to his ministers.
"This Prince Kuśadruma is your king until my return;
know this.
In this manner, govern the kingdom accordingly and protect the people of the city and the countryside with righteousness."
Then King Kuśa, having thus instructed his ministers and established his brother Kuśadruma on the throne,
paid homage to his mother, the Great Queen Alindā, circumambulated her, and taking up his seven-stringed lute,
set out facing north.
King Kuśa, providing for his own livelihood through various means, proceeded toward Kanyakubja, his father-in-law's residence, and in due course arrived at the territory of Kanyakubja.
There, having arrived to stay in a certain village, he was given shelter in the hall of an elderly woman.
Now, a festival was taking place in that village;
then King Kuśa was addressed by that old woman:
"Son, there is a festival taking place here in the village; go into the middle of the village, and there you will obtain some food and drink; then, having eaten, you shall return."
Then King Kuśa, having heard that from the old woman, went into the middle of the village.
Then King Kuśa played such a lute and sang such a song that all the people of the village were delighted.
Thereupon, the villagers, being filled with joy, gave to this Kuśa a cow-stall full of various kinds of snacks, a large earthen vessel full of boiled rice, a jar of curd, and various condiments.
Then King Kuśa caused all the solid and soft food to be brought into the hall for the elderly.
Then that old woman, seeing the abundant food and drink— a large basket filled with various kinds of snacks, a large vessel given full of rice, and various kinds of side dishes—
was struck with wonder upon seeing what had been brought in by King Kuśa.
She became delighted.
Today this musician, having taken a single meal, will depart during the final watch of the night; that remaining food—both hard and soft—will serve as my sustenance for two or three months.
While King Kuśa was conversing with that old woman, he ate half of that basket of snacks;
the old woman also knew this,
thinking, "Even now, in just a moment, he will give me the remainder of my snacks."
Then King Kuśa, being hungry, ate the entire basket of snacks; not even a single morsel of snack was left remaining.
To that elderly woman, this thought occurred:
When this musician has eaten all of that great basket of sweetmeats, he will be satiated;
he will not be able to eat more of these sweets from the bowl,
and thus my food will last for a long time.

Then King Kuśa, having set out on his journey while hungry, consumed that large platter of sweetmeats, the jar of curd, and all those various kinds of side dishes; he left nothing remaining for that old woman.
Then that old woman became despondent and cried out, "Help! Help! Enter! Run! A piśāca has entered my house in human form with his body inside; he wishes to devour me!"
King Kuśa said:
"Mother, why do you cry out? Why do you run away?
There is no one here in the village who is wicked; do not be afraid, do not cry out.
Having stayed for this one night, I shall depart tomorrow."
Then King Kuśa, having risen at the time of the first light of dawn, set out and in due course arrived at Kanyakubja;
he entered a florist’s workshop and approached the chief florist, saying, "I too shall dwell here; I am also skilled in this craft."
Now, in that flower-seller’s shop, necklaces for the royal ladies and fragrant crests were being fashioned into garlands.

Now King Kuśa produced such neck-ornaments, fragrant crests, and garlands—well-made, well-finished, most variegated, and shapely—that when all the florists saw them, they were struck with wonder, exclaiming:
"Oh, what a noble son of a teacher! What a magnificent craftsman! He who produces such neck-ornaments, fragrant crests, and garlands, so well-made and so well-finished!"
"We have never seen this before.
And King Kuśa wrote everything down in his own hand so that Sudarśanā would know, "This is the work of King Kuśa."
Those necklaces, fragrant crest-ornaments, and garlands were brought into the royal palace and presented to Sudarśanā.
"Look, Sudarśanā, at these varieties of flowers; how well-made, how variegated, how perfectly finished, and how many-colored they are!"
Then Sudarśanā, having taken whatever was most beautiful there—the neck-ornament, the crown, and the finest garland—thought, "I shall fasten them," when she saw the name of Kuśa upon them.
This thought occurs to her:
"This must be the deed of Kuśa; King Kuśa will have come here in an ordinary disguise."
Then Sudarśanā, having discarded those [garments] made by Kuśa, took up other ordinary ones.
Then Sudarśanā was addressed by her mother, by her sisters, and by the women of the inner apartments:
"Sudarśanā, why do you cast aside these most beautiful necklaces, crowns, and garlands to take up other, ordinary ones?"
She said to her:
Enough for me with these; let this alone be mine.
Whatever secret is therein, he does not disclose it to anyone.
Thus, King Kuśa, having stayed with the florist, did not find his purpose; thereupon, he departed and sought refuge with the head potter.
There too, various kinds of potter’s vessels were being made for the sake of the king’s harem.
Now, King Kuśa produced such well-made, well-finished, and shapely potter’s vessels that all the potters, upon seeing them, were struck with amazement, exclaiming:
"Oh, what a fine master’s son, what a splendid craftsman, who makes such well-made, well-finished, and shapely potter’s vessels as we have never before seen!"
These were all things he had seen before.
And on all of them, King Kuśa inscribed his own name by means of a mere mark, so that Sudarśanā might know: "This is the work of Kuśa."
Then those maidservants in the inner apartments brought those pottery vessels into the royal palace and presented them to Sudarśanā, saying:
"Look, Sudarśanā, at these pottery vessels—how beautiful, excellent, well-made, and perfectly finished they are! Take whichever one pleases you."
Then Sudarśanā, thinking, "I shall take whichever of these potter's vessels is most beautiful and most worthy of being seen," saw one bearing the name of Kuśa.
It occurred to her,
"This is the work of Kuśa."
Then, having discarded those, she accepted other ordinary ones.
Then Sudarśanā was addressed by her mother, her sisters, and the queens:
"Sudarśanā, such beautiful vessels as these have never before been brought into this royal palace;
why do you not take these beautiful vessels?"
Then she said:
Enough for me with this; let this alone be mine.
Whatever secret is therein, he does not disclose it to anyone.
Thus, King Kuśa, having stayed with the potter, did not find his purpose;
therefore, departing from there, he approached the chief carpenter.
There too, for the sake of the king’s harem, various kinds of carpenter’s goods were being made:
stools were being made, couches were being made, benches were being made, beds and seats were being made, and footstools were being made.
They are being made; auspicious seats are being made; iron pegs are being made; small boxes are being made; end-pieces are being made; and various other kinds of carpenter’s tools are being made.
Now King Kuśa fashioned such carpenter’s tools—well-made, well-finished, and shapely—that all the carpenters were filled with wonder upon seeing them.
"Oh! What a son of a master craftsman, what a fine artisan, who makes such tools, so well-made and well-finished, the likes of which we have never seen before!
And on all of them, King Kuśa inscribed his own name as a mere designation, so that Sudarśanā might know: "This is the work of King Kuśa."
Then those female slaves of the harem brought that carpenter’s equipment into the royal palace;
having selected all the most beautiful items among them, they were presented to Sudarśanā.
"Sudarśanā, look, look at these carpenter's tools; how beautiful and pleasing to behold they are!
Take whichever among them you desire."

Then Sudarśanā, thinking, "I shall take whichever among those things there is most beautiful— the stools, the couches, the benches, the footstools, the foot-slates, the bhadrapīṭhas, the ayakkas, the antakoṭas, the baskets, or the small boxes"— beheld the name of Kuśa.
Then this thought occurred to her:
"This is the deed of Kuśa."
Then, having let him go, she took hold of another common man.
Then Sudarśanā was addressed by her mother, her sisters, and those women of the inner apartments:
"Sudarśanā, why do you discard these such beautiful carpenter's tools and take up others that are common?"
Then she said:
Enough for me with those; let these alone be mine.
Whatever secret is therein, he does not disclose it to anyone.
Thus, King Kuśa, having stayed with the carpenter, did not find what he sought;
so, departing from there, he went to stay with a washerman.
There too, laundry was washed for the king’s harem, and Sudarśanā’s laundry was also washed right there.

Now King Kuśa recognized Sudarśanā’s garments. King Kuśa then washed those clothes for Sudarśanā in such a way that they were thoroughly rinsed, clean, spotless, and laundered, such that all the washermen, upon seeing the clothes, were struck with amazement.
"Oh, how excellent is the son of the virtuous teacher, this skillful artisan, who washes these robes— so well-washed, so thoroughly rinsed, so clean and stainless— which we have never seen before!"
King Kuśa wrote his own name with a marking-nut (*bhallātaka*) fruit as a mere sign, so that Sudarśanā might know, "This is the work of Kuśa."

Then those palace maidservants brought those garments into the royal palace; those which were the garments of the queens were presented to the queens, and those which were the garments of the women of the inner apartments were given to the women of the inner apartments.
Then those women of the inner apartments saw the garments of Sudarśanā—white, clean, and spotless.
Then they were filled with wonder at all those beautiful garments—well-washed, clean, and spotless—and they said, "Sudarśanā deserves a washing fee of two or three times [the usual amount].
And Sudarśanā, seeing those clothes so pure and stainless, became joyful.
Even in that remote region where a washerman would mark a garment with *bhallātaka* (marking-nut) merely as a sign and write the owner's name upon it, he wrote the name of Kuśa there.
Having seen this deed of Kuśa.
She did not receive it herself, but had her attendant take it.
All those women of the inner apartments gave the washermen’s fee for their respective garments into the hands of the maidservants;
however, Sudarśanā did not wish to give the washermen’s fee for her garments.
Then Sudarśanā was addressed by her mother, by her sisters, and by the women of the inner apartments.
Sudarśanā, when all your garments were well-washed, very clean, and entirely spotless, you did not give him any fee for washing them.
Sudarśanā said:
Why do you worry? He will give it at another time.
Whatever secret is therein, he does not disclose it to anyone.

Thus, King Kuśa, having stayed with the washerman, did not find his purpose. Thereupon, he departed and attached himself to the chief courtier; and there, in the laundry, the garments of the king’s harem were being washed, as were the garments of Sudarśanā.
Right there, King Kuśa recognized Sudarśanā’s garments.
Kuśa dyed those garments for Sudarśanā so beautifully, with such vibrant colors and such exquisite patterns that all those dyers were struck with amazement, exclaiming:
"Oh, how excellent is this son of a master dyer! He is a truly skilled craftsman who dyes these garments so beautifully and with such exquisite variety—colors never before seen by us!"
And on all of them, King Kuśa wrote his own name as a mere mark using *bhallātaka* [poison], so that Sudarśanā might know: "This is the work of Kuśa."
Then those female slaves of the harem gave back to the queens whatever robes belonged to the queens, and they gave to the women of the harem whatever robes belonged to the women of the harem.

When the women of the harem saw Sudarśanā’s robe, they were struck with wonder, saying: "These robes of Sudarśanā are so well-dyed, beautiful, and exquisitely variegated; they are twice or even three times as [fine] as these of Sudarśanā."
That which is to be colored should be given.
Then those robes were presented to Sudarśanā.

Then Sudarśanā, seeing those robes— well-dyed, beautiful to behold, and exquisitely variegated— became contented and filled with joy and gladness; she looked until she saw, in the place where the dyer was marking them with *bhallātaka* seeds, the name of Kuśa.
It occurred to her:
"This is Kuśa's deed.
She did not accept it herself, but gave it to her attendant.
Then those women of the harem gave the dyeing fee for their respective garments into the hands of the maidservants; but Sudarśanā did not wish to give the dyeing fee.
She was addressed by her mother, her sisters, and the women of the inner apartments:
"Sudarśanā, since your garments are so well-dyed, so variegated, and so beautiful, you ought to provide a dyeing fee twice or even three times as much; yet you do not wish to give it.
Sudarśanā said: "I will not give it."
Why do you worry? He will give it at another time.
Whatever secret is therein, he does not disclose it to anyone.
Then King Kuśa, having stayed with the washerman and not finding his purpose there, departed from that place and approached the chief of the mat-makers.
Thereupon, by the command of King Mahendraka, various kinds of vessels for food and vessels for drink, made of gold and silver and inlaid with jewels, were being fashioned for the sake of the harem.

Now King Kuśa had golden and jeweled vessels, inlaid with gems, for eating and drinking, which were so beautiful and well-fashioned that there was not even a single potter capable of making such vessels.
Then those coppersmiths, seeing such things,
were filled with wonder.
"Oh, how wonderful is the son of the virtuous teacher, this excellent artisan, who fashions such precious vessels as these, the likes of which we have never seen before!
And on all of them, King Kuśa inscribes his own name by way of a mere sign, so that Sudarśanā may know: 'This is the work of Kuśa.'"
Then, when all those royal vessels made of gold and silver were finished, they were presented by that chief master craftsman to King Mahendraka.
Then King Mahendraka, seeing those vessels which Kuśa had fashioned, was filled with wonder:
"Such are these vessels inlaid with jewels; they must have been made by this skillful master."
Then King Mahendraka gave those jeweled vessels into the hands of the eunuchs and chamberlains, saying:
"Go, enter the inner apartments; first give them as you please to the Great Queen and my daughter Sudarśanā, and afterwards to the other queens and the women of the harem."
Then those chief eunuchs and chamberlains brought those jeweled vessels into the inner apartments and presented them to the Great Queen, saying:

"Queen, these jeweled vessels have been sent by the King; let the Queen and your daughter Sudarśanā take them first as they desire, and afterwards they shall be given to all the other queens and to all the women of the harem."
Then Sudarśanā was addressed by her mother, by her sisters, by the women of the inner apartments, and by the eunuchs and chamberlains.

"Sudarśanā, these jeweled vessels and drinking cups have been sent for you by your father; you should take them first according to your wish, and afterwards they shall be given to the other queens and all the women of the harem; take as much as you desire."
Then Sudarśanā, thinking, "I shall take whatever there is most beautiful, well-made, perfectly finished, and well-formed," saw the name of Kuśa.
It occurred to her:
"This is the work of Kuśa."
Then, having discarded that, she took others made by an ordinary artisan.
Then Sudarśanā was addressed by her mother, her sisters,
the women of the inner apartments, the eunuchs, and the chamberlains.
"Sudarśanā, why do you discard such beautiful, precious vessels that are most excellent in every way, and instead take up other common ones?"
She then said:
Enough for me with this; let this alone be mine.
Whatever secret is therein, he does not disclose it to anyone.
Thus, King Kuśa, having stayed with the coppersmith, did not find what he needed;
so, departing from there, he attached himself to the chief goldsmith.
There too, by royal command, various kinds of golden ornaments were being made for the sake of the harem.
Head-covers are being made; foot-coverings are being made; golden garlands are being made; *kilañjaka* mats are being made; turbans are being made;

jeweled earrings are being made; caskets are being made; face-flower ornaments are being made; *bimba* ornaments are being made; bracelets are being made; anklets are being made; and hip-bands are being made.
Foot-covers are being made, anklets are being made, and toe-rings are also being made.

Now King Kuśa fashioned such golden ornaments— magnificent, beautiful, well-made, perfectly finished, flawlessly polished, with all impurities and dross removed, supple, workable, and radiant— such that when all those goldsmiths saw them, they were filled with wonder.

"Oh, how wonderful is the son of the noble teacher, this excellent craftsman, who fashions such golden ornaments so well-made, perfectly finished, and beautifully formed, the likes of which we have never seen before!
And King Kuśa inscribes his own name upon them all by way of a mere mark, so that Sudarśanā may know, 'This is the work of Kuśa.'"
Then, when those goldsmiths had finished the ornaments, they presented them all to King Mahendra.

Then the king, having seen the ornaments that had been fashioned by King Kuśa, was struck with wonder, thinking: "Oh, how well-made, how perfectly finished, and how beautiful these ornaments are, fashioned by the skillful son of a master!"
Then King Mahendraka sent those ornaments into the hands of the eunuchs and chamberlains.
"Go! First give these ornaments to the Great Queen and to Sudarśanā as they desire; afterwards, give them to the other queens and to all the women of the inner apartments.
Then those eunuchs and chamberlains, having entered the royal palace, presented those ornaments to the Great Queen and to Sudarśanā.
"Queen, this golden ornament has been sent to you by the King.
You and your daughter Sudarśanā should take it first as you desire;
afterwards, it shall be given to all the other queens and to everyone in the inner apartments."

Then Sudarśanā, thinking, "I shall take whichever of these golden ornaments is the most beautiful, well-crafted, perfectly finished, and shapely," saw one bearing the name of Kuśa; at that sight, it occurred to her:
"This is the work of Kuśa."
Then, having let go of that, she took ordinary items made by a common craftsman.
Then Sudarśanā was addressed by her mother, by her sisters, by the women of the harem, and by the eunuchs and chamberlains.

"Sudarśanā, why are you so perverse? Having set aside these all-beautiful golden ornaments— well-fashioned, well-finished, shapely, and made by a skilled master-craftsman— why do you instead take up other common ones made by a poor artisan?"
Sudarśanā said:
Enough for me with that; let this alone be mine.
Whatever secret is therein, he does not disclose it to anyone.
Thus, King Kuśa, having stayed with the goldsmith, did not find what he sought;
thereupon, having departed from there, he approached the chief of the jewelers.
There too, by the king’s command, [he was occupied] with the affairs of the harem.

For the sake of wealth, various kinds of ornaments were being made; necklaces of pearls, gems, beryl, conch, crystal, coral, quartz, emerald, and ruby were being made, as well as half-necklaces, jeweled earrings, jeweled breastplates, and armlets made of precious stones; bracelets were being made, and girdles made of jewels were being fashioned.
Now King Kuśa produced such well-crafted, perfectly finished, and shapely jeweled ornaments that all those jewelers were filled with wonder upon seeing them.
"Oh! What a noble master’s son, what a magnificent artisan, who produces such ornaments—so well-crafted, perfectly finished, and shapely—that we have never seen the like before!
And on all of them, King Kuśa inscribed his own name by way of a mere sign, so that Sudarśanā might know, "This is the work of Kuśa."
Then, at the time when those ornaments were finished by the jewel-workers, they were presented to King Mahendraka.
Then the king, seeing the ornaments that Kuśa had fashioned, was filled with wonder:
"Oh! How excellent is this son of a master craftsman; what a beautiful artisan he is!"
Then King Mahendraka, having sent those ornaments into the hands of the eunuchs and chamberlains, said:
"Go, first give these ornaments to the Great Queen and Sudarśanā according to their desire; afterwards, give them to all the other queens and to everyone in the inner apartments."
Then those eunuchs and chamberlains, having brought those ornaments into the royal palace, presented them to the Great Queen and Sudarśanā, saying:
"Queen, these jeweled ornaments have been sent by the King; you and your daughter Sudarśanā may take whatever you desire.
Afterwards, they shall be given to all the other queens and the women of the harem."

Then Sudarśanā, thinking, "I shall take whichever of these jeweled ornaments is the most beautiful there, well-fashioned, well-finished, and shapely," saw the name of Kuśa upon it; at that, she thought,
"This is the work of Kuśa."
Then, having let that go, she took other ordinary ones made by common craftsmen.
Then Sudarśanā was addressed by her mother, by her sisters, by the women of the harem, by the eunuchs, and by the chamberlains.

"Sudarśanā, why are you so perverse? Why do you cast aside these gemstone ornaments—which are well-crafted, well-finished, shapely, and made by skilled artisans—and instead take up others that are common and poorly made by unskilled craftsmen?"
Then Sudarśanā said:
Enough for me with these; let this alone be mine.
Whatever secret is therein, he does not disclose it to anyone.

Now, King Kuśa, having lived at the root of the jeweler’s, did not find his purpose there. So, departing from there, he went to the root of the chief shell-and-bracelet maker. There too, by royal command, various kinds of ornaments and vessels made of shell and ivory were being fashioned for the sake of the harem.

They also make ivory pegs, they make ointment boxes, they make ivory caskets, they make yellow pigment figures, they make ivory ewers, they make ivory combs, they make ivory footstools, they make lion figures, they make conch shells, they make conch-shell beds, and they make various objects made of conch shell.
Oil vessels, perfume vessels, and cosmetic boxes were being made; conch-shell lotus stalks were being made,
as well as conch-shell seals, conch-shell bracelets, conch-shell girdles, conch-shell necklaces, conch-shell palanquins, and conch-shell shields.

In this way, he fashioned various kinds of vessels and ornaments made of conch and ivory—well-crafted, well-finished, and beautifully shaped—such that all the artisans working with conch and ivory were struck with wonder upon seeing them.
