"Oh! What a noble master’s son, what a magnificent craftsman, who creates such ornaments and vessels of conch and ivory as we have never seen before! they exclaimed.
And on all of them, King Kuśa inscribed his own name merely as a designation, so that Sudarśanā might know, "This is the work of Kuśa."
Then, when those artisans who were shaped like conch shells and elephants had completed everything according to their instructions, they presented it to King Mahendraka.
Having seen that noble, beautiful, and well-executed work of Kuśa, which was worthy of a king, the king was struck with wonder:
"Aha! How marvelous are these things created by the virtuous son of the preceptor!"
Having seen the conch and ivory articles crafted by Kuśa, which were noticed by the princes, the ministers, and the king’s men, they were filled with wonder.
These were made by the virtuous son of the teacher.
King Mahendra sent those ornaments and vessels into the hands of the eunuchs and chamberlains, saying:
"Go, enter the inner apartments; first give them as you wish to the Great Queen and my daughter Sudarśanā, and afterwards to the other queens and the women of the harem."
Then those eunuchs and chamberlains took those ornaments and vessels and entered the inner apartments; they were presented to the chief queen.

"Queen," they said, "these ornaments and vessels made of conch and ivory have been sent by the king for you and for your daughter Sudarśanā. Take them first according to your wish; afterwards they shall be given to the other queens."
And of all the women of the inner apartments.

Then Sudarśanā, seeing those ornaments and vessels made of conch and ivory— seeing how well-crafted, well-finished, excellent, and beautiful they were, and seeing that they had been made by the son of a master craftsman and were being offered in her hand—
took them; however, when she saw the name of Kuśa upon them, this thought occurred to her:
Thinking, "This is Kuśa’s work," she then set that aside and took up other ordinary items made by common craftsmen.
Then Sudarśanā was addressed by her mother, by her sisters, by the women of the inner apartments, and by the eunuchs and chamberlains.

"Sudarśanā, why are you so perverse that, having rejected these all-beautiful, well-made, well-finished, and shapely pieces crafted by the son of a master artisan, you take up others that are common and made by a poor craftsman?"
Why do you not take these things that are all so beautiful?
Then Sudarśanā said:
Enough for me with these; let this alone be mine.
Whatever secret there was therein, he did not disclose it to anyone.
Now, King Kuśa, having stayed with the worker of conch-shell ornaments, did not perceive any special excellence there. Thereupon, departing from him, he approached a worker in leather (jantakāra).
There, by the king's command, various kinds of leather straps and staffs were being fashioned for the sake of the harem.
Various toys were made, including mechanical dolls;
fans were also made with mechanical dolls;

there were palm-leaf fans, peacock-feather fans, footstools, benches, and large chairs, all with legs consisting of mechanical dolls; there were bracelets, all of which had legs made of mechanical dolls.
And mechanical figures of various kinds of birds were made— parrots, starlings, mynas, cuckoos,
swans, peacocks, woodpeckers, water-fowls, pheasants, and pheasant-like birds; even oil-flasks were made as mechanical figures.
And various kinds of fruits and non-fruits are produced from the eight types of mechanical devices:
auspicious fruits, pomegranates, citron fruits, *vīrasenaka* fruits, grapevines, mangoes,
rose-apples, peepal trees, wood-apples, coconut palms, jackfruit trees, *kṣīrikā* trees, and *nīpa* trees.
And *kadamba* trees, and date-palm creepers;
in this way, various kinds of mechanical vessels are fashioned.
Then King Kuśa made such well-crafted, well-finished, and shapely mechanical vessels that all the machine-makers, upon seeing them, were struck with wonder, saying: "Oh,
what a fine master’s son, what a splendid craftsman, who makes such well-crafted, well-finished, and shapely vessels as these, the likes of which we have never seen before!"
And on all of them, King Kuśa inscribed his own name by way of a mere designation, so that Sudarśanā might know: "This is the work of Kuśa."
Then, when all the vessels had been completed by those artisans, they were presented to the king.
Then King Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, seeing those figures made of kuśa grass, was struck with wonder: "Aha!
What kind of mechanical dolls these are—so well-made, so perfectly finished, and so lifelike, crafted by the son of a master artisan!"
Then the king gave those articles into the hands of the eunuchs and chamberlains, saying:
"Go, enter the inner apartments; first give them to the Great Queen and to my daughter Sudarśanā, and afterwards give them to all the other queens and the women of the harem.
Then those eunuchs and chamberlains took the articles and entered the inner apartments; they presented them to the Great Queen and to her daughter Sudarśanā.

"O Queen, these eight vessels containing mechanical toys have been sent to you by the King. You and your daughter Sudarśanā should take them first according to your desire; afterwards they will be given to the other queens and to all the women of the harem."
Then Sudarśanā, seeing there that which was most beautiful, well-made, well-finished, and shapely, extended her hand toward it, thinking, "I shall take it," until she saw the name of Kuśa;
then this thought occurred to her:
"This is the work of Kuśa."
Then, having let that go, she took other ordinary ones.
Then Sudarśanā was addressed by her mother, by her sisters, by the women of the harem, and by the eunuchs and chamberlains.

"Sudarśanā, why are you so perverse? Why do you reject these well-made, well-finished, and beautifully shaped items crafted by the son of a master artisan, and instead take up other common objects made by inferior craftsmen?
Do they not all appear beautiful? Sudarśanā replied:
He said: "Enough for me with this; let this alone be mine."
Whatever secret was there, no one at all discovered it.
Thus, King Kuśa, having stayed with the mechanic, did not find his purpose;
thereupon, having departed from there, he approached the head of the reed-workers.

There, various kinds of royal bamboo wares were being made: fans, palm-leaf fans, umbrellas, umbrella-bearers, baskets, cane couches, cane frames, and cane chests— such various kinds of bamboo wares were being manufactured by royal command for the sake of the inner apartments.

There, King Kuśa, together with those reed-workers, fashioned various kinds of reed-articles for the harem such that not even a single one among all those reed-workers was able to make anything like them.
Then, at the time when all the reed vessels had been prepared exactly as commanded, they took those vessels and presented them to the king.
The king entrusted them into the hands of the eunuchs and chamberlains to be brought inside the inner apartments; first, they were presented to the chief queen and to Sudarśanā.
"Take these first, which have been sent by the king, according to your desires; afterwards, they shall be given to the entire harem."
Whatever was desired by the Mahādevī was taken; thus she is also called Sudarśanā.
"Take, O Aho Varuṭa, whatever vessels you desire."
Then, seeing those beautiful, magnificent, well-crafted, and noble articles of the reed-worker— which were worthy of a king,

causing great wonder among the people, and made by King Kuśa himself with his own name inscribed as a mark— she realized, "These were made by Kuśa," and having set them aside, she took other ordinary articles of the reed-worker. Then...
[Mvu 2.478] She was addressed by her mother, by her sisters, by the women of the inner apartments, and by the eunuchs and chamberlains:
"Sudarśanā, why do you discard these beautiful and magnificent varuṭa ornaments and take up others that are common?"
Then she said:
Let these be sufficient for me; I have had enough of them.
Whatever secret was there by which Sudarśanā did not take those royal vessels, and which they did not know—[that remained unknown].
Thus King Kuśa, having stayed there at the base of the reed-thicket as well, did not find his purpose.
Thereupon, he went out and entered the kitchen of Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, and approached the chief cook.
I too would have remained right here; I would have performed whatever task you commanded, for I am skilled in that work as well.
Then that chief cook stationed King Kuśa there in the kitchen and gave him this command:
"Perform your work here."

Then King Kuśa, in that royal kitchen during his royal duties, prepared such varieties of meats, condiments, vegetables, and foods— sour, salty, sweet, bitter, pungent, and astringent— as had never before been seen by anyone in all those royal kitchens, let alone prepared.

Furthermore, since King Mahendraka of the Madrakas was born, he had never before experienced such a flavor. Now, at the time when King Mahendraka was seated at the head of the meal, there were various kinds of meats, various kinds of side dishes, various kinds of vegetables, and various kinds of foods— noble and consisting of sour, salty, sweet, bitter, pungent, and astringent tastes.
King Mahendraka, while consuming those things which King Kuśa had mastered through his spiritual powers, was not satisfied.
Filled with wonder, the king asked the cook:
"O man, by which cook has my meal been prepared today?
For never since I was born have I tasted such a supreme flavor as this before on the tip of my tongue."
Then that chief cook, having joined his palms in reverence, made this request to the king.
"O Queen, another guest has arrived here and has set out for the kitchen;
by him, the meal for the Great King has been prepared."
Then it occurred to that king:
"That soup is skillfully prepared; it must be gathered together in various ways and cherished, so that it does not go anywhere."
Then the king addressed the chief cook.
"O, my man, bring that soup by which my meal today was completed; I will not eat until I have seen it."
Then, at the time when King Kuśa had sat down at the head of the meal, that chief cook presented him, saying, "This is that soup by which the food for the Great King was prepared."

Then Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, beheld King Kuśa—ugly to look at, ill-favored, with thick lips, a thick head and feet, a large belly, and black as a heap of soot; and having seen him, the king was struck with amazement: "Oh, how strange! One who is called 'Shobhana' (the Handsome) is actually of such a vulgar appearance, yet he possesses such a sense of taste, such a supreme appreciation of flavors!"
Then the king comforted him, saying,
"The livelihood provided for you is excellent, just as it has been arranged."
Having seated him in front of foods and drinks fit for a king, he was made to eat and drink, and a garland was bestowed upon him.
Then King Mahendra gave this command:
"Let this soup enter the royal palace through an open gate."
Thus, now, he dwelt in that royal household, honored and respected; he was dear to the king, and beloved, cherished, and pleasing to all the princes, the ministers, and the commanders of the army.
Then Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, addressed the eunuchs and the chamberlains.
"Friends, let this soup enter the inner apartments with confidence; let it become a source of play for the women of the harem."
Then King Kuśa entered the royal palace with full confidence; those women of the harem thought, "This one has been given to us by our king as a plaything.
Those women of the harem then played and sported with him confidently, mounting his back and riding him like various vehicles.
Then King Kuśa [was with] the women of the harem.
Being carried away by force, he was suddenly seen by Sudarśanā.

Then, upon seeing King Kuśa, Sudarśanā became frightened and terrified; she grew angry with those women of the harem, reviled them, and reproached them, saying, "Is it permissible for women to make a man carry them?"
Then those women of the harem said:
"Sudarśanā, why are you angry with us, wasting away and reviling us?
If we were to give this toy to him, and he were to become your husband, then you would be filled with jealousy."
Sudarśanā said:
"Let this jealousy of mine remain; however, you will not be able to drive him. I shall not be well-disposed toward whichever woman among you drives him."
Then Sudarśanā, seeing King Kuśa in the inner apartments, her facial complexion dejected and afflicted by grief, neither drew near to him nor uttered a word.
Then King Kuśa said:
O Sudarśanā, even here, having seen me, you are terrified.
Sudarśanā said:
"Why have you come here now? It would be a marvel if you had been seen coming by day or night; if you are not some forest *piśāca*, then you have not been killed by anyone.
Your kingdom is vast, your harem is vast; go to your own kingdom, play, enjoy yourself, and take your pleasure there. What will you do staying here?"
King Kuśa said:
"Sudarśanā, I will not go away without you;
the directions no longer appear clear to me, since it was from them that I came here."
Sudarśanā said:
What shall I do now, or whom shall I blame?
My heart trembles upon seeing him, like [the fear felt] toward a sea-rākṣasa.
What shall I do now, or whom shall I blame? My heart trembles upon seeing him, like a bewildered doe seeing a hunter.
Not reproaching him, [the king] followed him day and night as he went along, saying:
"Go back to your own kingdom, Kuśa; I do not desire you, who are so ill-favored."
The king said:
O large-eyed, dark-complexioned woman with beautiful hips and slender waist, I am indeed bewildered by your desires; I do not even aspire to the kingdom.
I will not go, O lady with well-rounded thighs;
I do not know the direction from which I have come. Confused in mind, I wander through the world.
I am intoxicated by sensual desires, O lady with eyes like those of a doe.
The goddess said:
This dissipation of your wealth— since you desire her who does not desire you, O King, since you lust after one who is unwilling— this is not the mark of a wise man.
Kuśa said:
Whether she is unwilling or willing, the man who obtains a beloved woman—there they praise the gain; there, lack of gain is considered evil.
The goddess said:
You are capable of delighting even a thousand women in a single night,
yet you undergo great suffering for the sake of one woman's desire.
The king said:
"I do not consider this to be suffering, O illustrious lady of beautiful complexion;
once my holy life has been well-practiced, you shall become my wife."
The goddess said:
"Shame on your religious life! Let this evil be yours:
in the next world, you shall desire either a female dog or a female jackal."
Kuśa said:
"Do not speak thus, O blessed lady, you of beautiful hips and slender waist;
we too are ascetics, and it is through holy conduct that we shine."
O noble lady, they too shine here because of their well-practiced conduct;
having been reborn in the heavens among the Thirty-three gods, they enjoy all their desires.
Therefore, O blessed lady, O fair-hipped one of slender waist, I tell you this: Kuśa, who possesses the voice of a lion, is your only husband; there is no other.
The goddess said:
If this speech of the fortune-teller should prove true, I will not be your wife; cut me into pieces as you wish.
The king said:
"I do not wish to cut you, O lady of beautiful hips and slender waist;
remaining uncut, O blessed one, you shall become my wife."
And my kingdom is great, with many horses and many men;
it is infinitely manifold, with abundant clothing and food.
Thus, having abandoned both my kingdom and my realm, I have come here;
deluded by desire for you, I do not even aspire to the kingdom.
The goddess said:
You dig a well in stone and seek an earring from a non-eared one; you attempt to bind the wind with a net—desiring that which does not desire you.
"You desire me though I do not desire you; you seek me though I am unwilling.
Go back to your own kingdom; why do you weary yourself?"
The king said:
"This is no hardship for me; this is my holy life (brahmacarya). But hereafter, O blessed lady, you shall indeed become my wife."
The goddess said:
Let this evil celibacy you have undertaken be yours;
instead, I seek after a female dog, a female jackal, or even a female donkey.
Then that heroic prince Kuśa, who was peerless in battle and possessed of ascended wisdom, spoke these words:
"If I were going, O blessed lady, with beautiful hips and slender waist, I would bind you with fetters; what could your kinsmen do for you?"
The goddess said:
That very same Dharma which was previously generated by you is now for another purpose.
I am mindful of that very same Dharma which you wish to bind me to.
The king said:
"I am able to adorn you, O blessed lady, O mistress of the household; once adorned, you may go wherever you wish. What will your father do?"
"I am able to delight even a thousand women in a single night;
you alone, O blessed one, O lady of pure teeth, O mistress of my household, are my choice."
The goddess said:
I know you, O Great King, that you are powerful, a bull among men;
yet you are ill-favored, difficult to look upon, and unpleasant to the touch, O Lord of the Earth.
With thick lips, a thick head, thick limbs, and a large belly, I do not wish to see you; do not weary yourself.
These high-walled enclosures, with their watchtowers and parapets,
will ward off those who would otherwise advance with elephants.
O Lord of Creatures, these men fight with spears, javelins, and arrows, and with very sharp swords; may they obtain you.
Thus, King Kuśa now conversed with Sudarśanā in various ways, one with the other;
yet no one knew that this was King Kuśa.
Now, the neighboring rival kings— those of great renown, great power, and great armies—
heard that Sudarśanā, the daughter of Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, who was gracious and beautiful to behold, had fled from King Kuśa and come into her father’s presence;
and that King Kuśa did not find her pleasing as a wife because she was so exceedingly beautiful.
Then those seven kings, having equipped a fourfold army—consisting of elephant corps, cavalry, chariot corps, and infantry—assembled for the sake of Sudarśanā.
Now, among those seven kings, the one who was the most noble of all was the king named Durmati; he was the strongest and the most illustrious of those seven kings.
Then all those seven kings, with great prosperity and great splendor, set out and in due course arrived at the park of Kanyakubja.
Then Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, dispatched a messenger to each of those seven kings, saying:
"This daughter of mine, Sudarśanā, is the wife of King Kuśa; therefore, she cannot be given by me to anyone else."

Then those seven kings, having heard the reply of Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, became enraged and incensed; they surrounded the city of Kanyakubja on all sides with their respective armies and took up their positions.
King Mahendraka, having entered the city and bolted the gates, remained shut inside.
Then this thought occurred to Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas:

"I am indeed besieged and held captive by these seven kings; all of them are renowned for their great power and strength, and I am not capable of giving them battle. Even if I give my daughter to one of them, the other six kings will be hostile toward me. What shall I do now?"
Then King Mahendraka, enraged at his daughter Sudarśanā, rebuked her.
"From whose master have you fled to come here, that for your sake I am confined and held captive by seven kings?
If anyone among these seven should cause me harm, then I will cut you into seven pieces and give one piece to each of those seven kings."
Then, having heard her father’s words, Sudarśanā became afraid, terrified, and filled with suffering and dejection; she addressed her mother.

"Mother, when these seven kṣatriyas, having become hostile toward one another, shall cause each other to be slain, then, having reduced them to ashes and gathered their bones, you must have a memorial mound (elūkā) erected for me.
And at the entrance of that mound, you must have a karṇikāra tree planted."
Then, after the passing of the summer and when the first month of the rainy season was occurring, that karṇikāra tree became fully blossomed, with a color like the luster of gold.
Then you will remember:
"My daughter Sudarśanā was such in her complexion."
Then that great queen, having heard the words of her daughter Sudarśanā, became afraid, terrified, and filled with suffering and dejection; with a choked throat and a weeping face, she said:
"How will there be separation from my daughter?"
Then it occurred to Sudarśanā:
"Since King Kuśa is endowed with such vigor, strength, and prowess, these seven kings are not capable of giving battle to Kuśa.
What if I were to seek my life from King Kuśa?"
Then Sudarśanā approached King Kuśa and performed various kinds of flattering gestures and spoke to him.
"Great King, my father threatens me thus: 'If these seven kings should cause you any harm, then I shall cut you into seven pieces and give one piece to each of these seven kings.'"
Then King Kuśa spoke to Sudarśanā in many ways.
If I were to desire you, I would show you great disrespect; what then would you do to me?

Thus King Kuśa sat conversing with Sudarśanā. When Sudarśanā’s mother heard this, and having heard it, she looked again at King Kuśa and thought: "Who is this? Where has he come from? Is he a bamboo-worker, a fowler, a leather-worker, a barber, an outcaste, or a *pukkasa*—he who [dares to take] my daughter?"
He reviles and threatens him.
Then Sudarśanā, having placed her hands in anjali before her mother, said:
"Mother, do not speak thus! This is certainly neither a bamboo-worker, nor a potter, nor a slave, nor a leather-worker.
He is named Kuśa, the eldest son of King Ikṣvāku and of his five hundred princes; Mother, do not think of him as a slave."
Resembling a white conch shell and attended by throngs of women,
you consider this prosperous kshatriya clan to be merely your slave.
Amidst a family of Kṣatriyas, flourishing and filled with throngs of women adorned with golden vessels, you indeed consider yourself a slave.
There are sixty thousand cities—prosperous, flourishing, and free from thorns—and a wealthy kṣatriya clan; yet you consider yourself a slave!
Sixty thousand elephants emerged, adorned with golden ornaments,
covered in gold, and possessing tusks as long as plowshafts.
Mounted by village chiefs with swords and spears in their hands,
you consider yourself a slave to this prosperous family of kṣatriyas.
There were sixty thousand chariots adorned with the sound of joy,
made of iron, well-fastened, and covered with leopard skins.
Mounted by village leaders with bows in hand and clad in armor—
[you who belong to] a prosperous kṣatriya clan— you indeed consider yourself a slave!
Sixty thousand thoroughbred horses, the best of steeds,
wearing golden girths and possessing bits made of jewels.
Mounted by village chiefs, armed with nooses and clad in armor—
though you belong to a prosperous kṣatriya family, you surely consider yourself a slave.
Ten thousand brahmins constantly eat at the king's house,
whether by day or by night, always treated with hospitality and honored;
yet you consider the family of this kshatriya to be prosperous and think of yourself as a slave.
Five hundred princes are your maternal and paternal kinsmen;
the kshatriya family is prosperous, yet you consider yourself a slave.
There were sixty thousand treasuries belonging to his father and his grandfather...
where the king named Kuśa, a lord of men, resided;
by virtue of his complexion and prowess, there was no one equal to him in the world.
Then, having heard these words from Sudarśanā’s mother, the Great Queen became filled with joy.
Such is my son-in-law, endowed with all virtues.
Then Sudarśanā’s mother, having heard her daughter’s words, informed Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas.
"O Great King, you should know that your son-in-law, King Kuśa, has arrived here."
Then the king, having heard the queen's words, became afraid, terrified, and agitated, with the hairs on his body standing on end.
The king said:
"O Queen, have you perhaps gone mad, or are you distracted in mind, that you speak thus, saying 'King Kuśa has arrived here'?
What is King Kuśa like, or where have you seen King Kuśa?"
The goddess said:
"Great King, I am neither mad nor deranged; rather, this is your son-in-law, King Kuśa, who cooks food for you in the kitchen and provides entertainment for those in your inner apartments."
Then the king, having heard this, became even more terrified and agitated, and was overcome by suffering and dejection.
"It is not that suffering which the seven kings inflict upon me by holding me captive that I consider such; rather, it is this suffering:
that the Great King Kuśa will come here out of anger toward Sudarśanā, and in his wrath at my being held against my will, he will cause some harm within the inner city."
Then King Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, terrified and trembling, entered his own inner apartments;
joining his palms toward King Kuśa, he asked for forgiveness, saying:
"Forgive me, Great King, for whatever offense I have committed against you."
Then King Kuśa comforted his father-in-law:
"Do not fear, Great King; there is nothing for which I must ask your forgiveness."

Then King Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, having ushered King Kuśa into the bathhouse for a moment, had his hair and beard trimmed by barbers; he was anointed with hundred-fold refined fragrant oils, bathed with royal bathing powders, smeared with royal unguents, and arrayed in royal garments and ornaments.
Adorned with ornaments, he sat upon a single seat together with his father-in-law,
and was served by a fivefold musical ensemble.
Now, the loud, great, and tumultuous roar of the military forces of those seven kings was heard.
Then King Kuśa asked his father-in-law:
"Great King, whose sound is this great clamor of a multitude of people that is heard?"
The king said:
"Seven kings have surrounded this city on all sides for the sake of Sudarśanā, and I am being held captive as their prisoner.
This was the report concerning the military force of those kings.
Then King Kuśa persuaded his father-in-law.
"Do not fear, Great King; I shall act in such a way that these seven kings will bow down and become obedient to your word."
Then King Kuśa addressed his father-in-law.

"Great King, have all these illustrious elephant-kings, all the horses, all the quadrupeds, and the entire multitude of people plug their ears with beeswax, lest they break their own army upon hearing my lion’s roar."
Then King Kuśa, having mounted a magnificent state elephant and accompanied by a great multitude of people, caused the city gate to be thrown open and rushed out.
King Kuśa let out a lion’s roar.
As he let out that lion’s roar, all seven kings, together with their armies and their mounts, were broken;
having captured them alive and bound them firmly by the back of the neck with their arms behind their backs, they were handed over to his father-in-law, Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas.
These are those great kings; all those seven kings prostrated themselves before Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas.
Victory to the Great King! We have come for refuge to the Great King; we shall be those who carry out your commands at the mere word.
Then Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, asked his son-in-law Kuśa:
"Son, what do these seven kings please you? What shall we do?
We will do exactly as you command."
King Kuśa said:

"Great King, you have many daughters in your harem, and all of them must certainly be given to husbands. Moreover, these seven kings are all Kṣatriyas of great strength, great vehicles, great fortune, and vast kingdoms.
Therefore, Great King, having adorned seven of your daughters with a thousand pieces of gold, give one daughter to each of these Kṣatriya kings."
"And these seven kings shall become your sons-in-law, and they shall be your powerful allies.

All those neighboring kings—being of great strength, with great vehicles, and great retinues—will bow down to you and follow your lead; no rival king whatsoever will oppose you," said Mahendraka, the King of the Madrakas.
"Son, he will certainly do exactly as you have commanded."

Then Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, having adorned each of those seven daughters individually with gold and having adorned each one with a thousand pieces of gold, gave one daughter to each of the kings; and with great royal majesty and great royal power, he established an alliance through sons and grandsons.
Then those seven kings were sent back to their respective kingdoms by Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, with great hospitality and honor.
"Go, sirs, and cause each your own kingdom to be governed."
[Mvu 2.491] Now, after King Kuśa had stayed for some time once those kings had been dismissed, he addressed his father-in-law, Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas:
"Great King, I take my leave; I too shall go to my own realm."
Mahendra, the king of the Madrakas, said:
"Son, do not go! My life has been given to you; my entire kingdom has been saved from peril.
I am worn out, aged, decrepit, and my youth has passed.
I am the father and you are the son; you must rule the kingdom—do not go!"
King Kuśa said:
"Great King, it has been a long time since I arrived; my kingdom is unsettled, and my mother will be filled with longing. I take my leave; I am going."
Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, said:
You must certainly go.
King Kuśa said:
"Great King, I must certainly go."
Then Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, summoned his daughter Sudarśanā and gave her these instructions:

"Daughter, your husband King Kuśa is endowed with such valor, so great in strength and majesty, that he has delivered both you, me, and the entire kingdom from peril. O daughter Sudarśanā, you ought to serve King Kuśa as your husband with love and reverence."
Then Sudarśanā, having joined her palms and responded "So be it" to her father’s words,
King Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, gave his daughter Sudarśanā to King Kuśa with great honor and a grand assembly,
accompanied by a fourfold army consisting of elephant corps, cavalry, chariot corps, and infantry.
"You have been dismissed from your own kingdom; go, my son, to your own kingdom."
Then King Kuśa, while traveling to his own kingdom, stayed in a grove on the outskirts of a city that had gardens; there was a great lotus pond there.
While bathing in that lotus pond, King Kuśa saw his own reflection in the water, which was so ill-colored, hideous, and unattractive.
Having seen it, his own body having become unpleasant to him, he spoke as follows:

"Or rather, this is the place where Sudarśanā, the daughter of Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, despises me on account of my misshapen form, my ugly complexion, and my hideous appearance; what if I were now to take my own life?"
Now, he desired to kill himself by means of self-inflicted violence.
Śakra, the lord of the gods, took note of King Kuśa’s state of mind in the realm of the Thirty-three, seeing that he desired to take his own life through fasting.
It occurred to Śakra:
"This King Kuśa is a Bodhisattva who has set out for the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings.
Thinking that he is ill-favored and unpleasant to behold, people will not wish to approach him; thus he will perish, and there will be calamity for the whole world."
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, taking a divine jewel-gem named Jyotīrasa from the midst of a single-strand necklace of divine red pearls, stood in the sky, in the air,
and addressed King Kuśa:
"Great King, do not harm yourself; rather, bind this single-string necklace containing the *jyotīrasa* gem upon your head.
Then, with it bound, no man in all Jambudvīpa will be your equal in complexion or form.
Furthermore, if you wish to assume your former complexion and form, then cover that *jyotīrasa* gem in the single-string necklace with a cloth; then your former complexion and form will return."
Then King Kuśa, having bathed there in the lotus pond, having anointed himself with ointments, and having put on robes worthy of a king, fastened that single-string necklace upon his head.
Then, in that lotus lake, he gazed at his own face until he realized there was some distinction.
As he examined himself, he saw that he was handsome and beautiful to behold, such that no man in Jambudvīpa had ever before been seen with such complexion and form.
Having seen himself thus possessed of such noble appearance, King Kuśa became joyful and delighted in heart.
No longer will Sudarśanā, the daughter of Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, treat me with contempt, nor any other person of poor complexion, thinking me to be such.
Then King Kuśa, standing at his own gate, thought, "I shall enter. Thereupon, he was stopped by the gatekeepers: "Who are you, man, who wishes to assault the royal palace?"
"You do not know that King Kuśa is difficult to approach and hard to withstand; do not fall into calamity and ruin this very moment!"
Then King Kuśa said:
I am your master; I am your king, Kuśa.
The gatekeepers said:
"O King, do we not recognize Kuśa, such as King Kuśa is?

May it be well! If King Kuśa were to become like this, then we would be favored with the highest favor; and the entire kingdom and the Ikṣvāku clan would be graced by a king so pleasing, handsome, and endowed with such supreme beauty and form."
Then it occurred to King Kuśa:
"He does not recognize me."
Then King Kuśa covered his single-string necklace of jyotīrasa gems with his own garment;
when the gatekeeper saw King Kuśa in his true form, he was terrified and trembling and prostrated himself before him.
"Great King, we do not know; you yourself, Great King, must know."
Then King Kuśa, having entered the royal palace, approached the queen;
but she warded him off.

"Who are you, man, and from where do you come, you who wish to violate the royal palace? You do not know that King Kuśa’s inner apartments are difficult to approach. Do not violate the royal palace; do not fall into misfortune and ruin."
Then King Kuśa said:
"O Queen, I am your husband; I am King Kuśa; know this!"
Then that queen said:
"You are not my husband, nor are you King Kuśa; or rather, do I not know what King Kuśa is like in complexion and form?
May it be well! If King Kuśa were such as this in complexion and form, then I would be favored with the highest favor."
Then King Kuśa covered that single-string necklace with the jyotīrasa gem with a cloth, and immediately his complexion and form returned to how they were before.
Then Sudarśanā said:
"Great King, why did you show this illusionist to me?"
King Kuśa said:
"O Queen, this man is no magician; rather, I was intending to kill myself by my own hand.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, gave me this single-stringed necklace and this *jyotīrasa* gem."
"Great King, do not destroy yourself! Instead, bind this single-string necklace of *jyotīratna* gems upon your head; then no other man in all of Jambudvīpa will be your equal in complexion and form.
If you wish to regain your former complexion and form, then have that single-string necklace of *jyotīrasa* gems covered with a cloth, and your former complexion and form will return.
This was a favor granted to me by Śakra, the lord of the gods."
Then Queen Sudarśanā said:
I have been favored by Śakra, the lord of the gods, by whom such a complexion and form as yours has been created.
The goddess said:
"Great King, never cover this single-string necklace of jyotīrasa gems; at all times let it remain for you in such a noble form.
You shall become even more delightful to the entire kingdom and to the whole body of people."
Thus, King Kuśa now travels along the road with such a complexion and form that he resembles a son of the gods.
Then, in Vārāṇasī, the four hundred and ninety-nine princes, all the ministers, and the entire vanguard of the army heard that King Kuśa was coming;
they all went out to meet King Kuśa.
King Kuśa also arrived, mounted upon the back of a noble elephant and surrounded by a fourfold army.
Then those princes and the elite of the army did not recognize King Kuśa;
they then questioned one another.

"Who might this king be who is so handsome, beautiful to behold, and of great majesty, coming along on the back of a noble elephant with such sublime complexion and form? Even King Kuśa is not to be seen."
It occurred to King Kuśa:
"These do not recognize me."
Then King Kuśa, while seated upon the back of his excellent elephant, covered the single-stringed *jyotīrasa* gem with his hand;
immediately, its color and form returned to how they were before.

Then those four hundred and ninety-nine princes, the ministers, and the army commanders, seeing King Kuśa’s own physical form and appearance, became afraid and terrified; they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and said to the king:
"Victory to you, Great King! We do not know, Great King, who this is."
Then King Kuśa informed his brothers, the ministers, and the army commanders of this matter:
"Sirs, Śakra, the lord of the gods, gave me this single-string necklace and a *jyotīrasa* gem; bind these upon your heads, and then no other man will be your equal in complexion and form.
Then those princes, the ministers, and the army commanders spoke thus to the king:
"We have been favored by Śakra, the lord of the gods, since such a complexion and form as this has come upon the Great King."
Thus, now King Kuśa, having arrived at Vārāṇasī with great royal majesty and great royal power, entered the royal palace;
and with his noble complexion and form, having saluted the Great Queen Alindā and bowed at her feet, he stood before her.
Then Queen Alindā did not recognize King Kuśa;
she asked, "Where is my son? Where is King Kuśa?"
King Kuśa said:
"O Ambā, I am your son; I am King Kuśa."
The Great Queen said:
"You are not my son; you are not King Kuśa.
"O King, do I not recognize King Kuśa?
Has King Kuśa been struck down or killed by someone, that he is not seen?"
Alas, what a death without a protector is this for me, that separation from my only son has come to pass!
Then the king, seeing his mother lamenting, covered that single-string necklace of jyotīrasa gems with his garment, and her complexion and form were restored to how they were before.
Then Queen Alindā, seeing her son with his own complexion and form, became joyful in mind and questioned that son.
"My son, by what means has such a complexion and form come to be yours?"
King Kuśa said:
"Mother, Śakra, the lord of the gods, gave me a single-string necklace with a *jyotīrasa* gem;
having fastened it on myself, my complexion and form have become like this."
Then Queen Alindā became joyful, filled with gladness and happiness, thinking:
"I have seen my son with such noble complexion and form, just as I had desired.
And all the women of the inner court, having seen such noble complexion and form of King Kuśa, became joyful, filled with gladness and happiness.

Now, whenever King Kuśa fastens that single-string necklace containing the *jyotīrasa* gem— which had been given by Śakra, the lord of the gods— a divine radiance proceeds from it; and whenever he covers that jewel with his hand, it returns to its former color and appearance.
Thus, King Kuśa, having defeated his adversaries and eliminated his enemies, now ruled the kingdom in Vārāṇasī with noble enjoyments and luxuries.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke this verse before the fourfold assembly and the great multitude of people:
Thus, for one possessing merit, all matters become favorable,
just as King Kuśa was reunited with his wife and kinsmen.

"O monks, it might occur to you that the king named Kuśa at that time and on that occasion was someone else; however, it should not be viewed in this way. At that time and on that occasion, I myself was the king Kuśa."
"That Mahendraka, the king of the Madrakas, was someone else"—
it should not be viewed in this way;
he was this very Śākya, Mahānāman.
That great queen named Alindā was another;
it should not be viewed in this way,
for she is Queen Māyā.
That Sudarśanā was someone else;
it should not be viewed in this way.
This is that Yaśodharā.
"Monks,
it might occur to you that at that time and on that occasion, the eldest among those seven kings named Durmati was someone else.
It should not be viewed in this way."
This is that Māra, the Evil One;
those other kings were also the retinue of Māra.

Even then, by the sound of my clearing my throat, this Māra, the Evil One, together with his army and his mounts, was defeated; and now too, monks, at the foot of the Bodhi tree, by the sound of my clearing my throat, this Māra, the Evil One—
He, together with his army and his mounts, was defeated.
In Vārāṇasī there was a king of the Ikṣvāku lineage, possessed of great power, great fame, and victorious; yet no son was born to him.
At that time, a thought occurred to him, who possessed great supernatural power:
"What if I were to release my women's quarters every three fortnights?"
On the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and up to the eighth day of the fortnight,
that lord of men would enter the women's quarters for the sake of offspring.
With joyful intentions and adorned with all their ornaments,
they approached every door like terrified does.
One woman entices while prattling, another laughs,
and yet another runs about, chasing after this and that.
All were shaken; all were overcome by fainting.
The city of King Ikṣvāku was rendered unconscious by the wives of the king. ...
At whatever time, whether the right or wrong hour, the brahmin would come into my presence.
Inform me quickly whether there might be a petitioner; for where a gift is given to a petitioner, it yields great fruit.
Then Śakra, the lord of the Thirty-three, reflected.
"O domestic priest, this is the task which the king wishes to perform."
And having become old and broken, leaning upon a staff with trembling limbs, he approached the king's gate.
Then the brahmin spoke thus to the messenger who was traveling there.
Inform him quickly; I wish to see the lord of men.
Then the messenger, the attendant, said this to the king:
"A brahmin has arrived at Your Majesty's presence and desires to see the king."
Welcome to you, Great Brahmā; you are most welcome. What do you desire? Seeking what? For what purpose have you come? What may I give to you?
"I have heard this being spoken here by the people of the Ikṣvāku clan:
'The king, the lord of men, empties his inner apartments every three fortnights.'"
On the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and up to the eighth day of the fortnight, the best of men who desires a son should practice; thus have I heard it spoken.
Having heard that sound, my senses thrilled and gladdened, I would go here seeking a woman; therefore, let him be a match for me.
The king said:
"Come quickly, chamberlain! Show me the women swiftly; whichever one you have in mind, show her to me today as a favor."
Then the chamberlain led the brahmin into that inner apartment.
Then his queen, Aliṇḍā, was told this.
The brahmin said:
Let this very woman be mine, she who stands there so proud,
standing with her faultless limbs, drenching her face with tears.
Kubjaka said:
"O Elder, do you desire to be attended by young women,
yet not a single young woman has even touched you with her hand?"
"Do you, O Elder, desire to be attended by young women?
Yet not a single young woman has even touched you with her foot."
Foul-smelling, with wrinkled skin and a gray-haired face, you dwell like a stinking jujube flower; like a goat reeking of odor, depart, for I have no need of you!
The king said:
"I will give you a livelihood, or wealth, or grain, or excellent villages;
enjoy that very thing now! What will you do with Alindā?"
The brahmin said:
"I am coughing and fainting, and I lose consciousness again and again;
I urinate upon my own bed—she will lift me up."
"Be silent, O hunchback; grind the cosmetic powder.
I am dear to Alindā; do not pay her any mind."
"Be silent, O hunchback! You hide even your garland.
I am dear to Alindā; you do not even take me into account."
The king said:
"O Brāhmaṇa, if you wish to eat alms-food in the royal palace, then eat that very food now; what will you do with Alindā?"
The brahmin said:
O King Ikṣvāku, do not regret what has been given! If you had chosen something else as a favor, you would later regret it. I bid you farewell and depart; since you do not grant what was invited.
The king said:
I do not regret my actions, O Brahmā; may you instead become Tuṣita once more, and let all these women, together with Aliṇḍā, attend upon you.
"And I give this low-caste hunchbacked woman to you for sexual pleasure;
let her be your slave, take her wherever you wish."
The hunchbacked woman said:
"I would rather eat poison and die, O Lord, if you would grant me this:
I shall kill this old man with broken limbs while he is alone in private."
The brahmin said:
I have enmity with all hunchbacks whatsoever who dwell upon the earth,
since this low-caste hunchback here desires to harm me.
The king said:
O Brahmin, we are the upholders of the Dharma for all living beings;
go away, do not revile me, and do not engage in quarreling with me.
O Brāhmaṇa, one who is dead, one who is decrepit, one who is ruined, and one who dwells with his teacher—
these are as disagreeable in this world as an enraged black serpent.
"If you, O brahmin, wish to eat alms-food even in the royal palace, then eat it there, O brahmin; what will you do with Alindā?
The brahmin said:
O Ikṣvāku, do not now choose a boon for us that you will later regret after having offered it to a woman.
I bid you farewell as I depart; having given, O King, do not regret it, you who, after being entreated by my wives, have rendered my request false.
The king said:
I do not regret my Brahminhood; become young again!
Let all these women, together with Aliṃdā, attend upon you.
"O auspicious one, O brahmin, enjoy this woman as long as you wish;
lie down upon this prepared bed, and she shall be subject to your will."
Taking her by the hand— she who possessed beautiful hips and a slender waist—
he emerged from the palace gate as she wept with a tearful face and a choked throat.
Having departed from the royal palace, a hut was constructed along the wall;
Śakra said:
"Having put on fine garments, come, O blessed lady, let us enjoy ourselves."
Turn toward me; do not turn away.
Rejoice with me with great joy; I am one who delights in you.
"Laughing, delight me; you have won the boon that I am delighted by you. Come, noble lady, delight me; you have won the boon that I am delighted by you."
"Rise up without weariness! I have been honored in the inner chamber;
go and inform the king: 'Be glad, for I have won!'"
Śakra, having caused that brahmin disguise to disappear, stood there in his own form.
Having remained there, illuminating all directions with his radiance,
Āliṃdā saw him and a state of mental confusion arose.
Then she was invited by Śakra to choose a boon;
she chose a son, saying, "Grant me the boon of a son. Śakra said:
"I am Śakra, the lord of the gods and sovereign of the Thirty-three;
choose a boon, O auspicious lady, whatever you desire in your heart."
The goddess said:
If Śakra, the lord of the Thirty-three, would grant me a boon, I request this boon:
a son; O Śakra, grant me this boon.
Śakra said:
If, with a well-disposed mind, you delight me in this chamber, may a son be born to me upon my request— one of noble birth who shall increase the kingdom.
A son shall be born to you, Siṃhabāhu, who is very strong, beautiful in complexion and form, well-born, and the enhancer of the kingdom.
That powerful and wicked one will be known as Siṃhāsuptapīḍa;
he will be called Kuśasamajña and Saprajñāna, and he will crush the kingdoms of others.
Śakra gave a medicinal pill to the queen, saying:
"Having rubbed this with your tongue, taste it with the tip of your tongue; then you will have a son."
Then that queen, having tied those medicinal pills into the corner of her silken garment, went to the royal palace;
having arrived, she informed the king.

"That was Śakra, the lord of the gods; he came in the guise of a brahmin and was well-honored by me. He gave me this medicinal pill, saying, 'Having rubbed it on your tongue, you shall taste its flavor; from that, a son will be born to you. " The king said:
Your facial complexion is serene, and you look upon us with a smile;
indeed, such perfection of complexion exists for the sake of the supreme goal.
The goddess said:
"O Great King, Indra has granted me a son who is possessed of great strength,
powerful like a lion, mighty, and a crusher of enemy kingdoms."
The king, enraged, said:
Having seized her by the throat, destroy her, for she has been defeated by me;
I do not wish even to look upon her who defies my command.
He then removed one pill and gave it to those four hundred and ninety-nine queens;
she alone did not receive one, [thinking], "A deformed son will be born to her."
She asks, "Where was that pill ground?
Here, in this mortar."
Then, having moistened it with water, she tasted a tiny fragment of the pill with the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass.

In this way, all five hundred queens conceived in their wombs; after the lapse of nine or ten months, all five hundred queens gave birth, and five hundred handsome princes were born. Eventually, when Ikṣvāku had passed away, Kuśa obtained the kingdom.
Then Kuśa spoke thus to his mother and his ministers.
Bring my wife, the chief queen.
His mother said to him.
"Who will give you a suitable wife for your wickedness? I shall bring you a wicked woman."
"O mother, if you bring a wicked woman to be my wife,
I shall not even touch that wicked wife with my hand."
O mother, you wish to bring back my wicked wife.
I would not even touch your wicked wife with my foot.
Aliṇḍā said:
O dear son, living together is happy when both possess identical characteristics;
when both are of equal status, neither reviles the other.
The virtuous woman feels contempt upon seeing her husband as wicked;
indeed, my son, it would have been better for you to have had a wicked wife, for you yourself are wicked.
The king said:
I have neither heard nor seen that kings are unfortunate,
nor that the bull among men consorts with wicked women.
"I am a king, a Kṣatriya, a conqueror, and possessed of great strength; I have abundant treasuries and power. For women indeed desire wealth."
Women adorned with every ornament, purchased with wealth, are brought from foreign kingdoms to those whose father’s home is far away.
He brought home as his wife the daughter of the King of Madra,
Prajāpatī, who was endowed with all proper conduct and possessed of all auspicious bodily marks.
Then that girl was addressed by her mother-in-law.
"In our Ikṣvāku lineage, it is the law that for twelve years a husband must not be seen [by his wife]."
Now, no lamps were burning in their sleeping quarters.
Sudarśanā said to King Kuśa:
This royal palace is prosperous, a mine of endless jewels;
yet, whether by day or by night, we find no lamp.
We do not see one another at all, by night or by day; seeing no one else, we remain here in solitude.
Here we dwell in a gathering of darkness, in the midst of gloom;
to me, this dwelling seems like the company of the blind.
The king said:
"I do not know this; what is its meaning, or for whom is it intended?
Go and ask my mother; she will explain it to you."
Then, when the night had turned to dawn, she bowed at her mother-in-law's feet and said:
This royal palace is prosperous, an inexhaustible mine of various jewels;
yet, whether by day or by night, we find no lamp here.
Neither by night nor by day did we see one another;
not seeing each other, we remained there in seclusion.
[Here we dwell together in this gathering of darkness, in the gloom;
like the dwelling of the blind, so does this appear to us.]
The mother-in-law said:
O Prajāpati, when you shall see your son after twelve years,
then, O gods, you shall see one another through my prayer.
Sudarśanā said:
O Noble One, it is an evil thing that the gods have granted this boon:
that for a long time we shall not see one another’s company again.
A sense of curiosity arose in the queen to see the king.
She then made a request to her mother-in-law.
She said to her mothers-in-law:
"Daughter, an audience with you has been granted for tomorrow; go and see him."
The *kuśa* tree from the veranda was made into a king and seated upon the royal throne;
Kuśa himself held the parasol, while the princes, ministers, and the people of the towns and countryside sat down each upon their own respective seats.
O King, having seen Sudarśanā and the entire assembly, [the king] was pleased; but seeing the bearer of the parasol, his mind became averse.
Then Sudarśanā said to her mother-in-law:

"The king is handsome, the princes are handsome, and the assembly is handsome; yet the parasol-bearer is not visible. Because of this, the splendor of that entire assembly, including the king, is marred. If this parasol-bearer were not seen here, then this assembly, together with the king, would be truly beautiful."
The mother-in-law said this to her.
"Do not speak thus, daughter! You do not know the greatness of this umbrella-bearer.
He is high-souled, he is of great strength, he is virtuous, and he is very wealthy; it is through his power that we are all happy."
Then, having gone to her bed, she said to the king:
Surely you do not find another umbrella-bearer in this world such as this one of yours, O King— shameless and lacking in modesty.
The king said:
Is it because of his beauty, O beautiful one, or is it because he is so very powerful that he is pleasing to us?
"O beautiful one, is it because of his beauty, or is it because he possesses great wealth?
It is precisely because he is so wealthy that he is pleasing to us."
"O beautiful one, what indeed does beauty matter? Moreover, he might even be a hero.
Considering him to be a hero, he is truly pleasing to us."
"O beautiful one, what indeed matters his appearance? Moreover, he is of virtuous conduct;
it is because he is of virtuous conduct that he is pleasing to us."
"O beautiful one, what indeed is his form, and why does he have such a great voice?
By his power alone do we all continue to live."
He is my friend of happiness and my companion, dear to me as my own life;
were I separated from him, neither of us would exist.
Then the queen and the entire female retinue went to see the lotus pond.
There, the king, by his very nature, had descended into the lotus pond and was sitting there. As soon as the queen had descended, she was seized by him;
the queen knew that he was a water-rākṣasa.
"She has been taken."
The women of the inner apartments also released a rain of flowers. The king said:
The queen went to the garden to look at the lotuses in the pond; she did not bring me any lotuses. Surely, my dear, you are not dear to me.
The goddess said:
"O King, I went to the park to bathe in the water of the lotus pond;
there I saw a piśāca, and I fell down in a deep swoon."
He who holds the parasol for you and he who was born in the lotus grove— I believe they were both born of the same woman, for such is his characteristic mark.
And at a later time, the queen went out with the ladies of the inner apartments to visit a mango grove.
The king, by his very nature, went to a mango grove and remained in that mango garden.
There, he seized the goddess Aṇvantī.
The queen knew she had been seized by the forest-rākṣasa;
the women of the inner apartments also released a rain of flowers.
In the bedchamber, the king said to the queen:
"O Queen, you went to the flourishing mango grove to look at it; yet you did not bring me any mangoes. Surely, my dear, you are no longer dear to me."
The goddess said:
"O King, while we were going to inspect the flourishing mango grove, we saw a piśāca there; we fainted and fell down violently."
I think that he who holds your parasol was born of the same mother as he who was in the lotus grove and he who was in the mango grove.
Now the elephant stable was set ablaze;
the king himself, having girt his loins, released the elephants,
cut their bonds with a sword, and cast the door-panels outward.
King Nārāyaṇasaṃghaṭana, by his strength, seized an elephant with his hand and hurled it; having been released from its trunk, Dīptakā was set free.
The women of the harem were speaking in praise of the king,
saying, "Oh, how great is the king's prowess!
Then, a certain hunchbacked woman also spoke in praise of the king.
Powerful, beautiful, vast, and great,
he shines like the full moon in the sky, radiant on all sides.
With eyes as copper-red as those of a cakora bird, he shines like the god of love;
the king, a bull among men endowed with great power, has set the elephants free.
The king said:
"This hunchback who praises the king is indeed fortunate;
I shall give you four garments from Kāśī."
Seeing the king, Mahendraka’s daughter was distressed;
she grieved, thinking, "This is indeed my husband, and he is of such a form."
The daughter of the king of Madra said:
There is no one who can cut out the tongue of this hunchback,
even with a very sharp weapon, as she praises the king.
The hunchbacked woman said:
Kings threaten with both imprisonment and execution;
therefore, I speak in praise of this [virtue] so that one may protect one's own life.
The goddess said:
I do not see, nor shall I see; what is the purpose of my life?
This very day I shall depart, before my vital breaths abandon me.
Then that queen, the daughter of the King of Madra, being angry,
went by carriage with her hunchbacked companion to her own family home.
The mother too, broken by grief for her son like a palm tree, fell to the ground;
she was like the trunk of a *sāla* tree cut down by an axe.
Thus, filled with grief for her son, she fell upon the earth.
The king, distressed by grief for his wife and desiring to go in search of her, was met by his mother, who was also sorrowful; she addressed King Kuśa with this verse:
"Alas! For me, so unfortunate, a great gain has been brought to my family:
the daughter of Mahendra has come here from five hundred yojanas away."
The people of that land always subsist on parched grain and are constantly clad in woolen blankets.
Eating coarse food and performing coarse labor, how will you travel the path?
The king said:
Or, through a hundred illusions of the mind— such as dancing, singing, instrumental music, and play—
I shall provide for my own livelihood by means of various such expedients.
The king, having established his brother Kuśadruma on the throne and having instructed his ministers, [departed].
Having saluted his mother and circumambulated her,
he then took up his lute and set out facing north.
Now, having arrived for lodging in another village of the Madra country, he was given shelter by a certain elderly woman.
On that very day, he was entertained in that village with the playing of the lute;
she gave him abundant solid and soft food, a large basket of snacks, a great vessel of boiled rice, a jar of curd, and various kinds of side dishes.
This thought occurred to the elder woman:
"Having taken this one meal, he will depart tomorrow, and this shall be my food for two months.
Meanwhile, while Kuśa was bringing a message to his grandmother, he ate the entire basket of sweets all at once;
and she ate the whole large bowl of rice, which was the cooking of eight or nine measures of rice.
And those condiments and that jar of curd were lost;
the old woman was left hopeless.
"Enter into every direction; Death has come here, a Piśāca in human form who desires to devour me."
Kuśa said:
All those who dwell in this village and commit evil with their bodies— having stayed for one night, O Mother, I shall depart tomorrow.
Having stayed there for one night, he then went to Kanyakubja and attached himself to a florist. Thus, first [he served] those of the artisan class, and afterwards the kitchen.
The king was also won over; because he had become dear to the king, he was introduced into the inner apartments by the women of the harem, thinking, "He shall be an entertainer."
The women of the inner apartments and even the daughters of Mahendraka were carried on his back;
even Sudarśanā, while being carried by him, felt discomfort and tried to stop him.
"What can I do now? Whom shall I blame? she thought.
Seeing him, he terrifies me, like sea-monsters in the ocean.
What shall I do now, or whom shall I blame? Having seen him, I am terrified like a bewildered doe seeing a hunter.
"O one devoid of vigor, you who have come following me day and night—go, Kuśa, to your own kingdom; I do not desire one of such ill-favored appearance."
The king said:
"O woman of beautiful hips and slender waist, may I be very dear to you;
for the sake of your desires, I would not even long for a great kingdom."
I shall not go, O lady of well-restrained thighs;
I do not know from which direction I have come. Confused in mind, I wander through the world.
I am intoxicated by desires, O lady with eyes like those of a deer.
The goddess said:
This distraction of your mind— that you desire one who does not desire you,
O King, that you lust after one who is unwilling— is not the characteristic of a wise man.
Kuśa said:
Whether she be unwilling or willing, if a man obtains a beloved woman, they praise that as a gain; failure to obtain her there is considered a misfortune.
The goddess said:
You are capable of delighting even a thousand women in a single night,
yet through desire for a single woman, you undergo great suffering.
The king said:
"O illustrious one, you who possess such beauty, I do not consider this to be suffering;
rather, it is that when the holy life has been well-practiced, you shall become my wife."
The goddess said:
"Shame on your celibacy! May you incur evil and sin!
In the next world, you shall desire either a female dog or a female jackal!"
Kuśa said:
"Do not speak thus, O blessed lady, fair-hipped one with a slender waist;
even for a female ascetic, the holy life shines forth beautifully."
O noble lady, they too shine here because of their well-practiced conduct;
having been reborn in the heavens among the Thirty-three, they enjoy all their desires.
"Therefore, O blessed lady, O fair-hipped one, O slender-waisted one, I tell you this:
there is no other husband for you than Kuśa, who possesses the voice of a lion."
The goddess said:
If the words of the diviners shall prove true, I will not be your wife; cut me into pieces as you wish!
The king said:
"I do not wish to cut you, O fair-hipped one of slender waist;
remaining uncut, O blessed lady, you shall become my wife."
And my kingdom was great, with many horses and many men;
it possessed infinite and abundant gifts, as well as plentiful clothing and food.
Therefore, having abandoned both my kingdom and my realm, I have come here;
I do not desire your kingdom along with its pleasures.
The goddess said:
You dig a well in stone; you seek a pericarp from a *karṇikāra* flower;
you try to bind the wind with a net—yet you desire that which does not wish to be desired.
Being unlovely, what do you desire? . . . . . . . . //
Go, Kuśa, to your own kingdom; why do you weary yourself?
The king said:
"This is no hardship for me; this is my holy life.
But in the future, O blessed lady, you shall become my wife."
The goddess said:
Let this celibacy of yours, which you have undertaken, become a source of evil;
I pray rather for a female dog, a female jackal, or a female donkey!
The prince Kuśa— heroic, valiant, and peerless in battle, possessed of perfected wisdom— spoke these words:
"O auspicious lady, O woman of beautiful hips and slender waist, as I was going along, I would have bound you with fetters; what could your kinsmen have done for you?"
The goddess said:
Having offended against that very same Dharma which was previously generated by you,
you now wish to bind me while merely recollecting that same Dharma.
The king said:
"I am able, O blessed lady, having bound you, O sovereign of creatures, to make you do whatever I wish; what will your father do?"
"You are able to delight even a thousand women in a single night;
you alone, O auspicious one, O lady of pure teeth, O mistress of the household, are my choice."
The goddess said:
I know you, O Great King, bull among men; you are powerful, yet you are ill-favored in color, difficult to look upon, and unpleasant to the touch, O Lord of the Earth.
"You have thick lips, a thick head, thick limbs, and a large belly;
I do not wish to see you, lest I afflict myself."
The goddess said:
These [guards], with their high walls, watchtowers, and parapets,
or those who ride upon elephants, indeed ward off whoever approaches here.
They fight with spears, javelins, and arrows.
And with very sharp swords, O Lord of Creatures, may I obtain you.
[_Mvu_3.20_] Now King Mahendraka reproached his daughter:
"Why have you come here, having abandoned such a king as he, before whom rival kings tremble?"
"And here I am, besieged by seven kings on your account;
now, having divided these [lands] into seven portions, I shall give them to these seven kings."
Then that frightened princess, with a throat choked with tears and a weeping face,
spoke these words with eyes full of water:
If, mother, the far-roaming Kṣatriyas should kill me,
have my bones collected and have them cremated in a secluded place.
Having had it burned in a secluded place, you should have an *elūka* tree planted for me;
having planted that *elūka* for me, you should then plant a *karṇikāra* tree.
And then, when spring has arrived at the end of winter and the flowers are in bloom, you will remember me, O Mother, thinking thus of my daughter of such a complexion.
Then that prince Kuśa, skilled in battle,
stood firm, having resolved that his fully developed wisdom must be applied.
Having bound these [enemies] and divided them portion by portion, O Kṣatriyas,
and having waged war, thereafter there will be peace.
Then that illustrious Kṣatriya queen, her limbs trembling, spoke these words to the prince:
I promise you this in truth, O mighty prince:
if any king should commit an offense against you or act improperly toward you, [I shall punish him].
Kuśa said:
I too know you, O Prajāpati of pure teeth.
If I should ever again act in this manner hereafter.
Then Prajāpatīmātā, with a tearful throat and a weeping face,
her eyes filled with water, spoke these words:
Who indeed was he—a bamboo-worker, a weaver, or perhaps even a Pukkasa?
In whose royal family was he born, and what did he do that his face is thus?
Sudarśanā said to her mother:
He is neither a bamboo-worker nor a Caṇḍāla, nor again is he a Pukkasa;
he is the son of King Ikṣvāku—yet you consider him a slave.
Resounding with the cries of peacocks and cranes and attended by the sound of musical instruments,
that flourishing family of a kṣatriya— you consider yourself its slave!
Resembling a white conch shell and attended by throngs of women,
you consider that prosperous Kṣatriya clan to be your slave.
This prosperous kṣatriya family, filled with throngs of women and adorned with vessels of gold— you consider yourself its slave.
Sixty thousand cities, a prosperous kingdom free from thorns,
and a flourishing kṣatriya lineage— yet you consider yourself a slave.
Sixty thousand elephants, adorned with golden ornaments,
with golden coverings and tusks as long as plowshafts, have emerged.
Mounted by village chiefs with swords and spears in their hands,
you consider that prosperous kshatriya clan to be your slave.
There were sixty thousand chariots, adorned with joyful sounds,
with rims firmly bound in iron and covered with leopard skins.
Mounted by village chiefs, armed with bows and clad in armor—
this is the flourishing clan of a kṣatriya, yet you consider yourself its slave.
There were sixty thousand horses, the best of steeds of noble breed,
wearing golden girths and bits made of jewels.
Mounted by village chiefs who are armored and hold whips in their hands—
you consider that prosperous kṣatriya family to be yours as a slave.
Twenty thousand brahmins constantly eat at the king’s expense,
whether by day or by night, always treated with honor and worshiped;
yet you consider that family of a kṣatriya, so prosperous, to be merely a slave.
There are five hundred princes, well-born on both the maternal and paternal sides; the lineage of this kṣatriya is flourishing, yet you consider him a slave.
Then the king heard that the son-in-law of the queen had arrived right here in the inner apartments.
Now, being afraid that there might be danger from kings outside, [he thought], "This danger has arisen within;
what will Kuśa do?"
"Why do you speak like one who is mad or of distracted mind?
What is this Kuśa like, and why should we look for him?"
The goddess said:
"O Lord, this prince stands within the inner apartments; having come forth, he now stands outside."
Having heard his words, he became afraid and agitated in mind; placing one shoulder bared as a mark of respect and with palms joined in reverence, he stood there.
Forgive us, O Great King; forgive us, O Bull among Men!
We did not know that you, with a voice like a lion’s, had come here.
Forgive us, O Great King; forgive us, O Bull among Men!
We did not know that you, O one of great voice, had come here.
Forgive us, O Great King; forgive us, O Great Charioteer!
We did not know that Mañjusvara had come here.
Then the king again reproached his daughter.
Such a long time has passed since my son-in-law arrived, yet you did not inform me.

Then, at that very moment, having been anointed with oils refined a hundred times and a thousand times, he was bathed, smeared with costly ointments, and dressed in magnificent garments; with a crown placed upon his head, he was attended by the fivefold musical ensemble.
Kuśa said to his father-in-law:
Let the ears of all those elephants and horses be covered;
let my own army not be broken by my lion's roar.
"Quickly harness the horses with their golden banners raised high;
depart from the inner palace following behind King Mahendra."
Like a hero and a lord in battle, he let out a lion’s roar;
having roared that lion’s roar, he took hold of the kṣatriyas.
Then those seven kṣatriyas, having seized him alive, brought him before their father-in-law.
The kings said to them:
"What shall I do? [he asked].
Kuśa said:
"Approach my father-in-law with your feet and cause him to prosper."
Then they approached King Mahendraka on foot, and he granted them victory and prosperity.
The King of Madrakara said:
"What shall I do? he thought.
Kuśa said:
You will do my bidding.
The father-in-law said:
"Intending to do."
"Do you have daughters? Adorn each one with a thousand pieces of gold and give one daughter to each king; let them become your sons-in-law, and you shall dwell in happiness and freedom from anxiety."
King Mahendraka gave to each one of those kṣatriyas a daughter adorned with a thousand pieces of gold, like a golden joint [passed down] through sons and grandsons.
Then they were dismissed to their own kingdoms.
When the seven kings had departed, Kuśa addressed his father-in-law.
"I too shall go."
The King of Madra said:

"Daughter Sudarśanā, you are worthy to serve with love and reverence this king, who is endowed with such prowess, heroic, far-sighted, a son of Ikṣvāku, possessed of great strength, and of noble lineage— by whom I,
along with my entire retinue and the whole city, have been liberated from doubt."
"So be it," the daughter replied, and she heeded her father's words.
Then King Mahendraka, having bestowed a great gift of jewels with grand hospitality, equipped a fourfold army for his son-in-law and Sudarśanā, and sent them forth.
Having now settled in the country he desired,
he descended there into a lotus pond to bathe.
While bathing there, he saw his own reflection.
Seeing that reflection of himself as ill-favored and unsightly, he became dejected, thinking:
"Because of this, Mahendraka’s daughter holds me in contempt."
I shall take action against myself.
Then he was attended upon by Śakra, the lord of the gods.
This Bodhisattva Kuśa, desiring to bring about his own disfigurement, gave him the *jyotīrasa* single-strand necklace jewel, saying:
"Bind this on; then in appearance you will have no equal anywhere in all of Jambudvīpa.
Whenever you desire your former appearance, cover this jewel with your hand."
Now, with that jewel-gem fastened upon him, he entered the royal palace; yet, because of his divine appearance, he was stopped by the gatekeeper who said, "Do not enter!"
Then he said:
"I am Kuśa."
The doorkeeper said:
"May King Kuśa be thus in form," he said. "May it be well."
King Kuśa covered that precious gem with his hand,
and its color and form returned to what they were originally.
Having seen him, the door-keeper prostrated himself with his head.
He then entered into the presence of the queen.
The goddess said:
"Do not trample upon the royal palace!
Why have you entered the royal palace?"
He said:
I am Kuśa.
The goddess said:
May King Kuśa come to possess such a form as this.
When the king touched that jewel with his hand,
it immediately became as it was before.
The goddess said:
Therefore, remove your hand from the jewel.
The king spoke, and the hand was removed; his divine form was restored once more.
Desiring to approach my very self,
Śakra then gave me this jewel-gem named Jyotīrasa.
Hearing that King Kuśa was approaching, four hundred and ninety-nine princes, the ministers, and the vanguard of the army all went out to meet him.
They beheld King Kuśa mounted upon the back of a noble elephant, possessing a divine form and blazing like the sun, coming forward surrounded by a fourfold army;
yet they did not recognize him.
Then the king covered [the bowl] with his hand, which was adorned with jewels, and its appearance returned to what it was before; thereupon, they all prostrated themselves.
Thus, with great ceremony, King Kuśa entered the inner apartments together with Queen Sudarśanā.
Thus, for one who possesses merit, all matters become favorable,
just as Kuśa was reunited with his wife and his kinsmen.
Recalling his former dwelling and former birth, the Blessed One,
the Teacher, related this Jātaka in the presence of the monks.
Those aggregates, those elements, and those sense-bases—
the Blessed One explained this matter for the sake of the self.
In this beginningless and endless saṃsāra where I formerly dwelt,
I was then Kuśa, and Yaśodharā was Sudarśanā.
Māyā was then the mother, and Mahānāma was Mahendraka; Māra was another king—thus you should remember this Jātaka.
Thus, this immeasurable and ancient cycle of many sufferings, with its high and low courses of conduct— having become free from fever, free from fear, and free from sorrow, [I have seen it].
He recited his own Jātaka in the midst of the community of monks.
The monks said to the Blessed One:
“Blessed One, as the ripening of that karma, King Kuśa became ill-colored, unpleasant to behold, and disagreeable to look upon.”
The Blessed One said:

Once upon a time, monks, in the past, in the city of Kampilla in the country of Pañcāla, there lived a husband and wife who were young, handsome, and deeply in love with one another. Their home was well-ordered and free from any thorns [of discord]. When Buddhas do not appear in the world, Pratyekabuddhas arise; they are beautiful in their silence, like the horn of a rhinoceros.
They tame themselves alone, they pacify themselves, and they attain final nirvana.
The food had been prepared there by that woman.
And a Pratyekabuddha, young and handsome, with a graceful deportment, entered that house for alms.
Gods and humans are gracious and full of faith.
Upon seeing the Pratyekabuddha, faith arose in that woman.
She also gave alms-food to that Pratyekabuddha.
Then her husband, having entered, saw both that Pratyekabuddha and his wife in the house.
Then a suspicion arose in him:
"This young renunciant must surely have been looking at my wife."
He spoke thus to his wife with harsh words.
This has been eaten by you before, just as you give him food.
She said:
"May evil be stilled! This highly fortunate one has gone forth; he is an unprecedented guest who has entered my home today. Out of faith, I have given alms to him."
Then that Pratyekabuddha, knowing the unwholesome thought that had arisen in that man, departed from that very house for the sake of his welfare, soaring through the air like a king of swans.
Then, seeing that Pratyekabuddha risen into the air, faith arose in that man: "This seer is one of great fortune."
He asked his wife for forgiveness and made a vow:
"In another birth as well, may you be my wife. Even when she went to another kingdom, she did not remain under the control of anyone else, but remained under his alone.
The Blessed One said:

It may be, monks, that you might think: "Was that man in the city of Kampilla at that time and on that occasion someone else who, out of a jealous nature and with a wicked mind, falsely accused the Pratyekabuddha? King Kuśa was that man in the city of Kampilla at that time and on that occasion.
She was another wife;
she was Sudarśanā, the daughter of Mahendranātha.
Monks, as the ripening of that karma, King Kuśa became deformed.
The Kuśajātaka is completed.
The monks said to the Blessed One:

"How was it, Blessed One, that Māra the Evil One, following closely behind the Blessed One while he was practicing austerities, seeking an opportunity and searching for a vulnerability, yet failing to find one, became despondent and withdrew?"
The Blessed One said:
On other occasions as well, this one followed closely behind me, seeking an opening and looking for an opportunity; but finding no opening, he withdrew in disappointment.
The monks said to the Blessed One:
At another time as well, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
On another occasion as well, monks.
Monks, in the past, in times long gone, there was a bull, a lord of cattle, followed by a herd of cows.
Now that bull’s testicles were pendulous and flaccid; with those pendulous testicles, he followed behind the herd of cows, keeping his back close to their backs.
And in that forest retreat lived a jackal named Girika.
By him that bull was seen wandering together with the herd of cows, possessing long testicles.
Thus, for many years, he followed closely behind him, back to back.
He had another jackal as a companion.
That [companion] saw Girika following closely behind the back of that bull, and having seen him, he addressed Girika with a verse:
For how many years, Girika, have you followed the lord of cattle?
Again and again you tremble, and you look about in utter terror.
"These are thick and these are long; these are well-fastened and these are loose.
These will not fall, therefore you shall have nothing to eat."
I too followed them for fifteen years;
whether they were loose or well-fastened, there was no fear for them as they flew.
The Blessed One said:
It may be, monks, that you might think that at that time and on that occasion the bull was someone else. [But it was not so.]
Thus, I became a bull.
This very jackal named Girika was Māra.
Even then, seeking an opportunity but not finding one, he departed in disillusionment.
Thus ends the Vṛṣabha-jātaka.
