The monks said to the Blessed One:
How is it, Blessed One, that Māra the Evil One is unable to find an opportunity against the Blessed One?
The Blessed One said:
Monks, it is not only now that Māra the Evil One is unable to find an opportunity to gain entry to me;
on another occasion as well, he was unable to find an opportunity to gain entry to me.
The monks said.
At another time as well, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
And at other times as well, monks.
Long ago, monks, in a region of the Himalayas, there was a monkey who led a large troop of monkeys.
In that Himalayan region there was a great lake where the monkey troop would frequently descend to drink water;
and in that lake lived a water-rākṣasa.
Whatever deer, bird, monkey, or human enters that pool of water to drink, the water-rākṣasa drags them down there.
That troop of monkeys also descended into that lake to drink water.
Then that water-demon, remaining within the water, watched those monkeys; unseen by them, he dragged one monkey toward him.
In this way, whenever those monkeys had descended to drink water, that water-rākṣasa would watch for them and, remaining unseen, drag them out from their dwelling place.
Now that lord of monkeys did not see those monkeys who had been dragged into the water-pool there;
it occurred to him: "Where are those monkeys? Have they perhaps gone elsewhere?"
He looked all around, yet he did not see [him].
That wise leader of the herd, as those monkeys were descending into the lake—
by whichever path they entered that lake to drink water— observed their feet as they descended and as they emerged; he saw that for those descending, the footprints grew larger,
while for those emerging, they diminished.
The thought occurred to him:
"These are being dragged away here by the water-demon; therefore, I do not see them. Enough of drinking the water myself with my own mouth."
And he saw that the monkeys were being dragged down into that water by a water-rākṣasa; then the rākṣasa gave orders.
"Go from this Nalavana forest and take stalks of reeds so that you may drink water;
then the water-rākṣasa will not be able to drag you back."
Having gone from the reed-thicket, they each took very long stalks of reeds so that, while standing at a distance and drinking water, the water-demon might not be able to pull them down.
Whenever the water-drinkers went, they would take their respective reeds and descend; then, staying at a distance, they drank the water through those reeds.
The water-rākṣasa was no longer able to drag the monkey back down.
The footprints of one entering [the water] are visible, but not of one emerging;
one should drink with a reed-pipe; for one who is vigilant, there is no fear.
The Blessed One said:
It may be, monks, that you think the lord of monkeys at that time and on that occasion was someone else;
however, it was I myself who was he then.
He who was the water-rākṣasa was none other than Māra himself.
Even then, he was unable to perceive the incarnation.
Thus ends the Vānarajātakam.
The monks said to the Blessed One:
How did the Blessed One transcend the realm of Māra through the excellence of his wisdom regarding unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now that I have safely transcended the realm of Māra through my excellence of wisdom; on another occasion,
even when I was a monkey, I safely transcended the realm of this very Māra by placing my feet upon his head through my excellence of wisdom."
The monks said.
At another time as well, Blessed One?
The Blessed One said:
On another occasion as well, monks.
Once upon a time, monks, in the distant past, a monkey was leading a large troop of monkeys in the Himalayas.
Now, in the last month of summer, having eaten various kinds of fruits from that Himalaya together with that troop of monkeys, he became thirsty and came to a lake to drink water.
And that lake was surrounded by steep banks; there was no place to descend or to emerge.
That leader of the herd, searching all around that lake for an opening and wandering about due to thirst for water, tore through a layer of rocks and fell into that lake;
within that water was the den of a python,
and in that den lived a great python.
While he was dwelling there, food arose for him with little difficulty;
whatever water-drinking animal, deer, bird, or monkey came there, he would eat it.
As he was falling into that water, the lord of monkeys saw him;
he then extended his neck out from the cave, thinking, "I shall seize this monkey," and addressed the monkey with a verse:
Moreover, this monkey who frequents the forest has appeared,
who now desires to drink water at the edge of the bank inside the cave.
Then that lord of monkeys could find no foothold at all in that water where he might set his foot and step from the water onto dry land.
This thought occurred to him:
If this python should turn its neck away, I would place my foot upon the head of this very python and step onto dry land.
He then addressed the python with a verse:
I myself am not to be devoured by you; do you not see these two broad [beings]? You who threaten me face-to-face, you speak these words.
Then that python turned its neck toward where those monkeys had been pointed out by the leader of the troop, in order to look at them.
Immediately, the python turned its neck away, and the lord of the monkeys placed his foot upon the head of that turned-away python and then safely stepped from the water onto dry land.
Then that python was struck with wonder at the monkey's extraordinary intelligence.
"This monkey has no foothold here in the water-pool where he might plant his foot and step from this water onto dry land.
Then he pointed out these monkeys to me;
thus he turned his face away from there, and my neck turned toward where those monkeys were.
And by his extraordinary intelligence, he placed his feet upon my very head and set out across the dry land.
He replied to that lord of monkeys with a verse:
And you quickly and swiftly restrained that thought again,
you who, knowing me to be turned away, were born as a hero and a warrior.
O Lord of Monkeys, he who possesses these four qualities— just as you do— namely, vigor, intelligence, mindfulness, and wisdom, shall turn back suffering.
"Furthermore, monks, it may be that you think: 'At that time, on that occasion, was the lord of monkeys in the Himalayas someone else?
But he, at that time, on that occasion, was I myself who was the lord of monkeys."
That water-snake in that lake was someone else;
indeed, it should not be viewed in this way. For what reason?
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, this wicked Māra was the resident python in that lake.
Even then, by means of my superior intelligence, I placed my foot upon his head and crossed over from that pool of water;
now too, by means of my superior intelligence, I have transcended the realm of this Māra.
The Vānarajātakam is completed.
The monks said to the Blessed One:
Behold how the Blessed One speaks in praise of meritorious deeds!
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now that I speak in praise of merits;
at other times as well, monks, I have spoken in praise of merits."
The monks said.
At other times as well, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
On another occasion as well, monks.

Long ago, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi, there was a king named Añjanaka who ruled the realm; he was one who had performed meritorious deeds, possessed great majesty, maintained a well-gathered retinue, was disposed toward giving and sharing, and possessed great strength, a great treasury, and many mounts.
His kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, well-supplied with food, crowded with people, and filled with happy subjects.
Now, King Añjana had a son named Puṇyavanta, a prince who at all times spoke in praise of meritorious deeds.
This prince had four sons of ministers as his companions.
One minister’s son, named Vīryavanta, always spoke in praise of vigor, saying that vigor is supreme in the world.
The second son of the minister was named Śilpavanta; at all times he was a proponent of the arts, [asserting] that the art is unsurpassed in the world.
The third son of the minister was named Rūpavanta; he was a proponent of beauty, asserting that beauty is supreme in the world.
The fourth son of the minister was named Prajñāvanta; he always spoke in praise of wisdom, for wisdom is supreme in the world.
Then they were addressed by that meritorious prince:

"There is no merit in this world equal to merit, it is unsurpassed. "If you are unable to find out [here], let us go to another kingdom; there we shall find out who excels—whether in merit, in vigor, in craft, in beauty, or in wisdom."
Then they went from Vārāṇasī to the city of Kampilla, thinking, "We shall find out who in the world is preeminent—whether in merit, in vigor, in craftsmanship, in beauty, or in wisdom."
Then, having departed from Kaṃpilla, they went to bathe in the Gaṅgā; and there, in the current of the river Gaṅgā, they saw a great log of wood floating down.
Then those sons of ministers and that meritorious prince spoke to that heroic son of a minister.
"O you who possess vigor, you must now display your vigor regarding this log of wood; exert yourself as much as you can to pull back this log of wood as it is being carried down by the river Gaṅgā."
Then that heroic one, having generated great strength and power by means of that [act], dragged that log of wood which was being carried away by the river Gaṅgā onto dry land.
Then they examined it and saw that it was a most precious sandalwood tree.
Then he was sold by that energetic son of a minister to the perfumers for one hundred thousand purāṇas.
Having brought a hundred thousand of those ancient [texts], he gave them to his companions and addressed those companions with a verse:
The world praises vigor; vigor is unsurpassed in the world. Behold how, through the power of vigor, this mass of wealth has been gathered by me!
Then they said:
The fruit of diligence has been seen;
we now behold the fruit of craftsmanship for Śilpavanta.

Then Śilpavanta, taking his lute, emerged from the presence of his companions and, together with the sons of ministers and the sons of guild-masters who were skilled in the lute, began to play the lute.
A great multitude of people gathered there; even all those in the city of Kampilla who were trained in the playing of the lute heard of it and assembled as well.
Together with that minister’s son, they played the lute in competition with one another;
yet no one at all was able to surpass that minister’s son on the lute.
Then indeed, that minister’s son Śilpavanta excelled all others in the playing of the lute.
Then, as that skilled artisan was playing that lute, one string of the lute broke, yet such a sound as before issued from that lute.
His second string broke, yet such a sound as before issued from the lute. His third string broke, yet such a sound as before issued from that lute.
In this way, one by one, six strings were severed until only one string remained;
then, from that single remaining string, exactly the same sound emerged.
The entire assembly was struck with wonder by the lute-playing of that son of a minister, Śilpavanta.
Then he obtained a great deal of silver and gold, as well as clothing.
Having brought that silver and gold, he gave it to his companions, saying,
"This too is the fruit of my craft."
He then addressed those companions with a verse:
In this world they praise craftsmanship; craftsmanship is unsurpassed in the world.
By my skillful training on the lute, a great mass of wealth has been acquired by me.
Then they said:
We have seen the fruit of this minister’s son’s craftsmanship;
let us now behold the fruit of his beauty as well.
Then that handsome minister’s son, having run out from among his companions, entered the street of the market stalls.

Now, as he was walking along the street in the marketplace, he was seen by a leading courtesan— handsome, beautiful to behold, with a noble presence, and endowed with the most excellent abundance of beauty.
At the mere sight of him, an exceeding love arose within her.
She sent a maidservant.
Go and summon this man in my name.
Then she was summoned by that maidservant: "Noble daughter, your noble son wishes to see you."
Then he entered the house of that chief courtesan together with her maidservant. The chief courtesan welcomed the minister’s son:
"Welcome, noble son! This house is yours; it is your supreme prize. Therefore, enjoy yourself, take your pleasure, and be entertained by me, provided with the five strands of sensual pleasure."
He was made to sit on a single seat by that leading courtesan and enticed with many kinds of wealth.

Having led him into the bathhouse, she gave him an oil massage with fragrant oils, bathed him with excellent bathing powders, anointed him with exquisite unguents, and clothed him in costly Kāśika garments.
As he sat together with that leading courtesan, a sumptuous meal was served to him.
Then, while sitting together with her, he said:
"In such-and-such a house of mine there are four friends; having summoned them, a measure of wealth should be given to them so that they do not suffer."
"By the mere word of the chief courtesan, a hundred thousand [pieces] were placed before you; give these to those companions."
Then those companions were summoned;
they arrived at the house of that leading courtesan and saw the handsome son of a minister sitting on the lap of the leading courtesan, who was endowed with great splendor.
Then, being handsome, he saw that female companion and addressed her in verse:
In this world they praise physical beauty; in this world beauty is unsurpassed. And from the lap of a courtesan, a mass of wealth was brought to me.
Take this hundred thousand and spend it.
Then, taking a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], they went to their own dwelling place.
Then they said:
The fruit of beauty has been seen even in the son of the minister;
likewise, the fruit of wisdom is to be seen even in one who possesses wisdom.
The wise man also, having departed from that warehouse, entered the street of the marketplace.
There he saw the son of a guild-president quarreling with a leading courtesan in the midst of a great crowd of people.
The son of the guild-president said to that leading courtesan:
"Come today and attend upon me for the night;
I shall give you a hundred thousand [pieces of gold]."
The chief courtesan said:
"Noble son, I have no leisure this night; I have already accepted wages for another night today.
We shall attend upon him today, and tomorrow, noble son, I will come into the presence of the noble son."
Then she went that night to serve as an attendant for that man.
The merchant’s son also lay down, thinking only of that preeminent courtesan.
Then, throughout the entire night, he sported, dallied, and enjoyed himself with that chief courtesan according to his desire, even within a dream.
Then that leading courtesan, having played, enjoyed herself, and dallied with that man during that night, went to the presence of the merchant’s son when the night had turned to dawn, saying:
"I have come here, O noble son, to serve you."
The merchant’s son said:
"Today, in a dream, I have spent the entire night with you, playing, delighting, and being entertained according to my desire; go, I have no need for you."
"If the noble son has spent the entire night with me in a dream, sporting, delighting, and enjoying himself as he desired, give me a hundred thousand [pieces of gold]."
The merchant said:
"Since you have spent the entire night with another man, why should I give you a hundred thousand?"
She said:

"Noble son, you yourself have said that throughout the entire night you played, dallied, and enjoyed yourself with me as you desired in a dream; therefore, the noble son must pay the fee of one hundred thousand."
There, he [heard] that dispute of theirs.
A great multitude of people had gathered, yet no one was able to resolve their dispute.
While he was standing there, that wise son of a minister was addressed by these merchants of Kampilla:
"Speak, young man, whatever occurs to you in this matter: should this guild-president’s son give a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] to this preeminent courtesan, or should he not?"
The wise one said:
Just as there was a union between the guild-president’s son and this courtesan, so too must the guild-president’s son pay the fee to this courtesan.
They said.
Let the prince explain how it should be given.
That wise man had a great circular mirror brought, as well as a hundred thousand [pieces of gold].
He was called the merchant’s son.
"Take this casket worth a hundred thousand and hold it facing this circular mirror."
The merchant’s son lifted up that casket worth a hundred thousand and placed it before this mirror-disk.
"Come, my lady, take this reflection of the casket worth a hundred thousand that appears here in the mirror-disk;
this is your fee."
When this had been explained to that wise son of a minister, a great roar of acclaim was raised by the multitude of people, and they covered him with abundant gold and bullion.
He gave that gold and bullion to those companions.
He addressed that female companion with a verse:
In this world, they praise wisdom; wisdom is supreme in the world. Through well-considered wisdom, I have gathered a mass of wealth.
Then those sons of the ministers said:
We have seen the power of the heroism of Vīryavanta, the son of the minister; the power of the craft of Śilpavanta; the power of the beauty of Rūpavanta; and the power of the wisdom of Prajñāvanta.
Now let us behold the power of the merit of the prince Puṇyavanta.
Then the meritorious prince, having run away from those companions, went toward the royal palace and prostrated himself there;
he remained in the vicinity of the royal palace.
He was seen by another son of a minister;
at the very moment of seeing him, affection for the prince Puṇyavanta descended upon that son of the minister.
He was invited by him to take his meal, led to his own home, and brought into the gymnasium.
Having exercised, he bathed, anointed himself, and sat down for his meal.
There, that prince, together with the minister’s son, attended upon him for that day with excellent food and drink fit for a king.
And that minister’s son, having been made to mount the royal carriage, was laid down to sleep;
and he was seen by the daughter of King Brahmadatta.
It occurred to her:
"This son of a minister has arrived."
Then, having departed from the royal palace at an improper hour and entered the carriage shed, she mounted the very carriage there where the meritorious prince was lying, thinking:
"He will now wake up in a moment;
then he will sport with me."

The prince, too, having eaten and drunk, lay down in comfort; and that princess, tormented by thoughts of sensual desire, thinking, "Now she will wake up," or "She will wake up even for a moment," fell asleep, overcome by the onset of the night.
Then, when the sun had risen, she descended from her carriage and entered the royal palace, where she was seen by the ministers.
This thought occurred to them:
"This princess has descended from the carriage shed and entered the royal palace while still awake; let it not be that she sat here in the carriage with any man."
And while they were searching in that manner, the meritorious prince then descended from his vehicle.
It occurred to those ministers:
"From where has this man come, that he is staying here in the carriage shed together with the daughter of King Brahmadatta?"
He was seized by those ministers, and having seized him, they presented him to King Brahmadatta:
"Your Majesty, this man lay with the king's daughter in the carriage shed."
He is asked thus:
"How is this so?"
He said:
"Your Majesty, I was invited to the house by a certain minister’s son; having eaten and drunk there, I was turned out at an improper hour and set out on my way home.

Because of that fault of departing at an improper hour, I climbed up here into this carriage-shed and lay down, having eaten and drunk, and no one else was known to be there with me as a second person."
The king also questioned his daughter:
"How is this so?"
She, moreover, reported it to Brahmadatta exactly as it was;
just as the man spoke, so she spoke, and not otherwise.
King Brahmadatta became pleased with Prince Puṇyavanta, and seeing that the prince was gracious, handsome, intelligent, and well-established, this thought occurred to him:
"This cannot be an ordinary man; this prince must be of noble lineage."
He then questioned the prince.
"O youth, from where have you come?"
The prince said:
He was the son of Añjana, the King of Kāśi, from Vārāṇasī.

Upon merely seeing Prince Puṇyavanta, King Brahmadatta of Kampilla was overcome with paternal affection for him; since that king had no son, he adorned his daughter with a thousand pieces of gold and, with great royal majesty and great royal power,
bestowed her upon Prince Puṇyavanta in the presence of the entire city, and established him in the kingdom.
And the king spoke to his ministers, as well as to the merchants and the people of the countryside.
"This son has been born to me; let him be the king for now, as I am old."
Then, having attained the kingdom, that Puṇyavanta summoned those companions and addressed them in verse:
In this world they praise merit; in this world merit is unsurpassed.
Through my merits, both sovereignty and a royal maiden have come to me.
The Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, monks, it might occur to you that at that time and on that occasion, the minister's son named Vīryavanta was someone else.
It should not be viewed in this way.
And why is that?"
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, this Śroṇakoṭiviṃśa was the minister’s son named Vīryavanta.
That minister’s son Śilpavanta at that time and on that occasion was someone else;
it should not be viewed in this way. For what reason?
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, this noble son Rāṣṭrapāla was the minister’s son Śilpavant.
It should not be viewed in this way that the minister’s son Rūpavanta was someone else at that time and on that occasion. For what reason? Because he was none other than I.
Monks, that elder Sundarananda was, at that time and on that occasion, the minister’s son Rūpavanta.
That minister’s son who was wise at that time and on that occasion was someone else;
it should not be viewed in this way. For what reason?
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, this very elder Śāriputra was the wise son of a minister.
It should not be viewed in this way that at that time, on that occasion, the son of Añjana, the King of Kāśī, named Puṇyavanta, was someone else.
For what reason? Because he was none other than I.
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, I was the prince named Puṇyavanta, the son of Añjana, the King of Kāśi.
Even then, I was one who spoke in praise of meritorious deeds.
Even now, I am one who speaks in praise of meritorious deeds.
Thus ends the Puṇyavanta-jātaka.
Moreover, monks, it is not only now that I speak in praise of meritorious deeds;
at other times as well, I have spoken in praise of meritorious deeds.
The monks said.
At other times as well, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
On another occasion also, monks.

Long ago, monks, in the past, in Mithilā, a king named Vijitāvin reigned. He was one who had performed meritorious deeds, possessed great majesty, and maintained his retinue well; he was disposed toward giving and sharing, and there was nothing he would not give to ascetics, brahmins, the destitute, or beggars. To anyone who needed an elephant, he gave an elephant.
To whoever has need of a horse, he gives a horse;
to whoever has need of a chariot, he gives a chariot;
to whoever has need of whatever kind of vehicle, he gives such vehicles.
To whoever has need of women, he gives a woman adorned with every ornament;
to whoever has need of female slaves, he gives female slaves.
To whoever has need of slaves, she gives slaves;
to whoever has need of garments, she gives garments;
to whoever has need of such-and-such vessels, she gives such-and-such vessels.
To whoever has need of a cow, he gives a cow;
to whoever has need of oxen, he gives oxen;
to whoever has need of gold, he gives gold.
To whoever has need of gold, he gives gold;
to whoever has need of silver, he gives silver;
to whoever has need of whatever thing, he gives that very thing to them.
And there is nothing that he does not relinquish, nor does any alteration of his state occur.
Moreover, while giving and relinquishing, he becomes joyful; having given, he does not later feel regret.
Indeed, he becomes full of rapture and gladness.
Now, because he was giving away excessive gifts and his treasuries were being exhausted,

the accountants, the high officials, the princes, the ministers, the townspeople, the countryfolk, and a great multitude of people assembled together; and having been banished from that kingdom, he went to a great forest thicket in the Himalayas.
Having gone there to that forest grove and having established a hermitage, he constructed huts of grass and leaves and made his dwelling.
Dwelling there in that hermitage as well, he would gather roots, leaves, flowers, and various kinds of fruits, first feeding the sages and afterwards taking food himself,
always desiring the Dharma.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, having approached the grove for the purpose of testing the king, stood in the sky with his divine splendor and sought to dissuade the King of Videha from giving.
"Great King, this kind of giving is not praised by the wise; at all times, such giving is censured by the wise."
He who gives such a gift suffers in this very life;
having passed away from among humans, he is reborn in the hells.

Just as the Great King, by means of this gift, has been exiled from his kingdom and is now deprived of sovereignty and joined with suffering in this present life, so too, by the power of this gift, he will be reborn in the hells in the future.

"O Great King, if you have faith in me such that you believe that by giving a gift here one will be reborn in the hells in the next world, I shall show it to you directly, O Great King, where the givers and masters of gifts are reborn;
there Śakra has conjured a great hell, set ablaze, burning fiercely, and emitting flames."
There, many thousands of living beings were seen being cooked, crying out with terrifying sounds.
He then said to the king:
"Great King, go and ask these beings who have been reborn in hell and are crying out: 'By what karma have you been reborn here in this hell?'"
The king questions those denizens of hell.
"What evil deed was committed by you while you were human beings, such that you now experience these sufferings in hell, crying out with such terrifying voices?"
Then those emanations said:
"Great King, we were donors and masters of giving in the world of men; by us, noble, abundant, and extensive gifts were given to ascetics, brahmins, the wretched, and beggars.
By the power of that, having passed away from among humans, we have been reborn here in these hells."
The king said:
"Friends, it is not as you say;
there is neither cause nor condition by which a donor or master of giving, having given a gift, would be reborn in the hells."
Then indeed, those donors and masters of giving, having given gifts, through the power of that giving, upon the dissolution of the body, are reborn in the heavens.
There they experience various kinds of divine pleasures.
Having experienced those divine pleasures among the gods, at the exhaustion of their lifespan, they pass away from the heavens and are reborn among humans in wealthy families.

Moreover, Kauśika, when those supplicants, having received their gains from me and with their intentions fulfilled, depart, then a sublime joy and gladness arise in me, and they too become joyful. Even if I am reborn in the hells, I still have the resolve to give gifts.
Thus Śakra, the lord of the gods, having inquired after that King of Videha, was gratified.
"Excellent, Great King! Noble is your intention; it was for the sake of testing you, Great King, that I came here."
Having spoken thus, Śakra, the lord of the gods, vanished from that grove and reappeared in the abode of the Thirty-three.
Now, in that kingdom of Mithilā, ever since the king was exiled, the rain has not fallen, a famine has occurred, and the land has been harassed by thieves and rival kings.
Then those princes, ministers, accountants, high officials, merchants, and countryfolk went to that forest grove,
asked the King of Videha for his forgiveness, and with great royal splendor and great royal majesty,
reinstated him in Mithilā; at that time, there was an abundance of food.
The Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, monks, it might occur to you that at that time and on that occasion, the king of Videha in Mithilā named Vijitāvin was someone else.
But it should not be viewed in this way. And why is that?"
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, I was the King of Videha named Vijitāvin in Mithilā.
Even then I was a speaker in praise of merits; even now I am a speaker in praise of merits.
There was once a king named Vijitāvin, the lord of Videha and ruler of Mithilā;
he was renowned throughout the quarters for his generosity, being one who gave freely and without envy.
He would not fail to relinquish anything—not even elephants, horses, chariots, and vehicles; nor women adorned with ornaments; nor gold and silver.
Abounding in joy and gladness, one should generate a state of mental well-being;
having given, one becomes joyful, and having given, one does not regret it.
Upon seeing a śramaṇa, a brāhmaṇa, a pauper, or a beggar,
he satisfied them with food and drink, as well as with clothing, bedding, and seats.
The accountants, the high ministers, the princes, the counselors, the merchants, and the multitude of people, having assembled together, shall banish him from the kingdom.
Having been exiled, he approached a forest grove;
having constructed a hermitage there, he made his dwelling.
And in that forest grove, having gathered various fruits and having satisfied the seers, he afterwards ate himself.
Śakra, with his divine splendor, approached the king;
standing in the air, he spoke these words.
The wise do not praise a gift that is always censured;
because of this excessive giving, you have been exiled from your kingdom.
In this very life you are suffering, O Kṣatriya, deprived of your kingdom;
having gone to the next world, O King, you will go to hell.
If you do not believe me as to where the donor goes,
I shall show you that very destination which is the goal of donors.
Śakra created a blazing hell filled with light,
and he showed many thousands of beings being cooked there.
Ask this yourself, O Great King: why are these subjects being consumed by fire? By what misfortune have they come to experience such painful sensations?
Wailing with a voice like Bhīṣma’s, you experience painful sensations;
ask him about this matter: what evil did you commit in the past?
They said:
O lord of men, we were once masters of generosity among humans;
yet, despite having given much in charity, we now experience this suffering.
The king said:
There is no such possibility, nor does such a situation exist,
that a virtuous donor, having passed away, should go to a state of misery.
Having passed away from among humans, the donors go to heaven;
there they personally experience superhuman miraculous powers produced by their own deeds.
O Lord of Men, even though the suffering in the hells is indeed manifold and of such a nature...
Having seen that beggar, I am not able [to refuse him].
How can he, whose every resolve and desire is fulfilled, speak such words?
Having obtained me, how could he, being so delighted, turn away from me?
O Thousand-eyed One, may that be my delight.
There is nothing that I would not give as a gift here; day after day, I shall fulfill and satisfy [all beings].
I am their ultimate refuge, I am that wish-fulfilling tree.
...devoid of leaves and fruit.
My mind does not become angry when asked; having given, I do not grieve nor do I regret.
I have never heard of a case where one should not give.
And whatever I have heard, I bring it quickly to fulfillment. In a single moment, all my desires are fulfilled; Saṃjaya has realized the truth for me.
For seven days the Sage remained seated comfortably upon his couch, as immovable as a mountain.
On the seventh day, the Lord, the Great Sage, emerged and uttered words that made known thousands of world-systems.
The ripening of meritorious deeds is pleasant, one's intentions are fulfilled,
and one swiftly attains supreme peace and liberation.
Thus ends the Jātaka of Vijitāvin, the King of Videha.

Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One’s disciple, the Venerable Ānanda, while wandering on a tour among the Magadhans together with a great community of monks, five hundred monks in all, arrived at Rājagṛha, the city of the Magadhans, and stayed right there in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, thirty of the Venerable Ānanda’s co-residents renounced the training, manifested their weakness, and returned to the lower life for the sake of sensual pleasures.

The Venerable Mahākāśyapa heard that thirty of the Venerable Ānanda’s co-residents, having renounced the training and manifested weakness, had turned back toward the inferior state for the sake of sensual pleasures.
Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa approached the venerable Ānanda; having exchanged greetings with the venerable Ānanda and engaged in pleasant and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the venerable Mahākāśyapa said this to Ānanda:
"Venerable Ānanda, we would like to ask you about a certain matter, if the Venerable Ānanda would grant us the opportunity to have our questions answered."
When this had been said, the venerable Ānanda spoke thus to the venerable Mahākāśyapa:
"Ask, Venerable Kāśyapa, whatever you desire; having heard it, I shall explain."
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda:

If you think so, venerable Ānanda, considering how many purposes did the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, perceive when he prohibited his disciples from eating in a group and authorized them to eat at most three times a day?
When this had been said, the venerable Ānanda spoke thus to the venerable Mahākāśyapa:
"Indeed, Venerable Mahākāśyapa, we have come from afar to ask the Venerable Mahākāśyapa about this matter."
It would be well if this meaning were to occur to the venerable Mahākāśyapa himself.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda.
"Venerable Ānanda, seeing two purposes, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, has prohibited communal meals for his disciples and permitted meals in groups of three.
What are these two?
[They are] for the protection, preservation, and comfortable dwelling of families, and for the cutting off of the faction of evil ones."
Those evil ones, having bound the community with worldly gain, would incite quarrels, disputes, strife, and contention within the Saṅgha, as well as legal issues and remorse.
"Indeed, Venerable Ānanda, seeing these two purposes, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has prohibited for his disciples eating in a group and has permitted eating in groups of three."

Therefore, venerable Ānanda, you are wandering on alms-round among families like a pestilence destroying the grain, amidst this assembly that is new, young, and youthful; whose sense-doors are unguarded, who lacks moderation in eating, who is not devoted to the practice of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night, and who shows no respect toward their fellow celibates— whether elders, juniors, or those of middle standing.
I think this young boy, while acting, did not recognize his own mother.
When this had been said, the venerable Ānanda spoke thus to the venerable Mahākāśyapa:
For indeed, venerable Mahākāśyapa, gray hairs have grown upon my head, yet you still think that I am to be addressed by the venerable Mahākāśyapa with the address "young man."
A second time and even a third time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa said this to the Venerable Ānanda:

In this way, venerable Ānanda, you wander among these assemblies— among those who do not guard the doors of their sense faculties, who lack moderation in eating, who do not apply themselves to the practice of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night, and who show no respect toward their fellow celibates, whether elders, juniors, or those of middle standing— and I consider you to be like one causing the destruction of a grain crop; yet I do not [reproach you].
The boy understood only his mother.
A second time and even a third time, the venerable Ānanda said this to the venerable Mahākāśyapa:
"Indeed, venerable Mahākāśyapa, gray hairs have grown upon my head; yet you, Mahākāśyapa, still think that I am to be addressed with the address 'little boy' even for a third time.
Now at that time, the nun Sthūlanandā was standing not far from the Venerable Ānanda.
Then the nun Sthūlanandā said this to the venerable Mahākāśyapa:

How much more so, then, would the noble Mahākāśyapa— who was formerly a follower of another sect— think it right to address the noble Ānanda, the sage of Videha, the attendant of the Blessed One, who moves in the presence of the Blessed One and is the recipient of the teachings directly from the Blessed One, with the address "young man" even for a third time?
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda:
"Indeed, Venerable Ānanda, this sister speaks as if she were unaware of her own form.

How much more so, then, could the noble Mahākāśyapa— who was formerly a follower of other sects— not recognize the noble Ānanda, the sage of the Vaidehas, the attendant of the Blessed One, one who dwells in the presence of the Blessed One, and the recipient of the Dharma directly from the Blessed One?"
He thought that he should continue to address him as "young man" even for a third time.
When this had been said, the venerable Ānanda spoke thus to the venerable Mahākāśyapa:
Venerable Mahākāśyapa, you must forgive this; women are foolish, untrained, unskilled, and ignorant of the proper field.
In this manner, up to the third time, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda.
"Indeed, Venerable Ānanda, this sister of yours must have spoken thus because she did not recognize him.
But how could the noble Mahākāśyapa [not know] the noble Ānanda, the sage of Videha, the attendant of the Blessed One?"
He thought that even toward one who dwells in the presence of the Blessed One, who receives the teachings face-to-face, he should address him up to three times as "young man."
For a third time, the venerable Ānanda said this to the venerable Mahākāśyapa:
"Venerable Mahākāśyapa, please forgive this woman; she is a fool, unrefined, unskilled, and ignorant."
When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda:

Indeed, venerable Ānanda, I do not recall ever before my going forth having gone forth and designated another teacher externally, other than that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One.
Indeed, venerable Ānanda, formerly, while I had not yet gone forth, this thought occurred to me: [text continues]
Furthermore, this household life is a confinement, an abode of dust; whereas the life of renunciation is like the open air.
It is not possible for one dwelling at home to practice the holy life (brahmacarya) that is utterly refined, utterly blameless, pure, and utterly pristine.
What if I were now to go forth from the home into the homeless state?
Indeed, venerable Ānanda, having abandoned the non-wasteful life of a householder, I left behind eighty cartloads of gold and bullion,
five hundred male slaves, five hundred female slaves, five hundred head of livestock, five hundred villages and fields,
and nine hundred and ninety-nine excellent golden ploughs from Kāpilavastu; I have now taken up only this single ragged garment of cotton cloth.
Having taken up [this path], I shall go forth following those who are Arhats in the world.
At that time, venerable Ānanda, there was indeed no other Arhat in the world except for that Blessed One, the Truly Self-Awakened One.
And so, venerable Ānanda, having thus gone forth, on the night of the final year, I saw the Blessed One at the Bahuputraka Caitya near Rājagṛha.
Upon seeing him, the perception of non-duality arose in me: "I see the Perfectly Awakened One;
I see the Blessed One alone; I see the All-Knowing One; I see the Blessed One alone; I see the All-Seeing One."
May I see him thus; may I see the Blessed One with his knowledge and vision that are without remainder; may I see the Blessed One alone.
"Indeed, venerable Ānanda, having approached the Blessed One and bowed my head at the Blessed One’s feet, I stood to one side. Standing to one side, venerable Ānanda, I said this to the Blessed One."
The Blessed One is my teacher; I am a disciple, O Sugata.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to me, the venerable Ānanda.
In the same way, Kāśyapa, I am the Teacher and you are my disciple.

For whoever, Kāśyapa, having obtained a disciple endowed with such a state of mind, while being himself only a perfectly awakened one, should claim to be a perfectly awakened one; or while being himself not omniscient, should claim to be omniscient—[he would be like that].
If one who is not all-seeing should claim to be all-seeing, or one who possesses only incomplete knowledge and vision should claim to possess complete knowledge and vision,
his head would split into seven pieces.

Furthermore, Kāśyapa, being indeed a perfectly awakened one (samyaksaṃbuddha), I claim to be a perfectly awakened one; being indeed omniscient (sarvajña), I claim to be omniscient; being indeed all-seeing (sarvadarśāvī), I claim to be all-seeing; being indeed possessed of knowledge and vision without remainder, I claim to be possessed of knowledge and vision without remainder.
"Kāśyapa, I teach the Dharma to my disciples out of direct knowledge, not without direct knowledge; I teach the Dharma to my disciples with its causal basis, not without a causal basis;
I teach the Dharma to my disciples with its miraculous power, not without miraculous power."

"Kāśyapa, I say that for me, who teaches the Dharma to my disciples with direct knowledge rather than without direct knowledge, who teaches the Dharma to my disciples with a causal basis rather than without a causal basis, and who teaches the Dharma to my disciples with miraculous power rather than without miraculous power, exhortation is to be performed and instruction is to be performed."
Therefore, Kāśyapa, you should train yourself in this regard.

But rather, I shall dwell restrained by the Prātimokṣa vows, perfected in conduct and range of activity, seeing danger even in the slightest faults, and training myself by undertaking the rules of training; endowed with pure action of body, speech, and mind, I shall be one whose livelihood is completely purified.
In this way, Kāśyapa, you should train yourself.
Therefore, Kāśyapa, you should train yourself in this way here.

However, thinking, "I shall dwell with the doors of the six sense-faculties guarded," he dwells with mindfulness as protection, mindfulness as constant observation, abiding in equanimity, seeing the danger [of sensual desire], and seeking the way of escape; being wise and endowed with a mind free from passion, having seen a form with the eye, he will neither grasp at its general appearance nor grasp at its secondary details.

"Since covetousness, dejection, and many evil, unwholesome states have entered my mind because I dwell with the faculty of sight unrestrained, I shall practice for their restraint; I shall guard it and attain restraint over the faculty of sight."
In this way, Kāśyapa, you should train yourself.

Having heard sounds with the ear, smelled odors with the nose, tasted flavors with the tongue, touched tangibles with the body, and cognized mental phenomena with the mind, I shall dwell neither grasping at their signs nor grasping at their secondary characteristics. For if I were to dwell with my sense faculties unrestrained, there would arise in me, on that basis, covetousness, dejection, and many other unwholesome states.
"Evil, unwholesome states have entered my mind; I shall practice for their restraint, I shall guard the faculty of the mind, and I shall attain restraint through the faculty of the mind."
In this way, Kāśyapa, you should train yourself.
Therefore, Kāśyapa, one should train oneself in this way here.
"What is my mindfulness directed toward the body, accompanied by happiness, such that I shall not abandon the body constantly and continuously?"
In this way, Kāśyapa, you should train yourself.
Therefore, Kāśyapa, you should train yourself in this way here.
"Whatsoever wholesome qualities I shall master, all that is for the sake of self-taming, tranquility, and final nirvāṇa.
In this way, Kāśyapa, you should train yourself.
Therefore, Kāśyapa, you should train yourself in this way: "How may there arise in me toward the four assemblies an exceeding degree of love, reverence, shame, modesty, and cultivation?"
In this way, Kāśyapa, you should train yourself.
Therefore, Kāśyapa, you should train yourself in this.
But rather, I shall dwell observing the arising and passing away of the five aggregates of clinging:

"This is form, this is the arising of form, this is the passing away of form; this is feeling, this is the arising of feeling, this is the passing away of feeling; this is perception, this is the arising of perception, this is the passing away of perception; these are mental formations..."
"The arising of volitional formations," "the passing away of volitional formations"; "consciousness," "the arising of consciousness," "the passing away of consciousness."
In this way, Kāśyapa, you should train yourself.

Indeed, venerable Ānanda, having been exhorted by the Blessed One with this exhortation, I remained a trainee with further work to do for exactly eight days; on the very ninth day, I attained full realization.
"Venerable Ānanda, after the Blessed One had exhorted me with this exhortation, he rose from his seat and departed."
Indeed, Venerable Ānanda, I followed closely behind the Blessed One as he was walking along.
Venerable Ānanda, as I was following closely behind the Blessed One, this thought occurred to me:
"Oh, let the Blessed One step off the path and stay by the foot of some tree;
I shall prepare for the Blessed One a patched outer robe made of cotton scraps."
Venerable Ānanda, having understood this reflection of my mind, the Blessed One stepped aside from the path and took his stand at the foot of a certain tree.
"Venerable Ānanda, I shall prepare for the Blessed One a saṃghāṭī made of scraps of cotton cloth; may the Blessed One sit upon the seat thus prepared."
Having sat down, O Venerable Ānanda, the Blessed One said this: "Gentle, Kāśyapa, is this outer robe made of tattered cotton rags;
soft, Kāśyapa, is this outer robe made of tattered cotton rags; smooth, Kāśyapa, is this outer robe made of tattered cotton rags."

“Kāśyapa, this robe made of scraps of cotton cloth is pleasant; Kāśyapa, this robe made of scraps of cotton cloth is thin; Kāśyapa, this robe made of scraps of cotton cloth is light; Kāśyapa, this robe made of scraps of cotton cloth is well-made; Kāśyapa, this robe made of scraps of cotton cloth is smooth.”
"Kāśyapa, this robe made of rags from a dust-heap of cotton cloth is beautiful; Kāśyapa, this robe made of rags from a dust-heap of cotton cloth is soft to the touch."
Indeed, venerable Ānanda, I said this to the Blessed One.
"It would be a gain for me, O Blessed One; it would be well-acquired by me, if the Blessed One would accept from me this outer robe made of rags from cotton cloth."
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to me, the venerable Ānanda.
"Do you, moreover, Kāśyapa, wish to wear in the presence of the Tathāgata a saṃghāṭī robe made of hempen rags?"
When this had been said, venerable Ānanda, I spoke thus to the Blessed One.
It would be a great gain for me, Blessed One, a truly well-obtained gain, if the Blessed One would grant me this outer robe made of hempen rags.
"Venerable Ānanda, the Blessed One indeed gave me this outer robe made of hempen rags; Venerable Ānanda, I accept this outer robe made of hempen rags from the Blessed One.

If, Venerable Ānanda, those speaking correctly were to say, 'A disciple of the Blessed One has accepted hempen rags in the presence of the Teacher,' it is precisely so that they would be speaking correctly."
For what reason?
Venerable Ānanda, I am the disciple who, in the presence of the Teacher, was the recipient of robes made of hempen rags.

Ānanda, those who would speak correctly would say: "The son of the Blessed One, born from his very breast, born from his mouth, born of the Dharma, fashioned by the Dharma, an heir to the Dharma and not an heir to material things"—it is in this way that they would speak correctly.
And for what reason?
"Venerable Ānanda, I am the Blessed One’s legitimate son, born from his mouth, born of the Dharma, fashioned by the Dharma, an heir to the Dharma, not an heir to material things."

Venerable Ānanda, he who would think to conceal my three knowledges (*tisro vidyāḥ*), the six superknowledges (*ṣaḍ abhijñāḥ*), and the mastery of powers (*balavaśībhāva*) might as well think to conceal a sixty-year-old elephant with a mere cloth.

Venerable Ānanda, he who would think to conceal my three knowledges, the six superknowledges, and the mastery of powers might as well think to block the current of the river Gaṅgā with a handful of dust.
Venerable Ānanda, he who would think to conceal my three knowledges, the six superknowledges, and the mastery of powers might as well think to bind the wind with a net.
Venerable Ānanda, I think that even space should be made five-fingerbreadths thick by anyone who thinks they can conceal my three knowledges, six superknowledges, and mastery of the powers.
Furthermore, Venerable Ānanda, if among these five hundred monks there should be any doubt or uncertainty regarding me, let him ask a question;
by answering that question, I thus roar this true lion’s roar.
When this had been said, those monks spoke thus to the venerable Mahākāśyapa.

Furthermore, Venerable Mahākāśyapa, if anyone should have any doubt or uncertainty, let that person, Venerable Mahākāśyapa, ask a question; we shall honor him, Venerable Mahākāśyapa, and we shall follow him even further than this, and even more excellently than this.

Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened those monks with a discourse on the Dharma, rose from his seat and departed. Not long after he had left, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa turned his entire body toward the direction of the nun Thūlanaṇdā with the gaze of an elephant, thinking, "Perhaps she might find faith in her heart," even though that [mass of flesh] was as large as a wagon wheel.
The earth shook, yet the nun Sthūlanandā did not develop a clear mind.
With a corrupted mind, the nun Sthūlanandā gave way to malice toward the venerable Mahākāśyapa;
immediately thereafter she passed away, having harbored resentment toward the venerable Mahākāśyapa, and was reborn in a certain [hell].
It is heard that they have been reborn in the great hell.
Thus concludes the Mahākāśyapa-vastu-pravrajyā-sūtra.
Half a yojana from Rājagṛha was a village named Nālandagrāmaka, which was prosperous, flourishing, and wealthy.

There lived a brahmin, a great landowner, who was opulent, possessed of great wealth and vast enjoyments; he had abundant diverse property, an abundance of money, grain, treasuries, and storehouses, an abundance of gold, silver, assets, and implements, an abundance of elephants, horses, oxen, cows, and sheep, and an abundance of female and male slaves, laborers, and servants.

Now, that brahmin mahāśāla had a wife, a brahmin woman named Śārī, who was gracious and beautiful to behold. By that brahmin woman Śārī, he had seven sons: Dharma, Upadharma, Śatadharma, Sahasradharma, Tiṣya, and Upatiṣya. Of these, six were married, while the seventh, Upatiṣya, the youngest, remained unmarried and stayed at the teacher’s house.
He studies the Vedic mantras.
Half a yojana from Rājagṛha was a village named Kolitagrāmaka, which was prosperous, flourishing, wealthy, and crowded with many people.

There also lived a great brahmin householder who was opulent, possessed of great wealth and vast enjoyments; he had abundant riches, grain, treasuries, and granaries; he possessed an abundance of gold, silver, assets, and implements; he had many elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep; and he had numerous female and male slaves, laborers, and servants.
By one of the Maudgalyāyana lineage.
He had a son named Kolita, who was gracious, handsome, wise, skillful, and intelligent;
he was studying the Vedic mantras at that very same school for teachers,
along with Upatiṣya and about five hundred other young brahmin students.

First of all, Kolita and Upatiṣya studied the Vedic mantras and were given their instruction; they served their teacher and offered him their teacher’s fee: an umbrella, sandals, a staff, a water-pot, a wooden bowl, and a hempen garment.
Now those two were friendly, affectionate, and well-disposed toward one another;
Upatiṣya would go from the village of Nālanda to the village of Kolita to see Kolita,
and Kolita would also go from the village of Kolita to the village of Nālanda to see Upatiṣya.
In Rājagṛha, there was being held a festival called Giriyagrasamāja, common to all, for five hundred ascetics.
Now, there were five hundred ascetics with five hundred parks;

all five hundred parks were filled with many thousands of people, where hundreds of spectacles were being held, hundreds of musical performances were underway, and there were hundreds of other actors, dancers, athletes, wrestlers, musicians, clowns, acrobats, and jugglers.

Then those sons of great brahmin householders, Upatiṣya and Kolita, surrounded by four thousand attendants and mounted on horse-drawn chariots yoked with teams of four horses, went to witness the festival at Giriya-gra.

Those beings were endowed with the roots of merit and virtue; they possessed excellent dwellings, had performed meritorious deeds under previous perfectly enlightened Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, and eminent disciples, had planted the seeds of truth and merit, had severed their bonds, and were destined for rebirth in higher realms.
Beings in their final existence who practice the course of causes and conditions for the sake of accomplishing the noble dharmas.
As those two groups were watching that assembly on the mountain peak, the causal condition was revealed through their former roots of merit.
When Śāriputra saw that multitude of people, the perception of impermanence arose in him: "Within a hundred years, through impermanence, this entire multitude of people will no longer exist."

As for Maudgalyāyana, as he too beheld the crowd of people laughing, shouting cries of derision, and showing their rows of teeth, the perception of bones arose within him. Then, seeing Śāriputra with a dejected facial expression, Maudgalyāyana said to him:
The sounds of charming lute strings and songs, resonating with the clear tones of the three-fold musical instruments,
are heard as sweet and delightful.
O venerable one, why is your face so dejected?
This is indeed not the time for one who is joyful to grieve, nor for one who is delighted to feel aversion; abandon your discontent and listen to this like the music of the apsarases.
With a joyful countenance, he was delighted by this delight of men.
Then the young brahmin Śāriputra said this to the young brahmin Maudgalyāyana:
These objects are stained with passion, and objects are both moving and unmoving; what delight can there be for those of childish intellect in worldly existences and material things?
Before long, O Sage, all those who are insatiable and greedy for sensual pleasures will go forth with their limbs scattered, dead, reduced to ashes.
Therefore, Maudgalyāyana, that perception does not delight me; I have no pleasure in it. Rather, my delight is in the vast image cultivated through the intellect.

Indeed, it is the right time to practice the Dharma; for even the Narakas, Kinnaras, Suras, and Asuras who move with ease, though agitated by the pleasures of desire and with insatiable minds, have gone to their destruction.
Even the gods long for him who, having reached the time of intoxication [with worldly life], delights in physical seclusion in the forest; for his practiced conduct is difficult to perform.
May I be one like Śāriputra, whom the discerning praise as being equal toward pleasure and pain, and toward delight and aversion.
Then the young brahmin Śāriputra addressed the young brahmin Maudgalyāyana.
Going forth is my intention; I shall go forth.
Maudgalyāyana said:
Whatever is desired by you is also desired by me; I too shall go forth into the religious life.
Maudgalyāyana said:
Whatever destiny is desired by you is pleasing to us as well;
death together with you is better than life without you.
Now at that time, in the city of Rājagṛha, a wandering mendicant named Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra was residing in a park for wandering mendicants with a retinue of fifty followers.
Then those young brahmin students, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, went to the Wanderers’ Grove and entered the wandering life under Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra, the wanderer.
Within seven days of his ordination, Śāriputra mastered all the treatises of the wanderers; within half a month, Maudgalyāyana also mastered all the treatises of the wanderers.
Then they said:

"This dharma is not conducive to liberation; it does not lead to the destruction of suffering for one who practices it. Let us go our separate ways and seek a well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, wherein the end of suffering is brought about.
Whichever of us first finds such a well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya must inform the other."
Then, together, we shall go forth into homelessness in the noble Dharma and Vinaya.
Having then compiled those wandering mendicants' treatises into a formal collection, they entered Rājagṛha; Śāriputra the wandering mendicant entered by one way, and Maudgalyāyana by another.

Now at that time, the Blessed One, having stayed as long as he pleased in the Yaṣṭīvana park on the slopes of the mountains, arrived at the Bamboo Grove and stayed there in the Kalandakanivāpa of the Bamboo Grove together with a great community of monks, numbering twelve hundred and fifty monks.
Then the venerable Upasena, having dressed early in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, set out for alms in the city of Rājagṛha.

The wanderer Śāriputra saw the venerable Upasena coming from afar, inspiring confidence through his dignified manner of advancing and retreating, looking forward and looking around, drawing in and stretching out [his limbs], and carrying his outer robe, bowl, and inner robes;
like an elephant who has completed its task, with his sense faculties withdrawn within, his mind not wandering outward, established, and having attained the nature of reality (dharmatā).
Looking only a yoke’s length ahead, and seeing this, his mind became exceedingly serene.
Moreover, this conduct of one who has gone forth is excellent;
what if I were now to approach him?

Then the wanderer Śāriputra approached the Venerable Upasena; having exchanged greetings with the Venerable Upasena and engaged in pleasant and courteous conversation, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, the wanderer Śāriputra said this to the Venerable Upasena:
Is it the Teacher, the Blessed One, or a disciple?
When this had been said, the venerable Upasena said this to the wandering ascetic Śāriputra:
"I am a disciple, venerable sir."
When this had been said, the venerable Śāriputra spoke thus to the wanderer Upasena:

"What does your teacher profess? What does he proclaim? Furthermore, how does he teach the Dharma to his disciples? And what kind of instruction and admonition does he frequently exercise toward his disciples?
When this was said, the Venerable Upasena spoke thus to the wanderer Śāriputra:
Having heard little, Venerable Sirs, I would merely speculate upon this matter.
When this had been said, the wandering mendicant Śāriputra spoke thus to the venerable Upasena.
"What business do I have with the letter?
It is the meaning that matters, for one who knows the meaning values the meaning; such a person seeks to accomplish the goal through the meaning."
We too, having grasped this mass of words—a meaningless collection of phrases—for many days, were deceived; we were previously deceived.
When this had been said, the venerable Upasena said this to the wanderer Śāriputra:
"Indeed, Venerable One, it is with reference to dependently arisen phenomena that the Teacher enjoins relinquishment."
Then, while the wandering ascetic Śāriputra remained right there on that spot of earth, the dustless, stainless Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena was purified.

Then indeed, the wanderer Śāriputra— having attained the Dharma, having abandoned [wrong] views, having crossed over doubt, being free from hesitation, with a straight mind, a gentle mind, a pliable mind, inclining toward Nirvāṇa and leaning toward Nirvāṇa— spoke thus to the Venerable Upasena:
"Venerable Upasena, where does the Teacher dwell?
When this was said, the venerable Upasena spoke thus to the wandering mendicant Śāriputra:
The Teacher was at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground in the Bamboo Grove.
Having spoken thus, the venerable Upasena went about for alms in the city of Rājagṛha.
The wanderer Śāriputra approached the wanderer Maudgalyāyana.
The wanderer Maudgalyāyana saw the wanderer Śāriputra coming from afar with a perfectly pure complexion, the color of a lotus, and with serene faculties; and having seen him, he...
He said this to the wandering ascetic Śāriputra:

The complexion of the venerable Śāriputra’s face is completely pure and radiant, and his faculties are serene. Surely, venerable Śāriputra, you have attained the Deathless and the path leading to the Deathless; like a blossomed lotus, your pure face is opened, your faculties are tranquil, and the Deathless has been reached.
In some places, by that [means], you spread out that double-layered, auspicious, and variegated net of light rays.
When this had been said, the wanderer Śāriputra spoke thus to Maudgalyāyana.
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, I have attained the Deathless and the path leading to the Deathless—
that which is heard of in the scriptures as being like the udumbara flower in the forest; the Buddhas,
masses of glory, arise, and now the Light of the World has arisen."
When this had been said, the wanderer Maudgalyāyana spoke thus to the wanderer Śāriputra:
"Venerable Śāriputra, what does the Teacher proclaim? What does he teach?"
When this had been said, the wanderer Śāriputra spoke thus to Maudgalyāyana:
Of those phenomena that arise from causes, the Tathāgata has declared their cause.
And the Great Śramaṇa is one who teaches that their cessation is thus.
Then, while the wandering mendicant Maudgalyāyana remained right there on that spot of earth, the dust-free, stainless Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena became purified.

Then indeed, the wanderer Maudgalyāyana— having attained the Dharma, having abandoned [wrong] views, having crossed over doubt, being free from hesitation, with a mind that was uplifted, gentle, and pliant, inclining toward Nirvāṇa, leaning toward Nirvāṇa, and tending toward Nirvāṇa— [became thus].
Then the wanderer Maudgalyāyana said this to the wanderer Śāriputra:
"Venerable Śāriputra, where does the Teacher reside?"
When this had been said, the wanderer Śāriputra spoke thus to the wanderer Maudgalyāyana:

"Venerable sir, this Teacher is dwelling in the Bamboo Grove at Kalandakanivāpa together with a great community of monks, numbering twelve hundred and fifty. Let us go and inform Sañjayin, and then we shall practice the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One, the Teacher, in the Bamboo Grove."
When this had been said, the wanderer Maudgalyāyana spoke thus to the wanderer Śāriputra:
Go, venerable Śāriputra, from here to the Bamboo Grove; what is the use of seeing Sañjayin with his evil views?
Śāriputra said to him:
"Indeed, venerable Maudgalyāyana, even Sañjayin was of great benefit to us, depending upon whom we went forth from the household life."
Then, having gone to the park of the wandering mendicants, they addressed Sañjayin.
"Let us go, O Blessed One; we shall lead the holy life under the Great Śramaṇa."
When this had been said, Sañjayin the Wanderer spoke thus to the wanderers Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana:
"Sirs, do not practice the holy life under the ascetic Gautama.
Here are my five hundred wandering mendicants; you may share half of their provisions."
They said:
Indeed, we shall not go; we will practice the holy life under the Blessed One, the Great Śramaṇa.
Well-expounded is the Dharma and Vinaya by the Blessed One, with its gates opened and its rags torn away; it is sufficient for one who desires [the goal] through heedfulness.
Then, having addressed Sañjayin, they departed from the wanderers' park toward the Bamboo Grove; those five hundred wanderers also went along with the wanderers Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana.
Sañjayin said to Śāriputra:
No longer taking just one, nor two, nor three, nor four, but rather all five hundred, Upatiṣya sets out, leading them away.
The Blessed One addressed the monks in the Bamboo Grove.

"Prepare seats, monks; these wanderers Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana are coming with a retinue of five hundred, desiring to lead the holy life in the presence of the Tathāgata. They shall become my foremost pair of disciples, a noble pair: one the foremost among those of great wisdom, and the other the foremost among those of great supernormal power."

The wanderer Śāriputra saw the Blessed One approaching from afar in the Bamboo Grove, honored and surrounded by a great assembly, teaching the Dharma— good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and the right phrasing.
He was proclaiming the holy life that is solitary, complete, pure, and pristine;

he was endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man, his body adorned with the eighty minor characteristics, possessed of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, powerful with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and [endowed] with the four grounds of self-confidence.

Confident, with senses calmed and mind at peace, having attained the supreme perfection of self-mastery and tranquility— like a serpent that has performed its duty, with senses withdrawn within, mind not turned outward, well-established, having attained the true nature of reality, upright, looking only a yoke’s length ahead— a guarded serpent with conquered senses, like a lake that is clear, undisturbed, serene, and filled with jeweled pillars.

He appeared as if risen like a golden image, shining like a mass of radiance, blazing with glory like a second rising sun; he was lovely to behold and not disagreeable to look upon— liberated with a liberated retinue, self-disciplined with a disciplined retinue, crossed over with a retinue that has crossed over, reached the further shore with a retinue that has reached the further shore, and established on firm ground with a retinue established on firm ground.

He has attained security and is surrounded by those who have attained security; he is a true ascetic and is surrounded by true ascetics; he has cast out evil and is surrounded by those who have cast out evil;

he is a true brahmin and is surrounded by true brahmins; he is learned in the Vedas and is surrounded by those learned in the Vedas; he is a bath-graduate and is surrounded by bath-graduates; he has cast out the defilements of unrighteousness and is surrounded by those who have cast out the defilements of unrighteousness.
Then indeed, the wanderers Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred, approached the Blessed One, bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the wanderer Śāriputra said this to the Blessed One:
We dwelt in the waters of the ocean; we dwelt in mountain caves and forest groves;
but because of not seeing you, O Sage, we have long dwelt among false teachers.

Having turned back from the wrong path, they have become serene on the true path; O Great Caravan Leader, having crossed over that wilderness of saṃsāra, those wise ones, being dispassionate, do not become attached again.
Then indeed, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, the wandering mendicants, said this to the Blessed One.
May the Blessed One let me go forth; may the Sugata ordain me.
Then the Blessed One addressed the five hundred wandering mendicants, headed by Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, with the call: "Come, monks!"
Come, monks, lead the holy life under the Tathāgata.

Now, as soon as they had been addressed by the Blessed One with the words "Come, monk," whatever marks of a wandering ascetic, whatever secret signs of a wandering ascetic, whatever banners of a wandering ascetic, and whatever accoutrements of a wandering ascetic they possessed all vanished completely; the three robes appeared upon them, along with sumbhaka bowls and hair established in its natural state, and their deportment became established just like that of [the other monks].
This is the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk for these five hundred venerable ones, headed by Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, who have been ordained for a hundred years.
Then, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One in this way:

"Bhagavān, what is it that, when being designated, is designated? What is it that, while persisting, persists? What is it that, when being broken up, is broken up? What is it that, when reconnecting, reconnects?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Śāriputra:

Śāriputra, when the four elements are being designated, they are designated as "the four elements"; while the four elements persist, they persist; when the four elements are being broken apart, they are broken apart; and when the four elements are reconnecting, they reconnect.
When this had been said, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One in this way:
"Blessed One, with what as its condition does it persist? With what as its condition is it broken? With what as its condition does it reconnect? And with what as its condition does it not reconnect?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Śāriputra:
“With what as its condition does it arise, Śāriputra? “With blame as its condition, with craving as its condition, with karma as its condition, and with this as its condition, Śāriputra, it arises.”
With what as its condition, Śāriputra, does it abide?
Śāriputra, it remains conditioned by the karma of lifespan and conditioned by food.
"Śāriputra, with what as its condition does it break?"
Through the exhaustion of the life-span, through the exhaustion of karma, and through the cessation of food, Śāriputra, this [body] breaks apart due to these conditions.
With what as its condition, Śāriputra, does one link up [in rebirth]?
Because ignorance has not been abandoned and because one is under the sway of craving, his karma becomes ripened; Śāriputra, through this condition, there is a rebirth-linking.
"By what condition, Śāriputra, does one not undergo rebirth?
"Because ignorance has been abandoned and craving has been brought to an end, karma no longer ripens for him; by this condition, Śāriputra, one does not undergo rebirth."
Śāriputra, when the internal sense-base of the eye is unimpaired and the external sense-base of forms comes into the range of vision,

there arises from that cause a delightful and refreshing state that gives rise to joy, happiness, and mental ease, and it gladdens the faculties. Śāriputra, those phenomena which arise dependently in this way give rise to joy, happiness, and mental ease, and they gladden the faculties.

Śāriputra, those phenomena as well are born, become, conditioned, felt, and dependently originated; they are neither self nor belonging to a self; they are empty of a self or of anything belonging to a self.
Thus, elsewhere it is likewise: both action and the maturation of action, as well as the cause and the phenomena arisen from the cause.
In the same way, Śāriputra, when the internal sense-bases— the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind— are unimpaired, and external phenomena come into the range of the mind,
there arises for him, based on that cause, a pleasant and gratifying state accompanied by joy and mental ease, which gladdens his faculties.

Śāriputra, those phenomena which, arising dependently, produce joy, bliss, and mental ease, and which gladden the faculties—those phenomena, Śāriputra, are born, become, conditioned, felt, and dependently originated; they are neither self nor belonging to a self; they are empty of a self or of anything belonging to a self.
Thus, in this way, elsewhere there is both action and the ripening of action, as well as causes and the phenomena arisen from causes.

The Blessed One spoke this. While this exposition was being delivered, the minds of all those hundreds of monks, headed by Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging.

And the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having been ordained for seven days, attained the power of psychic transformation and mastery over psychic transformation, and realized the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).

The Venerable Śāriputra, having gone forth for half a month and received full ordination for half a month, attained mastery over the higher knowledges and the perfection of wisdom, and realized the four analytical insights.

The Venerable Maudgalyāyana, having recently gone forth and recently received full ordination, realized the three knowledges: the divine eye, recollection of past lives, and the destruction of the outflows.
Thus this is heard.
The Sūtra of the Wanderer Dīrghanakha should be composed.
The monks said to the Blessed One:

Behold, Blessed One, how the Blessed One, having turned back the five hundred bhikṣus headed by the venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana from the harsh views of the wanderer Sañjayin, has delivered them from the dense wilderness of the cycle of birth, old age, and death that is without beginning or end.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now that these five hundred monks, headed by Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana,
have been turned away from the harsh views of the wanderer Sañjayin and delivered from the dense wilderness of the cycle of birth, old age, and death, which has no beginning or end."

On another occasion as well, these [beings] were rescued by me from the hands of the rākṣasīs on that dreadful island of rākṣasīs; having been brought safely across the great ocean, they were established back in Jambudvīpa.
The monks said.
At another time as well, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
On another occasion also, monks.
Once upon a time, monks, in the past, five hundred merchants from Jambudvīpa set out upon the great ocean in a sea-going vessel for the sake of wealth.
When their ship had gone into the middle of the ocean, it was wrecked by a *makara*, a species of sea-monster.
Now, with that ship having foundered, they paid homage to whichever god they were devoted to among the gods of gods:
some paid homage to Śiva, some paid homage to Vaiśravaṇa, some to Skanda, some to Varuṇa, some to Yama,
some to Kuvera, some to Śakra, some to Brahmā, and some paid homage to the ten directions.
So that we may cross over from this great ocean alive.
Now, when that ship had wrecked, they fell into the middle of the ocean taking various kinds of floats; some took a jar, some a plank, and some a series of gourds.
Some, having deprived one another of life, clung to that corpse; for the great ocean does not dwell together with a dead corpse, but rather quickly casts that corpse onto dry land or an island.
Then we too shall cross over to an island or to dry land together with this corpse.
Then those merchants, while floating upon that great ocean, were cast by the wind onto the island of the rākṣasīs.

There on that island of rākṣasīs, they see thousands of various kinds of trees. And in whatever way they are driven toward that shore by the wind, there they see hundreds of charming and beautiful women wandering about, dressed in garments dyed in various colors, adorned with ornaments, and wearing jeweled earrings.

Having manifested many hundreds of rākṣasīs in human form— some with the appearance of young brides, some with the appearance of women who have recently given birth, and some with the appearance of middle-aged women—
they descended into the ocean and seized each merchant one by one.

"Welcome, noble sons! You shall be husbands to us who are husbandless; you shall be protectors to us who are protectorless; you shall be kinsmen to us who have no kin. You are our masters, for we have all met with disaster and calamity at sea due to the failure of our ship.
Surely the Lord of the Waters has been gracious to us, since you have brought us to this island."
Having placed those merchants upon their shoulders, they brought them out from the sea and, having established them on dry land,
they comforted those merchants.

"Noble sons, do not grieve; do not despair! Noble sons, you have reached the great jewel-island, which possesses abundant jewels, infinite jewels, abundant food and drink, abundant flowers and fruits, abundant perfumes, garlands, and ointments, abundant clothing, and abundant rugs and coverings."
"Here, noble sons, playing, sporting, and enjoying yourselves, drinking honeyed wine and liquor, you experience pleasures with your backs turned toward the perception of danger."
Then those merchants said:
Be patient for a moment while we dispel our grief.
Then all those five hundred merchants, having departed from the presence of those women to a secluded place, went aside and wept, grieved, and lamented.
"Alas, mother! Alas, father! Alas, son! Alas, brother! Alas, sister! Alas, Citra-Jambudvīpa! Alas, my excellent park!"

Having wept, lamented, and wailed, and having consoled one another, they each clung to their own wives. Together with those women, they reached a great forest grove endowed with every kind of flower and fruit, by way of a magnificent path— covered in green grass, cleared of weeds, thorns, and stumps, free from pebbles and gravel, dustless, level, and even.
In that forest grove there are flowers of various kinds, fragrant and sweet-scented, belonging to all seasons and available at all times;

in that forest grove there are various kinds of leaf-powders endowed with fragrance and flavor, resembling fine honey; and there are ponds and lotus-pools of pleasant water, resounding with the cries of swans and ducks, and covered with blue, red, white, and yellow lotuses.
