Then, having emerged from that forest, they beheld the dwellings of those rākṣasīs—lofty, magnificent, white and pale, resembling snow; adorned with turrets, lion-ventilators, windows, and lattices like stars and the moon; and they saw the city of the rākṣasīs, which was like the palace of Vaiśravaṇa.
Then those merchants were led by those rākṣasīs into their respective dwellings on the island, which resembled divine celestial palaces.

Then those merchants saw in those abodes of the rākṣasīs couches well-prepared, with woolen rugs spread over them, covered with white cloth, having red pillows at both ends, made of gold, silver, and ivory.

There were exercise halls, delightful with their locations in the Aśoka grove and endowed with all kinds of flowers and fruits; and there were excellently prepared arrangements for food, drink, and meals, which were most charming.

Then, having had them seated upon auspicious thrones made of jewels, their hair and beards were trimmed by barbers; they were made to exercise in training halls, bathed in bathing halls, and once their limbs were washed and polished, their bodies were anointed with red sandalwood and kālānusāra paste, dressed in costly garments, and adorned with excellent garlands.
Adorned and most costly cushions filled with cotton were presented; fresh and exquisite foods, both hard and soft, were presented; various kinds of condiments were presented;
and various kinds of meats—exquisite in sugar, salt, sweetness, bitterness, pungency, and astringency—were presented.
Namely: pork, fish, partridge meat, quail meat, francolin meat, pheasant meat, and venison.

And they delighted them in various kinds of dance, song, and instrumental music; others played upon mṛdaṅga drums, āliṅga drums, sindhava drums, paṇava drums, ekādaśika drums, vīṇā lutes, nakulaka drums, sughoṣa drums, bhāṇḍaka drums, and veṇuka flutes.
But others sang sweetly.

When those rākṣasīs knew that the merchants had become fully confident, thinking, "These men are ours," they showed them their vast treasuries of jewels. They prepared excellent and choice food for the noble sons and arranged sweet seats for them.

"May the noble sons enjoy themselves here on this Jewel Island like the sons of the gods in the Nandana grove; nevertheless, even though the noble sons are heedless, they must not go by the road to the south of the city."
Then, monks, it occurred to the caravan leader among those five hundred merchants, who was wise and possessed of discernment:
"Why indeed are these women blocking our path from the south of the city?
Let me now find out what is there to the south of the city and how it is."
Then, monks, the caravan leader, perceiving that the women were either asleep or intoxicated and heedless, took his sword-belt, departed from the city, and followed that southern road.
As he went along, he saw a shelter in the sky and a great terror, and he heard the sound of many men crying out.
Then, following that sound of the men, he saw an iron city surrounded by a copper wall.
Now, searching for the gate of that city, he circumambulated it on all sides, yet he did not see that gate; however, he heard the sound of many men shouting.

Crying out, "Alas, mother! they wailed; crying out, "Alas, father! they wailed; crying out, "Alas, son! they wailed; crying out, "Alas, brother! they wailed; crying out, "Alas, sister! they wailed; crying out, "Alas, the best of gardens of Jambudvīpa! they wailed.
Hearing that sound and approaching that city, he saw on the northern side of the city, clinging to the wall, a tall *śirīṣa* tree.
Having then climbed that *śirīṣa* tree, he saw hundreds of men in the city who were fasting and whose hair, nails, and beards were long.
Clad in rags of putrid cloth, their skin and flesh scorched by the wind, blackened and filthy with soiled hair, they are overcome by hunger and thirst;
with their fingernails they dig the earth for water, but being dragged up from the ground by their weakness, they fall back down again onto the earth.
Then, hearing the sound of the branches, leaves, and foliage of that śirīṣa tree, they all stood up with their hands joined in reverent salutation.
"Who are you, noble son—whether a god, a nāga, a kinnara, a gandharva, a yakṣa, or a kumbhāṇḍa? We have gone to you for refuge.
Release us from this painful bondage; may I once again dwell in my own country and be reunited with my friends and kinsmen."
Then indeed, that caravan leader, having gone to the *śirīṣa* tree with eyes filled with tears, spoke thus to those merchants:

"I am neither a god, nor a yakṣa, nor a kinnara, nor a gandharva, nor Śakra, nor Brahmā, nor Virūḍhaka the Great King. We too, for the sake of wealth, had set out from Jambudvīpa by ship and entered the ocean; our ship was wrecked, and hundreds of merchants were rescued by these women."
Then they play, sport, and enjoy themselves together with us; and whatever is unpleasant to them, we do not do, nor do they desire to do anything unpleasant to us.
Then those merchants from within said:

"Venerable sir, we too set out from Jambūdvīpa on a ship for the sake of wealth and plunged into the ocean. When we had gone into the midst of the sea, our ship was wrecked. Then I was rescued by these women; five hundred merchants, like us, also sport, enjoy themselves, and take their pleasure with them, just as you do now.
When your ship was wrecked and cast by the wind toward the island of the rākṣasīs, then it was by these [women]..."
When you were seen by the rākṣasīs, they devoured two hundred and fifty of us five hundred merchants;
even those children who were born from our loins were devoured by them, and we remaining two hundred and fifty merchants have been cast here into this city of copper.
These, worthy sir, are not human women; they are rākṣasīs.

Then the caravan leader, having gone to the *śirīṣa* tree and heard those words of the inner merchants who had been cast into the copper city, became afraid, terrified, and agitated; joining his palms in reverence, he asked:
"Tell me what means there is so that I may be safely released from the presence of those rākṣasīs."
Then they said:

On the full moon day of the month of Kārttika, a king of horses named Keśī, having consumed uncultivated and unsown *śāli* rice—free from husks and powder, consisting of fragrant grains—from the continent of Uttarakuru, came here to this island of rākṣasīs; having arrived, he uttered a sound three times in a human voice:
"Who wishes to go to the further shore of the great ocean? I shall ferry you across in safety."
Take refuge in that king of horses;
he will lead you from this island of ogresses to the further shore of the ocean.
Of those five hundred merchants, whoever shall hold onto the tail of that king of horses,
or onto any other part of its limbs, and who shall also hold onto one another among those men, they will cling to its great back and,
by the hundreds or thousands, will gradually reach Jambudvīpa.
This is the means for you to go safely from this island of rākṣasīs to Jambudvīpa; there is no other.
Then that caravan leader spoke to those merchants who had been detained.
"Come, all of you as well; we shall go to Jambudvīpa.
In that case, either leap over the city wall or dig beneath it."
They said this to him.
"You do not know what the city of the rākṣasīs is like; therefore, we will not be able to leap over it.
But if you wish, you may flee, and in that way there will be liberation for you.
However, if you are now cast into the Copper City, there will be no liberation for you."
"Go in safety to your own country. In such-and-such a city, there are our paternal kinsmen; having inquired after them in our name, you should say to them: 'Give gifts, perform meritorious deeds!

Even with a broken potsherd, wander for alms from house to house and live in Jambudvīpa; do not descend upon the ocean again, where you would endure such sufferings as these, or else maintain your livelihood by performing the service of others. "And do not [do so]!"
Set your minds on crossing the ocean, wherein such sufferings as these exist.
Then he said:
"O noble one, I shall go by myself before the ogress wakes up; let her not know of my arrival here."
Then that caravan leader descended from that śirīṣa tree, while those merchants from within cried out, "We have been devoured by rākṣasīs! Avidhāvidhā! and "This is our last sight of our kinsmen!"
Then that caravan leader, having descended from that śirīṣa tree and gone by the path he had come, lay down there upon the bed of the rākṣasī.
Having gone there to his bed, he reflects.

"How can I bring this matter to the attention of these merchants so that they will understand it exactly as I have seen and heard it myself, yet without the rākṣasīs becoming aware of it, and so that this urgent task may be accomplished?"
If I were to inform these merchants of this matter right now, before the king of horses has even arrived,
then one or another of these five hundred merchants— whether distracted or intoxicated—
might tell the rākṣasīs; consequently, it would lead to regret, and we would all fall into misfortune and calamity through this error.
In this regard, the wise praise those for whom whatever secret has been disclosed; rare are those virtuous persons who are able to keep a secret.
"What if I were to keep this secret myself until the Kaumudī Cāturmāsī festival? Then, having arrived at this island of rākṣasīs with the king of horses, I shall explain this danger.
Thereupon, he kept that secret within his own heart and did not tell anyone until the Kaumudī Cāturmāsī.
The Kaumudī festival had arrived, and the king of horses reached the island of the rākṣasīs;
then the caravan leader informed those five hundred merchants.

"Do not be negligent today, whether with regard to women, or food and drink, or song and music. There is a certain matter of some importance that you must hear from me. There is a certain secluded place; all of you go there together once those women have fallen asleep."
Then all those hundreds of merchants, while those women were sleeping there in a secluded place, gathered together; having assembled, they questioned that caravan leader.
"Speak, O caravan leader, whatever you have seen or heard."
The caravan leader explained to those merchants their entire current situation.
"This thought arose in my mind: 'Why do these women ward off us from the southern road of our city?
Then, out of great curiosity, he took up a sword-leaf and went along the southern road of the city while his wife was sleeping.
There I saw a city made of copper that was gateless; I did not see any gate to it, yet I heard the sound of many people wailing.
Thus, while circumambulating that city clockwise,
he saw a tall śirīṣa tree on the northern side of that city.
Having climbed that śirīṣa tree, I looked down upon that city.
And there I saw many hundreds of merchants imprisoned, withered, their skin and flesh scorched by wind and sun until they were covered in a network of veins;
they were dark-skinned with filthy hair, and overcome by hunger and thirst, they were scratching the ground with their fingernails for the sake of water.
Furthermore, hundreds of skeletons were seen scattered and strewn about in the ten directions.
And there, such-and-such a merchant from such-and-such a city and such-and-such a merchant [arrived]; all those merchants indeed came, and it was announced to those merchants.
Those who lived there, remaining as the remnants after being devoured by the rākṣasīs, as well as another two hundred and fifty merchants who had been eaten by these rākṣasīs—[all were gone].
Therefore, none of these are human; they are all rākṣasīs.
If we do not make an effort to return to our own country, then all of us will likewise fall into calamity through this host of rākṣasīs.

If you desire liberation from the hands of the rākṣasīs and a safe journey to Jambudvīpa, [know that] Keśin, the king of horses, having eaten the rice grown without plowing or sowing in Uttarakurudvīpa— rice that is free of husks and powder, with fragrant grains— will come here to Rākṣasīdvīpa on the full moon day of the month of Kārttika, standing upon the shore of the ocean on the northern side of this Rākṣasīdvīpa.
"Who is it that proclaims, 'I am one who goes to the further shore'?
Therefore, let us go there to the presence of the king of horses;
he will bring us safely to our own country."
Then those five hundred merchants, together with the caravan leader, went to the northern side of the city of the rākṣasīs.
There they saw Keśin, the king of horses, standing on the seashore, having raised his neck and crying out, "Who is going to the other shore?"
Then all those five hundred merchants, with their hands joined in reverential salutation, approached Keśin, the king of horses.
O Greatly Compassionate One, we have come to you for refuge; please ferry us across, for you have reached the further shore.
Then that king of horses gave instructions to those merchants.
At the moment when I take you from this island of rākṣasīs and, having uttered the sound "hīṣ" three times, set out through the path of the birds,
then those rākṣasīs who have children— whether boys or girls— will come bringing them with them and will lament most piteously, saying: "Noble sons, do not abandon us at the word of another!"
And do not abandon this delightful jewel-island, which abounds in jewels and possesses infinite treasures.

Therefore, you must not place trust in the words of those rākṣasīs; and whoever among you places trust in their words will become full of longing, thinking, "This is my wife," "This is my son," "This is my daughter," and they will once again fall under the power of the rākṣasīs and fall to the ground behind me.
And those who do not believe the words of those rākṣasīs, thinking, "This is not my wife; this is not my son;
this is not my daughter," and those who remain indifferent—they, though clinging to me as a child, will go safely to Jambudvīpa.
Thus, monks, that horse-king Keśin, having instructed those hundreds of merchants and having neighed three times, set out through the path of the sky, taking the entire caravan with him.
Hearing the neighing sound of that horse-king Keśin, those rākṣasīs came, each bringing her own sons and daughters, saying:
"Noble sirs, do not abandon us on the word of another; do not abandon this delightful Jewel Island, which abounds in many jewels and infinite treasures."

Monks, those among the merchants who had felt attachment toward the rākṣasīs fell to the earth behind them; however, those who were free from attachment reached Jambudvīpa safely from the island of the rākṣasīs.
"Furthermore, monks, it might occur to you that at that time, on that occasion, the horse-king Keśin was someone else.
It should not be viewed in this way. For what reason? [Because he was I myself]."
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, I was Keśin, the king of horses.
"Furthermore, monks, it might occur to you that at that time and on that occasion those five hundred merchants were someone else.
But it should not be viewed in this way. And why is that?"
Monks, those five hundred merchants at that time and on that occasion were these very ones.
Even then, having rescued these people from that dreadful island of rākṣasīs and having safely ferried them across the great ocean, I established them in Jambudvīpa;

and now as well, having turned them back from their dreadful wrong views, I have delivered them from the dense wilderness of the saṃsāra of birth, old age, and death, which is without beginning or end.
Having generated a sense of spiritual urgency and stirred the mind,
listen with one-pointed attention and a perfectly serene heart.
Listen with a serene mind to the former life of the Blessed One, which is endowed with the Dharma and its meaning, and which produces horripilation in those who have faith.
Then at that time, I was the king of horses, a possessor of compassion;
I rescued the companies of merchants from the salt waters and the island of the rākṣasīs.
Now at that time, a group of merchants had approached the ocean,
which was garlanded with waves and crested with billows and possessed many jewels, for the sake of wealth.
Then that ship was shattered by a sea-monster in the salt waters;
it was driven on with great speed by the wind from the wings of a Garuḍa.
As that [treasure] is being scattered, they cry out with cries of distress in the midst of the ocean;
and they pay homage to the gods, each according to their own particular inclination.
Some [saw] Śiva, some Vaiśravaṇa, Skanda, Yama, and Kuvera;
others [saw] the Thousand-eyed One, Virūḍhaka, and others [the guardians of] the directions.
And for their sake, there were requisites in the bowl;
having taken them, they plunged into the salt-water ocean.
Some took rows of bottle gourds, others again planks made of *simbalī* wood;
others took fences, and still others heaps of cotton.
Another, having slain another, clings [to him] for the sake of his own life;
for the ocean does not dwell for a single night with a dead corpse.
While they were drifting there that night upon the salt waters of the ocean,
they then beheld on the shore the most excellent trees growing along the coast.
As they reach the shore accordingly, they behold hundreds of young women who resemble celestial damsels, clothed in garments of red silk.
Some resemble maidens, while others shine like newlywed brides;
with their heads adorned with choice garlands and wreaths, their faces graced by earrings blazing like Jāmbūnada gold,
and their eyes resembling tawny honey, they all shine upon the riverbank.
And having plunged into the water, they uttered words both piteous and sweet:
"O Noble Sons, do not depart so hastily, you who are the protectors of the protectorless!"
For us, who are without husbands, without kinsmen, and dwelling in the forest,
the cloud must surely have been gracious, since it has brought you to the shore.
Taking her by the shoulders, they lifted her up from the water one after another;
and they consoled her many times, saying, "Noble lady, you must not despair."
Dwell with us, O noble sons, together with these women; do not despair, even if you must abandon beloved kinsmen, friends, fathers, and sons.
Now, O hosts of gods, take your delight with us in the Nandana grove;
drinking honeyed liquor, enjoy the supreme pleasures of this island.
With eyes filled with tears, they said to that woman on the surge of the ocean:
"Wait for a brief moment while we dispel our grief."
Having gone not very far, those merchants met together;
they were comforted, yet they wept and wailed like those afflicted by separation.
Alas, mother! Alas, father! Alas, sons! Alas, my own beautiful homeland! Alas, Jambudvīpa! Alas, the most excellent gardens! Alas, the delightful [places]!
Happy indeed are those who, having once been united with their kinsmen and relatives,
shall dwell for a single night and then bring about the destruction of the body.
Is it possible, in the midst of the supportless salt-water ocean,
for those who are mindful of their karma and free from sorrow to dwell?
Having wept, cried out, and consoled one another,
they went to their delightful dwellings.
Having traversed the earth where deer-grass grows lushly, which is free from stones, pebbles, and gravel, and which is dustless, level, and even, they enter the forest.
It was filled with various trees—Aśoka, Atimukta, Campaka, Priyaṅgu, and Śāla; Tilaka, Vakula, and Kulavaka; and dense thickets of Puṃnāga and Tālīsa.
And here there are flowering *karīra* trees, as well as *kulattha*, *karamarda*, and *jīvaka* creepers;
there are delicate *navamālikā* vines, and groves of *pāṭala* and *kareṇuka* trees.
The seasonal grove was filled with *kārī*, *navamālikā*, and *mallikā* jasmine, as well as *priyaṅgu*;
it was beautifully adorned with various shrubs of *kupya*, annual *mallikā*, and *madagandhikā*.
Adorned with *sāra* and *tāra* flowers, and endowed with *campaka* blossoms,
it was set ablaze with red and yellow *aśoka* flowers.
The Suyāmas, far more beautiful than their own bodies, further adorn that excellent forest, which is graced by mango, karṇikāra, kuravaka, tilaka, and vakula trees.
There are *puṣpa* trees, *nāga* trees, *bhavya*, *pālevata*, *pippala*, and *kapittha* trees;
there are *mrotaka* and *saptaparṇa* trees, as well as the beautiful groves of *mucilinda*.
Campaka trees are in full bloom at their edges, and mango groves are covered in blossoms;
various trees are flowering, resonant with the songs of honey-bees and bumblebees.
The wood-apple, coconut, plantain, breadfruit, palmyra, and date-palm;
the citron and the citron-tree—none of these were seen for any length of time.
The akṣoḍa, tamāla, mocā, kiṃśuka, mṛdvīkā, bhavyā,
and pomegranate trees were never not to be seen at any time.
Some have their flower-tips bent down; others are ripe and withered;
still others have their branches in clusters, and they are not seen at any time.
And these and other flowers, blooming upon the best of trees,
belong to all seasons and are seen at no time whatsoever.
In that excellent grove, there are lotus ponds with pleasant waters, resounding with the cries of swans and cranes;
they are covered with red and blue lotuses, and others are likewise delightful to the eye.
Then some, adorned with black garments and beautiful blue tunics,
emerging from the water, dispel the long-standing sorrow.
And by those rows of forests, the flowering lotus ponds are beautified;
they dispel even greater sorrow and the destruction of the vehicle.
Having emerged from that excellent forest, they then beheld the dwellings of the rākṣasīs, which resembled masses of snow and were like the palaces of the gods with their apsarases.
Polished by friction, like the palace of Vāsava in the celestial realm of Maru,
the mansions of the rākṣasīs stand situated at the very summit of the sky.
With its balconies, lion-arches, windows, stars, and crescent moons, that most excellent city, the city of the rākṣasīs, appeared exceedingly beautiful.
Then, for those who had entered there and were seated upon great, magnificent thrones,
they brought forth bathing water for them whose nails, hair, and beards had been trimmed.
To those who have undertaken ritual bathing, who are adorned and wearing the *varadamudrā*,
they offer food provided with many flavors and condiments.
There were many wild boars, fish, buffaloes, kids, rams, chickens, peacocks, partridges, quails, water-fowl, francolins, and cranes as well.
There, those who understand [the instruments] play the mṛdaṅga, the āliṅga, the saindhava,
the paṇava, the eleventh, the vīṇā, and the vallakiguṇaka.
Some played the vallakī, tūlā, nakulakā, parivādinī, gomukhī, and even the flute; others played various instruments, while still others sang sweetly.
Knowing her to be trusting, they showed her excellent gardens,
as well as abundant jewels and the provision of beds, seats, and food.
May you and we both take delight in this, like the hosts of Maruts in the Nandana grove;
however, those who are heedless must not go upon the southern path.
The caravan leader among them, who is wise, skillful, and intelligent—
sitting alone in seclusion, what indeed is he preventing from the path?
"What if I were now to take a sword and, while Sahasopinī is asleep,
lead her to that path to the south of the city?"
While she was fast asleep,
he took his sword and went toward that narrow path to the south of the city.
Just as he proceeds along the path, he hears from afar a loud shout;
following that sound, he then beholds a city made of copper.
Having arrived, he searched everywhere for a door but did not see any;
yet he heard the sound of many people coming out.
"Alas, mother! Alas, father! Alas, sons! Alas, my beloved native land! Alas, Jambudvīpa! Alas, the excellent gardens!"... [and so forth].
Happy indeed are those who, having gathered with their kinsmen and relatives,
shall dwell for a single night and then bring about the destruction of the body.
How can we, while performing our duties with the mind, bring about the destruction of the body in the midst of the salt-water ocean which is without support?
Now, hearing those lamentations, the one of excellent wisdom and keen intellect looked up at a tall *śirīṣa* tree to the north of the city.
Having climbed that śirīṣa tree, he saw hundreds of men in the city who were fasting for a month,
with their nails, hair, and beards grown long.
Their limbs were covered with visible veins, their skin and flesh scorched by wind and sun;
they wore tattered, putrid rags, were tormented by thirst, and had filthy hair.
Some, for the sake of water, scratch the ground with their nails;
they rise up, they fall, and having fallen, they writhe upon this earth.
Having seen other skeletons scattered and strewn in all directions,
he remained seated upon the tree, established and composed in meditative concentration.
Having perceived that the leaves of that śirīṣa tree were being shaken by the wind,
and having beheld that best of trees, they all stood with palms joined in reverence.
"Who are you, noble son? Are you a god, a nāga, a garuḍa, a guhyaka, or a suvarṇa? Or perhaps you are the thousand-eyed Virūḍhaka, or some other yakṣa?"
Save us who are deeply afflicted; let there be compassion for you, O bull among men!
May these living beings once again find their own country and beloved kin.
With eyes filled with tears, the merchant Śirīṣagata replied:
"Noble son, I am neither a god, nor a nāga, nor a garuḍa, nor a guhyaka, nor a suvarṇa."
I am neither the thousand-eyed Indra, nor Virūḍhaka, nor even a yakṣa.
We noble ones have plunged into the lord of waters for the sake of wealth;
our ship was wrecked, and we were rescued by women.
They respond to me properly, like mothers to their sons who desire to serve them; those women do not wish for what is unpleasant, nor do they ever cause me displeasure.
Having heard these terrifying words, the merchants said this:
"We too have descended from Jambudvīpa into the lord of waters."
We have become divided in our vehicles; we have been led astray by women.
May they treat us properly, O worthy sirs, just as you do.
Of the five hundred merchants who were rescued by these [beings], only two hundred and fifty remained here; the others were devoured.
Even those sons of mine who were young children, sweet-voiced, they too have been devoured by these women, O noble sir, out of their greed for flesh.
"O worthy one, these are not human women; they are terrifying rākṣasīs.
Bearing swords as their girdles and hearts [of malice], these are rākṣasīs in the form of human women."
Then the merchant became even more deeply agitated;
that wise man questioned her about how one might escape from the island of the rākṣasīs.
"Come now, worthy sir, tell us how our liberation will come about;
how may we pass safely through this terrible time that ends our lives?"
And those who were well-wishers and compassionate told him exactly what they had seen and heard regarding the escape from the island of the rākṣasīs.
In the month of Kārttika, on the full moon day of Kaumudī,
the swift horse Valāha, the best of steeds with beautiful mane, will arrive.
With limbs gradually beautiful, a pure body, and fragrant, he was one who had shaken off his impurities;
powerful and endowed with speed, equal to the swiftness of the wind, he moved like the wind itself.
With a head like a crow’s and lotus-like eyes, he was born from the lineage of Vālāha;
resembling a peak of the Himavat mountains, his voice resounded like the drum of thundering clouds.
Having eaten the rice-grains grown on his own land— free from husk and free from powder—
he remained on the shore of the ocean, in the northern part of the city of the rākṣasīs.
Lifting up his noble head, the king of horses spoke these words:
"Who among you will go to the further shore of the salt-water ocean?"
Whom shall I lead to safety? Whose word shall be fulfilled for me?
Come to him for refuge; he will lead you safely to the further shore.
"Come here, worthy ones; you too must approach the city called Hayasāhvaya, the iron city, the copper one, and leap over the city of the rākṣasīs.
Then, dig from below, and from there you shall go in safety."
"Come now, friend, you do not know that even when they leap over it, it grows;
even when they dig into it, this city made of copper remains firm."
"O worthy one, there is no liberation for us from this state, bound as we are by our own karma; we have been dragged down from Jambudvīpa by the actions we ourselves have committed."
Sent by the messengers of Yama from your own minds, you have now received the command of Yama:
"Go now to your own homes with heedfulness."
And let your kinsmen say to you: "Give gifts, O worthy ones!
Let not the thought arise in you to plunge into the ocean."
Even if one begs from house to house with a broken bowl,
living together with one's own kin is not such a suffering as this.
Not having one's requests granted, nor being sent on errands,
nor living together with one's own kin— none of these constitute such suffering as this.
Come now, worthy sir, I shall depart before she awakens,
lest this cunning woman, having come here, should discover my stratagem and my manly prowess.
And as he was climbing down, he cried out, "Avidhāvidhā!";
having brought his own country to mind, he was pierced again by the arrow.
Having descended with his caravan and traveled back along the path by which he had come,
he lay down and fell asleep upon a seat made of *sahasopinī* grass.
And there he reflected: "How may I awaken the merchants?
These rogues do not understand this matter as it truly is."
The wise do not praise one who reveals what is secret;
those who are intoxicated or heedless may prattle, and such talk leads to regret.
And like a drop of oil, it expands when illuminated; that secret mantra... [is revealed].
Those men who can determine what is beneficial and what is harmful are difficult to find;
therefore, I shall surely keep this secret myself until the full moon.
Then, when the month of Jyeṣṭha had arrived and the time for the Horse Sacrifice (Aśvamedha) had come, I spoke to them.
The merchant companions said: "You must not be negligent;
regarding women, food, and drink, you shall have only as much as is necessary for your purpose."
When that day had passed,
all those merchants went to that secluded place while the women were still fast asleep.
And having gathered there, the merchants asked him:
"Noble sir, please tell us this matter exactly as it was seen and heard by you."
And he, seeking their welfare and full of compassion,
related to them exactly what he had seen and heard regarding the escape from the island of the rākṣasīs.
Then the merchants said: "All of these are a host of rākṣasīs;
[this is] Asipaṭṭahṛdayā..."
...in the northern part of the city of the rākṣasīs.
Standing on the shore of the ocean, the king of horses spoke these words:
"Who among you will go to the further shore of this salt-water sea?"
Whom shall I lead to safety? For whom among us shall my word be fulfilled?
Let us go to him for refuge; he will lead us safely to the further shore.
Having heard those words of the caravan leader, all the merchants, united and together, departed for the northern direction.
Having traveled not very far, those merchants saw that king of horses standing on the shore of the ocean, in the northern part of the city of the rākṣasīs.
With his head uplifted, the king of horses spoke these words:
"Who among you will go to the further shore of this salt-water ocean?
Whom shall I lead in safety? For whom shall my word be fulfilled?"
Having heard those words of the king of horses, the merchants,
raising their joined palms in reverence, spoke these words:
We all go to you for refuge, O bringer of benefit to the world;
lead us to the further shore, and may your word be fulfilled.
And the King of Horses said: "Now, having seized the tips of the hairs, I shall flee swiftly; this you must keep in mind."
If you should think thus: "This is my wife," or "This is my son," or "This is my daughter," you will again fall helplessly into the power of others.
Now, if it should occur to you thus: "This is not my wife, nor is this my son, nor is this my daughter," then you shall go safely to the further shore.
Having thus instructed the merchants, the supreme horse,
compassionate out of pity, spoke these words:
"Come, worthy sirs; may it be well with you, O merchants; may prosperity attend you.
I shall carry you across from this dreadful and terrifying danger."
Having taken up the merchants, he departed from the earth by way of the sky—
the path of birds in the supportless atmosphere, the realm of the wind and the winged creatures of the gods.
The hosts of gods, the hosts of dānavas, the hosts of bhujagas, and the yakṣas and rākṣasas in their abodes waved their garments, crying, "Excellent! Excellent, O Great Being!"
Without doubt, before long you will become a Teacher, a light for the world;
you shall ferry this world across to the further shore of the ocean of old age and death.
And those who thought, "This is my wife" or "This is my son" or "This is my daughter," were thrown from horseback and scattered across the earth on all sides.

And those who were there thinking, "This is not my wife, nor is this my son, nor is this my daughter," they have safely crossed to the other shore. ... [omission] ... In this very same way, those gathered here in Jambudvīpa...
Those who do not place faith in the words of the King of Dharma will meet with calamity, just as merchants [are seized] by rākṣasīs.
But those who shall have faith in the words of the King of Dharma will go in safety, just as merchants [travel] by means of the horse Bālāha.
Recalling his former dwelling and former birth, the Blessed One,
the Teacher, related this Jātaka in the presence of the monks.
Those aggregates, those elements, and those sense-bases—
the Blessed One explained this matter with reference to the self.
In this beginningless and endless saṃsāra where I formerly dwelt,
I was then Bālāha, the horse Mañjukeśa, the most excellent of steeds;
at that time, there were five hundred merchants who were guided by me.
Thus, this immeasurable and manifold suffering, this ancient cycle of high and low births—
[having transcended it,] he is free from fever, free from fear, and free from sorrow.
He recited his own birth story in the midst of the community of monks.
Thus concludes the Jātaka of the five hundred bhikṣus, headed by Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, who were cast onto the island of the rākṣasīs.
Then, indeed, the wanderer Sañjayin Vairaṭiputra spoke at the crossroads, the junctions of four roads, and the entrances for hearing the news in the city of Rājagṛha:
The ascetic Gautama has arrived at Girivraja of the Magadhas; having led away all [the followers] from Sañjaya,
whom indeed will he lead?
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
The Great Heroes, the Tathāgatas, indeed lead by means of the True Dharma;
for one who understands, what cause for resentment can there be toward those who lead by means of the Dharma?
The Blessed One, the perfectly awakened Buddha, having accomplished the purpose for which he had come forth, dwells at Rājagṛha as the teacher of gods and humans.
The Śākyas and Śākyāyanīs of Kapilavastu heard that the Blessed One,
having indeed set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dharma, was dwelling in Rājagṛha, practicing for the welfare of gods and humans.
Then the Śākyas of Kapilavastu approached King Śuddhodana and said this to King Śuddhodana:

"O Great King, the Blessed One, having fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and having set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dharma, dwells in Rājagṛha while practicing for the welfare of gods and humans.
It would be well, O Great King, if you were to send a messenger to the Blessed One;
the Blessed One has shown compassion toward gods and humans."
It would be well if the Blessed One would also have compassion for his kinsmen.
King Śuddhodana said:
So be it; let him be released.
It occurred to those Śākyas:
"Who would be a suitable and worthy messenger for the Blessed One?"
The Śākyas said:
"Great King, this Chandaka was indeed the attendant of the Blessed One while he was still a prince; by him the prince was successfully escorted forth.
This Udāyin, the son of the family priest, was also a childhood friend of the Blessed One while he was a prince, having played with him in the dust."
Let these be sent forth.
Then they were addressed:
"Chanda and Kālodāyin, go to Rājagṛha and approach the Blessed One; offer salutations to the Blessed One and say:
'The Blessed One has shown compassion for gods and humans; it would be well if the Blessed One would likewise show compassion for his kinsmen.'"
And whatever the Blessed One may say to you, that you should do.
Having given their word to King Śuddhodana, they then departed from the city of Kapilavastu and, traveling by stages, arrived at Rājagṛha, at the Kalandakanivāpa in the Bamboo Grove.
Then indeed, Chandaka and Kālodāyin approached the Blessed One, bowed their heads at the Blessed One’s feet, and stood to one side.
The Blessed One said to them:
Chandaka and Kālodāyin, why have you come?
They said:
"We shall lead the Blessed One to Kapilavastu."
On this matter, on this occasion, in this context, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses of the Dharma.
O Lord, for one whose conquest lives on, that conquest is not conquered by Death;
by what path can you lead that Buddha, whose range is infinite and who is trackless?
For one whose ensnaring craving has been utterly eradicated, there is no guide anywhere;
by what path will you lead that Buddha of infinite prowess, who is trackless?
Then they were addressed by the Blessed One.
Chanda and Udāyin, why will you go forth?

They were now no longer desirous of going forth; for they had been instructed by King Śuddhodana, "Whatever the Blessed One tells you, that you should do," yet they saw neither saffron robes there nor a barber who might shave off their hair and beards.
Then, out of reverence for the Blessed One, though against their will, they said:
"Lord, I shall go forth."
Then they were addressed by the Blessed One with the "Come, monk" formula: "Come, monks, Chandaka and Kālodāyin; lead the holy life under the Tathāgata."
Then, as soon as they were addressed by the Blessed One with the "Come, monk" formula, whatever marks of a householder, whatever concealments of a householder, whatever banners of a householder,

and whatever habits of a householder there were— all disappeared entirely; three-layered robes appeared, along with an alms bowl, and their hair remained in its natural state, while their deportment became established just like that of monks who had been ordained for a hundred years.
This is the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk for the venerable Chanda and Kālodāyin.
Since the Blessed One went forth and since he attained unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment,
the Blessed One has not even once sat facing his birthplace for seven years, not even for as long as it takes to breathe in and out.

After the passing of seven years, the Śākyas of Kapilavastu who were former paternal kinsmen and blood relations, having passed away from among humans, were reborn among the gods as a result of the ripening of their wholesome karma; having become gods, they entreated the Blessed One:
"The Blessed One has shown compassion toward gods and humans; may the Blessed One likewise show compassion toward his kinsmen."
It is the time for the Blessed One to show compassion toward his kinsmen.
The Blessed One consented to those deities by remaining silent.

Then, indeed, the deities, understanding through the Blessed One’s silence that he had consented, were satisfied and elated; they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One, and vanished right there.
Then the Blessed One had a seat prepared facing toward his native land.
Now the Venerable Udāyin was skilled in discerning signs;
this thought occurred to him:
Just as the Blessed One had the seat prepared facing Kapilavastu, desiring to show compassion toward his kinsmen.
He thus entreated the Blessed One.
Listen with an undistracted mind to this concerning the peerless and unassailable Victor,
having knelt down and bowed your head in salutation.
Kālodāyin requests the immeasurable.
Now, O Venerable One, these trees, seeking fruit,
are glowing like flaming fires.
O Great Hero, it is the time; the Blessed One is the possessor of flavors.
The blossoming and enchanting forests spread their fragrance in all directions;
having shed their flowers, they now take up fruit.
It is time for you, O Teacher, to depart from here.
May it be neither too cold nor too hot, but pleasant for the season, as you travel on the road;
may the Koliyas and Śākyas behold you.
His face was like Rohiṇī among the stars.
Then the Blessed One described to the venerable Śāriputra the wandering tour of the Blessed One Śikhin.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, in the past,
when the World-Leader Śikhin had set out upon his journey, it was sublime.
To whatever village or town that Leader approaches,
there at every such place, water for drinking becomes available, endowed with the eight qualities.
To whichever village or town that Leader approaches, there,
in every direction, a grove of *sumana* flowers shall arise to meet him.
To whatever village or town that Leader approaches,
the trees standing like pillars along the four directions burst into bloom and waft their fragrance.
At the foot of whichever tree the Leader stands,
that very best of trees releases its blossoms, having been illuminated.
At the foot of whichever tree the Leader stands,
that very tree releases its fruits in full abundance on every side.
And whatever human trees there were, with their flowers and fruits,
as well as the various sense-bases, appeared before Śikhin, the Leader of the World.
And when the World-Leader Śikhin was present, non-human trees, flowers, fruits, and pleasure groves were seen.
Then, as Śikhin, the leader of the world, set out upon his journey, this earth, along with its oceans and mountains, trembled.
Then the gods scattered mandārava flowers over Śikhin,
the Leader of the World, as he had set out upon his wandering.
Then the gods scattered great mandārava flowers over Śikhin,
the Leader of the World, as he had set out upon his journey.
Then the gods scattered *karkārava* flowers over Śikhin,
the Leader of the World, as he set out upon his wandering.
Then the gods scattered great karkārava flowers over Śikhin,
the Leader of the World, as he had set out upon his wandering.
Then the gods scattered radiant flowers over Śikhin,
the leader of the world, as he set out upon his journey.
Then the gods scattered great, radiant flowers over Śikhin,
the Leader of the World, as he had set out upon his wandering.
Then the gods scattered flower baskets over Śikhin,
the Leader of the World, as he set out on his journey.
Then the gods scattered great mañjūṣa flowers over Śikhin,
the Leader of the World, as he had set out upon his journey.
And then the gods scattered fearsome flowers over Śikhin,
the leader of the world, as he was wandering on his tour.
And then the gods scattered great, magnificent flowers over Śikhin,
the Leader of the World, as he was wandering on his journey.
Then the gods scattered flowers of universal fragrance over Śikhin,
the Leader of the World, as he was wandering on his journey.
Then the gods scattered great, all-pervading fragrant flowers as Śikhin,
the Leader of the World, was wandering on his journey.
Then the gods scattered *pārijāta* flowers over Śikhin,
the Leader of the World, as he was wandering on his tour.
Then the gods scattered golden flowers over Śikhin,
the Leader of the World, as he was wandering on his journey.
Then the gods scattered flowers made of silver over Śikhin,
the Leader of the World, as he was wandering on his journey.
Then the gods scattered flowers made of jewels over Śikhin,
the Leader of the World, as he was wandering on his journey.
And then the gods scattered powders of sandalwood over Śikhin,
the Leader of the World, as he was wandering on his journey.
Then the gods scattered powders of agallochum as Śikhin,
the Leader of the World, was wandering on his journey.
And then the gods scattered powders of saffron over Śikhin,
the leader of the world, as he was wandering on his journey.
Then the gods scattered powders of *tamāla* leaves over Śikhin,
the leader of the world, as he was wandering on his journey.
Then the gods scattered powders of divine jewels over Śikhin,
the Leader of the World, as he was wandering on his journey.
Thousands of millions of musical instruments resounded in the sky as Śikhin,
the leader of the world, was wandering on his journey.
In the sky, drums resounded without being struck,
as Śikhin, the Leader of the World, was wandering on his tour.
The gods, stationed in the sky, cast down their garments as the Leader of the World, Śikhin, was wandering on his journey.
The dragon kings, the garuḍas, and humans approached Śikhin,
the leader of the world, as he was wandering on his journey.
These many yakṣas, endowed with beauty and renown,
followed the wandering course of Śikhin, the Leader of the World.
Eighty-six thousand householders gathered together and followed the wandering course of the Leader of the World as he traveled.
Neither hunger nor thirst was experienced there, nor was any decline described for Śikhin,
the Leader of the World, as he was wandering on his journey.
There was neither cold nor heat there, nor were there gadflies or mosquitoes,
for Śikhin as he wandered on his journey, the leader of the world.
Having wandered on his journey and having disciplined many people,
the Perfectly Awakened One, the Seer whose rebirth is exhausted, passed into final nirvana.

Then the venerable Śāriputra rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
The Blessed One, moreover, possesses a morality equal to that of the Blessed One Śikhin, an identical wisdom, and the same powers, intrepidities, and Buddha-qualities.
The conduct of this Blessed One will also be exactly like that of the Blessed One Śikhin.

And the Blessed One went on his journey for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, welfare, and happiness of the great body of beings, both gods and humans.
Then, having adjusted his robe over one shoulder and extended his hands in reverent salutation,
Śāriputra requested the Tathāgata for a journey there.
Now is the time for the Blessed One,
the Teacher, to set out on his wandering out of compassion for living beings.
Those who have cultivated the Dharma and are in their final bodily existence, being entreated,
would grant an opportunity out of compassion for living beings.
Having observed the Upoṣadha fast for half a month from here,
I shall set out on a wandering tour out of compassion for living beings.
Then, having observed that upoṣadha for half a month,
the Teacher set out on his journey out of compassion for living beings.
To whatever village or town Gautama approaches, there,
in every direction, wholesome medicinal herbs spring up.
To whatever village or town Gautama approaches,
the flowering trees of that place waft their fragrance in the four directions.
Under whichever tree Gautama stands,
that very best of trees bends down and sheds its flowers.
At whatever tree's root Gautama stands, that very tree releases its fruits in full abundance on every side.
And whatever human trees there were, with their flowers and fruits,
they appeared to move along as the Leader of the World was walking on his journey.
And those trees that were non-human, as well as their flowers and fruits,
appeared to move along as the Leader of the World walked his course.
Then the earth, together with its oceans and mountains,
trembled as the Leader of the World set out upon his journey.
Then the gods scattered mandārava flowers as the Leader of the World was proceeding on his journey.
Then the gods scattered great mandārava flowers as the Leader of the World was proceeding on his journey.
Then the gods scattered karkārava flowers as the Leader of the World set out upon his journey.
Then the gods scattered great *karkāravā* flowers as the Leader of the World set out upon his journey.
Then the gods scattered radiant flowers as the Leader of the World set out upon his journey.
Then the gods scattered great, radiant flowers as the Leader of the World was proceeding on his journey.
Then the gods scattered flower baskets as the Leader of the World set out upon his journey.
Then the gods scattered great mañjūṣaka flowers as the Leader of the World was setting out upon his journey.
And then the gods scattered magnificent flowers as the Leader of the World was wandering on his journey.
And then the gods scattered great, magnificent flowers as the Leader of the World was wandering on his journey.
Then the gods scattered flowers of universal fragrance as the Leader of the World was wandering on his journey.
Then the gods scattered great universal fragrances and flowers as the Leader of the World was wandering on his journey.
Then, as the Leader of the World was wandering on his journey, the gods scattered fully blossomed flowers.
Then the gods scattered flowers made of gold as the Leader of the World was wandering on his journey.
Then the gods scattered silver flowers as the Leader of the World was wandering on his journey.
Then the gods scattered flowers made of jewels as the Leader of the World was wandering on his journey.
And then the gods scattered powders of sandalwood as the Leader of the World was proceeding on his journey.
Then the gods scattered powders of agallochum as the Leader of the World was wandering on his journey.
And then the gods scattered powders of keśara as the Leader of the World proceeded on his journey.
Then, as the Leader of the World was wandering on his journey, the gods scattered powders of *tāla* leaves over him.
And then, as the Leader of the World was wandering on his journey, the gods scattered divine powders of precious gems.
Thousands of millions of musical instruments resounded in the sky as the Leader of the World proceeded on his journey.
In the sky, drums resounded spontaneously, unstruck,
as the Leader of the World was wandering on his journey.
While the Leader of the World was wandering on his journey, the gods stationed in the sky scattered garments from above.
The dragon kings, the garuḍas, and humans followed the Leader of the World as he wandered on his journey.
These many yakṣas as well, handsome and renowned,
followed along on the journey while the Leader of the World was traveling.
These many gods as well— handsome and renowned—
followed along on the journey while the Leader of the World was wandering.
Three thousand gods, majestic, beautiful, and renowned,
followed the conduct of the Leader of the World as he was wandering.
Eighty-six thousand brahmins assembled and followed the journey as the Leader of the World was wandering.
Eighty-six thousand householders gathered together and followed the journey as the Leader of the World was traveling.
While the Leader of the World was wandering on his journey, neither hunger nor thirst, nor even any decline, is described as having occurred there.
Neither cold nor heat, nor gadflies nor mosquitoes,
afflict the Leader of the World as he wanders on his journey.
Having wandered on his journey and having guided many people,
the Lord of the World arrived at the Śākyas' city named Kapila.
Now the Blessed One was dwelling in the Nyagrodha Grove together with a great community of monks, numbering eighteen hundred monks.

King Śuddhodana heard that the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour among the Kośalas together with a great saṅgha of monks— eighteen hundred monks in all— had reached the city of the Kośalas and was staying right there in the Nyagrodha Grove.
Then all those Śākyans and Śākyanīs of Kapilavastu, desiring a vision of the Blessed One, each prepared their own carriage-teams,
thinking, "We shall go for a vision of the Blessed One."
King Śuddhodana heard that the Śākyans and Śākyan women of Kapilavastu were having their respective carriages yoked,
saying, "We shall go to the Nyagrodha Grove to see the Blessed One."
He then caused a proclamation to be made throughout Kapilavastu.
"No one should approach the Blessed One first;
everyone must go together with me to the Nyagrodha Grove to see the Blessed One."

Then indeed, King Śuddhodana, together with his entire harem headed by Yaśodharā, together with the princes and ministers, together with the Śākyas and their retinues, together with the archers, charioteers, and horsemen,
together with the merchants and caravan leaders, and together with the guild-leaders and the townspeople, [departed] with great royal majesty and great...
With royal splendor, he departed from the city of Kapilavastu in order to see the Blessed One.
King Śuddhodana, surrounded by the circle of Śākyas, set out from Kapilavastu in a chariot drawn by four horses to go and see the Blessed One at the Nyagrodha Grove.
At that time, the community of monks was entering the city of Kapilavastu for alms;
King Śuddhodana saw the community of monks.
He then questioned his ministers.
"O, my ministers, what are these wandering mendicants like this?"
The ministers said:
This is the retinue of the divine prince.

Then, seeing her with her emaciated body— a female ascetic who had gone forth as a seer, along with Uruvilvākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, Śāriputra, and Maudgalyāyana together with their retinues, all of whom were bodies scorched by austerity, shaven-headed, and carrying bowls in their hands— he became dejected in his facial expression.

"If my son does not go forth, he will become a universal monarch (cakravartin) ruling over the four continents; a conqueror, righteous, a king of dharma, endowed with the seven treasures, surrounded by a thousand kings, and he shall dwell upon the earth."
Turn back such a retinue as this; I do not wish to see him.
Then those monks were addressed by the ministers.
The king does not wish to see you; turn back.
Then, having turned back, they went to the Nyagrodha Monastery.
"O Blessed One, King Śuddhodana wishes to see you;
having seen you, he will then return to us."
The Blessed One said:
"In this very place, there will be food for the entire community of monks."
Uruvilvākāśyapa addressed the Blessed One.
"I am going, Blessed One; I shall turn back King Śuddhodana."
The Blessed One did not consent.
Nadīkāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, and Upasena—all these monks of great supernatural power—petitioned the Blessed One.
"Let us go, Blessed One; let us inspire faith in King Śuddhodana so that he may approach the Blessed One."
The Blessed One did not consent even to theirs.
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
Which monk does the Blessed One desire who might inspire faith in King Śuddhodana?
With his purified divine eye, which surpasses that of humans, Mahāmaudgalyāyana saw that the Blessed One’s mind was fixed upon the monk Kālodāyin:
"The monk Kālodāyin will inspire faith in King Śuddhodana."
Having seen him, he approached the venerable Kālodāyin and said this to the venerable Kālodāyin.
"It is a gain for you, venerable Udāyin; it is well-gained that you have a Teacher who desires this. The monk Udāyin will inspire faith in King Śuddhodana.
There are other elder monks who beg and do not receive; go, venerable Udāyin, and inspire faith in King Śuddhodana."
When this had been said, the venerable Kālodāyin spoke thus to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the consecrated Kṣatriya kings who have attained the power and heroism of their realms are difficult to approach."

Just as, venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, a blazing great mass of fire is difficult for a person to approach, even so, venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, anointed Kṣatriya kings who have attained power and prowess over their realms are difficult to approach.
Just as, venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, a sixty-year-old elephant is difficult to approach,
even so, venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, anointed Kṣatriya kings who have attained the strength and power of their realm are difficult to approach.

Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, just as a lion, the king of beasts, possessing fangs, strength, and a mane— the lord of wild animals— is difficult for a man to approach, even so, Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the anointed Kṣatriya kings, who have attained power and heroism over their realms, are lions among men and difficult to approach.
They come to approach [him].

Just as, venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, a tiger with its body crouched is heavy to behold and difficult for a man to approach, even so, venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, anointed kṣatriya kings who have attained the power and vigor of their realms— those tigers among men— are difficult to approach.
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Kālodāyin in verse:
Listen to me, Udāyibhadra; you are the foremost among those with supreme merit and faith.
Quickly inspire confidence in that best of kings, who brings joy to the Śākya clan.
Indeed, no other monk whatsoever is capable of pleasing the king's mind,
except for you, Udāyin, who share the same conduct as the Blessed One.
Long ago, Udāyin, in a past time, there was a lord of the earth named Satyavardhana, a protector of the world whose fame was far-renowned.
That righteous King of Dharma was honored by millions of billions of living beings;
he ruled this earth, bounded by the oceans, in accordance with the Dharma.
And that king had a son, Darśāvī, who had seen previous Buddhas;
his name was Matisāra, and his mind was cultivated by a multitude of virtues.
Seeing the faults in sensual pleasures and having no desire for any enjoyment of sense-objects,
one who has planted roots of merit does not delight in the household life, but finds joy in solitude.
Satyavardhana said to him: "Son, enjoy these exquisite sensual pleasures in this palace which resembles the abode of Vaiśravaṇa and is like the residence of the immortals."
Matisāra, having joined his ten fingers in salutation, said to him:
"O protector of the earth, these riches are not to be possessed by a wise man."
For those things are approved by ignorant people and are under the sway of passion. What is the reason? Would a man who is not blind take a wrong path under the influence of one who is blind?
How could one who has reached the shore desire that which is being carried away, unprotected?
How could one who is bound set out on the road to prison by word alone?
How could a wise man desire the company of one who stands in a precarious position?
O King, you appear to me like one who is blind, being carried away and lost for a long time;
you are swept along by the flood of desire, whereas I loathe desires.
And by the command of his powerful father, that Matisāra,
the prince, went forth into homelessness, abandoning the kingdom and disregarding sensual pleasures.
Like a snake casting off its worn-out skin, or like a mass of ripe phlegm,
he abandoned the entire earth bounded by the ocean, having perceived the defects in sensual pleasures.
Having transcended the realm of desire, the essence of wisdom practiced the divine abodes,
the prince [striving] for the attainment of the state of Brahmā.
When the prince had gone forth, the son of the family priest named Somadatta, who was devoted to him, followed Matisāra into the religious life.
When the prince had gone forth into homelessness, his father felt displeasure toward him;
having gone there, Somadatta pacified the protector of the earth.
What do you think, Udāyin? Was Matisāra someone else at that time, on that occasion? It was I myself who was indifferent to the enjoyment of sensual pleasures.
What do you think, Udāyin? Was that Satyavardhana someone else? That king Śuddhodana was indeed that very same person at that time.
"What do you think, Udāyin? Was that Somadatta, who was devoted to me, someone else? You yourself were he; I am indeed the Truth, and you have found faith in me."
Therefore, Udāyin, now win the favor of King Śuddhodana;
when that protector of the earth is pleased, there will be a great gathering of wealth.
O son of noble family, there will be an accumulation of infinite fruit for gods and humans;
through the grace of the excellent king, quickly inspire confidence in this best of men.
Now the Lord of the Śākyas, struck by excessive pride and agitated by discursive thoughts,
stands with a dejected mind like an elephant fallen upon a mountain slope.
Just as a powerful man surrounded by a life-force-sapping rākṣasa knows neither himself nor his subjects, so too does the lord of the earth know nothing but the enemy.
Reflecting upon the loss of sovereignty and contemplating sovereignty once more, why have you become displeased with me? Quickly restore your favor!
Then King Śuddhodana, having turned back from the city gate of Kapilavastu, together with the entire Śākyan assembly, took his place in his own audience hall.
Thereupon, King Śuddhodana addressed the Śākyas and the Śākyāyanīs.
Having fallen even from great sovereignty and lordship, the prince has gone forth into homelessness.

Had the prince not gone forth, he would have become a universal monarch (cakravartin), a conqueror of the four continents, righteous, a king of dharma, endowed with the seven treasures; these would have been his seven treasures.
Namely:
the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure—such are the seven treasures.
Furthermore, he would have a full thousand sons, who were brave, heroic, handsome in form, and crushers of enemy armies.

"Thus, having conquered these four great continents, bounded by the oceans and mountains— entirely without thorns, without punishment, without weapons, and without oppression— by means of Dharma alone, and having dwelt therein as king surrounded by thousands of kings,
the universal sovereignty would have come into our hands; yet we were left behind when the Prince went forth into homelessness."
They have been fallen from great sovereignty and lordship.
Then, indeed, the venerable Udāyin rose up into the air from the Nyagrodha Grove and stood in the sky at the height of a palm tree before King Śuddhodana, who was surrounded by a circle of Śākyas.
King Śuddhodana saw the venerable Udāyin standing in the sky at the height of a palm tree.

Upon seeing him, he was thrilled, delighted, and filled with joy; rising from his seat, he arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms toward the venerable Udāyin, and addressed the venerable Udāyin in verse:
From where have you come, O one clad in red robes?
For what purpose have you arrived here?
Or what do you desire here, Udāyin?
The sight of those who have accomplished their vows is very difficult to obtain.
"O glorious lord of the realm, it is a most rare gain for you that you have a son who is the supreme among men."
He illuminates the entire world with his splendor,
like the thousand-rayed sun rising over the earth.
Thus, now the Elder Udāyin, standing in the air at the height of a palm tree, proclaimed many glories of the Buddha's majesty; and King Śuddhodana, having heard them, became filled with joy.
He then addressed the Śākyas and the Śākyan women.

Just as, O Vāsiṣṭhas, when the sun is about to rise, this is its precursor and its sign— namely, the dawn— so too has Udāyin, the disciple of the Sugata, the son of the Buddha, the seer of the ultimate truth and the dispeller of all doubts,
arrived within the Śākya clan.
"I shall propitiate the Truth"—with such hope, [the farmer] is drawn to the field; with hope, the seed is sown;
with hope, merchants set out upon the ocean to carry away wealth.
Whatever hope I stand upon for anyone, may that hope of mine be fulfilled.
Again and again they quickly sow the seed;
again and again the King of the Gods sends down rain;
again and again the multitude of seeds grows.
The farmers obtain gain again and again.
Again and again beggars come;
again and again the virtuous give;
again and again, having given, the virtuous [remain].
Again and again they go to the heavenly realm.
A person of noble birth is rare; he is not born everywhere.
Wherever that hero is born, that family prospers in happiness.
For the Hero, possessed of vast wisdom, purifies seven generations in whichever family he is born;
the God of Gods leads the Śākyas like a father.
By you too, O Sage, one born with a true name has been produced.
The father of the Jina, the Buddha, was named Śuddhodana; his mother was indeed named Māyā,
who bore the Bodhisattva in her womb.
Upon the dissolution of the body, he rejoices in the heavens.
The Mother of the Buddha rejoices in the five desirable and lovely strands of sensual pleasure; she is exceedingly... one who desires merit.
She was surrounded by hosts of apsarases.
The Śākya father was pleased and filled with joy for his son, the Buddha, the invincible protector, the peerless Aṅgīrasa, the savior.
By virtue of the Dharma, Gautama, you are my noble kinsman.
The king said:
O monk, he under whom you have gone forth,
practicing the holy life with faith—
he is neither afraid nor does he fall into fear.
Even alone, he delights at the foot of a tree.
Udāyī said:
O King, he in whose presence I have gone forth out of faith practices the holy life;
he is neither afraid, nor does he experience fear.
Even alone, he finds delight at the foot of a tree.
Better than that is one who is vigilant, a sage unshaken by blame or praise,
not trembling at sounds like a lion.
O Śākyan, how can you call the Victor— who is like the wind unimpeded in a net, a leader among others who cannot be led by another, and one who is fearless— a coward?
I call him whose peerless wisdom you perceive my son;
you are the son of that son, who is my son.
Having eaten, O monk, take away the alms-bowl.
We too shall go to behold the Buddha, the unsurpassed one whose doubts have been dispelled;
that Essence of Beings has arisen in the world.
O monk, speak to my son as you have said.
Having eaten as much food as required— pure, excellent, and endowed with delicious flavors—
he set out, taking his alms-bowl.
He approached the place where the unconquerable Jina was.
Having approached that place,
he offered alms-food to the Victor;
having bowed at his feet, he spoke to the Tathāgata.
Your kinsmen will come to see you.

Having heard of such qualities, the protector of the earth uttered this exclamation three times: "Well gained are my gains, that within this triple-thousandfold world system there is such an infinity!"
While the Jina is still living in this world-system,
there will be a meeting with the Leader;
the trees and creepers will be in full bloom, strewn with flowers.
And even though it was resounded by throngs of brahmins,
my heart thus blossomed with joy upon hearing that my son was endowed with every virtue.
Then King Śuddhodana addressed a certain royal minister.

"O minister, it is said that Prince Sarvārthasiddha, having awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and having set in motion the supreme wheel of Dharma, has arrived at the groves near Kapilavastu;
therefore, I shall go out to meet my son, Prince Sarvārthasiddha."
Then, have a proclamation made in the city of Kapilavastu:
"All the Śākyas— brahmins, householders, musicians, guilds, and all those belonging to the various arts and crafts— must go out to meet Sarvārthasiddha along with me."
"Excellent, Great King!"

Having given his promise to Śuddhodana, the royal minister immediately caused a proclamation to be made throughout the city of Kapilavastu— at its crossroads, junctions, and the entrances to the marketplaces.
"Venerable sirs, the youth Sarvārthasiddha, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, has arrived at the groves near Kapilavastu.
Therefore, all of you must go together with King Śuddhodana to meet the Blessed One."
He who belongs to the lineage of the Śākyas will be his protector; one whose purpose is accomplished, whose mind is detached from the state of craving,
whose outflows are exhausted, who is free from passion, and who possesses all-seeing vision.
Then, in twelve years, we shall behold him of infinite wisdom.
Having heard the sound of the drum of bliss and the music played by hosts of gods at Lumbinī in the Śākya kingdom,
he for whom the vow was made: "I shall become a Buddha in the world."
Thus he will come, speaking the truth, free from darkness.
He who took seven steps here in Lumbinī, by which he awakened to the seven jewels of the factors of enlightenment;
he who roars the lion’s roar: "I am the eldest in the world."
Thus he will come, shattering the arguments of opponents.
By this [wisdom], that which has caused harm— the entirety of the bed of the womb— is destroyed, and the cause of further existence is completely dried up;
the creeper of craving, the root of suffering, is also withered away.
Thus he will come, effecting liberation from bondage in the world.

Then, having heard that report from Kapilavastu, the Śākyas and Śākyāyanīs quickly assembled at the gate of the royal palace, along with the princes, ministers, the elite of the army, and the brahmins headed by the domestic chaplain; the merchant community headed by the guild-leaders; and all those residing in Kapilavastu, such as the musicians—namely, the chariot-racers, bards, actors, dancers, wrestlers, boxers, hand-clappers, acrobats, tumblers, and jugglers.
Velambakas, storytellers, *paṃcavaṭukas*, singers, musicians, jesters, those who play the kettle-drum, conch, clay drum, and war drum, as well as those who play the *tūṇava*,
*paṇava*, flute, lute, *ekadaśī*, and *vīṇā*— many instrumentalists in all— gathered at the gate of the royal palace,
as did all the guilds of Kapilavastu.

Namely: goldsmiths, silversmiths, woolen-cloth makers, conch-shell workers, ivory carvers, jewelers, weavers, perfumers, shepherds, oil-pressers, butter-vessel makers, cow-dung sellers, water-sellers, cotton-merchants, curd-sellers, cake-makers,
sugar-candy makers, sweetmeat-makers, flour-grinders, firewood-sellers, roasted-grain sellers, merchants of fruits, merchants of roots, and perfume-grinding oil-merchants.
The makers of necklaces, the makers of earrings, the makers of molasses, the makers of candied sugar, the sellers of ginger, the distillers of *sīdhu* liquor,
and the merchants of sugar— these and many other traders, all of whom were artisans of Kapilavastu, assembled at the royal palace.
For example, there are smiths, copper-smelters, goldsmiths, workers in silver, makers of tin, makers of lead, makers of lacquer, potters, basket-makers, weavers, tent-makers,
makers of divine garments, washermen, dyers, clean-weavers, and painters.
Carpenters, craftsmen, blacksmiths, basket-makers,

bookbinders, those who work in leather, barbers, preparers, cutters, plasterers, master builders, architects, irrigators of fields, well-diggers, carriers of earth, wood-merchants, grass-merchants, sellers of posts, sellers of bamboo, sailors, ferrymen, gold-washers, and wrestlers.
These and other people— high and low, inferior, superior, and middling—
all gathered at the gate of the royal palace.
Thus now King Śuddhodana, together with this body of people, the women of the inner apartments, and surrounded by the princes and ministers,
mounted a chariot drawn by four horses along with the archers, charioteers, and elephant-riders; [he was accompanied by] the guild of merchants headed by the *śreṣṭhin*,
the community of traders headed by the caravan leaders (*sārthavāha*), the Brahmins headed by the royal chaplain (*purohita*), and the eighteen guilds.

Honored and surrounded by great royal splendor and great royal majesty, amidst the shouts of "Ha! and "Hi! from a vast multitude of people, and the resounding noise of kettledrums, clay drums, tabors, and conchs, he departed from the city of Kapilavastu and set out for the Nyagrodha Grove in order to see the Blessed One.
Then this thought occurred to the Blessed One:

The Śākyas are arrogant; if I were to greet them while they are seated on their own thrones, their minds would surely be disturbed. For how could it be otherwise? He who, having abandoned the sovereignty of a universal monarch, went forth into homelessness, and having awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, has realized the Dharma and declares himself the Lord of Dharma—how indeed could he be treated with such disrespect?
He does not rise up for his father, nor for those who are older, nor for those who occupy the position of a teacher.
There is no being, nor any assembly of beings, for whom the earth would not split into seven pieces at the head if they were to stand before the Tathāgata.
What if I were now to walk back and forth in a long promenade in the sky, a distance of a man’s height, high above the air?
Then the Blessed One, knowing the pride and arrogance of his father, King Śuddhodana, and the Śākya circle,
and perceiving their arrival, walked a long distance back and forth in the sky at a height of one man's stature,
his soles not touching the ground.
Then King Śuddhodana saw the Blessed One from afar in the Nyagrodha Grove, walking back and forth in a long promenade in the sky at a height of one man’s length, his soles not touching the ground;
and upon seeing him, his hair stood on end with joy at such a marvelous and wondrous thing, thinking, "How wonderful is the Dharma of the Prince!"
He has been approached as the supreme among bipeds in all the world.
Then King Śuddhodana, the Śākya, addressed the Śākyas.

"Behold, O Blessed Ones, the prince by whom this thought was conceived and prayed for, desiring to see the All-Knowing One whose resolve is realized regarding all dharmas and who is the perfected Lord of Men— may he behold Siddhārtha, who has attained all perfections.
Having seen his son with a fully perfected body...
His limbs were well-defined and adorned with a hundred thousand marks,
just like the moon in its fifth month surrounded by the stars of auspicious signs.
Having seen him of beautiful form, with a body beyond compare, long-eyed and blazing with splendor,
then indeed King Śuddhodana, having traveled by carriage as far as the ground was accessible to a carriage, [alighted] from the carriage.
Having descended from his carriage together with his own inner court and the Śākya circle, he entered the Nyagrodha Grove on foot;
approaching the Blessed One, he bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet and addressed him in verse:
O you of vast wisdom, O All-Seeing One, this is the third time I prostrate at your feet,
just as the fortune-tellers predicted for you.
And that which the shade of the rose-apple tree did not leave him.
Then the Blessed One, standing in the air at a height of a palm tree in the Nyagrodha Grove, performed various and manifold twin miracles (*yamakaprātihārya*).
His lower body blazed with fire, while from his upper body five hundred streams of cool water flowed;
when his upper body blazed with fire, five hundred streams of cool water flowed from his lower body.

Then the Blessed One, having manifested the form of a bull through his supernatural power— endowed with a moving hump and perfect color and shape— vanished from the eastern direction and appeared in the western direction;
vanishing from the western direction, he appeared in the eastern direction.
Vanishing in the northern direction, he appears in the southern direction;
vanishing in the southern direction, he appears in the northern direction.
In this way, the Great Miracle should now be performed in detail.

Then, having seen such a miracle of supernatural power by the Blessed One, many hundreds of thousands of millions of living beings became joyful, filled with gladness and happiness, and struck with wonder and amazement;
they set up thousands of shouts of acclaim.
Now, when the Blessed One had gone forth, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī’s eyes became covered as if by a film due to her weeping and grief, and she became blind.

While the Blessed One was performing various and manifold twin miracles in that Nyagrodha Grove, thousands of shouts of acclaim arose; Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī then asked Yaśodharā: [The rest of the passage continues with Yaśodharā describing the wonders.]
Why are these people making thousands of shouts of acclaim?
Yaśodharā said:
This Blessed One is performing various and manifold miraculous feats of double-appearances in the sky, the open air, yet you do not see them.
Yaśodharā said:
Come now; I shall act in such a way that you may see for yourself.

Then Yaśodharā, having filled her cupped hands with water from where five hundred streams were flowing from the body of the Blessed One as he was performing miracles, washed the eyes of Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī; and by the power of the Buddha, those cataracts were split apart.
Then, her vision became as it was before—pure and stainless.
Then the Blessed One, having performed various and manifold twin miracles in the sky above,
and having displayed many thousands of miracles of supernormal power to establish many thousands of living beings in the noble dharmas, sat down upon the very seat that had been prepared.

Then King Śuddhodana and the Śākyas, having bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and having greeted the Blessed One most courteously and thoroughly, sat down to one side. Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and Yaśodharā, together with the women of the inner apartments, having bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and having greeted the Blessed One, sat down to one side.
Then King Śuddhodana, overcome with agitation, asked the Blessed One about his welfare and well-being.
As he, possessing the complexion of a god and a delicate form,
was walking about the grounds of the pleasure grove,
his father approached him with palms joined in reverence.
O gods, [we invoke] Indra for you; O thirty [gods], [we invoke] Śakra for you.
This is the third [time], O one of vast wisdom; I bow at your feet, O All-Seeing One,
regarding that which the prognosticators have prophesied for you.
And the shadow of the rose-apple tree did not leave him.
Those two of divine appearance, having come together—
the Buddha and the King, the father of the Buddha—
shone resplendently as they sat in the Sāla grove.
Just as the moon is released from the mass of clouds.
Then, after a long time, the father Aprameya saw his own dear and pleasing son,
who was as dear to him as his own life, seated there.
Driven by an impulse, he asks what is beneficial and what is harmful.
Formerly, O Hero, you would mount your beautiful and fine woolen sandals placed upon delicate rugs and walk back and forth.
While that white parasol was being held over him,
he was [surrounded] by thousands of wheels with copper-colored, soft rims on all sides.
O Hero, as you tread upon the *kuśa* grass, thorns, and gravel, do your feet not suffer pain?
The Blessed One said:
I am the conqueror of all, the knower of all; I am unsullied among all phenomena.
Having abandoned everything, I am liberated through the destruction of craving.
One like me does not experience feelings with full awareness.
The king said:
