Formerly, at that time, with your red sandalwood— resembling the hue of the moon's blood,
possessing a pleasing fragrance and being most cooling—
Having bathed him, the bath-attendants anointed him.
Now, during the harsh nights of summer,
you wander from forest to forest, walking about,
with water that is bright and cool and pleasant.
Who now shall bathe you, who are exhausted?
The Blessed One said:
O Gautama, this river is pure, with its bathing-places consisting of virtuous conduct; it is untroubled and always praised by the righteous.
In its lake, the hosts of gods have bathed.
With my body plunged in, I cross over to the further shore.
The Dharma is a lake, O Gautama, with virtue as its bathing ford; it is untroubled and always praised by the righteous.
In this lake, the hosts of gods have bathed.
She carries away the earth, fragrant with her own merit.
The king said:
But when you, wearing garments of Kāśī cloth, have put on pure robes scented with lotus, water-lily, and campaka flowers;
Thus you shine within the Śākya circle, like Śakra in the midst of the thousandfold world-systems.
He now wears hempen garments, woven cloths, dyed robes, and tree-bark,
and he does so without feeling any disgust.
This too, venerable sir, is a marvel for you.
The Blessed One said:
O Lord of Men, the Jinas do not become obsessed with robes, bedding, or food,
whether they obtain what is pleasing or even what is unpleasant.
The Jinas are equanimous and discerning.
The king said:
Formerly, you possessed wonderful, noble chariots— exquisite, made of gold and bronze, and highly precious—
as well as a white parasol, jewels, a sword, and chowries.
They surely grasped the direction from which you were departing.
Formerly, your supreme steed Kaṇṭhaka was swift as the wind, exalted, rapid in his pace,
a well-bred horse covered with a golden net.
He constantly carries him wherever he desires.
You who are provided with vehicles for riding,
with chariots, horses, and elephants,
wandering from kingdom to kingdom—
Tell me now: are you not weary?
The Blessed One said:
The chariot for me is the basis of supernormal power, driven by my own mind;
fortitude, wisdom, and mindfulness are the charioteers; and the four right efforts are my horses.
I have proceeded evenly toward that well-prepared state.
The king said:
Formerly, you used to eat pure and exquisite food from silver vessels and golden bowls.
They attended upon him through the majesty of the king.
Now you consume both the salty and the unsalted, the coarse and the refined, the flavorless and the flavorful, while feeling aversion toward it.
This too, venerable sir, is a marvel for you.
The Blessed One said:
Those Buddhas who have passed away in the past, those yet to come, and I myself,
who am unshakable— whether it be coarse or not coarse, flavorless or flavorful.
One who seeks the ultimate truth enjoys [these things] for the benefit of the world.
The king said:
Formerly, you slept upon couches with golden legs, spread with cow-hides, cotton mattresses, and comfortable pillows of fine linen on great beds.
You rejoice in that place strewn with scattered flowers.
Now, having spread grass and leaves upon the rugged and harsh ground,
you rejoice, O Essence of Beings.
I hope your limbs do not ache, O wise one?
The Blessed One said:
O Śākyan, those like me do not sleep in suffering;
all my fevers of grief have been abandoned.
Thus, I am forever free from fever and free from sorrow.
I, who am compassionate toward all beings, shall take [it].
The king said:
Formerly, O Gautama, you were in your own home, within the inner apartments which resembled the celestial palaces of the gods,
illuminated by a multitude of lamps like fireflies.
In a gabled chamber with its windows closed.
Then women, adorned with various garlands and ornaments, resembling apsarases,
approached, eager and ready to perform whatever service was required.
They look toward his face, wondering, "What does the Noble One say?"
The Blessed One said:
Even today, in my own vihāra, the Śākyas, the gods, Brahmā, and the radiant ones—
even their minds function under my control.
And wherever I wish, there I place it.
The king said:
Accompanied by the sounding of kettledrums, clay drums, and lutes, and praised by those skilled in the sounds of cymbals and the telling of tales, you shine forth within the circle of the Śākyas.
Like Śakra in the midst of those who have gone to a thousand worlds.
The Blessed One said:
Challenged by the expounders of grammar in the discourses of the Sūtras,
I am the awakener of knowledge and liberation;
I shine resplendent in the midst of the community of monks.
He was like Brahmā in the midst of a thousand worlds.
The king said:
Formerly, O Bhīma, you were in your own palace within the inner apartments, which resembled a celestial chariot of the gods,
while armored men guarded you.
Well-trained, armed with swords, firm, and skilled strikers.
Now he dwells alone in the forest, where the cries of owls and jackals resound,
during nights frequented by many beasts of prey.
Tell me now, why are you not afraid in this place?
(The Blessed One said:
"Even if all the hosts of yakṣas were gathered together— fierce elephants roaming the mountain fastnesses— "
Those like me do not experience horripilation;
having abandoned fear, I have attained fearlessness.
I wander alone, a sage, heedful and unshaken by blame or praise,
like a lion that is not terrified by sounds.
O Śākyan, how can you call the Jina— who is like the wind unattached in its nets, a leader among others who cannot be led by another— a coward?
The king said:
The entire earth has been conquered by you throughout all eons; this city of yours is filled with thousands of sons,
and you have renounced even the seven precious jewels.
O Hero, you have indeed attained the state of a recluse.
The Blessed One said:
The entire earth has been conquered by me throughout all kalpas; I have a thousand sons who fill my city,
and these eight treasures exist for me.
There is no other such jewel as this.
To him who was free from passion, whose faculties were perfectly composed, who was rightly liberated, whole, and without outflows—
the father approached with palms joined in reverence.
Teach me the path for the benefit of humanity.
Having pervaded him with knowledge, the Teacher spoke thus to his father, Śuddhodana:
Constantly seek the sight of monks;
do not be negligent, for the Dharma will be yours.
Then, immediately after the Protector had described to his immeasurable father the sight of the monks,
that virtuous man began to attend upon them.
Then, one should purify the higher Dharma-eye.
Such was that joyful meeting between father and son at that time;
thus do I recollect the Sugata.
Who would not obtain spiritual joy that is free from worldly desire?
The Pitāputrasamāgama is completed.
The monks said to the Blessed One:
Behold, Blessed One, how King Śuddhodana has been inspired with faith by the Venerable Udāyin!
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now that this King Śuddhodana has been inspired with faith by Udāyin; on another occasion as well, he was inspired with faith by this same Udāyin."
The monks said.
At another time as well, Blessed One?
The Blessed One said:
On another occasion as well, monks.

Long ago, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi, a king named Brahmadatta reigned. He was one who had performed meritorious deeds, possessed great majesty, maintained a well-gathered retinue, was disposed toward giving and sharing, and possessed great strength, a great treasury, and a great army of mounts.

His city, Vārāṇasī, in the kingdom of Kāśi, was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, crowded with many people, populous, filled with happy inhabitants, free from riots and disturbances, with thieves well-restrained, and rich in commerce.
There dwelt a king of crows named Supātra, with a retinue of eighty thousand.
Now that king of crows had a crow-wife named Supārśvā;
she conceived a pregnancy-longing for the food of kings. She informed her husband, Supātra, the king of crows, of that longing.
He said:
"I shall have royal food sent; eat it."
Then that king of crows said to his minister:
"Command Supārśvā that she shall give instructions to the crows so that they will bring the king's food from the kitchen of King Brahmadatta."
Then that minister said:
"Master, I shall bring even the king's food.
Then that minister commanded those crows:
"Go to King Brahmadatta."
"Bring the king's meal from the kitchen; the wife of Supātra, the king of crows, shall partake of it."
Those crows said:
The royal palace is guarded by those trained in archery;
birds are unable to cross over it from any direction, and therefore we are not able to bring the king’s food from King Brahmadatta’s kitchen.
Others were also commanded, but they did not dare;
even by eighty thousand crows, no one dared to bring the king’s royal food from King Brahmadatta’s kitchen, fearing that having gone there, they might be struck with a shaft or a pellet.
Then, this thought occurred to the minister of that king of crows:

"I am the minister of Supātra, the king of eighty thousand crows; if I am unable to carry out this command of Supātra, the king of crows, it will not be a display of our manly prowess. I shall go and report this to my own king, Supātra."

"Great King, I shall bring you royal food from my own kitchen here; if I am killed, let it be a sacrifice offered with a single body, for this is not the food of Supātra, the wife of the king of crows. Then, without being noticed even by those royal guards trained in archery and weaponry whose minds were distracted, he took various kinds of fresh royal food, endowed with excellent color and flavor, from King Brahmadatta’s kitchen and departed with his beak.
Day after day, again and again, it carries [it] away.
[They went] to present those various soups to King Brahmadatta.
In this kitchen, a crow commits an offense: it makes the king’s food leavings, defiles it, and destroys it. We were engaged in our work and were driven away by those acts;
the king has commanded his ministers to restrain us.
"In this way, have the kitchen covered with a net, so that the crow will not be able to commit an offense in the kitchen."
"By the mind one [attains] the gods, by speech the rulers of the earth;
by action the wealthy, and by [the lack thereof] the poor."
At the mere word of King Brahmadatta, the entire great kitchen was covered with a net.
Thus, that crow was unable to alight there in the kitchen, nor was he able to commit any offense.
He too reflected: "How shall they carry away this royal food from here?"
This thought occurred to that crow:
"What if I were to guard this very path by which the king's food is brought from the kitchen?"
From whichever path he sees the king’s rice, sauce, various kinds of meat, snacks, sesame preparations, or any other edible being brought toward him,
he takes it from there with his mouth and goes on.
The king commanded: "Give covering lids to the food vessels of all these servers and eunuchs."
Then those servers, having covered that food with lids, approached the king from the kitchen.
Then that crow was no longer able to take it away.
Then this thought occurred to that crow:
"How might I be able to steal royal food once more for the wife of the king of crows?"
Now, whatever morsels of food King Brahmadatta sent by the hands of the maidservants to the queens, he would take back from their hands.
King Brahmadatta heard this;
therefore, as the morsels of food were being placed into the queens' mouths, that crow would snatch the food from the hands of the maidservants.
The king gave the command.
Give coverings for all the morsels being placed into the mouths of the maidservants.
And there, a heavy resentment arose in King Brahmadatta.
"Oh, what a crow this is! So audacious, talkative, impudent, and reckless that he cannot be kept away by those with bows in hand; having seen [food] from within, he swoops down."
The king gave the command.
Whoever should seize this crow of mine while it is still alive and bring it near me, to him I would give a generous covering.
"Such is the command for the entire retinue," King Brahmadatta spoke thus.
[ _Mvu_ 3.128] Now, another maidservant was going along, having taken a morsel of food from her own lady, the queen, and covering it with her garments to present it to King Brahmadatta.
She was seen by that crow,
and this thought occurred to him:
"How can I take the food from this maidservant's hand?
Suppose I were to stick myself to the tip of this maidservant's nose; then, terrified, she will drop this food, and I shall take that food and depart."

Then, having swooped down upon where the female slave was, he alighted on her nose; a wound was inflicted there on the nose. Terrified, the slave abandoned her food and seized that crow with both hands.
Then that maidservant, taking the crow with blood flowing from its nose, approached King Brahmadatta and said, "This is that crow you saw; it has been captured."
Then King Brahmadatta became pleased with that maidservant:
"You have done well in catching this crow."
Then King Brahmadatta gave that maidservant a generous reward.
And that crow was rebuked:
"It is not right that you should even assault the royal palace."
Then that crow addressed King Brahmadatta with a verse:
In Vārāṇasī, O Great King, there dwelt a king of crows named Supātra,
surrounded by eighty thousand crows.
His pregnant wife Supārśvā desired meat—
the freshly cooked royal food prepared in the king’s kitchen.
Having heard his words and carrying out his instruction, I paid honor to my husband by making a wound upon my nose.
Then, monks, King Brahmadatta became pleased with that minister of the crow-king;
for this minister of the crow-king received neither a village nor wealth from that crow-king, nor did he have any other means of livelihood.
Seeking their livelihood with their own beaks, they performed the task of sacrificing themselves for that king of crows.
Then, monks, King Brahmadatta addressed his ministers and retinue in verse:
For such a person as this deserves to enjoy royal luxury,
just as this twice-born man has been subservient to the king of crows until his death.
Then King Brahmadatta granted that crow daily royal food.

Having prepared a full meal consisting of various kinds of fresh royal delicacies, it was set aside for the sake of that crow in a secluded spot; thus, he would eat his own daily portion himself and take some to the king of crows.
An order was issued to the retinue:
"No one at all should cause any obstruction whatsoever to this crow as it goes to or comes from the royal palace."
The Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, monks, it might occur to you that at that time and on that occasion, the king of crows named Supātra was someone else.
But it should not be viewed in this way. And why is that?"
I was that king of crows.
She who was the wife of Kākarāja, named Supārśvā, was this Yaśodharā.
And he who was the minister of the king of crows, over the eighty thousand crows, was this very elder Kālodāyin.
He who was King Brahmadatta has become this King Śuddhodana.
At that time also he was propitiated by him, and now too he has been propitiated by him.
The Kākajātakam is completed.
The monks said to the Blessed One:
Behold, Blessed One, how this Mahāprajāpatī became blind through grief for the Blessed One, and having come to the Blessed One, has become sighted again.
The Blessed One said:
“Monks, it is not only now that Mahāprajāpatī became blind through grief and compassion for me, and was restored to sight by relying on me alone;
on another occasion as well, Mahāprajāpatī was restored to sight by relying on me.”
The monks said.
"At another time as well, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
At another time as well, monks.
Long ago, monks, in times past, on the slopes of the Himalayas there was a mountain named Caṇḍagiri.
On its side there was a great forest tract, covered with thousands of trees laden with flowers and fruits, provided with lotus ponds and hermitages, frequented by hosts of seers, remote and secluded.
There dwelt a large herd of elephants belonging to the six-tusked lineage.
There, a noble elephant calf was born, possessing six tusks, with a head like a *indragopaka* insect, well-established in its seven limbs, and the color of a white water lily (*kumuda*).
When he had grown up, he served his mother with profound respect and affection.
Having first given her food and drink, he would afterwards partake of them himself; and from time to time, he would groom and bathe her when her body was covered in the dust of the forest creepers.
In this way, that young elephant calf, with great attentiveness, faith, affection, and reverence, served his mother at all times.
Then, on one occasion, having bathed his mother and knowing that she had eaten and was resting, he went out by the outer gate while traveling together with a herd of elephants.
Now, he was seen by some deer-hunters while they were tracking the hunt; they went and informed the King of Kāśī:
"Your Majesty, in that forest thicket there dwells such a young elephant, handsome and beautiful to behold; he would be worthy of Your Majesty."
Then, monks, having heard those hunters, the King of Kāśi approached that forest grove with his army and his vehicles.
Having seized that young elephant from the forest grove, he was escorted into Vārāṇasī surrounded by other female elephants and stationed in the elephant stable.
Then it occurred to that king: "This vehicle of mine will be auspicious."
Now he was honored with every kind of hospitality; the king himself provided him with food and drink.
Yet he found no pleasure in all that honor; as he remembered his mother with grief, he sighed deeply, shed tears, and grew thin and withered away.
Then the king, moved by affection, raised his joined palms in reverence and questioned that young elephant.
"O best of elephants, I honor you with every form of hospitality; yet still you wither, fade, and decline in complexion and form. I do not see you uplifted, joyful, or with a cheerful countenance.
Speak to me; tell me what deficiency of provisions I shall provide for you. You are dear to me, O best of elephants, and pleasing to me; tell me why you are declining in your appetite."
And you do not accept water and drink.
Then that young elephant, being questioned by the king, spoke in human speech.

"Your Majesty, I lack no utensil whatsoever, nor do I have any need for such food. My mother dwells there in that forest grove; she is aged, elderly, advanced in years, deprived of sight, and weak of body. Whenever I am aware of it, I do not know how to enjoy food or drink myself without first giving some to my mother."
This is my vow: my death shall occur right here;
I will never again consume food or drink myself without first giving it to my mother.
Now, that King of Kāśī was righteous, compassionate, and devoted to benefiting others.
This thought occurred to him:
"It is marvelous how this young elephant calf is so filial toward its mother, so righteous, and so well-bred—that for all these days it has neither accepted food nor drunk water."
"Out of grief for our mother,
these qualities that belong to this young elephant are not easily found among some men.
It would not be good for us, nor would it be fitting, that we should harm such virtuous beings."
He then said to the high ministers:

"Release this young elephant; let him go to the forest thicket from which we brought him, so that he may reunite with his mother, for he who is devoted to his mother might die here from lack of food. Then we would be rendered useless and joined with unrighteousness."
Then, by the king's command, he was led to the vicinity of that very same forest grove and released.
Having gone to that forest grove, he now took neither food nor drink, but searched for his mother.
Then his mother, weeping out of grief and not seeing her little son, became blind.
Now, that young elephant, not finding his mother, climbed to the summit of a mountain and let out a cry like a great elephant.
As he was letting out that great cry of an elephant, his mother recognized that voice, thinking, "This is my son's voice," and she too let out a great roar.
Then, by him, his mother's voice was recognized.
He then approached the presence of his mother.
His mother was sitting at the edge of a pond, blind and wandering about with her body covered in dust, when she heard the sound of her son's voice.
Then that young elephant, having eaten tender forest creepers from here and there, would groom his mother and remove the dust from her body.
Then, filling his trunk with water from a lake, joyful, elated, and filled with gladness and cheerfulness, he would bathe his mother.
Now she had bathed, those eyes were washed, all impurity was rubbed away, and her filth had departed; her vision became completely pure.
Then that female elephant, seeing her little son, was filled with joy and gladness and asked:
"Son, where have you gone, leaving me behind—me who am helpless and of weak sight?"
He then related that matter in detail to his mother, explaining how he had been seized and how he had been released.
She said to that little son:
"O son, may the King of Kāśi, together with his retinue, rejoice just as I rejoice today upon seeing you."
"O monks, it may be that you think thus: 'At that time, on that occasion, the King of Kāśī was someone else.
But this is not to be viewed in such a way. For what reason? Because..."
This Nanda, my paternal nephew and brother, was formerly the King of Kāśī.
I myself was that very young elephant at that time.
She who was the mother of the young elephant was this Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī; even then she became blind through grief for me, and only by coming to me did she become sighted again.
Now too, this Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī has become blind through grief for me, and only by coming to me has she become sighted again.
Thus ends the narrative of the *Hastinikājātaka*.
Having abandoned all hindrances, listen all of you with one-pointed minds,
to how the conduct of a Bodhisattva is both extremely difficult to perform and truly inspiring.
Even for an elephant born in the animal realm, there was affection for its own mother;
how much more then should one who has become human attend upon his teacher, that brahmin?

Granted that Bodhisattvas are affectionate toward all living beings and naturally tender by nature, yet they are exceedingly affectionate toward their gurus; as it has been heard, so shall I proclaim.
On the slopes of the Himavat mountains, in the delightful Caṇḍogre Caṇḍa mountain,
which is here and there adorned with hermitages belonging to communities of ascetics.
It was frequented by throngs of kinnaras, elephants, monkeys, boars, śārdūlas, and tigers;
it was the haunt of ruru deer, buffaloes, and sarabhas, and was filled with bulls, camaris, and śambaras.
That excellent forest shines on all sides with pairs of peacocks, parrots, jīvajīvaka birds, cakoras, and karaviṅkas, as they warble sweetly.
In various places, lotus ponds filled with royal swans shine forth; in the city, they are graced by the playful movements of kalahamsa geese and stirred by herds of elephants.
In some places, near the trees, various delightful carpets were laid out by bees and honey-bees with their crushed flowers; there, deer and birds stood about, moving with playful grace.
In some places, that excellent forest shines with aged ascetics who delight in meditation, who have gone to the mountain streams, and with others devoted to the recitation of sacred texts.
In some places, the excellent forest shines with young men wearing long matted hair and deerskin bark garments, carrying various fruits and roots in their hands.
On that delightful slope,
the noble elephant, with his whole being, attended to his mother— who was blind, aged, and weak of limb.
While sporting together with the herd of elephants, he went a great distance away;
and the king, along with his army, arrived at the place where the elephant was being captured.
Having seen that excellent elephant, the king’s charioteer also spoke with joy:
"O King, this preeminent elephant in the herd is endowed with the marks of a supreme beast."
Having seen that noble elephant, the lord of elephants, who was moving among a herd of tuskers,
the King of Kāśī seized him from the forest and bound him to his excellent city.
He neither drank nor ate, yet he sighed repeatedly;
the protector of the earth spoke to that jewel among elephants with a sweet voice.
O best of nāgas, do not become emaciated; accept this food and drink this water.
I shall delight you here in this most excellent city, for you are truly radiant.
The best of elephants said:
"Indeed, O Lord of Men, I do not grieve for my bonds, nor for my confinement, nor for hunger and thirst;
rather, O Ruler of Men, I grieve because of that which is more painful than this."
The king said:
O noble elephant, what is more painful than this for you? Tell me of another even greater pain, because of which it does not occur to you to seek water and food.
The young elephant said:
"My mother is advanced in years, aged, and exceedingly affectionate; she is blind.
O Lord of Men, she will die without me, and for that reason I grieve."
I first brought lotus stalks and fibers for her who was without eyes; later, I myself ate them today, and thus I grieve, thinking, "I am fasting."
In the summer, when my limbs are scorched by heat, I offer her cool water shaded by the forest and bathe her; yet today I grieve, thinking, "She is without a protector."
Now she wanders in the forest, sightless and her body covered in dust;
crying out, "O my son! she has encountered a sorrow even more painful than before.
Having heard the words of the lordly elephant— so very sweet and full of compassion— the best of men, the lord of men, his face filled with tears, addressed the elephant:
Such qualities as these are very difficult to find among certain men;
it is because of them, O best of elephants, that this pain arises within your heart.
Release the noble elephant quickly; let him roam in the forest while attending upon his elders, so that his mother may be comforted and rejoice together with her jewel of a son.
The mother of that preeminent elephant, shattered by the arrow of grief and afflicted by suffering,
roams the forest crying out, just as a dark cloud thunders across the sky.
May the mother be with her calf; may the wild deer and the forest deities rejoice.
Now that it has been told, may my sightless mother rejoice because of this jewel.
Desired by hunters for the sake of its tusks, and by tigers for the sake of its blood and flesh, the best of elephants was led away like a tribute to the royal capital; thus did I enter Kāśī.
The forest deities said: "The king of Kāśi shall take this best of elephants, endowed with the most excellent marks, from the forest and bind him to his preeminent city."
Surely death will come to me, who am helpless and deprived of my eyes;
and that elephant, so very affectionate toward me, will also die out of grief.
He who roamed among the excellent mountains and the finest forests with their blossoming peaks—
that elephant shall surely die, grieving for me and my grove.
Furthermore, O best of elephants, your mother was never angry with you nor ever abandoned by you;
she followed you with love, so may there be liberation for you as well.
Furthermore, O Hero, never without first giving a portion of food,
or fruits and roots, to your mother, let your own meal take place.
Then the noble elephant, hastening to his mother, addressed her affectionately and stroked her,
who was purified of dust, with his delicate trunk.
I was bound by the King of Kāśī with cruel snares in that supreme city;
but for your sake, I have been released again by the King of Dharma.
Having heard the roar of that excellent elephant and having experienced its touch, she was joyful in mind and uplifted; having regained the elephant, her eyes filled with tears once more.
The little female elephant said:
Thus may the King of Kāśī rejoice along with his kinsmen,
just as I rejoice today because of my son and my eyes.
Today, together with her son, she beholds this excellent elephant— the very same son she formerly saw in the mountain forest filled with deer— with her own eyes.
Having directly known his former birth, the Perfectly Awakened One, the best of speakers,
the Teacher, related this Jātaka in the presence of the monks.
I was that excellent elephant, and she was that female elephant; for that reason, even today I am her son, and Gautamī is filled with deep affection for me.
In this long saṃsāra, you have been afflicted by attachment and aversion;
therefore, in order to abandon attachment and aversion, practice the Dharma free from the sense of "mine."
The Hastinī-jātaka is completed.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, discipline sentient beings by means of three miracles:
namely, the miracle of supernatural power, the miracle of instruction, and the miracle of teaching the Dharma.
By means of these three miracles, the Blessed One disciplined many thousands of living beings in the noble Dharma within the Nyagrodha Grove.
Then indeed Rāhu, the lord of the asuras, Vemacitrin, the lord of the asuras, and Mucilinda, the lord of the asuras, together with sixty nayutas of asuras, took abundant perfumes and garlands;
and many thousands of asuras and many thousands of asura maidens, adorned with every ornament and wearing jeweled earrings, [came] with great asura majesty.

With great asura-miraculous power, they approached the Banyan Grove at Kapilavastu; having arrived, they stood in the sky above the Banyan Grove in mid-air and performed worship and honor for the Blessed One with all kinds of perfumes,
all kinds of garlands, all kinds of dances, all kinds of songs, all kinds of instrumental music, and all kinds of orchestral performances.

Having honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated the Blessed One, they resolved their minds upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, thinking: "O, may we too in a future time become Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas, endowed with knowledge and conduct, Sugatas, knowers of the world,
unsurpassed charioteers of men to be tamed, teachers of gods and humans, just as this Blessed One is."

May we now likewise be endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, our bodies adorned with the eighty secondary characteristics, endowed with the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, powerful through the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and confident through the four grounds of self-confidence— just as the Blessed One is now— and may we likewise turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
"May we conduct ourselves just as the Blessed One does now;

and may gods and humans regard us as worthy of being heard and believed, just as they do the Blessed One now; and may we maintain this harmonious community of disciples just as the Blessed One does now."

"Thus, having crossed over, may we help others cross; being liberated, may we liberate others; having found rest, may we give rest to others; having attained final nirvana, may we lead others to final nirvana.

In this way, may it be for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of the great multitude of beings, both gods and humans."
Then the Blessed One, having understood this kind of mental aspiration of those asuras, manifested a smile at that very moment. Immediately upon its manifestation,
rays of light of various colors and many hues— blue, yellow, madder-red, crimson, white, and bright— issued forth from the Blessed One’s mouth.
Having illuminated the entire buddha-field with their golden color, as far as the Akaniṣṭha realm of the gods, they circumambulated the Blessed One three times and vanished before the Blessed One.
Then the venerable Aśvakī approached the Blessed One, and having extended his joined palms toward him, he said this to the Blessed One:
"Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not manifest a smile without cause or condition.
Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition for manifesting this smile?"
Then the Blessed One, having been questioned by the Venerable Aśvajit, and after the asuras— up to the Akaniṣṭha host of gods—
had circumambulated the Blessed One three times and vanished before him, explained the mental aspiration of the asuras through verses.
Then the Lord of Bipeds, having perceived the noble intention of the Dānava, manifested a smile;
Aśvaki, having joined his palms in reverence, asked him.
Having seen the smile from the mouth of the Sugata.
The Supreme Sage, the lamp of the world, does not manifest a smile here without cause;
O Best of Men, tell us the reason for this smile.
That which was performed by you, seeking the welfare of the world here.
Today, without a doubt, sublime awakening has been generated by someone within this assembly,
whose intention the Tathāgata, having understood, [recognizes].
He manifested a beautiful smile.
Even though he was filled with doubt here today upon seeing the smile from the Sugata’s mouth,
speak, O Supreme among Men; let there be no delay.
Cut away the doubt and the distress of those who are uncertain.
Since the Lamp of the World, having perceived this sublime offering from the Dānava, has manifested a smile,
speak a prophecy concerning the host of Asuras.
Or having heard which, one might become uplifted.
The Blessed One said:
Excellent, Aśvajit, are the questions you have asked regarding that for which the Benefactor of the World smiled;
I shall explain its fruit to you in its entirety.
Listen to me as I speak with a single-minded focus.
Wishing for unexcelled enlightenment, the asuras performed worship for me here;
they abandoned that asura body.
Having gone to heaven, they shall rejoice for a long time.
Having dwelt for a long time in the city of the gods,
fully endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure,
he returns once again to this human world.
They will worship the Jinas, the lords of bipeds.
Having performed worship toward the Jinas hundreds and thousands of times over many kalpas,
he now bears the marks resembling gold.
All shall become Jinas, conquerors of their enemies.
And having heard the prophecy concerning the asuras, the world with its gods— many hundreds of thousands of living beings— was satisfied and uplifted.
They have set out therein in the unsurpassed vehicle.
Then, at that time, Saṃbara, the lord of the asuras, spoke this verse:
May I always have association with such friends as these,
by relying upon whom and depending upon whom we may worship the Supreme among Bipeds.
Then the Blessed One, having prophesied those sixty million asuras for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment,
and having established many thousands of living beings in the noble dharmas, exhorted King Śuddhodana along with his retinue.
Then King Śuddhodana, together with his retinue, rose from his seat, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, and departed;
likewise did the entire multitude of people.

Then, indeed, King Śuddhodana, at the end of that very night, having prepared an abundance of solid and soft foods, had the city of Kapilavastu sprinkled and swept; he cleared it of dust and removed all stones, pebbles, and gravel; he scattered loose flowers, perfumed it with incense from censers, draped it with variegated hangings, stretched out canopies, and suspended bundles of silk ribbons and garlands.

From Kapilavastu as far as the Nyagrodha Monastery, having stationed throughout various regions actors, dancers, athletes, wrestlers, musicians, jar-bearers, acrobats, and performers of the *dvistvala* and *velambaka* dances, he caused the Blessed One to enter the city with great royal majesty and great royal splendor.
Then King Śuddhodana, having placed the Blessed One together with the community of disciples at the head [of the procession], led them into the royal palace.
Then the Blessed One, having entered the residence of Śuddhodana, sat down on the seat that had been prepared, as did the community of monks according to their respective seats.
Then King Śuddhodana, with his own hands, satisfied and served the Blessed One with abundant and exquisite solid and soft foods, as well as the assembly of monks including friends and ministers.

Then the Blessed One, having finished eating, washed his hands, and set aside his bowl, instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened King Śuddhodana with a discourse on the Dharma; thereafter, rising from his seat, he departed.

On another day, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī provided a meal for the Blessed One together with the community of disciples; on another day, Yaśodharā provided a meal; and on another day, the women of the inner apartments did so.
On another day, the Śākya community provided a meal for the Blessed One together with his community of disciples.
Now Yaśodharā has prepared sweetmeats for the Blessed One together with his community of disciples, and she has invited her entire circle of kinsmen.

The Blessed One, who knows the right time, the right hour, and the right occasion, and who discerns the superior and inferior qualities of individuals, dressed himself early in the morning, took his bowl and robe, and surrounded and preceded by the community of monks, entered the residence of Yaśodharā and sat down upon the seat prepared for him, as did the community of monks according to their respective seats.

Then indeed Yaśodharā, the mother of Rāhula, together with Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and her circle of kinsmen, satisfied and served the Blessed One, along with the community of disciples, with excellent solid and soft foods.
Then Yaśodharā gave a fresh, exquisite sweetmeat, endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and flavor, into the hand of Rāhula, saying, "Go, give this sweetmeat to your father."
Having gone there and placed it in the Blessed One’s bowl, he sat down in the shadow of the Blessed One and said this to his mother:
"Truly, Mother, this shadow of the ascetic is pleasant."
Then Yaśodharā spoke thus to the young prince Rāhula:
And whatever paternal wealth there is for the son.
Then indeed, the youth Rāhula said this to the Blessed One:
"Give me my paternal wealth, O ascetic!"
The Blessed One said:
"Rāhula, go forth into homelessness; then I shall give you your father's inheritance."

Then indeed, the king together with his harem and the Śākyas with their retinues became joyful, satisfied, and elated, thinking: "The Blessed One has accepted Rāhula as his son; what fault could there be in Yaśodharā?"

Then Yaśodharā, having adorned herself with all her ornaments, served the Blessed One. She wondered, "How is it that my noble son continues to dwell at home, yet there is no change in the mind of the Blessed One?

Then the Blessed One, having finished his meal, washed his hands, and set aside his bowl, addressed the King Śuddhodana together with his harem, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, and Yaśodharā, the mother of Rāhula, along with their retinues, with a discourse on the Dharma.
Having shown, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them, he rose from his seat and departed.
The monks said to the Blessed One:
"Behold, Blessed One, Yaśodharā is tempting you with sweetmeats."
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now that this Yaśodharā has enticed me with sweetmeats."
The monks said:
"Also at other times, Blessed One?"
The Blessed One said:
And at other times as well, monks.

Once upon a time, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi, to the north of that place, in the vicinity of the Himalayas, there was a hermitage named Sāhañjanī. It was peaceful, secluded, devoid of people, remote from men, suitable for solitary retreat, and well-supplied with roots, leaves, flowers, and water.
There dwelt a sage named Kāśyapa, who possessed the five superknowledges, had attained the four dhyānas, and was endowed with great supernatural power and great majesty.
In the last month of summer, he ate fruits that were not yet fully ripe and, being thirsty, drank a great deal of water.
His internal humors became congested by the wind and heat,
and he voided urine mixed with semen into a stone basin.
Another doe, being thirsty, drank that urine under the perception that it was water.
The doe, being in her season, licked the opening of her womb with her tongue—her muzzle being smeared with impurity—along with the semen;
having become intoxicated by that, she conceived in her womb.
And that seer dwelt in loving-kindness (*maitrī*); even the beasts and birds were not afraid of him.
Hundreds of beasts and birds roamed and lived around the precincts of the hermitage. That doe also roamed around the very same precincts of the hermitage and wandered about right there.
Then, in due course of time, she gave birth to a son.
When that seer saw her, this thought occurred to him:
"How can this human offspring belong to a female deer who has gone into the animal realm?"
The knowledge of the sages functions by means of focused attention.
Then that sage focused his attention:

"At such a time, I consumed an excessive amount of small, unripe fruits and drank a great deal of water; consequently, because my bodily elements were overflowing, [semen] was discharged into the *apalakuṇḍaka*."
She had urinated;
this thirsty doe, perceiving it as water, drank it while she was in her season, and consequently conceived in her womb.
[The woman thought: "This is my own discharge of semen."
Then, taking the infant in his deerskin garment, he brought him into that hermitage.
Then that doe followed behind him;
with that wooden board, he cut the umbilical cord of the infant, anointed it with oil, and washed away the impurities of the womb with warm water.
The seer pressed that infant form against the udder of that doe, and she suckled him;
the seer also placed the doe’s udder into the mouth of that boy.
Whenever that boy was sitting down, the doe would wander all around his hermitage, drink water, and then return to suckle him from her udder and lick him with the tip of her tongue.
At the time when that infant was even supported by her feet, he himself would take hold of the doe's teat and drink from it.
Because he was born as a one-horned being who wanders alone, that seer gave him the name Ekaśṛṅga.
Now, just as his mother roamed with the deer, so too did that young seer Ekaśṛṅga roam, playing together with the deer and fawns.

Wherever his mother roamed with the herds of deer, there also the young seer Ekaśṛṅga would roam. Playing together with the fawns and roaming again and again with the deer and fawns, he would return once more to that seer’s hermitage.
Then the seer gave him various small fruits, endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and flavor.
When that young seer was lying down in the hermitage, many deer and fawns would lie down surrounding that young seer.
Whenever those deer and fawns desired to graze, they would awaken that young seer as he lay sleeping by nuzzling him with their snouts.
Thus, those deer and fawns, as well as various kinds of birds, took delight there in that hermitage together with that young seer.
When that young seer Ekaśṛṅgaka had attained maturity, he would sprinkle and sweep the hermitage of that seer;
he would bring various kinds of roots, bring leaves, bring water, and bring firewood; he would massage the seer, bathe him, and tend to the sacred fire.
She served that seer with various kinds of preparations made from roots, leaves, flowers, and fruits, and offered him water to drink.
Having first served that seer and her mother, the doe, she afterwards took her own food.
That seer taught the path of meditative absorptions and supernormal knowledges to that young seer.

Then, as that young seer dwelt devoted to the practice of vigilance during the first and last watches of the night, striving and exerting himself, he produced the four meditative absorptions and realized the five superknowledges.

Now that young seer had become an attainer of the four dhyānas, possessed of the five superknowledges, a celibate from his youth, endowed with great psychic power and great majesty, renowned among gods and men.
The young seer Ekaśṛṅgaka dwelt in the Sāhañjanī hermitage on the bank of the river Gaṅgā in the Himalayas;
and in the city of Vārāṇasī, he was not the son of the King of Kāśi.
He then performed many sacrificial rites for the sake of obtaining a son, thinking, "May a son be born to me," yet no son was born to him; although his harem was extensive, he had only daughters.

Now, the King of Kāśī heard that on the bank of the Gaṅgā there was a hermitage named Sāhañjanī, where a seer named Kāśyapa resided; and while that royal seer was dwelling in that hermitage, a young seer named Ekaśṛṅgaka was born from a doe.
"What if I were to give my daughter Nalinī, the princess, to the young seer Ekaśṛṅga? He shall be both my son and my son-in-law."
Then, monks, that King of Kāśi said to his brahmin family priest:
There lived a seer named Kāśyapa.
While that royal seer was dwelling there in his hermitage, a young seer named Ekaśṛṅga was born from a doe.
"What if I were to give my daughter, Princess Nalinī, to the young seer Ekaśṛṅga? He would then be both my son and my son-in-law."
Then, monks, that King of Kāśi addressed his brahmin domestic priest and royal preceptor:
"Go, priest, give this Princess Nalinī to the young seer Ekaśṛṅga;
he shall be both my son-in-law and my grandson."

Then, monks, the brahmin chaplain and royal preceptor, having caused Princess Nalinī and her retinue to mount a horse-chariot, took abundant food and drink, sweetmeats, and various kinds of edibles and delicacies, and arrived at the Sāhañjanī hermitage.
Then, having gone to the hermitage site of Sāhañjanī, they arrived in its vicinity, not very far from the hermitage.
There, Princess Nalinī was playing and laughing together with her companions; seeing them thus sporting, the flocks of beasts and birds were terrified and fled in every direction.
Then, monks, this thought occurred to the young seer Ekaśṛṅga:
Why indeed are these beasts and birds today terrified and fleeing in every direction?
Then, monks, the young seer Ekaśṛṅga went to where the princess Nalinī was.
Monks, the young seer Ekaśṛṅga saw the maiden Nalinī playing with her friends;
she was well-adorned, beautifully decorated, and dressed in costly garments.
Upon seeing her, this thought occurred to him:
Truly, these young seers are handsome; their deerskins, their matted locks, and their girdles of antelope skin are magnificent.
He gazed upon the princesses;
he then beheld the deer-skin girdles of those princesses shimmering exceedingly upon their bodies.
Then Ekaśṛṅgaka asked Nalinī:
Beautiful indeed are your deerskins, matted hair, girdles, and necklaces.
Then the princess Nīlanī took the young seer Ekaśṛṅga by the hand and said:
Such are these our deerskins, girdles, neck-threads, and hand-threads.
Then she gave sweetmeats and a drink to that young seer, saying, "Please enjoy this sweetmeat from our hands."
Then he consumed those sweetmeats and drank the beverage as well.
While he was in that hermitage with his sense of taste repelled by bitter and astringent fruits, as he was eating those sweetmeats, an exceedingly great relish for flavors took hold of him.
And having drunk those drinks for quenching thirst, he then said:
"Beautiful indeed are these fruits and juices of yours, as well as the water, the deerskins, the girdles, the necklaces, and the bracelets; such noble foods are not found in our hermitage.
Then, monks, the princess Nalinī said this to the young seer Ekaśṛṅga:
"Come, young seer! These huts of ours are mobile; we shall take these huts wherever we wish and go. Come, enter our hut and I will show you the hermitage."
Then Nalinī, having mounted the vehicle there, extended her hand to Ekaśṛṅga and said, "Come, enter; let us go into this hut of ours, our hermitage."
Then, seeing horses harnessed to that carriage, he said:
"The doe was my mother, and deer carry this leaf-hut; I will not enter here."

Then Nalinī clung to the hand of the young seer Ekaśṛṅga, she clung to his neck, embraced him, kissed him, and seduced him; and the young seer, from the top of her head down to her feet, observed her marks:
he saw that his own matted locks were of one kind, while Nalinī’s were of another; he saw his own form was of one kind, while Nalinī’s was of another.
She saw her own girdle of muñja grass to be of one kind, and that of Nalinī to be of another; she saw her own hand-ornaments to be of one kind, and those of Nalinī to be of another.
Then, having engaged in conversation with the young seer, having established mutual trust, and having generated affection, she acted exactly as the Blessed One had said.
Whether through dwelling together in the past or through present benefit,
such love arises for him like a lotus in water.
Wherever the mind dwells or the consciousness finds clarity,
there the wise person should reach their goal, together with my city of contentment.

As they wandered through saṃsāra for a long time across thousands of millions of births, there was a mutual encounter between them as husband and wife; therefore, upon seeing one another, their mutual affection is rekindled.
Then Nalinī, with the intention of seducing the young seer Ekaśṛṅga, had him eat royal delicacies— sweetmeats, hard foods, and soft foods—
and had him drink excellent beverages; and having embraced him, kissed him, and pressed him close to her neck, she mounted a horse-drawn carriage and returned to Vārāṇasī.
He announces this fundamental nature in detail.

The young seer Ekaśṛṅgaka, having gone to the hermitage, sat there attending to the delightful signs from the crown of the head down to the feet of that princess Nalinī; he neither brought roots and fruits,
nor water, nor wood, nor did he sweep the hermitage grounds or tend to the sacred fire-offering.
Then that seer, seeing the prince lost in thought, asked him:
"You have not split the wood, you have not fetched the water, and the fire-oblation has not been offered; yet you are absorbed in meditation."
The young seer said:

"From another hermitage, a young seer has arrived here together with many other young seers; he is pleasing and handsome, adorned with beautiful matted hair, deerskins, beautiful necklaces, bracelets, and beautiful girdles of muñja grass.
Moreover, their fruits and drinking water are polished and refined, unlike our own, even in this hut provided for hunting."

"I have seen those fawns of yours in such-and-such a part of the hermitage, and through that young seer, affection has arisen within me. When he takes me by the neck and, placing his mouth against my mouth, makes a sound, it produces great joy in me. Remembering him, I am dejected of face; without him, I find no delight in the hermitage."
Then, having heard this from the young seer, it occurred to the seer:
Given the way this young seer describes their complexion and physical form, those young seers cannot possibly be women.
Then that seer said to the young seer Ekaśṛṅgaka:
"Son, those are not young women of the seers; they are women who entice the seers and cause them to turn away from their ascetic heat.
Those women must be avoided from afar by the seers, for they create obstacles for those living the holy life.
Do not associate with them; they are like venomous serpents, they are like poisonous leaves, and they are comparable to pits of glowing embers."
Then the King of Kāśi said to that priest:

"Having planted Aśoka groves in the boats with trees endowed with flowers and fruits, go upstream along the Gaṅgā to that hermitage together with Nalinī and her retinue; then, having placed that young seer on the boat, bring him back."

Then the domestic priest, having given his word to the King of Kāśi, had the princess Nalinī boarded along with her retinue on boats from Pūrvaṃtaka that were provided with canopies, draped with variegated cloths, hung with bundles of silk streamers and garlands, and strewn with loose flowers; and he went upstream on the Gaṅgā to that Sahya hermitage.
Then, having moored the boats near that hermitage, the princess Nalinī was sent into the presence of the young seer Ekaśṛṅga with the command: "Go, bring the young seer here."
Then Princess Nalinī, having disembarked from the boat, sat with her retinue in that hermitage, plucking various kinds of forest flowers and forest shoots.
And seeing her, the throngs of beasts and birds fled in every direction from that hermitage, uttering their respective cries.
The young seer, seeing those flocks of beasts and birds terrified, went to that place;
there he saw the princess Nalinī with her retinue, plucking forest flowers and forest shoots.
And having seen her, he approached where the princess Nalinī was.
The young seer was greeted again by Nalinī; she clung to his neck, embraced him, and kissed him.
Having eaten sweetmeats and various kinds of snacks, and having drunk beverages fit for a king, he boarded the boat together with Nalinī.
Nalinī said:
These move about in the water in our hermitage.
Having enticed her with that, he brought her to Vārāṇasī by means of a boat;
the domestic priest then gave Nalinī in marriage to the young seer.
He sat and played with that Nalinī, yet he did not enter into union with her;
for he knew, "This is a young seer, my friend."

Then, while he was on that boat together with Nalinī, he arrived at the hermitage of Sāhañjani; and there he saw the young seer Ekaśṛṅga coming along with Nalinī, the princess, and his mother, the doe.
Then she asked her son,
"Son, where have you been?"
Then he said:
"I have gone to the hermitage of this friend of mine."
"Friend, this is my fire which, having been circumambulated, was grasped by me with a hand moistened with water."

Then this thought occurred to that doe: "Indeed, this young seer does not know what a companion is, nor what a wife is; yet this maiden and this young seer are the best of men, and by him she has been taken as his wife—having circumambulated the fire and grasped her hand with water, she has been obtained as a wife."
In that regard, who could have informed the young seer of this matter, so that he would not think: "This young seer is the daughter of the King of Kāśi named Nalinī, given as your wife"?

And there, at the foot of that hermitage of Sāhañjana on the bank of the Gaṅgā, as a young seer was entering the hermitage of ascetic women who were devoted to their vows, he was stopped by those female ascetics.
"Do not enter this hermitage; you are a man, and this is the hermitage of women who are devoted to their vows and practicing celibacy—it is not permitted for a man to enter here."
Then that young seer questioned the female ascetic.
Who is it, whether woman or man?
That female ascetic explained the nature of women to him, saying: "This is not your companion; this is not a young seer.
This is a woman named Nalinī, a princess and the daughter of the King of Kāśi. You were born as a man from a doe;
therefore you do not know that she was given to you as a wife by means of water. You are her husband, and it is not permitted for you two to abandon one another."

Then, having heard those words of the female ascetics, the young seer went together with Nalinī to the hermitage of his father, the seer Kāśyapa; having prostrated at his father’s feet, he reported this entire matter to him in the presence of his father along with Nalinī.
This thought occurred to the seer:
The young seer is unable to dwell here in this hermitage without Nalinī; they have become bound to one another and have developed mutual affection.
Then he spoke to his son, the young seer Ekaśṛṅga.
"My son, this Princess Nalinī has been given to you; having made Agnideva her witness, she was taken by the hand with water and bestowed upon you.
She is your wife, and you are her husband. You two must not abandon one another."
Go together with her to the city of Vārāṇasī.
Then, having bowed at the feet of the seer and circumambulated him, and having paid homage to their mother, they went to Vārāṇasī; having arrived, they approached the King of Kāśi.
The king gave a suitable residence to the young seer, as well as a retinue, coverlets and rugs, and all manner of articles for enjoyment and use; he was then consecrated as crown prince.
All accumulations end in depletion; all elevations end in a fall;
all unions end in separation; and life ends in death.
Then that King of Kāśi, having been joined with the law of time, passed away; Ekaśṛṅga obtained the kingdom in Vārāṇasī.
Then, from the root of Nalinī, thirty-two twin sons were born;
and from the roots of the other queens as well, more than a hundred sons were born.
Having ruled the kingdom righteously for a long time, and having consecrated his eldest son in the kingdom, he again went forth into the wandering life of a seer.

Then, by devoting himself to the practice of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night, applying himself, striving, and exerting himself, he generated the four dhyānas and realized the five superknowledges (abhijñās) through the path that has been cleared away.
Having now transcended the realm of desire, at the breaking up of the body, he was reborn in the company of the Brahma gods.
The Blessed One said:
He who at that time was the seer Kāśyapa was Śuddhodana;
she who was the doe, monks, was Mahāprajāpatī; and he who was the King of Kāśi was this very Mahānāma the Śākyan.
And he who was the young seer Ekaśṛṅga was none other than I myself;
and she who was the princess named Nalinī was this very Yaśodharā.
Even then, she adorned herself and seduced me; even now, she has adorned herself and seduces me.
The Jātaka of the princess Nalinī is completed.
The monks said to the Blessed One:
"Behold, Blessed One, how this Yaśodharā has been sent away by King Śuddhodana to be executed—without having been interrogated, without having been investigated, and though she was innocent.
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, it is not only now that this Yaśodharā was sent away by King Śuddhodana to be executed without being interrogated and while being innocent; on another occasion as well, this Yaśodharā was sent away by this King Śuddhodana to be executed without being interrogated, without being investigated, and while being innocent."
The monks said:
At another time as well, Blessed One?
The Blessed One said:
On another occasion as well, monks.

In the past, in the region beyond the Himalayas, there was a great forest tract; therein was the hermitage of the seer Māṇḍavya, who had attained the four dhyānas and the five super-knowledges. It was a most auspicious place, provided with roots, fruits, flowers, leaves, and water, and frequented by hundreds of thousands of deer and birds.

Then, monks, in the last month of summer, after the seer Māṇḍavya had consumed small-fruiting fruits and drunk a great deal of water, his bodily elements became excessively moistened, and he discharged urine mixed with semen into a stone basin.
Then, monks, a certain doe in her season, wandering in thirst, mistook a stone basin for water and drank the urine mixed with semen from that seer.
With her muzzle smeared with the impurity, she licked her own vulva;
inconceivable is the ripening of the karma of sentient beings.
That doe, having conceived that semen and blood together, obtained a womb.
She then wandered and roamed about in the vicinity of that very hermitage.

Then, in due course of time, that doe gave birth to a girl who was beautiful to behold, with a noble countenance, endowed with the highest excellence of complexion, fair-skinned, and resembling a lump of fresh butter; and as soon as she had given birth to that girl, the seer beheld that object.
This thought occurred to him:
Whence could this doe, belonging to the animal realm, have a human offspring?
Having focused his attention, the knowledge of the seers possessing the five supernormal powers proceeds.
Then the seer Māṇḍavya, possessed of the five superknowledges and of great merit, applied his mind in contemplation.
"In this hermitage of mine, there is no passage for any other person.

This doe was born and raised right here in my hermitage, and likewise hundreds of other deer and birds have been raised here in this forest grove; not a single deer or bird of mine ever goes to another forest grove."
And no other deer or bird comes here from any other forest grove;
these herds of deer and birds were born, have grown, and have flourished right here in this forest grove, and they delight in this grove frequented by non-humans.
At such-and-such a time, during the last month of summer, I ate very ripe fruits and drank a great deal of cool water.
Then, because my elements were agitated, I discharged urine mixed with semen into a stone basin; that thirsty doe drank the urine mixed with semen, perceiving it to be water.
Consequently, she conceived in her womb. This is the discharge from my body.
There, the ṛṣi Māṇḍavya conceived an exceeding love for the girl.
Taking that girl with his deerskin garment, he brought her to the hermitage;
she, too, followed after him like a doe.
Then that seer cut the girl's umbilical cord with a fruit-blade. While she was being cherished by human care, she remained nursing at the teat of that forest doe;
and the seer would press small ripe fruits into her mouth from time to time, anoint her with oil, and bathe her with warm water.
As that girl grew up, she greatly beautified that forest with her mother, the doe, and the seer; and her mother would lick her with her tongue.
At the time when that girl, growing up, began to walk on her feet, wherever she placed her feet, there lotuses appeared for that girl as the ripening of wholesome karma accumulated in the past.

And all around that seer’s hermitage, as the girl wandered about, rows of lotuses sprang up; it shone like a grove of lotuses, and with those lotuses the girl played, picking them up with her hand and moving about.
Then, as a result of that girl’s wholesome karma, lotuses appeared at the steps of that seer;

seeing this, he was filled with wonder, thinking, "Oh, what supernatural power (ṛddhi) this girl possesses! Wherever she placed her feet, there beautiful and lovely lotuses appeared. He thought, "This girl must surely be one who has performed meritorious deeds."
Formerly, she had planted roots of merit among those worthy of offerings, by virtue of which she possesses such power as this.
Then that seer gave the girl the name Padumāvatī.
As she grew up, she wandered all around that hermitage together with her mother;
wherever the doe went wandering, there the girl also wandered with her mother, roaming about playing in the company of deer and fawns.
And whenever she became hungry, she would come to that hermitage together with her mother, surrounded by other deer, does, and fawns.
Then the seer would give the doe, who had arrived at the hermitage, the finest fruits and the finest drinks.
Now she herself ate various fruits and gave them to other young deer.

When that girl was lying down there in the hermitage, then those young male deer and female deer, having completed their walk about, would lie down; and when they wished to go for a walk, they would wake the girl by nuzzling her with their snouts.
Wherever those deer wandered as they roamed about, there that girl would wander along with them, playing together with the male fawns and the female fawns.
Wherever she wandered, there, upon every step in all directions, lotuses appeared.
That girl also, taking those lotuses from right there, fastened them on herself and fastened lotuses upon those young deer as well.
Thus, sporting together with them in that hermitage, she grew up; they did not find delight even for a moment apart from one another.

When that girl had reached maturity, she then sprinkled and cleaned the seer’s hermitage; she brought various kinds of root-preparations, she brought various kinds of leaf-preparations, she brought various kinds of flower-preparations, she brought various kinds of fruit-preparations, she brought water, or she brought wood and fuel.
She anoints that seer with oil and bathes him;
she tends to his sacred fire-offering and serves that seer with various kinds of roots, leaves, flowers,
and fruits, and brings him various kinds of fruit juices.
And wherever she wandered in that hermitage, and wheresoever she went— whether to gather roots, or leaves, or flowers, or fruits— she would return surrounded by those deer and birds.

Once, while Padumāvatī was going to fetch water surrounded by those deer and birds, King Brahmadatta of Kāmpilla, pursuing a deer on a horse as swift as the wind along with his vanguard, reached that region.
By that deer, King Brahmadatta was led to a forest grove.
As it was said by the Blessed One in the Dharmapada:
Leaping is the way of deer; the sky is the way of birds;
dharma is the way of the twice-born; and nirvana is the great way.
That deer disappeared there in the forest thicket.
While King Brahmadatta was searching for that deer in the forest thicket,
he saw Padumāvatī there at the water’s edge; she was dressed in a black antelope skin as an upper garment,
holding a water-pot and a beautiful lotus in her hand— graceful, lovely to behold, and supremely radiant.
She was endowed with an abundance of beauty;
and wherever she set her feet, there beautiful and lovely lotuses would appear.
And having seen this, monks, this thought occurred to King Brahmadatta regarding the seer’s daughter Padumāvatī:

"Oh, what a beautiful form and miraculous power this maiden possesses! Wherever she places her footsteps, lotuses appear there—exceedingly pleasing to the eye, serene, and lovely to behold. Who indeed might she be?
Is she a daughter of the gods, a daughter of the nāgas, a daughter of the kinnaras, a human woman, or perhaps a non-human being?"
What if I were now to approach him and ask?
Then, monks, King Brahmadatta approached the seer’s daughter Padumāvatī and said this to her:
"O blessed lady, who are you, and to whom do you belong?"
When this had been said, monks, the seer’s daughter Padmāvatī spoke thus to King Brahmadatta:
I am indeed a seer’s daughter named Padmāvatī, the daughter of the seer Māṇḍavya, who lives in the forest, subsists on roots and fruits, and observes the life of celibacy.
When this had been said, monks, King Brahmadatta spoke thus to the seer’s daughter Padmāvatī:

"O blessed lady, what kind of food preparations do you have while living in the grove, by which your body is so well-nourished? And what kind of garments do you wear, by which you possess such a delicate complexion?
When this was said, monks, the seer’s daughter Padumāvatī, touching the king’s garments, spoke thus to King Brahmadatta:
Roots and fruits are our food, and deerskins our clothing; yet these [skins] are so fine that they are not even true deerskins.
When this had been said, monks,
this thought occurred to King Brahmadatta:
"This young seer-maiden is ignorant of proper distinctions; she does not recognize the difference between the garments of a king or those worthy of a king and the garments of a seer,
nor does she know the difference between deerskins, nor the difference between garments worthy of a king, nor even the qualities of my horse."

"This seer’s daughter, this princess—she would be a suitable wife for me; yet, without the permission of the seer Māṇḍavya, I am not even able to take her hand, let alone lead her from this hermitage to the city of Kampilla. The illustrious seer Māṇḍavya might reduce me and my entire retinue to ashes with a curse."
"What if I were now to entice the seer’s daughter Padumāvatī by means of a stratagem?"

Monks, when the kings of old went out hunting, they would fill a *yamalaka* basket with barley-meal mixed with honey and ghee, as well as sweetmeats fit for a king and fried cakes, and fasten it behind the saddle-cloth on the back of the horse, thinking: "Lest the king, having been carried off alone and without a second into the forests by his horse, should perish from hunger."

Furthermore, monks, at that time, King Brahmadatta had a basket filled with barley meal mixed with honey and ghee, as well as sweetmeats and cakes, which was tied behind him on the horse's back beneath the saddle-cloth.
Then, monks, King Brahmadatta, having drawn out a sweetmeat from the casket, gave it to Padmāvatī.
"Come now, noble lady, these fruits are ours."
Then she said:
"I wonder which fruits are more beautiful, yours or ours?"
Having then consumed that sweetmeat, she said:
"O Blessed One, these fruits of yours are beautiful, sweet, and full of flavor; our fruits, however, are bitter and astringent."
The king said:
Such are the fruits upon the trees in our hermitage; if you wish to enjoy such as these, then go to my hermitage.
When this had been said, monks, the seer’s daughter Padumāvatī spoke thus to King Brahmadatta.
"I wish to enjoy such fruits as these; wait a moment. This hermitage of ours is not far away, so I will fetch this water, take leave of my father, and then I shall go to your hermitage."
Then, monks, King Brahmadatta gave other sweetmeats to Padumāvatī.
"Take these to your father and say this:
'I shall become the wife of that seer whose hermitage has such fruits as these. Then you must return quickly; here I am, sitting by the riverbank."
Then, monks, the seer’s daughter Padumāvatī went to the hermitage of Māṇḍavya; having set down her water vessel, she gave those sweetmeats to her father Māṇḍavya, saying:
"Father, eat these fruits. I shall become the wife of whichever seer has such fruits in his hermitage."
Then, monks, this thought occurred to the seer Māṇḍavya:

Surely King Brahmadatta of Pañcāla, while hunting deer, has arrived near this hermitage; it was he who gave these sweetmeats, which Padmāvatī has eaten— sweetmeats worthy of a king— and she will not be able to subsist any longer here in this hermitage on bitter-tasting fruits and berries, for Padmāvatī is a princess.
"What if I were now to give myself as a wife to this King Brahmadatta?"
Then, monks, the seer Māṇḍavya spoke thus to the seer’s daughter Padumāvatī.
"Indeed, Padumāvatī, fruits do not look like this; who is tempting you with these desires that are like a blazing fire?"
Then, monks, this thought occurred to Padumāvatī:
Those trees called "desires" must surely exist, whose fruits are such as these.
Then Padumāvatī spoke thus to her father.
"Father, if such is the taste of those fruits that grant all desires, then I shall enjoy them; these large fruits do not please me."
Then the seer Māṇḍavya said this to Padmāvatī:
"Padumāvatī, who gave these fruits to you? What is that young seer like, and in what region does he dwell?"
When this had been said, Padumāvatī spoke thus to the seer Māṇḍavya:
"Father, a young seer wearing a fine antelope skin stands on the riverbank riding a deer; he gave these fruits to me, and such are the fruits found in his hermitage, father."
Then the seer Māṇḍavya, together with Padumāvatī, approached King Brahmadatta; having greeted King Brahmadatta with friendly words, he gave Padumāvatī to King Brahmadatta with a libation of water.
"O Great King, let her be your wife; she is a worthy match for you, O Great King, and do not act unkindly toward her on the mere word of another without having investigated the matter."
Then King Brahmadatta, having mounted Padumāvatī upon the back of a horse and having paid homage to the seer Māṇḍavya, mounted the horse once more and set out for the city of Kampilla.
He saw the vanguard of King Brahmadatta’s army approaching from afar, and having seen it, he went toward where King Brahmadatta was.
Then King Brahmadatta, having descended from the back of his horse, mounted the back of an elephant together with the seer’s daughter Padumāvatī and set out for his own park in the city of Kampilla.

Padmāvatī heard the great clamor of a vast multitude of people in the city of Kampilla, and she beheld the city of Kampilla itself— charming, with its lofty walls, watchtowers, round turrets, and gateways.
And having seen King Brahmadatta again, you addressed him:
"Whose voice is this that is heard, indeed, in the midst of the forest? Is it the voice of sages, or do these tall leaf-huts of forest deer appear here?"
Then King Brahmadatta said this to Padmāvatī:
"This is the forest of the sages and the deer; these are our lofty leaf-huts that are visible."
Then King Brahmadatta, having approached his own park and dismounted from the back of an elephant, entered the park with Padumāvatī.
Then King Brahmadatta addressed his ministers and courtiers.
"O village headman," he said, "bring the family priest quickly.

Decorate everything in the interval between the royal palace and the garden for Padumāvatī’s sake— stretching out canopies, scattering variegated flowers, and hanging bundles of silk ribbons and garlands."

"In various places, you must provide incense that has been burned, ground that has been sprinkled and swept, and scattered loose flowers; and you must set out dancers, actors, athletes, wrestlers, musicians, panegyrists, *kadvistvalakas*, *velambakas*, and *naṭṭadharas*.
This is for the gods by thought, for kings by word, for the wealthy without delay, and for the poor by their labor."
By a mere word of the king, everything was prepared by the ministers exactly as commanded.
Then Padumāvatī said this to King Brahmadatta:
Where is that Blessed One? Where are the sacrificial fuel, the hot water, the water-pot, or the time for me to offer the fire-sacrifice?
Then King Brahmadatta said to Padumāvatī:
"Wait for a moment; fine antelope skins are being brought for you. Then, having bathed together in the Ganges, we shall offer oblations into the fire."
Then, at that very moment, at that very instant, the king’s ministers and courtiers brought the harem to that garden;
they brought Padumāvatī’s garments and ornaments; they brought the brahmin family priest and the royal preceptor;
and the entire city, headed by its guild-leaders, came forth, as did the community of merchants, headed by its caravan leaders—all of them.
And eighteen rows of people went forth.

The king’s ministers, courtiers, prominent citizens, brahmins, the royal chaplain, and the royal preceptor saw Queen Padmāvatī, adorned with all her ornaments, gracious, beautiful to behold, and endowed with the most excellent abundance of complexion.
Together with King Brahmadatta, she performed a circumambulation of the fire.
And wherever she set her feet down, there lotuses appeared—graceful and beautiful to behold.
Having seen this, thrilled, satisfied, and filled with joy, they addressed King Brahmadatta.
"O Great King, never before have we seen or heard of such supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) as that of this Queen Padumāvatī.
It would be well, O Great King, if Queen Padumāvatī were to enter the royal palace on foot; then the great multitude of people, having seen such supernatural power of the queen, would become joyful."

Then King Brahmadatta, together with his harem and Queen Padumāvatī, preceded by his ministers and courtiers, entered the royal palace from the park with a great multitude of people, accompanied by great royal splendor and great royal majesty.
That multitude of people saw lotuses, beautiful and lovely to behold, on both sides of Padumāvatī’s footsteps, extending as far as the park and as far as the royal palace.
Having seen this, the great multitude of people again uttered an inspired exclamation.
King Brahmadatta has performed meritorious deeds, for such a jewel among women as this has appeared to him.

Then the king, having gone up to the excellent upper palace together with Padumāvatī, being fully endowed and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure, played, delighted, and amused himself; and he instructed Queen Padumāvatī in intoxicants,
dice, and songs and instrumental music, being so infatuated with Padumāvatī that he paid no heed to the other queens.
And Padumāvatī, living together with King Brahmadatta, became pregnant.
When it was the time for the queen’s delivery, King Brahmadatta commanded those women of the inner apartments who were skilled in the duties of women: "Bring forth Padumāvatī.
And the king, placing gold and bullion before him as well as various kinds of garments, sat down and said, "I shall give a reward to those who inform me that Padumāvatī has been safely delivered.
Then this thought occurred to those queens:
"Ever since Padumāvatī was brought here on account of that [incident], our king has paid us no heed;
therefore, while she is about to give birth, we must bring her to ruin and disaster."
Then they questioned that Padumāvatī.
Do you know how women give birth?
Then she said:
"I do not know."
Then those female attendants said:
When a woman is giving birth, her eyes are bound with a cloth.
Then she said:
When I too am giving birth, you should bind my eyes with a cloth.
Then, at the very moment she was about to give birth, her eyes were bound with a cloth.
She then gave birth to two sons who were gracious and beautiful to behold.
Then this thought occurred to them:
"This queen was already beloved and highly esteemed by King Brahmadatta even though she was childless; how much more so now that she has sons?
Since this royal family was previously without heirs, with the birth of these two boys, she will become even more exceedingly dear to King Brahmadatta, and he will no longer pay attention to us."
Then those women of the harem spread a cloth over the hot ground and threw the children upon it.
Having made that heating-stone well-concealed and securely fastened, and having heated it with royal gold, they cast it into the river Gaṅgā;
and Padumāvatī’s face was smeared with the impurities of her own womb.
Then Padmāvatī asked the women of the inner apartments, "What has been born to me?"
Those women of the inner apartments also wiped the two placentas with the fetal membrane and presented them to Padmāvatī.
These have been born.
Then she said:
"Release these; what shall I do with them? he asked.
Then King Brahmadatta asked:
"Has the queen given birth? he asked.
They said:
"Great King, two children were born, handsome and beautiful to behold; yet as soon as they were born, they were eaten by her.
Great King, how could there be offspring for a celibate seer? This is a *piśācī* you have brought back; by good fortune you have escaped with your life."
"Come from the presence of that female piśāca and see her yourself, if you do not believe us."
Then, having entered to see that queen, he saw Padumāvatī smeared with blood, looking just like a rākṣasī.
Then, having seen them, he became afraid.
He spoke to his ministers.
"Go and have her executed, considering her to be a mere human woman; she was brought here by me, and whether she be a *piśācī* or a *rākṣasī*, I have no need for her."
Then she was expelled from that royal palace.
Then she questioned those ministers.
Where will you lead me?
They said:
"You have been sentenced to death by King Brahmadatta."
Then she questioned those ministers.
"What offense have I committed against King Brahmadatta that I have been sent forth to be executed?"
Those ministers said:
Having given birth to two boys, you ate them; therefore, the king, regarding you as a female piśāca, has ordered that you be executed.
She said:
