"No children have been born to me; I asked the women of the inner apartments, and they said, 'Two fetal sacs were born to you, and those too were discarded right there. I see no children at all, nor do I eat them."
Now those ministers were wise and possessed expert knowledge of the deceptions and guiles of women.
This thought occurred to them:
This Padumāvatī is beloved and highly esteemed by Brahmadatta; it is possible that she might have been humiliated or deceived by these women of the harem while she was unaware.
Then those ministers questioned that Padmāvatī.
"How have you given birth? he asked.
She then explained that matter in detail to those ministers.
By those women of my harem, while I was giving birth, my eyes were bound with a cloth so that I saw neither the children nor did I eat them.
And at the time when I had given birth, I asked those women of the harem, "What has been born to me? Then they presented two fetal membranes to me, saying, "These have been born."
Then this thought occurred to those ministers:

"This queen has been deceived by the women of the harem out of a jealous nature; furthermore, this queen is beloved and highly esteemed by Brahmadatta. Let it not be that later King Brahmadatta should feel remorse toward Padmāvatī from afar, or fall into illness through grief."
Then those ministers concealed Queen Padumāvatī in their own home and reported to King Brahmadatta, "The queen has been killed."
When those queens heard that Padumāvatī had been killed, they became agitated toward King Brahmadatta;
they sprinkled clarified butter and cast mustard seeds into the fire, offered oblations in the four directions,
and performed rites for pacification, saying, "By good fortune, O Great King, you have escaped alive from the hands of the rākṣasīs!"
During that moment, the king, having bathed and anointed himself, amused himself with a performance of dance performed by women alone;
meanwhile, some of the women of the inner apartments played the lute, some played the sughoṣaka, some played the mṛdaṅga drum, some played the flute, some danced, and some sang.
Then, monks, a certain deity who had gained faith in the seer Māṇḍavya stood in the sky, in the air, and said this to King Brahmadatta:

"You have not heard well, O Great King; you have not fully understood, O Great King; you have not comprehended, O Great King, since you, without having investigated and without having delved into the matter, cast away the innocent Padmāvatī as one to be executed, and do not remember the words of such a highly distinguished seer."

Then, having heard that sound from the deity situated in the sky, the women of King Brahmadatta’s harem sang and played musical instruments even more beautifully, so that King Brahmadatta would not hear what that deity was saying.
Then King Brahmadatta dismissed the women of the harem, saying, "Wait a moment until we know what this deity situated in the sky is saying."
Then those women of the harem became silent at the king’s word; the deity spoke to King Brahmadatta.

"You have heard poorly, O Great King, you who, without having investigated or delved into the matter, have ordered the execution of the innocent Padmāvatī; you do not even remember the message of such a highly distinguished seer. Then King Brahmadatta, having heard this from the deity, questioned the women of the inner apartments.
"Speak the truth: what are these children now, born of Padumāvatī?"
Then those women of the harem saw [him] being questioned by King Brahmadatta.
"Padumāvatī was killed by the king's command; the king has the power even to abandon us. Let us inform him of this truth exactly as it is."
Then those women of the inner apartments said:
"Your Majesty, two sons were born to Padumāvatī; we placed them in a chest, sealed it with the royal seal, and set it adrift upon the river Gaṅgā. Neither was she seen by her, nor was she eaten."
Then, dejection arose within that King Brahmadatta.

"O sons, such a jewel of a woman, though innocent, has been caused by me to be slain; and I have failed to carry out the command of such a highly fortunate seer; thus we are deprived of our children."
Then that chest, while being carried away by the river Gaṅgā, was pulled out by fishermen who were catching fish.
Then those fishermen saw that casket sealed with the royal seal.
This thought occurred to those fishermen:
"Lest the royal court suspect us of being thieves and these caskets be seized from us,
whereby all our secrets will be revealed— let us go and present these caskets to King Brahmadatta, so that we may not be punished with the highest penalty on account of being accused as thieves."

Then, taking that casket, they approached King Brahmadatta and said: "Great King, while we were catching fish in the river Gaṅgā, this casket was found floating with the water; it has been lifted out and sealed with the royal seal. May Your Majesty examine it."
Then, monks, King Brahmadatta addressed his ministers and courtiers: "Ho there!
Find out what is in this chest."
Then the ministers opened the chest and saw those two children of Padumāvatī, who were gracious and beautiful to behold.
They said:
"Great King, within this chest are two children, pleasing and beautiful to behold, the sons of Padmāvatī, who resemble the Great King himself.
Great King, Queen Padmāvatī is innocent; yet, without being questioned or investigated by Your Majesty, she has been sentenced to death."

Then King Brahmadatta, seeing those children and recollecting the many multitudes of virtues belonging to Padmāvatī, fainted and fell to the ground, crying out, "Alas! I have been deprived of this jewel among women.
Then, this thought occurred to those ministers:
Lest some affliction should indeed arise in the body of the king, who is so longing for his queen.
Then they said:

"Great King, do not grieve on account of Padumāvatī. Having understood the matter thus, O Lord, we did not commit an act of rashness; the Queen was spared and not slain, for we foresaw this future outcome."
Then King Brahmadatta, having heard these words of his ministers, became gladdened and filled with joy.
He spoke to his ministers.
"Where is Padmāvatī?"
The ministers said:
"In that house," he said.
Then the king went there into the presence of Queen Padumāvatī.

Having gone to Queen Padumāvatī, the king consoled her in many ways: "By good fortune, O Queen, you have today been delivered from such a calamity; by good fortune, you have been reunited with me and your sons.

Your co-wives had them executed—what was your intention? What shall I cause those enemies of yours to receive, or what kind of misfortune shall they undergo, so that it might be for your welfare, if only the king commands it and they are all bound in fetters?"
Clad in garments of hemp, let them wander about performing service.
Then, monks, Queen Padumāvatī, weeping, said this to King Brahmadatta:
O Great King, do not do anything displeasing to those queens.
"I am the eldest among these younger sisters; whatever livelihood has been assigned to them, increase it for them, do not let it diminish, and attend to all their needs."
Just as trees bear flowers and fruits in their due season, so do sentient beings experience the ripening of their actions when the proper time has arrived.
"By me alone, O Great King, were those deeds performed that I was honored and revered by you; by me alone were those deeds performed that I was released by you to be executed."
Then King Brahmadatta said this to Queen Padumāvatī:
"O Queen, do not shed tears; I relinquish my entire kingdom to you. Rejoice together with your sons and forgive this offense of mine."
Then Queen Padmāvatī said this to King Brahmadatta:
"O Great King, what use have I for sovereignty, or for a son, or for wealth, when I am fully aware? Having gone forth into the religious life, I shall return once more to my father's presence."

"I was told by my father, 'Padumāvatī, who is seducing you with desires that are like fire? By my father's words, I am now consumed with burning pain, just as I was told by my father at the hermitage: 'O Great King, this woman, innocent as a doe, is to be executed by you for departing from her father's hermitage.'"
Then Queen Padumāvatī, having again gone forth as an ascetic and donned robes dyed with mineral pigments, went to the hermitage of the seer Māṇḍavya.
And the seer Māṇḍavya passed away;
his grass hut and leaf hut fell into ruin.
Then, this thought occurred to Queen Padumāvatī:
Because of such persistence of mine, King Brahmadatta, my father, was rejected by these two who were destined for destruction; since he has passed away, I have fallen into this state of ruin.
"What if I were now to go on alms-round, wandering through the countryside and the royal capitals?"
Then Queen Padumāvatī, wandering through villages, market towns, and royal capitals, arrived at Vārāṇasī, the city of King Kṛkī.

The King of Kāśi, ruler of Vārāṇasī, saw Queen Padumāvatī within the city; having seen her, the King of Kāśi again attempted to seduce Queen Padumāvatī in many ways, saying: "What use have you, noble lady, for this life of renunciation—you who are young, of golden complexion, and beautiful?"
"These trees are flowering, in full bloom, lovely, pleasing, and heart-entrancing; come, let us enjoy ourselves within such-and-such a grove."
When this had been said, the female ascetic Padumāvatī spoke thus to the King of Kāśi.
"O Great King, you wish to enter the fire, with whom you wish to take delight as one who has gone forth and is established in the Dharma; O Great King, I have no desire for sensual pleasures."
The King of Kāśi said:
If you do not wish it, O blessed lady, then I shall take you by force.
Padumāvatī said:
If you seize me by force, then I shall consume you with my ascetic power, like fire consuming dry grass.
Then the king, having heard that, returned in fear, and she remained here in this kingdom at her ease and comfort.
I invite you with service for the benefit of all.
Then King Brahmadatta, having entered the house of the King of Kāśi in the guise of a brahmin, said, "I too, Great King, am skilled at dice.
While the king was playing with his queens, he played along and spoke to Padmāvatī:
"With what anger have you come here?"
Padumāvatī said:
It is solely by your fault, O Great King, that we have come here.
Then the King of Kāśi, being in doubt, questioned King Brahmadatta.
"Never before have I heard such a doctrine from Aṣṭāpada; who are you, and who is this woman of yours?"
King Brahmadatta said:
"I am Brahmadatta, the King of Pañcāla; this Padmāvatī here is my wife who has come with me."
When this had been said, the King of Kāśi spoke thus to King Brahmadatta.
Welcome to you, Great King; we welcome you, Great King. Bring the queen here, and I shall escort her along with the vanguard of the army.

Then King Brahmadatta, the king of Pañcāla, having had Queen Padumāvatī mounted upon the back of an elephant together with a fourfold army from Vārāṇasī, brought her back again to the city of Kampilla with great royal majesty and great royal power.
And for Queen Padumāvatī, who had been sentenced to death by King Brahmadatta,
those lotuses vanished from her footsteps;
yet when she was brought back from Vārāṇasī to Kampilla by King Brahmadatta, the lotuses appeared once more upon her footsteps.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, that seer Māṇḍavya was certainly not someone else; I myself was the seer Māṇḍavya at that time."
Indeed, monks, it was not anyone else;
this very Yaśodharā was at that time Queen Padmāvatī.
"Monks, that King Brahmadatta was indeed no other;
it was this very King Śuddhodana who at that time was King Brahmadatta."
Even then, this King Śuddhodana, without having investigated or scrutinized her, sent forth Yaśodharā to be executed;
and now as well, this King Śuddhodana, without having investigated or scrutinized her, has sent forth this innocent woman to be executed.
The imaginative narrative concerning Padumāvatī is completed.
The monks said to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, by the ripening of what karma do lotuses appear at Padumāvatī’s feet? And when she was released by King Brahmadatta after having been sentenced to death, those lotuses vanished;
yet when she was brought from Vārāṇasī to Kampilla by King Brahmadatta, lotuses appeared once more at her feet."
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, this was the ripening of the karma of this very Padumāvatī, by which lotuses appeared upon her feet; and when she had been delivered as a victim to be executed by King Brahmadatta, they vanished; yet when she was brought from Vārāṇasī to Kampilla by King Brahmadatta, they appeared once more while she was still alive."

Once upon a time, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a female servant of another householder was entering the city from outside, carrying a water-jar from a lotus pond with a lotus flower held in her hand.

And another Pratyekabuddha, having wandered for alms in the city of Vārāṇasī, was departing from the city toward the outside with a graceful deportment— graceful in his advancing and retreating— and gods and humans were filled with serene faith.
When that girl saw the pratyekabuddha, a serene faith arose in her mind. With a serene mind, she gave that lotus to the pratyekabuddha, who accepted it for the sake of showing her favor.
Then that girl saw that lotus looking exceedingly beautiful in the hand of that pratyekabuddha, and she saw her own hand as withered.
Then she requested that lotus again from the presence of that Pratyekabuddha, saying, "Venerable sir, give me that lotus once more."
The Pratyekabuddha gave that lotus back to the girl, saying, "Here, noble lady."
She took the lotus back from the hands of the Pratyekabuddha.
She then saw her own hand adorned with a lotus, while she saw the hand of the Pratyekabuddha withered;
remorse arose within her:
"I have done what is not good, in that, having given this lotus to this seer with a devout heart, I snatched it back again."
Then she gave that lotus back again to that Pratyekabuddha.
O Blessed One, out of compassion for me, please accept this lotus once again.
Then Paduma was seized again by that Pratyekabuddha from that girl.
The Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, monks, it may be that you think thus: 'At that time, on that occasion, she was some other girl in Vārāṇasī.
But it should not be viewed in this way. And for what reason?
Monks, this Padmāvatī was that very girl from Vārāṇasī.

Because she gave that lotus to the Pratyekabuddha with a devout heart, as the ripening of that karma, lotuses appeared upon the feet of Padumāvatī. Because she again snatched that lotus from the hand of that Pratyekabuddha, as the ripening of that karma, those lotuses vanished from her feet when she was ordered by King Brahmadatta to be executed.
Because she gave that lotus again to that Pratyekabuddha, as the ripening of that karma, lotuses appeared again in her footsteps when she was brought from Vārāṇasī to Kampilla by King Brahmadatta.
Thus concludes the *Pūrvayoga* of Padumāvatī.
The monks said to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, as the ripening of what karma did Prince Rāhula dwell in the womb for six years?"
The Blessed One said:
Monks, this is indeed the maturation of the ancient karma of this youth Rāhula.
Once upon a time, monks, in the past, in the kingdom of Videha at the capital city of Mithilā, there was a brahmin king.
He had two sons: a prince named Bhadra and a prince named Sūrya; Sūrya was the elder and Candra was the younger.
Then, monks, that Brahmin king of Videha passed away due to the exhaustion of his lifespan and the exhaustion of his karma.
The Moon said to the Sun:
"You are the elder; you should attain the kingdom.
I shall go forth into the wandering life of a seer."
Then the youth Sūrya said this to the youth Candra:
"What ought to be done for kings?"
The prince Candra said:
The king must issue a command to the people.
Then indeed, Sūrya spoke this to Candra:
"O Prince, I, as king, command you: you shall become king, and I shall go forth into the wandering life of a seer."
Then, monks, Prince Sūrya, having consecrated Prince Candra to the kingdom in Mithilā, went forth into the wandering life of a seer.

Then, as he dwelt devoted to the practice of vigilance during the first and last watches of the night, he accomplished the four dhyānas and realized the five super-knowledges; thus, he became a seer of great psychic power and great majesty.

Those who were among the inner circle of attendants of Prince Sūrya also went forth into the ascetic life with Sūrya; they all became attainers of the four dhyānas, possessed of the five superknowledges, and endowed with great psychic power and great majesty.
Then this thought occurred to the seer Sūrya:

"I am indeed an attainer of the four dhyānas and possessor of the five superknowledges, and this entire retinue of mine is likewise an attainer of the four dhyānas and possessor of the five superknowledges; what if I were now to strive for a further distinction?"
He then made this formal undertaking: "I shall not consume water or even a tooth-stick that has not been given."
Then, monks, at a later time, the seer Sūrya, through a lapse of mindfulness and confusion, drank water that had not been given from another seer’s water vessel.

When he had drunk it, mindfulness arose in him: "I have undertaken a vow that I must not consume water or even a tooth-stick that has not been given. Then, through a lapse of mindfulness, I drank water from this seer’s water-vessel without it being given.
The thought of remorse arose in him: "I am a thief; I have committed theft," because he had drunk water from another's vessel without it being given.
Then, overcome by suffering and dejection, he rose from his seat and sat down upon the ground.
Then those young brahmins approached the seer Sūrya and paid homage to the seer Sūrya.
Then, monks, the seer Sūrya said this to those young brahmins:
"Young men, do not salute me."
Then, monks, those young brahmins said this to the seer Sūrya:
"O Preceptor, why should we not pay homage to the Preceptor?"
The seer Sūrya said:
"Indeed, young men, I am a thief."
The young brahmins said:
Or what, or how, O Preceptor?
The sage Sūrya said:
The water was drunk from the water vessel of the young man named so-and-so without it being given.
Then those young brahmins said this to him.
May you, Preceptor, not speak thus.
"You are not a thief, sir; this water of ours belongs to our preceptor, so the water you have drunk is your own. Do not harbor any remorse."
The seer Sūrya said:
"Young men know my undertaking of the vow: never before have I consumed water or a tooth-stick that was not given; even water was never drunk by me previously unless it was given.
Yet I have become a thief; inflict upon me the punishment that is meted out to a thief."
The young brahmins said:
"O Preceptor, we do not venture to carry out the disciplinary punishment against you.
This King Candra is your brother; go into his presence."
He will inflict corporal punishment upon you.
Then the seer Sūrya set out for the royal capital of Mithilā, to the presence of King Candra.
King Candra heard that his brother, the seer Sūrya, was coming to Mithilā.
Then King Candra set out with a fourfold army to go forth and meet the seer Sūrya.
Then King Candra approached the place where the seer Sūrya was, descended from his vehicle, and paid homage to the seer Sūrya.
Then the seer Sūrya spoke thus to King Candra.
Furthermore, O Great King, do not indeed pay homage to me.
When this had been said, monks, King Candra spoke thus to the seer Sūrya.
"O Blessed One, why should I not salute my eldest brother, the seer Sūrya, upon seeing him?"
When this had been said, monks, the seer Sūrya spoke thus to King Candra.
"I am a thief, O Great King; I have drunk water that was not given. Inflict upon me the punishment that is meted out to a thief."
Then, monks, King Candra said this to the seer Sūrya.

"I grant you permission, Blessed One: the water that was drunk by you from your own domain has been drunk from my kingdom; whatever is my kingdom is also yours. Go wherever you wish; do not, Blessed One, harbor any remorse."
Then the seer Sūrya addressed King Candra with a verse:
"O Great King, I am not able to dispel my remorse;
let the punishment be duly inflicted upon me, just as it is inflicted upon a thief."
Then, indeed, the son and the nephew of King Candra of Videha said this to King Candra of Videha:
"O Lord, let the punishment for the seer be carried out for the sake of dispelling his remorse; let the seer not be tormented by remorse."
Then this thought occurred to King Candra:
"What kind of disciplinary action (*daṇḍakarma*) should I perform against the seer Sūrya, so that the seer might become free from remorse?"

Then King Candra, having had the Aśoka grove sprinkled and swept, having had excellent seats prepared and various kinds of food brought in, and having had sweetmeats fit for kings tied to the branches of the trees, spoke thus to the seer Sūrya:
"Go, Blessed One; sit here in the Aśoka grove. Whatever food, drink, and bedding arrangements are here, I authorize you to enjoy them as you please."
Then King Candra detained the seer Sūrya in the Aśoka grove for six nights.
Then, after the passing of six nights, this thought occurred to King Candra:
"How may I dismiss the seer Sūrya after making him free from remorse? he thought.
This thought occurred to him:
"What if I were now to cause the release of all those bound in fetters?"
Monks, on the seventh day, King Candra indeed caused the release of all prisoners;
and the seer Sūrya was addressed by the ministers.
"Go! The Blessed One has lifted the rod.
King Candra then ordered the release of all prisoners.
Now, being free from remorse, he returned once more to the hermitage.
The Blessed One said:
It may be, monks, that you might think: "That King Candra at that time and on that occasion was someone else. But he was none other than this very Prince Rāhulabhadra.
He who was the seer Sūrya was indeed myself at that time.
Because the seer Sūrya was confined within the Aśoka grove for six nights, as the ripening of that karma, Prince Rāhula remained in the womb for six years.
The former life story of the auspicious Rāhula.
[ Mvu 3.176 ] King Śuddhodana, having then assembled the Śākyas, said:
Sirs, if Prince Sarvārthasiddha had not gone forth from the home life into homelessness, he would have become a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*),
a lord over many thousands of kings, and you all would have been his followers; but since he has renounced the sovereignty of a wheel-turning king,
departed from the home life into homelessness from a kṣatriya family, and has awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*).
And if that kṣatriya were to have a retinue of brahmins, that would not be appropriate for him.
Then those Śākyas said:
"May Your Majesty command what is to be done."
King Śuddhodana said:
Let one Kṣatriya youth from each family go forth into homelessness;
however, where there is an only son, let him not go forth;
and where there are two brothers, let one of them go forth.
Even where there are many brothers, let but one from among them go forth into homelessness.
Cast the voting sticks so that the majority of the Śākya clan may arise to go forth as renunciants, O Śākya youths.
There, the voting sticks were distributed by a representative of the clan, and for the most part, they fell to the Śākya community.

When King Śuddhodana issued the command, "Let the Śākya youths go forth; however, whoever has an only son, let him be exempt," five hundred youths then went forth from home into homelessness by means of that exemption for an only son.
King Śuddhodana had two sons, the Blessed One and Sundarananda;
when the Blessed One had gone forth, Sundarananda was released.
The sons of Śuklodana were Ānanda, Upadhāna, and Devadatta;
among them, Devadatta went forth from home.
Ānanda also desired to go forth, but his mother, Mṛgī, a Śākya maiden, did not grant him permission.
Having gone to the country of Videha, he dwelt there observing a vow of silence. Of Śukrodana, two sons, Nandana and Nandika, went forth into the religious life;
his other two sons remained at home.
The sons of Amṛtodana were Anuruddha, Mahānāma, and Bhaṭṭika.
Anuruddha was asked by Mahānāma:
"Will you go forth into homelessness, or will you attend to household affairs?"

Thus Anuruddha, being possessed of merit, does not inquire what must be done by one dwelling at home, nor what must be done by one who has gone forth into homelessness; instead, he remains playing with a troupe of women devoid of men, fully endowed and immersed in the five strands of sensual pleasure.
After the sun has set, a thousand lamp-trees are lit for him at night.
In order to test Mohana, one thousand minus one lamp-trees were set ablaze.
At that time, his pure physical eye perceived that among those one thousand minus one lamp-trees, there was no complete set of one thousand lamp-trees in his mind.
His entire retinue of servants was struck with wonder.
"Oh, how pure is the prince's vision!
For even when there is one lamp missing from a thousand lamps of a lamp-tree, he perceives those lamps as impure."
Then he asked that elder brother, Mahānāma.
"What must be done by one dwelling in a household, or what must be done by one who has gone forth?"
He said to him:

One who dwells in a household should rise early in the morning and offer a "good night" greeting to the king; one should also offer a "good night" greeting to the Śākya elders. One should look after those who are dear; one should attend to the funeral rites for those who have passed away;
and one should provide food and clothing for the members of the household, as well as for the female and male slaves, laborers, and servants.

And during all festivals, you must attend to the expenditures—both those for the festival itself and those incidental to it—and ensure that the elephants, horses, goats, cattle, and sheep are properly cared for; the chariots, yoked vehicles, and carriages must be maintained; the villages and enjoyments must be protected; the various works must be supervised from time to time; and the fruits [of these labors] must be brought in.
Various kinds of grain species are to be sown, planted, and inspected.
From time to time, as each kind of grain ripens, it is to be harvested, gathered into threshing floors, and winnowed.
Whatever household task there may be, whether internal or external, all must be performed.
Anuruddha said:
Furthermore, what should be done by one who has gone forth?
Mahānāma said:

"An ordained person should seek alms in the forenoon; having performed the function of taking food with food, whether coarse or refined, he should discipline himself, pacify himself, and bring himself to final nirvāṇa," Anuruddha said.
"Enough for me with household affairs; you carry them out, while I shall go forth into the religious life."
Then those five hundred Śākya princes went forth with great royal majesty, great royal power, and their respective splendors:
some on the backs of elephants with golden parasols and trappings of hooves; some in golden palanquins covered with various jewels;
and some in golden chariots drawn by four horses, covered with nets of various jewels, adorned with victory banners, and accompanied by joyful sounds.
With umbrellas, banners, and flags raised high,
some went on the backs of horses adorned with every ornament and covered with golden nets;
and Devadatta, seated upon a high lion-throne on the back of a well-adorned elephant covered with a golden net, galloped forth.
As he was rushing out, his crown became caught on a hook at the top of the gateway.

By means of that hook, the crown was pulled off from Devadatta’s head. A great crowd of people broke into loud laughter, and the diviner and the astrologer prophesied the purpose for which Prince Devadatta was going forth.
"He will not accomplish that task;
he will fail in the supreme goal"—this is the crown which was lifted from his head by the hook from the top of the archway.

Then indeed those five hundred Śākya youths, with great royal majesty and great royal power, accompanied by all kinds of dances, all kinds of songs, and all kinds of musical instruments and cymbals, departed from the city of Kapilavastu and proceeded toward the Nyagrodha Grove.
Then those five hundred Śākya youths, having traveled by their vehicles as far as the ground would allow for them,
alighted from their vehicles and approached the Blessed One. Surrounded by many thousands of people,
they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.

Now, among those Śākya youths, there was a barber’s son named Upāli who served them; he had planted roots of merit under previous perfectly enlightened Buddhas, was perfumed by their influence, had severed his bonds, was no longer subject to rebirth, was in his final existence for the noble dharmas, and was a possessor of the meditative concentrations and the superknowledges.
He was now presented by his mother to the Blessed One with the thought, "This one shall shave off the Blessed One's hair," and the Blessed One gave his consent.
Then, Upāli, he shaved off the hair on the Blessed One’s head.
Then Upāli’s mother asked the Blessed One.
"It is easy, Blessed One; Upāli shaves off his hair."
The Blessed One said:
He combed his hair with ease and approached the Tathāgata.
Then she said:
"Child, do not approach the Blessed One."
He then entered the first dhyāna.
She then asked the Blessed One once more.
"It is well, Blessed One; the boy Upāli is letting his hair fall out."
The Blessed One said:
The boy Sukha was shaving off his hair, but he kept making a clucking sound with the razor.
Then she said:
Child, do not whet the razor.
He then entered the second dhyāna.
Then Upāli’s mother asked the Blessed One.
"It is well, Blessed One; the boy Upāli is shaving off his hair."
The Blessed One said:
The boy Upāli was shaving the hair comfortably, but he was distressing the Tathāgata with his inhalations and exhalations.
Then she said:
"Child, do not disturb the Blessed One with your inhalations and exhalations."
Having transcended those,
he entered the third dhyāna and the fourth dhyāna.
The Blessed One said to the monks:
"Monks, take this razor from Upāli's hand so that it does not fall to the ground."
Then that razor was taken from Upāli’s hand by the monks.
Then those Śākya youths, having cast aside their respective garments and ornaments, placed them before Upāli, saying:
"Upāli, let this be your wealth; we who have gone forth have no need for these."
"In the presence of the Blessed One, we shall go forth."
This thought also occurred to Upāli:

"These Śākya youths have abandoned their kingdom and, having given these garments and ornaments to me, are going forth from the home life into homelessness; why then should we, who subsist by the blade, not go forth? I too shall go forth."
I shall not consume these vomited [things].
Then Upāli the barber approached the Blessed One, bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet, and said this to the Blessed One:
May the Blessed One let me go forth; may the Sugata ordain me.
Then the Blessed One addressed Upāli the barber with the words "Come, monk," saying: "Come, monk Upāli; practice the holy life under the Tathāgata."
Then, as soon as the Blessed One had spoken the "Come, monk" formula, whatever marks of a householder, protections of a householder, banners of a householder,

or conventions of a householder he possessed all vanished; his three robes appeared, as did his sumbhaka bowl, and his hair was established in its natural state, while his deportment became established just like that of a monk who had been ordained for a hundred years.
The going forth, the full ordination, and the state of a monk of the venerable Upāli.

While the five hundred Śākya youths were in the midst of exchanging greetings with their parents, friends, kinsmen, and blood relations, Upāli was the very first among them to go forth into the religious life.
Then indeed, five hundred Śākya youths approached the Blessed One, bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, and said this to the Blessed One:
May the Blessed One let me go forth; may the Sugata ordain me.
Then the Blessed One, having set aside those five hundred youths, addressed Devadatta with the call, "Come, monk."
"Come, monks; O Śākya princes, practice the holy life under the Tathāgata."
Now, as soon as they were addressed by the Blessed One with the words "Come, monk," whatever marks of a householder, protections of a householder, banners of a householder,

or ornaments of a householder they had all vanished; three robes appeared upon them, along with sumbhaka bowls, their hair settled in its natural state, and their deportment became established just like that of [an ordained monk].
Indeed, for these venerable Śākya princes who have been ordained for a hundred years, this is their first going forth, their full ordination, and their status as monks.
Then they were addressed by the Blessed One:
"Upāli, the monk who is the eldest among you, having bowed at his feet, all of you should stand in order of seniority.
And whoever, having first bowed at the feet of the Tathāgata and Upāli, shall stand in that order, he shall be the eldest."
Then, having bowed at the feet of the Blessed One and of Upāli, all those hundreds of monks stood in order.
For indeed, the great multitude of people who had been conquered spoke thus.
The Śākyas have conquered pride and anger; the Śākyas have destroyed pride and arrogance.
King Śuddhodana, together with his retinue and the Śākyas, bowed at the feet of the monk Upāli and addressed the venerable Upāli in this way:
Welcome to King Śuddhodana; a warm welcome to King Śuddhodana.
Then, indeed, the ministers and courtiers of King Śuddhodana, seeing the Venerable Upāli speaking personally with King Śuddhodana, became aware of it.
How indeed can Upāli the barber, of low birth, speak thus to King Śuddhodana?
King Śuddhodana also said to those members of his assembly and ministers:
"Sirs, do not address the noble Upāli as being of low birth.
His former birth was one thing, but now, as a śramaṇa, he possesses royal majesty; he should no longer be called one of low birth."
The monks said to the Blessed One:
"Behold, Blessed One, how the feet of the Venerable Upāli, though of low birth, were venerated by the assembly including the king, because he had come to the Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, it is not only now that, because of me, this Upāli of low birth has had his feet worshipped by the assembly including the king; on another occasion as well, because of me, this Upāli of low birth had his feet worshipped by the assembly including the king."
The monks said to the Blessed One.
At another time as well, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
On another occasion as well, monks.

Once upon a time, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi, two poor boys were going out as wood-gatherers carrying baskets of boiled beans for food. At that time, a Pratyekabuddha was entering Vārāṇasī for alms, with a graceful deportment, moving forward and backward with composure, and looking ahead and around with dignity.

With his outer robe adjusted and his bowl and robes properly carried, like a well-trained elephant performing its task, with his sense faculties withdrawn and his mind withdrawn, established in the natural state of reality, mindful, clearly comprehending, concentrated, one-pointed in mind, with senses restrained and gaze undistracted.
Having seen him, they indeed approach with faith.
Then, with hearts full of faith, they spoke thus to one another:
Whatever boys there may be who live by harsh means, deprived of food and clothing, wretched among men, miserable among men, or pitiable among men—
just as we and all others have failed to plant roots of merit in such two-legged fields of merit;

and whatever people there may be who are wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments, whether they be great kṣatriya householders, great brahmin householders, or any others who are happy— all of them likewise [fail to do so] in regard to such two-legged fields of merit.
Having performed wholesome deeds, [they thought]:
"What if we were now to place this sour gruel into the bowls of this seer?"
Then they placed those boiled grains into the bowl of that Pratyekabuddha.
The Pratyekabuddha, having accepted that alms-food from those children, departed through the air like a king of swans.
Seeing that Pratyekabuddha traveling through the air, those boys were filled with joy and thought, "A highly fortunate seer has been honored by us with almsfood."
Then, filled with joy and gladness, they made this aspiration.
One said:
"By this root of merit, may I become a consecrated Kṣatriya king."
The second said:
"By this root of merit, may I be reborn in a great brahmin family of noble lineage, wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments."
For when one has serene confidence in the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, and in the disciples of the Buddhas, even a very small offering becomes great.
All accumulations end in depletion; all elevations end in a fall; all unions end in separation; for life indeed ends in death.
Then those boys, having passed away due to the exhaustion of their lifespan and the exhaustion of their karma, were reborn together in that very city of Vārāṇasī:
one was conceived in the royal palace in the womb of the king’s chief queen, and the second was conceived in the house of the domestic priest in the womb of the priest’s wife.
In the course of time, at a certain occasion, the king’s wife and the priest’s wife both gave birth;
two boys were born.

For both of them, delightful birth-rites were performed for seven days; at the end of the seventh day, the name Brahmadatta was given to the prince, and the name Upaka was given to the son of the domestic priest.
A suitable nurse was appointed, and the prince and the son of the family priest were raised together like blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water lilies, or white lotuses.
As it was said by the Blessed One:
For those who have performed meritorious deeds flourish like banyan trees grown in fertile soil;
whereas those with little merit are diminished, like trees growing by the roadside.
Then, when they had grown up and reached the age of discretion, they were instructed in writing, as well as in the arts of calligraphy, calculation, memorization, and sealing.
Prince Brahmadatta also became one who had attained mastery in every respect regarding elephants, horses, archery, swordsmanship, running, leaping, racing, and the sciences of weaponry.
And when his father had passed away, Prince Brahmadatta was consecrated to the kingdom in Vārāṇasī by the ministers.
And the young brahmin Upaka had his mind bound with passion for a certain young woman.
Now, at a certain place, he had been rebuked by that young woman for some time and would not look at her;
and when the Kaumudī festival of the fourth month was celebrated in Vārāṇasī, that young woman, being in love with the young man Upaka, returned to him.
"Young man, the Kaumudī Cāturmāsī festival is at hand; provide me with perfumes and garlands so that we may make the Kaumudī Cāturmāsī delightful."
Then that young man, having heard her, became pleased and joyful,
thinking, "By good fortune, my young woman has returned!"
Now, that young brahmin Upaka received a gift of beans from another man on the bank of the Ganges;
and he hid those beans right there on the bank of the Ganges.
Now, for the sake of that bean,
while it was midday and the clouds had gathered, he went along the bank of the Ganges, singing sweet songs of the Kinnarīs with joy, for the sake of that bean.
Monks, King Brahmadatta, while staying in his excellent upper palace, saw the young brahmin Upaka at midday, when the sky was cloudless,
singing with a sweet voice as he went from within the city to outside the city; and upon seeing him,
affection for the young brahmin Upaka arose within him.
As it was said by the Blessed One:
Whether through dwelling together in the past or through present benefit,
such affection arises for him like a lotus in water.
Wherever the mind settles or the consciousness becomes serene,
there the wise should reach their consummation, having previously lived in seclusion from me.
Thus, as soon as King Brahmadatta saw the young brahmin Upaka there, affection arose within him.
Then King Brahmadatta sent a messenger to the young brahmin Upaka.
"Go and bring this young brahmin who is going from inside the city to outside the city while singing."
Having gone there, he was rescued by them.
"Come, young man; the king summons you."
Then he was brought into the presence of the king by those royal officers.
"Your Majesty, this young brahmin has been brought here."
Then King Brahmadatta addressed the young man Upaka with a verse:
When the intermediate night has passed, the earth is like glowing embers;
yet when you sing your songs, the heat does not scorch your faces.
The sun blazes above, and the sand below is heated;
with an uplifted mind and a cheerful spirit, you then sing of the faces.
Then, monks, the young brahmin Upaka addressed King Brahmadatta in verse:
The sun does not scorch; it is the end-makers who scorch me.
Both the end-makers and the destroyers—they are what scorch, not the sun.
Trifling indeed is this heat that scorches the body;
it is disputes over what ought to be done that truly scorch one, not the sun's heat.
Then King Brahmadatta replied to the young brahmin Upaka with a verse:
Why does he produce such agitation, and by what is he tormented?
Tell me, when asked, why this body is afflicted by heat.
Then, monks, the young brahmin Upaka addressed King Brahmadatta in verse:
"O God, subduer of enemies, this low-caste woman, Kumbhadāsī, is my beloved;
I am entirely devoted to her and have been tormented by her."
Then, monks, King Brahmadatta addressed the young brahmin Upaka.
"Where will you go, young brahmin?"
Then, monks, the young man Upaka addressed King Brahmadatta in verse:
"I have a bean obtained through begging that I have hidden on the bank of the Ganges;
for its sake, I am going to the city ahead."
Then, monks, King Brahmadatta addressed the young brahmin Upaka:
"Wait a moment, young brahmin; you shall go when it is cool."
Then the young brahmin Upaka addressed King Brahmadatta in verse:

"O Great King, those things which stand still for one who is standing still when the vehicle is at rest, run ahead for one who is running while the vehicle is being drawn; for the sake of that bean, I shall go."
Then King Brahmadatta replied to the young man Upaka in verse:
"If you have need of a māṣa, I shall give you a māṣa. Accomplish your purpose with the māṣa; do not go out in the heat, young man."
The young brahmin Upaka said:
"If Veda will give me one bean, then with these beans I shall be satisfied even as a low-caste woman; furthermore, this Kaumudī festival will proceed without obstacle."
Then the young brahmin Upaka addressed King Brahmadatta in verse:
And whatever bean the king might give shall be the second;
with these two beans, that low-caste woman will be satisfied.
The king said, "Young man, I will give you two māṣas; do not go while being cooked by the heat."
King Brahmadatta addressed the young brahmin Upaka with a verse:
"If you have need of beans, I will give you two beans;
do what needs to be done with the beans, young man, do not go out in the heat."
Upaka said:
These two māsas and that third one shall constitute an invitation;
thus there will be a delightful Kaumudika festival for the low-caste woman.
And you have two māsas; that shall be the third.
With these three māsas, that low-caste woman will be satisfied.
King Brahmadatta spoke thus to the young brahmin Upaka.
"O young man, do not go in the heat; I will give you three māṣas.
If you have need of māṣas, I shall give you more māṣas.
Perform your business with the māṣas; O young man, do not travel in the heat."
The young man said:
"Your Majesty, these three māsas shall be yours, and that fourth one will be the invitation; there will be more to come.
In this way, you shall enjoy delightful moonlight festivals together with Vṛṣalikā."
"And you have three māṣas; that shall be the fourth.
O King, with four māṣas, a low-caste woman becomes exalted."
In this manner, King Brahmadatta gave a hundred thousand [pieces] to the young man Upaka, yet he would not relinquish that single bean;
even when offered the other half, he did not desist from that bean.
Then King Brahmadatta gave half of his kingdom to that young brahmin Upaka; half of the harem was given to him;
half of the treasury and granaries was also given, and half of the ministers, soldiers, and the vanguard of the army was likewise given.
Then those two both ruled the kingdom; both administered affairs of state together.

Then that young brahmin, provided with the five strands of sensual pleasure, played, delighted, and enjoyed himself. Now King Brahmadatta was exceedingly and intensely confident in the presence of the young brahmin Upaka; wherever he went, he would go to sleep with his head resting on the lap of the young brahmin Upaka.
Then, while King Upaka was lying down, this thought occurred to him:
"How can there be two kings over a single kingdom? What if I were to have this King Brahmadatta killed, so that I alone might become the king?"
Then this thought occurred to him again:
"It would not be good for me, nor would it be fitting, that I should be ungrateful toward King Brahmadatta, who is himself grateful."
A second and even a third time this thought occurred to him:
"It would not be good, nor would it be fitting, that there should be two kings in one kingdom; what if I were to deprive King Brahmadatta of life and become the sole King of Kāśi myself?"
Then for a second and even a third time, this thought occurred to him:
"It would not be good for me, nor would it be fitting, that I should be ungrateful toward King Brahmadatta, who is himself grateful."
Now, having gone forth [into homelessness] with the thought "it is not so, it is not so," King Brahmadatta woke up because of that.
He said this to him.
Upaka, you say, "I am one who knows neither the way nor the non-way."
Then he said:
"O King, such was my thought:
'What if I were to deprive Brahmadatta of life and become the sole King of Kāśī myself?'"
King Brahmadatta did not believe him.
Then Upaka said:
"It is even so, Your Majesty, as I have spoken."
Then King Brahmadatta addressed the young brahmin Upaka with a verse:
"O young man, I have given you half of my kingdom little by little;
yet you do not release even a single bean—how will there ever be an end?"
Then the young brahmin Upaka addressed King Brahmadatta with a verse:
Indeed, no end is found here for this infinite craving;
O King, I shall go forth into homelessness, for I find no delight in kingship.
Enough for me of many sensual pleasures, by which a fool is never satisfied;
enough for me of all sensual pleasures—I shall go forth from the home into homelessness.
O Desire, I know your root: you are born from volitional construction (*saṃkalpa*). I shall no longer construct desire; therefore, you shall not exist for me.
A fool is not satisfied with few desires, nor even with many;
having abandoned all desires, he sees like one who has awakened.
I desire that your desires may arise, yet they shall likewise become completely stilled;
having understood this to be the fruit of desire, [one should practice accordingly].
I do not pray for sons, cattle, or wealth.
Then the young brahmin Upaka spoke thus to King Brahmadatta.
"Grant me permission, O Lord; I shall go forth into the religious life."
The king said:
"Do not go forth; together we shall rule the kingdom."
Upaka said:
"O Great King, there is no purpose for me in kingship; grant me permission, for I shall go forth."
Now, having been granted permission by King Brahmadatta with the words, "If such is your intention, go forth into the religious life," he departed.
Now, to the north of that place in Kāśī, there was the hermitage of a renunciant seer who possessed the five supernormal powers, belonging to a potter.
Then the young brahmin Upaka, having gone to that hermitage, went forth as a renunciant in the presence of that potter who had become a seer.

Then, by dwelling devotedly, applying himself, striving, and exerting himself in the practice of vigilance during the first and last watches of the night, he produced the four dhyānas and became a seer of great supernatural power and majesty; while seated cross-legged in his hermitage, he stroked and touched the lunar and solar disks with his hand, and even brought the Brahma-world under his control with his body.
[_Mvu_3.191_] He causes it to turn. Then King Brahmadatta, longing for the young man Upaka, frequently recited this verse:
Upaka has attained this great result from a small [effort]; he has gained a vast benefit.
Truly, a great gain has been won by the young man.
He who has gone forth, having abandoned delight in sensual pleasures.
The women of King Brahmadatta’s harem heard this verse from King Brahmadatta again and again, yet they did not understand its meaning.
Now, King Brahmadatta had a barber named Gaṅgapāla;
being a trusted attendant, he would enter the king's inner apartments at his pleasure to perform services for King Brahmadatta.
Then he was addressed by King Brahmadatta:
"Gangapālaka, please trim my hair and beard."
Having spoken thus, he fell asleep.
While he was thus lying down, his hair and beard were trimmed; and when the king woke up, he said:
"Gaṅgapāla, come; perform my hair-cutting."
Gaṅgapāla said:
"O Lord, your hair and beard have been trimmed while you were asleep."
Then Gaṅgapāla, taking a mirror, approached King Brahmadatta and said, "May Your Majesty look into it.
As the king looked at his hair and beard in the mirror, he became pleased with the barber Gaṅgapāla.
The king said:
"Gaṅgapāla, I am pleased with this craft of yours; being satisfied, I offer you an excellent and superior village as a boon. Take the village, if you so desire."
Then he said:
"As soon as I have consulted [with them], I shall take an excellent village from the presence of Your Majesty."
Then Gaṅgapāla informed the women of King Brahmadatta’s harem.
"Today I have pleased King Brahmadatta with my craft, and he has offered me an excellent village; I shall accept this excellent village."
The women of the inner apartments said:
"Forgive him this excellent village; this king constantly recites this verse."
Upaka has attained this great result from a small [deed]; he has realized a vast benefit.
Truly, a great gain has been won by the young man.
He who has gone forth, having abandoned delight in sensual pleasures.
"And we do not understand the meaning of this verse;
therefore, go and speak to King Brahmadatta, saying: 'Enough for me, O Lord, with this excellent village, since Your Majesty constantly recites this verse.'"
Upaka has attained this great result from a small cause; he has realized a vast benefit.
Truly, a great gain has been won by this young man.
Whoever should go forth, having abandoned delight in sensual pleasures.
"O Great King, explain this matter to me."
Then Gaṅgapāla, having approached King Brahmadatta, said:
"Your Majesty, enough for me with this excellent village, since Your Majesty constantly recites this verse."
Upaka has attained this great fruit from a small [cause]; he has realized a vast benefit.
Truly, a great gain has been well-obtained by this young man.
Whoever should go forth into homelessness, having abandoned delight in sensual pleasures.
"O King, please explain the meaning of this verse."
"Let this be my boon. The king said:

"The young brahmin Upaka, having abandoned half the kingdom and seeing the peril in sensual pleasures, went forth into the ascetic life of a seer; he has become a highly fortunate seer possessing the five super-knowledges, while I have remained intoxicated by sensual pleasures."
Thus, longing for that young brahmin Upaka, I frequently recite this verse.
Then Gaṅgapāla, having heard this from the king, entered the inner apartments and comforted the women of the harem.
"Do not be anxious on his account; the king will not go forth into the religious life.
Out of longing for that young brahmin Upaka, the king frequently recites this verse:"
Now the women of the inner apartments, joyful, satisfied, and elated, having made a great heap of gold, bullion, garments, and ornaments, said to Gaṅgapāla:
"Gangapāla, may this be a covering for you."
Then this thought occurred to that Gaṅgapāla:
"If even this young brahmin Upaka, though wealthy, has abandoned his home and gone forth, why should I not go forth?
Let me indeed go forth; what need have I for the minds of others?"
Then she spoke to the women of the inner apartments.
"Enough for me with that gold of the doe; I too shall go forth."
Then, having approached Brahmadatta, he said:
"Your Majesty, grant me permission; I shall go forth into the religious life."
The king said:
In whose presence will you go forth?
He said:
"I shall go forth into homelessness in the presence of the seer Upaka."
The king said:
"I permit you; go forth!"
Then Gaṅgapāla went to Upaka’s hermitage and went forth as a monk.

By him also, dwelling devotedly to the practice of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night, applying himself, striving, and exerting himself, the four meditative absorptions were accomplished and the five super-knowledges were realized; he became a seer capable of wiping away the disks of the moon and the sun.
Monks, King Brahmadatta heard that all three of those seers had become possessed of the five super-knowledges and were of great psychic power and great majesty.
Then, a desire to see those seers arose within him. He then addressed his ministers and courtiers:

"Let us go to see those seers, to the hermitage of Upaka the renounced potter and Gaṅgapāla; for all three of those seers have attained the four dhyānas and the five superknowledges, possessing great psychic power and great majesty.
That is the time to approach, visit, and attend upon such worthy recipients of offerings."
The ministers and members of the assembly said:
Let the god not go into their presence; rather, they should be brought here by name.
Then Gaṅgapāla went to King Brahmadatta’s mango grove, hung up his barber’s equipment, and went forth into homelessness.
Then, indeed, a certain royal minister addressed King Brahmadatta with a verse:
"This is that very mango grove of the illustrious Brahmadatta, where [the King], having hung up his razor and his shaving kit, went forth into the religious life.
A king must not go into the presence of those of low birth."
They must indeed come into the presence of Your Majesty.
The king said:
"This is not the dharma that those worthy of offerings would say: 'Come here to see the king.
It is we who must go there to see the seers."
Then King Brahmadatta, surrounded by his princes and ministers, approached where those seers were.
Then the seer Gaṅgapāla approached King Brahmadatta and said this to King Brahmadatta:
Welcome to King Brahmadatta; let King Brahmadatta be seated.

Then indeed, the ministers and courtiers of King Brahmadatta rebuked the seer Gaṅgāpāla with their words and made him tremble: "What are you saying, Gaṅgāpāla? Being of low birth, how can you address King Brahmadatta by name?"
Then King Brahmadatta addressed that assembly of ministers with a verse:
Say nothing to Gaṅgapāla,
who is training in the states of silence of the sages;
he has crossed over that flood of the ocean.
Having crossed over that, they become free from passion.
Through austerity they abandon evil deeds;
through austerity they dispel darkness.
Having overcome [all] by means of the cultivation of austerity, Gaṅgapāla [attains liberation].
I address Brahmadatta by name.
Behold this visible result, even to this extent: the ripening of patience and gentleness,
which has led to the renunciation of the world including its gods.
Worthy of veneration by gods and humans.
Then King Brahmadatta, together with his ministers and courtiers, bowed his head at the feet of those seers and sat down to one side.
Now, she who had been the wife of that Gaṅgapāla while he was a householder was also devoted to her husband; she did not desire another man even in her mind.
Gangapāla, desiring to test her, assumed a divine form and approached her carrying a golden vessel; he enticed her, saying, "Take this golden vessel and enjoy yourself with me."
Then she said:
For a devoted wife does not sleep during the day.
Then that son of the gods, having been turned away on that day, approached on another day taking a silver vessel and said, "Accept this silver vessel and enjoy yourself with me."
Then she said:
For a devoted wife does not kill.
On that day as well, having been refused, he approached on another day taking a bronze vessel, saying, "Accept this bronze vessel; let us enjoy ourselves together."
Then that woman addressed that son of the gods with a verse:
Where a woman or a man makes his will, causing even an elephant to bend or to lift itself up—
that is indeed contrary to the nature of the gods.
This has been rejected by one who is very small.
Then the son of the gods addressed that woman in verse:
In the world of men, both the lifespan and the beauty of those with fair limbs perish;
yet by that very same beauty, wealth may also be acquired.
You are declining; today you are more decayed than before.
The Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, monks, it might occur to you that at that time, on that occasion, the seer named Upaka was someone else.
But this should not be viewed in such a way. And why is that?"
I was that seer named Upaka at that time.
That King Brahmadatta was no other;
at that time, this Śuddhodana was the King of Kāśī, Brahmadatta.
Monks, that barber named Gaṅgapāla who at that time went forth as a seer was none other than this Upāli; even then, because of me,
the entire assembly including the king paid homage to the feet of this man of low birth, and now too, because of me, the entire assembly including the king [pays homage].
The feet of the assembly were worshipped.
Thus concludes the Jātaka of Upāli Gaṅgapāla.
The monks said to the Blessed One:
Behold, Blessed One, how a great multitude of people followed after the Blessed One when he had gone forth!
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it was not only now that a great multitude of people followed me when I went forth."
The monks said:
At another time as well, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
On another occasion as well, monks.
"Once upon a time, monks, in the distant past, there was a king named Diśāmpati. [The Buddha] explained this in detail through the Mahāgovinda Sūtra.

The Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One, having accomplished the purpose for which he had come, was dwelling at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain as the teacher of gods and humans—honored, revered, esteemed, worshiped, and venerated. The introduction should be expanded in detail up until: "And the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have attained mastery over the mind."
In whichever dwellings they desire, in those very dwellings they abide.

Then indeed, Pañcaśikha, the son of the Gandharvas, possessing a most excellent complexion and a most excellent body, having illuminated the entire Gṛdhrakūṭa mountain with his radiance throughout the night, approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, he said this to the Blessed One:

"Venerable Sir, I would announce this to the Blessed One; Venerable Sir, I would report this to the Blessed One, namely, what was said by me when the gods of the Trayastriṃśa heaven, Śakra the lord of the gods, and Mahābrahmā were seated together in the Sudharmā assembly hall of the gods."
It was heard directly and received directly from those who were speaking.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Pañcaśikha, the son of the Gandharvas.

"Declare it to me, Pañcaśikha! Explain it to me, Pañcaśikha! Tell me what you heard directly from the presence of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, from Śakra the lord of the gods, and from Mahābrahmā, as they were speaking, and what you received directly from their presence."
When this had been said, Pañcaśikha, the son of the Gandharvas, addressed the Blessed One in this way:

Once, Blessed One, on a certain occasion, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, together with Śakra, the lord of the gods, and Mahābrahmā, were seated and assembled in the Sudharmā assembly hall of the gods for some business concerning the gods.

And in that regard, Blessed One, certain sons of the gods who have been reborn later surpass other sons of the gods who were reborn earlier in five divine respects: in longevity, in strength, in fame, in splendor, and in retinue.
Some sons of the gods spoke thus:

"Look at this first, worthy sir: those other sons of gods who were born previously are now surpassed by these others born later in five divine respects—in lifespan, in strength, in fame, in glory, and in retinue."
There, Blessed One, some sons of the gods spoke thus:
"Indeed, worthy sir, these were disciples of the Blessed One.
Having practiced the holy life, after the breaking up of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world, among the Trāyastriṃśa host of gods.

These, having been reborn later, greatly outshine the other sons of the gods who were reborn earlier by means of five divine qualities: in lifespan, in complexion, in strength, in fame, and in glory and retinue."
There, O Blessed One, some of the devas spoke thus:

"O worthy sir, it would be wonderful if four Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas were to arise in the world and teach together; it would be for the benefit of gods and for the benefit of humans, the hosts of Asuras would diminish, and the divine hosts would increase."
And there, O Blessed One, some sons of the gods spoke thus:
"Rare, O worthy sir, is the appearance in the world of four Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas.

Oh, if only three Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas were to arise in the world and teach the Dharma! That would be for the welfare of gods and for the welfare of humans; the hosts of Asuras would diminish, and the divine hosts would increase."
Thereupon, O Blessed One, some sons of the gods spoke thus:
"Rare, O worthy sir, is the appearance in the world of three Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas.

Oh, rather, O worthy sir, if two Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas were to arise in the world and teach the Dharma, it would be for the welfare of gods and for the welfare of humans; the hosts of Asuras would diminish, and the divine hosts would increase."
When this had been said, O Blessed One, Śakra, the lord of the gods, addressed the gods of the Trayastriṃśa heaven.
"It is indeed impossible, O worthy one, it is out of the question, that two Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas, should arise in the world at the same time and teach the Dharma."
When this was said, the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three became satisfied, elated, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and happiness.

Then, indeed, the Blessed One Śakra, lord of the gods, perceiving that the Trāyastriṃśa gods were satisfied, elated, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and cheerfulness, addressed them: "If, friends,
you would hear of the eight wonderful and marvelous qualities of that Blessed One, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One..."
Then you too would become even more satisfied, joyful, elated, delighted, and filled with gladness and cheerfulness.
When this had been said, O Blessed One, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods:
Therefore, worthy Kauśika, let it occur to you to cite the eight marvelous and wonderful qualities of that Blessed One, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One.
Then indeed Śakra, the lord of the gods, spoke eight marvelous and wonderful qualities of the Blessed One.
Indeed, friends, when the Blessed One, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has appeared in the world, the hosts of asuras diminish and the divine hosts increase.
And furthermore, my friend, I do not perceive any teacher arisen in the world for the benefit of many beings who is either past or present now, except for the Blessed One,
the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Furthermore, friends, the Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, is well-expounded;
it is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be personally realized by the wise.
This is the crushing of intoxication, the removal of thirst, the uprooting of attachment, the cutting off of the flow of phenomena, the destruction of craving, dispassion.
Cessation is Nirvana; such is this well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya.
Furthermore, my friend, I do not perceive any Teacher arisen in the world—neither in the past nor now in the present—who is other than that Blessed One, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One.
Furthermore, friends, the Blessed One, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, has indeed attained the path for his disciples who are still in training and for those Arhats whose nature is unshakable.

And even for them, that Blessed One, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, having dispelled [those distractions], dwells in forest lodgings— remote, secluded, devoid of people, hidden from men, suitable for retreat, and conducive to solitary meditation— alone, withdrawn from the crowd; he is called "one" because he is devoted to being named "One."
Furthermore, friends, I do not perceive any teacher arisen in the world who possesses such a single name as the past, nor one in the present, other than that Blessed One,
the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One.

"Friends, it is indeed a gain for the Blessed One, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one, that he receives exquisite foods, both solid and soft, of upright flavor and fresh flavor; and yet, that Blessed One, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one,
partakes of that food without being attached, without being infatuated, seeing the danger [in it], possessing the wisdom of renunciation, and free from intoxication regarding sensual pleasures."
Furthermore, friends, as I survey the world, past or present, I do not see any teacher who has arisen in the world who consumes food free from intoxication, other than that Blessed One, the Arhat,
the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Furthermore, friends, that Blessed One, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, teaches the Dharma to his disciples out of direct knowledge, not without direct knowledge;
it is by such direct knowledge, by such direct knowledge, that he has appeared in the world as a Teacher endowed with the path of teaching the Dharma.
I do not perceive anyone in the past, nor in the present, other than that Blessed One, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Furthermore, friends, that Blessed One, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, has indeed crossed over doubt; he is free from hesitation and has attained self-confidence regarding wholesome qualities. Moreover, friends, I do not perceive any teacher arisen in the world—neither in the past nor now in the present—who has crossed over doubt in such a way, other than that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One.

Furthermore, friends, the nirvana of that Blessed One, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, and the path leading to nirvana, truly flow together; just as, friends, the waters of the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā,
flowing together, merge into the great ocean, even so, friends, do they flow together for that Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One.
Nirvana and the path leading to Nirvana—

thus, friends, I do not perceive any teacher arisen in the world, whether in the past or now in the present, who is endowed with such a well-expounded and well-proclaimed path leading to Nirvana, other than that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat.
By the Perfectly Enlightened One.

When this had been said, O Blessed One, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven became even more satisfied, thrilled, elated, joyful, and filled with gladness and cheer; they addressed Śakra, the lord of the gods:
"Therefore, worthy Kauśika, let it occur to you once again to proclaim those eight marvelous and wonderful qualities of that Blessed One, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One."
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, indeed proclaimed once more eight marvelous and wonderful qualities of the Blessed One.

Furthermore, friends, when that Blessed One, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has appeared in the world, the hosts of asuras diminish and the divine hosts increase. Friends, regarding a Teacher who has thus set out for the welfare of many and thus set out for the happiness of many,
having appeared in the world, I do not perceive anyone else— whether past or even now present— who is equal to him.

By the Blessed One, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One— [and so on] as before— friends, the nirvāṇa of that Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One, and the practice leading to nirvāṇa, truly flow together. Just as, friends, the waters of the Gaṅgā and the waters of the Yamunā, flowing together, flow into the great ocean.

In the same way, friends, is the nirvāṇa of that Blessed One, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, and the path leading to nirvāṇa. And furthermore, friends, I do not perceive any teacher arisen in the world— neither in the past nor now in the present— who has practiced the teaching of the Dharma of nirvāṇa so well-expounded and well-proclaimed as by that Blessed One, the Arhat.
By the Perfectly Enlightened One.
When this was said, the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three were even more thrilled, elated, joyful, and filled with gladness and happiness.
Then, O Blessed One, the Great Brahmā, perceiving that the gods of the Thirty-three were even more thrilled, elated, and filled with joy and gladness, spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods:
Therefore, friend Kauśika,
let it occur to you to proclaim once more these eight marvelous and wonderful qualities of this Blessed One, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, indeed proclaimed once more eight marvelous and wonderful qualities of the Blessed One.
Furthermore, friends, when that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Enlightened One has appeared in the world, the hosts of asuras decline and the divine hosts increase.

"Friends, I do not perceive any teacher arisen in the world who has practiced for the benefit and happiness of many people, whether in the past or even now in the present, other than that Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha.
And so on, until: Furthermore, friends, the nirvāṇa of that Blessed One, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, and the practice leading to nirvāṇa, are indeed in perfect harmony."

Just as, friends, the waters of the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā flow together and merge into the great ocean, even so, friends, is the Nirvāṇa and the practice leading to Nirvāṇa of that Blessed One, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One. And furthermore, friends, when such a Teacher has appeared in the world— one who has well-taught, well-proclaimed, and entered upon the teaching of the Dharma of Nirvāṇa—
I do not perceive anything arisen that is past, nor even anything present at this time, other than that which was [taught] by the Blessed One, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One.
When this had been said, the gods of the Thirty-three became even more thrilled, elated, and filled with joy and gladness.
Then the Blessed One, the Great Brahmā, perceiving that the gods of the Trayastriṃśa heaven were even more thrilled, elated, joyful, and filled with gladness and happiness, addressed them in verses:
"O gods of the Trayastriṃśa, together with Śakra, rejoice!
Paying homage to the Tathāgata, [rejoice] in the blissful nature of the Dharma."
And then the deity became joyful, filled with gladness and mental well-being.

Then, indeed, the Blessed One Mahābrahmā, perceiving that the gods of the Trayastriṃśa heaven were even more thrilled, delighted, and filled with joy and gladness, addressed them: "If you, worthy friends, listen for a long time to the great proclamation of that Blessed One, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, you shall become pure, and you will be even more thrilled, elated, joyful, and filled with joy and gladness."
When this had been said, O Blessed One, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven said this to Mahābrahmā:
"In that case, friend Mahābrahmā, let it occur to you to recite the long-standing Great Declaration of that Blessed One, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One.
Then Mahābrahmā indeed recited the Blessed One’s long-standing Great Declaration.
Long ago, sirs, in a past time, there was a king named Diśāmpati.
Furthermore, sirs, King Diśāmpati had a brahmin named Govinda who served as his domestic priest; he was the king’s teacher, learned, skillful, and wise in various matters.
Furthermore, sirs, King Diśāmpati had a son named Reṇu, who was dear and beloved, wise, skillful, and intelligent in various matters.
Furthermore, sirs, the Brahmin Govinda had a young son named Jyotipāla, who was his only child, dear and beloved, wise, skillful, and intelligent in various matters.
Then, sirs, after the passing of a long time, the Brahmin Govinda died.
Then, indeed, sirs, when the brahmin Govinda had passed away, King Diśāmpati grieved, languished, lamented, beat his breast, wailed, and fell into a state of delusion.

"O sirs, at this very time when we, having properly fulfilled all the duties for Govinda, were provided with and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure, playing, enjoying, and diverting ourselves— that is the very moment the brahmin Govinda has passed away."
"Indeed, sirs, Prince Reṇu heard that King Diśāmpati, upon the death of the brahmin Govinda, was grieving, wearying, lamenting, beating his breast, wailing, and falling into a state of confusion."
Then, sirs, Prince Reṇu approached King Diśāmpati and said this to King Diśāmpati:
"Do not grieve, Great King; do not be distressed; do not lament; do not beat your breast and cry out; do not fall into despair.
Why is that?
Great King, the brahmin Govinda has a young son named Jyotipāla, who is dear and pleasing, wise, skillful, and intelligent, and who is even more learned than his father in various matters."
He was more skillful and more discerning;
moreover, whatever his father perceived, all of that was practiced in secret by the young brahmin Jyotipāla.
May Your Majesty establish him in his own ancestral position, namely, that of the family priest, Govindya.
Then, indeed, sirs, King Diśāmpati addressed a certain man.
"Come, man, go to where the young brahmin Jyotipāla is, and having approached him, speak thus to the young brahmin Jyotipāla:"
King Diśāmpati addresses you, Jyotipāla:
"May the venerable Jyotipāla approach where King Diśāmpati is."
"Very well, Great King," that man replied to Diśāmpatirāja; having heard this, he approached the young Brahmin Jyotipāla and said this to him.
King Diśāmpati addresses you, Jyotipāla: "May the venerable Jyotipāla approach King Diśāmpati, now that the brahmin Govinda has passed away."

"Very well, sir," the young Brahmin Jyotipāla replied to that man. Having approached King Diśāmpati and exchanged greetings with him, and having engaged in pleasant and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side.
When the young brahmin Jyotipāla was seated to one side, King Diśāmpati said this to him:
"May the venerable Jyotipāla exhort me; may the venerable Jyotipāla instruct me; and may the venerable one not delay in giving us exhortation and instruction.
And we shall establish the venerable Jyotipāla in his own ancestral position, namely, in the office of the domestic priest of the Gauvindas."
Then indeed, sirs, the young man Jyotipāla was established in his own paternal position as the domestic chaplain of Govinda;

whatever work his father caused to be done, that work he also caused to be done, and whatever undertakings his father accomplished, those undertakings the young man Jyotipāla also accomplished— just as his father did.
Jyotipāla the young brahmin instructs him for the sake of wealth; whatever his father accomplishes for the sake of wealth, Jyotipāla the young brahmin also accomplishes for the sake of wealth.
For indeed, the brahmins, householders, merchants, and countryfolk spoke thus: "Victory!"
Furthermore, sirs, the young Brahmin Jyotipāla was called Govinda, and Mahāgovinda was called Jyotipāla.
For indeed, the syllables "Govinda, Mahāgovinda" have fallen to the young Brahmin Jyotipāla as his own victory.
Then, indeed, venerable sirs, the brahmin Mahāgovinda approached those kṣatriyas and said this to them:
"Come, sirs, come! Approach Prince Reṇu and speak thus to Prince Reṇu."
"Whatever happiness Lord Reṇu has, that happiness we also have; whatever suffering Lord Reṇu has, that suffering we also have.

O Reṇu, this King Diśāmpati is aged, old, advanced in years, and has reached the end of his journey; he has arrived at the stage where life is difficult to overcome, O Reṇu, for this life indeed ends in death.
Now, O Reṇu, when King Diśāmpati passes away, if those who rule the kingdom consecrate you, Lord Reṇu, in the kingship, will you be able [to provide] for us as well?"
To share [it] with the kingdom.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the six kṣatriyas, Prince Reṇu and the others:
"If, sirs, you appoint me king after the passing of King Diśāmpati, I shall share the kingdom with you."
Now, no one else in our kingdom shall ever again attain such happiness as this, except through you.
Then, indeed, sirs, after the passing of a long time, King Diśāmpati passed away.
Then, indeed, O sirs, the royal officials approached Prince Reṇu and said this to him.
"O Prince, you have attained the kingdom; we shall consecrate you with the sovereignty."
When this had been said, sirs, Prince Reṇu spoke thus to those royal officials:
Therefore, sirs, may you be happy; do whatever you deem to be the right time for now.
Then indeed, King Reṇu, having been consecrated in his kingdom, being fully endowed with and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure, played, enjoyed himself, and amused himself.
Then, indeed, venerable sirs, the brahmin Mahāgovinda approached those six kṣatriyas and said this to them:
"Come now, sirs! For this King Reṇu, sirs, has been consecrated in the kingdom; endowed with and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure, he plays, enjoys himself, and amuses himself.
And these, sirs, are indeed the sensual pleasures that intoxicate."
"Come, sirs, go to King Reṇu and say this to King Reṇu: 'Does your majesty, Reṇu, remember those words?'"
Having given their assent to the brahmin Mahāgovinda, these six kṣatriyas went to King Reṇu and, having approached him, spoke thus to King Reṇu: "It is well."
Does your honor, Reṇu, remember those words?
When this had been said, sirs, King Reṇu spoke thus to those six kṣatriyas.
I remember those words, sirs:
"Who now shall divide this great earth into seven portions?"
When this had been said, sirs, the six kṣatriyas spoke thus to King Reṇu.
