"Now then, O Reṇu, who indeed is wiser or more discerning than that Blessed One Mahāgovinda, who shall divide this great earth into seven parts?"
Then, indeed, gentlemen, King Reṇu addressed a certain man.
"Come, my good man, go to where the brahmin Mahāgovinda is, and having approached him, speak thus to the brahmin Mahāgovinda:
'King Reṇu addresses the Blessed One Mahāgovinda.'"
"Very well, Great King," that man replied to King Reṇu, and having approached where the brahmin Mahāgovinda was, he spoke thus to the brahmin Mahāgovinda.
King Reṇu addressed the Blessed One Mahāgovinda:
"May the venerable Mahāgovinda approach King Reṇu."

Saying "So be it," the brahmin Mahāgovinda gave his assent to that man; he then approached King Reṇu, exchanged greetings with him, and after engaging in polite and friendly conversation, sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the brahmin Mahāgovinda said this to King Reṇu:
Sirs, this great earth extends over seven kingdoms.
To the south was Saṃkṣiptā, situated in the shape of a wagon's head;
in the middle of the Egg was the city of King Reṇu.
Of the Kaliṅgas and of us, [the city of] . . . . . . ;
and Māhiṣmatī . . . . . , and Roruka of the Sauvīras.
I shall have Mithilā built among the Videhas, and [a city] among the Aṅgas;
and Vārāṇasī among the Kāśis—this is what was planned by Govinda.
Then, indeed, gentlemen, the brahmin Govinda established those six kṣatriyas in their respective kingdoms.

Not long after his consecration, the six kings quickly assembled and, having approached the brahmin Mahāgovinda, spoke thus to him: [The blank line indicates the beginning of the sentence. Not long after his consecration, the six kings quickly assembled and, having approached the brahmin Mahāgovinda, spoke thus to him: "Brahmin Mahāgovinda, we have heard that you have renounced the world and gone forth into homelessness. "Friends, it is true that I have renounced the world and gone forth into homelessness. "Brahmin Mahāgovinda, since you have renounced the world and gone forth into homelessness, please teach us the Dharma as you know it. "Friends, I am indeed one who has renounced the world and gone forth into homelessness; however, I do not possess the knowledge of the Dharma to teach you. "Brahmin Mahāgovinda, we have heard that there is a recluse named Āḷāra Kālāma who has renounced the world and gone forth into homelessness. He is wise, learned, and possesses great wisdom. He knows the Dharma and is capable of teaching it. Brahmin Mahāgovinda, please go to the recluse Āḷāra Kālāma and learn the Dharma from him. "Friends, I have already gone to the recluse Āḷāra Kālāma and learned the Dharma from him. "Brahmin Mahāgovinda, what kind of Dharma did you learn from the recluse Āḷāra Kālāma? "Friends, the recluse Āḷāra Kālāma teaches the Dharma as far as the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*). "Brahmin Mahāgovinda, please teach us the Dharma as you know it. "Brahmin Mahāgovinda, please teach us the Dharma as you know it. "Friends, I am indeed one who has renounced the world and gone forth into homelessness; however, I do not possess the knowledge of the Dharma to teach you. "Brahmin Mahāgovinda, we have heard that there is a recluse named the Son of the Sakyans (*Sakyaputta) who has renounced the world and gone forth into homelessness. He is wise, learned, and possesses great wisdom. He knows the Dharma and is capable of teaching it. Brahmin Mahāgovinda, please go to the recluse the Son of the Sakyans and learn the Dharma from him. "Friends, I have already gone to the recluse the Son of the Sakyans and learned the Dharma from him. "Brahmin Mahāgovinda, what kind of Dharma did you learn from the recluse the Son of the Sakyans? "Friends, the recluse the Son of the Sakyans teaches the Dharma as far as the cessation of perception and feeling (*saññāvedayitanirodha*). "Brahmin Mahāgovinda, please teach us the Dharma as you know it. "Friends, I am indeed one who has renounced the world and gone forth into homelessness; however, I do not possess the knowledge of the Dharma to teach you. "Brahmin Mahāgovinda, we have heard that you have renounced the world and gone forth into homelessness. We wish to follow you and renounce the world with you. "Friends, I am indeed one who has renounced the world and gone

May the venerable Mahāgovinda exhort us; may the venerable Mahāgovinda instruct us. Just as the venerable Mahāgovinda instructs King Reṇu in matters of welfare and purpose, so may he likewise instruct us in these six kingdoms regarding matters of welfare and purpose.
Now at that time, the brahmin Mahāgovinda was instructing the seven kings in matters of state;
he was teaching the mantras to seven hundred thousand brahmins and teaching the mantras to seven hundred bath-graduated (snātaka) students.
"Repeat what I say."
For indeed, the brahmins, householders, merchants, and countryfolk all recognize the illustrious brahmin Govinda as one who has conquered.
The noble Mahāgovinda saw Mahābrahmā face to face, and having consulted with Mahābrahmā again and again on what was to be understood, he instructed him in matters of meaning.
"Venerable sirs, the brahmin Mahāgovinda indeed heard:

'The brahmins, householders, merchants, and countryfolk perceive me thus: "The noble and illustrious Govinda sees Brahmā face to face, and furthermore, he deliberates with Mahābrahmā regarding those matters of purpose that he instructs. "
Furthermore, I do not actually see Mahābrahmā face to face, nor do I instruct him on matters of meaning after repeatedly consulting with Mahābrahmā about what is to be known.
Indeed, it would not be right or fitting for me to accept praise that is false and non-existent.
Furthermore, I have indeed heard this from the presence of ancient teachers—those who were advanced in years, aged, decrepit, elderly, and had reached the end of their journey—who spoke thus:

"To one who remains in seclusion for the four months of the rainy season and meditates on the meditation of compassion, Mahābrahmā himself approaches him; and whatever purpose he has in mind, that is either granted to him or explained when he asks about it."
"What if I were to remain in seclusion for the four months of the rainy season and practice the meditation on compassion, provided that the Blessed One Reṇu grants me permission?"
When this had been said, sirs, King Reṇu spoke thus to the brahmin Mahāgovinda:
"In that case, O Mahāgovinda, may you be happy; do as you deem it the right time."
Then, indeed, venerable sirs, Mahāgovinda remained in seclusion for the four months of the rainy season and practiced the meditation on compassion.

Then, indeed, gentlemen, at the end of the four months of the rainy season, on that very day of the *poṣadha*— the fourteenth or the full moon— the Brahmin Mahāgovinda, having bathed his head and dressed in fresh, clean garments, with his body purified, stood between the altar and the fire upon a smooth slab of stone anointed with ghee and free from any intervening space, facing the fire.
Having lit it, one should sit facing north in the house of the faithful.
Then, indeed, sirs, before long, there appeared from the northern direction the manifestation of a great light.

"Friends, Mahāgovinda indeed beheld the appearance of a great light from the northern direction; and having seen it, he was struck with wonder and amazement, his hair standing on end, as if something never seen before were now being seen."
Then, indeed, sirs, the Great Brahmā, having come through the air from the northern direction not long after, stood in the sky above Mahāgovinda the brahmin, suspended in mid-air.

Indeed, the brahmin Mahāgovinda, looking upward, saw Mahābrahmā stationed in the sky above, suspended in mid-air; and having seen him, he extended his joined palms toward Mahābrahmā and addressed him in verse:
Whether you possess strength, fame, or splendor, what indeed are you, O worthy one?
Not knowing [this], I ask you: how may we come to know you?
When this had been said, sirs, Mahābrahmā replied to the brahmin Mahāgovinda in verse:
"Who they recognize as the Prince in the Brahma-world, eternal—even the gods recognize him thus; know it to be so, Govinda."
When this had been said, venerable sirs, the brahmin Mahāgovinda addressed Mahābrahmā in verse:
Accept from me, O Brahmā, a seat, water for the feet, and sweet rice-porridge; I offer this excellence to you.
Then, indeed, the Great Brahmā replied to the Great Brahmin Mahāgovinda with a verse.
I accept the seat, water for the feet, and the sweet rice-porridge; O Govinda, bring the best of these to me.
When this had been said, the venerable Mahāgovinda brahmin addressed Mahābrahmā in verse:
Whether for the sake of benefit in this present life or for happiness in the future world,
having been granted the opportunity, I shall ask that which is desired in my mind.
When this had been said, sirs, Mahābrahmā replied to the brahmin Mahāgovinda with a verse:
Whether for the sake of benefit in this present life or for happiness in the future world,
having been granted the opportunity, ask whatever you desire.
Then, indeed, it occurred to the brahmin Mahāgovinda: "What now?"
"I have indeed been invited by Mahābrahmā to answer a question; what now should I ask Mahābrahmā—concerning a matter pertaining to this present life, or rather, concerning the future life?"
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to the brahmin Mahāgovinda:
There is, first of all, this benefit pertaining to the present life, which concerns these five strands of sensual pleasure.
"What if I were now to ask Mahābrahmā a question concerning the matter of the future life?"
Then, indeed, the brahmin Mahāgovinda asked Mahābrahmā a question concerning the matter of the future life.
Desiring freedom from desire regarding all conditioned things, I ask Brahmā Sanatkumāra: "What should one do? How should one act? What should one practice?"
A human being attains the immortal world of Brahmā.
When this had been said, sirs, Mahābrahmā replied to the brahmin Govinda in verse:
Having abandoned the sense of "mine" among human beings, O Brahmin,
become one-pointed, compassionate, and secluded;
free from the stench of impurity, abstain from sexual intercourse.
A human being attains the immortal world of Brahmā.
When this had been said, sirs, the brahmin Mahāgovinda spoke thus to Mahābrahmā:
"Having abandoned the sense of 'mine'": this, sirs, is how we understand the meaning of what the Great Brahmā says,

when someone goes forth from the home life into homelessness, having relinquished a small mass of wealth or a large mass of wealth, and having relinquished a small circle of kinsmen or a large circle of kinsmen.

Whether born from a high family or a low family, having discarded the marks of a householder and taking up the outer robe, bowl, and monastic garments, he trains in the precepts, endowed with pure bodily and vocal action, possessing a completely purified livelihood,
and having abandoned the sense of "mine"— this, friends, is the meaning we understand when the Great Brahmā speaks thus.
"Venerable sirs, we understand this matter to be the state of unification with Great Brahmā."
"Because here a certain person, through the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, with internal serenity and one-pointedness of mind,
enters and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is free from applied and sustained thought, born of seclusion, and filled with rapture and happiness— and because he has become one-pointed—
this is the meaning we understand from what the venerable Mahābrahmā says."
"Compassionate and secluded"—this, venerable sirs, is how we understand the meaning of what the Great Brahmā has said.

In this case, a certain person dwells having suffused one direction with a mind imbued with compassion— vast, exalted, non-dual, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will— and likewise the second, the third, and the fourth;
thus above, below, across, and everywhere, throughout the entire world, he dwells having suffused it all.
"Compassionate and secluded"— this, venerable sirs, is how we understand the meaning of what the Great Brahmā has spoken.
"Sirs, we do not understand the meaning of what the Great Brahmā has spoken regarding the absence of the stench of raw flesh."
O Brahmin, what among men are the raw-smelling ones?
O hero, tell me this which I do not know: by what are the water-bearing channels covered with chaff?
Those bound for the states of woe have attained peace in the Brahma-world.
When this had been said, Mahābrahmā replied to the brahmin Mahāgovinda in verse:
Anger, false speech, and doubt;
arrogance,
envy, violence, and resentment toward the teachings of others.
O Brahmā, those foul odors among human beings,
by which the water-bearing rivers are choked like a pit of chaff, have ceased; the world of Brahmā has become tranquil.
When this had been said, the Blessed One Mahāgovinda spoke thus to Mahābrahmā.
"Raw stench," we understand this to be the meaning, venerable sir, of what the Great Brahmā is saying.

"It is not possible for one dwelling in a household to practice the holy life (brahmacarya) that is entirely refined, entirely blameless, entirely pure, and completely cleansed. Life is short; the world beyond must be traversed. For one who is born, there is no such thing as immortality. Therefore, one must know, reflect upon, and awaken to this: one must do what is wholesome, one must practice the holy life, and no evil deed whatsoever should be committed in the world."
"O Great Brahmā, I shall now go forth from the home into homelessness, if the Blessed One, the Great Brahmā, would grant me his instruction."
When this had been said, sirs, Mahābrahmā spoke thus to the brahmin Mahāgovinda.
Therefore, O Mahāgovinda, be happy; do now as you deem it timely.
And I have heard this: at that time, it is said, the Blessed One was a brahmin named Mahāgovinda; does the Blessed One remember?
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Pañcaśikha, the son of the Gandharvas:
"It is even so, Pañcaśikha; at that time I was the brahmin named Mahāgovinda.
And I remember it, Pañcaśikha, though you have not heard how that brahmin Mahāgovinda went forth from the home life into homelessness."
Indeed, Pañcaśikha, I am that brahmin Mahāgovinda; having approached King Reṇu, I addressed King Reṇu with a verse.
I address you, O Great King, Renu, lord of the earth:
having abandoned my kingdom and my office as domestic priest, I shall go forth into the religious life.
When this had been said, Pañcaśikha, King Reṇu replied to the brahmin Mahāgovinda in verse:
"If there is anything lacking for you in desires, we shall fulfill it for you;
or who is harming you that we should protect you? You are our father and we are your sons; O Govinda, do not go forth!"
When this had been said, Pañcaśikha, the brahmin Mahāgovinda approached King Reṇu and addressed King Reṇu with a verse:
There is no deficiency in desires, nor is there anyone who would cause us harm;
having heard the words of non-humans, how could we act otherwise?
When this had been said, Pañcaśikha, King Reṇu replied to the brahmin Mahāgovinda in verse:
What was the appearance of that non-human being, and what did he say,
hearing whose words you have abandoned our house entirely?
When this had been said, Pañcaśikha, the brahmin Mahāgovinda addressed King Reṇu with a verse:
While I was desirous of sacrificing on all sides and remained fasting,
the fire was kindled, clothed in a covering of kusha grass and bark.
Then the eternal Brahmā appeared in the world before me;
having heard his word, I abandoned both you and my entire home.
When this had been said, Pañcaśikha, King Reṇu replied to the brahmin Mahāgovinda with a verse:
We place our faith in you just as Govinda speaks;
having heard the words of a non-human being, how could we act otherwise?
Whatever words the venerable Mahāgovinda speaks, they are indeed concerning wholesome things;
and whatever shall be the destiny of you, Govinda, that shall also be our destiny.
Just as a pure and clear beryl gem in the sky,
so shall I conduct myself with purity according to the instruction of Govinda.
When this had been said, Pañcaśikha, the brahmin Mahāgovinda addressed King Reṇu with these verses:
If you would abandon those sensual pleasures in which ordinary people are attached, it would be well; therefore, become firm, established in patience and meditative concentration.
This is the path to the City of Brahmā; this is the eternal path proclaimed by those who know the True Dharma for the sake of rebirth in the world of Brahmā.
Pañcaśikha, those six kings indeed heard that the brahmin Mahāgovinda was going forth from the home life into homelessness;
they immediately assembled together.
Then, Pañcaśikha, the brahmin Mahāgovinda approached those six kings and said this to them:
"Go, sirs; go, sirs! Now seek another teacher who will instruct you, each in his own kingdom, in matters of statecraft."
For what reason?
I shall go forth from the home into the homeless state.
For I have heard from the presence of Mahābrahmā as he spoke of the "stench of raw flesh":

it is not possible for one dwelling in a household to practice the holy life (brahmacarya) that is completely refined, completely blameless, pure, and purified; life is short, the next world must be gone to, and there is no such thing as non-death for one who is born. Therefore—
That which is to be known, attained, and realized must be understood; one should practice the wholesome life of celibacy, and no evil deed whatsoever should be committed in the world.
Then, Pañcaśikha, this thought occurred to those six kings:
"For these so-called brahmins are indeed greedy for enjoyments;
what if we were now to invite the brahmin Mahāgovinda with enjoyments?"
Then, Pañcaśikha, those six kings invited the brahmin Mahāgovinda to enjoy their wealth.

"Mahāgovinda, in these six kingdoms there exist abundant human enjoyments— righteous, acquired through righteousness, gathered and amassed by righteous power; therefore, let Master Mahāgovinda take this wealth, and let Master Mahāgovinda not go forth from the home life into homelessness."
When this had been said, Pañcaśikha, the brahmin Mahāgovinda spoke thus to the six kings.

"Indeed, sirs, we too possess abundant human enjoyments— righteous, acquired through dharma, gathered and amassed by righteous power— and yet I shall renounce even these and go forth from the home into the homeless state."
For what reason?
For I have heard from the presence of Mahābrahmā as he spoke of the "stench of raw flesh":

it is not possible for one dwelling in a household to practice the holy life (brahmacarya) that is completely refined, entirely blameless, pure, and cleansed; life is short, the world beyond must be traversed, and there is no such thing as non-death for one who is born.
Therefore, that which is to be known, attained, understood, performed, and practiced as virtue—the holy life—must be undertaken;
nothing evil whatsoever should be done in this world.
Then, Pañcaśikha, this thought occurred to those six kings:
For these so-called brahmins are indeed lustful for women;
what if we were now to entice the brahmin Mahāgovinda with women?
Then, Pañcaśikha, the six kings invited the brahmin Mahāgovinda with women.

"O Mahāgovinda, in these six kingdoms there exist many women who are gracious, beautiful to behold, noble in appearance, and endowed with the highest excellence of radiant complexion; therefore, may the venerable Mahāgovinda take these women as his wives. Let not the venerable Govinda go forth from the home into the homeless state."
When this had been said, Pañcaśikha, the brahmin Mahāgovinda spoke thus to those six kings.

"Indeed, sirs, we too have forty wives who are similar to you—gracious, beautiful to behold, with ample space [for their needs], and endowed with the highest excellence of fair complexion; yet even having abandoned them, I shall go forth from the home into the homeless state."
For what reason?
For I have heard from the presence of Brahmā as he spoke of the "stench of raw flesh":

it is not possible for one dwelling in a household to practice the holy life (brahmacarya) that is utterly refined, utterly blameless, completely pure, and perfectly cleansed; life is short, the world beyond must be traversed, and for one who is born there is no non-death. Therefore, this must be understood.

That which is to be attained, that which is to be understood, that which is to be done, and the wholesome holy life (brahmacarya) must be practiced; and no evil whatsoever should be committed in the world.
When this had been said, Pañcaśikha, those six kings spoke thus to the brahmin Mahāgovinda:

"In that case, Mahāgovinda, wait for seven years until we have established our sons and brothers in our respective kingdoms and return; whatever destiny awaits you, Mahāgovinda, shall also be our destiny."
When this had been said, Pañcaśikha, the brahmin Mahāgovinda spoke thus to those six kings.
Indeed, it has been far too long for you that I have remained thus; after these seven years, I shall go forth from the home to the homeless life.
For what reason?
For I have heard from the presence of Mahābrahmā as he was speaking of the "stench of raw flesh" (āmagandha): "It is not possible to perform an evil deed."
When this had been said, Pañcaśikha, those six kings spoke thus to the brahmin Mahāgovinda:
"In that case, Mahāgovinda, wait for six years;
[and so on,] by repetition: five years, four years, three years, two years, one year;
wait for seven months, until we, Mahāgovinda, [have settled matters regarding] our respective kingdoms, sons, and brothers."
Having established ourselves, we shall come; whatever be the destiny of you, Govinda, that shall also be our destiny.
When this had been said, Pañcaśikha, the brahmin Mahāgovinda spoke thus to those six kings.
"Indeed, sirs, seven months is far too long; I shall go forth from the home life into homelessness."
For what reason?
I have heard from the presence of Mahābrahmā as he was speaking of the "stench of raw flesh" (āmagandha): it is not possible for one who has heard this to commit evil.

When this had been said, Pañcaśikha, those six kings spoke thus to the brahmin Mahāgovinda: "Therefore, Mahāgovinda, wait for six months until we have established our sons and brothers in our respective kingdoms and shall return.
"The same should be done in every case," [he replied], and so on, down to five months, four months, three months, two months, and one month.
"As soon as we have established our sons and brothers in our respective kingdoms and return, whatever destiny awaits you, Mahāgovinda, that same destiny shall also be ours."
When this had been said, Pañcaśikha, the great brahmin Mahāgovinda spoke thus to those six kings:
"Indeed, sirs, this half-month has been far too long; I shall go forth from the home life into homelessness."
For what reason?
For it has been heard that an evil deed should not be committed.
When this had been said, Pañcaśikha, those six kings spoke thus to the brahmin Mahāgovinda:

"Therefore, O Great Govinda, wait for seven days until we have established our sons and brothers in our respective kingdoms and return; whatever destiny awaits you, Govinda, that same destiny shall also be ours."
When this had been said, Pañcaśikha, the brahmin Mahāgovinda spoke thus to those six kṣatriyas:
"Indeed, sirs, this is but a short time—namely these seven days. Therefore, sirs, may you be happy; do whatever you deem to be timely now."
Then, Pañcaśikha, the brahmin Mahāgovinda approached those seven thousand great brahmin householders and seven hundred bath-graduates and said this:
"Come, sirs; come, sirs! Now seek another preceptor who will teach you the mantras.
As for me, I shall go forth from the home to the homeless state."
For what reason?
For I have heard from the presence of Mahābrahmā as he spoke of the "stench of raw flesh" (āmagandha), that evil karma must not be committed.
When this had been said, Pañcaśikha,
those seven thousand great brahmin householders and seven hundred bath-graduated brahmins said this to the brahmin Mahāgovinda:

"May the venerable Govinda not go forth from the home life into homelessness; for this so-called 'going forth,' O Mahāgovinda, brings little profit, little enjoyment, little renown, and little merit. But this state of being a brahmin, O Mahāgovinda, brings great profit, great splendor, great renown, and great merit."
When this had been said, Pañcaśikha, Mahāgovinda spoke thus to those seven thousand brahmins and seven hundred bath-graduates.

Sirs, do not speak thus. For this so-called going forth, sirs, is of great power, great gain, great renown, and great benefit; whereas this so-called brahminhood, sirs, is of little purpose, little gain, little renown, and little benefit—whatever you perceive at all, all that [is included in the former].
This is indeed our own cause.
When this had been said, Pañcaśikha, the seven thousand brahmins and the seven hundred bath-graduated (snātaka) brahmins said this to the brahmin Mahāgovinda:

"So it is, O Preceptor; so it is. This so-called renunciation is indeed of great power, of great gain, of great renown, and of great benefit. But this so-called Brahminhood, O Preceptor, is of little purpose, of little gain, and of little benefit.
Whatever we know at all, O Preceptor, all that has its origin in you, as does whatever belongs to your [teaching]."
Whatever is the destiny of our preceptor, that shall also be our destiny.
When this had been said, Pañcaśikha, the brahmin Mahāgovinda spoke thus to those seven thousand great brahmin householders and the seven hundred bath-graduates:
Therefore, sirs, may you be happy; do whatever you deem to be the right time for now.
Then, Pañcaśikha, the brahmin Mahāgovinda approached those forty wives of equal status and said this to the forty wives of equal status:
"Let all you women who wish do so: let those who wish go to their respective families of kin; let those who wish seek another husband; and let those who wish dwell right here in this brahmin family."
"In this brahmin family there exist abundant human enjoyments, righteous and acquired through dharma, gathered and amassed by righteous means;
I shall go forth from the home into the homeless state."
For what reason?

For I have heard from the presence of Mahābrahmā as he spoke of the "stench of raw flesh" (āmagandha): it is not possible for one dwelling in a household to practice the holy life (brahmacarya) that is utterly refined, utterly blameless, completely pure, and perfectly cleansed.
For what reason?

Life is short; one must depart for the next world, and there is no such thing as immortality for one who is born. Therefore, one should know, one should attain, one should awaken; one should do what is wholesome, one should practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and one should not perform any evil deed whatsoever in this world.
When this had been said, Pañcaśikha, those forty wives of similar appearance said this to the brahmin Mahāgovinda:

"Indeed, the noble Govinda is our master at the time he is a master, and our friend at the time he is a friend; whatever destination the noble Mahāgovinda shall have, that shall also be our destination.
When this was said, Pañcaśikha, the brahmin Mahāgovinda spoke thus to those forty wives who were his equals:
Therefore, ladies, may you be happy; now do whatever you deem to be timely.
Then indeed, Pañcaśikha, on that very seventh day, the brahmin Mahāgovinda had his hair and beard shaved off, donned saffron-colored robes, and went forth from the home into the homeless state.
Furthermore, when he had thus gone forth, seven kings followed him into the homeless life;

seven thousand great brahmin householders followed him into the homeless life; seven hundred bath-graduates (snātaka) followed him into the homeless life; forty wives of equal rank followed him into the homeless life—not to mention the rest of the people who came for a visit.
That assembly consisted of many hundreds and many thousands.

Furthermore, Pañcaśikha, the brahmin Mahāgovinda was an outsider who had become free from passion for sensual pleasures; he taught the Dharma to his disciples for the sake of attaining companionship in the Brahma-world.
Furthermore, Pañcaśikha, those disciples of the brahmin Mahāgovinda who understand the Dharma as it was taught in its entirety attain rebirth in the company of the Brahmā-world.
However, Pañcaśikha, those disciples of the brahmin Mahāgovinda who do not understand the Dharma as it was taught in its entirety are reborn among the gods of the desire realm.
Some are reborn to dwell together with the gods of the Four Great Kings; some are reborn among the gods of the Thirty-three;
some among the Yāma gods; some among the Tuṣita gods; some among the Nirmāṇarati gods;
and some attain rebirth to dwell together with the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods.
Furthermore, Pañcaśikha, those women or men who harbor harsh thoughts toward the brahmin Mahāgovinda and his disciples, upon the dissolution of the body after death, will be reborn in states of woe,
in miserable destinies, in perdition— in the hells.

Furthermore, Pañcaśikha, those women or men who have set their minds upon the brahmin Mahāgovinda and his disciples, after the breaking up of the body, after death, they are reborn in a good destination,
in a heavenly world, among the gods.
Furthermore, Pañcaśikha, in whatever village or town the brahmin Mahāgovinda dwells while relying upon it, there he becomes the king of the kingdom, a deity among householders,
or a Brahmā among brahmins.
Even where he enters upon the path of Nirūha, there he becomes either a king of a kingdom, or a deity for householders, or a Brahmā for brahmins.
For indeed, O brahmins and householders, the people of the towns and the countryside, being uplifted, utter this inspired exclamation: "Victory!"
Homage to that noble Mahāgovinda; homage to the noble Saptapurohita.
Thus spoke the Blessed One while staying at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain.

And while this exposition was being delivered, the dust-free, stainless Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena became purified in Pañcaśikha, the son of the Gandharvas. With a joyful heart, Pañcaśikha, the son of the Gandharvas, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.
The Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, monks, it might occur to you that the brahmin named Mahāgovinda at that time was someone else.
But this should not be viewed in such a way. For what reason?"
"Monks, at that time and on that occasion, I was the brahmin named Mahāgovinda.
Even then, when I had gone forth, a great multitude of people followed me in going forth;
and now too, when I have gone forth, a great multitude of people has followed me in going forth."
Thus concludes the Govindīya Sūtra concerning the Blessed One’s former abodes.

The Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One, having accomplished the purpose for which he had come, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery—the teacher of gods and humans, honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated. Having established the detailed introduction, [the text continues] as far as: "Furthermore, Buddhas have attained mastery over their own minds."
The Blessed Ones dwell in whatever dwellings they desire to dwell in— possessing upright minds, gentle minds, pliant and concentrated minds, minds of loving-kindness, tamed minds, peaceful minds,
liberated minds, pure minds, stainless minds, bright minds, radiant minds, and unobstructed minds.

They possess upright minds, stable minds, well-established minds, unattached minds, unclinging minds, non-defiled minds, undeluded minds; minds like the earth, minds like water, minds like fire, minds like wind, minds with a soft touch like *kācilindika* cloth, minds like Indra’s pillar, minds well-liberated, and wisdom well-liberated; they have cast away the moat and dismantled the ramparts.

They are without fetters, the foremost jewels on the tip of the banner of the Noble Dharma, the best of brahmins, the best of kṣatriyas, those who have completed their studies, those who have mastered the Vedas,
speakers of truth, speakers of what is meaningful, speakers of what is right, speakers of the non-perverted, speakers of the non-false, and speakers of the non-otherwise. (Therefore,
the Tathāgata is called "one who speaks non-otherwise.")
Then, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda.

"Ānanda, I shall sit for three months on a single alms-bowl; I will dwell according to the dwellings of the former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones. Let no one else approach me in any way."
"Very well, Blessed One," the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
Then indeed the Blessed One sat for three months, dwelling in the same manner as the former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, subsisting on a single alms-meal.
Then, indeed, at the end of the three months, during the evening time, the Blessed One arose from his seclusion, went out from the monastery, and sat down upon a couch.

The venerable Ānanda indeed saw the Blessed One seated on a couch in the hut for covering; having seen him, he approached the Blessed One, bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet, and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, he said this to the Blessed One:
The Blessed One’s faculties were tranquil and sublime; his complexion was perfectly pure, and the color of his face was radiant.
Indeed, the Blessed One was dwelling in sublime abodes.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Ānanda:
"It is so, Ānanda; if he so desires, Ānanda, the Tathāgata could sit for an eon, or for the remainder of an eon, on a single alms-bowl."
For what reason?

It is thus, Ānanda, with the former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who dwelt dwelling in those abodes, having attained the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom.
Then, Ānanda, in an incalculable eon, in an immeasurable and incalculable eon, there was a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Indradhvaja.
Furthermore, Ānanda, the capital city of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Indradhvaja was named Indratapanā.
It was twelve yojanas in length from east to west and seven yojanas in width; it was surrounded by seven walls made of gold, covered with gold.

Furthermore, Ānanda, the royal capital Indratapanā was surrounded by seven rows of palm trees, variegated and beautiful to behold, consisting of the seven precious substances: gold, silver, pearl, beryl, and crystal.
On the coral *tāla* trunk there were leaves of musāragalva and fruits of ruby; on the golden *tāla* trunk there were leaves of silver and fruits of pearl;
on the silver *tāla* trunk there were leaves of pearl and fruits of crystal; and on the crystal *tāla* trunk there were leaves of beryl.
The leaves and fruits of the palm trunk made of beryl were made of musāragalva;
the leaves and fruits of the palm trunk made of musāragalva were made of ruby; and the leaves and fruits of the palm trunk made of ruby were made of gold.

Furthermore, Ānanda, when those palm trunks are stirred by the wind and struck together by the wind, a sound issues forth that is lovely, charming, delightful, and not unpleasant to hear. Just as, for example, from a five-piece musical ensemble played perfectly by skilled musicians, a sound issues forth that is lovely, charming, delightful, and not unpleasant to hear— exactly so, Ānanda, it is with those palm trunks.
When stirred by the wind and struck together by the wind, a sound issues forth that is lovely, pleasing, enchanting, and not disagreeable to hear.

Furthermore, Ānanda, at that time in the royal capital of Indratapanā, those intoxicated men and women, by means of that sound like the rustling of palm leaves, became endowed with and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure; they played, rejoiced, and amused themselves.
Furthermore, Ānanda, the royal capital Indratapanā was indeed surrounded by seven networks of railings,
variegated and beautiful to behold, made of the seven precious substances: gold, silver, pearl, beryl, crystal, emerald, and ruby.
The gold foot had a silver pin as its support and base;
the silver foot had a pearl pin as its support and base;
and the pearl foot had a lapis lazuli pin as its support and base.
The needle, the support, and the base of the one made of beryl were made of crystal;
the needle, the support, and the base of the one made of crystal were made of emerald; and the needle, the support, and the base of the one made of emerald were made of ruby.
The footstool was made of ruby, while the needle-case, the support, and the base were made of gold.
Furthermore, Ānanda, those railings and lattices were covered with two sets of golden nets each;
the golden net that was made of gold had bells made of silver,
and the silver net that was made of silver had bells made of gold.
Furthermore, Ānanda, the royal capital Indratapanā had three gates all around that were variegated and beautiful, made of seven materials: gold, silver, pearl, beryl, crystal, musāragalva, and ruby.
Furthermore, Ānanda, the bricks of those two gates were of two colors: gold and silver.
Furthermore, Ānanda, those gates had staircases made of two materials: gold and silver.
Furthermore, Ānanda, those gates had two types of railings: of gold and of silver.
Furthermore, Ānanda, those gates were made of two kinds of materials, with an equal proportion of both gold and silver.
For those gates, there were two kinds of railings made of gold and silver.
Those gates were made of two kinds of materials, both of which were unfavorable to gold and silver.
Furthermore, Ānanda, the door-panels of those four gates were made of four kinds of materials: gold, silver, pearl, and beryl.
The panels covering those gates were made of two kinds of precious materials: gold and silver.
Furthermore, Ānanda, those gates had door-panels made of two materials: gold and silver.

In front of those gates, reed-fences were constructed, three men's height in depth, three men's height in elevation, and twelve men's height in thickness; they were variegated and beautiful to behold, made of seven precious substances: gold, silver, pearl, beryl, crystal, white coral, and ruby.
Furthermore, Ānanda, those gates were each covered with two golden nets: one made of gold and one made of silver.
On the golden net there were silver bells, and on the silver net there were golden bells.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when those golden nets are stirred by the wind and struck together by the wind, a sound issues forth that is lovely, charming, delightful, and not unpleasant to hear.

Just as, for example, when a five-piece musical ensemble is played correctly by skilled musicians, a sound issues forth that is beautiful, pleasing, enchanting, and not disagreeable to hear— even so, Ānanda, from those [bells] being struck together, there issues forth a sound that is beautiful, pleasing, enchanting, and not disagreeable to hear.
Furthermore, Ānanda, the royal capital Indratapanā was indeed not empty of such sounds as these:
namely, the sounds of elephants, the sounds of horses, the sounds of chariots, the sounds of infantry, the sounds of kettledrums,

the sounds of small drums, the sounds of conchs, the sounds of flutes, the sounds of lutes, the sounds of singing, the sounds of instrumental music, and the sounds of both singing and instrumental music.
"Eat, chew, drink, give gifts, and practice the Dharma toward śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; may it be well with you!"—with such words [he addressed them].
Furthermore, Ānanda, in the capital city of Indratapanā there was a pillar named Valayā; it was variegated and beautiful to behold,
made of seven precious substances— gold, silver, pearl, beryl, crystal, emerald, and ruby—
twelve yojanas in height and four yojanas in its base.
The Blessed One said this; having said this, the Teacher further spoke as follows:
"There was a teacher named Indradhvaja."
Golden-hued, endowed with the marks of a hundred merits.
The seer of great power, the leader of the community, disciplines seven hundred million [beings];
honored as the leader of the host of ascetics.
He entered the well-constructed Indratapanā cave.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Indradhvaja prophesied the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahādhvaja.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahādhvaja gave a prophecy concerning the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dhvajottama.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dhvajottama prophesied the Tathāgata Dhvajarucira.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Enlightened One Dhvajarucira prophesied the Tathāgata Dhvajaketu.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Dhvajaketu prophesied the Tathāgata Ketudhvaja.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha Ketudhvaja predicted the Tathāgata Dhvajadhvaja.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Dhvajadhvaja prophesied the Tathāgata Dhvajāparājita.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Dhvaja-aparājita prophesied the Tathāgata Aparājita.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Aparājita prophesied the Tathāgata Supratāpa.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Supratāpa gave a prophecy concerning the Tathāgata Pradīpa.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Pradīpa made a prediction concerning the Tathāgata Supratiṣṭhita.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Supratiṣṭhita prophesied the Tathāgata Nāgamuni.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Nāgamuni prophesied the Tathāgata Mahāmuni.
The Great Sage Ānanda, the Tathāgata, made this prediction concerning the Tathāgata Munipravara.
The eminent sage Ānanda, the Tathāgata, prophesied the Tathāgata Saṃvṛtaskandha.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Saṃvṛtaskandha made a prediction concerning the Tathāgata Bandhuma.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Bandhuma made a prediction concerning the Tathāgata Ariṣṭa.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Ariṣṭa likewise made a prediction concerning the Tathāgata Vijitāvin.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Vijitāvin made a prediction concerning the Tathāgata Krakucchanda.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Krakucchanda prophesied the Tathāgata Asamasama.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Asamasama prophesied the Tathāgata Prabhaṃkara.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Prabhaṃkara prophesied the Tathāgata Oghaja.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Oghaja prophesied the Tathāgata Mahābala.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Mahābala prophesied the Tathāgata Sujāta.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Sujāta made a prediction concerning the Tathāgata Pāraṃgata.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Pāraṅgata made a prophecy concerning the Tathāgata Mahāprasāda.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Mahāprasāda prophesied the Tathāgata Sukhendriya.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Sukhendriya prophesied the Tathāgata Nakṣatrarāja.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Nakṣatrarāja prophesied the Tathāgata Śatapuṣpa.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Śatapuṣpa made a prediction concerning the Tathāgata Viraja.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Viraja made a prediction concerning the Tathāgata Brahmasvara.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Brahmasvara prophesied the Tathāgata named Śiras.
Ānanda, when the Tathāgata named Śirasāhvaya appeared, there was a royal capital called Puṣpāvatī. It was twelve yojanas in length from east to west and seven yojanas in width from south to north.
It was surrounded by seven walls made of gold with golden roofs, and it was encircled by seven rows of palm trees.
It was variegated and beautiful with seven colors, as described previously, up to the point that the trunk of the golden palmyra tree had leaves and fruit made of silver.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when those palm trunks are stirred by the wind and struck together by the wind, a beautiful and pleasing sound issues forth.
Furthermore, Ānanda,

those people who were drunkards in that royal capital of Puṣpavatī played and diverted themselves, provided and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure by means of that sound of the palm-leaf fruit.

Furthermore, Ānanda, the royal capital Puṣpāvatī was indeed surrounded by seven networks of railings; it was variegated and beautiful to behold, with its seven colors like the capital city of Indratapanā.

There, in the capital city of Puṣpāvatī, it was not empty of such sounds as these: namely, the sound of elephants, the sound of horses, the sound of chariots, the sound of infantry, the sound of kettledrums, the sound of small drums, the sound of conchs, the sound of flutes, the sound of lutes, the sound of singing, and the sound of instrumental music; as well as the cries, "Eat! Feast! Drink! Give gifts! [Practice] the Dharma!"
"Practice [virtue] among the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; may it be well with you"—thus was the air filled with these words.
In that royal capital, there was a pillar named Valayā, variegated and beautiful to behold, made of seven precious substances: gold, silver, pearl, beryl, crystal, musāragalva, and ruby;
it was twelve yojanas in height and four yojanas in its base.
The Blessed One said this; having said this,
the Teacher then further spoke as follows concerning the succession of these Buddhas:
He who was named Śiras became the western one.
The rishi of great majesty, the leader of the community, disciplines seven hundred million beings;
honored as the leader of the host of ascetics, he guides them.
He entered the well-constructed Puṣpavatī.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Śirasāhvaya prophesied the Tathāgata Nāgakulottama.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Nāgakulottama made a prediction concerning the Tathāgata Kṣamottara.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Kṣamottara prophesied the Tathāgata Nāgottama.
The Tathāgata Nāgottama prophesied the Tathāgata Ānandāṅgottama.
The Tathāgata Aṅgottama gave a prophecy concerning the Tathāgata Vāsava.
The Tathāgata Vāsava gave a prophecy concerning the Tathāgata Candrima.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Candrima prophesied the Tathāgata Hetumān.
The Tathāgata has prophesied the Tathāgata Jina-indra as one who possesses a cause.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Jinendra prophesied the Tathāgata Jāmbūnada.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Jāmbūnada made a prophecy concerning the Tathāgata Tagaraśikhin.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Tagaraśikhin prophesied the Tathāgata Paduma.
The Tathāgata Paduma prophesied the Tathāgata Kauṇḍiṇyagotra.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata of the Kauṇḍinya clan made a prediction concerning a Tathāgata of the very same Kauṇḍinya clan.
The Blessed One said this; having said this,
the Teacher then further spoke as follows concerning the succession of these Buddhas:
The last one was of the Kauṇḍinya clan.
There were three hundred noble Buddhas,
all of whom belonged to the Kauṇḍinya clan.
These leaders of the assembly of sages, possessed of great majesty, were all in a single eon named Upala;
they numbered three hundred times ten million each.
There was a great assembly of disciples.
The lifespan of those disciples was three hundred and three years;
their [lifespan] was twenty-three thousand years.
The true Dharma remained for those who had attained final nirvana.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Paścimaka of the Kauṇḍinya clan made a prediction concerning the Tathāgata Candana.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Candana made a prediction concerning the Tathāgata Viraja.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Viraja predicted the Tathāgata Hiteṣin.
Ānanda, desiring their welfare, the Tathāgata prophesied that Supātra would become a Tathāgata.

Furthermore, Ānanda, during the time of the Tathāgata Supātra, there was a royal capital named Abhayapurā, twelve yojanas in length and seven yojanas in width from south to north; it was surrounded by seven golden walls and seven rows of palm trees, variegated, beautiful to behold, and of seven colors.
It is to be described in every respect as being like the royal capital Puṣpāvatī.
There too, there was a pillar named Valayā, variegated and beautiful to behold, with seven colors.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Supātra, remained for a full hundred kalpas while surveying the guidance of the Dharma.
He gave a prophecy concerning the Tathāgata Varuṇa.
The Blessed One said this; having said this,
the Teacher, the supreme preceptor of the worthy vessel, who is most compassionate for the welfare of others, spoke this further:
Beholding the guidance of the True Dharma,
he remained for no less than one hundred eons,
leading thirty-two *koṭī-nayuta* beings to liberation.
Having established the teaching that brings security and wide-reaching peace in the City of Fearlessness, he made a prophecy concerning Varuṇottama.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Varuṇottama prophesied the Tathāgata Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Dhṛtarāṣṭra prophesied the Tathāgata Śvetarāṣṭra.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Śvetarāṣṭra prophesied the Tathāgata Śikhin.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Śikhin made a prediction concerning the Tathāgata Śikhin himself.
In the succession of these Buddhas,
there were sixty-two Buddhas named Śikhin; all of them appeared in the Paduma eon.
Possessing great majesty and destroying the hosts of enemies, you have led your disciples onto the broad, true path.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Paścimaka made a prediction concerning the Tathāgata Virūḍhaka.
The Tathāgata Virūḍhaka made a prediction concerning the Tathāgata Sunetra.
The Tathāgata Sunetra prophesied the Tathāgata Sujāta.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Sujāta, having disciplined eighty-four thousand nayutas of disciples in a single day, passed into parinirvāṇa on that very same day.
Furthermore, Ānanda, the true Dharma of that Tathāgata remained for thirty thousand years.
The Blessed One said this; having said this, the Teacher further spoke as follows:
"Ānanda, the Tathāgata Sujāta has prophesied the Tathāgata Utpala."
The Tathāgata Utpala prophesied the Tathāgata Brahmottama.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Brahmottama made a prediction concerning the Tathāgata Sudarśana.

Furthermore, Ānanda, when Sudarśana was the Tathāgata, there was a royal capital named Devapurā, twelve yojanas in length and seven yojanas in width. It was surrounded by seven golden walls and seven rows of palm trees; it was variegated and beautiful to behold, and with its seven colors, it was as worthy of description as the City of Fearlessness (Abhayapurā).
In the succession of these Buddhas, Sudarśana was the last;
he was of great majesty, the leader of the multitude of men.
Surrounded by three hundred million followers,
that leader of the assembly of śramaṇas entered the well-fashioned city of the gods.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Sudarśana prophesied the Tathāgata Arthadarśa.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Arthadarśin made a prediction concerning the Tathāgata Mūla.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Mūla predicted the Tathāgata Auṣadhi.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Auṣadha predicted the Tathāgata Hitaiṣin.
Desiring their welfare, Ānanda, the Tathāgata made this prediction concerning the Tathāgata Jāmbūnada.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Jāmbūnada made a prediction concerning the Tathāgata Sāla.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Sāla made a prediction concerning the Tathāgata Abhijit.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Abhijit prophesied the Tathāgata Jinavarottama.
The Tathāgata Ānanda, the most excellent among the best of Jinas, prophesied the Tathāgata Samantabhadra.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Samantabhadra prophesied the Tathāgata Śaśivimala.
The Tathāgata Śaśivimala prophesied the Tathāgata Pauṇḍrīka.
The Tathāgata Pauṇḍarīka thus prophesied the Tathāgata Candrima.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Candrima prophesied the Tathāgata Bhāvitātman.
The Tathāgata Bhāvitātman made a prediction concerning the Tathāgata Oghaja.
The Tathāgata Oghaja made a prophecy concerning the Tathāgata Ānandābhaya.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Abhaya gave a prophecy concerning the Tathāgata Svayaṃprabha.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Svayaṃprabha gave a prophecy concerning the Tathāgata Mahābala.
The Tathāgata Mahābala made a prediction concerning the Tathāgata Āditya.
The Tathāgata Āditya prophesied the Tathāgata Pratāpavat.
The Tathāgata Pratāpavat then prophesied for the Tathāgata Hiteṣin.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Hiteṣī made a prophecy concerning the Tathāgata Dhvajottama.
The Tathāgata Dhvajottama prophesied the Tathāgata Dhvajadhvaja.
The Tathāgata Dhvajadhvaja made a prediction concerning the Tathāgata Ketu.
The Tathāgata Ketu prophesied the Tathāgata Ketūttama.
The Tathāgata Ketūttama gave a prophecy concerning the Tathāgata Asahya.
Asahya the Tathāgata made a prediction concerning Jāmbūnada the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata Jāmbūnada made a prediction concerning the Tathāgata Sālarāja.
The Tathāgata Sālarāja made a prophecy concerning the Tathāgata Akutobhaya, Ānanda.
The Tathāgata Akutobhaya prophesied a manifested Tathāgata.
The emanated Tathāgata made a prediction concerning the tranquil Tathāgata.
Upaśānta prophesied the Tathāgata Jinendra as a Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata Jinendra-ānanda prophesied the Tathāgata Jinendra himself.
In the succession of these Buddhas,
the last was named Jinendra; these three hundred noble Buddhas were [thus].
They were all named Jinendra.
These leaders of the assembly of sages, possessed of great majesty,
were three hundred times three crores in number during that single eon of great renown.
There was a great assembly of leaders.
The lifespan of those leaders was three thousand years;
their [lifespan] was thirty-three thousand years.
The true Dharma remained for those who had entered final nirvana.
The Tathāgata Paścimaka, the Lord of Jinas, prophesied the Tathāgata Sarvārthadarśin.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Sarvārthadarśin, surveying the guidance of the Dharma, remained in the world for a thousand eons and prophesied that Aśoka would become a Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata Aśoka prophesied the Tathāgata Dhvajottama.
The Tathāgata Dhvajottama prophesied the Tathāgata Nyagrodharāja.
The Tathāgata Nyagrodharāja made a prediction concerning the Tathāgata Vipulayaśas.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Vipulayaśas prophesied the Tathāgata Jayanta.
The Tathāgata Jayanta predicted the Tathāgata Śākyamuni.
Furthermore, Ānanda, during the time of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Perfectly Enlightened One, there was a royal capital named Siṃhapurī,
twelve yojanas in length and seven yojanas in width. It was surrounded by seven golden walls and seven rows of palm trees, variegated, beautiful to behold, and of seven colors.
As before, it is to be described as being like Indratapanā.
There, in Siṃhapurī, there was a sacrificial post named Valayā;
it is to be described as before.
In the succession of these Buddhas, Śākyamuni was the last;
he was of great majesty and the leader of the host of sages.
Preceded by three hundred million followers,
that leader of the assembly of śramaṇas entered the well-constructed city of Siṃhapurī.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni predicted the Tathāgata Sarvada.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Sarvadaya prophesied the Tathāgata Atyuttama.
The Tathāgata Atyuttama prophesied the Tathāgata Uttara.
The Tathāgata Uttara gave this prophecy concerning the Tathāgata Samitāvin.
The Tathāgata Samitāvin, surveying the guidance of the Dharma, remained in the world for a full thousand kalpas and then prophesied the Tathāgata Baladatta.
The Tathāgata Baladatta made a prophecy concerning the Tathāgata Bhāgīratha.
The Tathāgata Bhāgīratha thus prophesied the Tathāgata Aṅgīrasa.
The Tathāgata Aṅgīrasa prophesied the Tathāgata Nāgottama.
The Tathāgata Nāgottama prophesied the Tathāgata Nāgabala.
The Tathāgata Nāgabala made a prediction concerning the Tathāgata Puṣpa.
The Tathāgata Puṣpa made a prediction concerning the Tathāgata Puṣputtara.
The Tathāgata Puṣpottara made a prediction concerning the Tathāgata Meru.
The Tathāgata Meru prophesied the Tathāgata Ratnāgni.
The Tathāgata Ratanāgni made a prophecy concerning the Tathāgata Puṣpakṛta.
The Tathāgata Puṣpakṛta gave a prophecy concerning the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara.

Ānanda, when Dīpaṃkara was the Tathāgata, there was a royal capital named Dīpavatī; it was twelve yojanas in length and seven yojanas in width, surrounded by seven golden walls and seven rows of palm trees, variegated, beautiful to behold, and encircled by the seven precious colors.
Everything is to be described as before.
In the succession of these Buddhas,
Dīpaṃkara was the last;
he was of great majesty, the leader of the host of seers.
Accompanied by eighty thousand disciples and honored as the leader of the assembly of ascetics,
he entered the well-constructed city of Dīpavatī.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara prophesied the Tathāgata Sarvābhibhū.
The Tathāgata Sarvābhibhū made a prediction concerning the Tathāgata Padumuttara.
The Tathāgata Padumuttara made a prediction concerning the Tathāgata Atyuccagāmin.
The Tathāgata Atyuccagāmin gave a prophecy concerning the Tathāgata Yaśottara.
The Tathāgata Yaśottara prophesied the Tathāgata Śākyamuni.
The Tathāgata Śākyamuni prophesied for the Tathāgata Arthadarśin.
The Tathāgata Arthadarśin gave a prophecy concerning the Tathāgata Tiṣya.
The Tathāgata Tiṣya made a prediction concerning the Tathāgata Puṣya.
The Tathāgata Puṣya prophesied the Tathāgata Vipaśyin.
The Tathāgata Vipaśyin made a prophecy concerning the Tathāgata Śikhin.
The Tathāgata Śikhī made a prophecy concerning the Tathāgata Viśvabhū.
The Tathāgata Viśvabhū made a prediction concerning the Tathāgata Krakucchanda.
The Tathāgata Krakucchanda prophesied the Tathāgata Konākamuni.
The Tathāgata Konākamuni made a prophecy concerning the Tathāgata Kāśyapa.
The Tathāgata Kāśyapa prophesied the Tathāgata Śākyamuni.
I, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, have prophesied the Tathāgata Maitreya.

Furthermore, Ānanda, when Maitreya was the Tathāgata, there was a royal capital named Ketumatī, twelve yojanas in length and seven yojanas in width, surrounded by seven golden walls and seven rows of palm trees— variegated, beautiful to behold,
and encircled by the seven precious colors.
Everything is to be described as before.
In the succession of these Buddhas, Maitreya will be the last;
he will be of great majesty and the leader of the assembly of sages.
Honored as the leader of a host of ascetics, he will discipline seventy billion beings and enter the well-fashioned city of Ketumatī.
The Buddhas who are to be saluted have been proclaimed by the Charioteer of those to be tamed,
from Indradhvaja down to Maitreya who has not yet arrived.
The Teacher, like the sun, blazes with splendor; Ānanda questions the Conqueror, that lion among men who has conquered all afflictions, in the Aśoka Grove.

The fame of the Blessed One is wondrous, and his glory is marvelous throughout the ten directions. What deed has the Blessed One performed by which he shines with such austerity in the world, including the realm of the gods?
And having heard this, that great seer, the essence of beings who destroys the endless thorns of doubt, replied to Ānanda with unimpeded speech:
Ānanda, listen to me as to what kind of roots of merit were planted by me while wandering here and there among the Buddhas and their disciples.
By one who aspires to awakening, desiring the imperishable state.
With a joyful mind, I have performed very great services.
And under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, under the Buddha Sarvābhibhū, Ānanda,
and under the Buddha Padumottara and the one named Atyucca...
And in the time of Yaśottara, Śākyasiṃha, Arthadarśin, Tiṣya, Puṣya— the supreme among men— and also in the time of the perfectly awakened Vipaśyin.
Under Śikhin, Krakucchanda, Mahāprajña, Konākamuni, and Kāśyapa,
I performed very great services with a joyful heart.
"These beings of great power, infinite... renowned throughout the world, noble and honored by me—because of that, Ānanda, I am able [to do so]."
By that [merit], incomparable glory and renown have arisen throughout the ten directions;
by that, I shine resplendent in the world including its gods and its Brahmās.
And having heard the words of the Lord of the World, whose speech is never false, Ānanda, joyful and with a thrilled heart, asked further:
How long ago did those Perfectly Awakened Ones appear in the world? Let it be told;
how long did they remain for the benefit of the entire world?
Thus the Sambuddha, radiant as gold, joyful and with a gladdened mind,
proclaimed the Great Seers, the Buddhas, who had passed away long ago.
This seer of ultimate reality is equal and identical to the Buddhas;
he displays miracles in the same manner as all the Buddhas.
This domain of the Buddhas is inconceivable, incomparable, and incalculable;
O Blessed One, I am thrilled having heard these words which are like nectar.
The infinite goal has been realized for the world including its devas and Brahmās;
this is the domain of the Buddhas, inconceivable by others.
A single Śākya prince, son of the Śākyas, born of the most excellent Śākya lineage,
the bringer of joy to the Śākya clan— the Buddha— likewise awakens the world.
After the passing of Dīpaṃkara, Ānanda, when ten million eons had been fully completed,
Sarvābhibhū, the One Possessed of Ten Powers, appeared in the light of the island.
And when that leader, Sarvābhibhū, had passed away,
Padumottara, the Daśabala, appeared after a hundred thousand kalpas.
After that Sugata Padumuttara had attained final nirvāṇa,
the Blessed One Atyuccagāmin appeared after a hundred thousand eons.
Long ago, when the Lord Atyuccagāmin, renowned throughout the world, had entered final nirvana,
five hundred kalpas later, the Buddha Yaśottara appeared.
When Yaśottara had passed into nirvāṇa and the world was lost in blinding darkness,
the heroic Buddha Śākyamuni arose after a hundred eons.
When the perfectly awakened Śākyamuni had entered parinirvāṇa, Ānanda, I was reborn as Arthadarśin in this very ninety-ninth eon.
In the ninety-fifth eon, Tiṣya appeared as the illuminator of the world;
and in the ninety-second [eon], Puṣya, the bull among men, arose in the world.
In the eighty-ninth aeon, Vipaśyin appeared in the world;
and in the thirtieth aeon, Śikhin and Viśvabhū likewise appeared.
Krakucchanda, Mahāloka, Konākamuni, and the illustrious Kāśyapa— I myself, Ānanda, have arisen as these [Buddhas] in this Fortunate Aeon.
"I have prophesied that this great-souled one will become a Buddha in a future time;
Maitreya of great majesty, Ānanda, in this very eon."
The Blessed One, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, remained in the world for an entire eon;
and Sarvābhibhū also remained for an eon for the welfare of the world.
Padumottara also remained in the world for a full ten million years;
the Exalted One, traveling very high, remained for a hundred thousand years.
Yaśottara remained for ninety thousand years; Arthadarśin remained for ninety-five thousand; Tiṣya for ninety-two thousand; and Puṣya remained for ninety-two thousand.
In former times, the lifespan of the Buddha Vipaśyin was eighty thousand years;
at that time, the lifespan of Śikhin was seventy thousand years.
The former lifespan of Viśvabhū was sixty years, that of Krakucchanda fifty;
that of Konākamuni was thirty, and that of the illustrious Kāśyapa twenty.
For us too, Ānanda, at this time, in this world, the lifespan of the Śākya sovereign is merely a hundred years.
Some stood firm in supernatural power, some stood firm in their karma; having established themselves in both power and karma, they attained final nirvana in the interval.
Like the sun shining as it has risen into the sky in autumn.
Dīpaṃkara remained there, having pervaded a hundred yojanas with his radiance.
Illuminating the ten directions and teaching the Dharma, which is difficult to encounter, he lights up the worlds; therefore, his name is Dīpaṃkara.
The All-Conqueror, endowed with the ten powers, having overcome thousands of millions of living beings, leads them to the state of the Deathless; therefore, his designation is "Unconquered."
Padumottara, having gone to a park outside the excellent city,
was enjoying himself by the lake when he saw a lotus, as large as a chariot wheel, rising up from within the water.
Having ascended there, he sat down, having assumed the cross-legged posture;
while the great lotus was fading, he attained the five supernormal powers.
Having become possessed of the five superknowledges, he rose into the air by means of supernatural power;
having approached the foot of the Bodhi tree, the One Endowed with Ten Powers attained omniscience.
Having risen to the height of a palm tree, the Blessed One stood there, moving exceedingly high;
because of that, he was known by the name Atyuccasāhvaya (He of the Exceedingly High Name).
The teaching of the Blessed One, the tamer of the untamed, became widespread; because of his immeasurable fame, he was known by the name Yaśottara.
Having departed from a preeminent city that was wealthy and flourishing, the Śākyan of the Gautama clan abandoned the seven treasures; he became known as Śākyamuni.
Seeing the goal within the goal, you trained hundreds of disciples in Arhatship;
therefore, the world came to know you as the Jina Arthadarśin.
They were living during the time of Tiṣya; Tiṣya arose as the Light of the World.
Therefore, he was known in the world by the name Tiṣya, the Dispeller of Darkness.
They were abiding in the month of Puṣya, and the Light of the World was born under Puṣya;
therefore, he became known in the world by the name corresponding to that constellation as "Puṣya."
With unblinking, all-encompassing vision, Vipaśyin beheld forms without effort; because his eyes were pure, he became known by the name Vipaśyin.
The protector of the earth instructed him in matters of wealth and the methods for achieving them;
because of that, he became known as Vipaśyin, the Blessed One.
Having attained full awakening, the Victor Vipaśyin surveyed the world;
seeing the dharma of the one with a mane (the lion), he received the name Vipaśyin.
Because upon his birth the fire blazed up in the world like a flame fanned by the wind, and the cresting fire burned with exceeding brilliance, he was therefore given the name Śikhin.
And when the Lord of Jinas had arisen, the god then rained down an unceasing stream;
from that [rain] there arose a sound, and it was known as Viśvabhū.
The names of the mothers and fathers, beginning with their noble lineages, of the Blessed One Krakucchanda, of Konākamuni, and of Kāśyapaśiri.
Of the solar lineage, radiant, born of the Ikṣvāku clan,
a Kṣatriya by birth, foremost, the Blessed One, the supreme person.
In an unconquered brahmin family, a storehouse of many jewels,
this brahmin will renounce vast sensual pleasures and go forth into homelessness.
In the future, on this circle of the earth, Maitreya will appear in a family that is prosperous with miraculous powers and adorned with excellent wisdom.
In the first assembly, there will be ninety-six koṭis, all of them arhats who have attained mastery and shaken off the dust of passion.
In the second assembly as well, there will be ninety-four koṭis,
all of them arhats who have attained mastery and shaken off the dust of passion.
In the third assembly, there will be ninety-two koṭis of all those who are arhats, masters of themselves, and cleansed of passion.
Dīpaṃkara, possessed of great wisdom, was a kṣatriya by birth;
Sarvābhibhū, the possessor of the ten powers, was a brāhmaṇa by birth.
The Blessed One Padumuttara, the possessor of the ten powers, was by birth a kṣatriya;
the Blessed One Atyuccagāmin was by birth a brāhmaṇa.
Yaśottara, Śākyamuni, Arthadarśin, Tiṣya, and Puṣya were all of kṣatriya birth; these supreme among men were great seers who had cultivated their selves and were of brahmin birth.
Vipaśyin, Śikhin, and Viśvabhū were kṣatriyas;
Krakucchanda, Konākamuni, and Kāśyapa were also brāhmaṇas.
The son of King Śuddhodana of the Ikṣvāku lineage, born of Māyā,
was a Śākya youth who brought joy to the Śākya clan.
Surrounded by a retinue of a hundred million, having pervaded the world of the Lord of the Asuras, he will be stainless, liberated, with a liberated mind— the one known as Maitreya.
These supreme among men are born only from two types of families:
first, in a kṣatriya family, or else in a brāhmaṇa family.
For when the kṣatriyas become the foremost in the world,
then the Buddhas, the supreme among men, arise in a kṣatriya family.
But when those reckoned for their virtues become brahmins in the world,
then the Buddhas, the great seers, arise in a brahmin family.
Having seen Dīpaṃkara, the eldest in the world, at the crossroads of the four great paths,
he was filled with joy as he praised the matted-hair ascetic while aspiring for unsurpassed awakening.
Having taken golden flowers with palms joined in reverence,
he scattered them over Sarvābhibhū while aspiring for unsurpassed enlightenment.
Taking handfuls of flowers resembling masses of gold,
I scattered them over Padumuttara while praying for unsurpassed enlightenment.
The Blessed One, who goes exceedingly high and is compassionate toward the world,
I showered with gold while praying for unsurpassed enlightenment.
He honored the illustrious Yaśottara, who was preceded by the community of monks,
while aspiring for unsurpassed enlightenment through his service.
Taking fragrances— exquisite and most precious scents—
I scattered them over Śākyamuni, aspiring for unsurpassed enlightenment.
Taking gold, silver, and beryl, I joined my palms in reverence and scattered them over Arthadarśin, praying for unsurpassed enlightenment.
And I praised Tiṣya, the Lord of the World, face-to-face,
while seeking unsurpassed awakening through present application.
Having entered upon the Puṣya constellation, joyful and with palms joined,
I stood paying homage, aspiring for unsurpassed enlightenment.
Seeing Vipaśyin approaching like the full moon on the fifteenth day,
he spread out his deerskin on the path, seeking unsurpassed enlightenment.
Seeking supreme enlightenment, he gratified Śikhin— who was wandering for the sake of the world and was preceded by the community of monks— with various kinds of solid and soft food.
And with great joy, seeking unsurpassed enlightenment, he clothed Viśvabhū and his disciples in most precious robes.
And in the presence of the three Lords of the World, I practiced the holy life;
Kāśyapa prophesied of me: "You shall attain unsurpassed awakening."
Having performed the five deeds, I pray for nirvāṇa with three;
and by three I am perfumed in the world, and the group of thirty has been turned back.
When the world was being formed during the ninety-first aeon,
another bodhisattva then wandered through saṃsāra for nine aeons.
Endowed with a body of vigor, possessed of vast wisdom and meditative concentration,
that Supreme among Men shall remain for nine eons through his vigor.
Vigor is the chariot for awakening; it is the power spoken of by none other.
Yet vigor is not unpraised as a factor of awakening, a power, a faculty, and a limb of enlightenment.
Through renunciation, giving, self-control, and restraint, the supreme among men attain [their state];
when the world is turning back, they become once more the preeminent leaders.
Those supreme among men attain enlightenment after a hundred eons;
then, in the ninety-first eon, the Bull of the Śākyas became a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Having embraced the virtue of generosity, the highly renowned Bodhisattvas praise generosity, ethical conduct, and wisdom to the great seers.
The gift of the Buddhas was taught by the Sugata, who possesses peerless conduct and peerless wisdom; recollecting the Sugata in such a manner, [one should practice].
Who would not obtain spiritual joy that is free from worldly desire?
Thus spoke the Blessed One; the world with its gods, humans, and asuras rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
_____The Bahubuddhasūtra is completed.

Indeed, for the benefit of all sentient beings, the Venerable Sugata, the Perfectly Awakened One, has revealed this great accumulation of Dharma, which brings welfare to the great multitude, this Great Narrative, and this Great Wisdom.
Those who teach the true Dharma and those who hear it taught—
all of them attain the state of Nirvana, which is immutable.
In former times, there was a perfected birth of Sarvadada,
who, seeking the welfare of the world, practiced right conduct, generosity, and self-restraint;
Śakra then acted as an obstacle-maker to test him.
He will not cause me to fall from this position.
Having thus created that hell for every single one of them—
those who possess the virtues of heroes of generosity who fall into it—
he then withdrew that kind of suffering, O Hero.
Generosity is the foundation; may all sentient beings be happy.
Śakra said, "O Hero, through tranquility, generosity, and self-restraint, what would you pray for? [The attainment of] the bliss of the Blessed Lady in the next world.
He replied, "In the city of the Blessed Lady, there is no body."
How much more so, then, toward those who seek the city of the Blessed Lady!
Where one knows neither old age nor death, nor sickness,
nor separation from beloved ones;
[there is] peace, free from attachment, and liberation from incessant suffering.
I pray for the state of the Unfallen One and for final liberation.
For he indeed said: "This state, which awakens one to enlightenment, is extremely difficult to perform; it involves the abandonment of delight in sensual pleasures.
Turn back from your own intention and generate a desire [for worldly life]."
In sensual pleasure and in the delightful pleasure of enjoying sense objects, which are like poison.
Even if the throne of Śakra were mine forever, and I were never separated from all the delights of sensual pleasure,
my mind would never be bound by the happiness of the qualities of desire.
May I never turn back from my aspiration for omniscience.

May I be happy for hundreds of billions of trillions of eons with whatever divine and human pleasures exist in the world, and whatever happiness there is here in this birth, as well as that which lies beyond.
May I never turn back from my vow for omniscience.
Whatever sufferings exist here and whatever are heard of throughout many millions of billions of eons in their various forms—
may I experience all those millions of eons of suffering as my own suffering.
May I never turn back from my vow for omniscience.
If I must dwell in the Avīci hell for as long as it takes for me to become a knower of the ultimate truth,
my vigor shall not be possible to withdraw.
I shall not turn back from my vow for omniscience. ... Even if, O fool, one were to eat iron balls or drink molten metal...
May I never turn back from my vow for omniscience.
I would dwell in the midst of the netherworld together with executioners; even if my body were devoured again and again,
I would be capable of enduring such suffering.
May I never turn back from my vow for omniscience.
Even if one were to rain down a shower of sharp-edged arrows and spears,
and if that entire body were to be cut into pieces without exception,
one would be capable of enduring such suffering as that.
May I never turn back from my vow for omniscience.
If, having performed worship toward Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I were to obtain this supreme enlightenment only after five eons,
I would still be capable of wandering through that long cycle of existence.
May I never turn back from my vow for omniscience.
Even if I were to remain in the womb for many millions of great eons, and even if I were born a hundred times and my body were to become exhausted,
I would endure such suffering as that residing within my body.
May I never turn back from my vow for omniscience.
And whatever sufferings there are in hell, as well as those of many kinds in the animal realm and in the states of hungry ghosts and humans—
if all that suffering were to descend upon my body.
May I never turn back from my vow for omniscience.
For as many millions of living beings as I might discipline in this world, for that many millions of eons may I dwell in hell;
I am capable of enduring such suffering for that long.
May I never turn back from my vow for omniscience.
I am no longer able to turn back from this;
this resolve has been made for the sake of the welfare of the world,
until the full moon of the deathless has been attained.
May I never turn back from my aspiration for omniscience.
This armor of mine is firm and made of diamond;
I am girt for generosity, self-control, vows, and austerity, and I feel no weariness in liberating sentient beings from further becoming.
May I never turn back from my vow for omniscience.
Thus, with minds resolved and the meaning well-determined, they wander through the world with their hearts fixed on awakening,
like those who have crossed the ocean after many have failed.
They shall attain enlightenment after having defeated Namuci together with his army.
Then, when King Śuddhodana saw the Blessed One performing various and manifold twin miracles in the sky at a height of a man's stature in the Nyagrodha Grove, and when Rāhu the lord of the asuras,
Vemacitrin the lord of the asuras, Mucilinda the lord of the asuras, and sixty other millions of asuras had been prophesied for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
Having established many thousands of millions of living beings in the noble Dharma, and having himself realized the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala),

he— having seen the Truth and possessing an unerring perspective within the Teacher’s dispensation— rose from his seat, extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, and uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) in the presence of the Blessed One:
"O son, I have gained a great gain; I have truly gained a great gain, for I have such a son as you, the best among bipeds, endowed with all virtues.
It was not in vain, my son, that you renounced the fruitful sovereignty of a universal monarch and abandoned your vast circle of kinsmen to go forth into the homeless life.
It was not in vain that you practiced austerities for six years; oh, it was not in vain that through your fruitful deeds, awakening (bodhi) has been attained!"

"My life has become undeluded and fruitful, for whom such a Dharma has been revealed. There is no one equal to you in the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its recluses, brahmins, and mendicants, including gods, humans, and asuras.
For me too, my son, life is undeluded and fruitful, since in my realm such a son has arisen—one who is peerless in all the world and the foremost among gods and humans."

"Excellent, my son! You who seek the welfare and benefit of the whole world, being compassionate, out of compassion for me as well, my son, and out of compassion for [the people], you should eat daily at the royal palace for as long as you wish to dwell in Kapilavastu."
The Blessed One indeed consented by remaining silent.
Then King Śuddhodana, perceiving through the Blessed One’s silence that his request had been granted, became thrilled, joyful, and filled with gladness.
He bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated him three times,
extended his joined palms toward the community of monks, and departed.
Then, at the end of that very night, King Śuddhodana prepared an abundance of solid and soft foods; he had the city of Kapilavastu sprinkled and swept, cleared of dust, stones, pebbles, and gravel,
strewn with loose flowers, perfumed with incense burners, draped with variegated cloths, covered with canopies, and hung with bundles of silk ribbons and streamers.
From Kapilavastu as far as the Nyagrodha Monastery, along the way, actors, dancers, athletes, wrestlers, hand-clappers, drummers, lute players,

flute players, reed players, double-reed players, *śobhika* performers, ball players, storytellers, singers, and groups of five musicians were stationed at various places so that the Blessed One’s entry into the city might take place with great royal majesty and great royal splendor.
