Then, on the following day, the Blessed One— neither too early nor too late, having finished his Magadhan morning meal and having put on his robes, preceded by the community of monks and surrounded by the community of monks— with Śāriputra at his right, Maudgalyāyana at his left, and the monk Ānanda behind him— [proceeded].
They go with the gait of a king among two [ranks];
the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, go with the soaring flight of a swan.

Furthermore, it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) regarding the entry of the Blessed Buddhas into a city that when the Blessed One enters a city, horses neigh, elephants let out cries like those of cranes, peacocks dance, cuckoos warble "tuṇa-tuṇa," and musical instruments play even though they have not been struck, including those contained within their cases.
The ornaments resound;
the blind regain their sight for that moment,
and the deaf regain their hearing for that moment.
Those who were insane regain their mindfulness for that moment;
those who have drunk poison become free from poison;
and those people who were faithless and of weak devotion now become fully restored.
Then the Blessed One entered the city.

Immediately after the Blessed One placed the soles of his feet upon the gate of the city of Kapilavastu, this great earth shook, trembled, quaked, and convulsed in six ways: the east rose and the west sank;
the west rose and the east sank; the south rose and the north sank; the north rose and the south sank.
The south rises and the north sinks.
The Blessed One, having now entered the city of Kapilavastu, arrived in due course at his father’s residence.
Then those Śākyans of Kapilavastu, having assembled the Śākyans, caused a proclamation to be made: "Sirs, no one must inform Rāhula that 'You are the son of the Blessed One.
Whoever shall inform him, his punishment shall be death."
Now the Blessed One was eating regularly at the royal palace.
Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī made this request to King Śuddhodana.
"Great King, if it should be so agreeable, then may the Blessed One eat in my family."
The king said:
Gautamī, do so.
Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī approached the Blessed One, bowed her head at the Blessed One’s feet, and extending her joined palms toward the Blessed One, addressed him as follows:
May the Blessed One consent to take his meal tomorrow at his own residence.
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.

Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, understanding the Blessed One’s acceptance through his silence, prepared an abundance of hard and soft food. At the end of that very night, she had her own residence swept clean,
adorned with bundles of hanging silk ribbons and cords, strewn with loose flowers, and perfumed with incense.
A highly precious seat was prepared for the Blessed One, and likewise for the community of monks according to their rank.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One, having dressed early in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, entered the residence of Prajāpatī Gautamī, preceded by the community of monks.
The Blessed One sat down on the seat that had been prepared, and the community of monks sat according to their respective seats.
Then indeed, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, with her own hands, satisfied and served the community of monks headed by the Buddha with abundant solid and soft food.

Now, when the Blessed One had finished his meal, washed his hands, and set aside his bowl, as did the community of monks, the Blessed One offered a gradual teaching of the Dharma to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and the women of the inner court— namely,
that gradual teaching of the Dharma which is characteristic of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
Namely: a discourse on generosity, a discourse on ethical discipline, a discourse on heaven, a discourse on merit, and a discourse on the ripening of merit.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī was pleased; and to her, whose mind was thus serene, the Blessed One further revealed the Four Noble Truths:
suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path.
Then, as Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī sat upon that seat, the dustless, stainless eye of Dharma regarding all phenomena was purified.
Then Rāhula was touched by the Blessed One’s shadow;
at that moment, all his hairs stood on end, all his limbs were moistened with joy,
and his entire body was filled with bliss as he sat within the shadow of the Blessed One.
He gazed at the Blessed One with unblinking eyes.
Then Rāhula asked his mother.
"Mother, where has father gone?"
Yaśodharā said:
Son, he has gone to the southern region.
Rāhula said:
"Mother, for what purpose have you gone to the Southern Road?"
Yaśodharā said:
He went away on a trading expedition.
Rāhula said:
"Why then does my father not send me anything at all that is beautiful?"
Yaśodharā said:
My son, this path is contrary to that of the kṣatriyas.
Therefore, if he comes, then he will come in person.
Rāhula said:
"Mother, is this śramaṇaka a relative of mine?
Never before has my mind been so captivated as it is by this śramaṇa;
I think that now he steals away my entire heart."
"It cannot be without cause that, upon merely seeing this ascetic, such intense love has been produced in me as has never arisen for any other Śākyas;
therefore, I think he must be my father."
Then Yaśodharā said:
"Son, this is not your father."
Now Rāhula requested [it] with a throat choked by compassion for his mother.
"Mother, you must certainly tell me: who is this ascetic of mine?"
Yaśodharā’s heart was tormented by love and affection for him;
she thought, "What shall I do?
If I tell him now, it will result in the punishment of death."
"Now, if I do not tell him, my own son will be deceived;
I know what must happen—I shall tell him."
Granted, the Śākyas might indeed cut my limbs one by one with a sharp weapon and tear them apart, yet I would never have failed to look upon my own son, Rāhulaśiri.
"Granted, the Śākyans might indeed have torn my body with a sharp blade while it was bound with a cloth bandage; yet I would never have failed to speak to my own son, Rāhulaśiri."
"Granted, the Śākyans might indeed cut my body with a sharp weapon, selling it by the piece for copper coins; yet I would never have failed to announce the glory of Rāhula, my own son."
"Granted, the Śākyas might indeed tear hundreds of holes even in my body, but I would never fail to instruct my own son, Rāhulaśirika."
Then, seeing that lion among men approaching, surrounded by his excellent retinue, Rāhula, his pride vanished and his eyes closed in devotion, gazed intently upon the Sugata.
With eyes like those of a peacock or a cakora bird, and with joyful eyes filled with collyrium,
Rāhula gazes intently at the Sugata while looking toward his mother.
Seeing that lion among men seated there, surrounded by his excellent retinue, Vatsa,
like a calf still nursing, approached the Perfectly Awakened One.
And that supreme man, joyful and seated in the shadow of the Sugata, addressed his mother: "This shadow of the ascetic is pleasant."
I have seen many Śākya youths who have gone to the ten directions, burdened with the weight of their ornaments; my mind finds no peace.
Just as my body is quickly gladdened upon seeing this one wearing the saffron robe,
my body is gladdened upon hearing him speak sweet words.
With hands and feet as delicate as a web, he is serene in every way and beautiful to behold;
even in looking at him, I rejoice, for he is truly one whose sight is never satiated.
I am joyful upon seeing you approaching from afar with a golden complexion;
but when you depart, I become sorrowful due to your absence.
Seeing my golden-colored form, which is not without cause for this praise by Yama,
my mind becomes exceedingly serene at the very sight of it.
"I think that in various births here and there, this ascetic was my father and my brother; for thus does he gladden my body."
"O Mother, tell me if you have previously seen or even heard of anyone whose purpose makes my mind so exceedingly serene."
Having heard those words spoken by her own son, Rāhula’s mother, feeling as if she were fainting, then spoke thus:
My heart is burning as he asks with such sweet words;
it is not possible for me not to tell my own son, Rāhulaśiri.
"Granted, they might even cut my body with a well-sharpened weapon;
yet it is not possible for me not to tell my own son, Rāhulaśiri."
Granted, the Śākyas might have torn my body with a sharp blade;
yet it was not possible for them not to tell their own son, Rāhulaśiri.
"Even if they were to cut my body into pieces the size of a kahāpaṇa coin,
it would not be possible for me not to tell my own son, Rāhulaśiri."
Granted, the Śākyas might even tear hundreds of holes in my body;
yet it is not possible that I should not tell my own son, Rāhulaśiri.
This, my son, is your father whom you see from afar, golden-hued like a blossoming *karṇikāra* tree, possessing a beautiful golden color that inspires serene confidence.
"O son, he whose hair-tuft between the eyebrows is as white as a conch shell and curls to the right,
and from whom this radiance issues forth— he is your father."
"O son, this is your father whom you see from afar, golden-hued,
like a kālānusāri flower, wafting the fragrance of his virtue."
"O son, this is your father whom you see from afar, golden-hued,
established in the four meditations like Himavat, the king of mountains."
This, my son, is your father whom you see from afar, golden-hued like a golden mountain,
risen up before the noble Saṅgha like a Nāga.
This, my son, is your father whom you see from afar, golden-hued like a lion, powerful and fanged, surveying the ten directions.
"O son, this is your father whom you see from afar, golden-hued like a bull surrounded by a herd of cows, encircled by the noble Saṅgha."
This, my son, is your father whom you see from afar, golden-hued,
illuminating the world with his radiance like the full moon on the night of the fifteenth day.
"This is your father, my son, whom you see from afar with a golden complexion;
like the rising sun, he brings light to the blind."
"O son, this is your father whom you see from afar, golden-hued like Śakra, the king of the gods, surrounded by hosts of deities."
"O son, this is your father whom you see from afar, golden-hued;
like Brahmā in the Brahma-world, he utters a wondrous voice."
"Son, this is your father whom you see from afar, golden-hued,
with limbs beautiful with the thirty-two marks, like a *sāla* grove in full bloom."
This, my son, is your father, who departed from this excellent city, leaving behind both you and me, without regard for his circle of kinsmen.
"This, my son, is your father whom you see from afar, golden-hued;
having mounted Kaṇṭhaka, he departed while you were sleeping soundly on your bed."
For the deities of this world-leader opened the door,
and having made the sound vanish, no person heard the sound.
While seated there in the realm of the Mallas, he addressed Chandaka:
"This top-knot has been taken up; bring it to Śuddhodana."
"O Protector of the Earth, present these ornaments and Kaṇṭhaka;
and offer my salutations to my mother and to the king."

I shall go without turning back, and having accomplished my own purpose, I shall return; with the burden laid down and free from the arrow of defilement, I shall become a field of merit for the world.

Having laid down the burden, become free from the arrow, accomplished his own goal, and conquered the afflictions, the Kinsman has come here to Kapilavastu out of compassion for the community of his relatives.
Then Rāhula, having heard from his mother that "this is my father," clung to the corner of the Blessed One's robe and said: [“This is my father.”]
"Mother, if he is indeed my father, I shall go forth from the home into homelessness, seeking the path of my forefathers."
Immediately thereafter, Rāhula clung to the corner of the Blessed One’s robe;
then those women of the inner apartments raised a cry.
Then King Śuddhodana,
hearing that sound, became afraid and asked:
Whose is this evil sound, this roar of the great multitude, such as it was when Sarvārthasiddha went forth?
Then, others reported [this].
"Your Majesty, Prince Rāhula has clung to the corner of the Blessed One's robe, saying, 'I too shall go forth.'"
Now King Śuddhodana, being filled with longing, cast off that longing within the royal lineage.
Then King Śuddhodana wept; when the king wept, the entire circle of Śākyas wept.
Thus, both within and without, there was a single sound of lamentation.

King Śuddhodana, having wept and wiped away his tears, approached the Blessed One; he bowed at the Blessed One’s feet, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, addressed him thus:
"It is sufficient that the Blessed One, having renounced the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch and his great [retinue], has gone forth alone;
therefore, it would be well, Blessed One, if you would permit Prince Rāhula so that he does not go forth, lest this royal lineage be uprooted."
The Blessed One said:

"O Great King, this being is in his final existence; he has performed his duties and has been perfumed by the impressions of other Buddhas. He is incapable of dwelling amidst wife and children; he must attain parinirvāṇa with these very aggregates."
King Śuddhodana, too, being faithful and full of serene confidence, placed his trust in the Blessed One and said:
"Since the Blessed One has gone forth, we have not been able to perform any rite for Rāhula—not the birth-rite, nor the tonsure-rite, nor the ear-boring ceremony.
Since the Blessed One must certainly go forth with Rāhula, it would be well if the Blessed One were to wait for seven days;
on the seventh day he will perform his renunciation, and that itself shall be his birth-rite."
That very tonsure ceremony, that very growth of the earrings, and that very renunciation.
Then the Blessed One addressed Rāhula.
"Return, Rāhula; do as your noble father commands you."
Then Rāhula cast down the corner of the Blessed One’s robe.
Then Yaśodharā, having taken Rāhula by the hand, led him into the inner apartments; taking him onto her lap and sitting down, she said:
"Son Rāhula, do not go forth! Son, you think now that it is difficult to attain;

[you think] such fine Kāśī garments as these in this royal palace must be worn, such costly beds as these in this royal palace must be slept upon, and such refined foods as these in this royal palace must be eaten."
Moreover, son Rāhula, one who has gone forth must sleep on a bed of grass spread upon the ground; he must dwell at the foot of a tree as his seat and bedding;

he must go for alms among the families of Caṇḍālas and Pukkasas; he must look upon the faces of those who are angry or pleased; and he must eat even leftover food, even if it is as putrid as a dog's breath.
"Furthermore, one must collect discarded rags from the charnel grounds where jars are kept, and one must dwell in forest hermitages.
There, terrifying sounds are heard, such as the roars of lions, the roars of tigers, and the cries of jackals.
And you, son Rāhula, are delicate, accustomed to comfort, and have been raised in a royal palace; you, my son, are one who has been pampered."
Hearing the sweet sounds of lutes, flutes, and drums, how will you find delight? Where indeed will you go to encounter him?
"In this matter, it is well for you, my son Rāhula; here in this inner palace, play and enjoy yourself with the five strands of sensual pleasure. What is the use of this going forth?"
Rāhula said:
"O Ambā, he was not my father; he was raised in the family of a great king."
Yaśodharā said:
Thus it is.
Rāhula said:
"Mother, whoever speaks correctly should say that he is delicate, most delicate; for my father did not sleep on a bed of grass spread upon the ground, but made his bed and seat at the foot of a tree,
went for alms from house to house, ate leftover food, and dwelt in forest retreats."
Even he, who was so delicate and accustomed to such comfort, has achieved this; we shall not fail to achieve it.
Moreover, Mother, having abandoned sensual desires, I shall go forth from the home to the homeless life; we must certainly attain Nirvana.
Furthermore, Mother, if anyone here is steadfast and mindful, consider them as my very self: I alone shall go forth and seek the path of my forefathers.
Yaśodharā said:
"My son, you will certainly go forth into the religious life."
Rāhula said:
"Certainly; it is most necessary."
Yaśodharā said:
There is no liberation.
Rāhula said:
It does not exist.
Yaśodharā said:
You are abandoning me, as well as my grandfather and your circle of kinsmen.
Rāhula said:
"Certainly, I shall renounce it."
Yaśodharā said:

Listen, my son: if you must by all means go forth from the home into the homeless life, then you must dwell with the six sense faculties well-restrained and their doors guarded; you must practice moderation in eating;
and you must be devoted to the practice of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night.
You must be one who has initiated vigor;
you must dwell devoted to the practice of standing, walking, and sitting;
and even your own flesh and blood, my son, must be relinquished by you.
Furthermore, the training rules prescribed by the Buddha must not be transgressed;
and the training rule prescribed for you, my son, by the Blessed One must be maintained in its entirety.
Even for the sake of your life, my son, you must follow it.
And you, my son, must remain well-restrained in order to attain the unattained nirvana.
For what reason?

"For indeed, my son, there come women who are elderly, graceful, and beautiful, to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One; toward them, my son, you must maintain the perception of them as your mother.

My son, there come young women who are graceful, beautiful, and adorned with ornaments; in that regard, my son, you must not give rise to desire, but rather, my son, at that time you should dwell contemplating suffering and dwell contemplating impermanence."
If you are able, son Rāhula, to turn your mind away from the going forth, then be full of faith.
Then King Śuddhodana issued a command in the city of Kapilavastu:

"Whatever fragrance, garland, flower, or powder exists within the vicinity of the city of Kapilavastu for twelve yojanas, collect it all! Assemble all the actors, dancers, athletes, wrestlers, and musicians!"
By the mind one attains the gods, by speech the rulers of the earth,
by [right] action the wealthy, and by [wrong] action the poor.

At the mere word of the king, that city was adorned and cleansed; it was cleared of gravel and pebbles, perfumed with incense burners, hung with clusters of silk ribbons and garlands, surrounded by variegated cloth hangings, covered with canopies, and strewn with loose flowers. ...
For what reason? Because [the women] were adorned with various garlands and ornaments, and possessed the bloom of their first youth.
Many thousands of women were stationed at the crossroads.
At that time, there was a young girl dwelling within the interior of the palace;
like a doe, she ran away very hurriedly, looking back as she fled.
The son of the Buddha, the offspring of Śuddhodana, is named Rāhula;
having abandoned his [lineage], the Blessed One renounced the kingdom and went forth into homelessness.
They beat the drums and lutes, which emit excellent sounds;
they strike the mṛdaṅga drums: "The prince will not depart for long."
The lutes and harps, struck with their plectrums, hum sweetly;
the prince will not depart for long.
The chariot, variegated with leopard skins, resounding with joyful noise, and well-adorned—
having ascended this chariot, the haughty prince went forth.
Thousands of hand-drums, sounding auspicious cries of joy for sensual pleasures, resounded before Rāhula as he was departing, he of immeasurable fame.
O Prince, these people, born in the regions of Aṃśuka and Śikhī, clothed in fine garments and woolen blankets, and mounted upon the best of elephant-backs, follow after you as you depart.
These girls, born of the mountain peaks, clothed in fine garments and woolen blankets,
and possessing most sweet and varied speech, follow after the prince as he departs.
They beheld the array of chariots, yoked teams, and vehicles as if it were the very embodiment of glory;
yet once again, the women of the king’s inner apartments, their eyes filled with tears, were overcome with grief.
With eyes like those of an elephant or a cakora bird, he has now reached the city gate,
surrounded by his retinue of playful celestial nymphs like Indra among the gods.
Having approached his father, the supreme among men, the leader, the lion among men, who had gone to the Nyagrodha Grove and possessed a golden complexion, Rāhula [spoke].
Having attained renown himself, he who possesses supreme fame pays homage with his soft, webbed palms;
the bull among men strokes the head of the elephant’s son.
O Rāhulabhadra, has your contemplation of the observances borne fruit? Abandoning this compassionate form, become one who ends existence; touch Nirvāṇa.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Śāriputra.
"Ordain Rāhula, Śāriputra; he shall be your attendant."
Then the Elder asked the Blessed One.
"How, Blessed One, shall I go forth?"
The Blessed One said:
Just as, Śāriputra, for one who has gone forth in the noble Dharma and Vinaya while remaining a youth.
He says: "I, Rāhula, go for refuge to the Buddha; I go for refuge to the Dharma; I go for refuge to the Saṅgha.
A second time also, I, Rāhula, the Buddha is my refuge, with no other refuge; the Dharma is my refuge, with no other refuge; the Saṅgha is my refuge, with no other refuge."
"O Rāhula, for as long as life lasts, I shall abstain from taking life; for as long as life lasts, I shall abstain from taking what is not given;
for as long as life lasts, I shall abstain from sexual misconduct; for as long as life lasts, I shall abstain from false speech;

for as long as life lasts, I shall abstain from the use of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which are the basis of negligence. Please accept me as a lay follower on account of these [vows]."
By means of the five precepts.

"I, Rāhula, follow the Buddha, the Blessed One, who has gone forth, into the homeless life; for a second time, I follow the Buddha, the Blessed One, who has gone forth, into the homeless life; for a third time, Rāhula, I have followed the Buddha, the Blessed One, who has gone forth, into the homeless life."

"I, Rāhula, for as long as life lasts, observe the training precept of abstinence from taking life; I observe the training precept of a novice, up to the training precept of not accepting gold and silver.
These indeed are the ten training precepts."
Then the Elder, having shaved Rāhula’s hair and ordained him, took him by the right hand with Śāriputra and by the left hand with Maudgalyāyana, and they sat down upon a grass mat.

Thus now the Blessed One, the Daśabala, whose fame is renowned in heaven and on earth, who has a disciplined assembly of disciples, and who possesses vast wisdom, addressed the pair of chief disciples, Karakandika and Kāraka.
For Rāhula’s faculties are sharp; he will understand this Dharma.
Let the prince go forth into homelessness; let him be one who follows my example.
Knowing the proper time, Śāriputra spoke to the Leader of the World:
"How may I cause Rāhulaśrī, the son born of the flesh of the Jina, to go forth?"
Out of compassion for the world, the Leader, with the voice of Brahmā,
fully explains how one goes forth as a youth within the Noble Dharma and Vinaya.
Maudgalyāyana took him by the left hand and Upatiṣya by the right;
having ordained him, they sat down upon that grass mat.
He who removes the bracelets and the golden thread from his body shall no longer wander afflicted by suffering; in their distress, they remember the One Possessed of the Ten Powers.
Placing her son, whose eyes were like those of an elephant or a cakora bird and whose large eyes were coppery-red, upon her lap, his mother addressed him with these verses:
Wearing the finest robes and with your body perfumed by the scent of unguents,
you— though accustomed to ultimate comfort— are practicing the ascetic life, which is so difficult to lead.
One should rejoice in those who practice self-restraint; even if one must dig for scraps of cloth in the latrine, or eat the leftovers of a slave-girl carrying water-jars, O Rāhula.
You, with golden anklets...
[radiant] like refined gold, your kinsmen take delight in you.
What do you have to do with the forest, my son, having heard the sound of those lutes with their sweet and charming tones, like the songs of *nakula* birds?
"You do not uphold this teaching... Come, my son!
Go back with your face turned away; for the imperishable state is not easily attained."
Rāhula said:
If, Mother, there are any of quick understanding, count me among them;
for I too shall follow the ancestral path that crushes the afflictions.
At night the barber sharpened his razor, and Rāhula released Maṇicūḍa;
then Abhimanyu, recollecting the Best of Bipeds, [wept].
And seeing him thus intent upon the teaching of the One Possessed of Ten Powers, [the Buddha said:
"Attain that quickly; touch the blissful peace of Nirvana."
"O son, those qualities which transcend both birth and old age—attain them quickly! Thus he spoke also to Rāhula.
Taking those locks of hair— which were like the color of a peacock’s neck curved in a circle— into her lap,
his mother stroked them.
With eyes filled with tears, Yaśodharā beheld her own son, Rāhulaśrī, whose head was shorn of hair, as he was born from the impulse of the Dharma.
Maudgalyāyana and Upatiṣya ordained the young prince Rāhula, who was free from the marks of a householder, red as a tree, and clad in saffron robes.
Having gone forth from there, that son of the one who bears the thirty-two marks dwells,
desiring training, in reliance upon the elder Upatiṣya.
This is indeed worthy of you, that having gone forth out of faith,
you wander with a mind unstained, regardless of the qualities of sensual pleasure.
Having eaten pure rice from the Śākya clan, accompanied by many soups, curries, and side dishes, Rāhula wanders for alms.
Worship with both head and mind the son of the Buddha named Rāhula, who destroys the veil of the darkness of ignorance and has abandoned all outflows.

Then, indeed, when the Blessed One had finished eating among the women of the inner apartments, Yaśodharā, the mother of Rāhula, out of respect for those senior ladies, on the following day, extended her joined palms toward the Blessed One and invited the Blessed One, together with the community of disciples, for a meal on the morrow.
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then Yaśodharā, perceiving the Blessed One’s acceptance through his silence, became thrilled, filled with joy and gladness.
When that very night had passed,
having prepared an abundance of solid and soft food,
and having prepared many fresh and exquisite sweetmeats endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and flavor, at the end of that same night, he went to his own residence.
It was sprinkled and swept, made ready, draped with bundles of silk ribbons and garlands, strewn with loose flowers, and covered with canopies;
a costly seat was prepared for the Blessed One, and likewise for the community of monks according to their rank.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One, having dressed early in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, entered the inner apartments surrounded by the community of monks.
Then indeed Yaśodharā, the mother of Rāhula, having adorned herself with various kinds of garments and ornaments,
served the Blessed One and tempted him with sweetmeats, thinking: "Perhaps the noble son will return to the household life," yet there was no change in the mind of the Blessed One.

Then, when the Blessed One had finished his meal, washed his hands, and set aside his bowl— and the community of monks had done likewise— the Blessed One, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened King Śuddhodana, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, Yaśodharā the mother of Rāhula, and their retinues with a discourse on the Dharma, rose from his seat and departed.
Then the monks said to the Blessed One:

"Behold, Blessed One, how Yaśodharā, adorned with all her ornaments and having decorated herself, serves the Blessed One and tempts him with sweetmeats; yet there is no change in the state of the Blessed One's mind.
The Blessed One said: [as follows].

"Monks, it is not only now; on another occasion as well, this Yaśodharā, having adorned herself with all her ornaments, dressed herself up, served [me], and tempted me with sweetmeats. In the meantime, the Ekaśṛṅga-jātaka must be told again."

Having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, the Blessed One sat right there at the foot of the Bodhi tree upon a grass mat, remaining for seven days in the bliss of joy without breaking his cross-legged posture.
Here, at the Bodhi tree, I attained preeminence;
having completed seven days after awakening to perfect enlightenment, I brought an end to the dense wilderness of birth, old age, and death.
Here, I shattered the Māra of the afflictions and shattered the Māra who is a son of the gods; here, my immeasurable and incalculable vow, which had been made, was fulfilled.

Here, at the Bodhi tree, having awakened to the supreme enlightenment— the [enlightenment] of that which is without beginning or end— the Perfectly Awakened One did not rise from his seat for seven days, he who is the shrine for the entire world.
Thousands of millions of deities assembled in the sky and rained down a shower of flowers for no less than seven nights.
There the gods rain down divine blue lotuses, red lotuses, and beautiful white lotuses, each with a thousand petals and most lovely to behold.
And Māra was dejected; he scratched the earth with a reed, thinking:
"I have been conquered by the God of Gods, the Protector, the Lion of the Śākyas."
The gods of the Thirty-three, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, those who are Nirmita, and the Paranirmita gods— all established in the realm of desire.
Divine red sandalwood, aloeswood, and likewise campaka flowers,
as well as divine showers of blossoms, were scattered from the sky.
And divine jewel-powder was scattered from the sky;
it pervaded this entire buddha-field with streams as thick as axle-trees.
Thousands of millions of Brahmās have gathered in the sky;
they rain down a fine powder of divine red sandalwood.
Starting from the gods on earth up to the Śuddhāvāsa deities who are self-luminous,
this lineage was completely filled with deities.
With parasols, banners, and flags, they completely fill the sky and perform the most excellent worship of the glorious, perfectly awakened Buddha.
A vast radiance was released, completely illuminating the Buddha-field;
even the world-systems up to the peak of existence stood as bright as fire.
The hells became completely pacified by the rays of the Buddha;
their limbs were cooled, and everyone became happy.
For those whose hellish suffering has been completely exhausted,
immediately after passing away from the hells, they will be reborn among the gods.
In Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Tapana, Pratāpana,
and Raurava, the fire was extinguished by the rays of the Lord of the World.
Then, in the Avīci hell, in Saṃghāta, and in the individual hells,
the fire was completely extinguished by the rays of the Lord of the World.
In as many world-systems as there were individual hells,
the fire was entirely extinguished by the rays of the Lord of the World.
And those who belong to the animal realm and feed on flesh and blood were suffused with loving-kindness by the Buddha, so that they no longer harm one another.
The Bodhi tree was adorned with parasols, banners, and flags;
it was covered with gabled pavilions fashioned by the sons of the gods.
And pieces of broken ground and gravel and sand were spread all around the base of the seat of enlightenment, established upon the earth.
The seat of enlightenment was completely covered by ground made of jewels,
which had been fashioned by the sons of gods as the navel of the Buddha-field.
Thousands of sons of gods stood upon the earth;
taking up incense burners, they paid homage to the Leader of the World.
And the entire ground below was overspread with lotuses made of Jāmbūnada gold, which rose up through the splendor of the Buddha.
And those who were afflicted by the suffering of disease, without protection and without refuge,
became free from illness and happy, suffused by the light rays of the Buddha.
Those born blind shall see forms once they have obtained unimpaired vision;
and they shall speak to one another concerning the Protector who has attained enlightenment.
Passion, hatred, and delusion were brought to their end at that time when the Lion of the Śākyas, the Great Seer, attained enlightenment.
The palaces, celestial mansions, and delightful gabled chambers were all oriented toward the Bodhisattva, the Protector.
As many men, women, and kinnaras as there were within the Buddha-field,
they all turned their faces toward where the Great Sage’s enlightenment was located.
The deities, the sons of gods, and the beautiful daughters of gods all turned their faces toward that place where the Supreme among Men was.
Then the nāgas, gandharvas, yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, and rākṣasas—
all turned their faces toward where the Great Seer’s enlightenment was.
The boys and girls were placed upon the couch;
with their faces turned toward it, they remained facing the place where the Great Seer’s Bodhi tree stood.
And whatever divine ornaments, distinguished and made of jewels,
had been worn by the gods, they all turned their faces toward him.
Then all the ornaments of the nāgas, yakṣas, piśācas, and rākṣasas became motionless, directed toward the Bodhi tree.
Then the celestial palaces of the gods, the nāgas, the yakṣas, and the rākṣasas turned their faces toward where the Great Seer’s seat of awakening was located.
Ankle-bells, bracelets, or even armlets—
these were worn by the Buddha who had attained awakening, by whom awakening was rendered motionless.
Adorned with golden coins and beautiful necklaces,
they were bound upon the necks of men by whom unshakable awakening was attained.
A pearl necklace was fastened, variegated jeweled earrings were worn,
a veil and a finger-ring were present— by which the immovable state of awakening was attained.
However many inconceivable realms of sentient beings there are within the Buddha-fields—
whether they know or do not know— that by which unshakable awakening is attained.
And cool, delightful winds, fragrant and enchanting,
blow everywhere throughout the field of enlightenment of the Protector who has attained awakening.
The love and devoted service established toward that beloved only son were exactly the same as those felt by his parents immediately thereafter.
As many gods, nāgas, humans, asuras, kinnaras, and yakṣas as there are within the Buddha-field, they all behold the Leader.
Having taken up incense burners, they all remained there in comfort and paid homage to the Lamp of the World, who was established at the seat of awakening.
With palms joined they pay homage and praise him with verses;
established at the seat of awakening, they perform worship for the Buddha.
Everyone saw the Lord of the World, the Illuminator, standing nearby; no one perceived him as being at a distance, as if he were situated only a fathom away.
No one in the world-system sees the Buddha from behind;
for in every direction, one beholds the Buddha’s face all around.
No one perceives the Leader of the World from his left or right side;
everyone sees the Great Hero facing them directly.
Immediately thereafter, that Buddha-field was perfumed with incense;
by its fragrance, tens of millions of Buddha-fields in every direction were filled.
It is not possible to calculate how many millions of beings,
having beheld the glory of the Buddha, have set out toward enlightenment.
Whatever grasses and whatever medicinal herbs and forest trees there were,
they all turned toward that direction where the Great Seer’s seat of awakening was located.
Who, having heard such a Dharma as this taught by the Lord of the World, would not be satisfied, except for one who belongs to the faction of Māra?
It is not possible to describe in its entirety with words, even by one speaking through supernatural power,
the splendor that belonged to the Buddha, the Protector, when he had attained awakening.
Those who have seen the Perfectly Awakened One established at the seat of enlightenment, and who have honored the Great Hero— hearing this, those wise ones are filled with joy.
And those monks who are established in the aggregate of ethical discipline without flaw—
having heard this sutra, they will experience great joy.
Endowed with excellent patience and gentleness, and possessing undaunted minds,
they will find satisfaction in seeking the wisdom of a Buddha.
For those beings who have been comforted with the thought, "I shall liberate you from your afflictions," they will experience joy when I attain supreme enlightenment.
Those supreme among bipeds, those former Buddhas whom you have honored,
will experience great joy upon hearing this sutra.
Those beings by whom you were gladdened and satisfied with food and drink will,
upon hearing this sutra, show reverence toward the Buddha.
Those destitute beings who have been covered with wealth by you,
having heard this sutra, will show reverence toward the Buddha.
And those who have had beautiful stūpas built for previous Buddhas,
lofty and excellent palaces, they indeed shall be filled with joy.
Those who, having abandoned gain and honor, upheld the true Dharma while it was falling into decay for the sake of the Protectors of the World— they indeed shall become joyful.
Those who possess unconditioned life and are exempt from punitive actions will indeed rejoice upon the chest of the Lord of the World.
Those who shall behold the perfectly awakened Maitreya will become [enlightened].
Those who, having seen Maitreya, the perfectly awakened one, the supreme among bipeds,
shall perform extensive worship, for them there will be joy.
Those who, having seen you— the lion, the great elephant, the shrine of the world—
shall perform extensive worship, for them there will be joy.
Those who, desiring the wisdom of a Buddha, shall perform worship of Ketu, the Lord of the World, will experience great joy.
And those who shall perform worship for the Buddha Pradyota,
being seekers after the wisdom of a Buddha, will experience great joy.
And those who, having seen the Buddha Jyotīvara, the Unconquered,
shall perform a great worship, for them there will be joy.
Those who, having seen Sunetra, the illuminator of the world, shall honor him with reverence and worship,
will experience great joy.
There will be two Buddhas, Tathāgatas named Kusuma, who are Lords of the World;
those who see them and honor them will experience great joy.
Those who, having seen Meru— the best of bipeds, the perfectly awakened one, the foremost of speakers— shall honor him, for them there will be joy.
And those who, having seen the supreme Buddha, the best of bipeds,
shall offer him the highest worship, for them there will be great joy.
And those among the four lords of men who shall honor the Saṅgha in this Fortunate Aeon (bhadrakalpa) will become exalted.
Those who are greedy for gain and honor, relying on crooked wisdom,
will experience terror upon hearing this, for their desires are manifold.
And those who delight in company and are established in living in groups— upon hearing of seclusion from the Buddha, they experience joy.
And those who, though of immoral conduct, having heard what was thus spoken by the Buddha,
shall bow down before the Lamp of the World and show intense reverence.
Those future bodhisattvas who have been prophesied by the Buddha—
those who are gentle and pleasant to dwell with— they shall experience joy.
Those for whom there is no turning back from the Buddha-knowledge in any respect—
those people, having heard this sutra, will become happy.
For those who have honored, revered, respected, and worshiped the former Buddhas— the essence of beings and lords of men—
with a mind bowed in devotion, are instructed in the wisdom of the Buddha.
Having heard the supreme color of the Man, they become joyful.
Those whose faith is complete and universal, who are endowed with hundreds of millions of excellent qualities,
and who uphold the Dharma while it is being destroyed;
With a joyful mind, [he dwells] within the teaching of the Sugata.
And those who were not fickle, nor agitated, nor talkative, nor of confused speech; whose speech was very gentle and who were free from pride.
Having heard the supreme color of the Jinas, they become joyful.
Those who have not abandoned the wisdom of the Buddha—
such stainless awakening that is equal to the infinite—
and those who practice their vows with vigilance;
Having heard the wisdom of the supreme Victor, they become joyful.

Then, indeed, at the end of seven days, the Blessed One rose from his lion throne and, gazing at the Bodhi tree with the gaze of a nāga, remained for a second week without food, filled with joy and happiness,

watching the Bodhi tree with an unblinking gaze, [thinking]: "In this Bodhi tree of mine, [I have realized the end] of the dense wilderness of saṃsāra, which is beginningless and characterized by birth, old age, and death."
The Māra of the afflictions has been defeated by me here; the Māra of death has been defeated; the Māra of the aggregates has been defeated; the Māra of the son of a god has been defeated.

Here, my immeasurable and incalculable vows have been fulfilled; here, at the tree of awakening, I have attained preeminence in the world, I have attained excellence in the world, and I have attained the state of being the essence of sentient beings.
The Blessed One, having gazed at the Bodhi tree with an unblinking gaze for seven days with joy and happiness, spent the third week walking back and forth on a long promenade with joy and happiness.

Now at that time, Māra the Evil One was sitting not far from the Blessed One, miserable, dejected, and full of regret, scratching the ground with a stick, thinking: "The ascetic Gautama has transcended my domain; the ascetic Gautama has transcended my domain."
Then indeed, Tantrī, the daughter of Māra, and Aratī, the daughter of Māra, approached where Māra the Evil One was and addressed Māra the Evil One in verse:
"Father, though you are indeed dejected, I shall bring that man here,
having bound him with the snares of passion like an elephant from the forest."
Having bound it, I shall bring it here; it will become subject to you.
Then Māra the Evil One replied to his daughters with a verse:
The Worthy One, the Sugata in this world, cannot be led astray by passion;
he has transcended my domain, and therefore I grieve intensely.
Then those daughters of Māra, disregarding the words of their father Māra, approached the Blessed One where he was and followed after the Blessed One as he walked in meditation:
"We would serve your feet, O Blessed One; we would serve your feet, O Sugata."
The Blessed One paid no heed to her, for his mind was perfectly and completely liberated through the unsurpassed destruction of the substrata of existence.
Then those daughters of Māra, having approached a secluded place, consulted with one another:

"The inclinations of men are manifold; the inclinations of men are manifold. What if we were now, by means of our supernatural power, to manifest a hundred forms each—just like women about fifteen or sixteen years of age—and [approach him]?"
Having approached the place where the ascetic Gautama was, they walked back and forth following the ascetic Gautama as he was walking.
"O Blessed One, we would serve your feet; O Sugata, we would serve your feet.
Yet the Blessed One did not pay them any heed, for his mind was perfectly and completely liberated through the unsurpassed destruction of the substrates of existence.

Then those daughters of Māra, having approached one side, consulted together with these words: "The inclinations of men are manifold; the inclinations of men are manifold. What if we were each to create a hundred forms—just as if we were women who have given birth once or twice—and having created such forms, go to where the ascetic Gautama is?"
Having approached him, they walked back and forth following the ascetic Gautama as he was walking.
"We would serve your feet, O Blessed One; we would serve your feet, O Sugata.
Yet the Blessed One paid them no heed, for his mind was perfectly and completely liberated through the unsurpassed destruction of the substrates of existence (*anuttara upadhisaṃkṣaya*).

Then those daughters of Māra, having gone to a secluded place, consulted together with these words: "The inclinations of men are manifold; the inclinations of men are manifold. What if we were each, by means of our supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), to manifest a hundred women of such-and-such a form—just like middle-aged women—and then approach the Blessed One?"

They followed the Blessed One as he walked back and forth, saying, "We would serve at your feet, O Blessed One; we would serve at your feet, O Sugata. Yet the Blessed One paid them no heed, for his mind was perfectly and completely liberated through the unsurpassed destruction of the substrates of existence.
Then those daughters of Māra, having gone aside, consulted with one another: "Oh! Let us each manifest a form resembling the supreme excellence of youth;

let us rather manifest ourselves as aged, decrepit, elderly, with grey hair, hunchbacked like a curved roof-rafter, and leaning upon staffs, so that we may approach the ascetic Gautama where he is and [address] the ascetic."
Having bowed her head at the feet of Gautama, the Pratyekabuddha addressed the ascetic Gautama, saying, "We would ask you a question."

Then those daughters of Māra, having become aged, decrepit, elderly, grey-haired, and humpbacked like curved roof-rafter beams, approached the Blessed One leaning on staffs; having bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they stood to one side.
Standing to one side, Māra’s daughter Tantrī addressed the Blessed One in verse:
How dwelling and practicing much here does a monk cross over the five floods and cross the sixth?
How meditating and practicing much does he [cross] the perception of sensual desire?
He is excluded; he has not attained a firm [grasp].
Then the Blessed One replied to Tantrī, the daughter of Māra, in verse:
Having understood the Dhamma and meditating without discursive thought, he is neither attached nor does he harbor sloth here;
a monk who dwells thus frequently in this way—
Having crossed five floods, one crosses the sixth here.
With body pliant, mind well-liberated, mindful and unshakable, with pride removed;
he meditates fruitfully and frequently on the perception of the foul.
He is excluded; he has not attained firm [mastery].
Then indeed, Aratī, the daughter of Māra, addressed the Blessed One in verse:
Overcome by sorrow, you meditate in the forest,
longing for life; yet,
having encountered those of the village, you do not form a friendship with them.
Why do you not form friendship with people?
Then the Blessed One addressed Aratī, the daughter of Māra, in verse:
Having dug up the entire root of sorrow and having abandoned all greed for existence,
I shall attain the acquisition of the goal and peace of heart.
Devoted to meditation, my mind perceives the essence to be in bliss;
therefore, I do not form friendships with people, for no friendship exists for me in that regard.
Then indeed, the Māra goddess Arati addressed the Blessed One in verse:
Having cut off craving and moving amidst virtues, he will inspire great zeal in those who are attached to this world; indeed,
he will lead many people to true knowledge.
Having snatched it away, King Death will lead you to the unshakable state free from sorrow.
Then the Blessed One replied to those daughters of Māra in verse:
Dig up a mountain with your fingernails; chew iron with your teeth;
strike a mountain with your head; seek the deep when it is shallow! Why do you pursue such evil things, even harboring constant malice toward the Buddha?
Then those daughters of Māra, realizing "The ascetic Gautama knows us," became sorrowful, dejected, and full of regret; they approached their father, Māra, and addressed him with this verse:
"Today, Father, even my own death would not have been brought about by passion.
He has transcended my domain; therefore, I grieve most bitterly."
"Or rather, dear father, were any other man who was not free from attachment to see us endowed with such beauty, he would faint at the sight and fall down, or hot blood would issue from his mouth,
and by that very affliction he would meet his end or suffer the destruction of his mind. But as for the ascetic Gautama, dear father— "
He is worthy of offerings, free from passion, free from hatred, free from delusion, and has become one who has overcome all things.
Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, Māra the Evil One addressed the Blessed One in verse:
Having come here, the lute-like Arati and Rati cause delight;
the Great Hero should dispel them as the wind blows away drifting cotton.
Having spoken thus, Māra the Evil One, suffering, dejected, and full of regret, vanished right there.
When the Blessed One had set in motion the most excellent wheel of Dharma, the monks said to the Blessed One:

"How was it, Blessed One, that the daughters of Māra approached the Blessed One seeking an opportunity and searching for a vulnerability, yet, finding no such opportunity, became disillusioned and withdrew?"
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now that these daughters of Māra have approached me seeking an opportunity, searching for an opening, and having failed to find one, have turned back in disillusionment.
On another occasion as well, they approached me seeking an opportunity, searching for an opening, and having failed to find one, they turned back in disillusionment."
The monks said:
At another time as well, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
On another occasion as well, monks.
Once upon a time, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi, there was a merchant named Dharmalabdha.
That sea-born caravan leader set out upon the great ocean and returned with his ship successfully accomplished.
Then, about five hundred merchants approached him from Vārāṇasī and said,
"We too shall embark upon the great ocean together with you."
Dharmalabdha said:
"You are not able to go by that path by which I am going."
"I am traveling through the middle of the island of the rākṣasīs,
and those rākṣasīs entice the merchants with hundreds of stratagems;
there, many hundreds of merchants, lured by the rākṣasīs, fall into ruin and calamity."
It is not possible for you to go along with me as an equal.
Now, that caravan leader Dharmalabdha gave no opportunity to those five hundred merchants,
[thinking], "Lest you fall into misfortune and ruin there, enticed by the rākṣasīs."
Then those five hundred merchants, having gathered together, said:

"This merchant Dharmalabdha travels to the great ocean by a beautiful route; he goes in safety and returns in safety, he returns quickly and returns with his vessel successful. Furthermore, he leaves us no opportunity to go [with him]. Sirs, whatever merit this merchant Dharmalabdha possesses—being so meritorious and accumulating such merit—you too should accumulate that same merit, at the very time when he departs from here from Vārāṇasī."
At that time, we too shall set out.

Whatever merit Dharmalabdha accumulated, those five hundred merchants also accumulated exactly the same merit; and at the very time when the merchant Dharmalabdha set out for the ocean, those five hundred merchants also set out, traveling together with the caravan leader Dharmalabdha.
At the time when they reached that region where those rākṣasīs were, the caravan leader Dharmalabdha caused all those five hundred merchants to wake up by making a sound.
"Sirs, all these five hundred merchants have set out from Vārāṇasī together with me, and we must reach this very abode of the rākṣasīs.

There, those rākṣasīs will entice you in many ways: some will entice you with forms, others with sounds, others with smells, others with tastes, and others with touches; there are various [dangers] on that path."
They will manifest various kinds of beautiful objects of desire and will manifest market stalls set out along the roads;
yet wherever there may be some beautiful object of desire, you shall not see it there.
Therefore, none of you should feel greed for anything, none of you should take anything, and none of you should consume anything.

They will manifest thousands of various kinds of trees endowed with flowers and fruits, filled from their very roots up to their blossoms with *madana* flowers and *madana* fruits, so heavily laden with flowers and foliage that neither flower nor fruit may be plucked.

And they will manifest various kinds of lotus ponds— clear, beautiful, with cool water, strewn with golden sand, covered with blue, red, white, and fragrant lotuses, and possessing pleasant landing-stairs. Therein, none of you should approach [the water], nor should anyone from there taste the water, or the lotuses, or the blue lotuses, or the white lotuses, or the lotus stalks and fibers.
They will also manifest various other kinds of precious jewels;
and therein you must not give rise to greed for anything whatsoever.
Whoever among you gives rise to greed there shall no longer return to Jambudvīpa.
In that very place, he who is led astray will fall into calamity;
but he who departs from that dwelling of the rākṣasīs, being entirely free from attachment, shall go forth with his vessel accomplished and, having returned safely, will go back to his own country.
Having accumulated merit, the merchants from Jambudvīpa set out upon the great ocean, that mine of wealth and jewels.
Having embarked upon it and plunged into the ocean,
they took jewels from the islands and returned again in safety.
They had a caravan leader who was wise and discerning of their welfare;
known by the name Dharmalabdha, he instructed them.
On this merchant's road, there are terrifying rākṣasīs who have attained mastery through supernatural power and are trained in the practice of illusion.
The fool, being of a nature characterized by poor wisdom, who would set his heart upon those [celestial nymphs],
shall never again go to his own home in Jambudvīpa.
But that merchant here who shall indeed be free from longing for them will go safely to Jambudvīpa, to his own home.
They set out upon the path where the rākṣasīs were; and those rākṣasīs perceived them as merchants according to their respective inclinations.
The merchants perceived various and manifold sensual pleasures through forms, sounds, touches, smells, and tastes.
Therein, those merchants who were inclined toward forms were enticed by forms; those merchants who were inclined toward sounds were enticed by pleasing sounds of song and instrumental music;

those merchants who were inclined toward odors were enticed by various kinds of most delightful fragrances; those merchants who were inclined toward tastes were likewise enticed by various kinds of the finest flavors; and those merchants who were inclined toward tangibles were enticed by various kinds of tactile sensations.
All five hundred merchants said:
"For the sake of which we have been undergoing hardships day and night, performing various kinds of labor—those very forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles have now reached us here.
We shall play and delight in these very things; we will not go back to Jambudvīpa again."
They send word to the caravan leader Dharmalabdha.
"In our name, you should inquire after the health of our friends, kinsmen, and blood relations in Jambudvīpa; as for us, we shall take our delight right here."
The caravan leader said to them:
"Sirs, these are not human women; they are rākṣasīs.
I told you this from the very beginning:
tomorrow we shall pass beyond that abode of the rākṣasīs, and those rākṣasīs will try to seduce you in many ways."
In this matter, you must not harbor greed.
If you wish to go to your own country in safety, do not, sirs, conceive the thought that these rākṣasīs are human women; otherwise, you will all fall into calamity and ruin.
Now, though they were addressed in many ways by the caravan leader Dharmalabdha, they did not listen, being deluded by ignorance.
Then the caravan leader Dharmalabdha, having passed beyond that entire array of mansions created by the rākṣasīs with his own retinue, found them vanished as if they had been a dream.
Thereupon, five hundred merchants were all devoured by five hundred rākṣasīs, leaving nothing but their bones behind.
Having devoured five hundred merchants, that entire host of rākṣasīs gathered together;
having assembled, they said:

This caravan leader Dharmalabdha repeatedly descends upon the great ocean by this very route; having obtained his profit, he returns again and again to his own country in safety. He also warns other merchants, saying: "Do not come by this route, lest you be devoured by the rākṣasīs."
Who is able to covet and eat this which has been obtained through the Dharma?
There, a certain rākṣasī possessed of many illusions entered; she was one who, having enticed hundreds of merchants, had devoured them.
She was encouraged by those other rākṣasīs.
"Whatever is obtained through dharma shall become your food through greed."

Having magically transformed herself into a young and beautiful woman, she followed behind Dharmalabdha as he went along; she repeatedly crossed his path within the sight of that caravan leader, yet the caravan leader’s mind did not become attached to that woman.
The caravan leader, having disembarked at that port city on the ocean and taken various kinds of jewels, safely returned from the sea to Jambudvīpa.
That rākṣasī, in her form as a young and beautiful woman, followed closely behind the caravan leader Dharmalabdha, attempting to seduce him in many ways.

At the time when Dharmalabdha had safely reached the countryside from Vārāṇasī, a rākṣasī, having conjured up a boy resembling the caravan leader Dharmalabdha, presented him to the caravan leader, saying:
"If you go leaving me behind, take this little son; who will bring him up once you have gone?"
The caravan leader said:
"This is not my son, nor are you my wife; I am a human being and you are a rākṣasī. Many hundreds of merchants have been enticed by you and have thus fallen into calamity."
She censured the great multitude of people from the villages, the towns, the market towns, and the countryside.
"This Dharma which I have obtained was brought here to me from such-and-such a city by those with pleasant voices, yet they abandoned it here;
they do not accept this son of mine, nor do they acknowledge even me."
Then that caravan leader was addressed by the great multitude of women and men:
"Caravan leader, do not abandon this woman after bringing her here from the seaport; she is your son, resembling you."
The caravan leader said:
"This is not my son, nor is this my wife; she is a rākṣasī. Many hundreds of merchants have been enticed by these rākṣasīs and devoured."
That rākṣasī also said to that person:

Such are these men who acquire wealth: at the time when women are infatuated with them, they speak hundreds of virtues; but at the time when they have become dispassionate, we are treated like Piśācas and Rākṣasīs, and reviled with hundreds of insults.
In this way, the rākṣasī incited that multitude of people.
In this way, the caravan leader Dharmalabdha safely reached his own home in Vārāṇasī.
Then the merchants spoke incessantly to the caravan leader:
"For whose sake we strive day and night without weariness—
of what kind would those goods be that you have obtained here for us?"
"O noble one, you speak of health; our kinsmen are here in Jambudvīpa. We shall enjoy ourselves right here; there will be no returning there."
The caravan leader said:
"Surely you have no memory, or perhaps it is distorted, O worthy ones;
for you will before long become food for rākṣasīs."
Having drunk your skin, fat, flesh, and blood,
the rākṣasīs will be satisfied, provided with their food.
"He who does not do my bidding will come to regret it later. Immediately after that, other merchants spoke to the caravan leader.
"For whose sake we strive day and night without weariness—how might we attain those sounds? Yet even they have been attained by us here."
"O noble one, you speak of health among our kinsmen in Jambudvīpa;
we shall find delight right here, for there is no returning to that place."
[ Mvu 3.293 ] Immediately thereafter, other merchants said to the caravan leader:
"For whose sake we strive day and night without weariness—how shall we obtain those perfumes? They have been obtained by you here."
"O noble one, you speak of health among our kinsmen in Jambudvīpa;
we shall take our delight right here, for there is no returning there."
Then other merchants said to the caravan leader immediately thereafter:
"For whose sake we strive day and night without weariness—how might we obtain those flavors? Even those have not been obtained by us here."
"Relatives, you speak of health and water in Jambudvīpa;
we shall enjoy ourselves right here; there will be no returning there."
The caravan leader said:
"Indeed, you do not remember that, O worthy ones; you have fallen into delusion. Before long, you shall become food for the rākṣasīs."
Having drunk your skin, fat, flesh, and blood,
the rākṣasīs will become satisfied, being fully provided with their food.
"If you do not follow my word, you will come to regret it. Immediately thereafter, other merchants spoke to the caravan leader.
"For what purpose we strive day and night without weariness—how might we attain those [pleasures] of touch? Those have been attained by you here."
"O noble one, you speak of health in Jambudvīpa;
we shall enjoy ourselves right here; there is no going of ours there."
The caravan leader said:
Surely you have no mindfulness, or perhaps it is perverted, O worthy sirs;
for before long you will become food for the rākṣasīs.
Having drunk your skin, fat, flesh, and blood,
the rākṣasīs will be satisfied and fully provided with food;
since you do not carry out my word, you will later come to regret it.
Then, immediately thereafter, all those terrifying rākṣasīs established themselves within that dreadful iron city for the sake of the merchants.
Those rākṣasīs, having assembled, deliberated for some time:
"This lone merchant has come again and again;
he crosses to the other shore in safety, so it is not possible to devour him."
Then a certain rakshasi, wise and discerning of the matter,
having enticed many merchants, devoured them.
And she spoke to all those very cruel meat-eaters:
"I shall entice him; he will become my food."
The merchant crossed the ocean, and that ogress also crossed; she pursued him from behind, following closely at every step.
"This young son of yours will die from grief for you; take him back, for why would you abandon your own biological son?"
Dharmalabdha said:
"Release her whose wife she is; you speak of a son where there is no son.
You are not a protector of humans, nor will you be able to devour me."
And she proclaims among the people in the villages, towns, kingdoms, and provinces: "This man is abandoning my husband."
A great multitude of people, both women and men, having gathered together, reproached the man, saying: "Why do you abandon your wife?"
Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras have gathered here;
they revile him harshly, saying, "Whose wife are you abandoning?"
Dharmalabdha said:
"O worthy sir, this is not my wife; she is a terrifying Rākṣasī, a fierce devourer of humans—know this for certain."

When he is recognized by the great multitude as one who has obtained his status through merit, he does not desire it; he thinks, "This is not my son, nor is this my wife; she is a *rākṣasī*, a night-roaming demoness. He then informs that body of people:
"Such are these men who have obtained wealth; they become attached right there, and they become disenchanted right there."

At times when they are desirous, we constantly converse with women on hundreds of pleasant things; but at times when they become dispassionate, we are treated like ogresses or like female piśācas of low birth, and are reviled with hundreds of unpleasant things.
Then that woman was not desired by him because she had obtained the Dharma.
The ministers informed King Brahmadatta.

"Your Majesty, the great caravan leader Dharmalabdha brought back from the seaport a woman who was gracious, beautiful, endowed with supreme beauty, and of such peerless form that she could not be distinguished [from his daughter].
For some reason, Dharmalabdha desired neither that woman as a wife nor that son."
The king commanded his ministers.
"Call the caravan leader Dharmalabdha."
Then he was summoned by the ministers into the presence of the king, and that woman was also summoned.
When King Brahmadatta saw that woman—handsome, beautiful, and endowed with the most excellent form—an intense passion for her arose within the king.
Then he said to that caravan leader:
If you have no need for this woman, give her to me.

"O Great King, do not be negligent! This is not my wife, nor is this my son. She is a siren from the ocean who has followed behind me, clinging to my back for the sake of seduction. She is not a woman; she is a rākṣasī. O Great King, do not set your mind upon her."
Now that king was infatuated with that woman because of her youth and beauty; he did not listen to Dharmalabdha, as it was said by the Blessed One:
For one who is impassioned does not know the goal; one who is impassioned does not see the Dharma.
When passion overcomes a man, it becomes a blinding darkness.
By him, the rākṣasī was introduced into the inner apartments.
Having played, enjoyed himself, and amused himself with her, King Brahmadatta lay down to sleep.
That rākṣasī cast a sleep-inducing spell over the entire royal household;
together with her daughter, she devoured the king.
Having devoured the king, that son was sent to the lair of the rākṣasīs with the command:
"Come quickly; this royal palace must be devoured!"
Within a single muhūrta, he returned, having seized that host of rākṣasīs.
During that night, the entire royal palace—both inside and out, including the women, men, and maidens, as well as the elephants and horses—was all devoured; nothing remained but heaps of bones.
When the night had turned to dawn, the ministers went to the royal palace and saw that the gates were closed.

The chaplains arrived, the army commanders arrived, and the guilds of merchants arrived, headed by the caravan leader Dharmalabdha; all of them came to inquire after his well-being as they had done on other occasions, yet they saw those gates of the royal palace closed.
Those ministers questioned one another.
Why do they not open the gates of the royal palace today?
At other times, the gates of the royal palace are left open, the palace is sprinkled and swept, and the seats are prepared;

yet one does not hear the sound of anyone—neither the sound of women nor men, nor the sound of elephants nor horses—even though the royal palace is so vast and there is such a great multitude of people. Why is it that no one’s voice is heard?
A sound is heard.
The caravan leader Dharmalabdha said:
"Sirs, you shall no longer hear news from the royal palace;
for that fierce ogress, who feeds on flesh and blood, has been brought here.
She has caused great calamity to arise here."
"Open these gates so that we may know what is happening in the royal palace."
The ministers, having brought a ladder, had the men hoisted up and said, "Go and open the gates!"
The men who had entered the royal palace saw there the skeletons of elephants and the skeletons of horses,
and they reported this to the multitude of people.
This entire royal household has been devoured; nothing remains but skeletons.
Then they were told, "Having descended, open these gates."
Then, having descended, the gates were opened; the ministers, the army commanders,

and the citizens entered the outer gate of the royal palace and saw that in the elephant enclosure only skeletons remained, and in the horse enclosure likewise only skeletons remained, as well as the bones of those elephant-keepers and horse-keepers.
Just like a cemetery, so was that royal palace on the outside—fearful, terrifying, and foul-smelling.
Having opened the gates of the royal palace from within, they entered the gateway; there, only the bones of the king and the queens remained.
Thus, that royal palace, both inside and out, had become like a cemetery—frightful, terrifying, and foul-smelling.

Then those ministers and merchants, having assembled a great multitude of people, had that royal palace— both inside and out— cleaned, sprinkled, swept, and perfumed with incense; they performed funeral honors for the bodies of the king and all his queens, stationed guards all around the city, and deployed the fourfold army.
The elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry.
In this way, that city together with its countryside is protected so that no king might commit an offense against it.
Then those ministers, merchants, and countryfolk gathered together, maintained their counsel, and deliberated with one another.
"Sirs, who here in our Vārāṇasī will become king, who would be able to protect this kingdom in accordance with the Dharma?"
This thought occurred to all those kings, ministers, merchants, and country folk:
No other king is worthy [to rule] in Vārāṇasī except for Dharmalabdha, the caravan leader;
he is meritorious and vigilant,
and even the yakṣas and rākṣasas are unable to find an opportunity to harm him.
There, having entered the great ocean three times, he returned safely at all times with his vessel successful.
Those men, having caused that caravan leader Dharmalabdha to sit upon a great lion-throne made entirely of gold, consecrated him in the kingship.
The Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, monks, it might occur to you that at that time and on that occasion, the caravan leader named Dharmalabdha was someone else.
It should not be viewed in this way."
For what reason?
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, I was the caravan leader named Dharmalabdha.
She who was the senior rākṣasī is this daughter of Māra.
At that time, she was the senior among the rākṣasīs;
even then, she approached me seeking an opportunity to enter and looking for a way to gain access, yet she was unable to find an opening against me.
Even now, these women have approached me seeking an opportunity and looking for a way to gain entry, yet they were indeed unable to find any opening against me.
When King Dharmalabdha heard from his ministers that the woman was from across the great ocean, he did not desire her.
Immediately thereafter, the king commanded his great ministers:
"If he does not desire this woman, then cause her to enter my inner apartments."
Having recognized the obstacle, that rākṣasī did not eat them;
instead, she sent her son there as a messenger to inform the other rākṣasīs:
"The king has indeed been devoured by me; come quickly to take him!"
Five fierce rākṣasīs who feed on blood departed;
they all went to the royal palace and exerted their prowess as they had come.
Recalling his former dwelling and former birth, the Blessed One, the Teacher, recounted this Jātaka in the presence of the monks:
"Those aggregates, those elements, and those sense-bases."
Referring to himself, the Blessed One explained this matter:
"In the beginningless and endless cycle of existence where I formerly dwelt..."
"I was a merchant named Dharmalabdha, intent on my business;
the daughters of Māra were rākṣasīs—thus you should remember this Jātaka."
Thus, having been free from fever and free from sorrow, he beheld this immeasurable, ancient course of many sufferings, both high and low.
The Blessed One spoke in the midst of the community of monks.
The Jātaka of the caravan leader Dharmalabdha is completed.
The Naga king Kāla approached the Blessed One there at the great walking path.
Then, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he arranged his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms in reverence, and said this to the Blessed One.

“Blessed One, my abode was enjoyed by previous perfectly awakened ones—by the Blessed One Krakucchanda, by Konākamuni, and by Kāśyapa. It would be well, Blessed One, if you too would enjoy my abode out of compassion.”
There too, in the abode of Kāla the Naga king, the Blessed One spent the fourth week in the bliss of joy.
Then, at the end of that fourth week, the Blessed One arose from the abode of Kāla the Naga king.
The Naga King Mucilinda, who had seen previous Buddhas, approached the Blessed One.
He too, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, stood to one side with palms joined in reverence and made a request to the Blessed One.

"Blessed One, my abode was enjoyed by previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones—by the Blessed One Krakucchanda, by Konākamuni, and by Kāśyapa. It would be well, Blessed One, if you too, out of compassion, would enjoy my abode."
In the abode of the Naga king Mucilinda as well, the Blessed One spent the fifth week entirely without food, passing the time in the bliss of joy.

Then, an untimely storm arose there for seven days, and it rained day and night for seven days; the Naga King Mucilinda, having coiled his body seven times around the Blessed One with a circumference of half a yojana, covered him from above with his broad hood.

And just as the Naga King named Mucilinda, desiring that the Blessed One should not be afflicted by the stench of poison or the stench of evil, emerged from his own abode and covered him with his coils, shielding him with his hood made of dense, auspicious merit for seven days, thereby generating vast merit; so too did he act.
And by the nāga king Vinipāta, great merit was produced, for he surrounded it with a vast array of enjoyments for seven days.
When the Blessed One, the perfectly enlightened one, was practicing austerities on the bank of the river Nairañjanā, he was seen there by a goat-herder while he was performing those austerities.
Having seen the Blessed One performing fierce austerities, faith arose within him.
Then, with a mind full of faith, he planted a young *nyagrodha* tree dedicated to the Blessed One.
Having planted that young banyan tree, he approached the Blessed One and, with palms joined in reverence, said:

"Lord, this young banyan tree was planted by me with the Lord in mind, thinking: 'When this young banyan tree has grown up and the Lord has reached the completion of his life-span, then may you enjoy this banyan tree for my sake as a favor.'"
The Blessed One signaled his acceptance to that goat-herd by remaining silent.
Then, perceiving that silent acceptance, he became satisfied, elated, joyful, and filled with gladness and happiness.

Then, from time to time, he would dig around that young banyan tree, loosen it, turn it over, and break up the earth; and from time to time, he would sprinkle it, drench it, moisten it, and water it thoroughly with cool water.
Then, by the majestic power of the Blessed One’s splendor, that young banyan tree was quickly provided with many branches, becoming pleasing and beautiful to behold.
Then, seeing that young banyan tree with its trunk and branches, which was beautiful and inspiring of serene faith, the mind of that goat-herd became exceedingly clear.

Now, through that clarity of mind and that root of merit, upon the dissolution of the body, he was reborn in the realm of the Trāyastriṃśa gods as a son of the gods named Nyagrodha, possessed of great psychic power and great majesty.

Having been reborn later than others, he surpassed the other previously born sons of the Trāyastriṃśa gods in five divine respects: in divine lifespan, divine complexion, divine happiness, and divine sovereignty.
With a divine retinue.

Immediately upon being reborn there, this thought occurred to him: "What wholesome deed did I perform and accumulate while I was a human being, by the ripening of which karma have I been reborn here in this Trāyastriṃśa heaven?"
Then the divine son Nyagrodha, reflecting upon his roots of merit, saw that the Nyagrodha tree had been planted by him on the bank of the river Nairañjanā for the sake of the Blessed One.

Then the divine son Nyagrodha, surrounded by many thousands of divine sons, his complexion exceedingly radiant, having illuminated the entire palace of the Naga king Mucilinda with his sublime and magnificent splendor, approached the Blessed One; having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Standing with his palms joined in reverence, he addressed the Blessed One as follows.

"Lord, while I was a human being tending goats as a goat-herd, I planted this *nyagrodha* tree in honor of the Blessed One. By that root of merit, Lord, having passed away from among humans, I have been reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa host of gods.
It would be well, Lord, if the Blessed One would partake of this *nyagrodha* tree out of compassion, so that it may become even more fruitful for me."
The Blessed One consented to that son of the gods by remaining silent.

Then that son of the gods, perceiving his acceptance through silence, was satisfied, elated, joyful, and filled with gladness and happiness; he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated him three times to the right, and vanished right there.
The Blessed One, having risen from the abode of the Naga king Mucilinda, spent the sixth week without food at the foot of the Ajapala banyan tree, dwelling in the bliss of rapture.
Then, at the Ajapāla Nyagrodha tree,
after the passing of the sixth week, he spent the seventh week without food in the Kṣīrikā forest grove at the Bahudevataka Caitya, dwelling in the bliss of joy.
In this manner, the Blessed One remained without food for seven weeks, which is forty-nine days.
In the northern region, there was a city named Ukkala.

From that city of Ukkala, two caravan leaders named Trapusa and Bhallika— wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments, meritorious, and having a large retinue— were coming along that road from the southern region with five hundred wagons.
Among those auspicious bulls, one was born under the constellation Sujātā and the other under Kīrtika;
thus, by the names of those constellations, they were known as Sujāta and Kīrtika.
They carry the caravan leader’s vehicle in front of every other member of the caravan;

wherever there is any danger on the path— whether fear of lions, fear of tigers, fear of leopards, fear of bears, fear of elephants, fear of forest deities, fear of floods, or fear of thieves— they do not [fear] there.
Then those merchants, sensing that danger was imminent, withdrew their things and fled in all four directions, looking about on every side.
Then those oxen, Sujāta and Kīrtika, arrived at that Kṣīrikā forest grove;

there, by means of their supernatural power, they were restrained by the former kinsmen and maternal relatives of the merchants Trapuṣa and Bhalliya who had become gods, and they were unable to proceed.
