While they stood there, all those men, terrified of the caravan, took up their positions there in readiness.
Then their deities—former kinsmen and blood relatives—stationed in the intermediate space, raised a cry and made their voices heard.
"Do not fear, O merchants; no calamity shall befall you.

This Buddha, the Blessed One, dwells here in this forest grove, having appeared after seven incalculable eons for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, and for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of the great multitude of beings, including the gods."
Today marks the forty-ninth day—seven weeks—of that man’s being without food.
You should provide him with nourishment; from this, there will arise for you an immeasurable root of merit.
Then, having heard those words of the deities, the merchants Trapuṣa and Bhallika took refreshment mixed with honey and ghee.
Those deities went before those merchants,
saying, "Come this way."
Then those merchants were led into the presence of the Blessed One by those deities.
Taking that honey-refreshment, they approached the Blessed One and said,
"May the Blessed One partake of this honey-refreshment for the sake of showing us favor."
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to the Blessed One:
"Indeed, did the former Perfectly Enlightened Ones receive offerings with vessels, or did they receive them with their own hands? Did the Perfectly Enlightened Ones receive offerings with vessels?"

Simultaneously with the arising of that thought, the four great world-protectors approached the Blessed One, each carrying a golden bowl; thinking them to be bowls made of jewels, they were not suitable for a renunciant, so the Blessed One did not accept them.
Then, taking those bowls made of silver, they approached the Blessed One;
however, considering them to be bowls made of precious materials, the Blessed One did not accept them.

In this way, whether they were made of pearl, beryl, crystal, musāragalva, or ruby, the Blessed One did not accept them, considering them to be jeweled bowls and deeming them unsuitable for one who has gone forth.
Then those four, taking their stone bowls, approached the Blessed One.
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to the Blessed One:
"If I accept the bowl from only one world-protector, there will be a change of heart in the other three."
The Blessed One accepted the four bowls from all four world-protectors, pressed them down with his thumb, and consecrated them as a single bowl.
Those four bowls then became one bowl, yet the four rims of all four bowls remained visible.
There, the Blessed One partook of the honey-mixture offered by the merchants Trapusa and Bhallika.

Then the Blessed One, having drunk the honey-refreshment provided by the merchants Trapusa and Mallika—which was fresh, exquisite, and endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and flavor—pronounced a blessing.
That which is endowed with many excellent qualities is called "satisfying," being perfect in color, as well as in fragrance and flavor.
Fresh, exquisite, desirable, and permissible,
they first offered the Teacher satiated food consisting of *trapusa* and *bhallika* fruits.
Let that best of men drink it mixed with honey and ghee;
satisfied by these, the hero, having arisen from his meditative seclusion,
shall satisfy gods, gandharvas, and humans with a rain of Dharma.
I shall bestow upon you this divine *svastika* blessing, auspicious and effective in accomplishing all goals;
hearing which, everyone with a joyful mind will achieve every purpose.
May there be well-being for you bipeds; may there be well-being for you quadrupeds.
May there be well-being for those traveling on the road, and well-being for those who have returned.
May there be well-being at night and by day; may there be well-being when the midday stands firm. May there be well-being for you everywhere, and may no evil come upon you.
Glory is established upon your right shoulder, and glory is established upon your left;
glory is well-established in every limb of yours, like a garland.
May there be well-being for you, may there be auspicious glory for you, O merchants; may there be prosperity for you as you go toward the eastern direction for whatever business you have.
May the constellations that preside over that direction protect you:
Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, and Punarvasu.
Puṣya is the excellent lunar mansion, and Aśleṣā is the seventh.
Thus, these seven illustrious lunar mansions are the guardians of the world;
they are assigned to the eastern quarter, and the eastern direction belongs to them.
May these protect you both on the ground and within your dwellings;
may the directions be safe for you, and may no evil come upon you.
Having achieved your purpose, may you return home, guarded by those constellations.
In the eastern quarter, there are eight divine maidens:
Nandottarā, Nandiṣeṇā, Nandinī, and Nandirakṣitā.
Jayantī, Vijayantī, Siddhārthā, and Aparājitā—
their sovereign king was known by the name Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
The king who is the lord of the gandharvas is protected by the gods;
may he also protect you both on the earth and in your dwelling.
May the directions be secure for you, and may no evil come upon you;
having achieved your purpose, may you return protected by all the gods.
In the eastern quarter stands the shrine named Cāpala;
it constantly blazes with splendor and its prayers for truth are ever answered.
May it also protect you with its presence upon the earth and its dwelling place.
May the directions be secure for you, and may no evil come upon you;
having achieved your purpose, may you return, well-protected by all the shrines.
For whatever purpose you go to the southern direction,
may the constellations that preside over that direction protect you.
Maghā, both Phalgunīs, Hastā, Citrā as the fifth,
Svātī, and Viśākhā— these belong to the southern direction.
Thus, these seven illustrious lunar mansions are the guardians of the world;
they are assigned to the southern quarter, and this is their southern direction.
May they also protect you both on the journey and at home;
may the quarters be safe for you, and may no evil come upon you.
Having achieved your purpose, may you return, guarded by those constellations.
In the southern quarter are eight divine maidens:
Lakṣmīmatī, Śrīmatī, Yaśomatī, and Yaśodharā.
Established in virtue, radiant, perfectly pure, and well-prophesied—
may they also protect you by means of their ground and their dwelling.
May the directions be secure for you, and may no evil come upon you;
having achieved your purpose, return protected by the daughters of the gods.
Their sovereign is the king named Virūḍhaka;
may the king, the lord of the kumbhāṇḍas, protect [them] together with Yama.
May the directions be secure for you, and may no evil come upon you;
having achieved your purpose, return well-protected by the kumbhāṇḍas.
In the southern quarter, I beheld a shrine named Abhipaśya;
it constantly blazes with splendor and its prayers for truth are ever fulfilled.
May he also protect you with his presence upon the earth;
may the quarters be secure for you, and may no evil come to you.
Having accomplished your purpose, may you return well-guarded by the shrine.
Go toward the western direction for whatever purpose you have;
may the constellations that preside over that direction protect you.
Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Mūla are possessed of firm vigor;
both Āṣāḍhas, Abhijit, and Śravaṇā constitute the seventh [group].
May they also protect you both on the journey and at home;
may the directions be safe for you, and may no evil come upon you.
Having achieved your purpose, may you return, guarded by those constellations.
In the western direction, there are eight divine maidens:
Alambuṣā, Miśrakeśī, Ariṣṭā, and Suprabhāyakā.
...and Kṛṣṇā Śuklā Draupadī—
may they also protect you with health and auspiciousness.
May the directions be secure for you, and may no evil come upon you;
having achieved your purpose, return home, protected by celestial maidens.
Their sovereign king is named Virūpākṣa;
may that king, the lord of the nāgas, together with Varuṇa, protect you.
May he also protect you with his presence upon the earth;
may the quarters be secure for you, and may no evil come to you.
Having achieved your purpose, return protected by all the nāgas.
In the western quarter of the world is the mountain named Asta;
may the turning point of the moon and sun, Asta, grant you prosperity.
May he also protect you both by means of the earth and by his dwelling.
May the directions be safe for you, and may no evil come upon you;
having achieved your purpose, may you all return protected from thieves.
Go toward the northern direction for whatever purpose you have;
may the constellations that preside over that direction protect you.
Dhaniṣṭhā and Śatabhiṣā, both the Proṣṭhapadas as well,
Revatī and Aśvinī, and Bharaṇī is the seventh.
May they also protect you with the ground and with their dwellings;
may the quarters be secure for you, and may no evil come upon you.
Having achieved your purpose, return home, protected by those constellations.
In the northern quarter there are eight divine maidens:
the goddess Ilā, the goddess Surā, Pṛthivī, and Padmāvatī.
May Āśā, Śraddhā, Hrī, and Śrī, having come together,
likewise protect you both by means of the earth and by means of their own abodes.
May the directions be secure for you, and may no evil come upon you;
having achieved your purpose, return, protected by the daughters of the gods.
Their sovereign is the king named Kuvera;
may the king, lord of all yakṣas, protect [us] together with the rākṣasīs.
May he also protect you with his presence upon the earth;
may the quarters be secure for you, and may no evil come to you.
Having achieved your purpose, return, guarded by yakṣas and rākṣasas.
In the northern quarter lies the mountain named Kailāsa;
it is the abode of the hosts of yakṣas and the dwelling place of the rākṣasas.
May he also protect you both on the journey and at home;
may the directions be safe for you, and may no evil come upon you.
Having accomplished your purpose, return protected by yakṣas and rākṣasas.
There are twenty-eight constellations, seven in each of the four directions;
together with the moon and the sun, they total thirty, no less.
Thirty-two celestial maidens, eight in each of the four directions,
and the four illustrious Great Kings, the guardians of the world,
protect the four directions with their blazing radiance.
May the eight śramaṇas, the eight brahmins, the eight kṣatriyas of the [eight] regions,
and the eight gods together with Indra, always grant you protection.
Then the Blessed One gave them the three goings for refuge:
"Go for refuge to the Buddha; go for refuge to the Dharma; go for refuge to the Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples in the future."
They have now gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dharma, and gone for refuge to the Saṅgha.
Then they said:
“O Blessed One, we are merchants who travel through various lands and kingdoms.
It would be well if the Blessed One would grant us some relic that we might worship.”
Then the Blessed One, having pulled out the hair from their heads with his hand, gave it to them, saying, "Have this Hair-Stūpa built.
Having also pulled out the nails and given them, he said, "Have this Nail-Stūpa constructed. He added, "The stone will arrive;
you must install that stone [as the foundation]."
Then, they had a hair-stūpa constructed at the district called Keśasthālī;
they had a nail-stūpa constructed at the city called Vālukṣa;
and at the district called Śilukṣa, a stone was also installed there, which had been thrown by the Blessed One’s hand through his supernatural power.

Now, after forty-nine days—seven weeks—of being without food, the Blessed One drank a honey-refreshment from the merchants Trapuṣa and Bhallika; once he had drunk it, they were overwhelmed by the Blessed One.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, offered a myrobalan fruit to the Blessed One, saying,
"It shall be the gateway for the relics."
The Blessed One then consumed that myrobalan fruit, and he planted its stalk right there in that same spot.
On that very day, it grew with branches and twigs, becoming a great myrobalan tree endowed with flowers and fruit;
this was the Blessed One’s first “miracle-tree.”
And those myrobalans which were from that tree, they now recognize as the young sprouts of the myrobalan trees of Cetakī.
Then, at Uruvilvā, the Blessed One practiced austerities for six years.
At that time, in Uruvilvā, from the village of Senāpati, a hempen rag-robe was offered with a devout heart to the Blessed One while he was practicing austerities at Nagara-valambikā;
[she said], "When the Blessed One's resolve is fulfilled, then please accept and use this hempen rag-robe as a favor."

Perceiving the Blessed One’s acceptance through his silence, she was satisfied and joyful; she hung her rag-robe from a tree branch, bowed her head at the Blessed One’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.

Not long after that, she passed away with a mind full of serene faith, recollecting that gift of a rag-robe from the presence of the Blessed One. Immediately upon her death, she was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven among the gods,
as the most excellent of hundreds of thousands of apsarases in the celestial palace of a certain son of the gods of great psychic power and majesty.
Then that apsaras reflected:
"What root of merit did I, while being a human being, perform, and what kind of gift did I establish, by which I have been reborn in the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa gods?"
She then reflected and saw that in the village of Senāpati at Uruvilvā, there had once been a distressed woman named Gavā who was a supporter of the city.

At the time of my death, while the Bodhisattva was practicing austerities, she gave him a hempen rag-robe with a devout heart. By virtue of that root of merit, having passed away from among humans, I have been reborn here in this assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
And that gift of mine has not yet been enjoyed by the Blessed Ones;
if the Blessed One would enjoy this very gift out of favor toward me, that would be of even greater fruit for me.

Then that goddess, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of apsarases and with great divine majesty and great divine power, took that hempen rag-robe from the branch of a tree in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven and approached the Blessed One.

This hempen rag-robe was given by me with a devout heart to the Blessed One while he was practicing austerities as a human being. "When the Blessed One’s resolve is fulfilled, then, O Blessed One, please accept it for my sake. By that root of merit, having passed away from among humans, I have been reborn in the realm of the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
"May the Blessed One, out of compassion, please accept this hempen rag-robe from me, so that it may become of great fruit for me."
The gods, situated in the intermediate space, said to the Blessed One:
"May the Blessed One not accept this hempen rag-robe; we shall give the Blessed One divine, choice garments."
The Blessed One did not accept the offerings of fine garments from those deities;

however, he accepted the hempen rag-robe from Gavāṅgī, the city-dweller. Then, hundreds of thousands of deities from the sky threw down handfuls of cloth for the Blessed One and raised shouts of "Ha! and cries of joy.
The sovereignty of a universal monarch has been renounced; why does our mind not find delight in rag-robes?
Now the Blessed One, desiring to wash his hempen rag-robe, had need of water.
Then indeed, Śakra, the lord of the gods, dug a river with his hands; even today, that river is called "Hand-Dug."
Where there is need for a stone slab, he will wash that hempen rag-robe upon it.
The four Great Kings presented four stone slabs;
on one of those stone slabs, the Blessed One washed that hempen rag-robe.
On the second stone slab, that coarse robe was dried.
The Blessed One, by means of his supernormal power, lifted up the third stone slab there before Trapusa and Bhallika, who were staying in the town named Śilukṣa.
They established that stone slab right there at the stūpa;
even today, it is known as the seat named Śilā within the kingdom of Gandhāra.
On the fourth stone slab, the Blessed One sat down and sewed that hempen rag-robe;
even now, that stone slab bears the name "The Blessed One’s Sewing Seat."
All four stone slabs were consumed by the Blessed One, and they became objects of veneration for the world of gods and humans in Jambudvīpa.

The Blessed One, having now washed and sewn that hempen rag-robe, descended to the river Pāṇikhātā to bathe. Having bathed, as the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are untiring in body and untiring in mind, he intended to emerge from the river Pāṇikhātā; there on the bank was a tree named Kakubha, with spreading branches and twigs, beautiful and lovely to behold. Its name was—
There was a tree of that same name, and the deity of that tree was a son of the gods named Kakubha who resided there.
That son of the gods was addressed by the Blessed One as he was crossing over from that river.
Bring forth your hand, O Kakubha!
The divine son Kakubha, wearing excellent and stainless earrings, extended his arm toward the Blessed One.

The Blessed One took the divine son Kakubha’s arm and crossed the river Pāṇikhātā; and as soon as he had crossed, the Blessed One withdrew his own hand from the divine son Kakubha’s arm, and there, upon the branch of a tree—
A lotus is seen upon the palm of the Blessed One’s five-fingered hand.
"Now, that for the sake of which I [struck] the Bodhi tree with my hand—the beautiful *kakubha* tree, the *nadīkā*, the stone dug out by the hand—has been placed there by the gods.
Thereupon, the Blessed One went to the Goatherd’s Banyan tree.
While staying at the foot of the banyan tree of Ajapāla, the Blessed One investigated the world.

This Dharma that I have fully awakened to is profound, subtle, refined, difficult to understand, beyond the sphere of logic, to be realized by the wise, and contrary to the whole world. Furthermore, these beings delight in the *ālaya*, rejoice in the *ālaya*, and thrive in the *ālaya*; and for people who delight in, rejoice in, and thrive in the *ālaya*, this point is difficult to see—namely, dependent origination as "this being the cause, this being the condition."

The relinquishing of all acquisitions, the stilling of all volitional formations, the cutting off of the continuity of phenomena, the exhaustion of craving, dispassion, cessation, and Nirvana— if I were not to teach this to others, and others were not to comprehend it from me, that would be a source of distress for me.
"What if I were now to dwell alone, silent, on a mountain in the forest?
And at that moment, these verses occurred to the Blessed One:
My path goes against the current; it is profound and difficult to see.
Those stained by passion will not perceive it; enough now with further exposition.
It has been attained by me with great difficulty; enough now with proclaiming it!
For men, swallowed up by sensual desires, are carried away with the current.
The Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvilvā on the bank of the Nairañjanā river, at the foot of the Goatherd’s Banyan tree, having recently attained full enlightenment.
Then, while the Blessed One was alone, in seclusion, and in retreat, this reflection arose in his mind:

Since this Dharma which has been realized by me is profound, subtle, delicate, difficult to understand, beyond logic, outside the sphere of reasoning, to be known by the wise, and contrary to the whole world— if I were to teach it to others and they were not to comprehend it, that would be a supreme weariness for me.
"What if I were now to dwell alone in silence in a forest retreat?"
Then indeed, Mahābrahmā, having understood this kind of reflection in the mind of the Blessed One, approached Śakra, the lord of the gods, and said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods:
"Friend Kauśika, the Blessed One inclines his mind toward a state of little zeal, not toward setting the Wheel of Dharma in motion.
Nevertheless, friend Kauśika, let us approach the Blessed One and entreat the Blessed One to set the Wheel of Dharma in motion."
"Very well, worthy sir," Śakra, the lord of the gods, replied to Mahābrahmā.
Then indeed, Mahābrahmā, Śakra the lord of the gods, the divine son Suyāma, the divine son Sunirmita,

the divine son Vaśavartin, the four Great Kings, these ten lords of yakṣas, and ten senior yakṣas with retinues of many hundreds of yakṣas, when the night had passed, illuminated the entire vicinity of the foot of the Nyagrodha tree with their radiance.
They approached the place where the Blessed One was, bowed their heads at the Blessed One’s feet, and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, Mahābrahmā said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods:
And you, worthy Kauśika, entreat the Blessed One to set the Wheel of Dharma in motion.
Then indeed Śakra, the lord of the gods, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, approached the Blessed One and addressed the Blessed One in verse:
Arise, O conqueror in battle! You have fulfilled your burden; wander through the world free from debt, for your mind is as pure as the moon on the fifteenth night.
Then the Blessed One remained silent and did not consent to Śakra, the lord of the gods, turning the wheel of Dharma.
Then Mahābrahmā spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods:
Indeed, worthy Kauśika, the Blessed Ones, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones are not thus entreated to turn the wheel of Dharma;
nor do the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones turn the wheel of Dharma when so entreated.
When this had been said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, spoke thus to Mahābrahmā:
"Venerable Mahābrahmā, you have shown these former perfectly awakened ones; therefore, Venerable Mahābrahmā, you yourself should entreat the Blessed One to set the wheel of Dharma in motion."
Then Mahābrahmā, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder and extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One in verse:
Arise, O conqueror of battle! You have fulfilled your task; wander the world free from debt.
Teach the Dharma, O Sugata; there will be those who understand.
Then the Blessed One remained silent.

Then indeed, Mahābrahmā, Śakra the lord of the gods, the divine son Suyāma, the divine son Saṃtuṣita, the divine son Nirmita, the divine son Vaśavartin, the four Great Kings, and many hundreds of yakṣas with their retinues of many hundreds of yakṣas,
perceiving the Blessed One’s non-acceptance regarding the turning of the wheel of Dharma, became filled with suffering and dejection before the Blessed One.
Having bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and circumambulated him, they vanished right there.
In this regard, this is heard:
The Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvilvā, on the bank of the Nairañjanā river, at the foot of the Goatherd’s Banyan tree, having recently attained full enlightenment.
Then, indeed, Mahābrahmā, whose complexion was transcendent, when the night had passed, having illuminated the entire vicinity of the Goatherd’s Banyan tree with his radiance,
approached the Blessed One. Having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and circumambulated the Blessed One, Mahābrahmā stood to one side and addressed the Blessed One in verse:
Arise, O conqueror of battle! You have fulfilled your burden; wander through the world free from debt.
Teach the Dharma, O Sugata; there will be those who understand.
Then the Blessed One replied to Mahābrahmā in verse:
My path goes against the stream; it is profound and difficult to see.
Those who are stained by passion will not perceive it; enough, O Brahmā, with proclaiming it.

Then, having learned of the Blessed One’s refusal at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree regarding the turning of the wheel of Dharma, Mahābrahmā was filled with grief and dejection. He bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One,
circumambulated the Blessed One, and vanished on the spot.
In this regard, this is heard:
The Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvilvā on the bank of the river Nairañjanā, at the foot of the Goatherd’s Banyan tree, having recently attained full enlightenment.
Furthermore, at that time, such evil and unwholesome views as these arose among the brahmins and householders of Magadha.

The wind would not blow, the rivers would not flow, pregnant women would not give birth, birds would not fly about, fire would not burn, and the rising of the moon and sun would not be perceived; the world would become enveloped in blinding darkness.

Then, indeed, Mahābrahmā, having perceived that such evil and unwholesome views had arisen among the brahmins and householders of Magadha, and having surpassed [all others] in beauty, at the end of the night, illuminated the entire vicinity of the root of the banyan tree belonging to Ajapāla with his radiance, approached the Blessed One.
Having bowed his head at the feet [of the Buddha], he stood to one side and recited this verse:
In the past, an impure Dharma conceived by those with defilements appeared in Magadha;
now you have opened the door to the Deathless.
May they hear the Dharma, awakened to by the Immaculate One.

Then the Blessed One, having understood the request of Mahābrahmā and by means of his own personal knowledge of awakening, beheld the entire world with his unsurpassed Buddha-eye; he saw beings of high and low status, inferior and superior; he saw beings of ugly form, difficult to discipline, and difficult to purify; he saw beings.
He saw beings who were of good disposition, easy to discipline, and easy to purify; he saw beings of quick understanding, of analytical understanding, and those for whom the word is supreme.
He saw beings of sharp faculties and of powerful faculties. He saw the three groups of beings: the group fixed in rightness, the group fixed in falsehood, and the undetermined group.
Just as a man with sight, standing on the bank of a lotus pond, might see with little difficulty blue lotuses,

red lotuses, or white lotuses— some within the water, some level with the water, and others rising above the water— even so the Blessed One, surveying the entire world with his unsurpassed Buddha-eye, beheld it all.
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to the Blessed One:

Whether I teach the Dharma or do not teach it, those fixed in the group of the false (mithyātva-niyata-rāśi) are incapable of understanding this Dharma. Whether I teach it or do not teach it, those fixed in the group of the right (samyaktva-niyata-rāśi) will certainly understand whatever I may teach. As for those in the undetermined group (aniyata-rāśi), if I teach them the Dharma they will understand it; if I do not teach it, they will not know it.

Then the Blessed One, having understood that such evil and unwholesome views had arisen among the Magadhan brahmins and householders concerning the indeterminate group (aniyata-rāśi), and having understood the entreaty of Mahābrahmā, as well as his own vow fulfilled and brought forth over seven incalculable eons for the sake of sentient beings;

And having entered upon great compassion, these lords of gods of great majesty, the Lords of the World, approached me and entreated me to set in motion the Noble Wheel of Dharma. Then the Blessed One granted permission to Great Brahmā to set in motion the Noble Wheel of Dharma.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed Mahābrahmā in verse:
"The door to the Deathless has been opened for me;
O Blessed One, those who desire to hear this Brahman,
let them cast aside their lack of faith and their intent to cause trouble."
In Magadha, the Dharma was previously impure, characterized by harmful intent and lacking in excellence.
Then, indeed, when the Blessed One had granted permission to Mahābrahmā for the turning of the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, the gods of the earth raised a cry.
Thus, worthy sir, has the Blessed One granted the opportunity to Brahmā for the turning of the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.

That shall be for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, welfare, and happiness of the great multitude of beings—both gods and humans. The hosts of Asuras will diminish, and the divine hosts will increase.
Having heard the cry of the gods of the earth, the gods of the Four Great Kings, the gods of the Thirty-three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods,
and the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods raised their voices and made this sound heard.
Thus, worthy sir, the Blessed One has granted the opportunity for the Great Brahmā to set in motion the Wheel of Dharma.

This will be for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of the great multitude of beings, both gods and humans; the hosts of Asuras will diminish, and the divine hosts will increase.
Thus, at that time and on that occasion, a cry rose up as far as the Brahma-world.
In this regard, this is heard:
Then, at the time of setting it in motion, the Blessed One asked: "What kind of beings set the noble wheel of Dharma in motion?"
Those beings who are endowed with prior practice set in motion the noble wheel of Dharma. Indeed, I am endowed with prior practice; therefore, I am worthy to set in motion the noble wheel of Dharma.
Those beings who are endowed with unsurpassed conduct—beings of such a kind set in motion the noble wheel of Dharma.
Furthermore, I am indeed endowed with unsurpassed conduct; I am worthy to set in motion the Noble Wheel of Dharma.

Those beings who are endowed with the excellence of unsurpassed dwelling—such beings as these set in motion the Noble Wheel of Dharma. Those beings who are unique—such beings as these set in motion the Noble Wheel of Dharma.
Those beings who are endowed with a perfect passing away—such beings set the noble wheel of Dharma in motion.

Those beings who are endowed with a perfect descent into the womb—such beings set the noble wheel of Dharma in motion. Those beings who are endowed with a perfect stay in the womb, those beings who are endowed with a perfect birth—those [beings set the noble wheel of Dharma in motion].
Those beings who are endowed with the primary marks, those who are endowed with the secondary characteristics, those who are endowed with skillfulness,

those who are endowed with fortitude, those who are endowed with mindfulness, those who are endowed with the presence of the Dharma, those who are endowed with the qualities of a Sage, those who are preeminent in the world, those who are endowed with the discernment of the world, and those who are endowed with the essence of being— [they are such].

Those who, by means of right wisdom, understand what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible; those who, by means of right wisdom, understand as it truly is the path leading everywhere and the paths leading to various destinations;
those who, by means of right wisdom, understand as it truly is the world of diverse elements and the world of manifold elements; and those [who understand] other beings and other individuals...

Those who understand, as it truly is, the diversity of the faculties and the vigor of beings, they alone set the wheel of Dharma in motion. Those who, through right wisdom, understand as it truly is those in the world who have various inclinations and those in the world who have manifold inclinations, they alone set the wheel of Dharma in motion.

Those beings who correctly and thoroughly understand, as it truly is, the diversity of the ripening of all actions and undertakings of action— past, future, and present— that have been performed and accumulated, whose ripening has not yet matured, but whose ripening is imminent, and which will result in diverse ripenings in the future; they alone set the Wheel of Dharma in motion.

Those who, with respect to all meditations, concentrations, liberations, and attainments, understand as it truly is both affliction and purification; and those who, with the purified divine eye, which transcends that of humans, see sentient beings passing away and being reborn— be they beautiful or ugly, in happy states or miserable states, lowly or exalted— sentient beings according to their karma.
Beings of such a kind clearly understand as they set in motion the Noble Wheel of Dharma;

those who recollect their manifold former abodes, and those who, through the destruction of the outflows, clearly understand as they truly are the outflow-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and those who are long-lived and perfected in livelihood.

They become endowed with ethical discipline, endowed with meditative concentration, endowed with liberation, and endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation; they are endowed with renunciation, endowed with the attainment of great compassion, endowed with awakening, endowed with the knowledge of others' mental states, endowed with the miracle of supernatural power, endowed with the miracle of mind-reading, and endowed with the miracle of instruction; they are possessed of all wholesome qualities.

Those who have attained the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of language (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*);

those endowed with the noble five-limbed concentration (*pañcāṅgika-samādhi*), endowed with the fivefold wisdom-concentration (*pañcajñānika-samādhi*), and endowed with the noble great five-limbed right concentration (*mahāpañcāṅgika-samyak-samādhi*);
and those who have attained the noble great fivefold wisdom-right concentration, who are perfected in the powers (*bala*) and perfected in the faculties (*indriya*).

And those who are endowed with supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), and those who are also endowed with speech that is refined, distinct, and faultless, capable of making the meaning understood; those who are perfected in answering questions, and who are capable of cutting through the arguments of others out of confidence (*vaiśāradya*);
and those who are capable of rightfully subduing others who wish them harm.
In order to bestow happiness upon others, they set in motion such a noble wheel of Dharma;
those beings who are endowed with all the qualities of a Buddha, such beings set in motion the noble wheel of Dharma.
Furthermore, being endowed with all the qualities of a Buddha, I am indeed worthy to set in motion the wheel of Dharma.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One, having recognized this kind of undertaking of his own qualities, thought this:
"What if I were now to set in motion the noble, unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma?
Who indeed would be capable of understanding the Dharma first as it is taught by me, and who would not cause me distress regarding this teaching of the Dharma?"
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to the Blessed One:

Udraka Rāmaputra was pure, with little dust, of a nature beyond doubt; he had gone far and transcended, teaching the Dharma for the sake of dwelling in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Today, seven days after his passing, Udraka Rāmaputra has died—a great loss indeed for Udraka Rāmaputra!

"Indeed, who else is there among beings who is pure, with little dust in their eyes, of a nature not lacking in direct vision, who would be capable of understanding the first Dharma taught by me and would not cause me trouble while listening to this Dharma?"

Ārāḍa Kālāma was pure, with little dust in his eyes, of a nature with little dust, and capable of understanding the first teaching I proclaimed; he would not have disturbed me while listening to this Dharma. It is a great loss for Ārāḍa that he has passed away three days ago.

"But who else is there, another being, pure and of a nature with little dust, who is capable of understanding the Dharma taught by me for the first time, and who will not trouble me regarding this hearing of the Dharma?
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to the Blessed One.
The group of five auspicious companions— pure, with little dust, and of a nature possessing little dust—
are capable of understanding the Dharma when first taught by me, and they will not cause me any disturbance regarding this hearing of the Dharma;
for they have followed me even previously while I was practicing austerities.
And they were dwelling at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.
"What if I were now to go to Vārāṇasī and, at the Deer Park in Ṛṣipatana near Vārāṇasī, teach the Dharma for the first time to the group of five auspicious ones?"
Then, indeed, many powerful deities belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm approached the Blessed One; having bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they stood to one side.
Standing to one side, they said this to the Blessed One:

"Since it is well-known and thoroughly understood by the Blessed One's disciples, and since we are indeed capable of performing various and manifold miraculous feats of supernatural power for the Blessed One—
we shall follow the path by which the Blessed One will go from the place of awakening to Vārāṇasī, to the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana,
in order to set in motion the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma; therefore, we shall [follow] the Blessed One from the place of awakening as far as Vārāṇasī."

We shall prepare the road—level, even, and free of unevenness, like the palm of a hand; with canopies spread out, surrounded by variegated cloth hangings, draped with bundles of silk ribbons and streamers;

sprinkled and swept clean, perfumed with incense, strewn with loose flowers, covered with golden sand, covered with divine pearl dust, covered with divine crystal dust, and covered with divine musāragalva gemstone dust.
It shall be strewn with divine red powder.
And there, O Blessed One, along the path from where enlightenment is until Vārāṇasī, we shall manifest divine rows of palm trees—
transparent, level, like sand, providing comfort, variegated and beautiful, in seven colors.
Of gold, silver, pearl, beryl, crystal, emerald,
and ruby; and there, O Blessed One, we shall manifest divine rivers on both the left and right sides of the path— clear, level, sandy, pleasant, and strewn with golden sand.

Covered with blue lotuses, red lotuses, night-blooming water lilies, white lotuses, nalini-lotuses, and fragrant saugandhikas; and with mangoes, rose-apples, lakucas, jackfruits, coconuts, pālevatas, bhavyas, pomegranates, and vṛddhikas;

there, O Blessed One, along the road from [here] to Bodhi and as far as Vārāṇasī, we shall manifest divine parasols, we shall manifest divine banners, and we shall manifest divine gabled pavilions—wondrous and beautiful, made of the seven precious substances: gold, silver, pearl, beryl, crystal, and musāgalva.
Of Lohitikā.

As the Blessed One walks, they will walk; as he stands, they will stand; and before him, the sons of the gods who are rain-clouds will scatter divine flowers, and the gods will gently spread out their [garments].

When the Blessed One set out from Bodhimaṇḍa for Ṛṣipatana, the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī, in order to turn the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven prepared the path. Having conjured up a great fourfold army—a vast elephant corps, a vast cavalry, a vast chariot corps, and a vast infantry—they escorted the Blessed One as he proceeded toward Vārāṇasī;
even the lords of the Suvarṇas, the Suvarṇa kings—whether born from eggs, from a womb, spontaneously, or from moisture—did so.
Or they, having miraculously conjured a great fourfold army by their supernatural power, went before the Blessed One as he traveled.

Even the nāgas— the lords of nāgas and nāga kings, whether born from eggs, from a womb, from moisture, or by spontaneous birth— having miraculously conjured a great fourfold army by their supernatural power, went before the Blessed One as he was traveling toward Vārāṇasī.

The gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, the Nirmāṇarati, the Paranirmitavaśavartin, and the Brahmakāyika gods, having miraculously manifested a great fourfold army, escorted the Blessed One as he was going to Kāśī.

Then indeed the Blessed One, honored and surrounded by a great assembly of many hundreds, many thousands, and many hundreds of thousands, went from Uruvilvā to Gayā, and from Gayā he went to Aparagayā.
In Aparagayā there was a king of the nāgas named Sudarśana;
he invited the Blessed One to stay in Aparagayā and to accept a meal.
Having stayed there in the abode of the nāga king Sudarśana and having taken his meal, the Blessed One proceeded to Vaśālā.
In Vaśālā, there was a brahmin named Nadi who was said to be of a "huhunka" disposition; as the Blessed One was passing by, he circumambulated him counter-clockwise and uttered the sound "huhuṃ."
On this matter, on this occasion, on this account, at that time, the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance:
That brahmin who has warded off evil qualities, who is free from grumbling, free from impurity, self-restrained, whose taints are exhausted, and who bears his final body— him I call a brahmin.
In accordance with the Dharma, he would speak the Brahma-discourse to the Brahmins.
In Vaśālā, a certain householder invited the Blessed One for lodging and a meal. Having stayed there and finished his meal, the Blessed One departed from Vaśālā for the town named Cundadvīla.

Upaka the Ājīvaka saw the Blessed One coming from afar; having seen him, he approached the Blessed One, exchanged polite and friendly greetings with him, and after exchanging courteous words, stood to one side. Standing to one side, Upaka the Ājīvaka said this to the Blessed One:
The complexion of the Blessed Gautama is completely pure, perfectly bright, and his facial expression is serene.
Just as the stalk-attachment of a ripe palmyra fruit that has recently fallen from its stem is completely pure,
perfectly bright, and has a golden luster, even so is the complexion of the Blessed Gautama completely pure.
Today the facial complexion of the Blessed Gautama is purified and serene; the Deathless has been attained by the Blessed Gautama, as well as the path leading to the Deathless.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Upaka the Ājīvaka.
O Upaka, the Deathless has been attained by me, as well as the path leading to the Deathless.
When this had been said, Upaka spoke thus to the Blessed One.
Where, O Gautama, is your holy life lived?
When this had been said, the Blessed One addressed Upaka the Ājīvaka in verse:
I am the conqueror of all, the knower of all; I am unsullied by any phenomena.
I am omniscient, liberated through the destruction of craving.
Having directly known this, what indeed should I point out?
When this had been said, Upaka the Ājīvaka spoke thus to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One Gautama is not without a teacher; you do not understand this.
Then the Blessed One addressed Upaka the Ājīvaka in verse:
I have no teacher whatsoever; there is no one equal to me to be found.
I am the uniquely awakened one in the world, having attained supreme enlightenment.
When this had been said, Upaka the Ājīvaka said this to the Blessed One:
"Does the Blessed One Gautama acknowledge himself to be an Arhat?"
Then the Blessed One addressed Upaka the Ājīvaka in verse:
For I am indeed the Worthy One in the world; I am the unsurpassed one in the world.
In this world with its gods, no one equal to me is found.
When this had been said, Upaka the Ājīvaka spoke thus to the Blessed One.
"The Victor" refers to the Blessed One Gautama; he understands this.
Then the Blessed One addressed Upaka the Ājīvaka in verse:
For those like me become Jinas who have attained the destruction of the outflows;
evil states have been conquered by me, therefore, Upaka, I am a Jina.
Just as a white lotus is not stained by the mud, so am I not stained by the world; therefore, Upaka, I am a Conqueror.
That which is to be directly known has been directly known; that which is to be spoken has been well spoken;
that which is to be abandoned has been abandoned by me. Therefore, Upaka, I am a Victor.
When this had been said, Upaka the Ājīvaka spoke thus to the Blessed One:
"Where will the Blessed Gautama go?"
Then the Blessed One addressed Upaka the Ājīvaka in verse:
I shall go to Vārāṇasī; I shall beat the drum of the Deathless;
I shall set in motion the Wheel of Dharma, which is irreversible in the world.
This Dharma which I have realized— dispassionate, peaceful,
and auspicious— I shall set forth for the benefit of all living beings.
Those who were the perfectly awakened ones of the past, those who are the Buddhas of the future,
and those who are the perfectly awakened ones at present— removers of the grief of many—
they teach the Dharma to sentient beings; this is the nature of the Buddhas.
The deities spoke this verse from the midst of the sky:
Whoever, having seen such a great seer, the charioteer who tames men, should avoid him with their hands and feet, [they lose] that great glory.
I bow down to him to an exceeding degree.
In Cundadvīlā, there was a yakṣa named Cunda.
By him, the Blessed One was invited to dwell in his own residence and to partake of a meal.
Having stayed for one night in the abode of the yakṣa Cunda and having finished his meal, the Blessed One proceeded from Sārathipura to Lohitavastuka.
In Lohitavastuka there was a nāga king named Kamaṇḍaluka.
He invited the Blessed One to his own abode for lodging and a meal.
There too, the Blessed One, having stayed for one night and finished his meal, proceeded from Lohitaka to Gandhapura.
In Gandhapura there dwells a yakṣa named Kandha;
he invited the Blessed One to his own abode for lodging and a meal.
There too, the Blessed One, having stayed for one night and finished his meal, proceeded toward Sārathipura.
In Sārathipura, the Blessed One was invited by a certain householder for lodging and a meal.
There too, the Blessed One, having stayed for one night and finished his meal, arrived at the bank of the Ganges from Sārathipura.
Then the boatman said:
Give me the fare for crossing.
The Blessed One said:
How could there be a toll for me, who am equal toward a clod of earth and gold, and from whom the notions of "precious metal" and "silver" have departed?
The boatman said:
"If you give it to me, you will cross over; but if you do not give it, you shall not cross over."
The Blessed One said:
The swan does not ask the ferryman on the bank of the Narmadā;
by the strength of its own wings, the swan crosses the Narmadā.
Having spoken thus, the Fully Awakened One proceeded like a king of swans;
the Great Sage, having crossed the flood, stood upon the bank of the Gaṅgā.
The Blessed One, having now crossed the Gaṅgā, arrived at Vārāṇasī;
he stood at Saṃkhamedhīya, waiting for the time to go into Vārāṇasī for alms,
for Buddhas do not dwell abroad at an improper time.
At the proper time, they wander for alms in the village;
they dwell apart from those who roam at improper times.
Therefore, the Buddhas do not wander at the wrong hour.
At Ṛṣipatana, the group of five auspicious ones were dwelling: Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya, Aśvakin, Bhadraka, Vāṣpa, and Mahānāma.
The Blessed One, having wandered for alms in Vārāṇasī and finished his meal, proceeded toward Ṛṣipatana.
The Blessed One was seen by the group of five auspicious ones;
seeing the Blessed One approaching from afar, they made a pact among themselves.
"This ascetic Gautama is approaching—he is lax, indulgent in luxuries, and has abandoned his exertion in spiritual practice; no one should rise to greet him."
The Blessed One was approaching, and they found no pleasure in their own seats;
just as birds in their nests or on tree branches would fly up when scorched from below by fire,
even so did the group of five auspicious ones [react] upon seeing him approaching from afar at their respective seats.
Finding no pleasure [in staying], they rose up to meet the Blessed One and went out to greet him, saying:
"Come, venerable Gautama! Welcome to the venerable Gautama! A warm welcome to the venerable Gautama!"
The Blessed One said:
"Your vow, O monks of the Bhadravargīya group, has been broken. Monks of the Bhadravargīya group, do not address the Tathāgata by the title 'Venerable' (āyuṣmat)."
Now, as soon as they had been addressed by the Blessed One with words of instruction, whatever marks of the heterodox, whatever protections of the heterodox,

and whatever customs of the heterodox they possessed all completely vanished; the three robes appeared, as did the Sumbhaka bowls, their hair was restored to its natural state, and their deportment became established just like that of monks who had been ordained for a hundred years.
This is the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk for the five venerable ones of the auspicious group.
Then they invited the Blessed One with cooked oil.
There was a lotus pond named Buddhavicīrṇā; the Blessed One bathed there, for the Blessed Buddhas know all things.
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to the Blessed One:
On which spot of earth did the former Perfectly Enlightened Ones set in motion the wheel of Dharma?
Simultaneously with the arising of that thought, he bowed down to that spot of earth before the Blessed One.
Then, this occurred to the Blessed One:
Indeed, did the former Perfectly Enlightened Ones set the wheel of Dharma in motion while walking, or while standing, or while sitting, or while lying down?
Simultaneously with the arising of that thought, five seats appeared for the Blessed One at Ṛṣivadana.
The group of five auspicious ones questioned the Blessed One.
"For what purpose, Blessed One, are these seats?"
...the Blessed One said:
Monks, this auspicious eon is named Puṣpika, and in this auspicious eon, one thousand Buddhas are to arise.
Three are known; I am the fourth.
Krakucchanda has a radiance of nine yojanas; Konākamuni has a radiance of two yojanas; Kāśyapa has a radiance of four yojanas;
I, Sarvasiddhārtha, have a radiance of one fathom; Ajita has a radiance of twelve yojanas; Siddhārtha has a radiance of twenty yojanas;
Maitreya has a radiance of twelve yojanas; Maitrīyaśas has a radiance of eighteen yojanas; and Sarvaprabha has a radiance of ten yojanas.
Pṛthivīpāla had a radiance extending twelve yojanas; Pṛthivīvijaya had a radiance extending four yojanas; Pṛthivīpaśyin had a radiance extending three yojanas;

Jayamitra had a radiance extending four yojanas; Sugrīva had a radiance extending twelve yojanas; Sudarśana had a radiance extending ten yojanas; Supaśyin had a radiance extending ten yojanas; Sarvajaya had a radiance extending eight yojanas; and Sarvābhibhū had a radiance extending one krośa and one yojana.

Sarvābhibhū had a radiance of eight *yojanas*; Sarvamitra had a radiance of two *yojanas*; Abhinnābha had a radiance of twelve *yojanas*; Atisūrya had a radiance of four *yojanas*; Abhibhūyaśas had a radiance of one *yojana*; Sudaya had a radiance of one *yojana*; Sudarśana had a radiance of one *yojana*; Sarvābhibhū [again] had a radiance of sixty *yojanas*; Vairocana had a radiance of seven *yojanas*; and Sarvapaśyin [had a radiance of seven *yojanas*].
... [there was] one named Vairocanaprabha, whose radiance extended for ten yojanas.
Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana.
There the Blessed One addressed the venerable group of five auspicious ones: "O monks! "Venerable Sir," the monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this to them.
"Monks, there are these two extremes for one who has gone forth.
Which two?
That which is devotion to the pleasure of sensual desires—vulgar, common, ignoble, and unbeneficial—and [the other is]..."

This devotion to self-mortification— which is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial— does not lead to the future life of the holy life, nor to disenchantment, nor to dispassion, nor to cessation, nor to the state of a recluse, nor to perfect awakening, nor to Nirvana.
"Monks, these two are the extremes for one who has gone forth. Monks, having avoided both these extremes, the Tathāgata has awakened to the Middle Way in this Noble Dharma and Discipline;
it produces vision, leads to peace, to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to the state of a recluse, to full enlightenment, and to Nirvāṇa."

Monks, what is that Middle Way realized by the Tathāgata in this Noble Dharma and Vinaya, which produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to peace, to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to the state of a recluse, to enlightenment, and to Nirvana?

Monks, this Noble Eightfold Path— namely, right view, right intention, right effort, right action, right livelihood, right speech, right mindfulness, and right concentration— is that Middle Way realized by the Tathāgata in this noble Dharma and Vinaya; it produces vision, leads to peace, and results in disenchantment [with suffering].
It conduces to dispassion, to cessation, to the state of a recluse, to perfect enlightenment, and to Nirvana.
Furthermore, monks, there are these four noble truths.
Which four? Namely:
the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
The noble truth of the practice leading to cessation.
In this regard, monks, what is the noble truth of suffering?
It is as follows:
Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering, association with the unpleasant is suffering, separation from the pleasant is suffering,
not to obtain what one desires and seeks is also suffering;
form is suffering, feeling is suffering, perception is suffering, mental formations are suffering, and consciousness is suffering— in short, [all this is suffering].
The five aggregates of clinging are suffering;
this, monks, is the noble truth of suffering.
In this regard, what is the noble truth of the origin of suffering?
It is this craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there; this, monks, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering.
In this regard, what is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering?

It is the complete exhaustion, fading away, cessation, relinquishing, abandoning, and relinquishment without remainder of this very craving—which is accompanied by delight and lust, and finds delight here and there; this, monks, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.
In that regard, what is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering?
It is this very Noble Eightfold Path; namely:

right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, monks, is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
The noble truth of the path.
"‘This is suffering,’ monks— regarding these teachings unheard of before, through appropriate attention,
knowledge arose, vision arose, science arose, intelligence arose, vast wisdom arose, and insight arose."
"‘This is the origin of suffering’— monks, regarding these things unheard of before, through wise attention, knowledge arose, vision arose, science arose, intelligence arose,
vast understanding arose, wisdom arose, and light became manifest."
"Monks, regarding these things unheard of before, through wise attention, the knowledge arose in me: 'This is the cessation of suffering.
Vision arose, science arose, wisdom arose, vast understanding arose, intelligence arose, insight arose, and light became manifest."
And this is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering; monks, regarding these dharmas unheard of before, through wise attention, knowledge arose in me, up to the point that light appeared.

Furthermore, monks, regarding this noble truth of suffering as something to be fully understood, regarding these dharmas unheard of before, through wise attention, knowledge arose in me, up to the point that light appeared.

Furthermore, monks, regarding this noble truth of the origin of suffering as something to be abandoned, through wise attention to those teachings unheard of before, knowledge arose in me, and so on, until light appeared.
Furthermore, monks, this noble truth of the cessation of suffering was realized by me through wise attention to teachings unheard of before; knowledge arose, up to and including light.

Furthermore, monks, this noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering was cultivated by me through wise attention to teachings unheard of before; knowledge arose, up to and including the manifestation of light.

Monks, as long as I had not fully understood these four noble truths in this way— through their three turnings and twelve aspects— with right wisdom according to reality, I did not claim to have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; nor did the knowledge arise in me that my liberation of mind was unshakable and realized.

Monks, when I had thus thoroughly understood these Four Noble Truths in their three turnings and twelve aspects with right wisdom as they truly are, then I claimed to have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; knowledge arose in me, and my unshakeable liberation of mind and liberation through wisdom were realized.

Thus spoke the Blessed One while dwelling at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana. And upon this exposition, the dust-free and stainless eye of Dharma regarding all phenomena was purified for the venerable Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya and for eighteen koṭis of gods. And this great earth trembled, shook, and quaked violently in six ways, like a leaf severed from its stalk.

The eastern edge rises and the western edge sinks; the western edge rises and the eastern edge sinks; the southern edge rises and the northern edge sinks; the northern edge rises and the southern edge sinks; the center sinks and the edge rises; the edge sinks and the center rises.

And an immeasurable radiance appeared in the world, surpassing even the divine power of the gods, the power of the nāgas, and the power of the yakṣas— even those intermediate spaces between worlds that are shrouded in darkness, enveloped in gloom, desolate, and unknown, never before perceived, wherein even the moon and sun, despite such great supernatural power and such great majesty, cannot prevail.
Their own light did not reach the light [of others], nor did their radiance pervade the radiance; yet they were not obscured by that illumination.
Furthermore, those other beings who had been reborn there also recognized one another by means of that light, saying, "It seems, friends, that other beings have also been reborn here."
"Indeed, other beings as well have been reborn!
At that very moment, at that very instant, all beings—even those reborn in the great Avīci hell—became endowed with absolute happiness.
And the gods of the earth raised a cry and proclaimed this sound:

"Friends, this unsurpassed wheel of Dharma— having three turnings and twelve aspects— has been set in motion by the Blessed One at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana; it cannot be turned back by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or anyone else in the world in accordance with the Dharma."

It will be for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, benefit, and happiness of the great mass of people— both gods and humans— and the hosts of asuras will diminish while the divine hosts will increase.
Having heard the cry of the gods of the earth, the gods of the Four Great Kings raised a cry and made their voices resound;
the gods of the Thirty-three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, and the Brahmakāyika gods raised a cry and made their voices resound.

Thus, worthy sir, was the unsurpassed wheel of dharma— having three turnings and twelve aspects— set in motion by the Blessed One at Ṛṣivadana, the Deer Park in Vārāṇasī; it is not to be turned back by anyone, whether by a śramaṇa, a brāhmaṇa, a deva, a Māra, or anyone else in the world, in accordance with the Dharma.
That will be for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, benefit, and happiness of the great mass of people, both gods and humans;
the hosts of asuras will diminish, and the divine hosts will increase.
The venerable group of five, being uplifted in mind, rejoiced in what was spoken by the Blessed One.
The Blessed One, the perfectly awakened Buddha, having accomplished the purpose for which he had come, dwells at Vārāṇasī as the teacher of gods and humans.
There, the Blessed One addressed the venerable group of five auspicious companions.
"Monks, form is not-self; feeling is not-self; perception is not-self; mental formations are not-self; consciousness is not-self.

Monks, if this form were self, then form would not lead to affliction and suffering, and one could exercise power over form according to one's will, saying: 'Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus. But because, monks—"
Form is not-self; therefore, form leads to affliction and suffering, and herein one's willful agency does not prevail—that is, "let my form be thus, let it not be thus."
If, monks, this feeling were the self, then feeling would not lead to affliction and suffering; and one would have mastery over feeling, such that one could say: "Let my feeling be thus;
let my feeling not be thus.
But because, monks—
Feeling is non-self; therefore, feeling leads to affliction and the arising of suffering, and herein one's willful agency does not prevail—that is, "May my feeling be thus; may it not be thus."

"Monks, if this perception were the self, perception would not lead to affliction and suffering, and one could exercise mastery over it, saying: 'Let my perception be thus; let my perception not be thus.
But because, monks, perception is not-self, therefore perception leads to affliction and suffering, and one cannot exercise mastery over perception, saying: 'Let my perception be just so.'"

"Monks, conditioned phenomena are a source of affliction. Monks, if conditioned phenomena were the self, these conditioned phenomena would not lead to affliction and suffering; and one could exercise mastery over conditioned phenomena according to one's desire, such that:
'Let my conditioned phenomena be thus; let my conditioned phenomena not be thus.'"
Monks, because conditioned phenomena are non-self, they lead to affliction and suffering; and herein, one's own will does not prevail, such that one could say, "Let my conditioned phenomena be thus;
let them not be thus."
“Monks, if consciousness were the self, this consciousness would not lead to affliction and suffering, and one could exercise mastery over consciousness, saying: ‘Let my consciousness be thus;

let my consciousness not be thus. Monks, because consciousness is not-self, therefore consciousness leads to affliction and suffering, and one cannot exercise mastery over it, saying: ‘Let my consciousness be thus; let my consciousness not be thus.’”
So be it.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves in this way.

Whatever form there may be— whether internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, past, future, or present— all form should be seen as it truly is with correct wisdom: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self."

Whatever feeling, whatever perception, whatever formations, and whatever consciousness—whether internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, whether past, future, or present—all consciousness should be seen as it really is with right wisdom: "This is not mine; this I am not; this is not my self. Thus should it be viewed.
The Blessed One said this while staying at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana.

And while this exposition was being spoken, the mind of the venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya was liberated from the outflows through non-clinging; and for the four other monks, the dust-free, stainless Dharma-eye regarding phenomena was purified, as it was for the venerable Aśvajit.
In Bhadrika, Vāṣpa, Mahānāman, and thirty koṭis of gods, there arose the dustless, stainless, pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.
With uplifted minds, the venerable group of five auspicious ones rejoiced in what was spoken by the Blessed One.
The Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One, having accomplished the purpose for which he had come, was dwelling at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana.
There, the Blessed One addressed the venerable group of five auspicious ones.
"If you think so, monks, what is the root from which sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair arise; from what are they born, and from what do they originate?"
When this had been said, the venerable group of five auspicious ones said this to the Blessed One:

"Indeed, Blessed One, phenomena have existence as their root; they lead to existence, Blessed One; they originate from existence, Blessed One; they have existence as their refuge. It would be well, Blessed One, if you were to explain this matter to the monks.
Having heard it directly from the Blessed One and received it directly from him, the monks will retain it for the sake of suchness."
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the group of five auspicious companions:
Monks, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise rooted in form; they come into being born of form and originating from form.

Monks, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise rooted in feeling, rooted in perception, rooted in mental formations, and rooted in consciousness; they come into being born of consciousness. If you think, monks, that form is either permanent or impermanent—

"For that, Blessed One, is indeed impermanent. Furthermore, monks, having understood the impermanence of form— having understood its instability, its fragile nature, and its subject to change, fading away, and cessation— whatever taints, vexations, fevers, burning pains, and afflictions arise conditioned by form, which lead to renewed existence,"
They are obstructed from future birth, aging, and death.
Through their cessation, those taints (*āśrava*), vexations, fevers, burnings, and afflictions—which lead to renewed existence and result in future birth, aging, and death—do not arise.
"Monks, if you consider it, is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness permanent or impermanent?"
For that, O Blessed One, is indeed impermanent.
The Blessed One said:

Excellent, monks! Indeed, monks, having understood the impermanence of consciousness, and having understood its instability, its fragile nature, and its subjectivity to transformation, fading away, and cessation, those taints (*āsrava*), vexations, fevers, and burning pains— which are defiling, leading to renewed existence, and resulting in birth, aging, and death— that arise conditioned by consciousness, cease and are stilled.
They cease;

through their cessation, those outflows (*āsrava*), vexations (*vighāta*), fevers (*paridāgha*), and torments (*sajvara*)—which are afflictive (*sāṃkleśika*), leading to renewed existence (*paunarbhavika*), resulting in future birth, aging, and death, and which have consciousness as their root, are born from consciousness, and originate in consciousness—do not arise.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves in this way.
"Whatever form there may be— whether internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, past, future, or present— all such form is not mine,
this is not I, this is not my self. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves."

Whatever feeling, whatever perception, whatever formations, and whatever consciousness—whether internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, whether past, future, or present—all these are not mine; I am not this; this is not my self.
Thus, this should be seen as it really is with right wisdom.
Thus spoke the Blessed One while dwelling at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana. And while this exposition was being delivered, the venerable Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya attained mastery over the powers;

the minds of four monks—the venerable Aśvaki, Bhadrika, Vāṣpa, and Mahānāma—were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging; and for five crores of deities, their minds were freed from passion and free from stain regarding all phenomena.
The eyes of Dharma were purified;
the Venerable Five Companions of the Auspicious Group, being uplifted in mind, rejoiced in what was spoken by the Blessed One.
The Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One, having accomplished the purpose for which he had come, was dwelling at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana.
Now at that time, three monks set out for Vārāṓasī for alms.
The Blessed One, having directed his mind toward the minds of those monks, exhorted them and gave them instruction.

"Thus, monks, attend with the mind; thus direct the mind; reflect upon these reflections. Monks, dwell with yourselves as your island, not another as your island; with yourselves as your refuge, not another as your refuge;
with the Dharma as your island, with the Dharma as your refuge, not another as your refuge.
While those monks, O monks, were dwelling there with themselves as their island, not another as their island, with the Dharma as their island, and with the Dharma as their refuge..."

Those who have no other refuge should investigate thoroughly: what is the root from which sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair arise; from what are they born, and by what are they produced?
When this had been said, the monks said this to the Blessed One:
“O Blessed One, all phenomena have existence as their root; O Blessed One, they are led by existence, originate from existence, and have existence as their refuge.

It would be well if the Blessed One were to explain this matter to the monks; having heard it directly from the Blessed One and received it directly from him, the monks will retain it for the sake of suchness.”
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to those monks:
Monks, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise rooted in form; they come into being born of form or originating from form.
Monks, do you consider form to be permanent or impermanent?
"Form, indeed, is impermanent, Blessed One."

"Excellent, monks! Indeed, monks, having understood the impermanence of form, and having understood its weakness, its lack of radiance, its fragility, and its subject to transformation, fading away, and cessation—those taints (*āsrava*), vexations, fevers, and burning pains that arise conditioned by form, which are afflictive, leading to renewed existence, and resulting in future birth, aging, and death—they cease.
Monks, what do you think: is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness permanent or impermanent?"
For this, O Blessed One, is indeed impermanent.
The Blessed One said:
Excellent, monks! Indeed, monks, having understood the impermanence, weakness, and fragility of consciousness, they cease, become tranquil, are abandoned, and pass away.

Through their cessation, the taints, vexations, fevers, and burning pains—those defiled states leading to renewed existence and resulting in birth, aging, and death in the future—do not arise; they are brought to cessation.

The outflows, vexations, fevers, and torments—those which lead to affliction, to renewed existence, and to birth, aging, and death in the future—are rooted in consciousness; they are born of consciousness and originate from consciousness.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
whatever form there may be—whether internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior—[all such forms must be seen as they really are with correct wisdom].

Or whatever form—whether far or near, past, future, or present—all that form should be seen as it truly is with correct wisdom: "This is not mine; this I am not; this is not my self. Thus indeed should it be viewed.
The Blessed One spoke thus while dwelling at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana.
And while this exposition was being delivered, three monks attained mastery over the powers, and for eighty million deities, the dust-free and stainless Dharma-eye regarding phenomena was purified.
With uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.

Then indeed, on the twelfth day of the waxing moon in the month of Āṣāḍha, after the midday meal, while seated facing eastward in a shadow measuring one and a half man-lengths, under the constellation Anurādhā and during the auspicious moment called Vijaya, the Blessed One set in motion the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma.
Furthermore, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not set in motion a wheel of Dharma made of gold, nor one made of silver, pearl, beryl, crystal, musāragalva,
ruby, brass, copper, iron, stone, wood, or clay.
Now, indeed, these very four noble truths constitute the Wheel of Dharma with its three turnings and twelve aspects.

When the first discourse on turning the wheel of Dharma was set in motion, the dust-free, stainless eye of Dharma regarding all phenomena became purified for the venerable Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya and for eighteen koṭis of gods.
And this great earth shook, trembled, quaked, vibrated, resounded, and reverberated in six ways.
As it vibrated, he gazed toward the south, and he gazed toward the north, and he gazed toward both the north and the south;

it caused delight and made one tremble with wonder; it was beautiful to behold and made one tremble with joy; it was pleasing, gladdening, soothing, worthy of being looked upon, insatiable to the sight, not disagreeable, and inspiring serene confidence.

And the great earth—serene, free from agitation, and free from terror—trembled; yet as it trembled, it did not harm any living being, whether mobile or stationary. By the power of the Blessed One, an immeasurable radiance appeared in the world, surpassing the splendor of the gods, the splendor of the nāgas, and the splendor of the yakṣas.

Even those intermediate spaces between worlds— shrouded in darkness, plunged from darkness into darkness, desolate, unformed, and never before formed, where even the moon and sun, despite their great psychic power and majesty,
cannot reach with their radiance nor illuminate with their light— even those were pervaded by that illumination.
Even those beings who had been reborn there recognized one another, saying, "Indeed, friends, other beings have also been reborn here;
indeed, friends, other beings have also been reborn here. And at that very instant, at that very moment, all beings—even those reborn in the great Avīci hell—became endowed with absolute happiness.
As the Blessed One was turning the wheel of Dharma, he made himself understood by the sound of his voice throughout sixty-one triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems,

and beyond those as well. And those Blessed Buddhas who at that time were teaching the Dharma in their respective assemblies in other world systems remained silent before the Blessed One as he turned the wheel of Dharma.
They came into being.
The Perfectly Awakened One Duḥprasaha was teaching the Dharma to the assembly. The Blessed One Duḥprasaha remained silent, yet the sound of a Buddha issued forth.
The astonished assembly questioned the Blessed One Duḥprasaha.
The voice of the Buddha issued forth.

While it was issuing forth, the Lord of the World, Duṣprasaha, remained silent; the assembly was struck with wonder as the voice of the Buddha—sweet-toned like a kalaviṅka bird, approaching with the resonance of thundering clouds and the sound of drums—issued forth, yet the Blessed One, the most excellent of speakers, did not speak.
Duṣprasaha said:
In that world-system named Mahānāma, the Victor Śākyamuni turns the wheel of Dharma, from which this sound issues forth.
He proclaims throughout incalculable thousands of world-systems; the voice of the one of supreme intelligence is heard as if it were near, even though it is far away.
Thus, the Fully Awakened One, possessed of such great majesty and with his aspirations fulfilled, distributes [the fruits of his merit] to those who seek enlightenment.

The voice with which the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, at Ṛṣivadana in the Deer Park near Vārāṇasī, turned the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma in its three revolutions and twelve aspects, is endowed with sixty qualities.
By which sixty?
The voice of the Tathāgata is profound, awe-inspiring, intelligible, heart-reaching, lovely, inexhaustible, irresistible, released, and not discordant.

And it is faultless, flawless, unslanted, untarnished, like the sound of a chariot wheel-rim, with a voice like the thundering and roaring of clouds, with a voice like the simultaneous rumbling of wind, rain, and thunder, with the voice of a god, with the voice of Brahmā, with a favorable voice,
an uncorrupted voice, an undeluded voice, a voice that does not sink, a voice that does not swell, an unagitated voice, and a voice that conveys meaning.
And [he possesses] a true voice, a glorious voice, a bull-like voice, a lion’s voice, an elephant’s voice, a noble-bred horse’s voice,

a crane’s voice, a sparrow’s voice, a cuckoo’s voice, a beautiful voice, a sweet voice, a voice of discernment, one perfected in syllables, one perfected in discernment, one perfected in softness, and one perfected in extensiveness.
And he was endowed with the birth of wholesome qualities and endowed with the expansion of truth; endowed with the birth of roots of merit and endowed with a beautiful voice;

endowed with what is delightful, with the sound of strings, the sound of song, the sound of instrumental music, the sound of a jar, the sound of a man, the surpassing sound, the sound of a drum, the unsurpassed sound, and the voice of a Tathāgata.
Furthermore, the voice of the Tathāgata radiates throughout all directions and is not obstructed anywhere.

The voice endowed with which the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, turned the wheel of Dharma— threefold in its revolution and twelvefold in its aspects— at Ṛṣivadana, the Deer Park in Vārāṇasī, is endowed with these sixty qualities.
Then, at that time, Mahābrahmā praised the Blessed One to his face with appropriate verses.
By him, the foremost among the essence of beings, born in the Ikṣvāku clan,
who sets the wheel of Dharma in motion, the earth was made to tremble.
And eighty terrifying portents occurred,
and furthermore, eighty earth-born [omens] arose through the power of the Wheel of Dharma.
Clouds with limbs variegated by masses of flowers arose and showered the Lord,
the Supreme among Men, who brings benefit to Kāśī.
Like women with their braided hair loosened, the clouds rise up;
these formidable clouds, bearing golden conchs, are like heaps of flowers.
Having heard that the Dharma-body of the Lion among Men had arrived,
Sanatkumāra thought, "I shall pay homage to the Tathāgata."
And Brahmā, standing in the expanse of the sky, clearly recognized him by his true appearance and radiance as one who perceives all things.
O Gautama, you who sit upon the jewel-adorned earth as far as the ocean of Buddhas,
you cause the triple-thousandfold world system to tremble when you hurl your thunderbolt.
When that supreme among men had hurled his most excellent weapon, the ten directions all around were agitated by mere light.
Shaking off the perversions that rely on the thicket of views,
