the Jina— the King of Nāgas, the Foremost among the lords of men— possesses the gait of a lion.
Just as a fearless lion dwelling within the mountains terrifies all his enemies, so does the Jina, whose gait is like that of a lion, act as a king.
Having struck down the faction of Māra, O destroyer of Māra’s foremost army,
you raise the banner of the Jina while arraying it to the right.
Resounding with the sound of great jewels, that earth trembles yet does not sink;
when called forth by his voice and recollected, the Vasundharā rises up.
Residing upon the summit of Mount Meru, the supreme beings scattered from all sides the finest mineral, which possessed the radiant luster of refined gold, over the Sage.
With a serene mind and a joyful heart, my senses bowed with palms joined in reverence,
I have come here because I heard of the Wheel of Dharma.

In the Blessed One’s first discourse on turning the wheel of Dharma, Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya and eighteen koṭis of gods were disciplined; those gods, announcing [the news] in their celestial abodes, went to their respective dwellings.
"All aggregates are without refuge, burning with great fear,
unemancipated, and without essence"— thus speaks Gautama.
Enough of your [worldly] faith; approach for the sake of paying homage to the Buddha, who perceives the meaning of reality and has transcended enmity and fear.
Thirty koṭis of deities came to Ṛṣivadana;

when the second discourse on the turning of the wheel of Dharma was being spoken, they were disciplined, and even as they were expressing their delight in their respective abodes, they departed for their own dwellings.

Having heard of them, fifty koṭis of deities arrived; they too were disciplined by the Blessed One in the third discourse on the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and even as they were expressing their delight in the celestial abodes, they [departed] for their own respective [dwellings].
They went to their own abodes.

Having heard this, eighty koṭis of deities arrived; they too were disciplined by the Blessed One in the fourth discourse on the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma, and they also went to their respective abodes in the celestial palaces, proclaiming [this news].
Then indeed, the son of the gods named Śikharadhara, belonging to the Tuṣita host, praised the Blessed One—who had gone to Ṛṣivadana—with these verses in his presence:
Reverent and full of respect, Brahmā joined his palms in añjali.
Excellent is the fathom-wide radiance that issues from you, who possess such a virtuous form;
excellent is your speech, which is pleasing to the mind, meaningful, and purposeful.
Excellent is the union with dispassion, endowed with all the virtues of the joints;
excellent are the four truths, which you, O Sage, proclaim as the truth.
Excellent, O Deva and Gandharva! They drink in your sweet speech;
excellent, that you have set in motion the peerless wheel which cannot be turned back.
In this world, there is no one equal to you in form, complexion, or lineage, nor likewise in deportment, vigor, meditative concentration, or wisdom.
Today, O Hero, eighteen koṭis of sons of gods have been disciplined in the first fruit; this is the first seat, O Sage.
Furthermore, O Hero, thirty million sons of the gods were disciplined in the first fruit at the second seat, O Noble One.
Furthermore, fifty koṭis more were disciplined on the third seat;
the sons of the gods were liberated from the states of woe.
Furthermore, O Lord, eighty koṭis were led to the fruit of stream-entry at the fourth seat and liberated from the miserable states of existence.
Therefore, O Supreme among Men, there is no one equal to you in loving-kindness;
O Compassionate One, Bull among Men, you are fearless from any quarter.
By good fortune, O tiger among men, you have been born as one beautiful to the world;
for the benefit of all sentient beings, remain long, O Great Sage!
Not long ago, O bull among men, you were born as a prince;
you are the leader of those who have gone astray and the giver of sight to the blind.
May our teacher never depart from among us;
may your station be boundless, O Leader of the World.
The states of woe have been brought to an end there by your own splendor, O Self-Existent One;
and heaven has been rendered devoid of space upon reaching you, O Supreme Person.
O best among the bulls of men, this group fixed in falsehood will,
upon encountering you who belong to the undetermined group, fulfill its potential.
And you, O one praised by the gods, born of a royal lineage, having attained that indeterminate mass [of potential], will fulfill the mass of rightness.
And the increase of marvelous qualities is perceived upon reaching you, O Sun among Men, the infallible one who brings an end to darkness.
O beloved of the people,
O great sage, as you speak these true teachings, the world together with Indra rejoices in your words.
Thus do the hosts of gods praise the giver of boons, whose mind is full of joy,
who is endowed with infinite virtues, the caravan leader, the supreme among men.
The monks said to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, as the ripening of what karma was the Dharma first understood by the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya?"
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, this was indeed his former vow."
Monks, in the past, in times long gone, in the city of Rājagṛha, a Pratyekabuddha suffering from a bile disorder requested shelter in a potter’s workshop.
He was attended to by that potter and was freed from his affliction of bile.
Then those Pratyekabuddhas who had been his attendants came there to the potter’s workshop to inquire after the well-being of that Pratyekabuddha who was suffering from a bile disorder.
Having freed the Pratyekabuddha from that affliction of bile, the potter asked him:
"By whom was the Dharma first understood?"
That Pratyekabuddha said:
I first understood the Dharma, and afterwards these [others] did so.
Then that Bhārgava made this aspiration:

"By whatever root of merit I have accumulated through performing attendance and service for you, by that root of merit may I also be the very first to understand the Dharma taught by the Blessed Buddha."

I should not long for gain or honor; I should long for remote lodgings and be content with whatever alms-bowl I receive. I should dwell among waterfalls and forest groves as one who has become like a corpse, cast away from the world.
The Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, monks, it may be that you think thus: 'At that time, on that occasion, was that Bhārgava in the city of Rājagṛha someone else? But it should not be viewed in this way.
And why?
Monks, that elder Ājñātakauṇḍinya was at that time, on that occasion, the Bhārgava in Rājagṛha."
Because he gave shelter and performed service for that Pratyekabuddha who was afflicted by bile-fever,
and because he made this aspiration: "Just as you first understood the Dharma and afterwards others [did],
may I too be the very first to understand the Dharma taught by the Blessed Buddha"— by virtue of that karma...
By that ripening of karma, Ājñātakauṇḍinya was the very first to realize the Dharma, and afterwards the others.
By whatever root of merit has been accumulated for the sake of food, clothing, edibles, and service—
by that root of merit, may there be an encounter with the Best of Men.
Just as you first understood the Dharma and afterwards others did,
so may I first understand that which was taught by the Victor.
Having few desires and being content with whatever alms-food may come my way,
with a mind nourished by the bliss of tranquility, may I not long for gain or honor.
May my body be cast away there, upon the mountains frequented by herds of deer in the remote wilderness,
at the time of my death.
Whether treated with honor or dishonor, life-force, consciousness, and even body-heat depart;
for whom could there be joy when the dead body is like the dust of the earth?
The Jātaka of Ājñātakauṇḍinya is completed.
The monks said to the Blessed One:

Having performed renunciations of self, having performed renunciations of sons, having performed renunciations of wives, having performed renunciations of wealth, and having performed renunciations of kingdoms, the Blessed One fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and endowed the Venerable Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya with a great purpose.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now that I have endowed this Ājñātakauṇḍinya with great benefit;
on another occasion as well, he was endowed with great benefit by me through the sacrifice of my own life."
The monks said:
"At another time as well, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
On another occasion as well, monks.

Once upon a time, in the past, there was a king of Kośala who had performed meritorious deeds; he was renowned, possessed great strength, a vast treasury, and many mounts. His kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, crowded with people, and its inhabitants were happy. Punishment was mild, strife and civil unrest were absent, thieves were well-restrained, and it was rich in commerce, being governed righteously.

And in every region of that king’s realm, there arose a report of his virtuous fame and renown; he was honored by donors and masters of charity, devoted to the welfare of others, and possessed the vision of the world beyond.
Considering him to be righteous and having no regard for the world beyond, the King of Kāśi, desiring to seize that kingdom of Kośala,
mobilized a fourfold army— consisting of elephant corps, cavalry, chariot corps, and infantry— and marched upon the territory of Kośala.
The King of Kāśī was defeated by the ministers and the vanguard of the army of that King of Kośala; he fled alone, and his entire host was broken.
At a later time, he returned again with a fourfold army, but once more he was defeated and departed.
In this way, that King of Kāśi came again and again to that territory of Kośala with his fourfold army.
There, many thousands of living beings, on both sides, hurling swords, arrows, spears, and javelins at one another's bodies, fall into misfortune and ruin.

When that righteous King of Kośala— who was compassionate and possessed of vision regarding the world beyond— saw those thousands of living beings falling into ruin and calamity, a sense of spiritual urgency arose in his mind: "Having obtained this kingdom, I am committing such an unrighteous act through greed for sovereignty, resulting in the slaughter of people."
Deeply distressed, he abandoned that kingdom and went alone, without a companion, to the Deccan in disguise, thinking, "There, by whatever means possible, I shall provide for my livelihood.

As he was traveling, exhausted by the journey and scorched by the wind and sun, he sat down to rest beneath the cool shade of a banyan tree. At that time, another sea-faring caravan leader arrived, his ship having been wrecked, along with all his followers.
With his wealth lost at sea, he comes from the southern ocean to Kośala.

"The righteous King of Kośala, compassionate and intent on favoring others, hears that he rescues many thousands of people who have fallen into ruin and deprived of wealth, providing them with whatever means they require. He will give me such means by which I may once again engage in trade and rescue myself from my fallen state."
Having placed his hopes in that King of Kośala, he then traveled gradually from the southern region and arrived at the territory of the King of Kośala.
He went from there to the presence of the King of Kośala at the banyan tree.
The king asked that caravan leader:
"Dharma-brother, are you not weary or exhausted? Rest here in this cool shade of the banyan tree, for you are fatigued from the journey."
Then he said:
"May it be well with you, brother in the Dharma; I shall depart."
Then the king said:
"Where is your spiritual brother? What is the purpose of your swift departure, such that you do not even wish to rest?"
Then he said:
"Good sir, I am a caravan leader from such-and-such a city, one who travels by sea.
Having taken a great deal of wealth and various kinds of merchandise from my own city, I set out upon the great ocean with a well-equipped ship toward the seaports."
There, upon that great ocean, my ship laden with wealth was wrecked; by means of a plank, I emerged alive from the sea, though only with my body.
So I am going into the presence of the King of Kośala for the sake of some wealth, so that I might once again engage in trade and rescue myself from this fallen state.
It is with this hope that I have come, traveling such a great distance.
Then the King of Kośala, having heard those words of the caravan leader, wept and shed tears.
The caravan leader said to him:
"O gentle-faced one, why do you weep?"
The king said:

"I am weeping because you have come from afar, having lost your ship and filled with hope, thinking that the King of Kośala will provide me with the means for my livelihood so that I may once again engage in trade and rescue myself from this fallen state."
"My kingdom has been seized by the King of Kāśī, and I have departed for the Deccan with nothing but my body; I shall provide for my livelihood through whatever means possible.
It is for this reason that I weep—that you have come such a great distance at my voice, yet I am in such a state of misfortune, fallen away from my kingdom."
Then that caravan leader addressed the King of Kosala with a verse:
For having heard your renown from afar, O hero in renunciation, I have come here;
my hope for my heart's desire has been strengthened.
Hope was turned into despair by the sight [of him].
The king said:
I am the granter of hundreds of heart's desires;
there is no one equal to me among gods and men.
For your sake, I shall even sacrifice my life.
May my proclamation not prove false.

Then the king comforted the caravan leader, who had fallen to the ground in a faint, having lost all hope, saying: "You have come here from afar with me as your object of hope; I shall act in such a way that your journey will not be in vain."
For your sake, I shall sacrifice my own life.
"Bind my arm and present it to the King of Kāśī;
then the King of Kāśī, being pleased, will give you abundant wealth. I would rather sacrifice myself than let my hopes directed toward you be in vain."
Then that caravan leader said:
I do not venture to commit evil for the sake of wealth against this bull among men;
such as I have heard of you, O wise one of the world, such a sight of yours is most difficult to attain.
The king said.
What is the fruit of life for those whose fame is not great in the world?
Since my purpose has not been achieved, I shall turn back with my request frustrated.
I would gladly be slain by my enemies;
I would gladly have my limbs severed by my foe;
I would indeed endure even the most intense agony.
I shall endure suffering, and may you not fall into despair.
And that King of Kāśi delighted in the life of the King of Kośala, and every day he proclaimed thus: "To whoever brings the head of the King of Kośala, I shall give a great gift."
While the Kosalan king was being urged again and again by that caravan leader, the Kosalan king was subsequently bound hand and foot and handed over to the King of Kāśī.
The King of Kāśi said:
"Aha! This king is both a hero and one highly trained; how was he bound by you and brought here?"
When he had related the entire reason for his coming, the King of Kāśi was filled with wonder and said:
"It is not right for us to seize the kingdom of such a righteous king."
Having once again consecrated the King of Kośala in his own kingdom, he went to the kingdom of Kāśī;
meanwhile, that King of Kośala bestowed a great mass of wealth upon the caravan leader.
"It may be, monks, that it might occur to you: 'Was that King of Kośala someone else? It is not so, monks; at that time, I myself was that King of Kośala."
Ājñātakauṇḍinya was not anyone else; at that time, he was the caravan leader.

Even then, by sacrificing myself, I joined him with a great purpose; and now, too, having sacrificed hundreds of various sufferings and having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, I have joined him with a great purpose.
Thus ends the Jātaka of Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya.
The monks said to the Blessed One:

The Blessed One caused the five Bhadravargīyas, who were adherents of other sects and being swept away by a violent flood of views, to turn back from those courses of view; having rescued them from the terrifying and formidable ocean of saṃsāra, he established them in the secure ground, the auspicious, peaceful, fearless state of nirvāṇa.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now that the group of five auspicious ones have been delivered by me from the ocean of saṃsāra; on another occasion as well,

when their ship was wrecked in the great ocean and they were without shelter, without protection, without refuge, without a resort, fallen into distress, and come to ruin, I sacrificed myself and established them safely back across the great ocean."
The monks said.
At other times as well, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
On another occasion as well, monks.

[_Mvu_3.354_] Once upon a time, monks, in the past, merchants in Jambudvīpa set out upon the great ocean in a ship for the sake of wealth. Their ship was wrecked by a makara, a species of sea-monster;
there, whatever merchants were there... [they] swam with their arms, and the caravan leader also...
Having previously practiced something [of the path], he too floats upon the ocean with his arms.
Now, five merchants were floating upon the great ocean with their arms, together with that caravan leader.
This thought occurred to the caravan leader:

"It is not possible for us to cross this great ocean by means of our arms; we must all perish here. Furthermore, I have heard that the great ocean does not dwell for a single night with a dead corpse.
What if I were to sacrifice my own body so that these five merchants may reach dry land safely from this great ocean?"
And the caravan leader had a weapon in his hand;
he said to those five merchants:
"O all of you, I shall establish you safely on dry land from the great ocean."
Then, in that water which was without support or foothold, all five merchants clung to the caravan leader;
thereupon, the caravan leader cut his own throat with a weapon, for the great ocean does not dwell with a corpse even for a single night.
Then, monks, the great ocean very quickly cast that corpse onto dry land.
Then all those five merchants, together with the corpse Kuṇapa, were cast onto dry land by the force of the ocean.
This great earth trembled violently, and there arose a great roar of the beings.
The gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and asuras cried out, "What is this? in the great ocean?
The deity of the great ocean said:

This Bodhisattva, together with some merchants, had embarked upon the great ocean in a ship; their ship was wrecked by a makara, a species of sea monster. Those merchants who had previously practiced [virtue] were brought safely from the great ocean to dry land by the Bodhisattva through his self-sacrifice.
"We have lived negligently, for we did not take into account that Bodhisattvas perform such difficult deeds, being ever intent on the welfare of all sentient beings."
In the distant past, while practicing for enlightenment, the preeminent among speakers descended into the lovely salt ocean, which is frequented by whales and sea-monsters.
Then, his vessel having been wrecked by a fish in the form of a makara in the waters of the ocean,
that merchant, though deprived of his wealth, remained steadfast as he drifted upon the sea.
Having perceived those who were without protection, without refuge, and afflicted by suffering, Vāṇijā reflected upon a means: "How might I bring happiness to these beings who are in pain?"
Then this reflection occurred to him: "I have heard that the ocean, its salt waters inhabited by timi fish and makaras, does not dwell with a corpse for even a single night."
"I would rather sacrifice myself than let these merchants perish at sea"—
such was the firm resolve of Dṛḍhamati, who had reached the further shore of mental conduct.
This great compassion, which seeks the welfare of all sentient beings and has been accumulated over a long period of time, pervades his mental continuum.
He said to the group of merchants: "I shall sacrifice myself; cling to my body!
For the deity of the salt waters will not allow a dead corpse to remain for the night."
Taking up a sharp weapon, he turned back his own body;
all the merchants were quickly brought to the shore of the ocean.
The earth, together with its mountains, cities, and market towns, along with its hills, forests, and groves, was violently shaken;
the ocean, with its cities of the Dānavas and the abodes of the serpents, was thoroughly agitated.
"What is this? the people, the deities of the mountains and forests, and the serpents asked. Then the deity of the salt waters, being distressed, replied.
This essence of the elephant-being, the preeminent among speakers, was practicing for the sake of awakening;
he has crossed over the salt waters, yet this was not known by me in my heedlessness.
Thus, with his ship wrecked upon the ocean, that best of men filled it once more;
he sacrificed his own dear self for the sake of liberating other people.
By his very power, the earth, along with the oceans and Mount Meru, was shaken;
and the cities of the Guhyakas and Dānavas, together with the abodes of the serpents, were thrown into turmoil.

How indeed could all sentient beings ever be able to repay the debt of gratitude to those who are the essence of beings, while they are practicing for the sake of awakening, let alone once they have become omniscient?
But whoever practices within the teaching of the Jina with their whole being—
to that extent, indeed, has the essence of the elephant-being been repaid.
The Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, monks, it may be that you think the caravan leader at that time and on that occasion was someone else.
It should not be viewed in this way.
Why is that? Monks, I myself was that caravan leader."

Those five merchants were not others; they were those very ones of the auspicious group (Bhadravargīya). Even then, by sacrificing myself, I established them safely on dry land from the great ocean; and now as well, by sacrificing myself, I have delivered them across from cyclic existence (saṃsāra).
They were established in nirvāṇa.
Thus ends the Jātaka of the group of five auspicious ones.
The monks said to the Blessed One:
The Blessed One taught the Dharma to the assembly consisting of gods and humans.
The Blessed One said:
Monks, it is not only now that I have taught the Dharma to an assembly consisting of gods and humans; on another occasion as well, monks, I taught the Dharma to such an assembly.
The monks said.
At another time as well, Blessed One?
The Blessed One said:
On another occasion as well, monks.
Long ago, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi, a king named Kalabha reigned; he was fierce, merciless, and impulsive.
Now, having gone out to the park grounds in the inner apartments, he played at water-sports in the lotus pond together with the women of the harem.
Having broken off blue, red, white, and fragrant lotuses, and having played, enjoyed himself, and dallied with his harem, he became exhausted from the pleasure.
While the king was fast asleep, the women of the harem roamed through that garden grounds.
The seer Kṣāntivāda, having come from the continent of Uttarakuru by means of his supernatural power, was sitting there in that park.
Then he was seen there in the park by the women of the harem as they were wandering about.
Then, having seen the illustrious seer, they attended upon him with serene minds, saying: "O Blessed One, teach us the Dharma!"
Then that seer taught the Dharma to those women of the harem;

he proclaimed discourses on giving, discourses on morality, discourses on heaven, discourses on merit, and discourses on the ripening of merit. He revealed the danger, the degradation, and the defilement in sensual pleasures, as well as the excellence and purification of renunciation.
That most excellent of seers proclaimed to them the ten wholesome paths of action, which result in happiness for gods and humans in this world, being bright and resulting in a happy ripening.
Then those women of the inner apartments waited upon the seer with one-pointed minds.
When the king awoke, he did not see his harem. Enraged, he drew his sword from its scabbard and searched the harem step by step.
He saw those women of the harem sitting with the seer placed before them.
Having seen that seer, he became even more exceedingly enraged, thinking, "By this man my entire harem has been seen.
Then, in his anger and with a malevolent mind, he asked the seer:
"Who are you?"
The seer said:
I am a proponent of patience; let them rejoice.
Then, becoming even more malicious, he said:
If you are one who speaks with patience, then extend your finger in salutation.
The seer extended his finger.
The king cut off that finger of the seer with a sword-blade; then, through the mother’s love for her son, milk began to flow from her breasts, and likewise milk flowed from that finger of the seer.
Because of his mind of loving-kindness toward sentient beings, all five fingers on each of his hands were cut off one by one, and milk flowed from them all.
The king asked again.
What is your doctrine?
The seer prophesies only patience:
"I am a proponent of patience; let there be joy!"
By him the hand of that seer was cut off, and even from that, milk flowed forth.
The king asks the seer.
"What is your doctrine?"
The seer prophesies only patience:
"I am a speaker of patience; let them rejoice!"
Then, in that very same way, his second hand was also cut off, starting from the fingers up to the elbow; and from it, too, milk flowed from every part as it was being cut, piece by piece.
The king asked:
"What is your doctrine?"
The seer prophesies only patience;
I am a proponent of patience, so rejoice!
In this way, his feet were also cut off, starting from the toes up to the knees.
The king asked:
"What is your doctrine?"
The seer prophesies only patience:
"I am a teacher of patience; let them rejoice!"
Now one of his ears was severed, and from that severed [ear] milk flowed.
The king asked the seer:
"What is your doctrine?"
The seer explains only patience:
"I am a proponent of patience; let those who rejoice do so."
By him his second ear was cut off, yet from that too milk flowed forth, for his mind was free from malice.
Again the king asked the seer:
"What is your doctrine?"
The seer prophesies only patience;
I am a proponent of patience—rejoice!
By him the nose of that seer was cut off; nevertheless, from him who remained free from malice, milk flowed forth.
Again the king asked the seer:
"What is your doctrine?"
The seer prophesies only patience:
"I am a proponent of patience; rejoice!
Even if you were to cut my body into a hundred pieces with an axe and cast them down with a malicious mind, even then I would not abandon patience."
When the seer had been torn into pieces, the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and bhūtas were agitated and raised a great clamor; they caused living beings to experience great fear and terror.
When the people of the towns and countryside saw the great terror of the bhūtas and heard them crying out, they prostrated before the seer and asked for his forgiveness.
O Great Brahmā, do not be angry with him who cuts off your hands, feet, ears, and nose; may there be well-being for all other beings.
The seer said:
Even toward one who cuts off my hands, my feet, and my ears and nose,
I do not become angry, let alone toward other beings.
The devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas said:
"Let us incite the seer Kṣāntivādin; it is not possible for him to prosper this kingdom of King Kalabha along with its realm and its countryside.
Let the flourishing countryside be consumed by fire; let the kingdom perish!
[They acted] so as to harass the seer Kṣāntivādin, who is non-violent."
Let this city be set ablaze; let it be made a place for the dead.
Where they harassed the seer Kṣāntivādin, who was free from malice.
Let this king, together with his ministers and his assembly, be consumed by fire,
since they have harmed the seer Kṣāntivādin, who was free from fault.
Seeing that great upheaval of living beings, the people of the towns and countryside were terrified; they prostrated before the seer and entreated him.
O Great Brahmā, do not be angry with him who cuts off your hands and feet, and your ears and nose; may there be well-being for other beings as well.
The seer said:
"Do not be afraid; no harm whatsoever shall come to you, even from him who cuts off my hands and feet, and my ears and nose."
I do not even become angry with him, much less with other subjects;
the king himself will experience the ripening of his own actions.
The ṛṣis, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas said:
When the god does not rain in due season, the sown seeds do not sprout; scorched by heat and struck down by wind, they wither away.
Thus it was in the past: there was a seer who was an illuminator of patience;
while he remained established in that patience, the King of Kāśi had him executed.
The ripening of that harsh karma was bitter in its fruit,
which the King of Kāśi experienced when he was cast into hell.
Thus indeed did the seer who spoke of patience endure;
even as his limbs were being cut away, he did not become angry with anyone at all.
Then that King of Kāśi, Kalabha, having been consumed by fire, was reborn in the great Avīci hell.
In Hastināpura there was a king named Arjuna; having recognized those of virtuous appearance, he would pose questions to them.
Whoever was able to satisfy his mind was released alive and in safety, but whoever was unable to satisfy King Arjuna’s mind by answering his questions was himself slain with a spear by King Arjuna.

From the slopes of the Himavat mountains, a seer named Gautama arrived at Hastināpura; he possessed the five superknowledges, had attained the four meditative absorptions, was of great psychic power and majesty, and was free from passion for sensual desires.
Now, when that seer was questioned by King Arjuna, he gave an answer to that question here which was fraught with danger; and the king did not understand it.
Consequently, that illustrious seer Gautama was killed by the king himself with a spear, and King Arjuna was also consumed by fire and reborn in the Mahānaraka hell upon a spear-point.
In Kaliṅga there was a city named Dantapura;
there a king named Nārīkela reigned, who was wicked, disfigured, fierce, cruel, and impulsive.
Having invited śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, he feeds them to dogs;
and while they are being devoured by them, he laughs.
He too, having been burned by fire, was reborn in a great hell, where he is devoured day and night by dark and brindled creatures.
In the city of Kampilla, a king named Brahmadatta reigned.
That King Brahmadatta had a hundred sons who were princes; and the chaplain also had a son, a young brahmin student named Yajñadatta, who was the chaplain’s son.
In the southern region,
it was heard that in the city of Kampilla, King Brahmadatta had a hundred princes who were masters of archery and weaponry.
"I shall go there to the city of Kampilla; I will teach that hundred of princes the knowledge of archery and weaponry, and from that, my livelihood will come."
He then arrived at Kampilla and stayed with the domestic priest; he was also introduced by the priest to King Brahmadatta.
Brahmadatta said to him:
"Train these one hundred sons of mine in the science of archery;
I shall give you abundant wealth."
Now, that master of archery was teaching the science of archery, and Yajñadatta, the son of the domestic priest, was also training in the science of archery right there together with those princes.
Now they had all been trained in the entire science of archery, and among them all, Yajñadatta excelled in that knowledge of archery.
Having now been trained, they gave a demonstration before the entire assembly including the king and a great multitude of people.

A hundred youths shot arrows at Yajñadatta, and Yajñadatta, with the edge of his discus, cut all those arrows—shot by the hundred youths—before they had even reached his body; the entire assembly, including the king, was struck with wonder at Yajñadatta.
Thus, his name Śarabhaṅga came into being.

To the north of Vārāṇasī, in the Himalayan foothills, was the Sāhañjanī hermitage, well-supplied with roots, leaves, flowers, and fruits; abundant in *kodrava*, *śyāmāka*, *bhaṅga*, *prāsādika*, vegetables, and lotus roots; graced by many thousands of trees laden with flowers and fruits; and well-provided with water.
There dwelt a seer named Kāśyapa with a retinue of five hundred; they all possessed the five superknowledges, had attained the four dhyānas, and were of great psychic power and great majesty.
Śarabhaṅga, the son of a family priest, having gone there to the Sāhañjanī hermitage, went forth into the ascetic life under the seer Kāśyapa.
Dwelling thus, devoted to the practice of vigilance during the first and last watches of the night, applying himself, striving, and exerting himself,

he produced the four dhyānas and realized the five superknowledges (abhijñās). Having attained the four dhyānas and the five superknowledges, the seer Śarabhaṅga became one of great power, renowned and well-known throughout the world including the devas as a lifelong celibate who had relied upon fierce asceticism.
The Great Naga.
He has now gone to the southern region.
In the land of the Āsmakas is the river Godāvarī;
having established a hermitage named Kapitthaka on its bank, he dwells there.

A disciple of the seer Kāśyapa named Vatsa, with a retinue of five hundred, dwelt in a hermitage on the bank of the Gaṅgā in the Himalayas. They were all possessed of the five superknowledges, had attained the four meditative concentrations, were free from passion for sensual desires, lived by gleaning grains, and were of great spiritual power.
Now, at that time, a wind-related illness arose in the seer Vatsa.
Unable to endure the cold in the Himalayas, he went to the southern region to a city named Govardhana.

Now at that time, a king named Daṇḍakin ruled the kingdom; he was unrighteous, an unrighteous king, fallen away from right view, greedy for sense objects, deluded, possessing perverted vision, lacking filial piety toward mother or father, disrespectful toward ascetics and brahmins, cruel, merciless, and violent.
Having seen that seer, the calf was made to trample him with its dust; yet he remained unharmed, unoffended, and blameless.
Now, in that kingdom, there was a chief minister named Vighuṣṭa.
He had the seer quickly dug up alive from that heap of dust, and having prostrated himself, he asked for forgiveness, saying:
"Venerable sir, it was not pleasing to me that the king committed such a rash act."
It would be well, Blessed One; you should please forgive me.
The seer said:
"Minister, depart quickly from this kingdom!
On the seventh day I shall pass away; when I have passed away, there will be a most terrible danger here in this kingdom."
Then that minister, having heard [the words] of the seer Vatsa, departed from Daṇḍakin’s kingdom for another kingdom, together with his sons and wife, his retinue, and all his circle of kinsmen.

After the passing of seven nights, the seer Vatsa died. Immediately upon the death of the seer, there was a great upheaval among the spirits; by them, the entire kingdom and the city were reduced to ashes during the night.
Between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, the seer Kāśyapa was performing a sacrifice. There, ninety-eight...
A thousand ascetics had assembled there; they possessed the five superknowledges, had attained the four meditative absorptions, and were all of great psychic power and great majesty.
In Kaliṅga there was a city named Dantapura; there lived a king named Uggata. Having seen this terrible, great fear, and this great calamity of those kings, he went to Saṃjayantī to see the seers.
In Saṃjayantī there was a king named Bhīmaratha.
Having seen the misfortune of those kings, he became distressed and asked that King of Kaliṅga:
"Where will you go?"
He said this to him.
I shall go to see the sages.
In Hastināpura, a king named Aṣṭamaka ruled the kingdom.
Having witnessed the terrible misfortune of those four kings, he too became terrified and agitated; he set out as well to see the sages.
Śakra, the lord of the gods, having seen the calamity of those four unrighteous kings of lawlessness— who were corrupted by evil, merciless, cruel, and violent—
came with great divine power to see the sages.
On the slopes of the Himavat, five hundred sages who subsisted on roots and fruits, ascetics living by gleaning who were pure and austere, beheld him.
Well-restrained, practicing fierce austerities, and noble.
There was once a seer here of the Vatsa clan who became emaciated by wind-related ailments;
unable to endure the cold on the slopes of the Himalayas, he remained there.
He departed from the forest for the royal capital.
There lived a king named Daṇḍakin who practiced unrighteousness; having adopted a false view, he was settled in perverted conceptions.
He covered that seer with dust.
That very king had a chief minister known by the name Vighuṣṭa in the kingdom;
having rescued that seer, he said to him:
O Brahmā, please forgive me; it was not my pleasure, nor was it right.
The seer Vatsa said to that minister:
"Go from here, lest there be misfortune for you;
within seven nights from now, [you shall depart]."
A great danger of terrible form will arise.
And when the seer had passed away, there arose a great agitation among the spirits there;
his kingdom, along with its wealth and its realm, [was thrown into turmoil].
In a single night, they reduced it to ashes.
Then the ascetic Śarabhaṅga said to the assembled sages:
"Daṇḍakī has not done what is right."
Let us go; let us perform worship for the calf.
Then King Aṣṭamaka, King Bhīmaratha, the King of Kaliṅga, and Udgata,
both agitated and thrilled, spoke this:
"Let us go, O seers, to see him and to ask that by which it may come to pass."
Then those three lords of men,
adorned with earrings and fine garments, approached the presence of the seers, contented yet moved by spiritual urgency.
With lapis lazuli, pearls, and swords in their hands.
The seers said.
The king said to the seer: "Who are you, and how are you known in the world of men?"
The kings said:
King Aṣṭamaka, Bhīmaratha,
and King Kaliṅga, as well as Udgata,
went forth to see the well-restrained seers.
Having come here, we desire to ask questions.
The sages questioned Śakra as he was traveling through the atmosphere.
You stand in the sky, in the atmosphere, illuminating like the moon on the fifteenth day;
we ask you, O God of great majesty.
How do they know this in the world of men?
Śakra said:
"The gods know me as the Lord of Śacī; they call me Maghavan in the world of men."
"O Lord of Great Power,
he has come to see the well-restrained seers."
The seers said:
Puraṃdara, the Lord of Beings, who is again Indra, the sovereign of the thirty-three gods— he,
the crusher of the hosts of asuras, has arrived.
He seeks an opportunity to ask a question.
"O sages, we have come from afar;
O sages, we have arrived here with well-restrained minds. With hearts full of faith in the Noble One, we come to pay homage at your feet."
This one is the best among men in all the world.
The seers said:
The fragrance of the sages who have long practiced meditation wafts forth, stirred by the wind;
depart from here, Śakra, and sit down.
This fragrance is not easily endured even by the gods.
Śakra said:
The fragrance of the sages who have long practiced cultivation wafts forth, stirred by the wind;
it is pure and sweet-smelling, belonging to those who have long practiced cultivation.
This fragrance is not offensive to me.
The sages said:
This seer Sarabhaṅga is noble,
for since his birth he has abstained from sexual intercourse;
the Teacher Buddha is one whose form is well-disciplined.
Therefore, may he explain these questions here.
The sages said:
"O Vāsiṣṭha, answer the questions;
the sages of virtuous form entreat you."
For this is the duty for wise men:
that whatever tree one desires, its fruit is one's burden.
[Śarabhaṅga said:
Whatever question you desire in your minds, having been granted leave, you may speak.
I shall answer your questions,
for I have seen this truth and that which is beyond.
Then the king asked.
Just as there were Daṇḍakin, Nālikera, Arjuna, and King Kalabha—
tell me the destiny of those who committed such evil deeds.
Where have the sages been reborn after having harassed [us]?
Śarabhaṅga said:
Just as there were Daṇḍakin, Nālikera, Arjuna, and King Kalabha—
understand their destiny, who committed such extremely evil deeds.
Wherever they were reborn, they became harassers of the seers.
Because the seer Daṇḍakī stepped upon him with dust, he was uprooted along with his wealth and his kingdom,
and fell into the hell named Kukkula.
From that, masses [of fire] like a network of sparks arise.
Arjuna, having harmed Gautama of the lineage of Aṅgiras, fell into Naraka with his head downward and feet upward, pierced by spears and pikes.
The seer, an ascetic who has long practiced the life of celibacy.
He who harms those who are self-restrained and have gone forth after having invited them with food and drink—
those dogs will [eat] that coconut in the next world.
They devour him by force as he struggles.
He who should cause the execution of one who has gone forth in fragments,
a seer who preaches patience, an unoffending ascetic—
that Kalabha has fallen into the Avīci hell.
Greatly burning, pungent, and terrifying.
Having heard of such hells and having seen kingdoms utterly destroyed,
one should practice the Dharma toward ascetics and brahmins.
Acting thus, one shall attain the heavenly realm.
The kings said:
Since you have surpassed others in what I asked you, I ask you another thing; tell me that here:
having killed what does one never grieve?
Whose abandonment do the seers praise?
Śarabhaṅga said:
Having destroyed anger, one never grieves;
the seers describe the abandonment of envy.
One should endure all harsh words spoken by others.
The virtuous call this power invincible.
The kings said:
For it is possible to endure the speech of two people— either one who is superior or one who is equal;
but how could one endure the speech of an inferior?
Explain this matter to me, Kauṇḍinya.
Sarabhaṅga said:
For people endure the words of a superior out of fear,
and likewise those of an equal due to the cause of conflict;
but he who here endures the words of an inferior— [he is truly patient].
The virtuous call this the supreme power.
How can you recognize one whose form is concealed by four layers—
whether they are similar, superior, or inferior—
for the virtuous move about in various disguises?
Therefore, one should indeed endure the speech of everyone.
Even a vast army together with its king, though fighting, could not achieve this purpose that a patient person of noble character accomplishes.
The heroes bring peace to those who possess patience.
The kings said:
We rejoice in your well-spoken words; I ask you another question, so speak on this here:
how many kinds of one possessed of virtue do you describe?
How many kinds of wise person do you say there are? How many kinds of true person do you say there are? And how many kinds does glory not abandon?
Sarabhaṅga said:
He who is well-restrained in body and speech, and who commits no evil with the mind,
nor does anything harmful in the world—
One who is such as that, I call virtuous.
All objects of wealth perish again;
yet wealth that has come at the proper time does not depart. One should not act in such a way as to cause harm for the sake of one's own self.
Such a person as that, I call wise.
Indeed, that person who is grateful and appreciative of what has been done, who is a virtuous friend and firm in devotion,
performs his duty with respect even in times of adversity.
Such a person as that, I call a true man.
One who is endowed with these three qualities— being pleasant, amiable, and gentle in speech; being respectful, reverential, and possessed of a sense of shame— is [truly virtuous].
In such a manner, Fortune does not abandon him.
The kings said:
We rejoice in your well-spoken words; I ask you another question—speak on this here:
[of] ethical discipline, wisdom, glory, and gratitude.
What indeed do those skilled in the Dharma declare to be the most excellent?
Sarabhaṅga said:
The wise indeed declare that wisdom is supreme,
like the king of stars among the constellations; so too are ethical conduct, glory, and gratitude.
But those who possess wisdom are the most excellent.
The kings said:
We rejoice in your well-spoken words;
I ask you another thing—speak upon that here.
What should one practice, what should one cultivate, and by doing what does one become wise? This is what I consider.
Sarabhaṅga said:
Serving the elders, being skillful and learned, grasping the teachings and inquiring after them,
one listens with reverence to well-spoken words.
One who acts in this way, I believe, becomes possessed of wisdom.
Thus, through wisdom, he perceives the quality of sensual desire as suffering, impermanent, and subject to change;
perceiving it thus, he abandons longing for it.
Amidst great terrors that are like executioners.
Thus, free from passion and well-disciplined in his faults,
one should cultivate the meditation on loving-kindness with heedfulness;
with a mind of loving-kindness, one should be compassionate for the welfare of others.
Acting thus, one goes to the heavenly realm.
This verse of such a kind was spoken by that virtuous person for the sake of the well-spoken meaning;
whoever, my friend, should practice this accordingly.
May I go to the point where the King of Death is not seen.
Rejoicing in that well-spoken word,
Brahmā, Indra, and the gods of the Thirty-three,
filled with zeal and joy, joined their palms in reverence.
Those illustrious ones went to that city of the gods.
The arrival of Aṣṭamaka, Bhīmaratha, and Udgata, the king of Kaliṅga, was of great significance.
Or else, sensual desire has been abandoned by all of them.
The kings said:
For thus it is that you, who know the minds of others,
have seen that desire for sensual pleasures has been abandoned by all of us;
grant us the opportunity for your favor.
So that we may fully attain your course.
Sarabhaṅga said:
I grant you leave out of compassion; the passion for sensual desires has been abandoned by all of you. Make your bodies a source of vast joy.
So that you may fully attain my course.
The kings said:
"We shall do all these words of yours, O one of vast wisdom; whatever you shall say to us,
we shall fulfill with great joy."
So that we may fully attain your course.
And worship has been performed for the calf and the seer;
let those seers of virtuous form depart,
and you may dwell in the hermitage, delighting in meditation.
This is the supreme wealth for one who has gone forth.
Recalling his former dwelling and former birth, the Blessed One,
the Teacher, related this Jātaka in the presence of the monks.
And those aggregates, those elements, and those sense-bases—
the Blessed One would explain this matter with reference to the self.
In this beginningless and endless saṃsāra where I formerly dwelt,
there were Anāthapiṇḍika, Śakra the king of the gods and lord of Śacī, the King of Kaliṅga, Ānanda, Śāriputra, and Aṣṭaka.
Then King Bhīmaratha was the Maudgalyāyana of great supernatural power;
I was Sarabhaṅga—thus should you remember this Jātaka.
Even then the Dharma was taught by me to the assembly consisting of gods and humans; now as well, the Dharma is being taught by me to the assembly consisting of gods and humans.
The Sarabha-jātaka is completed.
In Vārāṇasī, thirty companions had gone out to a park; the mother of one among them had passed away and was reborn among the goddesses.
She had realized the Dharma at the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma.
She remembered that son;
then, because of her affection for her son, she felt toward all those companions the same love she felt for her son.
In Vārāṇasī, there was a courtesan named Kāśikā.
For what reason was that courtesan called Kāśikā?
Such a beautiful form, produced as the ripening of virtuous karma, was able to endure the entire land of Kāśi; therefore, it is called "Kāśikā."

Upārdhakāśikā was the sister of that very Kāśikā; her beautiful form, produced by her own previous karma, was just like that of Kāśikā, yet one of her eyes was tawny. For that reason, she was called Upārdhakāśikā.
Those members of the assembly said to that woman from Kāśī, "Come and serve us.
But she, being empowered by that deity, did not go, saying, "I have some household business; I am unable to come."
Then, taking half-Kāśika cloth, they went to that park.
That deity also approached within the range of vision of those members of the assembly, appearing in the guise of a woman from Kāśi.
Seeing her, they ran toward Kāśikā;
the goddess was seen going and coming by way of immeasurable paths.
Then that goddess, having led those members of the assembly from that park ground into Ṛṣivadana, vanished in the presence of the Blessed One.
Then those members of the assembly approached to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
What sport, what pleasure can there be while [the world] is thus constantly ablaze? Having been cast into darkness, why do you not seek a lamp?
What joy, what delight can there be when things are thus constantly aflame? Cast into darkness, you do not manifest light.
Then they were all disciplined by the Blessed One in the mastery of powers, and they were ordained and received full admission with the "Come, monk" formula.
This is the going forth, the full ordination, and the state of being a monk for the venerable thirty members of the assembly.
_____ Thus concludes the account of the going forth of the thirty companions.

The Blessed One was staying at Vārāṇasī, the teacher of gods and men; having related the introduction in detail, there were now thirty other people traveling along a road not far from Ṛṣivadana. Then the Blessed One sat down near the road for the sake of favoring them.

Then, having seen the Blessed One, they approached him to pay homage at his feet; and by the Blessed One, through the power of mastery over all, they were all disciplined, ordained with the "Come, monk" formula, and received full admission.
This was the going-forth, the full admission, and the status of monkhood for these thirty venerable persons.
The Blessed One was staying at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana, the teacher of gods and humans.

Having related the introduction in detail, [it is said that] in the Kośala country there was a village named Droṇavastuka; there lived another brahmin, a great householder, wealthy, of great fortune, of great enjoyment, possessing abundant wealth, possessing abundant property, and possessing abundant stores of money, grain, treasuries, and granaries.
He possessed abundant gold, silver, wealth, and requisites; he had many female and male slaves, laborers, and servants; and he owned many elephants, horses, goats, cattle, and sheep.
Now, that brahmin mahāśāla had a wife named Maitrāyaṇī, who was gracious, beautiful to behold, noble in appearance, and endowed with the highest excellence of radiant complexion.
This brahmin lady Maitrāyaṇī had a son, a young man named Pūrṇa, who was gracious, handsome, and youthful in form.

Having performed meritorious deeds, being of great renown, and having fulfilled his duties under previous perfectly enlightened ones, he has severed his bonds, realized the state of full knowledge regarding the noble dharmas, and is in his final existence.

He heard that King Śuddhodana had a son named Sarvārthasiddha, who was endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man— those thirty-two marks of a Great Man by which there are only two destinies for such a person, and not a third.

If he dwells at home, he becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin), a lord of the four continents, a conqueror, righteous, a king of dharma, endowed with the seven jewels. These are his seven jewels, namely: the wheel-jewel, the elephant-jewel, the horse-jewel, the gem-jewel, the householder-jewel, the woman-jewel, and the counselor-jewel as the seventh; and his army is complete with a full thousand [divisions].
Of sons who are heroes, valiant, of excellent form and appearance, and who cause the destruction of enemy armies—
he dwells in these four great continents, namely: Jambudvīpa, Pūrvavideha, Aparagodānīya, and Uttarakuru.

Having conquered this entire great earth, including Uttarakuru and bounded by the oceans and mountains— making it free from thorns, without punishment, without weapons, and without oppression— he dwells therein through Dharma alone. Furthermore, if he goes forth from the home to the homeless life, he becomes a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha.

Endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, one whose fame is proclaimed and whose renown is celebrated, not led by others, a conqueror, unconquered, a seer of the meaning of all that is known,
self-controlled, and a master of his own will— he, the Seer of great psychic power and great majesty, [spoke] categorically for four reasons.
"Buddha will appear in the world"—thus was he prophesied by other fortune-tellers as well.

When the Blessed One had gone forth, he too went forth on that very same day; having gone to a hermitage in the Himalayas, he entered the life of a wandering seer and became a seer of great psychic power and majesty, one who attained the four dhyānas and possessed the five superknowledges.

Now he had twenty-nine young seers as disciples; they were all masters of the Vedas with their six limbs, attainers of the four meditations, possessed of the five superknowledges, and endowed with great supernatural power and majesty.
He said to those disciples:

A Buddha has appeared in the world; he dwells at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana, teaching the Dharma to human beings— a Dharma that is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, with good meaning and well-expressed in phrasing, which reveals a holy life that is entirely complete, pure, and purified.
"All aggregates are without refuge, scorched by great fear,
untrustworthy, and devoid of essence," so Gautama declares.
"What if we young men were now to go toward Vārāṇasī, to the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana,
in order to see that Blessed One Gautama? It is indeed excellent to approach and attend upon such Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones."

"Excellent, Preceptor! those young brahmins said. [They saw] Pūrṇa... proclaiming the holy life (*brahmacarya*), endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, his body adorned with the eighty minor characteristics (*anuvyañjana*), possessed of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), and strong with the ten powers of a Tathāgata and the four [assurances].

Confident through his intrepidities, with senses calmed and mind at peace, he had attained the supreme perfection of self-mastery and tranquility, having reached the ultimate perfection of self-mastery and tranquility. With his senses withdrawn inwardly and his mind not wandering outward, established in the nature of reality (dharmatā), he was as clear, untroubled, and serene as a lake; he rose up like a pillar of jewels or a pillar of gold shining with splendor.
Blazing with splendor, he was lovely to behold and not disagreeable to look upon;
and having seen him, his mind became exceedingly serene.
With a serene mind, he then approached the Blessed One, bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet, and said this to the Blessed One:
"Let me go forth, O Blessed One; ordain me, O Sugata."
Then the Blessed One addressed the seer Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra and his thirty companions with the "Come, monk" formula.
"Come, monks; lead the holy life under the Tathāgata."
Now, as soon as they had been addressed by the Blessed One with the words "Come, monk," whatever marks of a seer, protection of a seer, banner of a seer,

or attire of a seer they possessed all vanished; the three robes appeared, along with sumbhaka bowls established in their natural state, and their hair and deportment became established just like those of monks who had been ordained for a hundred years.
This is the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk for the venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, including his thirty personal disciples.
Thus, having been disciplined by the Blessed One in the mastery of power,
he— now having attained that mastery of power— praised the Blessed One to his face with these appropriate verses:
That you, while dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven, having become an elephant resembling a peak of snow,
entered the final womb— O kinsman of the one with a thousand rays— that is dear to me.

And that both your mother and father in this world were endowed with such noble form— your father being born of a lineage of great lords and sharing the same clan as the thousand-rayed sun— that is dear to me.
O you who abide in the presence [of reality], who pass away from the world without touching anything,
and who are unsullied by bile, blood, and phlegm— O you of the same lineage as the one with a hundred rays, you are dear to me.
And beholding you, O one of golden complexion, my mind experiences supreme joy;
like snakes following a red thread, O kinsman of the thousand-rayed sun, you are dear to me.
That you were born for the welfare of many people, shaking the earth as you were born;
that you took seven steps upon birth, O kinsman of the one with a thousand rays—that is dear to me.
And that the lords of the Guhyakas held a parasol over the Sage at his birth, and that there were two fans on both sides— O you of the lineage of the thousand-rayed sun, that is dear to me.
And that at the moment of your birth, O kinsman of the one with a hundred rays, streams of water—both warm and cool—gushed forth from the wells; that too is dear to me.
That you went forth, having abandoned the very strands of sensual pleasure, the seven treasures, and the four great continents— O kinsman of the one with a hundred rays— that is dear to me.
Having abandoned the earth, kinsmen, and the seven excellent treasures, you have brought an end to birth and death; O kinsman of the one with a hundred rays, that is dear to me.
O Hero, when the Blessed One’s mind was then being liberated, a great radiance arose;
all became exclusively blissful, O kinsman of the one with a hundred rays—that is dear to me.

Today the noble assembly has been well-disciplined by the Jina, the Teacher; with minds supremely joyful, they have approached the time for the subduing of enemies. O you of the lineage of the thousand-rayed sun, that is dear to me.
Just as your vow was in the past, so have you now fully realized it, O Lord of the World;
that your vow and its attainment have been fulfilled, O kinsman of the one with a hundred rays, is dear to me.
Your renown has spread throughout the ten directions, and there is no one equal to you among the realms of beings;
you have reached the supreme goal through the nature of reality (dharmatā). O scion of the lineage of the hundredfold flavors, that is dear to me.
By good fortune the Blessed One is happy and free from illness; by good fortune this task of yours has been successfully accomplished.
By good fortune Namuci, along with his army, has been slain by you; by good fortune you have realized both this world and the world beyond.
By good fortune, O Lord of the World, you have requested it; by good fortune, O Hero, you grant your assent to him.
By good fortune, through the Dharma, I shall set in motion the Wheel of Dharma, endowed with twelve aspects.
By good fortune you have roared the lion’s roar; by good fortune there is no counter-argument to you anywhere.
By good fortune, O Best One, you have attained the Dharma of the Victor; by good fortune, you possess no stinginess.
By good fortune, divine vision has arisen for me; by good fortune, superhuman hearing has arisen for me.
Having seen Death on the Himalayas, it is by good fortune that you have been encountered by me.
[ Mvu 3.382 ] Herein, the five supernormal powers arose for me; by good fortune, my disciples became obedient.
By good fortune, we were not joined with evil; by good fortune, we experience the King of Dharma.
By good fortune we have come for refuge; by good fortune the Four Truths have been fully realized;
by good fortune you are perfectly confident in the Dharma; by good fortune we have attained mastery.
Thus, at that time, in the presence of the Jina, the Venerable Pūrṇa,
having attained the Dharma, was joyful and rejoiced, having received the path that had been taught in the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī.
The narrative concerning the Venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra is completed.

The Blessed One, the perfectly awakened one, having accomplished the purpose for which he had come, was dwelling at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana, as a teacher of gods and humans; [this being] the detailed introduction, in the region of Avanti, in a town named Markaṭa, there lived a wealthy brahmin householder of King Ujjhebhaka Toṇehāraka.

The royal preceptor was a man of great wealth and great enjoyment, possessing abundant resources, vast property, and an abundance of money, grain, treasuries, and storehouses; he had an abundance of gold, silver, wealth, and utensils, as well as many female and male slaves, laborers, and servants, and many elephants, horses, goats, cattle, and sheep; he belonged to the Kātyāyana clan.
He had two sons: one named Nālaka and the second named Uttara.
Uttara was the elder, while Nālaka was the younger; he was wise, skillful, intelligent, quick-witted, sharp-minded, and possessed of penetrating insight.

Their maternal uncle, a seer named Asita, dwelt in a hermitage on the Vindhya mountains in the land of the Avantis; surrounded by a retinue of five hundred disciples, subsisting on roots, fruits, and gleaned grain without cultivation, he was teaching the Vedas and mantras to five hundred young brahmins.
Having gone there to the north, he studied the Vedas;
then, having performed the communal recitation (*saṃgīti*), he returned to his father’s presence.
Then he gave instruction before his father and other brahmins who were masters of the Vedas;
as he was giving that instruction, Nālaka grasped all those Vedas.
He too, having heard the Vedas from his brother in the presence of his father and those brahmins who had mastered the Vedas, applied himself to their study.
His father and those brahmins who had mastered the Vedas were amazed, exclaiming, "Oh, the intelligence of this young man!"
Then his parents said to him, "The Buddha has appeared in the world; go forth into the religious life."
Having gone to the Vindhya Mountains, he entered the life of a wandering ascetic under the hermitage of his maternal uncle, the seer Asita.

By applying himself, striving, and exerting effort, dwelling engaged in the practice of vigilance during the first and last watches of the night, he produced the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and realized the five super-knowledges (*abhijñā*).
When the Blessed One had awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and set in motion the sublime wheel of Dharma...

While he was dwelling at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana, practicing for the welfare of gods and humans and leading hundreds of thousands of living beings to the deathless, his disciple was addressed by the seer Asita:
"A Buddha has appeared in the world; go, go forth toward the east."
Then, proceeding by stages from the hermitage of the seer, he arrived at Vārāṇasī.

In Vārāṇasī, six teachers who claimed the status of a teacher resided: Kāśyapa, Pūraṇa, Maskarī Gośāliputra, Ajita Keśakambalin, Kakuda Kātyāyana, Sañjayī Vairaṭṭikaputra, and the Nirgrantha Jñātiputra.
He approached those six teachers who claimed to be masters, yet he did not find satisfaction in their minds.
There are four great treasures: Śaṅkha in Vārāṇasī, Paduma in Mithilā, Piṅgala among the Kaliṅgas, and Elapatra in Takṣaśilā.
In Vārāṇasī, a monthly festival of Śaṅkha was being held;
there, the Naga kings who were lords of treasures arrived as invited guests.
And there, the Naga king Elapatra had established these questions: "To whoever shall answer these questions, his daughter shall be given and a thousand pieces of gold."
How is one a sovereign king? How does one become a ruler? How does one become free from passion? And how is one called a fool?
The Blessed One said:
The sixth is the sovereign king who rules over his kingdom with passion;
yet he who is without passion becomes free from dust, while he who is passionate is called a fool.
Elapatra said:
By what is that fool carried away, and what indeed does the wise person push aside?
How does one become secure in yoga? Tell this to me who asks.
The Blessed One said:
The fool is carried away by attachments; the wise man casts them off.
One who is unbound by all attachments is called a possessor of security.
Elapatra said:
You are addressed by the Buddhas and the awakened ones regarding dreams or visions;
having examined them, speak the truth—proclaim it and cut through our doubt.
The deity said:
The Great Hero was seen in person, dwelling within the Deer Park,
proclaiming the supreme Dharma like a lion in a mountain cave.
"Ah, after so long we shall behold him whose limbs are adorned with various marks like stars— the Buddha of supreme intelligence!"
After a long time, we shall hear your voice, which resembles the sound of Brahmā and shatters all afflictions by teaching that "all things are impermanent, suffering, and non-self."
Having heard this voice of fresh resonance, which resembles the sound of Brahmā,
we shall attain liberation from our worldly bonds upon reaching that bull among men.
Having seen the Great Seer, the illustrious Kāśyapa, who acts for the sake of the world and perceives the ultimate goal,
[he saw] the root of all that is auspicious.
We shall guard our virtue as the yak guards its tail.
Having cut off the path in the midst of the forest,
and having failed to make the Teacher, the Sage,
their guide, they have shattered the training of those who perceive the ultimate truth.
Fallen from the path, one enters the Avīci hell of great suffering.
Showers as vast as mountains, known as the "Infinite Piercing," fall upon his limbs;
they tear at the body of one afflicted by suffering.
Therefore, O you of vast renown, grant us liberation!
I hear the Dharma, yet I do not see it, for my eyes have been plucked out like the sun as it rises; O you with the splendor of the sun’s rays, grant me comfort!
When will there be liberation for those in the animal realm?
Seeing this terrifying transformation arising from immoral conduct, who that has a throat choked with tears and weeps would not practice moral discipline?
He indeed delights in pleasures, yet he shall not be unsteady; being of virtuous conduct, he is immovable like a mountain.
O wise one, draw forth the intellect that perceives the true goal.
Belonging to the lineage of Maitreya, he is the destroyer of the passion for existence.
Nālaka Kātyāyana, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, spoke thus to the Blessed One.
My father was the family priest of King Toṇehāra;
he was endowed with knowledge regarding the arising of stars and had attained mastery over the constellations.
My father, compassionate and desiring my welfare, said this to me:
"O son, a Buddha has indeed appeared; go to the east and go forth into the religious life."
Thus have I arrived, O Blessed One; please grant me the going forth.
The Tathāgata, endowed with the grounds of self-confidence, speaks these words.
He addressed the brahmin Kātyāyana, saying, "Come, monk!
This indeed became his going forth and his full ordination.
The Venerable Kātyāyana said:
You have understood this speech of Asita exactly as it is;
but I ask you, Gautama, who have reached the further shore of all phenomena.
To one who has gone forth as a homeless wanderer and desires to live by alms,
O Sage, proclaim the Dharma— the state of sagehood, the supreme goal.
The Blessed One said:
And you ask about this state of silence, which is not difficult nor hard to accomplish;
indeed, I shall explain it to you—steadfast yourself and remain firm.
You should make your portion equal toward those who revile or praise you in the village;
guard against mental malice, and remain patient and composed.
Various sounds issue forth like flames of fire in a forest;
let not that woman seduce you for the sake of luring the sage.
Abstaining from sexual practices, having abandoned both superior and inferior sensual desires,
he is neither hostile nor obstructive toward those beings who are mobile or stationary.
As it is with oneself, so it is with others; as it is with others, so it is with oneself.
Taking oneself as the measure, one should neither harm nor cause others to be harmed.
Having abandoned even this slight desire here, become one who is free from longing and at peace.
Abandon both desire and greed, wherein ordinary people are attached;
let the wise person practice accordingly and cross over this hell.
Then, after spending the night there, he should enter the village for alms;
he should not welcome invitations or offerings from the village.
Having entered a village, the sage should not wander impulsively among the families;
he should not be a seeker of food, nor one who interrupts conversation, nor should he speak with a desire for gain.
With bowl in hand, he should wander about, though not mute, appearing as if he were mute;
he should not disparage this or that gift, nor should he despise the donor.
"It was right that you gave; it was not right that you did not give. May it be well with you!
Since you are equal in both respects, I shall turn back your harshness."
Having wandered for alms, he should protect the edge of his bowl;
with an empty belly and moderate food, he should be one of few desires and free from greed.
Thus, having gone to the foot of a tree and taken his seat, the Sage meditates upon what is beneficial; he does not seek excessive gratification for himself.
For that monk, O monks, for whom there is no stream here, whose flow is severed,
and who has abandoned what is to be done and what is not to be done— for him no fever exists.
Thus has the refuge been declared by the Fully Awakened One who understands all things:
you shall delight in solitude, and thus you shall traverse the ten directions.
In this way you shall attain the state of a sage; be like the edge of a razor. Having brought the tongue against the palate, become thus restrained.
Free from the stench of raw flesh, unattached, and devoted to the foot of a tree,
you should train in sitting alone and in the service of the ascetics.
Having heard of the upright meditation of those meditators who have abandoned sensual desires,
my follower should then further train himself in moral shame and faith.
The further shore does not double, nor indeed does it multiply in this way;
manifold is the path revealed by the state of a recluse.
One recognizes that flood in rivers, in chasms, and in ravines;
yet it roars like a torrent, while the great ocean remains tranquil.
That which is empty makes noise; that which is full is indeed silent.
A fool is like an empty jar; a wise person is like a full pool.
The sage who speaks much that is appropriate and meaningful,
knowing well, speaks much in order to realize nirvana for himself.
But the wise one who speaks with moderation and does not speak much despite knowing [the truth]—that sage deserves the state of a muni; that sage has attained the state of a muni.
The Questions of Nālaka are completed.

The Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One, having accomplished the purpose for which he had come, was dwelling at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana, the teacher of gods and humans— having provided the detailed introduction—
the wealthy merchant in Mathurā, who was rich, of great wealth and great possessions, with vast assets and abundant stores of money, grain, treasuries, and granaries.
He possessed abundant wealth and resources consisting of gold and silver, as well as many elephants, horses, goats, and sheep, and a large number of female and male slaves, laborers, and servants.
Now, three daughters were born to that merchant.
Thinking that she was inauspicious, she was given to a female wanderer (parivrājikā), with the instruction:
"When she has grown up, then cause her to go forth; this shall be your means of livelihood."
A nurse was also given to raise that girl, and whatever expenses were incurred were provided by the merchant.

Then she grew up just like a blue lotus, a red lotus, or a white lotus; and when she reached the age of discretion, she was initiated by that female wanderer and trained in the ascetic practices, having mastered all the scriptures of the wanderers.
Now she engaged in conversation with various other female wanderers, and no one was able to provide her with a reply;
she alone was proclaimed as the foremost among speakers, a master of debate, and proficient in all treatises.
And another brahmin, a master of the Vedas, an expert in all the śāstras, a grammarian who had reached the furthest limit of his field, a debater and proponent of arguments,
arrived at Mathurā from the Deccan; having wrapped his side with a copper vessel and lit a great torch,
he entered Mathurā.
"Look out from the middle of this market street;
is there anyone skilled in description who might converse with us?"
Then he was addressed by the people of Mathurā:

"Extinguish this firebrand! [The man replied,] "There is a female renunciant here among us; she is foolish and young, but on the seventh day from now she will speak with you. If you are able to converse with her, then [you may do so]."
Then he said:
"So be it; on the seventh day from now, I shall speak with that female wanderer, and your honors should be present among them."
Those merchants and countryfolk from Mathurā summoned that female wanderer and said to her:

"A brahmin has arrived from the southern region, a debater who has mastered the Vedas and is intent on debate regarding grammar; you are able to engage in discussion with that brahmin on the seventh day."
Then she said:
"Certainly, I am able to converse with him or anyone else;
I too am intent on debate."
Having heard this from the Naigamas, the Naigamas caused bells to be sounded at the crossroads, junctions, streets, and gateways in Mathurā, proclaiming:
"On the seventh day, a discussion and debate will take place between such-and-such a female wanderer and a brahmin disputant from the southern region."
Whoever wishes to hear it, let him assemble.
There, platforms were constructed all around with colorful decorations;
having heard the news from the countryside, a great multitude of people came to Mathurā.
This thought occurred to that brahmin:
"What kind of female wanderer is she who will converse with me?
What if I were now to see that female wanderer?"
Then, out of curiosity and with a desire for further inquiry, he went to that dwelling place of the female wanderers; having arrived, he questioned them.
Who is that female wanderer who will debate with that brahmin from the southern region in the midst of a great assembly?
Those who were questioned by him pointed out that female wanderer, who was reciting her lessons in her own cell with a distinct voice and deliberate articulation.
Then that brahmin, having approached the female wanderer, asked her:
"Is it true that you speak with me in the midst of the assembly?"
Then she said:
"Certainly, there is no doubt; I shall speak with you in the midst of the assembly, or with any other person who speaks with faith."
Now that brahmin was young and handsome, and that female wanderer was also young and beautiful; from the very moment they saw one another, love fell between them.
Then that brahmin said to that female wanderer:
"I am one who has need of you."
That female wanderer said:
I am in need of you.
The brahmin said:
"If it be so, we shall act in such a way that there may be a meeting between us, yet others do not know of it. Having reached a mutual agreement there in the midst of the assembly, we shall converse;
whoever among us should be defeated must enter into discipleship under the other."
"There is no wonder here that a woman should be subdued by men.
But if you, lady, were to subdue me, then I would be despised and humiliated by the whole world, thinking: 'By a mere woman of two-finger-wisdom, you have been subdued!
Lady, act in such a way that I may subdue you; then you shall be my disciple."
"You shall become [a monk];
thus there will be a mutual meeting between us,
and no one at all will know of it."
Then that female wanderer said:
So be it.
Then that brahmin, having thus consulted with that female wanderer, rushed out.

Then, on the seventh day, many thousands of living beings assembled there from the fourfold army; King Māthura arrived, the princes and ministers arrived, the merchant guild headed by the guild-leader arrived,
the community of traders headed by the caravan leader arrived, the assembly of brahmins headed by the domestic priest arrived, and the eighteen guilds arrived.
Śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, tīrthikas, and courtesans had gathered together.
That brahmin also arrived, and that female wanderer also arrived together with many other female wanderers;
having arrived, they sat down on their respective seats in the midst of the assembly.
The brahmin rose and made a request to the assembly together with the king.
"Sirs, we have committed the folly of a young boy in that we, as women, entered into conversation with her.
It would not be surprising if I were to rebuke this female wanderer; for they would say, 'What is so wonderful in a man rebuking a woman?

But rather, if this female wanderer were to rebuke me, then I would be despised and humiliated by the whole world, thinking, 'You have been rebuked by a mere woman whose wisdom is only two finger-breadths deep.'"
Thus,
I made this request to the assembly together with the king:
"If I am able to refute this female wanderer in the midst of the assembly, then [I shall do so] to this female wanderer."
"I must become her disciple; then, when I have refuted this female wanderer in the midst of the assembly, she must enter into discipleship under me."
Then that female wanderer was questioned by that assembly.
"O Brahmin, this person speaks thus; how does it occur to you?"
Then she said:
"So be it."

Having made this agreement with the brahmin, the female wanderer took up her staff; the female wanderer also countered that brahmin with a superior argument for the sake of prevailing in the assembly.
Thus, with those words and counter-words, they spent that entire day, yet neither was able to refute the other, nor could the other refute the first.
In this manner, as it was for one day, so it continued for seven nights;
yet no one was able to subdue another, nor could anyone else subdue the other.
When those men had returned home from that assembly at every evening session, they were asked by their wives: "From where have you been coming every evening for these seven nights?"
