They said:
"You do not know for what purpose we have come at this unusual hour.

A brahmin from the southern region has arrived— one who has mastered the six limbs of the Vedas, attained proficiency in all treatises, and is a master of grammar— who has been conversing with that female wanderer for seven days now and is unable to defeat her."
Then they said to their masters:
Thus, since women are wise in this way, what man would place himself before a woman in terms of intellect and discernment?
The thought occurs to those people:
"If by some means that brahmin could be won over by that female wanderer, then these women of ours would always hold her in contempt and regard us as not even worth a blade of grass.
Thus, for the most part, that entire city became favorable toward that male wanderer and toward that female wanderer.

On another day, when the assembly had gathered, the brahmin gave a reply to the female wanderer; however, because she, though desiring it, did not respond to that reply, the people raised shouts of derision, declaring the brahmin victorious and the female wanderer defeated.

Then that brahmin had the female wanderer take up her triple staff and have her take her umbrella and sandals; he then expelled her from the midst of the assembly according to the rule for a disciple.
The brahmin also went to the female wanderer’s dwelling, and they met with one another according to their mutual desire.
Through frequent union, that female wanderer became pregnant.

Having now departed from Mathurā and wandering on a tour through the countryside in the southern region, after the lapse of nine or ten months, they arrived at Śvetavalākā; there, at Śvetavalākā, they stayed for the night.
In that assembly hall, the female wanderer gave birth;
a boy was born, handsome, beautiful to behold, and endowed with the most excellent excellence of complexion.
Because he was born in the assembly hall of those [gods], they gave the young brahmin the name Sabhika.
Then that young brahmin was raised by his mother and father.

When that young man had reached the age of discretion, he was taught writing, arithmetic, accounting, and depositing, and he was made to study all the treatises of the wandering mendicants; he became a master debater.
Then, having entered the interior of the ocean, he sought a Buddha where no Buddha existed.
Wandering through the sixteen great provinces, he eventually arrived at Vārāṇasī and approached the Blessed One at the Deer Park in Ṛṣivadana.
Then the wanderer Sabhika, having exchanged greetings with the Blessed One and having engaged in pleasant and courteous conversation, sat down to one side.
Seated there, the wanderer Sabhika asked the Blessed One a question.
"Filled with doubt and uncertainty, I have come desiring to ask a question;
thus was the question asked by that householder."
Blessed One, explain it in due order, in accordance with the sequence, with logical connection, and in conformity with the Dharma.
The Blessed One said:
You have come from afar,
desiring to ask a question here;
I shall be the one who brings an end to your questions.
I shall explain it in due order, in accordance with the truth, with logical connection, and in conformity with the Dharma.
When this had been said, Sabhika the Wanderer replied to the Blessed One in verse:
What has one attained to be called a monk of good vows? How and what is it that makes one "tamed"? And how is one called a "Buddha"?
"O Blessed One, being asked by me, please explain in due order, in accordance with the sequence, with logical connection, and in conformity with the Dharma."
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the wanderer Sabhika.
Having made himself ready with his feet, having reached final nirvana and crossed over doubt,
he has understood both non-existence and existence in the world.
Having lived [the holy life], that monk has exhausted rebirth.
Equanimous toward all things and possessed of mindfulness,
he does not harm anyone in the world; such a śramaṇa has crossed over and is unstained.
The exalted one who does not produce any influx.
He whose faculties are cultivated both internally and externally in the world,
having become weary of this world and the world beyond—
One who is cultivated and self-controlled guards the proper time.
Having scattered through many eons the various sufferings of saṃsāra, he attained the fourfold rebirth—
free from stain, free from dust, and free from blemish.
They call him a monk who has attained the destruction of birth.
Then the wandering mendicant Sabhika, having rejoiced in what was spoken by the Blessed One, asked the Blessed One a further question.
What has he attained that they call him a brahmin? What is a śramaṇa? How is one well-bathed? How is one called a pure nāga?
O Blessed One, having been asked this question by me, please explain it in due order, in accordance with the truth, with logical connection, and in conformity with the Dharma.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the wanderer Sabhika.
Having washed away all evils, stainless, well-composed, and established in self,
he has understood saṃsāra as it truly is.
Having lived [the holy life], with rebirth exhausted, he is a Brahmā.
The one who has practiced self-restraint, having abandoned the ripening of merit,
being detached, and having understood this world and the world beyond;
The ascetic who has transcended birth and death is called "such" because of his being thus.
Having washed away all evils,
both internal and external, throughout the entire world,
as conceived by gods and humans;
"An aeon is not [too long] for me, moreover, as one who has completed his studies."
He does nothing at all in the world,
having relinquished all bonds through every yoga; unattached to anything, he is liberated.
"A Nāga is called 'Protector' because of suchness.
Then the wanderer Sabhika said this to the Blessed One:
What has been attained do they call "one who knows"?
How do they describe one who has understood? How does one become "possessed of vigor"? And how is one called "a thoroughbred"?
O Blessed One, being questioned by me, please explain my question in due order, in accordance with the truth, with logical connection, and in conformity with the Dharma.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the wanderer Sabhika.
Having investigated the Vedas exclusively [for the sake] of the ascetics...
Thus, being free from passion toward all feelings, he is a feeler who has transcended all feelings.
Having eliminated conceptual proliferation and name-and-form,
as well as the passion that exists internally and externally—
he who is equanimous, liberated from the bond at the very root of passion.
The Worthy One is called "Tathāgata" because he has realized suchness.
He who has severed his bonds, who possesses abandonment, and having brought about the destruction of all suffering,
does not protect others anywhere else.
One who is free from passion and possesses vigor is called "suchness."
He whose bonds have been refined both internally and externally throughout the entire world,
and who is liberated from all bonds of passion—
Those of vast wisdom call him "one who is well-bred."
Then, indeed, the wandering mendicant Sabhika asked the Blessed One a question.
Furthermore, one might ask the Sage: "Indeed, how is it that you are called 'the Knower of the Field' (kṣetrajña)? Thus the Householder asked the question.
How is that name of yours, O Sage, explained?
O Blessed One, being questioned by me, please explain the question in due order, in accordance with the sequence, with logical connection, and in conformity with the Dharma.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the wanderer Sabhika.
The fields of total restraint—
whether divine, human, or that which is the Brahmā-field—
he is liberated from all bonds to the root-fields.
The Knower of the Field is called "Tathāgata" because of his suchness.
Having investigated the mere sheaths—
the divine, the human, and that which is the sheath of Brahma—
he is liberated from the bondage of all sheaths.
One who is thus is called "skilled" by the Tathāgata.
Having investigated both the internal and external roots of the white and the roots of the black, he has abandoned them and has transcended them.
One who acts accordingly is called wise.
Having understood the Dharma of both the existent and the non-existent, inwardly and outwardly, with a liberated mind,
he is worthy of worship by gods and humans alike.
That sage has transcended the impurity of attachment.
Then the wandering mendicant Sabhika said this to the Blessed One:
A learned scholar of the Vedas... [text fragment] ...a learned scholar of the Vedas.
"What indeed is it called?"—thus I have asked the Blessed One; please explain to me, in due order, in accordance with the truth, with logical connection, and in conformity with the Dharma.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the wanderer Sabhika.
Having heard all dharmas and having fully understood what is blameworthy and what is blameless in the world with its gods,
he is peerless, without grasping, and purified.
Free from suffering, they call him a learned master of the Vedas.
Having abandoned dwellings, attachments, and bonds, he has transcended them; being dispassionate toward all evils, he does not return to the bed of the womb.
The Noble One is called "the Protector" because of suchness.
He who has attained the goal through my teachings,
having approached all phenomena with right knowledge, is endowed with true insight and conduct.
One who possesses such conduct is called a protector because of their suchness.
Having avoided and fully understood whatever phenomenon there may be that results in suffering— whether above, below, across, or including the world of the gods.
One who has brought illusion, conceit, as well as anger and greed to their end—
that wanderer they call one who has attained what was to be attained.
Then Sabhika, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the well-spoken words of the Blessed One, praised the Blessed One with these appropriate verses:
O one of vast wisdom, those sixty-three doctrines of the ascetics' disputations are all dependent upon designations and the perception of syllables.
O Hero, you have opened up the paths of retreat.
You are the ender of suffering, you have gone to the further shore of all phenomena;
you are the perfectly awakened one, free from outflows;
you possess splendor, steadfastness, and abundant wisdom.
He who is free from passion shall indeed bring an end to suffering.
The Sage, who has attained the attainment of the states of silence, is unshakable;
he is incomparable, the kinsman of the sun, the bestower of liberation, and one whose vows are pure.
As that Naga of Nagas, the Great Hero, speaks,
all the deities rejoice, as do both Narada and Parvata.
I sought that which I desired, and the Visionary One explained it to me;
all your doubts have been shattered and rendered baseless.
Truly, you are a sage and a fully awakened one; there are no hindrances for you.
Thus, you are not defiled by either merit or evil.
"Cool, having attained self-control, radiant, and possessing true valor—O Hero, stretch out your feet; Sabhika pays homage to the Teacher."
Now, having been disciplined by the Blessed One in the mastery of the powers, he was ordained with the "Come, monk" formula and received full admission.
This was the going-forth, the full admission, and the state of a monk for the venerable Sabhika.
The story of Sabhika, the questions, the destruction of the outflows, and the going forth are completed.

The Blessed One was staying at Vārāṇasī on the bank of the river Varaṇā, as a teacher of gods and men; having established the setting in detail, there was then on the bank of that river Varaṇā a great nyagrodha tree, possessing roots, possessing a trunk, and possessing branches, leaves, and foliage— graceful, inspiring, and dark blue.
Resembling a cloud of collyrium.
There, a man had made a vow at that banyan tree by chance, and his prayer was fulfilled.
He performed a great festival and honored that banyan tree with offerings.
Then, seeing him, other men and women followed his example and [began to worship] there at that banyan tree.

Thinking, "It is a prayer for truth," all those in Vārāṇasī pray to that banyan tree; it is renowned for its prayers for truth, and whatever one prays for at that banyan tree, that prayer of theirs is fulfilled.
There was once a certain person who had practiced virtue in the past.
And this [person] bows down to the gods;
by chance he leads them to that state—
thus do false views proceed.

And in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a guild-president who was wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments; he had abundant property, vast granaries and treasuries, an abundance of gold, silver, wealth, and utensils, many elephants, horses, goats, and sheep, and numerous female and male slaves, laborers, and servants, yet he was childless.
Now, for the sake of a son, he has offered hundreds of sacrifices and prayers, thinking, "May a son be born to me," yet none is born.
Now, the merchant’s wife heard that on the bank of the Varaṇā River there was a banyan tree that fulfilled prayers; whatever anyone requested there, that prayer was granted.
Then the merchant’s wife informed her husband:
"Noble son, I have heard that on the bank of the Varaṇā River there is a great banyan tree called Satyopayācana; whatever anyone requests there, it is fulfilled for them.
Let us go to that banyan tree and petition it for a son."
The guild-president, together with his retinue, went to that banyan tree by means of great supernatural power and prosperity.
Having arrived there, he performed a great offering and honor for that banyan tree; then, together with his wife, the guild-president made this vow before the banyan tree:
"We desire a son from you. If a son is born to me, then I shall establish a temple here for you and perform great offerings and honors for you."
Women are capable of directing men;
therein, the auspicious woman is the very root.
And even those lords of men who have been slain in battle [are so through her].
For them as well, this [misfortune] has woman alone as its root.
That merchant’s wife also made a vow.
"O Nyagrodha tree, you are renowned as one who makes true requests.

Just as the merchant has promised you a temple and offerings of honor, so shall I fulfill them; however, if you do not give me your son, then I will have your roots cut down along with everything they hold.
A tree deity dwells there, bearing the same name as the tree itself.
There, in that banyan tree, dwelt a son of the gods named Nyagrodha.
Now, that son of the gods, being thus entreated by the merchant’s wife, became afraid:
"I do not take anything from anyone, yet this merchant’s wife makes such a request of me.
If she does not have a son, she will have this palace of mine cut down with an axe."
The divine son Nyagrodha requested Śakra, the lord of the gods:

"O Kauśika, I do not take anything from anyone by force, nor do I snatch it away; however, that merchant has performed worship and hospitality in my abode and made such a vow. I desire that it be fulfilled for that merchant of Vārāṇasī."
May he become my son; let not that residence of mine be destroyed.
Then that son of the gods was comforted by Śakra, the lord of the gods:
"Do not fear; I shall act in such a way that he will have a son who will not destroy your abode."

Now, at that time in the abode of the Thirty-three, there was another son of the gods who had performed meritorious deeds, who was renowned, possessed of great supernormal power and majesty, and who had rendered service under previous perfectly enlightened Buddhas; he whose roots of virtue were fully ripened, who was close to nirvana, bound by only one more birth, and subject to passing away from among the hosts of the Thirty-three gods.

Thus was he addressed by Śakra, the lord of the gods: "You are subject to the law of falling; since the signs of the law of falling have appeared for you, you shall fall and be reborn. Therefore, be reborn there in Vārāṇasī in the womb of the wife of a guild-leader."
Then that son of a god said to Śakra, the lord of the gods:
My intention is this: having been reborn among human beings, I shall go forth in the teaching of the Blessed Buddha, and having gone forth, I shall make an end of suffering.

Therefore, it is not possible for me to be reborn in that merchant’s family; for a merchant’s family is a source of great attachment and an obstacle to wholesome qualities (kuśaladharma). Instead, I shall be reborn here in this middle [class].
Therefore, having gone forth in the teaching of the Blessed One without hindrance and according to my pleasure, I shall make an end of suffering.
Śakra said to him:
"Make a vow there to be reborn in that merchant family; I shall act in such a way that you, having gone forth from that merchant family, will renounce the world in the teaching of the Blessed One.
At these words of Śakra, the lord of the gods, that son of the gods made a vow to be born there in the family of a certain merchant in Vārāṇasī.

Having now passed away from among the Trāyastriṃśa gods, he was conceived in the womb of the guild-president’s wife in Vārāṇasī; and after the lapse of nine or ten months, that guild-president’s wife gave birth.

A son was born to her, handsome, beautiful to behold, with no coarse features, endowed with the highest excellence of complexion. As soon as he was born, the guild-president performed delightful birth-rites for him;
food, drink, snacks, meals, perfumes, garlands, and ointments were distributed among ascetics, brahmins, the wretched, beggars, and other people;
and channels of oil, channels of ghee, and channels of drink were set flowing.
After the passing of seven days, an assembly of brahmins skilled in astrology was summoned and told, "Give a name to the boy."
When they were giving a name to that boy, they gave him the name Yaśoda.
Then, having satisfied and served those brahmins with that solid and soft food, and having given them hundreds of laps full of silver and gold, they were dismissed.
Four nurses were appointed for Yaśoda:
one anointed him and bathed him; another suckled him at the breast; another removed his excrement and urine; and another carried him on her hip.
In this way, the young Yaśoda grew up just like a blue lotus, a red lotus, or a white lotus.
As it was said by the Blessed One:
For those who have performed meritorious deeds flourish like a banyan tree in fertile soil;
one of little merit does not grow, like a tree by the roadside.
When the prince had reached the age of discretion, he was then taught writing—its composition, memorization, and practical application.
Furthermore, his father had three palaces built for him: one for winter, one for summer, and one for the rainy season; and sixty thousand women were established as his harem.

And in those palaces, staircases equipped with mechanical devices and spells were constructed; five hundred men would join them together and take them apart, and as those staircases were being joined and taken apart, the sound traveled for half a yojana.
The second Kulika, having gone to the eastern region on business, returned;
the merchant then sent a messenger to him.
"Come, behold the power of my son!"
Then that guild-president came into the presence of the merchant.
The merchant had that second guild-president seated upon a single couch;
he also summoned the youth Yaśoda,
who, having paid homage to both his father and the second guild-president, was made to sit right there on the couch.
All these three sat together upon a single couch.
The king sent a messenger to the merchant, saying:
"There is urgent royal business; come quickly!"
The guild-president said to the second nobleman:
"You were with the prince until I returned from the royal palace."
The merchant had gone to the royal palace, and the second guild-president, the householder, was sitting there together with Prince Yaśoda.
Then, having seen that prosperity of Yaśoda, the guild-president’s son, this thought occurred to him:
"Indeed, this household life is not to be desired for one who possesses such enjoyments and luxuries.

Without a doubt, this young man must have performed services toward the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and the great Śrāvakas; he must have offered every kind of gift, perfumed his mind with spiritual impressions, and cultivated previous roots of merit, being thus unique."
Having planted roots of merit,
if that prince were to see the Buddha, the Blessed One, the god beyond gods, he would then be endowed with great benefit.
The householder said:
"Prince, indeed all youth ends in old age; all health ends in illness;

all life ends in death; all prosperity ends in adversity. With all that is dear and beloved, there is separation, dissociation, and parting—either after a long time or soon; you will either abandon this father, or he will abandon you."
Or will you abandon existence?
Indeed, Prince, have you seen the Blessed One?
The prince said:
Of what nature is the Blessed One?
The householder said:
O Prince, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat,

the Perfectly Awakened One, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, the knower of the world, the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, the teacher of gods and humans, is possessed of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty secondary characteristics.

His body was adorned; he was endowed with the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; he was powerful through the ten powers of a Tathāgata; he was perfectly confident through the four grounds of self-confidence; he was gracious, inspiring faith, with tranquil faculties and a tranquil mind;
he had attained the supreme perfection of self-mastery and tranquility; like an elephant that has completed its task, his senses were withdrawn within and not directed outward.

With his mind established and having attained the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā), this guarded elephant—having conquered his senses—is as clear, undisturbed, and serene as a lake; he shines like a raised jeweled pillar or a golden pillar, blazing with a mass of splendor and glory. He is enchanting and not disagreeable to behold, and he dwells right here on the further bank of the river Varaṇā in Vārāṇasī.

He has reached the shore, surrounded by those who have reached the shore; he is peaceful, surrounded by those who are peaceful; he is self-controlled, surrounded by those who are self-controlled; he is a brahmin, surrounded by brahmins;

he is learned in the Vedas, surrounded by those learned in the Vedas; he is a bath-graduate, surrounded by bath-graduates; he is a knower, surrounded by knowers; he has gone to the further shore, surrounded by those who have gone to the further shore;
he has reached dry land, surrounded by those who have reached dry land; he has abandoned all unwholesome qualities and is endowed with all wholesome qualities.
The conqueror, unconquered, who has seen the meaning of what is to be known, who is self-controlled and exercises mastery, practices the conduct that benefits gods and humans.
Thus did the householder, the second nobleman, speak the praises of the Buddha in the presence of the youth Yaśoda;
and the youth Yaśoda was one perfected by his previous applications, in his final existence.

Then, a desire to see the Blessed One arose in him, and a sense of revulsion toward sensual pleasures was born; through proper mental attention, his mind flowed toward, settled upon, and became clarified by the thought of going forth.

Then, having awakened at the hour of midnight, he saw that inner apartment asleep: one woman was embracing a lute, another a flute, another a *sughoṣaka*, another a *nakula*, another a bamboo pipe, another a *mahatī*, another a *vādiśa*,
another a *vikuṭaka*, another a *bhramarikā*, another an *ekādaśikā*, and another a drum.

One woman was embracing another; one was playing a *paṇava* drum, and another a *dardura* drum; some had placed their arms upon each other's shoulders, while one held another's jaw, and from some saliva dripped down.

Seeing that transformation of the prince, the women of the inner apartments conceived the perception of it as a cemetery; and desiring to go forth, they thought, "In the presence of the Blessed One, we shall go forth from the home life into homelessness."
Śakra, the lord of the gods, surrounded by countless hundreds of thousands of deities, arrived bringing perfumes and garlands.

The sons of the gods set up stairways, and as Yaśoda placed his feet upon the lowest step, the gods released a rain of celestial flowers; in the house of the guild-leader, a flood of divine blossoms reached the height of the knees.
Surrounded by hundreds of thousands of deities, the prince departed from the city of Vārāṇasī and approached the place where the Blessed One was.
The Blessed One emitted a radiance.

The noble son Yaśoda saw the Blessed One on the far bank of the river Varaṇā, lovely and pleasing to behold; having seen the Blessed One, he stepped out onto jeweled sandals and addressed the Blessed One in verse:
"I am beset, O Śramaṇa; I am beset, O worthy sir!"
The Blessed One said:
"Come, young man, do not fear; this is a state free from affliction. In this well-expounded Dharma, you shall become free from passion."
Then indeed, Yaśoda, the son of the guild-president, approached the Blessed One, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, and sat down to one side.
To that son of a guild-leader, Yaśoda, the Blessed One delivered a discourse intended to inspire faith, namely:
a discourse on giving, a discourse on ethical conduct, a discourse on heaven, and a discourse on the ripening of merit.
Yaśoda, the son of the guild-president, gained faith; his mind was filled with serene confidence in the presence of the Blessed One.
Then, for that Yaśoda, the son of a guild-leader, the Blessed One revealed the four noble truths;
he explained, taught, established, disclosed, analyzed, clarified, illuminated, and proclaimed the noble truth of suffering,
as well as the noble truth of the origin of suffering.
He teaches, and even elucidates, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering and the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.

Then, indeed, Yaśoda, the merchant’s son, while seated right there on that very seat, realized the three superknowledges, the six superknowledges, and mastery over the powers, and he experienced manifold kinds of miraculous power.
Then, at the end of that very night, Yaśoda’s parents,

not seeing the merchant’s son Yaśoda, went forth from Vārāṇasī with their throats choked with tears and faces weeping, surrounded by a great multitude of kinsmen and many thousands of living beings; they approached the Blessed One where Yaśoda was.
While searching for the merchant’s son,
Yaśoda’s parents saw his jeweled sandals on the bank of the Varaṇā River;
having seen them, they took Yaśoda’s jeweled sandals and, kissing them with their mouths, wept and wailed.
They grieved and lamented.
Having wept, wailed, grieved, and lamented, he approached the Blessed One, bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet, and said this to the Blessed One:
The Blessed One saw Yaśoda, the son of a guild-president.
Yaśoda, the son of the guild-president, entered such a state of mental concentration that while he remained seated right there, his parents did not see him, nor did any other group of people.
Then the Blessed One addressed the parents of Yaśoda, the merchant’s son.
"Sit down, householder.
It is possible that you may see Yaśoda, the merchant’s son; and having seen him, O Yaśoda, the merchant’s son, you should inspire your hearts with faith."
Then indeed, Yaśoda’s parents, the son of the guild-leader, having bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, sat down to one side, as did the rest of the multitude.
Then the Blessed One addressed Yaśoda, the merchant’s son, with his mind:
"Display a miracle of supernatural power."
Then indeed, Yaśoda, the son of the guild-president, standing in the air at the height of a palm tree, displayed many kinds of miraculous feats of supernatural power: being one, he became many;
having become many, he became one;
he appeared and disappeared; and he passed through walls, through mountains, and through rocky crags without obstruction.
And upon this earth he performs the act of emerging and submerging;
just as if in water, he walks without breaking through it, just as if on earth.
Even these two, the moon and the sun, so powerful and so majestic, he touches and strokes with his hand while sitting cross-legged, and he exercises mastery with his body as far as the Brahma-world.

He performs various twin miracles (*yamaka-prātihārya*): his lower body blazes while from his upper body five hundred streams of cool water flow; his upper body blazes while from his lower body five hundred streams of cool water flow; his left side blazes while from his right side [cool water flows].
Five hundred streams of cool water flow from his right side, while his left side blazes; from that left side, five hundred streams of cool water flow.
Then indeed, Yaśoda, the merchant’s son, having miraculously transformed himself into a bull the color of blue collyrium, vanished in the eastern direction and reappeared in the western direction;
he vanished in the western direction and reappeared in the eastern direction; he vanished in the southern direction and [reappeared] in the northern direction.
It appears in the northern direction and disappears in the southern direction; it appears in the southern direction.

Then indeed, Yaśoda, the son of the guild-leader, having magically transformed himself into the lion, the king of beasts—powerful, with large fangs, and maned—he let out a lion’s roar three times and vanished in the eastern direction and reappeared in the western direction;
he vanished in the western direction and reappeared in the eastern direction; [and likewise] from the south...

Having vanished from the north, he reappears in the south; having vanished from the north, he reappears in the south; having vanished from the earth, he reappears in the sky; having vanished from the sky, he reappears upon the ground.

Then indeed, Yaśoda, the son of the guild-president, having magically transformed himself into a white elephant-king with six tusks, a head like an *indragopa* insect, seven well-placed limbs, and the color of a white water-lily, vanished in the eastern direction and appeared in the western direction; vanishing in the western direction, he appeared in the eastern direction.
Vanishing from the south, he appeared in the north; vanishing from the north, he appeared in the south;
vanishing from the earth, he appeared in the atmosphere; and vanishing from the atmosphere, he appeared upon the earth.

Then, indeed, the noble son Yaśoda, having manifested himself in the form of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) endowed with the seven jewels and surrounded by a fourfold army, vanished in the eastern direction and appeared in the western;
vanishing in the western, he appeared in the eastern; vanishing in the southern, he appeared in the northern.
Having disappeared in the north, he appeared in the south; having disappeared from the earth, he appeared in the atmosphere; having disappeared from the atmosphere, he appeared on the earth.

Then indeed, the noble son Yaśoda went, stood, sat, and lay down in the sky at the height of a palm tree; he emitted heat and moved about, just as in the last month of summer the winds called *saṃghaṭṭaka* blow; even so did Yaśoda, the merchant’s son, go, stand, sit, and lie down in the open air at the height of a palm tree.
He blazes forth and wanders about;
standing at the height of one palm tree, then two palm trees, he becomes many after being one, and becomes one after being many.
Just as it was performed in the first revolution, so it should be done up to the height of seven palm trees.
From a height of seven palm trees he stood at six, from six at five, from five at four,
from four at three, from three at two, from two at one, and from one he stood upon the ground; having become one, he became many, and having become many, he became one.
Thus, he appears and disappears; he passes through walls, through mountains, and through rocky peaks without obstruction; he emerges from and sinks into this earth;
having risen up from the ground, he walks, stands, sits, and lies down; he emits heat and wanders about.

Then indeed, the various non-Buddhist practitioners—namely the Carakas, Parivrājakas, Traidandikas, Ānandikas, Guruputrakas, Gautamas, Dharmacintikas, Vṛddhaśrāvakas, and the third group, the Ulūkapakṣika Bhaginī Śramaṇās—having seen these various and manifold miraculous feats of supernatural power performed by Yaśoda, the son of the guild-leader, were struck with wonder and amazement; they became deeply moved and their hair stood on end. Up to that point...

The Dharma and Vinaya of the Blessed Gautama are well-expounded, revealed, with the rod laid aside and the rags cast off; they are sufficient for adornment and sufficient for inspiration, in that even one who is a householder, wearing white garments, clad in pure Kāśī cloth, his body anointed with sandalwood, and adorned with armlets and earrings, can personally realize such a Dharma as this.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One, concerning Yaśoda, the merchant’s son, uttered this inspired utterance:

Neither the state of being shaven-headed, nor matted hair, nor mud, nor various postures, nor sleeping on the bare ground, nor dust and water, nor the practice of squatting— these are not the means of abandoning [defilements].
For by that, there is no liberation from suffering.
Or even if adorned, one may practice the Dharma—
patient, self-controlled, disciplined, and living the holy life—
having laid aside the rod toward all living beings.
He is a brahmin, he is a śramaṇa, he is a bhikṣu.
Then the Blessed One delivered an inspiring discourse to Yaśoda’s parents and that great assembly of people—
namely, a discourse on giving, a discourse on morality, a discourse on heaven, a discourse on merit, and a discourse on the ripening of merit.
Yaśoda’s parents and that great assembly of people directed their minds toward the Blessed One with deep faith.

The Blessed One proclaimed the Four Noble Truths—suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering—to Yaśoda’s parents and that great multitude of people.

Then, while Yaśoda, the merchant’s son, and his parents remained seated on those very seats, the dustless, stainless Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena was purified; and many thousands of living beings also attained the Dharma.
Then the mother and father of Yaśoda, the guild-president’s son, said this to the Blessed One.
"O Blessed One, let Yaśoda, the merchant’s son, go forth; O Sugata, grant full ordination to Yaśoda, the merchant’s son."
Then the Blessed One addressed him with the "Come, monk" formula: "Come, monk; practice the holy life under the Tathāgata."

Then, as soon as Yaśoda, the son of a guild-leader, was addressed by the Blessed One with the "Come, monk" formula, whatever marks of a householder, whatever secrets of a householder, whatever banners of a householder, and whatever attributes of a householder he possessed all vanished; his three robes appeared, along with a sumbhaka bronze bowl, his hair remained in its natural state, and his deportment became perfectly composed.
It was, for example, as if for a monk who had been ordained for a hundred years;
such was the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk for the venerable Yaśoda, the son of a guild-leader.
_____ Completed is the dwelling of Yaśoda, the son of a guild-president.
The monks said to the Blessed One:

"Blessed One, as the ripening of what karma was Yaśoda, the son of a guild-leader, born into a wealthy, affluent, and highly prosperous guild-leader family, and having become a householder, how did he so swiftly attain mastery over his own powers?"
The Blessed One said:
Monks, this was the former vow of this very Yaśoda, the son of a guild-leader.

[ Mvu 3.414 ] Once upon a time, monks, right here in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a man from a decayed family who lived in hardship and poverty, making his living through the labor of others. Since Buddhas do not appear [frequently], Pratyekabuddhas arise in the world as objects of veneration during the intervals between Buddhas; they are beautiful in their silence, wandering alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
They tame themselves alone and attain parinirvāṇa; they are worthy of offerings and fields of merit.

Then a Pratyekabuddha named Bhadrika, having dressed himself early in the morning from Ṛṣivadana and taking his bowl and robe, entered the city of Vārāṇasī for alms at a time that was neither too early nor too late, while the morning meal was still being served; he was well-restrained in body, well-restrained in speech, well-restrained in mind, possessed of well-established mindfulness, and composed in concentration.
With a one-pointed mind and well-restrained senses.

Then, while wandering for alms in the city of Vārāṇasī, he was seen by that man from a decayed family. Gods and humans, being gracious and full of faith, were deeply moved in mind upon seeing the Pratyekabuddha Bhadrika; with a serene heart, they entered their homes.

Having been honored with food at his home, he made this aspiration: "By performing such service toward one worthy of offerings, may I not go to any evil state or to ruin through this root of merit; may I never be reborn in poor families, but may I be reborn in families that are wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments."
Then, having understood this kind of aspiration, the Pratyekabuddha Bhadrika departed through the air like a king of swans.
Then that man, seeing Bhadrika the Pratyekabuddha traversing the air like a king of swans, and longing for that Pratyekabuddha, with a heart even more serene,
made this aspiration:
"May I become a possessor of those qualities which this renunciant possesses."
The Blessed One said:
Monks, at that time and on that occasion, this Yaśoda, the son of a guild-president, was a youth from a family of diminished means here in the city of Vārāṇasī.
It was because of the service he rendered there to the Pratyekabuddha and the vow he generated that, through the ripening of that karma—
As a result of that, having taken it as his basis, he was never reborn in the states of woe or the lower realms; having passed away among humans, he was reborn among the gods as one of great power,
and having passed away among the gods, he was reborn among humans as one of great power, and in this very last birth, having pleased the Tathāgata, he attained mastery over the powers.
The Yaśoda-jātaka is completed.
The Blessed One, the perfectly awakened one, having accomplished the purpose for which he had come, was dwelling at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana.
There, the Blessed One addressed the venerable group of five auspicious ones.
“O monks, I am liberated from all fetters, both those divine and those human.
Go forth, monks, on your journey; let not two of you go by the same way.”
"For there are, O monks, beings who are pure, with little dust in their eyes, and of clear birth; yet they are falling away because they have not heard the Dharma.
I too shall go to Senāpati Village in Uruvilvā out of compassion for the matted-hair ascetics."
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to Māra, the most evil one:
"Indeed, this ascetic Gautama is staying at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana. He addresses the group of five auspicious monks: 'O monks, I am liberated from all fetters, both divine and human.
You too, O monks, are liberated from all fetters, both divine and human. Go forth, O monks, on your journey; do not [delay]!'"

And two monks came to me; there were beings with little dust in their eyes, who, due to not hearing the Dharma, were falling away from the state of those who have seen the truth. I too shall go toward Senāpati Village in Uruvilvā out of compassion for the matted-hair ascetics;
what if I were now to approach them?
For the purpose of removing the cataracts of ignorance.
Then indeed, Māra the Evil One addressed the Blessed One in verse:
"You consider yourself liberated though you are not liberated; why do you think you are liberated?
You are bound by tight fetters; you shall not escape me, O ascetic."
Then the Blessed One replied to Māra the Evil One with a verse:
I am liberated from all fetters, both those divine and those human;
know this, O Evil One: you, O Ender, are defeated!
Then indeed, Māra the Evil One, realizing "The ascetic Gautama knows me," became distressed, dejected, and remorseful, and vanished right there;
thus is this heard.
The Blessed One, the perfectly awakened Buddha, having accomplished the purpose for which he had come, was dwelling at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana as the teacher of gods and humans.
Then, while the Blessed One was alone, in seclusion, and in meditative retreat, this reflection arose in his mind:
Sensual pleasures are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to Māra, the Evil One:

"This ascetic Gautama is dwelling at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana. While he was alone, in seclusion, and in retreat, this very reflection arose in his mind: 'Sensual pleasures are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change; what if I were now to approach him in order to confound his vision?'"
Then indeed, Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One and addressed the Blessed One in verse:
"A snare named 'Firm' is roaming within your mind;
with it I shall bind you, O śramaṇa—you shall not escape me."
Then the Blessed One replied to Māra the Evil One in verse:

In this world, the five strands of sensual pleasure are proclaimed, with the mind as the sixth; therein my desire has vanished, it is severed, destroyed, and rendered baseless. Know this, O Evil One: you are defeated, O Ender!
Then, it occurred to Māra the Evil One:
"The ascetic Gautama truly knows me.
Distressed, dejected, and full of remorse, he vanished right there.
In this regard, this is heard.
The Blessed One, the perfectly awakened Buddha, having accomplished the purpose for which he had come, was dwelling at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana.
Then, while the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, withdrawn in meditation, this very reflection arose in his mind: "Material substratum is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change."
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to Māra, the Evil One:

The ascetic Gautama is staying at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana. While he was alone, in seclusion, and in retreat, this reflection arose in his mind: "Basis-of-existence is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change;
what if I were now to go to him in order to confound him?"
Then indeed Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One and addressed the Blessed One in verse:
One with sons rejoices in his sons; likewise, a cowherd rejoices in his cattle; so too does a person rejoice in their acquisitions.
For he who is without substrate does not rejoice.
Then the Blessed One replied to Māra the Evil One in verse:
One with sons grieves because of his sons; likewise, a cattle-owner grieves because of his cattle.
People are oppressed by their acquisitions.
For he who has ceased does not grieve.
Then indeed, Māra the Evil One, perceiving "The ascetic Gautama knows me," became distressed, dejected, and full of regret, and vanished right there;
thus is this heard.
The stainless color of the Blessed One Gautama— pure, utterly pure, immaculate, and radiant— is celebrated;
he bestows that peerless state upon all sentient beings.
May all beings attain nirvāṇa through their activities.
The monks said to the Blessed One:
How does the Blessed One utter an inspired utterance?
In whom neither deceit nor pride dwells,
who is free from passion, free from affliction, and free from desire;
whose anger has been cast out and whose self is fully extinguished—
He is a brahmin, he is a śramaṇa, he is a bhikṣu.
"O Blessed One, how should we also go for alms? Should we say, 'Give us alms'?"
The Blessed One said:
One should not remain silent when there is a formal recitation;
such is the request made to the Noble Ones.
Once upon a time, monks, in the past, in this very city of Vārāṇasī, there was a friend of a prince named Asthisena, the son of a family priest.

Having seen the peril in sensual pleasures, he went forth into the wandering life of a mendicant; he lived as a celibate from his youth, practiced the ten paths of wholesome action, had mastered the Vedas, and had reached the furthest limit of the wandering ascetics' scriptures.
Then that prince, having attained the kingdom, addressed Asthisena, the son of the family priest, with a verse:
The wise do not hate a beggar who comes with a staff of bones;
you are dear to me as a practitioner of the holy life (brahmacārī), O Brahmin—ask for whatever you desire.
Then, monks, the mendicant Asthisena replied in verse:
One who begs becomes disliked; one who does not give becomes disliked.
Therefore, I do not beg from you, lest there be enmity toward me.
Then, monks, that King of Kāśi replied to the mendicant Asthisena in verse:
For when a petitioner, though being one who ought to ask, does not request what should be asked for,
he causes another to lose the merit [of giving] and he himself suffers a loss.
Then, monks, the mendicant Asthisena replied to that King of Kāśi.
They say that begging is weeping, and not giving is weeping in response;
therefore, I do not beg from you, lest there be weeping for me.
One who possesses wisdom does not beg, nor is it fitting for noble ones to know [by begging].
Noble ones abide in their formal instruction; this is the manner of begging among noble ones.
Then, monks, that King of Kāśi replied to the mendicant Asthisena in verse:
"I give you, O Brahmin, a full thousand of Rohiṇī cows together with a bull;
for how could a noble man not give to another noble man?"
Having heard this well-spoken verse that was recited,
The Blessed One said:

Monks, he who was then the son of the royal priest of the King of Kāśī, named Asthisena, and who was a wandering ascetic and a friend of the king, was none other than myself; at that time, I was that wandering ascetic Asthisena.
The Jātaka of Asthisena is completed.
The Blessed One said:
The wise man indeed does not beg, nor is it fitting for a noble one to make known [his needs];
the noble ones abide in detachment—this is the begging of the noble ones.
In this way, monks, one should go on almsround.
Then those monks said to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, when alms have been obtained by us, should we say, 'May it be well! May it be well!'?"
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, you must not point out [the food] when alms have been obtained."
To refrain from all evil, to cultivate the wholesome,
and to purify one's own mind— this is the instruction of the Buddhas.
Then those monks, having completed the rainy season retreat at Ṛṣivadana in the Deer Park, set out on a wandering tour in various directions.

In Ṛṣivadana, the deity, seeing that the dwellings, walking-paths, sitting-places, and sleeping-quarters of those monks were empty and joyless, and finding no delight there, approached the Blessed One and addressed him in verse:
Today, having seen this empty and secluded place devoid of people, a distaste for sense-objects arises in me;
[so too do] those various tales of yours, though you are so learned.
Where have those disciples of Gautama gone?
The Blessed One said:
Some have gone to Magadha, some to Kosala, and others have gone to the land of the Vajjis;
like deer, they wander without attachment.
The monks dwell in seclusion.
The Blessed One set out;
seeing the Blessed One approaching the bank of the Ganges, the boatman brought the boat alongside.
The Blessed One, having boarded the boat, said to the boatman:
"Empty this boat, O monk; when emptied with loving-kindness, it will become light for you. Having cut off passion and hatred, you shall thereafter attain nirvāṇa."
"Empty this boat, O monk; when it is emptied with compassion, it will become light for you.
Having cut off passion and hatred, you shall thereafter attain nirvana."
"Empty this boat, O monk; once emptied with joy, it will become light for you.
Having cut off both passion and hatred, you shall thereafter attain nirvāṇa."
Empty this boat, O monk; when emptied by means of equanimity, it will become light for you.
Having severed both passion and hatred, you shall thereafter attain nirvāṇa.
The monk who dwells in loving-kindness and has faith in the Buddha’s teaching attains the peaceful state, which is irreproachable and liberating.
The monk who dwells in compassion and has faith in the Buddha's teaching attains the state of peace, which is not frequented by ordinary worldlings.
The monk who dwells in sympathetic joy and has faith in the Buddha’s teaching attains the state of peace that is not frequented by base men.
The monk who dwells in equanimity and has faith in the teaching of the Buddha attains the peaceful state, the deathless state of Nirvana.
Delighting in the Dharma, rejoicing in the Dharma, reflecting upon the Dharma,
and constantly recollecting the Dharma, a monk does not fall away from the true Dharma.
With an uplifted mind and a serene heart, having overcome both the pleasant and the unpleasant,
the monk then abounds in joy in the vicinity of Nirvana.
Neither by mere moral conduct and observances, nor again by great learning, nor even by the attainment of meditative concentration, nor by dwelling in remote lodgings and seats.
Longing for the bliss of renunciation, which is not practiced by ordinary worldlings,
the monk places his trust [in it] even before the destruction of the taints has been attained.
One does not become a monk merely by begging from others;
one does not become a monk merely by adopting unwholesome qualities.
But he who, having taken up the holy life with regard for both sensual pleasures and evil,
has become a ladder and possesses wisdom— he indeed is called a bhikkhu.
Wherever I walk, wherever I stand, wherever I sit, wherever I lie down; wherever I contract my body, wherever I extend my body—therein [I remain mindful].
Moving with restraint,
sleeping with restraint, and dwelling with restrained intentions, one should meditate vigilantly, delighting in deep reflection and remaining concentrated.
One who is contented—him they call a bhikkhu.
Restraint of the eye is good; restraint of the ear is good;
restraint of the nose is good; restraint of the tongue is good.
Restraint of the body is good; restraint of the mind is good.
A monk who is restrained in every way is liberated from all suffering.
Then, having been disciplined by the Blessed One through his mastery,
as soon as he was addressed with the words, "Bhikṣu, bail out this boat," whatever layman's mark, layman's concealment, layman's banner,
or layman's appearance he had all vanished instantly, and there appeared for him the three robes and a well-fashioned alms-bowl.
His hair remained established in its natural state, and his deportment was such that it resembled that of a monk who had been ordained for a hundred years.
In this manner, there was the going forth, the full ordination, and the state of a monk for the venerable ferryman Gaṅgeyaka.
Thereupon, the Blessed One dismissed him.
Then he spoke to the Blessed One.
“Blessed One, if I were asked by someone, ‘Who are you?’, what, Blessed One, should I say?”
The Blessed One said:
You are a śramaṇa, you are a brāhmaṇa, you are a knower, you are a deliverer, and you are one who has gone to the further shore.
Śakra, the lord of the gods, having manifested himself through his supernormal power in the form of a young brahmin— gracious, handsome,
with beautiful matted hair as blue as the neck of a peacock, and carrying a golden staff and water-pot— followed behind the Blessed One, holding his bowl, robes, and water-strainer.
The people said:
"Who is this youth, so pleasing and handsome? He then said:
I am the attendant of that hero who is endowed with fortitude, a meditator, a peerless person, an Arhat, and a Sugata in the world.
Gautama, who ferries across those being swept away by means of the ship of Dharma—
he who has crossed over, reached the further shore, and awakened— I am his attendant.
The Blessed One also dismissed Śakra, the lord of the gods.
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to the Blessed One:

"What are these matted-hair ascetics devoted to? "They are indeed matted-hair ascetics, devoted to matted-hair ascetics. Having thus spoken, the Blessed One, having manifested a thousand matted-hair ascetics—gracious, inspiring, and of great majesty—surrounded by them, approached the matted-hair ascetic Uruvilvākāśyapa through the sky by means of his supernormal power.

When Uruvilvākāśyapa, together with his retinue and five hundred matted-hair ascetics, saw the thousand [ascetics] who were so pleasing and beautiful to behold, he became filled with apprehension, thinking:

"A great multitude of people will surely come to this hermitage of ours; they are devoted to us, and there is no one in the world equal to the seer Uruvilvākāśyapa and his retinue—yet this seer has a retinue of a thousand matted-hair ascetics."

"Today, this one of great supernatural power and great majesty has arrived here at the hermitage; the entire body of people will place their faith in this seer who possesses a retinue of a thousand followers and is endowed with great supernatural power and great majesty.
Having placed their faith, they will perform acts of devotion, honoring him, respecting him, revering him, worshipping him, and showing him honor, but not so toward me and my retinue."
They will attend to it with mindfulness.

Then the Blessed One, having understood this reflection in the mind of the seer Uruvilvākāśyapa, himself vanished from his matted-hair guise and manifested a thousand created figures in the form of matted-hair ascetics.

Then Uruvilvākāśyapa, seeing that the thousand matted-hair ascetics had vanished and beholding the Blessed One in his own form— the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata— [was struck with wonder].
The Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed Charioteer of men to be tamed,
the Teacher of gods and humans, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
his body adorned with the eighty minor characteristics, and possessed of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

He was endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, powerful; confident through the four grounds of self-confidence, inspiring confidence, and pleasing; with tranquil faculties and a tranquil mind; having attained the highest self-control and tranquility;
like an elephant who has completed his task; with senses not wandering outward and a mind not wandering outward, established and having attained the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Gupta the Naga, having conquered his senses, was as clear and untroubled as a lake, serene and tranquil; he was like a raised pillar of jewels,
shining like a golden image, a mass of splendor blazing with glory like a second rising sun— exquisite and pleasing to behold.
And having seen this, Uruvilvākāśyapa, together with his retinue, was struck with wonder:
"The ascetic Gautama possesses great supernatural power and great majesty; yet I am even more possessed of great supernatural power."

Then indeed, that multitude of people, arriving one after another, approached the Blessed One; having bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they placed the Blessed One at their very forefront, never satiated by the sight of the Blessed One.
Then, this thought occurred to the seer Uruvilvākāśyapa:
"Ah, would that the ascetic Gautama might depart from my hermitage by some other way!"
Then the Blessed One, having understood this reflection in the mind of the seer Uruvilvākāśyapa,
just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm,
in that same instant rose up into the air from the hermitage of the seer Uruvilvākāśyapa.
He stayed at Uruvilvā, in the village of Senāpati, on the bank of the river Nairañjanā, at the foot of a banyan tree belonging to a cowherd.
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to the matted-hair ascetic Uruvilvākāśyapa when the crowd of people had departed:
"Oh, if only the ascetic Gautama would come here; having come here, he might partake of this solid food and soft food."

Then the Blessed One, having understood this reflection in the mind of the matted-hair ascetic Uruvilvākāśyapa, just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, in that very instant rose up into the air from the foot of the banyan tree at Ajapāla and approached Uruvilvākāśyapa.
He stayed in the hermitage of Jaṭila.
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to the matted-hair ascetic Uruvilvākāśyapa and his retinue:

The ascetic Gautama possesses great supernatural power and great majesty; he knows the minds of other beings and other individuals with his own mind, yet we are even more possessed of great supernatural power.
Then indeed, the matted-hair ascetic Uruvilvākāśyapa satisfied the Blessed One with his own hands with excellent solid and soft food.

Then the Blessed One, having finished his meal, having washed his bowl, and having withdrawn his hand, expressed his appreciation for that gift of the matted-hair seer Uruvilvākāśyapa with this verse of rejoicing:
The Agnihotra is the mouth of sacrifices; the Sāvitrī is the mouth of the Vedic meters;
the king is the mouth of human beings; and the ocean is the mouth of rivers.
The moon is the foremost among the stars;
the sun is the highest among those that shine above, across, and below;
and the Perfectly Awakened One is the best among speakers for the world including the gods.

Then indeed, Uruvilvākāśyapa, together with his retinue, stood in the air above the sky offering oblations into the fire; yet that fire of theirs would not blaze up, and this thought occurred to them:
Whose power is this, by which the fire does not blaze?
Surely it is through the power of the ascetic Gautama.
Now, when that fire had blazed up, this thought occurred to them:
The ascetic Gautama possesses great supernatural power and great majesty, but we possess even greater supernatural power.
He cast an oblation into that fire, but it did not fall; then this thought occurred to them:
"Whose power is this, by which no oblation falls into the fire?
Surely it is by the power of the ascetic Gautama!
For as soon as it occurs to them, 'This is the power of the ascetic Gautama,' then that oblation falls into the fire-offering."
"Having offered oblations to Agni, we shall descend from the intermediate space," they said, but they were not able to descend.
This thought occurred to them:
"Whose power is this, by which we are unable to descend from the air to the hermitage?
Surely it is through the power of the ascetic Gautama."

Because it occurred to them, "This is the power of the ascetic Gautama," they then [thought], "We shall sit down in our respective palanquins which have been established in the sky," yet they did not see those palanquins.
This thought occurred to them:
"Whose power is this, by which we do not see the palanquin?
Surely it is through the power of the ascetic Gautama."
When it occurred to them, "This is the power of the ascetic Gautama," they then saw those palanquins.
This thought occurred to them:
"The ascetic Gautama possesses great supernatural power and great majesty, yet we possess even greater supernatural power.
Let us take our water-pots and go to fetch water," they said; however, they were unable to lift those pots.
This thought occurred to them:
"Whose power is this?
Surely it is the power of the ascetic Gautama, since they think, 'This is the power of the ascetic Gautama,' and then they each saw their own water-jars."
This thought occurred to them:
The ascetic Gautama possesses great supernatural power and great majesty, but we possess even greater supernatural power.
Taking their water-pots, they went to the Nairañjanā River to fetch water, but they were unable to fill those pots.
This thought occurred to them:
Whose power is this? Surely it is that of the ascetic Gautama.
When it occurred to them, "This is the power of the ascetic Gautama," they then filled those water-jars with water.
This thought occurred to them:
"This ascetic Gautama possesses great supernatural power and great majesty, but we possess even greater supernatural power."
They will intend to eat, yet they will not be able to eat.
This thought occurred to them.
Whose power is this? Surely it must be that of the ascetic Gautama.
When it occurred to them, "This is the power of the ascetic Gautama," they were then able to take food.
This thought occurred to them:
The ascetic Gautama possesses great supernatural power and great majesty, but we possess even greater supernatural power.
Having finished their meal, they thought, "We will fell some logs," but though they raised their axes, they were unable to set them down.
This thought occurred to them:
Whose power is this? Surely it is that of the ascetic Gautama.
When it occurred to them, "This is the power of the ascetic Gautama," they then set down those raised axes and let those pieces of wood fall.
This thought occurred to them:
"This ascetic Gautama possesses great supernatural power and great majesty, but we possess even greater supernatural power."
Thus the Blessed One, in the presence of Uruvilvākāśyapa, converted the three brothers along with their retinues by means of five hundred miracles;
this was the final miracle.
The Blessed One, desiring to retire into seclusion, said to Uruvilvākāśyapa:
"Kāśyapa, I shall rest here in this fire-hut of yours."
Uruvilvākāśyapa said:
Therefore, Gautama, this fire-sanctuary is not to be entered by anyone, whether human or non-human; for a wicked nāga dwells within this sanctuary.
Even we ourselves avoid this fire-sanctuary from afar out of fear of that wicked nāga.
The Blessed One said:
"Please grant me leave, Kāśyapa; I shall go into seclusion here in this fire-hut."
Uruvilvākāśyapa said:
"Venerable Gautama, I do not permit you to use this fire-shelter.
Indeed, a fault is reported regarding this fire-shelter and these many hundreds of grass huts and leaf huts; let the venerable Gautama hide himself wherever he finds pleasure."
Then the Blessed One, rising from his seat, entered the fire-hall of Uruvilvākāśyapa and sat down for the sake of seclusion.

The Blessed One then entered the fire-element concentration within the fire-hut. Unable to endure the Blessed One’s fiery power, he descended into the bowl that had been given to the Blessed One by the Four Great Kings.
There, he was suffused with the Blessed One’s loving-kindness, subdued, and rendered free of poison; he no longer gave way to anger.
The fire-sanctuary, through the Blessed One’s splendor, was seen to have become a single mass of flame.
This thought occurred to those matted-hair ascetics:
The wicked Naga has burned the ascetic Gautama, and the entire fire-hall is ablaze.
Then, taking water, they ran forth, thinking, "We shall extinguish the fire-shelter and we shall rescue the ascetic Gautama."
The Blessed One, having tamed that nāga and rendered him free of poison, took him in his alms-bowl and presented him to Uruvilvākāśyapa.
Uruvilvākāśyapa, along with his retinue, was struck with wonder when that nāga entered the Blessed One’s bowl.

"The ascetic Gautama possesses great supernatural power and great majesty," he thought, "for behold, Blessed One, that which could not have been entered by either a human or a non-human has now been overcome by the spiritual power of the ascetic Gautama."
Then, indeed, in the presence of Uruvilvākāśyapa, those three brothers together with their retinues were all inspired with faith by the Blessed One through this final miracle.
Having tamed the king of serpents at the fire-hut of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa,
he brought him out in his bowl and presented him to the venerable Kāśyapa.
Behold this, Kāśyapa: his splendor has completely consumed the splendor [of others], such that no one in this world is able to enter his abode.
With the hairs on his body bristling with joy, Uruvilvākāśyapa and his retinue saw that the elephant had been tamed and pacified by the Elephant among Men.
That nāga, for whose sake the abode of the great seer had been difficult to enter,
has now been tamed and rendered free of poison through the power of the Buddha.
The Blessed One said:
In one disciplined by me, there are no faults; here, O Kāśyapa, there is no lack of restraint. The sky might fall, the earth might shatter, but one tamed by the Buddha would never act with poison.
Dismissed by the Blessed One, that serpent named Saṃvartanāga,
having assumed a human body, prostrated at the feet of the Sugata.
Be my refuge, O best of men; this was no transgression on my part, O one of great wisdom, for it was my own mind that became corrupted and was cast away before your very eyes.
O Supreme among Men, whatever offense I have committed externally, whatever transgression I have committed—
that indeed, O Best of Guides, I go once more to you for refuge.
Having saluted him who is worthy of homage and having circumambulated him many times,
the Naga departed after paying obeisance with great reverence for his teacher.

The Blessed One, by means of five hundred miracles, brought all three brothers— Uruvilvākāśyapa with his retinue of five hundred, Nadīkāśyapa with his retinue of three hundred, and Gayākāśyapa with his retinue of two hundred— under his powerful mastery; he summoned them with the "Come, monk" formula, ordained them, and conferred full ordination upon them all.
Come, monks, lead the holy life under the Tathāgata.

Now, as soon as they were addressed by the Blessed One with the "Come, monk" formula, whatever marks of a seer, protection of a seer, banner of a seer, or attire of a seer they possessed all vanished; the three robes appeared upon them, along with sumbhaka bowls, and their hair settled into its natural state, while their deportment became established just like that of monks who had been ordained for a hundred years.
In this manner, the full ordination and the status of monkhood were attained by the three venerable brothers—Uruvilvākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, and Gayākāśyapa—together with their retinues.
Now, they had a nephew named Upasena who, having built a hermitage on the very bank of that river Nairañjanā— endowed with leaves, flowers, and fruits— dwelt there with a retinue of three hundred,
being an attainer of the four dhyānas, possessed of the five superknowledges, and endowed with great psychic power and majesty.
Then those monks, headed by Uruvilvākāśyapa, cast all their ascetic belongings—the deerskins, sandals, robes, wooden frames, and water-pots—into the Nairañjanā River, thinking:
"Our nephew Upasena, along with his retinue, will make use of these ascetic belongings."
When they saw that merchandise being carried away by the Nairañjanā river, they hauled up all of that merchandise.
Then this thought occurred to that seer Upasena:
"Could it be that my maternal uncles have been harassed by someone?"

Then, hurrying with great speed, the Blessed One together with his retinue arrived at the hermitage of Uruvilvākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, and Gayākāśyapa; meanwhile, the Blessed One and the community of monks, having finished their meal, were washing and scrubbing their bowls in the Nairañjanā River.
Then the seer Upasena approached where Uruvilvākāśyapa was and addressed the venerable Uruvilvākāśyapa in verse:
Your fire was offered to delusion; that austerity of yours was performed for delusion—[all] which you have cast off in your final time, like a snake its worn-out skin.
Then the Venerable Uruvilvākāśyapa replied to the seer Upasena in verse:
My fire was offered in delusion; my asceticism was performed in delusion—[all] that I have cast off in the final stage of life, like a snake sheds its worn-out skin.
And he too, along with his retinue, was disciplined by the Blessed One in the mastery of power; he was ordained with the "Come, monk" formula, received full admission, [and addressed:
"Come, monks! Practice the holy life under the Tathāgata."
As soon as they were addressed by the Blessed One with the words "Come, monk," whatever marks of a seer, protections of a seer, banners of a seer,

or accoutrements of a seer they possessed all vanished; the three robes appeared upon them, along with a sumbhaka alms-bowl, their hair settled in its natural state, and their deportment became established just like that of monks who had been ordained for a hundred years.
This is the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk for the venerable Upasena together with his retinue of two hundred and fifty.
This was the first assembly of disciples of the Blessed One, consisting of twelve hundred and fifty monks.
The monks said to the Blessed One:

"Lord, as the ripening of what karma did the three brothers—the venerable Uruvilvākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, and Gayākāśyapa—become so possessed of great supernatural power, great majesty, and swift realization?"
The Blessed One said:
Monks, it is the ripening of the roots of merit planted toward the Buddha through their former vows that these very individuals possess great psychic power, great majesty, and swift realization.

Long ago, monks, in the past, there was a king in Hastināpura named Mahendra. He was one who had performed meritorious deeds, was of great renown, righteous, a king of Dharma, and well-supported by his retinue; he was disposed toward giving and sharing.
Now, while that king reigned, a Tathāgata, Arhat, and perfectly enlightened Buddha named Puṣpa, together with his community of disciples, dwelt in Hastināpura as a guest.

In Kaliṅga there was a city named Siṃhapura, where three brothers born of one mother ruled the kingdom. Now, while they were in that kingdom, a jewel appeared; taking that jewel, they came from Siṃhapura to Hastināpura and presented that jewel to King Mahendraka.
Then King Mahendraka became delighted with those brothers because of that gift.
He said:
What shall I do for you?
Then they said:
"We desire, O Blessed One, that you should dwell for the rains-retreat in our city out of compassion for us;
we wish to perform a great meritorious deed by your arrival this very day."
Then King Mahendraka said:
Furthermore, the Blessed One will dwell in our city once again.
May you also be embraced by this merit.
Then those brothers requested the Blessed One Puṣpa, together with his community of disciples, to stay in their own city.
The Blessed One spent the rainy season retreat right there and passed into parinirvāṇa.
After the Blessed One Puṣpa had passed away, they performed the funeral rites for his body and erected a stūpa.
While King Mahendra was ruling the earth with righteousness and conducting himself by undertaking wisdom,
he had three brothers who were his companions in conduct.
And sons and wives likewise follow after him.
Once, practicing together in perfect harmony,
they indeed exercised sovereignty through righteousness;
possessing abundant enjoyments, they were endowed with jewels.
May I satisfy [him] for so many years.
Sharing equal food within a single kingdom,
they beheld the Buddha, the supreme among bipeds,
who had reached the perfection of the one named Nakṣatra.
Worshipped by gods and humans according to his own power.
When the Compassionate Teacher had entered final nirvana,
we, together with our wisdom, along with our sons, wives, kinsmen, and relatives, erected a stūpa.
And she is noble and preeminent among the women in the city.
With elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry;
with dance, song, and instrumental music;
and with perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
We performed worship for the great seer.
By the fruit of that worship of the stupa,
O Great Sage, for ninety-two kalpas they have not fallen into miserable states because of that very same karma.
We are all disciplined under your teaching, O steadfast one.
Thus ends the Jātaka of the Venerable Uruvilvākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, and Gayākāśyapa.
The Blessed One, together with a great saṅgha of monks numbering twelve hundred and fifty, went from the hermitage of Uruvilvākāśyapa to Dharmāraṇya, the hermitage site of the great seers.

There, seven hundred matted-hair ascetics were residing; they had all attained the four dhyānas and possessed the five superknowledges (pañcābhijñā), were two hundred years of age, and all had their roots of merit fully ripened, being in their final existence.
For the sake of favoring them, the Blessed One went to that hermitage;
there, the Blessed One spoke the Chapter on the Thousands among the Dharma-padas for those matted-hair ascetics.
Even a thousand words composed of meaningless phrases are not as good as a single meaningful word, hearing which one attains peace.
Even a thousand verses composed of meaningless words are not as good as a single meaningful verse, hearing which one attains peace.
He who conquers hundreds of thousands of men in battle is not the true victor;
rather, he who conquers himself alone is indeed the superior victor in battle.
Even one who might conquer hundreds upon hundreds of thousands month after month would not be worth a sixteenth part of the serene confidence placed in the Buddha.
Even one who might conquer hundreds upon thousands month after month,
does not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of serene confidence in the Dharma.
One who might conquer hundreds upon thousands month after month does not equal even a sixteenth part of the serene confidence placed in the Saṅgha.
One who might conquer hundreds upon hundreds [of foes] month after month is not worth even a sixteenth part of those who are perfected in virtue.
One who might conquer hundreds upon thousands month after month does not equal even a sixteenth part of those for whom the Dharma has been well-expounded.
Month after month, a fool might consume food with the tip of a blade of kusha grass;
yet he is not worth even a sixteenth part of the serene confidence placed in the Buddha.
Month after month, a fool might consume food with the tip of a blade of kusha grass;
yet he is not worth a sixteenth part of the faith placed in the Dharma.
Month after month, a fool might eat his food with the tip of a blade of kusha grass;
yet he is not worth even a sixteenth part of one who has faith in the Saṅgha.
Month after month, a fool might eat his food with the tip of a blade of kusha grass;
yet he is not worth even a sixteenth part of those who possess the clarity of meditative concentration.
Month after month, a fool might eat his food with the tip of a blade of kusha grass;
yet he is not worth even a sixteenth part of those who possess perfected virtue.
Month after month, a fool might eat his food with the tip of a blade of kusha grass; yet he is not worth even a sixteenth part of those for whom the Dharma has been well-expounded.
And one who might live for a hundred years, performing service to the sacrificial fire,
subsisting on leaves, dwelling in a cemetery, and practicing various forms of austerity;
Whoever should honor for even a moment one whose self is cultivated,
that single act of honoring is better than a hundred years of burnt offerings.
Whatever sacrifice or oblation one who seeks merit performs in this world for a year,
all of that does not equal even a fourth part [of the merit of one who has seen the Dharma].
Salutation toward those who walk uprightly is better.
Better than living for a hundred years immoral and unconcentrated is a single day's life of one who is virtuous and meditative.
Better than living for a hundred years lazy and lacking in vigor is a single day lived with firm exertion of energy.
Better than living for a hundred years without seeing the Buddha's teaching is to live for a single day seeing the Buddha's teaching.
Better than living for a hundred years without seeing the supreme Dharma is to live for a single day seeing the supreme Dharma.
Better than living for a hundred years without seeing the arising and passing away [of phenomena] is a single day's life for one who sees the arising and passing away.
Better than living for a hundred years without seeing the deathless state is a single day's life for one who sees the deathless state.
Better than living for a hundred years without seeing the deathless state is a single day's life for one who sees the deathless state.
Now they have all been disciplined by the Blessed One into the mastery of powers, and they have all attained final nirvana.
After the Blessed One had performed the funeral rites for their bodies and erected stupas, he departed from Dharmāraṇya and arrived at the banyan tree of Ajapāla.

The Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, having accomplished the purpose for which he had come, was dwelling at Uruvilvā on the bank of the river Nairañjanā at the foot of the Goatherd’s Banyan tree,
not long after his full enlightenment. Now at that time, King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra had a brahmin domestic priest.
The royal preceptor, having gone to the excellent upper terrace of the palace at the time of dawn during the night, was reciting aloud in detail the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.

King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra heard the brahmin priest and royal preceptor, who was situated in the upper story of the palace at the time of dawn, reciting aloud in detail the thirty-two marks of a Great Man; and having heard this, mindfulness of the Blessed One arose within him.

"O, may a Buddha, a Blessed One, arise in my realm; and may I behold that Blessed One, and having beheld him, may I have faith in him as he proceeds, and with a faithful mind may I attend upon him; and may that Blessed One teach me the Dharma, and having heard his Dharma, may I understand it."
Then, at the end of that very night, King Śreṇya Bimbisāra addressed a certain man.
"Come, man, quickly have the auspicious vehicles harnessed, and report to me when they are ready."
"Very well, Great King," that man replied to King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra, and having done so, he quickly harnessed the excellent vehicles; once they were harnessed, he informed him:
"The excellent vehicles are harnessed for you, Great King; do as you deem it the right time."

Then King Śreṇya Bimbisāra, having mounted a certain excellent vehicle, departed from the city of Rājagṛha with great royal splendor and great royal majesty, amidst the shouts of "Ha! and "Hi!", and the sounding of drums, kettledrums, cymbals, and conchs by a vast multitude of people, and proceeded toward a certain park.

Then King Śreṇya Bimbisāra proceeded by carriage as far as the ground was passable for a carriage; having descended from the carriage, he walked on foot through that park grounds, and while walking and wandering about, he sat down upon a golden couch facing the east, surrounded by his harem and attended by his ministers and courtiers.

Then, as King Bimbisāra gazed upon the city of Rājagṛha, and as he recollected the mountains of Rājagṛha, the lotus ponds, the ancient noble dwellings, and the dead and the departed, he felt revulsion toward sensual pleasures.
Right attention arises.
