Having emerged from the park grounds, the increaser of the kingdom of the Aṅgas sat upon a couch with a pure golden base.
Resounding with the sound of those three [instruments], providing the perfect awakening at the right time,
that excellent *sāla* tree was in full bloom, having produced its flowers at that moment.
He beheld those mountains frequented by wild beasts, inhabited by langurs,
and haunted by large lions.
The king sat down facing the east, recollecting the ancient legends;
with eyes filled with tears, he spoke this verse:
"May this white mountain remain as vast as Kailāsa;
yet my fathers and grandfathers have passed away as hungry ghosts, their craving still unextinguished."
The excellent, delightful forests, the various lotus ponds, and the mountain peaks—
wherever they may have gone, to what direction indeed have they departed?
In the same way, these kingdoms and these wide-flowing rivers which once reached these villages—where indeed have they gone? To what direction have they departed?
In the same way, where have those garments gone, these gold neck-ornaments with earrings, and these very sandals that they once wore? To what destination have they departed?
These lovely lotus ponds, resounding with the songs of various birds,
are covered with white lotuses, water lilies, and fragrant flowers.
As for those who bathed here, where indeed have they gone?
In that same way, these delightful, divine seats, covered with green grass,
surrounded by nearby water, and possessing cool shade, are enchanting;
those who would have frequented them here— where indeed have they gone?
Those very dwellings of hundreds of living beings are now mountains; and today these have been traversed by me, who has not seen his own birthplace.
Emptiness has been explained to me, and the directions have been traversed by me;
thus, what is this mortal life, so limited and joined with suffering?
Immediately following life comes death; death is certain for one who is born. There is no immortality for those who have been born, for such is the nature of living beings.
A living being who has set out upon the path may travel with weariness,
yet here the messengers of Yama, bearing his commands, traverse day and night.
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to a certain minister of the king:
It is said that a dejection arose in King Śreṇya Bimbisāra: "What indeed might be the means by which I could dispel this dejection of King Śreṇya Bimbisāra?
Then, this thought occurred to the king's minister:
It is said that for King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra, the city of Rājagṛha was dear and pleasing.
"What if I were now to describe the excellence of the city of Rājagṛha in his presence?"
Then that royal minister addressed King Śreṇya Bimbisāra with a verse:
These mountains are graceful, these mountain peaks are delightful—
those very ones in Rājagṛha that have been sprinkled with water by the celestial being.
And the streams flow with broken banks...
Then King Śreṇya Bimbisāra dismissed that royal minister.
You are indeed a deluded man, you who think that very thing which we censure is precisely what should be praised.
Then, indeed, in King Śreṇya Bimbisāra there arose an even greater degree of revulsion toward sensual pleasures, as well as mental suffering and dejection, through proper reflection.
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to the brahmin, the royal chaplain, the teacher of the king:
Sorrow and dejection arose in King Śreṇya Bimbisāra: "What indeed might be the means by which I could dispel the sorrow and dejection of King Śreṇya Bimbisāra?
Then, this thought occurred to the brahmin priest, the king's preceptor:
King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra indeed holds the Buddha, the Blessed One, dear and pleasing; what if I were now to speak the praises of the Buddha in his presence?
Then the brahmin household priest, the royal preceptor, addressed King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra with a verse:
It is a gain for the illustrious King Aṅga, the lord of the kingdom and sovereign of Magadha, that the Tathāgata has appeared within his realm.
The Himavat mountain resounds with its name proclaimed.
Endowed with virtue, patience, and austerity, he has lived the holy life that brings an end to the world.
Having gathered together in hundreds, thousands, and millions,
they attain the deathless, the peaceful, the unsurpassed security of yoga.
Then King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra addressed the brahmin royal chaplain and teacher with a verse:
I love to proclaim my fame in the kingdom; I love to proclaim my fame, O beloved one! [I love to proclaim the fame] of the beloved Buddha, who acts for the welfare of the world, O Brahmin.
I give you sixteen excellent villages, ten yoked chariots of noble breed,
a hundred female slaves, and a hundred cows.
For the sake of proclaiming the glory of the beloved Buddha.

Then indeed the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour among the Magadhans together with a great community of monks, numbering twelve hundred and fifty monks, proceeded toward Rājagṛha, the city of the Magadhans; having reached it, he stayed right there in the Yaṣṭīvana park at Antagiri.
King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra heard from his brahmin domestic priest and royal preceptor that the Blessed One,
while wandering on a tour through Magadha together with a great saṅgha of twelve hundred monks,
had followed the road toward Rājagṛha, the city of the Magadhans, and having arrived there, was staying right there in the Yaṣṭīvana Grove on Mount Antagiri.
Having heard this, you addressed a certain royal minister:
"O worthy minister, I shall go out to meet the Blessed Buddha; have Rājagṛha decorated, have excellent vehicles prepared, and [inform] all the brahmins and householders of Rājagṛha."
"Together with all the guilds of artisans and all the trade associations, I must go out to meet the Blessed One, the Buddha."

"Very well, Great King," replied the royal minister to Śreṇya Bimbisāra. Having given his assent, he immediately had excellent vehicles harnessed and caused a proclamation to be made throughout Rājagṛha at the crossroads, junctions, and market entrances:
"The Buddha, the Blessed One, has arrived at the Yaṣṭīvana park on Mount Antagiri near Rājagṛha; all of you, sirs, must go out to meet the Blessed One together with King Śreṇya Bimbisāra."

Having heard that proclamation, the princes, ministers, and courtiers, the brahmins headed by the domestic priest, the townspeople headed by the guild-leaders, the community of merchants headed by the caravan leaders, and all the eighteen guilds of Rājagṛha quickly assembled at the gate of the royal palace.

Namely: jugglers, palm-clappers, musicians, actors, dancers, wrestlers, boxers, hand-cymbalists, acrobats, tumblers, rope-walkers, pole-climbers, those who recite from memory, those who perform with five wooden blocks, singers, those who play the *guṇavarta* lute, those who perform the *tāṇḍava* dance,
fortune-tellers, courtesans, jesters, and those who play the kettle-drum, conch, clay drum, large drum, flute, small drum, lute, *vallakī* lute, and the eleven types of stringed instruments.

And many other makers of musical instruments gathered at the gate of the royal palace, as did all the guilds, such as: goldsmiths, silversmiths, cloak-makers, lapidaries, perfumers, dealers in woolen cloth, oil-pressers, butter-vendors, cowherds, curd-sellers, cotton-merchants, confectioners of sugar-candy, makers of sweetmeats, makers of *kaṇḍuka* sweets, makers of *samita* sweets, and makers of *śaktu* flour-gruel.
Fruit-sellers, root-sellers, powder-grinders, perfumers, oil-merchants, shopkeepers, weavers, molasses-makers, honey-producers, sugar-sellers,
and whatever other traders there may be, as well as all the various crafts, such as: smiths, copper-smelters, goldsmiths, silversmiths, and lapidaries.

[They were] makers of iron vessels, makers of tinware, makers of lead-glazed pottery, makers of mechanical devices, garland-makers, basket-makers, potters, leather-workers, makers of balls, weavers of chariot-fender cloth, dyers, spies, cotton-spinners,
painters, carpenters, sculptors, makers of black bowls, goldsmiths, book-makers, barbers, ritual experts, and cutters.
Plasterers, master builders, carpenters, basket-makers, well-diggers, clay-carriers, wood-carriers, dealers in bark,
dealers in timber, dealers in bamboo, sailors, ferrymen, gold-washers, and moṭṭikas— these and other people of various sorts, low, high, and middling, all assembled at the royal palace.

Then that royal minister, perceiving that the multitude of people had assembled, had auspicious vehicles prepared and approached King Śreṇya Bimbisāra; having approached him, he spoke thus to King Śreṇya Bimbisāra.
"O Great King, the auspicious vehicles are prepared and a great multitude of people has gathered; O Lord, do now as you deem it timely."

Then King Śreṇya Bimbisāra, having mounted a magnificent carriage and surrounded by twelve nayutas of Magadhan brahmins and householders, set out from the city of Rājagṛha with great royal splendor and amidst the clamor of a vast multitude— the shouting of "Ha! and "Hi!", and the resounding noise of drums, mṛdaṅgas, kettledrums, and conchs—
and proceeded toward the Yaṣṭīvana park on Mount Antagiri.

Then King Śreṇya Bimbisāra proceeded by carriage as far as the ground was suitable for a carriage; having alighted from the carriage, he approached the Blessed One on foot, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, and sat down to one side.
Some, having exchanged greetings with the Blessed One and engaged in polite and friendly conversation, sat down to one side.
Some, having announced their respective names and clans as their parents' names, sat down to one side.
Others, extending their joined palms toward the Blessed One, [sat down to one side].
They sat down to one side;
some of the Magadhan brahmins and householders sat down to one side in silence.
Now at that time, Uruvilvākāśyapa was sitting not far from the Blessed One.
Then, it occurred to those brahmins and householders of Magadha:
"Does Uruvilvākāśyapa lead the holy life under the ascetic Gautama, or does the Great Ascetic Gautama lead the holy life under Uruvilvākāśyapa?"
Then the Blessed One, having understood such a reflection in the minds of those brahmins and householders, addressed the venerable Uruvilvākāśyapa in verse:
Having seen what, O dweller of Uruvilvā, did you abandon the fire and speak as one who is emaciated? Kāśyapa, I ask you about this matter.
How has your Agnihotra sacrifice been abandoned?
When this had been said, the venerable Uruvilvākāśyapa replied to the Blessed One in verse:
They speak of foods, drinks, and flavors, as well as sensual pleasures and women, in the context of sacrifice; yet,
having understood these to be impurities within the acquisitions (upadhi), [one should renounce them].
Therefore, I find no delight in sacrifice nor in the oblation.
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Uruvilvākāśyapa in verse:
You did not set your mind upon these—
on food, drinks, and likewise flavors—
but rather upon that supreme among gods and men.
Wherever your mind, O Kāśyapa, finds delight.
Then the venerable Uruvilvākāśyapa replied to the Blessed One in verse:
Having seen the Sage— peaceful, free from acquisitions, possessing nothing, unattached to all states of existence,
unchanging, and not to be led by others—
Therefore, I do not delight in sacrificing or in offering oblations.
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Uruvilvākāśyapa with a verse:
In vain was the fire sacrificed for you; in vain was that austerity performed by you.
"He who has cast off [defilements] in his final time, like a snake shedding its worn-out skin"—
then indeed the Venerable Uruvilvākāśyapa replied to the Blessed One with this verse:
In vain was the fire offered by us; in vain was that austerity performed by me, which I have cast off in my final time, like a snake sheds its worn-out skin.
"By means of fire and sacrifices one is liberated"— this was my former view when I was ignorant,
blind, and following after birth and death.
Not seeing the supreme, imperishable state.
Now I behold that unclouded state well-taught by the Protector, the best of Nagas;
may I touch the state of ultimate perfection.
Having abandoned birth and death within saṃsāra.
Many beings are frustrated as they perform various austerities,
failing to reach the ultimate goal and remaining unable to cross beyond their doubts.
For a long time I have been defiled, bound by the fetters of views;
the Blessed One, the Seer, has liberated me from all my bonds.
The Blessed One is my teacher; I am a disciple of the Sugata.
Then the venerable Uruvilvākāśyapa rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One,
circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and stood behind the Blessed One, fanning him with a peacock-feather fan.
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to those Brahmins and householders of Magadha:
"Uruvilvākāśyapa is leading the holy life under the ascetic Gautama."
Then the Blessed One delivered a discourse on the Dharma to those brahmins and householders of Magadha.
Form arises and ceases for the brahmin householders; feeling arises and ceases; perception arises and ceases; volitional formations arise and cease; consciousness arises and ceases.
The noble disciple and the brahmins and householders, perceiving form as subject to arising and passing away, perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as impermanent.
Perceiving form as impermanent, and perceiving feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as impermanent;
perceiving form as suffering, and perceiving feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as suffering.
He correctly perceives that form is non-self; he correctly perceives that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-self.
Perceiving that form is non-self, and perceiving that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-self, he understands form as arising and passing away.
Understanding form as arising and passing away, one understands feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as arising and passing away.
Understanding them thus, one understands form as impermanent;
understanding them thus, one understands feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as impermanent.
Understanding, one understands that form is suffering;
understanding, one understands that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are suffering;
understanding, one understands that form is non-self.
Understanding that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not-self, one understands them as such.
Understanding this, one does not grasp at anything in the world.
Not grasping, one attains parinirvāṇa within oneself.
He understands: "Birth is exhausted for me; the holy life has been lived; what was to be done has been accomplished; there is no further state of being such as this."
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to those brahmins and householders of Magadha:

Since, indeed, O friend, form is not-self, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not-self, then who is there that acts or causes to act, that rouses or causes to rouse, that casts off or causes to cast off— [who] takes up these formations or casts them off, [and] for whom these formations are empty, devoid of self, or belonging to a self?
Then the Blessed One, having understood this very reflection in the minds of those brahmins and householders of Māgadha, addressed the monks.
"Monks, the fool designates [the self] by way of what has been accepted: 'Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are my self; my self is not, however, that which I speak of thus:

"I am the one here who is the doer, the one who causes to be done, the one who rouses, the one who takes up, or the one who lays down—that which lays down these formations and takes up others elsewhere. "
Furthermore, it is indeed conditioned phenomena that arise, and it is indeed conditioned phenomena that cease; and they arise with causes, and they cease with causes.
"Monks, the Tathāgata declares that the reconnection of the formative forces (*saṃskāra-pratisaṃdhi*) is with cause; he is the self, the appropriator."
I designate the passing away and rebirth of sentient beings.

"Monks, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, I see beings passing away and being reborn— beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, lowly and exalted; I understand how beings fare according to their karma, yet I do not speak thus."

"I am not the one here who is the doer, or the one who causes to be done, or the arouser, or the one who brings about, or the taker, or the depositor; rather, it is that which deposits these formations and takes up others.
Indeed, it is only formations that arise, and only formations that cease."
And they arise with causes and conditions, and they cease with causes and conditions.
The views of causality are the views of existence and non-existence.

“Monks, for one who sees with right wisdom, as it truly is, the arising of conditioned phenomena together with their cause, whatever view of existence or view of eternalism there might be, that does not occur.

And monks, for one who sees with right wisdom, as it truly is, the cessation of conditioned phenomena together with their cause, whatever view of non-existence or view of annihilationism there might be, that also does not occur.
Therefore, monks, having avoided both these extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma by the middle way.”

Conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations; conditioned by volitional formations is consciousness; conditioned by consciousness is name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases is contact; conditioned by contact is feeling; conditioned by feeling is craving;
conditioned by craving is clinging; conditioned by clinging is existence; conditioned by existence is birth; conditioned by birth...
Old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair—
thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.

Thus, indeed, from the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations; from the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness; from the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form; from the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases; from the cessation of the six sense bases comes the cessation of contact;
from the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling; from the cessation of feeling...
With the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth;
with the cessation of birth comes the cessation of old age and death; and with the cessation of old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
Thus occurs the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.
Thus spoke the Blessed One while staying at Rājagṛha in the Yaṣṭīvana grove on Mount Antagiri.

And while this exposition was being delivered, as King Śreṇya Bimbisāra sat right there on his seat, the dust-free, stainless Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena was purified; and for eleven *nayutas* [of beings], the dust-free, stainless [Dharma-eye] was likewise purified.
The eye of Dharma regarding all phenomena became purified.
Those twelve nayutas of chariot-keepers and vehicle-keepers also thereafter went for refuge to the Buddha, went for refuge to the Dharma, and went for refuge to the Saṅgha.
With uplifted minds, those monks, King Śreṇya Bimbisāra of Magadha, and the brahmins and householders rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.
The monks said to the Blessed One:
"Lord, why and how was such a vast gift bestowed by King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra upon this priest after he had come into the presence of the Blessed One to hear the Dharma?"
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now that this King Śreṇya Bimbisāra has given a vast gift upon hearing of me from his domestic priest; on another occasion, too, he gave one."
The monks said.
At another time as well, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
On another occasion as well, monks.
Once upon a time, monks, in the past, in the city of Mithilā, the great capital of the Videha country,
King Arindama reigned— a righteous king of Dharma, who maintained his retinue well, was disposed toward giving and sharing, and possessed great power and a vast array of vehicles.
He had sixty thousand elephants adorned with every ornament; sixty thousand horses adorned with every ornament;

sixty thousand chariots covered with leopard skins and lion skins, equipped with victory banners, making a joyous sound, highly magnificent, with flags and pennants raised high; and sixty thousand milch cows with their calves.
He had sixty thousand maidens and sixty thousand couches made of gold, silver, and ivory.
Furthermore, monks, King Arindama had sixty thousand golden bowls and sixty thousand silver bowls.
Furthermore, monks, King Ariṃdama had sixty thousand ancestral treasures and sixty thousand cities that were prosperous and free from thorns.

King Ariṃdama had a son of his domestic priest named Śroṇa, who was a master of the three Vedas— including the phonological analyses, the histories as the fifth, along with the Nighaṇṭus and Kaṭhas— as well as being skilled in etymology, prosody, and grammar.

Having undertaken the ten wholesome paths of action within the Brahminical Vedas, and having perceived the peril in sensual desires, he went to the Himalayas and went forth into the religious life of a seer.

Then, by practicing, striving, and exerting himself along that non-Buddhist path, he produced the four meditative absorptions and realized the five supernormal powers; he became a seer of great psychic power and great majesty.
Then, monks, after a long period of time had passed, this thought occurred to the seer Śroṇa:

King Arindama was my childhood friend, playing with me in the dust; today, as he has been exercising great sovereignty for eighty-four thousand years, it is surely the time for King Arindama to go forth into the religious life, so I should certainly urge him toward it.

Then, monks, just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, in that same moment, in that very instant, the seer Śroṇaka rose up into the air from his hermitage in the Himalayas and alighted in the Great Deva Mango Grove.

Monks, the brahmin family priest and royal preceptor of Arindama saw the seer Śroṇaka sitting at the foot of a certain mango tree in the Mahādeva mango grove; having seen him, he approached the seer Śroṇaka, greeted him with great kindness and courtesy, and paid homage to the seer Śroṇaka, and then [proceeded] where...
He set out for Mithilā because of King Arindama’s affliction.
And on that very day, monks, there arose in King Arindama a revulsion for sensual pleasures and a wise reflection, and a desire to see the seer Śroṇaka arose within him.
Then, monks, at that time King Arindama spoke this verse:
"I shall give him an excellent village and adorned women—
whoever tells me of Śroṇaka, my companion from playing in the dust."
And he had a brahmin who was of noble birth and a teacher;
seeing him so deeply distressed and dejected, he spoke these words:
"Give me an excellent village and well-adorned women;
I shall proclaim Śroṇaka as my companion for playing in the dust."
Indeed, within your own conquered realm, in your very garden grounds, there are mango trees in flower and fruit; it is there that the seer dwells.
Then that king, hurrying, addressed his minister.
"Quickly equip all our nāgas with their ornaments;
let the kettledrums and tabors be sounded, and let the single medium-sized conch shell be blown."
"I wish to see my friend Śroṇaka and attend upon him;
I am going to the forest, which is endowed with the fruits of various trees."
The king...
where Śroṇaka meditates.
And he saw that seer playing in the dust with his companion;
having seen Śroṇaka there, he spoke these words to him:
"O monk, why do you, though possessing a shaven head and a patched robe, remain meditating at the foot of a tree like a wretched man who has lost his father and mother?"
Then, monks, the seer Śroṇaka addressed King Arindama in verse:
A king does not become wretched, even through the splendor of his dharma-body,
if he approaches the Dharma and delights in that Dharma; but that man who, though devoted to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, does not delight in the Dharma, becomes a wretched king.
Then, monks, King Arindama replied to the seer Śroṇaka in verse:
How, Śroṇaka, do you sleep peacefully in the edge of the forest?
How is it that, dwelling alone in the wilderness, you find delight?
"How is it, Blessed One, that there is no affliction of the body?
Shall I provide protection for you, or shall I lead you to the city?"
Then, monks, the seer Śroṇaka replied to King Arindama in verse:
O King, what will my kingdom do for one who wanders alone?
Indeed, it is first and foremost a blessing for the poor monk who has no home.
When I depart from villages, kingdoms, and likewise market towns, I go forth without regard for anything; no one obstructs me.
This, indeed, is the second blessing for a poor, houseless monk.
For one traveling along the path, whatever obstacles there may be,
by taking up the bowl and robes, he goes happily everywhere;
this indeed is the third blessing for a poor monk who has gone forth from the home.
When Mithilā is burning, nothing of his is burned;
indeed, this is the fourth blessing of the poor, homeless monk.
They do not enter into a storehouse, nor do they go from house to house with a jar;
seeking their alms, those of noble vows travel on foot.
This is the fifth blessing of the poor, homeless monk.
Having gone forth from various families and residing in various regions, they love one another; behold the true nature of the Dharma!
Then, monks, King Arindama replied to the seer Śroṇaka in verse:
"Truly, there is constant welfare for those of whom you speak, Śroṇaka;
but we are greedy for sensual pleasures—what shall I do, Śroṇaka?"
Then, monks, the seer Śroṇaka addressed King Arindama with a verse:
O Great King, I shall provide a simile for you; listen to it from me.
For in this world, some wise people understand the meaning through a simile.
In the past, O Great King, there was an elephant sixty years of age who,
having fallen into mountain fastnesses, was being carried away by the force of the Ganges.
In that regard, Kāla reflects: "I am of little wisdom and lack intelligence;
yet this auspicious vehicle has been obtained by me through a small amount of auspicious exertion."
Day and night, his mind remained fixed there as he ate the flesh of nāgas, drank the waters of the Bhāgīrathī,
and beheld various wonderful sights; thus the bird continued his journey.
That Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā leads him, heedless and clinging to a corpse,
toward the ocean, where there is no refuge for birds.
Just as sea-monsters (*makara*) and *timiṃgila* fish devour a foolish creature after killing it,
so too, O King, do persons who are dependent on sensual pleasures fall into ruin.
I tell you this, O King: do not be negligent regarding the Dharma;
otherwise, you will fall headlong into a hell of terrifying form.
Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, and the two Rauravas; furthermore, Mahāvīci, Tapana, and Saṃpratāpana.
Thus these eight great hells have been described, difficult to escape;
they are teeming with fierce beings and each has sixteen secondary hells.
It has four corners and four gates, divided and measured into sections;
it rises a hundred yojanas and extends a hundred yojanas all around.
Then, for those who have been cast into hell and are contorted by iron,
there is a ground made of iron, blazing and filled with heat.
The torments of the miserly are terrible, radiant, and difficult to approach;
they are hair-raising in form, formidable, terrifying, and full of suffering.
All of them were most terrifying, filled with hundreds of flames,
and each one radiated light for a hundred yojanas.
Where many beings, fierce and doers of great evil,
are tormented for a long time, even for hundreds of years.
The guardians of hell strike with thick iron clubs those who have committed evil deeds, as if they were their enemies.
I shall proclaim that to you in successive verses;
lend me your ear and listen with attention as I speak.
And in the Saṃjīva hell, having suspended them with feet upward and heads downward,
they carve them with adzes and axes.
Then, driven by the power of their rage, they furiously tear one another apart with their own sharp, self-arisen iron claws.
And for those men who, with corrupted minds, cut one another down, sharp axes shall grow upon their hands.
As their limbs are being severed, a cool wind blows upon them,
arising from all their members as a result of the ripening of their former karma.
Having thus understood their [intentions], Śroṇaka spoke to that king of the dwelling place of evil-doers, calling it "Saṃjīvaka."
Released from Saṃjīva, plunge into the Kukkula [hell]; having come together with one another, you shall be of long duration and vast extent.
All of them indeed run for many yojanas,
being burned in the pits of embers and experiencing painful sensations.
Having escaped from the Kukkula hell, they plunge into a corpse-pit that is long,
vast, wide, and deep, reaching a hundred men in height.
Out of compassion for him, those harsh beings, who feed on flesh and blood, pierce his skin with sharp spears and devour him there.
Having emerged from the mire of corpses, those seeking happiness behold beautiful trees covered with green leaves and approach them.
Seeing him there, hawks, vultures, crows, and owls with iron-like beaks, smeared with blood, devour him like a bird perched high in a tree.
And when they have been devoured until only the bones remain,
then their skin, flesh, and blood are produced once more.
Terrified and having fled, perceiving a refuge where there was no refuge, they approached the horrific Forest of Sword-leaves while being tormented.
Then, wounded, afflicted, and smeared with much blood,
they leave the Forest of Sword-Leaves and go to the Vaitaraṇī River.
They plunge into that river of caustic water, and its waters pierce through their very limbs and members as they swell.
Then, having pierced them with iron hooks, the men of Yama lift them onto the riverbank and force them to eat iron balls.
And they cause them to drink molten, heated copper;
that [liquid], having seized their intestines, passes out through the lower part.
Thus, you who follow the path of desire, having failed to perform wholesome deeds, enter hell through your evil course of action.
And those humans who completely avoid evil deeds and whose conduct is exclusively wholesome do not go to an unfortunate rebirth.
Therefore, having understood that action— whether wholesome or evil— is difficult to master,
one should avoid all evils and practice what is wholesome and auspicious.
Or alternatively, having understood the Dharma that is free from acquisitions, one should cultivate the auspicious Noble Eightfold Path for the sake of abandoning all suffering.
"Great King, beings of such a kind experience such sensations in the hells— those who have ended in evil deeds, being heedless and of childish intellect."
Therefore, O King, I say this to you: do not be negligent regarding the Dharma;
lest you fall headlong into a hell of terrifying form.
With a mind deeply stirred, the king, having heard the well-spoken words of Śroṇaka,
experienced a sense of spiritual urgency that was marvelous and hair-raising.
Then the king, hurrying, addressed his minister:
"Quickly bring the prince, the long-lived one who increases the kingdom."
"I have a young son who is long-lived and will increase the kingdom;
I shall establish him in the sovereignty, and he shall be your king."
Then the king’s messengers and the compassionate ministers quickly brought back the prince, long-lived and the increaser of the realm.
Then, monks, King Arindama addressed Prince Dīrghāyu in verse:
I address you, sir: renunciation appeals to me. Lest I, like a foolish crow, fall under the sway of sensual desires.
"O son, take charge of these sixty thousand cities and this prosperous kingdom free from thorns; I entrust the sovereignty to you."
This very day I shall go forth into homelessness; who knows if death will come tomorrow?
For there is no avoiding union with that great army, Death;
let me not, like a witless crow, fall under the power of sensual desires.
Sixty thousand elephants were all there, well-adorned,
tuskers endowed with strength, clothed in garments fashioned of gold.
Mounted upon her, she is armed with spears, tridents, staffs, lances, and fetters;
O son, accept her, and I shall hand over the kingdom to you.
This very day I shall go forth into homelessness; who knows if death will come tomorrow?
For there is no avoiding that great army, Death;
let me not, like a witless crow, fall under the power of sensual desires.
Sixty thousand swift-coursing horses from the Indus region,
adorned with every ornament and mounted everywhere by heroes—
may I not, like the witless crow, fall under the power of sensual desires.
"Sixty thousand cows, all of them yielding milk when their calves are present—O son, accept these; I hand over the kingdom to you."
I shall go forth into homelessness this very day; for who knows if death will come tomorrow?
Lest I, like a witless crow, fall under the sway of sensual desires.
There are sixty thousand maidens adorned with jeweled earrings;
O son, accept them, for I entrust the kingdom to you.
I shall go forth into homelessness this very day; who knows if death will come tomorrow?
Lest I, like a witless crow, fall under the sway of sensual desires.
"O son, accept these sixty thousand couches made of gold and silver; I entrust the kingdom to you."
This very day I shall go forth; who knows if death will come tomorrow?
For there is no avoiding that great army, Death; let me not, like a witless crow, fall under the power of sensual desires.
"O son, accept these sixty thousand [villages] made of gold and silver; I entrust the kingdom to you."
I shall go forth into homelessness this very day; who knows if death will come tomorrow?
For there is no avoiding that great army, Death;
let me not, like a witless crow, fall under the sway of sensual desires.
"O son, take possession of these sixty thousand treasures of abundant gold; I now hand over the kingdom to you."
This very day I shall go forth into homelessness; who knows if death will come tomorrow?
For there is no avoiding that great army, Death;
let me not, like a witless crow, fall under the sway of sensual desires.
"O son, take possession of those sixty thousand treasures consisting of no small amount of the seven jewels; I hand over the kingdom to you."
This very day I shall go forth into homelessness; who knows if death will come tomorrow?
For there is no avoiding that great army, Death;
let me not, like a foolish crow, fall under the power of sensual desires.
Then, indeed, the youth Dīrghāyu replied to the king with a verse.
I have heard this clearly: my mother has passed away;
I shall not be able to live without the King.
Just as a hunter follows a wild elephant from behind, so shall I pursue you, carrying your *suṃbhaka* fruit.
Then, monks, King Arindama addressed his ministers and assembly in verse:
Just as when a sea monster tears apart a merchant ship belonging to traders seeking wealth, those traders fall into calamity.
May we not create an obstacle for myself... [and so forth].
"Take this prince— long-lived and the increaser of the kingdom—
and quickly lead him to the inner apartments and the pleasure-increasing palace;
there, beautiful women resembling celestial maidens will delight him."
Then, having taken the prince, the illustrious high ministers entered the city of Mithilā with great royal splendor.
Then, indeed, one royal maiden, adorned and wearing garlands and ornaments, rose up and spoke thus to the king:
Tell us that: are you a Gandharva, or are you Śakra Puraṃdara?
I ask you concerning the command of the King... [omitted]... . . . . . . . . //
How can you abandon us— the prosperous kingdom free from thorns,
as well as the long-lived prince, along with the ministers, wealth, and grain?
Then the king said to that princess:
I am neither a god, nor a nāga, nor a gandharva, nor Śakra, nor Purandara;
I am a human being, terrified of sensual pleasures, having heard the instruction of the seer.
May I not, like a foolish crow, fall under the power of sensual desires.
One should do what is beneficial this very day; for who knows if death will come tomorrow?
For there is no avoiding that encounter with Death and his vast army.
Having spoken thus, that king went forth into homelessness in the very presence of that seer Śroṇaka.
The Blessed One said:

"What do you think, monks? Was that seer named Śroṇaka at that time and on that occasion someone else? Indeed, it should not be viewed in this way. And why is that? Because at that time and on that occasion, I was that seer named Śroṇaka."
No other king is to be seen as Arindama;
this is that very King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra.
Even then, he gave a vast inheritance to the one who spoke of his son Śroṇaka;
now too, he has given a vast inheritance to the son of the family priest because he spoke in praise of me, the Buddha.
The Arindamarājajātakam is completed.
The Blessed One said this, and the gods, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and that entire assembly, as well as those monks, rejoiced and highly praised what the Blessed One had spoken.
Thus, according to the recension of the noble Mahāsāṃghikas, the Lokottaravādins, the glorious Mahāvastu-avadāna is completed.

Of those phenomena that arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has declared their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa. (The manuscripts add the following colophon:)
Whoever hears the Dharma of the Sage and, having heard it, adheres to it,
being liberated from all evil, goes to Sukhāvatī.
Therefore, this well-spoken word of the Sugata should be heard with faith;
it was previously taught by the Jina through various kinds of insights.
Thus, through devotion and by the power of the Sugata, I have completed this well-spoken work which points out the path to absolute liberation.
Therefore, may whatever merit I possess— which destroys all evils, is worthy of closing the gates to the lower realms, and teaches the path to enlightenment— [accrue to others].
By the power of this merit, may all beings in every way,
completely liberated from all afflictions, go indeed to Sukhāvatī.
Those beings who are blind, one-eyed, as well as hunchbacked or deformed, and others who are thirsty, hungry, and oppressed by every kind of suffering.
By that merit, may they all be endowed with every happiness;
having enjoyed various enjoyments, may they attain imperishable liberation.
May all those beings who are submerged in the six realms of existence and agitated by birth and old age,
all become travelers upon the path to enlightenment through my merit.
Those beings who are of a foolish nature, who are deprived of the true Dharma,
who are constantly attached to evils, and who are deluded by passion, hatred, and ignorance;
Through my merit, may they all then remember their past lives and,
endowed with generosity, ethical discipline, and the other perfections, practice the conduct of awakening.
May the king be possessed of security; may the ministers conduct themselves according to policy;
and may the heroes always be victors over their enemies in battle.
May the clouds rain in due season, and may the earth always be filled with grain;
by this merit that arises from my vow, may there be auspiciousness.
By the power of that merit, may I reach the further shore of enlightenment for the sake of crossing over the ocean of saṃsāra and for the welfare of embodied beings.
May there always be auspiciousness.
In the illustrious Nepāla year, when the moon was in the sign of Taurus,
in the month of Āṣāḍha, during the bright fortnight, on the conjunction of the full-moon day.
When the conjunction with Uttarāṣāḍhā occurs, during the meeting with Indra,
on that very auspicious day joined with a Sunday.
This auspicious collection of wise sayings, written by the venerable Nandācārya for his own benefit,
has reached completion through devotion to the illustrious Great Sage.
The extent of the work is 25,000 verses.
In the year 842, on the full moon day of the bright fortnight in the month of Āṣāḍha, under the lunar mansion Uttarāṣāḍhā, in conjunction with Indra, on Sunday—on this very day it was established.
This was written by the hand of Vajrācārya Kulisa Śrī Nanda Veda, a resident of the Jaśodhara Mahāvihāra in the great city of Lalitapattana; may it be auspicious!
He was ordained by the preceptor Śrī Gajendravajra.
May there be auspiciousness at all times.
Just as I saw the manuscript, so have I written it;
whether it be correct or incorrect, it should be purified by the great scholars.
May there be auspiciousness at all times.
